nodes.misconception: Texture describes something rough, bumpy or hard to touch.
nodes.response: Remind students that textures can be rough, hard and bumpy but they can also be smooth, soft and fuzzy.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Textured marks with charcoal

nodes.misconception: When drawing, artists only use their hands.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can use their whole body when creating marks.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: How artists make marks

nodes.misconception: Art materials must be bought rather than made.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can buy their ink from a shop, but they can also make their own from natural materials.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark-making with ink and water

nodes.misconception: Emotions can be shown through images but not through mark-making.
nodes.response: Remind children that different styles of marks can show the emotions of the artist, such as rounded lines showing that an artist might be feeling happy and calm. The artist does not need to create an image to express an emotion.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressive mark-making

nodes.misconception: Artists have to hold a drawing tool with their hands to make marks.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can make marks by holding a drawing tool but they can also make marks without directly touching the drawing tool.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Building drawing machines

nodes.misconception: Every mark or shape needs to be identical and placed in a perfectly regular sequence to make a pattern.
nodes.response: Remind children that patterns do not always have to be exactly the same each time, but they still follow a rule or idea.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark-making and patterns

nodes.misconception: If the model looks good, it doesn’t matter if it does not stand properly.
nodes.response: A successful architectural model is both visually creative and structurally sound. Aim to build with purpose to create stability.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make an architectural 3D model

nodes.misconception: As long as a model is shown, it doesn't need to be explained.
nodes.response: It’s important to explain your ideas clearly - your model shows the design, but your words help others understand why and how you made it.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Present a group design proposal

nodes.misconception: All buildings look the same because they follow similar rules.
nodes.response: While buildings need to be safe and follow certain rules, architects use creativity to make them unique.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate an architect

nodes.misconception: All the lines in a building should go straight up and sideways.
nodes.response: Some lines go towards a vanishing point to show how things look smaller as they get further away. That’s how we create perspective.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw buildings using simple perspective

nodes.misconception: Group work means I only do one small part and don’t need to help with the rest.
nodes.response: While roles may be shared, everyone in the group should contribute ideas and help make decisions together to ensure the final design feels like a team effort.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop a collaborative group design

nodes.misconception: Shading just means colouring in darker.
nodes.response: Tonal shading uses a range of light to dark tones to show how light hits different surfaces.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Tonally shade architecture

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that artists need to have directly experienced something or physically visited somewhere to be inspired to create an artwork.
nodes.response: Explain that artists can be inspired by the rainforest without being physically present there. Clarify that art inspired by rainforests could focus on plants, landscapes, or abstract interpretations.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Artists who use the rainforest as inspiration for their artwork

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that mixing in lots of colours makes a better brown.
nodes.response: Overmixing paint can lead to a muddy, unappealing colour, rather than a clean, rich brown.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore the shades, textures and colours of a rainforest

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that leaves are uniform in shape, when in fact rainforest leaves vary greatly in shape and size.
nodes.response: Highlight the diversity of plant forms and individuality of shape in the lesson.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw the rainforest: studies of plants and leaves

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use the same brush size for the entire painting.
nodes.response: Demonstrate how larger brushes are best for covering big areas like the background, while smaller brushes are ideal for details like leaves, veins, or animal features. Provide examples of how different brush sizes create varied textures and effects.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Paint a rainforest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they will need to always use leaves when creating a frottage. Pupils may think frottage involves drawing objects such as leaves.
nodes.response: Frottage involves rubbing over textures, not drawing them. It captures the texture of surfaces rather than depicting them with lines. While leaves are commonly used, frottage can be done with various textured objects like coins or wood.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make frottage leaf studies

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that texture is only about how something feels when touched.
nodes.response: Remind children that in art, texture can also be shown visually, like drawing rough bark or smooth leaves, even if you can’t physically feel it.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Collage skills using the rainforest as inspiration

nodes.misconception: Pupils may hold the camera or device in a  landscape grip instead of portrait.
nodes.response: Pupils should hold their device/camera with a portrait grip.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Take and edit a portrait photograph

nodes.misconception: You need to press down hard to engrave a design.
nodes.response: Children should be encouraged not to press too hard when engraving their design to avoid making holes in the matrix.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a print profile portrait

nodes.misconception: Students spread images individually out across the page without making visual connections.
nodes.response: Encourage students to use overlapping and layering with their images to create interest and visual connections.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create an identity mood board

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that, in a profile portrait, both eyes and ears are visible.
nodes.response: In a true profile portrait, only one eye and one ear are typically visible, as the subject is viewed from the side.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Profile portraits in art

nodes.misconception: Students may attempt to create a piece that resembles a two-dimensional image as a result of not layering the materials.
nodes.response: Students should be reminded to layer materials to create a three-dimensional piece.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Relief sculpture profile portrait

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the eyes are drawn towards the top of the face.
nodes.response: The eyes are halfway between the top of the head and the chin.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw a profile portrait

nodes.misconception: Typographic designs should be minimal because otherwise they are hard to read and do not communicate a clear message.
nodes.response: Typography enhances the clarity of a design, making text easier to read by arranging elements with a visual hierarchy.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create  expressive typographic work

nodes.misconception: The content of text conveys all essential information.
nodes.response: Typograhy, typefaces, and letterform designs can change the emotion and message of written text.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Learn to draw typographic letter forms

nodes.misconception: To create an expressive letterform you must have neat handwriting skills.
nodes.response: Expressive letterforms use drawing and designing skills to convey emotions and ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design an expressive letter form

nodes.misconception: Concrete poems are drawings decorated with words.
nodes.response: Concrete poems integrate text with a shape to convey meaning. They are not merely drawings decorated with words.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a concrete poem

nodes.misconception: Letters are only used for reading
nodes.response: Letters can be used to make interesting and beautiful designs
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Graphic design: the art of letters

nodes.misconception: Calligraphy is just decorative handwriting.
nodes.response: Calligraphy is an art form with specific techniques, not just decorative handwriting.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise calligraphic techniques

nodes.misconception: All street art is vandalism and illegal.
nodes.response: While some graffiti is done without permission, many street artists get permission or are commissioned to create their work. Street art can be a respected and impactful form of expression.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Artists who create street art

nodes.misconception: Graffiti art is only about using spray paint on walls.
nodes.response: Graffiti can be done using many mediums, including digital media, and digital tools allow us to explore and refine our designs without needing physical walls. Graffiti is about expression, regardless of the medium.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing graffiti letter designs using digital media

nodes.misconception: Street art has to be spontaneous and can't be planned or created digitally.
nodes.response: While street art often has a spontaneous nature, digital tools allow artists to plan and refine their designs before sharing them publicly. Digital art can provide more control and flexibility, allowing for thoughtful and intentional compositions.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Use digital techniques to make street art compositions

nodes.misconception: Graffiti letters are always supposed to be messy or hard to read.
nodes.response: While some graffiti can be abstract or complex, many styles focus on legibility and clarity, especially in tags and block letters. Graffiti artists often balance style with readability, making their work both creative and accessible.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketching street art and designing graffiti letters

nodes.misconception: Street art is just graffiti and vandalism, not real art.
nodes.response: While some street art is made without permission, many street artists communicate meaningful social or political messages. Street art is a legitimate and powerful art form that challenges societal norms and promotes dialogue.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring social messages in street art

nodes.misconception: Digital tools are not necessary for street art; real street art has to be done with spray paint on walls.
nodes.response: While spray paint is common in street art, digital tools are increasingly used in the design and creation process. Digital art allows artists to experiment, refine, and plan their murals before transferring them to large-scale physical surfaces.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a street art mural

nodes.misconception: Faces are symmetrical and all proportions should fit to set guidelines.
nodes.response: Most faces are asymmetrical with different proportions. Guidelines for drawing faces give only a rough estimation of where features might be placed, and will differ for each person, as we are all unique.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Painting: the foundations of a facial expression

nodes.misconception: Colours are neutral and do not evoke emotion.
nodes.response: Colours can evoke a wide range of different emotions. For example, blue might suggest calmness while red might indicate anger.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing: use tone and colour for facial expressions

nodes.misconception: All types of smile indicate happiness in a person.
nodes.response: There are many nuances in smiles, such as a polite smile versus a genuine smile, which can convey different feelings.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Analyse a facial expression through drawing

nodes.misconception: Only strong emotions can be seen as facial expressions.
nodes.response: Facial expressions can sometimes be subtle or mixed, making them challenging to identify accurately.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate facial expressions in portraits

nodes.misconception: Emotions are only conveyed through words and physical gestures.
nodes.response: Facial expressions are a universal way to communicate emotions, even without words.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital photography: creating a series of facial expression photographs

nodes.misconception: The largest features of a facial expression convey the most emotion.
nodes.response: Applying details and small adjustments to a facial expression such as tone, texture and highlights can make them more dynamic, expressive and realistic.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Painting: finalising a facial expression painting

nodes.misconception: Clay cannot be worked with unless it is very wet.
nodes.response: Clay can be worked with when it is leather hard. This means it has dried out slightly, so it can be stronger to work with.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a low relief ceramic tile: transfer and carve

nodes.misconception: Artists have group critiques to just suggest ways to make an artwork better.
nodes.response: Group critiques can be useful for an artist to get new ideas or suggestions, but are also useful for other artists to hear the reasons behind the artist's choices.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a low relief ceramic tile: decorate and evaluate

nodes.misconception: Artists can only take inspiration from the same features of a landmark.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can look at the same landmark, but choose to take inspiration from different features. Finding different things inspiring is an important part of being an artist.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a local landmark low relief tile

nodes.misconception: Landmarks are always human-made.
nodes.response: Remind children that some landmarks are made by humans but others are natural formations, such as cliffs, trees or waterfalls.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Photograph a local landmark

nodes.misconception: Responding to a subject is making  a copy of it.
nodes.response: Remind children that responding to an artwork means reacting to it, rather than just reproducing it.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Research and photograph a local landmark

nodes.misconception: The rolling pin does not have to rest on the guide sticks to ensure an even consistency of clay.
nodes.response: Remind children that the rolling pin should rest on both of the guide sticks.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a low relief ceramic tile: trace and transfer a design

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the shapes they use need to be perfect or uniform when sketching.
nodes.response: Remind children of the difference between organic and geometric shapes. Organic shapes do not need to be uniform or perfect.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a monster

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that storyboards need to be perfect and spend more time on the details of the drawing as opposed to thinking about the sequence of events of their animation.
nodes.response: Remind children that storyboards are rough sketches that help plan the sequence of the animation.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan a monster animation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that reviewing work after completing is not necessary.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that reviewing your work after finishing it is very important. It helps you spot any small mistakes, like jumps in the animation or unclear movements, which can make a big difference in how smooth and professional the animation looks.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Edit and complete a stop motion animation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that stop motion animation is the same as a video recording. They may think that you need expensive equipment to create stop motion animations.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that stop motion animation is created by taking individual still images. A video recording captures continuous motion. It can be created using simple and readily available devices.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make your monster move - stop motion animation

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that the characters are the only important part of the animation and that scenery doesn't matter. They also may believe that scenery is only for decorative purposes.
nodes.response: Addressing these misconceptions through discussion and reference to examples can help students understand the importance of scenery in clay animation and how it enhances storytelling.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a modelling clay monster

nodes.misconception: Monsters in myths and films are always portrayed as evil.
nodes.response: Monsters in myths and films are not always portrayed as evil. Creating monsters can involve using different features that portray a friendly or approachable character.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Monsters in myths and film

nodes.misconception: All architectural designs are symmetrical.
nodes.response: Some buildings are also asymmetrical.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing like an architect

nodes.misconception: Pupils may press too lightly and as a result their marks will not be clear.
nodes.response: Give plenty of oportunity to create drafts of their monoprint, improving the line quality each time.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a monoprint of a building

nodes.misconception: You need to press down hard when using charcoal.
nodes.response: Pressing down too hard will break the charcoal. You need to be much more gentle.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing buildings using charcoal

nodes.misconception: Students may think that all buildings are the same and don’t understand why some materials are better for the environment.
nodes.response: Some buildings waste energy, while others are designed to protect nature.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainable architecture

nodes.misconception: Any shape can make a strong building.
nodes.response: Architects select specific shapes and structures to make homes stable.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design and build a home using recycled materials

nodes.misconception: Artists always draw things exactly how they look in real life.
nodes.response: Artists sometimes draw things as they look in real life but can also draw things from their imagination.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing and painting my dream building

nodes.misconception: Paintbrushes can be left dirty and used again without cleaning.
nodes.response: Remind children that paintbrushes like to be cleaned and left on top of water pots so the next artist can use them.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketchbook experimentation: water-like marks

nodes.misconception: Artists always depict water using the colour blue.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can use blue to represent water, but they can use lots of other colours as well.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: How has water been depicted by artists, makers and designers

nodes.misconception: That portrait means the picture is always a person's face, and landscape means it can only be a big outdoor scene.
nodes.response: Remind children that portrait just means the paper is taller than it is wide, and landscape means it’s wider than tall. You can use both for many different kinds of pictures, not just faces or outdoor scenes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Painting with water as a subject

nodes.misconception: Artists will always depict the texture of water in the same way.
nodes.response: Remind children that although water itself always feels wet and smooth, artists might use their materials to show the water being bubbly, smooth or rough. Artists can describe this as the texture of the water.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Depicting water with watercolour and collage

nodes.misconception: That all artwork is permanent.
nodes.response: Remind children that some artwork can be made to be permanent, but other artwork can be made to only last a short time.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a collaborative mixed media collage

nodes.misconception: Artists always make artwork by themselves.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can choose to work by themselves, but they can also plan and make work collaboratively.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Watercolour water collaboration

nodes.misconception: Design thinking is only for artists or people who are good at drawing.
nodes.response: Design thinking is for everyone - it's more about problem-solving than creating beautiful artworks. Sketches help communicate ideas, and they don’t have to be visually striking to be effective.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to design thinking

nodes.misconception: Wild animals don’t belong in cities and can’t survive there.
nodes.response: While some wild animals struggle in cities, others adapt well if we design spaces with them in mind. Urban environments can become important habitats with thoughtful planning.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a space for urban wildlife

nodes.misconception: Urban art is just graffiti or vandalism.
nodes.response: Urban art includes many creative and meaningful responses to city life - from murals and installations to Fine Art inspired by architecture. It can be legal, expressive, and community-based.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching the urban environment

nodes.misconception: Urban design is solely about constructing buildings.​
nodes.response: Urban design encompasses the planning of entire city environments, including streets, public spaces, transportation systems and the relationships between different urban elements.​
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating urban design

nodes.misconception: Sustainable transport is just about electric vehicles.
nodes.response: Sustainability includes more than just power sources - it also involves materials, passenger capacity, energy use, and reducing pollution across a whole system.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a sustainable transport system

nodes.misconception: Urban design is only about buildings and roads.
nodes.response: Urban design includes public spaces, such as parks, playgrounds, and recreational areas. Urban design is about how people use and experience space, not just what gets built.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a space to play

nodes.misconception: Art is only about copying what things look like, rather than expressing feelings.
nodes.response: You can use colours, shapes, or lines to share your mood or ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing relationships

nodes.misconception: Children may rush through the drawing without observing carefully, believing that drawing quickly means drawing well.
nodes.response: Children could be reminded to take their time and look closely at the subject.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: People that are important to me

nodes.misconception: You always have to take a photograph from the front.
nodes.response: You can experiment with angles and frames to make your photographs more interesting.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Connections through photography

nodes.misconception: Symbols have to be detailed.
nodes.response: Symbols can be refined and made simple.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital printing

nodes.misconception: All joining methods are equally strong.
nodes.response: Some methods, like a tight twist are much stronger than others.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating an armature figure

nodes.misconception: The more clay you use, the better balanced your figure will be.
nodes.response: Using more clay does not always make your figure balanced. A figure is balanced when the weight is spread out evenly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sculpting Myself

nodes.misconception: Reflecting on your work only happens when you have finished making it.
nodes.response: Remind children that reflecting on the success of your work and areas that could be improved can happen both during and after the making of your work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Realise the details of a local landscape painting

nodes.misconception: A paintbrush can only be used for one effect.
nodes.response: Remind children that a paintbrush can be used to create many different effects, such as dry-brush and wet on wet.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore a variety of painting techniques

nodes.misconception: When artists look at the same landscape, their artwork will look similar.
nodes.response: Remind children that sometimes artists will make artwork that looks similar, but this is not always the case. Artists can interpret their inspiration using their own, individual style.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and applying the influence of other artists

nodes.misconception: Artists can only work in sketchbooks purchased from a shop.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can work in lots of different styles of sketchbook, including ones they have made themselves.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Lay the foundations for a local landscape painting

nodes.misconception: Urban landscapes cannot contain any natural features.
nodes.response: Remind children that both natural and urban landscapes can have a mix of natural and human-made features, but natural landscapes focus more on nature, and urban landscapes focus more on buildings and roads.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Photograph a landscape in your local area

nodes.misconception: In nature, patterns are perfectly repeated.
nodes.response: Remind children that in nature, patterns sometimes repeat but the shapes, colours or lines are slightly different.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Analyse a local landscape through the formal elements

nodes.misconception: Warp and weft threads are the same.
nodes.response: Remind children that the warp threads hold the weft threads in place. These are the first threads attached to the loom.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring weaving techniques

nodes.misconception: Evaluating is only saying what you like or dislike
nodes.response: Remind pupils that evaluation is more than just saying what we like or dislike about an artwork. It should help an artist improve their work over time.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Embellish and evaluate

nodes.misconception: Looms cannot be made from everyday objects.
nodes.response: Remind children that looms can be made on a wide variety of frames, including found sticks or paper plates.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Weaving using everyday objects as a frame

nodes.misconception: All textiles are fabric.
nodes.response: Remind children that fabric is one kind of textile. There are many different kinds of textiles including felted materials, waterproof materials and synthetic fibers.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The qualities of different textiles

nodes.misconception: All looms are rectangular.
nodes.response: Remind children that some weavings are made on square or rectangular looms, but weavings do not have to be made on looms with straight sides. Looms can be curved.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Circular weaving

nodes.misconception: Once  a design has been created, it cannot be adapted or changed.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can change their ideas as they go, making changes to their design as they continue through the design and making process.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design an underwater weaving

nodes.misconception: Objects in art are just for decoration.
nodes.response: Objects often have meanings. For example, a crown might mean power. When planning, think carefully about what each object could represent in your story artwork.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan a story artwork including character and objects

nodes.misconception: Characters just need to look good, they don’t need to mean anything.
nodes.response: Great character design includes meaning with symbols and design choices conveying personality and mood.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing: create a character for a story

nodes.misconception: Colouring everything in neatly makes a finished artwork.
nodes.response: Finishing an artwork isn’t just about colouring - it’s about choosing colours and adding details that help tell the story more clearly and powerfully.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Complete a story artwork: colour and detail

nodes.misconception: A symbol has only one meaning for everyone.
nodes.response: Symbols can mean different things in different cultures or to different people.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Symbolism and stories in art, craft and design

nodes.misconception: Any object can be used as it doesn’t have to mean anything.
nodes.response: Objects can be used to help tell stories and add depth and meaning through what they symbolise.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop understanding of symbolism: collect and draw objects

nodes.misconception: The environment can be anywhere; the most important clues for a story are from the characters and objects.
nodes.response: The setting is an important device for communicating a story. It shows where the story happens and adds clues about mood, time, or place.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop a story: creating a scenic composition

nodes.misconception: All 3D card designs require glue or tape to stick pieces together.
nodes.response: Techniques such as slotting can be used to create strong and effective 3D card structures, even without the use of glue.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sculpture: card construction techniques

nodes.misconception: Adding too many decorations will make the mask too busy or overwhelming.
nodes.response: It’s important to find balance in the mask’s design. Decoration can enhance the mask and highlight specific areas, such as the eyes or mouth, without overcrowding the mask’s overall look. Less can be more in some areas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface decoration and completion of a mask

nodes.misconception: All masks are used for disguise.
nodes.response: Masks can also be used for cultural ceremonies, art and storytelling.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mask designs: research and mood board

nodes.misconception: A mask shape must be perfectly symmetrical to look good.
nodes.response: While symmetry is often used, asymmetry can also be used to create dynamic and interesting designs.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a mask shape

nodes.misconception: A single thick layer of modroc will create a strong sculpture.
nodes.response: Modroc works best when thin layers are built up gradually. This allows the material to dry properly and allows the sculpture to become stronger.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mask construction using modroc

nodes.misconception: Sources should be copied from exactly to create a good design.
nodes.response: Sources are for inspiration, not replication. Great designs mix ideas from multiple sources and add personal creativity.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a mask using sources

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that tone is only about making things darker and that shading should be done with harsh, straight lines.
nodes.response: Tone includes both light and dark areas, and the goal is to show the full range of tones, from light highlights to deep shadows. Using the side of the pencil for softer shading, helps to avoid harsh lines.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a tonal study of a sculpture

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think sculptures can only be made from one material, like clay or metal, rather than a combination of assembled materials.
nodes.response: Show images of sculptures made from various materials (e.g. cardboard, wood, metal, plastic). Discuss with the class how combining materials can make sculptures more interesting or practical.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketchbook research: artists who have assembled materials to make sculpture

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that shadows are always black.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to cast shadows and to look at the tone of the shadow. Observe the tone on different coloured objects. Draw pupils' attention to the fact that shadows are not always black.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketchbook research: insect, animal and bird studies and designs

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think any material can be used for any body part, like using lightweight or flexible materials for the base instead of sturdy ones.
nodes.response: Show examples of sculptures with a sturdy base versus those with a weak base, using different materials (e.g., cardboard vs tissue paper).
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Select and assemble recyclable materials to make a creature

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a maquette is the final sculpture and needs to be large. They may also jump into adding small details before constructing the basic form.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a maquette is a smaller version to plan and test ideas before making a bigger sculpture. The main shape and structure need to be built first to support the details.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sculpture: make a maquette

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all parts of the sculpture must be detailed.
nodes.response: Remind children that  it’s better to focus on key features like the face, wings, or texture, rather than decorating every part. This keeps your design clear and makes your creature stand out.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sculpture: refine and finish creature creations

nodes.misconception: Complementary colours are located next to each other on the colour wheel.
nodes.response: Remind children that complementary colours are opposite each other on the colour wheel, not next to each other. This opposite placement is what creates their high contrast and visual vibrancy when paired.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Use monoprinting to create a self-portrait

nodes.misconception: Evaluation and reflection only takes place when the artwork is complete.
nodes.response: Remind children that reflecting upon your artwork can be useful at any stage of the creative process. It helps the artist recognise their successes and decide upon areas that could be improved.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemblage: exterior box design

nodes.misconception: Assemblage sculptures cannot contain drawn and collaged elements.
nodes.response: Remind children that assemblage is a form of sculpture that includes everyday objects but can also be made from natural materials, manufactured items, photographs, text and drawings.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemblage: interior box design

nodes.misconception: Assemblage sculptures are carved or moulded.
nodes.response: Remind children that an assemblage sculpture is not usually carved or moulded, but parts are assembled using glue, tape, wire or thread.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan for an assemblage sculpture

nodes.misconception: Including personal materials in artwork has no effect on how emotional or powerful the art feels.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists might use personal materials to tell a story, share a memory, or express emotions.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create an art box

nodes.misconception: You do not need to plan a self-portrait concrete poem. You should just start by writing.
nodes.response: Remind children that planning some descriptive words or phrases can help to ensure their emotions or message are communicated effectively in their concrete poem.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draft a self-portrait concrete poem

nodes.misconception: Primary colors are made by mixing other colours together.
nodes.response: Remind children that primary colours cannot be created by mixing other colours. Secondary colours are made by mixing two primary colours together. For example, blue and yellow make green.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mixing secondary colours: spring greens

nodes.misconception: Paint can only be mixed in a paint palette.
nodes.response: Paint can be mixed in a paint palette, but it can also be mixed on paper to create a blend.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mixing secondary colours: summer purples

nodes.misconception: All opinions should be the same.
nodes.response: Remind children that other people might disagree with you or have a different opinion. This is what helps to make art exciting.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Paint the seasons: plan a colourful work

nodes.misconception: Artists only use paintbrushes to apply paint.
nodes.response: Artists can use a paintbrush to apply paint, but they can also use other tools, such as leaves, sticks and pinecones.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mixing secondary colours: autumn oranges

nodes.misconception: That each part of a triptych is separate and unconnected.
nodes.response: Remind children that in a triptych, each panel shares ideas with the others to create one single artwork.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Painting the seasons

nodes.misconception: Hot or cold colours can change the temperature.
nodes.response: Remind children that these colours do not really change the temperature, but they can make people feel warmer by looking at them, as they remind them of hot things like the sun or a fire.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Hot and cold colours

nodes.misconception: Students may not consider how materials are joined together.
nodes.response: When constructing a structure, we must think carefully about how they are joined together.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Construct a paradise island base

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that once the base is painted the 3D artwork is completed.
nodes.response: Artists often reflect and revisit their work to add further detail and bring their artwork to life.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Decorate a papier-mâché paradise island

nodes.misconception: Everyone in the group has to have the same ideas.
nodes.response: It's okay to have different ideas as good teams listen, share, and find ways to combine or choose ideas together.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Invent a collaborative paradise island

nodes.misconception: Children may think that art is only about copying what you see, not what you feel or imagine.
nodes.response: Art can involve expressive mark-making, imaginative thinking and communicating mood or ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Imaginative memory drawing

nodes.misconception: When painting, pupils may try to paint everything at once without letting layers dry.
nodes.response: When painting, it is important to paint the background first and let it dry before adding other elements on top.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Respond to artists' visions of paradise

nodes.misconception: The pupils may think that one layer of papier-mâché is enough.
nodes.response: We need multiple layers to make it strong. Artists build layer by layer to shape and secure their sculpture.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a papier-maché paradise island

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all parts of the plate will print.
nodes.response: Show and remind pupils that only the raised parts of the plate will print, and the carved parts will stay blank.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Insect printmaking: block print

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that adding more detail will always make a print better.
nodes.response: While detail can be important in some art, too many tiny or delicate details can get lost or not transfer properly when printing. It’s actually more effective to use bold, simple shapes and lines to create a clear and striking print.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Refine and prepare drawings for print

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the insect needs to be in the centre of the page for a balanced composition.
nodes.response: Remind children that composition can be balanced even if the insect is placed off-centre. Balance is about how all elements (insect, plants, background) work together, not just where the main subject is.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw and observe insects in detail

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that monoprinting means making multiple copies of the same image.
nodes.response: Through discussion and observation, remind pupils that each print is slightly different because of the way ink is applied and removed.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Insect printmaking: monoprint

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a repeat pattern means just stamping the same image randomly.
nodes.response: Demonstrate how patterns can follow a structured repetition, showing examples of tiling techniques.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a repeat pattern print

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Chine collé is just gluing paper onto a print after it is finished.
nodes.response: Explain that the thin paper is applied before printing, so it bonds as part of the printmaking process.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Insect printmaking: Chine collé

nodes.misconception: It is easier to sketch an outline without first using shapes.
nodes.response: Remind children that if we use shapes to plan our drawing, it becomes much easier to achive the correct position and proportions with our outline.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a portrait of a sleeping person

nodes.misconception: Opinions about an artwork can only be shared through words.
nodes.response: Remind children that we can share our opinions about an artwork with both a verbal and a visual response. It is another way of telling others what interests us most about an artwork.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art about dreams

nodes.misconception: Artists need to observe from reality to make art.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that art can be an observation, but it can also be taking an idea we have in our heads and making it into an artwork.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Illustrate a piece of text about dreams

nodes.misconception: Shadow appears all around the object in a single, dark tone. Pupils may also draw shadows as a solid, dark shape.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to draw an arrow to show where the light is coming from. Remind pupils to look carefully at their object and consider where the shadow is darkest and where the shadow fades.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Add tone to your sleeping portrait

nodes.misconception: Photographic images always reflect reality.
nodes.response: Remind children that photographic images can be digitally manipulated using a computer or digital software, they do not always reflect reality.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a digital dreamscape

nodes.misconception: When cutting complex shapes, we move the scissors rather than the paper.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to move the paper, rather than the scissors when cutting, with their thumbs facing upwards towards the ceiling.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Surreal dreamscape collage

nodes.misconception: Templates do not need to be pinned to fabric.
nodes.response: Remind children that pinning before cutting allows you to adjust the placement of your templates.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating templates for fabric from drawings

nodes.misconception: Arpilleras generally avoid themes related to daily life or social issues.
nodes.response: Remind children that arpilleras are typically appliquéd textile scenes, showing everyday life, rural culture, or times of conflict. Arpilleras are sometimes used as activist art, especially in the context of human rights or social justice.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop a design for an arpillera

nodes.misconception: Artists rarely use their work to respond to conflict or explore its impact on people and society.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists have often responded to war and conflict by using their work to express the pain, fear, and devastation experienced by those affected.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art about conflict

nodes.misconception: Needle felting tools are easy to use without considering safety.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that felting needles are extremely sharp. They should be used with a high consideration of safety, particularly ensuring fingers and eyes are protected.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore needle felting

nodes.misconception: Stitches are just used to join materials together.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that while stitches can be used to join materials together, they are also used in a skilled and decorative way through embroidery.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Stitch an arpillera

nodes.misconception: Evaluation and reflection only takes place when the artwork is complete.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that reflecting upon your artwork can be useful at any stage of the creative process. It helps the artist recognise their successes and decide upon areas that could be improved and refined.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate and refine your arpillera

nodes.misconception: Pupils could think the maquette is the final version of their sculpture, rather than a starting point for refining and improving their design.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a maquette is a guide for their sculpture, not a final blueprint. Emphasise that it's okay to make changes as they work to improve stability and functionality.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Refine and evaluate a robot sculpture

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume robots have only one job, not understanding how versatile robots can be when designed for different tasks such as cleaning, farming, or saving resources.
nodes.response: Remind children that robots can have many different purposes! Show images of robots used in various ways, like cleaning oceans, planting trees, or sorting recyclables.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a robot

nodes.misconception: Some children might think cross-hatching is just drawing straight lines to create shading.
nodes.response: Show pupils different examples of cross-hatching and allow time to practise other shading techniques.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a tonal study of a robot sculpture

nodes.misconception: You can choose recycled materials randomly without considering your robot's purpose or the material's properties.
nodes.response: Encourage children to focus on the robot's main purpose first, like its key features (e.g. arms for cleaning). Once those are in place, they can add extra details. Remind them to refer to their maquettes to stay focused.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sculpt a robot using recyclable materials

nodes.misconception: Some children might not realise that robots are used in real life, such as in hospitals, factories, and homes.
nodes.response: Remind children that robots do appear in films and books, but they are also used in real life. For example, robots help doctors in hospitals, build cars in factories, and even explore space for NASA.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Research robots in art

nodes.misconception: A maquette is a finished sculpture, not a model for planning a design.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that building a maquette is an opportunity to test different elements of their design, allowing them to identify areas for improvement. A maquette does not need to be perfect as its purpose is to resolve issues before the final design.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a maquette of a robot

nodes.misconception: Patterns can only be made with shapes and lines.
nodes.response: Remind children that shapes and lines can be used to make patterns, but motifs can be used to create more complex patterns.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Print and pattern with vegetables

nodes.misconception: Tone is always achieved through pressure.
nodes.response: Remind children that tone can be achieved through adding pressure, but layers of material can also be built up or removed to vary tone.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Tonal flowers

nodes.misconception: Drawings always have to look exactly like the object the artist is observing.
nodes.response: Drawing exercises focus more on artists using their eyes to carefully observe lines and shapes, rather than trying to create a drawing that looks exactly like the object.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing flowers: shape and line

nodes.misconception: Texture can only be shown with drawing or painting
nodes.response: Remind pupils that artists might choose to use clay to represent textures as it can show a wide range of different surfaces.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make flower sculptures: texture

nodes.misconception: The petals of a flower are flat.
nodes.response: Remind children that the petals of a flower curve and bend, so are not flat shapes. They are a three-dimensional form.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine elements and create a flower garden

nodes.misconception: Artists can always match colours on the first attempt.
nodes.response: Remind children that it can take an artist several tries to make the correct colour. By practicing colour mixing, artists can improve over time.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Colour mixing for the garden

nodes.misconception: Artistic choices never change during the creative process.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists often make creative adjustments as they work, changing their ideas, materials, or processes based on how the artwork is developing.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make an abstract composition

nodes.misconception: Responding to an image means making an exact copy
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a response means taking an idea but changing it slightly to make it yours.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Observe and record microorganisms

nodes.misconception: Collages are always three-dimensional.
nodes.response: Remind children that collages can be three-dimensional, but can also be made on a flat surface.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Monoprint onto a collaged surface

nodes.misconception: Monoprinting is only about making a copy, not about creativity.
nodes.response: Remind children that monoprinting is a form of artistic expression. Artists can use monoprinting to create unique, creative works where textures, colours and styles can vary greatly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating monoprinted papers using different textures and surfaces

nodes.misconception: Artists can only use one material to create tone in an artwork.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists can use a range of materials within one artwork to show tone. This is called a mixed-media artwork.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Tonal studies of microorganisms

nodes.misconception: The fabric colour palette selected should precisely match the colours present in the petri dish.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists might choose to take inspiration from a similar colour palette of fabrics, rather than those that match exactly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Scrap fabric microrganism collage

nodes.misconception: Traditionally, all cultures use paintbrushes to paint.
nodes.response: Remind children that although paintbrushes are a popular artistic tool, they are not traditional for every community or culture.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Devise a mark-making toolkit

nodes.misconception: A paper-cut printing process cannot be used to create multiple prints from the same templates.
nodes.response: Remind children that artists might choose this process as they can make multiple prints from the same templates.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make an abstract print using a paper-cut technique

nodes.misconception: Abstract art copies exactly what something looks like.
nodes.response: Remind children that abstract art is art that does not try to represent something realistically, but instead focuses on emotions, shapes and movements.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring abstract art

nodes.misconception: All papers have the same texture.
nodes.response: Remind children that different papers have different textures. For example, tracing paper is smooth and thin, while watercolor paper is thick and textured. Materials can look and behave differently depending on the surface of the paper.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create an abstract composition

nodes.misconception: Stitching onto paper is exactly the same as stitching onto fabric.
nodes.response: Remind children that stitching on paper requires a few things to be mindful of, including preparing holes in your paper and not pulling your thread too tightly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make an abstract felt panel

nodes.misconception: Stitches are just used to join materials together.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that, while stitches can be used to join materials together, they are also used in a skilled and decorative way through embroidery.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design an abstract textile panel

nodes.misconception: Marbling was invented in Britain.
nodes.response: Art historians are not exactly sure where marbling was invented, but it was certainly popular in places such as Japan a long time before it was brought to Britain.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Chalk prints

nodes.misconception: Chalk pastels only come in black and white.
nodes.response: Chalk pastels come in black and white, but they also come in a wide range of bright and vibrant colours.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a chalk planet

nodes.misconception: Straight lines rather than curved lines are used to draw a sphere.
nodes.response: Remind children that if straight lines are used, the sphere can look flat even though the artist has used tone. Curved lines help the moon to look spherical.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw the moon

nodes.misconception: Marbling prints can only be made in one way.
nodes.response: Marbling can be made in lots of different ways, such as ink or chalk  floating on water. Marbling can also be made with shaving foam.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make decorative paper using marbling techniques

nodes.misconception: Backgrounds in artworks are not as important as the images within an artwork.
nodes.response: Remind children that backgrounds to artworks can make an image more interesting, or tell us more about the images within an artwork. They can also make an artwork look more three-dimensional.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a space inspired composition

nodes.misconception: Scissors should be held with the thumb  on the bottom, and the index finger on the top.
nodes.response: Remind children that scissors should be used with the thumb on top, nearest to the ceiling. Scissors should also be held in the same position, cutting away from the body with the paper being moved.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create planets and stars using collage papers

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think pressing down hard makes the print clearer.
nodes.response: Applying even pressure will result in a clearer print.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Print a repeat pattern using a motif

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that patterns do not need a grid to be structured.
nodes.response: While freehand patterns exist, grids help maintain consistency.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a pattern using a square grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all repeating patterns are natural patterns, even if they are man-made.
nodes.response: To help clarify, you could emphasise that natural patterns are found in nature. Nature walks can be a hands-on way to help students discover natural patterns.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Patterns in nature

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that intricate designs are necessary, however simple shapes with clear details often work best for creating patterns.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch a few different simple shapes and test how they repeat in a pattern. You can also cut out your motif and arrange multiple copies to see how they fit together.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Design and make a pattern motif

nodes.misconception: All kaleidoscope patterns are circular.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that while many have a circular appearance, kaleidoscope patterns can also be based on squares, triangles, and other geometric grids.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a kaleidoscope pattern

nodes.misconception: Patterns in art are always symmetrical and repetitive.
nodes.response: While many patterns do follow symmetrical or repetitive structures, patterns in art can also be organic, irregular, and asymmetrical.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating patterns in art

nodes.misconception: Once an idea has been drawn, it is finished.
nodes.response: Artists often revisit and refine their ideas. A first sketch is just the starting point - you can improve your work by trying different layouts, materials, and colour choices.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop a Pop Art piece

nodes.misconception: All Pop Art looks the same - it’s just bold colours and celebrities.
nodes.response: Each Pop artist had a unique message and approach. Some explored consumerism, others made emotional or political statements.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Pop Art: in depth artist study

nodes.misconception: Sketchbooks are for finished drawings only.
nodes.response: Sketchbooks are working spaces. They’re for exploring, not perfecting. Artists use them to test, plan and reflect, not to make polished work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Idea development: thinking through sketching

nodes.misconception: Pop Art is just cartoon drawing or copying famous things.
nodes.response: Pop Art uses familiar imagery to comment on culture, not just to copy it. Artists chose their subjects carefully to reflect society’s values and consumer habits.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The history of Pop Art

nodes.misconception: Researching means copying images exactly into your final artwork.
nodes.response: Research is about gathering inspiration and developing ideas, not copying. Artists reinterpret and combine sources in creative and personal ways.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Pop Art: finding sources and researching an idea

nodes.misconception: A final outcome must look identical to the original plan.
nodes.response: Artists adapt ideas during making. Their plan is a starting point - not a rule. Changing materials or layout during creation is part of the artistic process.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Pop Art: realise a final outcome

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that art has to last forever to be important or valuable.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that art can be ephemeral - meaning it lasts only a short time - and still be very important. Just like nature’s changes, temporary art helps us notice beauty, tell stories, and understand ideas about growth and resilience.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art that shows nature’s resilience

nodes.misconception: Art is only made from traditional art materials.
nodes.response: Art can be made from almost anything, including plastic waste, as in the case of Mandy Barker.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: An artist's respond to plastic waste

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that anything found outside is natural, even if it is actually human-made. For example, bricks, fences, playground equipment, or painted surfaces.
nodes.response: Remind children that natural means it comes from nature and wasn’t made by people. Human-made means humans designed or built it, even if you find it outside.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Recording environmental textures

nodes.misconception: Nature and cities can’t go together.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that many cities already mix nature into their design - with green roofs, gardens, trees, and wildlife spaces. Cities can be sustainable and nature-friendly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Imagining a better future

nodes.misconception: There is a right and wrong way in which to rearrange lines and shapes when making abstract art.
nodes.response: There is no right or wrong - in abstract art shapes and lines can be rearranged according to the intentions of the artist.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw fossils in an abstract style

nodes.misconception: Two pieces of clay can just be pressed together to attach them.
nodes.response: Clay needs to be scored and slip applied to create a strong bond, just like glue helps stick paper together.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Experimenting with clay for a cake sculpture

nodes.misconception: Even if the coils don't stick together, the pot will still hold together once it dries or after it's fired.
nodes.response: Coils need to be properly joined using slip to ensure they don’t separate during the drying or firing process.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Experiment with coil and pinch pot techniques

nodes.misconception: Charcoal is too messy to control, and mistakes can’t be fixed.
nodes.response: Charcoal is a flexible material. Smudging can be used to soften mistakes or use a rubber to refine shapes and add highlights.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing: observe and draw cakes using charcoal

nodes.misconception: If the clay is wet, it will stick together and hold without needing to apply slip.
nodes.response: Clay must be wet enough to join properly. Without slip, dry clay won't bond effectively, leading to cracks. The best way to stick together different pieces of clay is to score each side and use slip to ensure a secure connection.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Build a clay celebration cake

nodes.misconception: A cake design must be realistic to be good.
nodes.response: While realism can help in some design projects, creative and exaggerated designs can make cakes visually exciting and unique.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketching and designing a celebration cake

nodes.misconception: A good cake-inspired sculpture must look realistic.
nodes.response: Cake-inspired sculptures can be creative, experiment with textures, colours and other ideas, not just realistic depictions. Great art can be a combination of interpretation and imagination.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Ceramics: finalising a cake inspired creation

nodes.misconception: All maps have to look like the ones on phones or paper.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that some artists make maps with patterns, colours and memories.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Paint a walking line

nodes.misconception: You need special or expensive things to make fabric patterns.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that you can use natural objects, paper and wax to make patterns on fabric. You can use simple, safe materials to tell powerful stories through cloth.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Print a sea pattern on cloth – stories in indigo

nodes.misconception: We all feel the same about every colour.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that everyone feels colours differently.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art with music and colour

nodes.misconception: We can use as much clay from the Earth as we want!
nodes.response: Remind pupils that we share natural resources and use them carefully, so there is enough for everyone.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a clay picture

nodes.misconception: Beads are just for decoration.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that beads can tell stories, show who someone is, or carry messages. In many cultures around the world, beads are worn to remember, to celebrate, or to show strength. The patterns and shapes often have deep meanings.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Clay beads: meanings and patterns

nodes.misconception: Symbols are just pictures - they don’t really mean anything.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that symbols are pictures with power. People use them to show who they are, what they believe in, or what they want to change. On banners, every shape and colour can tell a story.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Printing symbols: banners and identity

nodes.misconception: My sculpture has to look like a real person to say something important.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that sculptures can be bold, simplified or abstract and still carry strong messages. Artists like Sokari Douglas Camp use pose, pattern and costume to express complex ideas about history, power and pride.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Masque: sculpture, clothes and messages

nodes.misconception: My sculpture needs to show action or be realistic.
nodes.response: Our sculpture can be still, soft, or bulky. It doesn't need to move or look like a real person to hold meaning. Wrapping and shaping can show something inside you, a memory, a feeling or a story, without using words.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Wrapping a sculpture: hidden stories

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think they can only use scissors to cut paper.
nodes.response: Model tearing and cutting and explain to pupils that choice between the two is important. Tearing makes soft textures like grass or clouds. Cutting makes sharp edges for shapes like windows. Think about which works best for your design.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a background using reclaimed materials

nodes.misconception: Silhouettes must be made of black card or paper.
nodes.response: Remind children that silhouettes are often made of black paper or card as this shows up well against a light background, but it is up to the artist which solid colour they will use to make their silhouette.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a silhouette scene

nodes.misconception: Pupils may paint the fox and background in similar colours, making the sculpture blend in.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the fox should stand out - encourage warm, bright colours for the fox against darker shades in the background.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Reclaimed materials: finalising a mixed-media piece

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel the need to cut the clay straight away before connecting the dots.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to connect the dots carefully first before cutting. Consider giving them a light pencil or tool to trace the outline before cutting.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Sculpture: make a simple clay animal

nodes.misconception: There is only one spiky texture on a hedgehog.
nodes.response: A hedgehog has a spiky texture, but also has soft, furry ears.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Respond to nocturnal animals through modelling materials

nodes.misconception: Once an artwork is finished, artists should never change or improve it.
nodes.response: Remind children that looking at your work and finding ways you could improve it is an important part of being an artist.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a silhouette plaque

nodes.misconception: Once a sculpture is built, it should always stay the same.
nodes.response: Some sculptures are meant to change over time. Artists might add to them, reuse parts or let nature affect them. Change can tell new stories and show that art is alive.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Clay landscapes: hand building towers together

nodes.misconception: Charcoal is just for colouring or outlines.
nodes.response: Remind children that charcoal is a powerful tool for mood and space – it can create atmosphere.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Charcoal worlds: draw, smudge, imagine

nodes.misconception: Sculpture has to be glued or stuck together to be finished.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that some sculptures are temporary – artists sometimes build things that can fall, change or disappear.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Balance and print: telling stories with everyday things

nodes.misconception: Some materials are too simple to be art.
nodes.response: Remind pupls that artists like El Anatsui use simple, reused materials to make powerful work about memory, movement and transformation.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art installation: sculpture you can walk through

nodes.misconception: Makeup is only used to cover imperfections and cannot be used to tell a story, represent a theme or have fun with one's appearance.
nodes.response: Remind children that makeup is much more than decoration. It is a powerful way to express identity, emotions and celebration, and it helps bring people together in shared joy and creativity.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative careers: makeup artist

nodes.misconception: All festivals are global events.
nodes.response: Remind children that while some festivals are celebrated globally, such as New Year's Eve, other festivals are celebrated only in particular areas or countries.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Festivals from around the world

nodes.misconception: It is not important to consider the identity of the festival when creating your logo.
nodes.response: Remind children that graphic designers should consider the unique character of their festival when creating their logo, so they can visually represent the ethos of the event in their design.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative careers: graphic designer

nodes.misconception: A content creator must always promote an event through posters and videos to be successful.
nodes.response: Remind children that while posters and videos are useful, an event can also be successfully promoted through spoken messages, social media, or written adverts. The key is to share clear and engaging information, not just the format used.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative careers: content creator

nodes.misconception: A fashion collection is an assortment of clothes and accessories with no common theme or coordinating colours.
nodes.response: Remind children that a fashion collection consists of clothes and accessories that share colours, fabrics, or themes designed to showcase the particular style of a fashion designer.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative careers: fashion designer

nodes.misconception: A game's aesthetic does not need to be consistent throughout the game.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that keeping the graphics, sounds, colours and feelings the same throughout the game helps players stay focused and understand the game better.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative careers: games designer

nodes.misconception: Recycled materials are rubbish, and art made from them is not important.
nodes.response: Artists turn everyday scraps into powerful pieces. Using waste shows we care for the planet and value every material, big or small.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Unweaving, wrapping, transforming: textile sculpture

nodes.misconception: History ended long ago; it has nothing to do with today.
nodes.response: History still affects life now. By talking about past injustice, maybe through art, we learn how to build a fairer present
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Shadow stories: silhouette, clay and light

nodes.misconception: All protests are loud and dangerous.
nodes.response: Protest can be peaceful and placards can be a safe way to share ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Cut, colour, speak: Pop Art placards for protest

nodes.misconception: Identity means one thing about you.
nodes.response: Identity is made of many parts - culture, hobbies, family, beliefs - and a collage can mix images to show all those layers of who you are.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Set the scene: collage, figure and symbol

nodes.misconception: A portrait has to look real or neat to show who someone is.
nodes.response: Portraits can show feeling, memory, or mood without looking realistic. Artists use colour, texture and shape to tell a story about the person.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Painting a portrait with colour and feeling

nodes.misconception: If the shapes look abstract, it seems like they don’t mean anything.
nodes.response: Artists often use abstract shapes and textures to suggest hidden meaning or feeling. Symbols and patterns can carry personal or spiritual meaning - and sometimes, part of the power is in the mystery.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Layers and symbols: surface, texture and identity

nodes.misconception: Western portraits are the artworks where artists represent stauts effectively.
nodes.response: Many artefacts and artworks around the world and throughout history do this.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Raised portraits: representation through dots and relief

nodes.misconception: Patterns in medieval paintings were just decoration.
nodes.response: Patterns actually had symbolic and spiritual meanings, helping people understand religious ideas when most couldn’t read.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Patterns in medieval art

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all art is still and that it doesn't show movement.
nodes.response: Artists have lots of ways to show change or movement such as using lines, colours, and even how they arrange things in the picture.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Abstract expression

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume that maps always have to be accurate like road maps or atlases.
nodes.response: Artists can creative in the way they express their ideas or experiences.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Places and migration

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they can't move away from their initial plan.
nodes.response: Artists change their artwork as they go by responding to reflection and feedback.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Layering and mixed-media

nodes.misconception: Pupils may spread their images separately across the page without using layering.
nodes.response: Layering is used in collage to create further meaning and depth to the artwork.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal geography

nodes.misconception: Children may think that maps show only real places, exactly as they are in real life.
nodes.response: Artists create expressive maps from their memory and imagination that may not look like real life.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Maps as art

nodes.misconception: Only men were important in history and trade.
nodes.response: Women played key roles such as making silk, running markets and sharing stories. Artists invite us to think about this through their work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Clay travellers: figures from the Silk Road

nodes.misconception: Africa is one country.
nodes.response: Africa is a continent made up of many different countries and cultures, past and present. Different maps from different times can show this.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Create a history map

nodes.misconception: All abstract symbols need to be explained to others.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that some abstract symbols hold personal or cultural meanings that don’t have to be explained. The West African Adinkra symbol Sankofa, literally means “go back and fetch it” and suggests that we carry our past with us.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Collage sails: pattern and identity

nodes.misconception: Artists only make artwork with images.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that artists can make artwork with images, but they can also create artwork with words.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Cutting stories with paper

nodes.misconception: Weaving is simply a way of creating fabric for clothing and has no connection to colour or culture.
nodes.response: Weaving goes beyond just making fabric; it’s a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring weaving

nodes.misconception: Appliqué is just a form of decorating fabric and has no connection to colour or culture.
nodes.response: Appliqué goes beyond just decorating fabric, it's a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring appliqué

nodes.misconception: Embroidery is a simple way of decorating cloth and has no cultural context.
nodes.response: Embroidery goes beyond just being a decorative process, it is a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring embroidery and stitch

nodes.misconception: Tie-dye is a modern European technique
nodes.response: Tie-dye or similar forms, such as Bandhani from India, originates from many different regions around the world and exists in multiple forms and styles. Tie-dye is a global textile technique that has existed for thousands of years.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring dyeing

nodes.misconception: In Tataki-zome, you should hammer the leaves and flowers as hard as possible to get the best results.
nodes.response: Hammering too hard can damage the fabric or crush the plant too much, causing it to bleed or smudge. In Tataki-zome, it’s important to tap gently and evenly so the natural colours and delicate shapes of the plants transfer clearly and beautifully.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring print design

nodes.misconception: Fashion illustrators make finished garments.
nodes.response: Fashion illustrators draw designs and ideas. They help fashion designers show what clothes will look like before they are made.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the creative industries

nodes.misconception: Lines create an edge but they don't create volume.
nodes.response: Contour lines and directional hatching lines can be used to describe the volume of a 3D object in a 2D drawing.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: volume

nodes.misconception: Depth can only be created in a realistic scene or in a realistic way.
nodes.response: Depth can be entirely imaginary or realistic. Artists can manipulate elements to create the illusion of shapes, colours and lines standing out or recessing in an image.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: depth

nodes.misconception: Asymmetrical designs don't balance.
nodes.response: Asymmetrical designs can use visual weight to create a type of balance even if the work is different on both sides.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: balance

nodes.misconception: In two point perspective, some lines don't need to recede to the vanishing point
