nodes.response: All lines recede to one of the vanishing points. Otherwise your drawing won't be realistic
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: perspective

nodes.misconception: An object has the same mass whether in real life or in a 2D representation.
nodes.response: Whilst an object in real life may have a certain physical mass, if it is depicted in an image its visual weight might not represent this physical mass accurately. Especially compared to other items. This is due to the use of visual elements.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: mass

nodes.misconception: For artwork to employ variety, it needs to be overwhelming or not unified.
nodes.response: Artwork that employs variety can do so in a unified way to still create work that is cohesive.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: variety

nodes.misconception: Scale means size.
nodes.response: Scale is specifically about relative size.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art:  scale

nodes.misconception: To create unity, all elements in a piece must look exactly the same or be repeated in a uniform manner.
nodes.response: Variety can still contribute to a cohesive composition, as does repeating elements in a non-uniform way.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: unity

nodes.misconception: Rhythm is just another way of saying pattern
nodes.response: Rhythm is a visual beat that utilises pattern and repetition across an artwork to direct your eye across the work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: rhythm

nodes.misconception: Proportions are set rules and always apply
nodes.response: Proportions are relative to the unique form you are observing. They relate to the different sizes of the different parts but may be different for each person, place or object
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of art: proportion

nodes.misconception: Documenting an artist’s journey is only about completed artworks.
nodes.response: Sketchbooks, notes, and drafts are just as important, showing the development of ideas, experimentation, and problem-solving along the way.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Documenting the creative journey

nodes.misconception: Artists always have a fixed idea before they start their work.
nodes.response: Many artists gather inspiration as they go. Collecting a wide range of visual sources lets ideas evolve naturally rather than sticking to a single idea.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Selecting inspirational visual source material

nodes.misconception: Distorting a photograph with manipulation techniques only damages it.
nodes.response: In art, photos are not just static records of the past; they are versatile tools that can be reinterpreted and manipulated to express new ideas and perspectives.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Manipulating photographs

nodes.misconception: Critical analysis in art is just about writing facts about artists.
nodes.response: Critical analysis goes beyond facts; it involves interpreting the artwork, understanding its context, and evaluating its impact and meaning.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The art of critique: analysing and interpreting artworks

nodes.misconception: Using unconventional materials doesn’t have a deeper purpose in the drawing process.
nodes.response: Unconventional materials can lead to unique textures, effects, and creative outcomes, challenging traditional drawing methods.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing for different purposes and needs

nodes.misconception: Using inspiration from artists means copying their work exactly.
nodes.response: The goal is not to copy an artist's work but to adapt their techniques, mark-making, or approach to develop your own creative style and ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing ideas for experimentation

nodes.misconception: Exploring different perspectives just means drawing the object from different angles.
nodes.response: To explore perspectives, you also need to change how you look at the object—by positioning yourself differently, changing your distance, or experimenting with different materials and techniques. It's about seeing the object in new ways.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Recording from observation and first-hand sources

nodes.misconception: Drawing always has to be neat, precise, and done with traditional materials like pencil.
nodes.response: Artists can experiment with non-traditional materials and looser techniques like splashes, drips and sprays to develop freedom and unexpected results.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Manipulating drawings

nodes.misconception: 2D drawings cannot be transformed into 3D forms.
nodes.response: 2D drawings are like a blueprint for 3D forms. By imagining how shapes in a drawing could extend into space, students can add depth, volume, and perspective to give their designs a 3D appearance.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: 2D into 3D

nodes.misconception: Art must be created with the hands.
nodes.response: Art is for everyone whatever their circumstances and is not always created through using hands. Artists can create art in innovative ways without using hands.  Art is a way for all of humanity to express their viewpoints and diverse experiences.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Viewpoints and techniques: disability and art

nodes.misconception: All artworks about causes are created to warn audiences.
nodes.response: There are many reasons why artists make artworks about causes including to bring joy, to celebrate and to inspire hope.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art can change the world: text based art

nodes.misconception: Art should be something we instantly recognise and physically last a long time.
nodes.response: Art may not be a recognisable image and may exist only in a specific timeframe.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: That's not art!

nodes.misconception: Art can only be made by one artist, working alone.
nodes.response: Art can be a collaborative process. When artists collaborate, they work together to communicate common meanings or achieve common goals.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: This is art: the power of collaborative making

nodes.misconception: All of the artwork held in public institutions within the United Kingdom originates from there.
nodes.response: Some artwork held in the collections of public institutions in the UK were created by civilisations that were colonised by the British Empire.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art, empire and museums: who owns art?

nodes.misconception: Drawing has to be a replica of what is being looked at.
nodes.response: Drawing can be detailed and replicate an object, but it can also be many other things. Artists often play with techniques and process to try out different ways of exploring drawing and this can lead to experimental and exciting discoveries.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: “I can’t draw!" Building confidence through drawing techniques

nodes.misconception: The way you show your work doesn't really matter so long as it's tidy.
nodes.response: A creative, careful presentation will support the idea, message or mood and help make your work impactful.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting artwork

nodes.misconception: The response from the timed period is marked as a stand alone outcome.
nodes.response: The marks are awarded holistically and take in the whole creative process. This period is a great way to resolve your ideas and spend time focusing on realising your intentions. It shouldn't be incredibly stressful or worry you!
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to make a response under timed conditions

nodes.misconception: You cannot remove any work from your book or portfolio.
nodes.response: You should select your work carefully and on rare occasions you might find work that doesn't add to the creative journey and is best left out. Discuss these pieces with your teacher to get guidance first.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a cohesive narrative: explaining the process

nodes.misconception: I can just make lots of different versions and present them as experiments.
nodes.response: Experimentation is about thinking through doing. It is only useful when it moves your creative journey forward.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and experimenting with materials and techniques

nodes.misconception: Every idea must be innovative and interdisciplinary.
nodes.response: Sometimes taking ideas and inspiration from others or following a tried and tested path moves you forward.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Taking the individual path, responding to collaborative work

nodes.misconception: You should take forward all of the suggestions from your critique to improve your response.
nodes.response: You should listen to and consider all suggestions carefully, but you are expected to respond in a personal and meaningful way, so trust in your own artistic voice. You should take the suggestions forward if they align with your vision and style.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: reflect and refine the response

nodes.misconception: Composition is more relevant to 2D work.
nodes.response: Composition is relevant to all areas of art practice as it's about deciding on the best arrangement for your work. It will be dictated by your intentions for the piece. In 3D, we consider the composition from all angles or in the round.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: plan a response

nodes.misconception: A group crit is only useful while the project is ongoing.
nodes.response: A group crit involves diverse perspectives. Even if you don’t incorporate it into your current work, it helps you understand different viewpoints to improve your skills and help you anticipate opinions in future projects, making you a better artist.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate artwork

nodes.misconception: I need new resources for my response.
nodes.response: You need suitable resources, ideally first-hand. They don't need to be new they can be sourced from bits of your project so far.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: first-hand resources

nodes.misconception: I should select an artist because their work looks like the work I would like to create.
nodes.response: This is one reason, but more in depth critique will help you select artists based on ideas and visual language that can help you make original work that is more personal and meaningful to you.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the work of artists and designers: key elements

nodes.misconception: Reimagining work means simply copying the original in a slightly different way.
nodes.response: Reimagining is about transforming the original work, changing materials, scale, techniques, or context to create something new that still connects back to the starting point.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing ideas collaboratively through manipulating source material

nodes.misconception: I should talk about all of the visual elements and principles of art in my evaluation.
nodes.response: Select and describe only the areas that are relevant, but consider them all to see if you notice anything new. Sometimes you make work instinctively and don't realise until later what techniques or principles you actually applied.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate use of materials and techniques

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about collaborative annotation is that it’s just about leaving individual notes side by side.
nodes.response: In reality, the purpose is not only to make comments but to interact with each other's ideas, responding, questioning and building connections so that understanding is developed collectively rather than in isolation.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective annotation: supporting each other to record the process

nodes.misconception: As I have to make something personal I can't copy an artist's ideas or techniques.
nodes.response: Copying or pastiche can help you learn techniques, but to create original work that meets the A04 objective, you must also add your own ideas and intentions.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Review developed ideas: trials and experiments

nodes.misconception: Everyone has to work on the same part of the collaborative art piece at the same time.
nodes.response: In reality, collaboration can also mean dividing tasks, working on separate elements that are later combined, or contributing in different ways, such as planning, designing, making, or assembling.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a collaborative still life

nodes.misconception: Collaborative artwork ends when the group finishes working together.
nodes.response: In reality, collaborative pieces continue to evolve as viewers engage with them, as participants reflect on the process and as the artwork is displayed or adapted in new contexts.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the work of artists and designers who work collaboratively

nodes.misconception: You don't need to record failures as it will lower your GCSE grade.
nodes.response: Record all of your experiments, but make it clear in your work that you know which ones were successful and take these forward in your creative journey. This is evidence of your informed and insightful approach. This will attract a higher mark.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop ideas: trials and experiments

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about collaboration is that everyone has to agree on every detail or work in the same style for it to succeed.
nodes.response: In reality, differing approaches and opinions can make the final artwork more dynamic and original.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Initial ideas: collaboration and generating ideas

nodes.misconception: Students often place the vanishing point too low or high, or forget to use it consistently, which causes the drawing to look distorted or unrealistic.
nodes.response: Remember: the vanishing point sits on the horizon line, which is your eye level. All diagonal lines must meet at the vanishing point—even if it’s off the paper!
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Technical drawing techniques to communicate ideas

nodes.misconception: All buildings have straight lines and are built out of box like shapes.
nodes.response: Buildings can come in many different forms, with influences coming from a range of different sources.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Becoming inspired: developing an architectural design

nodes.misconception: Some students think pitching means just reading out facts about the design.
nodes.response: A strong pitch is more than just facts. It’s a story with a clear beginning, middle and end that shows your idea solves a problem and stands out from the rest.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Telling a story: pitching ideas to an audience

nodes.misconception: Buildings are all rectangular in shape with pitched roofs and walls the same colour.
nodes.response: Buildings are made in lots of different shapes and sizes, and are often decorated in ways that are personal to their communities.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Architecture through time and place

nodes.misconception: Buildings are all made from solid materials, brick, stone or concrete.
nodes.response: Buildings can be constructed from different materials. These may include traditional stone and brick or modern sustainable materials.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Architectural materials: experimenting with form

nodes.misconception: Colour is just used to make a space look good.
nodes.response: Colour in a room can have a big impact on the way a space feels and how we feel in that space.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing with colour in architecture and interiors

nodes.misconception: Craft is only about making functional objects and is less important than Fine Art.
nodes.response: Craft is the creation of objects and artworks requiring both artistry and technical skill. It includes both functional and non-functional items and embraces contributions from all genders and communities.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: This is craft

nodes.misconception: Puppets are only used for children's entertainment.
nodes.response: Different cultures use puppets to tell important stories, share cultural traditions, perform rituals, and even address social or political issues. Puppets can express powerful ideas and emotions, not just for fun but also to convey deeper messages.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The curious art of puppetry

nodes.misconception: Quilts are just blankets or decorative items and don’t have any deeper meaning.
nodes.response: While quilts are often used for warmth or decoration, many artists use quilts to share powerful stories and messages. Quilts can be a way for artists to speak out about important issues and make sure voices are heard.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The subversive power of quilting

nodes.misconception: Weaving is simply a way of creating fabric for clothing and has no connection to storytelling or culture.
nodes.response: Weaving goes beyond just making fabric; it’s a powerful form of art that can tell stories and reflect cultural heritage.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The landscapes of weaving

nodes.misconception: Pottery is only used for making practical items like bowls and pots, and it doesn’t have any artistic or cultural significance.
nodes.response: While pottery is often associated with functional items like bowls and vases, it has been used throughout history and in contemporary times as a medium for artistic expression and storytelling.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The humble pot

nodes.misconception: Body adornment is only about appearance or fashion trends.
nodes.response: Body adornment often holds deep cultural, religious, or personal meaning. It can express identity, heritage, beliefs, or social status, connecting individuals to family traditions or cultural values— beyond just aesthetic appeal.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Body adornment

nodes.misconception: Making a portrait always means painting a face.
nodes.response: Artists use paper, cardboard, silhouettes and even walls to create bold, powerful and expressive figures. You do not need to only paint a face to create a portrait.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring power in the portrait

nodes.misconception: Portraits must always show the person directly.
nodes.response: A portrait can also include symbolic representations, like objects that reflect the person’s personality or even something as unique as a sample of their DNA.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a portrait?

nodes.misconception: Words don’t matter that much — it’s the drawing that tells the story.
nodes.response: Words can express things a face alone might not show — like beliefs, experiences, or emotions. The style of the text also adds meaning.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Words in portraits

nodes.misconception: Only large, figurative sculptures are considered 3D portraits.
nodes.response: 3D portraits can be created in various sizes and forms, not just large figurative sculptures. They can include small, detailed works or abstract representations.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring portraits through 3D

nodes.misconception: The painted portrait only focuses on realism and accuracy in depicting the subject.
nodes.response: While many portraits aim for realism, painting also allows for abstract and emotional interpretations, capturing the subject's personality, mood, and deeper meaning beyond just physical appearance.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring portraits through paint

nodes.misconception: Negative space just means there’s nothing there — it’s empty or unfinished
nodes.response: Negative space may look ‘empty,’ but artists use it intentionally to draw attention elsewhere — it helps us focus on shape, emotion, or story without showing everything. It’s a powerful choice, not a mistake.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Using portraiture to reveal and conceal identities

nodes.misconception: Texture is only a visual quality, it doesn't add meaning to your work.
nodes.response: Texture is one of the tools artists use as a visual language to communicate.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Texture

nodes.misconception: In 3D or sculptural work, mass is just about how much it weighs and its physical presence.
nodes.response: Mass can be symbolic due to the materials used. Materials can carry more or less visual weight.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mass, shape, volume and depth

nodes.misconception: The arrangement of the elements has no effect on the overall effectiveness of the composition.
nodes.response: A successful composition creates structure and activates the visual language to convey meaning.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Composition

nodes.misconception: Experiments should include radical or very exaggerated changes.
nodes.response: You can make very subtle changes and experiements and they can have a big impact on your work - that's the value of experimentation!
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Scale, proportion and perspective

nodes.misconception: Patterns need to be regular and ordered.
nodes.response: Pattern can be irregular or regular.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Pattern

nodes.misconception: Lines are only useful in drawing and painting
nodes.response: Lines are vital for all work across every specialism. There are many ways line can impact your work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Line

nodes.misconception: Hue and colour mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Colour is the overarching name for what we see but it is made up of hues and tones.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Tone, hue and colour

nodes.misconception: Your work needs to be full of obvious pattern for it to feel unified.
nodes.response: Pattern is an important element in art but unity can be felt without artwork looking like a repeat pattern.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Unity, variety, rhythm and balance

nodes.misconception: Shapes are only found in the positive space made by an actual object.
nodes.response: Shapes are inadvertently created all the time in the gaps between objects in your composition. We call this the negative space.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Shape and form

nodes.misconception: 3D drawings must look exactly like 2D sketches.
nodes.response: 3D drawing explores form and space - it’s about expressing line, contour and movement in three dimensions, not replicating flat sketches.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing skills: drawing with 3D

nodes.misconception: Any camera setting will capture light drawings.
nodes.response: Long exposure (slow shutter speed) is essential for creating light drawings, without it, the camera won’t capture light movement, only still images.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing skills: drawing with light

nodes.misconception: Digital drawing doesn’t require the same skills as traditional drawing.
nodes.response: Core artistic skills like proportion, tone and composition still apply in digital artworks. Digital tools simply offer new ways to achieve them.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing skills: digital drawing

nodes.misconception: Sculptures have to be heavy, strong objects which are fully free standing.
nodes.response: Some sculptures are delicate and light. Sculptural works can be presented in a range of ways including hung, free standing, stacked or in relief.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring biomorphic sculptures using papier mâché

nodes.misconception: If the surface is carved too deeply, layers can be glued back on later.
nodes.response: Soap is a soft material, and carving too deeply can cause unintended breakage. It’s important to carve in gradual layers, starting with rough shaping before adding finer details.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Thinking in 3D, carving with soap

nodes.misconception: Plaster and paper will behave the same way in a mould.
nodes.response: Plaster and paper have very different properties. Plaster sets quickly and picks up fine details. Paper air dries more slowly and shrinks more as it dries. It might not show fine texture as clearly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring 3D art materials with casting (paper and plaster)

nodes.misconception: Sculptures must take a long time to create.
nodes.response: Some sculptural works can be quick responsive works.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: 3D Design: displaying a sculpture

nodes.misconception: Clay work is only about making a vessel which is perfectly symmetrical and with a uniform form.
nodes.response: Clay is expressive! It doesn't have to be perfectly symmetrical or realistic. Many artists use bold designs, patterns, and personal storytelling in their work, imperfections add character and meaning.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring 3D construction techniques with clay

nodes.misconception: Aritsts can only take direct inspiration from nature, copying it exactly.
nodes.response: Artists have always taken inspiration from nature and can use this as a starting point to develop into complex works.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to organic forms with card, papers and modroc

nodes.misconception: That gender and sexuality are the same thing.
nodes.response: Gender is about your personal identity, how you see yourself, while sexuality is about who you are attracted to.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Gender and sexuality in art

nodes.misconception: Art only connects people if everyone understands it the same way.
nodes.response: Art connects people because it sparks emotions and ideas, even if everyone sees it differently. It’s the shared experience, not exact understanding, that brings people together.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal to universal: art as connection

nodes.misconception: All artists make art with the intention of sharing with an audience.
nodes.response: Some art is made as an act of pure self-expression. Even deeply personal works are shaped by history, identity, and society, meaning they can take on wider meanings even if the artist did not intend them to.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Identity, art and  self-expression

nodes.misconception: Religious art only includes paintings or sculptures.
nodes.response: Religious art isn’t just paintings or sculptures, it includes architecture, textiles, calligraphy and even temporary creations like Rangoli and sand mandalas, all used to express and connect with the spiritual.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Religion and belief in art

nodes.misconception: When artists make work about identity, they reveal all aspects of themselves.
nodes.response: Artists make selections about what to conceal or reveal in their work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Curating identity: choosing what to show in art

nodes.misconception: Maps in art are literal,
nodes.response: Artists might use mapping through literal geography, map-like work or more abstract or subjective representations of movement, memory, and relationships.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mapping identity

nodes.misconception: Printed textile is only for mass production.
nodes.response: Printed textiles can be produced in limited quantities or even one-of-a-kind pieces.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring printed textiles

nodes.misconception: Architecture is plain and without details.
nodes.response: Architects use many different patterns in their designs, both literal patterns and patterns through their use of form.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Architects who build communities

nodes.misconception: Fashion design is solely about trends and superficial appearances.
nodes.response: Fashion design is more than trends; it can challenge our understanding of fashion.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Fashion design for empowerment

nodes.misconception: The main role of graphic designers is to make work that is pleasing to the viewer’s eye.
nodes.response: Many graphic designers push traditional boundaries and shift the focus from creating purely aesthetically pleasing works to communicating messages about social justice.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Communicating ideas through graphic design

nodes.misconception: Set designers work only in theatre and film.
nodes.response: Set design is used in many different contexts, including theatre, film, fashion, art and music.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Imagining new worlds: set design

nodes.misconception: Design is about making things that have never been made before.
nodes.response: Design is about planning and making something.  It doesn’t need to be something that has never been done before, it can be to improve an existing object to make it work or look better.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Defining design

nodes.misconception: Changing the aperture or shutter speed only affects how bright the photo is.
nodes.response: While both aperture and shutter speed do affect exposure (how light or dark a photo is), they also have creative effects on how the photo looks, such as blur.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Picture taking: aperture and shutter speed settings

nodes.misconception: Lighting is just a technical tool in photography.
nodes.response: Lighting has the power to transform a photograph, shaping its mood, tone, and clarity.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Picture taking: lighting

nodes.misconception: Depth of field is only controled by moving the camera nearer or further away from the subject.
nodes.response: Depth of field is mainly controlled by adjusting the aperture (f-stop).
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Picture taking: depth of field

nodes.misconception: Photographers can't control the way movement is depicted in their photographs.
nodes.response: Photographers can freeze action sharply or blur it creatively, depending on the photographer’s intent.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Picture taking: motion

nodes.misconception: The safelight allows any kind of light to be on in the darkroom without damaging prints.
nodes.response: The safelight is not a “free pass” for unlimited light exposure and that all light exposure must be controlled and time-sensitive.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Darkroom processes: using an enlarger and developing a print

nodes.misconception: Research is separate from making work.
nodes.response: Research feeds directly into experimentation and outcomes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Photography: the influence of sources on photographic investigations

nodes.misconception: Editing an image always changes or damages the original file.
nodes.response: By using adjustment layers and layer masks, edits are non-destructive.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital processes: using digital media to layer an image

nodes.misconception: Photo editing is always obvious or “fake”.
nodes.response: In reality, edits can be extremely subtle and still have a significant impact on the final image.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital processes: using digital media to manipulate an image

nodes.misconception: Phones produce high quality photos, so photography with cameras is redundant
nodes.response: Phone cameras are powerful, but professional cameras give more control, lens options, and depth of field, which matters for creative and technical work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to the principles of photography

nodes.misconception: Collaborative art is just a group project with a leader.
nodes.response: Collaborative art is a collective process of co-creation where ideas and efforts are deeply intertwined.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a collaborative portrait

nodes.misconception: Artwork is often seen as a passive object that hangs on a wall.
nodes.response: Art can also be used to activate social change and is a process that can helps spark conversation and raise awareness. The act of creating and sharing the work is powerful in itself.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Repetition in art activism

nodes.misconception: Social action art must always make tangible improvements to an issue.
nodes.response: Social action art might make tangible improvements to an issue but might focus instead on sparking conversation or raising awareness.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: What is social action?

nodes.misconception: Street art is primarily an illegal activity or act of vandalism.
nodes.response: Street art is a legitimate and powerful form of artistic expression that addresses important social issues.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Street art: power to the people

nodes.misconception: Art about war mainly glorifies violence or heroism.
nodes.response: Much art inspired by war actually critiques violence, depicts the horrors of war, and emphasises the human cost.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art and war

nodes.misconception: Architects only consider one building, not the wider area.
nodes.response: Architects consider the built environment, the local area's history and needs and think outside the box to create connections between communities in their work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Belonging: a sense of place

nodes.misconception: You should only add layers to a painting with paint.
nodes.response: Dry materials can be used in a variety of ways to add detail and shading to an art work. Dry materials can be layered over the top of wet materials once dried. Examples include pastel over watercolour or pen over dried ink washes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Abstract art: dry materials in response to stimuli

nodes.misconception: All paintings are made with paint brushes.
nodes.response: Using different types of tools helps abstract artists create lots of different types of expressive marks and textures in their work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark-making using different tools

nodes.misconception: Abstract art is easy to create.
nodes.response: Abstract art does not try to show things as they look in real life. Instead, it focuses on expressing emotions, ideas, or movement which is not an easy task.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Abstract art: painting using different stimuli

nodes.misconception: Mark-making is only needed in abstract work.
nodes.response: Artists use different marks to express emotions, create mood, and bring their artwork to life.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Abstract marks: respond to stimuli by painting

nodes.misconception: When observing a stimulus, it is best to respond using pencil.
nodes.response: Different stimuli, call for different methods like, loose washes, impasto, detailed line work, collage, etc. Matching technique to stimuli ensures the artwork communicates its idea effectively.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark-making: matching technique to stimuli

nodes.misconception: Artists start a painting or drawing on a plain piece of paper
nodes.response: Often artists create surfaces and backgrounds to work on, it makes the piece have less gaps and is interesting to work over.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark-marking: preparing the surface for painting

nodes.misconception: The most technically perfect pieces should always be selected for exhibitions.
nodes.response: An exhibition’s power lies in how the works connect thematically, emotionally, and conceptually, not only in technical skill.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Selecting work and considering the audience

nodes.misconception: Artists only talk about their work to promote it in galleries and museums.
nodes.response: Artists might talk about their work for engagement and promotion, in a variety of contexts.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Talking about your work

nodes.misconception: Only professional curators decide what is exhibited.
nodes.response: Throughout history and globally, artists have curated their own work. Sometimes artists self-curate but sometimes this process can be in collaboration with professional curators.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Artists as curators

nodes.misconception: Reproduction is only possible with a photocopier/printer and reproductions are not as valid as originals.
nodes.response: Hand-made reproductions (drawn, traced, collaged, reinterpreted) are also valid artistic processes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Reproducing art: postcards, prints and artist editions

nodes.misconception: An artist statement has to be a long, formal piece of writing full of complicated words.
nodes.response: Artist statements can be short and simple, written in clear and honest language, and can also take other formats such as bullet points, spoken word, visual mind maps, captions, or short videos.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an artist statement

nodes.misconception: Making an exhibition is just about hanging art.
nodes.response: Curation requires skills and knowledge. Curation can create connections and a narrative between individual works.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The role and impact of curators

nodes.misconception: Promoting a show is just about putting up a poster or posting once online.
nodes.response: Effective promotion requires planning, multiple methods, and consistent communication.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Promotions: how to publicise a show

nodes.misconception: Presentation is just for decoration.
nodes.response: Presentation is part of communication, not decoration.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Presentation of work

nodes.misconception: A concept is entirely fixed.
nodes.response: A concept can develop and evolve but it should not completely change without very good reason.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a unique concept for a 3D project

nodes.misconception: There is one particular way to present art research and it has to look polished.
nodes.response: Artist research should be meaningful, it may look polished, but it may also just look purposeful and be presented with care.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching and presenting a 3D designer’s work

nodes.misconception: A designer's style is fixed and remains constant.
nodes.response: A designer will grow and develop and so their distinctive style will evolve over time as they experiment more and engage with new ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing your 3D design voice

nodes.misconception: A final piece must be large scale and completely finished.
nodes.response: A final piece or outcome is just the end point in your journey so far, it should resolve your ideas but it can do this in many ways and in different scales.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and creating a final 3D piece

nodes.misconception: Experimentation just means making new things each time.
nodes.response: When you experiment you are thinking and doing. Always think about what works and what new ideas are generated.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Refining your 3D style through experimentation

nodes.misconception: It should be obvious how to explore a theme and reponses will be similar.
nodes.response: Every person brings their own experiences to a theme so which aspect and how you explore it will depend on you, your background and your unique artistic voice.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting and responding to a theme in 3D design

nodes.misconception: Sketchbooks have a set format, and must be presented in the 'right' way.
nodes.response: Sketchbooks are a personal record of your own creative journey, but in the GCSE course they also allow you to gain marks, so sometimes we recommend working in a certain way to help you achieve.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of a sketchbook in developing your 3D practice

nodes.misconception: A repeated pattern is just the same shape copied over and over again.
nodes.response: While repeating the same shape is one way to create a pattern, artists and designers use a variety of methods to make repeated patterns more dynamic, engaging and sophisticated.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: pattern

nodes.misconception: Texture is only about how something feels, not how it looks.
nodes.response: Texture can mean how something feels, and we call that physical texture. But artists can also create the illusion of texture in drawings or paintings — that’s called visual texture.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: texture

nodes.misconception: Composition is only used in one way to express realistic images.
nodes.response: Composition is used by artists in many ways, and how composition is used can change across cultures.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: composition

nodes.misconception: Line is only used for drawing.
nodes.response: Artists create and apply lines in a multitude of ways across different mediums including sculpture and painting, as well as in drawing.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: line

nodes.misconception: Shape and form are the same thing.
nodes.response: Shape is flat and 2D, like a drawing. Form is 3D and has depth — you can see or feel it from different angles.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: shape and form

nodes.misconception: Colours carry the same meaning for everybody.
nodes.response: Colours can carry different meanings, and these can vary across people, places and cultures.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: Colour

nodes.misconception: Tone is all about smooth blending
nodes.response: Tone can be captured in a variety of ways and mediums
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The elements of art: tone

nodes.misconception: Critical thinking focuses on judging artworks as 'good' or 'bad'.
nodes.response: Critical thinking  helps artists and audiences to think deeply about art and respect different viewpoints.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Critical thinking: Western art

nodes.misconception: Artists work in one discipline.
nodes.response: Artists can make art using many different disciplines.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art movements, disciplines and multidisciplinary artists

nodes.misconception: Art movements came about in isolation from the world around them.
nodes.response: Art movements are often impacted by changes in the world around them.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The influence of technology on art movements

nodes.misconception: Iconic images come from across all areas of art history.
nodes.response: Iconic images mainly come from Western art history which can mean that the diversity of our world is often not reflected.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Iconic images from art movements

nodes.misconception: When artists respond to events, they always do so to document that point in history.
nodes.response: There are many ways and reasons why artists respond to events.  One of these can be to document that point in history but they can also do so to express their opinions, be a powerful voice for marginalised groups and to help fight for justice.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art in response to events

nodes.misconception: Manifestos are always communicated through text.
nodes.response: In art, manifestos don’t need to be written but can be multidisciplinary in their approach.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Start your own art movement: the role of manifestos

nodes.misconception: "Inside" and "outside" in design always refers to physical spaces, like buildings or rooms.
nodes.response: In photography, "inside" and "outside" can mean more than places - they can show how someone feels on the inside, how people hide emotions, or the contrast between personal and public life.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Inside and outside in photography

nodes.misconception: Light and dark are only used to make things look realistic, not to create mood.
nodes.response: This overlooks how contrast can be used to suggest emotion, tension, calm, or drama, not just realism.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Light and dark in photography

nodes.misconception: Landscapes are just pretty pictures of nature – there's not much meaning behind them.
nodes.response: While landscapes often show beautiful scenery, they can express powerful ideas, like climate change, migration, culture, or even identity. Photographers use landscapes not just to show what they see, but to say something about how they feel or value.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Landscapes in photography

nodes.misconception: Objects in photography are only depicted realistically.
nodes.response: Objects can be used in a range of ways in photography. Objects in photography can be used as a subject that might also contain symbolic meanings.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Objects in photography

nodes.misconception: Natural forms are always perfectly symmetrical, like leaves or flowers.
nodes.response: While some natural forms show symmetry, most have irregular, flowing shapes. Even symmetrical forms often have variations, this is part of what makes nature interesting to photographers.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Natural forms in photography

nodes.misconception: Portraits are just about what someone looks like on the surface with no deeper meaning.
nodes.response: While capturing someone’s physical appearance can be part of a portrait, photographers often go much deeper. Portraits can reveal who someone is, exploring culture, identity, relationships, life experiences and even social or political themes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Portraits and figures in photography

nodes.misconception: Once a print is made, it’s finished, and no further changes can be made.
nodes.response: Prints can be developed further using mixed media and physical alterations like cutting. The process of refining a print is an important step to enhance visual interest and highlight specific areas, creativity doesn't stop after the initial print!
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Working into and refining prints

nodes.misconception: All types of monoprinting follow the exact same process.
nodes.response: There are a number of methods for monoprinting that have different steps and outcomes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing with monoprint

nodes.misconception: Printmaking requires the use of specialist equipment to be successful.
nodes.response: High quality printing making can be achieved using a range of domestic materials and equipment.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing printing plates; transferring the design

nodes.misconception: Printmaking is only about making copies, not about creativity.
nodes.response: Printmaking is a form of artistic expression, artists can use printmaking to create unique, creative works where textures, colours, and styles can vary greatly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Artists that print from objects

nodes.misconception: Prints look exactly the same each time you repeat them.
nodes.response: No two prints are exactly alike, even if they come from the same plate or block. Factors like pressure, ink distribution, and the surface it’s printed on can make each print slightly different.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Selecting and rejecting ideas: using a gelli plate

nodes.misconception: Once ink is applied to the plate, the design is fixed and cannot be changed.
nodes.response: The printing process is about trying and adjusting. Artists can refine their design through trial and error, removing layers of ink or adding new ones to adjust their composition. It’s important to approach the process with flexibility and patience.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The printing of the plates: reduction printing

nodes.misconception: A crest is for royalty only.
nodes.response: Crests are symbols used by families, groups, or communities to represent their identity, values and stories. They are not only for royalty, but for anyone who wants to show their heritage or what they stand for.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Local areas and their migrations stories

nodes.misconception: Refugees are illegal and take jobs away from others.
nodes.response: Refugees are protected under international law and have the right to seek asylum. While they may need help when they arrive in a new country, many refugees go on to contribute positively to their communities.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Families and migration: refugee stories in art

nodes.misconception: Pets are not part of a family because they are animals.
nodes.response: Many people give their pets names, celebrate their birthdays, and care for them every day. Pets can be  part of the family.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The family in art

nodes.misconception: Your future identity is completely determined by your family roots.
nodes.response: A common misconception is thinking your family roots completely decide who you are, without any chance to grow or change. In truth, your identity is shaped by both your roots and your own experiences.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Roots: your connections and community

nodes.misconception: Every child has their own bedroom.
nodes.response: It’s a common misconception that every child has their own bedroom. In reality, many children share rooms, sleep in a living area or move around different homes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: A sense of place: your spaces

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about murals is that they are only decorative.
nodes.response: They often carry powerful social, cultural, or political messages.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Building community

nodes.misconception: Planning a collage or assemblage takes away creativity.
nodes.response: Planning provides structure but doesn’t mean the design is fixed. Many artists start with an idea but adapt it through experimentation. A plan helps build confidence, but the best results often come from unexpected discoveries along the way.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and developing collage inspired by our hobbies and interests

nodes.misconception: Collage landscapes should always look realistic.
nodes.response: Collage allows us to create landscapes that don’t have to follow real world rules. Surreal landscapes encourage imagination and creativity beyond what we see in everyday life.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing with collaging and relief through landscape

nodes.misconception: Abstract collages need to have perfect symmetry or recognisable shapes.
nodes.response: Abstract collages don’t need symmetry or recognisable images. The beauty of abstraction lies in experimenting to create something visually engaging which can express ideas or emotions and finding balance through the arrangement.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and refining an abstract collage

nodes.misconception: Collage is just about sticking random images together.
nodes.response: Collage is about careful selection, layering and composition to create meaning, tell stories, represent identity and explore social themes.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring collage and composition through portraits

nodes.misconception: Assemblage has to look like a recognisable scene to share meaning with the audience.
nodes.response: Meaning can be represented through objects, textures, and symbols. The way objects are arranged, and their relationships to each other can all convey emotions, experiences, and personality traits. Assemblage is about meaning, not just likeness.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring memory through the world of assemblage

nodes.misconception: Collage is a set process that cannot be modified or refined.
nodes.response: Collage is a flexible process. Rearranging elements helps refine ideas and create a stronger final piece. Professional artists often make changes mid-process to improve composition and meaning.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing and refining collages to represent home.

nodes.misconception: Artists always work alone to create their art.
nodes.response: Many artists collaborate with others, work in teams, or invite the community to be part of the process.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of relationships and connections through art

nodes.misconception: Memories cannot be used to express a person's identity
nodes.response: Memories play a key role in shaping who we are as they help us understand our past, influence how we view ourselves and guide how we express our identity over time.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art as self-discovery

nodes.misconception: Doodling is not a valid artform.
nodes.response: Doodling can express emotion, personality and imagination through simple lines and shapes. Many professional artists, illustrators, and designers start their ideas through doodling.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing emotion through art

nodes.misconception: Memories are always accurate and unchanging.
nodes.response: A common misconception about memories is that they are perfect and unchanging when in reality, memories can be inaccurate, influenced by emotions and change over time.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Transforming memories into art

nodes.misconception: Thinking that everyone else's emotional state is as it appear to be.
nodes.response: People can’t support you if they don’t know you need it. When someone wears an emotional mask, it’s hard to know the real person.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Making sense: art and wellbeing

nodes.misconception: Food is only for eating and cannot be used as an art medium.
nodes.response: Food can be used as an art medium because it evokes the senses and carries deep cultural and emotional meanings.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Food and personal narratives

nodes.misconception: The material an artist uses doesn’t matter as long as the subject or idea is strong.
nodes.response: The choice of materials greatly affects how an artwork looks, feels and communicates meaning. Materials can add texture, symbolism and emotional impact that deepen the viewer’s understanding.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The work of artists and designers: elements of art

nodes.misconception: Once a photo or drawing is finished, it can’t be changed or developed further.
nodes.response: A finished photo or drawing is just a starting point—artists often rework, edit, layer, or translate their images into new forms using different media to explore deeper meaning or fresh creative directions.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: appropriate resources and creating artwork

nodes.misconception: Balance means everything must be perfectly symmetrical.
nodes.response: Balance can be symmetrical, but it can also be asymmetrical or radial. Asymmetrical balance uses different elements on each side to create visual stability.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The work of artists and designers: principles of art

nodes.misconception: If you don’t use traditional art materials, your work won’t be taken seriously or get a high grade.
nodes.response: Art & Design encourages experimentation with a wide range of materials — not just pencil, paint and clay. Using unusual or personal materials can strengthen marks if they are purposeful, linked to ideas and part of a thoughtful process.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: layers and processes in different endorsements

nodes.misconception: All artists take inspiration from one source.
nodes.response: Artists might take inspiration from a wide range of sources including surroundings, objects, personal experiences, memories, artist's work or historical and contemporary movements.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying starting points

nodes.misconception: First-hand observations have to be drawings
nodes.response: First-hand observations can also include photography, sound recordings, writing, collected objects, or video — any direct response to real-life experiences.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: First-hand primary resourcing

nodes.misconception: Expensive or professional materials automatically produce better artwork.
nodes.response: The quality of the outcome depends more on how materials are used, combined, and manipulated, rather than their cost or brand.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate the use of materials and techniques

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about this lesson is that photography is just about capturing what you see, when in fact it involves making creative choices.
nodes.response: Photography is about deciding how to show the subject to communicate an idea or feeling. Understanding that really opens up creative possibilities.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Photographing for resources: what makes a good photograph

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about portfolios is that you need to include everything you've made.
nodes.response: It's much better to select work that clearly shows your ideas, development, artistic journey and skills.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting a portfolio: creating pages of documentation

nodes.misconception: Reflection is only about finding faults or criticising your work.
nodes.response: Reflection is about recognising both strengths and areas to improve in order to grow as an artist.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Self assessment techniques: evaluating your own work

nodes.misconception: A good portfolio presentation should be is highly decorative and colourful to be engaging.
nodes.response: While creative touches like washi tape or coloured paint can add personality, a clean and minimal layout can be just as effective, sometimes even more so. The goal is to curate a cohesive presentation that supports your work, not distracts from it
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Curating the artwork: selecting and arranging key pieces

nodes.misconception: Annotation has to be long, written paragraphs.
nodes.response: Annotation can be short notes, labels, sketches, diagrams, or even audio recordings. It’s any way you add extra information to explain your ideas clearly.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective annotation: different ways to present ideas

nodes.misconception: Only paper and canvas are proper or professional surfaces for making art
nodes.response: Artists have long worked on a wide range of surfaces, including wood, metal, glass, fabric, cardboard, plastic, ceramics, and more. The surface is a creative choice, not a limitation.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a surface, armature, background: preparing your personal response

nodes.misconception: More detail always makes an artwork better.
nodes.response: Too much detail—especially if it’s unfocused—can make an artwork feel cluttered, overwhelming, or take attention away from the focal point.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: how to judge quality and refining work

nodes.misconception: Art materials don’t matter beyond how they look or feel.
nodes.response: Materials can carry deep personal and cultural meanings that add important layers to the artwork’s story and message.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the work of artists and designers: materials and techniques

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about technical aspects in art is that technical skill only means making artworks look realistic.
nodes.response: Technical skill also includes mastery of materials, control of techniques and the ability to use those skills effectively in any style, whether abstract, expressive, or conceptual.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal response: finishing an artwork

nodes.misconception: Negative life experiences cannot be used as inspiration for creating artwork.
nodes.response: Many artists find that exploring difficult life experiences can lead to meaningful creative work.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Resourcing ideas through personal reflections, narratives and objects

nodes.misconception: A common misconception about paint pouring is that it’s purely random and anyone can do it without skill.
nodes.response: In reality, while paint pouring involves chance, artists use technique, colour theory and control to create intentional and successful compositions. It’s both creative and technical.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Connecting and combining: trials and experiments with materials

nodes.misconception: There are no new ways to be inspired by nature.
nodes.response: We can all find new things that inspire us in the world around us.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Nature and architecture

nodes.misconception: Animals are universially known for specific charatristics across all cultures.
nodes.response: Often how animals are linked to charateristics in the West is very different that other cultures across the world.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Animals depicted in art

nodes.misconception: Artists only make work that looks good and is uplifting.
nodes.response: Artists use the power of imagery to communicate difficult realities about the planet.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Art and environmental activism

nodes.misconception: The material of an artwork cannot communicate meaning.
nodes.response: Many artists carefully select materials to deepen the meaning of their work. The materials chosen for an artwork can often communicate meaning through common associations or contextual connections.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Artist responses to plastic pollution

nodes.misconception: Only complex images or shapes can create associations.
nodes.response: Simple images or shapes can create associations to themes or ideas.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: Nature and symbolism

nodes.misconception: Artists inspired by nature can only look carefully at natural forms and record them.
nodes.response: Artists can make art in and with nature as well as recording from nature.
nodes.subject: art
nodes.lessonTitle: The presence of nature in art

nodes.misconception: Rules are the same for everyone.
nodes.response: Rules may be different in different settings and situations, for example, you may have different rules at school and home. Laws are the same for everyone.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Why does society need rules and laws?

nodes.misconception: Democracy is just about voting for leaders and making decisions by majority rule.
nodes.response: Democracy is about fairness, equality and everyone having a voice in how their society is run.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a democratic community?

nodes.misconception: Fairness always means treating everybody the same.
nodes.response: Fairness may involve treating people differently based on their individual circumstances in order to achieve equitable outcomes.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What does fairness mean in society?

nodes.misconception: Only leaders, or those in power, can be active citizens.
nodes.response: Whilst leadership skills might help in some situations, many active citizens work behind the scenes, you don’t need to be a leader or in power to be an active citizen.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can we be active citizens?

nodes.misconception: Citizenship is only about legal status.
nodes.response: Citizenship is all about being part of a society and being an active citizen.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is citizenship?

nodes.misconception: To make a difference within the school community an active citizen has to make a big change.
nodes.response: Even small actions at school can make a meaningful change.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can we get involved in our school community?

nodes.misconception: Citizens aren't able to make a difference and hold leaders accountable.
nodes.response: Citizens hold leaders accountable through raising concerns, participating in inquiries and contacting MPs.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can we hold our leaders to account?

nodes.misconception: Media outlets are always factual and not bias.
nodes.response: Media outlets strive to report factual information. However, they can still exhbit media bias that can be linked to political affiliations and concentration of media ownership.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a free press and why is it important for democracy?

nodes.misconception: Only Members of Parliament (MPs) can be part of select committees.
nodes.response: The public can contribute to select committees by submitting evidence or attending public consultations.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can I take part in the democratic process? The role of select committees

nodes.misconception: All members of political parties share the same views.
nodes.response: Political parties generally align with core values and principles but will have varying opinions on certain issues.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is Parliament and what are its functions?

nodes.misconception: Devolution means the regional governments are independent.
nodes.response: Devolution allows more powers, but the countries still remain part of the UK.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How is devolution impacting the UK's democracy?

nodes.misconception: Low voter turnout means people are not interested in politics.
nodes.response: Voter apathy might play a part in low voter turnout but other reasons exist, such as feeling votes will not count.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can we tell if the UK is democratic?

nodes.misconception: Individual votes do not count so could be pointless taking part.
nodes.response: Marginal seats are an example of why every vote matters.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Are elections truly fair?

nodes.misconception: Democracy works exactly the same way in every country.
nodes.response: Democracy takes different forms across the world, for example, direct, full, flawed democracies and hybrid regimes.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is democracy?

nodes.misconception: The media should always be neutral.
nodes.response: Media freedom does not require journalists to be entirely neutral. It allows for a range of perspectives, such as investigative journalism and opinion pieces, as long as they are reported accurately.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Why is media freedom necessary in a democracy?

nodes.misconception: Democracy is not either strong or weak.
nodes.response: There are different features and areas of democracy, such as the type of democracy, electoral system, media and voting age. Each of these will have their own strengths and weaknesses that come together to form an overall judgement on democracy.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Does the UK’s democracy need reform?

nodes.misconception: A country just uses direct democracy.
nodes.response: Direct democracy can be used on its own or with other forms of democracy, such as representative democracy.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Is direct democracy better than representative democracy?

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the electorates.
nodes.response: The leader of each political party is voted in by members of that party. When the general election takes place, the party with the majority of seats forms the Government and the leader of that party becomes the Prime Minister.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can we improve democracy in the UK?

nodes.misconception: That government is the same thing as parliament.
nodes.response: Parliament is the law-making branch, made up of elected MPs. The Government, including the Cabinet, is in charge of running the country and implementing those laws. It is led by the Prime Minister. Parliament scrutinises Government actions/decisions.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is the difference between the Government and Parliament?

nodes.misconception: Political parties are all either left wing or right wing.
nodes.response: Many parties mix both views or focus on specific issues, like regional concerns. Some parties are centrist or have ideas that don’t fit neatly into either side.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What do political parties do?

nodes.misconception: Devolved governments can make laws on any issue.
nodes.response: The powers of devolved governments are limited to specific policy areas defined by devolution agreements.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How does devolved government work?

nodes.misconception: Civil servants and public sector workers make political decisions.
nodes.response: Civil servants and other public sector workers are neutral professionals who work to implement government policies and decisions made by elected ministers, but they do not make political decisions themselves.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How is the UK Government organised?

nodes.misconception: The party that wins the most seats will form the Government and have all the power.
nodes.response: If a party does not have the majority of seats (50%+1) in Parliament, they may not be able to form a government. They might have to form a formal coalition or a voting agreement with a smaller party to get the majority. Power may have to be shared.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What happens after a general election?

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the public during the general election.
nodes.response: The Prime Minister is not elected by the people; instead, they are the leader of the party that has the most seats in the House of Commons after the election.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How do elections work?

nodes.misconception: MPs only work in Parliament.
nodes.response: MPs spend a lot of time helping constituents, attending local events and managing casework.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What do MPs do?

nodes.misconception: An uncodified constitution means there are no rules or limitations on government power.
nodes.response: There are rules and limitations on government power in an uncodified constitution, e.g. the UK’s uncodified constitution is made up of various sources, including statute law and common law. Rule of law is a key principle that guides Parliament.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What are the advantages and disadvantages of an uncodified constitution?

nodes.misconception: Parliamentary procedures and traditions are old-fashioned and have no meaning in modern society.
nodes.response: The traditions in Parliament exist for important reasons and serve to highlight the democratic principles that shape our society.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Should parliamentary procedures be modernised?

nodes.misconception: Power is separated, therefore, each branch does not link together.
nodes.response: While power is separated, the branches are still linked and work together. Each branch has its own responsibilities but also checks and balances the others to ensure no one branch becomes too powerful.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Why do we have a separation of powers?

nodes.misconception: The Speaker is able to influence decisions in the House of Commons.
nodes.response: The Speaker is politically neutral and there to chair debates and keep order in the House of Commons.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Is the physical set up of the House of Commons fit for purpose?

nodes.misconception: The Supreme Court has the same powers throughout the UK.
nodes.response: While the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for most cases in the UK, its role in Scotland differs as Scotland has its own distinct legal system. In Scotland, the High Court of Justiciary is the highest court of appeal for criminal cases.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What does the supreme court do?

nodes.misconception: Both chambers in the UK's bicameral system have equal power and roles.
nodes.response: The House of Commons holds more legislative power, while the House of Lords primarily acts as a revising chamber, providing scrutiny and suggesting amendments, rather than making final decisions.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What are the benefits and drawbacks of a bicameral system?

nodes.misconception: Representative democracies take away the choices of citizens because the representatives make all the decisions on their behalf.
nodes.response: In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf, but they can also influence policies through voting in elections, contacting their representatives and sometimes even through referendums.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What are direct and representative democracies?

nodes.misconception: Becuase both countries are democracies, the UK and the US political systems are the same.
nodes.response: Both countries are democracies but they differ: for example, the UK has a parliamentary system where only the House of Commons is elected, while the US has a presidential system where voters elect both houses of Congress and the President separately.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What are the differences between the UK and US political systems?

nodes.misconception: Devolved governments can make laws and policies on any issue in their devolved region.
nodes.response: The powers of devolved governments are limited to specific policy areas defined by devolution agreements. Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales have some executive and legislative powers. English regional governments only have some executive powers.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What are the differences between local, regional and national governance?

nodes.misconception: The Civil Service is a political body.
nodes.response: The Civil Service is designed to be impartial, serving the Government of the day. Civil servants are expected to provide objective advice and implement policy without political bias. This allows for continuity even when political leadership changes.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What does the Civil Service do?

nodes.misconception: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet have total control over the UK.
nodes.response: The Prime Minister leads the Government but must answer to Parliament. Members of Parliament (MPs) debate and approve laws and can challenge a Prime Minister. The Cabinet makes decisions but is accountable to Parliament and the law.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How is the country run?

nodes.misconception: Democracy exists in all countries, just in different ways.
nodes.response: Democracy exists in many countries and the levels of it vary. However, in many countries, there is a large mix of democratic and non-democratic practices, and in others, there is no true democracy at all, with the government taking full control.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How does the UK political system compare to other systems?

nodes.misconception: Being involved in a community means only participating in big events or formal groups.
nodes.response: Community involvement can also be about smaller, everyday actions, like helping a neighbour or being part of a social group. It does not always require big events or formal organisations.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What is our local community and how am I part of it?

nodes.misconception: All migrants move by choice. For example, for work or a better life, rather than because they are forced to leave.
nodes.response: Not all migrants move by choice. Some, like refugees and asylum seekers, are forced to flee due to war or persecution.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: Why might people migrate to the UK?

nodes.misconception: Migration to the UK is only about people coming from other countries to live here.
nodes.response: Migration includes both people coming to the UK (immigration) and those leaving (emigration). It’s shaped by global and local factors and impacts communities, industries and the economy in various ways.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How has migration affected society?

nodes.misconception: Hate crimes only count if someone actually hurts you physically.
nodes.response: Hate crimes include any criminal act where someone is targeted because of their disability, race, religion, sexual orientation or transgender identity. The law protects people from all kinds of harm motivated by prejudice.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How can we maintain respect and understanding in society?

nodes.misconception: Migration only occurs because people are forced to leave their country due to negative reasons (e.g., war or persecution).
nodes.response: While people are often forced to migrate (due to push factors like war or persecution), others choose to migrate for reasons like better job opportunities, family reunification, or improved living conditions (pull factors).
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How and why do people migrate to and from different communities?

nodes.misconception: For communities to work together successfully everyone has to always agree.
nodes.response: Individuals can recognise and co-exist with beliefs, opinions and values that are different to their own. This allows people to peacefully live with others who we might disagree with, as long as they do not harm anyone through their choices.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What makes us feel like we belong?

nodes.misconception: The only election in the UK is the general election.
nodes.response: There are many different elections including: general, local government, PCC, Mayoral and devolved parliament elections.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How do elections in the UK work?

nodes.misconception: Local councils have full control of their spending so can make all decisions themselves.
nodes.response: Part of their funding comes from national government so they sometimes have to priorities government led initiatives over local need.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: What are local councils and what do they do?

nodes.misconception: Every local government runs in the same way.
nodes.response: Local governments do not all run in the same way. There are different type of councils including, county and district councils.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How is local government structured?

nodes.misconception: Local and national governments have the same powers.
nodes.response: The national government have broader powers and devolves some of this to local governments.
nodes.subject: citizenship
nodes.lessonTitle: How is local democracy different to national government?

nodes.misconception: Devolution means that areas become independent.
nodes.response: Devolution means powers are devolved but they are still part of the UK and Parliament still holds central power.
