nodes.lessonTitle: Reading text files

nodes.misconception: A project brief always includes success criteria.
nodes.response: Sometimes a project brief may not include success criteria, but a brief description of what the program needs to do. You may need to generate success criteria from the project brief.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project - dictionaries I

nodes.misconception: There is no way to store multiple records in one data structure in Python.
nodes.response: If you want to use multiple records in a database, then you can add multiple dictionaries to a list.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Records and dictionaries

nodes.misconception: A list index starts at 1 as that is the first element in the list and should be counted as the first item.
nodes.response: In most programming languages, list indexing is zero-based, which means the index starts at 0. The number indicates the position before the value is seen.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating lists in Python

nodes.misconception: Once an item is added to a list it is fixed in to the structure of the list and it cannot be altered.
nodes.response: Items can be removed, inserted and amended in a list using list methods. These methods change the structure of the list. Values of items can also be updated.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Python list operations

nodes.misconception: A for loop is the same as a while loop as they are both designed to repeat instructions. You should pick one and stick to it for all your programs.
nodes.response: Unlike a while loop, a for loop is count-controlled, meaning it will repeat a set number of times when the loop begins. In contrast, a while loop repeats instructions for as long as its condition is true. This can vary each time the loop runs.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using for loops to iterate data structures

nodes.misconception: Mathematical operations cannot be performed on items held in a list; the items must first be stored in a new variable.
nodes.response: Mathematical operations can be performed directly on list items by using an index value to reference the value used.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Mathematical operations in data structures

nodes.misconception: Strings are mutable meaning that any character within the string can be changed.
nodes.response: Strings are immutable. The elements of a string cannot be changed. If changes to the string are required, the whole string must be rewritten.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Iterating through data structures

nodes.misconception: Python will automatically round numbers to the nearest whole number.
nodes.response: Python will perform calculations based on the values that have been provided and generate an answer that can include fractional parts. If you want to reduce the number of digits, you can use the round() function.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data structure projects in Python

nodes.misconception: As long as a product is planned, it does not matter which type of planning document is used.
nodes.response: It is important to use the correct planning document to ensure the planning stage is useful for the creating stage.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Initiation and planning digital artefacts

nodes.misconception: Bitmap and raster are two different types of image.
nodes.response: They are the same and can be referred to as a raster or bitmap image.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating digital graphics

nodes.misconception: Websites require specialist knowledge to create and publish.
nodes.response: Drag-and-drop software and online platforms allow anyone to create and publish a website easily.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a multi-page website

nodes.misconception: A poster that is created using software is digital even when printed out.
nodes.response: The source of the design is digital if it was created using software. However, once that digital design is printed onto a physical medium like paper, the resulting poster itself becomes a physical artefact.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital artefact types and uses

nodes.misconception: The lifecycle is a plan you follow from start to finish in sequence.
nodes.response: Once you get to the testing and evaluation stage, you may move back to the execution stage until you are happy with the product.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Project lifecycle

nodes.misconception: Copyright only applies to the use of images.
nodes.response: Copyright refers to any creation by an original creator.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Legal and ethical considerations in creating digital artefacts

nodes.misconception: It does not matter how the camera is positioned as long as the action is captured.
nodes.response: The camera angle can help portray a key element of the moment to the viewer and help them understand the meaning of the clip.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating digital video

nodes.misconception: Once a product is completed it does not need to be improved if I am happy with it as the creator.
nodes.response: Listening to other opinions and referring to the success criteria of the client brief is essential to help develop a product that meets the client brief completely.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan and create a digital artefact from a given brief

nodes.misconception: Changing a shape's path doesn’t change how it behaves — it’s still just a shape.
nodes.response: Editing a path changes the shape’s structure. Moving nodes changes the outline, allowing for new and more complex designs.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Vector paths

nodes.misconception: Vector graphics are made from pixels and can lose quality when resized.
nodes.response: Vector graphics are made from lines and shapes. They do not lose quality when resized.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using vector tools to draw and modify shapes

nodes.misconception: SVG files are made of pictures, not code.
nodes.response: SVG images are stored as text-based code. Each shape is written with instructions that describe its appearance, such as its size, colour and position on the canvas.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Vector markup

nodes.misconception: Grouping objects is permanent.
nodes.response: Grouping objects can be reversed using ungroup. Combining objects is harder to reverse; only undo fixes combining.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Working with multiple objects

nodes.misconception: Vector images are better than bitmap images in every situation.
nodes.response: Vector and bitmap images are suited to different tasks. Vectors are best for simple, scalable designs like logos, while bitmaps are better for detailed images like photos.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing bitmap and vector graphics

nodes.misconception: You don’t need a plan before starting a vector design — you can just make it up as you go.
nodes.response: Planning helps you focus your design and choose the right tools and shapes before you start. Without a plan, it's easy to miss the goal or waste time making unnecessary changes.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a vector product

nodes.misconception: High-level languages are always better than low-level languages because they are easier to use.
nodes.response: High-level languages are generally easier to learn and use. However, low-level languages offer more direct control over the computer's hardware, which can be essential for certain tasks like writing operating systems or device drivers.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: High and low level languages

nodes.misconception: Input and output of a program happen automatically, without the need for coding. The computer uses it in the correct part of your program.
nodes.response: Computers process instructions in code that requires input and output. The programmer needs to specify exactly where and how it should be handled.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Input and output

nodes.misconception: You can define a constant in any programming language.
nodes.response: Python does not have constants. But if you want a value to be treated as a constant, it's a common naming convention for the identifier to be written in capital letters.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Variables and constants in programs

nodes.misconception: You must use an IDE to write and run programs.
nodes.response: You don’t need an IDE to write and run programs; you can use a simple text editor and a compiler or interpreter. However, an IDE makes the process much easier by providing tools such as autocompletion and error checking.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Features of an IDE

nodes.misconception: The order of instructions in a program doesn't really matter, as long as all the instructions are there.
nodes.response: Computers execute code line by line, in the order it's written. If you change the sequence, you're changing the steps the computer takes, and that will change the output.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Common data types

nodes.misconception: I can just start coding and figure it out as I go. Planning is a waste of time and boring.
nodes.response: Planning is like building a strong foundation. A good plan helps you write better code faster.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: sequence I

nodes.misconception: As long as all the necessary lines of code are present, the program will work, regardless of their order.
nodes.response: Computers run code line by line, in the order it's written. If you change the sequence, you're changing the steps the computer takes, and that will change the output.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing programs using sequence

nodes.misconception: Testing is just about making sure the program runs.
nodes.response: It's not just about running the program. We test to make sure the program does exactly what it's supposed to do, in all situations. This means checking if it handles correct input and incorrect input correctly.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: sequence II

nodes.misconception: Assembly language is only used for very old computers, and it's not relevant to modern programming.
nodes.response: It's true that assembly was used more in the past, but it's still relevant. It gives direct hardware control, crucial for things like embedded systems and device drivers. Understanding it helps you see how computers work at a low level.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Assembly language

nodes.misconception: Feedback is about telling people what has been done wrong and giving commands.
nodes.response: Feedback should be supportive and constructive. Feedback should include details of what has gone well as well as suggestions to help improve the product.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing a digital product

nodes.misconception: All content found on the World Wide Web is free to reuse.
nodes.response: Content on the World Wide Web is subject to copyright and can be reused subject to licence agreements. Content found on the World Wide Web should be carefully chosen to ensure it is trustworthy and accurate.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a slide deck

nodes.misconception: The format and layout of slide decks must always be created from scratch each time you start a new document.
nodes.response: Slide deck templates have pre-designed layouts and formatting that can be used as a starting point when creating new slide decks.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a slide deck template

nodes.misconception: A logo is a brand.
nodes.response: A logo is not a brand but a key part of a brand's or organisation's identity. A logo is a graphic that represents the visual identity of a brand or organisation.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Poster making

nodes.misconception: Plans cannot change as a project progresses.
nodes.response: Initial planning helps focus the purpose, content and layout of a product. However, due to feedback or changing needs, plans may need to be changed as a project progresses.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Poster planning

nodes.misconception: Posters and signs should include lots of text information for the viewer to read.
nodes.response: Posters and signs should avoid too much detail when using text and images. This helps to clearly get a message across to the viewer at a glance and does not rely on them having to spend time looking at the detail.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Features of a poster

nodes.misconception: The most detailed renders should always be produced.
nodes.response: Render engines and settings should be chosen with consideration to the requirements of the project. This may include considering factors such as time constraints and hardware limitations.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Render and export animations

nodes.misconception: 3D models are all made up of simple shapes that are scaled, moved and rotated.
nodes.response: Having only previously used object mode, learners may be unaware that geometry such as vertices, edges and faces can all be directly modified in edit mode. Working in edit mode gives a modeller greater freedom to create more complex models.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Complex models and colours

nodes.misconception: To create smooth organic surfaces and models, individual geometry such as vertices, edges and faces must be edited individually.
nodes.response: Free-form, organically shaped models can be created by using modelling tools such as proportional editing.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Organic modelling

nodes.misconception: The 3D viewport display in Blender is the view from the scene camera.
nodes.response: What is displayed in the 3D viewport in Blender is not what is viewed from the camera. The camera view must be enabled to look through the camera and set up composition.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Lighting and cameras

nodes.misconception: Detailed and complex 3D models are always created from scratch and therefore take a long time to create.
nodes.response: 3D models usually start off by using, adding and modifying simple 3D shapes. Further detail and complexities are then added to increase the realism of the model.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Move, rotate, scale, colour

nodes.misconception: Every frame of an animation needs to be created by the animator.
nodes.response: Most modern animations are created using tweening. Tweening creates the frames between keyframes and stitches them together. This reduces the time taken to create animations and can improve quality.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Keyframe animation and parenting objects

nodes.misconception: All network topologies work the same way and have the same benefits.
nodes.response: Different topologies connect devices in different ways. For example, star networks use a central hub, while mesh networks connect devices directly. Each has unique strengths and weaknesses depending on the situation.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network topologies

nodes.misconception: All devices on a network use the same IP address, so there’s no need for private or public IPs or DNS.
nodes.response: Each device needs a unique private IP address on a local network. To access the internet, the router uses a public IP address. DNS translates website names into IP addresses so devices know where to send data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network addressing

nodes.misconception: Network failure just means the internet stops working for a bit; it’s annoying but not serious.
nodes.response: Network failure can lead to data loss, financial damage and safety risks in sectors like healthcare. It is more than just an inconvenience and can impact lives and businesses.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of network failure

nodes.misconception: Wireless networks are always better than wired ones because they don’t use cables.
nodes.response: Wireless is more convenient, but it can be slower, less secure and more prone to interference. Wired connections are often better for speed, stability and data heavy tasks.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Wireless networks

nodes.misconception: All wired networks use the same type of cable.
nodes.response: Copper Ethernet and fibre optic cables have different speeds, distances and uses. For example, copper Ethernet is fine for short distances, but fibre optic is better for fast, long-distance connections.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Wired networks

nodes.misconception: All devices in a network do the same thing, they just send and receive data.
nodes.response: In a client–server network, devices have different roles. Servers provide services like file storage or email. Clients request and use those services, rather than providing them.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of network

nodes.misconception: All networks must have a server because a server is always needed to share files or printers between devices.
nodes.response: Not all networks need a server. In a peer-to-peer model, each computer can act as both client and server, sharing files directly. This setup is simpler but may lack central control and security.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network basics

nodes.misconception: All devices on a network share the same MAC address because they’re connected to the same router.
nodes.response: Each network device has its own unique MAC address assigned to its network interface card (NIC).
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network hardware and MAC addresses

nodes.misconception: The only factor that affects network performance is how fast your internet connection is.
nodes.response: Connection speed does affect performance, but it is also influenced by factors like bandwidth, latency, number of users, packet loss, hardware quality and interference on wireless networks.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network performance

nodes.misconception: A flowchart should always be created before writing a computer program.
nodes.response: For simple programs, a flowchart may not be needed and could add to development time. Sometimes the program code itself might be clear enough without a flowchart.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing algorithms using flowcharts

nodes.misconception: Computational thinking means writing code for everything.
nodes.response: While coding is a way to implement solutions, computational thinking can be applied to problems that don't require coding at all and should be seen as a set of processes that help people solve problems.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling a project using computational thinking

nodes.misconception: Computational thinking techniques are only related to solving problems with computers.
nodes.response: The underlying principles of computational thinking can be applied in various aspects of life, even without any digital technology.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Computational thinking

nodes.misconception: Using trace tables guarantees correct logic and code.
nodes.response: Trace tables can be subject to human error and can be impractical to use for complex algorithms.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Tracing algorithms

nodes.misconception: Arrays are always the best choice for storing and accessing collections of data.
nodes.response: While arrays offer efficient direct access to elements using their index, they have limitations, such as fixed size and potential inefficiency in terms of unused elements.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data structures

nodes.misconception: Pseudocode can be directly run or executed by a computer.
nodes.response: Pseudocode is a human-readable representation of an algorithm's logic but doesn't follow the syntax or rules of any particular programming language. It should only be used as a planning tool.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing algorithms using pseudocode

nodes.misconception: Algorithms and computer programs are actually the same thing.
nodes.response: A computer program is a specific implementation of an algorithm's logic. A clearly written algorithm provides instructions that can be implemented in various ways including, but not limited to, computer programs.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing algorithms to computer programs

nodes.misconception: Algorithmic bias can be completely eliminated.
nodes.response: It is extremely difficult, maybe impossible, for complex algorithms to be completely free from bias.  By aiming to understand sources of bias, actively working to reduce it, and being transparent, algorithmic bias can be reduced as much as possible.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Algorithmic bias

nodes.misconception: Bandwidth is the speed of data being transmitted across a network. The higher the bandwidth, the faster data can be transferred between points in a network.
nodes.response: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted at a time, not the time it takes to reach from one point to another. Higher bandwidth reduces the total transfer time of data but this is only noticable when there is a lot to transfer.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Wired and wireless networks

nodes.misconception: The internet is the same as the World Wide Web.
nodes.response: The World Wide Web is a service that is offered over the internet. The internet is the network that transfers data whilst the World Wide Web is the system of sharing information that people use.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The internet

nodes.misconception: On a network, servers, clients and routers have the same purpose.
nodes.response: Servers, clients and routers have distinct roles and functionalities in a network. They are not interchangeable and serve different purposes.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to computer networks

nodes.misconception: Data packets from a complete message always follow the same route to their destination. They are then put back together in the order they are received.
nodes.response: Data packets are split and will be sent using the most efficient route at the time which often changes. Packets include data parts so they can be reassembled at the destination as long as the order of the packets is identified before being sent.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the World Wide Web (WWW)

nodes.misconception: Computers only need protocols when sending emails or accessing websites.
nodes.response: Protocols are essential for all sorts of activities, not just email or browsing websites. Protocols are also needed for streaming movies, playing online games, making video calls, etc. Anything being sent across a network needs to follow a protocol.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Protocols and IP addresses

nodes.misconception: The internet of things (IoT) is only about smart homes and appliances.
nodes.response: IoT are everyday devices that are connected to the internet and can communicate with each other. They might not collect data for the same purpose but they can collect information about how people use the devices.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Internet of Things

nodes.misconception: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are the same thing.
nodes.response: Machine learning is a type of artifical intelligence that helps machines get better at tasks by learning from data, not just following pre-written instructions and rules.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Machine learning and artificial intelligence

nodes.misconception: All computers can do everything equally well.
nodes.response: General-purpose computers can run many programs, but single-purpose computers are designed to do one task very efficiently.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Traditional computer systems

nodes.misconception: The CPU is the only important part of a computer.
nodes.response: The CPU is an important part of a computer system but a computer also needs memory, input, output, and storage to work properly. All parts must work together as a system.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Computer architecture

nodes.misconception: The operating system is just what you see on the screen.
nodes.response: What you see on the screen is the graphical interface, but the operating system includes a lot more behind the scenes such as memory management, file systems, device control etc.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The operating system

nodes.misconception: Data science is just about collecting loads of data.
nodes.response: Data science isn’t just about gathering data, it’s about understanding data and using it to make decisions or discoveries.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data science

nodes.misconception: Boolean logic is about numbers
nodes.response: Boolean logic is about truth values such as yes/no, true/false or (1/0).
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Boolean logic

nodes.misconception: The sensor follows the line like a smart camera.
nodes.response: The sensor sends data back to the microcontroller to say whether light or dark is detected. The written code uses this data to decide how the buggy should respond.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Optical sensors for navigation

nodes.misconception: You can connect a motor directly to a microcontroller and it will work fine.
nodes.response: Microcontrollers send control signals, not power. Motor drivers act like electronic switches to take a signal and safely drive the motors with their own power supply.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Working with motors

nodes.misconception: Technical jargon impresses the audience and makes the presentation better.
nodes.response: Presentations should be clear and accessible, using simple language and examples that everyone can understand.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting a physical computing project

nodes.misconception: As long as the components are attached the buggy will work fine.
nodes.response: A good chassis design isn’t just about holding parts. Care should be taken when positioning and securing components to ensure the buggy is reliable, easy to fix and functions as intended.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Chassis design and build

nodes.misconception: Physical computing is just about programming robots.
nodes.response: Physical computing is much broader than just robotics. It includes any system where a computer interacts with the physical world through sensors and actuators, for example wearable devices, environmental sensors and smart home devices.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to physical computing

nodes.misconception: Ultrasonic sensors work like cameras and detect objects visually.
nodes.response: Ultrasonic sensors use sound not light to detect objects.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Ultrasonic sensors to measure distance

nodes.misconception: The microcontroller controls all systems at the same time.
nodes.response: In reality, most microcontrollers execute code sequentially, one line at a time. It may appear that microcontrollers are doing many things at once, but they’re actually switching between tasks quickly or handling them step by step.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating an autonomous vehicle

nodes.misconception: Adding more features always makes a product better.
nodes.response: Adding features should be done carefully, focusing on usefulness and how well they work together to solve a problem.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding additional features to your buggy

nodes.misconception: PANs are limited to Bluetooth or Wi-Fi connections.
nodes.response: PANs can use a variety of technologies, including wired connections like USB and FireWire, and wireless connections like Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and more.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal networks

nodes.misconception: Synchronous communication tools are better than asynchronous communication tools.
nodes.response: Neither type of communication can be deemed better than the other overall. Some forms of communication will suit different tasks better than others.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Tools for communication

nodes.misconception: When delivering a presentation you should read the slides out word for word.
nodes.response: Simply reading out the slides can disengage the audience and mean that your message can become lost.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Tools for presenting information

nodes.misconception: Working collaboratively is always positive and has an impact on productivity.
nodes.response: There are some disadvantages to collaborative working, for example complex decision making with multiple people can become a lengthy process and coordination of resources can be difficult.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Accessibility

nodes.misconception: Communication in the workplace is the same as communication with family or friends.
nodes.response: Communication in the workplace should be formal and professional. Slang language, abbreviations and emojis should be avoided.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Skills for the world of work

nodes.misconception: The cloud ensures everyone can access software and resources.
nodes.response: There are many different devices that can be used to access cloud services, and the functionality of each device will have an impact on the quality of service users will experience when using cloud based services.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Cloud computing

nodes.misconception: Supporting an employee's mental or physical wellbeing only costs an organisation.
nodes.response: Supporting an employee's mental or physical wellbeing can actually benefit an organisation through reduced time off and increased productivity.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Remote working

nodes.misconception: Modern technology has improved individuals' working lives in all aspects.
nodes.response: There are some negative impacts of modern-day technology on the workplace and individual workers. These include fewer opportunities for face-to-face communication and 24/7 connectivity.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The modern world of work

nodes.misconception: Gantt charts are more effective than Kanban boards because they show project dependencies.
nodes.response: Neither tool can be deemed more effective overall. A business should decide which of the tools will work well for them based on the needs of the project.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Tools for planning

nodes.misconception: If I change a few words from a website and use it as my own work it's not plagiarism.
nodes.response: Changing a few words isn't enough. Plagiarism is using someone's ideas without credit. Even if you rephrase, you must reference the original source.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Research and planning a blog

nodes.misconception: A rubric is just a checklist for the teacher. It doesn't help me write better blogs.
nodes.response: It's a guide to help you understand what makes a good blog post. It shows you the specific criteria, like clear writing or effective use of images, so you know what to focus on. Use it as a tool to improve your writing before submitting your work.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Use criteria to develop a blog

nodes.misconception: Success criteria are only for the teacher to use when marking work. They don't help me.
nodes.response: They're not just for marking. Think of them like a checklist or a guide to help you create your best work. They tell you exactly what you need to do to succeed.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Promoting a cause

nodes.misconception: Blogs are just like any other website; they're all the same.
nodes.response: Blogs are more like online journals or news sites. Blogs are updated regularly, while websites might not change as often.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Features of a blog

nodes.misconception: All information that is found on the internet is true.
nodes.response: Anyone can create a website. Check who wrote it, when and if the facts are correct. Don't believe everything you see without checking first!
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The credibility of sources

nodes.misconception: If I find an image online, I can use it however I want, as long as I don't say I created it.
nodes.response: Just finding an image online doesn't automatically mean you can use it freely. Think of it like this: someone created that image, and they have rights to it, just like an author has rights to their book.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using images appropriately

nodes.misconception: Just like addition, subtraction and multiplication there is only one type of division in programming.
nodes.response: There are three types of division in programming; real, integer and modulo division. Each deal with remainder values differently and will be useful in different ways in programming.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Arithmetic operators

nodes.misconception: Pseudocode is the same as a programming language and must follow a particular syntax.
nodes.response: Pseudocode is independent of a specific programming language and does not need to follow any particular rules. All that is required is that a programmer can read the pseudocode and understand how to implement it.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: selection I

nodes.misconception: Comments are added to code to help you understand your program.
nodes.response: Comments are used to make the code more readable to a programmer who seeks to understand it. The comments should be written in a style that would help them make sense of the program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Good programming practices

nodes.misconception: The = operator is used for comparison.
nodes.response: When using Python for programming the == operator is used for comparison and the = operator is used for assignment. Other languages may not always use these operators for these tasks.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Relational operators

nodes.misconception: If a program has a logic error it will not work and will give error messages.
nodes.response: Logic errors are errors that cause a program to work incorrectly or unexpectedly. With a logic error, the program can be run without failing, but it does not return the expected result. The user might not realise that there is an error.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: selection II

nodes.misconception: A program follows a sequence of instructions and will run all lines of code.
nodes.response: Selection statements can be used to control program flow, so some lines of code can be skipped to  follow a different path through the program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using selection when developing programs

nodes.misconception: A nested selection statement can only have one nested selection block.
nodes.response: Selection statements can can continue to be nested in further selection blocks to provide more complex conditions for which specific code will be executed.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Nested selection

nodes.misconception: All parts of a solution must be coded at the same time and tested that it works once coding has finished.
nodes.response: Individual subproblems can be approached separately and tested to ensure they work before moving onto the next part. It helps to know parts of a program work as intended.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Selection challenge

nodes.misconception: A logical expression can only check one value.
nodes.response: Logical expressions can combine relational and logical operators to check multiple values or inputs.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Logical operators

nodes.misconception: Pseudocode can be executed by a computer.
nodes.response: Pseudocode cannot be executed by a computer. Pseudocode must be translated into a real programming language such as Python, Java or C# for it to be executed by a computer.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Project design

nodes.misconception: Planning isn't needed for coding projects — you can just develop your code as you write.
nodes.response: If you plan out your algorithm first in human language, you can ensure each part is correct before writing any actual code. This reduces the likelihood of logic errors which could stop your code working as expected.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Approaching a programming project

nodes.misconception: Testing is something you only do at the end of a project.
nodes.response: Testing is carried out throughout the development process. There are also specific stages and methods of testing that can be adopted. An overall approach to testing should be agreed and planned depending on the requirements of the system.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing principles

nodes.misconception: You don't need to consider the inputs, outputs and processes of a program during the analysis stage.
nodes.response: Listing the inputs, processes and outputs before coding helps you clearly understand what the program needs to do, avoid mistakes and save time later. It breaks the problem into smaller steps, making it easier to solve and explain to others.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The project brief

nodes.misconception: If you are developing code for a project on your own, you don't need to worry about software design principles.
nodes.response: Even if your code isn't used by others, it is a good idea to follow software design principles in case you have to revisit or develop your code later on.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Software design principles

nodes.misconception: An evaluation just states if something works or not.
nodes.response: A strong evaluation should be specific and evidence-based, covering what works, how this was achieved and how it was tested.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating the success of a programming project

nodes.misconception: A function and a procedure are the same.
nodes.response: A function is different from a procedure because it returns a value or values to the main program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Refining code in a programming project

nodes.misconception: A function and a procedure are the same.
nodes.response: A function is different from a procedure because it returns a value or values to the main program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Refining code for a programming project

nodes.misconception: The append() method will replace the existing contents of a list.
nodes.response: The append() method will add an item to the end of an existing list but it will not replace or overwrite any existing items in a list.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing code for a programming project

nodes.misconception: A test plan should only include data that will cause a program to not work.
nodes.response: A test plan should contain a range of test data, including normal, erroneous and boundary.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing and refining a programming project

nodes.misconception: Conditional formatting needs to be applied each time a value in a cell changes.
nodes.response: Conditional formatting will automatically update if the value in a cell changes, as soon as a value meets the condition, the formatting will be appplied.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Formatting in a spreadsheet model

nodes.misconception: The IF function can only return the words True or False to the user.
nodes.response: The IF function returns a result of True or False, but you can set what message will be displayed to the user for each result within the function.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Lookup and reference functions

nodes.misconception: A spreadsheet can only be used to explore the costs of the event after it has happened.
nodes.response: A spreadsheet model can be used to predict and model the costs of the event before it happens to help the organisers make decisions about income and expenditure.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Spreadsheet project I

nodes.misconception: Data validation can only check values entered into a cell. It cannot be used to stop a user from leaving a cell blank.
nodes.response: Data validation can be used to prevent users from leaving required cells blank.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data validation in a spreadsheet model

nodes.misconception: The type of chart you select doesn't matter, all charts will represent data effectively.
nodes.response: Different types of chart present different types of data effectively. For example, a pie chart is used to represent data that makes up a whole part or 100%.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Visualising data using charts in a spreadsheet

nodes.misconception: The COUNTIF function is the same as the COUNT function.
nodes.response: A COUNTIF function returns the total number of cells based on a set criterion, whereas the COUNT function returns the number of cells that contain a number in a range.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Spreadsheet project II

nodes.misconception: A macro can only be used to clear data in a spreadsheet.
nodes.response: A macro is used to record and repeat tasks that can be automated in a spreadsheet. They are not just used to clear or reset data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving a spreadsheet model

nodes.misconception: Spreadsheet formatting is only used to make a spreadsheet look attractive.
nodes.response: Spreadsheet formatting is used to make information clearer but is also important to ensure data values such as currency are formatted correctly.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Spreadsheet modelling

nodes.misconception: The fill handle can only be used to replicate formulas.
nodes.response: The fill handle can replicate formulas, text and numbers.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Formulas in a spreadsheet model

nodes.misconception: Once AI is built, it can’t be changed and the risks are already set.
nodes.response: AI systems can and should be continuously monitored, tested and improved to reduce risks. Risk mitigation is an ongoing process, not a one-time fix.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Risk mitigation of AI

nodes.misconception: AI can think and make decisions like humans.
nodes.response: AI systems have no awareness or emotions and do not think or understand in the way humans do. AI systems process data and follow patterns or rules based on training data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: AI in our world today

nodes.misconception: Deepfakes are easy to spot because they always look fake or glitchy
nodes.response: Many deepfakes today are highly realistic and difficult to detect, especially when viewed quickly or shared on social media. As technology improves, deepfakes can mimic real people’s voices and faces with convincing detail.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Deepfakes and trust

nodes.misconception: Large Language Models (LLMs) understand what they’re saying, like a human does.
nodes.response: LLMs do not understand language or meaning. They generate responses by predicting the most likely next word based on patterns in the data they were trained on, not because they understand the content like a human does.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Chatbot applications and other LLMs

nodes.misconception: ML models are neutral and always give fair or accurate information.
nodes.response: ML models can reflect or amplify bias in their training data. If the data contains stereotypes or imbalances, the ML model can repeat or reinforce them.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Bias and accuracy in machine learning

nodes.misconception: AI image generators create completely original artwork from scratch.
nodes.response: AI image generators create new images by learning from and combining patterns found in millions of existing images. They don’t “imagine” or invent things like a human artist; they remix data they were trained on.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding image generators

nodes.misconception: Generative AI systems output is always accurate and based on facts.
nodes.response: Generative AI systems can produce convincing text but the output is not always accurate or based on facts. Fact checking is always important because AI systems generate content based on patterns in the training data, not verified information.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Uses of predictive and generative AI

nodes.misconception: You can just type anything into an LLM and it will always give the best answer.
nodes.response: LLMs work best when you give them clear, specific and well-structured prompts. The quality of the input directly affects the quality of the output; this process of designing and refining inputs to get better results is called prompt engineering.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Getting the most out of an LLM

nodes.misconception: The more data you include in a data visualisation, the better.
nodes.response: Removing unneccesary data from a visualisation can improve the quality of a visualisation.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using data to support decision making

nodes.misconception: Data is not important when presenting findings to support an argument.
nodes.response: Data makes your point stronger by showing real evidence.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Global data

nodes.misconception: Data capture forms are only electronic.
nodes.response: A data capture form can be designed and used on paper and data can be collected in person.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Capturing data to investigate an issue

nodes.misconception: If you have missing data and cannot find the original source, there is nothing you can do.
nodes.response: You could look at similar data and generate an average value to insert. For example, if the zoo is missing a weight for a lion, they could calculate the average weight of the other lions and enter this.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data cleansing

nodes.misconception: A visualiation will always tell you the information you need to know.
nodes.response: You may need to refine or collect more data to create visualisations which answer your questions effectively.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using data to make recommendations

nodes.misconception: A positive correlation means one variable has an impact on another.
nodes.response: Just because there is a correlation, it doesn’t necessarily mean that one things causes another to increase.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The investigative cycle

nodes.misconception: Closing tags are optional and are just used to make the code easier to read.
nodes.response: Most tags need to be closed and require the use of a forward slash. This marks the beginning and the end of the content that the HTML tag should be applied to.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Website building blocks

nodes.misconception: Search engines search the whole internet live.
nodes.response: Search engines use a pre-built index to deliver fast results.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Search engines and results rankings

nodes.misconception: Hyperlinks only work on the homepage.
nodes.response: Hyperlinks are used across all pages, creating a fully navigable website. Any object on any HTML page can be made into a hyperlink.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a custom website

nodes.misconception: Images are stored inside HTML files as one document that is downloaded and displayed.
nodes.response: HTML only references image files, which are stored separately. When a web page is downloaded, the linked images are downloaded separately.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding images to a web page

nodes.misconception: The more words I add to a search, the better my results will be.
nodes.response: Adding too many words can make a search too specific, limiting useful results. Use search operators like AND, OR, and NOT to refine the search and still find good information.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using search and web navigation effectively

nodes.misconception: CSS rules must always include < > like HTML tags.
nodes.response: CSS uses just the tag name, without brackets.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to CSS

nodes.misconception: A single audio file contains only one channel of sound.
nodes.response: Many formats (e.g., stereo or surround sound) contain multiple channels within one file. The information contained in the audio track can be reproduced on separate channels.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing sound with binary data

nodes.misconception: 1 bit is always used to represent 1 pixel.
nodes.response: While bits are used to represent the colour of pixels, it's not always a one-to-one relationship. The number of bits used can vary depending on the colour depth of the image.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: File size of digital images

nodes.misconception: The number of bits per pixel that represent the colour are always individual specific colours.
nodes.response: When RGB is used to define the colour of a pixel the bits represent different intesities of red, green and blue providing different colour mixes.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing images with binary data

nodes.misconception: Audacity project files can be listened to on all digital devices.
nodes.response: To listen to the audio on other devices, the file must be exported to a common format such as WAV (.wav) or MP3 (.mp3).
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing sound

nodes.misconception: Generative AI always has a negative affect on society.
nodes.response: Generative AI isn't always negative; it depends on its use. Generative AI tools can help artists, educators and scientists create innovative designs, engaging learning materials and advanced simulations.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Manipulating digital images

nodes.misconception: Compression always reduces quality or that compressed files are always lower quality than uncompressed files.
nodes.response: Lossless compression retains all original data by finding and storing repeated patterns more efficiently.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: File size and compression

nodes.misconception: More storage always means a faster computer.
nodes.response: Upgrading from a HDD to a SSD will improve speed, but simply increasing the capacity of the same type of drive does not make the computer faster.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Secondary storage

nodes.misconception: Data is stored "in the cloud", so it doesn't really exist physically or have an environmental cost.
nodes.response: The cloud is a network of large data centres. These are real, physical facilities that consume huge amounts of energy and water, and generate significant e-waste.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Environmental impacts of computing devices

nodes.misconception: The CPU decodes and understands the instructions.
nodes.response: The instruction is decoded and then executed. The process only executes the instructions received.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The fetch-execute (FE) cycle

nodes.misconception: All computers use the same operating system.
nodes.response: Different devices can run different operating systems, for example Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Operating system

nodes.misconception: Increasing cores and clock speed improves performance.
nodes.response: It can improve performance but not always, as other hardware components may not be able to work that way.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Computer specifications

nodes.misconception: The CPU is the brain of the computer and understands the instructions received.
nodes.response: The CPU is the core of the computer system and receives instructions that it then executes with the help of the different components.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The processor

nodes.misconception: RAM stores data and instructions when a computer is switched off.
nodes.response: RAM is volatile — when power is switched off, the data and instrucions are lost.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Main memory

nodes.misconception: Embedded system is a computer inside a computer / system inside a system.
nodes.response: Embedded systems are specific to a given task and often found within a machine.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Software and embedded systems

nodes.misconception: The value a variable holds cannot be updated and a computer remembers the previous values of variables.
nodes.response: A variable can be updated during a program. Once the value of a variable is updated in a program, the previous value is overwritten.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Program variables

nodes.misconception: A program can only follow one sequence of commands.
nodes.response: Selection allows for a program to follow alternative paths depending on the criteria of the selection statement.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Selection

nodes.misconception: Selection statements can only check one condition at a time.
nodes.response: Complex conditions can be built into selection using a combination of comparison and logical operators. Logical operators join separate conditions and provide one complete statement that still evaluates to only True or False.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Operators

nodes.misconception: Programming constructs cannot be combined in the same code block.
nodes.response: The programming constructs of sequence, selection and iteration can be combined within the same code block to make more complex programs.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving using programming constructs

nodes.misconception: A sprite in Scratch can only have one sequence of code blocks.
nodes.response: Sequences of code can be separated into subroutines and these subroutines can be called multiple times.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence

nodes.misconception: Iteration means a program will repeat something a set number of times.
nodes.response: Count-controlled iteration will repeat a sequence of commands a set number of times. Condition-controlled iteration will repeat a sequence of commands until a condition is met and so the number of times it will repeat can never be predicted.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Count-controlled iteration

nodes.misconception: The internet is built directly on the OSI 7-layer model, and its layers are actual physical hardware components.
nodes.response: The OSI model is a conceptual framework, not the internet's direct architecture. It helps to understand network functions.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network models

nodes.misconception: All the data from a website travels together in one file and always takes the same route through the internet to reach your device.
nodes.response: Data is broken into packets, and each packet may take a different route. This makes transmission faster and more reliable, because the network can avoid delays or busy routes.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: How data travels across the internet

nodes.misconception: Devices automatically know how to communicate to any other device, regardless of brand or type, without needing specific rules.
nodes.response: Devices rely on shared protocols to communicate and exchange data effectively, like a common language or set of rules. This ensures all devices follow the same process.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Protocols

nodes.misconception: The World Wide Web is a single entity stored in one place.
nodes.response: The World Wide Web is a vast collection of interconnected websites and documents hosted on servers all over the world. Your web browser accesses these different locations to display the information you see.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Internet fundamentals

nodes.misconception: Network threats and attacks come only from external hackers or from sources outside a network, while internal users or trusted software pose no risk.
nodes.response: Threats can be internal, like careless employees or malicious insiders, as well as external.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Threats to networks

nodes.misconception: Network security just stops viruses, so it’s only important for large organisations, not for individuals or small businesses.
nodes.response: Network security protects all users, not just large organisations. It prevents data theft, fraud, and service disruption. Individuals need protection from threats like phishing or ransomware.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Network security

nodes.misconception: You don’t need any hardware for the cloud — everything just happens online.
nodes.response: The cloud still relies on physical hardware, like servers, storage devices and networking equipment.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Hosting services

nodes.misconception: Students may think protocols like HTTP or FTP operate at all layers, or that TCP and IP are the only protocols in the model.
nodes.response: Specific protocols perform unique functions at dedicated TCP/IP layers.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The TCP/IP model

nodes.misconception: Search engines instantly know every website and search live each time you type in a query.
nodes.response: Search engines don’t search the web in real time. They use crawlers to index content in advance. When you search, they quickly scan this index to return the most relevant results.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Web technologies

nodes.misconception: Data is processed, organised and structured information that provides context and meaning.
nodes.response: Information is processed, organised and structured data that provides context and meaning. Data is facts and figures in their raw form.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing information

nodes.misconception: Once encrypted, a message cannot be decrypted.
nodes.response: A message can be encrypted and decrypted multiple times, this happens frequently during digital communications.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Turing's mug cryptography challenge

nodes.misconception: Computers process all types of information (text, images, video, etc.).
nodes.response: Ultimately, computers use sequences of symbols (0s and 1s) to represent all types of information.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Binary digits

nodes.misconception: Binary uses the same place value system as decimal.
nodes.response: Binary is a base-2 number system, whereas decimal is a base-10 number system.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers in binary

nodes.misconception: The representation length does not include any spaces.
nodes.response: The representation length is the total number of symbols in the sequence including spaces.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing characters

nodes.misconception: Mega is larger than giga.
nodes.response: The order of prefixes from smallest to largest is kilo, mega, giga, tera.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Measurements of data

nodes.misconception: Project management will not alter the outcome of a project or make it a success.
nodes.response: Project management will not guarantee success of a project, but effective project management will increase the likelihood of a project being successful.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to project management

nodes.misconception: Interaction can only occur between consecutive stages of the project lifecycle.
nodes.response: Interaction can happen across multiple stages of the project lifecycle.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Setting project aims and objectives

nodes.misconception: A feasibility report outlines the key requirements of a system.
nodes.response: A feasibility report is a document used in project management that assesses whether a project can be completed successfully.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting project briefs

nodes.misconception: Gantt charts are better than PERT charts.
nodes.response: Gantt charts may be deemed better than PERT charts in some instances, but not all. The choice of chart can depend on the project and what the team prefers to use.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Tools for project planning

nodes.misconception: The last stage of the project evaluation is the conclusion.
nodes.response: The last stage of the project evaluation is "recommendations".  It is important to reflect on and learn from your experiences and say what could be improved and how.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating the success of a project

nodes.misconception: It is better to check that hyperlinks work each time you add a link instead of checking them at the end.
nodes.response: You should check the hyperlinks as you go to fix errors immediately but also check the whole product is working once you have finished. This will ensure that the product meets the brief and works in its entirety.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Carrying out a project part II

nodes.misconception: You cannot prevent things from going wrong in a project.
nodes.response: Things can be done to prevent negative things happening during a project - these are called mitigations.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Start your own project

nodes.misconception: You should use all planning tools (Gantt, PERT and feasibility reports).
nodes.response: You don't need to use all planning tools; select the tools most suitable for a project.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Execute your own project

nodes.misconception: Testing should only be done at the end of a project.
nodes.response: It is good practice to test products during and at the end of a project.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate your project

nodes.misconception: Formulas can only be used on cells within one worksheet in a spreadsheet.
nodes.response: Formulas can work across multiple worksheets in a spreadsheet.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Carrying out a project part I

nodes.misconception: Because data is stored in the cloud, it doesn’t have a physical or environmental impact.
nodes.response: The term "cloud" sounds invisible, so many people assume their photos, videos and files are floating around in some harmless digital space. But in reality the cloud is made up of millions of physical data centres which are based across the world.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The environmental impact of data systems

nodes.misconception: Once data is stored in a database, it’s automatically safe and private.
nodes.response: Just storing data in a database does not make it secure. Data must be protected with proper privacy measures.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data and privacy

nodes.misconception: Big data can be stored in normal data strcutures like relational databases.
nodes.response: Big data is mostly unstructured, so it doesn't fit the row-and-column format of relational databases.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Big data

nodes.misconception: A DBMS is only used for storing data.
nodes.response: While storage is a major function, a DBMS also provides data security, integrity and querying capabilities.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Database design

nodes.misconception: You can delete data from a database using an SQL command without any consideration.
nodes.response: You should delete data using SQL commands carefully as data may be linked to other tables in the database.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: SQL fundamentals

nodes.misconception: SQL statements can only be used with exisiting tables.
nodes.response: SQL statements can be used to perform other actions on a databse such as creating new tables.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data management with SQL statements

nodes.misconception: Proprietary software always costs money.
nodes.response: Proprietary software is usually sold to end users, although sometimes it is available for free.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data protection, copyright and the law

nodes.misconception: A primary key and a foreign key are the same thing.
nodes.response: A primary key is an attribute that uniquely identifies a record in a database table, whereas a foreign key is an attribute in one table that is the primary key in another table and is used to link the tables together.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Database fundamentals

nodes.misconception: Using SELECT * is always the best method for returning data from a database table.
nodes.response: You should only use the SELECT * query when all fields are needed. Including unnecessary data can be frustrating for the person viewing and working with the results.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: SQL searches

nodes.misconception: Building a physical computing project is just about putting the parts together. The code is not that important.
nodes.response: The code tells the hardware what to do and how to interact with the world, without the code it wouldn't move or do anything interesting!
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a physical computing project

nodes.misconception: Sending and receiving radio signals broadcasts to all devices that have radio capability.
nodes.response: A radio channel can be set which means that only devices on that same channel will receive those broadcasts.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Connecting micro:bits to other hardware

nodes.misconception: There is no point in doing an evaluation once a project is finished as you are not going to go back and make any more changes.
nodes.response: Evaluations help learning by understanding your creative process and finding ways to improve. This often informs projects that you do in the future.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflecting on a physical computing project

nodes.misconception: Computers always have screens so that the user knows what processing has been performed.
nodes.response: Computers can carry actions using a variety of output devices. Physical computers are often used to carry out physical actions based on detected inputs so do not need a screen to display information.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating programs on a physical computing device

nodes.misconception: Planning a physical computing project slows you down and does not need to be thought of before starting what you want to make.
nodes.response: A plan helps you think through the steps, figure out what you need, and make sure your project turns out how you want it to. If you don't plan, you could end up making mistakes that will mean your project doesn't turn out how you would like.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing a physical computing project

nodes.misconception: The micro:bit can only show letters and numbers.
nodes.response: The micro:bit's LED display can show more than letters and numbers. It can show shapes, images, and patterns. The display matrix can be programmed to output any desired pattern.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using input and output

nodes.misconception: Variables always store numbers.
nodes.response: Variables can store different types of data, including text (strings), numbers or Boolean values.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: User inputs and variables

nodes.misconception: All screens run at the same time.
nodes.response: Only one screen is active at a time; users navigate between them when needed.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiple screens and navigation

nodes.misconception: Events happen automatically.
nodes.response: Events only trigger code if an event listener is attached. Without one, the app will not respond.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Events and interactions

nodes.misconception: You should start creating an app without planning.
nodes.response: Planning first helps avoid confusion and mistakes and helps you build apps more efficiently.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: App development project part 1

nodes.misconception: The user interface is only about how the app looks.
nodes.response: The user interface includes both how the app looks and how users interact with it. A good user interface is both visually clear and functionally simple.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to app design

nodes.misconception: Once the app runs it is finished.
nodes.response: Testing, debugging, and improving based on feedback are essential steps before finishing work on an app.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: App development project part 2

nodes.misconception: Social engineering involves technical skills and knowledge of computing concepts in order to carry out an attack.
nodes.response: Social engineering relies on manipulating a victim to steal their personal data. This is done by finding ways to trick the user in to handing over the data willingly.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Social engineering

nodes.misconception: You can only get malware on a computer if you download a file.
nodes.response: Malware can infect a computer in other ways, like visiting unsafe websites, clicking bad links, or through software flaws, not just by downloading files.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Malicious software

nodes.misconception: Hacking a computer system of someone you know as a joke is considered legal.
nodes.response: Even if there is no intention to commit a crime by accessing the computer system of someone you know, the fact that the access is unauthorised is considered a crime.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Hacking and brute force attacks

nodes.misconception: Using security measures will stop every cyber attack.
nodes.response: Security measures reduce the risk of cyber attacks but cannot stop all of them. New threats and advanced techniques can sometimes bypass even the best defenses.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting networks from security threats

nodes.misconception: As long as you use all security measures, a computer system connected to a network can be totally safe from cyber attack.
nodes.response: No computer system on a network can be completely safe, even with all security measures. Cybercriminals can find new ways to attack, so security only reduces the risk and doesn't completely eliminate it.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Preventing cyber attacks

nodes.misconception: Laws are put in place by Parliament to stop crimes from happening.
nodes.response: Laws don't completely stop crime, but act as a deterrent by outlining the consequences of committing crimes.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting personal data

nodes.misconception: I don’t need to follow the project brief to draw a flowchart.
nodes.response: The project brief gives you the purpose and requirements of the program. A flowchart must reflect those to show how the program will work step by step.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: iteration I

nodes.misconception: The condition in a while loop is only checked once. The loop will always run a fixed number of times.
nodes.response: Remind students that the condition is checked before each iteration. The loop repeats only while the condition is True. Variable changes inside the loop affect whether it continues or stops.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using trace tables

nodes.misconception: You have to write the full code for random number generation yourself.
nodes.response: Python's standard library includes the random module, which already has functions like randint() to generate random numbers. You just need to import it.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Randomisation

nodes.misconception: I finished the code and it runs, so I don’t need to test it.
nodes.response: Just because a program runs doesn’t mean it works correctly in all situations. Testing helps find hidden errors, especially with unusual or unexpected inputs that you might not think of.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: iteration II

nodes.misconception: A program will automatically ask people to try again if data is invalid.
nodes.response: The program will only ask for data to be input again if it has been programmed to do so; otherwise it will run with invalid data and may crash.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Validating data input in a program

nodes.misconception: Learners may think that the inner loop only runs once per program, rather than repeating fully each time the outer loop runs.
nodes.response: The inner loop runs completely every time the outer loop runs once. This means the code inside the inner loop is repeated multiple times depending on how many times the outer loop is executed.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Nested loops

nodes.misconception: Exception handling fixes the error in the code or stops it from happening.
nodes.response: Exception handling does not prevent errors but allows the program to detect them and continue running by managing the error appropriately.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing robust programs

nodes.misconception: Learners may think a for loop will always repeat forever unless they manually stop it.
nodes.response: A for loop repeats a set number of times, based on the range or count value given. The loop ends automatically when the final value in the range has been reached.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: For loops

nodes.misconception: A loop will always run at least once.
nodes.response: A loop only runs if the condition allows it. If the condition isn’t met initially, the code inside won’t run at all.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: While loops

nodes.misconception: A while loop is the most appropriate loop to use when you know exactly how many iterations will need to be performed.
nodes.response: While loops should be used when the number of iterations can change. Even though while loops can be used in this way, for loops are a more appropriate choice as they will track the number of iterations as part of their operation.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Iteration using while loops

nodes.misconception: Learners often get confused between the logic operators AND and OR.
nodes.response: For an AND statement to return True both inputs must be True. For an OR statement to return True either input can be True.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a program using control structures

nodes.misconception: The = symbol is used to check if a variable is equal to a value (comparison).
nodes.response: The = symbol is used in Python for assignment. The == operator is used for comparison.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Using selection

nodes.misconception: An if statement can only have two options.
nodes.response: An if statement can be paired with elif and else statements to create multi-path selection. This allows for multiple paths to follow in a program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Selection with multiple paths

nodes.misconception: Pupils often take user input for numerical values and then cannot perform arithmetic calculations on the data as the value is automatically stored as a string.
nodes.response: The int() function is used to convert a user's input to an integer so that calculations can then be performed. For example, age = int(input()) would allow a user to input their age in to a program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Working with numerical inputs

nodes.misconception: Pupils will modify their code to provide input directly in to the input() function, for example, user = input("Aisha"), rather than typing when asked as the program runs.
nodes.response: The computer follows the instructions of a program. Input that a user has to type in should only be entered when the program runs. This allows different users to provide different inputs without changing the program in any way.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a text-based program

nodes.misconception: Ciphers and encryption are the same thing.
nodes.response: Ciphers are one type of encryption method. Encryption includes ciphers but also involves algorithms, keys, and protocols used in modern digital security systems.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Common ciphers

nodes.misconception: Penetration testing is illegal or the same as hacking.
nodes.response: Penetration testing is legal and ethical when done with permission. It's a form of ethical hacking used to help organisations find and fix security weaknesses before real hackers exploit them.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing as a form of defence

nodes.misconception: Cybersecurity jobs are only for highly technical people who know how to code or hack.
nodes.response: Cybersecurity careers are diverse, and many roles value communication, analytical thinking, problem solving and ethical judgment just as much as technical skills.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Careers in cyber security

nodes.misconception: Installing antivirus software is enough to fully protect my device from malware.
nodes.response: Antivirus software is helpful, but it’s only one part of a broader defence strategy. Full protection also requires regular software updates, strong passwords, safe browsing habits and user awareness to avoid phishing and suspicious downloads.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Defence against malware

nodes.misconception: Malware only affects computers, not phones or tablets.
nodes.response: Malware can infect any idevice that is connected to the internet, including smartphones, tablets and smart TVs. Mobile malware is increasingly common and can steal data, track location or lock users out of their devices — just like on computers.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Malware: malicious software

nodes.misconception: Encryption makes data completely safe and unbreakable.
nodes.response: Encryption greatly improves security, but it is not foolproof. If encryption keys are weak, stolen or mismanaged, encrypted data can still be accessed by attackers.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Encryption tools to protect communication

nodes.misconception: Social engineering only involves technical hacking or complex cyberattacks.
