nodes.response: Social engineering mainly targets human psychology, not technical vulnerabilities. It's more about exploiting trust and human error than technical skills.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Social engineering techniques

nodes.misconception: Fake news is easy to spot because it’s obviously false or silly.
nodes.response: Fake news is often designed to look real and believable. It can mimic trusted sources, use partial truths, or appeal to emotions to trick people. It’s important to check information sources and think critically, even if a post seems convincing.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of fake news

nodes.misconception: All hackers are criminals trying to steal or destroy data.
nodes.response: Not all hackers are malicious. There are different types of hackers such as white hat ethical hackers, grey hat hackers who may break rules but not for personal gain and black hat hackers who are malicious hackers who exploit systems illegally.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The cost of cyber crime and hacker motivation

nodes.misconception: All artificial intelligence systems use machine learning.
nodes.response: No, some AI systems, such as rule-based expert systems or symbolic AI, use predefined logic and heuristics rather than learning from data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: AI and machine learning applications

nodes.misconception: More data is always better as it means the model can be better informed to make a prediction.
nodes.response: Poorly labelled or inconsistent data can make a model's predictions inaccurate. It is better to use a smaller amount of higher quality data to make more accurate predictions.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving a model

nodes.misconception: Building a machine learning app just means coding as you would do with any other programming project.
nodes.response: Building a machine learning app involves data collection, model training and coding the application. These facets are integral in developing a machine learning app.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a data-driven application

nodes.misconception: Users of a machine learning application do not need to be aware of how accurate it is.
nodes.response: Model cards are good practice when developing machine learning applications. A model card is a short report on how a machine learning model works, how well the model performs and what people should know before using the model.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Documenting and evaluating a machine learning model

nodes.misconception: The micro:bit understands movement like a human does.
nodes.response: The micro:bit records numbers (x, y, z acceleration) that are then interpretted using programmed instructions.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Gathering data for a model

nodes.misconception: More training makes a perfect model.
nodes.response: Not neccessarily - models can become too specialised and fail on new data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Training and testing a model

nodes.misconception: Pupils often find it difficult to know what order logic gates should be evaluated. Without brackets, there is still an order of precedence.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of how the order of precedence in maths is applied to calculations. In a similarway, logic gates should be evaluated in the order: brackets, NOT, AND, OR.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating logic circuits

nodes.misconception: A truth table can only have the column headings of single inputs like A, B, or X.
nodes.response: A truth table can have column headings that calculate the value of the expression, for example (A OR B).
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Truth tables

nodes.misconception: Each input can only be wired to one logic gate.
nodes.response: Logic gates can be combined to create complex circuits that represent any number of logic statements combined. This can involve the same input being connected to multiple logic gates.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Logic gate simulator software

nodes.misconception: All logic gates have two inputs and one output.
nodes.response: The number of inputs depends on the logic gate. The NOT gate is different in that it only has one input.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Boolean logic and logic gates

nodes.misconception: As logic gates are limited to two input, logic statements should also be limited in the same way.
nodes.response: Logic gates can be combined to created complex circuits that represent any number of logic statements combined.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to logic circuit design

nodes.misconception: Boolean logic is only used in logic circuits and logic gates.
nodes.response: The three fundamental Boolean operators are AND, OR and NOT. These are used in programs to perform selection and control program flow. In Python, these are written in words as: and, or, not.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Implementing Boolean logic in Python

nodes.misconception: Boolean logic statements should be processed in the order they are read (from left to right).
nodes.response: Boolean operators have an order of precedence that affects the which operator applies to which variable. If a different order is required, brackets should be used.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Logic statements and expressions

nodes.misconception: As logic gates are limited to two input, logic statements should also be limited in the same way.
nodes.response: Logic gates can be combined to created complex circuits that represent any number of logic statements combined.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to logic circuits

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that each time data is changed in a spreadsheet the formulas will also need to be changed.
nodes.response: Using cell references within a formula means that the formula will recalculate when the values in those reference cells change.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Spreadsheet calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that conditional formatting can only be used to add background colour to a cell.
nodes.response: Conditional formatting can be used to apply a range of formatting a cell including the text of the cell itself.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying conditional formatting to data

nodes.misconception: The order of column and row in a cell reference are unimportant as columns are labelled with letters and rows are labelled as numbers.
nodes.response: Spreadsheet cell references are presented as the combination of the column letter followed by the row number, (eg. A1, B2). If the order is interchanged any other part of the spreadsheet that references them will not be able to locate them.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Formatting data in a spreadsheet

nodes.misconception: When a filter is applied to a data set the data that is filtered is removed permanently.
nodes.response: A filter can be applied to data to remove selected data from a data set. However, this data is not permanently removed, if the filter is taken off the data will still be there.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Sorting and searching data

nodes.misconception: All range references in a spreadsheet needs to be the same as cell references in the format of column letter followed by row number (e.g. A1:A4).
nodes.response: If you want to reference the whole column you can remove the row numbers (e.g. A:A). Note that this is the only case where cell references do not have to follow the column:row convention.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing and visualising data

nodes.misconception: Data and information are the same thing.
nodes.response: Data and information are realted but are different. Data is raw facts and figures whilst information is data that has been processed to have meaning.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Collecting data for a purpose

nodes.misconception: A program must run line by line from top to bottom.
nodes.response: A subprogram is an 'out of line' block of code, which is typcially written at the top of a program and then called upon within the main program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Structured programs

nodes.misconception: A system should only be tested with normal data that will be expected. If it works with normal data it will work all the time.
nodes.response: A system should be tested with a range of test data, including erroneous data that is not meant to be accepted. Programs should make sure that there is no way to stop the software from working if invalid inputs are entered.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: subroutines II

nodes.misconception: When a function returns a value it can be used throughout the program that called it.
nodes.response: The return value needs to be stored if it is to be used later in the program that calls it. If it isn't stored, the value cannot be used again.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Functions

nodes.misconception: Functions and procedures are just different names for the same thing.
nodes.response: A function is a type of subroutine that returns a value whereas a procedure is a type of subroutine that does not return a value.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Procedures

nodes.misconception: When a function returns a value it can be used throughout the program that called it.
nodes.response: The return value needs to be stored if it is to be used later in the program that calls it.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Functions in programs

nodes.misconception: Assigning a variable inside a function automatically makes it global.
nodes.response: A variable is local, unless it is specifically set as a global variable.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Global and local variables in programs

nodes.misconception: A system should only be tested with normal data that will be expected.
nodes.response: A system should be tested with a range of test data, including erroneous data that is not meant to be accepted.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: subprograms II

nodes.misconception: Assigning a variable inside a function automatically makes it global.
nodes.response: A variable is local, unless it is specifically set as a global variable.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Global and local variables

nodes.misconception: A project brief is a set way to solve a problem.
nodes.response: A project brief outlines the requirements of a system, but there may be many ways to solve the problem.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: subprograms I

nodes.misconception: Functions and procedures are just different names for the same thing.
nodes.response: A function is a type of subprogram that returns a value whereas a procedure is a type of subprogram that does not return a value.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Procedures in programs

nodes.misconception: A program must run line by line from top to bottom.
nodes.response: A subrotuine is an 'out of line' block of code, which is typcially written at the top of a program and then called upon within the main program.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Structured programming

nodes.misconception: A project brief is a set way to solve a problem.
nodes.response: A project brief outlines the requirements of a system, but there may be many ways to solve the problem. The brief explains what needs to be solved, not how.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project: subroutines I

nodes.misconception: Python has a built-in XOR operator in the same way that it has AND, OR and NOT.
nodes.response: Unlike AND, OR and NOT, Python does not have a built-in operator for XOR and instead must be designed as part of and program that uses it.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating an XOR function

nodes.misconception: Divisions can only be arranged as regular rows and columns.
nodes.response: By using divisions within other divisions any layout of a page is possible.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: CSS for layout

nodes.misconception: Web page divisions all need to have unique labels. They can't be the same.
nodes.response: When designing divisions of a web page the same formatting may need to be applied to multiple divisions. In this case the labels would  need to be the same.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Web page layouts using CSS divisions

nodes.misconception: I don’t need a wireframe or site map, I can just start coding.
nodes.response: Planning is a key step in web development. A wireframe helps you decide where things go before writing any code, and a site map ensures you know how pages connect. Skipping planning often leads to messy code and confusing navigation.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Web based project I

nodes.misconception: Users don't ever see the underlying file structure of a website, so it's organisation is unimportant.
nodes.response: Organisation of resources can make the creation and maintainence of websites an easier task. The quicker a developer of website can find the component parts, the less time will be wasted when changes need to be made.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a mini website

nodes.misconception: JavaScript changes the original HTML file.
nodes.response: JavaScript only changes what the user sees in the browser. It does not change the actual HTML file saved on your computer or server.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: JavaScript

nodes.misconception: JavaScript only works after everything is perfect, I’ll fix it all at the end.
nodes.response: JavaScript is best written and tested in small steps. Writing a little, testing it, and debugging as you go helps avoid big problems later.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Web based project II

nodes.misconception: If someone cannot view an image on a web page it can be ignored as text on the page will be sufficient.
nodes.response: Images are used in web pages to provide the reader with extra context. By not describing them in some way the reader might not understand the information in the same way than if it was viewed.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Images and links

nodes.misconception: HTML is a programming language.
nodes.response: HTML is a markup language. It defines the structure and appearance of content on a web page, but does not not do any processing of data into information.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: HTML fundamentals

nodes.misconception: It is easier to apply CSS directly to the HTML tags as they are used.
nodes.response: There is little time saved by applying CSS directly to tags and it generates more work later if the same changes need to be made in different parts of a web page.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: CSS fundamentals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the place value for binary is the same as decimal in the fact each place value to the left is 10 times greater.
nodes.response: Binary place values double. So the first bit has the place value of 1 and the second has the place value of 2 and so on.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Number bases

nodes.misconception: Computers use binary for data and instructions but they can use other number systems just as easily.
nodes.response: Computers have to use binary as they are powered by electrical circuits which contain transistors which can be switched on and off using electricity. Using other number systems would require more complex circuitry.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Why do computers use binary?

nodes.misconception: Hexadecimal numbers are used to take up less memory on the computer.
nodes.response: Computers still only process and store binary data. Hexadecimal is used by humans to help them process long binary sequences more easily but the underlying number of bits is still the same.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Hexadecimal

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often default to decimal addition, in the fact that 1+1 = 2, whereas in binary 1+1 = 10.
nodes.response: Remind students that binary only has two digits; 0 and 1. Use the comparisons between binary and decimal addition in the slide deck to illustrate the differences.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Binary addition

nodes.misconception: When performing binary multiplication any result can be stored, regardless of how many binary digits are needed.
nodes.response: The size of a binary number that can be stored is allocated in memory. Sometimes the result of a binary shift may result in a larger binary number that can be stored in the number of bits available.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Binary shifts

nodes.misconception: You have to convert an 8 bit binary number in one go.
nodes.response: As a hexadecimal digit can be represented by 4 binary digits, it is useful to convert binary numbers in nibbles (4-bits at a time). This way each digit can be converted separately and then recombined for the final value.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Hexadecimal number conversions

nodes.misconception: The random module will only generate random numbers.
nodes.response: The random module can generate random characters as well as numbers.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: String manipulation

nodes.misconception: You must have the physical Sense HAT device to practice coding with the Sense HAT.
nodes.response: You do not have to have the physical Sense HAT to try this out. The Sense HAT emulator provides a digital representation of the device.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project - Sense HAT I

nodes.misconception: You cannot print a game board or table layout neatly in Python.
nodes.response: You can added spaces and | to format a game board or table in Python.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: 2D lists challenge

nodes.misconception: A function can only ever return one value.
nodes.response: A list can be used to return multiple values from a function.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: List methods

nodes.misconception: Arrays and lists behave in the same way.
nodes.response: An array has a predefined fixed size. A list can vary in size throughout program execution.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Arrays and lists

nodes.misconception: Arrays and lists behave in the same way.
nodes.response: An array has a predefined fixed size. A list can vary in size throughout program execution.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: 2D arrays and lists

nodes.misconception: Operations in programs can only be performed on numbers.
nodes.response: Operations can be performed on different types of data. What the operator does can change depending on the data type it is being used with.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: String handling

nodes.misconception: Indexing starts at 1 as that is the location of the first element.
nodes.response: In Python, and many other programming languages, indexing starts at 0.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Substrings

nodes.misconception: A list is static, so once it is created it cannot be edited or amended.
nodes.response: A list is a dynamic data structure that can change in size. The append() function can be used to add elements to a list.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Programming project - Sense HAT II

nodes.misconception: ASCII and Unicode are only used to represent the characters and symbols found in written communication across all languages in the world.
nodes.response: ASCII and Unicode include more than just characters from written languages. ASCII represents English letters, numbers and symbols. Unicode supports other symbols beyond written text, including mathematical symbols, emojis and non-text elements.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing text using ASCII and Unicode

nodes.misconception: Bitmap images that are large on screen are always poor quality.
nodes.response: The quality of a bitmap image depends on its resolution, not just its size on the screen. A high-resolution bitmap can appear sharp and detailed, while a low-resolution bitmap may look pixelated when enlarged.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing bitmap images

nodes.misconception: ASCII and Unicode are only used to represent the characters and symbols found in written communication across all languages in the world.
nodes.response: ASCII and Unicode include more than just characters from written languages. ASCII represents basic English letters, numbers, and symbols. Unicode supports a vast range of symbols beyond written text, including mathematical symbols and emojis.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing text using Unicode and ASCII

nodes.misconception: Binary is only used to represent numerical data.
nodes.response: Binary digits can be used to form sequences that can be used to represent any data. As long as it is identified what each sequence represents, binary digits can become any form of data or instructions.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representation using binary sequences

nodes.misconception: The sample rate and resolution of samples adjusts based on the sound that is being digitsed.
nodes.response: The digitsation of sound needs to be consistent so that the binary sequence represented can be processed as expected.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing sound

nodes.misconception: The sample rate and bit depth of samples adjusts based on the sound that is being digitsed.
nodes.response: The digitsation of sound needs to be consistent so that the binary sequence represented can be processed as expected.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Representation of sound

nodes.misconception: The same text entered into two separate text files will always result in the same file size.
nodes.response: How the text has been encoded will affect the file size of a text file. ASCII uses 8 bits per character whereas Unicode uses up to 32 bits. Therefore the choice of character encoding affects the overall file size of the same text.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Text file size calculation

nodes.misconception: Any sound that is digitised is going to be noticeably different to the original sound.
nodes.response: When sound is turned into digital form with a high enough sampling rate and sample bit depth, the difference from the original sound is too small for human ears to notice.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculation of sound file sizes

nodes.misconception: The same text entered into two separate text files will always result in the same file size.
nodes.response: How the text has been encoded will affect the file size of a text file. ASCII uses 7 bits per character whereas Unicode uses up to 32 bits. Therefore the choice of character encoding affects the overall file size of the same text.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Text file size calculations

nodes.misconception: Any sound that is digitised is going to be noticeably different to the original sound.
nodes.response: When sound is turned into digital form with a high enough sampling rate and sample resolution, the difference from the original sound is too small for human ears to notice.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculation of sound file size

nodes.misconception: Using a low resoultion or colour depth for an image makes it unusable.
nodes.response: A low resolution or colour depth does not necessarily make an image unusable. It depends on the purpose. Lower settings can be suitable for web use, icons or thumbnails, while higher quality is needed for printing or detailed graphics.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Bitmap file size calculation

nodes.misconception: Metadata is only used when a user needs to know when a file was made or changed.
nodes.response: Metadata can be used in a variety of ways. For example, software can be designed to make use of metadata for effective cataloguing and providing extra information about the properites of a file being used.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Metadata

nodes.misconception: The bubble sort algorithm stops on the last swap.
nodes.response: The pass through the list is repeated until no more changes are made on a pass. The last pass is needed to confirm the data is in order.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Bubble sort

nodes.misconception: A binary search can be performed on any data.
nodes.response: A binary search can only be performed on an ordered list as it finds the expected position of the search term based on a selected mid-point in the data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Binary search

nodes.misconception: An insertion sort is slower than other sorting algorithms.
nodes.response: While other algorithms offer better time complexity for large, unsorted arrays, insertion sort can still be faster in practice for smaller and partially sorted lists.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Insertion sort

nodes.misconception: A linear search can only be used on lists or sequences of numbers.
nodes.response: A linear search can be used on lots of different types of data, including strings.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Linear search

nodes.misconception: Merge sort is the most efficient sorting algorithm for all cases.
nodes.response: For smaller data sets, simpler algorithms such as insertion sort or bubble sort can be faster due to the overhead in merge sort of having to break apart the data to be sorted.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Merge sort

nodes.misconception: A linear search algorithm and binary search algorithm are equally complex to write.
nodes.response: Binary search algorithms are more complex to write due to the different paths that the algorithm can take rather than stepping through the search data in order.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing searching algorithms

nodes.misconception: Bubble sort is a fast and efficient sorting algorithm.
nodes.response: Bubble sort is considered inefficient for large data sets, but it can be made more efficient by using a flag to indicate when a swap is made in a single pass.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Code sorting algorithms

nodes.misconception: If your data is not sorted then you cannot use a binary search.
nodes.response: Data does need to be sorted to use a binary search, though use of a sorting algorithm first would allow binary search to be used. However, consideration must be given as to the benefit of this approach for searching.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Practice searching and sorting algorithms

nodes.misconception: Bubble sort is a fast and efficient sorting algorithm.
nodes.response: Bubble sort is considered inefficient for large data sets, but it can be made more efficient by using a flag to indicate when a swap is made in a single pass.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Coding sorting algorithms

nodes.misconception: Compression is only useful for pictures or photos.
nodes.response: Compression applies to many types of files such as MP3 for audio, MP4 for video, ZIP for grouped files.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: The need for compression

nodes.misconception: Lossy compression always results in a poor quality file that is not as usable as the original version.
nodes.response: Lossy compression removes data that is considered unnecessary or less noticeable, which may not impact the perceived quality of the file, especially to the human eye or ear.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Lossy and lossless compression

nodes.misconception: A higher compression ratio always means better quality.
nodes.response: A higher compression ratio actually means the file size has been reduced more. This often results in lower quality, especially with lossy compression.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Compression ratios

nodes.misconception: Compression is only useful for saving storage space.
nodes.response: While saving storage is one benefit, compression is also critical for faster transmission of files over the internet, reducing bandwidth usage on networks, and enabling smooth real-time communication.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Practical applications of compression

nodes.misconception: The best compression method is the one that makes files the smallest.
nodes.response: Smaller isn’t always better, sometimes important details are lost. The best method depends on the file type, quality needs, and purpose.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing compression algorithms

nodes.misconception: Bits and bytes are the same thing. They all refer to binary numbers.
nodes.response: A bit is the smallest unit of data. A byte is a group of 8 bits and is used to summarise larger sequences of bits in a more convenient way.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Measurements of storage

nodes.misconception: The Huffman tree is the compressed file.
nodes.response: The compressed file is a sequence of bits, and the tree is the representation of the coding system.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Huffman coding

nodes.misconception: Run length encoding always reduces file size.
nodes.response: Run length encoding only works well when data has long repeated patterns. If data is random or has frequent changes, RLE may not reduce the file size and can even make it bigger. For example, compressing "HELLO" with RLE results in "1H1E2L1O".
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Run length encoding

nodes.misconception: Neural networks offer transparency in terms of the decisions made by the algorithm.
nodes.response: It’s often hard to understand why a neural network made a particular decision which makes transparency difficult.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Machine learning engines

nodes.misconception: A classifier can be improved by providing more training data.
nodes.response: More data doesn't always mean improved predictions. The quality of data provided to a classifier is as important as the quantity.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification

nodes.misconception: In supervised learning, the model stores or "memorises" the training data to label new, unprocessed data.
nodes.response: A supervised learning model does not simply store or "memorise" training data. It detects patterns and relationships in the training data and stores these. If it only stored the training data, it could not accurately label new, unprocessed data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Approaches to training machine learning models

nodes.misconception: AI systems improve access to digital technologies.
nodes.response: Inequality of access to AI tools and systems is an ethical concern. Not everyone has equal access to AI tools which can actually increase the digital divide.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Social and ethical issues of AI systems

nodes.misconception: AI applications can think.
nodes.response: AI systems follow programmed rules or improve performance based on data, but they do not think or have emotions like humans.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to AI

nodes.misconception: A model can be improved by providing more training data.
nodes.response: Although a large data set is important, more data doesn't necessarily improve output. It is important that training data is high-quality, accurate and diverse.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Data driven models

nodes.misconception: Machine learning is the same as artificial intelligence.
nodes.response: Machine learning is one of the techniques that people can use to build artificial intelligence system models. It is a subset of artificial intelligence.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Machine learning

nodes.misconception: Only generative AI systems require training data to complete tasks.
nodes.response: All AI systems rely on training data to perform tasks by using patterns identified in the data.
nodes.subject: computing
nodes.lessonTitle: Predictive vs generative AI

nodes.misconception: All fruit and vegetables should be peeled before use.
nodes.response: Not all fruit and vegetables need to be peeled, such as apples and potatoes. The peel, or skin, can be tasty and be good for us. However, they should be washed to remove any dirt, insects and bacteria.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a poke bowl

nodes.misconception: For extra flavour in a recipe, only salt and pepper can be used.
nodes.response: There are lots of ingredients that could be used, such as spices, herbs, and other aromatic ingredients e.g. lemon grass, harissa.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Mexican pockets

nodes.misconception: No matter the size of the scones, they are baked for the same length of time.
nodes.response: The heat from the oven will take longer to penetrate and cook the scones the bigger they are. Therefore smaller scones will cook more quickly than bigger scones.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making fruit scone wedges

nodes.misconception: All sushi includes raw fish.
nodes.response: Although raw fish is a common ingredient, not all sushi includes fish. Other ingredients are used, such as vegetables, fruit, egg, and cooked fish and meat.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making simple sushi

nodes.misconception: Couscous is a grain.
nodes.response: Couscous is not a grain. However, couscous is made from semolina, which is coarsely ground durum wheat which is sprinkled with water and rolled to form small granules. It more closely resembles pasta.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a couscous salad

nodes.misconception: You do not need to get ready to cook every time you prepare and cook food.
nodes.response: We should always get ready to cook, so that we are hygienic (clean).
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making veggie dip and dippers

nodes.misconception: When cooking it is fine not to weigh and measure accurately, approximate measurements are fine.
nodes.response: It is important to weigh and measure ingredients accuarely, so that the recipe works well.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making veggie kebabs

nodes.misconception: Spring rolls are always fried.
nodes.response: Spring rolls can be oven baked or steamed. There are many different varieties.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making spring rolls

nodes.misconception: The dried fruit in rock cakes counts towards our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: The dried fruit does not count towards our 5 A DAY, as it is in small amounts. Rock cakes are sweet foods, containing sugar and fat. We need to eat less of these types of foods.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making rock cakes

nodes.misconception: The base of a pizza is always covered in a sauce made from tomatoes.
nodes.response: While a sauce made from tomatoes is traditional, the base can also be covered in pesto, a cheese sauce, or just garlic and oil.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a tear 'n' share pizza

nodes.misconception: Hands only need to be washed and dried before and after cooking.
nodes.response: Hands should also be washed and dried well after touching the bin, blowing your nose, and cleaning.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making patatas bravas

nodes.misconception: When baking, the baking trays (or foil trays) do not need to be greased or lined.
nodes.response: Baking trays (or foil trays) should be greased with a little oil, or lined with greaseproof paper, to create a barrier between the cake and the tray. The barrier helps to prevent the cake from sticking.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a UK seasonal fruit traybake

nodes.misconception: Hands can be washed in cold water with soap.
nodes.response: Hands must be washed in warm water with soap, then dried well.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Let's make a layered breakfast

nodes.misconception: Children have to use knives to cut food.
nodes.response: Kitchen scissors can be used to cut a variety of foods. Scissors are generally safer to use.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Let's make some veggie snacks

nodes.misconception: Hummus can only be made with chickpeas.
nodes.response: Hummus can be made with a variety of beans and legumes.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Let's make butter bean hummus on crackers

nodes.misconception: You can bake cookies of different sizes on the same tray, making a bigger one for yourself.
nodes.response: The cookies need to be the same size, for even cooking. If smaller, they will burn, if bigger, they will be undercooked.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making raisin and banana cookies

nodes.misconception: Sasusages contain meat, usually pork.
nodes.response: Many sausages contain meat, but there are many recipes that are vegetarian or vegan. Glamorgan sausages are vegetarian (as they contain cheese and egg).
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Glamorgan sausages

nodes.misconception: People with an allergy cannot eat bread.
nodes.response: Some people have an allergy to flour made from wheat, which many breads are made from. There are other flours that can be used, so they can eat bread.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Irish soda bread

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a sandwich always uses sliced white bread.
nodes.response: Sandwiches can use a range of breads from around the world and are eaten often in many countries.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a healthy wrap for lunch

nodes.misconception: The Eatwell Guide tells you exactly what foods to eat each day.
nodes.response: The Eatwell Guide shows that we should eat a wide variety of food from each food group.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing The Eatwell Guide

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that potatoes count as a vegetable.
nodes.response: In the Eatwell Guide, potatoes do not count as a vegetable. They are in the 'Potatoes, bread, pasta and rice' group.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy meal times

nodes.misconception: Curry powder is a spice from a plant.
nodes.response: Curry powder is a mixture of different spices blended together, not a single spice.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making curry in a hurry

nodes.misconception: Activity is about being sporty, being active.
nodes.response: Activity is all the things we do and movements we make, not only sports. It includes sports, but also reading, sleeping and watching TV.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Why we need energy and nutrients

nodes.misconception: If I have the same foods every day from the Eatwell Guide I will get all the nutrients I need and be healthy.
nodes.response: To be healthy and get all the nutrients we need, we should eat a wide variety of food from each of the Eatwell Guide food groups.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Sources of energy and nutrients

nodes.misconception: Being active is only good for my physical health, such as healthy bones, muscles and heart.
nodes.response: While being active is good for your bones, muscles and heart, it can also make you feel fitter and happier, make new friends and try something new.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Health and wellbeing

nodes.misconception: When using the hob, boiling and simmering cooking methods are the same.
nodes.response: Boiling is at the boiling point, bubbling rapidly. Simmering is below the boiling point, bubbling gently.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making bean and plantain stew

nodes.misconception: Traffic lights can be used to compare different types of foods for the healthiest option.
nodes.response: Traffic lights are designed to help people compare similar foods for the healthiest option, so they are comparing foods ‘like for like’.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food labels for health

nodes.misconception: We need six - eight glasses of water a day.
nodes.response: We need six - eight drinks a day. Water is a great choice, but other drinks count too, such as milk and juice.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Eat, drink and grow

nodes.misconception: People like and dislike the same foods.
nodes.response: There are no right or wrong foods to like to like or dislike. We all have different tastes.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food likes and dislikes

nodes.misconception: Only fresh fruit can be used for fruit saald kebabs.
nodes.response: A range of fresh, canned and dried fruit can be used for fruit salad kebabs. Go for a colourful variety.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Let's make some fruit salad kebabs

nodes.misconception: All fish is the same.
nodes.response: There are lots of different types of fish in the world. They look, smell and taste different. Tuna is one type of fish.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making tuna canapés

nodes.misconception: When planning healthy meals, you do not have to include drinks.
nodes.response: Healthy meals should always include a drink. Water is a great choice.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy meals

nodes.misconception: Everyone in a religion celebrates a festival in the same way.
nodes.response: The way religious festivals are celebrated varies based on where people live, their culture and denominational differences. For example, Christmas is widely celebrated by non-Christians, focusing on family, giving and joy.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food for special occasions

nodes.misconception: A diet means to lose weight.
nodes.response: The word ‘diet’ describes all the food and drink we consume.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: My meals the Eatwell Guide way

nodes.misconception: A healthy meal needs to have all the food groups from the Eatwell Guide.
nodes.response: We do not need to eat all the food groups at each meal. We can get all the food groups through different meals in the day.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Eat well every day

nodes.misconception: You do not need to wash your hands after touching a raw egg.
nodes.response: You should always wash your hands after touching a raw egg. This helps to prevent the spread of bacteria. Some bacteria can cause food poisoning.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making mini frittatas

nodes.misconception: We can make a recipe by guessing and judging the measures.
nodes.response: We weigh and measure ingredients to make sure the recipe is a success, and so we can make it the same again in the future.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Let's make a potato salad

nodes.misconception: There is a misunderstanding about the origin of food, and lack of awareness of where food comes from.
nodes.response: All food we eat comes from plants and animals. Food from plants includes fruit and vegetables. Food from animals includes milk, eggs, fish and meat.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant or animal?

nodes.misconception: Honey is made from a plant.
nodes.response: Honey is made by bees in the hive. It is a food made by animals.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food sources

nodes.misconception: Food waste happens mostly outside the home.
nodes.response: Food waste happens mostly inside the home - around 60%.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing food waste

nodes.misconception: Seasons do not matter, as you can always buy lots of different fruit and vegetables in any season.
nodes.response: While you can buy different fruit and vegetables, they might have to be imported from other countries as they cannot grow in the UK in certain seasons. We should also try and eat more seasonal fruit and vegetables from the UK.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Seasonal fruit and vegetables

nodes.misconception: UK seasonal fruit and vegetables tend to be more expensive.
nodes.response: UK seasonal fruit and vegetables tend to be less expensive, as there are lots of them.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a seasonal salad

nodes.misconception: Food can only be produced on a farm or in a field.
nodes.response: Food can be produced (grown) at home, such as fruit, vegetables and herbs. Some food can be foraged.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Producing our food

nodes.misconception: Cheese is only made with milk from dairy cows.
nodes.response: Cheese is made with milk from many animals, including goats, sheep, buffalo, reindeer and alpaca, as well as dairy cows.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making bruschetta

nodes.misconception: Food processing does not happen at home to prepare and cook food, only at a factory.
nodes.response: Food processing steps are used in the home to prepare and cook food, such as peeling, slicing, grating, mixing and baking.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Processing our food

nodes.misconception: 'Farm to fork' only applies to food produced on a farm and eaten with a fork.
nodes.response: 'Farm to fork' is a term used to describe the direct connection between food production (not just on farms) and its consumption (being eaten, not just with a fork).
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food origins

nodes.misconception: When making pâté, they must always be cooked.
nodes.response: Not all pâtés must be cooked first, some are non-cook. This pâté uses canned mackerel (which is already cooked), soft cheese and vegetables. Vegan and vegetarian pâtés can also be made.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a mackerel and tomato pâté, with celery sticks

nodes.misconception: Our food comes from shops and supermarkets.
nodes.response: While food is purchased from shops and supermarkets, plants are grown, animals are reared and fish is caught for us to eat.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Grown, reared and caught

nodes.misconception: There is a limited range of foods produced and made in the UK. This is why food from other countries are popular.
nodes.response: There is a huge range of food produced and made in the UK, including many traditional dishes. Food from other countries is often eaten to add variety to the diet.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food from around the UK

nodes.misconception: The flapjack recipe contains apple and sultanas, so must be part of our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: No, the flapjack does not count towards our 5 A DAY. There is not enough fruit, and they are high in sugars and fat (from butter). If we eat these types of foods, we should have them occasionally and in small amounts.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making apple flapjack bites

nodes.misconception: Recipes from around the world can only be cooked using ingredients from those countries.
nodes.response: We can prepare and cook recipes from other countries using ingredients grown, reared or caught in the UK. Sometimes there are ingredients that are not grown or easily made in the UK, so foods from other countries are used.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food from around the world

nodes.misconception: 'Use by' and 'best before' date marks are the same. The food is still safe to eat after the date passes.
nodes.response: 'Use by' and 'best before' date marks are not the same. After the 'use by' date passes, the food is not safe to eat. After the ‘best before’ date passes, the food will probably be safe to eat, but may not look or taste as good.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food labels for safety

nodes.misconception: Any Cornish pasties made and sold in the UK can use the name ‘Cornish pasty’, as it is based on a recipe.
nodes.response: Only pasties made in Cornwall to a specific recipe can be called a ‘Cornish pasty’; it is legally protected in the UK by Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Cornish pasties

nodes.misconception: Mould on fruit, yogurt or bread can be cut off, so the remaining food can be eaten.
nodes.response: If food has mould, the food should not be eaten, especially with soft foods like bread, yogurt or fruit. It is unsafe to eat and can cause illness.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making food safe to eat

nodes.misconception: Bread is only made from wheat (flour).
nodes.response: Other plants can be used to make flour such as maize, rye and chickpeas.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: World wide bread

nodes.misconception: A recipe cannot be changed, as it will not work.
nodes.response: Recipes can be changed, for example swapping chicken for chickpeas, or adding extra spices. The new recipe should be tested to make sure it works and tastes good.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a coronation chickpea pocket

nodes.misconception: Bread is complicated to make, so we can only buy bread from a bakery or shop.
nodes.response: Basic bread is made from flour and water, mixed together (sometimes other ingredients are added to make it rise and add flavour). Bread can easily be made at home.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Bread for all

nodes.misconception: Unfamiliar dishes or meals cannot be made in the UK, as they use unusual foods.
nodes.response: Although some dishes and meals look unfamiliar, they are all from plants and animals and can be  made in the UK. They are based on fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice or pasta; dairy and alternatives; beans, eggs, fish or meat.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Familiar and unfamiliar foods to me

nodes.misconception: A salad must contain lettuce, cucumber and tomato.
nodes.response: Salads can contain a wide range of different ingredients. We can take inspiration from around the world and choose different ingredients.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making an international salad

nodes.misconception: The term 'cooking' only means to add heat to food, such as baking, boiling and grilling.
nodes.response: The term 'cooking' includes: (1) the preparation of food, e.g. peel, slice and and mix; (2) heating food, e.g. baking, boiling and grilling. It is a term used to describe the entire process.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Ingredients, equipment and food skills

nodes.misconception: People eat the same types of food.
nodes.response: People eat different foods for a number of reasons. This includes time of day, occasions, likes/dislikes, where we live, who we live with, and tradition.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Family food

nodes.misconception: Graters are not sharp.
nodes.response: Graters are sharp, so we need to be careful. Be aware of your fingers and knuckles. Rub the food slowly and gently down the grater. You do not need to grate every bit of food.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Let's make a stripy salad pot

nodes.misconception: Most people have enough fruit and vegetables in their diet.
nodes.response: Most people need to eat more fruit and vegetables. We need at least 5 A DAY.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: My favourite fruit and veg

nodes.misconception: People in different communities follow different healthy eating advice.
nodes.response: Most people in the UK should follow the Eatwell Guide, and 8 tips for healthy eating, with the food and meals adapted for the needs of different groups.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy communities

nodes.misconception: Rice can only be cooked in a saucepan on the hob.
nodes.response: Rice can be cooked in different ways, such as on the hob, in a rice cooker, in the oven, and in a microwave. The hot water and steam  help to ‘cook’ the rice.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Baked savoury rice

nodes.misconception: Families from different cultures and communities only eat specific types of food.
nodes.response: Families from different cultures and communities enjoy a range of other foods, not just what is traditionally served.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Feeding communities

nodes.misconception: Recipes cannot be modified.
nodes.response: Recipes can be modified, for different occasions and the needs of people. Ingredients can be changed and other ingredients added.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making breakfast muffins

nodes.misconception: Who we are with does not affect what we eat and drink.
nodes.response: Who we are with often does affect what we eat and drink. For example, we might eat what our parents cook, or pick foods the same as friends.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Eat in, eat out

nodes.misconception: All snacks are unhealthy.
nodes.response: Not all snacks are unhealthy. We can use the Eatwell Guide to help us choose healthier snacks. We can choose snacks from each of the four biggest food groups.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy snack swaps

nodes.misconception: The cuisine, ingredients and food customs in different countries have not changed over time.
nodes.response: History has changed the cuisine, ingredients and food customs. This has happened because of travel, trade and wars.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Customs and traditions

nodes.misconception: Sensory evaluation can only help us decide whether we like a food or not.
nodes.response: Sensory evaluation can help us decide whether we like foods, but also allows us to describe and compare foods.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Food for the senses

nodes.misconception: Bread dough does not need to be kneaded.
nodes.response: Bread dough should be kneaded for 10 minutes, as it helps it to become smooth and elastic. Kneading helps the dough to rise.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making paska

nodes.misconception: A roux sauce can have all the liquid (milk) added at the same time, and whisked occasionally.
nodes.response: A roux sauce must have the liquid (milk) added gradually, and the sauce should be whisked continually to prevent lumps.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making green mac & cheese

nodes.misconception: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten in wheat flour only.
nodes.response: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten (a protein), which is found in flours from wheat, barley and rye.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making herby focaccia

nodes.misconception: Beans can count as many portions towards 5 A DAY, depending on the number of portions eaten.
nodes.response: Beans count as a maximum of one portion of 5 A DAY, no matter how much is eaten.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making cheesy bean burritos

nodes.misconception: Vegetables and fruit do not need to be washed before use as they look clean or have been taken from a packet.
nodes.response: Vegetables and fruit should be washed thoroughly before use. This removes dirt (soil/grit), insects and bacteria which could cause food poisoning.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making leek and potato soup

nodes.misconception: Sushi, raw fish, is the only common food eaten in Japan.
nodes.response: Japan has huge range of foods and dishes, of which sushi is one important aspect. There is a range of cooked dishes, including yakisoba (noodles), teriyaki (grilled with a glaze), yakiniku (grilled meat), and tempura (battered fried foods).
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making yakisoba noodles

nodes.misconception: Food lessons are just cooking.
nodes.response: Food lessons include cooking, which is important, but also applying healthy eating, where food comes from, safety (preventing accidents) and hygiene (making sure food is safe to eat), science, and consumer and food culture. Food is who we are.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a mini deli salad

nodes.misconception: Food hygiene is only about being clean when preparing, cooking and storing food.
nodes.response: Food hygiene is necessary in order to prepare and cook food which is safe to eat. It involves the 4Cs: cleaning (including personal hygiene), cooking, chilling and preventing cross-contamination.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a sweet & sour fakeaway

nodes.misconception: Any flour can be used to make a bread-like dough.
nodes.response: Although most flours will produce a dough, a strong flour is recommended as it is high in protein (gluten), which is needed to help trap the air and form the bread structure when baked.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Chelsea buns

nodes.misconception: Recipes cannot be modified for different budgets, as the stated ingredients must always be used.
nodes.response: Recipes can be modified for different budgets, using a number of strategies, such as comparing costs, buying own-brand items, and using seasonal fruit and vegetables.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making sweet potato katsu curry

nodes.misconception: Traditional fried falafel is healthy, as it is made from chickpeas.
nodes.response: While the chickpeas are a healthy choice, falafel is usually deep-fried, so less healthy. Alternative cooking methods could be used which use less oil, such as grilling, baking, or air-frying.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making pea and mint falafel, with tzatziki

nodes.misconception: Dietary Reference Values (DRVs), nutritional requirements, are intended for individual healthy people.
nodes.response: Dietary Reference Values (DRVs), nutritional requirements, are intended for different groups of healthy people. They are a series of estimates of the energy and nutrients required.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Nutritional needs throughout life

nodes.misconception: There is one form of malnutrition, intakes of energy and/or nutrients being below what is required.
nodes.response: There are two forms of malnutrition: undernutrition (intakes below what is required) and overnutrition (intakes above what is required).
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Health conditions

nodes.misconception: Potatoes can form part of our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: Potatoes do not count towards our 5 A DAY. They are a starchy carbohydrate in the Eatwell Guide.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making aloo gobi

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that the name of a food group from the Eatwell Guide is also the name of a nutrient.
nodes.response: A food group from the Eatwell Guide includes foods that contain various nutrients.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Eat well now

nodes.misconception: Everyone needs the same amount, or portion, of food.
nodes.response: Everyone needs slightly different amounts of food, depending on their age and activity levels.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making better food and drink choices

nodes.misconception: We should eat less starchy foods, as these are 'fattening' in the diet and provide little else.
nodes.response: Starchy foods should make up just over a third of the diet, as they are an important source of energy, fibre and micronutrients.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Macronutrients, fibre and water

nodes.misconception: The Eatwell Guide recommends a plant-rich, non-meat diet.
nodes.response: The Eatwell Guide recommends that we should have a plant-rich diet and reduce the amount of red and processed meat, if we eat too much.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making toad in the hole

nodes.misconception: An adequate intake of micronutrients is possible by always eating the same types of foods.
nodes.response: To ensure an adequate intake of micronutrients, it is important to have a varied diet. This is because different foods provide different types and amounts of vitamins and minerals.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Micronutrients

nodes.misconception: Following the Eatwell Guide is only about eating more healthily.
nodes.response: While following the Eatwell Guide will help people eat more healthily, it also has a 32% lower environmental footprint, compared to the current national diet, so can help us eat more sustainably too.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making bang bang veg, with an Asian slaw!

nodes.misconception: Biodiversity is not important in growing food, only the plants growing are important.
nodes.response: Biodiversity is important in growing food by promoting a healthy and balanced ecosystem, e.g. encouraging insects and birds to live near fields can help keep pests under control.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: One planet

nodes.misconception: Eating a limited range of fish is sustainable, as fewer species are caught.
nodes.response: 80% of the fish we eat comes from five species, which puts pressure on these fish stocks. We should eat a wider variety of fish to ensure more sustainable supplies.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Fish strips street wraps

nodes.misconception: Most of the food we eat is produced in the UK.
nodes.response: About 54% of the food on our plates is produced in the UK, the rest is imported from other countries.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Growing, rearing and catching our food

nodes.misconception: The 'all-in-one' method produces poor results, as the ingredients are not creamed together and/or whisked.
nodes.response: The 'all-in-one method' is a quicker cake making method, producing good results. Using self-raising flour and mixing throughly ensure the cakes rise well.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making mini carrot & orange cakes

nodes.misconception: Shortcrust pastry works best when cold butter (or baking fat) and water are used. If warm, the fat is harder to rub into the flour, and the pasty is hard to roll-out and use.
nodes.response: Make sure the butter or baking fat is cold, and that pupils use cold water, this helps to ensure that the pastry works better.  When rubbing-in the fat to the flour, use fingertips only, as less heat is passed from the hands to the fat.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making veggie tarts

nodes.misconception: Leftovers will still be safe to eat after 3 - 4 days, as they still look good.
nodes.response: Leftovers should be used within 48 hours from when it was made (24 hours for rice dishes). Longer periods of time increase the risk of food poisoning bacteria multiplying.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making beef and lentil cottage pie

nodes.misconception: When making two recipes at the same time, you should cook them separately in order. This takes longer, but the recipes are made well.
nodes.response: When making two dishes at the same time, read both recipes first to decide which order to complete the steps in each recipe - this is known as dovetailing. Dovetailing results in a better use of time, where tasks fit together easily.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making mushroom bean burgers, with flatbreads

nodes.misconception: Plant-rich means that we should not eat meat or dairy foods for healthier and more sustainable diets.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to cut out meat or dairy from our diet completely for healthier and more sustainable diets. Follow the Eatwell Guide: have plenty of fruit and veg; diversify sources of protein; and limit foods high in fat, salt and sugars.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant-rich and diverse

nodes.misconception: If a food is placed in the fridge, there is no need for it to be covered or placed in a container, as the fridge is a cold and safe storage area.
nodes.response: All food placed in the fridge must be covered or placed in a container to prevent cross contamination with other foods, preventing food poisoning. It also helps to stop the food drying out.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a Thai curry

nodes.misconception: A sponge and cake are the same.
nodes.response: Often the term ‘sponge’ and ‘cake’ are used interchangeably. However, sponges are traditionally made from eggs, flour and sugar (no butter), e.g. Swiss roll, and cakes are made from eggs, flour, sugar and butter, e.g. lemon drizzle cake.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making mini Victoria sponges

nodes.misconception: The UK produces all of its own food.
nodes.response: The UK produces 58% of the food it consumes, 42% is imported from other countries. This is due to season, cost, climate, and to add variety to the diet.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Eat local to taste the world

nodes.misconception: Rice should be stirred when cooked, so ensure it is covered in liquid.
nodes.response: It is best not to stir most rice dishes. Stirring breaks the rice and releases starch, making the rice feel mushy and ‘over cooked’. Risotto is stirred though, as the starch helps the dish have a creamy texture.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Jollof rice

nodes.misconception: We only make conscious food choices about what food we buy, cook and eat, based on a range of factors.
nodes.response: We make conscious and unconscious food choices about the food we buy, cook and eat.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Factors affecting food choice

nodes.misconception: Baking tins do not need to be greased and/or lined.
nodes.response: It is important to grease (with oil) or line (with greaseproof paper) a baking tin, as this acts as a barrier and prevents the food from sticking.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a Chicago style pizza

nodes.misconception: Cultural appropriation is just appreciation and admiration of other cultures.
nodes.response: Cultural appropriation can be the unacknowledged or inappropriate adoption or use of elements of a minority culture by members of the dominant culture, often in a way that is disrespectful, stereotypical, or exploitative.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Our dynamic food culture

nodes.misconception: Scotch eggs originate from Scotland.
nodes.response: While its name may sound Scottish, the Scotch egg has origins in 1738 London (a snack for travellers), India (nargisi kofta), and Yorkshire (a fish version).
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Scotch eggs, with a dipping sauce

nodes.misconception: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, have stayed the same over time.
nodes.response: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, continue to evolve (change over time) due to a variety of factors, such as history, culture, social media and health.
nodes.subject: cooking-nutrition
nodes.lessonTitle: Making Jerk veg and black bean curry, with rice & peas

nodes.misconception: Testing only happens at the end of the making process.
nodes.response: Testing should happen throughout the making process. This allows the designers and engineers to change / alter and improve any aspects as they move through the making process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing bridge structures

nodes.misconception: Testing needs to be completed at the end of the making task.
nodes.response: Through testing throughout the making process, any issues and changes can be addressed. This will make the product more successful.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a bridge structure

nodes.misconception: All bridges look the same.
nodes.response: All bridges are different. They use different materials, look unique (look different) and made by different designers and engineers.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop and finish a bridge

nodes.misconception: When gluing, always put the glue on the object that is being glued down.
nodes.response: By adding the glue to the backing instead of the object being glued down, it will prevent mess and reduce excess glue from being used. Additionally, use the a small amount of glue first as you can always add more glue.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating bridge collages

nodes.misconception: Bridges are only found over water.
nodes.response: There are different types of bridges, some carry people (footbridge), others allow vehicles to cross over water, roads or railways, some bridges carry trains and others carry boats (aqueduct).
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Bridges

nodes.misconception: Designs need to be decided upon and followed.
nodes.response: Final designs can be adapted and changed, even during the making process. This is because it is always good to be reflective throughout the making process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Generate ideas through talking and 2D drawing

nodes.misconception: Designers make a plan and follow this plan in the making stage.
nodes.response: Designers use their design brief to create a plan. This plan is important but changable depending on success of the project, alongside tools, skills and testing points along the way.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring bridge structures

nodes.misconception: The strongest materials make the best bridges.
nodes.response: Rather than using the strongest materials, sometimes it's better use materials the bend a little.  This is important in case it is windy or the ground shakes.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Reinforcing bridge structures

nodes.misconception: Sustainable buildings have to be buildings that are new.
nodes.response: Sustainable buildings can reuse materials from old buildings or be older buildings that have been redesigned.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainable housing

nodes.misconception: Tinkercad is a paid-for software that will cost schools money and is unsafe to use.
nodes.response: Tinkercad is free to use and schools can set up their own classrooms for pupils to work safely in.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: The TinkerCAD user interface

nodes.misconception: Shapes in Tinkercad can only be created from scratch.
nodes.response: The shape library has a range of prepared objects that can be added to a workplane.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manipulating 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Every shape must be moved on its own once on the workplane, so it is better to not make changes.
nodes.response: By grouping shapes that designers are happy with together, it makes it easier to move, rotate or scale them and make changes to the design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Compound 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Designs are drawn on paper and then manufactured.
nodes.response: Computer Aided Design helps designers accurately draw their ideas before manufacturing them.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Modify 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Design critique and design evaluation are the same.
nodes.response: Design critique evaluates a product to improve it, a design evaluation evaluates an end product against criteria.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Critique 3D eco-houses

nodes.misconception: Mirror is the same as rotate.
nodes.response: Rotating complex or compound shapes will not always have the same outcome as when mirroring a shape.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Complex 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Exploded diagrams have to be in perspective view.
nodes.response: Orthographic view is a better viewpoint for seeing the exploded parts of the eco-house.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploded diagrams in CAD

nodes.misconception: A disassembly is the same as an evaluation.
nodes.response: A disassembly focuses on the different parts and workings of the product. The evaluation focuses on views of what people like and dislike.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Disassemble products to inspire ideas

nodes.misconception: Envelopes have to be exactly the same size as the card that will go inside it.
nodes.response: A folded envelope needs to be slightly larger than the card.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Envelopes for moving cards

nodes.misconception: Slider mechanisms have a pivot points.
nodes.response: Slider mechanisms do not have pivot points and therefore do not use split pins. Slider mechanisms use a guide and a slot. They move in a straight line, rather than turning or pivoting.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Card slider mechanisms

nodes.misconception: A lever is just a seesaw mechanism and only moves up and down.
nodes.response: Levers move up and down and the end of the lever moves in a curved direction. Levers can be turned for different effects.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Card lever mechanisms

nodes.misconception: A common mistake is not understanding that different joining methods need to be used for different materials and reasons.
nodes.response: Some joining techniques such as PVA can be more messy and cause colours in materials to run, for example. Through adding PVA to the object being attached, this usually causes a neater, better presented outcome.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining materials in moving cards

nodes.misconception: Feedback has got to be positive.
nodes.response: Feedback can be positive and negative comments, which help the designer to constructively gain ideas for future projects.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Feedback and evaluation about materials and systems

nodes.misconception: All paper and card comes from trees.
nodes.response: Some paper and card can be from recyclable materials
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of paper and card

nodes.misconception: To help the split pin to turn, create a bigger hole.
nodes.response: If the hole is too big, this will allow the split pin to wobble and cause the mechanism to not work accurately. Use a standard pencil and turn the split pin when it is in place and this will help it the lever to move smoothly.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Mechanisms in moving cards

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter where you place the pivots on a lazy-tong linkage.
nodes.response: Where the pivots are placed is very important on a lazy-tong linkage.  If they are not placed correctly, the mechanism will not function correctly.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Bell crank and lazy-tong linkages

nodes.misconception: Evaluating a design uses only the user feedback.
nodes.response: Evaluations should be reflective and allow the designer to consider their thoughts as well as the user's.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Present the book to the user

nodes.misconception: Cutting and shaping are not the same.
nodes.response: Cutting can be a form of shaping.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan and make an interactive book

nodes.misconception: Open questions gather the users own personal views and may offer more ideas. Sometimes this leads to the user misunderstanding questions or providing answers which are not as expected.
nodes.response: All questions need to be specific and clear.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: User research

nodes.misconception: All linkages can be found in interactive books.
nodes.response: Not all linkages are suitable for use in an interactive book. Those that are used are chosen because they are the simplest, most functional option for the intended purpose.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Levers and linkages in products

nodes.misconception: Push-pull and parallel linkages are made of more than one lever.
nodes.response: Levers can be joined together to form a linkage. A parallel and push-pull linkage is made up of multiple levers.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Parallel and push-pull linkages

nodes.misconception: If the bridge is too tight over the mechanism, it will reduce the movement.
nodes.response: Make sure that when you attach the bridge, there is a gap to allow the mechanism to freely move underneath.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assembling components for an interactive book

nodes.misconception: Levers are always used to make things move easier.
nodes.response: Some levers are designed to to move things faster or further, a pair of tweezers for example.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Reverse motion levers and linkages

nodes.misconception: Finished products cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Adaptations can be made to individual components in a product to improve effectiveness.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Test and adapt cam mechanisms

nodes.misconception: All automata create the same up and down linear output.
nodes.response: The position of the follower and the size, shape and number of cams can create a range of movements.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Cams in a product

nodes.misconception: Force and pressure are needed to saw through wood.
nodes.response: Correct technique and posture allows the blade to work efficiently without force.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Wood construction and joining techniques

nodes.misconception: All cams create the same movement.
nodes.response: The size, shape and position of a cam will create different types of movement.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Cam mechanisms

nodes.misconception: Drilled and pierced holes can be any size.
nodes.response: Cam discs need to be tightly fitted to the axle so that they rotate with it. Holes for the axle and followers need to be loose to allow free movement.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemble cam mechanisms

nodes.misconception: All cross-section diagrams show the vertical plane.
nodes.response: Cross-sections diagrams can show the horizontal or vertical planes and these can provide very different views.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop ideas through cross-section diagrams

nodes.misconception: A common mistake is inaccurate measuring which means the box frame will not be square.
nodes.response: It is important to measure accurately to make sure the box frame is square.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Make an accurate box frame

nodes.misconception: All hardwoods are hard and all softwoods are soft.
