nodes.response: Balsa is very soft and light but it is a deciduous hardwood. Yew is heavy and hard but it is a coniferous softwood.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Wood functional properties

nodes.misconception: Windmills create wind, rather than being moved by it.
nodes.response: The wind pushes the windmill's blades to make them turn.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Using wind

nodes.misconception: Models need to work first time.
nodes.response: Through testing and repeat testing, models can be tried and adapted to work.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing wind sails

nodes.misconception: Rotary motion always produces electricity.
nodes.response: Rotary motion can be designed to lift objects, grind objects or produce electricity.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Rotary motion

nodes.misconception: An axle needs to be fixed.
nodes.response: An axle needs to be free moving, able to turn. The sails turn on the axle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Selecting an axle for a windmill

nodes.misconception: Windmills just need a wide base to stand by themselves.
nodes.response: When the wind catches them, they move or fall - windmills need ballast to secure them.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a windmill

nodes.misconception: Wind sails are always made of wood.
nodes.response: Wind sail structures may be made of wood, but will have fabric to catch the wind.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Select materials for wind sails

nodes.misconception: There is only one strategy to making a moving windmill.
nodes.response: There are multiple ways to make the windmill turn. It can be made using different materials - such as wood, card, straws, split pins and pins
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting final designs

nodes.misconception: Windmill have to be tested inside
nodes.response: The windmill can be tested inside or outside depending upon the conditions and supervision.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Finishing and testing windmill mechanisms

nodes.misconception: Circuits in the classroom are always safe to use.
nodes.response: Electricity is dangerous and needs to be carefully worked with. It can't always be seen and hazards need to be identified.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Connecting components safely

nodes.misconception: Ada Lovelace invented the first computer.
nodes.response: While Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm, she did not invent the first computer. Micro:bits demonstate the principles that Ada Lovelace worked on.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Ada Lovelace

nodes.misconception: Micro:bits can work on their own by being connected in a circuit
nodes.response: Micro:bits have to have a program downloaded before being connected into a circuit
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Micro:bit programs with variables

nodes.misconception: Cases are just boxes for a data logger to fit into.
nodes.response: Cases need to display the micro:bit, some of the components and fit the battery packs
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Data logger cases

nodes.misconception: Tally charts can only be completed on paper.
nodes.response: Data loggers can record tally charts electronically.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan and design a data logger case

nodes.misconception: Traffic surveys are only about collecting data.
nodes.response: Data collected from the data loggers can be used to understand what is happening in an environment and make suggestions for improvements.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Data logger tests and understanding the data

nodes.misconception: Micro:bits are not computers.
nodes.response: Micro:bits are small computers that have many different functions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Using Micro:bit inputs and outputs

nodes.misconception: To test simple circuits, you need to create a physical representation of the circuits.
nodes.response: Like many CAD applications, Tinkercad can simulate circuit operation within the circuit workspace.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Microcontrollers

nodes.misconception: Museum galleries are not organised in any order. Artefacts are displayed randomly.
nodes.response: Museum galleries are carefully designed and include thought about access and display of artefacts.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Museum gallery prototypes

nodes.misconception: Sensors on a micro:bit work automatically.
nodes.response: Micro:bits need a program to control the sensors.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Input and output design decisions

nodes.misconception: Museum galleries only contain paintings.
nodes.response: Museum galleries display a range of artefacts which include paintings and other physical objects.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Museum gallery artefacts

nodes.misconception: Crocodile clips have to be used to connect the components together.
nodes.response: Whilst crocodile clips can be used effectively, electrical wire from educational stockists can be used as a cheaper alternitive.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Integrate programmable systems in a product

nodes.misconception: Connected circuits will always work.
nodes.response: Circuits need to be checked that the connections are accurate and the components all work.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Museum alarm programming and fault finding

nodes.misconception: Only battery packs can be attached to micro:bits.
nodes.response: A variety of inputs and outputs can be attached to a micro:bit.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Offboard components

nodes.misconception: Exhibiting final products should always produce positive feedback.
nodes.response: By exhibiting our designs we can find out how to improve the products further.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great Exhibition and presenting museum alarms

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of switch.
nodes.response: Switches break the electrical flow of a circuit but they can be activated in different ways - they can be pushed, slid, twisted or pulled.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Push-to-make switches

nodes.misconception: Pulleys work under any amount of tension.
nodes.response: Pulleys will not work if the band is too tight (struggles to rotate) or too loose (falls off).
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemble an electric vehicle

nodes.misconception: The position of axle holes and axles doesn't need to be accurately measured.
nodes.response: Axle holes and axles need to be positioned accurately on order for the wheels and pulleys to rotate correctly and produce the correct movement. Accurate measuring is essential.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Make an electric vehicle chassis

nodes.misconception: All early engineers were men.
nodes.response: Many women have contributed to the development of engineering.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Dorothée Pullinger and car design

nodes.misconception: The shape of a vehicle has no effect on its speed.
nodes.response: Vehicle shape is considered in order to reduce air resistance (less drag).
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Aerodynamics

nodes.misconception: The size of a pulley does not effect the speed of rotation.
nodes.response: Smaller pulleys rotate faster than larger pulleys on the same system.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Pulley systems

nodes.misconception: All switches have to be pressed to work.
nodes.response: Switches control the flow of electricity in a circuit and can be pushed, slid, twisted or pulled.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Switches in simple circuits

nodes.misconception: Simple eletrical systems are not dangerous.
nodes.response: All exposed electrical wires need to be covered to prevent injury or fire.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Add a switch to a design

nodes.misconception: All circuits have multiple pathways (like the underground map).
nodes.response: A series circuit is a continuous loop where all the components are connected one after another along the same path.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Harry Beck and circuit diagrams

nodes.misconception: All vehicles are made from the same materials.
nodes.response: Discuss the diversity of materials used in vehicle construction and why different vehicles require different materials.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing a vehicle

nodes.misconception: An axle must hold two wheels.
nodes.response: The axle might hold one or two wheels. The axle can turn with the wheel.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design specification for wheeled vehicles

nodes.misconception: Completed vehicles are finished and therefore will not need any changes or alterations neeeded to them.
nodes.response: Testing and feedback is a good way to spot any problems with the vehicles and therefore time to correct, adapt and alter specific parts of the finished product and demonstrates that products always need reviewing and adapting to make them work.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Test a vehicle

nodes.misconception: A vehicle only has a chassis.
nodes.response: A vehicle has a chassis and a body.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Finishing a vehicle

nodes.misconception: Card and paper are the same.
nodes.response: Card is thicker and more durable than paper. Explain the differences in characteristics and uses.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Card properties and uses

nodes.misconception: Glue is the only way to join card sections.
nodes.response: Pupils might think that glue is the only joining technique. This lesson will explore other methods.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Card construction techniques

nodes.misconception: Axle holders can be placed at any angle.
nodes.response: Clarify that axles need to be parallel to ensure proper wheel function.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding wheels to a vehicle

nodes.misconception: Only cars have wheels and axles.
nodes.response: Highlight that many vehicles, including bicycles and toy cars, use wheels and axles.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Wheels and axles in vehicles

nodes.misconception: Air is empty because we can't see it.
nodes.response: Air takes up space and can make things move or change shape, such as when we inflate a balloon or a bike tyre.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Make things move with air

nodes.misconception: Design drawings must be technical and include detail.
nodes.response: Simple drawings can be annotated to add the extra information and detail needed to understand the design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop ideas through annotated sketches

nodes.misconception: Finishing techniques are just for decorative purposes.
nodes.response: Finishing techniques can be used to disguise working components.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemble a pneumatic animal

nodes.misconception: Air can only be directed to one place (output).
nodes.response: One input can affect multiple outputs by splitting the flow or direction of the air.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring pneumatic systems

nodes.misconception: Pneumatic systems always cause something to expland or inflate.
nodes.response: Pneumatic systems can cause directed movement of an object without inflation.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Pneumatic systems

nodes.misconception: Pneumatic systems will fit neatly into a product.
nodes.response: Systems and products will need to be adapted to ensure correct position and fit.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Make a pneumatic system

nodes.misconception: Finished products cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Finished products can be adapted to ensure they are fit for purpose.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate pneumatic systems

nodes.misconception: Action plans cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Action plans can be changed and adapted throughout the project.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan a pneumatic system

nodes.misconception: Packaging can only be reinforced from the inside.
nodes.response: Packaging can be reinforced on the inside and/or the outside using different methods.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Strengthen packaging

nodes.misconception: A brand logo needs to contain lots of information, colour and design.
nodes.response: Simple logos are often the most effective.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Branding packaging designs

nodes.misconception: Adverts are the only way to promote a product.
nodes.response: Products can be promoted through presentations, exhibitions, videos, posters and competitions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Promoting products

nodes.misconception: Design drawings have to be neat, fully completed and accurate.
nodes.response: Rapid sketches allows lots of ideas in a short space of time that can be developed later.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Annotated net sketches

nodes.misconception: Critiquing is negative and criticising.
nodes.response: Critiquing involves looking at the positive and negative aspects of a product.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainability and packaging design

nodes.misconception: A prototype doesn't need to be joined accurately.
nodes.response: Prototypes provide a good opportunity to test accurate joining techniques.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemble packaging

nodes.misconception: Packaging is constructed from lots of separate pieces.
nodes.response: Packaging is often one piece of material constructed as a net.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Shell structures

nodes.misconception: Packaging has always been the same.
nodes.response: Packaging has developed over time. The rise in plastic use has seen plastic replacing glass, increased use of recycled paper/card, less use of wooden crates used in the past.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Card functional properties

nodes.misconception: All fabric decorative techniques involve stitching.
nodes.response: Fabrics can be decorated using other techniques such as appliqué, fabric pens and paints.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop and finish an accessible product

nodes.misconception: An action plan is a list of instructions.
nodes.response: An action plan is more than a list of insructions; it provides a list of stages of making, sometimes in order but can also list the materials and tools needed.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design action plans

nodes.misconception: Curved seams require different stitches to straight seams.
nodes.response: The same stitches can be used on a curved edge as those used on a straight seam.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric seams and curves

nodes.misconception: Textile products are only designed for fashion.
nodes.response: Textile products can also serve functional and practical purposes, such as accessibility and user needs.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Accessible textile products

nodes.misconception: Impact statements only consider the design specifications.
nodes.response: Impact statements consider the outcome and the impact the product has had on the user.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Impact statements

nodes.misconception: Fabrics are only chosen for aesthetic reasons.
nodes.response: Fabric selection can be driven by function and aesthetics.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Select fabrics for functional and aesthetic properties

nodes.misconception: All pocket designs will be attached in the same way.
nodes.response: Different techniques, such as of loops and slots, should be chosen to suit the pocket type.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric pockets and slots

nodes.misconception: All fasteners are accessible to everyone.
nodes.response: The user needs should be considered when choosing fasteners so they are accesible to the individual.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Accessible fasteners

nodes.misconception: Polymers (plastics) are always in a solid state.
nodes.response: Polymers (plastics) can be heated to a liquid state, as in the process of injection moulding.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Ole Kirk Kristiansen and polymers

nodes.misconception: Fashion design only considers the aesthetic qualities of clothing and accessories.
nodes.response: Fashion designers must balance form and function when designing clothing and accessories.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Vivienne Westwood and fashion design

nodes.misconception: Prototypes are finished pieces that cannot be adapted.
nodes.response: Prototypes can help identify problems and prototypes made from card can be adapted easily.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Accessible design prototype

nodes.misconception: Product design, particulary functional furniture, does not the impact the wellbeing of society.
nodes.response: Design that is uplifting, inclusive and accessible can benefit society in a positive way.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Yinka Ilori and accessible design

nodes.misconception: Orthographic projections are just a plan view.
nodes.response: Orthographic projections have a plan or top view, side view and front view and are used for architects to show the different elevations of a building.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Architectural orthographic projections

nodes.misconception: Clothing is alway made from scratch using pattern pieces.
nodes.response: Existing clothing can be upcycled to make new items of clothing.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Upcycling fashion design

nodes.misconception: All design drawings are drawn from one angle, usually a front view.
nodes.response: Isometric drawings show three angles at the same time.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Graphic designs

nodes.misconception: All designers, architects and engineers sketch in 3D.
nodes.response: Designers, architects and engineers often use elevations to show different 2D views of 3D objects from the side, front and plan.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Zaha Hadid and architectural design

nodes.misconception: Feedback isn't helpful.
nodes.response: Feedback can be helpful if guided by questions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: User feedback to improve the pattern

nodes.misconception: Additional features need to be finished and functional.
nodes.response: Additional features on prototypes can be shown using mock-ups made from mixed materials.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop a fabric pattern in response to feedback

nodes.misconception: Prototypes are finished pieces that can't be adjusted.
nodes.response: Prototypes can be taken apart and adjusted.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Select and make a fabric pattern

nodes.misconception: A seam allowance is included in the sizing measurements.
nodes.response: A seam allowance needs to be added to the sizing measurements.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple pattern pieces

nodes.misconception: All hats are made the same way.
nodes.response: Different styles of hats require different patterns. These can also be adjusted to change the design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric patterns

nodes.misconception: Hat designs templates will fit all users.
nodes.response: Hats, and other items, can be tailored to fit an individual by taking measurements before planning a design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Research interviews

nodes.misconception: Fashion designers only design clothes.
nodes.response: Fashion designers can also design accessories, such as hats. Some fashion designers, such as milliners, specialise in one area.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Virgil Abloh and hat design

nodes.misconception: All fabrics have the same properties.
nodes.response: Different fabrics have different properties which must be considered when selecting fabrics for designs.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric functional properties

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to follow their design idea and chosen materials.
nodes.response: Please remind pupils that they can change their ideas and use alternative finishing techniques and joining techniques in their work. Designers are continuously reviewing and editing their designs to make sure that they meet the users' needs.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Finishing techniques for hand puppets

nodes.misconception: All of the detail of the puppet needs to be added to the template.
nodes.response: The template is the basic outline of the puppet. The extra detail, such as ears, can be added later.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan and make fabric templates

nodes.misconception: The whole puppet needs to be stitched.
nodes.response: There are other joining technqiues that can be used to join the felt together. The running stitch is one which is advised for this unit, however, staples or fabric glue / PVA can be used as an alternative.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining fabric to make puppets

nodes.misconception: All fabrics are the same.
nodes.response: There are lots of differnet types of fabrics, some are man-made and others are natural.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric properties

nodes.misconception: Design ideas cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Design ideas can be changed during the final design and the making tasks. Designs might be changed because something does not work, there are other ideas which will work better or testing shows problems with part of a design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketching ideas

nodes.misconception: All puppets are made the same way using the same materials.
nodes.response: Puppets can have different purposes/uses. Some use lollipop sticks, others have strings move each part. Puppets are used for storytimes, playtimes, concerts and on TV. Some talk with help from their puppeteers.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring puppets

nodes.misconception: Feedback has got to be positive.
nodes.response: Feedback can be positive or negative and aims to help the designer to improve on their design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Giving and receiving feedback

nodes.misconception: Children should use cotton to sew.
nodes.response: Using embroidery thread means that it is easier for smaller hands to use and it is also more resilient. It can be used with larger eyed needles too.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple sewing techniques

nodes.misconception: Decorations used are to make it look pretty.
nodes.response: As well as appearance, we need to consider usability and safety when choosing finishing touches.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding finishing touches to playground structures

nodes.misconception: Structures are all the same.
nodes.response: There are different types of structures - frame, shell and brick bonding structures. They are all used for different effects, purposes and reasons.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and reinforcing playground structures

nodes.misconception: Designers plan and follow their planning in the making stage.
nodes.response: Designers use their design brief to create a plan. This plan is important but changable depending on success of the project, alongside tools, skills and testing points along the way.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing playground structures

nodes.misconception: Feedback and testing can only be completed once the object is made and finished.
nodes.response: Testing and feedback can be a continuous process through the making and designing process. Pupils may reflect on the positives and negatives of any changes made in their final evaluation and feedback.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Test and talk about the final playground structure

nodes.misconception: Designs need to be decided upon and followed.
nodes.response: Final designs can be adapted and changed, even during the making process. This is because it is always good to be reflective throughout the making process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Making playground structures

nodes.misconception: Buttresses, bracing, anchors, wider bases and reinforced sides need to be on every single mock-up model for it to be freestanding.
nodes.response: Not all structures need a buttress, bracing, anchors, wider bases or reinforcing, it depends on the materials that are being used, the size, height and what the object is going to do.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing materials for playground structures

nodes.misconception: All play areas follow a similar design.
nodes.response: There are a wide variety of play area designs for different users that use different materials and shapes.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Shapes and materials used in playground structures

nodes.misconception: Structures that are anchored down are not freestanding.
nodes.response: Structures which are anchored down can be freestanding, such as play equipment. A structure which is joined to another structure, such as a radiator joined to a wall, is not freestanding.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple playground structures

nodes.misconception: Sewing is only used to join fabric pieces.
nodes.response: Sewing can be used to finish raw (cut) edges or add decorative detail to single layer fabric pieces.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric decorative techniques

nodes.misconception: Sewing consists of one type of stitch whereby the thread is passed in and out of the fabric.
nodes.response: There are different types of stitches, which require different movements of the needle and thread.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric joining and cutting techniques

nodes.misconception: Fabric and fasteners are chosen for aesthetic qualities alone.
nodes.response: Fabric and fasteners need to be selected carefully for their function and application.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design specification and fabric selection

nodes.misconception: Stitching size doesn't affect product outcome.
nodes.response: Large, uneven stitches will create gaps which will make the final product less effective.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemble a stationery storage product

nodes.misconception: Pupils often place pattern pieces in the centre of a piece of fabric.
nodes.response: Pattern pieces should be placed close to the edge and arranged so that they limit wastage.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Using stationery storage product patterns

nodes.misconception: Fabric patterns are the same size as the product dimensions.
nodes.response: A seam allowance must be added to allow for joining; retaining the product dimesions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric patterns and seam allowance

nodes.misconception: All products made for use in or around water need to be waterproof.
nodes.response: Clothing used for swimming ie, trunks, costumes, shorts and wetsuits, are not waterproof.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing fabrics

nodes.misconception: All fasteners perform in the same way.
nodes.response: There are positives and negatives with each type of fastener. The use of each depends on the product and user.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabric fasteners

nodes.misconception: Components all work however they are positioned circuit.
nodes.response: Some components are polarised and only work if they are the correct way round.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Electronic systems

nodes.misconception: Modern materials only provide advantages to designers and users.
nodes.response: Modern materials are often difficult and expensive to produce and are also difficult to recycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern materials

nodes.misconception: Increasing the size of the driven gear, increases the output speed.
nodes.response: Decreasing the size of the driven gear (or increasing the size of driver gear), increases the speed of the driven gear.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Gears

nodes.misconception: New and emerging technologies have only positive impacts.
nodes.response: New and emerging technologies can make some products obsolete. It can also mean that many workers with limited skills lose their jobs to robots. These workers may find it difficult, or may not want to, retrain.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: New and emerging technologies

nodes.misconception: The larger the diameter of a pulley wheel, the higher the output speed.
nodes.response: The smaller the pulley wheel, the quicker it will complete a rotation, therefore increasing the output speed.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Cams and pulleys

nodes.misconception: Textiles are not made from fossil fuels.
nodes.response: Synthetic fibres are usually made from fossil fuels such a polyester and ripstop nylon.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Material categories

nodes.misconception: Smart materials are only for fun products like colour changing mugs!
nodes.response: Smart materials give designers and engineers exciting possibilities when developing new products. Possibilities often focus on function and/or form. For example, thermochromic materials can be used to indicate a temperature and warn users of danger.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Smart materials

nodes.misconception: The only way to gain MA is by increasing the input force.
nodes.response: MA can be increased by increasing the distance from the fulcrum and the effort.  For example, increasing the arm length on the handle of a flat head screwdriver when opening a can of paint.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Levers and linkages

nodes.misconception: Renewable sources of energy do not have any negative impacts.
nodes.response: Renewable sources of energy have high initial set up costs, are often weather dependent and require effective storage of energy.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Energy generation and storage

nodes.misconception: Control systems are programmed with text-based languages.
nodes.response: Control systems can be programmed using different languages including text, blocks or flow charts.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Programmable systems

nodes.misconception: Environmental impact only occurs when products are disposed of.
nodes.response: Circular economy and LCA consider the environmental impact at every single stage of a product's life cycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Energy and the impact on designs

nodes.misconception: All new technology is good and we should use it.
nodes.response: New technology can be good but may also have negative consequences which responsible designers must consider.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: New and emerging technologies informing design decisions

nodes.misconception: Rendering is just adding tone.
nodes.response: Rendering should consider tone and depth but also the texture of the material the product is made out of.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced 3D sketching

nodes.misconception: Alessi is often thought of as a single designer.
nodes.response: Alessi is a group of designers.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: The work of other designers

nodes.misconception: Annotations can replace the need for a clear and accurate sketch.
nodes.response: Annotation provides further explanation or clarification on what is not visible in the sketch.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Mastering 3D sketching

nodes.misconception: All polymers are non biodegradable and can last for hundreds of year.
nodes.response: Polymers come in many forms including biodegradable and bio-based polymers that will break down more easily in the environment.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Polymer properties and processes

nodes.misconception: Data always involves numbers.
nodes.response: Data is information and can be recorded using both numbers and words.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing citrus fruit juicers

nodes.misconception: Designing products using the average measurements in an anthropometric data set will provide a successful user experience for all users.
nodes.response: Designing for the average person can diminish user experience and exclude a significant portion of the population from using products.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Anthropometrics and ergonomics

nodes.misconception: 3D sketching is just 2D sketching with an additional dimension.
nodes.response: To be able to sketch in 3D, we need to understand depth and perspective.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic 3D sketching

nodes.misconception: Possible outcome design fixation limits context exploration. Product analysis leads to copying.
nodes.response: Product analysis identifies successful features and those which can be improved.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Why and how designers analyse products

nodes.misconception: Recycling metals reduces their quality.
nodes.response: Most metals, including aluminium and steel, can be repeatedly recycled without negatively impacting their properties.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Metal properties and processes

nodes.misconception: It is often believed that focusing on form means sacrificing function, and vice versa. The assumption is that a product can't be both beautiful and functional.
nodes.response: Good design brings together both form and function. The form of a product can enhance the function of a product by making it more enjoyable to use.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Form versus function fruit juicers

nodes.misconception: All timbers are sustainable.
nodes.response: Timber can be a sustainable material if sourced from a Forest Stewardship Council certified supplier. FSC forests are managed to strict environmental, social, and ecological standards.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Timber properties and processes

nodes.misconception: LEDs are always used individually.
nodes.response: LEDs can be grouped in strips or matrices to create patterns or messages.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: LEDs

nodes.misconception: Physical sketching is the same as sketching in parametric CAD.
nodes.response: Sketches in parametric CAD need to be constrained in order to create accurate and error free models.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Create, modify and constrain 2D sketches in Fusion

nodes.misconception: Testing must always be done using a physical control system.
nodes.response: Testing a control system can be done using a physical control system and a multimeter or using a CAD simulation.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Virtual and physical testing of systems

nodes.misconception: A variable is a set piece of data that can not change once collected.
nodes.response: A variable is a named piece of data stored in a computer’s memory, accessed and changed by a computer program.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Data logging

nodes.misconception: Systems only use one input.
nodes.response: Systems often have multiple inputs. These can be switches and sensors.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Input components

nodes.misconception: 3D printing is sustainable because it is an additive manufacturing process with minimal waste.
nodes.response: 3D printing filament is a thermopolymer.  As with all manufacturing processes, there needs to be consideration of the materials used, their sources and disposal.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design for additive manufacturing with Fusion

nodes.misconception: When we select a component, they are all the same.
nodes.response: Different circuits and control systems require different value components. Changing one will affect the others.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Electronic calculations

nodes.misconception: A sketch is always needed to be able to use the Extrude command in Fusion.
nodes.response: Users can extrude from component faces and existing solid bodies.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: 3D model using Extrude and the Timeline in Fusion

nodes.misconception: Technical drawings created in CAD are always correct and error-free.
nodes.response: Using CAD reduces human error; however, users must add correct and relevant dimensions. Incorrect constraints can also result in errors.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Technical drawings in Fusion

nodes.misconception: Testing only happens when the final prototype has been made.
nodes.response: Testing should happen throughout the iterative journey, so that design decisions are made to meet design requirements and produce a successful design solution.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assemble, test and refine systems

nodes.misconception: Adding physical materials to components in Fusion is for aesthetic purposes only.
nodes.response: Adding physical materials to components alters their appearance and properties.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical materials and appearances in Fusion

nodes.misconception: All motors operate in the same way.
nodes.response: DC motors use open-loop systems, and servo motors use a closed-loop system.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Motors

nodes.misconception: Buzzers all work in the same way.
nodes.response: Different buzzers work in different ways.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Buzzers

nodes.misconception: Components can be placed by eye when assembly modelling in Fusion.
nodes.response: To create assemblies in Fusion, the correct joints should be used to replicate how components are assembled in the real world.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Assembly modelling in Fusion

nodes.misconception: All CAD modelling is the same, whether working in Tinkercad or Fusion.
nodes.response: Different CAD applications work in three distinct ways, constructive solid geometry, solid modelling and parametric modelling.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fusion fundamentals

nodes.misconception: Systems are simple with just one input, process and output.
nodes.response: Systems can be complex with multiple inputs, processes and outputs, feedback and variables.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Systems approach to design

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy, and repeatability.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Reforming manufacturing processes for timbers

nodes.misconception: All joining methods work the same for every material.
nodes.response: Different materials need different joining methods based on their properties.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining processes for timbers

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy and repeatability.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Deforming manufacturing processes for timbers

nodes.misconception: A mould and a former are the same thing.
nodes.response: A mould contains the material and shapes it as it sets or solidifies. A former is a shape around which a material is bent or stretched.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Production aids

nodes.misconception: Physical properties and working properties are the same thing.
nodes.response: Physical properties describe inherent features (like density, colour, or conductivity), whereas working properties describe how a material behaves under stress (like flexibility, toughness, or hardness).
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical and working properties of materials

nodes.misconception: All materials are ready to use in their natural state.
nodes.response: Raw materials need to go through a range of processing stages to make them usable.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Sources and stock forms of timbers

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy, and repeatability.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Wasting manufacturing processes for timbers

nodes.misconception: Quality control is only about looking at the product at the very end of production.
nodes.response: Quality Control can happen throughout production (in-process checks, sampling, functional tests), not just at the end.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Quality Control methods

nodes.misconception: Mass production and continuous production are the same thing.
nodes.response: Mass production stops and starts, but continuous production never stops.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Scales of production in manufacturing

nodes.misconception: The environmental impact of a material only happens when the product is thrown away.
nodes.response: A material’s environmental impact occurs at every stage of its life cycle; during manufacture, use, and disposal.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Environmental impact of materials

nodes.misconception: The same tools and methods are used for both small-scale and industrial manufacturing.
nodes.response: The scale of production heavily influences tool choice, speed, accuracy, and repeatability.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Finishing processes for timbers

nodes.misconception: A material's properties are fixed and cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Many materials can be altered after they are made to improve their properties, e.g. strength.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Enhancing the properties of timbers

nodes.misconception: Product safety is only about consumer protection.
nodes.response: Industry safety also includes protecting workers.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Health and Safety

nodes.misconception: Design briefs are only used in creative fields like product or graphic design.
nodes.response: Design briefs are crucial across many industries, including engineering, architecture, and product development.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design brief

nodes.misconception: The cost of a product only concerns raw materials.
nodes.response: Other factors like labour, overhead, distribution, and economies of scale affect the cost of a product.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Costing

nodes.misconception: Research is only conducted at the beginning of a project.
nodes.response: Research is involved in several stages of the design process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Research

nodes.misconception: Product analysis is only about identifying flaws or problems in a product.
nodes.response: In reality, product analysis is used to improve design, meet user needs, and stay competitive.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Product analysis

nodes.misconception: Design specifications and technical specifications are the same.
nodes.response: Design specifications focus on the overall concept, user needs, and appearance. Technical specifications detail the materials and measurement requirements needed to build a product.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design specification

nodes.misconception: Manufacturing process selection is solely based on cost.
nodes.response: Factors like product complexity, material properties, production volume, and lead time also play crucial roles.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacturing considerations and selection

nodes.misconception: Feedback is only used to fix problems.
nodes.response: Industries use feedback not just to solve issues but also to innovate, improve efficiency, enhance customer satisfaction, and stay competitive.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Feedback and evaluation

nodes.misconception: QA and QC are the same thing.
nodes.response: QA (Quality Assurance) focuses on preventing defects by improving the production process, while QC (Quality Control) focuses on identifying and fixing defects in the finished product.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Quality

nodes.misconception: Factories always produce goods in large amounts.
nodes.response: Factories are responsive and often adjust production methods based on demand.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Efficient manufacturing systems

nodes.misconception: The cheapest material is always the best choice.
nodes.response: Material selection involves balancing multiple factors, such as strength, durability, weight, sustainability, and ease of manufacturing; in addition to cost.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Material considerations and selection

nodes.misconception: Industries only modify products to make them cheaper.
nodes.response: Industries also improve products for better performance, sustainability, customer satisfaction, safety and compliance with regulations.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Modifications and improvements

nodes.misconception: Envionmental impact can only be assessed after a product has been manufactured.
nodes.response: Environmental impact can be assessed at every and all stages of the iterative design process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify environmental impact

nodes.misconception: Any marking tool will work on any material.
nodes.response: Using the wrong tool (e.g a pencil on metal) can result in unclear or inaccurate marks. Different materials require specific marking tools, such as pencils for paper and boards and marking knives for wood.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark out and prepare materials: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Choosing materials is always based on aesthetics.
nodes.response: Many factors determine the material choice, such as the purpose and environment of the product. For example, MDF is absorbent and not suitable for damp or humid places, unless finished with a waterproof layer.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Materials and manufacturing processes: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Using machinery results in greater accuracy.
nodes.response: Machinery or hand tools can result in accurate manufacturing. Accuracy is achieved with careful planning and execution with skill.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Equipment and machinery: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Innovation has to be revolutionary and entirely original.
nodes.response: Innovation can be revolutinary like the 'cats eye' or evolutionary where ideas change gradually and evolve over time.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Innovation when generating ideas

nodes.misconception: Orthographic projections are completed after manufacture.
nodes.response: Orthographic projections are known as a working drawing. These are sent from a designer to a manufacturer before manufacturing to enable them to manufacture the product or component.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan manufacture using orthographic projection: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Biomimicry is using nature to inspire aesthetics.
nodes.response: Biomimicry uses nature to inspire solutions to problems, biomorphism is about nature inspiring aesthetics.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Biomimicry

nodes.misconception: Development of design ideas is coming up with a completely new idea or the idea has to be changed significantly.
nodes.response: Developing an idea can be changing and altering very small things such as function, materials, size, proportion or aesthetics.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Using feedback to develop ideas

nodes.misconception: Using AI when designing is cheating.
nodes.response: AI can be used to help inspire us and is used to develop our own ideas. We must just be open and honest in our use of it.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: AI to develop ideas: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Quality control checks are performed on products after they are made to ensure they meet the required quality standards for sale or use.
nodes.response: Quality control checks are performed throughout the process to ensure quality remains constant.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Quality control: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: All prototypes must be life size.
nodes.response: It is not always possible to manufacture life size prototypes. The space to manufacture and store may be limited plus the materials may be expensive. A smaller scale product saves space and materials but still allows for a product to be manufactured.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Proportions and scale: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Once a final product is complete no further iterations or improvements are needed.
nodes.response: Designers constantly seek to improve and develop their designs and products. No product is ever perfect.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate with user feedback: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Using sources of inspiration when designing is copying.
nodes.response: When using sources of inspiration, they are usually not solutions or similar products but instead any image or product that inspires a spark of creativity.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating design ideas using SCAMPER

nodes.misconception: Parts lists are only needed for materials or components which need to be bought in.
nodes.response: A parts lists supports the thinking needed in preparation of manufacture for all components of a design. They help identify quantities and can highlight mistakes. A well-structured parts list speeds up production and ensures cost efficiency.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Parts lists: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Practice using the tools is not needed when working with polymers and timbers as they are easy to cut.
nodes.response: Practice is needed when using tools to cut all materials. Polymers and timbers are easy to cut, but complete control can be lost if cut too quickly. It can be challenging to keep on the line, so practice is needed.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Tools and processes: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: All specifications must use the same subheadings.
nodes.response: Specifications must be specific to the context, design opportunity and design brief.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Product requirements

nodes.misconception: Once a final product is complete, no further iterations or improvements are needed.
nodes.response: Designers constantly seek to improve and develop their designs and products, no product is ever perfect.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing and modifications: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: Gantt charts are used to plan out the whole design project.
nodes.response: Gantt charts can be used as a tool to plan out the whole design project. However it can be beneficial to use Gantt charts for the individual phases within the project, like the manufacturing stage. This can improve efficiency at crucial stages.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Time planning: polymers and timbers

nodes.misconception: A design brief should be very specific and identify a product that will be designed and manufactured.
nodes.response: To avoid design fixation, a design brief should be non-specific and open. A design brief should focus on the context and the problem, and not name a product that will be designed and made.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Write a design brief based on research

nodes.misconception: Fixating on one idea or existing ideas will lead to innovative designing.
nodes.response: Design fixation is the opposite of being innovative and is focussing or fixating on one idea or existing ideas. This can limit creativity and innovation.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Bisociation

nodes.misconception: Using closed questions in an interview will provide enough effective information to support further developments.
nodes.response: Using open-ended questions in an interview will allow for more detailed and flexible reponses, providing oppotunites for effective outcomes to support further developments.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Interviews

nodes.misconception: Questionnaires are only used to present data in graphs when investigating a context.
nodes.response: Questionnaires inform designing and provide evidence to justify design decisions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Questionnaires

nodes.misconception: It is only possible to present quantitative data.
nodes.response: Qualitative data can be presented in other formats to summarise findings.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Data analysis

nodes.misconception: Branding and logos are the same thing.
nodes.response: Branding is the way of making a company’s product or service more visible and recognisable. A logo is just a small part of branding and is a simple symbol or design that represents a business or brand.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Branding

nodes.misconception: Socioeconomic status is just about a person's income.
nodes.response: It is a combination of things such as income, education, occupation and even influence.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Economic viability

nodes.misconception: Patents and trademarks are the same thing.
nodes.response: Trademarks protect brand names and logos whilst patents protect inventions and new technologies.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design security

nodes.misconception: All data can be presented as a graph or chart.
nodes.response: The way in which data is presented will depend on whether the data is quantitative or qualitative.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Present data

nodes.misconception: When investigating a context you should only consider the users preferences.
nodes.response: There are many different groups of people from different places that should be considered when investigating a context. These different groups of people like stakeholders all have different preferences which the designer should consider.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: People and places

nodes.misconception: A specification is written after research and then referred to once the product is manufactured.
nodes.response: Design requirements should be used throughout the iterative journey (not just at the end!) to test concepts and make effective design decisions to creatively develop the product into a successful design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Define a specification

nodes.misconception: Pupils will know who their primary user is and will want to start designing.
nodes.response: Pupils need to find out more about the primary user and stakeholders so that they can define suitable and researched design requirements. This subsequently leads to successful design solutions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: User needs and wants considerations

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think they they need to know what they are designing and making straight away.
nodes.response: Pupils need to explore the context fully first to identify lots of possible design problems to solve before narrowing it down.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design opportunities

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will assume that they know how to manufacture their design without the need for a manufacturing specification.
nodes.response: Designs are rarely understood by verbal explanation, they need visual representations with specific details of materials, dimensions, finishes and suitable processes. Communication methods will vary depending on your design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacturing specification

nodes.misconception: Pupils often already know what they want to design and feel that their first prototype is the final solution that doesn't need further development.
nodes.response: The iterative journey transforms an idea into a successful product. Pupils should carefully explore, experiment, test, and develop ideas while keeping design requirements central to the process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Iteration

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to define a product that they wish to design and make at this point. They become fixated on a design.
nodes.response: Pupils need to keep their design brief open so that it does not create design fixation.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Define a design brief

nodes.misconception: Sketching is the only way to iterate design ideas.
nodes.response: Design ideas and iterations can be communicated using various techniques, such as sketching, CAD, prototyping, and AI.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Communicate ideas

nodes.misconception: Three design ideas are enough to avoid design fixation.
nodes.response: There are many ways to generate design ideas that avoid design fixation and produce a range of successful ideas that pupils can develop on their iterative journey.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Innovation

nodes.misconception: Modifications are often quickly generated by the student's personal opinions, rather than their evaluations.
nodes.response: Modifications should be informed from thorough testing and evaluation against design requirements with feedback from the primary user/stakeholders/experts.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluation and modifications

nodes.misconception: Testing only happens when the final prototype has been made.
nodes.response: Testing should happen throughout the iterative journey, so that design decisions are made to meet design requirements and produce a successful design solution.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing

nodes.misconception: Research only needs to take place at the start of the iterative design process.
nodes.response: Research is vital throughout the iterative design process and is not a linear activity. Pupils can research at any point to aid their design decisions and provide inspiration throughout the iterative process.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Research techniques

nodes.misconception: Students become so busy manufacturing their design solution that they often forget to evidence their manufacture.
nodes.response: It's easy to overlook the effort behind a product from the final photo. Documenting the manufacturing process highlights the skills, techniques, safety, and quality checks students use, proving their work, not the technician's.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacture

nodes.misconception: Pupils will use only their manufacturing specification when making.
nodes.response: Many pupils will struggle with time managment when manufacturing. Pupils need to plan out their time so that they can keep on track to meet their deadline whilst thinking about the operational elements.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning manufacture

nodes.misconception: External components must be used with microcontrollers to create control systems.
nodes.response: Microcontrollers have on board inputs and ouputs and connection points for additional external components.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Micro:bits in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: A light dependant resistor (LDR) only senses light levels.
nodes.response: An LDR's resistance changes depending on the amount of light it is exposed to. As the light level increases, the resistance decreases. This change in resistance can create a voltage change, which can be used as a signal to control an output.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Code and simulate Micro:bits in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: Designing with electonics must always involve physical components and circuits.
nodes.response: Designing with electronics can use physical components, schematics and CAD to test and iterate ideas.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Circuits in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: Iterations are only needed when a system doesn't work.
nodes.response: Systems are iterated to modify, fix, develop and improve.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop and modify code

nodes.misconception: Evaluating is one person's opinion.
nodes.response: Evaluating is most effective if it involves more than one person's opinion and data gathered from testing.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Test and evaluate a wearable product

nodes.misconception: Quality is only considered when the product has been completed.
nodes.response: Quality is considered at all stages of manufacture.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacture a wearable product

nodes.misconception: Only one method of integrating the components in a control system is used.
nodes.response: Different methods of integrating components can be combined, depending on the device's function and features.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Integrate a Micro:bit into a wearable product

nodes.misconception: Fabrics are always joined by stitching.
nodes.response: Fabrics can be joined using stitching, adhesives and mechanical fixings.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainable fabrics for wearable technology

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to define a product that they wish to design and make at this point. They become fixated on a design.
nodes.response: Pupils need to keep their design brief open so that it does not create design fixation.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Define a brief from design opportunities: saving space

nodes.misconception: Research into existing products is a secondary research task.
nodes.response: Primary research through the disassembly of a product can be extremely beneficial to really understand a product, its materials and how it is manufactured.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Disassemble flat pack furniture

nodes.misconception: Quality control and quality assurance is the same thing.
nodes.response: Quality control focuses on identifying defects in finished products, while quality assurance is about preventing defects through planned processes and systems during production.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Quality assurance when manufacturing: saving space

nodes.misconception: Using machinery to manufacture requires little skill when compared to using hand tools.
nodes.response: Using machinery to manufacture products takes skill and effort to achieve a high quaility finish, much like using hand tools.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Specialist techniques and processes for manufacture: saving space

nodes.misconception: Laser cutting is about cutting out simple shapes and only really works for 2D products and designs.
nodes.response: Laser cutters can be used to develop and manufacture effective and complex 3D products.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Laser cutting

nodes.misconception: Modelling only takes place with physical materials.
nodes.response: Virtual modelling using 3D drawing software can help to see ideas in 3D and enables quick and easy iteration.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design development with CAD: saving space

nodes.misconception: Once a design has been decided upon, it cannot be altered.
nodes.response: A design can continue to be altered, even when at the manufacturing stage.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design for manufacture: saving space

nodes.misconception: Modelling using CAD is the final step in the development of designs.
nodes.response: CAD is part of the iterative process. CAD should be used as a way to develop your idea by viewing it virtually and analysing the idea. Sketching over your CAD drawings can help to develop the idea before going back to make those improvements in CAD.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Iterate with CAD: saving space

nodes.misconception: Hand tools are outdated and less accurate than power tools.
nodes.response: Hand tools offer high precision when used correctly, especially for detailed work.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Specialist tools and equipment for manufacture: saving space

nodes.misconception: Design ideas are produced through sketches and drawings.
nodes.response: 3D or physical modelling is a great way to get design ideas out of your head. It is sometimes easier to work out your idea in 3D rather than worrying about whether you can draw it in 3D, especially if its form is complex.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketch modelling: saving space

nodes.misconception: The final evaluation is based upon the designer's perspective of the prototype and design process.
nodes.response: Testing and evaluations from the user and target market are essential to ensure the product meets the clients needs but is also commercially viable.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluation of market and user testing: saving space

nodes.misconception: A design portfolio should only include your best work and your best ideas.
nodes.response: A design portfolio should show the journey of the designer including all of the ideas that were not taken through or were not successful.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital Media Presentation: saving space

nodes.misconception: Timbers need a varnish to protect them.
nodes.response: There are many different options to finish the surface of timber and these are chosen depending on the type of timber, intended use, planned aesthetics etc.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface treatments and finishes: saving space

nodes.misconception: Using standardised components limit creativity and originality in design.
nodes.response: Standardised components can actually enhance innovation by allowing designers to focus on customisation, functionality, and efficiency while reducing costs and production time.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Standardised components

nodes.misconception: Pupils may come with an idea or even a solution at this stage and stick with it as they feel they do not need another idea.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to explore a range of ideas and possibilities to avoid design fixation and prepare them for the NEA.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore the context and avoid fixation

nodes.misconception: The life cycle in product design ends once the product is sold to the consumer.
nodes.response: The product life cycle includes stages beyond purchase such as: use, maintenance, and disposal or recycling. Sustainable design considers the entire life cycle to minimise environmental impact.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Life cycle assessment of flat pack furniture

nodes.misconception: Iterations of models are purely based on the thoughts of the designer.
nodes.response: Iterations can be based off a range of analysis and evaluations such as evaluating against the users needs and wants as well as direct feedback from the user.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Iterate with modelling: saving space

nodes.misconception: Commercial viability only relates to how well a product works.
nodes.response: A product can work well or be aesthetically pleasing, but if it’s too expensive to make, doesn’t meet market demand, or won’t sell at a profit, it isn’t commercially viable.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Commercial viability: saving space

nodes.misconception: Once a final product is complete, no further improvements are needed.
nodes.response: Designers constantly seek to improve and develop their designs and products, no product is ever perfect.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluate and refine processes

nodes.misconception: When you are creating a batch of the same design then you have to consider quality control checks as much as when you are creating a one off design.
nodes.response: Quality control is just as important in batch production as it is in one-off designs. Consistency across all items in the batch depends on regular checks to ensure each piece meets the same standard.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Batch production

nodes.misconception: Using a hot glue gun to join timbers for a final assembly is a durable method of joining.
nodes.response: Hot glue is not strong enough for a final timber assembly. It is more suitable for temporary joins, as it can weaken over time. For secure, durable joints, use screws, joints or wood glue instead.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Batch assembly

nodes.misconception: Pupils should design individually, and time should be taken when creating and thinking about design ideas.
nodes.response: Designers work in teams and collaborate to create design ideas. Working quickly when generating design ideas can prevent overthinking and allows freedom and creativity to lead the way.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Collaborative design for batch production

nodes.misconception: Quality control are checks that are done on products once made to ensure they are a high enough quality to be sold or used.
nodes.response: Quality control checks are done throughout the process to ensure quality is a constant.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Quality control and production planning

nodes.misconception: Manufacturing specifications only include dimensions and materials.
nodes.response: Manufacturing specifications also include finishes, safety requirements, assembly instructions and what tasks need completing. These details ensure that a product is made correctly, safely, and consistently.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacturing specifications

nodes.misconception: Softwoods are soft and light, hardwoods are hard and heavy.
nodes.response: The terms softwood and hardwood don’t refer to how soft or hard the wood is. They classify trees based on their seed type. Many softwoods are softer than hardwoods but it's not a strict rule. Balsa is a hardwood, but it’s one of the softest woods.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Timbers properties, sources and stock forms

nodes.misconception: All products are made in a factory on a production line using machines in their thousands.
nodes.response: Products can be maufactured in a factory using machines. They can also be manufactured by hand or using machines in a workshop. Products are made in varying amounts, this depends on their function, purpose and materials used.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Scales of production

nodes.misconception: Exploring the context should happen quickly so that you can get to the most important phase of designing.
nodes.response: Designing is an important phase. However, taking the time to really explore the context and understand the users needs and wants will provide solid foundations for successful designing.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore contexts and empathise

nodes.misconception: User feedback is just opinions, it’s not useful when developing designs.
nodes.response: Feedback is largely based on opinions. However, it provides real world insight into how people interact see, understand and would use a design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop ideas using feedback

nodes.misconception: Design optimisation is the same as design development.
nodes.response: Design development is the bigger process of taking an idea and turning it into a final product. Optimisation is the specific part of development where you focus on preparing the design for making, creating the best version of your existing design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design optimisation

nodes.misconception: Product analysis leads to copying of designs.
nodes.response: Product analysis identifies successful features and those which can be improved, this can lead to inspiration for new or improved ideas.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Product analysis and quality standards

nodes.misconception: When your final design has already been decided, it is a waste of time reflecting back on the design journey.
nodes.response: Even though the final design may be decided, reflection is not about changing the outcome, it's about understanding how you got there, what you learned, and how you can improve in the future.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Present an idea

nodes.misconception: Redesigning and evolving existing products is not really designing and does not show any creativity or innovation.
nodes.response: Redesigning existing products is a part of design work and often requires significant creativity, insight, and innovation. Some of the most impactful design breakthroughs came not from inventing something new, but from improving what already exists.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Redesign

nodes.misconception: Smart materials are only for fun products like colour changing mugs.
nodes.response: Smart materials give designers and engineers exciting possibilities when developing new products. Possibilities often focus on function and/or form. For example, thermochromic materials can be used to indicate a temperature and warn users of danger.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Smart materials in design

nodes.misconception: Designing is only creative when innovative ideas are produced.
nodes.response: Designing is creative at every stage, not just when coming up with brand-new ideas. Creativity is also shown in solving problems, improving existing products, and making designs more user-friendly, sustainable, or affordable.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Product evolution and development

nodes.misconception: High-fidelity prototypes are only about appearance and surface finish.
nodes.response: High-fidelity prototypes are about realism in both look and function. They should operate as closely as possible to the intended product - or convincingly simulate that functionality.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: High-fidelity prototyping

nodes.misconception: Medium-fidelity prototypes are just “tidier” versions of low-fidelity ones.
nodes.response: Medium-fidelity is not about neatness - it’s about using stronger materials and semi-functional builds to test ergonomics and usability.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Medium-fidelity prototyping

nodes.misconception: Empathy just means “feeling sorry” for others.
nodes.response: Empathy is understanding someone’s perspective and experience to inform design.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Empathy and user understanding

nodes.misconception: Inclusive design and accessible design are the same thing.
nodes.response: Accessible design is about making sure people with disabilities can use something. Inclusive design is about making sure everyone can use it, by thinking about all kinds of differences, including mental health and wellbeing.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: What is inclusive design?

nodes.misconception: Prototypes must be polished or look like the final product.
nodes.response: Early prototypes are rough and quick - their purpose is to test ideas, not show perfection.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Low-fidelity prototyping

nodes.misconception: Refinement is just “making it look nicer.”
nodes.response: Refinement is purposeful change based on evidence; it improves inclusivity, usability, and overall function, not just appearance.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Iteration and refinement

nodes.misconception: Testing is only to prove that a design works.
nodes.response: Testing is equally about finding flaws and learning what doesn’t work; failures provide insight.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic testing and feedback

nodes.misconception: Testing is a one-off activity that only happens at the end of designing.
nodes.response: Testing is an iterative process - it happens throughout development. Each round of testing reveals new insights and informs further refinement.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced testing and feedback

nodes.misconception: Mental health and wellbeing challenges are too personal or 'invisible' to be designed for.
nodes.response: Designers don’t solve mental health itself, but create supportive products, services, or environments that ease challenges.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying challenges and opportunities

nodes.misconception: The first idea is always the best.
nodes.response: Creativity improves with divergent thinking and iteration - the first idea is rarely the final one.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Idea generation

nodes.misconception: If a prototype works, it can definitely be manufactured successfully.
nodes.response: Functionality doesn’t guarantee feasibility or success. A design might work in one-off form but fail in cost, scale, or sustainability when made commercially.
nodes.subject: design-technology
