nodes.lessonTitle: Considerations for production

nodes.misconception: Research is just “copying” existing designs.
nodes.response: Designers critically analyse existing solutions to understand strengths/weaknesses for inspiration of new ideas.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Using research to inform design requirements

nodes.misconception: The most aesthetically-pleasing idea is the best.
nodes.response: Strong design choices balance creativity with inclusivity, feasibility, and impact - aesthetics alone aren’t enough.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Idea evaluation and selection

nodes.misconception: Inclusive design only applies to disability or accessibility-related products.
nodes.response: Inclusive design applies to everyone. It’s about designing for human diversity - age, ability, background, culture, and mental wellbeing - across all industries.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Inclusive design in industry

nodes.misconception: Polymers can all be recycled and are therefore environmentally ok.
nodes.response: Polymers are usually made from non renewable resources and even if recycled, are not sustainable.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Polymers properties, sources and stock forms

nodes.misconception: Inclusive design only benefits users with a disability.
nodes.response: Inclusive design benefits all users, not just those with disabilities. It aims to create products that as many users as possible can use.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Anthropometrics

nodes.misconception: Models are the final design.
nodes.response: Iterative design uses prototypes to model and test ideas, gather feedback and improve.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Foam modelling techniques

nodes.misconception: Designers can create successful products based on their preferences and abilities.
nodes.response: To have empathy for someone helps designers create better products because they understand users' needs, challenges, and feelings, leading to more useful and user-friendly designs.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Empathy

nodes.misconception: User needs and wants are the same thing.
nodes.response: Needs are the essential features required for the product to function, while wants are additional features that aren't necessary but would enhance the product if included.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Model accessible controllers

nodes.misconception: Cardboard is a weak material that is not suitable for modeling.
nodes.response: Cardboard has a fluted layer that increases its strength and rigidity. Modelling techniques, such as layering, can be used to increase its strength further, making it a versatile and very good material to model with.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Cardboard modelling techniques

nodes.misconception: Iteration is only needed for poor designs.
nodes.response: All designs can benefit from testing, feedback and iteration.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Ergonomic testing and design development

nodes.misconception: Ergonomics is just about the size of a product.
nodes.response: Ergonomics is the relationship between the user and the product, including its size, how well it fits and interacts with the body, and how easy and comfortable it is to use.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Ergonomics

nodes.misconception: Reforming is the same as deforming.
nodes.response: Reforming changes the state AND the shape; solid, liquid and back to solid. Deforming only changes the shape; the materials always remain a solid.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Reforming manufacturing processes

nodes.misconception: Cutting is the only form of removing material.
nodes.response: Removing material can include cutting, drilling and the use of abrasive papers and tools.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Wasting manufacturing processes

nodes.misconception: Wood, plastic and fabric are the correct terminology
nodes.response: Timbers and boards, polymers and textiles are the correct terms
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Materials in design

nodes.misconception: There is only one suitable material for each product.
nodes.response: There are many different materials which can be suitable once a choice has been made; it is important to explain and justify this.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Material selection

nodes.misconception: Recycling is good for the environment.
nodes.response: Recycling ensures that materials are useful for longer before being discarded, but the processing is an envionmental cost.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Material sustainability

nodes.misconception: Glue guns are a better adhesive than PVA glue for timbers.
nodes.response: This is not always true. PVA absorbs into the timbers and creates a good bond. Glue guns may add thickness to the join.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Fabricating manufacturing processes

nodes.misconception: Minimising waste means reducing the size of a product.
nodes.response: Using materials efficiently can be achieved by reducing size, but also by working accurately. This can be done by using stencils / templates, tesselation and nesting.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Minimising material waste

nodes.misconception: Laminating is when paper or card are covered in clear polymer.
nodes.response: Laminating means sticking several layers of material together, the clear polymer coated paper or card process is encapsulation.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Deforming manufacturing processes

nodes.misconception: Environmental impact only occurs when products are disposed of.
nodes.response: Circular economy and LCA consider the environmental impact at every single stage of a product's life cycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Life Cycle Assessment

nodes.misconception: Circular economy only means recycling.
nodes.response: The circular economy can be defined as products and materials being kept in circulation and not becoming waste. Design decisions within circular economy can be generated through consideration of 6 Rs: recycle, reuse, rethink, refuse, repair, reduce.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Linear versus circular economy

nodes.misconception: The only environmental decision at the manufacture and materials processing stage is the choice between renewable/non renewable sources of energy.
nodes.response: Environmental decisions include sources of energy, use of recycled materials, sustainable land management such as deforestation, pollution including water pollution and transportation. During manufacture, ethical impacts should also be considered.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacture and materials processing

nodes.misconception: The only way to reduce environmental impact at the distribution stage is through using electric vehicles.
nodes.response: There are many ways such as designing flat pack, stackable and lightweight products, packaging materials options and choosing where to locate manufacture.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Distribution

nodes.misconception: Considering a product's energy use is the only way to design a sustainable product.
nodes.response: There are many other ways to design a product to be sustainable when in use, including designing products to grow with users, be adjusted, modularity, reused etc.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Product in use

nodes.misconception: Repair, maintenance and recycling is the sole responibility of the user.
nodes.response: Design decisions made at the design/redesign stage can determine the ease and ability of a product to be repaired, maintained and recycled.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Repair, maintenance and recycling

nodes.misconception: Sustainability decisions happen after the product has been designed.
nodes.response: At the design stage, designers have a huge responsibility to influence many other stages of a product's life cycle through their design decisions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design

nodes.misconception: Redesigning a product for the circular economy only means making it recyclable.
nodes.response: Redesign in the circular economy involves designing products to last longer, be repaired, reused, or upgraded to reduce waste throughout the product’s entire life cycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Redesign and rethink

nodes.misconception: Paper and boards are often seen as weak materials.
nodes.response: Many types of paper and boards are designed to be robust and durable, such as corrugated cardboard used for packaging.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Paper and boards properties, sources and stock forms

nodes.misconception: The only way to gain MA is by increasing the input force.
nodes.response: MA can be increased by increasing the distance from the fulcrum and the effort. For example, increasing the arm length on the handle of a flat head screwdriver when opening a can of paint.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Movement with mechanisms

nodes.misconception: Laser cutters burn or melt the materials they are cutting.
nodes.response: Laser cutters actually vaporise the material with high precision.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: CAM, automation and laser cutting

nodes.misconception: All models can be simulated successfully in Sim Lab.
nodes.response: Before being simulated in Sim Lab, models need to be well-designed and stable, considering static and moving parts.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design and simulate in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: Robots will take all human jobs in the future.
nodes.response: Robots can sometimes replace people in certain jobs, especially when the work is dangerous, boring, or very hard for humans to do. People will still be needed to design, build and program robots.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Modelling and assembling complex shapes in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: Any model can be 3D printed using fused filament fabrication 3D printing.
nodes.response: Design for manufacture rules need to be considered when 3D printing. Not all models are suitable.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: CAD to CAM in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: Simulating in Tinkercad is exactly like physical testing.
nodes.response: Tinkercad is excellent for digitally testing ideas, but you should always expect to make adjustments when you build the physical models.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Model a moving part in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: CAD applicatons like Tinkercad just allow you to recreate an idea or design as a digital version.
nodes.response: CAD applications like Tinkercad are great for creating ideas and designs in a digital 3D world. They can also help you test your design and even simulate how it could work.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: 3D Modelling in Tinkercad

nodes.misconception: Fairtrade is just the label on bananas.
nodes.response: Fairtrade is a system that ensures farmers and workers receive fair prices, decent working conditions and support for sustainable community development through trade.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Manufacture and materials processing: Fairtrade

nodes.misconception: Considering a product's energy use is the only way to design a sustainable product.
nodes.response: There are many other ways to design a product to be sustainable when in use, including designing products to grow with users, be adjusted, modular, reused etc.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Product in use: S H E uniform and Hippo Roller

nodes.misconception: Repair, maintenance and recycling is the sole responsibility of the user.
nodes.response: Design decisions made at the design/redesign stage can determine the ease and ability of a product to be repaired, maintained and recycled.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Repair, maintenance and recycling: Energee Saw

nodes.misconception: Environmental impact only occurs when products are disposed of.
nodes.response: Circular economy and LCA consider the environmental impact at every single stage of a product's life cycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Circular economy and LCA

nodes.misconception: Sustainability decisions happen after the product has been designed.
nodes.response: At the design stage, designers have a huge responsibility to influence many other stages of a product's life cycle through their design decisions.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Design: Spider boot and Jaipur foot

nodes.misconception: The only way to reduce environmental impact at the distribution stage is through using electric vehicles.
nodes.response: There are many ways such as designing flat pack, stackable, lightweight products, and location of manufacture.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Distribution: Better Shelter and wind-up radio

nodes.misconception: Redesigning a product for the circular economy only means making it recyclable.
nodes.response: Redesign in the circular economy involves designing products to last longer, be repaired, reused, or upgraded to reduce waste throughout the product’s entire life cycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Redesign: The Washing Machine Project

nodes.misconception: Students often 'think' they understand a context without having fully explored it.
nodes.response: Students need to be encouraged to fully explore a context so to understand it fully before moving onto designing. This is great practice for the NEA.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating contexts

nodes.misconception: Modern materials only provide advantages to designers and users.
nodes.response: Modern materials are often difficult and expensive to produce and are also difficult to recycle.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern material properties

nodes.misconception: Physical and working properties are the same.
nodes.response: Physical properties are the characteristics of a material, such as appearance and features.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical properties of materials

nodes.misconception: Hardness testing is destructive.
nodes.response: Although an indentation is left in the test piece, hardness testing is less destructive than many other working property tests, such as tensile testing.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing working properties of materials

nodes.misconception: The environmental impact of a material only happens when the product is thrown away.
nodes.response: A material’s environmental impact occurs at every stage of its life cycle; during manufacture, use and disposal.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: The environmental impact of materials

nodes.misconception: The cheapest material is always the best choice.
nodes.response: Material selection involves balancing multiple factors, such as strength, durability, weight, sustainability, and ease of manufacturing; in addition to cost.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Selecting materials for manufacture

nodes.misconception: All metals have similar properties.
nodes.response: When metals are grouped into ferrous, non-ferrous, and alloy metals, their properties are different.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Metal properties, sources and stock forms

nodes.misconception: Absorbent materials hold water on their surface.
nodes.response: Absorbency involves the liquid being drawn into the material.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Testing physical properties of materials

nodes.misconception: Physical properties and working properties are the same thing.
nodes.response: Physical properties describe inherent features (like density, colour, or conductivity), whereas working properties describe how a material behaves under stress (like flexibility, toughness, or hardness).
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Working properties of materials

nodes.misconception: The front view is always the most detailed side of the shape being drawn.
nodes.response: The front view is chosen based on the most informative and clear perspective, not necessarily the most detailed one.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw orthographic projections

nodes.misconception: When rendering the light source, location might not be correctly identified.
nodes.response: Start with real objects and a light source to help students visualise where the shadow and highlight would be. Get students to label where the light source is.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Rendering techniques

nodes.misconception: A cross-sectional drawing is just another drawing view, such as front or side.
nodes.response: A cross-sectional view is an internal view showing what the inside looks like when sliced through. It is is meant to reveal hidden details inside an object.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Cross-sectional drawings

nodes.misconception: Students might confuse isometric drawing with oblique drawing.
nodes.response: Use side by side comparisons to allow students to see the distinct differences.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Crating techniques

nodes.misconception: Orthographic views are are separate drawings and do not connect.
nodes.response: Explain that each view (top, front, and side) represents a different perspective of the same object.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret orthographic projections

nodes.misconception: The vanishing point can be anywhere on the page.
nodes.response: The vanishing point represents where everything in the distance seems to disappear to your eye. It's usually on the horizon line, which is where the ground and the sky meet.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: One point perspective

nodes.misconception: Rendering and sketching are the same process.
nodes.response: Sketching is like creating the blueprint or the structure of the 3D model. Rendering happens afterward and focuses on adding realistic appearances to the sketch, like making glass look transparent or wood look grainy.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Realistic rendering techniques

nodes.misconception: The parts in an exploded diagram can be positioned anywhere.
nodes.response: Parts should be placed along a centre line, positioned vertically or horizontally away from the centre.
nodes.subject: design-technology
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploded diagrams

nodes.misconception: Pupils may suggest ideas for main or non-finite clauses that cannot be done simultaneously.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to imagine the two actions and consider whether they can be done at the same time.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A new sentence structure: the non-finite complex sentence

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not include the subject of the non-finite clause at the start of the main clause.
nodes.response: Explain that the person doing the non-finite clause must be mentioned at the start of the main clause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the comma rules in non-finite complex sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that any use of a co-ordinating conjunction creates a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that sentences like 'We ate cheese and ham.' cannot be a compound sentence because it does not contain two main clauses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Four sentence types

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that commas are only used to demarcate clauses or for 'pauses'.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about the specific rules for comma use, including for clauses, in lists and between adjectives in ENPs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comma rules in four sentence types

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any sentence beginning with an -ing word contains a non-finite clause.
nodes.response: Emphasise that a non-finite clause is a subordinate clause so cannot make complete sense - 'Singing is great!' is not a non-finite clause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A new subordinate clause: the non-finite (-ing) clause

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that relative and adverbial clauses are two types of subordinate clause.
nodes.response: Emphasise that relative and adverbial clauses are both subordinate, but they are differentiated by their starting word and use in sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Two types of clause

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just retell the nursery rhyme exactly as it is in four sentences.
nodes.response: Explain that we are retelling 'Humpty Dumpty' as a story and need to add our own storytelling language and detail.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retelling a story

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often answer questions with one word answers.
nodes.response: Model to pupils speaking in full sentences and always provide speaking frames (this can be verbally) to support pupils answering in full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Asking and answering questions

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to give short, simple instructions and may add in too many steps.
nodes.response: Model short, simple instructions before children are asked to complete Task B. Share some non-examples of long or complicated instructions. Remind children to always stop and wait after each instruction.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Giving and following instructions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think verbs can only show 'doing'.
nodes.response: Verbs can show 'being' and 'having' as well as 'doing'. These are sometimes 'hidden' in contractions (I'm, she's, they've, we've).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Two types of clause, including subordinate clauses

nodes.misconception: Children may be unsure which noun or noun phrase the relative clause should be placed after.
nodes.response: The relative clause is placed after whichever noun or noun phrase it provides extra, relevant information about.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A new sentence structure: the relative complex sentence

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe using a co-ordinating conjunction always creates a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Using a co-ordinating conjunction only creates a compound sentence if the conjunction is joining main clauses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Three sentence types

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that using 'before' and 'after' always creates an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.response: These words often create phrases, rather than adverbial clauses; a clause requires a verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Two types of conjunction

nodes.misconception: Children may believe relative clauses can only be placed in the middle of sentences.
nodes.response: Relative clauses follow nouns/noun phrases; although we focus on the middle position in Y4, it can vary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A new subordinate clause: the relative clause

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that commas indicate a 'pause' in sentences, or 'taking a breath'.
nodes.response: Commas have a number of specific functions, several of which are covered in this lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comma rules in three sentence types

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that a relative clause starts with a being verb e.g. 'who is' or 'which was'.
nodes.response: We can use a whole range of verbs to start the relative clause e.g. 'who has', 'which sits', 'who likes'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the comma rules with relative complex sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that longer sentences are always preferable to short ones.
nodes.response: Emphasise that text cohesion is best served by variety and that short sentences have a significant role in writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Five sentence types

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have previously only seen a relative clause interrupting a main clause.
nodes.response: A relative clause can be placed after any noun it refers to, including at the end of a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New subordinating conjunctions and relative pronouns

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think any group of words following a verb is an object.
nodes.response: A noun, noun phrase or pronoun that directly follows a verb can be an object.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subject and object

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that any group of words that is not a main clause is a subordinate clause.
nodes.response: Emphasise that knowing the difference between clauses (groups of words that contain verbs) and phrases (groups of words that do not) is key.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Clause structure

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse an exclamatory phrase with an exclamation sentence.
nodes.response: A phrase is a group of words with no verb. Any simple sentence must include a verb. Verbs in exclamation sentences are often being verbs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Four types of simple sentence

nodes.misconception: Pupils add a word after the co-ordinating conjunction not a main clause.
nodes.response: A co-ordinating conjunction in a compound sentence must join two complete main clauses. Any main clause must make complete sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the comma rule in compound sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not recognise that different subordinating conjunctions have different meanings and uses.
nodes.response: Each subordinating conjunction has a specific meaning. Each subordinating conjunction is useful for different sentence contexts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subordination with 'as' in adverbial complex sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not know when to use a comma to demarcate between the adverbial and main clause.
nodes.response: If the adverbial clause is first in the sentence, a comma is placed after it. If the main clause is first, no comma is placed after it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the comma rule in adverbial complex sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils are confused with when to use a comma and when not to use a comma.
nodes.response: A comma is used before "but" and "or" co-ordinating conjunctions. A comma is used after the adverbial clause if it is first in the sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Compound and adverbial complex sentences revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that "because" is a co-ordinating conjunction.
nodes.response: There are three co-ordinating conjunctions that are most frequently used in English. These are "and", "but" and "or".
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Three ways for co-ordination in compound sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the adverbial clause always comes second in an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.response: The position of the adverbial clause can swap. The adverbial clause can come first or second in an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the comma rule in adverbial complex sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not recognise that an adverbial clause is one type of subordinate clause.
nodes.response: "Subordinate clause" is an umbrella term. Any subordinate clause is a group of words that contains a verb and does not make complete sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adverbial complex sentences

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they have written a compound sentence just because they have included 'and'.
nodes.response: Look at sentences on a balancing scale with 'and' in the middle. Highlight that both ideas either side of 'and' must make complete sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining with 'and'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that 'and', 'but' or 'or' in sentences always make a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that to be a compound sentence, each idea on either side of 'and', 'but' or 'or' must have equal weight.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Co-ordination three ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils might struggle to know whether 'and', 'but' or 'or' is best in a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Share and discuss many examples and non-examples where 'and', 'but' or 'or' works best in a sentence in comparison with the other options.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Co-ordination for text flow

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise when 'or' is joining two main clauses and when it is joining two words.
nodes.response: Show, explain and say aloud many examples of 'or' joining two main clauses in compound sentence examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining with 'or'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse commands and exclamations particularly if a command ends in an exclamation mark.
nodes.response: Spend time unpicking the features of both commands and exclamations in order to highlight the difference between the two.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exclamations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that 'but' can be used in any sentence and may not recognise where it is suitable.
nodes.response: Show compound sentence examples that use the same first idea and let pupils hear the different joining words in action with the second idea.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining with 'but'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to know when a command ends in an exclamation mark and when it doesn't.
nodes.response: Choose clear examples that model strong emotion and calm emotion and use tone and intonation to support understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Statements, questions and commands

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that whenever we use 'those' or 'this', we are using a determiner.
nodes.response: Demonstratives are only determiners if they are introducing a noun in a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Determiners: quantifiers and demonstratives

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to connect the determiner to the noun when adjectives are in between.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that adjectives describe nouns - can they spot the noun the adjectives describe to help them find the determiner?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Determiners: articles and possessive pronouns review

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that the function of some words (e.g. before/after) depends on context.
nodes.response: Emphasise that sometimes these words are acting as subordinating conjunctions and sometimes they start phrases.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Fronted adverbials: single words, phrases and clauses

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that using a being or having verb means they've written a sentence in each tense.
nodes.response: Being verbs as auxiliary verbs are for progressive tenses; having verbs as auxiliary verbs are for perfect tenses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Progressive and perfect tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all verbs are formed the same.
nodes.response: Some verbs in English are irregular like 'be', 'say', 'come', 'bring', 'catch', 'choose', 'do', 'drink', 'eat', 'find', 'keep' and 'leave'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any time a word ends with -ing, it is a verb in the progressive tense.
nodes.response: Sometimes, words ending -ing are acting as adjectives. We must look at the word before the word ending in -ing to check if it's a verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Progressive present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils might presume that the past participle is always the same as the simple past tense.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to hear what sounds correct, for example, 'it has flown off', 'it has flew off'. This should be 'it has flown off'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Perfect present tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think they have used the progressive tense simply by using a being verb like 'am'.
nodes.response: 'I am happy today.' Ask pupils why this is not written in the progressive tense. The being verb must help the main verb that ends in -ing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple and progressive tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe dashes and commas are used interchangeably in fiction writing.
nodes.response: We favour using dashes when we are showing a dramatic effect and commas when simply adding detail.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Parenthesis: brackets, dashes and commas

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to vary both words/phrases/clauses and time/manner/place/cause.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have access to examples of both the different structures and purposes of fronted adverbials.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Single words, phrases and clauses in fronted adverbials

nodes.misconception: The same words act as prepositions and adverbs or as prepositions and subordinating conjunctions.
nodes.response: Prepositions are followed by nouns; subordinating conjunctions are in clauses; adverbs modify verbs and adjectives.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Synonyms, antonyms, prepositions and adverbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that determiners always come directly in front of a noun.
nodes.response: Adjectives may be placed between the determiner and the noun to provide description.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Determiners: articles, possessive pronouns, quantifiers and demonstratives

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that any use of 'have' shows the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Remind children that 'have' can be used as a main verb as well as an auxiliary verb. For example, 'I have three pets' = main verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sentences in the perfect present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that there can only be one verb in a sentence.
nodes.response: Auxiliary verbs are 'helping' verbs that connect to the main verb to help change the tense or meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sentences in the simple present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that every single verb in a sentence always carries the same tense.
nodes.response: Avoid teaching that all verbs in a sentence always carry the same tense; maintaining tense does not always require this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sentences in the progressive present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe using a co-ordinating conjunction always creates a compound sentence.
nodes.response: Using a co-ordinating conjunction only creates a compound sentence if the conjunction is joining main clauses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subordination and co-ordination

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an idea starting with 'because' makes complete sense on its own.
nodes.response: Make sure that 'because' always begins the second idea so that pupils can hear that the idea does not make complete sense by itself.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subordination with 'because'

nodes.misconception: It can be difficult to think of sentences with 'so' and 'that'.
nodes.response: Provide lots of examples before expecting pupils to do this for themselves.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subordination with 'so' and 'that'

nodes.misconception: Some subordination joining words can join the same sentences as others e.g. 'because', 'so', 'when'.
nodes.response: Discuss this with pupils if it arises in the lesson and explain that they have different purposes within the sentence but can both function.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subordination five ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an idea starting with 'when' or 'if' makes complete sense on its own.
nodes.response: Make sure 'when' and 'if' are always presented as part of the second idea so that pupils can hear the idea does not make complete sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subordination with 'when' and 'if'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think expanded noun phrases are full sentences.
nodes.response: Clearly highlight that these groups of words are called phrases. Provide lots of exposure to phrases not sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adjectives: expanded noun phrases

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that proper nouns only have a capital letter at the start of a sentence.
nodes.response: Pupils will be exposed to a range of sentences in which proper nouns feature at the beginning, middle and end.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Nouns: common and proper

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any noun ending is 's' is a plural noun.
nodes.response: Pupils are exposed to singular nouns that end in the letter 's'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Nouns: singular and plural

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse adverbs with adjectives.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils are exposed to both throughout the lesson so that you can discuss the differences. Only focus on -ly adverbs to begin with.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adverbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with verbs being used in different tenses.
nodes.response: When introducing verbs, keep it simple by using the simple present tense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Verbs: doing verbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils might struggle to identify adjectives within a sentence and confuse them with other words.
nodes.response: They will only be exposed to adjectives that come before nouns initially so that they become confident in identifying and using them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adjectives: to describe

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to think of adjectives to compare two nouns.
nodes.response: Make use of physical objects, images and word banks to support them with generating vocabulary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adjectives: to compare

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to recognise 'being' verbs in sentences.
nodes.response: Identify being verbs by showing them in their simplest form, then eliminating the nouns and adjectives from the same sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Verbs: doing and being verbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused by the presence of modal verbs at the start of questions.
nodes.response: Explain that in questions the modal verb can come first followed by the person we're referring to, then the main verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using modal verbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe all verbs in a sentence are always in the same tense.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the lesson to draw out the point that to maintain sense, we sometimes vary the tense of verbs in a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing sentences in the simple present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spot progressive tenses in negative forms like 'won't be waiting'.
nodes.response: Highlight that we still have an auxiliary verb and an -ing verb even when a negative interrupts like in 'were not watching/aren't looking'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing sentences in the progressive present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the progressive and perfect tenses as both use an auxiliary verb.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the progressive uses 'being' auxiliary verbs and the perfect uses 'having' auxiliary verbs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing sentences in the perfect present tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the concept of 'obligation' tricky to grasp.
nodes.response: Explain that obligations are things we think we should do or that should happen or that others think we should do or should happen.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Modal verbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the concept of 'obligation' in relation to modal verbs.
nodes.response: Talk about how sentences are showing that the speaker thinks they or someone else are 'obliged to' do something.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Further study of modal verbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe any words after a verb are an object.
nodes.response: An object must be a noun, noun phrase or pronoun that the verb is done to directly.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the active and passive voice

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to maintain the correct tense when converting between active and passive.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider the different tense options and find the one that sounds best.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the active and passive voice

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that verbs based on 'to have' and 'to be' are **always** auxiliary verbs.
nodes.response: Emphasise that when these verbs are on their own, they are just a main verb - they only change the tense when acting as an auxiliary verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sentences in the simple, progressive and perfect present, past and future tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think some phrases are sentences because they can look longer than full simple sentences.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that simple sentences must contain a verb in order to make sense. Note that phrases are often adjectives and nouns.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Present tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to know the difference between facts and opinions.
nodes.response: Provide lots of examples and opportunities for pupils to share different opinions about things they are familiar with like TV programmes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Statements and questions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to link related ideas together.
nodes.response: Give some non-examples to show what it sounds like when two ideas are unrelated e.g. Dad baked bread and she missed her sister.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Joining using 'and'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think you use exclamation marks at the end of every command.
nodes.response: Clearly show pupils when and why an exclamation mark is needed with some commands but not others.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Questions and commands

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to change the verb into the correct form to fit the rest of the sentence.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities to practise saying and reading present and past tense sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Present and past tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recognise that an idea must make sense on its own.
nodes.response: Model identifying the two ideas lots of times throughout the lesson before challenging pupils to do this themselves.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Co-ordination with 'and'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure about the past tense form of some verbs, particularly irregular verbs.
nodes.response: Use a range of past tense irregular verbs in modelled sentences. Give pupils a sentence scaffold including past tense verbs for Task B.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Past tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to remember where to place the apostrophe when contacting some 'not' words.
nodes.response: All 'not' words lose the letter 'o' between 'n' and 't'. Check that pupils are not putting the apostrophe before the 'nt e.g. don't/do'nt.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for contraction and singular possession

nodes.misconception: Pupils can muddle which letters in the words the apostrophe should appear between.
nodes.response: Look at correct examples alongside non-examples and show and read non-examples so pupils can see or hear that they do not sound right.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for contraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify which noun belongs to another noun.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have a solid grasp of what a noun is and that they always identify the nouns in any example.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for singular possession

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly place the apostrophe in the singular or plural noun that possesses the second noun.
nodes.response: An apostrophe is placed before the s at the end of the first noun when it is a singular noun that owns the second noun. An apostrophe is placed after the s at the end of the first noun when it is a plural noun that owns the second noun.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for singular possession and for plural possession

nodes.misconception: All words that end in -s need an apostrophe before the -s.
nodes.response: An apostrophe before the 's' is only used for indicating possession in singular nouns, not for all words ending in 's'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for contraction and singular possession review

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the apostrophe is placed before the s at the end of the first noun.
nodes.response: Repeat many times that an apostrophe is placed before the s at the end of the first noun only when it is a singular noun owning something. An apostrophe is placed after the s at the end of the first noun when it is a plural noun that owns something.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for plural possession

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the informal term 'speech marks'.
nodes.response: 'speech marks' is a term that signals the same thing as 'inverted commas' i.e. the dialogue in a sentence, but it is better to use the grammatical term 'inverted commas'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Direct speech: inverted commas

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what 'speech first' means.
nodes.response: Explain that if the direct speech opens or comes first in the sentence with the reporting clause afterwards or second, this can be referred to as a speech first sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speech first: punctuation rules

nodes.misconception: Children may believe all plural nouns end in 's'.
nodes.response: Discuss the plural nouns that do not end in 's' such as children, women, mice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes for contraction, singular possession and plural possession

nodes.misconception: Pupils may omit the comma after the reporting clause, or they may use a comma to end the sentence.
nodes.response: Reinforce the point that commas are never used to close a sentence, even in speech second sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speech second: inverted commas and punctuation rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that both the reporting clause and the direct speech begin with a capital letter.
nodes.response: Emphasise that when the speech comes first, the reporting clause has no capital.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speech first: inverted commas and punctuation rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that words stay as prepositions irrespective of what follows them.
nodes.response: Some words are prepositions when followed by a noun phrase, but they can be conjunctions or adverbs in other circumstances.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Prepositions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe all words have an antonym e.g. chicken/duck; tree/plant.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that these are not strictly opposites - they are just different! Most antonyms are nouns and verbs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Synonyms and antonyms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may create what they believe are fronted adverbial clauses, but they may omit the verb.
nodes.response: It is not wrong to omit a verb (this creates a phrase), but encourage pupils to circle or highlight the verb in a clause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Fronted adverbials: phrases and clauses

nodes.misconception: Pupils may create a clause instead of a phrase by using a verb in their fronted adverbial.
nodes.response: This is not wrong, but explain to children we are focusing on phrases and words today.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Fronted adverbials: single words and phrases

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not spot a determiner if adjectives are used between the determiner and the noun.
nodes.response: Emphasise that adjectives can be placed between the determiner and the noun.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Determiners: articles and possessive pronouns

nodes.misconception: Pupils might use 's after words ending in 'ch', 'sh', 'ss' or 'x'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that apostrophes are used for contraction or possession and to make these nouns plural we need to add the correct suffix.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply turning nouns from singular to plural using the suffix "-es"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think 'y' is removed and replaced with an 'i', like with the suffix -ed.
nodes.response: Show that we end up with two 'i's in a row if this happens: fly becoming fliing, so we keep the 'y'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix "-ing", using alternative rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the ending is spelt how it sounds: 'iz'.
nodes.response: Show pupils that the ending is spelt with the suffix -es, even though it can sound different.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing nouns from singular to plural using the suffix "-es"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to change the letter 'f' to 'v' and may just add the suffix -es.
nodes.response: Share lots of examples and give pupils the chance to say the plurals aloud so that they can hear the different sounds e.g. wolfs, wolves.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing nouns from singular to plural using alternative rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that all verbs ending in 'y' follow the rule remove the 'y' and add -ied.
nodes.response: Look at examples that add -ed and remove the 'y' and add -ied.  Focus on the sound the 'y' is making and see if it is part of a digraph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix "-ed", using alternative rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying all of the rules for the suffix "-ing"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the -es suffix is always pronounced as 'is'.
nodes.response: Model saying words like 'dominoes' (domino-is) and 'wishes' (wishs) incorrectly. Talk about making meaning when we read and spell.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise changing nouns from singular to plural using alternative rules

nodes.misconception: Children can spell past tense verbs how they sound, ending them with 't', 'd' or 'id'.
nodes.response: Explicitly discuss the examples of words where the ending sounds different and remind pupils that the spelling is still -ed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix "-ed"

nodes.misconception: Children often make mistakes in their repeat copying of spelling words by not checking properly.
nodes.response: Show children how to check by moving a finger along each letter of the word, checking the original against the newly written version.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying all of the rules for the suffix "-ed"

nodes.misconception: Pupils often assume words ending in the suffix -ing indicate the present tense.
nodes.response: Refer to the Year 3 grammar lesson on 'being' verbs and give plenty of examples to show the verbs in both past tense and present tense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix "-ing"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all nouns can be made plural by adding an 's'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there are some other ways to show more than one, such as one mouse, two mice or one child, two children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing nouns from singular to plural

nodes.misconception: Pupils may add -es or -ies to all words ending in the letter 'y'.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that words ending in a vowel, then a 'y', follow a different rule. Remind them we just add -s to make them plural.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply turning nouns from singular to plural

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start using hyphens for all prefixes.
nodes.response: Emphasise that not all prefixes require a hyphen - some prefixes frequently use them, but others rarely do.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Hyphens and ellipsis

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use commas instead of semi-colons to separate detailed list items.
nodes.response: Reinforce the idea that it would be confusing to separate items containing commas using commas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Semi-colons: second function

nodes.misconception: Pupils may give a consequence instead of an explanation after the colon.
nodes.response: Ask the question 'why?' about the part of the sentence before the colon - the answer should be an explanation not a consequence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Colons: second function

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not place a main clause before the colon.
nodes.response: Emphasise that for questions and lists, we always have a main clause before the colon; for questions, we also have one after the colon.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Colons: first function

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to choose a position in which to interrupt a speech sentence.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think of the complete sentence they want to say and interrupt it at a comma.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speech three ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to place the apostrophe correctly after the 's' for plural possession.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the apostrophe is placed after the 's' when showing possession for plural nouns that already end in 's'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes: for contraction, singular possession and plural possession 2

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the concept of ideas being 'closely related'.
nodes.response: Semi-colons don't need to show cause and effect or contrast; they are versatile and we should interpret 'closely-related' broadly.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Semi-colons: first function

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the flexibility of punctuation for bullet points - often, it is optional.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of consistency - choosing a method and sticking to it. Only complete sentences require capitals and full stops.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Bullet points

nodes.misconception: Pupils may omit the commas from a speech interrupted sentence or include an extra capital letter.
nodes.response: Use the graphic included in the slides as a visual prompt for pupils when writing speech interrupted.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speech interrupted: inverted commas and punctuation rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include within brackets information that is essential to the sentence's coherence.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to cover the parenthesis in a sentence and see if what's left makes complete sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Parenthesis: brackets

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify where to add parenthesis in a sentence.
nodes.response: It is easiest to add parenthesis after nouns or verbs - encourage children to identify these if needed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Parenthesis: dashes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe all plural nouns end in s.
nodes.response: Emphasise that several very common plural nouns do not end in s - make a list of these to keep.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using apostrophes for contraction, singular possession and plural possession

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused with which direction to go when 'going over' for the m, n and r.
nodes.response: Explicit modelling and using a point in the classroom to direct the children. Check teacher tip.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of m, n and r

nodes.misconception: There is a tendency for children to form the letter z backwards.
nodes.response: Model with directions in the room -  'straight across towards the door, diagonally back to the window, straight across to the door again'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of v,w, x and z

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused about the direction to take when forming the letters o, g and q.
nodes.response: Be very explicit about going anti-clockwise, use a clock to emphasise this to the children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of o, g and q

nodes.misconception: Direction of movement for the s and e can be challenging.
nodes.response: Use the clock in the classroom to remind children of the anti-clockwise direction. Put arrows on the children's page to support.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of e, s and f

nodes.misconception: That g, y, p and q are x-height letters.
nodes.response: Model through the lesson that although part of the letter is x-height, they are not x-height letters as they have descenders.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practice of letters with descenders

nodes.misconception: Some children may ask why b, d, g, p, q and y are not x-height letters.
nodes.response: Use pictures of these letters to emphasise to the children that they have ascenders or descenders.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practice of x-height letters

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused about which of the tramlines to start and end b and p on.
nodes.response: Explicit naming of the start and end points and modelling of this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of b and p

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused about the direction to take when forming this letter.
nodes.response: Be very explicit about going anti-clockwise, use a clock to emphasise this to the children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of c, a and d

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off the page for the letter k.
nodes.response: Emphasis should be placed on 'keep your pencil on the page' when modelling this letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of h and k

nodes.misconception: That the letters h, b, d and k are x-height letters.
nodes.response: Modelling through the lesson that although parts of the letter are x-height, they are not x-height letters because they have ascenders.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practice of letters with ascenders

nodes.misconception: Confusion on the direction for the 'curl up' on the y and j.
nodes.response: Be consistent with wording and modelling. Left direction is 'curl up' whereas 'flick' is when the direction is to the right.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of u, y and j

nodes.misconception: Letter families are letters that appear close to each other within the alphabet.
nodes.response: Letters are within the same letter family if they are formed in a similar way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of i, l and t

nodes.misconception: Many children will not securely use the correct pencil grip.
nodes.response: Ensure to spend sufficient time checking children's pencil grip and intervening where they need extra support.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to skills and patterns

nodes.misconception: The 'ee' sound can also be spelt 'ei' as opposed to 'ie' e.g. receive. This is far less common.
nodes.response: Children will learn the 'i before e except after c' rule later, but there are other exceptions. e.g. caffeine, protein, either.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'ee' spellings, including 'e', 'y', 'ie' and 'ey'

nodes.misconception: Common exceptions words which are hard to sound out e.g. 'could' , 'would' and 'should'.
nodes.response: Mnemonic devices such as 'Oh (o) you (u) lucky (l) duck (d)' can support memorising these trickier spellings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'igh' spellings, including 'ie', 'y' and 'i'

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘a’ in it e.g. shared.   ‘A’ can be pronounced in different ways.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to stretch each word when reading to help hear the 'ay' sound e.g. s-t-a-b-le vs sh-are-d
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'ay' spellings, including 'a', 'eigh' and 'ey'

nodes.misconception: Common exceptions words which are hard to sound out e.g. 'great' 'break' 'steak'.
nodes.response: Put these words into sentences and explain that often we have to learn to spell them by sight because spellings rules don't apply.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'ay' spellings, including 'a', 'eigh' and 'ey'

nodes.misconception: The 'oo' and 'yoo' sound are often confused.
nodes.response: Show examples of words where the same grapheme is making the 'oo' and the 'yoo' sound. Give practice reading aloud to hear the difference.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'oo' spellings, including 'ue', 'ui' and 'ou'

nodes.misconception: 'oe' and 'o' can be commonly confused because they often appear at the end of words.
nodes.response: Draw attention to how rare the 'oe' spelling is and that the 'o' spelling at the end has limited use in high frequency words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'oa' spellings, including 'o' and 'oe'

nodes.misconception: Confusion of 'now'/'know' and 'new'/'knew'. 'Ow' can be pronounced in different ways.
nodes.response: Teach examples of silent letters explicitly and get children to keep an eye out for them in their wider reading.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'oo' spellings, including 'oo', 'ew' and 'u-e'

nodes.misconception: Spelling rules are often found within root words, leading to confusion when suffixes are added.
nodes.response: Show examples of root words alongside words with suffixes added e.g. float and floating.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings 'oa', 'ow' and 'o-e' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: The 'ea' and 'ee' spellings are commonly confused.
nodes.response: Be clear that these spellings cannot be used interchangeably. It's important to learn the spellings of words individually to avoid mistakes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'ee' spellings, including 'ee', 'ea' and 'e-e'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may read the 'ow' in words such as 'below' and 'snow' as an 'ou' sound, such as in 'growl'.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that when the 'ow' digraph appears at the end of the word, it is typically making an 'oa' sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'oa' spellings, including 'oa', 'ow' and 'o-e'

nodes.misconception: Some children will not see connections between words in word families, like friend and friendship.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the link between friend and friendship.  If you can spell friend, you can also spell friendship.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'er' spellings, including 'or' and 'ear'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spell 'put' and 'Christmas'.
nodes.response: Point out the naughty letter 'u' in put and 't' in Christmas. The root word 'Christ' is in Christmas, but it's pronounced differently. In some accents, the 'u' in 'put' may not be an exception.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings 'oo', 'ew' and 'u-e' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: Common exception words which are hard to sound out e.g. 'there' and 'where' may be misspelt.
nodes.response: Put these words into sentences and explain that often we have to learn to spell them by sight because spellings rules don't apply.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings ‘igh' and ‘i-e' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘e’ in it and associate it with the long vowel 'ee'.
nodes.response: Teach that ‘e’ can be pronounced in different ways. Emphasise that in most words, the 'e' is making an 'e' phoneme.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'ee' spellings, including 'e', 'y', 'ie' and 'ey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘i’ in it e.g. carried. ‘I’ can be pronounced in different ways.
nodes.response: Always tell children to read the word with the most common phoneme for the grapheme and check if it makes sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'igh' spellings, including 'ie', 'y' and 'i'

nodes.misconception: Even is an exception to the rule when looking at generalisations for the e-e split digraph.
nodes.response: Explicitly refer to this during teaching and ensure practise is given to spelling exception words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings 'ee', 'ea' and 'e-e' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: The 'ou' and 'ui' spelling can be pronounced in different ways e.g. suit vs build or soup vs shout.
nodes.response: Be explicit with children about these different pronunciations and give them the opportunity to read words out loud to check.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'oo' spellings, including 'ue', 'ui' and 'ou'

nodes.misconception: Homophones - using the wrong spelling of a word containing the 'ay' sound e.g. plain vs plane.
nodes.response: Use of images alongside sentences and contexts containing the correct spelling is helpful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings ‘ay', ‘ai' and ‘a-e' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: There are certain spelling exceptions to the general rules taught in this lesson.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach some of these exceptions ('crayon') and explain the addition of suffixes to root words ('playing' or 'rained').
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The ‘ay' spellings, including ‘ay', ‘ai' and ‘a-e'

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think spelling generalisations are always true e.g. 'er' found at the end.
nodes.response: Careful with wording.  Say 'ir' and 'ur' are 'often' not 'always' found in the middle.  Show a familiar exception to the rule if necessary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'er' spellings, including 'er', 'ir' and 'ur'

nodes.misconception: There are a number of homophones in this lesson. Time and thyme. Sight and site.
nodes.response: Do explicitly teach these to children if they come up. Use images and sentence contexts to show how each spelling can be used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'igh' spellings, including 'igh' and 'i-e'

nodes.misconception: The digraph 'or' and trigraph 'ear' also make different long vowel sounds.
nodes.response: Remind children that the same grapheme (digraph and trigraph) can represent different sounds.  Say the words out loud to check.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'er' spellings, including 'or' and 'ear'

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘o’ in it and associate it with the long vowel 'oa'.
nodes.response: Teach that ‘o’ can be pronounced in different ways. Emphasise that in most words, the 'o' is making an 'o' phoneme.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'oa' spellings, including 'o' and 'oe'

nodes.misconception: In the dictated sentence, pupils may write the word 'its' with an apostrophe for posession.
nodes.response: Explain this word is an exception and an apostrophe is only used for the contracted form of 'it is'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings  'er', 'ir' and 'ur' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think 'y' is removed and replaced with an 'i', like with the suffix -ed e.g. carry
nodes.response: Show that we end up with two 'i's in a row if this happens: fly becoming fliing, so we keep the 'y'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ing to verbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think that all verbs ending in 'y' follow the rule remove the 'y' and add -ied.
nodes.response: Look at examples that add -ed and remove the 'y' and add -ied. Focus on the sound the 'y' is making and see if it is part of a digraph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ed to verbs

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may overgeneralise applying regular -ed rules to irregular verbs such as 'buy' -'buyed'.
nodes.response: Expose pupils to irregular past tense verbs in reading activities, encourage them to use mnemonics and hunt for words in sentences together.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling further words with the suffix -ed

nodes.misconception: You can hear the 'ee' in all words ending in -ious and -eous.
nodes.response: You cannot hear the 'ee' in words ending -geous, like 'courageous' (the 'e' is making the 'soft g' sound) or words with 'xi' or 'ti'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -ous, including -ious and -eous

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling further words with the suffix -ing

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to spell the root word or stem.
nodes.response: Ensure to focus on all the difficult elements of the words presented, not only the -ous ending that demonstrates the spelling rule.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ous to words

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the meaning of words encountered in the lesson.
nodes.response: Ensure to gloss the meaning of all vocabulary used in the lesson and say in full sentences to help embed the meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ate to words

nodes.misconception: Children cannot remember the dictated sentence because it is too abstract.
nodes.response: Give context to the sentence, such as imagine someone is applying to be part of a netball team. This is what the coach asks. Add images.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ify to words

nodes.misconception: Children may spell words with the suffix -en as they sound with 'in' or 'n'.
nodes.response: Explicitly draw comparisons to how words encountered are spelt and how they sound, particularly when there are differences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -en to words

nodes.misconception: Children do not know the associated root words.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand the meaning of all root words used with the suffix -ous and practise saying them in sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -ous

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know or understand the meaning of many words encountered in the lesson.
nodes.response: Put all unfamiliar vocabulary into simple sentences to expose children to the meaning.   Make links to root words where possible.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and applying all the rules for the suffix -ous

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the spelling 'ize' to represent the -ise suffix.
nodes.response: Explicitly reference the difference between how the word is spelt and how it is pronounced. In American English, the spelling -ize is used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ise to words

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused by sounds that use the same spellings, such as 'ar' and 'or'.
nodes.response: Remind children that the same sound can be represented in a number of ways and the same spelling can represent a  number of sounds.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the new 'or' spellings, including 'ore', 'ough' and 'a'

nodes.misconception: Children can confuse 'th' with 'f' and 'v' in some words because they pronounce it that way.
nodes.response: Focus on pronunciation of the sounds before spelling, and show the tongue moving forward for words with 'th' in them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling the 'o' sound after 'w' or 'qu'

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the 'rules' for the spelling will always help to choose the right spelling.
nodes.response: Explain that rules can help us a certain amount.  We also need to use our judgement of 'what looks right'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'or' spellings, including 'or', 'oor', 'au' and 'aw'

nodes.misconception: Autumn can also be assumed to have a capital letter, as the name of a season.
nodes.response: Explain that convention is generally not to capitalise the names of the seasons.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the spellings 'or', 'oor', 'au' and 'aw' in familiar words

nodes.misconception: Children may think 'ce' represents the 's' sound in 'ice' and 'face'.
nodes.response: Use sound buttoning as a strategy when you know it will reinforce the spelling pattern (it doesn't always work).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 's' spellings, including 'ss' and 'c'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to distinguish between decodable and common exception words.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the difficulties in spelling these words and give time to practise spelling these common exception words. Supplement the slides with any visuals linked to your school's SSP to support building on any learning from Rec and Y1.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling homophones and near-homophones

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure about what constitutes a long or short vowel sound.
nodes.response: Be very explicit about what is the short vowel sound, like 'e' in 'ledge' and what is a long vowel sound, such as 'ar' in 'large'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the 'j' spellings, including 'g', 'ge' and 'dge'

nodes.misconception: Children can often spell the past tense how it sounds, e.g. with a 'd' at the end rather than 'ed'.
nodes.response: Before writing the sentence, remind children that the suffix 'ed' can sound like 'd' or 'id' or 't'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Silent letters: the 'kn' spelling

nodes.misconception: Children can mix up the meaning of 'bought' and 'brought'.
nodes.response: Say the words in sentences several times to establish the meaning, and link to the present tense 'buy' and bring'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: New 'or' spellings, including 'ore', 'ough' and 'a'

nodes.misconception: When identifying spellings for 's', 'ce' and 'c' can be mixed up.
nodes.response: Use sound buttoning to help, especially when looking at words with split digraphs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 's' spellings, including 'se' and 'ce'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the vowel sound preceding the 'l' will always determine the spelling.
nodes.response: Showing examples of incorrect use of 'el' and 'le' alongside the correct can be very useful for children to spot the correct spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'l' spellings, including 'le' and 'el'

nodes.misconception: Some children might overemphasise the w in words containing 'wr' e.g. w-right for the word write.
nodes.response: Treat 'wr' as a digraph of the 'r' sound to avoid this confusion and orally segment and blend some words with the 'wr' spelling in.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Silent letters: the 'wr' spelling

nodes.misconception: 'ea' can be pronounced in a number of different ways (/ee/, /ay/, /e/)
nodes.response: Explicitly teach the most common spellings of the 'ea' spelling for the 'e' sound. Give time to practising both reading and writing them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling the 'e' phoneme with 'ea' and the 'ch' phoneme using 'tch'

nodes.misconception: Children can often spell the past tense how it sounds, e.g. with a 'd' at the end rather than 'ed'.
nodes.response: Remind children that the suffix 'ed' is often used to mark the past tense, even though it can sound like 'd' or 'id' or 't'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Silent letters: the 'mb' spelling

nodes.misconception: Children may be using 'ge' and 'dge' interchangeably.
nodes.response: Be very explicit about 'dge' being found alongside the short vowel and the 'ge' spelling being found alongside other vowel sounds.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'j' spellings, including 'g', 'ge' and 'dge'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the 'al' and 'il' spellings with other similar-sounding endings or 'l' spellings.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the irregularities and exceptions in English and use phonics, word games and pattern spotting to reinforce spellings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The 'l' spellings, including 'il' and 'al'

nodes.misconception: The 'gn' digraph does not always use the 'g' as a silent letter.
nodes.response: Expose children to words with 'gn' where the 'g' is both silent and not silent.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Silent letters: the 'gn' spelling

nodes.misconception: Many of these words are high frequency and common exception words.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the difficulties in spelling these words and give time to practise spelling these common exception words. Supplement the slides with any visuals linked to your school's SSP to support building on learning from Rec and Y1.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling more homophones and near-homophones

nodes.misconception: Forming a capital letter is just doing the lower case letter formation bigger.
nodes.response: Highlight every time the lower case and capital letter is different so it is clear the formation is different not just the size.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Matching lower case letters with their capital letters

nodes.misconception: Children may not use or know the letter names and rely on the phoneme the letter makes instead.
nodes.response: Use the teaching of the formation as an opportunity to revisit letter names vs. letter sounds (e.g. M vs. mmmm)
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of M, N, W and V

nodes.misconception: That capital letters are just bigger versions of the lower case letters.
