nodes.response: Emphasise that some lower case and upper case are similar but some look completely different.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of C, G, O and Q

nodes.misconception: Sometimes children can think days of the week are only capitalised if at the beginning of a sentence
nodes.response: Model and show examples of the days of the week in the middle of a sentence with a capital letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practice of capital letters and days of the week

nodes.misconception: The height of the vertical line is sometimes too short or too tall.
nodes.response: Emphasise starting the vertical line on the ascender line and finishing on the baseline.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of I, E, F, and L

nodes.misconception: Children recognise how 'Y' is typed on the computer and try to write it like that.
nodes.response: Discuss and show children different fonts and compare to how letters should look when we are writing them by hand.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of X, Y and Z

nodes.misconception: The capital letter 'K' may look like a lowercase 'k' (without the loop).
nodes.response: Emphasise where the diagonal lines need to go to and model using the capital 'K' in words, such as 'Kevin' or 'Kick the ball!'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of A, H, K and T

nodes.misconception: Drawing a large size j and dotting it to form the capital J.
nodes.response: Reminder that the capital J has a horizontal line across the ascender line.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of S, J and U

nodes.misconception: Sometimes these letters get reversed.
nodes.response: Emphasise the starting position and direction for each letter.  You could use 'landmarks' in your classroom, such as "Start by the window."
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of B, D, P and R

nodes.misconception: Pupils keep the 'e' when adding -y to words ending in 'e', writing 'slimey' or 'stoney'.
nodes.response: Focus on the rule, remove the 'e' and add -y, and make links to other suffixes that use the same pattern.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling adjectives with the suffix "-y"

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the spellings of homophones: eight and ate, weight and wait.
nodes.response: When you review the spellings of these words, ensure to identify that they are homophones and suggest ways to remember which is which.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling adverbs using the suffix "-ly"

nodes.misconception: All root words can take both suffixes -ful and -less.
nodes.response: Show a variety of words with suffixes -ful and -less.  Choose ones familiar to the pupils and put into sentences to demonstrate the meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes "-ful" and "-less"

nodes.misconception: Children see words as unconnected and so don't see the link between 'write' and 'wrote'.
nodes.response: Explicitly show how the spelling of connected words is linked, such as 'know' and 'knowledge' and 'write and 'wrote'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: spelling words with silent letters: "b", "w", "k" and "g"

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to double the consonant when adding the suffixes -er or -est.
nodes.response: Show non-examples when the consonant has not been doubled after a short vowel sound (hot-hotest). Explain how this alters our pronunciation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -er and -est using alternative rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to double the consonant after a short vowel, such as fun - funny.
nodes.response: Make links to other suffixes used, such as -ed or -ing, when the consonant is also doubled.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling adjectives using the suffix "-y"

nodes.misconception: Remind pupils to use the root word to help them spell the new word created by adding the suffix.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have a good understanding of the vocabulary. If they do not know the root word, they will find it harder to spell. Use images.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling -er and -est words with alternative rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that you can add -er or -est to any adjective and use it to make comparisons.
nodes.response: Make pupils aware that we cannot always add the suffix -er or -est to compare. For example, good - better - best or bad - worse - worst.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling words with the suffixes "-er" and "-est"

nodes.misconception: Children write words like 'basically' how they sound: 'basicly'.
nodes.response: Show the root words ending in 'ic' and how -ally is added.  Say the words how they are spelt to help remember.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix "-ly"

nodes.misconception: When practising spellings, children can practise wrong by copying out incorrectly.
nodes.response: Ensure to place emphasis on carefully looking and checking the spellings when practising.  This can be done individually or in pairs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling words with the silent letters "b", "w", "k" and "g"

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the -est suffix is spelt 'ist' or 'st' because that is what you can hear.
nodes.response: Review pupils' misconceptions after practice tasks. Even though the word can sound different, -est is always spelt in the same way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -er and -est

nodes.misconception: Children may spell words with the suffix -ful using a double 'l'.
nodes.response: Explicilty make the distinction between the word 'full' and the suffix -ful, which only has one 'l'.  Practise spelling both in a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling words with the suffixes "-less" and "-ful"

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not know the related root word or see how they are connected.
nodes.response: Put the /shun/ word and the associated root word into a simple sentence to help secure their meaning. This will help pupils see the connections in meaning and spelling between the words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffixes -cian, -sion and -ssion to represent /shun/

nodes.misconception: Children misspell the 'ough' letter string, like in 'thought' or 'fought'.
nodes.response: Use the phrase 'oh you grumpy hippo' to remember the sequence of letters: o u g h.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -ed to make the past tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the suffix is spelt with a double 'l' like the word 'full'.
nodes.response: Explicitly point out the difference between the spelling of 'full' and the suffix 'ful'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating adjectives using the suffixes -ful and -less

nodes.misconception: Pupils may spell words with -ize, how the suffix sounds and in the American spelling.
nodes.response: Discuss the difference between the American and British spelling of the suffix -ise.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Turning nouns and adjectives into verbs using the suffixes -ify and -ise

nodes.misconception: Children mix up the -ible and -able spellings.
nodes.response: Use the rules shown in the lesson: Is there is a recognisable root word without the ending? Is this a modern word?  Is there a related word ending in -ation? These will all help to identify the -able spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -able

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume all words ending in -ible do not have a root word.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that some words such as sensible do have a recognisable root word in English (sense).  However, other -ible words do have roots (stems) but not whole 'words' from English, they may be Latin roots, such as 'vis'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -ible

nodes.misconception: Many pupils misspell words with multiple syllables when choosing to double or not double the consonant.
nodes.response: Start off with simple examples of the rule, using single syllable words with short vowels to secure the doubling first, before moving on to multisyllabic words. Focus on the most commonly used words first.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix "-ing" to make the present and past tenses

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that all nouns are a person, place or thing that you can touch.
nodes.response: Show a range of different nouns, including common and abstract nouns. Show that they can be described with an adjective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Turning adjectives into nouns using the suffixes -ity and -ness

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use 'ck' to representing the 'c' phoneme at the end of the word after a short vowel, like 'stick' and 'trick'.
nodes.response: Explain that in most words where the 'c' is at the end, it is represented as 'ck'. As this is a suffix, it doesn't follow usual rules. If we can spot a root word, and know that the new word is an adjective it will most likely be spelt 'ic'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating adjectives using the suffixes -al and -ic

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to know which /shun/ spelling to use.
nodes.response: If needed, refer back to the Year 4 content where the /shun/ spellings are introduced initially. Emphasise that -tion is the 'best bet' and most common spelling and use that as the focus for the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -tion to represent /shun/

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss out the 'e' or 'a' in words ending in  -ery or -ary, as they are not always clearly pronounced.
nodes.response: Identify the endings -ary and -ery in focus words.  Say the words how they are spelt to help emphasise the vowel spellings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -ary and -ery

nodes.misconception: Children often use an apostrophe s, when they hear an 's' at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Remind children of the rules for using apostrophes.  Only use an apostrophe if you can name and recognise the rule - for omission or possession.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making plurals using the suffix -es and -ves

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to spell the root word of plural nouns in focus.
nodes.response: For children who need more support, provide the root word (singluar noun) as a starting point for Practise Task B, so they can focus on securing the rules around plurals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making plurals using the suffixes -s and -ies

nodes.misconception: Children mix up the vowel spellings in the words 'desperate' and 'separate'.
nodes.response: Saying the words slowly how they are spelt can help: sep-ar-ate, des-per-ate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Turning nouns and adjectives into verbs using the suffixes -ate and -en

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the correct punctuation for bullet points.
nodes.response: There are very few hard-and-fast rules; the key is to select consistent punctuation throughout the list.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Colons, semi-colons, hyphens and bullet points revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that only single main clauses can be joined by co-ordinating conjunctions.
nodes.response: Co-ordinating conjunctions can join groups of words that might be sentences on their own, including at least one main clause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple and compound sentences revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not grasp that the different types of subordinate clause are all subordinate clauses.
nodes.response: Reinforce the point that these are sub-types of subordinate clause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adverbial, relative and non-finite complex sentences revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that a passive sentence always contains the old subject of the active sentence.
nodes.response: Sometimes the old subject is removed completely like in this example: 'We passed the ball.' > 'The ball was passed.'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Subject, object, active voice and passive voice revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a comma to separate any main and subordinate clause.
nodes.response: When an adverbial subordinate clause comes after a main clause, no comma is needed; relative subordinate clauses don't always need commas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Commas, brackets and dashes revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to correctly use the apostrophe for plural possession.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that whenever the noun doing the possessing ends in s, the apostrophe goes after the s.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Apostrophes and speech punctuation revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all verbs in a sentence are always kept in the same tense.
nodes.response: Constantly encourage children to think about what 'sounds right' in a sentence and to try out different verb forms orally to see what works.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple and progressive tense revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see adverbs as doing more than saying 'how' verbs are done.
nodes.response: Adverbs modify verbs by saying when, where, how or to what extent they are done - encourage pupils to look for words that modify the verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Word class revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused between progressive and perfect tenses.
nodes.response: Focus on the auxiliary verbs and main verb forms - 'to be' vs 'to have' and -ing forms vs past tense forms.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Perfect tense revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify prepositions within a sentence & distinguish them from determiners.
nodes.response: Prepositions always come before a noun or noun phrase to say when, where or why; they are distinct from determiners, which show specificity.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Further word-level revision

nodes.misconception: Pupils often don't notice that they have written a phrase showing belonging.
nodes.response: Give chances to edit looking explicitly for where an apostrophe for possession is missing. Spot apostrophes in sentences when reading.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the apostrophe for singular possession

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all nouns can be made plural by adding an 's'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there are some other ways to show more than one, such as one goose, two geese or one child, two children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding '-es' to nouns ending in 'y'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the connections between words with the same root and mis-spell them.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the root word when spelling the new word.  'Happy' is connected to 'happier'.  They both have a double 'p'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -er

nodes.misconception: Children may form the apostrophe incorrectly - back to front or locate it at the wrong height.
nodes.response: Spend time practising how and where to write the apostrophe, so that it is the correct height and orientation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with contracted forms

nodes.misconception: Children hear 'd', 't' or 'id' at the end of the word and spell it that way.
nodes.response: Explain that sometimes the ending sounds like ‘t’, ‘d’ or ‘id’ but it is still spelt with the suffix -ed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -ed

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the suffix only has one 's', like the suffix -ful, which only has one 'l'.
nodes.response: Draw a direct comparison: '-less' is how we would expect it to be spelt, whereas '-ful' is surprising and only has one 'l'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -less

nodes.misconception: Children may assume the rule applies to all verbs with no exceptions.
nodes.response: Remind children that rules are for most spellings, but not all. There are exceptions to the taught rule such as I play - She plays.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding '-es' to verbs ending in 'y'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all words ending in -ly are adverbs.
nodes.response: Explain there are also  adjectives that end in -ly, like friendly, lonely, or lovely.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -ly

nodes.misconception: Children can think the suffix is spelt like the word 'full' with a double 'l'.
nodes.response: Explicitly discuss the difference in spelling, and provide opportunities to look at words and identify those with the suffix in them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -ful

nodes.misconception: Some children will think that all words ending in -tion should have a recognisable root word.
nodes.response: Show some words ending in -tion that don't have recognisable root words, e.g. potion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the 'tion' spelling

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to generate a sentence with these nouns in, such as improvement or darkness.
nodes.response: Model all the focus words simply and clearly in sentences to help demonstrate the meaning and their place within a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -ment and -ness

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't see the spellings of words with the same root word as connected.
nodes.response: Explicitly show how the spelling of the root word stays the same when the prefix is added.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling the prefix un-

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the -est suffix is spelt 'ist' or 'st' because that is what you can hear.
nodes.response: Review pupils' misconceptions after practice tasks.   Even though the word can sound different,  -est  is always spelt in the same way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -est

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Doubling the consonant with suffixes: -ing, -ed, -er, -est and -y

nodes.misconception: Children may think the 'y' should be replaced with an 'i' when the suffix is added.
nodes.response: Show that we end up with two 'i's in a row if this happens: fly becoming fliing, so we keep the 'y'. Regularly repeat the rules as chants.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and spelling suffixes: -ing

nodes.misconception: Children might confuse pairs of words against compound words. e.g. bus stop.
nodes.response: Give examples of both and model mistakes. e.g. write butterfly as butter fly and discuss.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling compound words

nodes.misconception: Children may use an apostrophe for plurals ending in 's'.
nodes.response: Explicitly look at non-examples where the apostrophe isn't used. Help the children to  identify when and why the apostrophe isn't used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words using the apostrophe for possession or contraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spell the root word.
nodes.response: As we are adding new learning, it's key to refer back to prior learning (in prior Y2 units as well as Rec and Y1). Refer back to learning in line with your school's SSP to support cognitive load, so pupils can focus on the suffix.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling 'tion'

nodes.misconception: Children cannot see how the words 'grave' and 'gravity' are connected.
nodes.response: Explain the different meanings of the word 'grave', including serious or heavy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -ity

nodes.misconception: Children may not know the meaning of some words reviewed, such a 'precision' or 'beautician'.
nodes.response: Explain the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary by giving a simple definition and applying in the context of a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: All of the /shun/ suffixes, including -tion, -cian, -sion and -ssion

nodes.misconception: Pupils mix up the double letters in 'disappear'.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that 'disappear' is made of the prefix dis- and appear.  That way, you know there will only be a single 's'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -al

nodes.misconception: Pupils spell the ending of professions 'cion'.
nodes.response: Focus on the difference between -ion and -ian endings.  Say the word how it's spelt to reinforce this: mu -si -ci -an.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The /shun/ suffixes, including -cian

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up the representations of 'l' and forget the representations which are most likely.
nodes.response: Frame the new learning on -al in the context of prior knowledge around representations of 'l', highlighting the most common representations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -al

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misspell the root of the word, rather than the suffix.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing what is unexpected or challenging about the stem of the focus words as well as the -tion endings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -tion

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that all nouns are a person, place or thing that you can touch.
nodes.response: Show a range of different nouns, including common and abstract nouns.  Show that they can be described with an adjective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating nouns with the suffixes -tion, -ity and -ness

nodes.misconception: Children may think the root word will help determine the spelling, but this does not always help.
nodes.response: Review links to root words when helpful, but encourage use of the rule about vowels and consonants to determine the spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The suffixes -cial and -tial

nodes.misconception: The children mis-spell words ending in -ness with root words ending in 'y'.
nodes.response: Focus on the pronounciation of the word.  Stretch it slowly: happ-i-ness. The 'i' can be heard clearly making the 'ee' sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -ness

nodes.misconception: Pupils miss out letters in 'century' because they cannot hear all the sounds.
nodes.response: Say the word slowly, as it is spelt, in order to empahsise all the letters: cen -tur -y.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The /shun/ suffixes, including -ssion

nodes.misconception: The wrong vowels are used in curriculum words: separate, popular and opposite.
nodes.response: Saying the words slowly 'how they are spelt' is a useful strategy to remember these tricky spellings, e.g. sep -ar -ate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffixes -cial and -tial

nodes.misconception: The curriculum words 'reigh', 'island' and 'February' can be mis-spelt, without the silent letters.
nodes.response: Practise saying the word how it is spelt, e.g. Feb-ru-ar-y.  Use the 'naughty letters' strategy to emphasise unusual letters in the words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The /shun/ suffixes, including -sion

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the -est suffix is spelt 'ist' or 'st' because that is what you can hear.
nodes.response: Review pupils' misconceptions after practice tasks. Even though the word can sound different, -est is always spelt in the same way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the superlative suffix -est

nodes.misconception: You can hear the 'ee' in all words ending in -ious and -eous.
nodes.response: You cannot hear the 'ee' in words ending -geous, like 'courageous' (the 'e' is making the 'soft g' sound).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -ous and -tious

nodes.misconception: Pupils will mistakenly use -ce endings for verbs instead of -se endings or vice versa.
nodes.response: Look at a selection of words that fit this spelling pattern and help them to recognise that -ce typically indicates a noun, whilst -se indicates a verb.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling more homophones

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the vowel sound preceding the 'l' will always determine the spelling.
nodes.response: Showing examples of incorrect use of 'el' and 'le' alongside the correct use can be very useful for children to spot the correct spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the spellings -le, -el and -il

nodes.misconception: Homophones sound the same so pupils may rely on previous spelling rules and so, spell them the same.
nodes.response: Spend time showing each word in a sentence, use images to support understanding and make sure each homophone is practised using a strategy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling further homophones

nodes.misconception: Children may think the root word will help determine the spelling, but this does not always help.
nodes.response: Review links to root words when helpful, but encourage use of the rule about vowels and consonants to determine the spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -cial and -tial

nodes.misconception: Pupils often incorrectly use an apostrophe when they hear an 's' at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the rules for using apostrophes. Only use an apostrophe if you can name and recognise the rule - for omission or possession.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming plural nouns using the suffix -es and -ves

nodes.misconception: Pupils will apply common plural rules to singular nouns that have irregular plural patterns.
nodes.response: Use spelling strategies such as 'big letters' or 'colour blocks' to help pick out the tricky elements of irregular plural spellings and embed them in the memory.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming irregular plural nouns

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to double the consonant when adding the suffix -er.
nodes.response: Show non-examples when the consonant has not been doubled after a short vowel sound (hot-hoter). Explain how this alters our pronunciation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the comparative suffix -er

nodes.misconception: Children misspell the 'ough' letter string, like in irregular past tense verbs 'thought' or 'fought'.
nodes.response: Use the phrase 'oh you grumpy hippo' to remember the sequence of letters: o u g h.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -ed to form the past tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know or understand the meaning of many words encountered in the lesson.
nodes.response: Put all unfamiliar vocabulary into simple sentences to expose children to the meaning. Make links to root words where possible.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -ous and -cious

nodes.misconception: Often the root of the word is hard to spell so this leads to incorrect spellings.
nodes.response: Discuss words that children find hard and look for root words that you recognise, or parts of the word that are difficult.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and applying the suffixes -cial and -tial

nodes.misconception: Pupils may pronounce homonyms incorrectly in sentences.
nodes.response: Show pupils that we can use the context of the sentence to help us uncover the meaning of the homonym and therefore its pronunciation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling homonyms

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to know which /shun/ spelling to use.
nodes.response: If needed, refer back to the Year 4 content where the /shun/ spellings are introduced initially. Emphasise that -tion is the 'best bet' and most common spelling and use that as the focus for the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -tion and -cian

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to spell the root word of plural nouns that are being focused on.
nodes.response: For pupils who need more support, provide the root word (singular noun) as a starting point for Practise Task B, so they can focus on securing the rules around plurals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming plural nouns using the suffix -s and -ies

nodes.misconception: Many pupils misspell words with multiple syllables when choosing to double or not double the consonant.
nodes.response: Start off with simple examples of the rule, using single syllable words with short vowels to secure the doubling first, before moving on to multisyllabic words. Focus on the most commonly used words first.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the suffix -ing to form the progressive tense

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up the representations of 'l' and forget the representations which are most likely.
nodes.response: Frame any new learning on -al in the context of prior knowledge around representations of 'l', highlighting the most common representations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words including the suffix -al

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not know the related root word or see how they are connected.
nodes.response: Put the /shun/ word and the associated root word into a simple sentence to help secure their meaning. This will help pupils see the connections in meaning and spelling between the words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -sion and -ssion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may select the wrong spelling for the wrong sentence.
nodes.response: Spend time talking about the meaning of the words as you come across them. Show pupils how to use the context of the sentence to help you decipher the meaning and if relevant, discuss its etymology.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling further near-homophones and homophones

nodes.misconception: Some children may think a letter string can only represent one sound.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the key phonics principles: a sound can be represented by more than one letter,  one sound can be represented by more than one spelling and one spelling can represent more than one sound.  It is why the English language is so hard!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Other sounds represented by the letter string ‘ie’

nodes.misconception: Homophones sound the same so pupils may rely on previous spelling rules and so, spell them the same.
nodes.response: Spend time showing each word in a sentence, use images to support understanding and make sure each homophone is practised using a strategy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling a selection of homophones

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the 'ei' spelling only represents the 'ee' phoneme.
nodes.response: Show a range of words with 'ei' representing different sounds.  You can stretch and sound button to show the direct phoneme - grapheme correspondence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Other sounds represented by the letter string ‘ei’

nodes.misconception: Children may find it very difficult to identify when 'fer' is stressed or unstressed.
nodes.response: Model saying the words with 'fer' aloud and stressing the appropriate syllable.  Ask pupils to copy you.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating the letter string ‘fer’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may select the wrong spelling for the wrong sentence.
nodes.response: Spend time talking about the meaning of the words as you come across them. Show pupils how to use the context of the sentence to help you decipher the meaning and if relevant, discuss its etymology.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling further homophones and near-homophones

nodes.misconception: When sorting 'ee' spellings, children can assume all the identified graphemes are making the 'ee' sound.
nodes.response: Stretch the 'red herring' words with an identified grapheme that makes a different sound e.g. qu-i-e-t.  The same spelling can represent a range of sounds.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating the ‘ee’ sound spelt ‘ie’ or ‘ei’

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to think of related words to create word maps independently.
nodes.response: Use a dictionary to support generating words and to check spelling.  This will help pupils to find words with different suffixes as the start of the spelling will be the same.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -ence and -ency

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think all words ending in -ent are the same word class.
nodes.response: Whilst the suffixes -ent and -ence can change word class, not all words ending in -ent are the same word class.  Give examples in a sentence to demonstrate, using the words contentment, (to) frequent, and silent.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -ent

nodes.misconception: Pupils may easily confuse the vowels in -ant and -ent spellings.
nodes.response: Say the word clearly how it is spelt in order to emphasise the vowel spellings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffix -ant

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty identifying the word class of focus words in the lesson.
nodes.response: Help the children to put the words into simple sentences in order to help identify the word class.  Is it a naming word for a person, place, thing or idea?  Is it describing a noun? etc.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -ance and -ancy

nodes.misconception: Children may not know how to pronounce focus words within the lesson, meaning they can't identify the stressed syllable.
nodes.response: Use 'my turn your turn' to ensure children can pronounce focus words correctly, and also put into sentences so they can understand the meaning and word class in context.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying spelling rules with the letter string ‘fer’

nodes.misconception: Children may choose the wrong spelling strategy to practise a particular word.
nodes.response: Help pupils to make informed choices about which spelling strategy is best to learn particular types of words.  For example, 'naughty letters' is useful to learn those with unusual spelling patterns.   Pupils will also develop their own favourites.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the rule ‘i before e except after c’

nodes.misconception: Pupils misspell the words with prefixes because they cannot spell the root word.
nodes.response: Draw attention to tricky elements of the root words as necessary, e.g. the 'ea' in healthy - unhealthy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling words with the prefixes "dis-", "non-", "mis-" and "un-"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start using these spellings in place of the most common spellings.
nodes.response: Emphasise that 'ay', 'ai' and 'a-e' are the most common spellings and tell pupils to try those out first.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling the 'ay' sound with 'a', 'eigh' or 'ey'

nodes.misconception: Every word with a prefix will have a root word that is recognisable, such as 'stroy' in 'destroy'.
nodes.response: Some words have roots that we will not recognise or no longer use.  Recognising the prefix can still help to spell and understand the word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes "de-", "re-", "sub-" and "super-"

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the difference between 'homophone' and 'homonym'.
nodes.response: Give specific examples of homophones (e.g. hair and hare) and homonyms (e.g. bark) and discuss the differences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and spelling homonyms

nodes.misconception: Children may forget the most common spellings and use the most recently learnt spellings.
nodes.response: Always emphasise prior learning. Show examples of words including incorrect and correct spellings to discuss (e.g. train and trean).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling the 'ay' sound with 'ei' or 'ea'

nodes.misconception: All words with a suffix will have a recognisable root word.
nodes.response: Show that not all words with suffixes or common word endings will necessarily have a root word that we can recognise.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling words ending in "-sure" and "-ture"

nodes.misconception: Children might confuse pairs of words with compound words. e.g. bus stop.
nodes.response: Give examples of both and model mistakes e.g. write butterfly as 'butter fly' or bus stop as 'busstop' and discuss.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling more compound words

nodes.misconception: Many homophones are common exception words and pupils often confuse homophones within sentences.
nodes.response: Give pupils the chance to choose the spellings they find most difficult and give them the strategies to help them practise.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling homophones

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the difference between 'homophone' and 'homonym'.
nodes.response: Give specific examples of homophones (e.g. hair and hare) and homonyms (e.g. bark) and discuss the differences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling homonyms

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think words are compound words if they can spot one word within another word.
nodes.response: Show examples e.g. 'yesterday'. Whilst it has the word 'day' in it, if you were to separate this, the word 'yester' would not make sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling compound words

nodes.misconception: The ending -ture can be easily mixed up with (t)cher.
nodes.response: Help pupils to spot words with a root ending in 'ch' or 'tch' with the suffix -er.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words ending in  -sure and -ture

nodes.misconception: Not all words have a word hidden in a word.
nodes.response: Show that this is a useful strategy to use when you can spot a word in a word, but it isn't always suitable.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply spelling words with the prefixes "de-", "re-", "sub-" and "super-"

nodes.misconception: Many of these words are high frequency or common exception words.
nodes.response: Be explicit about the difficulties in spelling these words and give time to practise spelling these common exception words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and spelling homophones

nodes.misconception: Children can often misspell words with prefixes as they spell them how they sound.
nodes.response: Help children to recongise when a word has a prefix and use that to support this with spelling, e.g. the prefix mis- has one 's'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes "dis-", "non-", "mis-" and "un-"

nodes.misconception: Children often put a large gap between the two digits when forming the number 10.
nodes.response: When modelling, emphasise that these two digits are 'friends' and like to be close together but not touching.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of numerals 6-10

nodes.misconception: Often students will struggle with which direction to go to form the numerals 2, 3, 4 and 5.
nodes.response: Model clearly using physical things in the room to show which direction they will be drawing. 'To the left, towards the window' for example.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Formation of numerals 0-5

nodes.misconception: It can be hard to identify the sounds a word makes when looking at the spelling.
nodes.response: Encourage children to listen to the word without looking at the spelling.  Stretch the word and identify each sound in turn.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words using hard c

nodes.misconception: Children may use the wrong vowel letter when spelling words with unstressed vowels.
nodes.response: Stretching the word and saying it slowly, how it is spelt, can help pupils to remember the correct spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling polysyllabic words with unstressed vowels

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all words with prefixes must have a recgonisable root word.
nodes.response: Look at some words with the focus prefixes that do not have a recognisable root word.  Discuss how the meaning of the prefix can still support children with understanding the meaning of the word, e.g. translate or transmit.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes bi-, trans-, tele- and circum-

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think every word with a prefix will have a recognisable root word.
nodes.response: Show that some roots we don't recognise may have Latin roots that we don't know.  We can call this a 'stem' or a 'root'.  Recognising the prefix can still help with spelling and understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes de-, re-, sub-, super-, inter-, anti- and auto-

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be familiar with the 'ff' and 'gh' digraph so may spell words contain 'ph' making the /f/ sound incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words and draw links between spellings containing the 'ph' spelling sounding like the /f/ sound and where it's most likely to go in the word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words of Greek origin that use 'ph' to make a /f/ sound

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be familiar with the 'ck' digraph so may spell words containing 'ch' making the /k/ sound incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words and draw links between spellings containing the 'ch' spelling sounding like the /k/ sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words of Greek origin that use 'ch' to make a /k/ sound

nodes.misconception: Children may not remember double letters at the start of some words with prefixes, such as illogical or dissatisfied.
nodes.response: Help the children to see that if they recognise the prefix and the base word, they can work out the spelling of the new word, as prefixes do not change the spelling of the root word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes co-, pre-, pro- and sus-

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a word can only contain a hard c or a soft c.
nodes.response: Look at some words that contain a soft c and a hard c, such as bicycle or access.  Use sound buttoning to help identify the phoneme grapheme correspondences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words using soft c

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 's' at the beginning and 'ss' in the middle of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between words containing the 'sc' spelling and looking at examples where it appears at the beginning and in the middle of a word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words of Latin origin that use 'sc' to make a /s/ sound

nodes.misconception: Children can confuse the homophones 'stationary' and 'stationery'.
nodes.response: Use the mnemonic 'the stationer sells stationery' to help remember.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling more polysyllabic words with unstressed vowels

nodes.misconception: Children may think all words with the letters strings have prefixes.
nodes.response: Discuss words using the letter sequence but not as a prefix, e.g. disturb, imp and uncle.  Reinforce the definition of 'root word' and 'prefix'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes meaning not

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that for every word with a prefix the meaning of the prefix will be very literal.
nodes.response: Show a range of words with the focus prefixes in.  Whilst with some words the meaning of the prefix may be clear, with others it is not.  Explain this is linked to the complex way that language develops over time.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the prefixes ad- and al- and hyphens

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to describe themselves.
nodes.response: Before describing themselves, model sentences by describing your pupils providing them with vocabulary, 'You are...'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing yourself

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unfamiliar with terms such as setting and plot.
nodes.response: Spend time contextualising the terms using stories they will know well, such as the deep, dark woods as the setting for 'The Gruffalo'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The theme of community in 'A Superhero Like You'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may attach stereotypes or preconceptions around the idea of a superhero.
nodes.response: As well as the images shown, supplement with more images to show a representative idea of a superhero, relevant to children's interests.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the idea of a superhero and predicting

nodes.misconception: Children may have already thought about a different aspiration (e.g. footballer, singer etc.)
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to choose a different job if they have requested and work with them to find a suitable adjective, such as 'unstoppable footballer' instead of 'helpful footballer'. The purpose of the task is about aspiration, so any job is suitable.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing about your future job

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to spell more complex adjectives or nouns, such as soldier or ambulance.
nodes.response: Provide a word bank for more complex words to encourage pupils to use if necessary. Provide sentence stems and scaffolds if necessary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing simple sentences about people who help us

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to generate adjectives.
nodes.response: The adjectives in this lesson have been deliberately chosen. Repeat the adjectives together and emphasise them when reading.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing adjectives to describe people who help us

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of what a noun is and so, unable to understand their caption is a noun.
nodes.response: Teach the 'Year 1 Word Class Grammar Unit' at the same time as this so the children can have explicit teaching of nouns and word class.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing captions about people who help us

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to think from someone else's perspective.
nodes.response: Use the 'I do, We do' to model turning yourself into the character. You could include props or masks to support as well as providing the stem sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Characters in 'A Superhero Like You'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume any combination of words they create forms a compound word.
nodes.response: Look at some non-examples such as 'starwhere' and 'somefish' to teach them that not every combination makes a compound word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating compound words

nodes.misconception: Children may not know the spelling due to not always being able to rely on rules.
nodes.response: Remind children of the range of spelling strategies they could use to remember the spellings, such as naughty letters or big letters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling homophones

nodes.misconception: It can be difficult to know when words should be hyphenated and when they should not.
nodes.response: Notice patterns such as vowel sounds and encourage the use of dictionaries to check words pupils are unsure of.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling further compound words

nodes.misconception: Pupils often miss the double letters in the middle of words that have a suffix.
nodes.response: Drawing attention to the patterns of how words are spelt when suffixes are added will help them to remember the double letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Doubling the consonant in polysyllabic words

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be used to the 'ck' representing the 'c' phoneme when at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Explain that in most words where the 'c' is at the end, it is represented as 'ck'. As this is a suffix, it doesn't follow usual rules.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ic

nodes.misconception: Children may think words such as 'feathery' have the -ery suffix.
nodes.response: Reinforce that most words ending in -ery have a root word. Encourage children to spot the root word before the -ery.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ery

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with the 'sh' digraph so may spell words containing 'ch' incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between spellings containing the 'ch' spelling sounding like the /sh/ sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: French derived spelling: 'ch' (sh)

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the difference on where you can and cannot find a root word.
nodes.response: Show examples of where an obvious root word can support spelling. Words without an obvious root word need to be practised.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding the suffix -ary

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to spell the root word or stem.
nodes.response: Ensure to focus on all the difficult elements of the words presented, not only the -ic ending that demonstrates the spelling rule.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the suffix -ic

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume that every word with a short vowel sound should have a double consonant.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that this is not always the case and give them examples of words such as 'hot' not 'hott' and 'shut' not 'shutt'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practise and apply doubling the consonant in contrasting words

nodes.misconception: Homophones sound the same, so they may rely on previous spelling rules and so, spell them the same.
nodes.response: Spend time showing each word in a sentence, use images to support understanding and make sure each homophone is practised using a strategy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating homophones

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 'g' and 'ck' at the end of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between words containing the 'gue' and 'que' spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: French-derived spellings: 'gue' (g) and 'que' (k)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that all curriculum words are common exception words.
nodes.response: Discuss that the list is made up of words with the rules they have learnt or should have come across. Discuss the rules some words use compared to words that may be exceptions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words from the Y5/6 curriculum list

nodes.misconception: Some children may think a letter string can only represent one sound.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the key phonics principles: a sound can be represented by more than one letter, one sound can be represented by more than one spelling and one spelling can represent more than one sound. It is why the English language is so hard!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the 'ee' sound spelt 'ie'

nodes.misconception: When starting a strategy, pupils may have copied the spelling down incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model the process of looking at it, considering what's difficult about the spelling and thinking about it. Then, model copying it for the first time, carefully checking each letter and verbalising what you notice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling key curriculum words

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think letters are silent in some digraphs for example, the 'h' in 'ch'.
nodes.response: Discuss difference between silent letters and digraphs. In 'chaos' the letter 'h' is silent but the other letters make a sound. Whereas, in the word 'clench' the 'h' is part of the 'ch' digraph where the two letters together make one sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the silent letters 'h', 'p', 'n', 'l' and 's'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that all words with the letter strings 'ough' and 'au' are pronounced the same way.
nodes.response: Show pupils that these letter strings can sound different depending on the word they are in. Explore different words and talk about which sounds are the most and least common.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognising the different sounds made by the letter strings 'ough' and 'au'

nodes.misconception: Spellings such as 'practice', 'advice' and 'device' can be more difficult for children.
nodes.response: Explore words ending in -ice and words ending in -ise. Listen to the difference in pronunciation of these words and discuss the difference in word class too e.g. practice, advice, device = nouns, practise, advise, devise = verbs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognising the different sounds made by the letter strings "ou", "ear" and "ice"

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the 'ei' spelling only represents the 'ee' phoneme.
nodes.response: Show a range of words with 'ei' representing different sounds. You can stretch and sound button to show the direct phoneme - grapheme correspondence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the 'ee' sound spelt 'ei'

nodes.misconception: Children mix up the -ible and -able spellings.
nodes.response: Use the rules shown in the lesson: Is there is a recognisable root word without the ending? Is this a modern word? Is there a related word ending in -ation? These will all help to identify the -able spelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the -able suffix

nodes.misconception: Pupils may easily confuse the vowels in -ant and -ent spellings.
nodes.response: Say the word clearly how it is spelt in order to emphasise the vowel spellings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -ant and -ance

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think all words ending in -ent are the same word class.
nodes.response: Whilst the suffixes -ent and -ence can change word class, not all words ending in -ent are the same word class. Give examples in a sentence to demonstrate, using the words contentment, (to) frequent, and silent.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the suffixes -ent and -ence

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 's' at the beginning and 'ss' in the middle of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: Talk about the origin of words drawing links between words containing the 'sc' spelling and looking at examples where it appears at the beginning and in the middle of a word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with Greek and Latin etymology

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start using hyphens for all prefixes.
nodes.response: Emphasise that not all prefixes require a hyphen - some prefixes use them more frequently, but others rarely do.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using hyphens to join prefixes to root words

nodes.misconception: Pupils will be more familiar with 'g' and 'ck' at the end of words so may spell words incorrectly.
nodes.response: The ‘gue’ and ‘que’ sounds nearly always appear at the end of words e.g. vague and antique. The ‘g’ and the ‘k’ sound with the more common spellings, can appear anywhere within a word e.g. eagle, kid and back.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with French etymology

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume all words ending in -ible do not have a root word.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that some words ending in '-ible', like 'sensible', are derived from recognisable English root words. However, there are also '-ible' words whose roots are not complete English words but may originate from Latin, like 'vis' to 'visible'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the -ible suffix

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse 'silent letters' and 'digraphs'.
nodes.response: 'kn' is a digraph making the /n/ sound but, in general, silent letters are individual letters in a word that are not pronounced, whereas digraphs are pairs of letters that represent a single sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spelling words with the silent letters 'b', 'k', 'g', 'w' and 't'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might assume any combination of words can create a compound adjective.
nodes.response: Look at some non-examples such as 'blood-paced' and 'fast-splattered' to teach them that not every combination makes a compound adjective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using hyphens to create adjectives

nodes.misconception: For these letters, children may finish on the baseline and forget the curved stroke as the lead out
nodes.response: Emphasise to the children through modelling that there has to be a 'tail' for the letter to join to the next letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of c, a and d

nodes.misconception: The lead out on the pre-cursive letter g and q can be challenging for children at first.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and opportunities to trace the grey examples will support correct formation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of o, g and q

nodes.misconception: The two loops on the pre-cursive letter f can be challenging for children at first.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and opportunities to trace the grey examples will support correct formation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of e, s and f

nodes.misconception: The lead out on the pre-cursive letter r can be challenging and children can sometimes dip too far.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and opportunities to trace the grey examples will support correct formation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of m, n, and r

nodes.misconception: Children may assume all pre-cursive letters have a lead out.
nodes.response: When modelling the break letters, ensure to emphasise 'break' to remind the children not to add a lead out.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of v, w, x and z

nodes.misconception: Children may form the print version of the letter and then add the 'lead in' separately.
nodes.response: Model and emphasise saying 'Ready, line, go' to remind them that the letter starts with the lead in on the baseline for pre-cursive letters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of b, p, h and k

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle with the shape and size of the loop at the end of the descender.
nodes.response: More tracing practice will support children to get a feel for the size and shape of the loop.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of u, y and j

nodes.misconception: Many children will not securely use the correct pencil grip.
nodes.response: Ensure to spend sufficient time checking children's pencil grip and intervening where they need extra support.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to handwriting skills and patterns

nodes.misconception: Children may form the print version of the letter and then add the 'lead in' seperately.
nodes.response: Model and emphasise saying 'Ready, line, go' to remind them that the letter starts with the lead in on the baseline for pre-cursive letters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pre-cursive formation of i, l and t

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off to form the join.
nodes.response: Emphasise the flowing motion of cursive writing. The letters need to be joined together so the pencil needs to stay on the page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The first join: in, ig, ed, eg, aw, ap, an, ar

nodes.misconception: Children will often remember one of the loops for the f but forget the other.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and emphasising that the letter f needs to 'hold hands' with the letter in front and behind it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The second join: ck, ch, if, il, it

nodes.misconception: The dip down for the third join can be challenging at first, especially when joining to the letter e.
nodes.response: Model with emphasis the dip down so that children can see its importance and purpose. Give them time to really look at the join to the letter e. Allow them to realise themselves that the dip down begins the formation of the letter e.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The third join: oe, we, os, rs

nodes.misconception: Children will often remember one of the loops for the f but forget the other.
nodes.response: Provide lots of modelling and emphasising that the letter f needs to 'hold hands' with the letter in front and behind it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The fourth join: wl, of, rt, ok

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle to get the gap size between the letters correct with this join.
nodes.response: Model this join lots emphasising 'we dip down and across and then form the next letter so they can still hold hands, we don't want them to be far away from each other'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The third join: oo, wa, wo, on, om, ow

nodes.misconception: At first, children might find writing a full sentence in cursive overwhelming and forget the correct joins. This would result in the words being joined in a random manner.
nodes.response: Give them time to think about their sentence before starting. Model writing a sentence slowly and thinking out loud about which joins to use. This will encourage the children to do the same.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing sentences with all four joins, using lead-ins

nodes.misconception: Children may want to take their pencil off before forming the suffix as they see it as separate to the root word.
nodes.response: Encourage children by modelling and emphasising that the pencil only comes off the page once the letter string is complete. Getting them to identify the last letter before starting can help to remind them of this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Suffixes: -ed and -ing

nodes.misconception: Children can sometimes see the word ending as a separate word and lift their pencil which disconnects the letter string.
nodes.response: Remind the children to look and read the word before writing it. Get them feeling confident that this is one word and the flow needs to continue until the last letter in the letter string.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Word endings: -sure and -ture

nodes.misconception: Some children will lift their pencil before the letter string has completed.
nodes.response: Remind the children that the letters want to hold hands and if they lift their pencil then the connection is broken. Speaking out loud, while modelling, to highlight this will support the children to apply it in their practice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Suffixes: -y and -ly

nodes.misconception: Children may want to take their pencil off after forming the prefix as they see it as separate to the root word.
nodes.response: Encourage children by modelling and emphasising that the pencil only comes off the page once the letter string is complete. Getting them to identify the last letter before starting can help to remind them of this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Prefixes: un-, non-, mis- and dis-

nodes.misconception: The lead out for the letter r can be challenging for children.
nodes.response: When introducing the suffix -er and its formation, take time to allow the students to investigate and practise the 'dip down' for the lead out.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Suffixes: -er and -est

nodes.misconception: The cursive formation of the letter f, with the lead in and lead out loop, can be challenging for students.
nodes.response: When modelling, ensure to include examples of words with the letter f at the beginning of the word and in the middle. Remind pupils that the letter f is the only letter in the alphabet with an ascender and a descender, therefore two loops.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Suffixes: -ful and -less

nodes.misconception: Children will often remember one of the loops for the f but forget the other.
nodes.response: Lots of modelling and emphasising that the letter f needs to 'hold hands' with the letter in front and behind it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The second join: if, il, it with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off to form the join.
nodes.response: Emphasise the flowing motion of cursive writing. The letters need to be joined together so the pencil needs to stay on the page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The second join: ck, ch with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle to get the gap size between the letters correct with this join.
nodes.response: Model this join lots emphasising 'we dip down and across and then form the next letter so they can still hold hands, we don't want them to be far away from each other'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The third join: us, rs and ws with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle to get the gap size between the letters correct with this join.
nodes.response: Model this join lots emphasising 'we dip down and across and then form the next letter so they can still hold hands, we don't want them to be far away from each other'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The third join: on, om, ow with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off to form the join.
nodes.response: Emphasise the flowing motion of cursive writing. The letters need to be joined together so the pencil needs to stay on the page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The fourth join: wl, ok, rt and rl with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off to form the join.
nodes.response: Emphasise the flowing motion of cursive writing. The letters need to be joined together so the pencil needs to stay on the page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The fourth join: ob, of, ot, oh with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle to get the gap size between the letters correct with this join.
nodes.response: Model this join lots emphasising 'we dip down and across and then form the next letter so they can still hold hands, we don't want them to be far away from each other'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The third join: oo, wa, wo with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off to form the join.
nodes.response: Emphasise the flowing motion of cursive writing. The letters need to be joined together so the pencil needs to stay on the page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The first join: in, ig, ed, eg with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children will often want to take their pencil off to form the join.
nodes.response: Emphasise the flowing motion of cursive writing. The letters need to be joined together so the pencil needs to stay on the page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The first join: aw, ap, an, ar with lead in

nodes.misconception: Children can struggle to get the gap size between the letters correct with this join.
nodes.response: Model this join lots emphasising 'we dip down and across and then form the next letter so they can still hold hands. We don't want them to be far away from each other'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The third join: oe, we, ve and re with lead in

nodes.misconception: As children start to write longer paragraphs in cursive handwriting their hands can get sore which can lead to them making mistakes.
nodes.response: Model to the children that it is good practice to take a break when writing to stretch your hand if it is becoming sore.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising handwriting in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Children may conclude that they can't make any mistakes with pens.
nodes.response: Emphasise to the children that pencils are used if there are going to be a lot of mistakes or changes like a sketch or a calculation. Explain that it's OK to make some mistakes with a pen and that these will need to be crossed out neatly.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making choices between pen or pencil

nodes.misconception: Some children might forget to add the capital letter for the direct speech within a speech second sentence or might try to join the capital letter to the other letters.
nodes.response: Model the habit of looking and thinking about your sentence before you write it. Where will my punctuation be? Where will my capital letters be? This way children will have the time to think about it before they start writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising handwriting by writing dialogue

nodes.misconception: Children may focus so much on the speed of their writing that they use the incorrect cursive joins.
nodes.response: When modelling, emphasise that the flow is smooth because the correct joins are being used. Clear reminders about letter formation and joins will support the children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building speed in handwriting

nodes.misconception: Sometimes when writing quotations, the children may forget to start with a capital letter as they are concentrating on using the inverted commas.
nodes.response: Model clearly by saying your thought process out loud to remind the children that a capital letter is needed. For example, 'quotation mark, capital letter, lift my pencil...'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising handwriting with more famous quotations

nodes.misconception: Children can get confused when writing the headline and start to join the capital letters to the lower case letters.
nodes.response: Model to the children that you think about the headline before writing it. Which words will have capital letters? When forming the capital letter, exaggerate the action of lifting your pencil after the formation to remind the children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising handwriting in journalistic writing

nodes.misconception: Some children may think a letter string can only represent one sound.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the key phonics principles: a sound can be represented by more than one letter, one sound can be represented by more than one spelling and one spelling can represent more than one sound. It is why the English language is so hard!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising spelling patterns linked to sounds

nodes.misconception: Pupils new to school may have missed or not secured prior learning, so will struggle to access the review lessons.
nodes.response: Ensure you have a grasp on the coverage of the spelling content. Depending on your pupils' acquisition of spelling, you may wish to use these lessons as a basis for re-teaching or reviewing prior learning. Use the starter quiz to inform planning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising spelling patterns linked to suffixes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the meaning of words or root words.
nodes.response: Spend time in the lesson discussing the meanings and links you can make between words and languages.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising spelling patterns linked to etymology

nodes.misconception: Sometimes children will forget to add the lead in for the first letter in the letter string or the first letter after the capital letter.
nodes.response: Use the 'Ready, line, go' technique to remind children to start on the baseline.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising handwriting with a poem

nodes.misconception: Children can forget the lead-in loop for the letter f when it is at the beginning of a word.
nodes.response: Model and remind children that every lower case letter starts on the baseline for cursive handwriting. This will remind the children to add the lead in loop.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing and writing homophones

nodes.misconception: The words in this lesson are over five letters long, so children might struggle to be consistent with the letter formation or the joins used.
nodes.response: Model looking at the words carefully before writing them. Point out which letters have ascenders or descenders and what that will mean for the formation of the letters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing the suffixes -tion, -cian, -sion, -ssion

nodes.misconception: Sometimes when writing quotations, the children may forget to start with a capital letter as they are concentrating on using the inverted commas.
nodes.response: Model clearly by saying your thought process out loud to remind the children that a capital letter is needed. For example, 'quotation mark, capital letter, lift my pencil...'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising handwriting with famous quotations

nodes.misconception: Some children might get confused with which join to use and try joining letters with the incorrect join.
nodes.response: Showing the children a visual of the four joins can help them to decide which join should be used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing the four joins

nodes.misconception: As the words get longer, children can rush, causing the letter spacing to become uneven and the writing illegible.
nodes.response: Remind and model to the children that the flow and movement of the pencil is the same at the end of the word as it is at the beginning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising common exception words

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to generate individual sentences per event.
nodes.response: Refer to the story mountain that the children made in a previous lesson and make that available. When retelling and reading the story, refer back to the model story mountain to refer to those points. Explain that each picture is one sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing about characters, setting and plot: 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify features of traditional tales independently.
nodes.response: Use tales that are relevant to your curriculum, including tales they already know well. If pupils know stories well, they will find it easier to make links and will find it easier to spot other similar features.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to traditional tales

nodes.misconception: Children may already know the story, so therefore will be unable to make a prediction.
nodes.response: Celebrate if children have heard a version before. Play a game to imagine that memory has gone from their heads and just get them to use the front cover as clues imagining they are detectives.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate vocabulary to explain the expressions and movements.
nodes.response: The purpose of learning cycle 1 is to provide the children with vocabulary. Narrate how the children are feeling in their freeze-frames and get them to repeat. For example, you may say 'You look horrified.' and the children repeat 'We are horrified'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Imagining you are the characters: 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might be able to think of adjectives, but they may not be specific to the character of the goats.
nodes.response: Share examples and non-examples of adjectives that can be used to describe the goats. Read extracts of the story to help pupils to understand that a character can be described in a certain way because of their actions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing the goats in 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to generate appearance words and may use words like 'scary' to describe his appearance as well.
nodes.response: Provide images to support them with generating ideas and explain that they can describe the appearance of specific parts of the troll e.g. 'bushy hair', 'sharp teeth', 'jagged claws', 'green skin' etc.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing the troll in 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: When you are modelling your write, continuously refer back to the success criteria yourself. Adapt the success criteria accordingly to help pupils experience success.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the end of the story: 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify the main events in a story and they may try and include too much on their story mountain.
nodes.response: Explain that the main events are the most important moments in the story. Without these moments, the story would not flow. Pick out some elements of the text that are minor moments and share these as non-examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequencing and making a story mountain: 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff'

nodes.misconception: Children will sometimes lift their pencils part way through the letter string.
nodes.response: Model to the children that they should look at the word first and plan for when they will be lifting their pencil: usually at the end of the word or after a break letter. Model writing the word, emphasising the flow as the letters connect.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing homophones

nodes.misconception: Children may lift their pencil in the middle of the letter string to 'dot' the letter i or put the 'cross' on the letter t.
nodes.response: Model to the children that you wait until the end of the letter string before adding the 'cross' or the 'dot'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing common exception words

nodes.misconception: When copying a poem, children can forget where the new line is or where a capital letter is needed.
nodes.response: Model to the children that you must take time to review the poem first before copying it. Where are the new lines? Where are the capital letters? Is there any punctuation needed? This will help to prepare them for copying.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing handwriting using another poem
