nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the opening of 'A Christmas Carol'

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that a story can contain multiple themes which sometimes overlap.
nodes.response: Discuss a simple but well known tale and its many themes in advance of the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'A Christmas Carol'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to write ideas for Scrooge's inner thoughts in this lesson.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have a plan to use with ideas for Scrooge's inner thoughts and model how to write these.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the climax of  'A Christmas Carol'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the editing process is just about correcting mistakes.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that all writers use editing as opportunity to improve their work as well as correcting mistakes. Even renowned authors make changes to their writing (vocabulary choice/sentence structure) in order to improve it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the build-up of 'A Christmas Carol'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to think of reasons for their opinions.
nodes.response: Give pupils some different possible reasons based on evidence from the text allowing them to choose from a list of reasons if necessary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing an opinion about events and themes in ‘Jack and the Beanstalk’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use an exclamation mark for every sentence or overuse them.
nodes.response: When you introduce exclamation marks, 'give' each child one exclamation mark to put in their pockets. Tell them they can only have one, so they should only get it out of their pocket when they think it is the best place to use it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the middle, building suspense: 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate descriptive language for Task B.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a word bank that includes two columns: expanded noun phrases and verbs. Encourage pupils to pick at least one from each column and add it it to their story mountain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retelling 'Jack and the Beanstalk' and using a story mountain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just use 'and' to add on another word or phrase rather than another sentence.
nodes.response: Show two different sentences as two complete ideas. Ensure pupils understand that each sentence needs to make sense on its own.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the beginning of a story, introducing character and setting: 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: When you are modelling your write, continuously refer back to the success criteria yourself. Adapt the success criteria accordingly to help pupils experience success.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the end of the story, building suspense: 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate vocabulary to explain the expressions and movements.
nodes.response: The purpose of learning cycle 1 is to provide the children with vocabulary. Narrate how the children are feeling in their freeze-frames and get them to repeat. For example, you may say 'You look famished.' and the children repeat 'We are famished'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Thinking from different perspectives: 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recognise that an idea must make sense on its own.
nodes.response: Support pupils using a sentence scaffold that guides them to join another complete simple sentence with 'and' rather than using 'and' followed by another phrase or expanded noun phrase.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Character description of the giant in 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to generate appearance words and may use words like 'curious' to describe his appearance as well.
nodes.response: Provide images to support them with generating ideas and explain that they can describe the appearance of specific parts of Jack e.g. 'yellow wellies', 'brown eyes', 'wavy hair', 'long legs' etc.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Character description of Jack in 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to compare fairy tales.
nodes.response: Use fairy tales that are relevant to your curriculum, including tales pupils already know well. If pupils know stories well, they will find it easier to make links and to spot other similar features.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the genre of fairy tales in 'Jack and the Beanstalk'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the difference between layout features and linguistic features.
nodes.response: This lesson focuses primarily on layout features to support children in understanding how to organise and structure information in an information text. Explain that the linguistic features refer to the type of language used and explore examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features of an information text to prepare for writing our own

nodes.misconception: The last sentence of the modelled paragraph is a command and an exclamation. Children may form the misconception that a command is always an exclamation or visa versa.
nodes.response: Explore examples of imperative verbs used to form a command and show examples of commands without an exclamation. Explore examples of exclamations that are not a command.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the introduction of an information text about an author

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to incorporate linguistic features that highlight chronology in their plan.
nodes.response: Highlight the use of 'after education' and 'eventually' in the model notes on slide 17 as examples of language that support in communicating the chronology of the author's career. Ask the children to brainstorm other examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the second section of an information text about an author

nodes.misconception: Children may find the use of subordination more difficult in their writing, especially finding ways to use subordinating conjunctions other than 'when'.
nodes.response: Focus more heavily on subordination than coordination during teaching. It is appropriate to focus on the subordinating conjunction 'when' as this is the most valuable for the text's purpose, but model the use of other subordinating conjunctions too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first section of an information text about an author

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to write concise notes that also contain appropriate detail and description.
nodes.response: Developing precise adjectives for their writing is important but the main focus should be on recording precise and accurate information. You may wish to provide them with a structured planning frame.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first section of an information text about an author

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate and include the different types of fronted adverbials.
nodes.response: Create a shared bank of fronted adverbials that are appropriate for the text type and make sure these are available for children to support them in their writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second section of an information text about an author

nodes.misconception: Children may be unfamiliar with the meaning of some of the vocabulary involved in exploring these author's lives. E.g. 'immerse', 'boarding school', 'hijab'.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for children to highlight any words they do not know the meaning of within each cycle of the lesson and explain the meaning (providing visual aids where appropriate) to support children in understanding each author's life.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating information about authors to prepare to write an information text

nodes.misconception: Children can think that there is only one way to respond to a poem and you can have the right or wrong understanding of it.
nodes.response: Avoid posing questions which may lead children to the idea that there is a right or wrong answer when discussing the poem. Try to encourage open responses to the poem, celebrating each unique response from individuals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Wide Open' by Rachel Rooney

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the poet is limited to putting real items into the box.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that with poetry the possibilities are endless and a good poet is creative.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'The Magic Box' by Kit Wright

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that performing poetry is something that does not require rehearsal and careful consideration beforehand.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that to have the greatest impact on the audience, you should look through your poem and consider how you will perform it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing your own imaginative poem

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to read the poem aloud and with expression.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have an understanding of what the poem means and some of the key vocabulary that they may not know. Model reading the poem aloud with expression for the children to get ideas and talk through the different ways to use your voice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'If You Could See Laughter' by Mandy Coe

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to think of imaginative ideas.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in pairs or small groups to generate ideas for their poems. You may also wish to do some further work on adjectives to describe and come up with a class word bank of adjectives to refer to.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing your own imaginative poem

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand what a fronted adverbial is.
nodes.response: Refer to the Year 1: Grammar: Word Class unit and teach alongside this unit.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequencing events in a recount

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to know what questions to ask someone about a trip.
nodes.response: Provide question prompt words and model these words being used to pose questions in full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using question prompts to plan a recount

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to speak correctly in the past tense, particularly with irregular verbs (e.g. saying 'sawed' or 'seed' for saw).
nodes.response: Use this lesson as an opportunity for as much oral rehearsal as possible to support children's errors in the moment. Repeat and re-model sentences back to them. Model incorrectly and ask the children to spot your mistakes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a recount?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may tick their success criteria without checking and correcting.
nodes.response: When you are modelling your write, continuously refer back to the success criteria yourself. Adapt the success criteria accordingly to help pupils experience success.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the middle and end of a school trip recount

nodes.misconception: Pupils may just use 'and' to add on another word or phrase rather than another sentence.
nodes.response: Show two different sentences as two complete ideas. Ensure pupils understand that each sentence needs to make sense on its own.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the beginning of a school trip recount

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all forms of poetry must have to rhyme.
nodes.response: Before the lesson, you might share examples of a range of poems in both fixed verse and free verse.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing understanding of 'Swallow's Kiss' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make a wish for themselves personally in Task A.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to consider the impact that they could have on their local community and wider world when discussing their wishes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'Swallow's Kiss' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have negative attitudes towards publishing their work.
nodes.response: Publishing becomes highly motivating when there is a real audience for the work - for instance, you could copy the reports and illustrations and gather them into a presentation book that can be taken home by each child in turn.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing a non-chronological report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may lose sight of the overall structure of the planned report.
nodes.response: Constantly refer back to the idea of paragraphs focusing on a given theme (diet, habitat) after a general introduction, using the stag beetle model as needed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching information about a penguin's habitat and diet

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to write their 'notes' in full sentences.
nodes.response: Oral rehearsal of sentences using very short notes will help them in writing tasks using these facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching information about a penguin's appearance and adaptations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty recognising that there are different types of complex sentence.
nodes.response: Different types of complex sentence contain different types of subordinate clause, each starting with a different type of word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring cohesive devices in a model non-chronological report about an insect

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty in making edits to their work in a practical way - where to write extra words etc.
nodes.response: Writing double-spaced is a good way of allowing room for editing - or you may want to have pupils re-draft the report completely, depending on your own school approach.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing a non-chronological report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident with the idea of paragraphs being composed of several linked sentences.
nodes.response: As you read, draw out the idea that all the sentences in each section are related to each other and deepen the reader's understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of a model non-chronological report about an insect

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with generating an introductory sentence for each section.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to think about the main point of the paragraph, e.g. What is most obvious about the penguins' appearance? Are penguins well-adapted? If so, to what?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing specific sections of a non-chronological report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to keep language formal when generating expanded noun phrases relating to the penguins.
nodes.response: Model out loud the thought process of selecting and rejecting different adjectives, bearing in mind formality - e.g. rejecting 'cute' and selecting 'instantly-recognisable'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching information about threats to a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to decide where to insert parenthesis into a sentence.
nodes.response: The parenthesis will usually follow the noun or noun phrase it adds extra information about.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating ideas for parenthesis in a report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have negative attitudes towards editing their work.
nodes.response: Encourage a growth mindset, modelling the idea that all work can be improved and avoiding negative responses to mistakes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of a non-chronological report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to choose appropriate cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.response: Give pupils access to the Cohesive Devices Bank throughout their writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing further specific sections of a non-chronological report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to select which facts to connect using cohesive devices.
nodes.response: Give pupils plenty of time to orally rehearse grouping information together using different cohesive devices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a non-chronological report about a penguin

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to attribute a feeling or emotion to a metaphor.
nodes.response: Some pupils could have visuals of the imagery contained in the poem, to support when attributing the change in emotional state of the speaker from verse 1 to verse 3.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading, responding to and performing ‘My Heart is a Volcano’

nodes.misconception: Not all pupils may be familiar with symbolism, especially common symbols.
nodes.response: To support pupils, adults could model out loud the associations that can be made about the objects .
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes of hate and anger in 'The Wall'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may initially think that 'Mum Says She Loves Me' is a poem which conveys a negative emotion.
nodes.response: 'Mum Says She Loves Me' depicts love in a different family structure. This does not mean that the love is any less than the love depicted in 'You Are'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes of love in 'You Are' and 'Mum Says She Loves Me'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it more challenging to identify themes of hope and belonging in 'The Colours of My Dreams' due to its more abstract imagery.
nodes.response: Explore how dreams are often seen as symbols of hope. Belonging can link to human experiences and emotional connections.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes of belonging and hope in 'Forest' & 'The Colours of My Dreams'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find understanding the symbolism in both poems challenging.
nodes.response: Pupils may benefit from additional images to support understanding and help with representation of emotions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring connections to ‘I Opened the Door’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect all experiences with deafness and the Deaf community to reflect this text.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that the text explores an individual’s recount of their experiences; it is not reflective of every experience within the Deaf community. Pupils could read additional texts to develop greater awareness and empathy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'El Deafo' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may list emotions when referring to a character trait.
nodes.response: Emotions are temporary. Explain that character traits are linked to characterisation. They are relatively stable over time. Examples of common character traits could be shared with the children prior to Task A.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'El Deafo' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to differentiate the use of 'euphoric' and 'cheerful' in sentences.
nodes.response: 'Euphoric' means extreme happiness. Share examples with pupils of when you may feel 'euphoric' compared to when you may feel 'cheerful'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing vocabulary associated with happiness

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to know what or who inspires them.
nodes.response: When introducing 'inspired', talk about pupils' different sources of inspiration and how this impacts them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing vocabulary associated with inspiration

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to agree on where each word should be placed on the scale of 'angry to angriest'.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that this is subjective and some people may think 'grumpy' is more angry than 'annoyed'. Encourage pupils to justify their point using the conjunction,' because'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing vocabulary associated with anger

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to use 'sulky' as an adjective and 'sulking' as a verb in sentences.
nodes.response: Model sentences using both 'sulky' and 'sulking'. Use this an opportunity to recap word classes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing vocabulary associated with sadness

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused by the adjective 'included' and use it as a verb.
nodes.response: Model using 'included' in sentences as a verb and also as an adjective. This is a good opportunity to recap word classes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing vocabulary associated with friendship

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the text has autobiographical features due to its tone and form.
nodes.response: 'Walter Tull's Scrapbook' is a biography. It is a non-fiction text with factual evidence. It is presented as a fictionalised scrapbook.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to Walter in 'Walter Tull's Scrapbook'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not think that Walter was paid well as a footballer. The value of currency was different.
nodes.response: In the 1900s, Walter's signing-on fee and weekly wage was very competitive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding words and phrases from context in 'Walter Tull's Scrapbook'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include any information that mentions keywords in the question stem.
nodes.response: It is important to model re-reading the question and answer, checking evidence for accuracy and context in answers.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Answering questions using evidence in 'Walter Tull's Scrapbook'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to draw out the most significant moments when summarising.
nodes.response: Model eliciting the key parts of Walter's life - using the contents page to support. Have these accessible during the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Summarising Walter’s life using ‘Walter Tull’s Scrapbook’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to draw similarities between Walter's home life and life at war.
nodes.response: Modelling a few additional examples will support pupils e.g. he excelled in football and at war.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making comparisons in 'Walter Tull's Scrapbook'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to provide two contrasting impressions of a character.
nodes.response: It may be helpful to visually mind map how readers might describe a character (using adjectives). Impressions can also be modelled verbally to develop pupils' understanding of character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'The Unforgotten Coat' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that there are multiple answers to open-ended or personal reflection questions.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to refer to the text as they discuss the questions. If a pupils' perspective can be justified by evidence in the text, it is a valid response.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'The Unforgotten Coat' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: The narrator in a story always remains the same.
nodes.response: There can be more than one narrator in a story. A change in narrator can demonstrate a shift in time or offer a different perspective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the main idea of 'The Pebble in my Pocket'

nodes.misconception: You should always look at an illustration first to identify what is happening in a text.
nodes.response: Illustrations can be very helpful for supporting understanding, but using strategies to understand vocabulary first is really important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring vocabulary in 'The Pebble in my Pocket'

nodes.misconception: Children might think that the story is only about a pebble being found and its story.
nodes.response: The author conveys the deeper meaning that everything that exists has a story to tell and builds our understanding of the world.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Summarising the key events and ideas in 'The Pebble in my Pocket'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there is no description in non-fiction texts.
nodes.response: In narrative non-fiction texts authors use literary devices such as imagery, similes and metaphors to enhance a reader's understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the author's choice of vocabulary in 'The Pebble in my Pocket'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that they can only find out information explicitly written in a non-fiction text.
nodes.response: Using inference skills and having rich discussion can allow students to draw greater conclusions about the information given.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'The Pebble in my Pocket'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might recognise common features or character types from other fairy tales leading them to think that the characters must conform to a stereotype.
nodes.response: 'Blackberry Blue' uses a range of fairy tales for inspiration. Use the text to discuss how characters do not always conform to stereotypes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and engaging with 'Blackberry Blue'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all traditional fairy tales include stereotypes.
nodes.response: Explain that stereotypes are formed as a result of many stories including similar features. Not all traditional tales include them. Stereotypes can also be found in contemporary texts too, which could be explored with pupils.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in 'Blackberry Blue'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a range of different answers for the final question in Task B.
nodes.response: If pupils' responses can be justified with evidence from the text, they are likely to be good justifications. It may be beneficial to share an example for each option verbally.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Blackberry Blue' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to agree on the placement of the statements in Task A.
nodes.response: Consider printing the statements and the Venn diagram, to allow pupils to move them as they discuss and work in small groups or pairs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making connections to 'Blackberry Blue'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to retrieve personality traits from the book that aren't explicitly mentioned.
nodes.response: Refer to things that Ada does, what she is interested in and model how to retrieve this from the text and then infer what type of person this makes her.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using evidence from 'Ada Twist, Scientist' to write a character description

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain of what some of the scientific vocabulary means, making the story difficult to follow.
nodes.response: As you are reading, gloss over key vocabulary, such as "research" and "hypothesis" by providing a definition linked to the events in the story using the illustrations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The theme of resilience in 'Ada Twist, Scientist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to know when to separate nouns with a comma and when to use 'and'.
nodes.response: Get a list of nouns and discuss where the commas and 'and' will go. Move the nouns into a scaffold to ensure it is structured correctly. Spend more time on this as it is newer learning. If needed, remove expectation to include adjectives in the list.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using descriptive language to describe yourself

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to link their own knowledge of the world to the texts to support their predictions.
nodes.response: Link the titles of the texts to what you have done in school, e.g. 'We drew symbols in our science experiment', 'A president is someone who leads something like our headteacher or the pupil council' etc.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Characters and plot in the story 'Ada Twist, Scientist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to share what their aspiration is.
nodes.response: As well as listing the jobs referred to in the lesson, refer to jobs or careers that your pupils have specific interests in, such as sports people, authors, singers as well as jobs that parents or family members may have.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring aspirations and the future: 'Ada Twist, Scientist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to give extended reasons for their opinions and then lose their full sentence structure.
nodes.response: Provide clear speaking frames and model sentence stems for the children to encourage them to speak in full, clear sentences. They only need to give one reason for each opinion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Our likes and dislikes

nodes.misconception: There may be pupils who do not know a nursery rhyme by heart.
nodes.response: Use the Y1 'Nursery rhyme' unit prior to this lesson to familiarise children with a range of nursery rhymes. Spend time in class singing and reciting nursery rhymes together. Children may wish to choose their favourite nursery rhyme to perform.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing a poem for an audience

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not have sufficient knowledge of different fairy tales and characters from them to be able to answer the questions.
nodes.response: Read and discuss the classic children's fairy tales regularly as part of story time with your class. These books could also be sent home. You could add more images to the slides as a prompt.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sharing our opinions about a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak too quietly and find it hard to speak in full sentences.
nodes.response: Display the visuals for successful speaking and listening in your classroom. Ensure pupils are confident in what they are going to say - they could practise their show and tell at home or with a teacher prior to delivering it in front of the class.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Standing to speak in 'show and tell'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to turn a simple past tense sentence into a perfect present tense sentence, especially when this involves changing the main verb.
nodes.response: Explore simple past tense examples where the main verb needs changing as well. E.g. 'It was' becomes 'It has been'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of a diary entry based on 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to come up with ambitious vocabulary for each part of their plan.
nodes.response: Come up with precise and ambitious vocabulary as a class first and create a word bank for display. Pupils could work in pairs or small groups to complete their plans.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the final paragraph of a diary entry based on 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to avoid repetition for describing each encounter.
nodes.response: Model a range of ways for saying the same thing. For example 'bumped into', 'came across', 'encountered', 'stumbled across', etc. Create a class bank of phrases and ideas they can use in their plan.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a paragraph of a diary entry based on 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to embed a relative clause and they may forgot the necessary commas needed to demarcate a relative clause.
nodes.response: Ensure there is a model of a relative complex sentence where the relative clause follows the main clause and one where the relative clause is embedded. Write the relative clause and commas in a different colour to make them visually stand out.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a paragraph of a diary entry based on 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to determine which suffix or word to use to turn an adjective into its superlative form.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to practise saying the superlative form of an adjective out loud to check it sounds right. Model and demonstrate the rules for how to turn adjectives into their superlative form.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for a diary entry based on 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to identify which familiar fairy tale characters the boy encounters in the forest.
nodes.response: Ask questions to prompt children, e.g. 'Which fairy tale character do you know who sold a cow?' Also encourage children to look for further clues in the illustrations, e.g. There is a beanstalk in the illustration on page 10.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the plot of 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Children might struggle to identify how to transition into the present tense smoothly in a way that supports text flow.
nodes.response: Highlight the use of the compound sentence using 'but' to contrast between past and present emotions. Encourage children to orally rehearse a similar sentence as their transition point to the present tense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the final paragraph of a diary entry based on 'Into the Forest'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify informal language.
nodes.response: Spend some time examining different ways informal language appears in the model diary entry (e.g. exaggeration, contractions, capitalised words, informal vocabulary).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing features of a diary entry

nodes.misconception: Children may have questions about the genre that the story belongs to and be unsure of what constitutes mythology. Children may also notice elements within the story that are similar to fairytales.
nodes.response: Explore examples of myths that the children have been previously exposed to and ask them to identify any commonalities within 'The Moon Dragons'. Explore which features of the story are reminiscent of fairy tales.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with 'The Moon Dragons'

nodes.misconception: Children may have questions or misconceptions around how the 'red-headed female heroine' is portrayed within stories.
nodes.response: It is important to explain that in life we do not judge somebody's qualities or traits based on their appearance. However, authors do sometimes use appearance to communicate certain messages.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making comparisons across books

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is a 'right' or 'wrong' answer when identifying themes within a text.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that different people will identify different themes within the same text. As themes are not explicitly stated within a text, pupils may interpret them differently. Share everyone's ideas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes in 'The Moon Dragons'

nodes.misconception: Children may develop simple questions where the answer can be retrieved from the text rather than involving inference to uncover.
nodes.response: Model the difference between a retrieval and an inference question. E.g. For page 13, a retrieval question could be 'How did the King speak to Alina?' whereas an inference question could be 'What did the King think about Alina's declaration?'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'The Moon Dragons' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Some of the vocabulary used to describe Alina's connection to nature and the moon dragons may be unfamiliar, e.g. 'intuitive'.
nodes.response: Explore the word 'intuitive' and its definition. Ask the children to consider moments that they feel a sense of intuitiveness and how this guides them to make decisions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a character profile for Alina in 'The Moon Dragons'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that bats are not nocturnal because they can be seen at zoos during the day.
nodes.response: Explain that zoos use carefully planned changes of lighting to help the bats think that it is night during the day.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating information about bats to be used in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Children may write in full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Model to the children how to use bullet points for notes and give them lots of examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning to write a section about bats in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that hedghogs can eat milk and bread, due to children's stories depicting this.
nodes.response: Explicitly teach the pupils that hedgehogs cannot eat milk or bread and instead eat insects and fruits. Watch videos online to support.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating information about hedgehogs for a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the vocabulary of 'chronological' and 'non-chronological' challenging.
nodes.response: Using examples that pupils are very familiar with, such as the events in a school day, will help to explain the concepts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning the features of a non-chronological report on nocturnal animals

nodes.misconception: Children may write detailed information and facts about nocturnal animals in their introduction.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the introduction gives general information. Give examples of general vs specific information for children to identify
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a non-chronological report about nocturnal animals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a joining word can be used at the start of a sentence.
nodes.response: Teach that the joining word acts as the link between two simple sentences and so no full stop is needed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a section about hedgehogs in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: The teacher says a word or phrase in a loud, clear voice, and the children have to echo it back as loudly and clearly as they can.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Delivering a presentation of a non-chronological report about nocturnal animals

nodes.misconception: Children may write in full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Model to the children how to use bullet points for notes and give them lots of examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning to write a section about hedgehogs in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that apostrophes for possession are only used for physical nouns.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that nouns such as skills or senses can also be possessed, or owned. E.g. a bat's eyesight.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a section about bats in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use apostrophes incorrectly when indicating possession.
nodes.response: Supplement the content in Learning Cycle One with further teaching of the rules associated with using apostrophes for singular and plural possession.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a setting and character description based on 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have incorrectly structured clauses or adverbial detail within speech sentences.
nodes.response: Repeatedly remind pupils which is the direct speech part of a speech sentence and which is the reporting clause part of a speech sentence. Knowing where the reporting clause is will help eliminate mistakes within it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the speech section of ‘The Highwayman’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to use all recital skills.
nodes.response: Each skill of using projection, diction and body language should be explicitly modelled. Modelling non-examples is useful for pupils to see and hear what works and what doesn't in performance.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning and reciting stanzas four to six of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to use all recital skills.
nodes.response: Each skill of using projection, diction and body language should be explicitly modelled. Modelling non-examples are useful for pupils to see and hear what works and what doesn't in performance.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning and reciting stanzas one to three of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up different poetic devices.
nodes.response: The tasks in learning cycles one and two explicitly model how each poetic device is used in each stanza.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing stanzas three and four of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find correctly punctuating speech first and speech second sentences challenging.
nodes.response: Use visual speech scaffolds to support pupils with correctly punctuating speech first and speech second sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the third part of the build-up of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recall, define and use different figurative language structures.
nodes.response: Use Joseph Coelho's 'MORERAPS' poem to provide additional examples of effective figurative language.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a setting and character description based on 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to describe a range of aspects of Tim's appearance and feelings.
nodes.response: Explicit modelling of adjectives, including compound adjectives, and show-not-tell will help pupils with their descriptions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the second part of the build-up of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to place the time period in which the poem is set.
nodes.response: Explicit discussion of features of the 18th Century and visual representations on a timeline will help pupils' understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the context of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only include direct speech sentences from their plans.
nodes.response: One of the elements of the success criteria directs pupils to use adverbial detail and subordination in each reporting clause. This helps pupils remember to stretch their initial ideas in their plans when independently writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the third part of the build-up of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush through the planning process and miss opportunities to describe and extend key moments.
nodes.response: The planning worksheet breaks down each section into smaller parts, prompting pupils to focus on key details.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first part of the build-up of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand some of the vocabulary in stanzas one and two.
nodes.response: Reading and listening to unfamiliar vocabulary should not put us off studying poetry or texts that contain it!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing stanzas one and two of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to put the Highwayman's words into their own.
nodes.response: Key unfamiliar language is explained in the previous lesson (L10) and paraphrasing the Highwayman's words is modelled in this lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using drama to analyse the next section of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which elements of their writing to edit.
nodes.response: Learning cycles explicitly model how to edit different aspects of writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the build-up of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget all elements of punctuation in speech first and speech second sentences.
nodes.response: Speech first and speech second sentence scaffolds are referred to throughout both learning cycles to support pupils.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing speech punctuation to write the next section of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the vocabulary, particularly in stanza six.
nodes.response: Give explicit definitions for any unfamiliar language, using visuals to support the explanations, to help pupils' understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing stanzas five and six of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use repetitive language choices.
nodes.response: Exposure to a range of compound adjectives and synonyms in the teacher model will support with language variation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first part of the build-up of 'The Highwayman'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that characters' traits and behaviours remain fixed within a narrative.
nodes.response: Discuss that several characters evolve emotionally over the narrative. Governor Adori begins the text very commanding, authoritative and selfish - he ends up redeeming himself by giving his daughter and Isabella time to escape.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing understanding of 'The Girl of Ink and Stars' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that character traits remain fixed throughout a narrative.
nodes.response: The characters in 'The Girl of Ink and Stars' are complex. Governor Adori's decision in the climax of the story is very different to decisions he made at the beginning of the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'The Girl of Ink and Stars' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they should always have the same answer as their partner.
nodes.response: Teach the pupils that when retrieving information, there is likely only one answer. However, discussion questions, like in Task B 4, the children's answers may be different and that is what makes the reading experience unique.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'The Owl Who Was Afraid of the Dark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to think of reasons they like the dark.
nodes.response: Brainstorm ideas beforehand as a class and if possible use two adults to model hot-seating before the children start the task.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Character, setting and plot in 'The Owl Who Was Afraid of the Dark'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to identify character traits for Plop for the inside of the owl template.
nodes.response: Reread specific pages aloud to the children and discuss Plop's actions and what this tells us about his character e.g. when he hears noises he goes down from his tree to explore - this tells us he is curious.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding character in 'The Owl Who Was Afraid of the Dark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Plop was not brave because he was scared of the dark.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that bravery/ courage is all about facing your fears and doing something even though it might frighten you.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes in 'The Owl Who Was Afraid of the Dark'

nodes.misconception: Children may not know or understand that owls are nocturnal and therefore not find it unusual or funny for an owl to be scared of the dark.
nodes.response: Allow the children to research owls ahead of the lesson, using non-fiction texts and the internet.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the opening of 'The Owl Who Was Afraid of the Dark'

nodes.misconception: Children may have questions around who the 'good' vs 'evil' characters are.
nodes.response: Goldilocks is the one who breaks into the bears' home and uses their things, therefore she would be considered the 'evil' character. However, ask/discuss whether her behaviour actually constitutes 'evil' and what her motivations might have been.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning a story to retell it

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to combine all elements of oral presentation successfully. E.g. When focusing on projection, they may lose some of their expression.
nodes.response: Ensure children practise the difference between projection and shouting. As they become more comfortable with projection, they should be able to juggle and maintain more elements of oral presentation successfully.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retelling a story with charisma

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult or forget to switch from a character voice to a narrator voice when they have finished saying the speech and they are saying the reporting clause.
nodes.response: Print a copy of the speech section of the story that shows the speech and reporting clause in different colours to support children in their oral rehearsal for different character's voices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Telling a story with charisma

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only want to use vocabulary from the original story.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we are retelling our own version of the story and therefore we can include our own precise and descriptive vocabulary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing storytelling vocabulary

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only consider themes that are universally understood.
nodes.response: Highlight that there are many possible themes that can be drawn out from a text; readers may interpret these differently.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'Shackleton's Journey'

nodes.misconception: Impressions can only be formed from what readers have understood from the text.
nodes.response: Explain that impressions can also be based on a reader's prior experience, however reasoning should be supported with factual evidence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Answering a range of comprehension questions on 'Shackleton's Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect to see features from other non-fiction texts they have read.
nodes.response: Non-fiction texts can vary greatly, both in terms of layout as well as form.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Examining the layout of 'Shackleton's Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused with the northern and southern polar regions.
nodes.response: Reiterate that Antarctica is the southern polar region, the Arctic, the northern.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'Shackleton's Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may form predictions without basing their ideas on evidence within the text.
nodes.response: Model making predictions based on information provided in the text or wider reading and research.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Shackleton’s Journey' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find creating their own repeated phrase during Task A challenging.
nodes.response: Adults may wish to provide a scaffold for pupils with some example lines.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a poem about a personal experience

nodes.misconception: In Task A, pupils may find it challenging to predict what might happen after a poem has seemingly ended.
nodes.response: Adults could verbally model possibilities, linking back to the poem. These are largely based on the speaker leaving their hometown or becoming trapped there.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes of resilience in 'One of These Days' and 'Being Heard'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have much experience associating colours with feelings and emotions.
nodes.response: To support pupils, adults could discuss feelings and emotions and their associations to colour prior to the lesson. The Disney Pixar film 'Inside Out' would be a suitable starting point for this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes of sadness in 'The Land of Blue'

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not be able to think of a text that they have an emotional connection with.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of texts that they have shared in class during the year or previous years. Model an example using a shared text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading, responding to and performing 'In the Heart of a Book'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not notice the patterns that can be associated with each poem when reading aloud.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to think about rhythm and rhyme when considering how to interpret a poem to be read aloud. Do they notice a particular rhythm when they read?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes of identity in 'Back to Me', 'Find Me', 'Friend' and 'Everyone'

nodes.misconception: Illustrations should merely echo or repeat what the words convey.
nodes.response: Illustrations can be an extension of the poem, adding layers of meaning or emotion beyond what words convey.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing and performing a free verse poem in the style of John Lyons

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to read a poem aloud.
nodes.response: Reading poetry aloud invites the reader to inject their own emotions, personal interpretation and expression into it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Carib Nightfall' by John Lyons

nodes.misconception: Using 'good vocabulary' automatically makes writing better.
nodes.response: There are no 'good' and 'bad words' in English. Rather, some are more precise and appropriate in certain contexts than others.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for a weather-themed poem

nodes.misconception: There is only one correct interpretation of a poem.
nodes.response: Emphasise to pupils that each reader brings their unique perspective, experiences and emotions to the poem. There is no 'right or wrong'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to John Lyons' poem 'Granny's Sugarcake'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may wish to directly replicate the language, style and vocabulary used in the poem.
nodes.response: The process of generating vocabulary from another poem is a source of inspiration to expand one's own vocabulary in a meaningful manner.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing 'Carnival Dance Lesson' by John Lyons and generating vocabulary

nodes.misconception: Performance of poetry must be done only one way.
nodes.response: Whilst poetry performance should adhere to the poem's original structure and rhythm, it is an art form that invites personal interpretation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing poems written by the poet John Lyons

nodes.misconception: There is only one correct interpretation of a poem.
nodes.response: There can be various ways to understand and appreciate a poem, making it a rich and subjective experience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning about the poet John Lyons

nodes.misconception: Free verse allows for entirely random writing without any consideration for form or craft.
nodes.response: Successful free verse poetry involves deliberate choices regarding line breaks, rhythms and imagery to create a meaningful poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a free verse poem about weather inspired by John Lyons' poems

nodes.misconception: There is a set of rules to follow when comparing poems.
nodes.response: Comparing poems often involves exploring similarities and differences, but remind pupils that it is a subjective process.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing John Lyons' poems ‘Happy Hummingbird Food’ and ‘Tadpole Comets’

nodes.misconception: The focus should be on finding rhyming words.
nodes.response: Poets should aim for natural and purposeful rhymes that complement the poem's intent rather than forcing words to fit a specific pattern.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a free verse poem inspired by John Lyons' poem 'Carnival Dance Lesson'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that alliteration only occurs when the words are next to one another.
nodes.response: Words do not necessarily have to be right next to each other, but the repeated consonant sounds should occur in close proximity.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Examining structure and language in 'The Listeners' by Walter de la Mare

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused by some of the antiquated language. This might impact reading fluency.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use reading strategies to support them in their initial understanding of the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: First impressions and engaging with 'The Listeners' by Walter de la Mare

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that imagery appeals to just one of the senses.
nodes.response: Through interpretation, imagery in the poem may fall under more than one sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying key themes in 'The Listeners' by Walter de la Mare

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any word can replace an unknown word.
nodes.response: Replacement words should be based on contextual clues, which can be supported through inferring and reading around a word.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding new vocabulary in 'The Listeners' by Walter de la Mare

nodes.misconception: Many readers might interpret the poem literally.
nodes.response: The listeners are non-human objects, described as phantoms by Walter de la Mare.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'The Listeners' by Walter de la Mare

nodes.misconception: During the writing process, pupils may find it hard to come up with adjectives to describe the nouns they are using.
nodes.response: Teach the pupils that first we select a noun that will need to be described, then we select the most suitable adjectives to describe them. Encourage pupils to plan their expanded noun phrases first, so they can easily put these into their recount.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning to write a recount about a school trip

nodes.misconception: Pupils make think that fronted adverbials of time can be used in any order.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that while some fronted adverbials of time are interchangable, there are still many others which must be carefully positioned within a piece of writing e.g. First, Finally.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a recount about a school trip

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a recount needs to include every single detail rather than just the most important moments.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to be selective about the most important parts when recounting. This could be taught by playing a game looking at a school day and choosing the most important parts (lunch, playtime, home time) compared to the least important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features of a recount on a school trip

nodes.misconception: Children may have misconceptions around the Iron Man's character arc and think that this focuses on how he changes as a character.
nodes.response: Explain that the main focus of the Iron Man's character arc is not how he changes, but how the way in which he is perceived by others changes. You can also explore the concept that acceptance allows people to show the best of themselves.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes in 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused about whether to put their ideas about Hogarth on the inside or the outside of the character outline.
nodes.response: Model completing the activity as a class and allow children to work in pairs or small groups using big sugar paper.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Chapter 3 and characterisation in ‘The Iron Man’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain of the different elements of a science fiction text.
nodes.response: You may wish to have a selection of science fiction texts available in the classroom for pupils to explore. Spend time talking through the different features of this genre.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the opening chapter of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the emotions that often exist beneath anger. They may also find it difficult to distinguish between 'feeling' anger and 'responding with' anger.
nodes.response: Ask the children to consider a time they have felt angry and what emotions may have triggered the anger. E.g. loneliness or sadness. Explain that anger is a normal emotion to feel but understanding the cause of it can help us respond differently.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Chapter 2 and humanity's response to the Iron Man

nodes.misconception: Children may assume 'evolution' refers to an internal or physical change in the Iron Man.
nodes.response: Ask the children to consider whether they think the Iron Man always had the positive qualities we witness at the end. This is a great opportunity to explore the concept of 'perception'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Chapters 4 & 5 and the evolution of the Iron Man

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to choose appropriate cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.response: Emphasise that often, we can choose from a wide range of cohesive devices that serve the same purpose; it is simply the writer's choice. Allow plenty of time for oral rehearsal before writing and give access to the bank of cohesive devices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first part of a journalistic report about a climate protest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may need support with punctuating direct speech in different forms.
nodes.response: Visual structures to support punctuating direct speech can be found in our KS2 Grammar lessons.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second part of a journalistic report about a climate protest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may provide 'answers' to the journalist's questions rather than a full quotation that stands alone.
nodes.response: You may wish to model writing one of the quotations to show pupils that it needs to stand on its own without the questions as prompts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating a fictional protest in role as a journalist

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel that they need to record the direct speech in full to ensure it is 'accurate'.
nodes.response: Although real journalists would want to keep the quotations exactly the same, it is fine for us to write notes in a plan.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a journalistic report about a climate protest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to punctuate direct speech correctly.
nodes.response: Visual prompts for punctuating different types of direct speech can be found in our KS2 Grammar curriculum.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Linguistic features of a journalistic report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the distinction between fact and opinion.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on the way information is presented: some things are adopted as fact by the journalist and others are presented as the perspectives of certain individuals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the structure of a journalistic report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they can simply read out their written journalistic report.
nodes.response: A radio broadcast will likely be shorter, more succinct and more informal than a written journalistic report. We also have the chance to include interviews directly with the people involved.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing a radio broadcast based on a journalistic report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that 'bad' weather is evidence against any drastic change in the climate.
nodes.response: Temperatures are rising, which leads to more extreme weather generally - not just to more dry and hot weather.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a speech about environmental issues

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that finishing a piece of writing is the end of the writing process.
nodes.response: When adults model enthusiasm for editing and improving, pupils will follow. Giving pupils a real outcome and audience for their writing also hugely increases the motivation to edit and improve.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Concluding and editing a journalistic report about a climate protest

nodes.misconception: Children may identify rhyming words that are not subject appropriate for the slogan.
nodes.response: Model examples and non-examples in context. E.g. 'hall' would not be a relevant rhyming word for 'ball'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children may try to include too many persuasive linguistic techniques in one sentence.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that their sentences still need to make sense, so focus on one linguistic technique per sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first paragraph of a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children might not understand the nuance involved in forming alliteration.
nodes.response: Not all of the words in the phrase need to begin with the same letter/sound and the words don't always have to be 'next door neighbours'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there is one right way to deliver a presentation of a persuasive advert.
nodes.response: Discuss how the target audience impacts the delivery. E.g. difference in delivering to investors (Dragon's Den style) or potential consumers
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children might think that an advert is always to sell a product.
nodes.response: Expose children to a variety of adverts that have different purposes, e.g. to change behaviour (environment, diet, health, etc.).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the features of a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with using a formal fronted adverbial to contrast appropriately.
nodes.response: Model a formal fronted adverbial of contrast used incorrectly (reiterate same point in main clause). Ask children to analyse and correct it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second paragraph of a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children might find it difficult to grapple with morphology that supports forming a headline.
nodes.response: Provide examples of catchy headlines and model using words in different ways e.g. bliss, blissful, blissfully.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating a headline and opening for a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Children find it hard to determine which suffix or word to use to form comparatives and superlatives
nodes.response: Encourage children to orally rehearse the comparative and superlative forms of adjectives to check that they sound correct.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating phrases for a persuasive advert

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the difference between the different types of fronted adverbial.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that an ‘and’ formal fronted adverbial builds on a point, a ‘but’ formal fronted adverbial introduces a contrasting idea to the previous sentence and a fronted adverbial of cause tells the reader the cause and effect of something.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing involves re-writing most or all of the text.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that editing involves checking for mistakes and making small tweaks to the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an introduction involves explaining their points in detail.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that an introduction only needs to be three sentences long and it provides a general overview of the letter, rather than specific facts and details.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the introduction of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they can place the sender's and recipient's address wherever they like.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there are strict rules to follow in terms of the layout of a formal letter.  Provide pupils with a range of examples of formal letters for them to explore in groups.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that points should involve full and long explanations.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that points are only one sentence long and use the word 'because' to give one reason to justify an opinion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating points to use in a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a conclusion simply summarises what has already been said, in the same way as the summary section of the PEPS structure.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the conclusion can continue to have a persuasive impact by using linguistic techniques such as presumption and veiled threats.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the conclusion of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that their second point can be similar or a continuation of their first point.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the two points used as arguments in their persuasive lettter should be different and appeal to the reader in different ways.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the second argument of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may become confused and try to use a conditional clause without a main clause.
nodes.response: Use the visuals of the superheroes to help emphasise that the conditional clause needs the main clause to make the sentence make sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second argument of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that it is not important to following a structure when writing their argument.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that by following a structure, such as PEPS, their argument will be more professional and flow better.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first argument of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use fronted adverbials inaccurately by getting the 'and' and 'but' adverbials mixed up.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to say their sentences out loud so they can hear if the fronted adverbial they've chosen to use sounds right.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first argument of a persuasive letter about school uniform

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand that the physical features of a book can be used as a storytelling tool.
nodes.response: Authors and illustrators use a variety of techniques to tell stories. Show children a physical copy of the book and how the line is used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing an opinion about 'Don't Cross the Line!'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that breaking rules is always a bad thing.
nodes.response: Help the children to understand appropriate examples of when breaking rules or challenging authority is appropriate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Linking to personal experiences and feelings in 'Don't Cross the Line!'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not fully understand the context in which the song was written.
nodes.response: It would be useful to complete/recap the unit 'Coming to England: reading' prior to starting this unit, to further contextualise the experience from a biographical perspective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'London is the Place for Me'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel that the Windrush experience was overly negative. Many people from the Caribbean experienced racial discrimination and found themselves in very challenging circumstances.
nodes.response: There were some positives that occurred as a result, including the setting up of the Notting Hill Carnival. Pupils may wish to explore this further.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering perspective in 'Sweet Jamaica'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may discuss other similarities and differences between the songs (such as song structure, genre).
nodes.response: Verbally model examples based on themes and imagery used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and contrasting 'London is the Place for Me' and 'Sweet Jamaica'

nodes.misconception: Based on the lyrics and music, pupils may have a solely optimistic view of the UK.
nodes.response: Reiterate that many people from the Caribbean experienced challenges and barriers, including discrimination.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the purpose and audience of 'London is the Place for Me'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may over-rely on one method for developing comprehension of new or unfamiliar words.
nodes.response: Explain that words can be understood in different ways (e.g. “sociable” could be understood by 'reading around the word' or 'identifying the word class'). Encourage pupils to use a range of methods where applicable.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring structure and language in 'London is the Place for Me'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate a range of precise and ambitious vocabulary in order to avoid repetition in the build up.
nodes.response: Model the use of a thesaurus for uplevelling vocabulary. E.g. Instead of 'ran', when describing the movements of Hogarth and his father, show other examples like 'raced', 'sped', 'sprinted', 'hurried', 'darted'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the build-up of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Children may not notice the subtle shifts in intensity and suspense at different points, e.g. how emotions may have shifted when the farmers waited and the Iron Man didn't arrive.
nodes.response: Ask children to imagine or act out how they would have felt as the farmers at each point to support them in incorporating the appropriate 'show and tell' throughout.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the build-up of 'The Iron Man' (part two)

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that any mention of character speech is direct speech because that has been the focus of their learning.
nodes.response: Model how speech is still indirectly reported within the climax alongside direct speech. E.g. 'Hogarth opposed hurting the Iron Man and he told the farmers he had a plan to protect everyone.'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the climax of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they need to write full sentences on their plan.
nodes.response: Plans are written to support pupils with future writing. Plans include ambitious vocabulary in note form.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the opening of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to generate varied speech ideas for Hogarth and ambitious vocabulary for the reporting clause that conveys the appropriate tone.
nodes.response: Get children to hot seat as Hogarth and imagine what they would say to the Iron Man in order to persuade him and win his trust. Ask children to consider how they said it in order to generate ideas for the reporting clause. Create a shared bank.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the climax of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with switching the order of the clauses in an adverbial complex sentence and remembering the comma rule.
nodes.response: Provide a model of an adverbial complex sentence. Example: 'His pulse raced as he sprinted home.' Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause in order to switch the clauses. Ask them where the comma goes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the build-up of 'The Iron Man' (part one)

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify or generate appropriate exaggerated synonyms.
nodes.response: Model the use of a thesaurus to identify appropriate exaggerated synonyms and create a shared bank of appropriate vocabulary for the children to use when writing their notes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the resolution of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to determine which suffix or word to use to form superlatives.
nodes.response: Encourage children to orally rehearse the superlative forms of adjectives to check that they sound correct.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the resolution of 'The Iron Man'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to stop retelling at the end of Chapter three and may continue to retell the rest of the story.
nodes.response: Make it clear that we are only focusing on the first part of the story for this narrative writing unit. Model retelling the story first.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequencing and retelling the story of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Children may forget to refer to the Iron Man using a variety of nouns.
nodes.response: Ask children to brainstorm a variety of different nouns for the Iron Man. They can use their plan to help them with this. Create a shared bank for children to refer to during writing. Examples: figure, creature, lifeform.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may consider Chaos to be a Greek god.
nodes.response: Chaos is considered a primordial being. It represents the formless, shapeless state from which everything else emerged.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the myth 'The Beginning of the World'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think retelling involves reciting the myth word-for-word.
