nodes.response: Explain that pupils should use summary skills to include key information, such as crucial characters, main events and significant settings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the myth 'The Trojan Horse'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think all non-fiction texts are entirely factual.
nodes.response: 'A Journey Through Greek Myths' is a non-fiction text that includes fictional retellings of ancient Greek myths.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the genre of 'A Journey through Greek Myths'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may initially get Cronus confused with Chronos who they were introduced to in Lesson 2.
nodes.response: Cronus was the leader of the Titans. Chronos was the god of time.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the myth 'The Birth of Zeus'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a theme of a myth is literal.
nodes.response: Themes usually have to be inferred by reflecting on the myth's complete narrative.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes in 'A Journey through Greek Myths'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may describe the setting solely based on what can be seen.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to use more than just one of their senses to create a more detailed description.  Provide additional support e.g. playing beach sounds, bringing in sand for children to feel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary to describe the setting of the story ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to describe the setting and the reader may struggle to picture it in detail.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that describing the setting using expanded noun phrases will help to add detail. Refer back to Lesson 2 where children will have created a sensory map of the setting.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all words are ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there can be multiple options when selecting vocabulary and they need to carefully choose the most precise words in their writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the opening of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to sequence the events/ images after watching the animation once.
nodes.response: Provide an opportunity to re-watch the animation. For Task A, print off the images and children can work in pairs or small groups to sequence the story on large sugar paper.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequencing and retelling the story of 'Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they have no errors if they have checked for mistakes in the writing lesson.
nodes.response: Teach them that editing is a part of the writing process that needs time dedicated to improving the word choices and spotting mistakes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the climax and resolution of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may choose inappropriate fronted adverbials of manner, which do not describe the verb in the most effective way.
nodes.response: Give children printed sentences and printed fronted adverbials of manner and allow them to choose the most appropriate one to start each sentence. Children work in pairs and then compare with another pair.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the climax of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to remember all the action in the climax.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to break down the climax into smaller sections and then focus on what happened in that section. Provide children will printed images from the animation, to support them with planning their climax.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the climax of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to generate ambitious verbs, adverbs, nouns and adjectives all at once.
nodes.response: Depending on the abilities in the class, you may wish to focus on just one of these aspects in the plan e.g. only adjectives and nouns. Alternatively, children could work in pairs or small groups to generate their plans.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the build-up of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all fronted adverbials of time do the same job.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that different fronted adverbials of time can have different impacts on the writing. In parituclar, to speed up or slow down the action.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the build-up of ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it harder to describe a character's personality, especially from an animation with nothing written down.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to analyse the character's actions in the animation carefully, thinking about what this tells us about their personality. Model some examples e.g. Emily leaves her parents and enters the arcade alone - this tells us she is brave.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary to describe the characters in the story ‘Lucky Dip'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that immigration is only **to** the UK and not into other countries **from** the UK.
nodes.response: Part of the reason for the post-war labour shortage was that Britons emigrated in vast numbers to other Commonwealth countries.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the Empire Windrush and the experiences of its passengers

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that every single verb in a past or present tense paragraph has to stick to that tense.
nodes.response: We're writing from a present or a past tense perspective, but the way that language works means that not every verb will be in the same tense in a paragraph. Encourage the children to think about what 'sounds right' and to orally rehearse sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the diary entry of a Windrush passenger after their arrival in the UK

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe they are expected to say their text map the same each time they repeat it.
nodes.response: The purpose of the text map is to remember the events; ideally, pupils would have repeated opportunities to rehearse the text map, trying out different language each time. You will find pupils readily copy language you used in your own retelling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retelling a Windrush story

nodes.misconception: Pupils will have been taught that exclamation sentences must contain a verb, as in 'What a mess there is!'
nodes.response: We use the term exclamative to include verbless construction like 'How cool!' alongside 'proper' exclamation sentences like 'How warm it is!'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the diary entry of a Windrush passenger before their arrival in the UK

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe a diary entry can only use the past tense.
nodes.response: The diarist will also explain what they are doing and feeling in the present moment.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the diary entries of an imagined Windrush passenger

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not take drama activities seriously or may give only surface-level responses.
nodes.response: Model the standard of response you expect and clarify expectations; remind pupils that we are empathising with real people and we should respect their experiences. Constantly showcase good examples from the class.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating ideas for the diary entries of a Windrush passenger

nodes.misconception: Explanation texts  can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Explanation texts are written in chronological order; they explain a process in the order in which it happens.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of an explanation text in preparation for writing

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-form using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first section of an explanation text about how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to remember the order in which the steps happen.
nodes.response: Review the steps in order lots of times together before completing the ordering board.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding and ordering how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that describe the personality of the bee.
nodes.response: Adjective choices are formal and technical in an explanation text rather than descriptive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for an explanation text about how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that take place inside the hive.
nodes.response: This section explains the first two steps of the honey-making process that take place outside the hive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first section of an explanation text about how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that take place outside of the hive.
nodes.response: This section explains the final three steps of the honey-making process that take place inside the hive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second section of an explanation text about how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the second section of an explanation text about how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: Emphasise that an introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of an explanation text about how bees make honey

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make generalisations based on the gender of the parents.
nodes.response: Explain that it can be harmful to make assumptions based on gendered stereotypes. Family structures are different and unique. Explain that both mothers and fathers can perform a variety of actions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Inferring meaning from images in 'Mirror'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have encountered many wordless or silent texts.
nodes.response: Have a range of wordless or silent texts accessible in the class or school library.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the text and author of 'Mirror'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have familiarity with either setting.
nodes.response: Use Google Earth to explore the satellite view of the Valley of the Roses in Morocco and Rozelle, Sydney (which the city suburb is based on).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using images to make comparisons and predictions in 'Mirror'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the clothing mentioned in the slides are the only styles worn in Australia and Morocco.
nodes.response: Both countries have other forms of dress/attire - seen in the two scenes (hardware store, market). You could ask pupils to conduct more research into both cultures.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making connections in 'Mirror'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to reflect on a character's identity and sense of belonging in Task B.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that identity and belonging can be shown through the boys' character traits, their relationships with their families and the actions they perform.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'Mirror'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand the plot due to all the nonsense words.
nodes.response: The nonsense words do not have a definition. We can read them alongside the real words to understand the plot.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the plot of 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving punctuation, language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the final two paragraphs of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing the opening of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only log key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the build-up of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that are not precise enough or appropriate for this narrative.
nodes.response: Create a shared word bank for the characters and setting that pupils can refer to.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary to write a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with remembering the punctuation rules in speech second sentences.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of the speech second punctuation rules. Encourage pupils to use this when writing direct speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the climax of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Notes in a plan can be written in any order.
nodes.response: The key moments in the opening are written in chronological order. Notes in the plan should be concise and follow this chronological order.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the opening of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can write a narrative by briefly explaining each key moment.
nodes.response: It is important we choose a range of adjectives, verbs and adverbs to include in our plan that create a full, descriptive narrative. The reader needs to be able to 'see' the pictures we paint with our words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the climax of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with how to apply the comma rule in a relative complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of a relative complex sentence. Ask children to identify the relative pronoun that begins the relative clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the build-up of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to use accurate punctuation when writing direct speech that is part of a complex sentence.
nodes.response: Refer to the Year 4 Grammar unit 'Apostrophes and speech punctuation' to support pupils with writing direct speech correctly. Remind pupils to start a new line each time there is a new speaker.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the resolution of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with using accurate punctuation in direct speech sentences.
nodes.response: Give pupils an opportunity to practise writing speech on mini-whiteboards and provide a visual scaffold to support them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can write a narrative by briefly explaining each key moment.
nodes.response: It is important we choose a range of adjectives, verbs and adverbs to include in our plan that creates a full, descriptive narrative. The reader needs to be able to 'see' the pictures we paint with our words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the resolution of a narrative based on 'Jabberwocky'

nodes.misconception: Children might think that a narrative fiction is always a completely made up story.
nodes.response: Explain that authors often taken inspiration from real life events to develop narrative fiction texts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Character, setting and plot in 'And Tango Makes Three'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to understand how the concept of identity links to family.
nodes.response: Explain that our family is a big part of who we are and can influence our identity. Offer a variety of examples demonstrating this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the meaning of family in 'And Tango Makes Three'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps in the process from when the food arrives in the mouth.
nodes.response: This section of the explanation text is about what happens after the food leaves the stomach.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second section of an explanation text about the digestive system

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that explanation texts can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Explanation texts are written in chronological order; they explain a process in the order in which it happens.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The features of an explanation text

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include information about food travelling into the intestines.
nodes.response: This section explains the process of food entering the body, moving through the oesophagus and to the stomach.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first section of an explanation text about the digestive system

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the conclusion should review every detail of the digestive process.
nodes.response: It is important not to repeat the explanation, but to highlight the key parts by reviewing the most important subject-specific vocabulary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of an explanation text about the digestive system

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: Emphasise that an introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of an explanation text about the digestive system

nodes.misconception: Children may only understand the term 'strength' in relation to physical strength.
nodes.response: Clearly explain the meaning of strength in terms of characters and provide children with examples. Pupils could discuss every day examples of strength of character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Anansi and the Antelope Baby' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Children may include unnecessary details when summarising the story.
nodes.response: Model non-examples when summarising the story. For example, model a sentence where an unnecessary detail has been included and ask the children to spot which piece of information could be taken out.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the folktale 'Anansi and the Antelope Baby'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to retrieve an answer if it is not in the sentence that the keyword is in.
nodes.response: Model checking the sentence before and after. E.g. For Task B 1. b), the answer to the question is in the sentences that follows the one with the keywords.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Anansi and the Antelope Baby'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to infer or justify an appropriate moral for the tale.
nodes.response: Model linking examples back to the story to ensure it is an appropriate inference. E.g. I think the moral of the story is that good deeds are returned because after Antelope did a good deed for Anansi, Anansi returned the favour.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing conclusions and making comparisons 'Anansi and the Antelope Baby'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the difference between stories within the genre of folklore.
nodes.response: Explore the differences between folktales and fairytales. For example, fairytales are more likely to involve magical or enchanting elements whereas folktales tend to reflect real-world settings and events.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the genre of 'Anansi and the Antelope Baby'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might spend too much time on their sketch, not leaving them with enough time for their annotations.
nodes.response: Model drawing a sketch yourself. You could also give pupils a timer of two minutes to complete their sketch in. For pupils who are struggling, you might provide a printed sketch of the witches to support them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part two of the opening of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Shakespeare's plays are too difficult to understand or inaccessible due to the language used.
nodes.response: Many of Shakespeare's themes, emotions and characters resonate universally across time.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the context of Shakespeare's 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think the more edits they make the better.
nodes.response: Praise pupils not on the amount they have edited, but on how well they are working as a team to find things that need correcting or improving.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing a soliloquy based on 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to convert notes into complete sentences.
nodes.response: Provide lots of time for oral rehearsal at each stage of the lesson and ensure children have access to vocabulary and plans used earlier in the unit.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part one of the opening of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to recall, define and use different figurative language structures.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of additional examples of effective figurative language. A display board or working wall of the different types of figurative language with examples that match the text type will be helpful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part one of the opening of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might spend too long drawing in Task A, which is not the point of the task.
nodes.response: You could set a one-minute timer for pupils to draw. You could also model sketching a dagger yourself so that they see that it does not need to be perfect.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the closing thoughts of Macbeth's soliloquy

nodes.misconception: 'Macbeth' solely depicts the triumph of evil.
nodes.response: Shakespeare depicts the intricacies of the human condition and the multifaceted motivations behind characters' actions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding themes, characters and plot in Shakespeare's 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may describe the setting solely based on what can be seen.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to use more than just one of their senses to create a more detailed description. Provide additional support, for example playing eerie sounds of the wind howling for them to hear or bringing in a gnarled piece of wood for them to feel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for the opening of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include the part where Macbeth sees the dagger, which is what they will write in the closing in the subsequent lesson.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils understand that they are writing about the visualisation of the dagger in the next section of the soliloquy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the 'for' section of Macbeth's soliloquy

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty making edits to their work in a practical way - where to write extra words etc.
nodes.response: Writing double-spaced is a good way of allowing room for editing - or you may want to have pupils re-draft the opening completely, depending on your school's approach.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing the opening of a narrative based on ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Pupils could get carried away with using Shakespearean style language and use it too frequently, taking away from them showing their understanding of the character of Macbeth.
nodes.response: Use your shared writing section to exemplify only using a few words or phrases to give it a 'Shakespearean feel'. Remind pupils that we still want to include different sentence types to achieve text flow.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the 'against' section of Macbeth's soliloquy

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find the concept of 'manipulation' difficult to understand.
nodes.response: You could provide pupils with a context that they might understand, for example, imagine a friend doesn't want to take someone else's packed lunch, but you want them to. How could you manipulate them? What could you say to convince them?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing a scene in the build-up of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: In Task A, pupils might need support in identifying what each still from the animation is showing.
nodes.response: Look at each image and prompt pupils with questions such as 'Who is this character?'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the main character in 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils will find this lesson difficult if they do not have a secure understanding of what a syllable is.
nodes.response: Ahead of the lesson, ask pupils to show you how many syllables there are in three different words (using their hands to 'clap the syllables') so you can assess if there are any pupils who need support prior to the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features of a soliloquy

nodes.misconception: Pupils might be confused by the crossover between a fronted adverbial of manner or time and a non-finite or adverbial clause, for example, 'Hunching over,...' or 'As soon as they had spoken, ...'.
nodes.response: Whenever a fronted adverbial of manner is also an adverbial or non-finite clause, make this explicit. For example, in slide 19, you could say 'Leaning towards her sisters,' is a fronted adverbial of manner, but it is also a non-finite clause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part two of the opening of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Play scripts dictate every aspect of a performance down to the smallest detail.
nodes.response: Actors and directors have creative freedom to interpret the text, bringing their own insights and ideas to the characters and scenes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characters and setting in the opening scene of 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they can simply read out their soliloquies.
nodes.response: Explicitly model the difference between reading and performing. You could also find some clips of actors performing in a Shakespeare play and discuss why their performance was strong and how that helped us to understand how the character is feeling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing a soliloquy in character as Macbeth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have the misconception that the Windrush Generation's experience of life in Britain was very positive.
nodes.response: The 'Life in Britain' learning cycle explores the challenges and discrimination faced by the Windrush Generation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching the Windrush in preparation for writing an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly include information that is not relevant to section one.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 explicitly outlines which aspects of prior research are appropriate for this section.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the first section of an essay about the Windrush

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use specific facts from their research in the introduction.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to 'general information' with clear modelling of what this looks like as exemplified in learning cycles one and two.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the introduction of an essay about the Windrush

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that essays are an opportunity for writers to share their own opinions.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to the word 'arguments' rather than 'opinions' or 'viewpoints'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of an essay in preparation for writing about the Windrush

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include information that is too specific for the conclusion.
nodes.response: Explicit reference to 'general information' must be made and visual prompts across planning slides will help remind pupils.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the conclusion of an essay about the Windrush

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write the full section as one paragraph.
nodes.response: Parts of the plan are explicitly allocated into paragraphs one and two. This is also modelled in the second learning cycle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the second section of an essay about the Windrush

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Re-read the final pages from the text to discuss how she is feeling at the end of the story. Model making notes and identifying which thoughts and feelings are the most important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the second paragraph of  a diary entry based on 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify informal language.
nodes.response: Spend some time examining different ways that informal language appears in the model diary entry (e.g. exaggeration, contractions, capitalised words, informal vocabulary).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the features of diary entries

nodes.misconception: Pupils may shift into writing from the third person perspective.
nodes.response: Pause at regular intervals during the writing process and have pupils read back and check for consistent use of the first person.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first paragraph of a diary entry based on 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Re-read the corresponding pages from the text to highlight which part we are using for our diary entry. Model making notes and identifying which events, thoughts and feelings are the most important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first paragraph of a diary entry based on 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their diary entry.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing a diary entry based on 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to switch fluently between tenses.
nodes.response: Practise saying sentences aloud to check tense is used accurately.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second paragraph of a diary entry based on 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it hard to understand the girl's comparison to the migrating birds at the end of the story.
nodes.response: The girl is comparing the birds' journey to her family's journey. The birds are also migrating to another country, but the difference is that the birds didn't have any difficulty crossing borders. Explore this comparison with pupils in detail.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the characters and key themes in 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might be confused by the difference between a refugee and a migrant.
nodes.response: Explain that a refugee is  a person who has been forced to leave their country in order to escape war, violence or natural disaster. A migrant moves from one place to another usually to find work or better living conditions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the plot of 'The Journey'

nodes.misconception: We can only find out information that is written in the text.
nodes.response: You can infer greater meaning about a person or event by looking for clues within the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Summarising 'Emmeline Pankhurst, Little People Big Dreams'

nodes.misconception: All narratives are fiction stories.
nodes.response: Some narratives tell the story of real life events, making them a non-fiction text. A biography is an example of this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to 'Emmeline Pankhurst, Little People Big Dreams' and features of a biography

nodes.misconception: I only need to read a story once to understand it.
nodes.response: Often stories have lots of new vocabulary and important information. Re-reading a story helps us with fluency and greater understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Emmeline Pankhurst, Little People Big Dreams'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to understand archaic language.
nodes.response: Use your teacher assessments to inform how you have pupils read; you may wish to have the majority of the class reading in mixed-ability pairs while you read to a small group, having them say the next word when you pause to ensure engagement.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Beowulf begins his quest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the concept of 'fate' raised in the lesson.
nodes.response: Discuss the idea of being 'fated' to experience something, using examples - for instance, happening to meet a partner in a particular place might be described as 'fated' to happen.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Beowulf completes his Danish mission

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the effect of the kennings in the second task.
nodes.response: You may want to complete this task orally with partner talk, or as a class discussion, rather than as independent work.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Beowulf faces a new foe

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that a prediction is a pure guess.
nodes.response: Our predictions are educated guesses based on what we have read already; when we make a prediction, we should explain how it connects to what we know about characters and plot.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Beowulf and the dragon

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that reading with an angry expression involves shouting or being loud.
nodes.response: Model the fact that you can show an angry tone of voice using even a very quiet voice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Beowulf's burial

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find evidence within the text to support an idea.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have read or followed the text themselves before attempting the tasks so that they are familiar with where to look for information.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Beowulf among the Danes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the concept of characterisation.
nodes.response: Explain that the author is trying make us feel certain things about the characters; characterisation is just the process of doing that. If the author wants us to think Grendel is scary, they have to make that happen through their descriptions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Characterisation of Beowulf and Grendel

nodes.misconception: Everyone is treated fairly and equally.
nodes.response: By exploring the text and reading the author's note, it is clear that not everyone has equal rights. Pupils could explore charities like Amnesty International who campaign for equality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'Front Desk' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: A favourite character is always someone who embodies positive character traits.
nodes.response: Favourite characters can be characters involved in key moments in the text; characters who change the most in the story; or, characters who remind readers of someone they know.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'Front Desk' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to infer why citizens might take little or no notice of the tremors.
nodes.response: Explain that the scientific study of volcanoes was not as it is today. Being near to a tectonic plate, Italy would have experienced earthquakes. Therefore, many people would have not treated the first signs of eruption as the danger it was.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Escape from Pompeii' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: During Task A, pupils may not find an example of each of the tension-building techniques.
nodes.response: Different techniques may be used on each page. You could share examples for the three double-page spreads after the task.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Turning points in 'Escape from Pompeii'

nodes.misconception: Less confident readers may find reading aloud challenging in a whole class context.
nodes.response: More confident readers could be partnered up with lesser-confident pupils, with a copy of the two double page spreads to refer to.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'Escape from Pompeii'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may encounter new or unfamiliar vocabulary in the additional material resources.
nodes.response: Pre-teaching specific terms with definitions or visuals will support less confident readers.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'Escape from Pompeii'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to think of character traits to describe Tranio in Task B.
nodes.response: A list of common traits could be displayed or printed for pupils to refer to. These could include traits such as: courage, selflessness, honesty, compassion, integrity, determination and leadership.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in 'Escape from Pompeii'

nodes.misconception: Children may try to include every detail when summarising the story.
nodes.response: Model how to summarise effectively, choosing only the key pieces of information from the plot. You may add some illustrations from the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with 'The Sheep Pig'

nodes.misconception: In Task A, pupils may place character traits both on the inside and outside of the outline.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that inner emotions and feelings remain inside, attributes that other characters can see go on the outside.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding character relationships in 'The Sheep Pig'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a climax and a turning point are exactly the same thing.
nodes.response: As you continue to read the text, discuss the climax with pupils as the highest point of tension and discuss differences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Sheep Pig' and discussing a turning point

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the confusion between 'ewe' and 'you' on p. 33.
nodes.response: Ask the children to explain the confusion. If they do not know, explain to them that a 'ewe' is a female sheep.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'The Sheep Pig' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that their oral rehearsal has to be perfect or excessively detailed.
nodes.response: The oral rehearsal is a first attempt; it may not be perfect. It reduces the cognitive load when writing, allowing extra details to be added more easily.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first half of the build-up of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to see the distinction between the overall story structure and the structure of the mini-stories.
nodes.response: As pupils will be writing events from only one mini-story in this unit, focus on the idea of each of these as a complete, resolved story in itself. The larger, overall structure is less significant for our writing in this unit.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the historical context and the plot of 'Beowulf'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe they are expected to tell a detailed story using various sentence types at this stage.
nodes.response: The oral storytelling here is the basis on which the more detailed, varied writing will be built - pupils should try to make their storytelling 'interesting', but it doesn't need to use all the grammatical structures they know at this point.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for the climax of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to remember the events of the narrative.
nodes.response: You may wish to work with a group of pupils to create a shared text map together, meaning it will be easier for you to rehearse with these pupils, modelling the process using a shared text map instead of individual ones.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retelling the story of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that they can **only** include the narrative elements in their writing.
nodes.response: There are other things we can write about - for instance, thoughts the characters have - but the narrative elements are a helpful structure we can use to generate ideas. There is no need to limit pupils to just these categories.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the build-up of ‘Beowulf and the dragon’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe they can only use the words provided in the tasks.
nodes.response: You may wish to list the words provided on a whiteboard during the lesson, but then encourage children to apply their own ideas in the tasks or to use a thesaurus to explore deeper.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for the build-up of ‘Beowulf and the dragon’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to integrate techniques for increasing pace into their writing.
nodes.response: Model during oral rehearsal and shared writing how we can do this. For instance, ask pupils to consider what characters might be thinking at different points to generate rhetorical questions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second half of the climax and resolution of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas with appropriate cohesive devices.
nodes.response: When completing shared writing, model considering and rejecting different ways of combining or connecting ideas; there is almost always more than one 'right' way and it is up to us to decide which we want to use.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second half of the build-up of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel tempted to rush through the plan with too little detail in each paragraph.
nodes.response: This is the purpose of encouraging pupils to engage with the narrative elements - model and encourage reflecting on each event through these four lenses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the climax and resolution of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be tempted to over-use short sentences in their writing.
nodes.response: Show in your shared writing that short sentences are impactful **because** they contrast with the longer or more complex sentences we tend to use in formal narrative writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first half of the climax and resolution of 'Beowulf and the dragon'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the author's life experience with those of the protagonist.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 draws explicit comparisons and discussion around the similarities between the two.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the context of 'Front Desk'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unaware of the layout features of a formal letter.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know that a persuasive letter starts with the date, a greeting, is organised by paragraphs and ends with a sign-off.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the purpose, layout and features of a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up physical and mental health benefits, leading to an unclear argument in the main body paragraph.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle task involves pupils categorising key arguments across the two main body paragraphs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part one of the main body of a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which elements of their writing to edit.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know the difference between different punctuation marks, different sentence structures, the meaning of 'ambitious vocabulary' and age-appropriate spelling rules.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the main body of a persuasive letter, inspired by a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to use too many persuasive techniques all at once in the introduction.
nodes.response: Explain that evidence and veiled threat are not appropriate to include in the introduction because they are too specific.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a persuasive letter, using inspiration from a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when reading aloud their persuasive letter.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading aloud a persuasive letter, inspired by a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to include information in the introduction that is too specific.
nodes.response: 'General information' is explicitly referred to throughout both learning cycles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the introduction of a persuasive letter, using inspiration from a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up linguistic features with persuasive techniques.
nodes.response: Linguistic features and persuasive techniques are addressed in isolation through the two distinct learning cycles. Build in more time for checking pupils' understanding if their knowledge is still not secure at the end of each.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying linguistic features and persuasive techniques

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of how to use different types of complex sentences.
nodes.response: Learning cycle one models different complex sentence types that can be used in the main body of pupils' letters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part two of the main body of a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not back up their points or arguments using evidence.
nodes.response: Learning cycle one reiterates the importance of writing credibility and how using evidence can enhance the credibility of the argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part two of the main body of a persuasive letter, inspired by a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use veiled threat as a persuasive technique, but they may use it clumsily or inappropriately.
nodes.response: The scaffolding and modelling of what appropriate veiled threat looks and sounds like is explicit in the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part one of the main body of a persuasive letter, inspired by a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to add additional, new and specific information into the conclusion.
nodes.response: Information in the conclusion must be kept general and it must summarise the rest of the letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the conclusion of a persuasive letter, inspired by a text

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that every detail in the text needs to be literally depicted in the illustration.
nodes.response: Effective illustration often involves capturing the feeling or atmosphere of the writing rather than just visualising specific objects.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Illustrating descriptive scenes

nodes.misconception: Similes must compare two similar things.
nodes.response: While similes often compare two things with some shared characteristics, they can also highlight differences for emphasis or contrast.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Linguistic features of descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a stormy scene

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log precise and ambitious vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note form.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a stormy scene

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a desert island scene

nodes.misconception: More figurative language in descriptive writing is always better.
nodes.response: Overuse of personification, similes or other figurative devices can overwhelm the reader or dilute the impact of the description.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising using figurative language

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log precise and ambitious vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a desert island scene

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use viewpoint fronted adverbials inaccurately by selecting the wrong intensity. For example, using 'shockingly' before a piece of information that isn't shocking.
nodes.response: Teach children to accurately guage the intensity of a statement or fact and then choose the right viewpoint fronted adverbial to match.  You could turn this into a game they play in pairs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a section about Florence Nightingale in a non chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the joining words used in compound sentences can also be used in complex sentences.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there are only certain joining words that can be used to join subordinate ideas to main ideas. Remind pupils that a compound sentence is made up of two ideas that make complete sense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a section about Mary Seacole in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: The teacher says a word or phrase in a loud, clear voice and the children have to echo it back as loudly and clearly as they can.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Delivering a presentation of a report on Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that hospitals have always been clean and organised as they are today.
nodes.response: Show pupils images of hospitals during the Crimean war and hospitals today and allow them to explore and make comparisons.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating knowledge of Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole for a report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include every detail when writing their plan.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a plan will help them when writing by guiding them on what content to include in each sentence. Model a written plan.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning to write a section about Florence Nightingale in a report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a conclusion is for summarising the key information from the report. Give children a range of sentences and ask them to sort into those you would or would not find in a conclusion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of a report on Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include every detail when writing their plan.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a plan will help them when writing by guiding them on what content to include in each sentence. Model a written plan.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning to write a section about Mary Seacole in a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all relationships within the text remain fixed or static.
nodes.response: It may be beneficial to verbally model an example for Task A to support pupils in their understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'The Wild Robot' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that illustrations always depict exactly what is mentioned in the words the author writes.
nodes.response: Show examples throughout the illustrated chapter book where the illustrations add in additional details, such as the double page spread on 158 and 159 where Roz is switched off.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'The Wild Robot' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write full sentences in their plan.
nodes.response: Teach children how to write notes which are short and capture key vocabulary and important information. Encourage children to include adverbs and joining words that they want to use, but written out of full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the second entry of Florence Nightingale's diary

nodes.misconception: Children may just think that writing a diary is just another task they have to do, rather than a personal and creative outlet.
nodes.response: Teach the children the benefits of keeping a diary. Link this to their mental health and how this will help them to maintain positive mental health.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features of a diary entry

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to include details in their plan from other times in Florence's life.
nodes.response: Ensure the children are clear that this entry is about just one day, the day she arrived at the hospital in Crimea. Use the three sections in the planning form to reiterate the key moments - arriving, seeing soldiers on the floor, the hospital food.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first entry of Florence Nightingale's diary

nodes.misconception: Pupils may inaccurately use an apostrophe for contraction by not removing letters and just putting the words together with an apostrophe.
nodes.response: Teach them that the apostrophe indicates where letters have been omitted. Give children examples and non-examples to sort and explain why they are right/wrong.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second entry of Florence Nightingale's diary

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to maintain a consistent tense in their writing. Usually, this is moving betwen past and present tense.
nodes.response: Teach children that words such as 'was' and 'had' can change the tense of verbs to the past tense. Play a game where children have to change present tense verbs into past tense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first entry of Florence Nightingale's diary

nodes.misconception: Children might think there is only one right answer to what message a story is trying to convey.
nodes.response: Authors understand that readers infer different meaning from their stories and are able to develop their own responses and opinions to them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a personal response to 'Marcy and the Riddle of the Sphinx'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to distinguish which features within the story are modern or traditional.
nodes.response: The illustrations within the story are a powerful tool for guiding students to identify modern versus traditional mythical features.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'Marcy and the Riddle of the Sphinx'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that character traits remain fixed throughout the narrative.
nodes.response: Character traits do not usually stay static. You could use Fagin as an example of this. His character changes within the chapter as Oliver understands what his real intentions are.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in 'Oliver Twist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that life for all Victorians was positive.
nodes.response: Depending on social class, life was very different. There was a big divide between rich and poor, with many people living in poverty.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'Oliver Twist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a character's emotions have to change drastically throughout a chapter.
nodes.response: In some chapters and with some characters, there will be less change as events that happen to them may not affect their emotions. You can explore this through the use of an emotions graph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Turning points in 'Oliver Twist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify keywords in the question.
nodes.response: Rehearse answering retrieval questions by modelling the process out loud. Encourage children to underline the keyword in the question and use skimming and scanning to find the answer.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Oliver Twist' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find discussing a character's search for identity challenging.
nodes.response: Discuss identity in relation to other characters that pupils have experienced in texts they have in common. Links can be made across lessons, particularly Lesson 1 and 2.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'Oliver Twist'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may consider the text as telling Omar's story in one continuous narrative.
nodes.response: The graphic novel has two significant jumps in time, page 114 (two years later) and page 221 (four years later). The afterword and author's note both describe what happened to Omar after arriving in the United States.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing understanding of 'When Stars are Scattered' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is one correct answer in relation to the question posed in Task A.
nodes.response: Explain that texts can offer us philosophical questions, which ask readers to reflect on their own opinions. Links could be made to the author's note and afterword to deepen understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'When Stars are Scattered' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that every mission succeeds in its aims due to the time, money and investment from scientists.
nodes.response: Draw reader's attention to the amount of time the team took to test the rover and the several failed attempts. Adults could link these processes to the processes the pupils complete in science (e.g. fair testing, hypothesising).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the story 'Curiosity: The Story of a Mars Rover'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to remember features found in non-fiction texts.
nodes.response: Display/print out common non-fiction text features, alongside layout features, to support pupils when comparing and contrasting.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading around the text 'Curiosity: The Story of a Mars Rover'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise non-fiction texts in picturebook form.
nodes.response: Non-fiction can take many different forms. If possible, have a range of non-fiction texts accessible in the book area or school library for children to explore and compare.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the context of 'Curiosity: The Story of a Mars Rover'

nodes.misconception: There are a few possible answers to the question about the "perfect" landing (in the 'Landing on Mars' cycle).
nodes.response: If pupils can justify how the landing went well, with evidence from their reading of the text, it is likely an appropriate justification.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Curiosity' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to think of themes.
nodes.response: During Task B, discuss common themes and model thinking out loud some suggestions (e.g. collaboration, determination).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'Curiosity: The Story of a Mars Rover'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think reading with expression is purely about volume.
nodes.response: Model reading words, phrases or sentences with and without expression and varying volume, pitch and speed. Then model your thought process about why you read it that way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Children of Lir' with expression

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to read words that are unfamiliar or not always decodable with phonics strategies e.g. 'jealous'.
nodes.response: Firstly, ensure that your school's chosen SSP has covered the GPCs covered in the book. Before independent reading, pull out words that you think the pupils may struggle with or are common exception words to practise strategies.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Children of Lir' and building fluency

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify the main events in the story and they may try to include too much information.
nodes.response: Explain that the main events are the most important moments in the story. Without these moments, the story would not flow. Pick out some elements of the text that are minor moments and share these as non-examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequencing and making connections about 'The Children of Lir'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to make inferences.
nodes.response: Lots of inference skills are based on our knowledge and understanding of the world or prior experiences. Provide pupils with the knowledge to model the thought processes to then help them form their answers.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing opinions about 'The Children of Lir'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all traditional tales have exactly the same features.
nodes.response: Talk about different traditional tales and examine similarities and differences, such as some traditional tales contain magic, some do not. Make use of physical and visual copies of traditional tales children are familiar with.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revisiting the genre of traditional tales

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the paragraph about exercise and sleep

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what 'lifestyle' means.
nodes.response: Explain that 'lifestyle' encompasses all the ways that humans choose to live, from what they choose to include in their diet to how much exercise and sleep they get.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Recalling facts about healthy lifestyle for a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the paragraph about a healthy diet

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a non-chronological report about healthy lifestyle

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that non-chronological reports can be informal.
nodes.response: Identify key linguistic features, such as subject-specific vocabulary and fronted adverbials, which contribute to a formal tone. You could keep a lot of these on a classroom display or English-themed table.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of a non-chronological report in preparation for writing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing the paragraph about diet

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting a non-chronological report about healthy lifestyle

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the paragraph about a healthy diet

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to repeat facts that were included earlier in the report.
nodes.response: Detailed facts about a balanced diet, exercise and sleep come in the earlier themed sections.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of a non-chronological report about healthy lifestyle

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the paragraph about exercise and sleep

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log key vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a section about Anglo-Saxon settlements for a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and plans should be written in full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should log key vocabulary, linguistic devices and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a section about Anglo-Saxon farming for a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include subject-specific information in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a non-chronological report about Anglo-Saxons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their report.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting a non-chronological report about Anglo-Saxons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously through the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of a non-chronological report about Anglo-Saxons

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a section about Anglo-Saxon settlements for a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Non-chronological reports can be written in first person
nodes.response: Non-chronological reports are only written in third person. A non-chronological report is not a biography or recount.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Linguistic features of a non-chronological report about Anglo-Saxons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means only correcting spelling and improving handwriting.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving punctuation, language choices and sentence structure to ensure that the writing meets its purpose.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the second half of a non-chronological report about Anglo-Saxons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means only correcting spelling and improving handwriting.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving punctuation, language choices and sentence structure to ensure that the writing meets its purpose.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing the first half of a non-chronological report about Anglo-Saxons

nodes.misconception: Pupils copy notes directly from their plans without forming full sentences.
nodes.response: Pupils should say the sentence aloud first, then write it out. Finally, pupils should check their writing for sense and punctuation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a section about Anglo-Saxon farming for a non-chronological report

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see the word 'relationships' as referring to romantic relationships.
nodes.response: Explore the different layers of relationships we all have; note that sometimes it's our closest relationships that are most turbulent or 'love-hate' because we can be more 'free' within them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring relationships and perspectives

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the idea of a 'concept'.
nodes.response: Spend a moment coming up with a list of concepts like 'hope', 'fear' and 'happiness' that you can refer back to.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring concepts and themes in 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all autistic people will be similar to Addie in the book or that all autistic people will experience the world in the same way.
nodes.response: Explain that autistic experiences are diverse and that Addie's experiences are not universal. The book is written by an autistic writer, who drew on her own experiences when writing the book. No autistic person 'represents' all autistic people.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Gathering evidence about characters and their relationships

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think an inference is just a guess.
nodes.response: Inferences are built on evidence, but they also make use of empathy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Inferring characters’ thoughts and motives

nodes.misconception: Pupils may label characters like Emily and Miss Murphy as simply 'bad', instead of trying to see their motivations.
nodes.response: Emphasise that giving reasons for someone's actions is not the same as excusing them; most things we do have a reason - that reason might just be a bad one!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making comparisons

nodes.misconception: Children may retrieve partial answers if they do not skim and scan properly.
nodes.response: Example: 'The Ganges River in India is sacred to Hindus' might lead children to think this is its only location. Check the spotlight box.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retrieving information from the non-fiction book 'Rushing Rivers'

nodes.misconception: Children find the difference between an index and a contents page confusing.
nodes.response: Clearly explain the key differences and look at examples of contents and index pages from a range of non-fiction texts to highlight this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the features of the non-fiction book 'Rushing Rivers'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which words should be included in bullet-point notes.
nodes.response: Model non-examples, e.g., 'downhill' and ask which keyword might be missing. 'Flows downhill' summarises appropriately.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading a section of the non-fiction book 'Rushing Rivers'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that pollution of rivers only affects the animals and plants that inhabit it.
nodes.response: Model examples of how food chains are broken for other animals and humans if living things in rivers are destroyed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of rivers through our reading of 'Rushing Rivers'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a poem cannot be written from the perspective of an object that isn't alive.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that personification is a fun and imaginative poetic technique to know and use.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Home Time' by Rachel Rooney

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to emphasise the different people in the conversation when reading aloud.
nodes.response: You may wish to act out the poem using two people so the pupils can see it performed as a conversation. Model changing your voice and using gestures to show the pupils how this has an effect.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to 'What Did You Do at School Today?' by James Carter and other poems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that performing a poem is the same as reading a poem aloud.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that performing a poem involves carefully considering how to use volume and gestures to bring the poem to life for an audience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing the poem 'The Morning Rush' by John Foster

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that poems are always about imaginative things and based in fantasy worlds.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that poems can also be about everyday experiences and familiar scenarios.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'The Morning Rush' by John Foster

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to work together as a pair to perform the poem.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that performing 'Please Mrs Butler' as a pair will help to create the scene and express how the characters are feeling. Model with another adult how to work together to perform and react to what the other one is saying.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Please Mrs Butler' by Allan Ahlberg

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that words can only rhyme if they are spelled the same.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that sometimes words have different spellings at the end, but can still be rhyming words as they make the same sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Please do not feed the animals...' by Robert Hull

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to think of authors, illustrators and books that inspire them.
nodes.response: Ensure your classroom has a diverse range of texts on display for children to explore. Regularly discuss text choices with pupils. You may want to refer to 'Developing Reading preferences in Year 4' to inspire some discussions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning about the author and reflecting on 'Arthur and the Golden Rope'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may place character traits both on the inside and outside of the character outline.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that inner emotions and feelings remain inside, attributes that other characters can see go on the outside.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing comprehension of 'Arthur and the Golden Rope' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may need some support in role playing as a Norse god.
nodes.response: Teachers could go over some drama strategies/tips, alongside exploring how pupils could use 'show not tell' to explore character traits.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with 'Arthur and the Golden Rope'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that a text only has one theme or main idea.
nodes.response: Texts often contain multiple layers of meaning and can address various themes simultaneously. They will be personal to each reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes in 'Arthur and the Golden Rope'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to distinguish between a traditional myth and a modern myth.
nodes.response: Create a short list of the features of both genres. Draw out the contemporary adaptations in modern myths.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the genre of 'Arthur and the Golden Rope'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect heroes to embody all of the heroic traits.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that heroes can go against stereotypes and expectations. These make characters complex and multi-faceted.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in 'Arthur and the Golden Rope'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that deforestation is unique to the Amazon, or that it is purely done for destructive reasons.
nodes.response: Emphasise that many countries (including the UK) have been heavily deforested over history; usually, this has been a result of increasing agricultural production.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching deforestation in the Amazon rainforest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that a modal verb 'helps' another verb.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the fact that a modal verb comes before a main verb to modify it, e.g. 'will show', 'might help', 'should do' or 'would lead'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the conclusion of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that only statistics are forms of evidence.
