nodes.response: Explanations and facts, as well as expert views and references to official reports, can be used as forms of evidence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the introduction to an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may notice that you could start off by discussing climate change, instead of deforestation, in this essay.
nodes.response: This is correct - we could come at it from either angle; however, since we are emphasising the Amazon rainforest in particular, it makes sense to start by referring to deforestation first.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Setting out a logical argument in response to an essay title

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect complex ideas with appropriate linguistic features.
nodes.response: Model and encourage oral rehearsal and use shared writing to model the process of selecting between various possible linguistic features you could use.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the first main paragraph of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that an essay is always a two-sided discussion leading to the writer's own conclusion.
nodes.response: In this unit, we will write a one-sided essay which makes the argument posed in the title; we will avoid presenting this as the writer's own opinion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to adopt the formal tone required for an essay.
nodes.response: You may wish to provide a bank of 'essay phrases' like 'contributes to', 'has strengthened' and 'is driven by' to support some pupils.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the second main paragraph of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils who are Christian may find it hard to connect their faith to the one depicted here.
nodes.response: Explain to children that religions evolve over time and that beliefs are not always fixed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the historical context of the Scottish witch trials

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to show elements of Maggie's story that are gratuitously graphic or violent.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that we are talking about real people and that we should consider how Addie reacted to this in the story.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the final sections of the climax, including a flashback

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to convert their plan into complete sentences.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils have plenty of time to orally rehearse using their plans.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second half of the build-up of 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see the structure within such a long narrative.
nodes.response: Note that structure is somewhat subjective, but that a lot of the plot will be taken up with the build-up towards the climax. Many plots intertwine and build tension.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Addie's character

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be accustomed to teacher modelling of written work.
nodes.response: Ensure plenty of time for oral rehearsal and encourage pupils to constantly refer back to their plan.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first half of the build-up of 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any piece of first person writing is internal monologue.
nodes.response: Internal monologue is first person writing that focuses on the inner thoughts of the person.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adopting different perspectives

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to adopt a positive mindset towards editing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to see this as an opportunity to push themselves towards producing a polished piece of work that shows off all their skills. Having a real audience for the text in mind will help them with this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Self-editing the climax of 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they have to stick rigidly to the dialogues and Addie's thoughts as shown in the book.
nodes.response: Explain and model how we can use our own imagination to build on the ideas in the book and make the drama our own.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using drama to explore a character 'low'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to adopt a positive mindset towards editing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to see this as an opportunity to push themselves towards producing a polished piece of work that shows off all their skills. Having a real audience for the text in mind will help them with this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Self-editing the build-up of 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel they have to cover every event from this part of the book in this piece of writing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to zoom in on just two moments, drawing out all the details from these; this will allow them to really focus on the quality of writing rather than the plot details.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the build-up of 'A Kind of Spark' including switches in perspective

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse this first person writing with internal monologue and focus only on Addie's thoughts.
nodes.response: Here, we haven't used the term 'internal monologue' because we are describing events and observations from Addie's perspective and not just thoughts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first section of the climax of 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to segment Addie's speech into three sections.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about past drama tasks where they looked at Addie's feelings before, during and after her speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the climax of 'A Kind of Spark' including flashbacks

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to respect the sensitivity of the subject matter.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils throughout to view the accused people as real people. You may want to refer to Addie's response to the school trip to help children understand this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring a historical scenario linked to ‘A Kind of Spark’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the key thrust of Addie's speech and instead focus on minor details.
nodes.response: When reading the text, say aloud your thoughts as a reader, for instance 'Ah, I can see Addie is trying to show the connection between what happened in the past and what's happened to Bonnie ...'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Addie's speech in the climax of 'A Kind of Spark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to punctuate direct speech correctly.
nodes.response: You may wish to select a few slides from our KS2 Grammar lessons on speech if appropriate to remind children of the punctuation rules.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the next two sections of the climax, including a flashback

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused as to why Joseph is heading into the city instead of away from it.
nodes.response: Explain that evacuation was not compulsory and many children stayed behind in the city (or were called back home after the 'phony war').
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in ‘When the Sky Falls’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that finding evidence that shows a person is feeling a certain way is the same as finding the motives behind their actions and feelings.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are clear that, for instance, finding evidence that a character is sad is different to explaining why they are sad (the motive).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining characters’ motives

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see the evidence on which they have based their inferences about characters' emotions.
nodes.response: We automatically infer as we read; encourage pupils to look back and think, 'What made you think that? What clues did the author give us?'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characters’ emotions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify concepts from the story.
nodes.response: You may prefer to provide a longer list of abstract nouns and allow children to make their own connections.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring concepts and themes in ‘When the Sky Falls’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see connections between Joseph and Adonis in the second task.
nodes.response: You may wish to discuss the idea of a metaphorical 'cage' midway through pupils' discussions, discussing ways in which Joseph is 'caged' by his difficulties.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making comparisons and connections

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they should only read a story once.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of reading and re-reading texts to develop greater fluency and understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring vocabulary in 'Grandad's Island'

nodes.misconception: Children might think that all families look like their own.
nodes.response: Emphasise the idea that all families are different and families go beyond just the people you live with.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The theme of family in 'Grandad's Island'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there can only be one setting in a story.
nodes.response: Explain that the setting may change in a story and talk through the different settings in 'Grandad's Island'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Character, setting and plot in 'Grandad's Island'

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only log key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the build-up of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing a piece of narrative writing based on 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can write a narrative by briefly explaining each key moment.
nodes.response: It is important we choose a range of adjectives, verbs and adverbs to include in our plan that create a full, descriptive narrative. The reader needs to be able to 'see' the pictures we paint with our words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the climax and resolution of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand the characters' emotions.
nodes.response: Tell pupils that exploring what the characters say and how they act helps to infer what they are feeling.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the moral and characters in 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused by how the statue can speak and used to be a living person.
nodes.response: 'The Happy Prince' is a fictional text so the characters act in ways that are not usual for humans.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the plot of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only log key vocabulary and it should be written in note-form using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the opening of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with remembering the different punctuation rules in speech first and speech second sentences.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of the speech first and speech second punctuation rules. Encourage pupils to use this when writing direct speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the climax of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with how to apply the comma rule in a relative complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of a relative complex sentence. Ask children to identify the relative pronoun that begins the relative clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the resolution of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with remembering the comma rule in an adverbial complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of an adverbial complex sentence. Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with how to apply the comma rule in a relative complex sentence.
nodes.response: Provide a visual scaffold of a relative complex sentence. Ask children to identify the relative pronoun that begins the relative clause and ensure that the visual highlights the comma rule.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the build-up of 'The Happy Prince'

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-form using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an explanation text about mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to remember the order in which the steps happen.
nodes.response: Review the steps in order lots of times together before completing the ordering board.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the process of mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that come in section 1 of the explanation text.
nodes.response: This section explains the final three steps of the mummification process, starting from when the body was covered in oil.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second section of an explanation text about mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of an explanation text about mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils might include steps of the process that come in section 2 of the explanation text.
nodes.response: This section explains the first three steps of the mummification process, up to where the body was covered in natron salt.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first section of an explanation text about mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously through the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of an explanation text about mummification

nodes.misconception: Explanation texts can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Explanation texts are written in chronological order; they explain a process in the order in which it happens.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features for an explanation text on mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use adjective choices that are descriptive and subjective.
nodes.response: Adjective choices are formal and technical in an explanation text rather than descriptive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating vocabulary for an explanation text on the process of mummification

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to note two different impressions when asked in Task B.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about Emmeline from Sophia's perspective. Verbally model rephrasing Sophia's thoughts into an impression a reader might make about Emmeline.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building comprehension of 'Princess Sophia Duleep Singh: My Story' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: A question in the first cycle explores the letter that Sophia's father writes to Queen Victoria. Pupils may find it hard to think of persuasive techniques that he uses to appeal for forgiveness.
nodes.response: It would be useful to link to prior learning to remind pupils of some techniques (such as emotional language, flattery, rhetorical questions etc.), alternatively adults could model some of the key points aloud.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in 'Princess Sophia Duleep Singh: My Story'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Abdul Karim's description of India is fully linked to his own experiences.
nodes.response: Explain that Abdul Karim was born in the village of Lalitpur in the North Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. His family background was modest. His description is likely influenced by who he is talking to.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring perspective in 'Princess Sophia Duleep Singh: My Story'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not fully understand the legacy of people, events or actions that happened in the past.
nodes.response: Refer pupils to examples that they have studied so far of people, events or actions that have left a legacy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring legacy and the suffragette movement in 'Princess Sophia Duleep Singh: My Story'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to note down qualities for each of the Duleep Singhs.
nodes.response: Mind maps could be displayed for each family member with information added as pupils read.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'Princess Sophia Duleep Singh: My Story'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the story structure within such a long novel.
nodes.response: Emphasise that different problems may be resolved at different points in a story, but we can identify the air raid as the overall climax because it is the point of highest tension.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the structure and historical context of ‘When the Sky Falls’

nodes.misconception: Integrating factual information into the main paragraphs can be challenging.
nodes.response: We can't tell the whole story in the introduction; the story of what happened is gradually revealed as the perspectives are given.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a journalistic report based on 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to integrate direct and reported speech into a paragraph that also contains factual information.
nodes.response: During shared writing, model how we can switch between direct and reported speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second half of a journalistic report based on 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have all characters using the same language in direct speech.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about the 'voice' of each character - how might they speak?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Self-editing a journalistic report based on 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to use the full range of cohesive devices and punctuation expected from them.
nodes.response: Our Y6 Grammar 'Revision' unit covers the full range of cohesive devices and punctuation expected of pupils in Year 6. You might wish to use these lessons to remind pupils of certain features they may wish to include.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first half of a narrative climax scene in 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate ideas for role play.
nodes.response: You might choose to hot seat each character in turn as a whole class, choosing children who feel confident sharing ideas to play each role.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating ideas for a journalistic report based on 'When the Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may 'start from scratch' with their notes in this lesson.
nodes.response: Pupils have already generated ideas for descriptive and emotive details ready to use in this lesson and they should feed these details and ideas into their plans today.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a narrative climax scene in 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to generate ideas for Joseph's feelings and emotions at different points of the climax.
nodes.response: You may want to add in role-play tasks as a 'way in' to the different points, modelling your thoughts in role as Joseph before giving pupils the chance to do the same.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating ideas for a narrative climax scene in 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to cover the 'events' of the story while focusing on descriptive and emotive details.
nodes.response: Ensure that you emphasise the need to move the action forwards and that you model this in oral rehearsal.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second half of a narrative climax scene in 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to choose appropriate cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.response: Emphasise that often, we can choose from a wide range of cohesive devices that serve the same purpose; it is simply the writer's choice. Allow plenty of time for oral rehearsal before writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first half of a journalistic report based on 'When The Sky Falls'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify informal language.
nodes.response: Spend some time examining different ways informal language appears in the model diary entry (e.g. exaggeration, contractions, capitalised words, informal vocabulary).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the features of a diary entry

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the concept of a stereotype.
nodes.response: Explore stereotypes for the traditional roles played by women and men. Ask children to compare this to the roles they see men and women playing today.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring character relationships in 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the distinction between hyperbole and metaphors.
nodes.response: Explain that hyperbole always uses exaggeration and doesn't need to be metaphorical. E.g. 'That is the best news I have ever heard.' Metaphors can involve exaggeration but do not need to. E.g. 'That is music to my ears.'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first diary entry based on 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to convey certain emotions without explicitly stating the feeling.
nodes.response: Explore common informal phrases used for certain emotions. E.g. "I am down in the dumps" to convey sadness.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring emotions in the opening of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the plan.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities for identifying appropriate note examples and identifying which events, thoughts and feelings are most important. Model taking notes and just capturing the most important information.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the second diary entry based on 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Students may find it difficult to understand elements from the opening due to unfamiliar vocabulary, specifically vocabulary that is culturally specific (e.g. 'rupee' or 'rickshaw').
nodes.response: Pre-teach unfamiliar vocabulary from the opening using visual images to support student understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the opening of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to identify which key information should be included in the notes.
nodes.response: Re-read the corresponding section from the text to highlight which part we are using for our diary entry. Model making notes and identifying which events, thoughts and feelings are most important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the first diary entry based on 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may include elements of Chulak's interaction with Lalchand in their recount because they know this as the reader but Lila only knows what Chulak tells her.
nodes.response: The diary is written from Lila's perspective. From her perspective, Chulak said he would visit her father and she doesn't find out anything about the interaction until he returns.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second diary entry based on 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to understand the nuanced difference between feelings and character traits.
nodes.response: Distinguish between a temporary feeling and a character trait. Explain that feelings become character traits if they are persistently displayed. E.g. Lila does not always feel frustrated but she has always shown determination.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a character profile for Lila from 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: All reasons to support an opinion are equally convincing.
nodes.response: Pupils should know that some reasons are more convincing than others and the one used should be the most convincing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Convincing an audience to agree with your opinion

nodes.misconception: Children in KS1 might not project their voices or speak loudly.
nodes.response: Show children a simple volume scale or traffic light system to visually represent the desired volume level.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sharing an opinion by speaking loudly and clearly

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to think of reasons for their opinions.
nodes.response: Give children the option of choosing from a list of reasons to help generate ideas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Giving a reason to explain an opinion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may refer to Tubman's activism and later life experiences in this section.
nodes.response: Explicit re-exposure to the information learned about Tubman's early life occurs in Learning Cycle 1 to keep pupils focused on this aspect of her life.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the section about Harriet Tubman's early life

nodes.misconception: This lesson contains a lot of subject-specific language and information related to the civil war in America.
nodes.response: Information is chunked into small, accessible parts and subject-specific vocabulary is explicitly defined.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching Harriet Tubman in preparation for writing a biography

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to use the most accurate, precise vocabulary when describing the historical and social context at the time.
nodes.response: Information about Tubman's activism and subject-specific vocabulary are reviewed and explicitly re-taught.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the section about Harriet Tubman's activism

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use facts that are too specific in the introduction.
nodes.response: General facts and information should be explicitly shared. Visuals that represent **general** versus **specific** information should be referred to throughout the planning process. Visuals help pupils 'see' which information belongs where.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the introduction of a biography about Harriet Tubman

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify which elements of their writing to edit.
nodes.response: Learning cycles explicitly model how to edit different aspects of writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing the early life section of a biography about Harriet Tubman

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly introduce new information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: Specific reference to keeping information in the conclusion general and teacher guidance on appropriate information to include is given in learning cycle one.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the conclusion of a biography about Harriet Tubman

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find identifying linguistic features of the text type challenging.
nodes.response: Explicit explanations are given for key linguistic features and modelled in the example biography.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the features of a biography

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a lot of subject-specific vocabulary without clearly explaining its meaning to the reader.
nodes.response: Pupils should be taught how to use parenthesis demarcated using brackets to add additional information to sentences. Brackets are a great tool with which to explain meaning of tricky vocabulary to the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the section about Harriet Tubman's activism

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find identifying a moral message from the text challenging.
nodes.response: You could support identification by drawing pupils' attention to moral messages they might have gained from previous texts shared with the class.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and engaging with themes in 'Greenling’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find thinking of connections between 'Greenling' and the rewilding non-fiction text challenging.
nodes.response: Model making connections aloud, focusing on character, setting and plot. Some pupils may benefit from printed double-page spreads of certain illustrations to support.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading around the text 'Greenling'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to find synonyms and antonyms of words.
nodes.response: It would be useful to pre-teach or practise a word explosion before commencing the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the story 'Greenling'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficulty understanding characterisation through body language.
nodes.response: Play a game where children use body language to convey different feelings and thoughts and their partner needs to guess.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characterisation in 'Greenling'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be used to analysing picturebook texts in finer detail.
nodes.response: Adults could model text marking - asking questions and interrogating certain pages. Thoughts could be verbalised to model possible processes that you would encourage the pupils to use.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making predictions about 'Greenling'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to record themselves during the second strategy.
nodes.response: Pupils could find a recording of the poem online. Hearing different interpretations of the poem from other performers can expose them to various styles and emotional expressions, which can inspire and inform their own recitals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning animal poetry by heart

nodes.misconception: The poem contains some examples of antiquated / archaic language.
nodes.response: A definition sheet could be provided to support pupils in understanding what happens in each verse.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to 'The Tyger' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find some examples of imagery and language challenging to understand.
nodes.response: It may be useful to provide a visual sheet accompanying the poem, exploring some of the more complex terms (anvil, furnace).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'The Tyger' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overuse gestures and movement when performing poetry.
nodes.response: Gestures and movement used in the performance should add rather than detract from the focus, which is the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing 'The Tyger' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise that a poem's structure can also convey meaning to a poem.
nodes.response: Highlight how the poem's lines in 'The Panther' form bars, similar to the ones imprisoning the panther in the poem. Pupils could read additional poems (such as concrete/shape poetry) to explore this feature further.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring human relationships with animals through poetry

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find some of the language new or unfamiliar to them.
nodes.response: An extended definition list could be created to support pupils in understanding. Explain that it is normal to not understand all the language in a poem, especially when we first read it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Pike' by Ted Hughes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know the birds described prior to reading the poems.
nodes.response: Pupils could research the three species before reading. Alternatively, the poem could act as a stimulus to prompt further reading.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'The Invaders' and 'Kingfisher' by John Foster

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to discuss how perspective can have an effect on their understanding of the poem and its themes.
nodes.response: It may be useful to remind pupils of the different perspectives that writing can take and the effect they can have on a reader or listener.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing 'Blackbird' by John Foster &'Hawk Roosting' by Ted Hughes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect alliteration to be when words are placed next to one another.
nodes.response: Alliteration also includes words that are placed close together. Pupils could text mark a copy of the poem to identify cases where the poetic device is used in the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing 'The Snow Leopard' by Philip Gross

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise all of the rhyming words.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that some words may not rhyme based on the accent of the person reading them. Likewise, other words may rhyme when read in Dickinson's native American accent.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading, responding to&performing 'A Bird came down the Walk' by Emily Dickinson

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'tired', children might use 'exhausted', 'fatigued' or 'worn out'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part 1 of the build-up of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'hot', children might use 'scorching', 'blistering' or 'burning'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part 2 of the build-up of the 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate synonyms for 'said'.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to use character perspective to understand how Lila and Razvani felt when they were speaking. Provide opportunity for partner talk and develop a shared bank of synonyms for 'said'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part 2 of the climax of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to remain connected to the different strands of the story. E.g. Lila has made it to the Grotto safely, but Chulak and Hamlet's journey is still crucial.
nodes.response: Ask children to consider why a huge element of suspense remains even though Lila has made it to the Grotto. Answer: She may have overcome the challenge of getting there but if Chulak doesn't get the magical water to her then she is still in danger.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the build-up in 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may have questions or misconceptions around the 'illusion' element of the special ingredient and how Lila was still successful in completing her quest.
nodes.response: Do not delve too deeply into the 'illusion' element as it is not key for the writing of the climax. We can summarise that the true quest was to show no fear in facing fire in order to pursue her dreams which Lila demonstrated.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the climax of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to generate some of their own ideas for precise and ambitious vocabulary.
nodes.response: Model use of a thesaurus to up level simple pieces of vocabulary. For example, instead of 'fell', children might use 'crumpled', 'collapsed' or 'sunk'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning part 1 of the climax of  'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that any mention of character speech is direct speech, because that has been the focus of their learning.
nodes.response: Model how speech can still be indirectly reported within the climax alongside direct speech. E.g. 'Lila pleaded for Razvani to help her.'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part 2 of the climax of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to develop 'show and tell' ideas without stating the emotion.
nodes.response: Act out different feelings to encourage children to consider what happens in their bodies when they feel that emotion.E.g. What do you think or physically feel when you experience frustration? Answers could include 'chest tightens' or 'jaw clenches'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding Lila's feelings in the build-up of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with remembering punctuation rules for direct speech.
nodes.response: Leave a modelled example of correctly punctuated direct speech in view for children. Provide them with the speech first punctuation rules to follow as they write.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using speech in the climax of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with switching the order of the clauses in an adverbial complex sentence and remembering the comma rule.
nodes.response: Provide a model of an adverbial complex sentence. Example: 'Her heart raced as she tumbled backwards.' Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause in order to switch the clauses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part 1 of the climax of 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with switching the order of the clauses in an adverbial complex sentence and remembering the comma rule.
nodes.response: Provide a model of an adverbial complex sentence. Example: 'Her heart raced as she tumbled backwards.' Ask children to identify the subordinating conjunction that begins the adverbial clause in order to switch the clauses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part 1 of the build-up in 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with developing an appropriate rhetorical question and writing it in the correct tense. E.g. 'Will she make it?'
nodes.response: Model appropriate examples in the past tense and highlight the ways in which it sounds like Lila is asking the question herself (despite the use of the 'she' pronoun). E.g. She decided to brave the heat. After all, wasn't she used to fire anyway?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing part 2 of the build-up in 'The Firework Maker's Daughter'

nodes.misconception: An emotive piece of narrative can sometimes overuse melodrama, exaggerating characters' feelings and actions too much.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils' representations of characters’ emotions and reactions are believable and consistent with their personalities.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an emotive narrative scene in 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have key vocabulary and be written in note-form using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the resolution of 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: One character (Paikea or Koro)'s perspective is entirely right or wrong.
nodes.response: Both Paikea and Koro have valid reasons for their beliefs and actions because of their backgrounds, experiences and the cultural context of their community.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring characters' perspectives

nodes.misconception: Maori culture is confined to historical practices and traditions only. It is not present in contemporary society.
nodes.response: Maori culture continues to adapt and thrive in contemporary society. Maori people are active in politics, arts, business and academia, contributing to the broader New Zealand society and global community.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning about the context of 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Internal thoughts are rhetorical questions only.
nodes.response: Internal thoughts can be questions and statements. Ensure pupils use their plans with ideas for Paikea's internal thoughts and model how to write these in the third person.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing paragraph one of an emotive narrative scene in 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their writing.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing and reading my 'Whale Rider' narrative aloud

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to know what makes certain vocabulary ambitious.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that there can be many options when selecting vocabulary and they need to carefully choose the most precise words for each part of their writing. This is best explained by what effect they want to create for the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the opening of 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Sequencing and retelling a story only involves recounting the events in the exact order that they occurred.
nodes.response: Effective sequencing and retelling requires pupils to know the plot deeply and to understand some key themes that are threaded through it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Retelling the story of 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that punctuation rules in direct speech are optional or may apply them inconsistently.
nodes.response: Explain that the reader must know where the direct speech begins and ends to understand what is being said. Display examples of speech with and without punctuation to emphasise this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising writing direct speech for 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse speech punctuation rules when writing speech first and speech second in a narrative.
nodes.response: At the end of speech first, a full stop must not be used. At the end of speech second, a full stop can be used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a narrative scene with direct speech in 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Direct speech should mimic real-life conversation exactly.
nodes.response: Direct speech should serve specific purposes, such as advancing the plot, developing characters or providing necessary information.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a narrative scene with direct speech in 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not write about all the key moments from the resolution.
nodes.response: The resolution follows a chronological order that includes four key moments that are detailed in pupils' plans.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the resolution of 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write about moments that take place later in the narrative.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know to focus on the three key moments from their plans from the previous lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Internal thoughts are always written from the first person perspective of the character.
nodes.response: In this piece, pupils will not switch between the third person and the first person perspective. Ensure pupils use their plan with ideas for Paikea's internal thoughts and model how to write these in the third person.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing paragraph two of an emotive narrative scene in 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Editing writing only involves correcting grammatical errors and spelling mistakes.
nodes.response: Effective editing goes much deeper. Ensuring the overall structure is logical and the content flows smoothly is crucial. This involves checking the organisation of ideas, the coherence of paragraphs and the transitions between them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing paragraphs of a narrative in 'Whale Rider'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel anxious that they are not themselves doing enough to tackle climate change.
nodes.response: Reassure pupils that their efforts are important, but that it is adults' responsibility to resolve the problem; take some time to discuss children's worries about this if needed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching the threats to the polar regions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to include the full details from their research notes in their oral rehearsal.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the purpose of the first task is to practise giving a summary of the whole argument, not to give all the evidence that supports it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to write an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to summarise the main points of their essay into their speech.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add to their notes as they orally rehearse their speech, jotting down additional thoughts that come to them as they practise.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a speech about the effects of climate change on the polar regions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to connect ideas with appropriate linguistic features.
nodes.response: When completing shared writing, show how the same ideas can be connected in different ways; focus on looking at the relationship between the ideas being connected.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first half of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may need support in understanding how the Arctic and Antarctica differ.
nodes.response: Use maps and images to show that the Arctic is circled by land while Antarctica is land surrounded by sea.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching the polar regions and their importance

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only include the information in their research notes and not draw ideas together into a conclusion.
nodes.response: While shared writing this section, constantly refer back to the essay question to ensure the conclusion addresses it head-on.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second half of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that an essay is always a two-sided discussion leading to the writer's own conclusion.
nodes.response: In this unit, we will write a one-sided essay, which makes the argument posed in the title; we will avoid presenting this as the writer's own opinion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the structure, features and purpose of an essay

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that you can only reply or respond when asked a question.
nodes.response: Give examples of how to respond to statements as well as questions. For example, how could you respond if someone said 'I love your coat'?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Conversation building

nodes.misconception: Pupils might struggle to see the difference between a fact and an opinion.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that if something is a fact, we can find out the answer because there will only be one correct answer. You could give additional examples to those at the start of Learning Cycle 2.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining why you disagree with an opinion

nodes.misconception: In Learning Cycle 2, pupils might think you are asking them if they agree, rather than asking them to identify who agrees out of the 3 characters - Aisha, Sofia and Alex.
nodes.response: Read each of the opinions in the speech bubbles out and ask the pupils who agrees that the class should get a pet.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining why you agree with an opinion

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that this poem is inaccessible because the language is difficult to understand.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that poems can be easier to understand once we work out the meaning of each line and explore the vocabulary used.  This is modelled in LC1.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Ozymandias' by Percy Bysshe Shelley

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to come up with their own ideas for kennings.
nodes.response: Brainstorm ideas about their object first (as shown in LC2), then support them to transfer these ideas into kennings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning how to write a kenning poem about big and small objects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to choose appropriate synonyms for the precise context in LC2.
nodes.response: Allow children to work in pairs or small groups to generate ideas. Mind map some more synonyms together as a class before they complete the task.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to write a poem about big objects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that poems are punctuated like prose.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that different types of poetry follow different patterns. Punctuation is still used to help the reader and lines in poems often start with a capital letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning how to write a haiku

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that free verse poems must not contain any poetic techniques such as rhyming words.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that although free verse poems do not follow set poetic structures and rules, they may still contain a range of poetic techniques. Allow the pupils to choose which techniques they want to include in their free verse poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a free verse poem about big objects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get stuck on trying to make every line rhyme.
nodes.response: Explain that free verse poems may use rhyme, but it's usually irregular and doesn't follow a particular pattern. Encourage pupils to include two rhyming words if they wish, but not to make this a focus of the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a free verse poem about small objects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person can be 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill. By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them. You could show videos of real poets performing their own poetry.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing your own poem inspired by big and small objects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any small object can be a good subject for poetry.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that the subject of a poem should be something that inspires poetry and will be interesting to write about. Provide children with a range of ideas for them to decide whether they are inspiring or not.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to write a poem about small objects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that illustrations are always drawn in pencil.
nodes.response: Include access to a wide range of materials which pupils can use to create an illustration for their poem. This might include colouring pencils, charcoal, watercolour, oil pastel, clay etc.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing an original poem

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of some of the definitions and synonyms of words associated with rain.
nodes.response: Dictionaries, thesauruses and rhyming dictionaries would support pupils when completing Task B.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to write poetry inspired by rain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to generate rhyming words associated with the heat.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in partners, or as a whole class, to create a list of rhyming words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a poem about the heat

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify different poetic techniques or examples of figurative language.
nodes.response: Pupils could text mark a physical copy of the poem with their thoughts and ideas. Highlighters could be used to mark rhetorical questions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'First Snow' by John Mole

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person can be 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill.   By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them.  You could show videos of real poets performing their own poetry.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing ‘Cosmic Disco’ by Grace Nichols

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to generate rhyming words associated with rain.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in partners, or as a whole class, to create a list of rhyming words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a poem about the rain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that every poem has to include rhyme.
nodes.response: Rhyme does not have to be included in each poem. Should pupils wish to include rhyme, a list of rhyming words can be generated with the whole class, in line with the positive imagery.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'When the Wind Blows' and 'Heatwave' by John Foster

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find counting syllables challenging.
nodes.response: Adults can model appropriate methods for syllable counting (including clapping, humming, tapping wrist).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a poem about the snow

nodes.misconception: Children can think that there is only one way to respond to a poem and you can have the right or wrong understanding of it.
nodes.response: Avoid posing questions which may lead children to the idea that there is a right or wrong answer when discussing the poem.  Try to encourage open responses to the poem, celebrating each unique response from individuals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to ‘Cosmic Disco’ by Grace Nichols

nodes.misconception: Children may think rhyming words have to have the same spelling of the repeated sounds.
nodes.response: Explain that rhyme is repeated sounds, not spelling.  Highlight the rhyming sections of the rhyming words within the poems.  Look at the different spellings.  Generate further rhyming words and identify the same or different spelling patterns.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to ‘Who Has Seen the Wind?’ by Christina Rossetti

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure of some of the definitions and synonyms of words associated with the heat.
nodes.response: It would be beneficial to have completed the Y4 Mrs Wordsmith vocabulary unit on 'Weather: wind and hot words' ahead of this lesson, to support children with generating vocabulary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to write poetry about the heat

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse a metaphor with a simile.
nodes.response: Explain that both metaphors and similes are ways of using language to compare.  Metaphors compare by saying something 'is' somthing else, whilst similes use the word 'as' or 'like'.  There are no similes in this poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Poetic devices used in ‘Cosmic Disco’ by Grace Nichols

nodes.misconception: Children may think characters can only be portrayed in one way, e.g. either as safe or dangerous.
nodes.response: A character can be described in a variety of ways. This can signal a change in their circumstances or demonstrate different impressions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring vocabulary in 'Leaf'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know that a fiction text can be based on real themes, events and issues.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that although the story 'Leaf' is a made up story, it is based on the real-life issue of climate change.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to the story 'Leaf'

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand what they are able to do to protect the environment and animal habitats.
nodes.response: Explain to the children the different ways in which humans can make positive choices to combat climate change.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The theme of belonging in 'Leaf'

nodes.misconception: When completing Task A, pupils may struggle to generate ideas.
nodes.response: Adults could provide a word bank and work with pupils to create a mind map of ideas. Examples can be included from 'Tempest Avenue' to further support.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'Tempest Avenue' by Ian McMillan

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find identifying individual aspects of the personal response challenging.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils who may need greater scaffolding to discuss similar quotes or moments to the examples given.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'No. 115 Dreams' by Jackie Kay

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find identifying examples of imagery/language challenging.
nodes.response: Pupils could use the modelled examples and further discuss the imagery and language used in those examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring imagery in 'London' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to come up with imagery to describe their individual settings.
nodes.response: It would be useful to have a word bank with specific words or phrases to describe some key settings (for example, city, rural and coastal).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a poem about a place

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find describing the impact of the poem's imagery and structure challenging.
nodes.response: Pupils could use the modelled example and elaborate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring impact in 'London' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find clapping the beat of the poem challenging.
nodes.response: A metronome could be used to support the reading. This would work best in 4/4 - four beats per measure.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring form in 'London' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find learning the entire poem off by heart challenging.
nodes.response: The lesson focuses on learning the first two verses by heart. If pupils are successful, they could try committing the entire poem to memory.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing the poem 'London' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: There is archaic and unfamiliar language that pupils will not recognise or understand in the poem.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it is normal to not understand all the language in an archaic text, especially when we first read it.  That is OK.  There will be lots of opportunities to build our understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing background knowledge about 'London' by William Blake

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to visualise the two settings being described by the poets.
nodes.response: Additional photographs could be provided to develop understanding of the two locations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing two poems on similar themes, 'Richmond Park' & 'The Old Farmer's Song'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand abstract imagery.
nodes.response: It may be useful to discuss abstract nouns before the session. Abstract imagery can be defined as descriptions that evoke ideas, emotions or concepts rather than concrete, physical objects.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring imagery in 'Eastbourne' by Joseph Coelho

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what free verse poems are.
nodes.response: Explain that free verse poems have no fixed rhyme scheme or structure. However, this doesn't mean they can't include rhyming words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring imagery in 'The City of my birth' by Karl Nova

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that free verse poems have no structure to them.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils read and re-read the poem many times. Each time they do so, they will hear more of the natural rhythms, beats and flow within it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing the poem 'The City of my birth' by Karl Nova

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a favourite character should always be someone who embodies positive character traits.
nodes.response: Explain that favourite characters can be characters involved in key moments in the text; characters who change the most in the story; or, characters who remind readers of someone they know.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'Wonder' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that disability and deformity are interchangeable.
nodes.response: August's facial deformity does not directly impair his physical abilities or cognitive functions. The email conversation between Julian's mother and Mr. Tushman explores this on pages 162 and 163.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'Wonder' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly include information that is not relevant to section one.
nodes.response: Learning cycle 1 explicitly outlines which aspects of prior research are appropriate for this section.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing section one of an essay about early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to understand the chronology of events within the time period.
nodes.response: Ensure that you use explicit modelling and give opportunities to pupils for them to be re-exposed to this chronology through tasks.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Researching early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use specific facts from their research in the introduction.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to 'general information' with clear modelling of what this looks like as exemplified in learning cycles one and two.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan and write the introduction of an essay about early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when presenting their learning.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective presenting are explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting our knowledge related to early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that essays are an opportunity for writers to share their own opinions.
nodes.response: Make explicit reference to the word 'arguments' rather than 'opinions' or 'viewpoints'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of an essay for writing about early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may include information that is too specific for the conclusion.
nodes.response: Explicit reference to 'general information' must be made and visual prompts across planning slides will help remind pupils.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing the conclusion of an essay about early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write the full section as one paragraph.
nodes.response: Parts of the plan are explicitly allocated into paragraphs one and two. This is also modelled in the second learning cycle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing section two of an essay about early Islamic civilisation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to include every one of these features in their speech.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that a speech does not need to contain all of these features. Encourage pupils to choose three features to include.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: What makes a successful speech?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know what 'feminism' or 'feminist' means.
nodes.response: Ensure that before beginning this lesson, you have developed pupils' understanding of what feminism is. You could use PSHE sessions to explore this in more depth.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How Emma Watson connects with an audience

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know about the differences in children's rights to education around the world.
nodes.response: Ensure that before beginning this lesson, you have developed pupils' understanding of how children's rights to education are different around the world. You could use PSHE sessions to explore this in more depth.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How Malala Yousafzai uses humour and anecdotes in a speech

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that provoking an emotional response in an audience is about making them sad.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know there is a wide range of emotional responses that audience members may have - and they may vary from person to person. These include anger, frustration, enthusiasm, determination, sadness, joy, hope and belief.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How Greta Thunberg provokes an emotional response from an audience

nodes.misconception: Pupils speak too fast.
nodes.response: Pupils can use note cards to remind them when to pause for emphasis and to control speed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Delivering a speech to an audience

nodes.misconception: Children may think that speeches do not need to have a specific purpose.
nodes.response: A speaker must consider their purpose for speaking before they write their speech so they know what impact they wish to have on the audience
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Deciding the purpose of a speech

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that speeches do not need to follow a particular structure.
nodes.response: Following a structure, such as PEPS, can help a speech to flow and make it easier to follow for an audience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a speech

nodes.misconception: All speeches must include all of the features included in this lesson.
nodes.response: A good speech may include some of these features but it is not essential that all are used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the features of a successful speech

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they need to include all the explanation for their opinion in their point.
nodes.response: A point is just the speaker saying what they think or believe and giving one short reason to justify that opinion using the word because.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding structure to organise a speech

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only adults make speeches.
nodes.response: It is very important for children to know how to share their opinions and feelings and making a speech is a good way to do this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding what speeches are and why they are important

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want more time to practise their performances.
nodes.response: You could teach the lesson across two lessons, with one lesson given for rehearsing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'Hide and Seek' by Matt Goodfellow

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident in identifying or discussing the sounds that a river makes.
nodes.response: Play pupils a video of river sounds before reading and exploring the poem. If you have access to the book 'Caterpillar Cake' by Matt Goodfellow, it would be beneficial to share the illustrations accompanying the poem with the children.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'River Lullaby' by Matt Goodfellow

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be nervous to perform in front of the class.
nodes.response: Pupils can work in pairs or in small groups to perform the poem. You could teach the lesson across two lessons and provide pupils with more time to practise their performances.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'A Ticket to Kalamazoo!' by James Carter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to identify the rhythm of the poem.
nodes.response: The best way to model this is through clapping or marching out the rhythm and letting them hear the beat.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'Elephant Beat' and 'Night Soup' by James Carter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that illustrations always depict exactly what is mentioned in the words the author writes.
nodes.response: Show examples throughout the illustrated chapter book where the illustrations add in additional details, for example, the depiction of a car on pages 90 and 91.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an understanding of 'Varjak Paw' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that how a character looks determines whether they are friend or foe.
nodes.response: When discussing the character of Sally Bones, focus on character traits that intimidate Varjak, not solely her appearance.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'Varjak Paw' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to use new ideas when publishing their non-chronological report.
nodes.response: Pupils should use the sections they have written in previous lessons that have been planned, drafted and edited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Publishing a non-chronological report about the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the paragraph about houses in the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that non-chronological reports can be informal.
nodes.response: Identify key linguistic features, such as subject-specific vocabulary and fronted adverbials, which contribute to a formal tone.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Linguistic features of a non-chronological report about the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the paragraph about diet in the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the paragraph about artefacts in the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Planning needs to be detailed and include full sentences.
nodes.response: Planning should only have keywords and be written in note-from using bullet points.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning the paragraph about artefacts in the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to include specific facts in the introduction.
nodes.response: An introduction's purpose is to introduce the topic and should only include general facts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the introduction of a non-chronological report about the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the paragraph about diet in the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils write facts in a non-coherent order.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are following the order of the facts on their plans when writing full sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the paragraph about houses in the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to introduce new ideas or information in the conclusion.
nodes.response: A conclusion does not introduce new information. Its purpose is to summarise the key points made previously through the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the conclusion of a non-chronological report about the Stone Age

nodes.misconception: A stereotype always has to link to someone's race or cultural background.
nodes.response: Stereotypes do not always relate to race or cultural background. Stereotypes can also be based on various other factors such as gender, age, religion, physical appearance and other protected characteristics.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing understanding of 'Danny Chung Does Not Do Maths' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: Friendships within texts are always positive throughout.
nodes.response: The friendships and relationships within 'Danny Chung Does Not Do Maths' are complex. They could be explored during a PHSE lesson - looking at how some friendships are not equal or balanced.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'Danny Chung Does Not Do Maths' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify visual, narrative and contextual elements in Task A.
nodes.response: Task A could be done in pairs or small groups, with adults supporting with modelled examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing a scene in 'No Country'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise the meaning associated with body language.
nodes.response: Pupils could model some key aspects (such as eye contact, open/closed postures) beforehand to better understand underlying emotions that the characters in the text exhibit.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identity and characterisation in 'Frizzy'

nodes.misconception: The quote on page 3 refers to violence, war and persecution. Pupils may be unsure about some/all of these terms.
nodes.response: Depending on the context of the class, appropriate definitions can be provided to better contextualise the introduction to the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'No Country'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find thinking and speaking in role as the father or Beatrice challenging.
nodes.response: Drama activities, such as 'thought tapping' or 'hot seating' may be useful to provide pupils with examples of thoughts and speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identity and characterisation in 'No Country'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to discuss themes part way through a narrative.
nodes.response: Model examples of themes with how they are portrayed in the graphic novel text. For example, war and politics can be seen in the newspaper clippings and the discussion between Beatrice's parents.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring themes in 'No Country'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify visual, narrative and contextual elements in Task A.
nodes.response: Task A could be done in pairs or small groups, with adults supporting with modelled examples.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing a scene and exploring themes in 'Frizzy'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may expect direct translations for Spanish text.
nodes.response: Explain that untranslated Spanish is the author and illustrators intention. Meaning can be inferred by exploring the surrounding panels for clues and context.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the context of 'Frizzy'

nodes.misconception: Edward isn't a likeable protagonist.
nodes.response: Edward Tulane is an anti-hero. An anti-hero is a flawed protagonist, often with ambiguous morals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'The Miraculous Journey of Edward Tulane' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to remember the order of Edward's owners.
nodes.response: You may want to note down the order of owners. This could be represented visually as a timeline within the classroom.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing understanding of 'The Miraculous Journey of Edward Tulane' through rich discussion

nodes.misconception: A verse novel has to be fixed or free verse. It cannot contain both.
nodes.response: 'Cloud Busting' has fixed and free verse poetry. The text includes a range of forms, including haikus, concrete poems and limericks.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing understanding of 'Cloud Busting' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: The friendship between Sam and Davey is wholly positive or negative.
nodes.response: The relationship between both boys is complex. You may wish to explore the theme of bullying in a separate lesson (e.g. PSHE) to acknowledge the traits that Sam exhibits and what could be done to resolve or address the behaviour.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing responses to 'Cloud Busting' through rich discussions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a character in a book has to be a person or animal.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that objects can be personified; the illustrations visually bring to life the personalities and emotions of each crayon character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging with the plot of  'The Day the Crayons Quit'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that simple sentences that are statements can only give facts.
nodes.response: Simple sentences can be used to state facts, opinions and emotions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the characters' emotions in 'The Day the Crayons Quit'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may shift into writing from the third person perspective.
nodes.response: Pause at regular intervals during the writing process and have pupils read back and check for use of the first person.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the first paragraph of a persuasive letter
