nodes.misconception: Pupils may shift into writing from the third person perspective.
nodes.response: Pupils are going to be writing a persuasive letter written from the first person perspective of the red crayon in ‘The Day the Crayons Quit’. Ensure that pupils have a word bank or display with 'I', 'me', 'my', 'we', 'us' and 'our' prompts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the second paragraph of a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may speak very quickly, quietly and not look up from their page when reading aloud their letter.
nodes.response: Techniques for effective reading aloud should be explicitly identified, explained and modelled throughout both learning cycles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading aloud a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to write in the character of the red crayon.
nodes.response: Ensure that you have additional resources like word banks for pupils to refer to that reference 'I', 'me', 'my', 'we', 'our' and 'us' words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify opinions and reasons in a persuasive letter.
nodes.response: Look for sentences where the writer expresses their emotions and a reason for why they are feeling that way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The features of a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that editing means correcting spelling and handwriting only.
nodes.response: Editing involves improving language choices, sentence structure and enhancing the overall quality and effectiveness of the writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer editing a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they should always compromise to solve a dispute.
nodes.response: Emphasise that compromise is used when **both parties** have something they can give up or offer.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Disagreeing with someone

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see conversations as only a way to share their interests with others.
nodes.response: Remind them that conversations are about 'receiving' as well as 'transmitting' and that listening is a big part of what makes good conversation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speaking socially

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they are either a 'good communicator' or a 'bad communicator'.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils have a growth mindset when it comes to developing presentation and communication skills. All the presentation skills showcased in this lesson can be practised, including those that pupils feel confident in!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting effectively

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that advocating for yourself means that you will always get what you want or that it is always appropriate to do so.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to remember that their perspective is not the only one; they may be in the wrong! This is why being polite and respectful is so important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Articulating yourself

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is always necessary to give advice when someone shares their feelings.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider that they may not be well-placed to advise in some situations; it can be absolutely fine to just show that you understand the person's feelings and that you will support them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Talking about transitions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that an opinion has to include 'my' or 'I'.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that an opinion is a view or belief that a person has. 'Tennis is the best sport' is an opinion because it is not a fact. Someone else may think differently.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a debate?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to think of a counter-argument.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think of one strong point. When thinking of a counter-argument, pupils should consider the opposite idea to their point.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Agreeing and disagreeing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to explain why a motion is not effective.
nodes.response: Explain thoroughly the criteria of an 'effective motion': it should be clear and easy to understand; both sides must  have an opportunity to make a fair point; it must be relatable, important and respectful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A motion to debate

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel unprepared for the debate as the tasks leading up to Task C are verbal discussions.
nodes.response: Plan an additional lesson where pupils prepare their speech using the PEPS structure and give them time to rehearse and write down their ideas. Then, conduct the debate in a separate lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An informal debate

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that repetition involves repeating just one word.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that repetition is often most impactful when repeating a phrase at the start of a sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How Martin Luther King engages an audience

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to think of orators they know within certain professions.
nodes.response: Give supportive clues, e.g., "Which young Swedish girl has done a lot to tackle climate change?".
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Speaking to an audience

nodes.misconception: Children may think that their speech should be purely made up of rhetorical questions.
nodes.response: Highlight and explain how rhetorical questions can be interspersed with statements and information that reinforce the point and help to achieve the purpose too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How Michelle Obama addresses an audience

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the points being used to justify an opinion in a speech.
nodes.response: At the start of LC1, watch the speech together and pause to identify the following: 1. the main opinion or argument 2. the points being used to justify. Focus on how information is used to persuade.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a speech?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find some of the langauge in the poem hard to understand.
nodes.response: Talk through any new or unfamiliar language with pupils. Explain that this is not langauge we would use with each other, but is included in the poem for comic effect.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'Compliments of Shakespeare'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to mark up their own poems.
nodes.response: Model marking up the poem as a class, highlighting the different areas you might annotate. Pupils could mark up the poem in pairs or small groups.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing 'I'm an Orchestra' by Laura Mucha

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person is either 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill. By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'Night Flight' by Laura Mucha

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to use too many gestures throughout their performance.
nodes.response: Gestures used in poetry performance should add depth and visual interest rather than overshadowing the spoken words of the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'Doing Nothing' and 'Travel by Book' by Laura Mucha

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to identify the differences between the original Cinderella and the one in the poem.
nodes.response: Recap the traditional Cinderella story and how Cinderella is made to do all the chores. Highlight that she needed a prince to save her whereas in the poem she takes control of her own future.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to the poet Laura Mucha

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that improvising a scene means taking a long time rehearsing it before a performance - like a normal play.
nodes.response: A cast of actors do not usually rehearse an improvised scene. They might spend only 30-60 seconds organising themselves on the stage and telling each other a very brief idea about how they are going to act.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they are either 'good' or 'bad' at acting.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils know that **performance techniques** can be learnt, practised and developed and that 'real' actors work hard on their craft.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing a script based on 'Charlotte's Web'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plays are put on quickly without much preparation or work.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand how much work from a dedicated team of actors, directors and stage crew goes into putting on a play. You could tell pupils that professional theatre companies take, on average, between 8-16 weeks to put on a play.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing a script based on 'The Owl who was Afraid of the Dark'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it is **always** easier to perform a play with a small number of characters.
nodes.response: The difficulty of a play is not just down to the number of characters in it. Often, the most difficult plays are the ones with the most troubling or complicated themes - central messages that the playwright wants the audience to think deeply about.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing a script based on 'The Iron Man'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to find examples of personification and explain the impact of using this.
nodes.response: You could show the whole poem on the slides and work as a class to find different examples. Then children can work in pairs to find more examples at their tables.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and responding to 'There are things that lurk in the Library' by Joseph Coelho

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that all poems must include rhyming words.
nodes.response: Use 'Teetering Towers' to exemplify that not all poems include rhyming words, but they can still follow a pattern and have a rythmic, musical quality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing Joseph Coelho's poems 'Teetering Towers' and 'City Kids'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person can be 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill. By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing 'There are things that lurk in the library' by Joseph Coelho

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a person is either 'good' or 'bad' at performing.
nodes.response: Explain that successful performances need practice, like any skill. By identifying the elements that contribute to a successful performance, we can then practise them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and performing 'A Book for a Daughter' by Joseph Coelho

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all writers start writing and are successful from a young age.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that Coelho wrote poems for a long time before he became successful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to the poet Joseph Coelho

nodes.misconception: You can't prepare in advance for a discussion.
nodes.response: Developing an effective strategy and learning some phrases, will enable you to take part in discussions successfully and confidently. These can help you feel more prepared in discussion scenarios.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Moving discussions forward by responding and asking questions

nodes.misconception: You can't prepare for discussions, so it's not really something you can practise.
nodes.response: Just like writing, you can learn phrases and strategies that can help you to respond and develop comments in a discussion, especially when offering evidence. These can help you feel more prepared in discussion scenarios.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using evidence to elevate discussions

nodes.misconception: As long as I am being quiet, I am listening.
nodes.response: Although being quiet is an effective way to show you are listening, there are many other things to consider to ensure you are 'actively listening'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Working together: productive discussions and active listening skills

nodes.misconception: Evaluating is about simply identifying whether something is good or bad.
nodes.response: The best evaluation will involve looking closely at something, thinking about its strengths and weaknesses, and explaining why it works well or not. It’s about making a thoughtful judgement based on evidence, not just a simple 'good' or 'bad' label.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating and practising discussion skills

nodes.misconception: Priestley suggests that all gender roles have been successfully challenged by the end of the play.
nodes.response: A more nuanced view is that argaubly Priestley shows both progress and resistance, suggesting that while some characters challenge gender roles, societal change is slow and not fully realised.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Contextualising gender expectations in ‘An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: Mrs Birling is a woman and therefore she automatically shares the same struggles as Eva Smith.
nodes.response: While both are women, Mrs Birling's high class gives her power to uphold societal norms, whereas Eva, from a lower class, is oppressed by them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding gender and class through Mrs Birling in 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: Eva Smith doesn’t have dialogue and therefore she can’t be analysed in depth.
nodes.response: Eva’s lack of dialogue actually makes her more powerful to analyse. Her silence and absence force the audience to focus on how others speak about her.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Eva Smith in 'An Inspector Calls': representation and symbolism

nodes.misconception: Planning an essay just means listing points I want to cover and then writing a draft straight away.
nodes.response: Whilst this can work, clearly understanding your argument, structuring your ideas, and deciding what evidence or quotations to use before you start writing can be much more efficient and effective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an essay on societal expectations in ‘An Inspector Calls’

nodes.misconception: The male characters fully embody societal expectations of masculinity.
nodes.response: Both Gerald and Eric's remorse reveal internal conflict, showing the struggles and complexities inherent in societal expectations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring interpretations of masculinity in 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: All quotations in an essay require analysis.
nodes.response: Some quotations are useful for supporting your argument but do not require detailed analysis. These should be embedded directly into pupils' sentences
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using quotations and context effectively in an 'An Inspector Calls' essay

nodes.misconception: Sheila’s transformation at the end of the play is entirely optimistic, showing that she has completely embraced responsibility and will lead a future free from societal inequality.
nodes.response: While Sheila's growth is significant, her awareness is limited and she’s still part of the system she criticises. Priestley uses her character to show potential for change, but also highlights the ongoing challenges of inequality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Sheila and changing attitudes toward gender and class in 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: That the animals feel negatively towards the rituals and ideas put forward by the pigs.
nodes.response: Think about the response to Beasts of England. Is this same atmosphere created by Napoleon's parade? Why are the pigs' rituals different?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Symbolism in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: Planning takes too long.
nodes.response: A detailed plan will speed up the writing process and ensure a cohesive and well structured argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an 'Animal Farm' Essay

nodes.misconception: The pigs immediately set about taking control of the farm.
nodes.response: The pigs' increasing power and control is a gradual process, relying on incremental changes in the commandments to gain overall control.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading and discussing Chapter 3

nodes.misconception: Napoleon's move towards autocracy is a sudden process.
nodes.response: It is gradual. Each chapter sees the spirit of the revolution and 'Animalism' further degraded by the actions of Napoleon and the pigs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 5 and Napoleon's rise to power

nodes.misconception: That context refers only to historical facts.
nodes.response: Interesting context also includes different attitudes and values. How would different audiences respond to the text and why?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using context effectively in 'Animal Farm' essays

nodes.misconception: That the revolution is a complete failure.
nodes.response: Explore the quote "the farm was more prosperous now, and better organised". Who has benefitted? Would some consider this a success?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 10 and considering the novella's structure

nodes.misconception: Spending too much time reading the question wastes time when you could be writing the essay.
nodes.response: It gives time to select what is relevant. It is just as important to know what **not** to include in a well argued response.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Essay writing: unpacking questions and writing theses on 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That quotes need to be long.
nodes.response: Explore the purpose of quotes and how efficiency is key. What is considered an effective use of quotes?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Essay writing: selecting and exploring quotes from 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That the animals could not have stopped the revolution.
nodes.response: How does Orwell describe Boxer? He is physically powerful and commands respect. If he had intelligence could he have made a difference?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 9 and exploring the character Boxer

nodes.misconception: That everyone in power sees education as a way to better society.
nodes.response: How does it feel when you don't understand something? Confusing? Scary? Disorientating? How could the pigs use this to their advantage?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the different methods of control and leadership in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That Napoleon and Old Major are completely different.
nodes.response: Look closely at their speeches. Interestingly they are very similar in their uses of devices, delivery and how they motivate the animals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal Farm: the pigs and the power of rhetoric

nodes.misconception: Once an essay is completed it's not worth thinking about again.
nodes.response: Revisiting our own essays can make feedback become really personalised and allow you to work and focus on your own targets.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising and editing 'Animal farm' essays

nodes.misconception: Benjamin is a minor character in 'Animal Farm' and doesn't represent much.
nodes.response: Could Benjamin make a difference? Could he have used his intelligence? Benjamin's apathy has a key role in the pigs' reign.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The characters in 'Animal Farm' and who they represent

nodes.misconception: That Snowball really is responsible for the windmill collapsing and other events on the farm.
nodes.response: Explore the question, how do you know if propaganda is working effectively? When there is unwavering belief in its messages.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 7 and Napoleon's culture of fear

nodes.misconception: The animals' apparent support for the pigs is genuine loyalty.
nodes.response: The reality is that this is manipulation, fear, and the pigs' gradual control over them. Examine the pigs' tactics.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 8 and the pigs' corruption

nodes.misconception: There is no benefit in looking at other people's responses.
nodes.response: How do you feel looking at your own work? It is quite difficult to be critical of your own work, practising on model essays helps this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating and improving model essays on 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That the animals are always equal, even from the very start.
nodes.response: Focus on the positioning of the animals and how they enter the barn. Orwell is already beginning to make distinctions between the animals.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading and discussing Chapter 1

nodes.misconception: Introductions and conclusion aren't important.
nodes.response: An effective introduction and conclusion means that a written response is more likely to be well considered and cohesive throughout.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Essay writing: creating introductions and conclusions on 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That there are "good" pigs and "bad" pigs.
nodes.response: For Orwell, all are susceptible to power and corruption. Orwell uses the pigs to critique the subtle and overt ways that this can be done.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the presentations of the different pigs in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: All animals were equally responsible for the defence of Animal Farm.
nodes.response: Snowball and Boxer were instrumental in the victory. Mollie deliberately shied away and Napoleon was curiously unmentioned.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 4 and considering Snowball as a leader

nodes.misconception: George Orwell was a communist.
nodes.response: Although Orwell wanted an equal society, he viewed communism as corruptible and idealistic.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': exploring Orwell's influences and purpose

nodes.misconception: Orwell offers a solution to the problems he explores.
nodes.response: Explore the idea of "resolution" in terms of 'Animal Farm'. Does Orwell offer any resolutions? Does the story feel finished?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Tracking important events and characters in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That quotes in essays need to be long and are difficult to remember.
nodes.response: Can you remember anything Boxer says? How about words used to describe characters? Any of the commandments? These are all key quotes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing an 'Animal Farm' essay

nodes.misconception: That the animals are happy in the work and with the sacrifices they are making.
nodes.response: Link back to Orwell's purpose about manipulation and propaganda. Their reality does not match the promises of the revolution.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading and discussing Chapter 6

nodes.misconception: Old Major invents Animalism.
nodes.response: The three pigs invent Animalism in response to Old Major's speech. What might Orwell be commenting on here or trying to reveal?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': reading Chapter 2 and exploring the three pigs

nodes.misconception: That Orwell offers a solution to the problems he highlights.
nodes.response: Focus on the cyclical structure and lack of resolution. How does this reflect Orwell's purpose? Is he just being critical and cynical?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal Farm: Orwell’s structural and stylistic choices

nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Symbolism in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.response: A detailed plan will speed up the writing process and ensure a cohesive and well structured argument.

nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an 'Animal Farm' Essay

nodes.response: Focus on the cyclical structure and lack of resolution. How does this reflect Orwell's purpose? Is he just being critical and cynical?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal Farm: Orwell’s structural and stylistic choices

nodes.misconception: 'Leave Taking' was written about the Windrush scandal.
nodes.response: Pinnock explains that she wrote 'Leave Taking' decades before the Windrush scandal, but some themes, like the precarious position of immigrants, happened to resonate with contemporary events when the play was revived.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock on writing 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: The play is only about the past or historical events.
nodes.response: Pinnock emphasises that the play connects past and present. It explores immigrant experiences, cultural identity, and family relationships, showing issues that are still relevant today.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock introduces ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Enid and other immigrants came to Britain fully aware of the challenges and were prepared for discrimination.
nodes.response: Pinnock explains that many, like Enid, saw themselves as British subjects and expected a “homecoming”, so the hostility and racism they faced were a shock.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock on the characters in 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: The general statement about the text in the introduction can be any fact you know about it.
nodes.response: The general statement, the first sentence of your introduction, should still connect to the essay question.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introductions and conclusions in a ‘Leave Taking’ essay on the character of Mai

nodes.misconception: Brod is not religious.
nodes.response: Consider the admiration Brod has for Pastor Chully Johnson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Scene Three of Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Context must be included in every paragraph.
nodes.response: Context must be included in essays, but where it is relevant and develops your analysis - not as a tick box exercise for each paragraph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using context effectively in 'Leave Taking' essays

nodes.misconception: Enid's husband never loved her. They had a terrible relationship.
nodes.response: Whilst there are descriptions of conflict in their relationship, the description of their moving to England shows their initial devotion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Scene Four of Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Del hates the education system and school.
nodes.response: Whilst Del did not have a positive school experience, she knows the value of education, hence her extreme reaction to Viv skipping an exam.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Scene Five of Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’: the relationship between Viv and Del

nodes.misconception: Every quotation you write about should be analysed in detail.
nodes.response: Main quotations should be analysed, but you should also include supporting quotations that are embedded into sentences without analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an essay on the theme of belonging in Winsome Pinnock's  ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Enid doesn't think England is racist.
nodes.response: Enid is very private about her views: we see only her reaction to the discrimination she faces. Consider if her dialogue reveals more.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the presentation of 1980s Britain in Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Del is uninterested in obeah until Mai realises it is her calling.
nodes.response: Del's interest in obeah is foreshadowed from Scene One onwards.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’: the character of Del

nodes.misconception: All planning should be in note form.
nodes.response: Foundations of your essay - thesis and topic sentences - should be written in full so you know they are powerful, precise and purposeful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a ‘Leave Taking’ essay on the character of Viv and ideas of belonging

nodes.misconception: You don't need to plan topic sentences in full.
nodes.response: Write topic sentences in full when planning. They give the essay structure and make sure you develop and support your thesis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Model responses for a ‘Leave Taking’ essay about identity and belonging

nodes.misconception: Context can't be included in a topic sentence or analysis. It must be confined to its own sentences.
nodes.response: Context can be woven into any moment in a paragraph; you must decide where it will be most purposeful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring model responses to an essay about Viv and belonging in ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Enid wants to move back to Jamaica.
nodes.response: Enid is full of inner conflict; it is not as simple as wanting to move back to Jamaica, or wanting to stay in England.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking': Enid’s relationships with Jamaica and England

nodes.misconception: Each production of a play is the same because the play's script is always the same.
nodes.response: The production of a play is always unique. The choice of director, producer, theatre, cast and the nature of its audiences all contribute.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Why did Winsome Pinnock write ‘Leave Taking’ and how do audiences respond to it?

nodes.misconception: Concluding sentences are the same as conclusions.
nodes.response: Concluding sentences conclude a single paragraph. Conclusions come at the end of a full essay.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an essay about the character of Brod in ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Mai's desire that people "invest" in themselves is just a way for her to make more money.
nodes.response: Whilst Mai is determined to be paid for her services, she takes her calling seriously.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between Mai and Del in Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: Brod contrasts Enid in every way.
nodes.response: Brod and Enid clash over education, Jamaica and England, but they also have many commonalities: their past and their migration.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking': the character of Brod

nodes.misconception: The Windrush generation were illegal migrants.
nodes.response: Those coming from the British Commonwealth were considered citizens.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The significance of Windrush to Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: You can't analyse stage directions in depth.
nodes.response: The closing stage directions of 'Leave Taking' are integral in understanding Pinnock's final messages about the characters and themes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the character of Del across the eight scenes of ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: The play is set over a series of days so Del's character development is rapid.
nodes.response: The stage directions at the beginning of each scene show that sometimes a few days have past, and sometimes much longer.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Scene Eight of Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: Brod's drinking is appropriate and meant to be funny.
nodes.response: Both Enid and Del challenge Brod's drinking, and his scenes expose his unhappiness, isolation and vulnerability.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Scene Seven of Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: The poverty Enid faced in Jamaica is equivalent to the poverty she faces in England.
nodes.response: Enid faced rural poverty where she "lived off the land". Farming is unreliable, and her family could feasibly become destitute.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Leave Taking': an exploration of shame and guilt through the character of Enid

nodes.misconception: Brod is Enid's husband.
nodes.response: Brod is a family friend. Enid's husband is mentioned in the play, but he left her and his two children when they were little.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Mai's son emigrated with her.
nodes.response: Mai's son was born in Britain, but his cultural identity is important to him and he doesn't feel at home in Britain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Scene Six of Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’

nodes.misconception: Del is as rude as ever about obeah.
nodes.response: Del is rude in this scene, but she also asks questions and watches Mai's practices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Scene Five of Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: Enid's life in Jamaica was terrible. It wasn't hard for her to leave.
nodes.response: Enid faced limited opportunities in Jamaica, but leaving also meant she forever altered her relationships with her family and community.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Winsome Pinnock’s ‘Leave Taking’: the character of Enid

nodes.misconception: Thesis statements and topic sentences are synonymous.
nodes.response: Thesis statements are supported by the whole text. Topic sentences give direction and purpose to individual paragraphs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Leave Taking’: annotating essay questions and writing thesis statements

nodes.misconception: Students may think the boys all feel the same about the killing of Simon.
nodes.response: Focus on words used: Some talk about "murder," some call the killing an "accident" or pretend that they left "early".
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 10 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students may see the rescue as wholly positive.
nodes.response: Draw your pupils' attention to the lack of understanding of their ordeal. Also, to the fact rescue comes on a warship and the officer is carrying a revolver.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 12 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the island is presented as idyllic in the first chapter.
nodes.response: Whilst there are aspects of the description that present the island as idyllic, Golding's descriptions are characterised by a sense of threat in more ominous undertones. He achieves this through his use of dark and light and through his use of verbs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Golding's use of setting in 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students might try to draw parallels between Jack and the snake from the Garden of Eden.
nodes.response: Arguably, the temptation is not Jack himself, but the savagery and evil that resides within him. It is the "beast" within him that tempts him to evil.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering and understanding allusions in Golding's 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that characters are not methods. They tend to think of methods as just 'similes' or 'metaphors'.
nodes.response: Any choice that the writer makes consciously is a method. This includes their use of characterisation. Anything the character says or does is a method.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a written response on human nature in Golding's 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the rift in the novel is only between Ralph and Jack.
nodes.response: Draw attention to how the boys are increasingly living separately: Piggy is on his own, the "littluns" are a group by themselves and Simon sneaks away to be alone.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 3 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Lots of students do not realise that this novel was actually inspired by an earlier, 19th century novel called 'Coral Island' by Ballantyne.
nodes.response: Golding uses the established genre and subverts its conventions to create a horrifying exploration of what evil truly is and where it comes from.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring structure, allegory and genre in Golding's 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students have a tendency to view Ralph as a morally-virtuous character who does no wrong.
nodes.response: Ralph does behave immorally and wickedly in the text - he is mean to Piggy about his asthma and he participates in the murder of Simon. What separates Ralph from the others is the remorse he shows for his actions and how he learns from them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering the presentation of Ralph in Golding's 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students may be confused about what is actually happening in the encounter between the beast and Simon.
nodes.response: Remind them that Simon has a tendency to lose consciousness. They need to be able to interpret this encounter on multiple levels.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 8 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students think that Golding sits on the 'nature' side of the nature/nurture debate.
nodes.response: Golding does not provide us with a concrete answer- he suggests that we all have the capacity (or the impulses) to behave sinfully, but it takes the right circumstances for brutality to emerge.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Golding's message about human behaviour in 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to recognise Ralph's role in the ostracism of Piggy.
nodes.response: Ralph is the first person to ostracise Piggy, by banning him from accompanying the boys on their expedition. He also calls Piggy by the name he begged Ralph not to use - Piggy. Once Jack senses Piggy's vulnerability within the group, he exploits it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The dehumanisation and death of Piggy in Golding's 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be puzzled by Ralph's seemingly sudden descent into the violence and savagery that seems to have captured the other boys.
nodes.response: Point out how Jack's more aggressive behaviour appeals to the boys.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 7 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Ralph doesn't blow the conch to summon the boys back because he is afraid of Jack.
nodes.response: Ralph is not afraid of Jack. He is afraid that if he blows the conch and the boys don't return, he will have lost his authority.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 5 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often judge Piggy by the critical standards employed by the other boys.
nodes.response: Pick out examples of how sensible and intelligent Piggy is and how his judgement is usually sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 2 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often overlook Simon's significance in this novel.
nodes.response: Simon is a very important character because he shows us that, in a world of evil, we can still act in a compassionate and civilised manner. Through Simon, Golding reminds us that our behaviour is a choice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Simon's role as an outsider and as Jack's foil in 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students may not understand that Sam and Eric have not actually seen the parachutist.
nodes.response: Unpick the description given by Sam and Eric. Were we (the reader) actually shown the different aspects of the beast?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 6 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students might think that Golding's reference to a world order in "ruins" refers to the damaged sandcastles and their ruined life on the island.
nodes.response: Remind students of Golding's wartime experiences and the events of WWII.  Golding is referring to the world the boys left behind as well as the world on the island.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 4 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: When pupils think about the role of rules in society, they tend to focus on the role of more punitive rules and argue that rules are restrictive.
nodes.response: Try to get pupils to understand the necessity for rules and laws - particularly those that ban harming others. Get students to imagine what life would be like if harming others was not prohibited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering ideas of rules and human nature in relation to 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the first attempt at their response is the finished version.
nodes.response: Redrafting your work has many benefits and the second attempt is always superior. Taking time to reflect on  your work and identify areas for improvements allows you to recognise any lack of clarity in your explanations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a response on human nature in Golding's 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the island in the novel is like a tropical paradise.
nodes.response: Draw their attention to the suggestion of danger in the language used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 1 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students think that symbols in a text have to be physical objects that represent ideas.
nodes.response: Symbolism is the use of images, words or nouns to represent abstract ideas or qualities - symbols do not have to be physical objects that can be picked up and held.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Golding's use of symbolism in 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think that only Jack's hunters are involved in the killing of Simon.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the one sentence where Golding says that Ralph and Piggy want to be part of the group.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 9 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the island turned Jack into the cruel and bloodthirsty leader he is by the end of the novel.
nodes.response: From the very beginning, Jack was characterised as unpleasant and egomaniacal. He treats the choir terribly in the first chapter. Jack arguably always had the traits of a dictatorial leader. The island has exacerbated these traits, not created them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering Jack's dictatorial leadership and antagonism in 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Students may think that Piggy's death is an accident, similar in kind to Simon's, an example of boys getting carried away.
nodes.response: Draw pupils' attention to the fact that Roger is compared to a hangman. A hangman kills intentionally.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An exploration of Chapter 11 of 'Lord of the Flies'

nodes.misconception: Annotating means highlighting everything you think is important in a text.
nodes.response: Annotating is a skill that requires time and thought. Using symbols and short notes makes your annotations helpful and understandable, even if you come back to them at a much later date.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Madeline Miller's 'The Song of Achilles': understanding the extract

nodes.misconception: The term complex sentence is a synonym for a long sentence.
nodes.response: A complex sentence is a technical term. It refers to a sentence that has a main clause and a subordinate clause. Sentences can be long but if they don't have a subordinate clause, they are not a complex sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing inspired by ‘Skin of the Sea’: varying sentence types to create rhythm

nodes.misconception: A Mami Wata is always presented as a mermaid who saves the souls of enslaved people.
nodes.response: Mami Wata is a water spirit and has a rich tradition in West, Central and Southern Africa. Bowen has used the deity in her novel and presented her as a mermaid with a specific task, but the goddess is presented in different ways in other art.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Natasha Bowen's ‘Skin of the Sea’: understanding the extract

nodes.misconception: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by someone or something.
nodes.response: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by a piece of art, and they describe that piece of art in the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring William Carlos Williams’s poem ‘Landscape with the fall of Icarus’

nodes.misconception: You have to include each aspect of characterisation in the same paragraph, and always in the same order.
nodes.response: Chaucer has a particular way of introducing and describing his characters. However, this is one way to do it, amongst many. You will see lots of different writers use the same methods of characterisation, but in different orders and structures.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating convincing characters using ‘The Canterbury Tales’ as stimulus

nodes.misconception: Using onomatopoeia is the only way to create a sense of sound in a piece of writing.
nodes.response: Onomatopoeia can be a helpful tool to rely on in some pieces of writing. However, alliteration, plosives and sibilance are often more sophisticated and more subtle. They also allow for a greater range of sounds to be generated.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing and refining descriptive writing: alliteration, plosives and sibilance

nodes.misconception: You should use an adjective to describe every noun.
nodes.response: Adjectives can help add interest and atmosphere to your writing. But not every noun needs an adjective. This can become overwhelming for the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective sensory language using ‘The Execution of Lady Jane Grey’ as stimulus

nodes.misconception: Flashback is the only way to include information about a character's past.
nodes.response: Flashback is a powerful method and one which lots of writers rely on. However, there are many other ways to include details about a character's past. For example, explanation from a character or dialogue between characters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Use of flashback in Natasha Bowen's 'Skin of the Sea'

nodes.misconception: Once you have used an image or idea in a piece of writing, you can't reuse it in the same piece.
nodes.response: Sometimes repeating an idea or image throughout a piece can help give it a sense of structure. You might change certain details, but you can repeat them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a full descriptive piece: ‘The Execution of Lady Jane Grey' as stimulus

nodes.misconception: Each section of the five part narrative structure equals one paragraph in your writing.
nodes.response: The five part narrative structure is a helpful way to help plan plot and character. However, some sections might be longer than others. Some might require multiple paragraphs, others just one.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a narrative using the five part narrative structure

nodes.misconception: When annotating, you should highlight, underline and circle interesting things. You don't need to write anything down as you will remember what you thought.
nodes.response: Symbols, highlights and underlinings are all useful, but only if accompanied by short written notes which remind you what it was you found interesting. Otherwise your symbols become meaningless.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Pat Barker's 'The Silence of the Girls': understanding the extract

nodes.misconception: All the Greek myths have morals.
nodes.response: The Greek myths are not all moralistic. Indeed, the gods, mythological creatures and mortals often act in cruel, reactive, vengeful and immoral ways.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Bruegel's Landscape with the Fall of Icarus: how the myth inspired the painting

nodes.misconception: 'The Fisherman the and Jinni' is a framing story because there is a story within it.
nodes.response: The story of King Yunan and his sage is a story within a story. In 'One Thousand and One Nights', the frame story is only that of Shahrazad and Shahrayar. This frame story punctuates all the tales, with dialogue between husband and wife throughout.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Hanan Al-Shaykh's ‘The Fisherman and the Jinni’: understanding the story

nodes.misconception: The Lady of Shalott chooses to take her own life on the way to Camelot.
nodes.response: The Lady of Shalott realises that, because she got up from her loom, she is now cursed. Knowing she will die from this curse, she gets into the boat to sail to Camelot. She realises she will not make it there alive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Alfred, Lord Tennyson's 'The Lady of Shalott': understanding the ballad

nodes.misconception: Auden is saying suffering is unimportant.
nodes.response: Auden presents extreme suffering, but he is exploring how, inevitably, when something terrible is happening, something ordinary is happening at the same time too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring W.H. Auden's poem 'Musée des Beaux Arts'

nodes.misconception: Proofreading and rewriting are the same thing.
nodes.response: Proofreading is the final stage of the writing process. It is about checking for small errors - often grammatical. Rewriting is a larger task which requires you to think about the effects you want to create.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving and proofreading a piece of narrative writing

nodes.misconception: You can't talk about two different texts in the same paragraph.
nodes.response: It can be tricky to talk about two texts in one paragraph, but it often makes for a stronger comparison. A good way to start is to consider one aspect of the texts you wish to compare, and then draw out the differences in your analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing poems: 'Brueghel's Winter' and 'The Hunters in the Snow'

nodes.misconception: The five part narrative structure is the only way to structure a story.
nodes.response: There are lots of ways to create a story that is structured. This is one example. The most important thing to remember is that whatever your structure, it should be considered and carefully planned.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The five part narrative structure

nodes.misconception: The folktales have no connection to the frame story.
nodes.response: The folktales are being told by Shahrazad. The fact that she is trying to save her life by telling the stories is important. But more than this, you can also make connections between the ideas, plot and characters in the folktales to the frame story.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the theme of power in Hanan Al-Shaykh's ‘One Thousand and One Nights’

nodes.misconception: We have two different presentations of Achilles. One of them must be right, and one must be wrong.
nodes.response: What Miller and Barker do with their novels is show how important perspective is. For Patroclus, Achilles is awe inspiring and innocent. For Briseis, he is quite the opposite. Their perspectives are based on their relationship with him.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparative paragraphs: 'The Silence of the Girls' and 'The Song of Achilles'

nodes.misconception: Writers can use any object to symbolise any idea.
nodes.response: Writers can get their messages across via inventive and innovative methods. However, there are some key symbols in literature which have a generally accepted meaning. For example, a rose to symbolise love, or a pearl to symbolise perfection.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Descriptive writing using Lord Tennyson's 'The Lady of Shalott' as stimulus

nodes.misconception: Middle English is the same as Old English. Both are general terms, and mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Middle English was spoken from about 1100-1500. Old English was spoken before 1100. Both are technical terms and have a specific meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Geoffrey Chaucer's ‘The Canterbury Tales’: compelling characterisation

nodes.misconception: The use of adjectives is a simple technique, so there isn't much point analysing a writer's use of them, or planning for them in your own writing.
nodes.response: Adjectives are a wonderful way to express tone, nuanced meaning and atmosphere. As such, they can be rich for analysis, and have a powerful effect on your own descriptive writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Walter de la Mare's poem 'Brueghel's Winter'

nodes.misconception: A third person omniscient narrator must develop each character in the same amount of detail.
nodes.response: Whilst a third person omniscient narrator can develop many characters, they don't need the same amount of space, detail and time in a written piece. You can still have a central character, and minor characters who are more or less important.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Third person omniscient writing: ‘The Execution of Lady Jane Grey’ as stimulus

nodes.misconception: You can't include quotations when exploring enjambment.
nodes.response: If analysing enjambment, you must include a specific example. Just as you would include a quotation to explore a simile (for example) so must you include a quotation to explore enjambment.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring enjambment in Alfred, Lord Tennyson's ‘The Lady of Shalott’

nodes.misconception: If you are in solitude, you feel lonely.
nodes.response: Solitude can be a pleasant state, one that lots of people seek out. It is different from feeling lonely or isolated.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Symbolism in Alfred, Lord Tennyson's ‘The Lady of Shalott’

nodes.misconception: You can't repeat any ideas in creative writing. Once you have used them once, you must create new ideas in every successive paragraph.
nodes.response: Repetition of certain ideas or images can give your writing a sense of structure. This is particularly true in your final paragraph where repeating ideas from your first paragraph can alert your reader to the idea that you are about to finish.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a full narrative piece using the five part narrative structure

nodes.misconception: Williams didn't use any methods in his poem because he is just describing a painting.
nodes.response: Every word in a poem is carefully selected. Williams could have made any number of choices about what he depicted in terms of focus, structure, tone and language. We can explore these methods, and add layers of meaning to the painting.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring William Carlos Williams's poem 'The Hunters in the Snow'

nodes.misconception: That 'Animal Farm' is a simple story about leadership and power.
nodes.response: Stylistically it is simple, but why does Orwell do this? What does he hope to achieve by making his novella accessible?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing form and structure in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: Writing essays is not like creative writing, it doesn't matter how you write things so much.
nodes.response: Not writing clearly and accurately can mean excellent ideas can be lost once written down.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': writing with clarity in essays

nodes.misconception: That Orwell presents "good" leaders and "bad" leaders.
nodes.response: Think about the impact of Mr. Jones and the pigs on the animals' lives. Is it easy to distinguish which one is better or worse?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using critical quotations and evaluating the leadership of 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: You need to learn lots of quotes to write a successful essay.
nodes.response: Picking a few 'hard working', analytically rich quotes is a better strategy. It's what you do with them that counts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing analytical paragraphs on 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That Boxer is only presented as naïve and gullible.
nodes.response: Why does Napoleon set the dogs on Boxer? There are moments when Boxer begins to challenge what he is being told by the pigs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Boxer and the theme of education in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That there are clear distinctions between good leaders and bad leaders in 'Animal Farm'.
nodes.response: Although 'Animal Farm' is simply written, its messages are complex. What is Orwell wanting to reveal about leadership in general?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The leadership of Mr. Jones in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: I don't need to bother with a conclusion.
nodes.response: Who will be reading your response? Imagine them reading your final sentence, how do you want them to feel?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing effective introductions and conclusions on 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: You must analyse every quotation at word level.
nodes.response: Sometimes exploring individual words can be helpful, but more often than not it makes for shallow analysis which is not helpful in answering the question. Look at 'bigger' methods than single words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': reviewing and refining an essay about Puck

nodes.misconception: Puck tries to create more chaos after realising his mistake.
nodes.response: Puck is consistently shown to follow Oberon's orders in relation to the Athenian nobles, and to try and do so correctly. However, he does find it very funny, even though he didn't deliberately create the situation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': How is Puck presented in Act 3, Scene 2?

nodes.misconception: It is not significant that Puck performs the epilogue. It could have been any of the characters.
nodes.response: There are many different ideas to explore in terms of why Puck performs this epilogue. It could speak to his centrality to the plot, his infamous reputation amongst the play's first Elizabethan audiences, and the way we should interpret key themes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': Puck's epilogue in Act 5

nodes.misconception: You should only analyse one quotation per paragraph.
nodes.response: Analysing multiple quotations, and exploring the connections between them, makes for the most powerful analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Puck's epilogue in Act 5 of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: You should only ever consider one Shakespearean play at a time. Comparing plays and characters is irrelevant and confusing.
nodes.response: Comparing characters can be an excellent way to deepen your understanding of Shakespeare as a writer, and to understand the significance of how a particular character has been created.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’: Shakespeare and the supernatural

nodes.misconception: Introductions are the same as thesis statements.
nodes.response: An introduction includes a thesis statement. However, an introduction should include a more general statement about the text, as well as a more general statement about the given character or theme as well as the thesis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introductions to essays about Puck in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Using one quotation per paragraph is enough.
nodes.response: Using multiple quotations per paragraph can be effective if you select quotations which link. Select quotations from across the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How is Puck presented in Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'?

nodes.misconception: You can't compare one scene to another. You must focus on one at a time.
nodes.response: A play is not a sequence of unconnected scenes and characters. They all work together to present and explore particular ideas. You should compare characters and scenes in order to understand a play, its characters and ideas more deeply.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’, Act 2, Scene 1: Titania and Oberon’s conflict

nodes.misconception: Paragraphs can only focus on one character at a time.
nodes.response: Comparing characters can be a useful way to deepen your understanding and analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': powerful topic sentences about Puck

nodes.misconception: If a play is a comedy, it won't have any moments of sadness in it.
nodes.response: When thinking about genre, we consider the overall tone, plot and features of a play. However, many comedies have moments of sadness, just as many tragedies have moments of humour.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the genre of William Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Puck is a disrespectful character.
nodes.response: Puck's disrespect is targeted at particular characters. He is shown as respectful to Oberon, for example, and other high status characters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’: Puck - obedient servant or irreverent joker?

nodes.misconception: The characters in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' are Elizabethan.
nodes.response: The play's first audiences were Elizabethan, and Shakespeare explores Elizabethan attitudes and ideas in the play. But the play is set in Athens many centuries before the Elizabethan period.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of Egeus in Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: The magical potion is removed from everyone's eyes at the end of the play.
nodes.response: Demetrius still has the magical potion on his eyes. This is why he is in love with Helena.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The plot of William Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: If you are writing about a character, you should just write down everything you know about them.
nodes.response: When writing about a character, you should consider how you interpret them and why. You should explain this main idea in your thesis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating an argument about the character of Puck in ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’

nodes.misconception: Oberon asks Puck to turn Bottom's head into that of a donkey.
nodes.response: Puck follows Oberon's orders, but in his own time, he gets up to his own mischief. He decides to transform Bottom and Oberon does not set out for Titania to fall in love with this particular character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the character of Puck in Acts 2 and 3 of ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’

nodes.misconception: Titania, Lysander and Demetrius have the antidote applied to them.
nodes.response: So that the play can end in happy marriages between all four Athenian nobles, only Lysander has the antidote applied to him. Demetrius is still under the influence of the magical potion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Act 3, Scene 2 of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': order is restored in the forest

nodes.misconception: It isn't important that Puck's mistake is genuine.
nodes.response: Without understanding what happens, and why, in Act 2, Scene 2, we won't have an accurate understanding of Shakespeare's characterisation of Puck which deepens and develops throughout the play.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How is Puck presented in Act 2, Scene 2 of ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’?

nodes.misconception: Oberon knows Titania will fall in love with Bottom.
nodes.response: Oberon hopes Titania will fall in love with something "vile" but he doesn't know about Bottom, or his transformation, until Puck tells him the joke he has played.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the magical potion in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: There is one interpretation of Puck (either malevolent or mischievous) and you have to work out which one is correct.
nodes.response: A play, and its characters, can be interpreted in many different ways. Different performances will draw out particular interpretations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The character of Puck in Shakespeare’s ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’

nodes.misconception: Every quotation in a main body paragraph should be analysed.
nodes.response: Some quotations should be analysed, but others you can simply embed into sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analytical paragraphs: Puck and the supernatural in ‘A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: A theme is any idea or plot point in a text.
nodes.response: Themes are the most important ideas in a text. There may be multiple. The most important themes are the ones that are returned to over and over again, and explored in a number of different ways.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring key themes in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': love, power, disorder

nodes.misconception: Context should be included in one sentence at the end of each analytical paragraph.
nodes.response: You can include contextual ideas where relevant - this could be at the start, middle or multiple times in a paragraph. Contextual ideas will often help you develop your analysis of a particular quotation or character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Including context when writing about Puck in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Oberon and Puck deliberately try and create disorder between Hermia, Lysander, Helena and Demetrius.
nodes.response: Oberon orders Puck to put the magical potion on Demetrius so that he falls in love with Helena. Puck makes a genuine mistake by putting it on Lysander.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The significance of the magical forest in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Oberon's commands, status and dominance in the dialogue mean he can only be interpreted as powerful.
nodes.response: There is much to suggest Oberon's power in this scene, but dialogue can be interpreted in many ways, and performance can affect how we perceive a character. There is no single reading of the play.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The character of Oberon in Act 2, Scene 1 of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Oberon finds the disorder between the Athenian nobles funny.
nodes.response: As soon as Oberon realises Puck's mistake, he swiftly tries to correct it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Act 3 of ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’: disorder in the forest

nodes.misconception: Analysis means zooming in to individual words and explaining what they mean.
nodes.response: Exploring quotations is more than just looking at individual words and offering paraphrase or synonym. Your exploration of the quotation should develop your ideas about the question, and look at dramatic methods (more than just individual words).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Model paragraphs about Act 2, Scene 1 of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Titania seems to have some power, but Hermia has none.
nodes.response: Hermia defies her father by saying that she will marry Lysander, and refusing to marry Demetrius. She is also willing to leave her father, and the place she was born rather than obey her father.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The patriarchal world of William Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'

nodes.misconception: Conclusions should include quotations.
nodes.response: Conclusions are about summing up your overall argument (your thesis) rather than continuing to develop it via analysis of new quotations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Conclusions to essays: Puck and the supernatural in ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’

nodes.misconception: Pankhurst and the suffragettes were peaceful protesters.
nodes.response: How does Pankhurst's speech convey some of the radical tactics or attitudes employed by the suffragettes? Pankhurst and her followers pushed boundaries and challenged societal norms to fight for women's rights.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and analysing a writer’s perspective

nodes.misconception: That memorising the speech, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
nodes.response: An effective speech will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing and delivering a powerful speech

nodes.misconception: Autobiographies are not considered literary or forms of literature.
nodes.response: Just like other forms of writing, writers of autobiographies will use literary devices to convey emotions and document events in detail.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring autobiographical texts

nodes.misconception: You should select one quotation from each text in a comparative paragraph.
nodes.response: Like in a powerful analytical paragraph, selecting multiple quotations from each text will help strengthen your argument. Selecting these quotations in the planning stage is key.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating comparative analytical paragraphs

nodes.misconception: That life was simply bad 'then' and 'good' now.
nodes.response: Exploring the similarities between the past and now, can help draw out the nuances of societal expectations and stereotypical representations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring historical attitudes and perspectives in non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: Evidence, or quotations, need to be long when used in an analytical paragraph or response.
nodes.response: If you select the right words, single words can provide an opportunity for rich analysis. Layering your comments means you can say a lot about a little!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating layered language analysis

nodes.misconception: You can't compare different text types to each other. For example, an article to a memoir.
nodes.response: By comparing different forms, we can often come to understand why a writer chose a particular text type more deeply - what this particular text type allowed them to do or convey to the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and evaluating non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: The only perspective presented in a text is the writer's.
nodes.response: Texts can also include viewpoints of characters, experts or sources the writer references. In this article we also hear the subject's perspective through the use of quotations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring a non-fiction text with multiple perspectives

nodes.misconception: Opinions are just what you think and don't need to be informed by anything.
nodes.response: Opinions should be informed by available information or evidence. For example: prior knowledge, contextual information and the writer's language choices, can all help to create informed opinions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and forming opinions on a 19th century text

nodes.misconception: A persuasive speech needs to be angry and aggressive.
nodes.response: What is Watson's tone? How does she motivate and persuade her audience without being confrontational? You don't want to alienate any audience members.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding what makes a persuasive speech

nodes.misconception: Content alone is enough for an effective speech.
nodes.response: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Giving a speech is so much more than just the words on a page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering non-verbal features in presenting a speech

nodes.misconception: When writing persuasively you should use as many rhetorical devices as possible.
nodes.response: Whilst using rhetorical devices is a great way to engage your audience, they need to be used sparingly and crafted carefully to ensure they don't lose their impact.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Persuasive writing: using credible and effective rhetorical devices

nodes.misconception: Planning isn't a useful step in the writing process and it takes too long.
nodes.response: How might planning help to organise our thoughts into a coherent response? How can planning improve the efficiency of the writing process?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an analytical response

nodes.misconception: As long as I am comparing the key points of two sources that is enough.
nodes.response: Using both comparative and correlative conjunctions will ensure there is nuance in your comparisons. They will also help keep your comparisons succinct.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the presentation of perspectives in non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: Only soldiers on the front line had direct experiences of conflict.
nodes.response: Who does war impact? Besides being a soldier, what other roles do people have in war?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering alternative perspectives of war in non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: I don't have time to write an effective closing, I just need to get my work finished!
nodes.response: The ending is arguably the most important part of the piece of writing. You need to leave your audience with a clear message that is memorable. You will get quicker at writing effective closings the more you practice using specific strategies.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a speech: openings and closings

nodes.misconception: When used, rhetorical devices have only one possible effect or outcome.
nodes.response: Writers can craft rhetorical devices to create different tones and match their purpose, audience and form. For example, direct address can be used to sound confrontational or it can create an intimate and personal tone.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing tone and language choices in non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: That historically, societal expectations were focused on women.
nodes.response: Both men and women were subject to societal expectations. However, men had much more freedom and power and it's important to acknowledge this difference.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring historical perspectives of men

nodes.misconception: Mind mapping is the only way to plan a piece of writing.
nodes.response: Mind mapping is a good place to start, but isn't always useful for considering structure. Using single paragraph outlines is an effective way to ensure a cohesive stricture and a clearly developed line of argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to write a persuasive speech

nodes.misconception: That discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
nodes.response: Think about all of the times you may need to use your verbal skills e.g. an interview or presentation. Being able to articulate yourself well verbally is an important skill to have.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Discussing historical and societal attitudes

nodes.misconception: As long as I can back up my answer, I can put forward any interpretation of the text.
nodes.response: Using tentative language can lead to a more exploratory approach, rather than presenting 'right' or 'wrong' interpretations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing analytical responses

nodes.misconception: In persuasive writing, I just need to include a range of rhetorical devices and sophisticated vocabulary.
nodes.response: Whilst it is important to use rhetorical devices and choose interesting language, you must also consider the structure of your writing. This ensures that your argument has a clear progression and your message doesn't get lost.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a viewpoint using structural features

nodes.misconception: Historical texts only portray stereotypical representations of women.
nodes.response: Even though societal expectations and stereotypes exist, this does not mean that all people conform to these standards - even in the past!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and exploring complex ideas in a text

nodes.misconception: When writing about serious issues, the main tone of your writing should be angry and confrontational.
nodes.response: Think about what engages you. An audience is far more likely to be engaged if they feel like they have a rapport with the speaker.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Varying sentences and using anecdotes to express a viewpoint

nodes.misconception: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time
nodes.response: How does the process of revising and rewriting develop vocabulary use? How does rewriting support the writing of future responses?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Re-drafting a persuasive speech

nodes.misconception: That everyone considers 'Romeo and Juliet' to be about love.
nodes.response: Some critics consider 'Romeo and Juliet' to be primarily about violence and society instead.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': contextualising violence and honour in Elizabethan society

nodes.misconception: Lord Capulet and Tybalt share the same views on all the Montagues.
nodes.response: While Lord Capulet wishes to join the fight in Act 1, Scene 1, he encourages Tybalt to leave Romeo alone at the Caplulet ball.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': violence, honour and social hierarchy in Act 1, Scene 5

nodes.misconception: Lord Capulet only considers Juliet to have dishonoured herself through her refusal of the marriage to Paris.
nodes.response: Arguably, Lord Capulet also thinks he and the Capulet family are also dishonoured by Juliet's refusal.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Lord Capulet's honour and violence in Act 3, Scene 5 of 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: Any quotation from the text adds weight to your argument.
nodes.response: For a quotation to be effective, it has to be relevant to the point you are making.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': selecting effective quotations and using context effectively

nodes.misconception: That men were supposed to be the 'bigger man' and act rationally in the face of a challenge to their honour.
nodes.response: In Elizabethan England, men were expected to defend their honour.
nodes.subject: english
