nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of violence and honour in Act 3, Scene 1 of 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: That the male characters in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet' are always keen to fight.
nodes.response: In Act 5, Scene 3, Romeo and Paris both seem reluctant to fight.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': honour, violence and masculinity in Act 5, Scene 3

nodes.misconception: Benvolio is a peaceful character in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
nodes.response: While Benvolio calls for peace, he engages in violence when he thinks it is necessary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': violence, masculinity and society in Act 1, Scene 1

nodes.misconception: Pupils think Macbeth has all of the characteristics of a tragic hero.
nodes.response: Use learning cycle 2 to draw out a debate about whether Macbeth actually learnt a lesson, highlighting where pupils may not agree.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': exploring Macbeth as the tragic hero

nodes.misconception: Thesis statements have to be very general.
nodes.response: Thesis statements can be specific, but they should offer opportunity to consider different interpretations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': exploring the theme of internal conflict

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe Lady Macbeth is solely responsible for the downfall of her husband.
nodes.response: When discussing Macbeth's intrigue in the prophecies, challenge pupils to question whether Lady Macbeth is responsible at this point.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Macbeth’: the witches’ prophecies in Act 1, Scene 3

nodes.misconception: There is only one plot point that fits to each part of Freytag's structure.
nodes.response: When discussing climax, ask pupils if any other events in the play could be considered the climax.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': the play as a Shakespearean tragedy

nodes.misconception: A thesis statement is just a rewording of the essay question.
nodes.response: The essay question is useful in formulating a thesis, however try using key question vocabulary and using it to form your own argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an analysis of Macbeth as a tragic hero

nodes.misconception: Students become over-reliant on the quotation: "Is this a dagger which I see before me?"
nodes.response: Draw attention to other quotations which both illustrate Macbeth can see a dagger, but also demonstrate the flaws in his character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth' Act 2 Scene 1: the dagger hallucination

nodes.misconception: All audiences will feel the same about Macbeth's death.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the joy of literature is exploring different responses to the same text. Use LC1 to identify these differences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': exploring Macbeth's death in Act 5

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth doesn't think guilt is a powerful emotion.
nodes.response: Lady Macbeth acknowledges that guilt can make people 'mad' or 'brainsickly' in 2.2. This is why she tries to reject the emotion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Lady Macbeth's feelings of guilt in ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: The only argument about Lady Macbeth involves her being subversive.
nodes.response: Characters can be interpreted in different ways. Your role is to construct a strong argument, not the 'right' argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the relationship between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth in Act 1, ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: There is just one reason that Macbeth doesn't want to commit regicide - his loyalty to Duncan.
nodes.response: Macbeth's soliloquy explores crime but significantly earthly punishment. For Macbeth, the consequence on earth is what frightens him.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth in Act 1, Scene 7 of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Malcolm is an immoral person.
nodes.response: Malcolm pretends he is filled with lust and greed, but this is to test Macduff's loyalty.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 4, Scenes 1 to 3

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is next in line to the throne.
nodes.response: Malcolm has been named Duncan's heir. However, he flees to England and thus Macbeth is crowned King.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 2, Scenes 3 and 4

nodes.misconception: Banquo's ghost is definitely a figment of Macbeth's imagination.
nodes.response: It's up to directors whether Banquo's ghost should appear on stage; an actor could play this part, or Macbeth could be scared of nothing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Act 3, Scene 4, ‘Macbeth’: Macbeth’s fears, and Lady Macbeth’s diminishing power

nodes.misconception: The murder of Banquo and Fleance (attempted) is the same as the murders that have preceded it.
nodes.response: Macbeth doesn't tell Lady Macbeth his plan, he hires murderers rather than doing it himself, and Fleance is a child.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the presentation of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth in Act 3 of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: The witches are presented solely as women, threatening women but women nonetheless.
nodes.response: Look at the language in Act 1, Scene 3: Banquo and Macbeth see the witches as unnatural, not just strange women.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The witches in Act 1, Scene 3 of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: The witches are presented in one way; any new interpretation supersedes the one before.
nodes.response: The witches are presented as supernatural, women, masculine and genderless. Paragraphs can explore all these; rely on LC2 to draw this out.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of the witches in Act 1, Scene 3 of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: A theme is any moment or idea in a text.
nodes.response: A theme is an idea that is explored in multiple different ways - it has to come up more than once in a text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 5, Scenes 6 to 9

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth doesn't value loyalty.
nodes.response: Lady Macbeth does value loyalty, but loyalty to herself and her ambitions, not the chivalric code.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: How does Lady Macbeth undermine Macbeth in Act 1 of 'Macbeth'?

nodes.misconception: The first scene is an exciting spectacle but not important to the rest of the play.
nodes.response: Despite its length, this scene grounds us in the atmosphere and main themes of the play.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the opening of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: The imaginary blood on Lady Macbeth's hands could symbolise Duncan's blood.
nodes.response: Symbols represent an idea that doesn't have a physical existence. Guilt is not a physical thing so the object, blood, is used.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 5, Scenes 1 to 5

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is solely worried about Banquo and Fleance in this scene.
nodes.response: Macbeth's focus is Banquo and his son, but his language reveals his worries about the regicide, his soul and his immediate future.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 3, Scenes 1 to 3

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth's presentation is the same in both Act 1, Scene 5 and Scene 7.
nodes.response: There is an increase in urgency, violence and strategy in Act 1, Scene 7.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Lady Macbeth’s character development across Act 1 of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is a Jacobean.
nodes.response: 'Macbeth' is set in 11th century Scotland. However, it was first performed in 1606 in front of a Jacobean audience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 1, Scenes 1-4

nodes.misconception: Thesis and topic sentences are the same thing.
nodes.response: A thesis must be overarching. A topic sentence can be much more specific.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an analytical essay about Lady Macbeth in ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Macbeth is a tyrannical ruler, and enjoys his tyranny.
nodes.response: Macbeth is a tyrant, but doesn't enjoy his reign. He is also self-aware: "I am in blood Stepp'd so far" or calling the witches "the worst".
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 3, Scenes 4 to 6

nodes.misconception: The Macbeths invite Duncan to their castle so they can kill him.
nodes.response: King Duncan is honouring the Macbeths by staying with them; he is honouring them because of Macbeth's performance in the recent battle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': An exploration of Act 1, Scenes 5 to 7

nodes.misconception: Hamartia is a synonym for excessive ambition.
nodes.response: Consider if students have read any other tragedies. Ask them to consider Othello's hamartia, for example.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Lady Macbeth's role in the downfall of Macbeth in 'Macbeth'

nodes.misconception: Shakespeare was a misogynist or, conversely, Shakespeare was a feminist.
nodes.response: We don't know about Shakespeare's political or social beliefs. The text is there for us to interpret, not define Shakespeare's views.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating the character of Lady Macbeth in ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me' here means she wants to be a man.
nodes.response: Whilst she might want some masculine qualities, there are more implications to this. She could be calling for supernatural qualities too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of Lady Macbeth in Act 1, Scene 5 of ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Contextual information in an essay should comprise of one final sentence in each paragraph.
nodes.response: Context should be weaved throughout an essay to help explore a writer's intentions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Macbeth’: exploring evidence and including context in an essay on Lady Macbeth

nodes.misconception: Analysis can only include a language focus, especially single word analysis.
nodes.response: You should analyse a range of writer's methods; this analysis should support your thesis or topic sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an analytical essay about Lady Macbeth as a Machiavel in ‘Macbeth’

nodes.misconception: Macbeth actually sees a dagger.
nodes.response: Shakespeare signals the dagger is a hallucination, and that Macbeth is aware it is a hallucination too: 'a dagger of the mind'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': an exploration of Act 2, Scenes 1 and 2

nodes.misconception: Lady Macbeth's rejection of guilt in 2.2 means 5.1's characterisation is inconsistent.
nodes.response: The language in 2.2 foreshadows what is to come.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Act 2, Scene 2 of ‘Macbeth’: characterisation and foreshadowing

nodes.misconception: Creative writing is more effective when it focuses on something extraordinary.
nodes.response: Describing something very well known to you can be more effective as you're able to spend the time focusing on the little details.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrasting the familiar and the unknown in your descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: That we will all have the same response to certain words.
nodes.response: Our response to words depends on our own individual experiences and memories and therefore we are likely to all get different connotations from words.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing your explanation of quotations from 'The Wonderful Wizard of Oz'

nodes.misconception: That descriptive writing is all about telling the reader what's in the image.
nodes.response: Descriptive writing is about showing the reader what's in the image through sensory and figurative language.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using sensory language and figurative language to create an atmospheric setting

nodes.misconception: That you should use generic sensory language to create an effective description.
nodes.response: You need to use sensory language tailored to the atmosphere that you want to create in order for it to be effective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using figurative language and structure to create an unsettling atmosphere

nodes.misconception: That you always have to plan before a piece of creative writing.
nodes.response: While a plan is very useful, and should be used in most cases, sometimes free writing can be a way of unleashing creativity that can then be revised.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering strategies for refining and editing your descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: Everyone will respond to an image in the same way.
nodes.response: How you respond to an image, and what you choose to zoom in on, will be different for each person since we're all unique with different memories and experiences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising planning and writing a detailed description based on an image

nodes.misconception: That you should choose the quotation with the most techniques as your evidence.
nodes.response: You need to select a quotation that matches the point of your topic sentence rather than simply being the one with the most techniques.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising topic sentences and selecting precise evidence from 'The Dark Lady'

nodes.misconception: That a pattern within a text is random and just happened by chance.
nodes.response: Patterns are a way for writers to emphasise certain information or convey importance onto a concept because our brains are wired to recognise and remember patterns.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining how Akala uses patterns of language for effect in 'The Dark Lady'

nodes.misconception: That we will all have the same answer to a question about how a writer presents a particular character or theme.
nodes.response: The way we respond to how a writer presents a particular character or theme will be very individual since our responses depend on our own experiences or memories.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Meeting a fantastical creature in Bilan's 'Asha and the Spirit Bird'

nodes.misconception: That looking at punctuation is very dry and has no impact on the way you see a text or a character.
nodes.response: The way that writers use and play with punctuation can have a profound impact on the way we view a text or character's emotions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using dashes, colons, and commas for effect in descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: That using similes is in itself effective descriptive writing.
nodes.response: You should aim to have a simile that creates a specific emotion and avoids clichés.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using ambitious language and colour imagery to improve your descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: That you shouldn't judge a book by its cover.
nodes.response: If we consider a literal book cover, it has been chosen to introduce the reader to the tone of the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to an unseen extract from Burnett's 'The Secret Garden'

nodes.misconception: That the choice of sentence type isn't important as long as the grammar and punctuation is correct.
nodes.response: The choice of sentence type can impact the way that a reader responds to your writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using simple, compound and complex sentences in descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: That you should put literary analysis in every part of your analytical writing.
nodes.response: You shouldn't put literary analysis in your topic sentence - it should just explain the main idea of the paragraph concisely.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using precise evidence from Burnett's 'The Secret Garden' to support an idea

nodes.misconception: That the reader will automatically be able to follow your train of thought.
nodes.response: We all have different connotations from words; you need to clearly explain how you have reached your idea in order for the reader to be able to understand your argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing explanations in analytical writing about Akala's 'The Dark Lady'

nodes.misconception: You can only describe light in a two-dimensional way.
nodes.response: There are many ways to describe light to have an effect. You can talk about the dawn, the twilight or the way the light gleams or flickers in order to influence the reader's perception.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining and emulating how Bilan uses light in 'Asha and the Spirit Bird'

nodes.misconception: That we will all respond to a description in the same way.
nodes.response: The way we respond to a description and the language devices will always be unique because we all have different experiences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining how Burnett presents the garden setting in 'The Secret Garden'

nodes.misconception: That prepositions aren't an important focal point for descriptive writing.
nodes.response: Not only do prepositions indicate the relationship between words, but they also influence our perception of people based on their body language and positioning in a scene.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering sentence structures in Bilan's 'Asha and the Spirit Bird'

nodes.misconception: That you should use definitive, authoritative language in your analytical writing to prove to the reader that you are right.
nodes.response: You should use tentative language because we can never be truly sure of the writer's intentions - you should use evidence and clear explanations to prove your idea to the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing clear analytical paragraphs about Bilan's 'Asha and the Spirit Bird'

nodes.misconception: That meeting someone unknown in a strange place will always be scary.
nodes.response: Instead of feeling scared, you might also feel excited or intrigued and you can use language to have this effect on the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing and emulating Baum's use of unknown characters in 'The Wizard of Oz'

nodes.misconception: That the subject of a sentence is always the person in the sentence.
nodes.response: A subject is the person, place, or thing that is performing the action of the sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing complete sentences and correcting sentence fragments

nodes.misconception: That a piece of writing is completely finished once you have written it.
nodes.response: The first time you complete a piece of writing is it in its draft form. You want to go back and continually revise it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Drafting a piece of descriptive writing on 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland'

nodes.misconception: That magic in stories always happens in a make-believe, faraway world.
nodes.response: Magical-realist stories are set in the real world but magic and fantastical events happen.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing character in an unseen extract from Bilan's 'Asha and the Spirit Bird'

nodes.misconception: That pathetic fallacy can only be used to give emotion to the weather.
nodes.response: Pathetic fallacy is where human emotions are given to any non-human object or thing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and emulating Baum's use of pathetic fallacy in 'The Wizard of Oz'

nodes.misconception: That it's impossible to guess what will happen in a text.
nodes.response: While we can't know for certain, we can pick up on clues that the writer gives us to make predictions about what will happen in a text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to key images in an unseen extract from Akala's 'The Dark Lady'

nodes.misconception: Creating an effective piece of descriptive writing is all about using linguistic devices.
nodes.response: Varying your sentences can also be a very effective way of conveying emotion and detail to help the reader visualise the scene.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using adverbs, subordinate clauses and compound sentences in descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: You should always use the most impressive sounding words in your description.
nodes.response: While you should reach for ambitious words, you want to ensure that all the words you use are creating a consistent atmosphere.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using adjectives and semantic fields to plan and write descriptive paragraphs

nodes.misconception: That you should immediately start trying to spot language devices when reading an unseen extract.
nodes.response: It's better to take the time to understand what is happening before starting to think about how the writer creates meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to an unseen extract from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland'

nodes.misconception: That the unknown is always scary.
nodes.response: While we typically think of the unknown as something scary and overwhelming, it can also be something exciting and refreshing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrasting the everyday and the unknown settings in Baum's 'The Wizard of Oz'

nodes.misconception: That there is a set formula to follow when it comes to choosing what to focus on in an image.
nodes.response: When looking at an image for descriptive writing, you should think about what catches your eye and then focus on those elements.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using vocabulary choices, similes, and metaphors to plan descriptive writing

nodes.misconception: That textures aren't an important detail in descriptive writing.
nodes.response: The textures that writers choose to use can help us to make inferences about the nature of the object or place.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering sensory language in Bilan's 'Asha and the Spirit Bird'

nodes.misconception: That stories are purely intended to entertain us.
nodes.response: While stories are entertaining, often there is also a message or a purpose behind the story that is designed to teach us something.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Dorothy's return from the unknown in Baum's 'The Wizard of Oz'

nodes.misconception: An effective essay includes all of your thoughts on the subject.
nodes.response: An effective essay is structured cohesively rather than including every thought.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing analytically about Shakespeare's presentation of Romeo and love

nodes.misconception: That people generally believe in free will and always have.
nodes.response: In Elizabethan England, people typically believed that fate controlled their lives - they believed they did not have free will.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an essay on the role of fate in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: That just identifying a method in a quotation is effective.
nodes.response: To be effective, you need to analyse the effect of the method in the quotation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an essay on the role of fate in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: Romeo is more impulsive than Juliet in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet'.
nodes.response: Arguably, Juliet's actions are also impulsive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the development of Romeo and Juliet's relationship in Act 2, Scene 2

nodes.misconception: Romeo is often said to be 'in love with love' and this is consistent throughout the play.
nodes.response: In Act 3, Scene 1, Romeo expresses negative feelings towards the concept of being in love.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring love, masculinity and fate in Act 3, Scene 1 of 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: That women were slaves in patriarchal societies.
nodes.response: While women had less legal power in patriarchal societies, they could still be very influential and powerful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Lady Capulet and the Nurse’s views on marriage in Act 1, Scene 3

nodes.misconception: That good vs. evil is easy to recognise in characters when reading stories or watching plays.
nodes.response: In tragedies, sometimes a character can embody both good and evil or there could be different perceptions of a character's nature.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the conventions of Shakespearean tragedy in 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: That light always symbolises hope and optimism in literature.
nodes.response: While light typically symbolises hope and optimism, for Romeo and Juliet it symbolises loss and separation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring symbolism in Romeo and Juliet's last meeting in Act 3, Scene 5

nodes.misconception: That Romeo and Juliet's first conversation exclusively focuses on the physicality of their love.
nodes.response: While Romeo and Juliet's first conversation contains many references to "lips" and "palms", the religious imagery also implies their spiritual connection.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring love and foreshadowing in Act 1, Scene 5 of 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: Juliet was Romeo's only love in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet'.
nodes.response: Before Juliet, Romeo believes himself to be in love with Rosaline.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing Romeo’s love for Juliet with his love for Rosaline

nodes.misconception: That characters either fully conform or fully subvert stereotypes.
nodes.response: Characters often exist within a grey area - they might conform to some aspects of a stereotype but subvert others - just as real people do.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Lord Capulet's views on women and marriage in Act 3, Scene 5

nodes.misconception: That Juliet is Romeo's only love in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
nodes.response: Before meeting Juliet, Romeo was in love with Rosaline.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Romeo's unrequited love for Rosaline in 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: That everyone in Elizabethan England thought dreams were profound and important.
nodes.response: Mercutio's 'Queen Mab' speech implies that dreams are inconsequential and merely wish-fulfillment.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Benvolio and Mercutio as Romeo's counsellors in Act 1, Scene 4

nodes.misconception: That everyone believes they have control over their lives.
nodes.response: Some people believe that their lives are controlled by fate and destiny.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring how the prologue sets up the theme of fate in 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: That people in Elizabethan England share the same ideas about religion as we do in modern society.
nodes.response: Religion was central to people's lives in Elizabethan England in a way that it is not in modern society.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the role of Friar Lawrence in Act 2, Scene 3 of 'Romeo and Juliet'

nodes.misconception: The role of comedy is merely to make people laugh.
nodes.response: Comedy can be a way of revealing information about characters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the role of the Nurse and comedy in Act 2, Scene 4

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that descriptions of setting only serve as background and do not contribute to character development or tone of a piece of writing.
nodes.response: Settings are integral to storytelling as they can reflect and enhance a character's emotions, personality, and the overall tone of the scene. For example, a gloomy, rainy setting can mirror a character's sadness or create a foreboding atmosphere.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing setting and developing tone

nodes.misconception: Pupils will sometimes overload the physical description of their character and list each individual detail, often using cliches.
nodes.response: Describing every part of a character’s appearance in detail can overwhelm the reader. It's better to provide purposeful descriptions that integrate physical appearance with personality to create an engaging and convincing character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Crafting physical description for malevolent characters

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a physical description of a character is enough to help the reader understand what the character's personality is like.
nodes.response: Though physical description is really useful, considering verb and adverb choices in particular allows the reader to really imagine a character. For example, how they walk, talk and behave around others are all telling of their character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using vocabulary effectively in fiction writing

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that using contrast and juxtaposition in character descriptions means simply listing opposing traits without showing how they interact or affect each other.
nodes.response: It's important to show how the contrasting traits of characters impact each other. For example, instead of just stating that one character is kind and the other is cruel, describe a scene where their actions and behaviors directly conflict.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrasting characters: using juxtaposition

nodes.misconception: Pupils often don't see the value in editing work and think once the first draft is finished, the work on it is done.
nodes.response: Writing is a process that involves multiple stages. Revising and editing are crucial steps to refine your work, enhance clarity, and improve overall quality. Even professional writers revise their drafts several times before publishing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing fiction about a malevolent character

nodes.misconception: Malevolent characters are always obviously and outwardly evil characters.
nodes.response: Ask pupils whether they can think of any characters from literature where their malevolence is implied or not explicitly stated at first. These characters are often dangerously deceptive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Crafting malevolent characters

nodes.misconception: Some pupils think that planning isn't a helpful or worthwhile exercise.
nodes.response: Planning allows us to carefully consider our ideas before writing and allows us to work out what ideas work best for the task we've been given. Planning often results in a final stronger piece of work so is very worthwhile!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning fiction writing about a malevolent character

nodes.misconception: As long as similes or metaphors follow the correct rules they will be effective.
nodes.response: Many comparisons in similes and metaphors are clichéd and this often takes away from a description and makes it unimaginative. The challenge is to try be original in your thought!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using figurative language effectively for character description

nodes.misconception: The most important part of dialogue is what is inside the speech marks.
nodes.response: What is said through dialogue is really important, but it's also crucial to consider how that dialogue is to be said. Careful selection of verbs and adverbs give the reader a crucial insight into how dialogue should be read.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Crafting character through dialogue

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think it doesn't always matter where paragraphs go as long as the text is broken up in places.
nodes.response: Effective paragraphing is important to the reader's experience of the text. It helps them to follow what they're reading more easily and well crafted paragraphs allow the writer to reveal information in a way that suits their writing best.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using paragraphs effectively

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think they have to come up with new ideas for each essay question they attempt.
nodes.response: Highlight similarities between the modelled plan on 'hypocrisy' and their own ideas relationing to 'duality'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': writing an analytical response about duality

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the genre of this novella is solely Gothic fiction.
nodes.response: Even without the presence of a detective character, the use of concealment and a carefully crafted mystery make this detective fiction too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': Chapters 3 and 4

nodes.misconception: Hyde is solely presented as a dangerous character from the start to the end of the novella.
nodes.response: Through the character of Hyde, and others' interactions with him, we can explore Stevenson's wider cautionary message.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': examining Mr. Hyde as a dangerous character

nodes.misconception: Utterson, as a lawyer, is a man of great curiosity and honour.
nodes.response: Utterson is both curious for the truth, but cautious about ruining the reputation of his peers. This leads to important clues being missed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 6: Remarkable Incident of Dr. Lanyon

nodes.misconception: The end of Chapter 8 implies Jekyll regretted creating Hyde.
nodes.response: Jekyll is a very complex character, his actions need to be explored with nuance. The best responses will consider Jekyll's joy and regret.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

nodes.misconception: Chapter 9 takes place after the events in Chapter 8.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if they were going to put the chapters in chronological order, how would this chapter be numbered? (Answer: Chapter 6)
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon's Narrative

nodes.misconception: Pupils must work through the text chronologically when selecting supporting evidence.
nodes.response: Pupils need to think of the logical order they should analyse evidence from the text - which section of the novella is strongest at proving their topic sentence?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': developing analytical paragraphs about Mr. Hyde

nodes.misconception: The story takes place in a dark, gloomy and traditionally Gothic setting.
nodes.response: Stevenson deliberately juxtaposes the building Hyde enters with the pleasant and well-to-do neighbourhood.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 1: The Story of The Door

nodes.misconception: Students might think that "third person limited" means the narrative is limited in scope or detail.
nodes.response: "Third person limited" means insight into one character's thoughts, not a story's limited scope.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 1: Meeting Mr Utterson

nodes.misconception: Using tentative language makes you sound unsure in your analysis.
nodes.response: Tentative language allows pupils to be more evaluative, exploring alternative viewpoints.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': refining written responses on duality

nodes.misconception: When analysing, all pupils need is a clear viewpoint.
nodes.response: A clear viewpoint is important, but adding nuance will improve the quality of pupil responses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': writing about Jekyll's culpability in the novella

nodes.misconception: All Christians were against scientific development.
nodes.response: Within all religions (or groups in society) there will be plurality of thought, including progressive viewpoints.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': the importance of science and religion in the novella

nodes.misconception: Any quotation that supports your argument can be used.
nodes.response: Select a quotation from learning cycle 1, such as "it wasn't like a man" and ask how much pupils could say about the quotation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': examining Mr. Hyde as the embodiment of evil

nodes.misconception: All quotations in an essay require analysis.
nodes.response: Some quotations are useful for supporting your argument but do not require detailed analysis. These should embedded directly into pupils' sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': exploring duplicity in a model essay

nodes.misconception: Just mentioning Stevenson's choices surrounding form and structure is valuable analysis.
nodes.response: All comments regarding Stevenson's use of form and structure should be tied back to Stevenson's purpose.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': examining the novella's structure

nodes.misconception: 'Jekyll and Hyde' is a stereotypically 'Gothic' novella.
nodes.response: Whilst certain elements of 'Jekyll and Hyde' do follow the conventions of the Gothic, others subvert it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the Gothic in 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: Character is more important than setting when trying to solve mystery.
nodes.response: Jekyll tells Utterson there is nothing he should worry about - this is not true. Ask pupils how the setting indicates that Jekyll is lying.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 5: Incident of the Letter

nodes.misconception: Stevenson was extremely critical of science.
nodes.response: Stevenson certainly plays on contemporary fears over unfettered scientific development. Whilst his novella could be seen as a criticism of this, the extent to which which Stevenson uses the text as his own personal criticism is arguable.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': examining Lanyon as a foil to Jekyll

nodes.misconception: Jekyll is the only character responsible for the crimes of Hyde.
nodes.response: A more nuanced understanding of the text explores the complicity of other characters and the decisions they make.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': exploring the duplicity of the upper class characters

nodes.misconception: The case is over now Hyde has been found dead.
nodes.response: Get students enthused about the final mystery - how has Jekyll disappeared from a room locked from the inside?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 8: The Last Night

nodes.misconception: Henry Jekyll is responsible for the death of Mr. Hyde. Jekyll is the 'self-destroyer.'
nodes.response: Hyde uses Jekyll as his protection from the gallows. When Jekyll is no more, it is Hyde who chooses death over punishment.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 10: responding to Jekyll's confession

nodes.misconception: Concluding sentences are the same as conclusions.
nodes.response: Concluding sentences conclude a single paragraph. Conclusions come at the end of a full essay.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': planning a successful essay

nodes.misconception: Liminal spaces are things that are unnerving in a mysterious way.
nodes.response: Liminal spaces often do create a unnerving tone, but this is due to them being the boundary to two opposing states.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 7: Incident at the Window

nodes.misconception: Stevenson encourages the reader to be critical of Jekyll due to the dual nature inherent inside of him.
nodes.response: Stevenson appears to embrace duality, through his rejection of Calvinism and alleged behaviour at university. He is critical of the hypocrisy that arose from those who harboured secrets as a result of duality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': duality as a theme in the novella

nodes.misconception: Students might think Stevenson's ambiguity about Hyde's appearance is due to insufficient detail.
nodes.response: Stevenson keeps Hyde's description vague to engage readers' imaginations, amplifying the character's eeriness.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde' Chapter 2: Search for Mr Hyde

nodes.misconception: When including 'the impact of the text today' in your conclusion, you just need to explain why the book is still studied today.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to 'step outside the text' and think about why themes, characters or moral messages might resonate with readers today.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Jekyll and Hyde': writing introductions and conclusions

nodes.misconception: In a debate you can only argue a stance you truly believe in.
nodes.response: Part of the skill of debating is being able to create, justify and convincingly present an argument that might not reflect your own personal viewpoint.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and presenting opening arguments for a debate

nodes.misconception: I do not need to plan for a debate.
nodes.response: To participate effectively in debate you will need to have clear arguments and rebuttals, that are backed up with evidence. Planning will ensure you can do this confidently.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Time to debate: planning, evaluating and participating

nodes.misconception: You always have to show both sides of the argument in a debate or discussion.
nodes.response: In a debate, it is much more skilfull to present a single line of argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding in debates: effective rebuttals

nodes.misconception: There are no rules in debating. It is just another way to argue or have an argument and does not need preparation.
nodes.response: Formal debating is an important part of society and allows important issues to be discussed in a constructuve way. It takes consideration and preparation to be involved in an effective debate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: What is a formal debate?

nodes.misconception: That Shakespearean theatre didn't have special effects.
nodes.response: Although they didn't have access to modern technology, the theatre used many special effects to help make the production more realistic.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Shakespearean theatre as a sensory experience

nodes.misconception: That Ariel is a female character.
nodes.response: There is no gender assigned to Ariel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing the role and presentation of Ariel in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That being an outsider is always a negative thing.
nodes.response: Sometimes people are considered outsiders because they don't fit society's expectations of normal and that's not necessarily negative.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the perspective of an outsider in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That the modern experience of going to the theatre is the same as in Shakespearean times.
nodes.response: The experience was very different - the modern theatre experience is quiet and respectful while the Shakespearean experience was riotous.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the Shakespearean theatre experience with modern theatre

nodes.misconception: That our feelings towards characters must be consistent.
nodes.response: Our feelings towards characters can change depending on what is happening during the plot.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the characters of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That Caliban and Prospero always have a negative relationship.
nodes.response: When Prospero first arrived, Caliban showed Prospero how to survive on the island so it began as a positive relationship.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding Caliban's role and presentation in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That an argument only means a heated, angry exchange.
nodes.response: An argument about a text means presenting your idea and your points to prove that your idea is correct.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an essay on Prospero's power over Caliban in 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That creative writing should be in present tense.
nodes.response: Because diaries are records of events that have happened, they should be written in past tense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a diary in the voice of Miranda from Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That a theatre performance is all about actors interacting with each other on the stage.
nodes.response: Often the most memorable moments from a performance are the actors' monologues where they express their character's inner thoughts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Crafting a monologue in Ariel's voice from Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That you should quote entire sentences of text in order to prove your point.
nodes.response: Often, individual words and short quotes are more effective in analytical writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing about Prospero's treatment of Ariel in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That we know for certain how Shakespeare intended his characters to be seen.
nodes.response: We don't know how Shakespeare intended the audience to perceive his characters - we can just look at the language and decide from that.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing a debate on the presentation of Caliban in 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That an analysis of a play only consists of the word the characters say.
nodes.response: The amount of lines a character has as well as stage directions are also important aspects of analysing a play.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the power dynamics between Prospero and Ariel in 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That pathetic fallacy is only about using the weather to express emotions.
nodes.response: Pathetic fallacy is a type of personification where emotions are given to a setting, an object or the weather.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the monologue of an outsider in relation to Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that women in Shakespeare's time always obeyed the male figures in their life.
nodes.response: There are many examples of women being disobedient and not following the rules of the male figures in their life.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Prospero's power over Miranda in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That planning is a pointless endeavour.
nodes.response: Planning is a really important aspect of any writing task as it makes the process easier and allows you to organise your thoughts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a monologue in Ariel's voice from Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That images and sentences always need to be varied in writing.
nodes.response: Repeated images and sentences can be an effective way of crafting a convincing character voice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Crafting a monologue from the perspective of Caliban from 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That symbols in literature mean the same to everyone.
nodes.response: Our responses to symbolism depend on our experiences as well as exposure to certain concepts so we might all have very different responses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Structuring an imaginative monologue in relation to Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that women were completely powerless in Shakespeare's time.
nodes.response: While there were legal restrictions and social pressures on women in Shakespeare's time, there were some women who had power and influence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the portrayal of Miranda in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That an argument needs to present a balanced viewpoint for both sides of the argument.
nodes.response: An argument needs to give your reasons behind your answer to the question.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering Caliban as an outsider in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That characters are only meant to be read as themselves.
nodes.response: Often in literature, the characters are the writer's way of commenting on something happening in the world.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Prospero's power over Caliban in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That calling someone a 'monster' means that you find them terrifying.
nodes.response: While calling someone a 'monster' can mean you find them terrifying, it can also be a way of ridiculing someone and showing your dislike.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the treatment of Caliban in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That it's obvious how a character should be interpreted by the audience.
nodes.response: The staging of a performance from body language to costuming can make a huge difference in how different audiences interpret a character.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Prospero and Caliban's relationship in Act 1 Scene 2 of 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That people didn't believe in magic in Shakespeare's time.
nodes.response: In Shakespeare's time, most people believed in magic and thought it could bring ill luck and misfortune.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Consolidating our understanding of the plot of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That proofreading is a waste of time.
nodes.response: Proofreading helps you to spot errors that might hinder the readers' understanding of your work.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving an essay on Prospero's power over Caliban in 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That we can't do anything to help control our nerves.
nodes.response: While we can't stop the feeling of nervousness entirely, we can trick our body into relaxing more by smiling and using deep breathing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering how to use body language and voice to perform a convincing monologue

nodes.misconception: Characters in literature are just there to create a good story.
nodes.response: Characters in literature often represent things bigger than themselves such as colonialism or gender inequality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising the theme of inequality in Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That you don't need to use quotes in your essay.
nodes.response: Quotes act as textual evidence and are needed to write a successful analytical essay.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an essay on Prospero's treatment of Caliban in 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: The defining feature of a comedy play is that they are funny.
nodes.response: While Shakespeare's comedies do employ humour, the defining feature is that everything is resolved at the end of the play.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the plot of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'

nodes.misconception: That Dr. Jekyll enjoys the experience of being Mr. Hyde.
nodes.response: Encourage students to notice the different ways that Dr. Jekyll has declined.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Detailed analysis of an extract in 'The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'

nodes.misconception: Students think that the fog is purely designed to create an eerie Gothic atmosphere.
nodes.response: Be clear about the symbolic nature of fog. The fact that it can allow for partial visibility.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering Stevenson's use of fog as a motif in 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: Students think the novel is entirely about secrets.
nodes.response: Remind them how often Hyde is observed committing crimes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering Stevenson's use of time and weather in 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: That Stevenson presents good and evil as complete opposites.
nodes.response: Remind students how easily Hyde and Jekyll blur into one.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering doors and windows as key motifs in Stevenson's 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: Students may think that the novel is Gothic in the typical sense.
nodes.response: Be clear about subversion and how it works in the novella. Although Stevenson uses some Gothic elements they are not always used in the typical way for the genre.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering Stevenson's subversion of Gothic setting in 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: That the dream is only caused by Utterson being in a state of distress.
nodes.response: Unpick the details of the dream to show the parallels with the plot.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Mr Utterson's dream in Stevenson's 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that setting is used solely to create atmosphere.
nodes.response: Encourage students to see Stevenson's use of setting as figurative as well as literal.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing atmospheric settings in Stevenson's 'Jekyll and Hyde'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the Ghost of Christmas Present is actually holding Plenty's horn.
nodes.response: Dickens carefully clarifies that the torch is "in a shape not unlike Plenty's horn", showing that the torch is not actually Plenty's horn.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': the ghosts and Dickens' use of allusion

nodes.misconception: Students try to include as much knowledge as possible in their responses.
nodes.response: Encourage students to be selective in their choice of ideas and to explain their choices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': constructing an argument about the ghosts

nodes.misconception: Students often don't realise that Dickens' deliberately capitalised on a popular genre.
nodes.response: Dickens wanted the novella to become a bestseller, as this would give his message the best chance of reaching as many people as possible.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': a Victorian ghost story

nodes.misconception: Students think that Scrooge's visit with the Ghost of Christmas Present is limited to Christmas Day.
nodes.response: Scrooge's time with the spirit goes beyond Christmas Day - to the Twelfth Day of Christmas, showing how time is manipulated in the novella.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': Dickens' ghosts as agents of time

nodes.misconception: Students might think that Scrooge is evil.
nodes.response: Scrooge is not evil - he is immoral. A distinction between the two needs to be clarified.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': the novella as a Gothic text

nodes.misconception: Students think they should present lots of different ideas in an essay.
nodes.response: Whilst you should present lots of different knowledge, the knowledge should all form part of the same idea or argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': conceptualised responses

nodes.misconception: Pupils think there are only four ghosts in the novella.
nodes.response: Pupils forget about the numerous ghosts that Scrooge sees when he looks out of the window at the end of Stave 1.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': the entrances and exits of the four ghosts

nodes.misconception: Students think that once they have put their pen down and stopped writing, that they have finished.
nodes.response: Students should think of their first attempt as simply a first draft. The second redraft is their chance to fine tune their argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': improving analytical writing

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Father Christmas was always pictured wearing red.
nodes.response: Victorian depictions of Father Christmas show him wearing green, with a wreath of holly around his head.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 3: the second of the three spirits

nodes.misconception: Students think that, in Stave 4, Scrooge is frightened of dying.
nodes.response: Scrooge is not frightened of death. He is frightened of dying without leaving a legacy because he has not contributed anything to society.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 4: Scrooge's fears

nodes.misconception: Students believe that the ghost shows Scrooge his future and that this will be Scrooge's fate.
nodes.response: The ghost shows Scrooge the "shadows of things that may be". The word "may" is vital, as he suggests that it is never too late to change.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 4: the last of the three spirits

nodes.misconception: Students think that Dickens' message about Christmas is focused solely on the importance of charity.
nodes.response: Dickens uses the many Christmas scenes in this section of the novella to emphasise the importance of community and human connection.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 3: Christmas around the world

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Dickens is solely emphasising the value of human life.
nodes.response: Dickens is also emphasising the importance of what we do with our lives - how we use them to enrich other people's human experience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 4: death in the novella

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Scrooge keeps his money to himself so that he can spend it on himself.
nodes.response: Scrooge's frugality also extends to his own existence: Scrooge refuses to spend money even on himself, choosing to live a meagre lifestyle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 1: Scrooge the Miser

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Dickens harshly condemns the wealthy.
nodes.response: Dickens only condemns people with money, who choose not to share it with those in need. This is exemplified in the character of Fezziwig.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 2: Scrooge's childhood and Fezziwig

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Dickens only offers a condemnation of the immorality exhibited by Mrs. Dilber.
nodes.response: Dickens, though he doesn't condone the character's behaviour, does empathise with her, and illustrates that she is the product of injustice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 4: a significant death

nodes.misconception: Students often believe that Bob Cratchit represents the most poor group of people in society.
nodes.response: Whilst Bob Cratchit certainly struggles for money and has to be resourceful to feed his family, he still has a job and a home.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 3: the Cratchits' Christmas

nodes.misconception: Students believe that Belle was never interested in having any money.
nodes.response: Belle was interested in having money - she just wanted to earn it with Scrooge over time.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 2: Belle

nodes.misconception: Students think that it doesn't matter which quotations they select for use.
nodes.response: It can be difficult to bring any new interpretations to commonly-used quotations, so try to pick some lesser-used ones.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': planning an extended argument

nodes.misconception: Students do not understand that an argument should build in complexity.
nodes.response: Students should consider the structure of their argument. Which ideas need to come first in order to foreground other ideas?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': writing an extended argument

nodes.misconception: Students often talk about Marley and Marley's Ghost as if they are the exact same character.
nodes.response: Marley in life held very different beliefs from Marley's ghost; his ghost acts as Scrooge's redeemer and represents something different.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 1: Meeting Marley's ghost

nodes.misconception: Students think that Scrooge hates Christmas because it marks the anniversary of Marley's death.
nodes.response: Scrooge hates Christmas because he views it as a crime against oneself. He resents that people spend money they don't have at Christmas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 1: The Characterisation of Scrooge

nodes.misconception: Students do not take the time to plan properly before writing.
nodes.response: Not taking the time to plan a response properly makes your argument less concise and less coherent.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': planning an essay on Scrooge

nodes.misconception: Students tend to 'bolt' irrelevant context onto the end of analytical paragraphs.
nodes.response: Context should be integrated into students' responses and should enhance or support their arguments.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': writing about Stave 2

nodes.misconception: Students fail to recognise that Scrooge doesn't just buy the Cratchits any old turkey.
nodes.response: Scrooge buys the Cratchits the "prize" (or most expensive) turkey. This shows that he is truly generous, as he goes above and beyond.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 5: the change in Scrooge

nodes.misconception: Students think the novella's title was chosen simply to reflect the festive period it covers.
nodes.response: The title is more symbolic of Dickens' intentions - he intended for the message from this text to be spread far and wide, much like a carol.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': symbolism in the novella

nodes.misconception: Students tend to struggle to understand how Scrooge has metaphorically fathered Ignorance and Want.
nodes.response: By being ignorant, Scrooge has neglected his social responsibility and nurtured inequality and injustice - the two children represent this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 3: Ignorance and Want

nodes.misconception: Students think that the writer's method is just similes/metaphors etc.
nodes.response: The writer's method is anything that they do consciously - it's any conscious choice that they make.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': writing about the presentation of children

nodes.misconception: Students do not embed their quotations.
nodes.response: If students don't embed their quotations, the response is not as concise as it could be. Being concise makes your response sophisticated.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': writing about Stave 1

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Fred making fun of Scrooge is mean.
nodes.response: Fred is shown to have a great sense of humour and this is what he's expressing when talking about his uncle. It is this sense of humour that enables him to remain optimistic despite financial struggle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 3: Scrooge and Fred as opposite characters

nodes.misconception: Students might think that because this is an 'old book', it might not still bear a relevant message.
nodes.response: The novella is a timeless classic because its message is universal. As long as there is injustice in the world, the text remains relevant.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': Scrooge's redemptive journey

nodes.misconception: Students think Scrooge is just a wicked character who hates other people, especially the poor.
nodes.response: Scrooge is a product of his environment and exemplifies the attitudes of many Victorian employers and wealthy citizens.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol': Scrooge as a very Victorian character

nodes.misconception: Students think that Scrooge is selfish and miserable because he is a wicked person.
nodes.response: Scrooge's miserliness comes from his deep-rooted fear of being poor.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'A Christmas Carol' Stave 2: the first of the three spirits

nodes.misconception: That simple poetry is not as good as complex poetry.
nodes.response: Arguably, good poetry creates an emotional response in the reader and evokes a particular image or impression.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Clare presents nature in 'Sunday Dip'

nodes.misconception: That you need to know the exact rhythm to analyse it.
nodes.response: Determining whether a rhythm is regular or irregular can be a way of analysing the structure.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Clare presents nature in 'Sunday Dip'

nodes.misconception: That a poet can only be a part of one literary movement.
nodes.response: Often, we can see poets as referencing more than one literary movement and that can help us understand the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Hood presents the past and present in 'I Remember, I Remember'

nodes.misconception: That 'temper' means anger.
nodes.response: While we might associate 'temper' with a 'temper tantrum', 'temper' can refer to any emotional frame of mind.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Wordsworth presents nature in 'To My Sister'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not initially link all of the examples of personification together.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that finding patterns in the text can be very useful to help create a thoughtful idea about the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'The Emigree'

nodes.misconception: That poems always consider the speaker's individual feelings and emotions.
nodes.response: Poems often use the speaker as a way of observing life around them and commenting on wider society.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Blakemore presents multiculturalism in 'Peckham Rye Lane'

nodes.misconception: That Romantic poems always present nature in a positive light.
nodes.response: Sometimes Romantic poets may show the devastation that humanity has caused nature or talk about nature in a grieving way.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the tone of Brontë's 'Mild the Mist Upon the Hill'

nodes.misconception: That using your imagination to create imaginary games is a way of withdrawing from the world.
nodes.response: While imaginary games can be used to withdraw from the world, our imaginations come from things we have seen or experienced and therefore imaginary games can be a way of connecting to the world and finding your place in it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Landon presents childhood in 'Captain Cook (To My Brother)'

nodes.misconception: That society has always considered childhood as a space for play and exploration.
nodes.response: Before the Enlightenment, children were generally considered small versions of adults.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing childhood in 'Sunday Dip' and 'Mild the Mist Upon the Hill'

nodes.misconception: That an anthology only explores the title theme.
nodes.response: An anthology could also explore the inverse of the title theme in order to highlight particular ideas or concepts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Conceptualising and exploring the Edexcel Belonging anthology

nodes.misconception: That a home is just a set of bricks and mortar.
nodes.response: A home offers us a place of refuge and safety - without a home we feel lost and unsure.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Hardi presents ideas of displacement in 'My Mother's Kitchen'

nodes.misconception: You should always write about the poem you know best.
nodes.response: You should write about the two poems that form the best complementary pairing for the question.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a written response on Edexcel’s Belonging anthology

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the speaker is Rumens herself.
nodes.response: Rumens herself did not experience the emigration that the poem describes. She may have written the poem based on her fascination with people and culture. She may have written the poem to appeal to all that have experienced a story of emigration.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'The Emigree'

nodes.misconception: That the form of a poem doesn't influence our analysis.
nodes.response: The chosen form can influence our perception of the theme of a poem and give us a clue into the writer's intentions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Blakemore presents multiculturalism in 'Peckham Rye Lane'

nodes.misconception: That comparing poems means focusing on their similarities.
nodes.response: The most effective comparisons look for subtle differences within wider similarities.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring ideas of cultural belonging in the Edexcel Belonging anthology

nodes.misconception: That refugees come from places that have always been war torn and a disaster zone.
nodes.response: Refugees can come from anywhere - places that used to be beautiful but have changed through war, regime change or natural disaster.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of oppression, heritage and place in Zephaniah's 'We Refugees'

nodes.misconception: Context should be used in every paragraph of a comparative analytical response.
nodes.response: While it is extremely important to use relevant contextual information to shape interpretations of the two poems being compared, it isn't necessary to include it in every paragraph unless it is relevant to the overall argument you are making.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Building analytical paragraphs about Edexcel's Belonging poetry

nodes.misconception: That dreams aren't based on reality.
nodes.response: Dreams often draw on our previous memories or experiences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Nichols presents memories of home in 'Island Man'

nodes.misconception: That the use of sibilance creates a harsh, sinister atmosphere.
nodes.response: While the hissing sound of sibilance can create a harsh atmosphere, we can also interpret it as a shushing sound that creates a calm atmosphere.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Wordsworth presents nature in 'To My Sister'

nodes.misconception: Thinking that every poem in the anthology is equally suitable for every potential question.
nodes.response: While there are common links between the poems, some have more tenuous connections than others.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing ideas of nostalgia in the Edexcel Belonging anthology

nodes.misconception: That an economic migrant and a refugee are the same thing.
nodes.response: A refugee is someone who has been forced to leave their country in order to escape war, persecution or natural disaster.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of humanity and oppression in Zephaniah's 'We Refugees'

nodes.misconception: That there is one accepted interpretation of a poem.
nodes.response: People may interpret and respond to poetry differently because poetry is, at its core, about emotion and we all have different emotion responses to stimuli.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of conflict and acceptance in Antrobus' 'Jamaican British'

nodes.misconception: That analysing punctuation isn't an effective way to approaching a poem.
nodes.response: Punctuation can affect a reader's journey through the poem as well as their emotional response.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Hood presents the past and present in 'I Remember, I Remember'

nodes.misconception: That the Romantics only wrote about nature.
nodes.response: Often Romantic writers also wrote about a nostalgia for the past.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing nostalgia and melancholia in Brontë's 'Mild the Mist Upon the Hill'

nodes.misconception: That material possessions don't matter.
nodes.response: While material possessions can be replaced, nevertheless they do provide a sense of safety and comfort for us.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of home, upheaval and heritage in Hardi's 'My Mother's Kitchen'

nodes.misconception: You should analyse one poem and then analyse the second, making your comparisons at this point.
nodes.response: The best analysis writing weaves comparisons throughout. A great way to practise this is by beginning each paragraph with a topic sentence that uses correlative conjunctions (e.g. both ... and ...).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing excellent model answers on Edexcel's Belonging anthology

nodes.misconception: That our identities are a singular, unchanging thing.
nodes.response: Our identifies are made up of many things that can change and evolve over time.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Antrobus presents identity and heritage in 'Jamaican British'

nodes.misconception: That all types of negative feelings are the same.
nodes.response: There are nuances within negativity - some negative emotions might stem from fear, anger, jealousy or uncertainty.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing ideas of displacement and belonging in the Edexcel Belonging anthology

nodes.misconception: That idyllic settings stay the same forever.
nodes.response: Arguably, Landon's 'Captain Cook (To My Brother)' suggests that an idyllic place does not last forever.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Landon presents childhood in 'Captain Cook (To My Brother)'

nodes.misconception: That idleness means laziness.
nodes.response: Idleness can also mean enjoying periods of rest and relaxation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Bridges presents nature in 'Clear and Gentle Stream'

nodes.misconception: Sibilance is only used to create a sinister atmosphere.
nodes.response: The repetition of 's' sound could also create a calming, soothing sound.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Bridges presents nature and belonging in 'Clear and Gentle Stream'

nodes.misconception: That imagery has one set meaning and connotations.
nodes.response: The connotations of an image can change depending on the language used in relation to it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Nichols presents ideas of belonging and place in 'Island Man'

nodes.misconception: It isn't important to consider the ethics of writing about war. It is a topic just like any other.
nodes.response: There are important questions to be asked when considering writing about any harrowing experience, particularly war.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding why people write about war

nodes.misconception: Those living in Britain during World War One faced no threat or privation other than their loved ones being far away.
nodes.response: World War One was what is known as 'total war' meaning that those in Britain felt its impact in their day to day life.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Ian Beck's ‘Propping Up The Line’: Alice’s experiences on the Home Front

nodes.misconception: Commas and full stops are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Full stops divide independent clauses and create a longer pause than a comma. Full stops divide ideas and create clear writing. Commas divide subordinate clauses and lists. They create a shorter pause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using sentence structure to create rhythm in writing about World War One

nodes.misconception: You can't compare different text types to each other. For example, a short story to a memoir.
nodes.response: By comparing different forms, we can often come to understand why a writer chose a particular text type more deeply - what this particular text type allowed them to do or convey to the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing texts about World War One using comparative topic sentences

nodes.misconception: Word choice is more important than rhythm.
nodes.response: Word choice and powerful literary methods (for example metaphor) are hard things to craft and deserve time and attention. But so too does your sentence construction. Consider if you heard one of your favourite songs but there was no rhythm to it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving the style of a letter: sentence structure and rhythm

nodes.misconception: If you are writing in third person, then you can't know the internal feelings of characters because you are not inside their head.
nodes.response: Writers that use a third person narrative voice can still explore and present the internal thoughts and feelings of one or more of their characters. You can develop their psychology without having to use the pronoun 'I'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative writing in the third person inspired by Katherine Mansfield's 'The Fly'

nodes.misconception: 'Testament of Youth' is fictional.
nodes.response: A memoir is an account of something based on a person's memories. They are examples of nonfiction.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Skim reading and close reading: 'Testament of Youth' by Vera Brittain

nodes.misconception: You can only use single paragraph outlines to plan analytical writing.
nodes.response: We structure so much of our writing using paragraphs. All paragraphs, whether creative or analytical or something else, require a clear and carefully planned structure.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Vivid descriptive writing using Ian Beck's ‘Propping Up The Line’ as stimulus

nodes.misconception: You can't use words, phrases or methods from other people's writing in your own writing.
nodes.response: Plagiarism is when you use someone's work or ideas without their consent. This is not allowed. However, you can use texts that inspire and excite you to inform your own writing. This might be a piece of powerful vocabulary or a powerful method.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Letter writing: planning, using Vera Brittain’s ‘Testament of Youth’ as stimulus

nodes.misconception: You must analyse every quotation.
nodes.response: There are some quotations that you will want to analyse in depth, and consider their methods and the range of ways they might be interpreted. However, there will also be quotations that link to your topic sentence, but don't need to be analysed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the presentation of the boss in 'The Fly' by Katherine Mansfield

nodes.misconception: You can't link quotations from across a text in a short story.
nodes.response: Being able to link quotations from any text together is a key skill in English. It helps make your analysis thoughtful and convincing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the presentation of the gas attack: Ian Beck's 'Propping Up the Line'
