nodes.misconception: There is one interpretation of a text and it is your job as a student of English to find the correct interpretation.
nodes.response: Texts rarely have one interpretation, and part of your job as a student of English is to consider the range and then select which one you think is the strongest, whilst still allowing for the idea that some might disagree with you.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Debating different interpretations of Katherine Mansfield’s ‘The Fly’

nodes.misconception: Skimming and scanning means you just aren't reading a text properly.
nodes.response: Reading is a skill and, often it is good not to dive into its most difficult skill - analysis - immediately. Instead, giving yourself some time with the text, its title and overall ideas can allow for a deeper understanding in the long run.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Skim reading and close reading: Wilfred Owen’s 1917 letter to his mother

nodes.misconception: There are no common symbols across literature.
nodes.response: There are many common symbols across literature which writers use knowing that many of their readers will know what they mean. For example, a crown to symbolise power. A rose to symbolise love. Birds to symbolise freedom.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Symbolism and motif in Ian Beck's short story, ‘Propping Up The Line’

nodes.misconception: Anyone who breathed in gas died immediately.
nodes.response: Gas attacks killed about three percent of people immediately, but there were long term physical and psychological effects for those who experienced gas attacks.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'Propping Up the Line', a short story about World War One by Ian Beck

nodes.misconception: You can't refer to other writers or texts in your analysis.
nodes.response: Often, you will be asked to write about a text, and that text should certainly be your focus. However, you can refer to other writers or texts if they help develop your analysis and understanding. This is called literary context.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of trauma in Ian Beck's short story, 'Propping Up the Line'

nodes.misconception: It is important to focus on the creation of complex methods like metaphor or anaphora. Verbs don't matter.
nodes.response: Every sentence should contain a verb. As such, choosing them requires careful thought, and can dramatically impact the tone and pace of your writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving a letter: deliberate verbs and precise adjectives

nodes.misconception: People don't use literary methods in nonfiction writing.
nodes.response: Whenever you write any thing - even a shopping list - you are employing methods. Every word is a choice, thus every choice can be evaluated. In nonfiction writing (even nonfiction writing by people who aren't writers) methods will be used for effect.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a letter as a soldier in the trenches of World War One

nodes.misconception: Trench warfare was fighting characterised by intense and constant action.
nodes.response: Trench warfare was characterised by intense periods of action, but also long periods of inaction which could be demoralising, boring and harrowing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: World War One: propaganda and trench warfare

nodes.misconception: Poems are carefully crafted and use methods, but nonfiction letters won't have a structure or include methods.
nodes.response: Almost all writing follows some sort of structure even, for example, a shopping list. Methods are tools writers use to convey their messages. Every single word, technically, is a method.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Letter writing: planning, using Wilfred Owen’s 1917 letter as stimulus

nodes.misconception: Working out the tone, audience and purpose is an unnecessary step in planning. These things are always really obvious.
nodes.response: The foundations of convincing writing comes in the planning stage. This includes thinking carefully about tone, audience and purpose. Having a deep, rather than superficial, understanding of each will allow for a compelling piece of writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a letter from the British home front: tone, audience and purpose

nodes.misconception: Every character is a foil to another because all characters are different.
nodes.response: Whilst characters, like humans, are unique, not every character serves as a foil. Strangely, character foils often have similarities in terms of who they are, and what has happened to them, but their reactions to these things are different.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Katherine Mansfield's 'The Fly' (1922): exploring character foils and symbolism

nodes.misconception: You should select one quotation from each text in a comparative paragraph.
nodes.response: Like in a powerful analytical paragraph, selecting multiple quotations from each text will help strengthen your argument. Selecting these quotations in the planning stage is key.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing texts about World War One in comparative analytical paragraphs

nodes.misconception: Mr. Woodifield intentionally tries to upset the boss.
nodes.response: Mr. Woodifield seems unaware that he has upset the boss, and his cruelty in mentioning his son's grave in Belgium is thoughtless rather than deliberately cruel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading Katherine Mansfield’s short story, ‘The Fly’ (1922)

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that Brooke fought and died in the war because he wrote a war poem.
nodes.response: Although Brooke bravely volunteered to fight in the war, he never actually engaged in any military action. Unfortunately, Brooke died from septicaemia on a ship en route to battle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of patriotism and optimism in Brooke's 'The Soldier'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the dying soldier was already dead when he was thrown into the wagon.
nodes.response: It is important that students understand that the soldier was still half-alive when he was tossed, dying, into the body wagon. This needs to be understood for students to grasp the brutality of war and the lack of respect soldiers were shown.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the realities of war in Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est'

nodes.misconception: Romantic literature is about love and romance.
nodes.response: Romantic literature is concerned with human emotion but Romanticism was a movement that rejected the principles of the Enlightenment period.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the connections between Romanticism and Shelley's 'Ozymandias'

nodes.misconception: The Romantics were known for writing about love and romance.
nodes.response: The Romantics are not to be confused with 'romantics' who may write love poetry. The Romantics most commonly wrote about nature and were known for critiquing the direction of society's progress.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Critical attitudes to powerful institutions in 'London' and 'Ozymandias'

nodes.misconception: Students think that the entire poem is in rhyming couplets.
nodes.response: Only the beginning of the poem is written in rhyming couplets. The couplets fade to pararhymes and then to non-rhyming couplets by the end of the poem, possibly to reflect the soldier's pain fading and the healing process.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Armitage presents the effects of war in 'The Manhunt'

nodes.misconception: Students do not think that they can analyse the poem's title.
nodes.response: In analytical responses, students can absolutely analyse the poem's title!  This can be a great way to start a response or comparison.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Byron presents the woman in 'She Walks in Beauty'

nodes.misconception: Students might think that Brooke fought and died in the war because he wrote a war poem.
nodes.response: Although Brooke bravely volunteered to fight in the war, he never actually engaged in any military action. Unfortunately, Brooke died from septicaemia on a ship en route to battle.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Brooke's presentation of England and patriotism in 'The Soldier'

nodes.misconception: Most poems are deeply personal or emotional and written spontaneously from the heart.
nodes.response: Armitage suggests that writing poetry about traumatic events can be a methodical process. He states that keeping some emotional distance can be helpful.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing interpretations of ‘The Manhunt’ with Simon Armitage

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the speaker does not love their partner very much.
nodes.response: The speaker does love their partner - very much. The speaker, unlike other lovers, refuses to make promises that they aren't 100% sure they can't keep - they arguably find promising 'forever' unrealistic.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding 'Valentine' by Carol Ann Duffy

nodes.misconception: Students think that Dharker is critical of the structures in the slums.
nodes.response: Though Dharker portrays how dangerous these buildings are, she also shows great admiration of the slum community's resourcefulness in building theses structures - she celebrates their fortitude and resilience in the face of adversity.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of community and resilience in Dharker's 'Living Space'

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think there is a 'right' answer when it comes to poetry - that the poem has to have one meaning.
nodes.response: The beauty of poetry is that it means something different to everybody - there is no 'right' answer - there are a series of possible answers.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the Eduqas poetry anthology

nodes.misconception: Students might think that they can only compare two poems from the same thematic cluster within the anthology.
nodes.response: Students can compare any pair of poems as long as the poems have some similarities.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a written response on poetry from the Eduqas anthology

nodes.misconception: All war poems from the anthology are equally comparable.
nodes.response: Some war poems are more suitable for comparison, depending on which question you are asked. You should make your decision based on which ideas and themes you want to discuss.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing how poets explore the experience of war in the Eduqas anthology

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that the poet does not support the idea of love.
nodes.response: In the poem, the speaker is expressing their love for their partner. The speaker does support love, and acknowledges the benefits it can bring - they just also acknowledge the great harm it can cause.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing 'Valentine' by Carol Ann Duffy

nodes.misconception: Students fail to recognise that the poem itself is a kind of memorial for the 38th division in the Battle of Mametz Wood.
nodes.response: The poem immortalises the Welsh soldiers in the 38th division, who lay undiscovered for decades, their stories untold. In this sense, the poem itself has become these soldiers' legacy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Sheers presents the brutality and legacy of war in 'Mametz Wood'

nodes.misconception: Students think that Dharker is critical of the structures in the slums.
nodes.response: Though Dharker portrays how dangerous these buildings are, she also shows great admiration of the slum community's resourcefulness in building these structures - she celebrates their fortitude and resilience in the face of adversity.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of community and faith in Dharker's 'Living Space'

nodes.misconception: Students often fail to appreciate the significance of the speaker being the soldier's wife.
nodes.response: The perspective the poem is written from is deeply significant. Perhaps Armitage chose to write the poem from the perspective of the wife because the soldier is too traumatised to speak of his own experiences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Armitage presents the effects of war in 'The Manhunt'

nodes.misconception: Students often make the mistake of thinking that, like many of the other war poems, this poem was written by a soldier at the time of the war.
nodes.response: This poem is not a personal account; Sheers wrote this poem in 2005. He wanted to raise awareness about the loss of Welsh lives in Mametz Wood and illustrate how destructive war is.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering the context of Sheers' 'Mametz Wood' and the futility of war

nodes.misconception: Students recognise that the hawk is powerful and don't explore this any further.
nodes.response: The significant question in the poem is arguably what makes the hawk powerful? Is it nature? Instinct? His physical strength? His intelligence?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Hughes presents the power of nature in 'Hawk Roosting'

nodes.misconception: Students think that Hughes wrote this poem about fascist dictators like Hitler.
nodes.response: Hughes stated that this was not his intention. Though the poem can be interpreted in this way, this was not what Hughes set out to convey - he wanted to convey the power of nature.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Hughes presents the power of nature in 'Hawk Roosting'

nodes.misconception: Students think that they can only discuss the similarities OR the differences between poems.
nodes.response: Though they should approach the comparison by identifying key or significant similarities or difference, within that, they can also explore the subtle variations between poems too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing how poets explore relationships in the Eduqas anthology

nodes.misconception: Students may fail to recognise that arguably, this poem is a series of stories instead of one 'big' story.
nodes.response: Dove arguably tells several small stories which all contribute to our understanding of the depth of love between her and her husband - Fred.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing 'Cozy Apologia' by Rita Dove

nodes.misconception: Students might think that this poem was written from one lover to another.
nodes.response: This poem is about Lord Byron's first encounter with his cousin's wife - as far as we know, he doesn't interact with her or pursue her - he merely observes her beauty from afar.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how the woman is presented in Byron's 'She Walks in Beauty'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that, because society was very religious in the 18th century, that Blake must have been a devout Christian too.
nodes.response: Blake was extremely opposed to mass worship and hated the fact that religion was allied with the Government - he felt this gave institutions the ability to control and oppress people.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of power and corruption in Blake's 'London'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to notice or appreciate how defiant this poem is at the end.
nodes.response: In saying that she will love her future husband "better" after death, Barrett Browning defies her father and any cosmic force which may try to prevent the couple from being together. Barrett Browning's passion and commitment to Browning is evident.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Browning presents love in 'Sonnet 43'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they need to 'zoom in' on every word when analysing a quotation.
nodes.response: Often, it can be useful to discuss the 'bigger' method that the poet is using e.g. their use of personification. By thinking about bigger methods, the students may be more focused on the themes of the poem and the poet's intentions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing excellent comparative essays on poetry from the Eduqas anthology

nodes.misconception: Students might think that this sonnet was written whilst Barrett Browning was married.
nodes.response: This poem was written before the pair were married. Barrett Browning knew of her father's disapproval, but loved Robert Browning very much.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the presentation of love in Browning's 'Sonnet 43'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that there is only 'one right interpretation' of a poem.
nodes.response: Students are shown in this lesson that poetry can be read in several different ways and that any interpretation is valid. Students should be encouraged to explore multiple interpretations when discussing poetry.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding 'Cozy Apologia' by Rita Dove

nodes.misconception: Students often want to be told the 'right' answer in English and think there is a right answer for every question.
nodes.response: There are no 'right' answers in this lesson - this lesson asks students to consider different possibilities and interpretations and to make up their own minds about the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of time and loss of innocence in Larkin's 'Afternoons'

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the wife receives two letters.
nodes.response: The wife receives a telegram and a letter. Both the irony and the tragedy are in the fact that, due to the quick nature of telegrams, the wife receives news of her husband's death before she receives his letter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding how Hardy presents the consequences of war in 'A Wife in London'

nodes.misconception: Students often use context as a 'bolt-on'.
nodes.response: Context is a valuable additional source of evidence for your argument. Context should be relevant, specific and support your argument. It should be 'peppered' throughout your essay and not 'bolted-on' at the end.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing model answers on poetry from the Eduqas anthology

nodes.misconception: Students often think that Larkin must have had a hostile relationship with his family because of this poem and some of his other poems.
nodes.response: Larkin didn't have a hostile relationship with his parents - he was just a cynical man who held quite bleak views. This doesn't mean he hated his parents - he just recognised that people are products of their own parents.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of time, family, and pessimism in Larkin's 'Afternoons'

nodes.misconception: Students are quick to identify a poem's rhyme scheme, but they often fail to explain its effect or why it has been used.
nodes.response: In this poem, Hardy arguably uses the same rhyme scheme throughout to reflect the inevitability of death and grief as a result of war. The rhyme scheme becomes a pattern in the same way that death and devastation becomes a pattern in war.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Hardy's presentation of the consequences of war in 'A Wife in London'

nodes.misconception: The structure of the poem is entirely predictable.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that Blake does break his rigid structure e.g. iambic tetrameter at times.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of power and conflict in Blake's 'London'

nodes.misconception: The form of poem an author might choose means little to the message
nodes.response: Poets pick their forms carefully, as we can see in 'Ozymandias' even the slight tweaking of form can impact the reading of the poem and its meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the concept of power in Shelley's 'Ozymandias'

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes fail to recognise that the tense shifts as the poem progresses.
nodes.response: Owen includes three tenses in his poem, perhaps to illustrate that the impact of war has, is and will be felt in his past, present and future.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how Owen presents the realities of war in 'Dulce et Decorum Est'

nodes.misconception: Shelley's poem presents a purely positive view of love.
nodes.response: Interspersed among his speaker's overblown philosophical descriptions focused around the beauty of natural symmetry, it's possible to read an element of frustration that the speaker's feelings of desire are unrequited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying how poets reflect desire in natural settings

nodes.misconception: In 'Mother, any distance', the 'child' figure yearns for independence while the parent isn't ready to let them go.
nodes.response: It is possible to interpret the poem in this way but it is also possible to infer that the speaker feels nervous about the prospect of their independence, worrying whether they will succeed or "fall".
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying how poets present relationships that change over time

nodes.misconception: The mother feels a loss of her her beauty, confidence and independence after having a child.
nodes.response: It's important to remember that the 'voice' we hear this from is the speaker's (the daughter). In this way, the negative connotations associated with motherhood could be interpreted as the speaker's guilt for taking her mother's freedom.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Before You Were Mine' by Carol Ann Duffy

nodes.misconception: Analytical paragraphs should be led by identification of writer's methods.
nodes.response: An effective analytical response avoids 'feature-spotting'. Paragraphs should be led with a comparison of key ideas in each poem, followed by a detailed analysis of how the writers use methods to convey these ideas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how poets convey heartbreak in natural settings

nodes.misconception: Sheers tells us that the couple have been arguing before heading out for their walk.
nodes.response: Sheers doesn't explicitly tell us that the couple have been arguing but subtly implies this using personification and pathetic fallacy in the first two stanzas. He describes how the couple are "silent and apart" to show their fragmented relationship.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing 'Winter Swans' by Owen Sheers

nodes.misconception: Ambivalence means you do not care either way (similar to indifference).
nodes.response: Ambivalence is when someone has mixed or conflicting feelings about something or someone.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Climbing My Grandfather' by Andrew Waterhouse

nodes.misconception: A poet will always make choices with a clear intention or meaning.
nodes.response: Armitage reveals that poetic choices can be deliberately ambiguous, allowing for multiple interpretations and personal responses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing interpretations of ‘Mother, any distance’ with Simon Armitage

nodes.misconception: The speaker is actually climbing a mountain.
nodes.response: The speaker compares the experience of climbing up his Grandfather's body as a child to climbing up a mountain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Climbing My Grandfather' by Andrew Waterhouse

nodes.misconception: Form and structure are the same thing.
nodes.response: Form deals with the 'poetic rules' that govern a poem and helps us to categorise it along with other similar poems whereas structure deals with how the ideas in the poem are ordered and organised.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding 'Winter Swans' by Owen Sheers

nodes.misconception: All three poems convey a negative view of romantic relationships.
nodes.response: All three poems begin by conveying a negative view of romantic relationships. This continues throughout 'Neutral Tones' and 'When We Two Parted' however 'Winter Swans' undergoes a shift to a hopeful tone by the end as the couple are unified.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying how poets convey heartbreak in natural settings

nodes.misconception: Every analysis paragraph should link to the wider context.
nodes.response: Effective analysis links to context only when relevant to the discussion of key ideas/methods and avoids 'bolt-on' sentences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how poets reminisce and remember loved ones

nodes.misconception: Analysis paragraphs should lead by 'feature-spotting' a technique and then linking it to key ideas.
nodes.response: The most effective analysis paragraphs lead with key ideas supported by evidence from the text, analysis of writer's methods, a justification of ideas and a link to the writer's intentions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem ‘Walking Away’ by Cecil Day-Lewis

nodes.misconception: All three poems reflect on memories of a loved one who is now dead.
nodes.response: Causley's use of an uncanny setting implies that the two parents are now in the afterlife, guiding the speaker's "[c]rossing", however Duffy and Waterhouse use language linked to death/loss ("ghost", "pulse") but do not imply the relative has died.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying how poets reminisce and remember loved ones

nodes.misconception: It's important to include a contextual link in every analytical paragraph.
nodes.response: Although it is important to include links to wider context in your overall response, it isn't necessary to include a contextual link in every analytical paragraph. In fact, 'bolt-on' contextual links should be avoided.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how poets present relationships that change over time

nodes.misconception: The speaker explains how having children ruined her mother's life.
nodes.response: While Duffy does explore how motherhood has contributed to her mother's loss of confidence and freedom, the final stanza of the poem shows them both having fun together so it is evident that there are many positive aspects to motherhood as well.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Before You Were Mine' by Carol Ann Duffy

nodes.misconception: You should decide on one main interpretation of text and focus on that in your analytical writing.
nodes.response: Effective analytical writing often includes multiple interpretations of a text and careful consideration of the wider context.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Eden Rock' by Charles Causley

nodes.misconception: Students may think that in the last two lines of the poem, the father now follows behind the son while he is out ploughing a field.
nodes.response: Although their roles have reversed, there is no indication that the last two lines involve the father and son ploughing. The echoes in the language merely symbolise that their roles have reversed as the son has grown up.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Follower' by Seamus Heaney

nodes.misconception: This poem is written in the form of a sonnet: it has 14 lines and a regular rhyme scheme.
nodes.response: This poem does not strictly follow the sonnet form but does use many of its conventions. It contains 15, not 14 lines and doesn't use a regular rhyme scheme. It does however end with a rhyming couplet and uses iambic pentameter in places.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Mother, any distance’ by Simon Armitage

nodes.misconception: The speaker mourns the growing distance between him and his mother.
nodes.response: This is just one interpretation of the text; we could also infer that the speaker has felt stifled by their mother's involvement in their life until now and yearns for their independence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Mother, any distance' by Simon Armitage

nodes.misconception: Eden Rock is a real place.
nodes.response: Eden Rock is a fictional place, devised by the poet Charles Causley. Causley confirms this but does suggest that he based the location on the Cornish landscape where he grew up.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Eden Rock’ by Charles Causley

nodes.misconception: This poem is an autobiographical account of one of Heaney's childhood memories.
nodes.response: This collection, 'Death of Naturalist', is semi-autobiographical since it reflects on aspects of Heaney's childhood, growing up in a rural Irish farming community, but the poet has never confirmed that this particular memory is from his childhood.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Follower' by Seamus Heaney

nodes.misconception: The poem is set by a pond where a couple are walking.
nodes.response: The poem is set in the present day (for the speaker) and the speaker is looking back on the memory of walking around a pond with their ex-partner.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Neutral Tones’ by Thomas Hardy

nodes.misconception: Shelley was a Romantic poet which meant all of his poems were love poems.
nodes.response: Romantic poetry did sometimes focus on themes associated with love, but not exclusively. Romantic poetry is instead characterised by its dramatic approach to exploring abstract and emotional concepts such as a love, nature or the supernatural.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Love’s Philosophy’ by Percy Bysshe Shelley

nodes.misconception: The poem is about a long-distance romantic relationship.
nodes.response: The relationship between the speaker and the man who sends her letters is ambiguous; it could be platonic, romantic or familial.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Letters from Yorkshire’ by Maura Dooley

nodes.misconception: Analysis should be led by identification of the writer's methods.
nodes.response: Effective comparative analysis should be led by key ideas and then supported by textual evidence and identification of the writer's methods and intentions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how poets reflect desire in natural settings

nodes.misconception: This poem is only about a Romantic view of love (from an abstract, philosophical perspective).
nodes.response: This poem appears to have an ulterior motive. Shelley uses language, form and structure to subtly persuade the listener to enter into a romantic relationship with him.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Love's Philosophy' by Percy Bysshe Shelley

nodes.misconception: In this poem, the speaker mourns for their lover after they have died.
nodes.response: This could be a valid interpretation but there is no evidence to suggest the lover is definitely dead. In fact, the volta in L.9 has the speaker demand he return which implies that there is a chance they could be reunited with one another.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Sonnet 29’ by Elizabeth Barrett Browning

nodes.misconception: The speaker of the poem has unrequited romantic feelings for the man and yearns to be with him.
nodes.response: This is only one interpretation of the poem. Alternatively, the reference to "romance" in L.5 could imply that the speaker romanticises the natural world that she is so distanced from in her urban landscape and yearns to return to nature.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem ‘Letters from Yorkshire’ by Maura Dooley

nodes.misconception: This is an account of Byron's affair with Lady Frances Webster.
nodes.response: It is believed that is poem is inspired by Byron's affair with Lady Webster. It is not a factual account, only perhaps a creative interpretation of his feelings about this and other affairs he was known to have had.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'When We Two Parted' by Lord Byron

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think the parent and child never spoke or saw each other again after this moment in the poem.
nodes.response: The separation described in the poem isn't just physical but rather emotional. Day-Lewis describes a moment where the speaker feels like they lost a part of their son because he had grown up and gained his independence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem ‘Walking Away’ by Cecil Day-Lewis

nodes.misconception: You need to include a reference to the wider context in every analytical paragraph.
nodes.response: The best analytical responses only include relevant pieces of context and weave it subtly throughout. It is important to include context in your answer but it isn't necessary to include it in every paragraph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem ‘Neutral Tones’ by Thomas Hardy

nodes.misconception: The lines, "They know not I knew thee, / Who knew thee too well" refer to the close emotional relationship the couple had since they knew everything about each other.
nodes.response: These lines can also be read as a euphemism for the couple's sexual relationship, since 'know' was a term often used in the Bible to refer to sexual intercourse.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem  ‘When We Two Parted’ by Lord Byron

nodes.misconception: The extended metaphor of trees and vines represent her absent lover.
nodes.response: The extended metaphor of a tree symbolises her absent lover whereas the extended metaphor of the vines symbolises her fantastical thoughts of her lover while he is away from her.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Sonnet 29' by Elizabeth Barrett Browning

nodes.misconception: Lines 9-16 of the poem use abstract imagery to convey the moment of the birth in the hospital room.
nodes.response: While this is one way of interpreting these lines, others have argued the abstract images could reflect society's unfair expectations of mothers and the nature of the developing maternal relationship.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Catrin' by Gillian Clarke

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not notice the significance of the textile imagery.
nodes.response: The textile imagery was carefully chosen for the poem, Jane Weir would have been very conscious of putting this in as she was a textile designer.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Poppies'

nodes.misconception: This poem is entirely autobiographical, written about Clarke's experiences of motherhood.
nodes.response: This poem was written just after the birth of Clarke's fist daughter so does reflect on her experiences of motherhood but the later scenes of a older child playing out are necessarily fictional.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Catrin' by Gillian Clarke

nodes.misconception: Students may associate war poetry with soldiers of the first world war and not consider other perspectives.
nodes.response: Many other people were affected by war in less obvious ways than the soldiers themselves.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Poppies'

nodes.misconception: We no longer experience gender inequality in today's society.
nodes.response: Although today's society is much more progressive than Victorian society, there are still areas where gender inequality is experienced, although it is usually much more subtle and institutionalised.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing women's conflict in the Edexcel 'Conflict' anthology

nodes.misconception: Context is required in every paragraph of a comparative analytical response.
nodes.response: Context is important to include in your response but it isn't necessary in every paragraph. In order to avoid 'bolt-on' context, it should only be used when it is relevant to the point you're making in that paragraph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing an extended and developed response on Edexcel 'Conflict' poetry

nodes.misconception: Effective comparative analysis leads by comparing the poets' use of literary methods.
nodes.response: The most effective comparative analysis writing should lead by comparing key ideas of attitudes in both poems.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making connections between poems in the Edexcel 'Conflict' cluster

nodes.misconception: The speaker feels as though her cousin Kate has ruined her life completely.
nodes.response: While the speaker does feel that Kate has stolen the life she deserved/desired, she also feels that she can have the 'last laugh' since she has given birth to the nobleman's son.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Cousin Kate' by Christina Rossetti

nodes.misconception: This poem is primarily about familial conflict.
nodes.response: Although the speaker and Kate are family relations, the conflict between them is focused on their shared love interest and so their family connection is inconsequential.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Cousin Kate' by Christina Rossetti

nodes.misconception: Analytical paragraphs should lead by comparing how the writers use language, form and/or structure.
nodes.response: The best comparative analytical writing begins by exploring connections between the key ideas or attitudes in a poem, supported by analysis of how writers use language, form and/or structure to convey these ideas or attitudes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an extended and developed response on Edexcel 'Conflict' poetry

nodes.misconception: Poppies is a poem about a mother whose son died during WWI.
nodes.response: Although Poppies are a symbol of remembrance for those who died in WWI, Weir uses her poem to draw attention to the many conflicts that have occurred throughout history. It isn't clear which conflict the son is heading off to fight in.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A comparison of ‘Poppies’ by Jane Weir with other Edexcel 'Conflict' poems

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter which two poems you choose to compare as all of them can be compared with each other.
nodes.response: In theory, you can compare any two poems from the anthology however it's important to remember that some have more connections than others. You should aim to select two poems with a range of connections to avoid tenuous links.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an extended and developed response on Edexcel 'Conflict' poetry

nodes.misconception: Knowing that the Brownings were married to each other is an important piece of contextual information.
nodes.response: Although it is relevant to know they were married, it is in linking their own unconventional marriage to the subversive presentation of love and relationships in their poems that the best contextual points can be found.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The poetry of Robert and Elizabeth Browning and Victorian values

nodes.misconception: All Victorian poets held the same views and attitudes towards societal issues.
nodes.response: Victorian poets had diverse views. Some challenged norms, others reinforced them. Consider each poem's own unique perspective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective context: Victorian poems in the 'Love and Relationships' anthology

nodes.misconception: All of these poems present relationships which are dysfunctional in some way.
nodes.response: Although 'Porphyria's Lover' and 'The Farmer's Bride' appear to show abusive, controlling relationships, the relationship in 'Singh Song!' is presented as a much more conventionally loving one.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing unconventional relationships in the 'Love and Relationships' anthology

nodes.misconception: The speaker kills Porphyria out of love, and his actions can be seen as a romantic gesture.
nodes.response: The speaker's actions aren't a romantic gesture but a sign of his disturbed mind. His love is possessive and obsessive, shown by his desire to control Porphyria. The calm tone he uses to describe the murder show his detachment from reality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Porphyria's Lover' by Robert Browning

nodes.misconception: Analysis should focus on the bride.
nodes.response: Although there is lots to say about the bride - and her treatment in the relationship - the farmer also presents a rich source of analysis through his often contradictory actions throughout the poem (explored in the written task in Learning Cycle 2).
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'The Farmer's Bride' by Charlotte Mew

nodes.misconception: Singh's wife is presented exclusively as a sweet and gentle character.
nodes.response: Although Singh does speak softly of his wife, she also has a fierce streak. This is shown when her eyes are described as like 'guns' and through the description of her arguments with Singh's parents.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'Singh Song!' by Daljit Nagra

nodes.misconception: Porphyria is entirely passive and without agency.
nodes.response: Porphyria displays agency by actively seeking out the speaker and initiating intimacy. Her actions challenge societal norms, reflecting her independence and desire, despite her eventual victimisation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Porphyria's Lover' by Robert Browning

nodes.misconception: Students might think Romantic poems are only about love and beauty.
nodes.response: Romantic poems also explore deep emotions, the sublime in nature, individualism and sometimes darker themes like sorrow and longing, reflecting the complexity of human experience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Romantic poems in the 'Love and Relationships' anthology

nodes.misconception: Students may think context should be mentioned separately at the end of their paragraphs, rather than integrated throughout their analysis.
nodes.response: Context should be woven into your analysis to enrich your interpretation e.g. 'Nagra's depiction of family duties versus personal desires draws from his British-Indian experience, showcasing challenges faced by second-generation immigrants.'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective context: modern poems in the 'Love and Relationships' anthology

nodes.misconception: Comparative responses are just a list of similarities and differences.
nodes.response: While identifying similarities and differences is essential, your comparative response should also articulate a clear argument that ties these observations together.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing unconventional relationships in the 'Love and Relationships' anthology

nodes.misconception: The farmer is simply trying to care for his wife, his actions are well-intentioned and innocent.
nodes.response: The farmer's attempts to care for his wife may initially seem genuine, but the poem suggests a deeper complexity to their relationship. The bride's evident distress and desire to escape challenge the notion of the farmer's benevolence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'The Farmer's Bride' by Charlotte Mew

nodes.misconception: The poem doesn't rhyme.
nodes.response: Although the poem doesn't follow a conventional and predictable rhyme scheme, it does have some irregular and half rhymes (e.g. "chapatti" and "chutney"). This structure imitates the playful and joyous content of the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Singh Song!' by Daljit Nagra

nodes.misconception: Students can think a motif is a symbol used once or think it is deployed in the same way as a semantic field.
nodes.response: Remind them of the etymology - there has to be movement and change of the motif.  A semantic field does not have to be symbolic.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The use of a motif in Hillary Clinton's speech

nodes.misconception: Students often think they need to be balanced in their writing and discuss both sides of a debate.
nodes.response: Teach the difference between opinion writing and argument writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing an opinion article about protecting the greenbelt

nodes.misconception: That you need to be personally affected by something to make a speech about it.
nodes.response: Draw attention to Hillary Clinton as an advocate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Hillary Clinton's passionate speech about women's rights

nodes.misconception: It is easy to confuse motifs with extended metaphors.
nodes.response: A motif uses recurring elements that can employ a range of techniques. An extended metaphor is a sustained comparison across a text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using a motif in your writing

nodes.misconception: Students think of speeches as being a form of protest, but poems or songs.
nodes.response: Emphasise the wide range of text types used in the lesson.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing convictions

nodes.misconception: Content alone is enough for an effective formal presentation.
nodes.response: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Delivering a presentation is so much more than just the words on a page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Delivering a formal presentation

nodes.misconception: Students often think that to evaluate something is to say whether or not you like it.
nodes.response: Keep reminding them of the criteria. Does a text measure up to a standard being set?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating how two non-fiction writers express their opinions

nodes.misconception: Memorising a presentation, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
nodes.response: An effective presentation will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing presentation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to deliver a presentation

nodes.misconception: Students often think that serious topics need serious text types such as articles or speeches.
nodes.response: Encourage students to consider why a writer might choose to use a poem to write about a serious topic and take a stand.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘The Chimney Sweeper’: a protest against child labour

nodes.misconception: Students often think they have to be balanced when they deliver persuasive presentations.
nodes.response: Be clear about taking a stand and picking a side. A presentation which is clear in its stance has much more impact.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning content for a presentation

nodes.misconception: Figurative language, like metaphors, is not used in presentations.
nodes.response: Stress how much stronger presentations can be when it allows the audience to make associations with objects and items they are familiar with.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating content for a formal presentation

nodes.misconception: Students may think that there is a very clear distinction between poetry and music lyrics.
nodes.response: Encourage students to consider what the poetry and song lyrics have in common. For example the use of verses and refrains, as well as the use of figurative language, often crosses over.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Where Have All the Flowers Gone?’: a song of conviction

nodes.misconception: Fairy tales are written solely for children.
nodes.response: Fairy tales are primarily stories about transformation and therefore this form appeals to many writers, especially those who are interested in social issues.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a fairy tale about a social issue

nodes.misconception: Students often don't value their own knowledge or experiences when aiming  to persuade.
nodes.response: Encourage students to use examples that they are familiar with.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Aristotle's triad

nodes.misconception: Students may not immediately understand the title if they have never come across 'colonialism' before.
nodes.response: Take some time unpicking why Clarke equates colonisation to stealing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ‘This Poem is Taking Place on Stolen Land’

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the same punctuation rules apply in poetry and other types of writing (e.g. full stops are needed at the end of lines).
nodes.response: Poems are not bound to formal punctuation rules. Having flexibility allows the poet to shape their poem based on emotion rather than grammar rules.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using punctuation in poetry

nodes.misconception: The poem 'Island Man' only tells the story of someone that misses the Caribbean.
nodes.response: The poem 'Island Man' can help to tell the story of any migrant who experiences nostalgia for their home country.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'Island Man' by Grace Nichols

nodes.misconception: Students may not realise the importance of listening in discussions, as they may be thinking about what they have to say next.
nodes.response: Explain the importance of listening. Model a discussion with a pupil where you are not listening, ask them how it made them feel and ask the class how it affected the quality of the discussion.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the link between place and identity

nodes.misconception: Students may think George The Poet's attitude towards his city is wholly negative.
nodes.response: George The Poet critiques certain aspects of London, particularly inequality and the way in which people often do not acknowledge the poverty in London.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering the nature of home

nodes.misconception: Students may not at first understand that they must use a parallel sentence structure when using correlative conjunctions e.g. Both 'Island Man' uses imagery as well as 'Search for My Tongue'.
nodes.response: Model a few sentences with correlative conjunctions to show that parallel structures are needed. e.g. Both 'Island Man' and 'Search for My Tongue' use imagery.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing poems about place and home

nodes.misconception: Students may be unfamiliar with the term 'region'.
nodes.response: Help students recognise and learn about their own region.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring regional pride in the poem ‘Anthem of the North’

nodes.misconception: Students may misconceive what the phrase "my tongue" means initially.
nodes.response: Explain the figurative language involved in the phrase "my tongue" and the link to language.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing 'Search for My Tongue'

nodes.misconception: As long as the content of a poem is good, the performance will automatically be good.
nodes.response: Performance requires practise in a unique set of skills which are worth practising as a good performance can enhance the poem content.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing our poems about place and home

nodes.misconception: Students may not understand the subtle difference between imagery and figurative language.
nodes.response: Whilst imagery can include figurative language and vice versa, imagery does not always have to be figurative.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning ideas for a poem about your home

nodes.misconception: Students may not immediately think they can relate to the poem, if their own home does not have distinct elements of their culture or heritage.
nodes.response: Explain how everyone can relate to the idea of having a filter on. Whilst Subramaniam takes off her filter and reveals her heritage at home, your students might reveal their true personality or hobbies through home.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring what home means through the poem ‘Filter’

nodes.misconception: A poem has to follow a similar rhythm the whole way through.
nodes.response: By creating two different rhythms, we can juxtapose two places.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring example poems about place and home

nodes.misconception: The most important thing in a poem is the words.
nodes.response: Structure is important, it can help tell your story. Not considering the structure of your poem is like an author not considering the beginning, middle and end of a novel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing our own poetry about home

nodes.misconception: Students may be used to starting any sensory language sentences with 'I can see, I can hear ...'
nodes.response: Poetry allows us to innovate with traditional writing structures to help a rhythmic flow and sense of nostalgia; help students recognise the difference between 'I can see ...' and 'Seeing ...'
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring memories of home in the poem ‘Childhood Tracks’

nodes.misconception: You have to be writing in the C18th to use Romantic conventions in your writing.
nodes.response: While Romanticism was a predominant movement in the C18th and C19th, more modern poets can also adhere to Romantic conventions and present a Romantic view of the world.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing belonging in 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' and 'I Shall Return'

nodes.misconception: You should ignore any parts of the poem that don't fit with your overall interpretation.
nodes.response: To create a nuanced argument, you want to think about why the poet may have chosen not to present a cohesive whole to the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of belonging and heritage in McKay’s ‘I shall return’

nodes.misconception: There is only one valid interpretation of a method.
nodes.response: There might be several different ways of interpreting a method.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of belonging in Wordsworth's 'I wandered lonely as a cloud'

nodes.misconception: Typically, literature presents the idea of a simple life as dull and monotonous.
nodes.response: Literary movements such as the Romantics presented an idealised view of a simple, rural existence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of belonging in McKay’s ‘I Shall Return’

nodes.misconception: Art is always meant to be beautiful.
nodes.response: Art can be a means of sparking discussion, representing political views, or addressing problems in society.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of dehumanisation and apathy in Ghose’s ‘Decomposition’

nodes.misconception: Taking a photograph of someone's suffering is an effective way of showing their suffering to others.
nodes.response: Arguably, both Duffy and Ghose reveal the futility of using art as a means of showing their suffering to others.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing ideas of art in Duffy's 'War Photographer' and Ghose's 'Decomposition'

nodes.misconception: The final word of a poem is an unimportant detail.
nodes.response: The final word of the poem offers us the lasting impression of the poem's message.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing ideas of dehumanisation and apathy in Ghose’s ‘Decomposition’

nodes.misconception: Adding an alternative interpretation weakens your argument.
nodes.response: Showing how you can reach the same conclusion about a text through multiple interpretations strengthens your argument.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an extended written response on the Eduqas 2025 poetry anthology

nodes.misconception: While comparing poems, you should only look for similarities between them.
nodes.response: To create an effective comparison, you want to find nuanced differences within overall similarities.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an extended written response on the Eduqas 2025 poetry anthology

nodes.misconception: You cannot be both respected and feared.
nodes.response: The Romantic sublime was the concept that we should feel awe towards nature - a mixture of both fear and respect.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of belonging in Wordsworth's 'I wandered lonely as a cloud'

nodes.misconception: Students may zoom into the suffering within the photos and not realise the complex emotions in the photographer himself.
nodes.response: Duffy, having seen  her friends do the job of photojournalism, may have been privy to the complex and difficult emotions involved in this job. This could be why she focuses on the quiet trauma within the photographer.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the poem 'War Photographer'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the concept of photo developing when initially reading the poem and thus not realise what the poem is about.
nodes.response: Explain the process of photo developing film photographs in a dark room - the dark room is because photographs are light-sensitive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the poem 'War Photographer'

nodes.misconception: The pronoun "you" is the only example of direct address.
nodes.response: Direct address is any way in which a writer directly addresses their audience. This could be a title, name or term.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Summarising a non-fiction text: 'a letter to my son' (the Guardian, 2014)

nodes.misconception: Inference and analysis are the same thing.
nodes.response: Inference is about reading between the lines. Analysis focuses on unpicking writer's methods and explores their effects.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a summary of a non-fiction text by including inferences

nodes.misconception: That perspectives are simply positive or negative.
nodes.response: Positive and negative can be useful words to initially consider a perspective, but then you must become more nuanced and use specific adjectives to identify feelings and perspectives.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing texts about drug misuse: ‘Confessions’ (1821) and ‘A letter to’ (2014)

nodes.misconception: Choosing vocabulary and ideas is the most important part of the writing process.
nodes.response: Structural features can really elevate your writing, making it more cohesive and impactful so that your reader doesn't lose interest.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using structural features effectively in non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: Placing ambiguous, short questions with direct address at the end of sentences is an effective rhetorical question. For example: 'Do you/don't you agree?'
nodes.response: Think about the purpose of a rhetorical question and why we use them. Is this the best way to challenge and provoke thought or get a reaction from your audience?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading an opinion article and creating rhetorical questions

nodes.misconception: Writing down any number in a piece of non-fiction writing is enough to show you know how to use statistics.
nodes.response: Statistics need to be credible. When creating your own statistics, you need to think carefully about how to make them sound believable by giving details like their source, date and data sample size.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using credible statistics in a piece of non-fiction writing

nodes.misconception: That Mayhew describes everything in the prison in a negative light.
nodes.response: Focus on the descriptions of the prisoners. Why does Mayhew present them in this way? What is he trying to say about prisoners?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and comparing two texts about prisons: London (1862) and Norway (2013)

nodes.misconception: When writing an extended piece of fiction or non-fiction, you should include every single method you know.
nodes.response: Different texts are read for different reasons and by different audiences. It is your job, as the writer, to consider which are the best methods for your particular text. Just because you know how to use a method, doesn't mean you have to include it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an open letter using single paragraph outlines

nodes.misconception: You can only use figurative language in fictional writing.
nodes.response: Non-fiction writers, just like fiction writers, are trying to create interesting, original and compelling ideas that their readers will remember, enjoy and learn from.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using figurative language in non-fiction writing

nodes.misconception: Websites don't need to be engaging if they only provide information.
nodes.response: What is the purpose of a website? If you want people to read the information, how are you going to engage your reader?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing website content

nodes.misconception: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time.
nodes.response: How does the process of revising and rewriting develop vocabulary use? How does rewriting support the writing of future responses?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising and editing non-fiction writing

nodes.misconception: The language and structure of an informative website is always unexciting and dull.
nodes.response: What is the best way to remember information? Are you more likely to remember if it is presented in an interesting and engaging way? Informative websites still need to engage their audience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the conventions of website content creatively

nodes.misconception: That only men from England fought for Britain.
nodes.response: Men from all over the British Empire fought for Britain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering the relationship between the poetry of WW1 and the context

nodes.misconception: That a poet had to experience actual fighting to write war poetry.
nodes.response: Though part of the Royal Navy Volunteer Reserve, Brooke saw no military action.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding patriotism in Rupert Brooke’s ‘The Soldier’

nodes.misconception: That you should always select quotes with the most linguistic features to talk about.
nodes.response: You should select the quote that best matches the point of the sentence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing about John McCrae’s ‘In Flanders Fields’ as a call to arms

nodes.misconception: That natural imagery is only designed to help paint a picture to the reader.
nodes.response: Natural imagery can also be used to suggest a concept is natural or make a comment about the relationship between humans and nature.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing John McCrae’s call to arms in ‘In Flanders Fields’

nodes.misconception: That only soldiers from England fought for Britain in WW1.
nodes.response: Soldiers from all over the British Empire fought for Britain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ideas of Empire and colonialism in Naidu’s ‘The Gift of India’

nodes.misconception: That all war poetry is designed to dissuade people from fighting.
nodes.response: Pro-war poetry is designed to encourage people to volunteer to fight.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the concept of remembrance in John McCrae’s ‘In Flanders Fields’

nodes.misconception: A comparative essay should deal with each poem separately in the body of the essay.
nodes.response: While one method of comparison might be to deal with each poem separately, you might also consider comparing the poems throughout the essay and instead splitting up the essay thematically or by methods.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a comparative response on perspectives of war and sacrifice in WW1 poems

nodes.misconception: That an answer should include all of the interesting details about a text.
nodes.response: An answer should only include details that are relevant to the question.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing about patriotism in Rupert Brooke’s ‘The Soldier’

nodes.misconception: That comparative essays should only focus on the differences between poems.
nodes.response: The most successful comparative essays focus on both the similarities and the differences between the poems.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing views in ‘The Soldier’, ‘In Flanders Fields’ and ‘The Gift of India’

nodes.misconception: That you cannot analyse words in structural analysis.
nodes.response: Analysis of where certain words appear in a poem is a valuable structural analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the humanity and fragility of soldiers in Naidu’s ‘The  Gift of India’

nodes.misconception: That analysing word choice is exclusively part of language analysis.
nodes.response: Analysing where certain words appear in a poem is an effective structural choice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the presentation of patriotism in Rupert Brooke’s ‘The Soldier’

nodes.misconception: That your feelings about a poem are irrelevant.
nodes.response: How you respond to a poem forms the basis of your argument about a poem - it helps you to understand how a poet has created meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a personal response to an unseen poem

nodes.misconception: That there is one correct way of organising your thoughts for a plan.
nodes.response: Creating a plan is designed to help you see what your argument is - there is no definitive way of how you should organise your thoughts.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a response to an unseen poem by collecting and organising your thoughts

nodes.misconception: That using tentative language makes your argument seem less convincing.
nodes.response: Using tentative language acknowledges that we are exploring poets' intentions and that there are many valid interpretations of a text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a comparative response to ideas of transience in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That comparing language is the best way to compare poems.
nodes.response: As well as comparing the language, you can also compare the use of form, structure and voice in poems.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing how poets present ideas of transience in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That you should consider the bigger picture of a text rather than minute detail.
nodes.response: Zooming in on individual words is a powerful analytical tool that allows you to see patterns in meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying and analysing semantic fields in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That you should only look for differences between poems in a comparative response.
nodes.response: A comparative response involves analysing and exploring the similarities and differences in how two poems present an idea or concept.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a comparative response to ideas of transience in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That you can only analyse what techniques a poet chooses to use.
nodes.response: Sometimes it's very powerful to analyse why a poet may have chosen not to use a technique in contrast to one who did choose to use it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing a comparative response to ideas of transience in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That the speaker of the poem is the poet.
nodes.response: A poet may talk about their own experiences through the speaker, or they may be exploring another aspect of the human psyche and experience through the speaker.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Conceptualising and analysing speaker and voice in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That the idea of life being temporary must always be a sad notion.
nodes.response: The idea of life being temporary might inspire us to live life to the fullest.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing ideas about transience in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That the tone and mood of the poem are the same thing.
nodes.response: Tone refers to the attitude of the writer towards the subject matter while mood refers to the effect the writing has on the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing tone in an unseen poem

nodes.misconception: That comparison involves spotting the differences between poems.
nodes.response: Arguably, the best comparisons are where there is an exploration of subtle differences within similarities.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing how poets present motherhood and maternal stereotypes in unseen poems

nodes.misconception: That considering which poem you have a stronger emotional reaction to is not worthwhile.
nodes.response: Comparing your personal responses to poems can help you to see how the poet has managed to create meaning and mood through their writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing personal responses to unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That sibilance only creates a sinister atmosphere.
nodes.response: Sibilance can also create a soothing atmosphere.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing use of sound in an unseen poem

nodes.misconception: That you should take imagery at face value.
nodes.response: Imagery in poetry is often metaphorical and symbolises a deeper meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding sub-text in unseen poems

nodes.misconception: Analysing a text is an individual exercise.
nodes.response: Having discussions around a text can help us build on our ideas and reconsider different ways of interpreting the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing and developing a response to an unseen poem

nodes.misconception: That you should select quotations by spotting methods within a poem.
nodes.response: While analysing methods is an important part of understanding a text, selecting quotations should focus on which word(s) create an evocative impression.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Selecting and using quotations from an unseen poem

nodes.misconception: That structural choices happen accidentally.
nodes.response: Structural choices are consciously made by the poet in order to influence the meaning of the poem.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Structural analysis of unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That titles shouldn't form a part of your analysis.
nodes.response: The title forms our first impression of the poem and therefore is a rich area for analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring titles in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That personal responses involve making guesses about the writer's context and state of mind.
nodes.response: Personal responses consider how and why a poem might create a certain emotion in the reader or what they say about society in general.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing extended responses to ideas of transience in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: That similes and metaphors are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Similes and metaphors are conceptually different since, in a simile, one thing does not become another while in a metaphor they do become each other.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining comparative imagery in unseen poetry

nodes.misconception: Julia Stoner's death was accidental.
nodes.response: Explain that the point of a mystery story is for the detective to use clues to solve it and usually find a perpetrator.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making predictions about ‘The Speckled Band’ mystery

nodes.misconception: It is better to know everything about a character or text before reading.
nodes.response: Making predictions can help us with our comprehension of complex texts and independent thinking.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Making predictions about Sherlock Holmes

nodes.misconception: As long as I keep my headline and subheading short, they will be effective.
nodes.response: Headlines and subheadings must be crafted to fit the purpose of the article.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating newspaper headlines and subheadings

nodes.misconception: Details of a crime can be reported in any part of an article.
nodes.response: Explain to students that more and more information is revealed as an article develops.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing the opening of an article on ‘The Speckled Band’ case

nodes.misconception: Students may be confused about Turner's fate at the end of the story.
nodes.response: Explain that no two Sherlock Holmes mysteries are the same. Two perpetrators can face different fates.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving 'The Boscombe Valley Mystery'

nodes.misconception: Conan Doyle creates a scary atmosphere all the way through 'The Speckled Band'.
nodes.response: If you look carefully, Conan Doyle carefully alters the atmosphere in order to build tension in the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading about Stoke Moran and analysing atmosphere in ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: An introduction can be written without thoughtful planning
nodes.response: To make an introduction worthwhile, and for it to effectively introduce an essay, it requires thoughtful planning
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘The Speckled Band’ and ‘The Boscombe Valley Mystery’: a written comparison

nodes.misconception: It does not matter who you interview for your article.
nodes.response: You should choose your interviewee carefully depending on the effect you want to have.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘The Speckled Band’ case: writing a newspaper article body

nodes.misconception: All victim profiles are similar.
nodes.response: Conan Doyle manipulates his presentation of victims depending on how he wants the reader to view them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the victims in ‘The Speckled Band’ and ‘The Boscombe Valley Mystery’

nodes.misconception: Each piece of evidence can be looked at in isolation when thinking about the crime.
nodes.response: Question your students' explanations to help them acknowledge where they have failed to consider certain pieces of evidence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating Julia’s death in ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: Some students think that villains are one dimensional.
nodes.response: Villains have their own struggles.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing John Turner from ‘The Boscombe Valley Mystery’

nodes.misconception: The tail functions as a summary of the events.
nodes.response: Although a conclusion in any other form of writing would contain a summary, an article summary usually goes at the beginning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Speckled Band' case: concluding newspaper articles

nodes.misconception: Students may not immediately piece together all of the pieces of evidence throughout the case.
nodes.response: Break the conclusion down for students with a visual depiction or flow diagram if necessary, explain that some clues were red herrings.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and summarising the conclusion of ‘The Speckled Band’ mystery

nodes.misconception: The police force we have today is the one society has always had.
nodes.response: Explain that the police force was a new concept to Victorians and thus civilians had a lot of anxiety around crime.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Helen Stoner’s presentation in ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: That a modern reader and Victorian reader perceive the text and characters in the same way.
nodes.response: Use Victorian context to explain the difference between our attitudes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an argument about Dr. Roylott from ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: Rhetorical devices can be used randomly throughout work with little thought.
nodes.response: Show that rhetorical devices have to be used for precise effect otherwise there is no point in using them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using rhetorical devices in newspaper articles

nodes.misconception: A newspaper article can be written in the same style as a story retelling.
nodes.response: Newspaper articles must have different elements to show they are an article - interview quotes and a concise way of writing things are key.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing your own newspaper article about Sherlock Holmes

nodes.misconception: McCarthy's son is definitely guilty.
nodes.response: It is suspected that McCarthy's son is responsible for the murder of McCarthy, however Holmes still has a lot of investigating to do.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Boscombe Valley Mystery'

nodes.misconception: Planning is not necessary before writing.
nodes.response: Planning is important in helping us structure our work and keep a clear focus.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a newspaper article about the solved  case of ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: Planning can often be seen as a waste of time.
nodes.response: You must take time to make notes and gather ideas so the analysis you write is strong.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing atmosphere and character in ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are almost identical.
nodes.response: Whilst all Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are part of the detective fiction genre, the stories can differ a lot.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing ‘The Speckled Band’ and ‘The Boscombe Valley Mystery’

nodes.misconception: Connotation is the definition of a word.
nodes.response: Connotation is a feeling that a word gives .
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Dr. Roylott in ‘The Speckled Band’

nodes.misconception: Poems are meant to be read in your head.
nodes.response: When poets write poems, they play close attention to their sounds and rhythm. As such, it's often important and desirable to hear poems aloud.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou’s ‘Phenomenal Woman’

nodes.misconception: You can't plan a poem. Poems are inspired, and just flow from the heart.
nodes.response: Poems, just like paragraphs, can be planned. You can consider ideas and methods. Indeed, because poems are often shorter than other texts, planning each idea and method is even more important - no word can be wasted.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding my own voice: planning a poem inspired by Maya Angelou

nodes.misconception: Figurative language and metaphors are synonyms.
nodes.response: All metaphors are examples of figurative language. But not all figurative language is a metaphor. For example, personification, hyperbole and simile are also examples of figurative language.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou's figurative language in ‘Phenomenal Woman’

nodes.misconception: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
nodes.response: Watching people perform poetry is very popular. The most engaging performers carefully consider how they will say the poem, and how they will engage with their audience.
