nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding my own voice: performing a poem

nodes.misconception: You can't plan a stanza of a poem. It's not like a paragraph or an essay.
nodes.response: Stanzas are like paragraphs. They need structure and focus. Spending time planning their methods, vocabulary and ideas make writing the stanza easier.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding my own voice: writing a poem inspired by Maya Angelou

nodes.misconception: Personal opinions about texts are not valid. Only analysis is valid.
nodes.response: Being a student of English can often feel like this. But expressing your opinions about your feelings towards a text - those you read in and outside the classroom - is very important and just as much a part of the subject of English as analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou’s ‘Still I Rise’

nodes.misconception: The caged bird is presented as completely powerless.
nodes.response: Although the bird in the cage is confined, he still has power, through his song which speaks to his unbroken spirit. We are meant to draw a parallel to the strength of the Black community.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou's 'Caged Bird'

nodes.misconception: Single paragraph outlines take too long to plan. You should just start writing.
nodes.response: Single paragraph outlines give you time to think and prepare. Spending time on these means that you will be able to write your paragraph efficiently knowing that it has a clear focus with well-selected supporting detail.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analytical paragraphs: Maya Angelou’s poetic voice

nodes.misconception: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
nodes.response: Watching people perform poetry is very popular. The most engaging performers carefully consider how they will say the poem, and how they will engage with their audiences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing Maya Angelou's ‘Caged Bird’

nodes.misconception: Comparing a poem's beginning and end doesn't count as analysis. It's too simple to be interesting.
nodes.response: At its most basic (and often most powerful), a text's structure is its beginning, middle and end. Commenting on the journey - emotional or physical - that a writer has taken us on is a great way to start exploring structure.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou's 'Woman Work'

nodes.misconception: Figurative language is a synonym for a metaphor or simile.
nodes.response: Metaphor and simile are both specific examples of figurative language. Figurative language is a broader term. Allusion, personification and hyperbole are other common examples of figurative language.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou’s use of figurative language

nodes.misconception: You shouldn't talk about poems as a group. This will make your comments too general.
nodes.response: You can make clear comments about a poet's work as a whole, as long as these comments are supported by specific examples from specific poems.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Maya Angelou's poetic voice

nodes.misconception: Every American president has a poem read at their inauguration.
nodes.response: Presidents have choice over some elements of their inauguration. President Clinton was only the second president to have a poem read at his ceremony, and he specifically asked for Angelou to write and perform it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou’s ‘On the Pulse of the Morning’

nodes.misconception: 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me' is saying that life isn't scary.
nodes.response: The poem lists many scary and frightening things. It presents some of the world's dangers. The speaker, however, is not frightened of life despite these dangers.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to Maya Angelou's distinctive voice: ‘Life Doesn’t Frighten Me’

nodes.misconception: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
nodes.response: Watching people perform poetry is very popular. The most engaging performers carefully consider how they will say the poem, and how they will engage with their audiences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing Maya Angelou's ‘Still I Rise’

nodes.misconception: A poem with a good rhythm always rhymes.
nodes.response: Rhythm is about the flow, beat and sound of a poem. Rhyme can sometimes develop rhythm, but it is not necessary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Refining poems: harmony and dissonance

nodes.misconception: Angelou copied Dunbar. Copying is not allowed.
nodes.response: Many writers learn from, and are inspired by, others. Angelou's poem is very different to Dunbar's - her personal style and voice come through - but the central metaphor 'speaks' from one poem to another, developing a relationship between them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Maya Angelou’s influences: exploring ‘Sympathy’ by Paul Laurence Dunbar

nodes.misconception: Personal opinions in English don't matter. Only analysis is valid.
nodes.response: Being a student of English can often feel like this. But expressing your opinions about your feelings towards a text - those you read in and outside the classroom - is very important and just as much a part of the subject of English as analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou's 'Equality'

nodes.misconception: Angelou's poem is unstructured - the stanzas are uneven and she talks about lots of different things.
nodes.response: Every piece of writing has a structure - even a shopping list. Structure is about the how a text is put together - at its most simple, beginning, middle and end. But we can also look for other structural features. In this case, stanzas and a refrain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a poem inspired by Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me'

nodes.misconception: The speaker in 'On Aging' doesn't think aging affects you.
nodes.response: The speaker lists some of the things that happen to you physically when you get older - she faces the reality. However, what she does want to change are people's reactions and perceptions of what these changes mean.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring Maya Angelou's 'On Aging'

nodes.misconception: 'Everyone is entitled to their own opinion', therefore there is no need to justify our opinions.
nodes.response: Although we are all entitled to our opinion, justifying your opinion allows people to trust and listen to your opinion more carefully.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Suite Française’: forming opinions on fiction

nodes.misconception: Students may think that they only way to evaluate is to write whether they 'agree' or 'disagree' with something.
nodes.response: In Learning Cycle 2, students learn that they can phrase and signpost their evaluations in a more sophisticated way, directly commenting on the writer's craft with evaluative adverbs.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Suite Française’: evaluating ideas about a writer’s craft

nodes.misconception: Students may think that being critical means to talk about the negative aspects of something.
nodes.response: We can be critical by judging something positively or negatively.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Cellist of Sarajevo': expressing a personal and critical response to a text

nodes.misconception: Students may be confused about when the extract is taking place or what war the extract is about as it references multiple moments of time.
nodes.response: The novel opening takes place during the siege of Sarajevo in the 1990s. However, the reference to the aftermath of WW2 is significant in universalising the themes and messages of the novel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing images of hope and destruction in Galloway's 'The Cellist of Sarajevo'

nodes.misconception: Proofreading your work is not important if you plan it.
nodes.response: Proofreading is equally important as planning. In pressured writing environments, we can easily make mistakes that we are not aware of.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Crafting an engaging narrative

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use objects to symbolise ideas but the object may not quite match the idea e.g. violence represented by a flower.
nodes.response: Thinking about the feelings that an object makes us feel might help us to decide whether it will be an appropriate symbolic object.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and emulating Galloway's use of symbols in ‘The Cellist of Sarajevo’

nodes.misconception: We can only manipulate time in one way in a narrative.
nodes.response: When we know the effect that we want our flashbacks and flashforwards to have, we can use both.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the use of time in Galloway's ‘The Cellist of Sarajevo’

nodes.misconception: Planning each paragraph to describe a different aspect of the scene will always create an engaging description.
nodes.response: Describing something different in each paragraph does not necessarily lead to an interesting description - it is the way in which the paragraphs link and build curiosity and tension that can make it more engaging.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Structuring paragraphs effectively in creative writing

nodes.misconception: Lists cannot add sophistication to your writing.
nodes.response: Varying the way we write lists can make our writing more sophisticated.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using inversion and asyndeton to craft interesting sentence structures

nodes.misconception: Students may misinterpret Murakami's semantic field and assume the text is a horror, mystery or thriller story.
nodes.response: If you really break down Murakami's use of semantic field, his word choice is more centered around dynamism of a living organism.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘After Dark’: exploring Murakami’s extended metaphor

nodes.misconception: Students may find it difficult to harmonise their perspective choice with appropriate metaphors.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing less effective pairings e.g. a tree would would not perceive people in a city as 'ants' but an airplane might.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Emulating Murakami’s craft to write a descriptive opening

nodes.misconception: We need to describe sounds in a scene merely to tick off the fact we have used sensory language.
nodes.response: Thinking of scenarios where sound is particularly important can help us to use sound imagery more effectively.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using onomatopoeia and alliteration to craft interesting sound imagery

nodes.misconception: The traditional story arc can only be applied to full narratives.
nodes.response: You can find elements of the traditional story arc in writing of any length.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Emulating Saramago's use of structure in 'Blindness'

nodes.misconception: Students may assume that they need to identify and name specific structural devices in their structural analysis.
nodes.response: An answer simply referencing 'the beginning, middle and end' can make for a successful structural analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing Saramago's use of structural devices in 'Blindness'

nodes.misconception: Students may confuse language and structural features.
nodes.response: Getting into a habit of asking a range of questions interrogating perspective, repetition, beginnings and endings can help students ease into the analysis of structure.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring structure in Murakami's ‘After Dark’

nodes.misconception: When we read something for the first time, we are able to take in all of the important information.
nodes.response: We may need to read something over and over again to fully comprehend it. Using active reading strategies can also help us to fully engage with a new text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing reading skills by responding to Murakami's 'After Dark'

nodes.misconception: A response is successful if it includes relevant quotes.
nodes.response: We should aim high in our language analysis. That means going a step further to use the most meaningful evidence as well as looking for patterns in the text that help us gather a collection of evidence.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'After Dark': selecting evidence to support language analysis

nodes.misconception: The Birlings are not guilty of any crimes in 'An Inspector Calls' because they do not face legal consequences.
nodes.response: While the Birlings do not face legal prosecution, Priestley uses their moral failings to argue that crime is not only a legal matter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the presentation of crime 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: Justice is exclusively linked to legal punishment.
nodes.response: In 'An Inspector Calls', Priestley challenges the idea that justice is solely legal. He presents moral and psychological punishment, showing that guilt and self-reflection drive real change, not just legal consequences.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring how Priestley portrays punishment and justice in 'An Inspector Calls’

nodes.misconception: The play is definitely a religious allegory, and all interpretations align with this view.
nodes.response: While the religious allegory is a valid interpretation, it’s important to consider it as one lens. Focussing on one interpretation may limit a deeper analysis of the text’s complexity.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Religion: sin, morality and punishment in 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: Rewording or summarising the main points of a question will lead to a developed response.
nodes.response: A nuanced response goes beyond rewording the question. It requires you to engage deeply with the text, offering detailed analysis and considering multiple layers of meaning.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'An Inspector Calls': writing an essay on punishment, justice and The Inspector

nodes.misconception: Writers always create entirely original characters, and using similar character types or archetypes makes a story unoriginal.
nodes.response: Archetypes explore universal themes, evolving with context. Writers reshape them, making characters unique while keeping familiar depth.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the Inspector as an archetype in 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: Labeling literary features like "metaphor" or "imagery" is enough to demonstrate analysis.
nodes.response: Feature spotting is not analysis. You need to explain how the writer's choices create different meanings and link to the writer's intention and wider themes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing nuanced analysis of  'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: The Inspector is a ghost and his supernatural qualitites should be interpreted literally.
nodes.response: Whilst this is one interpretation, it must be considered alongside the symbolic value of the Inspector’s supernatural elements and Priestley’s purpose.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The Inspector as a supernatural figure in 'An Inspector Calls'

nodes.misconception: The windmill is only presented as a negative.
nodes.response: Explore Snowball's initial plans. How does he view the role of the windmill? Orwell is showing how industry and progress can be exploited.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of the windmill in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That thesis statements and topic sentences are the same.
nodes.response: Differentiate; the thesis statement is a comment on the text as a whole, and a topic sentence has a focus on a specific part of the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an  excellent 'Animal Farm' essay

nodes.misconception: Mollie is the only character interested in sugar as a luxury.
nodes.response: Napoleon orders sugar for his table and his consumption alone. What does this tell us about the hypocrisy of the pigs?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of food and drink motifs in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: That Snowball isn't deceptive.
nodes.response: Does Snowball enjoy the "milk and apples" too? What is he awarded after the Battle of the Cowshed and how does this position Snowball?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The theme of deception in 'Animal Farm'

nodes.misconception: Snowball isn't to blame for the failed revolution.
nodes.response: How many examples can you find where Snowball supports hierarchical ideas that go against the ideals of equality?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': selecting judicious quotes and tracking a character in an essay

nodes.misconception: The characters are referred to as real people. For example "Old Major describes himself as ..."
nodes.response: Think about the purpose of the characters and why Orwell has constructed them the way he has.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Animal Farm': developing analytical paragraphs on Squealer

nodes.misconception: Context must be included in every paragraph.
nodes.response: Context must be included in essays, but where it is relevant and develops your analysis - not as a tick box exercise for each paragraph.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Weaving context into 'Animal Farm' essays

nodes.misconception: Viv, Del and Enid are not British citizens.
nodes.response: All three women are British citizens. Enid relocated from one part of the Commonwealth to another. During this post war period, this ensured legal status in Britain. Viv and Del were born in Britain.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of Black British experiences in Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: There is no point talking about the minor characters in a play - they are not important.
nodes.response: Each character, no matter how seemingly insignificant, is crafted by the writer and placed in the text for a specific purpose. It is your job to consider what their purpose is.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: In what ways is ‘Leave Taking’ a social commentary on 1980s Britain?

nodes.misconception: Context can't be used in a thesis statement. It must be saved for main body paragraphs.
nodes.response: Including context in a thesis statement is a powerful way to start an essay. It shows you understand the writer's intentions with their work.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using context in a 'Leave Taking' essay about intergenerational conflict

nodes.misconception: 'Leave Taking' is either universal, or about specific experiences and characters.
nodes.response: Like with many texts, we must hold both the idea of Leave Taking's universal themes with the specific experiences of its characters.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding intersectionality in Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: Ideas for one essay question can't be used in any other essay on the same text.
nodes.response: By the end of exploring and writing about a text, you will realise that there are certain ideas and references which you can rely on over and over.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an essay about coming of age in Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: You can't explore the dramatic function of off stage characters.
nodes.response: Off stage characters can help develop a world beyond the stage itself, grounding the play in its own reality.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of the male characters in Winsome Pinnock's in 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: 'Leave Taking' is a commentary on the experiences of all women.
nodes.response: Pinnock presents the unique stories of her created characters. The centrality of women suggests she is making some sort of social comment, but she is not generalising about every single woman's experience of the world.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The presentation of the matriarchy in Winsome Pinnock's 'Leave Taking'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might confuse compound and complex sentences, thinking that any sentence with more than one clause is a complex sentence.
nodes.response: A compound sentence has two main clauses that can each stand alone as separate sentences, joined by a coordinating conjunction. In contrast, a complex sentence has one main clause and at least one subordinate clause that cannot stand alone.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': writing an article about Mormor's death

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that writing a summary means including all details from the story.
nodes.response: Explain that a summary should only include the most important events and main ideas in a concise manner. Remind them that the goal is to capture the essence of the story, not every detail.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': Consolidating knowledge of the plot

nodes.misconception: The front cover is just for 'show' and a way to identify a book.
nodes.response: The images and font on a front cover can give you lots of clues about themes and genre.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': exploring the opening

nodes.misconception: Settings are only there to provide a backdrop for the story.
nodes.response: Setting plays a crucial role in shaping the mood and atmosphere of a novel. It can also help us gain a deeper understanding of the characters and themes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': introducing the setting

nodes.misconception: Including the theme of fate means that characters have no choice or control over their actions and are simply puppets of destiny.
nodes.response: While fate in 'The Twisted Tree' suggests that certain events and abilities are predestined, characters still have the power to make choices that shape their journey.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': the theme of fate

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think symbols in the novel have only one clear meaning.
nodes.response: Explain that symbols often have multiple meanings. For example, Martha's blindness can represent family secrets, vulnerability and hidden truths. Encourage looking for different interpretations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': symbolism

nodes.misconception: A theme is any idea or plot point in a text.
nodes.response: Themes are the most important ideas in a text. There may be multiple. The most important themes are the ones that are returned to over and over again, and explored in a number of different ways.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': identifying key themes

nodes.misconception: A script is just dialogue between characters and doesn't need any other elements
nodes.response: While dialogue is a crucial part of a script, it's not the only component. A script also includes stage directions, which provide important instructions on how actors should move, behave, and speak.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': introduction to script writing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a headline alone is enough to convey the entire story of an article.
nodes.response: Explain that while a headline grabs attention and hints at the article's content, it's the subheading and body text that provide the full details and context. Emphasise the importance of each element working together to inform the reader.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': creating a newspaper headline about the draugr

nodes.misconception: Gothic literature is only about horror and scary elements.
nodes.response: While Gothic literature often includes elements of horror, such as supernatural occurrences and eerie settings, it also explores complex themes like human psychology, societal anxieties and the supernatural as a metaphor for deeper fears or desires.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': the novel as a Gothic text

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that inferences are just guesses without any evidence.
nodes.response: Inferences are not guesses; they are conclusions drawn from evidence in the text. For example, Burge describes the fog as "snaking" around Martha. We infer that it is dangerous and sinister because the word "snake" often implies danger and malice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': Revising inferences

nodes.misconception: A thesis statement only needs to focus on one part of the book.
nodes.response: A thesis statement should address the overarching argument of your essay, which means it needs to consider the entire text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': introducing thesis statements

nodes.misconception: Students might think that making an inference is the same as guessing randomly without any evidence.
nodes.response: Inferences are not random guesses. They are logical conclusions drawn from clues or evidence presented in the text or context.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': making impressive inferences about the tree

nodes.misconception: The Norns are whimsical and conventionally beautiful.
nodes.response: Look at the descriptions of the Norns. Their beauty lies in their power and wisdom.  They are "gnarled" and "wrinkled", which adds an air of authority to their presence. They are also described as "fierce".
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading ‘The Twisted Tree’: Martha and Stig’s relationship

nodes.misconception: That discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
nodes.response: Think about all of the times you may need to use your verbal skills e.g. an interview or presentation. Being able to articulate yourself well verbally is an important skill to have.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading ‘The Twisted Tree’: the presence of the tree

nodes.misconception: All quotations need to be analysed in depth.
nodes.response: Not all quotations need the same level of analysis. Main quotations are central to your argument and should be analysed to show how they support your thesis. Supporting quotations are used to reinforce the point made with the main quotations.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘The Twisted Tree’: selecting excellent quotes when writing about the novel

nodes.misconception: Newspaper articles must strictly adhere to factual reporting without any creative elements.
nodes.response: While newspaper articles are based on factual reporting, they often incorporate language devices like puns, alliteration and sensationalist language in headlines and sometimes throughout the article. These elements are used to engage readers.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': planning a newspaper article about the dreadful draugr

nodes.misconception: The resolution of a story will leave no unanswered questions and all conflicts resolved.
nodes.response: Sometimes there can still be a few things left open or unresolved. This can make the story more interesting and leave readers thinking about what might happen next.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The resolution of 'The Twisted Tree'

nodes.misconception: The climax comes at the end of a story.
nodes.response: The climax is actually the high point of tension and action in a story, not necessarily at the end. It usually occurs towards the end but is followed by the resolution where the remaining conflicts are settled.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': the climax

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the conclusion should introduce new ideas or quotes.
nodes.response: Explain that a conclusion should summarise the main points and restate the thesis in a new way, rather than introducing new evidence or arguments. Its purpose is to reinforce what has already been discussed, reinforcing the main arguments.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': expressing my ideas about the novel

nodes.misconception: Stage directions are just suggestions and don't need to be followed exactly.
nodes.response: Stage directions are essential parts of the script that provide important guidance on how the scene should be performed. They help create the atmosphere, convey emotions and ensure the story is told as the writer intended.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': scripting a scene from the novel

nodes.misconception: Writers will not use stories or characters that already exist. This is copying!
nodes.response: Storytelling is an ancient form. Many writers and artists are inspired by stories that have existed for thousands of years. This is because of their universal characters and timeless themes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the use of mythology in 'The Twisted Tree'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that using exclamatory sentences is appropriate in a newspaper article about Mormor's death to express strong emotions.
nodes.response: Explain that while exclamatory sentences express sudden or strong emotions, they are not appropriate for a factual newspaper article. Instead, emphasise using emotive language and other devices that convey the community's feelings respectfully.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reporting on Mormor's death in 'The Twisted Tree'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that tension in a story is only created through dramatic events or actions.
nodes.response: Tension can also be built through subtle elements like descriptive language, sensory details and the anticipation of what might happen next.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': how the writer builds tension

nodes.misconception: Students might think that all stories fit perfectly into a traditional narrative arc with only one climax.
nodes.response: While many stories follow a traditional narrative arc, some can have multiple climaxes or may not fit perfectly into the structure. The narrative arc is a helpful guide, but it's important to recognise that stories can vary and still be effective.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted  Tree': understanding narrative arcs

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that the use of a formal tone and third person point of view is only necessary for professional journalism and not applicable to other forms of writing.
nodes.response: Explain that while formal tone and third person are essential in professional journalism, they are also important in many other types of writing, including more localised articles like this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': writing an effective article about the draugr

nodes.misconception: Villains are easily identifiable and will be always be introduced from the outset of a text.
nodes.response: Consider the draugr's subtle and encroaching presence. Burge uses this slow reveal to create tension.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': the draugr as a villain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all draugr are depicted in Norse mythology and in 'The Twisted Tree' in the same way.
nodes.response: While draugr in Norse mythology generally share traits their specific appearances can vary between stories. Rachel Burge's portrayal in 'The Twisted Tree' offers her unique interpretation, reflecting the novel's narrative and atmosphere.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': Norse mythology

nodes.misconception: Letters are only used in novels to drive the plot forward.
nodes.response: Letters can also give a reader an insight into a character's thoughts and feelings, as well as background information. They can also be used as an effective way to create dramatic irony.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading ‘The Twisted Tree’: Mormor’s letter

nodes.misconception: Tension is only about scary or dangerous situations.
nodes.response: While scary or dangerous situations can create tension, tension can also arise from emotional conflicts, difficult decisions, or unresolved mysteries. It's about keeping readers eager to know what will happen next.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading ‘The Twisted Tree’: explaining the creation of tension

nodes.misconception: As long as I have used "like" or "as", I have created an effective simile.
nodes.response: Consider this simile: 'Her voice was like a salad.' The comparison is unclear and doesn't enhance understanding.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Twisted Tree': exploring and creating similes

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that the draugr is simply a physical monster with no deeper significance or symbolism.
nodes.response: While the draugr is indeed a fearsome physical entity, it also symbolises deeper themes such as death, decay and the persistence of fear. In Norse mythology, draugrs are more than just monsters; they embody the fears and anxieties of the living.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'The Twisted Tree': analysing the dreadful draugr

nodes.misconception: Identifying language devices is the most important skill when analysing author's language choices.
nodes.response: When looking at the question, ask pupils whether 'Guthrie uses a simile' would be an appropriate response to the question. If not, why not?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Education for poor Victorian children

nodes.misconception: Comparisons are either clear similarities or clear differences.
nodes.response: Use examples from slides to demonstrate how comparisons are often more complex than ideas being completely similar or completely different.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the experience of child workers in the Victorian era

nodes.misconception: As long as I am being quiet, I am listening.
nodes.response: Although being quiet is an effective way to show you are listening, there are many other things to consider to ensure you are 'actively listening'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing active listening skills

nodes.misconception: Topic sentences are only used in essay writing.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that topic sentences are signposts for readers, indicating to them the direction our writing will be travelling in.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing a speech about supporting Victorian working class children

nodes.misconception: Clear and confident delivery of speeches requires a consistent pace of delivery throughout.
nodes.response: Model the delivery of a sentence which starts at pace, but slows down to draw attention to particular vocabulary choices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Delivering speeches about supporting Victorian working class children

nodes.misconception: The working class are the social class most likely to commit crime.
nodes.response: What types of crime are more likely to be committed by the wealthy? Why might they be less likely to be punished?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring youth justice in the Victorian era

nodes.misconception: Pupils start a speech by directly addressing the audience and explaining the purpose of the speech.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if the best method of getting your own way is by stating what you want straight away.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing speeches about supporting Victorian working class children

nodes.misconception: "You" is the only form of direct address when addressing a reader/audience.
nodes.response: When teaching the over reliance on direct address, rapidly fire questions to one pupil, addressing them as 'you'. Ask them how this feels.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a persuasive speech about supporting Victorian children

nodes.misconception: Slam poetry doesn't have any rules or conventions, so anything goes. It's just speaking to an audience.
nodes.response: While slam poetry encourages creativity and self-expression, it does follow certain conventions, like using sound techniques, imagery and themes. These conventions help poets effectively communicate their messages and engage the audience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to slam poetry

nodes.misconception: Pupils get too nervous to perfom and find public speaking really daunting so they can't do it.
nodes.response: Even the most confident speakers feel nervous! It is completely natural to feel nervous when public speaking. Practising and using specfic strategies will mean they will gradually begin to understand how to work with them.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a dynamic slam poetry performance

nodes.misconception: Adding "bang" or "crash" to the end of a line or stanza is an effective way to use onomatopoeia.
nodes.response: Although onomatopoeia might seem like an easy device to use, it still needs careful consderation and crafting to be used effectively and creatively.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing and emulating the use of sound in slam poetry

nodes.misconception: Slam poetry always has to be serious and about personal or social issues.
nodes.response: While slam poetry often tackles serious personal and social issues, it can also be playful, humorous or lighthearted. Slam poetry is about expressing yourself in an engaging and authentic way. You can write about anything that matters to you.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and creating a slam poem

nodes.misconception: That everyone believes we all have control over our life and decisions.
nodes.response: If you believe in fate, then you believe that our life is predetermined and our decisions ultimately don't matter.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': exploring Juliet's agency in Act 5, Scene 3

nodes.misconception: That forgiveness is always a personal choice.
nodes.response: Sometimes people feel societal pressure to forgive someone.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': exploring ideas of sex and forgiveness in Act 3, Scene 2

nodes.misconception: Women were completely powerless in patriarchal societies.
nodes.response: While women's lives were restricted, they were not completely powerless.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': exploring Juliet's character and conceptualising agency

nodes.misconception: We can get a definitive idea of the writer's intentions from the text.
nodes.response: We can never truly know what the writer's intentions were but we can tentatively explore ideas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': using tentative language to write about writer's intentions

nodes.misconception: That Paris is an unimportant plot device in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
nodes.response: Paris' interactions with Lord Capulet and Juliet arguably reveal contemporary stereotypes of relationships between men and women.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': exploring Juliet's agency in Act 4, Scene 1

nodes.misconception: That the rhythm of a character's speech is unimportant.
nodes.response: Exploring the rhythm of a character's speech can reveal their emotional state.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': exploring Juliet's agency in Act 4, Scene 3

nodes.misconception: That women always took a passive role in relationships in the Elizabethan era.
nodes.response: Arguably, Juliet takes an active role in her relationship with Romeo.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Romeo and Juliet': Juliet's agency in Act 1, Scene 5 and Act 2, Scene 2

nodes.misconception: I don't have time to write an effective closing, I just need to get my work finished!
nodes.response: The ending is arguably the most important part of the piece of writing. You need to leave your audience with a clear message that is memorable. Writing effective closings will get quicker the more you practice using specific strategies.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Engaging your audience: creating effective opening and closing paragraphs

nodes.misconception: Sometimes students think that a focused summary requires analysis of language.
nodes.response: Analysis requires you to zoom in and comment in detail about language choices. Why might this not be useful for a summary, where the aim is to be succinct and give a brief overview of a text?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding and summarising perspectives

nodes.misconception: Persuasive, issue based speeches have to maintain a serious tone.
nodes.response: Look at Malala's use of humour and anecdote. By engaging the audience in this way she holds their attention enough to make them listen to the serious messages.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding what makes a powerful speech

nodes.misconception: Content alone is enough for an effective speech.
nodes.response: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Giving a speech is so much more than just the words on a page.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using non-verbal features to present a speech effectively

nodes.misconception: Looking at other essays is cheating or copying.
nodes.response: Working with model responses helps develop your critical skills in order to evaluate your own work. Using and adapting others' ideas is a great thing to do!
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating and improving model responses on non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: As long as I am comparing the key points of two sources that is enough.
nodes.response: Using both comparative and correlative conjunctions will ensure there is nuance in your comparisons. They will aslo help keep your comparisons succinct.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: Talking about why you like something is a good topic for a speech.
nodes.response: Although it is important to choose something that interests you, you need to ensure the topic that you choose will enable you to present some complex ideas and use sophisticated vocabulary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Spoken language: choosing a topic and developing ideas for a speech

nodes.misconception: That discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
nodes.response: Think about all of the times you may need to use your verbal skills e.g an interview or presentation. Being able to articulate yourself well verbally is an important skill to have.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Having productive discussions in response to a non-fiction text

nodes.misconception: That spotting lots of different features makes a good analysis.
nodes.response: Simply spotting a feature is too superficial. The best analysis will say a lot about little. Being able to develop multiple comments on a single feature, creates a much better more in-depth analysis.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing a persuasive speech

nodes.misconception: Rhetorical devices always have the same effect.
nodes.response: Although we can make some assumptions about the effect of devices, considering specific information like the writer's intention and form will give a much more detailed and nuanced explanation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing tone and methods in non-fiction texts

nodes.misconception: Placing ambiguous, short questions with direct address at the end of sentences is an effective rhetorical question. For example: Do you?/Don't you agree?
nodes.response: Think about the purpose of a rhetorical question and why we use them. Is this the best way to challenge and provoke thought or get a reaction from your audience?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using rhetorical devices effectively

nodes.misconception: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time.
nodes.response: How does the process of revising and rewriting develop vocabulary use? How does rewriting support the writing of future responses?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Proofreading and redrafting a speech

nodes.misconception: That memorising the speech, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
nodes.response: An effective speech will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing speech.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to deliver a powerful speech

nodes.misconception: You don't need to, or shouldn't, use rhetorical devices in your topic or concluding sentences.
nodes.response: Just because the topic sentences introduce the main idea for the paragraph, that does not mean the topic sentence can't be really creative and engaging. It's crucial that it is engaging to motivate the reader to learn more about the topic.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing a persuasive speech

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to consider the symbolic importance of Duncan and, in particular, Malcolm in the play.
nodes.response: Ask pupils what the moral message of the play would be if Malcolm did not end the play as king.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Macbeth’: exploring King Duncan and leadership

nodes.misconception: Pupils often get mixed up between a noun appositive and a relative clause.
nodes.response: The relative pronoun 'who' could lead to pupils trying to add too much extra detail about a character, a noun appositive encourages brevity.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': the importance of kingship

nodes.misconception: Macduff acts as a foil to Macbeth solely because he is noble and courageous.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if Macbeth had dealt with his grief/devastation like Macduff would there have been different outcomes?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': masculinity as Macbeth's hamartia

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that all exam questions need unique ideas and responses.
nodes.response: When looking at the question in the first learning cycle, ask pupils if they can use ideas/arguments from previous 'Macbeth' essays.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Macbeth’: writing nuanced responses about the role of masculinity in the play

nodes.misconception: Banquo's main purpose in the play is to act as a foil, highlighting Macbeth's treachery.
nodes.response: Explore the purpose of Fleance, by asking pupils how they think events would have unfolded if Fleance had been killed too.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': exploring Banquo and the chivalric code

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe Lady Macbeth holds most of the responsibility for Macbeth's actions.
nodes.response: When considering the witches' role, ask pupils which ideas can be used to counter the significance of Lady Macbeth's role in his downfall?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Macbeth': exploring the external feminine influences in the play

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume Macbeth and his wife have never had children.
nodes.response: Remind pupils about Lady Macbeth's "I have given suck" (1.7). Explore the idea that the Macbeths may have had a child die in infancy.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: ‘Macbeth’: understanding the significance of a lack of a male heir

nodes.misconception: Introductions and conclusions aren't important.
nodes.response: An effective introduction means you can impress your reader from the outset and clearly layout your overarching argument for your essay.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Introductions and conclusions in a 'Small Island' essay

nodes.misconception: Gilbert shouting at Hortense shows he doesn’t respect her or care about their relationship
nodes.response: Gilbert’s anger reflects his frustration and the pressures he faces in a racist society. His harsh words mask his deep care and protectiveness, and the scene later shows their developing understanding and connection.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching and discussing 'Small Island' Act 2 Scenes 2 to 6 with Rufus Norris

nodes.misconception: The director just tells the actors where to stand and how to say their lines.
nodes.response: According to Norris, that’s only the simplest description. A director also creates an atmosphere of confidence, supports actors, makes key creative decisions, and ensures the whole production comes together smoothly.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Rufus Norris on directing and adapting 'Small Island'

nodes.misconception: The Pathé news clips are just old videos used as a backdrop and don’t add meaning to the play.
nodes.response: The Pathé clips set the historical context and show a biased view of the British Empire. They contrast with the characters’ real experiences, deepening our understanding of the story’s themes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching and discussing 'Small Island' Act 1 Scene 1 with director Rufus Norris

nodes.misconception: The ending is happy because everything works out perfectly and offers hope for the future.
nodes.response: Edmundson says the ending is hopeful, but not perfect. There’s pain, loss, and compromise (Queenie gives up her baby), but real progress comes from facing reality with care and honesty.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Helen Edmundson on the context, characters and themes of 'Small Island'

nodes.misconception: The fixed setting in Act 2 means the play is less interesting or creative.
nodes.response: The fixed setting in Act 2 shows how the characters feel trapped or confined by their situations, which makes the story more powerful and emotional.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching and discussing 'Small Island' Act 2 Scene 1 with Helen Edmundson

nodes.misconception: That only people born in Britain were part of the British Army that fought in WWII.
nodes.response: The British Army contained a huge number of soldiers from different countries. For example, over two and a half million men from the Indian subcontinent volunteered for service, producing the largest volunteer army in history.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring 'Small Island' and the Windrush context

nodes.misconception: All relevant information comes only from the dialogue in plays.
nodes.response: What is the role of stage directions? Explore how they are crafted to further characterisation. What extra information do they give us?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading the start of Act 1 Scene 1

nodes.misconception: There isn’t any humour in plays like 'Small Island' because the subject matter is too serious.
nodes.response: Humour is used in 'Small Island' to make the characters more relatable and to provide moments of relief during tense scenes. It helps the audience connect with the story while still exploring serious issues.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching and discussing 'Small Island' Act 1 Scene 2 with director Rufus Norris

nodes.misconception: Adaptations just copy the story from the book. The writer doesn’t have to change much or make many decisions.
nodes.response: Adaptations need big changes to work on stage! Edmundson tested scenes in workshops, adjusted them in rehearsals, and watched audience reactions in previews to make sure the story was clear and powerful in performance.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Helen Edmundson on adapting 'Small Island' for the stage

nodes.misconception: The best endings are always neat and fully resolved, tying up every storyline.
nodes.response: While neat endings can feel satisfying, 'Small Island' shows powerful endings often include uncertainty. Edmundson says the play balances hope and love with an unclear future, making it realistic and thought-provoking.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching 'Small Island' Act 2 Scenes 7-11 with Rufus Norris and Helen Edmundson

nodes.misconception: A flawed character is someone who is always unlikeable or hard to relate to.
nodes.response: In reality, flawed characters often have human weaknesses that make them more believable or even sympathetic, much like the character of Hortense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching and discussing 'Small Island' Act 1 Scenes 4-8 with Rufus Norris

nodes.misconception: Because Gilbert jokes and is confident, it means he isn’t really affected by racism or hardship.
nodes.response: Gilbert uses humour to hide pain. Arguably, his confidence masks his struggle, making his experience more powerful and real. Consider this when you watch the perfomance.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Watching 'Small Island' Act 1 Scene 3 with Rufus Norris and Helen Edmundson

nodes.misconception: Edmundson did not write 'Small Island'.
nodes.response: Explore the conventions of a play. What would Edmundson have to have added to re-imagine the novel?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': from page to stage

nodes.misconception: Bernard completely rejects Queenie's baby due to his racial prejudices.
nodes.response: What does the baby symbolise? How does Edmundson use Benard's behaviour to hint at the potential for reparation and change.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 2, Scenes 7 and 8

nodes.misconception: That segregation only happened in the United States.
nodes.response: This in the most part is true and Britain certainly didn't have any segregation laws. However, as we see in the play, some individuals and institutions still upheld these ideas of segregation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading the end of Act 1 Scene 3

nodes.misconception: That planning is not something that needs to be practiced.
nodes.response: What are the benefits of practising planning over writing whole essay responses? Not only is planning a very important part of the writing process, but an efficient way to practise essay writing.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding questions and writing thesis statements on ‘Small Island’

nodes.misconception: Hortense is the main protagonist.
nodes.response: Look at how many scenes other characters are in and the importance of their journeys. Why might Levy choose to have multiple protagonists? Think back to her original intentions.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Tracking characters and tension in 'Small Island'

nodes.misconception: Many students often think that planning isn't a useful step in the writing process and that it takes too long.
nodes.response: How might planning help to organise our thoughts into a coherent response? How can planning improve the efficiency of the writing process?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning and writing a 'Small Island' essay

nodes.misconception: The Windrush generation entered Britain illegally.
nodes.response: Those coming from the British Commonwealth were considered citizens. Migrants like Hortense and Gilbert were actively encouraged to believe that Britain was their 'home'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 2, Scenes 2 to 4

nodes.misconception: That all writers use only original ideas and if they don't they are bad writers.
nodes.response: Explore the idea of a literary trope and how writer's use these to elicit specific responses from readers. How do recognisable conventions work to appeal to us as readers?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': the significance of the hurricane

nodes.misconception: The Jamaican characters all have a cynical view of Britain and the British empire.
nodes.response: The reality is more nuanced. Whilst characters like Elwood are openly critical, some characters (like Gilbert) are more positive, buying into wartime narratives of fighting for their 'mother country'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading the beginning of Act 1 Scene 3

nodes.misconception: That Edmundson reveals that dreams are futile and hopeless.
nodes.response: Examine the purpose of the idealistic view of England, what does it allow Hortense and Gilbert to do? What reaction do these moments of humour and hope have on the audience?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 2, Scenes 5 to 6

nodes.misconception: That only the women in Act 1 consider marriage almost like a business transaction.
nodes.response: What does Gilbert gain from his marriage to Hortense? How does he describe his feelings towards Hortense and what does this tell the audience?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 1, Scenes 7 and 8

nodes.misconception: Michael and Hortnese have the same upbringing.
nodes.response: As well as exploring the different ways their lives are described, think back to how Mr. Philip reacts to Hortense climbing the tree. Why does he find it so problematic? This reveals a stark difference between Michael and Hortense.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': exploring the theme of power through Little Hortense

nodes.misconception: In 'Small Island' England is presented as a bad place and Jamaica as a good place.
nodes.response: Look at what is happening at the start of Scene 6, why is the situation volatile? What does the discussion between Gilbert and Elwood reveal about the realities in both Jamaica and England?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 1, Scenes 4-6

nodes.misconception: That 'Small Island' finishes with a perfect resolution.
nodes.response: What issues are addressed in these scenes? Is Edmundson suggesting that these have all been solved? Why is the theme of hope so important?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 2, Scenes 9 to 11

nodes.misconception: That Hortense is only motivated by heartbreak.
nodes.response: How does Hortense view herself, even from a young age? She does at times view herself as superior. Furthermore, she has lived in the house for a long time and has perhaps internalised the moral and religious standards that Mr. Philip holds.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': tracking the events of Act 1 Scene 1

nodes.misconception: That context refers just to historical facts.
nodes.response: Think about the 'big ideas' in the text and what has influenced and informed these. This all comes under the umbrella of context.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Essay writing: using context in responses to ‘Small Island’

nodes.misconception: Planning is not necessary to write an effective response.
nodes.response: Not only is planning an efficient way to consider different questions and arguments, it also leads to more cohesive, well sequenced responses.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': creating topic sentences and using quotes in essays

nodes.misconception: That Hortense is simply ungrateful.
nodes.response: Think about the promises and expectations that were used to encourage migration. View Hortense's and Gilbert's interaction in light of this betrayal.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 2, Scene 1

nodes.misconception: The Windrush generation entered Britain illegally.
nodes.response: Those coming from the British Commonwealth were considered citizens.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': exploring Act 1 through the context of Windrush

nodes.misconception: Once an essay is completed it's not worth thinking about again.
nodes.response: How does rewriting support the writing of future responses? Consider the strategies, tips and phrases explored. Revisiting our own essays can make feedback become really personalised and allow you to work and focus on your own targets.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Refining and improving an essay on 'Small Island'

nodes.misconception: That Queenie and Bernard's relationship is only a marriage of convenience.
nodes.response: How do Queenie and Bernard interact with each other? Can you find any clues where love or affection might be present?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Small Island': reading Act 1 Scene 2

nodes.misconception: That you should not use your own opinions or perspectives when exploring a text.
nodes.response: Being able to articulate your own opinions and perspectives is an important skill to have. They should be rooted in evidence from the text and should avoid speculation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring and evaluating the importance of Act 1

nodes.misconception: You can create tone via 1-3 words.
nodes.response: Show that tone is established through consistent effort and crafting throughout the writing process - every word is picked precisely.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using semantic fields to create a clear tone in dystopian writing

nodes.misconception: Students may think that complex sentences are superior to other sentences.
nodes.response: Show the effect of all sentences working in harmony via a model.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using complex sentences to describe dystopian settings

nodes.misconception: Compound sentences are better than simple sentences all of the time.
nodes.response: Make it explicit to students that sometimes simple sentences can be more suitable in their writing; long does not equal better.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using compound sentences to describe dystopian settings

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistake dystopia and utopia as the words are similar
nodes.response: Explicitly explain the difference between the two and explain that they are antonyms
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding dystopias

nodes.misconception: That the first draft is the final draft.
nodes.response: The best writing is achieved through a cycle of initial creation, feedback and re-drafting.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using feedback to improve dystopian descriptions

nodes.misconception: Action is a key part of a description.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the purpose of a description is to focus on certain aspects of a scene in order to set the tone and genre.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a description of a dystopian setting

nodes.misconception: Pupils might mistake a simile for metaphor and vice versa.
nodes.response: Go through simile and metaphor definitions and examples slowly and explicitly.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using vivid imagery to describe dystopian settings

nodes.misconception: As long as a similes compare something similar it is effective.
nodes.response: Similes are much more powerful when used alongside vivid description. Work through example in learning cycle 1 to help unravel this.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using similes to create atmosphere in dystopian descriptions

nodes.misconception: Students may use sentence fragments in their work
nodes.response: Showing exactly how sentence fragments obscure meaning and explaining why they should not be used
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using accurate sentences to describe dystopian settings

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that dystopian societies only involve dilapidated settings.
nodes.response: Explain that there are two sides in a dystopia: those with power and control who live in luxury and ordinary citizens in run down areas.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing a setting to reflect dystopian themes

nodes.misconception: Students add sophisticated punctuation as a tick box exercise.
nodes.response: The inclusion of sophisticated punctuation should always be driven first and foremost by effect. What effect will this punctuation achieve?
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Revising sentence and punctuation types for a dystopian description

nodes.misconception: Students may overuse exclamation marks because they think it adds sophistication
nodes.response: Show pupils that exclamation marks are best used for dramatic effect
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using punctuation accurately in dystopian descriptions

nodes.misconception: Exclamatory sentences are the only sentences that express emotions
nodes.response: Interrogative sentences can also effectively show some emotions e.g. confusion, despair, by the character asking themselves questions
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using a range of sentence types to describe dystopian settings

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that using any verb that is associated with people makes good quality personification.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a choices of verbs, including incongruous ones, to allow them to identify high quality personification.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating atmosphere in dystopian descriptions

nodes.misconception: Using semicolons and colons interchangeably
nodes.response: A semicolon always has to have an independent clause on either side of it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using sophisticated punctuation in dystopian descriptions

nodes.misconception: You do not need to check your work after writing it.
nodes.response: Show pupils the value of checking and editing their work - show the transformation from first draft to final draft.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a description of a dystopian setting

nodes.misconception: Students think that Frankenstein is the name of the creature.
nodes.response: Frankenstein is the name of the scientist who created the hideous creature that students are often familiar with.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying features of the Gothic genre in the plot of ‘Frankenstein’

nodes.misconception: Students think that using lots of the pronoun 'you' is an effective use of direct address. They tend to do this a lot in rhetorical questions.
nodes.response: Using 'you' too many times can create an accusatory tone that can actually make the reader defensive. Sometimes, it can be better to approach direct address more subtly, by speaking to an imagined reader or addressing the readers collectively.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving your opinion article on Gothic literature

nodes.misconception: Students panic about unseen activities and think that there is a 'right' or 'wrong' answer.
nodes.response: The text is unseen - students are not supposed to be experts on it. They just need to read the text and give their opinions about it - any well-evidenced opinion is the 'right' answer.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to 'Jane Eyre': Analysing an unseen extract

nodes.misconception: Students might not recognise this as a Gothic setting, as it is not overtly frightening or eerie.
nodes.response: Brontë's use of contrasting colours, isolation and cold make this a Gothic setting. Gothic descriptions do not have to be terrifying at all times.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading an extract from Charlotte Brontë’s ‘Jane Eyre’

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget that the description of the Creature is written from Frankenstein's perspective.
nodes.response: Shelley describes the Creature so horribly through the eyes of Frankenstein to show his disgust with his creation.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Frankenstein's reaction to his creation

nodes.misconception: Students often think that scientific advancements have always been celebrated.
nodes.response: In reality, scientists faced a lot of backlash for their ideas, mostly because many of them contradicted the teachings of the Bible.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Context for Gothic literature: science and religion in the 19th century

nodes.misconception: Students often rush the ending of their work - particularly if they are writing in timed conditions.
nodes.response: The ending is arguably the most important part of the piece of writing. Students need to leave their reader with a clear message that is memorable. The ending ties together the threads of the argument and reinforces the writer's viewpoint.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The structure of an opinion article

nodes.misconception: Students do not recognise the value in using semantic fields - they think that semantic fields are just a method that they can spot in other writers' texts.
nodes.response: Using semantic fields can help us to include figurative language, such as extended metaphors. They are means of including other methods - they are not necessarily a stand-alone method.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using semantic fields to create a gothic atmosphere

nodes.misconception: In descriptive writing, students often just describe what their protagonist can see. They often neglect the other senses.
nodes.response: To create the most vivid description possible, students should focus their description on the five sense, subtly moving between exploring how the scene feels, smells, looks, tastes and sounds.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a gothic description

nodes.misconception: Students tend to think of humans as being good and monsters as being evil.
nodes.response: In this novel, the line between good and evil is blurred. Shelley forces us to question who the real monster is in the novel.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Frankenstein' and the Gothic context

nodes.misconception: Students think that if they write a horror story that is full of blood and gore, that this makes it Gothic.
nodes.response: Gothic literature is about unsettling and mystifying the reader - not traumatising them with gory descriptions and extreme violence. There can be more fear in what is not revealed, than what is revealed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a Gothic description inspired by 'A monster within'

nodes.misconception: Students think that atmosphere is created purely through the description of a physical setting.
nodes.response: Atmosphere can also be created through characters interacting with one another, as we see in Chapter 11 of 'Jane Eyre'.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing the atmosphere at Thornfield Hall in ‘Jane Eyre’

nodes.misconception: Students often think that tone and voice are the same thing.
nodes.response: Voice is the identity of the writer and the beliefs they convey, whereas tone is the way in which these beliefs are conveyed.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing effective opinion articles

nodes.misconception: Students often think that once they have written their first draft, the piece is finished.
nodes.response: Writing is a process that involves several drafts of the same piece. Each time, editing and rewriting the draft makes the piece of writing better.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Editing descriptive writing based on ‘A monster within’

nodes.misconception: Pupils often reveal things early-on in descriptions by saying things like 'it was a painting' and then proceeding to describe it.
nodes.response: It can be much more effective to describe your narrator's view before revealing what the view actually is. This way, the reader is kept in a state of anticipation, as they try to work out what the view is.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Organising our gothic writing to build tension

nodes.misconception: Students often simply 'method spot' in analytical responses.
nodes.response: The writer's intention should form part of students' analysis of the text, as they should be outlining why the writer has used the method.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A written analysis of 'Frankenstein'

nodes.misconception: Students think that the first version of their work is the finished piece.
nodes.response: Redrafting work improves its quality, depth and coherence. Students should be encouraged to appreciate, and embrace the value of redrafting their work.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: A written analysis of 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

nodes.misconception: Students often make the mistake of using a new word they have just learned inaccurately, in an attempt to show off their knowledge.
nodes.response: The point of learning new vocabulary is to give students options and choices so that they can select the most specific and useful word in their writing. Sometimes, the most specific word choice isn't the new vocabulary.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using ‘Jane Eyre’ to inspire our use of gothic vocabulary

nodes.misconception: Students often think of methods exclusively as 'similes/metaphors' etc.
nodes.response: The writer's method is anything they do consciously. This could be choosing one, single word over another.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a cohesive argument about 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not appreciate the extent of Frankenstein's immorality.
nodes.response: In pursuit of knowledge, Frankenstein broke natural and political laws. He robbed graves and tortured live animals to achieve his ambition.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring the character of Victor Frankenstein in Mary Shelley’s ‘Frankenstein’

nodes.misconception: Students might not recognise that there is a possibility that the sound of the old man's heart beating, may be the sound of the narrator's own heart beating.
nodes.response: Some may interpret the sound of the old man's heart beating as the sound of the narrator's own heart beating, with anticipation and excitement at the prospect of the imminent murder.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

nodes.misconception: Students might think that they only need to plan one single paragraph outline.
nodes.response: Students will need to plan one paragraph outline per section of their response.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a written analysis of 'Frankenstein'

nodes.misconception: Students often don't think to include rhetorical devices within their topic sentences.
nodes.response: Just because the topic sentences introduces the main idea for the paragraph, that does not mean the topic sentence can't be really creative and engaging. It's crucial that it is engaging to motivate the reader to learn more about the topic.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning an opinion article about Gothic literature

nodes.misconception: Students often think that the Creature did something to terrify/hurt Victor.
nodes.response: Victor takes an instant dislike to the Creature because of its ugliness. Victor shuns the Creature immediately, purely because of its looks.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading an extract from 'Frankenstein': A fateful night

nodes.misconception: Students might think that irony is a term only used in comedy.
nodes.response: There is a dark comedy to this story, created through the use of irony, whereby the narrator insists that he is not 'mad' but then proceeds to murder and dismember an old man simply because he hates one of the old man's eyes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: The creation of suspense in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Gothic settings have to be utterly terrifying to count as Gothic.
nodes.response: Gothic settings are not about frightening the reader as much as possible. They are about making the reader feel unsettled and creating an atmosphere of mystery and dark intrigue.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Lowood Institution: Gothic settings in 'Jane Eyre'

nodes.misconception: Students often think that they have to write from their own perspective - that the 'voice' in the article has to be their own.
nodes.response: Students can create a voice. For example, they could write the article from the perspective of a teacher or a parent. This is still voice.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an opinion article on Gothic literature

nodes.misconception: Students often do not use descriptions in functional writing frequently enough.
nodes.response: Descriptive language massively enhances functional writing. Anecdotes are a brilliant example of how descriptive writing can be used to connect to the reader/audience.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using description in functional writing

nodes.misconception: Students think that Shelley was opposed to scientific advancement.
nodes.response: Shelley was not opposed to scientific advancement; she was opposed to unethical and limitless scientific practices.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Frankenstein's regret and the scientific revolution

nodes.misconception: Students do not appreciate the Creature's eloquence and the fact that he has educated himself.
nodes.response: The Creature is a persuasive and eloquent character who manages to convince Victor to begin making him a mate.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Regret in Mary Shelley’s 'Frankenstein'

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not understand that they have to think carefully about their use of figurative language and plan it before they begin writing.
nodes.response: Students need to consider carefully what kind of atmosphere they are trying to create. When comparing their setting to something else, the 'something else' needs to fit with the atmosphere they are aiming to create.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using figurative language to create a gothic atmosphere

nodes.misconception: Students often do not understand the depth of meaning that symbolism can provide.
nodes.response: Symbols communicate hidden or deeper meanings to the reader, so that they can better understand the characters or themes of the text.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Symbolism in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

nodes.misconception: That you should be very direct, almost aggressive in your persuasive writing.
nodes.response: While directness can convey confidence, an overly direct tone can be off-putting for the recipient and cause them to become defensive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Using modality, personification and active voice to write a persuasive letter

nodes.misconception: Some people might think that letter writing has no place in modern society.
nodes.response: While other forms of communication have overtaken letter writing in popularity, letter writing is still necessary for many professional purposes.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Conceptualising letter-writing and understanding the letter form

nodes.misconception: That you should always use words with high modality (must, need, have to) to make your writing seem persuasive.
nodes.response: Exclusively using words with high modality can make your tone seem too direct and, therefore, make the reader feel defensive.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering and evaluating persuasive letters

nodes.misconception: That the connection between the subject and object of a sentence doesn't matter in persuasive writing.
nodes.response: Using active or passive voice can affect the tone of your writing and how the reader responds to it.
nodes.subject: english
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering and using active and passive voice in persuasive letter writing

nodes.misconception: Any use of personification will be effective in your writing.
