nodes.response: Months of the year start with lowercase letters in French, unless at the start of a sentence.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Months of the year

nodes.misconception: The indefinite article 'des' changes based on gender as do the indefinite articles 'un' and 'une'.
nodes.response: The indefinite article 'des' does not change based on gender. 'Un pied' - 'des pieds'. 'Une main' - 'des mains'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: My monster: numbers 1-12, 'des', 'combien'

nodes.misconception: Expressions such as 'I am cold' must use the verb 'être' (to be) when translated into French, as in English. The verb 'avoir' can only be translated as 'to have'.
nodes.response: Certain expressions that use 'to be' in English, such as 'I am cold', actually use the verb 'avoir' in French: J'ai froid. 'Avoir' means 'to have' but it can also be translated as 'to be' with set expressions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: I'm sick! 'Avoir' meaning 'be'

nodes.misconception: Like in English, we use 's to show possession in French.
nodes.response: In French, unlike English, there is no possessive apostrophe. Use the preposition 'de' (of) to show possession: Pierre's brother - le frère de Pierre.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Menton Carnival: uses of 'de'

nodes.misconception: Accents are interchangable and do not change the pronunication of a letter. For example, [é] and [è] make the same sound.
nodes.response: Accents are not interchangable, they can change the pronunication of a letter. For example, [é] and [è] make different sounds.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Family activities: translating French present tense into English

nodes.misconception: Add an 'e' to all adjectives in French, in the feminine form.
nodes.response: Some adjectives in the feminine form are irregular. They do not follow the normal pattern of adding an 'e' to the masculine form. E.g. beau (m) and belle (f).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Menton Carnival: singular adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: There are two ways of referring to the present tense in French, as in English. For example: I watch and I am watching.
nodes.response: There is only one way to refer to the present tense in French: je regarde. This can be translated as both 'I watch', and 'I am watching'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Family activities: singular regular -er verbs

nodes.misconception: Questions using intonation or 'est-ce que' have different meanings: Tu aimes l'histoire ? vs. Est-ce que tu aimes l'histoire ?
nodes.response: 'Tu aimes l’histoire ?' and 'Est-ce que tu aimes l’histoire ?' mean the same thing, they are two different ways of asking the same question (using intonation or 'est-ce que').
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Presentation about Haiti: est-ce que questions

nodes.misconception: An accent does not change the pronunciation of a letter, [e], [é] and [è] sound the same.
nodes.response: An accent can change the pronunciation of a letter. [e], [é] and [è] make different sounds in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La Chandeleur: negation, -er singular verbs

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is just one way of saying 'you' in French.
nodes.response: In French there are in fact two ways of saying you. Use 'tu' when talking to one young person or to an adult you know well. Use 'vous' when talking to more than one person or to one adult you do not know well.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: New Year's traditions: 'vous' meaning formal you

nodes.misconception: We can add just one word to make a sentence negative in French, like the English word 'not'.
nodes.response: In French, we have to add two words to make a sentence negative, these are sandwiched around the verb: 'ne' and 'pas' (je ne chante pas).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mardi gras: negation, singular verbs

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is only one way to refer to 'they' in French.
nodes.response: In French there are in fact two ways to say they: ils and elles. Use ils when referring to a group of boys, or a group of boys and girls (masculine form). Use elles when referring to a group of girls (feminine form).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: 1st January in Haiti: -er verbs 'ils' and 'elles'

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [é], [er], [et] and [ez] have different pronunciations.
nodes.response: The SSCs [é], [er], [et] and [ez] are in fact pronounced exactly the same, as in: répéter.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas in Haiti and France: -er verbs 'nous' and 'vous'

nodes.misconception: Consonants at the end of words are pronounced in French.
nodes.response: Often, consonants are silent at the end of words in French, such as the letters d, s, t and x. These are called SFCs (silent final consonants).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas: practice with key sounds

nodes.misconception: You read French in the same way as you read English.
nodes.response: French is pronounced, and therefore read, differently than English. This can be seen with the five vowel sounds which are pronounced and read differently in French and English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Practice with French vowels and verbs for the classroom

nodes.misconception: Changing intonation doesn't affect meaning.
nodes.response: If you raise your voice at the end, you can turn a statement into a question.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: In class: intonation questions

nodes.misconception: Vowels are pronounced the same in French and in English.
nodes.response: The vowels [a] [e] [i] are pronounced differently in French and English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The vowels in French: [a] [e] [i]

nodes.misconception: Changing intonation doesn't affect meaning.
nodes.response: If you raise your voice at the end, you can turn a statement into a question.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What is he or she like? Intonation questions

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [an/en] make different sounds.
nodes.response: The SSCs [an/en] make the same sound.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What you are like: 'tu es'

nodes.misconception: Adjectives already ending in -e follow the pattern of adjective agreement and change in the feminine form.
nodes.response: Adjectives already ending in -e do not change.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Friends: adjectives ending in -e

nodes.misconception: Consonants at the end of words are pronounced in French.
nodes.response: Often, consonants are silent at the end of words in French. The exception to this rule are the letters c, r, f and l, which are pronounced.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Greetings: 'je suis' and 'il, elle est'

nodes.misconception: French adjectives never change form.
nodes.response: French adjectives do change; this is called adjective agreement. One change is to match the gender of the person described.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What you are like: singular regular adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: French adjectives never change form.
nodes.response: French adjectives do change; this is called adjective agreement. One change is to match the gender of the person described.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Introductions and taking the register: singular regular adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: 'Ça va ?' means 'How are you?' - it can only be a question.
nodes.response: ‘Ça va ?’ with raised intonation at the end of the sentence is a question and means ‘is it going OK?' or ‘how’s it going’?. ‘Ça va’ without intonation is a statement and means ‘it’s going OK’.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Is it going OK? 'Ça va ?'

nodes.misconception: Days of the week start with a capital letter in French, as in English.
nodes.response: Days of the week start with a lowercase letter in French, unless at the start of a sentence.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: It's Monday! 'C'est' and days of the week

nodes.misconception: An adjective agrees with the person who is talking, not the person being described. For example, if a boy says to a girl 'you are happy', 'happy' will be in the masculine form.
nodes.response: An adjective agrees with the person who is being described, not the person who is talking. For example, if a boy says to a girl 'you are happy', 'happy' will be in the feminine form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: I'm brave! Adjectives ending in -eux, -euse

nodes.misconception: Adding an -e to an adjective is the sole way to change an adjective from the masculine to the feminine form.
nodes.response: There are different ways to change a masculine adjective to a feminine adjective; adding an -e to the end being the most common. When an adjective ends in -eux in the masculine form, however, it changes to -euse in the feminine form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Poem: Matthieu le merveilleux

nodes.misconception: To say 'to (the) ...' in French before a masculine noun, use 'à le'.
nodes.response: There is no such thing as 'à le' in French; it becomes 'au'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Places in town: 'tu vas'

nodes.misconception: Directions in French use lower case letters like in English.
nodes.response: Directions in French use capital letters: 'le Nord, l'Est, le Sud et l'Ouest'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Canada: 'je vais' and 'il, elle va'

nodes.misconception: I use 'à' for 'to' with cities and 'en' for countries.
nodes.response: We use 'en' to say 'to' for feminine countries e.g. Je vais en France. If a country is masculine however we use 'au' e.g. Je vais au Portugal.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Canada: 'dans' and 'à' both meaning 'in' and 'to'

nodes.misconception: I have to pronounce every syllable of 'qu'est-ce que'.
nodes.response: When you say it slowly there are five separate syllables in 'qu'est-ce que' but in conversation we should naturally speed up the pronunciation and pronounce four syllables, we leave out the 'ce'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at home: questions with 'qu'est-ce que …'

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' means 'to do, doing' in French.
nodes.response: The verb 'faire' means 'to do, doing' and 'to make, making' in French. 'Je fais le lit. ' (I make the bed). 'Je fais du sport.' (I do sport).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at home: 'je fais' and 'il, elle fait'

nodes.misconception: My friend (girl) is 'ma amie' in French.
nodes.response: Even though 'amie' is feminine in this example, we use 'mon amie' because the word 'amie' starts with a vowel and this makes the pronunciation smoother.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Sports: intonation questions with 'quel' and 'quelle'

nodes.misconception: To say 'I'm eating pizza' in French it's 'je mange pizza'.
nodes.response: In English we often leave out the article, but in French we must use the partitive article when referring to an unspecified amount of food or drink. So we would say: 'Je mange de la pizza' because 'pizza' is feminine.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Summer time: understand a longer text

nodes.misconception: To express 'I play tennis' I say 'je joue le tennis'.
nodes.response: To express 'I play' with any singular sport, you use 'à + le, la' after the verb e.g. 'je joue au tennis', 'je joue à la pétanque'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Sports: 'jouer' singular persons

nodes.misconception: To say 'I do sport' in French, I use 'je fais sport'.
nodes.response: When using the verb 'faire' with sports we use the preposition 'de' afterwards, e.g. 'I do sport' is 'je fais du sport'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Sports: 'faire' singular persons with sports

nodes.misconception: In French 'il fait' always means 'he does, makes'.
nodes.response: In French 'il fait' often means 'he does, makes' but when referring to the weather it means 'it is' e.g. 'Il fait froid.' (It is cold.).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather: 'il fait'

nodes.misconception: To make sentences negative in French, you need to put the equivalent of 'don't' before the main verb.
nodes.response: To make sentences negative in French, you 'sandwich' the main verb between 'ne' and 'pas'. There are two elements which need to be in place. For example: 'je fais le ménage' (positive) 'je ne fais pas le ménage' (negative).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at home: negation

nodes.misconception: The SSC [s] always sounds like the English 'z'.
nodes.response: The SSC [s] sounds 'hard' (like the English 'z') when it is between two vowels. It sounds 'soft' at the beginning of a word/syllable, before or after a consonant and when there is a double [ss].
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: My friends: 'mes' and 'tes'

nodes.misconception: The letter 'c' is always soft (like the 's' in English) in French.
nodes.response: The letter 'c' is naturally soft before 'e' and 'i'  e.g. 'c'est', but hard before 'a', 'o' and 'u' e.g. 'carte'. The cedilla 'ç' is used to soften it before 'a', 'o' and 'u', e.g. 'français'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at home: 'tu fais'

nodes.misconception: The preposition 'à' has only one translation in English: at.
nodes.response: The preposition 'à' has in fact different meanings in English, it can be translated as at, in or to.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: My friend: singular -er verbs

nodes.misconception: The sound-symbol correspondences [ai] and [è] make different sounds.
nodes.response: The sound-symbol correspondences [ai] and [è] in fact make the same sound as in 'paire' and 'père'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Likes: 'aimer', 'mon', 'ma' and 'ton', 'ta'

nodes.misconception: There are two ways of referring to the present tense in French, as in English, e.g. 'I watch' and 'I am watching'.
nodes.response: There is only one way to refer to the present tense in French: 'je regarde'. This can be translated as both 'I watch' and 'I am watching'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Preferences: singular verbs of opinion

nodes.misconception: The verb 'aimer' means 'to like', and 'adorer' means 'to love'.
nodes.response: The verb 'aimer' means both 'to like' and 'to love'. 'Adorer' does also mean 'to love', but can be translated as 'to adore'. When saying 'I love you' in French, we say 'je t'aime'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Preferences: extending my sentences

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [eau], [au] and [o] are spelt differently therefore they make different sounds.
nodes.response: The SSCs [eau], [au] and [o] are spelt differently however they make the exact same sound.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: In class: 'il y a' and 'ce sont'

nodes.misconception: Like in English, adjectives do not change spelling based on the number of the noun described: a blue book - some blue books.
nodes.response: Unlike in English, adjectives change spelling based on the number (and gender) of the noun they describe: un livre bleu - des livres bleus.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: My ideal teacher: singular and plural adjectives

nodes.misconception: Like in English, adjectives go before the noun in French: a fast car.
nodes.response: Unlike in English, most adjectives go after the noun in French: une voiture rapide.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A horrible week! 'avoir' singular persons and adjectives after the noun

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in French: un chien noir.
nodes.response: Some adjectives go before the noun in French. These are prenominal adjectives that refer to beauty, age, good/bad or size (BAGS): un petit chien.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Our own space: 'ils ont', 'elles ont' and adjectives before the noun

nodes.misconception: Confusion between 'il a' and 'il est' as 'il est' is pronounced similarly to the English 'a'.
nodes.response: 'Il a' and 'il est' are pronounced differently and have different meanings: 'il a' is he has and 'il est' is he is.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: To have or to be: 'avoir' and 'être' singular

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is no article when making physical descriptions, e.g. 'I have blond hair'.
nodes.response: In French, we use definite articles when making physical descriptions, e.g. 'J'ai les cheveux blonds'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Hair and eyes: singular and plural adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: We use the verb 'je suis' ('I am') with ages in French.
nodes.response: When giving ages in French, we in fact use the verb 'j'ai' ('I have'), e.g. 'j'ai neuf ans' ('I have nine years').
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: All about me: presenting myself in French

nodes.misconception: The letter 's' is always a SFC (silent final consonant) in French.
nodes.response: When 's' is followed by a word starting with a vowel, the s is no longer silent, there is a liaison: 'nous avons'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Exchange school in England: 'nous avons' and 'vous avez'

nodes.misconception: Once you've learnt a new word, you remember it forever.
nodes.response: New vocabulary has to be practised regularly or you might forget it.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What is it? Intonation questions and 'quoi'

nodes.misconception: The 't' in c'est is always a silent-final consonant.
nodes.response: The 't' in c'est is pronounced if it is followed by a word beginning with a vowel like 'un' or 'une'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What is it? C'est and liaison

nodes.misconception: I can use 'avoir' as it is with any pronoun to mean 'have' or 'has' in French.
nodes.response: You have to use the different forms of 'avoir' depending on who you are talking about. For I have it is 'j'ai', for he has it is 'il a' for she has it is 'elle a'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What I and others have: 'j'ai' and 'il, elle a'

nodes.misconception: I can only use the words I have learnt in lessons when speaking and writing in French.
nodes.response: Reference resources like bilingual dictionaries give you the freedom to look up new words that are important to you, and include them in your work. You can build up a treasure trove of vocabulary this way.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Packing a bag: singular 'avoir'

nodes.misconception: I have to know every word in a story in order to understand it.
nodes.response: To understand a story which contains a few unfamiliar words, you can use the surrounding words that you do know to work out the probable meanings of unfamiliar words. There may be other visual cues as well.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Story: Lulu, la tortue

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [o], [au] and [eau] are spelt differently so they must be different sounds.
nodes.response: There are three different ways to spell the same [o] sound. You have to be careful and learn the spelling of words in French,  as well as being able to read them aloud correctly.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A strange dream: practice with key sounds

nodes.misconception: We have to translate the word 'do' into French to ask the question 'do you have?'
nodes.response: There is no word for 'do' in French. We use intonation to change the statement 'you have' into the question 'do you have?'
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: An excursion: 'tu as' and intonation questions

nodes.misconception: The verb 'avoir' in 'tu as' and 'il, elle a' and the verb 'être' in 'tu es' and 'il, elle est' sound the same and so must be spelt the same.
nodes.response: It is important to understand that they don't sound the same and are not spelt the same. Some forms of avoir sound the same due to SFCs. These singular forms of 'avoir' and 'être' should be learnt off by heart as they are extremely frequent.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Who has what? Singular 'avoir' and 'être'

nodes.misconception: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as female, if it is masculine we think of it as male.
nodes.response: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender. All French nouns are either masculine or feminine, whether they name people, places or things.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What is it? Naming belongings with 'un' and 'une'

nodes.misconception: I will just remember the new French words I learn.
nodes.response: When learning a new language, it is important to practise vocabulary regularly to strengthen your memory.  It's hardest to remember the words we learnt some time ago, so we need to practise them often.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Who has what? Singular 'avoir' and intonation questions

nodes.misconception: When referring to who or what somebody is in French, we must use 'il est' or 'elle est', like in English: she is my cousin.
nodes.response: When referring to who or what somebody is in French, we can use 'il est' or 'elle est', like in English. We can also use 'c'est': c'est ma cousine - she is my cousin.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Tintin: person nouns, 'avoir', 'être'

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go before the noun in French, as in English: 'a grey bike'.
nodes.response: Most adjectives go after the noun in French: 'un vélo gris'. These are postnominal adjectives.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What it is like: adjectives after the noun

nodes.misconception: The adjective 'cher' simply adds an -e in the feminine form.
nodes.response: The adjective 'cher' does add an -e in the feminine form, but there is an additional change as the first e changes to è in the feminine form: 'chère'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe what you have: speaking in sentences

nodes.misconception: When saying your favourite animal in French, use the article 'an/an' as in English: my favourite animal is a dog.
nodes.response: When saying your favourite animal in French, we in fact use the article 'the': mon animal préféré est le chien.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At the zoo: writing from a word list for reference

nodes.misconception: 'Il a' and 'il y a' sound similar and can be confused.
nodes.response: 'Il a' and 'il y a', despite sounding similar, are in fact different and have different meanings. 'Il a' means 'he has', 'il y a' means 'there is' or 'there are'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe what you have: adjectives after the noun

nodes.misconception: There is one form of the possessive adjective 'my' in French, as in English.
nodes.response: There are two forms of the possessive adjective 'my' in French: 'mon' (masculine) and 'ma' (feminine).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mother's day in 'la Francophonie': 'mon', 'ma' and 'ton', 'ta'

nodes.misconception: The pronouns 'il' and 'elle' can only mean 'he' and 'she' in French.
nodes.response: The pronouns 'il' and 'elle' mean 'he' and 'she', they can also be translated as 'it' as all noun have a gender in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mother's day in 'la Francophonie': 'il' and 'elle' meaning 'it'

nodes.misconception: The 'e' at the end of a word in French is pronounced.
nodes.response: The 'e' at the end of a word in French is silent, it is an SFe (silent final 'e'), e.g. 'timide'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What do you have? 'J'ai' and 'tu as'

nodes.misconception: Animals are referred to as 'it' in French, as they are in English: 'look at the tortoise, it is green'.
nodes.response: As all nouns have a gender in French, animals are referred to using 'il' and 'elle', depending on the gender of the noun (not the gender of the animal). Animals are therefore referred to using 'il' and 'elle': 'regarde la tortue, elle est verte'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At the zoo: 'il, elle' (it) and adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: All verb forms have the same ending.
nodes.response: A useful way to embed the pronoun-verb form-meaning connection is in reading activities that omit the pronouns; pupils are compelled to focus on the verb ending to complete the task.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At school: singular -er verbs

nodes.misconception: l' is only for feminine nouns.
nodes.response: l' is the article for all nouns starting with a vowel sound.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A birthday: -er verbs 'she, he'

nodes.misconception: 'The' is always 'le'.
nodes.response: There are three ways to say 'the' in French in the singular. 'Le' is used in front of masculine singular nouns. 'La' is used in front of feminine singular nouns. 'L'' is used in front of singular nouns starting with a vowel.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A family: singular definite articles 'le' and 'la'

nodes.misconception: [er] in French sounds the same as in English; as in the word 'colder', for example.
nodes.response: [é] and [er] have the same sound in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: In class activities: -er infinitive verbs

nodes.misconception: The verb ending for 'tu' is -e not -es.
nodes.response: The 's' in the -es ending is not pronounced. A useful way to embed the 'tu' - es form-meaning connection is in reading activities that omit the pronouns 'je' and 'tu'; pupils are compelled to focus on the verb ending to complete the task.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At school: -er verbs 'I' and 'you'

nodes.misconception: [é] and [er] make the same sound as [e].
nodes.response: [é] and [er] make the same sound, which is different from [e].
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: In-class activities: translating -er infinitive verbs into English

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is just one way of saying 'please' in French.
nodes.response: There are in fact two ways to say 'please' in French. Use 's'il te plait' with friends, family and people your own age and use 's'il vous plait' with adults outside of your family.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Friendship: plural definite article 'les'

nodes.misconception: The SSC [-tion] makes a 'sh' sound, like in English.
nodes.response: The SSC [-tion] makes a 's' sound in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at school: -er 1 and 2-verb phrases

nodes.misconception: Like in English, adjectives go before the noun in French: a grey bike.
nodes.response: Unlike in English, most adjectives go after the noun in French, these are postnominal adjectives: un vélo gris.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: All about me: intonation questions, adjectives and -er verbs

nodes.misconception: Like in English, we use the verb 'I am' ('je suis') with age.
nodes.response: In French, we use the verb 'I have' ('j'ai') with age, e.g. 'j'ai huit ans' - 'I am (have) eight (years)'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Message to a friend: writing words and phrases

nodes.misconception: The 's' is pronounced at the end of plural nouns in French.
nodes.response: The 's' is not pronounced at the end of plural nouns in French, it is an SFC, a silent final consonant.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers: 1-12, 'des'

nodes.misconception: The indefinite article 'des' changes based on gender as do the indefinite articles 'un' and 'une'.
nodes.response: The indefinite article 'des' does not change based on gender. Un livre - des livres. Une orange - des oranges.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers: plural indefinite article 'des', 'combien'

nodes.misconception: 'Il y a' and 'il a' can both be used to say what there is/are.
nodes.response: 'Il y a' and 'il a' sound similar but have different meanings. 'Il y a' means 'there is' or 'there are' and 'il a' means 'he has'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers: 'il y a', liaison

nodes.misconception: The French sound [oi] starts with a 'w'.
nodes.response: The French SSC [oi] does is spelt 'oi' and does not start with a 'w'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers: 1-12, plural nouns, 'il y a'

nodes.misconception: The pronouns 'y' and 'en' go after the verb, as 'there' and 'of it/them' do in English.
nodes.response: 'Y' and 'en' go before the verb in a present tense sentence e.g. 'elle y va' and 'elle en boit'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: À table ! Partitive and indefinite articles, preverbal use of 'y' and 'en'

nodes.misconception: All verbs in French can be used before an infinitive without a preposition.
nodes.response: Certain verbs require 'à' or 'de' before a an infinitive. Learning which verbs this applies to is helpful. Teachers might like to point out the more frequently occurring verbs of this type to help students develop their confidence in using them.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Vive la République : present tense,  prepositions 'à' and 'de'

nodes.misconception: French indirect object pronouns are all the same as direct object pronouns.
nodes.response: While some object pronouns are the same when used both indirectly and directly (e.g. me, te), there are some differences that students need to learn. It is a good idea to provide plenty of practice in this area to help students gain confidence.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Joyeuses fêtes : indirect object pronouns 'me', 'te', 'lui', 'vous'

nodes.misconception: There are separate indirect object pronouns in French to replace masculine and feminine nouns.
nodes.response: French indirect object pronouns make no distinction for gender (unlike direct object pronouns). 'Lui' means both '(to) him' and '(to) her'. 'Leur' means '(to) them' and can refer to both masculine and feminine nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le 14 juillet : indirect object pronouns me, te, lui, vous, nous, and leur

nodes.misconception: The ideas 'to', 'in', 'of' always have the same translation in French.
nodes.response: Prepositions are tricky to master in another language. Students should be given plenty of practice of 'à', 'en' and 'de' to see how their use varies according to context.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un pays francophone : present tense, prepositions 'à', 'de' and 'en'

nodes.misconception: Cognates are pronounced the same way in French as they are in English.
nodes.response: Cognates are often pronounced very differently in French.  Students should not overlook the importance of practising pronunciation of cognates in order to better respond to listening stimuli as well as to develop a more authentic pronunciation.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La diversité religieuse dans les pays francophones : extending vocabulary

nodes.misconception: The preposition 'à' is used to mean 'to' or 'in' for both cities and countries.
nodes.response: Prepositions can be tricky to master. Students must practise them carefully and thoroughly. Use 'à' before a city or town. Use 'en' before a feminine country or region. Use 'au' before a masculine country or region and 'aux' before a plural country.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'Hexagone : present tense, prepositions 'à' and 'en'

nodes.misconception: In the perfect tense, the pronouns y and en go before the past participle.
nodes.response: Both y and en go before the auxiliary verb in the perfect tense e.g. il y est allé, il en a mangé.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des plats typiques : use of 'y' and 'en'

nodes.misconception: It doesn't matter if you address a stranger in France as 'tu' or as 'vous'.
nodes.response: Using the correct register of address is very important for students. Practising role-plays in both formal and informal settings allows students to understand when to use the appropriate form of 'you'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Aller au restaurant : dictation, role-play

nodes.misconception: I want to avoid using object pronouns because my writing will be longer and therefore better if I just repeat all the nouns.
nodes.response: Although object pronouns use fewer words, it is much better style to use them to avoid repeating nouns. Appropriate use of object pronouns is also positively rewarded in exams as an example of complexity.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une fête culturelle/religieuse : extended writing, speaking, photo description

nodes.misconception: 'Il', 'elle', 'ils' and 'elles' only refer to people and not things. 'Il' therefore only means 'he' and 'elle' only means 'she'.
nodes.response: It is useful to keep in mind that 'il, elle' and 'ils, elles' can refer to things as well as people.  In this case, 'il, elle' means 'it' rather than 'he, she'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mon temps libre: subject pronouns, -er verbs and 'aimer' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: All -re verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, just like regular -er verbs.
nodes.response: -re verbs can be divided into four groups, following the patterns of entendre, prendre, traduire and écrire.  Encourage learners to be able to categorise -re verbs and to draw comparisons between the groups.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Qui fait quoi ? : -re verbs like 'prendre' and 'entendre'

nodes.misconception: [s] is always a silent final consonant.
nodes.response: [s] is usually a silent final consonant, but is pronounced when between two vowels. It's helpful to look out for verbs that start with a vowel. With such verbs in the third person plural, the 's' on 'ils' and 'elles' is pronounced.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une personne intéressante : -re verbs like 'traduire' and 'écrire'

nodes.misconception: Languages don't change; they have a fixed number of words in them.
nodes.response: Languages are not fixed; they are changing all the time, adopting new words to reflect how people live and speak.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Two musicians: singular 'être', singular adjectives

nodes.misconception: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' and can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' but 'on' is used more to talk about people generally, 'nous' is always used to talk about yourself and another person/people. The verb endings are different, 'on' uses il/elle verb endings and the 'nous' ending is -ons.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Dieppe festival: plural -er verbs, 'est-ce que' questions

nodes.misconception: When you add a question word at the end of a question, there is no need to change your intonation.
nodes.response: It is important to use your intonation by raising the pitch of your voice at the end of all questions in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Dieppe festival: singular -er verbs, 'pour' and 'sans', intonation questions

nodes.misconception: Add -s to make all adjectives plural.
nodes.response: Regular adjectives usually need -s adding in the plural form, however there are other patterns and differences between the masculine and the feminine form with adjectives ending in -x and -al.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Rock en Seine : plural 'être', plural adjectives

nodes.misconception: Use the same articles after 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'.
nodes.response: Use the indefinite article, depending on gender and number after 'il y a' but after 'il n' y a pas', always use de regardless of gender/number and d' for any nouns starting with a vowel.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: How do you say that? Articles, 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'

nodes.misconception: 'Ma' is the possessive adjective for all feminine singular nouns.
nodes.response: Use 'mon/ton' before all nouns starting with a vowel/h.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: How do you spell that? Alphabet, 'ils', 'elles' meaning 'they', 'mon, ma, mes'

nodes.misconception: I use the French present participle -ant to translate -ing in English.
nodes.response: The present participle -ant is not the only way to translate -ing in English. Sometimes the French infinitive is needed, where English uses the -ing form as a noun, e.g., 'visiter le Maroc aide à mieux connaître sa culture'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Au Maroc : regular present tense verbs, present participle with 'en'

nodes.misconception: There is only one word in French to translate 'mine', 'yours', 'his', 'hers'.
nodes.response: In French, possessive pronouns match the gender and number of the noun they replace in a sentence. They are formed of the definite article and the pronoun, for example: 'les chocolats, ce sont les miens,' meaning 'the chocolates, they are mine'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un portrait francophone : possessive adjectives, emphatic pronouns

nodes.misconception: Direct object pronouns can be used with verbs followed by 'à' like 'demander' and 'donner'.
nodes.response: Indirect object pronouns should be used with these verbs because you ask 'of' and give 'to' someone in French. In English, the 'to' is often dropped with these kinds of verbs e.g. 'je lui donne un cadeau' I give (to) him, her a present.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un portrait coloré : extended speaking

nodes.misconception: To make comparatives and superlatives in French, add suffixes -er and -est to adjectives.
nodes.response: Suffixes -er and -est do not exist in French. To form comparatives, use the forms 'more', 'less ... than' - 'plus ... que' and 'moins ... que'. To form superlatives, use the forms 'the most', 'the least' - 'le, la, les plus' and 'le, la, les moins'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une équipe accomplie : present participle adjectives, comparatives, superlatives

nodes.misconception: When making suggestions, 'let's' needs to be said in French as a separate idea.
nodes.response: In French, use the imperative in the 'nous' form to create the phrase 'let's + verb', e.g. 'allons ...' means 'let's go ...'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite en ville : role-play

nodes.misconception: The superlative in French always goes before the noun it describes, like in English.
nodes.response: Superlatives may go before or after the noun they describe. The rule that applies is BRAGS - if an adjective goes before the noun according to the BRAGS rule, its superlative form will also go before the noun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une sportive qui m'intéresse : extended writing

nodes.misconception: 'Nous' always means 'we'.
nodes.response: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun, but it means 'us' when used as a direct object pronoun and '(to) us' when used as an indirect object pronoun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Qu'en penses-tu ? Possessive adjectives, direct & indirect object pronouns

nodes.misconception: Present participles are always preceeded by 'en'.
nodes.response: The present participles 'ayant', 'étant' and 'faisant de' can be used without the preposition 'en' e.g. 'Ayant une grand-mère musulmane, je sais beaucoup sur l'Islam' - having a muslim grandmother, I know a lot about Islam.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Au Maroc : read and respond to texts

nodes.misconception: A subject pronoun or noun is always required when using a verb in French.
nodes.response: When using the imperative, neither subject pronoun nor noun is required. Match the spelling of the verb to the person or people who are being instructed.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Montréal, une ville francophone : the imperative

nodes.misconception: The imperative can only be used in the 'tu' and 'vous' forms in French, to instruct others to do something.
nodes.response: The imperative can be used in the 'nous' form in French. In this case, the imperative is suggesting what we should do, and is translated as let's in English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Allons-y ! The imperative

nodes.misconception: All agent nouns in French end in -eur, e.g. 'joueur'.
nodes.response: Many French agent nouns have the '-ateur' ending, for example 'consommateur', which means 'consumer'. This is because these agent nouns are linked to the original Latin forms that French has maintained today.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le conseil de la vie scolaire : extended speaking

nodes.misconception: Some nouns ending in -ion or -ation are masculine.
nodes.response: Every noun ending in -ion and -ation is feminine. There are no exceptions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une démocratie : creating nouns by adding -ion or -ation to the verb stem

nodes.misconception: There are two present tenses in French, simple present and present continuous, like English.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in French, which is used to communicate both English present tenses. For example, 'je joue au foot' can be translated as both I play football and I am playing football.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La diversité culturelle : regular present tense

nodes.misconception: All agent nouns are formed by adding either -eur or -ateur to the stem of the verb.
nodes.response: Most agent nouns follow this rule but there are exceptions, for example éduquer - to educate, becomes éducateur - educator. A stem change is needed here.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Pourquoi voter ? Creating nouns by adding -teur or -ateur to the verb stem

nodes.misconception: To make a comparative adjective in French, add the suffix -er to an adjective.
nodes.response: Most comparatives are formed using 'plus ... que' (more ... than), 'moins ... que' (less ... than), and 'aussi ... que' (as ... as). The adjective to compare goes in the middle and agrees with gender and number of the noun being compared.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une équipe francophone : adjective agreement, making comparisons

nodes.misconception: 'Il y a' always means 'there is'.
nodes.response: 'Il y a' can mean 'there is' or 'there are' and can be used with singular or plural nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des monuments historiques : 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'

nodes.misconception: Reflexive verbs and pronouns are only used when a physical action is done to oneself.
nodes.response: Reflexive verbs and pronouns indicate that the subject and object are the same person, but do not always represent a physical action. Sometimes there is no direct translation for the French reflexive pronoun in English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On organise des visites : reflexive pronouns, direct object pronouns

nodes.misconception: When forming yes/no questions, we need to translate the English 'do' or 'does' into French.
nodes.response: There is no equivalent to 'do' or 'does' in French. Use inversion, intonation or 'est-ce que' to form yes/no questions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un nouvel élève : yes/no questions with inversion, intonation and 'est-ce que'

nodes.misconception: -ir verbs have the same verb endings in the present tense as -er verbs.
nodes.response: Only verbs like 'ouvrir' have the same endings in the present tense as -er verbs. There are also verbs like 'choisir', verbs like 'partir' and verbs like 'venir' which have different endings.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Au château de Versailles : -ir verbs like 'ouvrir' (singular)

nodes.misconception: The pronouns ils and elles can only refer to people.
nodes.response: Ils and elles can refer to things as well as people. They are still translated as 'they'. We must use context and surrounding language to work out who or what they are referring to.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite scolaire : -ir verbs like 'ouvrir' (plural)

nodes.misconception: 'à' is always translated as 'to' or 'at'.
nodes.response: 'à' can be translated as 'to', 'at', 'in', 'on' or 'about', depending on the context. Particular care should be taken with verbs followed by 'à', e.g., 'réfléchir à' could be translated as 'to think about' or 'to reflect on'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des monuments commémoratifs : contraction of definite article after 'à'

nodes.misconception: French adjectives always come after the noun they are describing.
nodes.response: There are five categories of adjectives which come before the noun: beauty, rank, age, good/bad, size/quantity. Practise using these before the noun alongside other adjectives which come after the noun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des endroits touristiques : -ir verbs like 'venir', position of adjectives

nodes.misconception: All -ir verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, like -er verbs.
nodes.response: -ir verbs can be grouped into verbs like 'choisir', verbs like 'partir', verbs like 'venir' and verbs like 'ouvrir'. By learning the stem formation and endings for these four verbs, students should be able to use wide range of -ir verbs.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On part pour la France : -ir verbs like 'choisir' and 'partir', adjectives

nodes.misconception: The verb jouer is always followed by the preposition à.
nodes.response: Use jouer à for sports but use jouer de for instruments.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une nouvelle vie en France : liaison, questions, jouer à/de, negation

nodes.misconception: All verbs in French end in -er, -ir or -re.
nodes.response: Only infinitive verbs end in -er, -ir, or -re. When categorising words according to word class in Task A, draw attention to the different verb endings and discuss the possible subjects of each verb.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On va à un concert : direct object pronouns, reflexive pronouns and negation

nodes.misconception: The subject of a sentence precedes the verb and the object of a sentence always follows the verb.
nodes.response: When using direct object pronouns, the object precedes the verb.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ça ne vous intéresse pas ? Direct object pronouns, negation

nodes.misconception: All negative structures go around the short form of the verb only in two-verb structures.
nodes.response: Most negatives, such as 'ne...pas', 'ne...jamais' and 'ne...rien', go around the short form of the verb in two-verb structures. 'Ne...personne', however, goes around both verbs.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une nouvelle vie en France : negation

nodes.misconception: All questions in French must have a question word or start with a verb.
nodes.response: Statements can be made into questions in French by changing the tone of your voice.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ask about someone: yes/no intonation questions

nodes.misconception: Adjectives in French have only one form that can be used to describe any noun, like English.
nodes.response: In French, adjectives may change their spelling and/or sound when describing a woman, girl or feminine noun. This is called the feminine form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe a person or thing: regular gender adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: Final consonants that are pronounced in English are also pronounced in French.
nodes.response: The letters d, s, t and x are usually silent at the end of words in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Me and you: être 1st and 2nd persons singular

nodes.misconception: 'Elle' meaning she is pronounced with an [i] sound at the start.
nodes.response: 'Elle' is pronounced with a hard e sound like in egg.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe a person or thing: être 1st and 3rd persons singular

nodes.misconception: 'Il faut' works like modal verbs, it changes for different subject pronouns.
nodes.response: 'Il faut' is only used in the 3rd person singular and it is impersonal, it is used to talk about what it is necessary for people in general to do or what they must do.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Instructions at work: 'il faut' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: All adverbs that tell us how and how often something happens come straight after the verb and we add -ment to all adjectives to make them adverbs.
nodes.response: There are exceptions to the adverb placement and adverb formation rules. For example 'parfois' usually comes at the start of a sentence. 'Dur' is an adjective which often doesn't change even when it is used as an adverb with certain verbs.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Future goals - Eduardo Camavinga: modals + infinitive, '-ment' adverbs

nodes.misconception: [ou] and [u] are both the same 'u' sound.
nodes.response: Be careful not to mix up the similar but not identical sounds, people may not understand you or you could be saying a different word to the one you mean.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Work experience: modals 1st and 2nd persons plural

nodes.misconception: All modal verbs follow the same pattern in the 3rd person plural.
nodes.response: 'Devoir' and 'pouvoir' are formed the same way, 'vouloir' is the same with the addition of an 'l' instead of a 'v' and 'savoir' is different; it follows the same pattern as the 'nous'/'vous' forms.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Work experience: modals 3rd person plural

nodes.misconception: [en/an] and [on] sound the same in French.
nodes.response: Although the sounds are simililar and both nasal vowels, [en/an] is a nasal 'a' and [on] is a nasal 'o'. The mouth should be wide for [en/an] and almost closed for [on].
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Future goals - Taïs Vinolo: 'aller' + infinitive, negation

nodes.misconception: Add an -e to all adjectives to make them agree with feminine nouns.
nodes.response: The majority of adjectives need an -e adding in the feminine form but there are other patterns and exceptions to the rules. A common pattern is that adjectives ending -x change to -se in the feminine form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Jobs: feminine adjectives

nodes.misconception: Add an -e to all person nouns to make them feminine.
nodes.response: The most common way to make a person noun feminine is to add an -e to the masculine version. If nouns already end in -e, person nouns usually stay the same but the article changes. Jobs ending in 'eur' usually change to 'rice' in the feminine form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Jobs: feminine nouns

nodes.misconception: There is no need to use intonation when using inversion and 'est-ce que'.
nodes.response: Even when we form questions with inversion or 'est-ce que', it is still important to use intonation to signal that it is a question.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Jobs: singular 'avoir' or 'être', questions with 'est-ce que'

nodes.misconception: 'Ils ont' and 'ils sont' sound the same.
nodes.response: Although these two verbs sound similar, there is a distinction between the 'z' sound created by s-liaison in 'ils ont' and the 's' sound at the beginning of 'sont' after the silent 's' on 'ils'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Jobs: plural 'avoir' or 'être', article use with professions

nodes.misconception: Just add 'ne ... jamais' around the verb to say 'never'; the rest of the sentence stays the same.
nodes.response: Add 'ne ... jamais' around the conjugated verb, but in addition, change any indefinite/partitive articles to de/d' after a negative.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Canada: negation with 'ne…jamais'

nodes.misconception: Conjugate 'mettre' and 'remettre' exactly like 'entendre'.
nodes.response: 'Mettre' and 'remettre' do take the same verb endings as 'entendre'; however, they also drop a 't' in the singular present tense forms.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Canada: verbs like 'entendre'; 'mettre' and 'remettre'

nodes.misconception: The sound-symbol correspondences [ai] and [é/er/ez] sound the same in French.
nodes.response: The letters 'ai/ay' are the same as the SSC [é/er/ez] in French but [ai] is pronounced as in 'vrai' with slightly more relaxed lips than 'ai/ay' in English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Countries and states: 'à' and 'en'

nodes.misconception: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know' so they can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know', but 'connaitre' is used for being familiar with people/places/things, whereas 'savoir' usually means 'to know how to' or used on its own/with 'que'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Quebec: 'connaitre' and 'savoir'

nodes.misconception: I use 'notre' to mean 'our' in French just with masculine nouns.
nodes.response: The possessive adjective 'notre' is used before masculine and feminine singular nouns to mean 'our' in French. We use 'nos' when the 'possessed' noun is plural.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Special occasions: 'notre' and 'nos'

nodes.misconception: When I am forming information questions with 'est-ce que' I put the question word after it.
nodes.response: When forming information questions with 'est-ce que', the question word must come before it, e.g example: 'Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire demain ?' 'What are you going to do tomorrow?'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Celebrations: information questions with question word + 'est-ce que'

nodes.misconception: The possessive adjective 'son, sa, ses' matches the person who owns the noun that follows. So 'his' is 'son, 'her' is 'sa' and 'their' is 'ses'.
nodes.response: In French, the possessive pronoun matches the noun that follows it, not the person to whom the object belongs. This is why sometimes you cannot tell whether the owner is male or female because the words for 'his' and 'her' are the same in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: How people celebrate: 'son, sa, ses' meaning 'his', 'her', 'your (in general)'

nodes.misconception: Combination numbers in French are written like this: 'dix sept', 'vingt deux'.
nodes.response: French numbers which are made up of a combination of more than one number must be hyphenated, e.g. 'dix-sept' (17), 'vingt-deux' (22), and 'trente-et-un' (31).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Celebrations: numbers 13-31

nodes.misconception: 'On' is equivalent to 'one' in English and is therefore is very formal and rarely used.
nodes.response: 'On' is very commonly used in French and can mean 'everyone', 'people', 'you' and 'one'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: How people celebrate: 'on' for people in general

nodes.misconception: To express the date I use 'de' for 'of' so 2nd January would be 'le deux de janvier'.
nodes.response: There is no need to translate 'of' into French to express the date. For example 2nd January would be 'le deux janvier'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: When people celebrate: dates

nodes.misconception: In French, there is a separate word for 'would'.
nodes.response: The conditional verb form expresses the idea of 'would + verb' in its spelling. Students should be encouraged to used the conditional form of verbs instead of being over reliant on 'vouloir' in the conditional.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Tu aimerais ? Future and conditional with -er verbs (singular)

nodes.misconception: It isn't important to answer both bullet points in the longer writing task equally.
nodes.response: Students should plan carefully to address both bullet points in an equal manner, giving detailed answers and using a rich selection of language. Using the BORDER acronym helps students to fully answer the task.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La famille de mes rêves : extended writing

nodes.misconception: There is a separate word for 'will' in French when talking about the future.
nodes.response: The spelling of a verb in the 1-verb future form contains the idea of 'will' + verb e.g. il visitera = he will visit.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On ira en vacances : future with aller, avoir, être and faire

nodes.misconception: Only the present tense is required when performing the photo description task.
nodes.response: The present tense will mostly be used to describe a photo; however, other tenses are required for the follow-up questions based on the topic of the photo. Students should be able to use future and conditional verbs to discuss future plans.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ce serait parfait : photo description, extended writing

nodes.misconception: The conditional can always be used on its own without a prior conditional being described.
nodes.response: Apart from the verbs 'aimer' and 'vouloir', always use the conditional form of verb with a 'si' + imperfect sentence. It is not logical to say in French 'I would buy a villa' without an accompanying condition e.g. if I had lots of money.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Avec des si ... : future and conditional with -er verbs (plural)

nodes.misconception: A separate word for 'will' and 'would' needs to be translated into French when using future or conditional verbs.
nodes.response: The 1-verb future and conditional verb forms express 'will' and 'would' in their spellings. No separate word is required.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Où se loger ? Future and conditional with -er verbs (plural)

nodes.misconception: There are distinct words required in French to translate 'will' and 'would'.
nodes.response: The 1-verb future tense describes 'will + verb'. The conditional describes 'would + verb'. Students should be aware that both verb forms are 'simple' forms as all the meaning is contained within a single word.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Futurs divers : future -er verbs (singular), conditional vouloir (singular)

nodes.misconception: Use the present tense after 'si' and before the conditional to say what you would do.
nodes.response: French uses the combination of 'si' + imperfect + conditional to express what would happen if a certain condition occurred e.g. If I won the lottery, I would move to France.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Village, ville ou ile ? 'Si' + imperfect with conditional -er verbs (plural)

nodes.misconception: In French, there is a separate word for 'would' that is used with an infinitive to express what someone 'would' do.
nodes.response: The conditional form of verbs expresses 'would' + verb e.g. je visiterais - I would visit. There is no word for 'would' in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: À l'étranger : future and conditional with aller, avoir, être and faire

nodes.misconception: In French, 'to you' is translated literally from English e.g. I say to you 'je dis à toi'.
nodes.response: In French indirect object pronouns  to me and to you are translated by single words: 'me' and 'te'. They go before the verb, not at the end of the sentence.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ça t'intéresse ? Direct and indirect pronouns me and te

nodes.misconception: When using the verb 'rappeler', you need to have a suitable word for 'about', e.g., 'I am reminding you about the party'.
nodes.response: When using the verb 'rappeler', there is no need to include a word for 'about'. 'Rappeler' contains this idea within the verb.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une famille française : indirect object pronouns 'lui' and 'vous'

nodes.misconception: There are different words in French for the indirect object pronouns 'to him' and 'to her'.
nodes.response: There is just one third person singular indirect object pronoun in French, 'lui' , which means both 'to him' and 'to her'. It follows the same rule as other object pronouns - it precedes the verb.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une famille multiculturelle : direct and indirect object pronouns

nodes.misconception: The words 'le', 'la' and 'l'' can only mean 'the' in French.
nodes.response: The meaning of 'le', 'la', and 'l'' depends on where they are in the sentence. When before a noun, they mean 'the', but when before a verb, they mean 'him', 'her' or 'it'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une soirée chez amis : Direct object pronouns (le, la and l')

nodes.misconception: In France, the famous painting is called Mona Lisa, just like in English.
nodes.response: The French have their own name for the Mona Lisa, 'la Joconde', taken from the name of the lady in the painting - la Gioconda in Italian.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Les musées français : Indirect object pronouns me and te

nodes.misconception: French object pronouns go after the verb in place of the object, just as in English. e.g. The museum interests me.
nodes.response: French object pronouns go before the verb.  e.g. Le musée m'intéresse.  When speaking and writing French we have to take care to use the correct word, especially for object pronouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un musée décolonisé : Indirect object pronouns me and te

nodes.misconception: Adjectives usually come before the noun they are describing like in English.
nodes.response: Adjectives in French usually come after the noun they are describing.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Belongings: adjective position after nouns and the alphabet

nodes.misconception: 'Avoir' only means 'to have' in English.
nodes.response: 'Avoir' can be translated both as 'to have' or 'having'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What someone has: avoir 1st and 3rd persons singular

nodes.misconception: To ask 'do you have ...?' questions we need to know 'do you ...?' in French.
nodes.response: There is no phrase for 'do you ...?'. We use intonation to ask 'do you have ...?' questions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ask what someone has: 'avoir' 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say 'a' in French.
nodes.response: All nouns have a gender in French. We use 'un' for all masculine nouns and 'une' for all feminine nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What is that? C'est and singular indefinite articles

nodes.misconception: 'Qui' always means the question 'who?'.
nodes.response: When used in an interrogative sense, 'qui ?' means 'who?'. As a relative pronoun, 'qui' introduces more information about the subject in the main clause and can be translated as 'who', 'which' or 'that'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Qui a fait le ménage ? Perfect tense, relative clauses, negation

nodes.misconception: There is a French verb 'to can'.
nodes.response: The English idea of 'can' is translated in French by the verb 'pouvoir' meaning 'to be able to'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On peut acheter : present tense modal verbs

nodes.misconception: The same amount of words are used when translating between French and English.
nodes.response: Due to the nature of the languages, there may be differences in how some words or ideas are translated e.g. I need is 'j'ai besoin de' in French. More or fewer words might be necessary to complete an accurate translation.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On fait les magasins et les courses : extending vocabulary

nodes.misconception: All verbs using reflexive pronouns are reflexive.
nodes.response: Reciprocal verbs use the reflexive pronouns 'se', 'nous' and 'vous'. They are used to express actions that two or more people perform with, or for, each other, e.g. 'nous nous écrivons souvent' - 'we often write to each other'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ils s'entendent bien : reflexive pronouns

nodes.misconception: Reflexive pronouns are only used to talk about actions done to oneself.
nodes.response: Reflexive pronouns are also used with verbs to indicate a reciprocal (shared) action between two or more subjects. Verbs can only be reciprocal with plural subjects, i.e. 'nous', 'vous' and 'ils/elles'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ils m'inspirent : extended writing

nodes.misconception: Answers to conversation questions should only be given in the same tense as the question.
nodes.response: Students should develop answers to conversation questions in order to give additional information and detail. Using different tenses allows students to give a more detailed and complex answer.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La vie quotidienne : perfect and imperfect tenses, relative clauses and negation

nodes.misconception: There are always the same number of words used when translating between languages.
nodes.response: As languages are complex, many ideas are expressed differently in different languages. When translating, more or fewer words might be needed to convey the information e.g. avant de passer un examan - before sitting an exam.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On est prêt à tout : avant de, après avoir

nodes.misconception: French uses the present participle after the preposition 'sans'.
nodes.response: 'Sans' is followed by an infinitive in French where in English the present participle would be used e.g. without knowing, without looking.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Avant de passer un examen : prepositions with the infinitive

nodes.misconception: It is easy to predict the past participles of irregular verbs.
nodes.response: The past participles of irregular verbs must be learnt carefully. There are, however, similarities that are worth noting e.g. many irregular past participles end -u e.g. pu, voulu, cru, su.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On a fait les courses : irregular past participles, perfect tense modal verbs

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only used to describe how things were or used to be in the past.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense is also used to say what was happening when another thing occurred where it is used in combination with the perfect tense e.g. il regardait la télé quand son portable a sonné.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Je sortais la poubelle quand ... :perfect, imperfect, relative clauses, negation

nodes.misconception: The 'après avoir' + past participle structure applies to all verbs.
nodes.response: Verbs which take 'être' in the perfect tense use the structure 'après être' + past participle. The past participle must agree with the subject of the sentence e.g. Après être arrivée, elle a fait ses devoirs.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Après avoir préparé : après avoir + past participle

nodes.misconception: Verbs in French that relate to personal actions are only composed the same as in English.
nodes.response: Many verbs relating to daily routine are reflexive in French and require a reflexive pronoun to be used, e.g., 'je me lève'. This reflexive pronoun is not always used in English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une journée dans la vie d'un groupe francophone : reflexive pronouns

nodes.misconception: You must only use verbs in the same tense as the task question in your answer.
nodes.response: Students should practise combining different tenses of verbs when giving their answers (ensuring they give a relevant response to the task) in order to demonstrate a wider knowledge of language and to give a richer response.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: J'ai dû attendre : irregular past participles, modal verbs present and past

nodes.misconception: Verbs never change their spelling to agree for gender or number.
nodes.response: Past participles with 'être' verbs do agree for gender and number. Embedding this knowledge requires practice, a component of which can be practice of sound-symbol correspondences [i], [u], [é], [SFC], and [SFE].
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des auteurs francophones : perfect tense with 'être'

nodes.misconception: All French verbs use 'avoir' as the auxiliary to form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Verbs expressing changes of state, location or condition often use 'être' to form the perfect tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Qui a écrit ... ? Perfect tense with predictable and irregular past participles

nodes.misconception: The second element of the negative structure goes after the past participle when forming past tense phrases.
nodes.response: The second element of the negative structure is always placed after the auxiliary verb and before the past participle. This requires practice as students are likely to misapply the negative structure learned with present tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Qui a gagné ? Yes/no questions in the perfect tense

nodes.misconception: The negative structure ne ... personne is formed the same way as ne ... pas and ne ... jamais in the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Ne ... personne is unusual in that the second component (personne) comes after the past participle in the perfect tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Les champions du monde: negation in the perfect tense

nodes.misconception: The negative structure ne ... personne is formed the same way as ne ... pas and ne ... jamais in the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Personne goes after the past participle instead of after the auxiliary verb. Careful study and practice is required to master this structure.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le sport pour tous: negation in the perfect tense

nodes.misconception: Only irregular verbs such as 'faire' and 'avoir' have unusual past participles.
nodes.response: Verbs like 'ouvrir', 'traduire' and 'écrire' form their past participles differently to regular IR and RE verbs and should be seen as different types of verb when learning verb patterns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une écrivaine francophone: perfect tense verbs like ouvrir, écrire & traduire.

nodes.misconception: 'C'est' only translates to 'it is/that is'.
nodes.response: When talking about objects, 'c'est' translates to 'it is/that is' but when applied to people it can also mean 'he/she is'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Read about friends: feminisation of person nouns

nodes.misconception: In French, like in English, there is only one way to say 'the'.
nodes.response: There is more than one word to say 'the' in French. For singular masculine nouns, use 'le', and for singular feminine nouns, use 'la'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The person or a person? Singular definite articles 'le' and 'la'

nodes.misconception: There are just two words for 'the': a masculine and feminine version.
nodes.response: There are four different ways to say 'the' in French: 'le', 'las', 'les' and 'l'' (masculine singular, feminine singular, plural and preceding a vowel/h).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: More than one: plural nouns and plural definite article 'les'

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say 'it' in French.
nodes.response: In French, the word for 'it' changes depending on the grammatical gender of the noun it is replacing.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Write about a friend:  'il' and 'elle' meaning 'it'

nodes.misconception: There is no difference in French between the present and perfect tense forms 'I do' and 'I did', 'I say' and 'I said', because they sound the same.
nodes.response: The spellings of the past participles 'fait' and 'dit' are different to the first person (I) present tense but sound the same because of silent final consonants. Another difference is using 'j'ai' before past participles to say 'I did'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Today and yesterday: perfect tense with 'faire' and 'dire'

nodes.misconception: If you use inversion and add a question word, you don't need to change your intonation.
nodes.response: Even when using inversion and/or question words, still raise your voice at the end of a sentence in French when asking a question.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Weekday routine: inversion questions, negation

nodes.misconception: It is fine to use the infinitive next to the subject pronoun.
nodes.response: The infinitive is the dictionary form of the verb but verbs change ending to match their subject (I, you, she, he etc.). Regular -er verbs always add the same set of endings.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Weekday routine: -er verbs singular and plural

nodes.misconception: The perfect tense is made up of one part like it is in English.
nodes.response: You must have both parts of the perfect tense; the present tense of 'avoir' and a past participle. Regular past participles end in é.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Today and yesterday: perfect tense with 1st person -er verbs + avoir

nodes.misconception: There is just one equivalent tense in English to the perfect tense in French.
nodes.response: There are in fact two equivalent tenses in English to the perfect tense in French: the present perfect and the simple past. 'J'ai voyagé au Sénégal' can mean both 'I travelled to France' and 'I have travelled to France'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Senegal: perfect tense, inversion questions, negation 'ne... pas', 'ne … jamais'

nodes.misconception: The 'il' in 'il faut' means 'he'.
nodes.response: 'Il faut' is from the impersonal verb 'falloir' - 'to be necessary'.  'Il' does not mean 'he'; we translate 'il faut' as 'it is necessary' or 'you must'. It works like a modal verb in that it is usually followed by a 2nd verb in the infinitive form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Senegal: modals, 'il faut', possessive adjectives

nodes.misconception: Like non-person or object nouns, identity nouns exist in only one form and gender.
nodes.response: Unlike non-person or object nouns, identity nouns can have both masculine and feminine forms: le chrétien - la chrétienne. This is the same as other French person nouns you may know, e.g. le directeur/la directrice.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Religion in Francophonie: feminine and plural nouns

nodes.misconception: Like nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use lowercase letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un anglais.
nodes.response: Unlike nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use capital letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un Anglais.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Religion in Francophonie: singular 'croire', adjectives used as nouns

nodes.misconception: There is only one translation of a French infinitive into English.
nodes.response: An infinitive can be translated into English using the -ing form or 'to ...': conduire - to drive, driving.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Travel in France: more infinitive uses

nodes.misconception: Words ending in -c (like historic) also end in -c in French.
nodes.response: Words ending in -c in English often end in -que in French: historique.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Travel in France: infinitive used as a noun

nodes.misconception: Like the possessive adjectives 'mon' and 'ton', the possessive adjective 'leur' changes in the singular form based on the gender of the noun possessed.
nodes.response: Unlike the possessive adjectives 'mon' and 'ton', the possessive adjective 'leur' does not change in the singular form based on the gender of the noun possessed, it remains the same: leur chien, leur souris.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At a restaurant: possessives 'leur', 'leurs'

nodes.misconception: There is one way of saying 'your' in French.
nodes.response: 'Your' in French changes, depending on who you are talking to and what you are talking about. Use 'ton' (m), 'ta' (f) or 'tes' (pl) when talking to someone you know well. Use 'votre' (m/f) or 'vos' (mpl/fpl) when talking to someone formally.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At a hotel: possessives 'votre', 'vos'

nodes.misconception: 'Avoir' always means 'to have/having'.
nodes.response: Most of the time, we translate 'avoir' as 'to have/having' but there are expressions, where we would use the verb to be in English, where French uses 'avoir', usually expressing feelings/states e.g 'avoir froid', to be cold.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: My everyday: 'avoir' and 'être' for feelings and states

nodes.misconception: Knowing the lower numbers is enough to be able to tell the time in French.
nodes.response: As French uses 24-hour clock more than English and gives the minutes after the hour, you need to know numbers 1-59 well.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: My everyday: numbers 32-69, time

nodes.misconception: When using 'venir de' (to have just), the next word needs to be a past participle, like in English.
nodes.response: In French, 'venir de' is like every other French verb followed by 'de'. It is always followed by a second verb in the infinitive.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Notre planète est en crise : infinitives as nouns, 'en train de' and 'venir de'

nodes.misconception: When writing, talking about what someone does, has done using a text written in the first person for information, only the subject pronoun needs to be changed in each sentence.
nodes.response: When writing, talking in the third person using a text in the first person for information, change the subject pronoun, verb, object pronouns and possessive adjectives (words like 'my', 'your', 'his', 'her').
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La journée d'un jeune migrant : Extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: The subject of a sentence can only be a noun or pronoun.
nodes.response: A verb can be used as the subject of a sentence. In French, it must be in its infinitive form. When translated to English, use the -ing form of the verb.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Il faut agir : Infinitives as nouns

nodes.misconception: Silent final consonants are always silent.
nodes.response: The liaison rule means that Silent Final Consonants are pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel sound (including silent h).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mon voyage dangereux : Direct and indirect object pronouns in the past tense

nodes.misconception: The noun 'un être', meaning 'a being', changes to 'une être' when referring to a girl or woman. 'Un être humain' changes to 'une être humaine' in the feminine.
nodes.response: The noun 'être' is masculine, even when referring to a girl or a woman. The phrase 'un être humain', 'a human being', refers to both genders.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mon voyage dangereux : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: When using 'depuis' (for, since), sentences are framed in the past in French.
nodes.response: In French, when using 'depuis' to describe an action that started in the past but continues today, frame the sentence in the present tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des histoires diverses : Present tense with 'depuis'

nodes.misconception: There is only one word for "it" in French.
nodes.response: Nouns are either masculine or feminine. "It", when replacing a noun, also has a masculine and feminine form. Use 'le' for masculine nouns and 'la' for femnine nouns. 'Le' and 'la' shorten to 'l'' when the next word starts with a vowel sound.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Il m'a aidé : Direct and indirect object pronouns in the past tense

nodes.misconception: All similar looking French and English words have the same meaning.
nodes.response: Often, French words have multiple meanings and it is important to choose the right one for the given context e.g. 'durable' means durable and sustainable.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un problème écologique : Extended writing and speaking, photo description

nodes.misconception: The perfect tense can only be translated as what happened in French.
nodes.response: The perfect tense refers to the past in two ways: what happened and what has happened. Context tells us the intended meaning. 'Hier, je suis allé en ville' - yesterday I went to town. 'Je suis déjà allé à Paris' - I have already been to Paris.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ils sont venus à Paris : Present perfect

nodes.misconception: The singular forms of the verb 'faire' are spelled the same way because they are pronounced the same way.
