nodes.response: The singular forms of the verb 'faire' are spelled differently, but sound the same because the 's' and 't' are silent final consonants (SFC).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What someone does: 'faire' singular persons

nodes.misconception: The verb 'faire' only has a single definition.
nodes.response: The verb 'faire' is used to translate two key verbs in English, both 'to do' and 'to make'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What someone does: intonation questions with 'quoi'

nodes.misconception: I need to translate the word 'did' when I form a question in French.
nodes.response: To form a question in French, you can either raise your voice at the end of a statement to form an intonation question, or you can add 'est-ce que' at the beginning of a sentence. There is no French equivalent for 'did' in a question.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Geneva: perfect tense intonation and 'est-ce' que questions

nodes.misconception: I don't need to plan my written work before I start writing in French.
nodes.response: Planning is essential for success in any written task. Using a content and language checklist helps us to plan, improve and check our drafted written work.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Astronauts and French cuisine: writing an article

nodes.misconception: I can express 'this' for all masculine nouns with 'ce'.
nodes.response: There is another way of expressing 'this' in French for masculine nouns, which is 'cet', this is for masculine nouns beginning with a vowel or an 'h'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Brussels: perfect tense intonation questions

nodes.misconception: I pronounce [r] the same in French as in English.
nodes.response: The SSC [r] is very different in French. It is a raspy sound from the back of your throat like the [r] in 'rue'. It does require quite a lot of practice to master this sound.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Brussels: perfect tense -er verbs 1st and 2nd persons singular

nodes.misconception: The [o] sound in French is only pronounced one way.
nodes.response: The [o] sound in French can be open, like the [o] in 'porte' and 'd'accord' or closed like the [o] in 'radio' or 'dos'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Astronauts and French cuisine: extended reading

nodes.misconception: The closed [eu] and the open [eu/œu] sounds are the same.
nodes.response: There are open vowel sounds and closed vowel sounds in French. The closed [eu] sound is like the [eu] in 'peu', it is short and sharp. The open [eu/oœu] sound is a longer sound like the [œu] in 'sœur'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Switzerland: perfect tense singular -er verbs

nodes.misconception: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is and there was in descriptions of singular things.
nodes.response: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is or there are and there was and there were. They stay the same if you are talking about one thing or more than one.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Geneva: 'il y a' and 'il y avait'

nodes.misconception: I have to translate 'didn't' into French.
nodes.response: There is no direct translation for 'didn't' in French. Using 'ne ... pas' with the perfect tense expresses the equivalent of  'didn't' in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Switzerland: perfect tense negation

nodes.misconception: All regular verbs have a past participle ending in 'é', 'u' or 'i'.
nodes.response: There are other groups of regular verbs with different endings to the main -er, -re, -ir groups. These verbs are very commonly used and students should practise them regularly.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le langage cinématographique : past participles of regular verbs

nodes.misconception: There is no agreement needed with 'avoir' verb past participles in the passive voice.
nodes.response: Because the passive voice uses 'être', all past participles used must agree in number and gender with the noun subject, including 'avoir' verbs. E.g. La fille est choisie par le réalisateur.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une critique d'un film : extended writing

nodes.misconception: Past participle agreement only occurs in the perfect tense.
nodes.response: In the passive voice, all past participles are combined with a form of 'être'. As such, past participle agreement rules apply to all verbs. E.g 'La scène est critiquée par le journaliste'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Les thèmes du film : the passive voice

nodes.misconception: You can just learn set sentences by heart and produce them mechanically when requested.
nodes.response: Both writing and speaking must be adapted to the question and have a level of personalisation and spontaneity.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un membre de la famille que j'admire : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: Adjectives ending in -al take -s to create the masculine plural form.
nodes.response: Adjectives ending in -al need a spelling change to create the masculine plural form. Remove the -l and add -ux for example 'familial' - 'familiaux' in the masculine plural form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La valeur de la famille : feminine adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: Plural possessive adjectives agree with gender.
nodes.response: Plural possessive adjectives only agree with number.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'arrivée d'un réfugié chez nous : articles and possessive adjectives

nodes.misconception: The verbs refuser, demander, essayer, laisser and éviter, are followed directly by an infinitive e.g. éviter faire (to avoid doing), refuser faire (to refuse to do).
nodes.response: These verbs are followed by 'de' plus an infinitive e.g. éviter de faire (to avoid doing), refuser de faire (to refuse to do).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Conflits et solutions en famille : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: The only way to form the singular of a feminine noun is to add -e. The only way to form the plural of a noun is to add -s.
nodes.response: There are 4 ways to form feminine nouns which need careful practice. Similarly, there is more than one way to form plural nouns depending upon the final letter of the singular noun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: C'est de famille ! Gender and number agreement with nouns

nodes.misconception: Adjectives only have one possible translation.
nodes.response: In French, adjectives can be used as a noun. When preceded by a definite article, they are often translated as the (adjective) one e.g. le bleu is translated as the blue one, not blue or the blue.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un bon déjeuner familial : adjectives used as nouns and position of adjectives

nodes.misconception: You need to include 'pas' when using a negative subject pronoun.
nodes.response: The whole negative meaning is contained in the negative subject pronoun (rien or personne) with 'ne' before the following verb. An additional negative element is not necessary e.g. Personne ne mange sainement - nobody eats healthily.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Manger équilibré : negative subject pronouns

nodes.misconception: 'Plusieurs' and 'chaque' have singular and plural forms.
nodes.response: 'Plusieurs' is always written with an 's' and introduces a plural noun e.g. plusieurs problèmes. 'Chaque' is always written in the singular and introduces a singular noun e.g. chaque problème.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Il faut éviter : indefinite, demonstrative and interrogative adjectives

nodes.misconception: The expression 'j'ai mal' only means 'I have a pain'.
nodes.response: The French expression 'avoir mal' covers a number of symptoms which might be variously translated into English as an ache, a pain and sore or hurting body parts. Students should think about what sounds most natural when translating into English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: J'ai mal ... : irregular verbs in the present tense

nodes.misconception: 'Il' always means 'he' in English.
nodes.response: Impersonal verbs nearly always have the subject 'il'. This translates as 'it' instead of 'he' e.g. il fait beau - it is nice weather.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On se bouge ! Impersonal verbs

nodes.misconception: Use 'ne ... pas' to mean 'no, not one, not any'.
nodes.response: The structure 'ne ... pas' is used to negative a verb. To say that there was 'no, not one, not any' of a noun, use the structure 'ne ... aucun/e' e.g. il n'y a aucun fruit ici.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La santé n'a aucun prix : negative adjective determiner

nodes.misconception: An extended 150-word writing task should be planned as one complete task.
nodes.response: It is helpful to break down an extended writing task into two paragraphs and then to further break down those paragraphs. This allows students to manage the length of the task by treating it as four smaller connected tasks.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Faire de bons choix : extended writing

nodes.misconception: Word order with adverbs is the same in French and English.
nodes.response: Word order with adverbs is sometimes the same and sometimes different in French and English. Think about whether the adverb is a how/how often or a where/when adverb to know where to place it in French.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: When, where and how? Singular verbs like 'sortir', 'venir', adverb placement

nodes.misconception: All adjectives come after the noun they describe in French.
nodes.response: Most adjectives follow the noun they describe, but not adjectives of beauty, age, goodness and size, which come before like English adjectives.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What is it like? Singular verbs like 'dire' and 'prendre', adjectives

nodes.misconception: After faire, use the definite article in French.
nodes.response: Many activities such as doing homework or cooking are followed by the definite article, but sports activities with faire are followed by the partitive article e.g. 'je fais du vélo'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Shopping and other activities: 'faire' and 'de', questions with 'quels, quelles'

nodes.misconception: Articles can be missed out in French like in English.
nodes.response: Articles can't be omitted in French. Use the definite article with specific nouns/giving opinions and the partitive article with uncountable and non-specific nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Food and drink: definite and partitive articles

nodes.misconception: The sound 's' is always pronounced the same in French.
nodes.response: There are two 's' sounds, the hard 's' sound which sounds like a 'z', found between two vowels, including in liaisons and the soft 's' found in other words, often at the beginning, of words, between consonants and as a double 's'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Where is that? prepositions with 'de'

nodes.misconception: Ne ... pas goes around the main verb (the past participle) in perfect tense sentences.
nodes.response: Just like in other double verb sentences, ne...pas goes around the first verb; in the perfect tense, that's the conjugated form of 'avoir'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A typical day: partitive, liaison, perfect tense questions

nodes.misconception: 'Des' always means 'some'.
nodes.response: 'Des' is the word for 'some' but is also a form of the preposition 'de' before plural nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Who likes doing what? 'jouer' with 'à' and 'de'

nodes.misconception: Always use the partitive article after food and drink items, even with negative sentences.
nodes.response: The partitive article changes to 'de' to say what you don't eat and drink e.g. 'je ne mange pas de pizza'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Food and drink: 'boire' singular, write about own eating routines

nodes.misconception: Only change your main verb into a past verb in French like we can do in English to form the past tense, e.g. I do → I did.
nodes.response: In French you need two verbs in the perfect tense for it to make sense; the correct part of 'avoir' and the past participle.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A typical day: perfect tense, 'jouer', 'faire', jobs

nodes.misconception: 'Some' can be left out in French just like it can in English.
nodes.response: Always use an article before food nouns in French, if it is a whole item, use the indefinite article and if it's uncountable or part of an item, use the partitive article du, de la or de l'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Food shopping: partitive articles 'du, de la, de l', des'

nodes.misconception: Use the partitive article with all uncountable nouns, even negatives.
nodes.response: After quantities and negatives use 'de/d' instead of the partitive article. E.g Il y a beaucoup de riz. Il n'y a pas de riz.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Winter celebrations: partitive articles

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in French.
nodes.response: Most adjectives go after the noun they describe but there are a group of adjectives (BRAGS adjectives) that go before the noun. We call these pre-nominal adjectives.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas around the world: adjectives, comparatives

nodes.misconception: The articles le/la/l'/les and un/une can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use the definite article (le/la/l'/les) for specific nouns and the indefinite article (un/une) for non-specific nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Write a poem: using 'comme' in French similes

nodes.misconception: Colours are always nouns.
nodes.response: Colours can be used as nouns or adjectives. When used as adjectives, they must agree with the noun they are describing e.g. une chose bleue.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Sept Couleurs Magiques (Mymi Doinet)

nodes.misconception: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French reading exam.
nodes.response: Regularly revising vocabulary is an excellent method of preparation for the reading exam as well as being mindful of strategies such as spotting distractors and using synonyms to find the correct answer.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'histoire du Québec : pronouns, extended reading (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Use the same articles for nouns after negative structures.
nodes.response: After a negative structure (e.g. 'je n'ai pas'), indefinite and partitive articles change to 'de', e.g. 'je n'ai pas d'information' - 'I don't have any information'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'histoire du Québec : articles and imperfect tense, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: It is acceptable to only give short answers in the conversation element of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: Students should focus on giving answers in conversation that include at least three verb clauses. They should also regularly practise developing their answers with different verb tenses, subjects, opinions and reasons.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un ado francophone : present and perfect tense, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can't use the imperfect and perfect tenses together.
nodes.response: The two past tenses work together well to give a full description of past events. Use the perfect tense for completed actions and the imperfect to describe what things were like.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le Québec : relative clauses, perfect and imperfect, extended writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can't use the imperfect and perfect tenses together.
nodes.response: The two past tenses work together well to give a full description of past events. Use the perfect tense for completed actions and the imperfect to describe what things were like.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le Québec : relative clauses, perfect and imperfect, extended writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: The present continous in English has a direct translation in French.
nodes.response: Students need to take care to translate both the simple present and the present continous with the present tense in French e.g. I listen and I am listening are translated exactly the same way: j'écoute.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un ado francophone : present tense, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: All masculine nouns are made feminine by adding 'e' and plural by adding 's'.
nodes.response: A masculine noun can be made feminine by changing the article, adding 'e', changing 'eur' to 'ice' or 'n' to 'nne'. Nouns can be made plural by adding 's' or 'aux'. Nouns ending in 's' or 'x' don't have a plural form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Cannes : noun formation, extended reading (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can only answer conversation questions in the same tense as the question.
nodes.response: After responding appropriately to the initial question, it is a good idea to use different tenses in your answer to develop your response and to give interesting detail.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Cannes : past versus present, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Use the same articles for nouns after negative structures.
nodes.response: After a negative structures (e.g. 'je n'ai pas'), indefinite and partitive articles change to 'de', e.g. 'je n'ai pas d'information' - 'I don't have any information'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'histoire du Québec : articles and imperfect tense, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Cannes : reflexive verbs, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: All masculine nouns are made feminine by adding 'e' and plural by adding 's'.
nodes.response: A masculine noun can be made feminine by changing the article, adding 'e', changing 'eur' to 'ice' or 'n' to 'nne'. Nouns can be made plural by adding 's' or 'aux'. Nouns ending in 's' or 'x' don't have a plural form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Cannes : noun formation, extended reading (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: It is acceptable to only give short answers in the conversation element of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: Students should focus on giving answers in conversation that include at least three verb clauses. They should also regularly practise developing their answers with different verb tenses, subjects, opinions and reasons.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un ado francophone: present and perfect tense, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: There are only three types of regular verbs and they form their past participles in the same way.
nodes.response: There are distinct groups of 'ir' and 're' verbs which form their past participles differently from the regular pattern (-i, -u). Students will find it beneficial to learn these verbs together as a group.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un ado francophone : perfect tense, dictation, listening (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Cannes : reflexive verbs, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The present continous in English has a direct translation in French.
nodes.response: Students need to take care to translate both the simple present and the present continous with the present tense in French e.g. I listen and I am listening are translated exactly the same way: j'écoute.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un ado francophone : present tense, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French reading exam.
nodes.response: Regularly revising vocabulary is an excellent method of preparation for the reading exam as well as being mindful of strategies such as spotting distractors and using synonyms to find the correct answer.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'histoire de Québec: subject, object, and emphatic pronouns (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: There are only three types of regular verbs and they form their past participles in the same way.
nodes.response: There are distinct groups of 'ir' and 're' verbs which form their past participles differently from the regular pattern (-i, -u). Students will find it beneficial to learn these verbs together as a group.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un ado francophone : perfect tense, dictation, listening (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can only answer conversation questions in the same tense as the question.
nodes.response: After responding appropriately to the initial question, it is a good idea to use different tenses in your answer to develop your response and to give interesting detail.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Cannes : past versus present, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: In French the idea of 'best' and 'worst' is translated as 'plus bon' or 'plus mauvais'.
nodes.response: Just as in English, the French for 'best' and 'worst' are irregular adjectives and need to be learned carefully to avoid misunderstanding.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: C'est ma passion: comparative and superlative adjectives

nodes.misconception: Superlative sentences have the same word order in English and French.
nodes.response: Take care when writing or translating superlative sentences as the French word order differs quite significantly from English, e.g., 'the most interesting lesson' > 'the lesson the most interesting'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mes préférences au collège : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: 'Mieux' and 'plus mal/moins bien' can be used interchangeably with 'le mieux' and 'le plus mal' or ''le moins bien'.
nodes.response: 'Le mieux' and 'le plus mal'/'le moins bien' are superlative adverbs to describe actions as '(the) best' or '(the) worst'. 'Mieux' and 'moins bien'/'plus mal'  describe actions as 'better' or 'less well'/'worse' and are comparative adverbs.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mieux et le mieux : comparative and superlative adverbs

nodes.misconception: [qu] is pronounced the same in French and in English.
nodes.response: [qu] is pronounced differently in French and in English. It is important to to recognise and pronounce sound-spelling links correctly to understand and be understood by other French speakers.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Les matières les plus utiles: comparative and superlative adjectives

nodes.misconception: Students should develop their answers in role play tasks.
nodes.response: In role play tasks, students should concentrate on clearly communicating the stated information in a complete phrase and with conjugated verbs. There is no advantage to developing their answer further than is required.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: L'école chez nous: extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: The words 'meilleur' and 'mieux' can be used interchangeably as they both translate the English word 'better'.
nodes.response: 'Meilleur' is an adjective and can only be used to describe nouns. 'Mieux' is an adverb and can only be used to describe verbs.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Forces et faiblesses au collège: comparative and superlative adverbs

nodes.misconception: French infinitive verbs can only be translated by the 'to - ' structure in English.
nodes.response: The infinitive verb can be translated as 'to -' or '-ing' e.g. 'to do' or 'doing'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people like doing: 2-verb phrases with 'aimer'

nodes.misconception: It is possible to leave 'que' out in French like it is in English.
nodes.response: Even if we would not translate 'que' (that) in English, in French we always need to put it when we mean 'think that'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions towards others: Malala, singular -er verbs with preposition 'à'

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' always means 'to do' or 'to make'.
nodes.response: 'Faire' has lots of different meanings, including 'to go, going'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do: 'faire', meaning 'go'

nodes.misconception: Use the infinitive with 'je'.
nodes.response: The long form of the verb (infinitive) means -to or -ing so it needs changing for the correct subject pronoun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do: regular singular -er verbs

nodes.misconception: 'En' always means 'in'.
nodes.response: Many words in French have more than one meaning. 'En' means 'in' and 'by'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do: 'en', meaning 'in' and 'by'

nodes.misconception: Like in English, French has two present tenses.
nodes.response: There is no 'be -ing' in French. There is only one present tense for both the simple present and continuous present.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions: singular -er verbs in simple present and present continuous

nodes.misconception: Like in English, 'sans' is followed by the -ing form of a verb in French.
nodes.response: In French, 'sans' is followed by the infinitive form of a verb, e.g. 'elle part sans dire un mot' - 'she leaves without saying a word'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: plural verbs like 'sortir' and 'venir', 'sans' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: We need to use the future tense in French to describe future activities.
nodes.response: The present tense can be used with time adverbs to describe a future activity. For example, 'Mardi je vais chez Léa.' means: 'This coming Tuesday I am going to Léa's house.'. This is a future activity but the present tense has been used here.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Every week and this weekend: present tense with future meaning, 'choisir' verbs

nodes.misconception: The 3rd person plural 'they' form of the verb 'sortir' is 'sorent' and of the verb 'venir' is 'vienent'.
nodes.response: The verb 'sortir' keeps its 't' to become 'sortent' and the verb 'venir' doubles its 'n' to become 'viennent'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: more practice with plural -IR verbs

nodes.misconception: The [y] sound is the same in French as it does in English.
nodes.response: The English [y] has two different sounds, as in 'myth', a short 'i' sound, and 'cycling' where it sounds like the word 'eye'. The French [y] sounds like the SSC [i] as in 'midi'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: School life: singular verbs like 'choisir', questions with 'qui'

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to say please to a person in French: 's'il vous plait'.
nodes.response: There are two ways to say please in French: 'sil vous plait' for someone you don't know very well or someone in a position of responsibility like your teacher. But for friends and family you use 's'il te plait'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: formal 'you' and informal plural 'vous'

nodes.misconception: The pronoun 'on' only means 'people in general'.
nodes.response: The pronoun 'on' does mean 'people in general' but it is often used to mean 'we' in informal conversations, like when you are talking to friends. You will have seen this meaning before in the phrase 'on y va !' which means 'let's go!'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: 'on' meaning 'we'

nodes.misconception: All school systems are roughly the same.
nodes.response: School systems around the world can be quite different. For example in France you don't go to school on a Wednesday afternoon and you don't wear school uniform!
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: School life in France

nodes.misconception: All I need to know about [h] in French is that it is silent.
nodes.response: The rules of liaison and elision apply to the French silent [h]. Before a word starting with [h], if a word ends with an SFC, the consonant is pronounced (liaison) and words like 'le' and 'que' replace their final letter with an apostrophe (elision).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Every week and this weekend: more practice with plural verbs like 'choisir'

nodes.misconception: 'Qui' is always used as a question word.
nodes.response: 'Qui' is a question word meaning 'who' but is also used as a relative pronoun to introduce a relative clause, for example 'L'homme qui est grand est mon papa', meaning 'the man who is tall is my dad'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Free time: relative pronoun 'qui'

nodes.misconception: The letter 'e' is always pronounced the same in French.
nodes.response: The letter 'e' is often pronounced as the 'e' in 'je' is but can be pronounced like [è/ê]. Pronounce 'e' like [è/ê] before double consonants and the letters c/l if they are in the last syllable.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: New Year: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'

nodes.misconception: Always use the verb 'avoir' to help you form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Remember - for movement verbs and 'rester' use 'être', instead of 'avoir', to help you form the perfect tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Song: J'ai cherché

nodes.misconception: Use subject pronouns after prepositions to link nouns/pronouns.
nodes.response: Use the emphatic pronouns 'moi' and 'toi' instead of subject pronouns to link and emphasise nouns/pronouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A theft: emphatic pronouns 'moi' and 'toi' after prepositions

nodes.misconception: 'Mettre' is a verb like 'entendre' and it follows the same pattern.
nodes.response: 'Mettre' has the same present tense endings as verbs like 'entendre' but the stem is different in the singular forms. Drop one of the 't's from the infinitive, leaving the remaining 't' as a silent final consonant.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Free time: verbs + 'de' or 'à' + noun

nodes.misconception: Learning genders is not as important as learning the noun itself.
nodes.response: Leaning the genders of words is essential because it affects other parts of the sentence such as which form of 'à/de' to use before a noun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A theft: verbs with 'à' and 'de' before the noun

nodes.misconception: 'S' always sounds the same in French.
nodes.response: The 's' at the beginning of words and double 's' is a soft sound but 's' between two consonants is [s], pronounced as in 'maison'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Accidents and emergencies: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'

nodes.misconception: Always use the verb 'avoir' to help you form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Remember - for movement verbs and 'rester' use 'être', instead of 'avoir', to help you form the perfect tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: New Year in Algeria: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'

nodes.misconception: Adverbs always come in the same place in a sentence.
nodes.response: The type of adverb tells us where to place it. When and where adverbs usually come at the beginning or end of a sentence and how (often) adverbs usaully come straight after the first verb in a sentence.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The French Revolution: present and perfect tenses, 'ne…jamais'

nodes.misconception: Every 's' at the end of a word is silent because of the silent final consonant rule.
nodes.response: Usually 's' is silent at the end of a word but if the next word starts with a vowel, you usually hear liaison, whereby the final consonant is pronounced.  When the final consonat is 's', it sounds like the hard 's' in 'maison'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Emergency services: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'

nodes.misconception: All past participles are formed in the same way.
nodes.response: Regular -er verb past participles are formed by changing the -er at the end of the infinitive to é but there are other past participle patterns such as verbs like prendre changing to 'pris' and some irregular past participles.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The French revolution: perfect tense, questions, 'ne … pas'

nodes.misconception: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
nodes.response: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mes études : present and future, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Infinitive verbs are only used when they follow a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: When an infinitive is used at the start of a clause, it becomes a noun, e.g. 'Étudier est un bon moyen de trouver un meilleur emploi.'. ('Studying is a good way to find a better job.')
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: À l'université : infinitive as noun, conditional verbs, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French listening exam.
nodes.response: Students with a firm knowledge of French SSCs and strong vocabulary recall will find the listening exam less daunting. It is important to listen actively and use strategies for success such as awareness of distractors and synonyms.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Au collège : prepositions, transcription and listening (AQA)

nodes.misconception: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
nodes.response: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Mes études : present and future, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French listening exam.
nodes.response: Students with a firm knowledge of French SSCs and strong vocabulary recall will find the listening exam less daunting. It is important to listen actively and use strategies for success such as awareness of distractors and synonyms.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Au collège : prepositions, transcription, listening (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Infinitive verbs are only used when they follow a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: When an infinitive is used at the start of a clause, it becomes a noun, e.g. 'Étudier est un bon moyen de trouver un meilleur emploi.'. ('Studying is a good way to find a better job.')
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: À l'université : infinitive as noun, conditional verbs, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Verbs with 'de' e.g. 'persuader de', 'conseiller de' do not need to be followed by a second verb in its infinitive form.
nodes.response: All French verbs with 'de' are always followed by a second verb in its infinitive form. There may be a preposition or an object pronoun between the two verbs but a second verb in its infinitive form will always follow.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une orientation qui m'attire : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: All words ending in -ment are adverbs.
nodes.response: Whilst many words ending in -ment are adverbs where the feminine form of the adjective has been taken and -ment added to create the adverb, not all words ending in -ment are adverbs. Some nouns end in -ment e.g. 'le règlement' rule, regulation.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On cherche un boulot : adjectives into adverbs

nodes.misconception: 'Devoir' (must) and 'pouvoir' (can) do not require the second verb to be in the infinitive form because an infinitive is not required in English.
nodes.response: 'Devoir' means to have (to) and 'pouvoir' means to be able. Therefore, when followed by a second verb, this verb must always be in the infinitive form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un travail bien fait : modal verbs in present tense

nodes.misconception: When saying what you would like to do, a French word for 'would' is needed before the verb 'aimer' to like.
nodes.response: In French, to say what you would like to do, use the conditional stem of the verb vouloir together with the appropriate ending - -ais for 'je' and 'tu', -ait for 'il' and 'elle'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Les orientations professionnelles : present modals, conditional with vouloir

nodes.misconception: To create antonyms in French, always add the prefix in- to the start of an adjective or adverb e.g. 'utile' becomes 'inutile'.
nodes.response: Some antonyms are formed by adding the prefix im-. This is when the original word begins with p, b or m: possible become impossible; buvable (drinkable) becomes imbuvable (undrinkable); 'mature' becomes 'immature'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Les pour et les contre d'un travail : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: The letter x in the words 'sixième' and 'dixième' is pronounced the same as in English.
nodes.response: The letter x is pronounced as z due to liaison in these words and should be carefully practised to develop an authentic pronunciation.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Comment se mettre au travail ? Word patterns

nodes.misconception: There is just one way of saying 'you' in French like in English.
nodes.response: There are two ways of saying 'you' in French. We use 'tu' for 'you singular' and 'vous' for 'you plural'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Talk to others: -er verbs 2nd persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is pronounced.
nodes.response: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is not pronounced. It is therefore difficult to tell the difference between the 'il/elle' form and the 'ils/elles' form of verbs when spoken.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand what others do: -er verbs 3rd persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: When forming questions, we have to translate 'do you' into French.
nodes.response: There is no phrase for 'do you' in French; we can use intonation instead to form questions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ask others: -er verbs 2nd persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: All verbs in the 'nous' form end in -ons.
nodes.response: Some verbs like 'manger' behave a little differently. The 'nous' form of 'manger' is 'mangeons' so that the g sound remains soft.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What you do with others: -er verbs 1st persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: Préféré(e) is often spelt wrong, with not enough, or indeed too many accents!
nodes.response: 'Préféré' is favourite in its masculine form. The e that is added in the feminine form does not have an accent; 'préférée'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What you do with others: -er verbs and favourite things

nodes.misconception: I still need to use the subject pronoun even if I am using a name or a noun before the verb form.
nodes.response: A noun or name can replace a subject pronoun. So 'ils chantent ensemble' could be changed to 'les garçons chantent ensemble' or 'David, Robert et Jacques chantent ensemble'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Talk about what others do: -er verbs 3rd persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense formation is different for ir/re verbs.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense is formed exactly the same way as with -er verbs. Take the present tense nous form, remove -ons and add the imperfect endings.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Childhood: then and now: key - RE and -IR verbs in the imperfect tense

nodes.misconception: 'Il y a' always means 'there is/are'.
nodes.response: 'Il y a ' does mean 'there is/are' when followed by a noun but it means 'ago' when it is followed by a time like in the sentence 'Il y a deux ans, j'ai visité Londres' meaning 'Two years ago, I visited London'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Childhood: present and imperfect tenses, 'il y a' meaning 'ago'

nodes.misconception: Add 'ième' to make all ordinal numbers.
nodes.response: Add 'ième' to make the majority of ordinal numbers but 'first' (premier/première) is an exception and cardinal numbers ending -e, drop the final -e before adding 'ième'. There are a few other spelling exceptions like 'neuvième' and 'cinquième'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Primary and secondary school: -er verbs imperfect tense, ordinal numbers

nodes.misconception: [ai] and [é] sound the same in French.
nodes.response: In some regional accents  [ai] and [é] can sound similar.  Officially there is a difference in pronunciation and meaning as the ending of the imperfect tense is supposed to be pronounced [ai], whereas a common ending of the past participle is [é].
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Montreal - a diverse city: imperfect tense singular

nodes.misconception: All -re and -ir verbs follow the same pattern.
nodes.response: There are different groups of -ir and -re verbs that follow slightly different patterns. It's good to revisit these regularly in their own right and because they can help with other tenses.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Celebrities: perfect and imperfect

nodes.misconception: School years work the same in English and French.
nodes.response: French uses 'la' before ordinal numbers for school years, the lower the number, the higher the school year e.g. 'sixième' is equivalent to Y7 and 'cinquième' is Y8. Use 'en' to say you're in a school year e.g. 'en sixième'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: School in France - then and now: -er verbs imperfect tense

nodes.misconception: Past participles with 'être' don't change, just like past participles with 'avoir'.
nodes.response: Past participles with 'être' always agree in gender and number with the subject. Add 'e' to agree a feminine past participle and 's' to agree a plural past participle.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Spring holidays: perfect tense with 'être', pronouns 'moi', 'toi', 'qui'

nodes.misconception: You can use a time phrase to show whether you mean a completed action in the past or a regular past event/activity.
nodes.response: In French, the verb alone already shows whether you mean a completed action in the past (use the formation rule for the perfect tense) or a regular past event/activity (use the formation rule for the imperfect tense). Time phrases can also be added.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Montreal - habitual and one-off past events: imperfect and perfect

nodes.misconception: Add -s to all adjectives in the plural form.
nodes.response: Most adjectives do need an 's' in the plural form, but there are exceptions. Masculine adjectives ending -eux don't change at all and those ending -al change to -aux in the plural form. The feminine plural versions of these adjectives are regular.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Fire at the zoo! Plural adjectives

nodes.misconception: All adjectives are postnominal in French; they come after the noun.
nodes.response: Most adjectives in French come after the noun but there are a group of prenominal adjectives. We use BRAGS to remember that adjectives of Beauty, Rank, Age, Goodness and Size come before the noun like adjectives in English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: In the headlines: pre- and postnominal adjectives

nodes.misconception: Add -s to make all nouns plural in French.
nodes.response: Many nouns do need an -s in the plural form but masculine nouns ending in -eau or -eu need -x adding in the plural form, and there are other exceptions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: A day in the life of a journalist: plural masculine nouns '-x' and '-aux'

nodes.misconception: Adjectives follow the same order and punctuation as in English.
nodes.response: If there is more than one adjective in a sentence, adjectives after the noun are separated by ‘et’. BRAGS adjectives go before the noun and do not need ‘et’. In some sentences, there are adjectives surrounding the noun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Descriptions with multiple adjectives

nodes.misconception: 'Que' can be used in a subject-relative clause, e.g. 'le prof que s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.'.
nodes.response: 'Que' introduces an object-relative clause where a new subject and verb is used, e.g. 'la voiture que je voudrais est très chère'. 'Que' shortens to 'qu'' in front of a vowel.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des industries françaises : relative clauses

nodes.misconception: The relative pronouns 'qui' and 'que' can be used interchangeably to translate 'that', 'which' or 'who/whom'.
nodes.response: Use 'qui' to introduce a subject-relative clause. Use 'que' to introduce an object-relative clause.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une industrie qui m'intéresse: extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: 'Chaque' and 'plusieurs' change form and can be written as 'chaques' and 'plusieur'.
nodes.response: The indefinite adjectives 'chaque' and 'plusieurs' are invariable and only have the one form. As they are highly useful, encourage students to use them frequently in their work.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Quelques difficultés au travail : past tense questions, indefinite adjectives

nodes.misconception: Que can be used in a subject relative clause e.g. le prof que s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.
nodes.response: When the relative clause introduces a verb to describe a subject, 'qui' must be used and not 'que'. E.g. le prof qui s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Travailler en France: questions in present tense, relative clauses

nodes.misconception: The 'vous' form of address is only used for plural situations.
nodes.response: In formal situations, it is essential to address somebody as 'vous' in order to be polite and to show respect. Careful consideration of the context of a conversation is very important.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Je voudrais postuler : extended speaking, role-play

nodes.misconception: The same imperative form of a verb is used for both 'tu' and 'vous'.
nodes.response: There are separate imperative forms for 'tu' and 'vous' which must be used in exactly the same way as in conversation i.e. formal or information situations and singular and plural subjects.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Le chef : voir, boire, croire and faire in present, the imperative

nodes.misconception: The subject pronoun is used with the verb to make an imperative.
nodes.response: Imperative instructions do not include the subject pronoun e.g. Écoute ! Écoutez !
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Collègues et amis : the imperative

nodes.misconception: [ch] is pronounced the same in French as it is in English.
nodes.response: [ch] is a softer sound in French and students will need directed practice in order to pronounce it correctly. It is more like the sound 'sh' in English.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Au boulot : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: [qu] is pronounced the same way in French as in English.
nodes.response: In French, [qu] is always a hard sound and must be carefully practised in order to ensure clear communication with French speakers.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Quel boulot ? past tense questions; interrogative and demonstrative adjectives

nodes.misconception: Use one preposition for 'in' like in English.
nodes.response: There are a number of prepositions for 'in', depending on the number and gender of the noun. Use 'en' for feminine countries, à for cities, au with masculine nouns, à la with feminine nouns and aux with plural nouns and countries.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: New places: 'aller' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: Adverbs have the same word order in French as they do in English in two-verb sentences.
nodes.response: Adverbs that tell us 'how' and 'how often' come before the infinitive e.g. 'Elle peut souvent visiter les musées'. 'Tu ne peux pas encore visiter Alger.'
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: In Paris: 'vouloir' and 'devoir'

nodes.misconception: There is a direct translation in French of the English verbs 'must' and 'can'.
nodes.response: The idea of 'must' is conveyed by the verb 'devoir' (to have to do something). 'Can' is expressed with 'pouvoir' (to be able to do something).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: En ligne : Impersonal and modal verbs, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: The more times I read the text, the better I’ll understand it.
nodes.response: Re-reading without purpose doesn’t necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc., are more effective.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: En ligne : Reading aloud, extended reading (AQA)

nodes.misconception: There is a direct translation in French of the English verbs 'must' and 'can'.
nodes.response: The idea of 'must' is conveyed by the verb 'devoir' (to have to do something). 'Can' is expressed with 'pouvoir' (to be able to do something).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: En ligne : impersonal and modal verbs, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The more times I read the text, the better I’ll understand it.
nodes.response: Re-reading without purpose doesn’t necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc., are more effective.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: En ligne : Reading aloud, extended reading (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: In French there is a word for 'do/does' in yes/no questions.
nodes.response: The English verb 'do/does' isn't translated directly into French when asking a yes/no question. Instead, use intonation, inversion or 'est-ce que' to ask yes/no questions, e.g. 'Aimes-tu les réseaux sociaux ?' - 'Do you like social media?'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: En ligne : questions in three tenses, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: In French there is a word for 'do/does' in yes/no questions.
nodes.response: The English verb 'do/does' isn't translated directly into French when asking a yes/no question. Instead, use intonation, inversion or 'est-ce que' to ask yes/no questions, e.g. 'Aimes-tu les réseaux sociaux ?' - 'Do you like social media?'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: En ligne : questions in three tenses, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: There is always a liaison when an 's' is followed by a vowel.
nodes.response: The liaison between a verb and an article (nous avons un chien) is in fact optional. An optional liaison is often used in a more formal setting, for example when reading aloud a prepared speech rather than in a more formal conversation.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people have: 'avoir' 1st and 2nd persons plural

nodes.misconception: The indefinite article 'des' changes based on gender as do the indefinite articles 'un' and 'une'.
nodes.response: The indefinite article 'des' does not change based on gender: 'un livre' - 'des livres'; 'une gomme' - 'des gommes'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Family activities: plural indefinite article 'des'

nodes.misconception: Numbers ending in 's' and 'x' followed by nouns beginning with a vowel are pronounced the same as numbers followed by a noun beginning with a consonant.
nodes.response: Numbers ending in 's' and 'x' followed by nouns beginning with a vowel are pronounced with a liasion; the final consonant of the number is pronounced. 'Trois oranges' has a liaison, 'trois chiens' does not.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers 1-12: 'il y a'

nodes.misconception: Adjectives do not change spelling based on gender or number, as in English.
nodes.response: Adjectives do change spelling based on gender or number, for example: 'un chien amusant', 'deux tortues amusantes'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe people: 'être' 1st and 2nd persons plural and regular plural adjectives

nodes.misconception: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 's'.
nodes.response: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 'z'. This is distinguishable to 'ils sont' and 'elles sont' which have the pronounciation of an English 's' (no liaison).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people have: 'avoir' 3rd persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: There is just one way of referring to 'they' in French, as in English.
nodes.response: There is both a masculine and feminine form of the pronoun 'they'. Use 'ils' when referring to a group of boys or a group of boys and girls, and use 'elles' when referring to a group of girls.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe people: 'être' 3rd person plural and regular plural adjectives

nodes.misconception: All verbs can be followed by a direct object.
nodes.response: Not all verbs can be followed by a direct object; J'habite dans une maison; 'une maison' is connected to the verb by the preposition 'dans'. The verb 'j'habite' (I live) stands alone and does not have a direct object; we cannot say: I live a house.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading habits: verbs like 'prendre' and 'lire', direct objects

nodes.misconception: The direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you' are always 'me' and 'te' in French.
nodes.response: The direct object pronouns 'me' and 'te' change before a vowel in French, they become 'm' and 't'. This is an elision.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: At school and university: direct object pronouns 'me' and 'te'

nodes.misconception: The direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la' change to 'l' ' if the noun starts with a vowel or a 'h': Je lis l'histoire.
nodes.response: The direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la' change to 'l' ' if the verb starts with a vowel or a 'h', not the noun: J'achète le chapeau - je l'achète.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Shopping: direct object pronoun contraction 'l''

nodes.misconception: Numbers 70, 80 and 90 are one word numbers in French, just like 20 (vingt), 30 (trente), 40 (quarante) etc.
nodes.response: In French, the numbers 70 (soixante-dix), 80 (quatre-vingts), and 90 (quatre-vingt-dix) are not single-word numbers. Unlike 20 (vingt), 30 (trente), and 40 (quarante)—which are single words—70, 80, and 90 are constructed using compound expressions.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Shopping: direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la', numbers 70-99

nodes.misconception: The letter 'h' is pronounced like in English.
nodes.response: The letter 'h' is in fact often silent in French: j'habite.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Helping others at school: direct object pronouns 'me' and 'te'

nodes.misconception: 'Il' and 'elle' mean he and she and can only refer to people.
nodes.response: Every noun has a gender in French. Therefore 'il' and 'elle' can mean 'it', and 'ils' and 'elles' mean 'they' (people and things).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading habits: pronouns 'il(s)' and 'elle(s)' meaning 'it' and 'they', 'faire'

nodes.misconception: Idioms are the same in different languages.
nodes.response: Idioms can be specific to a language, culture or group of people. They are often impossible to translate directly. Their use adds variety and authenticity to students' work but it is necessary to discuss the idiom carefully when it is taught.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Projets pour le week-end: extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: The subject pronoun 'il' always means 'he'.
nodes.response: There are a number of impersonal verbs such as 'il faut', 'il neige' and 'il pleut'. Verbs such as 'il fait' and 'il est' can also be used in an impersonal sense. In these cases, the English meaning is 'it' or impersonal 'you', 'we' as appropriate.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ce week-end: impersonal verbs

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense only has one translation e.g. 'used to'.
nodes.response: Students must be aware that the imperfect tense can be translated differently according to context and intended meaning e.g. 'used to', 'was doing' or 'did'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Activités avant et aujourd'hui: extended speaking, photo description

nodes.misconception: There are two present tenses in French.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in French which translates both the simple present (I do) and the present continous (I am doing).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Avec mes amis : extended writing and speaking

nodes.misconception: French word order is the same as English to express something being missing.
nodes.response: Take care to model 'il manque' with students. 'Il manque' is followed by a noun and the English translation is inverted. 'Il manque une personne' means 'a person is missing'. 'Il manque' is also used with plural nouns and translates as 'are missing'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: On se retrouve : impersonal verbs

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only translated by 'was doing' in English e.g. I was listening to the radio.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense has more than one translation in English according to its use in French. Students need to be aware of the different meanings that might be conveyed when they encounter the imperfect tense e.g. I listened, I used to listen.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Quand j'étais petit : the imperfect tense with regular verbs ('used to')

nodes.misconception: The letter 'o' is consistently pronounced in French words.
nodes.response: An 'o' sound can be open or closed. 'O' is open when it is followed by a consonant (votre). 'O' is closed when it is written with a circumflex (ô), it is the last sound in a syllable (trop) or is followed by a 'z' sound (rose).
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une rencontre : verbs like connaitre in present tense

nodes.misconception: All verbs ending 'aitre' form the perfect tense in the same way.
nodes.response: Whilst this group of verbs behaves very similarly, the verb 'naitre' is irregular in the perfect tense. Students should be aware that it uses 'être' to form the perfect tense and its past participle is 'né'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Avec mes amis: verbs like connaitre in present and perfect tense

nodes.misconception: The ending -aient is pronounced differently to -ais and -ait.
nodes.response: Although the third person plural ending of the imperfect tense contains a lot of letters, it is pronounced the same way as -ais and -ait. Students will need a lot of practice saying the -aient ending out loud to become confident with this verb form.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Que faisais-tu quand ... ? : the imperfect tense with regular verbs ('BE' + ing)

nodes.misconception: I only use adjectives with comparative structures like 'plus ... que'.
nodes.response: Adjectives help us to compare two nouns with comparative structures such as 'plus ... que'. For example, 'Emily est plus petite que Lucy'. We can use adverbs in the same way to compare how people do things. For example, 'Emily va plus vite que Lucy'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: How people do things: comparative adjectives and adverbs

nodes.misconception: There is only one word for 'better' in French: 'meilleur'.
nodes.response: The adjective 'meilleur(e)' means 'better' in French and describes a noun, e.g.'il a un meilleur ordinateur' ('he has a better computer'). To describe an action as 'better' we use the adverb 'mieux', e.g. 'il chante mieux' ('he sings better').
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: How people do things: comparative adverbs

nodes.misconception: There is an equivalent way to add -er onto adjectives to make comparisons like in English.
nodes.response: We cannot change adjectives to make comparisons in French. To compare two people or things, we instead have to say that one is more or less 'something' than another. For example: 'Elle est plus grande que son frère.' She is taller than her brother.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparisons: 'plus…que', moins…que', 'aussi…que'

nodes.misconception: The SSCs [om] and [on] always sound the same.
nodes.response: When [om] or [on] appear at the end of a word or before a consonant, they have a nasal sound and are pronounced the same. However, before a vowel their sounds are oral, the 'm' and 'n' are pronounced more clearly, making these SSCs sound different.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Good and bad experiences: feminine adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: All two-verb sentences have à (to) before the infinitive.
nodes.response: Modal verbs, verbs of like/dislike and 'aller' are followed directly by an infinitive to form two-verb structures but some verbs form two-verb structures with 'à' + infinitive; for example, 'aider', 'apprendre' and 'commencer'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday activities: verbs with 'à' before the infinitive

nodes.misconception: 'Il est' always means 'he is'.
nodes.response: 'Il est' can be used as an impersonal verb where 'il' means 'it' and is not referring to a specific thing but talking about 'it' in general. e.g. 'Il est difficile de croire' means 'It is difficult to believe'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Pandemic in France: impersonal expression 'il est + adjective + de'

nodes.misconception: 'De' is always translated as 'to' in English.
nodes.response: 'De' is often translated as 'to'. However, it can be translated as 'from' and is sometimes not translated at all.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Decisions for the future: verbs with 'à' and 'de' before the infinitive

nodes.misconception: 'Il' always means 'he' in English.
nodes.response: In impersonal phrases, ‘il’ never means ‘he’. It often means ‘it’, but does not refer to a specific person or thing. It is often used in weather phrases, saying what time it is and what you must (not) do.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Pandemic in France: impersonal expressions including weather

nodes.misconception: Words will stick in my memory if I read them enough times.
nodes.response: It is the act of reaching for words that roots them deeper in memory, so testing oneself or working in pairs to try to recall words from memory is the most effective learning strategy for holding onto words in your long term memory.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des francophones célèbres: reading aloud, reading comprehension (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in French.
nodes.response: While the majority of adjectives are placed after the noun, certain types of adjective go in front. Students should be aware of which adjectives go where in order to speak and write with greater accuracy.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Bruxelles: position of adjectives and adverbs, writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Always use the infinitive to translate the '-ing' verb form into French.
nodes.response: The infinitive used as a noun in French translates the idea of 'doing' something, e.g. 'fumer est mauvais' ('smoking is bad'). The present participle translates the present continuous in English, e.g. 'étant célèbre' ('being famous').
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des francophones célèbres: imperative, present participle, writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: All adjectives go after the noun in French.
nodes.response: While the majority of adjectives are placed after the noun, certain types of adjective go in front. Students should be aware of which adjectives go where in order to speak and write with greater accuracy.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Bruxelles : position of adjectives and adverbs, writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: It is better to give long answers in the role-play task than short responses.
nodes.response: The role-play task is a short exercise requiring relevant answers to each bullet point that contain a verb. Longer answers are not appropriate to this task.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des francophones célèbres : word pattern rules, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can only prepare for the listening exam by learning vocabulary and grammar.
nodes.response: While a strong grasp of grammar and excellent recall of vocabulary is essential, there are also strategies to help students achieve success in the listening exam. Prediction of words and phrases is one method to actively engage with listening.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Bruxelles : transcription, extended listening (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The only way an adjective is made feminine is by adding the letter 'e' to a masculine adjective.
nodes.response: Although many feminine adjectives are formed by adding 'e' to a masculine adjective, there are other feminine endings and rules governing these, e.g. -se, -elle, -enne, -ve, -ère.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Bruxelles: negation, adjective agreement, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: It is better to give long answers in the role-play task than short responses.
nodes.response: The role-play task is a short exercise requiring relevant answers to each bullet point that contain a verb. Longer answers are not appropriate to this task.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des francophones célèbres : word pattern rules, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can only prepare for the listening exam by learning vocabulary and grammar.
nodes.response: While a strong grasp of grammar and excellent recall of vocabulary is essential, there are also strategies to help students achieve success in the listening exam. Prediction of words and phrases is one method to actively engage with listening.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Bruxelles : transcription, extended listening (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: The only way an adjective is made feminine is by adding the letter 'e' to a masculine adjective.
nodes.response: Although many feminine adjectives are formed by adding 'e' to a masculine adjective, there are other feminine endings and rules governing these, e.g. -se, -elle, -enne, -ve, -ère.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Une visite à Bruxelles : negation, adjective agreement, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Words will stick in my memory if I read them enough times.
nodes.response: It is the act of reaching for words that roots them deeper in memory, so testing oneself or working in pairs to try to recall words from memory is the most effective learning strategy for holding onto words in your long term memory.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des francophones célèbres : reading aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Always use the infinitive to translate the '-ing' verb form into French.
nodes.response: The infinitive used as a noun in French translates the idea of 'doing' something, e.g. 'fumer est mauvais' ('smoking is bad'). The present participle translates the present continuous in English, e.g. 'étant célèbre' ('being famous').
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Des francophones célèbres : imperative, present participle, writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' always means 'to do' or 'to make'.
nodes.response: 'Faire' has multiple meanings. 'To do' and 'to make' are the most common, but it can also mean 'to go' and 'to have', and it has other meanings in different verbal phrases.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do: 'faire' 1st and 2nd persons plural

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is just one word for 'my' in French.
nodes.response: French has 3 words for 'my' and the gender of the possession determines which 'my' to use; 'mon' for masculine singular nouns, 'ma' for feminine singular nouns and 'mes' for plural nouns.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Belongings: possessive adjectives 'mon', 'ma', 'mes' and 'ton', 'ta', 'tes'

nodes.misconception: 'Faire' always means 'to do' or 'to make'.
nodes.response: 'Faire' has multiple meanings. 'To do' and 'to make' are the most common, but it can also mean 'to go' and 'to have', and it has other meanings in different verbal phrases.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do: 'faire' 3rd persons singular and plural

nodes.misconception: Once you 'know' some vocabulary, you should move on.
nodes.response: Vocabulary and grammatical concepts need consistently revisiting in order to move it in to your long term memory. Work out what learning techniques work for you but the most important thing is repetition.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Family: extended practice

nodes.misconception: The letters 'ain' and 'aim' are always pronounced the same way.
nodes.response: Before a consonant or at the end of a word, [ain] and [aim] are nasal but before a vowel, they are non-nasal sounds.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Occupied France: perfect tense with verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir'

nodes.misconception: All -ir verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense.
nodes.response: There are different groups of -ir verbs. Learn which verbs act like 'sortir', 'choisir' and 'venir' in the present tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Concorde the history: 'sortir', 'choisir', 'venir' verbs, -ion/-ation nouns

nodes.misconception: When forming inversion questions in the perfect tense, you just have to swap the subject and the verb.
nodes.response: Swapping the position of the subject and the verb is an important step in forming inversion questions but remember to add a hyphen and -t- in the third person singular e.g. 'A-t-elle vendu sa maison ?'
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The French colonial empire: perfect tense with verbs like 'venir' and 'entendre'

nodes.misconception: Words with [tion] are cognates, therefore pronounced the same in English and French.
nodes.response: Although [tion] words are usually cognates, the sound is different and useful to revisit regularly.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Concorde the history: prepositions of place and movement

nodes.misconception: The verbs 'entendre' and 'venir' have the same auxiliary verb.
nodes.response: Although their past participles are formed in the same way (ending in u), ‘venir’ is always formed with the auxiliary verb 'être' and never with ‘avoir’.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The French colonial empire: more practice of verbs like 'entendre' and 'venir'

nodes.misconception: Verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir' follow the same patterns in the present and perfect tenses.
nodes.response: Verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir' follow the same patterns in the perfect tense - they need an auxiliary verb and a past participle ending in -i but follow different patterns in the present tense.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: The French Resistance: perfect tense with verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir'

nodes.misconception: The letter combinations [en] and [an] are pronounced differently in French.
nodes.response: The letter combinations [en] and [an] make the same sound in French, as can be heard in the word 'enfant'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Chez moi, chez toi : prepositions and emphatic pronouns moi, toi ...

nodes.misconception: 'Elle' only means she and 'elles' only means they when naming a group of girls or women.
nodes.response: When used as emphatic pronouns, 'elle' means her and 'elles' means them.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ma ville, mon pays : prepositions and emphatic pronouns lui, elle, eux, elles

nodes.misconception: 'Elle' only means she and 'elles' only means they when naming a group of girls or women.
nodes.response: When used as emphatic pronouns, 'elle' means her and 'elles' means them.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La vie quotidienne ici et ailleurs : extended speaking and writing

nodes.misconception: Sentences such as 'when I was little, I would do the shopping with my mother' can be translated by using both the imperfect tense and the conditional mood.
nodes.response: In French, when writing or translating sentences about what used to happen, all verbs should be in the imperfect tense. 'Used to' and 'would' (meaning habitually) are translated by the imperfect.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Où habiter : extended writing

nodes.misconception: 'Nous' always means 'we' in French.
nodes.response: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun. 'Nous' means 'us' when used as an emphatic pronoun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Découvrir d'autres pays : prepositions and emphatic pronouns nous and vous

nodes.misconception: When speaking or writing about what you did regularly in the past, use the perfect tense to state the action of the sentence.
nodes.response: When speaking or writing about what you did regularly in the past, use the imperfect tense to state the action. This is because you are talking about something that didn't have a clear start and end point. Perfect tense is not appropriate.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La transformation des villes : imperfect of être, avoir and faire

nodes.misconception: 'Être' is used to translate the phrase 'there used to be'.
nodes.response: Although in English, 'there used to be' has the idea of being, this is not the case in French. The phrase 'il y a' means there is but the verb is 'a' which comes from avoir. It's the same with there used to be: 'il y avait'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ma ville avant : imperfect of être, avoir and faire

nodes.misconception: 'Nous' always means 'we' in French.
nodes.response: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun. 'Nous' means 'us' when used as an emphatic pronoun.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Découvrir de grandes villes : prepositions and emphatic pronouns nous and vous

nodes.misconception: Only the near future and future tenses can be used to refer fo the future.
nodes.response: It is possible to refer to the future using the conditional mood: phrases like 'je voudrais' and 'il voudrait' which are followed by an infinitive. This creates the idea of what someone would like to do, clearly referring to possible future events.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: La vie en ville : extended writing and speaking, photo description

nodes.misconception: I should start transcribing as soon as the dictation begins.
nodes.response: It is useful to listen to the full sentence once before transcribing to get an idea of its meaning. This will help you write the sentence down and check it during the second and third times that the audio is played.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle d'écoute: dictation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: The word 'actuellement' means 'actually'.
nodes.response: The word 'actuellement' means 'currently'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle de lecture: extended reading and translation into English (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Answers in listening comprehension questions are usually obvious.
nodes.response: Listening comprehension passages do not always make answers obvious, often containing synonyms and distractors to test your attention to detail.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle d'écoute: extended listening (AQA)

nodes.misconception: When describing the photo in the writing exam, I should develop my sentences with justified opinions and a range of verb tenses.
nodes.response: You should keep photo description sentences short and simple in the writing exam.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle écrit: photo description, essay and translation practice (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can choose which bullet points I answer for the essay questions in the writing paper.
nodes.response: You must answer all bullet points for the essay questions in the writing paper.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle écrit: short and long essay practice (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should develop my answers as much as possible for all parts of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to develop your answers extensively for all parts of the speaking exam. Remember to keep your answers short and succinct in the role-play section.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle oral: role-play, read aloud, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Answers in listening comprehension questions are usually obvious.
nodes.response: Listening comprehension passages do not always make answers obvious, often containing synonyms and distractors to test your attention to detail.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle d'écoute: extended listening (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should develop my answers as much as possible for all parts of the speaking exam.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to develop your answers extensively for all parts of the speaking exam. Remember to keep your answers short and succinct in the role-play section.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle oral: role-play, read aloud, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: When describing the photo in the writing exam, I should develop my sentences with justified opinions and a range of verb tenses.
nodes.response: You should keep photo description sentences short and simple in the writing exam.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle écrit: photo description, essay and translation practice (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The word 'actuellement' means 'actually'.
nodes.response: The word 'actuellement' means 'currently'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle de lecture: extended reading and translation into English (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should start transcribing as soon as the dictation begins.
nodes.response: It is useful to listen to the full sentence once before transcribing to get an idea of its meaning. This will help you write the sentence down and check it during the second and third times that the audio is played.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle d'écoute : dictation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can choose which bullet points I answer for the essay questions in the writing paper.
nodes.response: You must answer all bullet points for the essay questions in the writing paper.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrôle écrit: short and long essay practice (AQA)

nodes.misconception: 'Ou' means 'or' and 'where' in French.
nodes.response: 'Ou' without an accent means 'or' and 'où' with an accent means 'where'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Ask where: 'vas', intonation questions with 'où', 'comment', 'quand'

nodes.misconception: 'à' + 'le' = 'à le'.
nodes.response: When 'à' is followed by 'le' it becomes 'au'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Places in town: 'aller' 1st and 3rd persons singular, 'au' and 'à la'

nodes.misconception: Add -e to all adjectives to make them feminine.
nodes.response: Some adjectives follow different patterns. 'Heureux' changes to 'heureuse' and 'naturel' changes to 'naturelle'.
nodes.subject: french
nodes.lessonTitle: Un poème familial: read and read aloud

nodes.misconception: When I combine 'à' with a plural noun with 'les', it becomes 'à les'.
