nodes.response: Use and share diverse examples of landmarks and their meanings, include those relevant and personal to pupils.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Local and national landmarks

nodes.misconception: As pupils first encounter the idea of climate they confuse it with weather.
nodes.response: Keep offering different examples and talk about weather being a snapshot of a moment in time but climate is a long-term trend of weather.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The weather where I live and in the UK

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the local area is either one particular place or has a particular size.
nodes.response: Share examples of where we go, and think about this in the context of everyday lives in urban and rural areas, using different examples.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Mapping places to visit in our local area

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that some jobs are gendered - e.g. tractor drivers or lifeboat crew are men.
nodes.response: Model jobs being done by a variety of people showing diversity where appropriate, in terms of gender, age, ethnicity and ability.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Key features of our local area

nodes.misconception: Sustainability is just to do with the environment.
nodes.response: Sustainability takes into account the long term needs of people, the economy and the environment.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing a new settlement

nodes.misconception: Some children may struggle to understand the concept of countour lines.
nodes.response: Showing animations and models of land in 3D with contour lines marked on can help.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Location and growth of settlements

nodes.misconception: Some children might assume any photograph in black and white is from a very long time ago.
nodes.response: Show children a black and white photo of their local settlement today.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Change in our local area

nodes.misconception: Cities are only places where people work.
nodes.response: Remind students that cities are places that people live and work as cities include residential areas.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Settlement features

nodes.misconception: All settlements grew in the industrial revolution because factories were built to provide jobs.
nodes.response: There are a variety of reasons settlements grow including developing as a tourist location or market town.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Our local town

nodes.misconception: Pupils often read four figure grid references the wrong way round.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they find the easting first by reading along the corridor, then read the northing by going up the stairs.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Villages, towns and cities in the UK

nodes.misconception: Difficulties in using digital mapping tools.
nodes.response: Provide additional teaching input to support learners in using digital mapping tools.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: A town in northern Italy

nodes.misconception: Limited understanding of what misconceptions and stereotypes are and the possible impacts of these.
nodes.response: Discuss examples of misconceptions and stereotypes that learners have encountered in their own lives.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing northern Italy with my UK region

nodes.misconception: A limited understanding of the concept of sustainability. It doesn't mean humans need to stop all activity, they need to change how they use the environment.
nodes.response: Sustainability doesn't mean humans need to stop all activity, they need to change how they use the environment.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Venice: A popular tourist destination

nodes.misconception: Difficulties in using digital mapping tools.
nodes.response: Provide additional teaching input in the use of digital maps.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geographical features in northern Italy

nodes.misconception: Lack of understanding about what a carbon footprint is.
nodes.response: Provide additional teaching input about carbon footprints and their link with climate change.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Location and transport

nodes.misconception: All villages in northern Italy are the same.
nodes.response: Villages in northern Italy have different climates, architecture and culture.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Village life in northern Italy

nodes.misconception: Children may think that older parts of a place have not changed since they have been built.
nodes.response: Use the photographs and evidence from fieldwork to challenge these misconceptions.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Mapping changes

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the time periods discussed in this lesson.
nodes.response: You could make a washing line timeline in the classroom with dates familiar to the children as markers then add the maps to the timeline.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring settlement change

nodes.misconception: Children may not be familiar with tally charts as a method of recording.
nodes.response: Practise reading and writing tallies prior to the lesson would support their understanding.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring change in a day

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that all change involves places becoming urbanised or developed.
nodes.response: Show children examples of areas that have been re-greened.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Our changing place

nodes.misconception: Children may require some support to generate their own yes/no questions.
nodes.response: You could play the yes/no game to get children thinking about how to elicit answers of just two words.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Recording local views

nodes.misconception: When planning their route children may not have any concept of distance.
nodes.response: Use the map scale to estimate how far the route is. An average walking speed is around 12 minutes per km.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Evidence from fieldwork

nodes.misconception: Some learners may be less confident with the use of aerial images, maps and data.
nodes.response: Spend additional time recapping and consolidating learners' geographical skills in using maps and other sources of information.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geographical skills: Describing the UK

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the country of Australia and the continent of Oceania.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring a map of Oceania and identifying the different countries and dependencies that make up this continent.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tourism: Oceania

nodes.misconception: That nobody is taking action to protect the environment.
nodes.response: Find out about ways in which people are taking action to protect the environment in learners' communities and elsewhere in the world.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Environmental geography: focus on North and South America

nodes.misconception: Not fully appreciating the huge size and diversity of Asia and the variations in climate and climate zones.
nodes.response: Use a globe/world map to highlight the size of the continent and the wide range of latitudes it covers.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrasting climates: Asia and Antarctica

nodes.misconception: Geography is something that happens in other parts of the world not in the place where we live.
nodes.response: Investigate the geography in local news stories as well as stories from elsewhere in the UK and other countries.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geography in the news

nodes.misconception: Geography is only something we learn at school.
nodes.response: Geography is all around us. We might learn it in school, at home and in many other places.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geography is all around us

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not fully appreciate the wide range of landscapes, physical features and biomes in Africa.
nodes.response: Spend some time exploring different countries and regions, including major cities and different types of biome.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Natural resources and sustainability: focus on Africa

nodes.misconception: People may have stereotypes about different places.
nodes.response: Discuss where people's stereotypes come from and emphasise the importance of using multiple sources of information to build up a more accurate picture of what a place is like.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of geographers: focus on Europe

nodes.misconception: Special places or landscapes all look the same.
nodes.response: Special landscapes can look and feel very different to each other. They are special because they make you feel different things like awe and wonder.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The seven wonders of the natural world

nodes.misconception: Special places have to be famous sites or those you visit on holiday.
nodes.response: Special places can be places that make you feel different emotions, they can include a range of places like your home, school, family home, place of worship etc. They're places that make you feel happy and positive and evoke memories.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Annotating our map of the school grounds

nodes.misconception: Landmarks are only new, futuristic buildings.
nodes.response: Historical architecture and buildings linked to past cultures and places are also landmarks. These buildings represent places and evoke memories and feelings just as much as modern and futuristic buildings.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Human wonders of the world

nodes.misconception: The best place I've ever been to has to be in another country.
nodes.response: The best place you have been to can be abroad but it doesn't have to be, it can be somewhere you have visited with family or to see family like another town or can be a place you went to on a day trip like a theme park, museum or zoo.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing and locating our favourite places

nodes.misconception: Believing that sustainability is only about the environment.
nodes.response: It relates to the social, economic and environmental impact of a city. This lesson focuses mainly on environmental issues but a city would not be judged to be sustainable if its citizens did not have their basic economic or social needs met.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Making cities more sustainable

nodes.misconception: Children may have heard about the ozone layer and think this is the main cause of climate change.
nodes.response: Whilst ozone depletion and climate change are linked, it is not a major cause of climate change.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Carbon footprints

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that renewable resources are 'safe'.
nodes.response: Explain that even water - a renewable natural resource - could become too polluted to use or if trees are cut down quicker than they can be replanted then that supply of wood will be exhausted.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing sustainability

nodes.misconception: Children might be under the impression that all agricultural crops are grown for human consumption.
nodes.response: In fact the vast majority of European cereal crop production is used to feed animals (and create biofuels, rather than feeding people.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling food waste

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that net zero means zero carbon emissions.
nodes.response: Net zero actually refers to a state in which the greenhouse gases going into the atmosphere are balanced by their removal out of the atmosphere.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using energy wisely

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that biodiversity means the total population of a species.
nodes.response: Biodiversity is  is the variety of all living things on Earth.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Biodiversity and sustainability

nodes.misconception: All roads in the UK were built for cars to travel on them.
nodes.response: Many of our roads were built before cars were invented. They were originally built for people walking, horses, and carts. Cars came much later, and the roads were changed over time so cars could use them safely.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using digital maps to explore changes in our local area

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all questionnaires have to be multiple choice selected from given responses.
nodes.response: Explain that sometimes it is necessary to ask opinions in an open question so that people can submit their own ideas.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork tools and techniques

nodes.misconception: Children need to understand that evidence can become dated - especially mapping and media evidence.
nodes.response: You could present some media reports of an issue which has been resolved (e.g. a new road crossing).
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Change in a local area

nodes.misconception: Not all data may fit the pattern they have identified.
nodes.response: These are called anomalies and can sometimes be explained away but individual anomalies would not disprove a pattern exists.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting data

nodes.misconception: Children may not see it as their 'job' to think about risk assessemnts.
nodes.response: Risk assessments conducted by children are very effective as children begin to look at their environment in a different way.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Risk assessment and staying safe

nodes.misconception: Recommendations might not have been enacted or responded to but the enquiry was not a failure
nodes.response: Highlight the cost of enacting changes and the restrictions on budgets and resources.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Future changes

nodes.misconception: Children might think these results will be permanent.
nodes.response: If time allowed you could repeat the fieldwork on a different day, or send groups out a different times then compare the results.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Active fieldwork

nodes.misconception: Learners may have limited knowledge about the jobs that people do.
nodes.response: Spend more time at the start of the lesson discussing the different jobs that people do in the UK.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Jobs in Arusha, Tanzania

nodes.misconception: Learners may have difficulties in identifying different features in satellite images and aerial photographs.
nodes.response: Use Google Earth to first locate and zoom in on features near your school that are already familiar to learners.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical and human features of Tanzania

nodes.misconception: Learners may think that the life of every child in Tanzania (and Africa) is like the life of Zahra.
nodes.response: Spend more time discussing the similarities and differences between people in the UK to help learners appreciate that there will be many similarities and differences in people's lives both within and between countries and places.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Daily life near Arusha

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have stereotypical views about what Tanzania is like and may not be aware of its geographical diversity.
nodes.response: Additional photographs of Tanzania could be found online to further emphasise the geographical diversity of this country.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tanzania's climate and landscapes

nodes.misconception: That Africa is a country not a geographically diverse continent.
nodes.response: Recap the names of the seven continents and five oceans. Spend more time using a map to identify different countries in Africa.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The location of Africa and UK connections

nodes.misconception: Learners may not fully appreciate the diversity of places within countries.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring a range of settlements in different parts of the UK.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Similarities and differences: Arusha in Tanzania

nodes.misconception: Solar panels do not work in the shade.
nodes.response: Solar panels do work in the shade and on cloudy days but they are less efficient in these conditions.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning to do fieldwork

nodes.misconception: All geographical questions make good fieldwork enquiry questions.
nodes.response: Fieldwork enquiry questions have to be answerable within the practical realms of data collection. Therefore some brilliant geographical questions might not be good fieldwork enquiry questions.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing a fieldwork enquiry question

nodes.misconception: Geographers should try to hide the things that do not go to plan in their fieldwork.
nodes.response: An important part of being a geographer is to be reflective and to take opportunities to improve on your practice.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflecting on our fieldwork enquiry

nodes.misconception: Geographers are only concerned with the data that shows the maximum scores.
nodes.response: Geographers do often use the maximum scores to show the best option, but they also look within the data to see how some variables compare with others.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Examining our geographical data

nodes.misconception: Maps are only used to help us find out where places are.
nodes.response: Maps are a brilliant tool that geographers can use to record and present information as well as use for navigation.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting our geographical data

nodes.misconception: Numerical data is more valuable to geographers than text data.
nodes.response: All data is valuable to geographers, providing it is fair and unbiased.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Collecting our geographical data

nodes.misconception: Understanding IMD rankings and comparing them with primary data can be challenging.
nodes.response: Make sure students are aware of the challenges of ranking and other attributes where a low number can be a positive thing (similar issue with some measures of development such as IMD).
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS for human geography fieldwork

nodes.misconception: Missing a small step in procedural knowledge for GIS.
nodes.response: Emphasise the most likely pitfalls e.g. toggling 'Time'; configuring symbols and pop-ups
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using 3D GIS for physical geography fieldwork

nodes.misconception: Systematic and stratified sampling are 'better' than a random sampling strategy.
nodes.response: There is no hierarchy of effectiveness in sampling strategies. The best strategy to use depends on the dynamics of the location, the size of the overall population of data, and what geographical conclusions one hopes to be able to make from the data.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Collecting physical geographical data

nodes.misconception: Secondary crime data tells us about the economic prosperity of a place.
nodes.response: Crime data can be misinterpreted. The data does not give any details about the economic status of the victim or the perpetrator. It is also assumes that the perpetrator lives in the area where they committed the crime, for which there is no evidence.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Urban fieldwork

nodes.misconception: A good enquiry question is answered in the data collection stage.
nodes.response: A good enquiry question guides you through all stages of the enquiry to help you find an answer.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Formulating an enquiry question

nodes.misconception: River processes are independent variables that shape river features.
nodes.response: Rivers are complex systems where processes and features both affect each other at different times. This means that students need to disengage with the idea that one variable is going to be independent of another as they present and analyse data.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: River fieldwork

nodes.misconception: Highlighting the flaws in a geographical enquiry shows that I am a poor geographer.
nodes.response: Good geographers take time to be deeply reflective of their work and will present their findings honestly and transparently, even if they show errors that affect the final outcome. Good geographers also show how a study can be improved and extended.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating geographical enquiries

nodes.misconception: Geographers present data to make it look more attractive.
nodes.response: Geographers present data so that it becomes more meaningful. It allows geographers to see patterns and relationships in the data that will help them answer their enquiry question.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting geographical data

nodes.misconception: Secondary data has to be collected by geographical experts.
nodes.response: Secondary data is often collected by experts or professional geographers but it can also be the data collected by other students in a different time frame.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Collecting human geographical data

nodes.misconception: Enquiries that focus on coastal management have to discuss effectiveness.
nodes.response: While many coastal enquiries focus on how effective management strategies are, the concept of effectiveness is far broader. Enquiries could study how coastal defences look, if they prevent access to the beach, or how sustainable it is to build them.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Coastal fieldwork

nodes.misconception: There are not enough issues in rural areas to make it worth studying fieldwork enquiries there.
nodes.response: Rural areas have a lot of issues around inequality and access to services as well as interesting cultural geography to study.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Rural fieldwork

nodes.misconception: A geographer has to be good at maths to successfully analyse quantitative data.
nodes.response: Successful analysis in geography means correctly understanding what numerical values mean, not necessarily being able to process and manipulate data.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing geographical data

nodes.misconception: Students will sometimes select basemaps because they like their appearance.
nodes.response: Students need to appreciate that some of the basemaps which may be least appealing at first sight provide much more effective visualisation. They are like the canvas for a painting.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to visualise data in a webmap

nodes.misconception: It is better to use the mean value rather than the mode or the median values.
nodes.response: The mean, median and mode have different purposes but none of the methods produce a result that is thought of as more reliable than the others.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using statistical data in geography

nodes.misconception: All contour lines have their height marked on them.
nodes.response: Most contour lines will show their height, but in very steep areas, where contours are close together, some will be omitted as there is a lack of space. The height of these lines can be calculated by looking at the height of the surrounding lines.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using OS maps to analyse physical features

nodes.misconception: A sketch map needs to be an artistic representation of a place.
nodes.response: A sketch map looks like a map as it has a plan orientation but it is not a work of art. It uses simple, clean lines to communicate the main features of a map.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketch maps and cross sections

nodes.misconception: Students frequently confuse the aerial images seen through software such as Google Maps as a map, partly because they are frequently displayed alongside actual maps.
nodes.response: Maps are representations of the world and use symbols and cartographic language to present certain characteristics of a place (and not others). Aerial photographs are indiscriminate views of the world and do not select certain aspects of geography.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and interpreting photographs

nodes.misconception: An anomaly in a data set means that an error was made in the way the data was collected.
nodes.response: Anomalies could be found in data sets for many reasons, including human error during data collection. It is more likely however that a variable that was not investigated is having an influence on that particular value, causing it to seem 'wrong'.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting graphs in geography

nodes.misconception: A six figure grid reference refers to only one point in the UK.
nodes.response: A six figure grid reference will be specific to a larger grid square in the OS National Grid. Each of these 100km2 squares are denoted by a two letter code, often seen in faint blue on the map. This means it refers to more than one point in the UK.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using OS maps to locate places

nodes.misconception: Any form of data presentation can be applied to any data set.
nodes.response: There are many different types of data. Accurate data presentation means that appropriate graphical data presentation techniques are matched with the particular characteristics of a data set.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing graphs in geography

nodes.misconception: White space on a map means there is nothing there.
nodes.response: White space means that the land cover there is grassland or farmland.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing landscapes using maps

nodes.misconception: Atlases specialise in large scale maps.
nodes.response: A large scale map means the map shows a large amount of detail but covers a small area. Therefore, atlases tend to use small scale maps that show a large area of land in limited detail.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using atlases

nodes.misconception: GIS and long-hand, paper-based mapping have the same value.
nodes.response: While it is very possible to create representations of spatial data on paper using layers of tracing paper over a base map, the real value of GIS is its ability to analyse data quickly and be edited once the map has been digitally  created.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and interpreting spatial data

nodes.misconception: All of the world is equally interconnected.
nodes.response: Some parts of the world are more interconnected than others. It is influenced by many factors including wealth and size.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing patterns of globalisation using digital maps and data

nodes.misconception: The Suez Canal is only important for the Middle East.
nodes.response: The Suez Canal is important globally as 30% of all global container traffic and 12% of all global trade passes through the canal.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Global transport routes

nodes.misconception: TNCs sell the same products in different countries.
nodes.response: TNCs can sell different products in different countries.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Transnational corporations

nodes.misconception: Supply chains start at the manufacturing stage.
nodes.response: Supply chains start when raw materials have been taken from the earth.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Food production and supply chains

nodes.misconception: Jeans come from one place.
nodes.response: Jeans come from many different places.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The globalisation of jeans

nodes.misconception: Living standards and quality of life are the same.
nodes.response: Living standards are about the the level of necessities and comforts of daily life that is available to and affordable by a person.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: TNCs: Advantages and disadvantages

nodes.misconception: Most of our imports in the UK come from China.
nodes.response: Most of our imports in the UK come from the US and EU countries.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The UK's imports and exports

nodes.misconception: You can only trade goods.
nodes.response: You can trade goods and services such as education and finance services.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of trade

nodes.misconception: Western culture refers to only North America.
nodes.response: Western culture refers to North America, Europe and Australia.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Globalisation challenges

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is about the world developing.
nodes.response: Globalisation is about the world becoming more connected.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The drivers of globalisation

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is the world becoming more developed.
nodes.response: Globalisation is the world becoming more interconnected.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Globalisation: An introduction

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is only beneficial to large companies.
nodes.response: Globalisation can improve the quality of life of people.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Globalisation opportunities

nodes.misconception: Flooding only happens close to rivers.
nodes.response: Flooding can also happen away from rivers, especially after heavy rainfall. When the ground can't absorb the water fast enough, surface water builds up and causes floods — even in places far from rivers.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: GIS: Analysing flood risk

nodes.misconception: Field sketches are artistic impressions of a geographical scene.
nodes.response: Field sketches are about clearly representing the geographical features of a place, not about the artistic skills of the geographer.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Planning a river enquiry and collecting data

nodes.misconception: Hard engineering is always very effective at protecting from flooding.
nodes.response: Channel straightening, dredging and embankments can all make flooding worse downstream, as the channel can hold more water and speed up the flow.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: River management

nodes.misconception: Attrition is where rocks and sediment carried by the river collide with the bed and the banks causing pieces to break off.
nodes.response: Abrasion is where rocks and sediment carried by the river collide with the bed and the banks causing pieces to break off.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: River processes

nodes.misconception: Flooding only has negative effects.
nodes.response: Flooding is a natural process; it can have positive environmental effects, such as soil replenishment.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The effects of flooding

nodes.misconception: Around one quarter of water is found on land.
nodes.response: Only 0.9% of water is stored on land.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The hydrological cycle

nodes.misconception: There is one source to a river.
nodes.response: There can be many different sources within a drainage basin system.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Drainage basins

nodes.misconception: Points in a channel profile should be joined using a ruler.
nodes.response: Points in a channel profile should be drawn with a slight curve to more accurately represent the shape of the river channel.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Presenting river data

nodes.misconception: Levees are man made.
nodes.response: Levees can be built as a flood defence but they can also be created naturally.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The middle and lower course of a river

nodes.misconception: Flooding is only caused by physical factors such as heavy rainfall.
nodes.response: Human factors can lead to flooding too, such as deforestation.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The causes of flooding

nodes.misconception: The angle of the line of best fit tells geographers how strong the correlation is between two variables.
nodes.response: The strength of the correlation is decided by how close the plots are to the line of best fit.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating river data

nodes.misconception: Only governments help make decisions on where flood protection is used.
nodes.response: Many stakeholders are invloved in making decisions on flood defences.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning river management

nodes.misconception: A river has the most energy in the upper course.
nodes.response: The river does not have that much energy in the upper course as there is not a lot of water in the river.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The upper course of a river

nodes.misconception: The 'global shift' of manufacturing industries from developed to emerging and/or developing countries was a one-off movement of jobs.
nodes.response: TNCs continue to seek locations with the lowest wages, meaning the loss of manufacturing jobs from emerging countries is possible; so some of the benefits of FDI may only be short-term.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Top-down strategies to reduce global inequalities

nodes.misconception: Aid is something given in the event of an emergency.
nodes.response: It is not always provided in the event of an emergency. Aid may be given to support the sustainable development of a community, e.g improving health or educational services in an area, to benefit local people in the longer term.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Bottom-up strategies to reduce global inequalities

nodes.misconception: Chart axes for 'Immigration numbers trend' show numbers are similar for many countries.
nodes.response: Chart axes appear to be comparable at first, the numbers on the vertical axis differ widely. It is therefore essential to look at the numbers carefully.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS maps to analyse links between inequality and migration

nodes.misconception: That everyone in a country with a high GNI is well off, with a good quality of life.
nodes.response: A country’s income is not equally divided by everyone who lives there. This is why GNI per head should be used along side other measures in order to understand differences in quality of life.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring development

nodes.misconception: That there are few people who live to 65 years and beyond in LICs and NEEs.
nodes.response: It is the proportion of the population that is small not the actual number of people. Some LICs and NEEs have large populations so there are millions of people who reach the age of 65 years plus.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Development and demography

nodes.misconception: There are more people living in poverty today than there once were.
nodes.response: The share of the global population living in extreme poverty has dramatically fallen in the past decades.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Rostow’s and Frank’s theories about development over time

nodes.misconception: That the benefits of international migration are limited to the country of origin (such as remittances).
nodes.response: Destination countries experience a wide range of social and economic benefits as a result of immigration.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Consequences of global inequalities

nodes.misconception: That a single image can help us to understand how quality of life is different in distant places.
nodes.response: While images can be of use they can not depict all aspects of life, moreover each image can only ever show a single place or group of people. Within any country there is a diversity of lived experience.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Defining development

nodes.misconception: That the physical environment is the key cause of global inequalities.
nodes.response: Physical geography is a cause of inequality but human factors, past and present, are as influential in affecting the pattern of trade and development.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Causes of global inequalities

nodes.misconception: Students will sometimes select basemaps because they like their appearance.
nodes.response: Students need to appreciate that some of the basemaps which may be least appealing at first sight provide much more effective visualisation. They are like the canvas for a painting.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to visualise data in a webmap

nodes.misconception: It is better to use the mean value rather than the mode or the median values.
nodes.response: The mean, median and mode have different purposes but none of the methods produce a result that is thought of as more reliable than the others.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using statistical data in geography

nodes.misconception: All contour lines have their height marked on them.
nodes.response: Most contour lines will show their height, but in very steep areas, where contours are close together, some will be omitted as there is a lack of space. The height of these lines can be calculated by looking at the height of the surrounding lines.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using OS maps to analyse physical features

nodes.misconception: A sketch map needs to be an artistic representation of a place.
nodes.response: A sketch map looks like a map as it has a plan orientation but it is not a work of art. It uses simple, clean lines to communicate the main features of a map.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Sketch maps and cross sections

nodes.misconception: Students frequently confuse the aerial images seen through software such as Google Maps as a map, partly because they are frequently displayed alongside actual maps.
nodes.response: Maps are representations of the world and use symbols and cartographic language to present certain characteristics of a place (and not others). Aerial photographs are indiscriminate views of the world and do not select certain aspects of geography.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and interpreting photographs

nodes.misconception: An anomaly in a data set means that an error was made in the way the data was collected.
nodes.response: Anomalies could be found in data sets for many reasons, including human error during data collection. It is more likely however that a variable that was not investigated is having an influence on that particular value, causing it to seem 'wrong'.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting graphs in geography

nodes.misconception: A six figure grid reference refers to only one point in the UK.
nodes.response: A six figure grid reference will be specific to a larger grid square in the OS National Grid. Each of these 100km2 squares are denoted by a two letter code, often seen in faint blue on the map. This means it refers to more than one point in the UK.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using OS maps to locate places

nodes.misconception: Any form of data presentation can be applied to any data set.
nodes.response: There are many different types of data. Accurate data presentation means that appropriate graphical data presentation techniques are matched with the particular characteristics of a data set.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing graphs in geography

nodes.misconception: White space on a map means there is nothing there.
nodes.response: White space means that the land cover there is grassland or farmland.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing landscapes using maps

nodes.misconception: Atlases specialise in large scale maps.
nodes.response: A large scale map means the map shows a large amount of detail but covers a small area. Therefore, atlases tend to use small scale maps that show a large area of land in limited detail.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using atlases

nodes.misconception: GIS and long-hand, paper-based mapping have the same value.
nodes.response: While it is very possible to create representations of spatial data on paper using layers of tracing paper over a base map, the real value of GIS is its ability to analyse data quickly and be edited once the map has been digitally  created.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using and interpreting spatial data

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that mass movement only occurs in mountainous areas or during extreme weather events.
nodes.response: Mass movement can happen anywhere there are slopes, even in places with mild weather conditions. While extreme weather can trigger events, even light rainfall can cause mass movement if the slope is steep or the material is already weathered.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Mass movement

nodes.misconception: The UK doesn't experience volcanic activity today, so volcanoes are not important to the UK's geological history.
nodes.response: The UK was once a volcanically active region due to its position near tectonic plate boundaries millions of years ago. Evidence of past volcanic activity includes: the Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland and the volcanic rocks in Snowdonia.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The geology of the UK

nodes.misconception: If we run out of oil, we can just make more.
nodes.response: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form – much longer than a human lifetime. We can’t just “make” more. Once we use them up, they’re gone. That’s why we need to balance using them with finding cleaner, renewable alternatives.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geology and the economy

nodes.misconception: Soil is just dirt.
nodes.response: Soil is a complex and vital resource made of minerals, organic matter, water, and living organisms. It is important for growing food, storing carbon, and maintaining ecosystems. Without healthy soil, agriculture and natural habitats wouldn't survive.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of soil

nodes.misconception: Geological timescales go back as far as human history.
nodes.response: Geological timescales are much greater than human history.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geological timescales

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of rock, and rocks can't change.
nodes.response: Students will explore the three main types of rock found on Earth, and understand how rocks are recycled through the rock cycle.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The rock cycle

nodes.misconception: Large soil particles means there are smaller pores between them.
nodes.response: Soil that is made-up of small particles has a structure where the particles can fit together more easily reducing the pore size between them.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Planning a soil enquiry and collecting data

nodes.misconception: Some students may think that grykes and clints are type of rock, rather than being a feature of limestone landscapes.
nodes.response: Students will be taught what clints and grykes are in relation to limestone.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Limestone landscapes

nodes.misconception: Proportional data can only be presented using a pie chart.
nodes.response: A pie chart is by far the most common method that geographers use, but any shape can be split into proportional sections.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Presenting soil data

nodes.misconception: All rocks formed during the same geological period will be similar.
nodes.response: Although many rocks formed during the same geological period will be similar, volcanic processes may be creating rocks at the same time as sedimentary rocks are being created. These rocks will be very different and create contrasting landscapes.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: GIS: Visualising the geology of the UK

nodes.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same process.
nodes.response: Students will be informed that erosion is the process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away and transported from its original site, whereas weathering is the process of wearing or being worn by long exposure to the atmosphere.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Weathering and rocks

nodes.misconception: Geological resources are all bad because they damage the environment.
nodes.response: While they can cause environmental harm, they also provide essential materials and economic benefits. The key is understanding both advantages and disadvantages—which is what geographers evaluate.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The impacts of using geological resources

nodes.misconception: Anomalous data can be ignored in the data analysis stage as it is due to human error in the data collection stage.
nodes.response: Geographers will always try to find explanations for data that does not fit the general trend before they dismiss it as being caused by human error during the data collection stage.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating soil data

nodes.misconception: Boycotting palm oil helps stop deforestation.
nodes.response: Experts recommend supporting certified sustainable palm oil, as palm oil is the most land-efficient oil crop. Replacing it with less efficient crops like sunflowers could cause more deforestation.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The palm oil dilemma

nodes.misconception: Hydroponic and aquaponic systems are completely self-sustaining or maintenance-free.
nodes.response: Require regular monitoring, energy inputs and human intervention to stay productive.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The future: hydroponics and aquaponics

nodes.misconception: Customer decisions don’t make a difference to global fish populations.
nodes.response: Eating fish from well-managed fisheries helps prevent overfishing, protects marine biodiversity, and ensures fish populations remain healthy for future generations.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainable fishing

nodes.misconception: All natural resources are natural and untouched by humans.
nodes.response: Many natural resources have been heavily managed, modified, or even created by humans, such as: managed forests, fish farms, or reservoirs.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Natural resources: The things we use

nodes.misconception: Methane from cow flatulence causes global warming.
nodes.response: Ruminant animals (like cows and sheep) produce methane during digestion, 90–95% of this is released through eructation (burping). Methane is a greenhouse gas, which insulates our planet.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Consumption and climate change

nodes.misconception: Any energy source can be produced anywhere.
nodes.response: Human and physical geography must be considered when locating energy sources.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Energy in the UK

nodes.misconception: Wind farms are best located as remotely as possible.
nodes.response: Wind farms should be located far from densely populated areas but close to the electricity grid. If they are too remote, the cost of connecting them to the grid will be high.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Windfarms: Decision making exercise

nodes.misconception: Rare earth materials are rare.
nodes.response: Despite their name, they’re not actually rare in quantity, they’re just rarely found in concentrated, economically viable deposits.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Rare earth materials

nodes.misconception: There are plenty more fish in the sea.
nodes.response: In 2018, nearly 90% of the world’s marine (sea) fish stocks were fully exploited, overexploited or depleted.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fish resources

nodes.misconception: Nuclear energy is either a renewable source of energy or a fossil fuel.
nodes.response: Nuclear energy is a non-renewable energy source but is not a fossil fuel.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Energy use around the world

nodes.misconception: It is not possible to be overweight and undernourished at the same time.
nodes.response: Undernourishment occurs when someone isn’t receiving enough calories or essential nutrients to grow and function well. So it is possible to over eat but not eat enough of the right foods to acquire sufficient nutrients.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Food resources

nodes.misconception: All the tests run on GM crops have found that they create no health issues.
nodes.response: Most major scientific bodies find no conclusive evidence of harm from approved GM foods, which have all been tested. However, some animal studies raise questions, and critics argue that long-term human studies are limited.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: A solution: genetically modified crops

nodes.misconception: Aid is separate from globalisation and has nothing to do with how Indonesia connects to the world.
nodes.response: When countries like Australia or organisations like the EU give aid to Indonesia, they are building connections through education and infrastructure. This support helps Indonesia grow economically, attract investment, and take part in global trade.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Globalisation in Indonesia

nodes.misconception: Development in Indonesia only has positive effects, like job creation and economic growth.
nodes.response: While development brings economic benefits, it also causes environmental problems like deforestation, water pollution, and loss of biodiversity, which can harm people and ecosystems in the long term.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Environmental impacts of economic development in Indonesia

nodes.misconception: ASEAN is only focused on trade and does not deal with other important issues like politics or security.
nodes.response: ASEAN focuses not only on trade but also on political stability, security, and regional cooperation to maintain peace in Southeast Asia.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to Indonesia

nodes.misconception: Economic development in Indonesia benefits everyone equally.
nodes.response: Economic development in Indonesia is mostly focused in urban areas like Jakarta and Java. Rural areas often miss out on investment, leading to unequal access to jobs, services, and infrastructure.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Effects of economic development on people in Indonesia

nodes.misconception: Indonesia is choosing between China and the USA and will eventually have to pick a side.
nodes.response: Indonesia works with both to stay neutral: to gain investment from China and to cooperate on security and trade with the USA. This helps it stay independent and build global influence.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Effects of economic development on the geopolitical influence of Indonesia

nodes.misconception: In Indonesia, agriculture remains the dominant sector in the economy.
nodes.response: Agriculture was once Indonesia’s economic backbone, but its role has declined since the 1990s. Today, industry and services dominate GDP, with manufacturing, finance, tourism, and digital sectors growing.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Key economic trends in Indonesia since 1990

nodes.misconception: Foreign companies always take profits back home and give nothing to locals.
nodes.response: Many TNCs invest in local jobs, training, and infrastructure, though some profits do return to the home country.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Costs and benefits of changing international relations

nodes.misconception: Tectonic plates float like rafts on liquid magma.
nodes.response: The mantle is semi-solid rather than a sort of liquid sea of magma.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Plate tectonics theory

nodes.misconception: Volcanoes only occur on land.
nodes.response: In fact, volcanoes occur underwater as well as on land, especially at constructive plate margins and hot spots.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Processes at constructive/divergent plate margins

nodes.misconception: That volcanoes occur directly above where the oceanic plate starts to subduct.
nodes.response: In fact, the melting of the oceanic plate occurs deep in the mantle, so magma rises to the surface some distance away from the plate margin.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Processes at destructive/convergent plate margins

nodes.misconception: Volcanoes occur at all plate margins.
nodes.response: While volcanoes are a feature of both destructive and constructive plate margins, there are no volcanic eruptions at conservative margins because no magma is produced.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Processes at conservative plate margins

nodes.misconception: The inner core is hotter than the outer core so the inner core must be liquid (molten rock) while the outer core is solid rock.
nodes.response: In fact, although the inner core is hotter than the outer core, the inner core is solid while the outer core is molten and liquid. This is because the pressure is so great in the inner core that it prevents the rock from melting.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The structure of the Earth

nodes.misconception: Tsunamis and landslides are primary impacts of earthquakes because they can cause massive damage to people and property.
nodes.response: Tsunamis and landslides are secondary impacts of earthquakes because they happen as an indirect result of an earthquake. For e.g, ground shaking destabilises slopes, making a landslide more likely, especially if there is then also heavy rain.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Impacts of earthquakes in a developed and a developing country

nodes.misconception: Japan’s tsunami evacuation failed because it had not invested in a tsunami warning system.
nodes.response: Japan had invested in a tsunami warning system, but due to how close the epicentre was, there were only 30 minutes before tsunami waves arrived, meaning that not everyone was evacuated safely. The height of the tsunami was not accurately predicted.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Examples of management of earthquake hazards

nodes.misconception: Because we know the location of plate margins, scientists can predict when earthquakes will happen.
nodes.response: While scientists can identify areas that are at high risk of earthquakes, exact predictions for when and where an earthquake will occur (or what magnitude it will be) are not possible.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing risks from earthquakes and volcanoes

nodes.misconception: People in developing countries are less prepared because they lack understanding of volcanic hazards.
nodes.response: People in developing countries have expert understanding of volcanic hazards and local communities are fully aware of hazards. Management problems are often due to lack of resources for effective prediction, preparation and relief.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Examples of management of volcanic hazards

nodes.misconception: That both volcanoes and earthquakes occur at all types of plate margin.
nodes.response: While earthquakes are produced by tectonic movements at all plate margins, volcanoes are not found at conservative plate margins.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes

nodes.misconception: Impacts of volcanic eruptions are always more severe in developing and emerging countries than in developed countries.
nodes.response: A lot depends on the eruption type and factors such as population density. Economic impacts are often highest in developed countries because of the higher value of the property impacted by the eruption.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Impacts of volcanoes in a developed and an emerging country

nodes.misconception: Students can find it difficult to grasp that Earth's crust and tectonic plates include the ocean floor, which has topography (e.g. mountains including volcanoes, valleys) just like the land areas.
nodes.response: Remind students (often!) that tectonic plates include the ocean floor. Apps such as 3D Scene can help to visualise this underwater topography, which we learn about by bathymetry. The story of Marie Tharp provides excellent disciplinary knowledge.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to visualise physical processes at different types of plate margin

nodes.misconception: Fairtrade is small-scale and mostly based in the UK.
nodes.response: The Fairtrade movement involves the trade in 300 different commodities and global networks of consumers as well as producers.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Strategies to reduce the development gap: Fairtrade, debt relief and aid

nodes.misconception: Chart axes for 'Immigration numbers trend' show numbers are similar for many countries.
nodes.response: Chart axes appear to be comparable at first, the numbers on the vertical axis differ widely. It is therefore essential to look at the numbers carefully.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS maps to analyse links between inequality and migration

nodes.misconception: The development of new jobs in industry occurs at a large scale, involving huge factories and investment by a transnational corporation.
nodes.response: Microfinance loans can also support the development of new jobs in industry, at a smaller scale.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Strategies to reduce the development gap: industry and investment

nodes.misconception: That everyone in a country with a high GNI is well off, with a good quality of life.
nodes.response: A country’s income is not equally divided by everyone who lives there. This is why GNI per head should be used along side other measures in order to understand differences in quality of life.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring development

nodes.misconception: Tourism has only brought benefits to the island of Bali and its people.
nodes.response: Tourism has various positive and negative impacts - while the economy has grown and some public services have improved, others have declined (e.g. the water supply) and so many people visit Bali each year its environment has suffered in the South.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Example of how tourism can reduce the development gap

nodes.misconception: That there are few people who live to 65 years and beyond in LICs and NEEs.
nodes.response: It is the proportion of the population that is small not the actual number of people. Some LICs and NEEs have large populations so there are millions of people who reach the age of 65 years plus.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Development and demography

nodes.misconception: That the benefits of international migration are limited to the country of origin (such as remittances).
nodes.response: Destination countries experience a wide range of social and economic benefits as a result of immigration.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Consequences of global inequalities

nodes.misconception: That a single image can help us to understand how quality of life is different in distant places.
nodes.response: While images can be of use they can not depict all aspects of life, moreover each image can only ever show a single place or group of people. Within any country there is a diversity of lived experience.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Defining development

nodes.misconception: That the physical environment is the key cause of global inequalities.
nodes.response: Physical geography is a cause of inequality but human factors, past and present, are as influential in affecting the pattern of trade and development.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Causes of global inequalities

nodes.misconception: Maps always have the same symbols.
nodes.response: You find different symbols depending on the scale of your map.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Features of an OS map

nodes.misconception: Contours are only used to show hills and mountains.
nodes.response: Contours are used to show the height of the land at 10 metre intervals above sea level.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Showing height and relief on OS maps

nodes.misconception: Geography is learning about the natural world.
nodes.response: Geography has many different aspects and includes learning about the natural world and learning about society.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Geography in secondary school

nodes.misconception: Digital maps are only used to locate places.
nodes.response: Digital maps are used in many different jobs and used to present data.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using a GIS to locate and analyse places around the world

nodes.misconception: OS maps all use the same scale.
nodes.response: OS maps have different scales.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Scale and distance on OS maps

nodes.misconception: All maps are the same.
nodes.response: Different maps aim to show different things such as country borders, the location of physical features and the height of the land.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Locational knowledge of the world

nodes.misconception: Fieldwork must take place in an unfamiliar location.
nodes.response: While it can be exciting to do fieldwork in a new place, fieldwork actually can take place anywhere.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Planning and collecting survey data

nodes.misconception: Subjective data is automatically invalid and should be ignored.
nodes.response: Geographers use subjective data a lot as they value people's, and their own, opinion about something.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Analysing, concluding and evaluating survey data

nodes.misconception: Northings come before eastings.
nodes.response: Eastings come first, then northings.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Four and Six Figure Grid References

nodes.misconception: Latitude lines run vertically down the Earth.
nodes.response: Latitude lines run horizontally while longitude lines run vertically.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Latitude and longitude

nodes.misconception: The purpose of data presentation is to make the data more attractive.
nodes.response: The purpose of data presentation is to allow geographers to identify patterns and relationships in the data.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Presenting survey data

nodes.misconception: Maps are always accurate.
nodes.response: Maps are never completely accurate.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Different map projections

nodes.misconception: A natural hazard is the same thing as a natural disaster.
nodes.response: A natural hazard is a potentially harmful event, a natural disaster is when a natural hazard event significantly affects humans.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to natural hazards

nodes.misconception: Tectonic plates float like rafts on liquid magma.
nodes.response: The mantle is semi-solid rather than a sort of liquid sea of magma.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Plate tectonics theory

nodes.misconception: Volcanoes only occur on land.
nodes.response: In fact, volcanoes occur underwater as well as on land, especially at constructive plate margins and hot spots.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Processes at constructive/divergent plate margins

nodes.misconception: That volcanoes occur directly above where the oceanic plate starts to subduct.
nodes.response: In fact, the melting of the oceanic plate occurs deep in the mantle, so magma rises to the surface some distance away from the plate margin.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Processes at destructive/convergent plate margins

nodes.misconception: The earthquake caused most of the destruction in the 2011 Tohuku disaster.
nodes.response: While the magnitude 9.0 earthquake was powerful, Japan’s strict building regulations meant that most modern buildings withstood the shaking. It was the 10-metre-high tsunami that caused the majory of the destruction.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: An example of effects and responses to a tectonic hazard in an HIC

nodes.misconception: Volcanoes occur at all plate margins.
nodes.response: While volcanoes are a feature of both destructive and constructive plate margins, there are no volcanic eruptions at conservative margins because no magma is produced.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Processes at conservative plate margins

nodes.misconception: Primary effects always cause the most damage.
nodes.response: Sometimes it is the secondary effects of a hazard that cause the most destruction, for example mudslides following a volcanic eruption.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Primary and secondary effects and responses to tectonic hazards

nodes.misconception: The extreme destruction in Haiti was the result of the earthquake magnitude being unusually powerful.
nodes.response: The earthquake had a magnitude of 7.0, which is not unusually powerful. The high death toll and destruction were due to Haiti’s poor infrastructure, weak building regulations and lack of preparedness, not just the earthquake’s strength.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: An example of effects and responses to a tectonic hazard in an LIC

nodes.misconception: Because we know the location of plate margins, scientists can predict when earthquakes will happen.
nodes.response: While scientists can identify areas that are at high risk of earthquakes, exact predictions for when and where an earthquake will occur (or what magnitude it will be) are not possible.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing risks from earthquakes and volcanoes

nodes.misconception: The bigger the hazard event is, the higher the hazard risk will be.
nodes.response: The size of the hazard event is not the only factor that affects hazard risk. For example, a higher income country may have a lower hazard risk for a magnitude 6.5 earthquake than a lower income country, even though the earthquakes have equal power.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Factors affecting hazard risk

nodes.misconception: That both volcanoes and earthquakes occur at all types of plate margin.
nodes.response: While earthquakes are produced by tectonic movements at all plate margins, volcanoes are not found at conservative plate margins.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes

nodes.misconception: Students can find it difficult to grasp that Earth's crust and tectonic plates include the ocean floor, which has topography (e.g. mountains including volcanoes, valleys) just like the land areas.
nodes.response: Remind students (often!) that tectonic plates include the ocean floor. Apps such as 3D Scene can help to visualise this underwater topography, which we learn about by bathymetry. The story of Marie Tharp provides excellent disciplinary knowledge.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to visualise physical processes at different types of plate margin

nodes.misconception: A dangerous earthquake event is when the ground shakes, once. Then the danger is over.
nodes.response: Further sizeable earthquakes may occur in the days, weeks and months after a big earthquake, known as aftershocks, and these can be as dangerous for people and property, especially given the damage already done.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The effects of earthquakes

nodes.misconception: The oceanic plate subducts at a destructive plate margin and melts to form magma.
nodes.response: The water in the oceanic plate lowers the melting point, helping mantle rocks above to melt and form magma, not the subducting plate itself.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Plate boundaries

nodes.misconception: There are no plate boundaries in Africa.
nodes.response: Mount Nyiragongo is on a constructive plate boundary known as the East African Rift System, where the African plate is splitting into the Nubian and Somali plates.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The eruption of Mount Nyiragongo

nodes.misconception: If someone survives and is not injured during the earthquake, they are then safe.
nodes.response: Since many survivors had to stay in crowded shelters or sleep outside, the risk of diseases increased. In addition, strong aftershocks hit the area, damaging buildings that were already unstable.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The 2025 Myanmar Earthquake

nodes.misconception: People do not live on volcanoes because it is too dangerous.
nodes.response: One in twenty people live close to an active volcano, as there are many attractive qualities to living there, e.g. fertile soils, tourist income and geothermal energy.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Living close to volcanoes

nodes.misconception: Lava is the only dangerous aspect to a volcanic eruption and you can just run out of the way.
nodes.response: Ash, lahars and pyroclastic flows are all extremely dangerous volcanic hazards. Pyroclastic flows can reach speeds of 435 mph, which is faster than a car.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Volcanic hazards

nodes.misconception: Earthquakes and volcanoes happen on tectonic plates.
nodes.response: Tectonic plates cover the whole world, this would mean they happen everywhere. The majority of earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries (where two plates meet), though there are some which happen away from boundaries.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Inside Earth

nodes.misconception: Tsunamis are just big waves.
nodes.response: Tsunamis are caused by displacement of the ocean, not wind blowing over the surface. Tsunami waves don’t break, they come as a fast-moving wall of water, which can be far bigger and faster than a normal wave. They can also flood kilometres inland.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The 2018 Sunda Strait Tsunami

nodes.misconception: Plate boundaries are clean cuts through the ground which separate two plates.
nodes.response: There is not one fault but many, which make up a plate boundary and the rock is locked together across the two plates.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Earthquakes

nodes.misconception: Earthquakes can be predicted a few weeks or days before they happen so that people can evacuate.
nodes.response: Humans can calculate the probability of an earthquake happening within a region, over a long period of time. It is not possible to predict exactly when or where earthquakes will occur, or of what size.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Living in earthquake regions

nodes.misconception: Lava and magma can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Magma is molten rock underground, whereas lava is molten rock above Earth's surface.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of volcanoes

nodes.misconception: South America and the South American plate are the same thing.
nodes.response: South America is a continent (land), whereas the South American plate also includes part of the Atlantic ocean.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: The movement of tectonic plates

nodes.misconception: The global atmospheric circulation systems controls the temperature of different climate zones.
nodes.response: Global circulation system redistributes heat received at the Equator, but latitude controls temperature of each climate zone. The amount of solar radiation received at each latitude is due to the curvature of the Earth.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Global atmospheric circulation model, pressure belts and surface winds

nodes.misconception: Immediate responses only happen during the tropical storm.
nodes.response: Immediate responses happen before, during and immediately after the storm.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tropical storms – responses

nodes.misconception: Climate change is only caused by human activity.
nodes.response: Human activity has been significant in recent climate change, but natural factors have caused changes to the climate over millions of years.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Natural and human causes of climate change

nodes.misconception: It is very easy to miss important small steps in GIS.
nodes.response: Take students through each step and check for understanding very regularly.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to map the track of a tropical storm

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms only affect coastal areas.
nodes.response: Explain that tropical storms can impact inland areas as well due to heavy rainfall and flooding.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tropical storms – hazards and effects

nodes.misconception: Climate change has only happened recently.
nodes.response: The Earth's climate patterns have changed numerous times in the past, for example there have been around 50 cycles of glacial (cold) phases and interglacial (warmer) phases in the Quaternary period.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Evidence for climate change in the Quaternary period

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms can form over land.
nodes.response: Tropical storms form over warm ocean waters where they can draw energy from the heat and moisture. Once over land, they lose their energy source and weaken.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tropical storms – distribution, formation and development

nodes.misconception: All regions will be equally affected by climate change.
nodes.response: Different regions experience the effects of climate change differently due to environmental, economic and social factors.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Effects of climate change on people and the environment

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms cannot be accurately predicted.
nodes.response: While it is challenging, advances in technology and meteorology have improved the accuracy of tropical storm predictions.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing risks from effects of tropical storms

nodes.misconception: All countries prepare and respond  to tropical cyclones in the same way.
nodes.response: The level of development, amount of governmental planning as well as a country's location and experience of tropical cyclones, will affect how they prepare for and respond to them.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Examples of preparation and responses to tropical cyclones

nodes.misconception: Glacial landforms are not created by climate change.
nodes.response: Glacial landforms are often linked to climate change. In many areas we can only see glacial landforms because the ice sheets and glaciers which created them have melted. Climate change also causes glacial processes which modify the landscape.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to visualise climate change impacts

nodes.misconception: The global atmospheric circulation systems controls the temperature of different climate zones.
nodes.response: Global circulation system redistributes heat received at the Equator, but latitude controls temperature of each climate zone. The amount of solar radiation received at each latitude is due to the curvature of the Earth.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Global atmospheric circulation model, pressure belts and surface winds

nodes.misconception: Immediate responses only happen during the tropical storm.
nodes.response: Immediate responses happen before, during and immediately after the storm.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tropical storms – responses

nodes.misconception: Weather hazards don't badly affect the UK population .
nodes.response: The UK experiences weather hazards that have serious social, economic and environmental impacts, the Beast from the East killed 10 people and cost the UK £1 billion per day.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: An example of a recent extreme weather event in the UK

nodes.misconception: It is very easy to miss important small steps in GIS.
nodes.response: Take students through each step and check for understanding very regularly.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to map the track of a tropical storm

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms only affect coastal areas.
nodes.response: Explain that tropical storms can impact inland areas as well due to heavy rainfall and flooding.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tropical storms – hazards and effects

nodes.misconception: The UK has a moderate climate and doesn't experience weather hazards.
nodes.response: The UK experiences a range of different weather hazards which can have serious impacts.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather hazards in the UK

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms can form over land.
nodes.response: Tropical storms form over warm ocean waters where they can draw energy from the heat and moisture. Once over land, they lose their energy source and weaken.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Tropical storms – distribution, formation and development

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms cannot be accurately predicted.
nodes.response: While it is challenging, advances in technology and meteorology have improved the accuracy of tropical storm predictions.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing risks from effects of tropical storms

nodes.misconception: Tropical storms only affect people during and immediately after they make landfall.
nodes.response: Due to improved monitioring and prediction, people may evacuate high-risk areas before a storm hits, and the effects of the storm can last for months afterwards as people repair and recover their homes, environments and livelihoods.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Example of a tropical storm

nodes.misconception: When using filters, selecting the incorrect 'condition'; when configuring pop-ups, using the incorrect formula of words to link with attribute titles.
nodes.response: Advise caution when selecting the 'condition' for a filter; take care when typing text and typing or selecting attribute titles.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Using GIS to visualise global trends in urbanisation

nodes.misconception: Those in informal employment are unskilled.
nodes.response: Just because work is unregulated it does not mean that the workers are unskilled. While some workers may not have official certification of skills, they still possess expertise.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrasting urban economies in developing, emerging and developed countries

nodes.misconception: Migrants all have similar reasons for migrating.
nodes.response: Migration is a deeply personal decision. Migrants will have many different, and sometimes contradictory, reasons for migrating.
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.lessonTitle: Factors affecting the growth of cities

nodes.misconception: The first cities to become megacities are now the largest global cities.
