nodes.response: Do not use a question word to translate 'which' when adding information about the noun in the main clause. ‘Was’ can be used as a relative pronoun meaning ‘that' or 'which’ when referring to a whole clause, not a specific noun.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Berühmte Deutsche: subject relative clauses, wh- pronouns in relative clauses

nodes.misconception: Use 'mehr' with adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons.
nodes.response: Use the comparative form of adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons, e.g., 'interessanter als', not 'mehr interessant als'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Traditionen in Österreich: comparative adverbs, postnominal superlatives

nodes.misconception: Only verbs expressing a change of state take 'sein' in the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Verbs referring to motion, which don't require a direct object (e.g., 'gehen'), take 'sein' in the perfect tense. Most verbs meaning 'happen' (e.g., 'geschehen', 'passieren') and the verbs 'bleiben' and 'sein' also use 'sein'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Bertha von Suttner: perfect tense change of state verbs, superlative adjectives

nodes.misconception: All nouns ending '-n' must be in the dative case.
nodes.response: The definite article 'den' shows the dative plural form as well as the '-n' added to the end of the dative plural. However, a number of nouns form their plural by adding '-(e)n' and are not in the dative case.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die Brüder Grimm: plural nouns, weak masculine nouns

nodes.misconception: 'Lieber' means 'love'.
nodes.response: It is easy to confuse the words 'Liebe', 'liebe' and 'lieber', particularly in spoken German. Pay careful attention to pronunciation and listen out for [er]. 'Liebe' is a noun (love), 'liebe' is a verb (love) and 'lieber' is an adverb (more gladly).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die Vennbahn: perfect tense, imperfect tense, weak past participles

nodes.misconception: Adjectival nouns do not require a capital letter because they come from adjectives.
nodes.response: Adjectival nouns require a capital letter, just like all nouns in German.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Traditionen in der Schweiz: abstract adjectival neuter nouns

nodes.misconception: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender.
nodes.response: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender, i.e., not all nouns referring to a female are gramatically female (for example, 'das Mädchen' = 'girl').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Narrating with nouns: singular definite articles

nodes.misconception: Word order is the same in German and English.
nodes.response: Word order is not always the same in German and English. Pay close attention to the position of different sentence parts (subject, verb, nouns, adverbs).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at home: verb infinitives and singular persons

nodes.misconception: [ch] is pronounced as in the English 'cheese'.
nodes.response: [ch] is soft in German after [i] or [e]. It is hard after [a] [o] or [u]. This is because [a] [o] and [u] are pronounced with a more open mouth whilst [i] and [e] have a more closed mouth.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you do at home: present tense (weak verbs) 1st and 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: There are two present tenses in German, as in English.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in German. 'Ich lerne' means 'I learn' and 'I am learning'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Life at home: building sentences, present tense singular

nodes.misconception: Word order is the same in German and English.
nodes.response: German sentences containing adverbs have a different word order to English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Activities at home: build sentences from infinitive verbs, word order

nodes.misconception: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’ as in English.
nodes.response: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you do at home:  questions with 'wer', 'was', 'wo' and 'wie'

nodes.misconception: 'Damit' always means 'with it' or 'with them'.
nodes.response: 'Damit' has a double identity! It can be used as a conjunction meaning 'so that' as well as a da-compound meaning 'with it' or 'with them'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Diskriminerung im Alltag: damit da-compound vs damit conjunction

nodes.misconception: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in all present tense forms.
nodes.response: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in the first person singular of the present tense only.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Das Leben mit Behinderung: stem changes in present tense weak verbs

nodes.misconception: You can only succeed in listening comprehension if you know all the vocabulary.
nodes.response: Whilst vocabulary knowledge is the most important element for success, other strategies can help, for example, close pre-reading of the questions, predicting vocabulary, avoiding distractors and checking answers carefully.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Welt - Platz für alle: extended listening and spoken production

nodes.misconception: Whenever two-verb structures are used, the second verb - the infinitive or the past participle - always goes to the end of the clause or sentence.
nodes.response: The second verb goes to the end with normal word order and WO1 conjunctions like 'und', 'aber', 'oder' and 'sondern'. But with WO3 conjunctions, the main or finite verb is sent to the end of the clause.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Du siehst nicht krank aus: word order in 2-verb structures with conjunctions

nodes.misconception: Vor' and 'bevor' and 'nach' and 'nachdem' are interchangeable because they mean 'before' and 'after'.
nodes.response: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions and are followed by a noun, 'bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions which link clauses and trigger word order 3.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gemeinsam statt einsam: prepositions vor, nach and conjunctions bevor, nachdem

nodes.misconception: Always use 'würd-' and a 2nd (infinitive) verb at the end of the sentence to mean 'would'.
nodes.response: This works for many verbs, but 'haben' and 'sein' have their own forms - 'hätte' ('would have') and 'wäre' ('would be'). No second infinitive is required.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Energiekrise in Deutschland: future vs conditional, 2-verb rule

nodes.misconception: 'Bis' always means 'until'.
nodes.response: 'Bis' has several meanings and uses. As a preposition it can mean 'until', 'up to' or 'by'. As a conjunction it usually means 'until'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Armut in Deutschland: 'bis' as preposition, 'bis' and 'wenn' as conjunctions

nodes.misconception: All prepositions are followed by only one case - for example, the accusative or the dative.
nodes.response: The prepositions 'an, 'auf', 'in',  ‘über’, 'unter', ‘vor’, 'hinter', 'neben' and ‘zwischen’ are used with the accusative case when there is movement, but the dative case when there is no movement.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Biodiversität: definite and indefinite articles after prepositions, da-compounds

nodes.misconception: All questions in German invert the subject and verb. Apart from that the word order is the same as English.
nodes.response: Subject and verb are inverted, but word order differs from English for a verb with a preposition - 'What are you talking about?'. In German, a preposition never ends a question. Use 'wo(r)' + preposition to start the question - 'Worüber redest du?'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die Umwelt: word order with questions, questions with wo-compounds

nodes.misconception: When saying the time, 'half past' is expressed the same way in German as in English, i.e., half past the current hour.
nodes.response: In German, 'half past' is expressed as half of the next hour, e.g., 'halb neun' is half of nine o'clock, or half past eight.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Famous festivals and traditions: plural reflexive verbs, 12-hour clock

nodes.misconception: Saying times in 24-hour format in German works in exactly the same way as in English.
nodes.response: Saying the time in 24-hour format uses numbers like in English. The difference is that German needs 'Uhr' - 'o'clock' - between the hour and the minutes, e.g., 21:50 is 'einundzwanzig Uhr fünfzig'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday routine: using verbs reflexively, 24-hour clock

nodes.misconception: 'Mich' and 'dich' are only direct object pronouns meaning me and you.
nodes.response: 'Mich' and 'dich' can also be reflexive pronouns and then mean myself and yourself. Reflexive pronouns are required when using a verb reflexively.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday actions and routines: using singular verbs reflexively

nodes.misconception: The meaning of all German phrases should be taken literally.
nodes.response: Just like English, German contains idioms, phrases that mean something other than their literal meaning, e.g., ‘da haben wir den Salat’ - 'we have the salad there', which should be understood as 'now we have a problem'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Festivals and traditions: using plural verbs reflexively

nodes.misconception: In a written dictation in German, the only thing that matters is the correct sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs).
nodes.response: SSCs are important, but the text needs to make sense grammatically. Check for correct spelling of known words, verb forms and tenses, and singular or plural nouns. Encourage students to check the details and to read back the texts in their head.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Marietta Slomka: dictation, extended translation

nodes.misconception: Past participles of -ieren verbs start with 'ge-' like most other past participles.
nodes.response: Unlike most other past participles, most German -'ieren' verbs act like some other weak German verbs, meaning that they do not have 'ge' at the beginning of their participles (for example, verbs beginning with 'be', 'er', and 'ver').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Heidi: perfect tense -ieren verbs, perfect tense with adverbs

nodes.misconception: Asking yes/no questions in the past is much more complicated than the present tense, as the rules are different. You need to translate 'did'.
nodes.response: The English 'did' isn't needed. Swap subject and verb for a yes/no question. 'Er sprach' (imperfect) becomes 'Sprach er?'. In the perfect tense, the past participle stays at the end of the sentence: 'Er hat gesprochen' - 'Hat er gesprochen?'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Matthias Maurer: yes/no questions in the perfect and imperfect tenses

nodes.misconception: All nouns change in their plural form.
nodes.response: Different nouns have different rules for forming plurals. It is important to learn these and acknowledge that there will always be exceptions to any rule.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas: 'Es gibt' with plurals, the song 'O Tannenbaum'

nodes.misconception: All nouns change in their plural form, and they all change in the same way.
nodes.response: Different nouns have different rules for forming plurals. It is important to learn these and acknowledge that there will always be exceptions to any rule.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas: definite article 'die', plurals with umlaut +e, no change -el/-en/-er

nodes.misconception: 'Sie' always refer to feminine 'it' when used as a subject pronoun.
nodes.response: 'Sie' means 'it' in the feminine form and 'they' in the plural form. 'Sie' is used for all plural forms.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you and others have and what it is like: subject pronoun 'sie' for 'they'

nodes.misconception: 'Er' and 'sie' only mean 'he' and 'she'.
nodes.response: Whilst 'er' and 'sie' do mean 'he' and 'she', they are also the masculine and neuter words for 'it'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Saying what something is like: subject pronouns 'er', 'sie', 'es' for 'it'

nodes.misconception: Feminine noun plurals are the same as masculine and neuter noun plurals.
nodes.response: Most feminine nouns add either an -e or an -en to the end of the noun in its plural form. Feminine nouns ending in -el or -er also add an -n unlike in the masculine and neuter form where nouns ending in these letters don't tend to change.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas traditions: 'sein' 3rd person singular and plural, plurals - +(e)n

nodes.misconception: All nouns change when they are in their plural form.
nodes.response: There are three different plural rules. 1. Most masculine and neuter nouns add -e to the end and an umlaut to the vowel; 2. M. and nt. nouns ending in -el, -er or -en often stay the same when plural; 3. Most feminine nouns add -n or -en to the end.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas traditions: singular and plural nouns

nodes.misconception: All plurals are formed in the same way.
nodes.response: Nouns have different rules for plurals depending on their gender and spelling.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: How many? Ask questions and give statements with plural nouns

nodes.misconception: The same plural rules apply to nouns of all three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter).
nodes.response: There are different rules for different nouns. It often depends on whether the noun is masculine, feminine or neuter. It is important to learn the plural noun form when learning a new noun.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers 1-12: plurals adding umlaut + -er

nodes.misconception: When talking about travel, where and how you went can be given in any order, as is the case in English.
nodes.response: When using adverbs to say where and how you went in the same sentence, manner (how) always comes before place (where).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Where did you go? How did you travel? Word order, manner before place

nodes.misconception: To talk about the past using the perfect tense, we always use the present tense of ‘haben’ with a past participle.
nodes.response: Some verbs require the present tense of ‘sein’ with a past participle when forming the past perfect tense. These are mostly verbs of movement to a destination, e.g., ‘fahren’ to travel, ‘fliegen’ to fly.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Where I went: singular perfect tense 'sein' vs 'haben', 'mit' + dative

nodes.misconception: The words for 'the' and 'a' are always the same after prepositions.
nodes.response: Prepositions take a specific case, e.g., 'durch' always takes the accusative. Some prepositions take different cases to create different meanings, e.g., 'in' and 'auf' can take the accusative, to show movement to, or the dative, to show location.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: The Black Forest: prepositions, perfect tense questions

nodes.misconception: The perfect tense in German is always formed with a part of 'haben' to express what someone has done.
nodes.response: Some verbs require a part of 'sein' to form the perfect tense, often with verbs of movement to a destination.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: The Black Forest: singular perfect tense with 'haben' and 'sein', 'durch'

nodes.misconception: 'Es' is the only German word for 'it'.
nodes.response: Object pronouns such as 'es' tell us the grammatical gender of the object of the sentence. German has three words for the object pronoun 'it' - masculine 'ihn', feminine 'sie' and neuter 'es'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: School subjects: singular 'mögen', object pronouns 'ihn', 'sie', 'es'

nodes.misconception: 'Sie’ always means ‘she’.
nodes.response: To say 'them' in German, use the plural object pronoun 'sie' for all genders.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: School subjects: 'mögen' singular persons, object pronoun plural 'sie'

nodes.misconception: [s] is pronounced the same as the English 's'.
nodes.response: [s] is pronounced like the English 'z' when it comes before a vowel. Elsewhere, both [s] and [ß] are pronounced like the English 's'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Opinions about school: 'finden' singular persons, object pronouns

nodes.misconception: [ß] is a capitalised letter 'B'.
nodes.response: [ß] is a symbol representing 'ss' and is called 'Eszett' or 'scharfes s'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Opinions about school: singular 'finden', 'ihn', 'sie', 'es', 'sie' (plural)

nodes.misconception: Da-compounds can always be translated literally, with the preposition retaining its usual meaning.
nodes.response: German verb and preposition combinations need to be learnt. We often use different prepositions after verbs in English and in German. Some da-compounds have also taken on slightly different meanings when used as adverbs or in idiomatic phrases.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Eine Online-Welt. Toll, oder? Prepositional verbs, da-compounds

nodes.misconception: We need to use the present continuous in German when describing photos.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in German. The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'. When translating English present continuous sentences, use the simple present.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Was machen sie online? Revisiting vocabulary, describing pictures

nodes.misconception: When writing in German, accuracy is the most important thing, so it's best to keep sentences short and clear.
nodes.response: When producing written work in German, try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity. This must, of course, be balanced with accuracy, which enables you to communicate your ideas clearly.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesundheit: read and respond to texts

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is never used in spoken German.
nodes.response: The irregular verbs 'haben' and 'sein', modal verbs and 'es gab' are all common in spoken German. Other verbs in the imperfect mainly appear in written texts.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Medizin früher und heute: 'es gibt' vs 'es gab', imperfect

nodes.misconception: You always leave out the subject pronoun when using the imperative.
nodes.response: The 'du' and 'ihr' forms of the imperative omit the subject pronoun, but the 'Sie' form retains it.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Seien Sie sicher online! Using 'Sie' in statements, questions and the imperative

nodes.misconception: 'Können' and 'dürfen' both mean 'can' in English.
nodes.response: Whilst we often use 'can' to translate both verbs in English, they are different in meaning.  'Dürfen' refers to permission - 'may I/am I allowed to?'. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something - 'can I/am I able to?'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Ab wann darf man wählen? Present and past modal verbs

nodes.misconception: The German subject pronoun 'man' must always be translated using the English subject pronoun 'one'.
nodes.response: 'Man' has a range of possible translations, including 'people' and 'you'. It can also be used to say what 'is done' or 'was done' by people in general.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Das Leben in anderen Ländern: adjectives with '-los', uses of 'man'

nodes.misconception: If we see a reflexive pronoun, e.g., 'uns' or 'sich', this always means that the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the verb are the same.
nodes.response: Some plural reflexive verbs are reciprocal, meaning the action of the verb is done 'to each other' rather than 'to oneself'. The word 'gegenseitig' can be used to emphasise reciprocal use. Otherwise, use context to work out which meaning is intended.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Denken Jugendliche heute global? Accusative and dative reflexive verbs

nodes.misconception: The conjunction 'obwohl' has the same effect on word order whether it starts the sentence or a second clause in a sentence.
nodes.response: The conjunction 'obwohl' always triggers word order 3 in a clause. However, if the sentence starts with the 'obwohl' clause, we then use the verb-comma-verb rule, meaning the second clause starts with the verb.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Beim Arzt: word order with 'obwohl', role-play

nodes.misconception: 'Gern' is a verb meaning 'to like, liking' and can be used in front of the noun in sentence, e.g., 'ich gern Fußball'.
nodes.response: 'Gern' is an adverb meaning 'gladly'. It is used to express liking doing an action and follows the verb that names the action, e.g., 'ich spiele gern Fußball'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Favourite activities in Vienna: present tense, 'gern',  inversion

nodes.misconception: The terms 'weak verb' and 'strong verb' refer to whether the action is powerful or not.
nodes.response: The term 'weak verb' is used to describe verbs that follow a regular pattern across all tenses. The term 'strong verb' describes verbs that have a stem change in either present or past tenses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Things you like to do: adverb 'gern'

nodes.misconception: 'Nicht' goes before the verb like 'not' in English.
nodes.response: In German, 'nicht' usually goes before the element it negates — unless it's negating the whole sentence, in which case it tends to go at the end, e.g., 'Ich kaufe das Auto nicht' - 'I'm not buying the car'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: In Vienna: present tense, negation with 'nicht'; question forming

nodes.misconception: All verbs only need the -en ending changed to match the subject in the present tense.
nodes.response: Some verbs need a change to the vowel in the stem in addition to the change to the -en ending, but only for 'du', 'er' and 'sie' (she).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Favourite activities: questions with 'welch-', answers with 'gern'

nodes.misconception: German forms comparatives in the same way as English.
nodes.response: Use 'als' to compare things that are different and 'so ... wie' to compare things that are the same.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutsche Influencer: comparatives, adding -keit and -heit

nodes.misconception: I should use word order two after phrases of opinion.
nodes.response: Use word order two after 'meiner Meinung nach' and word order three after 'ich denke, dass' and 'ich glaube, dass'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Wie sind deine Familie und Freunde? Adding un-, word order, superlatives

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives don't need endings.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives take the same endings as 'ein'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Familie: possessive adjectives, extended reading

nodes.misconception: Add -er to form all comparative adverbs.
nodes.response: Some comparative adverbs are irregular.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Freunde: 'gern' and 'lieber', dictation, comparative adverbs

nodes.misconception: When answering conversation questions, it’s good to keep answers as short as possible, as in a role-play task.
nodes.response: To give strong answers in conversation, it’s important to answer in full sentences and give details in our answers, including opinions and reasons, where appropriate.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Familie und Freunde: translation, comprehension, conversation

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives don't change their endings, like in English.
nodes.response: German possessive adjectives change their endings based on case and gender.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Familie: possessive adjectives, dictation

nodes.misconception: 'Zu', meaning 'to', is always needed as part of two-verb infinitive structures, e.g., 'Ich hoffe, mehr in die Schule zu lernen.'.
nodes.response: 'Werden' and modal verbs do not need 'zu' before the second verb: 'Ich werde mehr in der Schule lernen'. Other verbs that do not require 'zu' include 'helfen', 'lassen' and 'mögen'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: New Year's resolutions: future tense

nodes.misconception: When using two-verb constructions, the second verb is always in the infinitive and comes at the end of the clause.
nodes.response: When a two-verb construction follows a subordinating conjunction like ‘weil’, the short form of the verb moves to the end, after the infinitive (WO3), e.g., ‘Ich hoffe, dieses Jahr zu feiern, weil es Spaß machen wird.’.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: New Year's resolutions: word order with two-verb structures

nodes.misconception: Always use 'werden' and a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future ideas.
nodes.response: In German future ideas can be expressed by the present tense with a future time phrase. They can also be expressed by 'werden' plus a 2nd verb, or by 'möcht-' to say what you would like to do in the future.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: An der Universität: present vs future, 'möchte', extended writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: All German past participles start with 'ge-'.
nodes.response: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Schultag: perfect tense, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
nodes.response: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Schultag: nouns and plurals, present tense, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: An der Universität: verbs, nouns, adjectives with prepositions, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: An der Universität: read aloud, reading comprehension (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Tag: dictation, listening (AQA)

nodes.misconception: All German past participlies start with 'ge-'
nodes.response: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Schultag: perfect tense, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
nodes.response: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Schultag: nouns and plurals, present tense, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: An der Universität: verbs, nouns, adjectives, prepositions, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Tag: dictation, listening (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: An der Universität: read aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Always use 'werden' and a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future ideas.
nodes.response: In German future ideas can be expressed by the present tense with a future time phrase. They can also be expressed by 'werden' plus a 2nd verb, or by 'möcht-' to say what you would like to do in the future.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: An der Universität: present vs future, 'möchte', extended writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: German has one general verb meaning 'to put, putting'.
nodes.response: German has three placement verbs that translate into English as 'to put, putting'. 'Stellen' - to make something stand (vertically), 'setzen' - to make something sit, 'legen' - to make something lay down (horizontally).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Party plans: separable verbs, placement and position verbs, 'während'

nodes.misconception: All separable verbs in German have their word-for-word English equivalent, e.g., 'stattfinden' - 'to take place', 'mitbringen' - to bring with, along'.
nodes.response: Many two-part separable verbs in German have single word English translations, e.g., 'einkaufen' - 'to shop', 'anfangen' - 'to start'. It is especially important with these verbs not to forget the separable prefix in German.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Party plans: separable verbs in the present tense

nodes.misconception: We always use accusative reflexive pronouns ('mich', 'dich', etc.) with reflexive verbs.
nodes.response: If there is already an accusative object in the sentence, we use dative reflexive pronouns ('mir', 'dir', etc.) instead, e.g., 'Ich wasche mir die Hände'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Junge Pflegende: accusative and dative reflexive pronouns, 'welch-'

nodes.misconception: Verbs have the same meaning whether they are used reflexively or non-reflexively.
nodes.response: Some verbs have the same or similar meanings when used reflexively and non-reflexively, e.g. nennen, to call, sich nennen, to call oneself. However, some verbs completely change their meaning e.g. anziehen, to attract, sich anziehen, to get dressed.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Beziehungen: reflexive and non-reflexive verbs, reciprocal verbs

nodes.misconception: Verbs are only followed by the dative case if we translate the verb with 'to' or 'for' in English.
nodes.response: There are several impersonal verbs in German which require the dative case, e.g., 'gelingen' (to succeed).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Karneval: indirect object pronouns, verbs with indirect objects, 'bei', 'beim'

nodes.misconception: Questions words all have fixed spellings.
nodes.response: 'Wer', meaning 'who', changes spelling according to its case. This also used to be the case in English, but the 'whom' form is often not used nowadays.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Freunde: 'wen' and 'wem' - interrogative, word order with reflexive questions

nodes.misconception: Da-compounds can be used to refer back to any noun already mentioned.
nodes.response: Da-compounds can only be used with inanimate nouns. For people and animals, use object pronouns.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Frauen im Motorsport: da-compounds, wo-compounds

nodes.misconception: 'Damit' always means 'with it' or 'with them'.
nodes.response: 'Damit' has a double identity! It can be used as a conjunction meaning 'so that' as well as a da-compound meaning 'with it' or 'with them'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Traditionen: da-compounds, 'damit' as conjunction and wo-compounds

nodes.misconception: The present continuous in German is different to the simple present.
nodes.response: The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Weltreligionen und ihre Feste: expanding vocabulary, describing photos

nodes.misconception: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' and object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie' can only refer to people.
nodes.response: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' can mean 'he' and 'she' or they can refer to masculine and feminine nouns, meaning 'it'. The same is true for the object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie', which can mean 'him' and 'her' but also 'it'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Familie: direct object pronouns, singular and plural

nodes.misconception: All verbs in German are followed by the accusative case, apart from 'sein' which takes the nominative case.
nodes.response: A number of verbs are followed by the dative case. These must be learnt and carefully identified when translating into German.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Traditionen: 'jed-', dative verbs, translation

nodes.misconception: English verbs followed by prepositions can be directly translated into German.
nodes.response: Whilst many of the same verbs are followed by prepositions in both languages, different prepositions are often used, so these must be learnt.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Vorbilder: accusative definite articles, verbs with accusative prepositions

nodes.misconception: Form closed questions in German by adding 'do you ...' or 'are you ...', as in English.
nodes.response: Swap only the position of the subject and verb in a German statement to form a closed question.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Yourself and others: present tense questions and answers

nodes.misconception: You translate the English present continuous with a form of 'sein', e.g., 'Ich bin machen ...'.
nodes.response: There is only one present tense in German. 'Ich mache' means 'I do' and 'I am doing'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Famous German speakers: present tense weak verbs, singular persons

nodes.misconception: You can add the suffix -los to any German noun to make an adjective.
nodes.response: You can't just add -los to any noun to form an adjective. It only works if the result makes real sense - usually where there’s a natural English -less equivalent (like 'hairless', 'hopeless', 'windowless').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A murder mystery party: relative clauses

nodes.misconception: German [d] is always pronounced as English [d].
nodes.response: German [d] at the beginning of a word or syllable sounds like English 'd'; [d] at the end of a syllable sounds like -t. For example, the sentence 'die Landschaft in Deutschland ist wunderschön' contains examples of both [d] sounds.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Work placement as a stagehand: relative clauses

nodes.misconception: The word for 'who' in German is 'wer'.
nodes.response: We use 'wer' to ask or report a question: 'Wer ist das?', 'Ich weiß nicht, wer das ist.' But in sentences like 'that is someone, who ...' we use a relative pronoun - 'der', 'die', 'das' - which matches the gender of noun it refers to.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: People and things: relative clauses to define who, which, that

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Online Leben: questions, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
nodes.response: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Online Leben: questions, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
nodes.response: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Online Leben: questions, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Online Leben: questions, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Online Leben: dictation,  listening (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Online Leben: dictation, listening (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Verbs are only followed by the dative case if we translate the verb with 'to' or 'for' in English.
nodes.response: Some verbs are impersonal, and take the dative, and are usually used with 'es'. For example, 'gelingen' - 'es gelingt mir' (I succeed).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Berufserfahrung: verbs with indirect objects, dative pronouns

nodes.misconception: Use 'würd-' whenever you want to say 'would'.
nodes.response: 'Würd-' works for very many cases and is easy to remember because it sounds like the English 'would'. But 'haben' and 'sein' are important exceptions, especially in spoken German. 'Hätte' means 'I would have' and 'wäre' means 'I would be'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Wenn ich 16 bin: würd- with gern and lieber, imperfect subjunctive hätte, wäre

nodes.misconception: 'Solange' and 'sobald' have to be used with 'als' to translate the 'as' in 'as long/soon as'.
nodes.response: The single word 'solange' is the translation for three English words - 'as long as' - and the same for 'sobald' - 'as soon as'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Pläne: word order with 'sobald', 'solange' and 'wenn'

nodes.misconception: 'Können' and 'dürfen' both translate as 'can' in English.
nodes.response: 'Können' and 'dürfen' are often used incorrectly in both German and English. 'Dürfen' refers to permission - 'may I/am I allowed to?'. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something - 'can I/am I able to?', whether or not permission is given.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Was darf man ab wann? 'Dürfen' vs 'können', wh- questions and modal verbs

nodes.misconception: All sentences with 'wenn' use word order 3 and send the verb to the end.
nodes.response: Distinguish between a clause and a sentence. 'Wenn' clauses need a second clause to complete a sentence. A clause starting with 'wenn' sends the verb to the end. If the 'wenn' clause is first, the second clause (after the comma) uses inversion.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Das Pfandsystem: word order with 'wenn', inversion, plural nouns

nodes.misconception: In German, you always use 'müssen' to say what you have to do.
nodes.response: The verb 'sollen' is another way of expressing an obligation, something you have to do. It has several uses, including strong commands (e.g. 'you should ring the doctor straightaway'), which are similar to the 'have to, must' meaning of 'müssen'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Hitzefrei: 'müssen' vs 'sollen', 'sollen' vs 'sollte'

nodes.misconception: To say 'it' in German, always use 'es'.
nodes.response: As a pronoun, 'es' only replaces a neuter noun. 'Das Buch? Ich lese es gern.' ('A book? I like reading it.'). Use 'ihn' or 'sie' for masculine and feminine nouns. 'Der neue Film? Ich finde ihn (it) toll.'. 'Berlin? Ich besuche sie (it) gern.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Junge Deutsche: telling the time, uses of 'es'

nodes.misconception: Use 'wer' in German whenever you want to say 'who'.
nodes.response: There are 3 different forms of 'who' in German, which should be used correctly to match the case required in each sentence. There are different forms in English (who, whom), but we don't often use 'whom'. The rules in German are stricter.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Berufserfahrung: 'Sie', 'Ihnen', interrogatives 'wer', 'wen', 'wem'

nodes.misconception: 'Ich will' in German means 'I will' in English.
nodes.response: 'Ich will' (from the verb 'wollen') means 'I want to', but is a common false friend. The future tense in German needs 'werden' with a 2nd verb in the infinitive.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Berufe: 'werden' + infinitive, wh-questions in future and conditional tenses

nodes.misconception: 'z' is pronounced the same way in both English and German.
nodes.response: German [z] sounds like the English 'ts'. German [s-] is pronounced like the English 'z'. Use example words to remind you of the difference, e.g., 'Zug' (train) and 'Suche' (search).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Pläne: adding -er to verb stems for male agent nouns, extended writing

nodes.misconception: When an adjective follows 'ein', always add 'en'.
nodes.response: Adjective endings reflect the case and gender of the word they refer to. Dative case adjectives end in -en. In nominative and accusative, use -e for feminine and -es for neuter. Masculine -er  and -en match (d)er (nominative) and (d)en (accusative).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Junge Deutsche: neuter adjectival nouns, nominalisation, adjectival agreement

nodes.misconception: Alll German words of foreign origin form their plural by adding 's'.
nodes.response: Inanimate nouns add 's': 'Interviews', 'Songs'. Person nouns ending in -er (e.g., 'Reporter') do not change in the masculine plural. Weak masculine nouns (e.g., 'Journalist') add -en in the plural. Feminine plurals add -nen (e.g., 'Journalistinnen').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Junge Deutsche: weak plural masculine nouns, feminine person nouns

nodes.misconception: There is one verb meaning 'to like' in German, and that is 'mögen'.
nodes.response: 'Mögen' is 'to like', e.g., 'ich mag Mathe' ('I like maths'). However, 'gefallen' is another verb for expressing 'liking'. Its literal meaning is 'to please', so it's used with an indirect object, e.g., 'Mathe gefällt mir' - 'I like maths'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Opinions: verbs with indirect objects

nodes.misconception: After an opinion verb (e.g., 'denken') and the conjunction 'dass', we use normal subject-verb word order.
nodes.response: To say 'I think that ...' in German, we use the conjunction 'dass', which triggers word order 3 (WO3); e.g., 'Ich denke, dass Rapmusik toll ist.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Thoughts and opinions: opinion verbs with 'dass', word order

nodes.misconception: If we want to say 'her' in German, the word is always 'ihr'.
nodes.response: After many verbs, the word for 'her' is 'sie'; same as the word for 'she', e.g., 'ich frage sie'. The word 'ihr' means 'her' after a dative verb, e.g., 'ich antworte ihr'. 'Ihr' is also the possessive adjective 'her', e.g., 'ihr Lieblingsgeschenk'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Exchange gifts: 'von' and 'für', possessive adjectives (accusative and dative)

nodes.misconception: The German pronoun for singular informal 'you' is always 'du'.
nodes.response: German uses 'du' as subject pronoun, 'dich' as direct object pronoun,  and 'dir' as indirect object pronoun. There are also two object pronouns for 'me'. E.g., 'Du fragst mich.' ('You ask me.'), 'Du antwortest mir.' ('You answer me'.).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Exchange gifts: verbs with indirect objects

nodes.misconception: The subject pronoun 'sie' always means 'she'.
nodes.response: The subject pronoun 'sie' means 'she' when used with a 3rd person singular verb ending or 'they' when used with a 3rd person plural verb ending. If written as 'Sie' and is used with a 3rd person plural verb ending, it can mean 'you (formal)'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Childhood experiences: imperfect plural forms of 'sein' and 'haben'

nodes.misconception: Stress is always placed on the first syllable in German words.
nodes.response: Most German words place stress on the first syllable, but the 2nd syllable is stressed in words beginning with inseparable prefixes. Borrowed words stress the 2nd or final syllable.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Famous people and their languages: perfect tense with 'sein', calendar years

nodes.misconception: The sound-symbol correspondence [ie] is always pronounced as in 'Liebe'.
nodes.response: When [ie] is the final but unstressed syllable in a word, pronounce [i] and [e] as separate vowel sounds, e.g., 'Familie'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Migrant experiences: noun suffixes, ‘welch-’

nodes.misconception: Modal verbs require a 'zu' before the infinitive.
nodes.response: Two-verb structures without a modal verb require 'zu' before the infinitive, e.g., 'Ich habe Lust, schwimmen zu gehen.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Migration: imperfect modal verbs, word order with two-verb structures

nodes.misconception: At the end of a word, [e] sounds the same as short [e].
nodes.response: Final [e] sounds like 'uh', as in 'danke', 'Klasse'. Short [e] sounds more like 'eh' as in 'denken'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Migration: imperfect modal verbs 'konnte', 'musste', 'wollte'

nodes.misconception: Modal verbs don't require a 2nd verb in the infinitive unless they are in the present tense.
nodes.response: Modal verbs require a 2nd verb in the infinitive in other tenses, including the imperfect tense, e.g., 'ich konnte schwimmen'. They do not require a preceding 'zu' before the infinitive. Other verbs do.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Childhood experiences: imperfect modal verbs 'konnte', 'musste', 'wollte'

nodes.misconception: Separable prefixes always move to the end of a clause.
nodes.response: Separable verbs have a prefix that goes to the end of the clause in word order one clauses (standard word order), but in word order three (verb to end) the prefix and the verb reunite. Separable prefixes are always joined to the past participle.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Language and identity: separable verbs, cardinal and ordinal numbers

nodes.misconception: There are no rules to help you learn which verbs are strong and have a vowel change in their stem.
nodes.response: Only verbs with an 'a' or 'e' in their stem can be strong.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare lifestyles: present tense strong verbs 1st and 3rd person singular

nodes.misconception: 'Sie' always means 'she'.
nodes.response: As a subject pronoun, 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they'. As an object pronoun, 'sie' means 'her' or 'it'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Narrate other people's actions: present tense weak and strong verbs

nodes.misconception: Always use the word 'nicht' to negate a statement.
nodes.response: Use the correct form of 'kein' to translate 'not a/any' with nouns. Use 'nicht' with verbs and adjectives.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Can and can't: singular 'können' + infinitive and negation

nodes.misconception: The infinitive comes directly after the form of 'können', as in English: 'I can play guitar'.
nodes.response: The infinitive comes at the end of the sentence in German when used with a modal verb such as 'können', as in 'Ich kann Gitarre spielen'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Can and able: singular 'können' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: You have to use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun.
nodes.response: Do not use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun, e.g., 'Ich bin Sänger'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What we do together: present 1st person plural weak verbs and 'sein'

nodes.misconception: Compound nouns take the gender of their first noun.
nodes.response: Compound nouns take the gender of their final noun.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare activities: strong verbs 1st and 3rd person singular, compound nouns

nodes.misconception: A bilingual dictionary lists words from A-Z in one long list.
nodes.response: A bilingual dictionary is split into two sections. These is German to English, and English to German. Each section lists words from A-Z. To find the English meaning of a German word, look for it in the German to English section, and vice versa.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you and others do: strong verbs 1st and 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: There is no vowel change in the 2nd person singular 'du' present tense forms of strong verbs.
nodes.response: The vowel in the stem of strong verbs with an 'a' or 'e' in their stem will change in the 2nd person singular 'du' present tense form.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Ask about activities: present tense strong verbs 1st and 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: [v] is pronounced like the English 'v'.
nodes.response: [v] is pronounced like an English 'f'. [w] sounds like an English 'v'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What I do and what we do: present tense 1st person plural weak verbs

nodes.misconception: Umlauts do not make a difference to the pronunciation of a letter.
nodes.response: German vowels (with or without umlauts) can be short or long. Vowels are short when followed by more than one consonant. Vowels are long when there is a double vowel, followed by 'h', or a single consonant.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Other people's actions: singular present tense strong verbs

nodes.misconception: Verbs that are reflexive in English must be reflexive in German and vice versa.
nodes.response: Different verbs are reflexive in different languages. For example, 'sich erinnern' is not reflexive in English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Lebenserfahrung: simple past with früher, gern, lieber, am liebsten, reflexive verbs

nodes.misconception: Modal verbs must add ge- in the imperfect tense.
nodes.response: Modal verbs are normally used in the imperfect to describe past events. The imperfect is a different tense from the perfect and is formed differently.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Ich bin Ingenieurin: imperfect modals

nodes.misconception: I can answer a role-play question with one or two words.
nodes.response: Role-play questions need to be answered in full sentences with at least one verb.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die Ferien: perfect tense with adverbs

nodes.misconception: I should use the same word order in German as in English.
nodes.response: German word order is different from English word order. In word order 2, the subject and verb are inverted.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Es war toll! Perfect tense with 'sein', 'haben' and questions, inversion

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense of the modal verb 'mögen' is formed like other modal verbs.
nodes.response: The stem of 'mögen' in the imperfect tense is 'moch-'.  It is normally followed by a noun rather than a second verb in the infinitive.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Karrieregespräche: perfect tense strong verbs, 'mochte', 'gefallen' vs 'gemocht'

nodes.misconception: 'Aber' and 'sondern' mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
nodes.response: Use 'aber' to contradict a preceding statement that does not contain a negative. Use 'sondern' to mean 'but' or 'rather' following a negative statement.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Der Hund ist frech! Negation with 'nicht' and 'sondern', determiners

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Salzburg, Österreich: read aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. You should not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Salzburg, Österreich: modal verbs present vs imperfect, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutschland: negation, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutschland: negation, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutschland: adjective endings, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only ever written.
nodes.response: Whilst the imperfect tense is mainly used to narrate past events in written German, some forms are regularly used in spoken German, such as 'es gab', 'war' and 'hatte'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Salzburg, Österreich: imperfect tense, extended writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutschland: adjective endings, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only ever written.
nodes.response: Whilst the imperfect tense is mainly used to narrate past events in written German, some forms are regularly used in spoken German, such as 'es gab', 'war' and 'hatte'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Salzburg, Österreich: imperfect tense, extended writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Salzburg, Österreich: read aloud, reading comprehension (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutschland: read aloud, reading comprehension (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. You should not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Salzburg, Österreich: modal verbs present vs imperfect, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Deutschland: read aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The grammatical gender of feminine nouns changes to masculine in the dative case.
nodes.response: Feminine nouns are always feminine, no matter what case their article may change to.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: In and into places: prepositions 'in' and 'auf' (accusative and dative)

nodes.misconception: Nouns in German have capital letters in the same situations as English nouns.
nodes.response: German nouns are always capitalised, no matter where or how they are used in a sentence.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you and others do and when: time phrases as nouns and adverbs

nodes.misconception: 'Auf' always means 'on' or 'onto'.
nodes.response: 'Auf' sometimes means ‘at’ or ‘to’, especially with events or open spaces.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Where are you and where are you going? 'In' and 'auf' (accusative and dative)

nodes.misconception: Word order tells you if a sentence is a question or a statement.
nodes.response: Use clues such as intonation and vocabulary meanings to help you decide if a sentence is a question or a statement, as the word order in questions is similar to word order 2.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Who does what and when? 'Wann?' and inversion

nodes.misconception: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] make the same sound in English as they do in German.
nodes.response: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] sound the same in German. Even though many words with these spellings come from English, German pronounces 't' and [th] in the same way.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What others do and when: main clause word order and  inversion

nodes.misconception: In word order 2, all the words in a sentence change position from word order 1.
nodes.response: The verb remains in the same position in word order 2 as in word order 1. If emphasis is on the adverb, the adverb and subject swap position.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What I do and when: inversion in statements with adverbs of time

nodes.misconception: If a verb is 'strong', its past participle always has a vowel change.
nodes.response: In German, a strong verb has a stem change in one or more tenses. Some strong verbs have a stem change in the present tense but not in the perfect tense, e.g., 'sehen' - 'er, sie, es sieht' - 'hat gesehen'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Narrate a new experience: perfect tense with 'haben'

nodes.misconception: It is only the verb in a sentence that can tell us whether the action of the verb implies movement towards a destination or a static location.
nodes.response: The case (form of the article 'the' or 'a') used after prepositions 'in' and 'auf' tells us whether movement or location are implied, e.g., when the article is in the accusative case ('in den', 'in die', 'ins') it means 'into' and indicates movement.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A new experience: perfect tense with 'haben' and 'sein', 'in' and 'auf'

nodes.misconception: The comparative form of 'gern' is 'besser'.
nodes.response: The comparative form of 'gern' is 'lieber'. 'Besser' is the comparative form of 'gut'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Places you like and prefer: suffix -ung, comparatives, questions

nodes.misconception: I have to understand every single word in a text in order to understand its general meaning.
nodes.response: It is difficult to know all of the words in any given language! Use the words you do know and other contextual and linguistic clues to help you decipher the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Volunteering: discuss photos, word order with two-verb structures

nodes.misconception: The German number ‘Billion’ means billion in English.
nodes.response: The German word for 'billion' is ‘Milliarde’; ‘Billion’ in German means 'trillion' in English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Like and would like: 'mögen', 'möcht-', plural rules, large numbers

nodes.misconception: 'Gefallen' means ‘to like’ and works like a normal verb where I am the subject that does the action of ‘liking’.
nodes.response: 'Gefallen' means ‘to please’, so works differently. You are not doing the ‘liking’, the thing you like is ‘pleasing’ you. E.g., 'das Kleid gefällt mir' - literally, 'the dress pleases me'. More naturally translated - 'I like the dress'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Places you like and prefer: verbs + indirect object, 'gefallen', 'mögen'

nodes.misconception: When saying your occupation, use an indefinite article, like in English.
nodes.response: In German, when saying what your occupation is or what you would like to become, an indefinite article is not needed, e.g., 'Ich möchte in Zukunft Lehrer werden.' - 'In the future, I would like to become a teacher.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: School and future ambitions: plural 'mögen' and 'möcht-'

nodes.misconception: The word 'gefallen' always means 'fell'.
nodes.response: The past participle of 'fallen' ('to fall') is 'gefallen', as is the past participle of 'gefallen' ('to please'). The difference is that the auxiliary verb 'haben' is used with 'gefallen' (to please), but 'sein' is used with 'fallen' (to fall).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Volunteering: revisit perfect tense

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the person who owns the noun.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives must agree with the gender of the noun that follows, not with the person who owns the noun.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Families: possessive adjectives 'mein', 'dein', 'sein', 'ihr' (nominative)

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the person who possesses the noun.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the noun they describe, not the person who possesses it!
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A family in Namibia: possessives 'mein', 'dein', 'sein', 'ihr' (nominative)

nodes.misconception: Don't change the possessive pronoun used in a question when you give your answer.
nodes.response: If a question is addressed to you (i.e., uses a form of 'dein', as in 'Was ist dein Lieblingssport?'), respond with the correct form of 'mein' in the answer.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Ask about families: possessives 'mein', 'dein', 'sein', 'ihr' (nominative)

nodes.misconception: All plural nouns are formed the same way in German.
nodes.response: Nouns can form their plural in different ways in German. There are rules to help you learn this.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A day in my life: present tense, plurals and adverbs

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, pupils should keep their answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: word patterns, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfully answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: dictation, listening comprehension (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When taking part in a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: compound nouns, word patterns, role-play (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
nodes.response: When taking part in a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: compound nouns, word patterns, role-play (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfully answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: dictation, listening comprehension (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, pupils should keep their answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: word patterns, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Plural adjectival nouns always end in '-en'.
nodes.response: All plural adjectival nouns preceded by 'die' and all in the dative end in '-en', but for plural adjectival nouns without articles, use '-e' in the nominative and accusative.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Nach der Schule: abstract neuter adjectival nouns, plural adjectival nouns

nodes.misconception: All verbs with prefixes are separable.
nodes.response: Some prefixes are separable in some verbs but inseparable in others. For example, 'wieder' in 'wiedersehen' is separable, but not in 'wiederholen'. The stress always falls on the separable prefix.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gruppenzwang: word order with separable verbs in single and 2-verb clauses

nodes.misconception: Adjectives in German don't have endings.
nodes.response: Adjectives have endings when they precede a noun. Compare 'der Hund ist groß' with 'der große Hund ist schwarz'. Adjective endings agree in case, gender and number with nouns. There are useful tables that can be learned to support correct usage.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Das deutsche Schulsystem: adjective agreement

nodes.misconception: [qu] sounds the same in English and German.
nodes.response: In German, the SSC [qu] is pronounced 'k' then 'w' (which in German is like the English 'v' sound). Avoid confusion with English - for example, 'Qualität' vs 'quality'. In German, 'kw' appears only in complound words, e.g., 'Trinkwasser'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Therapiehunde: nouns and adjectives with prepositions

nodes.misconception: Many English superlatives use 'most', so you need to use 'meist' in German.
nodes.response: German superlatives use 'am -sten'. 'Most interesting' ist 'am interessantesten', and 'most difficult' is 'am schwierigsten'. No additional German word is required for 'most'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: In der Schule: superlative adjectives and adverbs

nodes.misconception: 'Bis' always means 'until'.
nodes.response: 'Bis' has several meanings and uses. As a preposition it can mean 'until', 'up to' or 'by'. As a conjunction it usually means 'until'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Schule - dieses Jahr: 'bis' preposition vs conjunction

nodes.misconception: Time, manner, place adverbs must always be used in the order TMP.
nodes.response: When using WO1, the order TMP applies. However, each of the elements can be used at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis. In that case, use WO2 and put the remaining elements in the order time before manner before place.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Kleine Schule: time, manner, place, present tense with gern, lieber, am liebsten

nodes.misconception: Definite and indefiniete articles are used the same way in German as in English.
nodes.response: Differences occur with some country names, some abstract nouns and professions: e.g., 'die Schweiz' (Switzerland), 'die Freiheit' (freedom). It's 'Er ist Arzt' (He is a doctor), but an article is needed before the adjective - 'Er ist ein guter Arzt'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Kleider machen Leute: definite and indefinite articles, extended speaking

nodes.misconception: All past participles in German start with 'ge-'.
nodes.response: Verbs beginning with 'be-', 'ent-' or 'er-' do not require 'ge-' at the beginning. Past participles of separable verbs have the prefix first then the past participle of the main verb. They are written as one word, e.g., 'eingeladen', 'ausgegangen'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Schule - letztes Jahr: nouns without plurals, past participles

nodes.misconception: Adjectives work the same way in German as in English and do not change their spelling.
nodes.response: German adjectives change their ending when placed before the noun, depending on the case needed, and the gender of the noun they describe.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What was it like then? Imperfect tense: 'war, hatte, gab, damals, früher'

nodes.misconception: The German verb for 'use' is needed when saying what used to happen.
nodes.response: 'Used to' in German is communicated by using the adverb 'früher' - 'in the past', 'in former times'. There is no need to include a German verb for 'use'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: This year and in the past: perfect tense with 'früher' and 'noch nicht'

nodes.misconception: 'Was' and 'had' have different forms in German for 'ich' and 'er, sie'.
nodes.response: In German, 'war' means 'was', 'hatte' means 'had'. Both forms remain unchanged for 'ich' and 'er, sie', like in English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Places and people: now or then? Imperfect tense: 'war', 'hatte', 'gab'

nodes.misconception: Like in English, a word for 'more' is needed in German when making comparisons like 'more difficult' or 'more interesting'.
nodes.response: German adjectives form comparatives by adding -er; there is no need to include 'more', e.g., more interesting > 'interessanter'; more difficult >'schwieriger'. English does this with 1- and some 2-syllable adjectives, e.g., 'small' > 'smaller'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Then and now: the comparative

nodes.misconception: Final [e] is a long vowel sound in German.
nodes.response: Final [e] is a short [e] sound, as in 'Liebe'. Final [er] is a longer sound, as in 'lieber'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Then and now: comparatives and plurals

nodes.misconception: German has one general verb meaning 'to put, putting'.
nodes.response: German has 3 placement verbs meaning 'to put'; 'stellen' - to make something stand (vertically), 'setzen' - to make something sit, and 'legen' - to make something lay down (horizontally). Equivalent position verbs are 'stehen', 'sitzen', 'liegen'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Make changes at home: prepositions and verbs of location and movement

nodes.misconception: Although some German words have more than one meaning, most of them have a main meaning and it's not important to know the other meanings.
nodes.response: Some very frequent words have several different meanings, all of them commonly used. It is important to know the meanings and to use context to select the right meaning. For example, 'vor' can mean 'in front of', 'before' and 'ago'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Journeys past and present: time-manner-place in the perfect tense

nodes.misconception: In 2-verb structures, the 2nd infinitive verb is always followed by 'zu'.
nodes.response: When followed by a 2nd verb in the infinitive, modal verbs and 'werden' never take 'zu'. Many other verbs do, for example 'versuchen, etwas zu tun' and 'helfen, etwas zu tun'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Answering the question 'Why?': two-verb structures with 'um ... zu'

nodes.misconception: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
nodes.response: German sentences can start with any adverb to emphasise that element. The TMP order is then retained for any other adverbs in that sentence. For example, 'Mit dem Zug (M) fahren wir morgen (T) nach Liechtenstein (P).'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Journeys past and present: time-manner-place word order in the present tense

nodes.misconception: To answer the question 'why' you have to use 'weil' or 'denn', which mean 'because'.
nodes.response: The structure 'um ... zu' followed by an infinitive verb means 'in order to' and can be used to give a reason or say why something is done. This structure is the same for any tense.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Why? Two-verb structures with 'um ... zu', imperfect modals 'durfte', 'sollte'

nodes.misconception: All prepositions are followed by either the accusative or the dative.
nodes.response: The prepositions ‘hinter’, ‘neben’, ‘unter’, ‘über’, ‘vor’, ‘zwischen’ and ‘in’ are used with the accusative case when there is movement but the dative case when there is no movement.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Freizeit: prepositions, da-compounds

nodes.misconception: We use 'wann' to say what we did, do or will do 'when'.
nodes.response: 'Wann' is a question word and means 'when' in questions and indirect questions. Use 'als' for 'when' when referring to specific past events or points in time and 'wenn' for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Alltag jetzt und früher: '-chen' and '-lein', 'wenn' and 'als'

nodes.misconception: If we see a reflexive pronoun, e.g., 'uns' or 'sich', this always means the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the verb are the same.
nodes.response: Some plural reflexive verbs are reciprocal or two-way, meaning the action of the verb is done 'to each other' rather than to oneself. Use context to work out whether reflexive or reciprocal meaning is intended.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Wir treffen uns: reflexive verbs past and present, forming adverbs, role play

nodes.misconception: The phrase 'zu Hause' means 'to home' because 'zu' means 'to'.
nodes.response: 'Zu Hause' means 'at home' and 'nach Hause' is used for 'going (to) home'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Ich fahre in die Schule: words for ‘in’ and ‘to’, wo-compounds

nodes.misconception: 'Um' always means 'at' and is used with clock times.
nodes.response: Whilst 'um' is used commonly with clock times to mean 'at', it can also mean 'around' when referring to places, e.g., 'around the corner', or 'about, approximately' with numbers, e.g., 'about 10km'. It also follows some verbs, e.g., 'es geht um'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Mein Alltag: telling the time, prepositions ‘um’, ‘seit’ and ‘vor’

nodes.misconception: 'Vor' and 'bevor' and 'nach' and 'nachdem' are interchangeable because they mean 'before' and 'after'.
nodes.response: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions and are followed by a noun, 'bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions which link clauses and trigger word order 3.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Vor und nach der Schule: word order with 'nachdem' and 'bevor'

nodes.misconception: All German-speakers speak the same way. There aren't different accents, unlike in the United Kingdom.
nodes.response: There are both different accents and different dialects in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. This means there are different ways of saying sounds, and different vocabulary. ‘Standard German’ is the version of German taught in schools.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What there is in different places: inversion with adverbs

nodes.misconception: 'Viel' and 'viele' are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Use 'viel' with uncountable nouns (i.e., you cannot put a number in front of it) and use 'viele' with countable nouns (i.e., you can put a number in front of it).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Berlin: inversion with adverbs of time and place, and  'viel' and 'viele'

nodes.misconception: The infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause when using two-verb structures.
nodes.response: In standard word order (word order 1), the infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause. However, after certain conjunctions (word order 3), the conjugated verb is sent to the end of the clause.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einflüsse und Ereignisse: word order in 2-verb clauses, extended writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: The infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause when using two-verb structures.
nodes.response: In standard word order (word order 1), the infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause. However, after certain conjunctions (word order 3), the conjugated verb is sent to the end of the clause.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einflüsse und Ereignisse: word order 2-verb clauses, extended writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einflüsse und Ereignisse: read aloud, reading comprehension (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: All conjunctions cause the verb to be sent to the end of the clause.
