nodes.response: Subordinating conjunctions, such as 'weil', 'dass', 'ob' and 'obwohl' send the verb to the end of the clause. Coordinating conjunctions, such as 'und', 'aber', 'denn' and 'oder' are followed by word order 1 (standard subject-verb-object word order).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einflüsse und Ereignisse: word order, picture task (AQA)

nodes.misconception: All conjunctions cause the verb to be sent to the end of the clause.
nodes.response: Subordinating conjunctions, such as 'weil', 'dass', 'ob' and 'obwohl' send the verb to the end of the clause. Coordinating conjunctions, such as 'und', 'aber', 'denn' and 'oder' are followed by word order 1 (standard subject-verb-object word order).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einflüsse und Ereignisse: word order, picture task (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einflüsse und Ereignisse: read aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Words which look the same in English and German will have the same meaning.
nodes.response: There are many false friends in German. These are words that look exactly the same but do not have the same meaning: for example, 'bald' means 'soon'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What makes us happy? Authentic texts, relative pronouns and comparatives

nodes.misconception: English verbs use the same prepositions as in German.
nodes.response: German verbs often use different prepositions from those used with English verbs; for example 'ich hoffe auf' - 'I'm hoping for' (not 'hoping on').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: verbs with 'an', 'auf', 'für', 'vor', reflexive verbs

nodes.misconception: The prepositions 'auf' and 'an' are always followed by the accusative case.
nodes.response: 'Auf' and 'an' are followed by the accusative case when there is movement. They are followed by the dative case when a location is being described.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: verbs with prepositions 'an', 'auf', 'für', 'vor'

nodes.misconception: The direct object precedes the indirect object in a German sentence.
nodes.response: If there are two objects in a sentence and one is a pronoun, the pronoun will precede the noun, regardless of whether it is the direct or indirect object. However, if both objects are nouns, the indirect object is first.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A school exchange: plural direct and indirect object pronouns

nodes.misconception: When two object nouns are in a sentence, the word order is the same as English: direct object - indirect object.
nodes.response: When two object nouns are in a sentence, the indirect object (in dative) precedes the direct object (in accusative). This is different from English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: At school: word order in sentences with two objects

nodes.misconception: A word for 'do', 'does', 'is' or 'are' is needed when forming yes/no questions in German.
nodes.response: In German, yes/no questions can be formed simply by inverting the subject and the verb. There is no need for a word like 'do' or 'are' at the start, e.g. 'Läufst du schnell?' - 'Do you run fast?'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday experiences: present tense separable verbs, questions

nodes.misconception: Separable verbs work exactly the same as all other verbs in the present tense.
nodes.response: Separable verbs use the same endings as all other present tense verbs, but in most sentences the separable verb prefix moves to the end of the sentence, e.g., 'anrufen' - 'ich rufe meinen Freund an'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday experiences: present tense separable verbs, 'gern'

nodes.misconception: Word order in German remains the same as English after ‘weil’ ('because').
nodes.response: When using ‘weil’ to give a reason, the verb moves to the end of the clause, e.g., ‘ich spiele gern Fußball, weil es Spaß macht'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What I prefer to do and why: 'weil', 'denn' and 'lieber'

nodes.misconception: German [st] and [sp] sound the same as in English, wherever they appear in the word.
nodes.response: At the start of words, German [sp-] and [st-] are pronounced 'schp-' and 'scht-'. If [sp] and [st] occur in the middle or end of a word, pronounce them as in English, except for compound nouns and separable verbs, which are also 'schp-' and 'scht-'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What I and others prefer to do: 'gern' and 'lieber' with present tense

nodes.misconception: To form the imperative, simply remove the subject pronoun and say the present tense verb form on its own.
nodes.response: To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative, simply remove the pronoun 'ihr' and say the verb form, e.g., 'Kommt!'. To use the 'du' form of the imperative, remove the pronoun 'du' but also remove the '-st' verb ending, e.g., 'Komm!'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Schreib eine E-Mail: informal imperatives, present tense verbs

nodes.misconception: 'Darum' is a da-compound and its meaning is always directly related to the preposition 'um'.
nodes.response: 'Darum' can be used as a da-compund, meaning 'around it' or 'about it' but it is also a conjunction meaning 'therefore' or 'that's why'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Eine Nachricht: 'worum' and 'darum', genitive prepositions

nodes.misconception: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
nodes.response: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Technologie der Zukunft: 'du' & 'ihr' questions with reflexives, modals, future

nodes.misconception: To mean 'for' with a period of time, use 'vor' in German.
nodes.response: 'Vor' means 'ago', e.g. vor zwei Jahren - two years ago.  To mean 'for' with a period of time in the present tense, use 'seit'; in the past, add 'lang' after the time phrase, but don't use a preposition for 'for'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Since, when and for how long? 'seit' with present, 'vor' with perfect tense

nodes.misconception: There is only one word in German for 'our' and 'their', just like in English.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives like 'unser' and 'ihr' change the spelling according to the gender of the noun and the case that is needed e.g.  'unser Hund', 'unsere Katze'; 'ihr Vater', 'ihre Mutter'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare school experiences: possessive adjectives 'unser' and 'ihr'

nodes.misconception: 'Seit' is always used with the continuous past, like in English e.g. I have been learning German since June.
nodes.response: In German, 'seit' is used with the present tense to say 'for' e.g. 'Ich lerne seit vier Jahren' 'I have been learning for four years'  as well as  'since' e.g. 'Ich lerne seit Juni Deutsch', 'I have been learning since June'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Since when? 'seit' with dative and present tense

nodes.misconception: Object pronouns like me, him, they are always the same in German, like English.
nodes.response: German object pronouns can be direct or indirect; they change their spelling depending on the case needed, e.g. direct object pronoun 'dich' - you is accusative; indirect object pronoun 'dir' - you is dative. The case is often determined by the verb.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: English and German schools: pronouns 'uns' and 'ihnen'

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: role-play, picture task, conversation (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: The only way to extend my sentences to add complexity is to add a subordinate clause with 'weil'.
nodes.response: There are many ways to add complexity, including using subordinate clauses with a wide range of conjunctions, as well as adding relative clauses or infinitive constructions.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: extended writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
nodes.response: Conversation answers following the picture task should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: picture task, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: When translating into English from German, I only need to understand the gist of the sentences.
nodes.response: When translating, it's important to ensure that you have accounted for the meaning of every German word, even though you might not translate word-for-word into English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: reading, translation into English (AQA)

nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: role-play, picture task, conversation (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Like in a picture description and conversation, I should develop my role-play answers as much as possible.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should be a short phrase or sentence. Pupils should not add too much unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: role-play, read aloud (AQA)

nodes.misconception: Like in a picture description and conversation, I should develop my role-play answers as much as possible.
nodes.response: When performing a role-play, answers should be a short phrase or sentence. Pupils should not add too much unnecessary detail.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: role-play, read aloud (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: When translating into English from German, I only need to understand the gist of the sentences.
nodes.response: When translating, it's important to ensure that you have accounted for the meaning of every German word, even though you might not translate word-for-word into English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Prüfungsvorbereitung: reading, translation into English (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: 'I am doing' is translated as 'Ich bin machen'.
nodes.response: There is no present continuous ('-ing' form) tense in German, and therefore no use of the verb 'sein'. Use a time adverb to express what you are doing right now in German, e.g., 'Ich mache jetzt ...'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Talking with friends: questions, simple present and present continuous

nodes.misconception: 'Haben' is a weak verb.
nodes.response: 'Haben' is an irregular verb because it does not follow a regular pattern of changes in the same way a weak verb does, even if the 'ich', 'wir' and 'sie' (they) forms look like weak verbs.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Talking with friends: 'haben' and 'sein'

nodes.misconception: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in all present tense forms.
nodes.response: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in the first person singular of the present tense only.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Mannschaft: stem changes 't' not 'st', 'e' before 't'/'st', 'el' stem

nodes.misconception: Strong verbs never keep their stem changes in the 'du' form of the imperative.
nodes.response: Strong verbs keep stem vowel changes, e.g. 'e' to 'i', 'e' to 'ie', but omit the umlaut ('ä') in the imperative.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Liest du Romane? Questions and informal imperatives with strong verbs

nodes.misconception: Only the tense of the verb can tell us whether a sentence is referring to present, past or future events.
nodes.response: Adverbs of time are also very important in helping us to identify time frames, particularly when the present tense is used for future meaning.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Freizeit: present tense for future meaning, extended writing

nodes.misconception: You can use conversational language (an informal register) whenever you want to.
nodes.response: A situation affects the register we use when speaking (i.e., the words we use). You use an informal register with friends, but a formal register with a teacher. Using formal register in formal situations is important in German-speaking communities.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Rules of a game: modal verbs, 'jeder', 'jede', 'jedes', conversational words

nodes.misconception: The infinitive follows the conjugated verb, as in the English 'I can play'.
nodes.response: In German, the infinitive is placed at the end of a sentence when used with a modal verb, as in 'Ich kann spielen.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Improve your lifestyle: modal verbs 'müssen', 'dürfen', 'wollen' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: Always use 'können' to translate 'can' into German.
nodes.response: 'Can' is often used with two different meanings in English - ability or permission. Use 'können' to express ability (e.g., 'Kannst du schwimmen?') and 'dürfen' to express permission (e.g., 'Darfst du schwimmen?').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Improve your lifestyle: modal 2-verb structures and pronoun 'man'

nodes.misconception: Strong verbs have a vowel change in all parts of the verb.
nodes.response: Strong verbs have a vowel change in the 2nd and 3rd person singular forms of the verb only (e.g., 'ich werfe', 'du wirfst', 'sie wirft').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Rules of a game: modal verbs, 'jeder', 'jede', 'jedes', dictogloss skills

nodes.misconception: All opinions phrases can be followed by 'dass' and word order 3 (subordination).
nodes.response: Whilst many opinion verbs, including 'meinen', 'glauben' and 'denken' are usually followed by 'dass' and word order 3, this is not always the case. 'Meiner Meinung nach' must be followed by word order 2 (inversion).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Discussion: opinion verbs, word order with 'dass', 'doch'

nodes.misconception: We can use a da-compound to refer back to any object noun already mentioned.
nodes.response: We can only use a da-compound to replace inanimate (non-living) nouns. For animate objects (people and animals), we use direct or indirect object pronouns to replace the noun.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: The environment: verbs with prepositions,  da-compounds

nodes.misconception: Form questions with prepositions in the same way as in English, by adding a preposition at the end, e.g., 'What is he interested in?'
nodes.response: German doesn't leave prepositions hanging at the end of questions like in English. Form questions by placing the prefix 'wo-' or 'wor-' before the preposition at the start of the question.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: The environment: wo- and da-compounds

nodes.misconception: I can use 'an' and 'auf' interchangeably to mean 'on' or 'onto'.
nodes.response: We use 'an' to mean 'on' or 'onto' when the position is vertical, e.g., 'on the wall' - 'an der Wand'. We use 'auf' to mean 'on' or 'onto' when the position is horizontal, e.g., 'on the table' - 'auf dem Tisch'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: In the news: 'an' vs 'auf' (accusative and dative)

nodes.misconception: Cognate recognition is the only strategy I need to understand texts in German.
nodes.response: Cognates are helpful, but not always enough.  You will understand much more if you know some common word and spelling patterns in German, and if you use your vocabulary and grammar knowledge creatively to work out the meanings of unfamiliar words.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: News article: 'gegen', 'laut'

nodes.misconception: German verbs always stress the same syllable.
nodes.response: Generally German infinitive verbs stress the first syllable; however, words starting with inseparable prefixes be-, er-, ge-, ver-, ent- stress the 2nd syllable, which includes most past participles; -ieren verbs stress the 'ie' in present and past.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A charity concert: past participles, verb stress, 'kein' vs 'nicht'

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is used in written, but not usually in spoken German.
nodes.response: The imperfect tense forms of 'sein', 'haben' and 'es gibt' are widely used in spoken German, along with imperfect modal verbs which, combined with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, are used to say what you and others wanted, were able or had to do.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A new place: time-manner-place, imperfect modal verbs

nodes.misconception: When we speak, the pitch of our voice rises and falls in the same way in German and English.
nodes.response: The rise and fall of our voice is similar in German and English sentences, but more marked in German and more noticeable with one-syllable words. Note the larger fall when saying 'gut' in German compared to 'good' in English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A charity concert: sentence intonation, object pronouns

nodes.misconception: The only way to communicate about past events in German is by using the 2-verb perfect tense, e.g., 'Ich bin nach Deutschland gefahren. Ich habe dort einen Strandurlaub gemacht.'.
nodes.response: We also use the single verb imperfect tense - 'war', 'hatte' and 'es gab', and imperfect modal forms - 'musste', 'konnte', 'wollte', with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, to talk about events in the past.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Travels and places: present and imperfect modal verbs

nodes.misconception: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive stays with the subject of the action.
nodes.response: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive goes to the end of the sentence. This is different word order to English and is called the ‘two-verb rule’.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Plans for the week ahead: modal verbs in present tense (future meaning)

nodes.misconception: The German 'Ich will' means 'I will'.
nodes.response: The German 'will' comes from 'wollen' and means 'want'. Do not confuse this with the future tense. 'Ich werde' means 'I will'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you want to and will do: future tense singular (will) vs 'will' (want to)

nodes.misconception: The 'k' in [kn] is silent.
nodes.response: Both sounds in [kn] must be pronounced. This is different from English. Compare English 'knee' and German 'Knie'. Remember to pronounce the 'k' in German words containing [kn].
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Who is supposed to do what? Modal verbs, two-verb structures, question words

nodes.misconception: You can only begin an inversion sentence  (word order two) with a time phrase, nothing else.
nodes.response: The emphasis is on whatever comes first in the sentence when using inversion (word order 2). It is acceptable to put the object of the sentence before the verb. For example, 'Den Kaffee trinken wir heute'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Plans for this weekend: present tense (future meaning), 'nach' vs 'zu' (dative)

nodes.misconception: Always add 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
nodes.response: Some verbs, like 'werden' and modal verbs, do not require 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Future plans: future tense 'werden' + infinitive vs 'planen' + 'zu' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: Always use 'müssen' in negative sentences to translate the idea of 'must not' in English.
nodes.response: English often uses 'must not' in lieu of 'don't have to', 'not allowed to' and 'should not'. However, you should use the correct modal verb in German to express these ideas, e.g. 'du musst nicht', 'du darfst nicht', 'du sollst nicht'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Who should do what? Meanings of  'sollen', 'müssen', 'dürfen'

nodes.misconception: Nouns created from verbs are always formed from the infinitive and are always neuter.
nodes.response: Nouns can be formed from the infintive and those nouns are always neuter. However, other nouns can be formed from the verb stem rather than the infinitive. Nouns ending in the suffix '-ung' are always feminine.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Zukunftsentscheidungen: nominalisation of infinitives, adding '-ung'

nodes.misconception: When developing a conversation about future plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
nodes.response: Whilst it is important to be able to refer to the future confidently, it is also helpful to add in different time frames to give more detail and to develop your sentences.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Was will ich lernen? Present modal verbs, describing photos, extended speaking

nodes.misconception: The subject and verb in a 'zu' clause must match the subject and tense of the linked clause.
nodes.response: We always use the infinitive and never a subject and finite verb in constructions with 'zu'. This applies to all tenses.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Abitur oder Ausbildung: ohne...zu..., entweder...oder..., weder...noch...

nodes.misconception: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make different sounds.
nodes.response: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make the same sound, but write 'ss' after a short vowel, 'ß' after a long vowel.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Summer plans: present tense (future meaning) 1st person, 'nächst-'

nodes.misconception: Use the simple present to translate future plans from German into English, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I play tennis.'.
nodes.response: Use the present continuous in English when translating future plans (that are expressed in the present tense) from German, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I am going to play tennis.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Summer plans: contrasting uses of the present tense, 'nächst-'

nodes.misconception: Add '-s' to form the plural of all nouns in German.
nodes.response: There is a set of rules that help you know how to form plural nouns in German. Not all nouns form their plural in the same way, so the rules need to be learned.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Poems: plural nouns, responding to a poem

nodes.misconception: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
nodes.response: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. This can be very confusing for English speakers. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Make plans: present tense (future meaning), numbers 13-31, dates

nodes.misconception: 'Zu' always means 'to'.
nodes.response: 'Zu' can also mean 'too', 'closed', 'off' and 'shut'! Context is important when translating into English.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Where people go: 'zu' vs 'nach', present tense (future meaning)

nodes.misconception: As long as we know the meaning of a noun, we don't need to worry about its grammatical gender.
nodes.response: Knowing the grammatical gender of a noun is very important, because the gender affects the form of other parts of a sentence, such as the article or preposition. This in turn affects the clarity and comprehensibility of the message.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Poems: prepositions 'in' and 'auf' (accusative and dative)

nodes.misconception: When a sentence contains both a direct object and an indirect object, the indirect object always comes first.
nodes.response: When a sentence contains both a direct object noun and an indirect object noun, the indirect object always comes first. When a pronoun is used to replace either noun, the pronoun comes first.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Psychische Gesundheit: position of indirect and direct objects

nodes.misconception: Adjectival nouns behave like adjectives in every way.
nodes.response: Adjectival nouns, like adjectives, change endings according to gender, case and the article used with them. However, like nouns, they have a grammatical gender and a capital letter. Abstract adjectival nouns are neuter.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund bleiben: abstract adjectival neuter nouns, adding '-los'

nodes.misconception: The verb 'mögen' takes regular verb endings.
nodes.response: The verb 'mögen' is irregular in the singular present tense forms, and the first and third person singular are identical: 'ich mag', 'er mag'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Was möchtest du? Present and conditional 'mögen'

nodes.misconception: The present tense in German can only be used to refer to the present.
nodes.response: The present tense can also be used with appropriate adverbs of time to refer to the near future, e.g., 'Am Samstag spiele ich Tennis.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesund und ungesund: expanding vocabulary, reading skills, role play

nodes.misconception: German question words, like English, do not change their spelling.
nodes.response: Whilst most question words, such as 'wo', 'was' and 'warum' have a fixed spelling, 'welch-' changes according the gender and case of the noun that follows.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Einkaufen: 'welch-' and 'dies-' in nominative, accusative, dative

nodes.misconception: Use 'würde' whenever you want to say 'would'.
nodes.response: 'Würde' works in most cases, but for the conditional with 'haben' and 'sein', we usually use 'hätte' ('I would have') and 'wäre' ('I would be').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Würdest du Veganer werden? Conditional with 'würde', 'hätte', 'wäre', 'sollte'

nodes.misconception: Indirect object nouns are always preceded by the words 'to' or 'for' in English, and this tells us we need to use the dative case for the indirect object in German.
nodes.response: Whilst the inclusion of 'to' or 'for' in English can be a helpful indicator that the dative case is needed in German, not all verbs require this in English, and many can use the same word order as German.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Gesundheit: position of indirect and direct objects with two nouns

nodes.misconception: 'Viel' and 'viele' and 'wenig' and 'wenige' are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Use 'viel' and 'wenig' with uncountable nouns (i.e., you cannot put a number in front of it) and use 'viele' and 'wenige' with countable nouns (i.e., you can put a number in front of it).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Isst du gesund? Nouns without plurals, plural rules

nodes.misconception: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
nodes.response: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: KaDeWe: cardinal and ordinal numbers

nodes.misconception: Adjectives and adverbs which are identical in German can be translated identically into English.
nodes.response: English adjectives and adverbs differ, often with the adverb ending in '-ly', so care must be taken when translating German adjectives used as adverbs.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Neue Schüler: adding '-keit' and '-heit', adjectives as adverbs

nodes.misconception: The only versions of Grimm brothers' fairy tales that exist are written in the imperfect tense.
nodes.response: There are many versions of the Grimm brothers' fairy tales. Many are written in the imperfect tense but there are also simpler, modern adaptations written in the present or perfect tenses, especially in children's books.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Der Rattenfänger: understanding a Grimm brothers' fairy tale, imperfect tense

nodes.misconception: Form questions with prepositions in the same way as in English, by adding a preposition at the end, e.g., 'What does he find out about?'.
nodes.response: German doesn't leave prepositions hanging at the end of questions like in English. Form questions by placing the prefix 'wo-' or 'wor-' before the preposition at the start of the question.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Fairy tales and poetry: da- and wo- compounds, imperfect

nodes.misconception: Make the imperfect stem of strong verbs just by removing -en and changing the stem vowel.
nodes.response: Many strong verbs form their imperfect stem in this way: 'lesen' - 'las', 'geben', 'gab'. Other verbs have other small changes too: 'kommen' - 'kam', 'essen' - 'aß'. Others are more irregular: 'gehen' - 'ging', 'sein' - 'war', 'haben' - 'hatte'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Fairy tales: diminutives, singular imperfect tense

nodes.misconception: All German words that look or sound similar to words in English are cognates.
nodes.response: Similar looking and sounding words are only cognates if they share the same meaning in both languages. When the meaning is different, similar words are called false friends.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A house move: adjective endings with definite articles (accusative)

nodes.misconception: German [v] is always pronounced like English [f].
nodes.response: In many words, German [v] sounds like English [f]. However, in German words of foreign origin, [v] usually sounds the same as English [v], e.g., 'Universität', 'November', 'Aktivität'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A new neighbourhood: accusative and dative prepositions

nodes.misconception: German word order is just like English - it's always subject-verb-object.
nodes.response: In English, word order is usually fixed: subject-verb-object, e.g., 'she eats an apple'. In German, the word order is more flexible because in main clauses the verb must be in second position. Any element can start a German sentence for emphasis.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A new home and new neighbours: word patterns and word order

nodes.misconception: After all prepositions, the case used depends on whether the verb describes 'location in' or 'movement to'.
nodes.response: Some prepositions always require dative endings regardless of the verb meaning; e.g., 'aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu'; other prepositions are only ever used with the accusative, e.g., 'durch, für'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A new home: dative adjective endings with definite and indefinite articles

nodes.misconception: When producing written work in German, I should stick to short simple sentences.
nodes.response: When producing written work in German, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Kommunikation online: extended writing

nodes.misconception: If you know the usual meanings of prepositions, choosing which preposition to use with each verb is straightforward, as we translate the preposition directly from English.
nodes.response: Verb and preposition combinations need to be learnt. The prepositions often lose their usual meaning when combined with verbs, and we often use different prepositions after verbs in English and in German.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die digitale Welt: verbs with prepositions, 'da-' and 'wo-' compounds

nodes.misconception: Infinitives and nominalised infinitives look exactly the same.
nodes.response: Infinitives can be turned into nouns by capitalising the first letter, so although they sound the same, they look different. They are always neuter. Use surrounding words, such as 'beim' and 'am' to identify nominalised infinitives when listening.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Magst du Musik? Nominalisation of infinitives with 'beim' and 'am'

nodes.misconception: Question words can replace definite articles as relative pronouns in relative clauses.
nodes.response: Question words, such as 'wo', can be used as pronouns in relative clauses, but they should not be used to translate 'who' or 'which' when adding information about the noun in the main clause.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Nachhaltige Mode: relative pronouns, question words in relative clauses

nodes.misconception: Always use the comparative form of an adjective as the starting point for forming the superlative.
nodes.response: Superlatives can change in the same way as comparatives, such as adding an umlaut, (alt, älter, der/die/das älteste). Where the comparative removes ‘e’, use the original adjective to form the superlative (teuer, teurer, der/die/das teuerste).
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Meine Lieblingssänger: 'wenn' and 'als', superlatives

nodes.misconception: Always use the imperfect tense to translate the English simple past, e.g., 'I chatted online.'.
nodes.response: The perfect tense is far more common in German and is used for both the English simple past and perfect tense in speaking. The imperfect is used mainly to narrate past events in writing. However, 'hatte', 'war' and 'es gab' are used in speaking too.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Digital Detox: perfect tense, imperfect tense, 'gerade'

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense in German is only used in writing.
nodes.response: Whilst the imperfect is largely used in writing, modal verbs are also used in speaking, along with verbs like 'war', 'hatte' and 'gab'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Ambitions of famous young Germans: reading skills, questions, imperfect modals

nodes.misconception: To talk about the future in German you have to use the future tense with 'werden'.
nodes.response: In German, you can use the present tense and a future time phrase to talk about the future: 'ich spiele nächste Woche Tennis' - 'I'm playing/going to play tennis next week'. 'Planen' and 'vorhaben' in the present tense also express future intentions.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Past and future goals: revisiting tenses and word order, translation skills

nodes.misconception: Giving the time as half past the hour works the same in German as it does in English, e.g., ‘halb neun’ is 'half past nine'.
nodes.response: In German, half past is expressed as half of the next hour, so 'half past nine' is 'halb zehn', or 'half way to ten', the next hour.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What you did when on Sylt: perfect tense, telling the time: half past the hour

nodes.misconception: Adjectives only change their spelling according to the gender of the noun they describe.
nodes.response: Adjectives change their spelling to match both the gender of the noun and the case, e.g., 'das ist ein lustiger Hund', 'ich habe einen lustigen Hund'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A music festival: perfect and imperfect, adjective endings

nodes.misconception: When addressing questions to someone, I can just use 'du'.
nodes.response: Questions often need to be asked using 'Sie', in situations where respect should be shown, such as when asking a teacher or an unknown adult.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: A music festival: perfect and imperfect tenses, question forming

nodes.misconception: To greet German speakers, use either ‘hallo’ or ‘guten Tag’.
nodes.response: Greetings in German-speaking countries vary depending on time of day, country/region and level of formality, e.g., ‘hallo’ in Germany but ‘servus’ in Austria and ‘hoi’ in Switzerland.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Where you went and where you were: 'in', 'an', 'auf', time with 'vor' and 'nach'

nodes.misconception: Poetry is always descriptive and doesn't tell stories.
nodes.response: Ballads are poems that tell stories with a sequence of events. They include scene-setting, action, change moments and a conclusion. Ballads are also lyrical - they use poetic language, imagery, rhythm, rhyme - and dramatic - often with direct speech.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Poetry and prose: understanding and creativity

nodes.misconception: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
nodes.response: German sentences can start with any adverb to emphasise that element. The TMP order is then retained for any other adverbs in that sentence. For example, 'Mit dem Zug (M) werden wir morgen (T) nach Wien (P) fahren.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Wiener Festwochen: inversion, time-manner-place

nodes.misconception: Saying or writing years in German is the same as in English, e.g., 1066 is 'zehn sechsundsechzig'.
nodes.response: Block the numbers in pairs as in English, but in German you must use 'hundert' or 'tausend'. 1066 is 'zehnhundertsechsundsechszig'. 2025 is 'zweitausendfünfundzwanzig'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Eine Reise durch Europa: dates

nodes.misconception: In the future tense and other 2-verb structures, the 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence.
nodes.response: The 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence in WO1 and 2. In WO3, where the main verb goes to the end of the sentence, the 2nd (infinitive) verb is in 2nd-last place - 'Ich weiß, dass du nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren wirst.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Interrailing: future tense, 2-verb structures, present tense with future meaning

nodes.misconception: Always use 'zu' to mean 'to'.
nodes.response: 'To' is expressed in different ways in German. 'In' and 'nach' also mean 'to'. 'Zu' can also mean 'shut', 'closed' or 'off'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: 16 Bundesländer: numbers, articles following 'in', 'zu', 'nach'

nodes.misconception: 'Wissen' and 'kennen' are interchangeable.
nodes.response: Use 'wissen' with facts (e.g., 'Ich weiß nicht!') and 'kennen' with people or things you are familiar with ('Ich kenne deinen Freund.').
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Berlin: 'wissen' vs 'kennen'

nodes.misconception: All verbs use the auxiliary verb 'haben' to form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: A small number of verbs use the auxiliary verb 'sein' to form the perfect tense. These verbs usually refer to movement or a change of physical state.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die Wuppertaler Schwebebahn: past tense, past participles, time-manner-place

nodes.misconception: All verbs with prefixes are separable.
nodes.response: Some prefixes are separable in some verbs, but inseparable in others. For example, 'wieder' in 'wiedersehen' is separable, but not in 'wiederholen'. The stress always falls on the separable prefix.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Eine Reise: present tense, separable verbs, possessive adjectives

nodes.misconception: 'Es ist' means 'there is'.
nodes.response: Use 'es gibt' to translate 'there is, there are' when making a general statement that something exists. Use 'da ist' when referring to a particular thing in a particular place at a particular time; for instance, in a photograph: 'Da ist die Kirche.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Bern: 'es gibt' vs 'da sind', determiners and prepositions

nodes.misconception: 'Denn' triggers word order 3.
nodes.response: Not all conjunctions trigger word order 3. 'Denn' means 'because' and is followed by word order 1. 'Weil' also means 'because', but triggers word order 3.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Graz: word order rules, possessive adjectives

nodes.misconception: A possessive adjective must match whoever possesses the noun in gender, number and case.
nodes.response: A possessive adjective matches the gender, number and case of the noun it describes, not the person possessing it, e.g., 'his school' - 'seine Schule'. The possessor is male but the noun they possess is feminine.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Badeschiff Berlin: possessive adjectives, modal verbs, 2-verb structures

nodes.misconception: Questions are formed in the same way in both German and English.
nodes.response: English uses 'do you ... ?' or 'are you ... ?' when forming questions. German inverts the position of the subject and verb in a statement to form a closed question. Add a question word at the start to change it into an open question.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Düsseldorf: past participles of strong and irregular verbs, questions

nodes.misconception: 'Ich will' in German means 'I will' in English.
nodes.response: 'Ich will' (from the verb 'wollen') means 'I want to', but is a false friend. The future tense in German needs 'werden' with a 2nd verb in the infinitive.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Romantische Straße: future tense, present tense with adverbs to express future

nodes.misconception: Cognates are pronounced the same as the English words.
nodes.response: Cognates may share similar spelling and meanings, but it is important to remember German pronunciation rules.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Die Sächsische Schweiz: 'man' + verb, 'Lieblings-' and 'Haupt-'

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is only ever written.
nodes.response: Whilst the imperfect tense is mainly used to narrate past events in written German, some forms are regularly used in spoken German, such as 'es gab', 'war' and 'hatte'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Das Ruhrgebiet: perfect tense irregular verbs, imperfect tense, 'früher'

nodes.misconception: Adjectives don’t have capital letters in German, so to say ‘the green ones’ in German, no capital letter is needed.
nodes.response: Whilst adjectives don't have capital letters, adjectival nouns always have capital letters; ‘die Grünen’ - 'the green ones'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Frankfurter Buchmesse: uncountable quantifiers, abstract adjectival neuter nouns

nodes.misconception: If I don't have a dictionary in an exam, I won't be able to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words.
nodes.response: If you cannot use a dictionary, look at the surrounding words. Is the word part of a compound noun? Is it a cognate? Using the words and grammar you know, generate a working translation and try to fill the gap. Consider the topic of the text, too.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Reisen: extending vocabulary

nodes.misconception: 'Wenn' can be used in question words to ask 'When?'.
nodes.response: Use the question word 'Wann?' to ask 'When?' in German. Use 'wenn' to say 'when' in a present tense statement.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Dreams and future goals: 'aus', 'wenn' + word order

nodes.misconception: 'Es' is the only word used to translate 'it' in German.
nodes.response: 'Es' is for neuter nouns or abstract ideas. Use the correct subject or object pronouns according to the grammatical gender of the noun they replace.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: What is important to you? Revisit subject and object pronouns

nodes.misconception: Use the same word order as English when using indirect object pronouns.
nodes.response: In German, the indirect object pronoun comes straight after the verb, not at the end of the sentence. For example, 'Musik ist mir wichtig.' - 'Music is important to me.'.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Tips for a happy life: read and respond to a text

nodes.misconception: Always add 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
nodes.response: Some verbs, like 'werden' and modal verbs, do not require 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
nodes.subject: german
nodes.lessonTitle: Future plans: 'zu' + infinitive, 'werden' + infinitive

nodes.misconception: That our knowledge of the past is factual.
nodes.response: Explain that our understanding of the past is based on evidence that helps to build up a picture. New discoveries are made all the time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Life at the end of the last Ice Age

nodes.misconception: Dates of artefacts are exact and precise.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that archaeologists use a variety of strategies to estimate an approximate date.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Significant Stone Age artefacts

nodes.misconception: All humans living in the Stone Age were Homo sapiens.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that there were different types of humans such as Neanderthals.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The evidence of the Paleolithic Era

nodes.misconception: That a campsite is used for holidays.
nodes.response: Discuss the difference between campsites in the Mesolithic Era and a campsite today to highlight the differences.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Settlement during the Mesolithic Era

nodes.misconception: That all Neolithic houses were built from stone.
nodes.response: Explain that many Neolithic house in Britain were built from wood and daub. Houses at Skara Brae were built from stone as no wood was available.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Skara Brae and life in the Neolithic Era

nodes.misconception: That there has only ever been one type of human.
nodes.response: Explain there was more than one type of early human but they are all extinct now. All modern humans are Homo sapiens.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The big picture of the earliest humans in Britain

nodes.misconception: There was no change in Elizabeth's education after she became an heir and she continued as she was.
nodes.response: Reinforce the events before and after this significant turning point in Elizabeth's life.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth's childhood education and interests

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Archbishop of Canterbury is a part of the royal family.
nodes.response: Reinforce the fact that the Archbishop of Canterbury works with the royal family and is also very important, but is not related.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth's childhood character

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused that the Archbishop of Canterbury is the leader of the Church of England.
nodes.response: Teach pupils that Elizabeth was symbolically the governor of the Church of England and the coronation emphasised this.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth II's public duties and service

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Princess Anne would be queen after Elizabeth.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that it is the eldest child who inherits the throne and therefore Charles, Prince of Wales, became King of England.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth II's reign comes to a close

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that Elizabeth was only queen of England.
nodes.response: Reinforce that she was queen of four nations - the United Kingdom.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Queen of four nations

nodes.misconception: Philip was always the Prince of Greece and Denmark.
nodes.response: Philip gave up his titles in 1947 so that he could marry Princess Elizabeth.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth's marriage to Philip

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused between Britain and United Kingdom.
nodes.response: Reinforce that Britain is the landmass where the three countries of England, Wales and Scotland are located.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Head of the Commonwealth

nodes.misconception: Elizabeth was queen whilst King George VI was alive because she took on some responsibilities.
nodes.response: King George VI was still alive and therefore still king. It is only after his death that she became queen.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth II's accession and coronation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Malta is close to the UK.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils how long it would take to travel there in the past (by boat) and today (by air).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth's first children

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Elizabeth fought actively during the war.
nodes.response: She contributed remotely but played a role that was just as pivotal.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth and Britain during WW2

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that Elizabeth was always going to be an heir.
nodes.response: The abdication had to happen in order for Elizabeth to be an heir.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 1936 - a momentous year for Elizabeth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Elizabeth was born a queen.
nodes.response: There was already a king and queen in throne. There cannot be more than one king and queen at a time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The baby Elizabeth

nodes.misconception: It is only WWI soldiers who are remembered with memorials.
nodes.response: All those who lost their lives in WWI are remembered through memorials (medical staff, civilians, animals etc).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Remembering those who gave their lives in WWI

nodes.misconception: Only people who were killed in WWI are remembered by street names and buildings.
nodes.response: Many people made a significant contribution to WWI in their local area and are remembered for this with street names and buildings.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Local communities and the Great War

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the word 'Great' when referring to WWI may mean that the war was a great idea.
nodes.response: To remind pupils that 'Great' in this context refers to the both the size and scale of the war.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great War

nodes.misconception: Medals were only awarded to leaders who fought in WWI.
nodes.response: Medals were awarded for acts of bravery across all ranks of soldiers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Captain Noel Chavasse

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think trenches were dug like long, straight ditches.
nodes.response: Trenches were dug in a zig zag shape for better protection.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Trench warfare on the Western Front

nodes.misconception: The war was only fought by soldiers and won on battlefields.
nodes.response: Civilians at home did much work to support the war effort and this was known as 'the Home Front'.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Home Front in WWI

nodes.misconception: The changes between the Bronze Age and the Iron Age happened instantly.
nodes.response: Explain that the changes between the Bronze Age and Iron Age happened gradually over time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and contrasting Bronze Age and Iron Age Britain

nodes.misconception: Farmers in the Iron Age had the same tools farmers have today such as tractors.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that farming was done by hand with a few iron tools to help. New tools such as the ard plough and iron sickle made a huge impact on farming.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing agriculture in Britain during the Iron Age

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that everything was made from bronze during the Bronze Age.
nodes.response: Items such as jewellery were often made from gold.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How bronze changed life in Britain

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand that the Iron Age coins were not just different to modern day coins but the first coins ever used in Britain.
nodes.response: Explain that during the Iron Age was the first time coins and the concept of money was used in Britain. Previously, people would have traded by swapping different goods.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing settlements and trade in Iron Age Britain

nodes.misconception: Bronze is a natural resource (metal) and not man-made.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that bronze is a product that was made by humans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The first use of bronze

nodes.misconception: That Celts and Iron Age people were two different things and there was a Celtic Era.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that the Celtic people lived during the Iron Age.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The beginning of the Iron Age

nodes.misconception: That photographs are the only way to find out about the 1960s and 1970s.
nodes.response: Explain that photographs are one source that historians can use. They also look at written evidence such as newspaper articles and diaries. They can talk to people who were alive in the 1960s and 1970s and look at artefacts.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Photographs of Britain in the 1960s and 70s

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that people in the past used phones and tablets to take photographs.
nodes.response: Show pupils the various devices that have been used in the past to take photographs and how they have evolved.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The challenges of early photography

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that people have always been able to take photographs.
nodes.response: Explain that photography was invented 200 years ago and, before that, photographs did not exist. People would have drawn or painted to record what they could see in front of them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The invention of photography

nodes.misconception: Trains were the same in the Victorian times as today.
nodes.response: Explain that the trains in the Victorian times were run on steam. They would have been very dirty, noisy and bumpy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Late Victorian seaside photographs

nodes.misconception: That all families were the same 140 years ago and life was the same for everyone.
nodes.response: Explain that while the photograph gives us some clues to life in the past, just like now, all families were different.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: A family portrait from 140 years ago

nodes.misconception: The Second World War was happening in the 1950's.
nodes.response: Explain to the children that the Second World War ended half way through the 1940's. In the 1950's people and cities were recovering from the effects of the war. New houses, technology and transport was available.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Photographs of Britain in the 1940s and 50s

nodes.misconception: Evidence of Christianity from the 4th century is definitive proof of when it was introduced to Britain.
nodes.response: The evidence of Christianity found in Britain dates back to the 4th century and this gives historians reason to believe this is around the time Christianity was introduced and became popular in Britain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Roman Christianity in Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think monasteries were only a place for prayer.
nodes.response: Monasteries were places for learning and culture where people could pray, study the bible and create things.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of Irish monasteries

nodes.misconception: It is widely believed that St Patrick brought Christianity to Ireland.
nodes.response: Christianity had reached Ireland through contact with Roman Britain and as a result some Irish people converted to the religion.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: St Patrick and Christianity in Ireland

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all Britons became pagans.
nodes.response: It is likely that some Britons adopted pagan beliefs when the Anglo-Saxons settled. Some may have continued to follow Christianity.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the Romans' withdrawal on religion

nodes.misconception: The missionaries found it easy to convert people to Christianity.
nodes.response: The missionaries like St Columba and St Columbanus experienced resistance from kings and bishops which sometimes led to major problems and even battle.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Irish missionaries

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Christianity survived because of one reason.
nodes.response: Christianity survived because of a few reasons. It survived in the places the Anglo-Saxons did not settle. It also survived because monasteries were set up and missionaries spread the the religion to other places.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How Christianity survived the Romans' departure

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think archaeologists only find out about the past through excavation.
nodes.response: Archaeologists use a range of ways to find out about the past which include excavation, field walking, surveying and aerial photography.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Discovery at Coppergate

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not grasp that artefacts act like pieces to a puzzle that help us learn about how people lived in a specific time or place.
nodes.response: The more artefacts archaeologists uncover, the more opportunity there is to study them carefully to learn about how people lived in a specific time or place.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How we know so much about Viking York

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think York was only strategically important because the rivers acted as a natural defence.
nodes.response: York was strategically important because the rivers were a natural defence, but they were also key routes for trade.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: York's importance to the Vikings

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have perceptions of Vikings as only fierce fighters.
nodes.response: Evidence shows that the Vikings who settled in York were peaceful; they farmed the land and were known for being great craftsmen, traders, artists, engineers and ship builders.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: A journey through Viking York: Houses, halls and craftspeople

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how the objects prove the trade links around the world.
nodes.response: Particular objects during this time could only come from certain places. For example, silk was only made in China and travelled via the Silk Road to the Middle East and onto Europe.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: A journey through Viking York: Merchants and traders

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that what archaeologists learn from artefacts is definitive knowledge.
nodes.response: Archaeologists carefully study artefacts to learn how people lived in specific times and places. New knowledge can be discovered and can change their understanding of how people lived.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The artefacts of Viking York

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that it was a combination of factors that led to laying the foundations of England.
nodes.response: Aethelflaed and Edward were able to lay the foundations for England by establishing strongholds to protect their towns and cities, combining their forces and leading campaigns together.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Aethelflaed and Edward

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all leaders are recorded in history.
nodes.response: Female leaders, like Aethelflaed, are often written out of history as there was prejudice towards women. Despite Aethelflaed's success and the respect she gained, she was likely erased from history so it did not undermine male leaders at the time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Aethelflaed's forgotten history

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise the significant leading role Aethelflaed had during this time.
nodes.response: Aethelflaed was thought to have been a strong, independent and well-educated woman. She had learnt a great deal about military leadership and strategy by watching her father King Alfred.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Aethelflaed and Aethelred

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Ethelred's reign was completely unsuccessful.
nodes.response: Although Ethelred made some poor decisions during his reign, evidence from his charters and coins suggest that Ethelred’s government was more effective than was once believed.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing rulers in the 11th century

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Britain only changed for the worse because of the Vikings.
nodes.response: Britain changed in multiple positive ways because of Viking invasion and settlement through trade, changing place names, creating a new generation and even creating the England we know today.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How the Vikings changed Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Athelstan easily united the kingdoms to create England.
nodes.response: It is likely that Aethelstan was able to achieve so much due to the success and influence of his father, Edward, and aunt, Aethelflaed.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Athelstan and the making of England

nodes.misconception: That everything we read about the past is always true.
nodes.response: Historians try to tell as accurate a story about the past as possible by carefully investigating and studying evidence. Sometimes though, historians do not always agree with each other especially about finer details, and so make generalisations.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What we know about Ancient Greece

nodes.misconception: The city-states had only differences; they had nothing common with each other.
nodes.response: The biggest link between the city-states is that they were all part of Ancient Greece. They must have had similarities as well as differences because they were all part of the same ancient civilisation.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The city-states of Ancient Greece

nodes.misconception: That all city-states in Ancient Greece had the same structure, and the people in each state had the same roles and values. That the city-states were peaceful and lived happily alongside each other.
nodes.response: Although there were some similarities across Ancient Greece, each individual city-state had differences. Societies in Athens and Sparta were very different. Sometimes, the city-states fought each other for the right to rule over all of the lands.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Sparta's rivalry with Athens

nodes.misconception: Ancient Greece and Greece are exactly the same place.
nodes.response: Modern-day Greece is part of the area that made up Ancient Greece, but it is smaller than Ancient Greece; the extent of the spread of Ancient Greece changed over time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Ancient Greece's location and history

nodes.misconception: That a country having a democratic government involves all the people in the country having a say.
nodes.response: In Ancient Greece, only men were allowed to be part of the Assembly and take part in votes. Women were not allowed to vote, the men made the decisions and the women had to abide by them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The city-state of Athens

nodes.misconception: That the Ancient Greeks could go up Mount Olympus to find the gods or see the gods and talk to them there.
nodes.response: Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, reaching almost 10,000 ft. There were no paths and there was no climbing equipment like we have today. Climbing the rough, rocky terrain was so dangerous it could cost the life of anyone who tried.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What Greek myths can tell us about Ancient Greece

nodes.misconception: The Silk Roads were specific, defined roads.
nodes.response: The Silk Roads were not actual roads nor a single route; it was in fact a network of trade routes running between China and Europe.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The geography of the Umayyad Caliphate

nodes.misconception: Baghdad was a city where everyone was expected to follow Islam.
nodes.response: People from all over the world visited Baghdad and practising other religions was tolerated.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How Baghdad became the ‘City of Peace'

nodes.misconception: Baghdad was a place of unrest.
nodes.response: Baghdad was a wealthy and populous city, often referred to as the City of Peace.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad, the ‘City of Peace'

nodes.misconception: The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was the founder of Islam.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was messenger sent to deliver the message of Islam.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Muhammad, the Qur'an and the rise of Islam

nodes.misconception: The people living on the Arabian peninsula have always followed Islam.
nodes.response: Pre-Islamic Arabia followed a mix of Judaism, Christianity and polytheism (the belief in many gods).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The early success of Islam

nodes.misconception: Muslims were intolerant of other religions.
nodes.response: People living in Muslim-controlled territories were allowed to follow their own religion.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The early caliphates and the spread of Islam

nodes.misconception: Baghdad was only connected to the East through trade.
nodes.response: Baghdad was also a centre for cultural, scientific, and intellectual exchange. It housed the House of Wisdom where scholars translated and studied works from other cultures and facilitated an exchange of ideas and knowledge, not just goods.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad's connections to the East

nodes.misconception: The House of Wisdom was exclusively Muslim.
nodes.response: The House of Wisdom was inclusive and multicultural, attracting scholars from various religious and ethnic backgrounds, including Christians, Jews, and Zoroastrians. This diversity helped in the exchange of ideas and knowledge.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad and the spread of ideas

nodes.misconception: Al-Mansur planned Baghdad as a circle solely because of his love for the Ancient Greek science of mathematics.
nodes.response: While Al-Mansur did have an interest in maths, the circular design of Baghdad was likely influenced by a combination of factors, including practical considerations such as defence and urban planning, as well as symbolic and religious significance.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad's connections to the West

nodes.misconception: Baghdad and Cordoba were identical in their cultural and architectural influences during their respective golden ages.
nodes.response: Baghdad was influenced by Persian, Greek, and Indian cultures. In contrast, Cordoba, part of Al-Andalus, had a unique blend of Islamic, Christian, and Jewish influences, contributing to its distinctive architectural styles and cultural heritage.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad and Cordoba

nodes.misconception: Europe, the Mediterranean, and Asia in the early 9th century were largely isolated, with minimal contact and influence between these regions.
nodes.response: There was much interaction between the regions during this period with extensive trade networks, such as the Silk Road, connected them and political leaders across these regions often maintained diplomatic relations.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia in the early 9th century world

nodes.misconception: Baghdad, especially during the Abbasid Caliphate, was an isolated or insular city.
nodes.response: Baghdad was a major hub of trade, communication, and intellectual exchange, connecting the Islamic world with both Asia and Europe.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad's connection to the medieval world

nodes.misconception: That life was the same 750 years ago as it is today.
nodes.response: Explain to children that lots of things were very different 750 years ago. For example, there were no cars, planes or trains and it would have taken Owain a long time to travel to Scotland and London. People would have travelled by horse or walked.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Wales, England and Owain Glyndwr

nodes.misconception: That legends are true.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that legends are stories that are often told verbally and may change over time. Play a game to demonstrate this; children sit in a circle and pass a message around by whispering to each other. Does the messgae change?
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Robert the Bruce and the spider

nodes.misconception: The names Aethelflaed and Aethelred are very similar and may be mistaken for the same person.
nodes.response: Highlight that the two names are very similar but that Aethelflaed was the daughter of Alfred the Great and became Lady of Mercia, whereas Aethelred was the king of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Aethelflaed and the bones of Saint Oswald

nodes.misconception: Robert the Bruce is a fictional character in a story.
nodes.response: Ensure that children understand that Robert the Bruce was a real person from the past.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Scotland, England and Robert the Bruce

nodes.misconception: The Welsh lords were chanting 'Owain Glyndwr, Prince of Wales' because he was the Prince.
nodes.response: Ensure children know that the Welsh lords were chanting because they wanted Owain to become the Prince of Wales and their leader.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Owain Glyndwr, Prince of Wales

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxons only had one king in Britain.
nodes.response: The Anglo-Saxons had different kingdoms in Britain, each with its own king.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Aethelflaed, Lady of Mercia

nodes.misconception: That philosophical questions, like all questions, must have answers.
nodes.response: Questions that relate to factual information usually do have answers. Philosophical questions are not about facts. Philosophical questions are about people's opinions, feelings and perspectives on life, so they can have many and varied responses.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Famous Ancient Greek philosophers

nodes.misconception: That Olympia and Mount Olympus are either the same thing or in the same place.
nodes.response: There are approximately 200 miles between the locations of Olympia and Mount Olympus. Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, whereas Olympia was a large flat plain. Mount Olympus was the mythical home of the 12 major gods, Olympia was not.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Ancient Greek Olympic Games

nodes.misconception: That people spoke a totally different language in Ancient Greece than they speak today in modern Greece.
nodes.response: The Greek alphabet has been in use for more than 2,000 years; the same alphabet that was used in Ancient Greece is used in Greece today. Much of the Greek language stems from or is the same as Ancient Greek.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The legacy of Ancient Greek language and architecture

nodes.misconception: That there is categorically one thing that can be considered the most significant legacy.
nodes.response: Significance differs according to perspective and context. Something that is of great significance to one person may be of little significance to another, it all depends on the criteria that it is being judged against.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The most significant legacy of Ancient Greece

nodes.misconception: Elections are the most fair and just way to make decisions.
nodes.response: Elections, when they are run honestly, are a fair and just way to make decisions. However, sometimes people can interfere with results of elections or try to sway people to vote in a certain way which means the outcome can be predictable.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Athenian democracy and modern Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Troy was a real place and that the Trojan War was a real conflict.
nodes.response: The story of the Trojan War is from Greek mythology. Myths are stories that people have told by word of mouth for thousands of years, some people do claim that myths are true but they are in fact fictional stories - they did not happen in real life.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Trojan War and 'The Iliad'

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that pagan beliefs were polytheistic and all non-pagan beliefs are monotheistic.
nodes.response: Though many pagan religions were polytheistic, there are non-pagan religions that are polytheistic such as Hinduism.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The conversion of the British Isles

nodes.misconception: King Offa was solely responsible for Mercian supremacy.
nodes.response: Although it was mostly King Offa, the supremacy of Mercia was already beginning before his reign and continued for a short while afterwards.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The rise of Mercia

nodes.misconception: As Christianity was popular in Roman times before its return, pupils may think this isn't a change.
nodes.response: Due to two forms of Christianity being practiced before the Synod of Whitby, there was a significant change to religion in Britain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How Britain changed after the Romans

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may believe the kingdoms were part of one united kingdom of England.
nodes.response: The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms had their own ruler and England was not a united kingdom or nation at this point.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxons are called that because only Angles and Saxons came to Britain.
nodes.response: 'Anglo-Saxon' is a term historians use to describe all the groups of tribes who came to Britain from Europe around this time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Anglo-Saxons come to Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe the Scots tribe were originally from Scotland.
nodes.response: The Scots tribe originated from Ireland but the name 'Scotland' comes from the tribe after they migrated there.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Britain at the end of Roman rule

nodes.misconception: The Benin Bronzes were created for trade with Europeans.
nodes.response: The Benin Bronzes were created to serve as significant cultural and religious artefacts within the Benin Kingdom and made from the manilla used as payment for goods.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Why arguments have broken out about the Benin Bronzes

nodes.misconception: All Obas of Benin were male.
nodes.response: While historically most Obas were, indeed, male, there were exceptions, and a few female rulers, known as "Queen Mothers," held significant influence and power. The Queen Mothers often acted as regents for young kings or played advisory roles.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Oba of Benin

nodes.misconception: Benin City was a primitive or undeveloped society.
nodes.response: Benin City was a thriving metropolis with well-planned streets, organised urban spaces, and impressive architecture.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Benin City

nodes.misconception: The modern republic of Benin and the kingdom of Benin are the same place.
nodes.response: The modern republic of Benin has no historical relation to the kingdom of Benin.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Benin Bronzes

nodes.misconception: The Oba in Edo society was merely a religious figure.
nodes.response: While the Oba did have significant religious functions and was seen as having a special connection to the divine, his role also extended to that of political leader, responsible for governance, justice, and maintaining order within the kingdom.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edo religion

nodes.misconception: The Kingdom of Benin's trade with Europe solely revolved around the transatlantic slave trade.
nodes.response: While the Kingdom of Benin did participate in the slave trade to some extent, it also engaged in other forms of trade, including the exchange of goods such as ivory, pepper, cloth, and brassware.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Benin and Europe

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think because European seafarers were using the navigation tools, they invented them too.
nodes.response: European seafarers didn't invent the astrolabe or compass. Many ancient people navigated by the stars like the Polynesians and Vikings.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Seafaring 550 years ago

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that archaeologists only dig up bones, like dinosaurs or extinct creatures.
nodes.response: Archaeologists work with all sorts of objects from the past, many of the items in museums have been dug up by an archaeologist.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Viking navigation and expansion

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it confusing that John Cabot sounds like a very English name yet he was Italian.
nodes.response: John Cabot is the English version of the name he was born as, Giovanni Caboto. He lived in England for so long he was known by John Cabot.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: John Cabot's journeys across the Atlantic

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that in the past ships only carried sailors, captains or other people working on the ship.
nodes.response: About 200 years ago, people began to travel through choice. People that travel on ships but do not work on them are called passengers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Life aboard the SS Great Britain

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the ship was called 'The Fighting Temeraire'.
nodes.response: 'The Fighting Temeraire' was the name of Turner's painting, the ship was called HMS Temeraire.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: From sail to steam power

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Zheng He went on his voyages by himself.
nodes.response: He was admiral of the Chinese fleet. He took many ships and lots of sailors on the voyages.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The incredible voyages of Zheng He

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the 'race across the Atlantic' was an actual race, like on school sports day.
nodes.response: At around the same time, people in different places were trying to achieve the same thing, so whoever achieved it first won the 'race'.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Brunel's race to cross the Atlantic

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have the impression that all Vikings were fierce, scary warriors.
nodes.response: Some Vikings were warriors, but not all. Vikings were also traders, farmers and settlers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Vikings and their longboats

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Mediterranean is a single country.
nodes.response: The Mediterranean is a large area surrounding and including the Mediterranean Sea. Many countries are part of this area.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Seafaring in the early Mediterranean world

nodes.misconception: Chinese ships must have had engines.
nodes.response: Engines had not been invented yet. Chinese sailing ships relied on the wind and power of the sea to make long journeys.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Chinese innovation in seafaring

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Polynesia is a country.
nodes.response: Polynesia is not one single country. It is a large area of the Pacific Ocean containing lots of different islands.
nodes.subject: history
