nodes.lessonTitle: How Polynesian explorers travelled and navigated

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that explorers always use a map.
nodes.response: Early explorers did not have maps. They often used natural features to navigate by such as rivers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early explorers and their boats

nodes.misconception: That only Egyptian people who were related by blood to the previous pharaoh could become a pharaoh.
nodes.response: Alexander was an ancient Greek. He was not Egyptian by birth or by blood but the Egyptian people still made him a pharaoh after Alexander drove the Persians out of Egypt.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Alexander's conquests

nodes.misconception: That the historical places named still exist today.
nodes.response: Over time, names and boundaries of places can change. Some places cease to exist entirely while the locations of some places do still exist but they have a different name today. A large area of Persia for example is in the modern-day country of Iran.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Persian Empire

nodes.misconception: Alexandria is a city in Greece.
nodes.response: Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria in Egypt, not on the mainland or any island of Ancient Greece. There is still a city called Alexandria on the original site in Egypt today; some ruins of the ancient city can be visited by tourists.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Alexander's achievements

nodes.misconception: That the Kingdom of Macedon and the modern republic of North Macedonia are the same place.
nodes.response: Although North Macedonia's name stems from Macedon, they are not exactly the same location. Most of North Macedonia was part of Macedon, but Macedon also covered large parts of what is now northern Greece, southern Bulgaria and eastern Albania.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Alexander's journey from boy to king

nodes.misconception: Alexander 'The Great' was the title that Alexander had when he was a living ruler.
nodes.response: 'The Great' is not a title. It is a type of nickname called an epithet. Epithets are only used to refer to people that have died and they tell us more about something significant the person did or what the person was like.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Why Alexander is called 'The Great'

nodes.misconception: That battles are always fought on land, by soldiers or warriors who are physically fighting each other.
nodes.response: Battles can be fought many ways - some Ancient Greek battles were land based and warriors used chariots and weapons like javelins. Other battles were at sea using boats that would be rammed into the enemy and archers that would fire arrows at them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The wars between Greece and Persia

nodes.misconception: BCE and CE denote times before and after the year 0.
nodes.response: There is no year 0. BCE denotes the time before the year 1 and CE denotes the time from the year 1.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Roman kings

nodes.misconception: Julius Caesar was an emperor of the Roman Empire.
nodes.response: Julius Caesar was not an emperor of the Roman Empire but a dictator of the Roman Republic.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The rise of the Emperors

nodes.misconception: People in Byzantine times never called themselves Byzantium.
nodes.response: People in Byzantine times always called themselves Roman.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The division of the Roman Empire

nodes.misconception: In ancient times, being Roman meant being from the city of Rome.
nodes.response: Initially, being Roman meant being from the city of Rome but later it included people who followed Roman ideology all over the Roman world.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What it meant to be a Roman

nodes.misconception: The fall of the Western Roman Empire happened when it was sacked in 410 CE.
nodes.response: The fall of the Western Roman Empire happened gradually over time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The fall of the Western Roman Empire

nodes.misconception: Rome was always an Empire.
nodes.response: Before the Roman Empire was founded, Rome was first ruled by kings and then Rome became a republic.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Roman Republic

nodes.misconception: Students may think that for something to be taught as history, all historians have to agree on it.
nodes.response: Historians do not always agree about the past and what sources tell us. It is important to remember this when being historians ourselves!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How we know about life in Anglo-Saxon England

nodes.misconception: Students may think that we only know about the Anglo-Saxons because of written history.
nodes.response: We know mostly about the Anglo-Saxons because of grave goods and other archeological finds.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Anglo-Saxon grave goods

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that as soon as Christianity returned to Britain, pagan traditions disappeared completely.
nodes.response: Paganism did not completely vanish. Though the majority of Anglo-Saxons were Christians, pagan beliefs and traditions were still present.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Religious buildings and artefacts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that Offa was the only Anglo-Saxon king to mint coins.
nodes.response: Offa was the first, but other kings minted coins with their head on too. The Archbishop of Canterbury has also been found on coins as well as Offa's queen: Cynethryth.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Anglo-Saxon coins

nodes.misconception: Widow is a gender neutral term.
nodes.response: Widow is a gendered term for a woman whose husband has died. A widower is a husband whose wife has died.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Anglo-Saxon law codes

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused by the etymology of 'girdle-hangers' .
nodes.response: Though they symbolise keys, girdle-hangers are called this because they hang from the girdle (belt or sash).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The graves of Anglo-Saxon women

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only women from Britain served in the armed forces.
nodes.response: Highlight how thousands of women from across the British Empire at the time joined organisations like the ATS to help the British war effort.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Women in the armed forces

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that life returned to normal for everyone after the war was over.
nodes.response: Emphasise how the changes brought by the Second World War were permanent.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How experiences differed during the Second World War

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that children were only evacuated to areas in Britain during the Second World War.
nodes.response: Children were sent to other countries like Australia and South Africa in 1940.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Bombing and evacuation

nodes.misconception: Only British people fought for Britain during the Second World War.
nodes.response: Highlight how millions of men and women from around the world helped the British armed forces.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The outbreak of the Second World War

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that the fighting in the Second World War only happened in Europe.
nodes.response: Discuss how the fighting was global and happened across three different continents with millions of people worldwide involved.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: A global war fought by an imperial army

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that nurses only did tasks like cleaning wards and providing meals.
nodes.response: Nurses did three years of training and had to pass exams in anatomy and physiology. They handled weapons on the front line and ran the hospitals caring for the injured in Britain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The experiences of nurses during the Second World War

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to comprehend the slow and painstaking nature of carrying out excavations.
nodes.response: Carter began excavating the Valley of the Kings many years before finding Tutankhamun's tomb; they were about to give up when they found it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Howard Carter and the Valley of the Kings

nodes.misconception: That mummification is just a case of wrapping a body in bandages and burying it.
nodes.response: There are several stages in the mummification process, each of which must be done precisely and carefully in order to be successful.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Death and the Ancient Egyptians

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the River Nile is a river found only in Egypt.
nodes.response: The River Nile does flow through Egypt, but it also flows through 10 other countries in east Africa. It is Africa's longest river.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The River Nile

nodes.misconception: That there was one hieroglyph (picture) equivalent to each letter of the English alphabet.
nodes.response: The Ancient Egyptians did not have an alphabet in the same way we do today. Hieroglyphs represented sounds and sometimes whole words. There were a lot more hieroglyphs than there are letters of the alphabet.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Rosetta Stone and Egyptian writing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the kingdoms are places in Egypt.
nodes.response: Kingdoms are are periods of time in Egyptian history; the Old Kingdom, the Middle Kingdom and the New Kingdom.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The three kingdoms of Egypt

nodes.misconception: It can be difficult for young learners to grasp how long 3000 years actually is and therefore appreciate just how long standing and important the Ancient Egyptian civilisation was.
nodes.response: Draw a timeline with 1AD in the middle, 2086 BCE on the left end and 2024 on the right end. Use this to demonstrate that the Ancient Egyptians existed for even longer than the time that has passed since 1 AD to today.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Change and continuity in Ancient Egypt

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all people in Roman Britain lived in Roman towns.
nodes.response: Make it clear to pupils that although many people came to the towns, Britain remained largely rural, with lots of small Celtic settlements.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Towns in Roman Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the people of Britain formed a united kingdom at this time.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that 1st century CE Britain was made up of various Celtic people, kingdoms and tribes.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Roman invasion of Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Hadrian's Wall was not very high, as the remaining stretches have been damaged.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that Hadrian's Wall is over a thousand years old, and any sections still standing were much taller in the past.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The buildings of Roman Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Caratacus' resistance and Boudica's rebellion took place at the same time.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that roughly 20 years had passed since Caratacus' defeat when Boudica rebelled.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Boudica's rebellion against Roman rule

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all aspects of religion, or all aspects of buildings changed.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that within an area of study that we define, there can be elements of both change and continuity.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The changes to life brought about by Roman settlement

nodes.misconception: Pupils may gain the impression that the Ancient Romans destroyed all aspects of Celtic worship.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that although the druids were wiped out, the worship of Celtic gods was tolerated as long as Ancient Roman ones were also respected.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How far religion changed under Roman rule

nodes.misconception: Writing is only created with pens or pencils.
nodes.response: Discuss different forms of writing such as print on a poster, graffiti, and lettering on clothing.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of trade, construction and writing in Mesopotamia

nodes.misconception: Art is only drawings or paintings.
nodes.response: Look at lots of different examples of ancient art, such as sculpture, textiles, jewellery, decorated household objects, weapons and armour.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The art and artefacts of the earliest civilisations

nodes.misconception: Nomadic lifestyles no longer exist.
nodes.response: Discuss the fact that many people in different parts of the world still live a nomadic lifestyle, some through choice and others as part of a continuing and ancient tradition.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the earliest civilisations

nodes.misconception: Egypt and Mesopotamia are the only places to have had early civilisations.
nodes.response: Look at a map of the world and point out the locations of the Indus Valley and Shang civilisations.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Other 'cradles of civilisation'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think floods are only destructive.
nodes.response: Explain that floodwaters can be very dangerous and cause much damage, but they also bring water and nutrients to the land for growing crops.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Mesopotamia, the land 'between two rivers'

nodes.misconception: Ancient writing was only for stories about rulers and gods.
nodes.response: Discuss the four different uses of ancient writing: trade, laws, religion and rulers. Discuss how these are similar to modern use, like laws needed for an ancient civilisation to develop, and think about the kinds of laws they would have needed.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Similarities between the earliest civilisations

nodes.misconception: That a turning point is a temporary change.
nodes.response: A turning point is usually a major, decisive and permanent change.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The ways in which Britain changed after the Second World War

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Churchill was unpopular because the majority of the British public did not vote for him in 1945.
nodes.response: Churchill was a popular individual. It was the lack of promises of his political party to make social changes that lost him the election in 1945.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The condition of Britain at the end of the Second World War

nodes.misconception: Students may think that National Insurance before WWII allowed men to receive healthcare without paying for it.
nodes.response: They had to pay with some of their wages to be entitled to the benefits of healthcare.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The creation of the National Health Service

nodes.misconception: People from the Caribbean travelled to Britain without being invited.
nodes.response: These people were invited to become British citizens by the government in 1948 to help the country recover and lots had contributed in the armed forces during the war too.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Windrush generation

nodes.misconception: That being a housewife was an easy role.
nodes.response: Working in the home on domestic tasks for 70 hours a week was more than a full time working week with a paid job.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of rapidly changing technology

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that the Vikings came to Britain for different reasons over a long period of time.
nodes.response: The Vikings first came to Britain to raid monasteries; they then invaded and settled in some Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. Finally, they tried to capture all of Britain but were unsuccessful. However, they were able to stay and control the Danelaw.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Why the Vikings came to Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that Britain was formed of separate Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
nodes.response: At this time, Britain was formed of four separate kingdoms: East Anglia, Northumbria, Mercia and Wessex.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great Heathen Army

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that the Viking army was so large it was able to split its forces which led to its success across Britain.
nodes.response: The Viking army was so large, it could split into different sections and fight in different parts of Britain at the same time. The army could also send reinforcements from one section to support another section in need.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Aethelred, Alfred the Great and Wessex

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that dividing England was a clever move for Alfred to make.
nodes.response: Alfred divided England and allowed the Vikings to control some areas. Alfred knew he could not get the Vikings to leave Britain as too many had already settled.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Anglo-Saxon fightback

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Vikings' motivation to raid Lindisfarne was to murder the monks rather than it being a consequence of the raids.
nodes.response: The Vikings raided monasteries because they were easy targets on the coast and they had many valuable objects they could steal.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early Viking raids

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the Vikings only raided places and left.
nodes.response: Vikings expansion involved sailing to explore new places which they often raided for goods. The Vikings then began to settle and trade in these places.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Seafaring Vikings

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the relics of St Columba were valuable.
nodes.response: The relics of St Columba were an important symbol of the Christian faith throughout the kingdom of Alba.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Constantine II, the Vikings and St Columba's relics

nodes.misconception: Some may think that John's sisters would be in line to the throne before him.
nodes.response: Explain that this is the case today in the UK - Princess Charlotte became the first female royal to benefit from The Succession to the Crown Act in 2013. The Act stated that girls born into the Royal Family will not be overtaken by younger brothers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: John and the 'Lionheart'

nodes.misconception: All Romans allowed Prasutagus and Boudica rule the east of England.
nodes.response: When Prasutagus died, the Roman Emperor Nero did not want to share power and control of the land with Boudica and her daughters.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Boudica and Prasutagus

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think there can only be one legend about Boudica.
nodes.response: There are many legends about Boudica's death. Historians from the past have told different stories but we do not know which is the truth.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Boudica meets her end

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the failure to capture Vienna meant Suleiman was a failure.
nodes.response: Emphasise that setbacks are normal and Suleiman was still able to extend the Ottoman Empire to its greatest ever reach.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Suleiman the general

nodes.misconception: Some may think that 'Suleiman the Lawgiver' and 'Suleiman the Magnificent' are different people.
nodes.response: Explain that these are different names used for the same person to remember different elements of his time as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Suleiman and the Ottoman 'Golden Age'

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Athelstan controlled Scotland because he defeated Constantine.
nodes.response: Although Constantine lost, Athelstan only remained king of England. He became overlord of Scotland but failed to unite England and Scotland under one kingship.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The rise of Alba under Constantine II

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the buildings commissioned by Suleiman are not used or in existence today.
nodes.response: Many of them still exist 500 years later and can be seen today, particularly the mosques and religious buildings which have been continually renovated over time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Suleiman the Lawgiver

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think women were not able to lead rebellions.
nodes.response: Boudica was a strong leader and the tribes respected her. The tribes were happy to follow her as part of the rebellion against the Romans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Boudica the warrior

nodes.misconception: Some may think that kings and queens after King John forgot about Magna Carta.
nodes.response: Kings and queens after King John still followed Magna Carta and it remained as a very important document of rights for the people. Today, there are still four of the original 63 clauses in use in England.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: King John and Magna Carta

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the Church is the same as a church building.
nodes.response: The Church is the name of the organisation that includes all the people who lead the Christian religion. Buildings are also called churches.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: King John and his barons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think revenge always involves killing people.
nodes.response: Revenge is the act of getting back at someone for something they did to you. This may involve stealing something or destroying something like property.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Constantine II's early life and exile in Ireland

nodes.misconception: Women could not hold positions of power in the Shang Dynasty.
nodes.response: The tomb of Fu Hao tells us that she was a powerful queen and one of the most successful and important army generals of her time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What archaeologists have found out about the Shang

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the Shang Dynasty symbols are exactly the same as the modern Chinese written symbols.
nodes.response: There are lots of similarities between them but they are different. Lots of the modern Chinese symbols are clearly based on the ancient Shang Dynasty ones.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Oracle bones and writing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all these ancient civilisations existed at separate times.
nodes.response: Although beginning thousands of years apart, by the time of the Shang Dynasty, the Ancient Sumerian, Ancient Egyptian and Indus Valley civilisations were still going!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Who were the Shang?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that sacrifices were only offered to gods.
nodes.response: The belief that the ancestors held power over the living family was very strong in the Shang Dynasty. The people wanted to remember them, keep them happy and asked for blessings for their actions in life.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Bronze dings

nodes.misconception: Some might assume that jade is always green in colour.
nodes.response: Jade is a natural stone and so the colour varies greatly. It can appear as many colours including black, brown, yellow, white, green and blue. Different colours have been more desirable at different points in Chinese history.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Jade artefacts

nodes.misconception: Ancient generals were only men.
nodes.response: The story of Fu Hao as one of the best Shang Dynasty generals at this time disproves this. There are records of around 600 women in the army at this time too.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The discovery of Fu Hao's tomb

nodes.misconception: Christianity is a Western religion.
nodes.response: Christianity originated in the Middle East and quickly spread across various regions, including Africa.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Christian Church in Aksum

nodes.misconception: The early Christian councils selected the books of the New Testament.
nodes.response: Though various local regional councils published lists of Old and New Testament books, there is no evidence of councils meeting to vote on the New Testament canon.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Christianity in Western Europe

nodes.misconception: The only Church to emerge from the Roman Empire is the Roman Catholic Church.
nodes.response: Two Christian Churches with slightly different ideologies emerged: the Roman Catholic Church was a product of the Western Roman Empire and the Eastern Orthodox Church developed in the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early Christianity's story

nodes.misconception: The Byzantines weren’t Roman.
nodes.response: The Byzantine Empire, also known as the Eastern Roman Empire, was a continuation of the Roman Empire. The term "Byzantine" is a modern designation used by historians, but the people of that time considered themselves Romans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Christianity in the Eastern Roman Empire

nodes.misconception: Constantine forced everyone in the Roman Empire to be Christian during his rule.
nodes.response: Constantine issued a law, the Edict of Milan, that protected all faiths from religious persecution so that everyone in the Roman Empire could practise the religion they wanted.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Constantine's conversion to Christianity

nodes.misconception: Christianity started with the birth of Jesus Christ.
nodes.response: Christianity developed after the death of Jesus when his followers continued to spread his teachings.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early Christianity

nodes.misconception: That archaeologists and historians are always right. That information about the past is always factual.
nodes.response: Explain that archaeologists and historians use clues to piece together what they think the past was like. These views and opinions can change over time as more sources or information is discovered.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What historians have learnt about Iron Age Britain

nodes.misconception: That by connected we mean geographically or physically rather thank via communication and trade.
nodes.response: Discuss the meaning of the word connected. Explore maps of the areas concerned. Explain that Britain and Europe were connected by communication and trade.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Iron Age Britain's connections to the wider world

nodes.misconception: Some may think that Celtic people and Iron Age people lived in different time periods.
nodes.response: Celtic people lived during the Iron Age.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The women of Iron Age Britain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all of our knowledge of the Iron Age is definitely correct.
nodes.response: Explain that archaeologists use artefacts to learn about the past, they get ideas and clues from the artefacts and build up a picture of what they think the past was like. There is very little written evidence about the Celts.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Celtic art, the Snettisham Great Torc and the Battersea Shield

nodes.misconception: That the archaeologists used the actual artefacts found in the grave to make the reconstruction of the chariot.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that archaeologists used new materials to make a replica chariot based on the evidence in the grave.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Wetwang chariot and Celtic warfare

nodes.misconception: That all bodies remain in a preserved state after death.
nodes.response: Explain that after death the body normally decomposes and a skeleton remains.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The discovery of Lindow Man

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only adults worked at jobs in factories in Victorian times.
nodes.response: In Victorian times, there were no laws stopping children working. Children had to earn money to live, so many of them worked in factories. Since they were young and small, children were useful for getting into tight spaces to clean or fix machines.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Factories in Britain during Victorian times

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Crystal Palace is still standing or that it can be seen or visited today.
nodes.response: The Crystal Palace was a temporary structure built for the exhibition. It was relocated and rebuilt in another part of London but was later destroyed by fire. The surrounding area was then named Crystal Palace to show how important the structure was.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great Exhibition

nodes.misconception: Pupils can struggle with the fact that the United Kingdom is a country made up of four separate smaller countries. Furthermore we also refer to Great Britain - which can again be confusing for pupils.
nodes.response: The UK's full name is The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland make up the UK. Great Britain is only the mainland countries of England, Wales and Scotland that share land borders.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victoria, Scotland and John Brown

nodes.misconception: That 'South Africa' refers to the southern half of the continent of Africa.
nodes.response: 'South Africa' is one single African country, which is located in the south of the continent of Africa. The south of africa (the part that sits in the southern hemisphere) covers a much larger area and includes 15 other individual African countries.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Alice Kinloch and the Victorian British Empire

nodes.misconception: That inventions are always things like machines, robots, computers and so on.
nodes.response: Inventions come from ideas, and people can have ideas about so many different situations in life. The invention here for example is a type of pain relief for childbirth, a medical invention.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victoria's children

nodes.misconception: That Victoria and Albert only married because they were made to do so, not because they loved each other.
nodes.response: Victoria and Albert had a strong connection from the first time they met. Written evidence tells us that the two were very much in love and their marriage was a happy, loving relationship.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victoria's proposal and marriage to Albert

nodes.misconception: That when Queen Victoria died, then Queen Elizabeth II became queen.
nodes.response: There were other monarchs in between Queen Victoria and Queen Elizabeth II. Queen Elizabeth II was the next female monarch but she did not become queen until 50 years after Queen Victoria died.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Britain at the time of Victoria's death

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Britain still rules over or controls India today.
nodes.response: Britain does not rule India today. Britain ruled India and much of the surrounding land for over 300 years, but this ended in 1947 when the territory was partitioned into two separate independent countries which became India and Pakistan.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victoria, Empress of India

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all Victorian children worked, or that no Victorian children had an education.
nodes.response: Children from wealthy families were educated at home or sent to schools that were paid for. Some children went to small local schools on some days of the week and worked on other days. Some of the least fortunate children did not go to school at all.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victorian childhood

nodes.misconception: That a coronation ceremony is when a person becomes a monarch.
nodes.response: The person who is first in line to the throne becomes monarch the minute that the previous monarch passes away. It happens in an instant. The coronation is an official ceremony, held later where the monarch receives their crown in front of people.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victoria's accession to the throne

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that classes in society are small groups, like classes at school.
nodes.response: Classes are groups of people, but classes in society include thousands, sometimes millions of people and they are not age related like school classes, they depend on other factors like wealth or profession.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victorian society

nodes.misconception: That nothing is known about Victoria (or indeed other monarchs) before becoming Queen.
nodes.response: There is a lot of historical evidence about Victoria's childhood including written accounts and artefacts that tell us a great deal about what her early life was like.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victoria's 'melancholy' childhood

nodes.misconception: Some may think that Emily Davison and Paul Stephenson were fighting for the same thing.
nodes.response: Emily Davison and Paul Stephenson were fighting for different change to happen in Britain at different times, around 50 years apart.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing Paul Stephenson and Emily Davison

nodes.misconception: Some may think that Emily Davison quit her job to join the Suffragettes.
nodes.response: Emily joined the Suffragettes in 1906 and did not quit her job to fight for women's suffrage full time until 1908.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Emily Davison and the Suffragettes

nodes.misconception: Some may think that women were not allowed to go to university at all in Victorian Britain.
nodes.response: Women were allowed to study at university, work very hard and take all of the same exams as men, but they were not allowed the degree at the end of it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Emily Davison's early life and education

nodes.misconception: Some children might think that militant tactics are a good way for them to get the things that they want to.
nodes.response: The Suffragettes used extreme tactics because they felt that it was their only option. Going on hunger strike is dangerous. For the issues that children might face, there are many safer and less harmful ways to make a change.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Stories from Emily Davison's activism

nodes.misconception: Some may think that thousands of people attend funerals usually.
nodes.response: Emily Davison's funeral was an exception. Usually funerals are only attended by people who knew the person.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Emily Davison's funeral

nodes.misconception: Some may think that as soon as someone is arrested, they go to prison.
nodes.response: This doesn't happen and is not what happened to Paul Stephenson. He was kept in a holding cell in the police station until midnight.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Paul Stephenson and The Bay Horse pub

nodes.misconception: That evacuation was a negative experience for all children.
nodes.response: Lots of children had healthier diets, more freedom and enjoyed their lives in the countryside.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Paul Stephenson's early life and evacuation

nodes.misconception: Some may think that the only people not allowed to work for the Bristol bus companies in 1963 were black people.
nodes.response: The bus companies did not allow anyone who was not white to work for them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Paul Stephenson and the Bristol Bus Boycott

nodes.misconception: Some may think that people only came to Britain from the Caribbean.
nodes.response: People from all over the world came to Britain, including from places like India and Poland.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Paul Stephenson arrives in Bristol

nodes.misconception: Some may think that Emily Davison died on the day of the Epsom Derby.
nodes.response: Emily Davison died four days after the race at Epsom, on the 8th of June 1913.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Emily Davison and the tragedy at Epsom Racecourse

nodes.misconception: Some may think that only Paul Stephenson's actions directly led to the 1965 law.
nodes.response: Paul's actions had an impact as did many other people's in the 1960s.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Paul Stephenson's legacy in Bristol and Britain

nodes.misconception: That certain jobs are for men only or women only.
nodes.response: Just like during the war, anyone should be able to and can do any job.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes for women following Emily Davison's death

nodes.misconception: Christianity is a single religion.
nodes.response: There are more than 45 000 different Christian denominations around the world today: although most of them believe the same fundamental things, there are stark differences between many of them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great Schism

nodes.misconception: Different religious denominations believe very different things from each other.
nodes.response: Different denominations within a religion will almost certainly believe the same fundamental things about their religion, but will differ over the details of belief or liturgy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Eastern Orthodox Church

nodes.misconception: Catholic priests have never been allowed to get married.
nodes.response: Catholic priests today are not allowed to get married, but in the past a great many were, even though it went against their rules. Some popes even had wives and children!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Background to the Great Schism: the Roman Catholic Church

nodes.misconception: Kings have the power to do whatever they want in their own countries.
nodes.response: For a great deal of English history, the power of the kings has been restricted by English laws and religious laws issued by the pope in Rome.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Henry VIII and the King's Great Matter

nodes.misconception: The Protestant Reformation was a single event.
nodes.response: The Protestant Reformation happened over a long period of time and happened differently in different countries. Some countries moved swiftly away from Catholic beliefs, whereas in others the pace of change was slower or even reverted backwards.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The English Reformation in its European context

nodes.misconception: There has always been a large variety of names that people could be called.
nodes.response: In societies that do not experience a great deal of immigration, the pool of names that people can be called can be limited. This was the case for hundreds of years in England, causing many people to share the same names (e.g. Thomas!).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Thomas Cromwell and the Reformation Parliament

nodes.misconception: A single person cannot shape history by themselves.
nodes.response: The Great Man Theory in History - the idea that a single person is responsible for important events - is somewhat outdated, but occasionally, as is the case with Martin Luther, an argument can be made that individuals can radically shape events.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Martin Luther and the Lutheran Reformation

nodes.misconception: Protestantism is a single unified religion.
nodes.response: There are, today, thousands of different Christian denominations that can be considered versions of Protestantism. Almost from its very inception, Protestantism split into a variety of competing belief systems.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Zwingli, Calvin and the Swiss Reformation

nodes.misconception: People decide for themselves what religious beliefs they hold.
nodes.response: For much of English history, people had to believe what the monarch told them to believe, else they would be killed. This insistence upon belief became more relaxed only in the relatively recent past.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The beliefs of the Church of England 1534-1558

nodes.misconception: Toussaint L'Ouverture was fighting against the French during the entirety of the Haitian Revolution.
nodes.response: He first fought Saint-Domingue's ruling French elites and slave-owners. He then fought Spanish troops after invading Spain's territory on the island. He then defeated a British invasion and became Haiti's official governor until France betrayed him.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Toussaint L'Ouverture and the fight for independence

nodes.misconception: The Haitian Revolution directly inspired the abolition of slavery everywhere.
nodes.response: The events of the Haitian Revolution strengthened Britain's abolitionist movement and helped France to initially abolish slavery in 1794; but under Napoleon the threat of enslavement returned.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of the Haitian Revolution in the abolition of the slave trade

nodes.misconception: The 1807 Slave Trade Act freed all enslaved people in the British Empire.
nodes.response: The 1807 Slave Trade Act did not free all enslaved people in the British Empire, but did ban the buying, selling and transportation of enslaved individuals from that point forward.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The 1807 abolition of the slave trade

nodes.misconception: Abolition of slavery in Britain and its colonies was a response to a single event.
nodes.response: Abolition of slavery in Britain and its colonies was a response to a number of events and an ever-growing public demand for change.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Abolitionist movements in Britain

nodes.misconception: All the peoples who revolted in Saint-Domingue were enslaved people.
nodes.response: The revolutionaries of Saint-Domingue were comprised of a combination of enslaved people, free people of African descent and free indigenous people.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The causes of the Haitian Revolution

nodes.misconception: Sait-Domingue was independent from France under Toussaint L'Ouverture's leadership
nodes.response: Toussaint L'Ouverture was technically the French Governor of Saint-Domingue due to his leadership during the slave uprising there during the 1790s. His attempt to establish the colony as a free country though in 1801 was a step too far for Napoleon.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Napoleon and the re-establishment of slavery

nodes.misconception: Everyone in Elizabethan England was Protestant.
nodes.response: Protestantism in Elizabethan England was the norm by the end of Elizabeth's reign, but England was religiously divided during her reign.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth I and the Church of England

nodes.misconception: Mary, Queen of Scots and 'Bloody Mary' were the same person.
nodes.response: The two Marys were cousins, not the same person.  Mary was a very common name at this time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth I and Mary, Queen of Scots

nodes.misconception: The English navy destroyed the Spanish Armada.
nodes.response: Most of the ships lost from the Spanish Armada were sunk in storms after the battle against the English navy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth I and the Spanish Armada

nodes.misconception: Elizabeth was the first female ruler of England.
nodes.response: There were female rulers before Elizabeth, including her sister Mary I immediately preceeding her.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth I and the succession: The Virgin Queen

nodes.misconception: Historians all agree about what happened in the past.
nodes.response: Historians are constantly arguing and changing their minds about events in the past as new evidence comes to light.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Popular depictions of Elizabeth I

nodes.misconception: The Elizabethan period was a 'Golden Age'.
nodes.response: Whilst there were many positives that came about during the Elizabethan era, many people suffered from poverty and starvation.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Elizabeth I's later years

nodes.misconception: Because the Abbasid Caliphate was large, the caliphs must have retained a lot of power.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the caliphs had little effective power beyond Baghdad itself by the 11th century and the Seljuks became de facto rulers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Baghdad in the 11th century

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that all medieval Islamic states must have been identical to one another.
nodes.response: Islamic states had similarities and differences (i.e. Cordoba had many Mediterranean influences; Persian influence was stronger in Baghdad).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Cordoba in the 11th century

nodes.misconception: As a Muslim island, there was little diversity in 11th century Sicily.
nodes.response: Sicily was amongst the most diverse places in Eurasia during the 11th century with a population of Muslims, Christians and Jews.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Sicily and other Islamic worlds in the 11th century

nodes.misconception: The Industrial Revolution led to a decline in living conditions across all parts of Britain.
nodes.response: The decline in living conditions during the Industrial Revolution was generally confined to industrial towns and their poorest areas.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Industrial Revolution and urban migration

nodes.misconception: Students assume the Agricultural Revolution was predominantly facilitated by changes in technology.
nodes.response: Farming tech in common use didn't change much. Improvements in agriculture occurred mainly because of the use of new farming methods.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Agricultural Revolution

nodes.misconception: Radicals encouraged the use of violence to solve the problems that industrial workers faced.
nodes.response: Radicals like Cobbett and Hunt emphaisised the importance of peaceful protests and the need to persuade government to extend voting rights.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Political radicals and the Peterloo Massacre

nodes.misconception: The Industrial Revolution affected all aspects of life in Britain equally.
nodes.response: The impact of the Industrial Revolution may be measured differently depending on which aspects of life historians focus their attention on.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Industrial Revolution and change in Britain

nodes.misconception: Most campaigners for reform like the BPU wanted all adults in Britain to be enfranchised.
nodes.response: The BPU campaigned for tax-paying males to be enfranchised, which would have continued to exclude many poor workers as well as women.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Calls for reform and the 1832 Great Reform Act

nodes.misconception: That the Industrial Revolution was only about the use of steam power.
nodes.response: Many key changes in the Industrial Revolution related to developments beyond the use of steam power, such as the exploitation of water power.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Inventions of the Industrial Revolution

nodes.misconception: That the Bayeux Tapestry is a 'biased' source and therefore not useful to historians.
nodes.response: Although all sources were produced in a particular context, historians can ask careful questions of them to learn about the past.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Battle of Hastings (1066)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that power associated with land ownership was a Norman import to England.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that Anglo-Saxon England was a society largely based on land ownership and the power that this brought.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Norman changes to English land holding

nodes.misconception: Pupils may consider sources to be inherently useful or not useful and make statements about bias.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that all sources are useful for investigating something, and that the questions we ask of them are important in this process.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the Norman Conquest on England

nodes.misconception: Students may think that 'eyewitness' accounts produce a more reliable picture of historical events.
nodes.response: Although 'eyewitness' accounts are valuable, they were produced for a particular purpose which may distort their contents.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 1066 and claims to the throne

nodes.misconception: The written word is the only useful source for the study of the past.
nodes.response: Although written sources are useful, material remains can reveal much about past societies - it depends on the questions historians ask of the source.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Norman changes to the English landscape

nodes.misconception: Students might think that 'the Church' is a physical building in which people pray.
nodes.response: Explain that 'the Church' refers to the wider organisation of the Christian faith, including all buildings and people which belong to it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Norman reforms to the English Church

nodes.misconception: Farmers will not starve because they grow their own food.
nodes.response: Poor harvests can put a great deal of strain on the amount of food a farmer can grow, even food for subsistence.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Growing population in Elizabethan England

nodes.misconception: Laws are regularly scrutinised and updated by the government.
nodes.response: Many laws remain unchanged and in place for an exceedingly long time. Sometimes new laws are created which make the old ones redundant, but other times there is no need to replace the existing law if it is still relevant.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the Elizabethan Poor Law

nodes.misconception: Historians all study the same things in history.
nodes.response: There is a large and ever-growing variety of themes that historians look at in history that shape the way we view the past, e.g. military history, economic history, women's history and many more.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Was there a ‘Golden Age’ for the poor in Elizabethan England?

nodes.misconception: The government is there to help people when they are in need.
nodes.response: Throughout much of history, governments have regularly failed to support the most vulnerable in society, as many of them did not see that as their function.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The problem of poverty in Tudor England

nodes.misconception: Governments and societies have generally been sympathetic to people in extreme poverty who may have been reduced to begging.
nodes.response: Throughout much of history, there has been little sympathy for people in extreme poverty from the majority of governments and societies, even when the circumstances that drove people into poverty are clearly out of their own control.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Tudor attitudes to poverty and the Elizabethan Poor Law (1601)

nodes.misconception: The English have always been a nation of animal lovers.
nodes.response: Blood sports were a very popular form of entertainment for hundreds of years. A large variety of animals were killed for our entertainment, such as bulls, bears and badgers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Social life for the poor in Tudor England

nodes.misconception: All working class men gained the right to vote due to the 1867 and 1884 Reform Acts.
nodes.response: As property qualifications remained in place, a significant proportion of working class adult men remained unable to vote even after 1884.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Widening the franchise in 19th century Britain

nodes.misconception: Europeans conquered the Americas easily because they had better weapons and technology.
nodes.response: European diseases killed and weakened many Native Americans, undermining indigenous resistance to European conquest.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Impact of Europeans on Native Americans

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that England was a comparable colonial power to Spain in the 16th century.
nodes.response: English colonisation attempts began much later than Spain’s, and occurred on a much smaller-scale with less government involvement.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: English settlement at Roanoke

nodes.misconception: John Rolfe’s marriage to Pocahontas represented goodwill between colonists and the Powhatan tribe.
nodes.response: Pocahontas' marriage involved her capture and forced conversion to Christianity. Pocahontas was used by the English for their own advantage.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: England's first successful American colonies

nodes.misconception: All Native American were the same and part of a single society.
nodes.response: There was a wide range of indigenous nations in the Americas, with many differences between their sizes, social structure and cultures.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Americas before the arrival of Europeans

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that America was ‘discovered’ by Europeans or that it was a 'new' place.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there were long-established communities in the Americas before European arrival - they did not need to be discovered.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: European arrivals in the Americas

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that European settlement completely destroyed indigenous communities.
nodes.response: Native Americans were devastated overall by European colonisation but indigenous communities persisted and were never completely overwhelmed.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Impact of European settlement in the Americas

nodes.misconception: Towns and cities are called by the same name as they were given when they were founded.
nodes.response: Towns and cities all over the world have changed their name repeatedly for a wide variety of reasons. For example, York was called Eboracum by the Romans, Eoforwick by the Saxons and Jorvik by the Vikings!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Background to the Crusades: the Byzantine Empire

nodes.misconception: Records of speeches from previous time periods are accurate representations of what these people actually said.
nodes.response: Accurate recording of speeches was not a priority for many historians or record keepers up until fairly recently. It was seen as acceptable to put words into the mouths of past people based on what happened after or to reflect present sensibilities.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Pope Urban II's call to crusade

nodes.misconception: Christians 'saved' the Holy Land from barbaric Muslim conquerors.
nodes.response: Muslims had generally treated Christians very well during the 400 or so years that they had controlled the Holy Land. In contrast, when the Christian crusaders arrived in the Holy Land they engaged in barbaric acts.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The First Crusade

nodes.misconception: The only reason why crusaders went on the First Crusade was to capture Jerusalem for Christianity.
nodes.response: People went on crusade for a wide variety of reasons; for some people, capturing Jerusalem from the Muslims was important, but it was almost certainly not the reason why the First Crusade was called in the first place.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The causes of the First Crusade

nodes.misconception: The medieval Islamic world was a single entity.
nodes.response: The Islamic Empire started as a single entity, but by the 11th century had fragmented into several competing nations.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Background to the Crusades: the Seljuk Empire

nodes.misconception: The pope has always been the most powerful person in the Roman Catholic Church.
nodes.response: For much of the medieval period, a power struggle between the pope and local kings took place for control of religion within each country.  In the early medieval period the pope had very little power at all.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Background to the Crusades: the medieval Western Church

nodes.misconception: Parliament fought both Civil Wars to remove Charles I from power
nodes.response: The majority of people in Parliament wanted to change how Charles I behaved but only a minority wanted to remove the king from power.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The execution of Charles I

nodes.misconception: Parliament ruled the country for the whole Interregnum period.
nodes.response: Parliament ruled the country at the start of the Interregnum but was dismissed, recomposed, and ruled without at other times after 1652.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Oliver Cromwell: The Interregnum and Protectorate

nodes.misconception: Parliament in the 17th century was similarly superior to the monarch as it is today
nodes.response: Parliament was there to assist the monarch but they could rule without it and did not consider it an equal to themselves
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The causes of the English Civil War

nodes.misconception: Primary sources are inherently useful because they were published at the time of an event.
nodes.response: Sources are produced for a variety of purposes which can affect what they say. Propaganda sources might falsify information to persuade.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Royalists and Parliamentarians

nodes.misconception: That all contemporary sources can be accepted based solely on the value of their content.
nodes.response: Historians must consider how the provenance of a source may have affected the way it discusses and portrays a historical issue.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Popular political pamphlets in seventeenth-century England

nodes.misconception: The Restored monarchy acted exactly the same way as it had before the Civil War
nodes.response: Charles II made a great effort to work with Parliament more co-operatively than his father. He let Parliament sit continuously for 18 years.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Charles II and the restoration of the monarchy

nodes.misconception: Governor Grant's reforms after the Morant Bay Rebellion reduced the problem of poverty for Black Jamaicans.
nodes.response: Grant tackled discrimination and other issues but did not provide the financial assistance needed to help many Black Jamaicans escape poverty.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The British Empire in Jamaica

nodes.misconception: The Indian and Jamaican rebellions triggered complete change in those colonies.
nodes.response: Major changes were introduced after these rebellions although little was changed to address the problem of poverty in either Jamaica or India.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Transformation in the British Empire

nodes.misconception: Britain ruled over large areas of Africa throughout the 19th century.
nodes.response: British colonies were mainly confined to coastal areas in the first half of the 19th century. It was only later that British rule extended into the African interior.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The British Empire and the Scramble for Africa

nodes.misconception: Ideas of racial superiority were the only justification for British imperialism.
nodes.response: Cultural and religious beliefs such as a belief in the superiority of Christianity helped to justify an encourage British imperialism throughout the 19th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Social Darwinism and race in the British Empire

nodes.misconception: British victory in the Opium wars allowed it to conquer large areas of China and establish many new colonies.
nodes.response: Hong Kong was gained as a new British colony but Britain used its victory in the Opium Wars to force the Qing empire to change its behaviour, rather than to create new colonies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Gunboat diplomacy and the British Empire in East Asia

nodes.misconception: All parts of the British Empire were always governed directly by the British government.
nodes.response: In the first half of the 19th century, India was ruled by the British East India Company, not by the British Government.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The British Empire in India

nodes.misconception: Surnames have always been used and they generally aren't changed from one generation to the next.
nodes.response: During the medieval period, people went by their first name and one or more given names. These given names could be nicknames based on their place of origin or occupation or a distinguishing feature. Some people chose their own given names.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The life of Matilda and medieval women

nodes.misconception: Women were forbidden from ruling in their own right in England during the medieval period.
nodes.response: The first time the concept of a woman ruling in her own right in England occurred it took everyone by surprise. No one had considered that a woman might rule alone, so there was no law preventing it from happening.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Matilda and the succession crisis

nodes.misconception: Women in England were not allowed to fight in wars.
nodes.response: We have many examples of women leading the defence of castles throughout English history, and occasionally leading the attack on enemy territory as well.  It was uncommon, but not unheard of.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Matilda's claim and campaign

nodes.misconception: Once a king dies or is taken prisoner, that is the end of the war.
nodes.response: Although a king is very important, there are many examples throughout history of a king's followers continuing to fight on successfully after their leader has been killed or captured.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Matilda's battles

nodes.misconception: It has always been illegal for children to get married.
nodes.response: Throughout history, royal children were regularly betrothed at a young age in order to secure alliances between nations. Marriage followed later when the children had grown up, although they regularly still married younger than we do today.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Matilda's early life: Empress of Germany

nodes.misconception: Barons must obey the their monarch's orders.
nodes.response: Although this is true in theory, in reality the barons and their monarch worked as a partnership: the monarch relied upon the barons and if they weren't doing a good enough job, they could expect to lose the support of their barons.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Matilda's later life: supporting Henry II

nodes.misconception: Monarchs need to secure their positions by imprisoning or killing any claimants to the throne.
nodes.response: Although many monarchs have acted in this way, there are countless examples of monarchs who tolerated the freedom of strong claimants to the throne in order to not appear despotic. William III of Orange is a good example.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Bill of Rights and constitutional monarchy

nodes.misconception: The past never changes.
nodes.response: Our understanding of the past changes frequently, which causes us to look at events in different ways. As such, how we view the past is constantly changing.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How historians' views differ regarding the Glorious Revolution

nodes.misconception: All Scottish people at the time followed the same type of Protestantism.
nodes.response: Scotland at this time was experiencing a serious split in the Protestant religion between Episcopalians and Presbyterians. The Episcopalians supported James while the Presbyterians supported William III.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Glorious Revolution in Scotland and Ireland

nodes.misconception: The 'Whigs' gained their name because of the fancy wigs and hairstyles that were the fashion in the 17th and 18th centuries.
nodes.response: 'Whigs' has nothing to do with hairstyles, but was instead originally a derogatory term used to describe the 'Country Party', as they were originally known. 'Whig' was a sound Scottish drovers shouted when controlling cattle on the way to market.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Whig interpretation of the Glorious Revolution

nodes.misconception: Only children of the monarch are next in line for the throne, not siblings.
nodes.response: As Charles II did not have any legitimate children, his heir was his brother, James II.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: James II's troubled early reign

nodes.misconception: Interpretations of history are set in stone.
nodes.response: Many aspects of history face regular revisions as more research is conducted.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Revisionist interpretations of the Glorious Revolution

nodes.misconception: History is not relevant to today.
nodes.response: Henry II’s reforms to the English legal system established the foundation of English common law, still in use today.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Henry II's legal reforms

nodes.misconception: The murder of Thomas Becket was the undoing of Henry II.
nodes.response: Long-term it increased Henry’s control over the Church. Bishops’ opposition decreased, while the Pope gave support after 1172.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The murder of Thomas Becket

nodes.misconception: Students may think that the role of the medieval monarch is comparable with today's monarchy.
nodes.response: A medieval king was judged by his ability on the battlefield. Success in battle was the best way for a king to become powerful.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How successful was Henry II as king?

nodes.misconception: That France existed as a unified nation.
nodes.response: "Modern-day France" did not exist yet, instead the area we know as France, was actually a collection of separate lands/duchies .
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Henry II and the Angevin Empire

nodes.misconception: Medieval queens had little influence.
nodes.response: Eleanor was an intelligent and powerful queen, acted as regent, and was a key conspirator of the revolt.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Eleanor of Aquitaine and the end of Henry II's reign

nodes.misconception: Medieval and modern Church power is equivalent.
nodes.response: Explicitly outline the Church's organisational power: land ownership, clergy social status, and spiritual authority.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Henry II's church reforms

nodes.misconception: The trend of British imperial decline was caused by foreign policy and external threats.
nodes.response: There is a link between foreign and domestic policy, both of which contributed to imperial decline.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Imperial decline

nodes.misconception: The rise of Germany and the USA and the growth of nationalist movements in the late 19th century contributed to imperial decline.
nodes.response: The British Empire responded to this rise in anxiety by showcasing their supremacy at Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Imperial anxiety and celebration of Empire

nodes.misconception: The effects of decolonisation were positive for countries newly independent from the British Empire.
nodes.response: For many newly independent nations, freedom brought many difficulties as well as benefits.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Decolonisation and contesting empire

nodes.misconception: The Great Exhibition was located in the Crystal Palace.
nodes.response: The Great Exhibition, which became known as the Crystal Palace, was located in Hyde Park.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great Exhibition and the British Empire

nodes.misconception: Historians have finished debating the legacy of the British Empire.
nodes.response: Historians continue to debate the legacy of the British Empire as new information emerges.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Commemoration and contestation of the British Empire

nodes.misconception: It is possible to view the British Empire as either a force for good or bad.
nodes.response: The enormity of the British Empire and number of individuals involved means that to attach a simple label to the British Empire is an impossible task.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: New imperial history

nodes.misconception: Britain was the first country to give women the right to vote.
nodes.response: New Zealand was the first country in which women gained the right to vote, in 1893. Australia was the next, nine years later.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The government's response to the suffragettes

nodes.misconception: The suffrage movement always involved violent or illegal tactics as well as peaceful and legal ones.
nodes.response: The early suffragist movement was committed to peaceful tactics, even among the so-called 'radical suffragists'.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Campaigns for women's suffrage

nodes.misconception: The view that it was the work women did to support the war effort which gained them the right to vote.
nodes.response: Many people were convinced women should be entitled to vote before 1914; however, the violence of the suffragettes and the interruption of WW1 delayed this.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Why it took so long for women to get the vote in Britain

nodes.misconception: The belief that all women supported the war, and that women were immediately involved in war work from 1914.
nodes.response: Some women were pacifists and did not support the war effort.  Women were only brought into the workforce from 1916 due to labour shortages.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The contribution of women during WW1

nodes.misconception: Victorian women played no political role in Britain in the 19th century.
nodes.response: Women were increasingly politically active in Britain, for example, through their involvement in the abolitionist movement and through their participation in trade unions, despite being unable to vote.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The position of women in the early twentieth century

nodes.misconception: Suffragists were the same as suffragettes.
nodes.response: One way for pupils to remember the difference is that the suffraGETtes wanted to GET things done - deeds not words.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The suffragettes

nodes.misconception: The nobility in England identified as English.
nodes.response: This period marks a time when the nobility, who had their ancestral roots in France, had now come to see themselves as English.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Henry III and the 1225 Magna Carta

nodes.misconception: Parliament is a powerful organisation that rules the country.
nodes.response: At this point in history, the role of parliament was to advise the king.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Simon de Montfort and the First Parliament

nodes.misconception: King John signed the Magna Carta.
nodes.response: A modern misconception is that King John signed Magna Carta, this is untrue, royal documents were not signed but sealed.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 1215 and Magna Carta

nodes.misconception: All kings are adults and are the ultimate decision makers.
nodes.response: Henry III became king when he was nine-years-old. As he was too young, regents were appointed to rule on Henry’s behalf.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The First Barons' War and Magna Carta reissued

nodes.misconception: Magna Carta was a singular event which resulted in a powerless monarchy and human rights for all.
nodes.response: Magna Carta started a process of struggle. The medieval monarchy remained powerful, and it did not grant freedoms to everybody.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The survival of Magna Carta

nodes.misconception: King John only ruled England.
nodes.response: King John inherited the Angevin Empire which stretched across England and France.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: King John and the causes of Magna Carta

nodes.misconception: No one challenged the Portuguese when they began buying enslaved people to take to the Americas.
nodes.response: Many rulers and local people in West Africa were opposed to the trading of enslaved people from the very beginning.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The arrival of European traders in West Africa

nodes.misconception: All kingdoms in West Africa saw the same changes as a result of the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
nodes.response: Some kingdoms were weaker as a result of wars between kingdoms, others were weakened because of alliances and others continued to thrive.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the Transatlantic Slave Trade on West African society

nodes.misconception: The triangular trade was a simple trading route with three main points.
nodes.response: The triangular trade was a complex system of trade, that is often simplified to help us better understand it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The structure of the Transatlantic Slave Trade

nodes.misconception: Britain was always involved in the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
nodes.response: Britain became involved in the trade in the 1500s, initially selling enslaved people onto plantations in Spanish and Portuguese colonies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: British involvement in Transatlantic Slave Trade

nodes.misconception: European merchants arrived in West Africa with the intention of starting to enslave people.
nodes.response: European merchants were attracted by the potential amount of gold they would be able to trade in West Africa.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The kingdoms of the Sahel

nodes.misconception: All African kingdoms and rulers willingly participated in the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
nodes.response: Some kingdoms did cooperate, but many - like the Kingdom of Benin - also tried to resist by refusing to trade enslaved people.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The expansion of the Transatlantic Slave Trade

nodes.misconception: Expansion of an empire always means that is growing stronger.
nodes.response: As the Mughal Empire expanded, the costs of maintaining its rule across India also increased and new tensions were created with groups who lost out from extended Mughal control.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Mughal empire in the 17th century

nodes.misconception: Students assume political instability is only the result of foreign powers challenging the leaders of a country.
nodes.response: Political instability at the start of Humayun's reign partly occurred because of rebellions by his younger brothers and political instability in the 1550s was created by descendants of Sher Shah fighting one another for power.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early Mughal rule

nodes.misconception: Violence was not important during the reign of some monarchs such as Akbar the Great.
nodes.response: Violence was consistently part of the reigns of Mughal emperors. Akbar ordered the massacre of 30 000 people living in Mewar after they resisted the Mughal army in 1568.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Mughal rule in India

nodes.misconception: Akbar is remembered as a strong military leader because he only used violence to expand the Mughal Empire.
nodes.response: Akbar used a variety of methods to expand the Mughal Empire. In some cases, such as to gain control over the Rajput states, diplomacy was more important for expansion under Akbar than violence.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Akbar the Great

nodes.misconception: Akbar's religious tolerance was absolute throughout his reign.
nodes.response: Akbar made some exceptions to his general policy of religious tolerance, such as when he declared a jihad against the Hindu Kingdom of Mewar.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Governance and religious policy under Akbar

nodes.misconception: Prior to the Mughal conquest, India was all ruled by a single state.
nodes.response: Multiple states ruled over India prior to Babur's successful invasion from 1525-27. In northern India this included a mix of Muslim and Hindu-led states.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The foundation of the Mughal Empire

nodes.misconception: The war had very little impact on Ireland.
nodes.response: Irish calls for independence were delayed by the outbreak of war, and then further delayed in 1918.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of WW1 on the British Homefront

nodes.misconception: The British army went into the war confidently, with a large number of troops.
nodes.response: The British army had no more than 700 000 men in August 1914, they would need to use mass recruitment and colonial armies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Western Front in WW1

nodes.misconception: The impact of WWI was limited to Europe, and those directly affected by the deaths of troops.
nodes.response: The impact of WWI can be seen in Britain across different groups in society, but also within British colonies across the world.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of WWI across the Empire

nodes.misconception: Historically the contribution of colonial troops to the war effort has been overlooked.
nodes.response: Colonial troops made significant contributions to the war, both within Europe and across the world.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The First World War in the colonies

nodes.misconception: That the assassination of Ferdinand led to the inevitable, immediate outbreak of a global war
nodes.response: The outbreak of the war was the result of a series of context-dependent events, including the Austrian ultimatum and the Schlieffen Plan
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The outbreak of war in 1914

nodes.misconception: Everyone knew what was agreed by countries which had made alliances before the start of the war.
nodes.response: Explain that important parts of the alliance agreements were not made public so other countries did not know about them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Growing international tension in the early 1900s

nodes.misconception: There is a belief that Edward I's military strength alone was sufficient to ensure long-term control and unity of Britain.
nodes.response: Edward I's approach was often brutal leading to ongoing resistance and ultimately limiting his ability to achieve lasting unification.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward I's failure to unite all of Britain

nodes.misconception: Britain and England are terms which describe the same area.
nodes.response: Britain is the name for England, Scotland, and Wales.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward I’s first campaign in Wales

nodes.misconception: Edward I always intended to conquer Scotland and add it to his kingdom.
nodes.response: Edward I's initial aim was to have the Scottish pay him homage as their overlord.
nodes.subject: history
