nodes.lessonTitle: Edward I and Scotland

nodes.misconception: Involving Parliament with the rule of the land meant there would be more fairness and justice.
nodes.response: Parliament passed discriminatory laws: handing more power to parliament did not necessarily mean a growth in rights and freedoms for all.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward I: warrior and just ruler

nodes.misconception: Students may assume that the English army only comprised English soldiers.
nodes.response: The English forces also included Welsh and even some Scottish soldiers. This reflects the complex political and military alliances of the time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Scottish resistance to Edward I’s rule

nodes.misconception: The Welsh resistance was always a unified movement.
nodes.response: Many Welsh princes cooperated with Edward's Welsh campaign in 1277. Edward’s army also included 9000 Welsh soldiers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Welsh revolt and Edward I’s conquest of Wales

nodes.misconception: Increased powers of self government in Norwich gave all locals more control over decision-making.
nodes.response: Only freemen had real political power in Norwich but very few women and almost no poor people were able to become freemen.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Local elites in medieval Norwich

nodes.misconception: Students think that medieval churches only focused on prayer and religious services.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the Cathedral and other groups of churchmen in medieval Norwich also provided charity, education and hospital care.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Churchmen in medieval Norwich

nodes.misconception: All people from the same social group had the same experiences.
nodes.response: Experiences could vary even between people from the same social group, especially if there were differences between their wealth and class.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Life in medieval Norwich

nodes.misconception: That all people in the medieval period completed the same type of work as one another.
nodes.response: Remind students that a wide range of different jobs and industries existed in medieval Norwich, even after it focused more on wools.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Trade in medieval Norwich

nodes.misconception: All women in medieval Norwich had the same experience as one another.
nodes.response: Female experiences were varied, especially by wealth and social class. Those from wealthier backgrounds were more likely to be literate.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Women in medieval Norwich

nodes.misconception: The poor always accepted their position in medieval society.
nodes.response: The poor challenged the social order in Norwich violently in 1381 and had to be actively managed by the elites.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Treatment of the poor in medieval Norwich

nodes.misconception: Only Britain and Europe engaged in empire building.
nodes.response: In fact, empires have existed across the world since at least the ancient period: several dynasties ruled across China, the Ottoman Empire spanned across Asia, Africa and Europe, and the Mali Empire controlled extensive territories in West Africa.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: England's Empire at the beginning of the 'long eighteenth century'

nodes.misconception: Empire was always about conquest.
nodes.response: In fact, empire was often an ad-hoc private affair. For example, the East India Company had taken control over large parts of India - an expansion driven by opportunistic officials largely acting independently of the British government.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Britain's Empire at the end of the 'long eighteenth century'

nodes.misconception: The Transatlantic Slave Trade made up a large percentage of Britain’s national income.
nodes.response: The direct profit from the trade in enslaved people was 1% of Britain’s national income. However, much more wealth was generated in Britain from the trade in products produced by enslaved labour, and by provisioning the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of Britain's economy and empire

nodes.misconception: Changes in the leadership of Russia led to complete change in the country's politics.
nodes.response: Both tsarist rule and Communist rule led to severe restrictions on political freedoms, including use of secret police to remove opposition.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Soviet Russia in the 1920s and 1930s

nodes.misconception: Students assume that revolutions lead to complete change.
nodes.response: Emphasise that there were significant changes in Russia after 1917 but similarities remained, such as the lack of freedom for opposition.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The extent to which communism changed Russia

nodes.misconception: Students assume all communists and socialists shared the same ideas.
nodes.response: Marx's ideas were interpreted differently by different groups of socialists. In Russia, this led to the split of the Social Democratic Party.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Karl Marx and communism

nodes.misconception: People only died in the Russian Civil War as a direct result of the fighting.
nodes.response: Millions of ordinary Russians died as a result of methods like the Red Terror and War Communism used by the Reds during the war.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Russian Civil War, 1918-21

nodes.misconception: Revolutions always involve the execution of the previous leaders of government.
nodes.response: Although there was violence during the February Revolution, Tsar Nicholas II agreed to abdicate.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Tsarist Russia

nodes.misconception: The Bolsheviks revolutionary background meant that they were completely different to the tsar.
nodes.response: The Bolsheviks treated opposition similarly to the tsar, using a secret police and re-introducing censorship.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Bolsheviks

nodes.misconception: The successor states completely ignored the Mughal Emperor's authority.
nodes.response: Successor states took a lot of power for themselves but still claimed to be loyal to the Mughals.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Challenges to Mughal rule

nodes.misconception: Aurangzeb was completely intolerant towards and alienated all non-Muslims.
nodes.response: Aurangzeb continued to support non-Muslim places of worship and to promote non-Muslim officials in the empire, leading to increased numbers of Hindus and Sikhs serving the Mughal Empire by the end of his reign.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Religious tensions in the Mughal Empire

nodes.misconception: Europeans were more powerful than other states and social groups in the 17th century.
nodes.response: Although European groups like the EIC were powerful, the Mughal Emperors retained greater power in the 17th century. Aurangzeb comprehensively defeated the EIC's military challenged during Child's War.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The arrival of the East India Company

nodes.misconception: The East India Company relied entirely on European soldiers.
nodes.response: The EIC increasingly recruited sepoy soldiers to serve in its army from the late-1740s onwards.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of the East India Company as a private army

nodes.misconception: Mughal authority collapsed in the 17th century.
nodes.response: Mughal rule faced challenges, but the emperors still had enough military power and political control to maintain their authority during the 17th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Mughal authority and the East India Company

nodes.misconception: EIC victory in the Battle of Plassey only relied upon its own strengths.
nodes.response: The EIC army benefitted from Indian support, including its secret agreement with Mir Jafar who refused to let his troops participate in the battle.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Plassey Revolution

nodes.misconception: Hitler was always an unpopular dictator.
nodes.response: Hitler often attracted enthusiastic crowds to his speeches. By January 1933, the popularity of Hitler and the Nazi Party had turned into an electoral success.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The rise of fascism in Europe

nodes.misconception: America and Britain won the war by defeating the Nazis in Berlin.
nodes.response: The Soviets had pushed the Nazi army back across eastern Europe; four out of five German soldiers killed in WW2 were killed on the Eastern Front.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: America's entry into the war and the D-Day landings

nodes.misconception: At the time, everyone knew Hitler was a tyrant, so appeasement was clearly wrong.
nodes.response: The international community was divided. Many wanted to avoid a repeat of World War One. Furthermore, many thought that Germany had been treated harshly after WWI, and it seemed fair for Germany to take back some of its territory.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Appeasement and the declaration of war

nodes.misconception: British troops began fighting against Nazi Germany immediately after war was declared.
nodes.response: For eight months, there was very limited British, French and German military land operation on the Western Front. This became known as the 'Phoney War'
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Blitzkrieg and the Battle of Britain

nodes.misconception: That the sole turning point of the Second World War was due to America being brought into the conflict.
nodes.response: America's entry into the conflict was an important turning point, however, another significant turning point occurred with the first defeat of the Nazi army in the Soviet Union.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 1941-2, a pivotal period of the Second World War

nodes.misconception: The atomic bombs dropped on Japan only had immediate impacts.
nodes.response: The bombs had unprecedented destructive power. They sent out a shock wave that incinerated everything within a four-mile radius and in the weeks that followed, people died from radiation poisoning despite having survived the initial blast.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The last days of the Second World War

nodes.misconception: The Ghana Empire was located in the modern-day country of Ghana.
nodes.response: The Ghana Empire was located in the Sahel, north of the Niger River, which is nowhere near the modern-day country of Ghana.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Trade routes throughout West Africa

nodes.misconception: Empires have to own land in order to control it.
nodes.response: Control can be gained through a variety of indirect means, such as through trade or tribute.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Gold and the West African economy

nodes.misconception: It is impossible for large numbers of people to cross the Sahara Desert.
nodes.response: Although extremely dangerous, the Sahara Desert has been crossed many times by large groups of people. Large amounts of provisions are needed though, which is why it is not a common occurrance.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage

nodes.misconception: Successful empires dominate and subjugate the conquered people within the empire in order to keep them loyal.
nodes.response: The Mali aristocracy adopted a successful 'hands off' approach to governance, allowing the different kingdoms within the empire a great degree of autonomy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The successful expansion of medieval Mali

nodes.misconception: All followers of the same religion practise their religion in the same way.
nodes.response: There are often large differences between followers of the same religion: people include elements of their own culture in their worship.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: New civilisations in the Sahel

nodes.misconception: Muslims mainly live in the Middle East.
nodes.response: Islam is the second most popular religion in the world, with Muslim-majority countries spread as far as Morocco in the west to Indonesia in the east.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Islam in medieval West Africa

nodes.misconception: The Black Death only affected Europe.
nodes.response: European records from the time are numerous and detailed, so we have a very clear idea about the impact of the Black Death on Europe. However, the Black Death affected a large geographic area, including places without detailed records of the impact.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The arrival of the Black Death

nodes.misconception: Only silk was traded along the Silk Road.
nodes.response: Silk was a primary commodity for a long time along the Silk Road, but there were many different goods and ideas that were traded between East and West along the trade route.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Silk Road

nodes.misconception: The Black Death was a terrible one-off event.
nodes.response: Although the Black Death was a one-off event, the plague, the disease that was the Black Death, continued to afflict Europe for hundreds of years after it first came to Europe in the 14th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the Black Death in Europe

nodes.misconception: Walpole created the role of Prime Minister and the idea of Cabinet.
nodes.response: Walpole's leadership saw him become de-facto Prime Minister and he formalised the idea of Cabinet which already existed in a loose, unofficial form.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Robert Walpole and 'Cabinet' government

nodes.misconception: The 1701 Act of Settlement meant that parliament no longer needed to worry about a Catholic taking the throne in the future.
nodes.response: Although the 1701 Act of Settlement stipulated a Catholic or the spouse of a Catholic could never succeed to the throne of England, parliament remained worried that a succession crisis could still ensue if a monarch died childless.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Hanoverian Succession

nodes.misconception: Resistance always involves the use of violence.
nodes.response: Jews adopted many nonviolent forms of resistance. Actions like smuggling resisted Nazi attempts to starve Jews and continuing education secretly resisted Nazi attempts to destroy Jewish culture.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Jewish resistance to the Holocaust

nodes.misconception: The Holocaust was confined to Germany.
nodes.response: The Nazis and their collaborators murdered 6 million Jews from across Europe and aimed to eliminate Jews from the entire continent.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Holocaust in context

nodes.misconception: Most Jews murdered during the Holocaust were killed in gas chambers in concentration camps.
nodes.response: Gas chambers were set up in specially constructed extermination camps for Jews and killed millions, but roughly half of all Holocaust victims were killed by other means.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Ghettos and the 'Final Solution'

nodes.misconception: Shared Jewish heritage meant that all European Jews lived similar lives.
nodes.response: Jews made individuals choices and were affected by factors such as wealth which led to the Jewish population living many different types of lives.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Jewish life in Europe before WW2

nodes.misconception: Leaders in the Lodz Ghetto made 'bad' choices for choosing to comply with German orders.
nodes.response: Leaders in the Lodz Ghetto, like many other Jews, faced multiple poor choices - or 'choiceless choices'. The decisions they made occurred in extreme circumstances where they had little real control over their own survival.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 'Choiceless choices' during the Holocaust

nodes.misconception: Only German Nazis were involved in the Holocaust.
nodes.response: Examples such as the Vel' d'Hiv Raid in France, carried out in 1942, show that other Europeans collaborated and helped to perpetrate the Holocaust.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Victims and perpetrators

nodes.misconception: Nazi antisemitism meant they were immediately violent towards Jews.
nodes.response: Open violence as a part of Nazi persecution only became common in 1938.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Nazi persecution of Jewish people

nodes.misconception: The French Revolution only occurred because of the Enlightenment.
nodes.response: The French Revolution occurred for a myriad of reasons. These include causes such as the Enlightenment, the influence of the American Revolution, the lavish spending of the monarchy and their supposed indifference to the plight of the Third Estate.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Enlightenment ideas and the causes of the French Revolution

nodes.misconception: All the Haitian rebels were enslaved people.
nodes.response: Many of the Haitian rebels were free people.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the French Revolution in the Atlantic world

nodes.misconception: All Enlightenment thinkers were racist.
nodes.response: Some Enlightenment thinkers promoted racist theories while others advocated for equality.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Enlightenment ideas: science and politics

nodes.misconception: The Declaration of Independence was signed after the settlers defeated the British in the Revolutionary War.
nodes.response: The Declaration of Independence was signed early on in the Revolutionary War and the US Constitution was signed after the war had concluded.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The American Revolution and Enlightenment ideas

nodes.misconception: All Enlightenment philosophers were atheists and rejected religion entirely.
nodes.response: Enlightenment philosophers wanted to reshape and redefine the role religion and the Church played in society.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The background to the Enlightenment

nodes.misconception: That the Statute of Labourers immediately forced all peasants to return to their home manors and to cease negotiating higher wages.
nodes.response: Through the interpretations section of the lesson, draw out the point that the Statute of Labourers was unenforceable in many cases.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Statute of Labourers and the response to the Black Death

nodes.misconception: Medieval people called their social system 'the feudal system'.
nodes.response: In fact, the term feudal system or feudalism did not start to be used until the 17th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The decline of the feudal system

nodes.misconception: That the main aim of the rebels in the Peasants' Revolt was to overthrow the king.
nodes.response: In fact the rebels' grievances were against local officials and the king's advisers, who they believed were misleading the king into acting against the interests of his people.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The causes of the Peasants' Revolt

nodes.misconception: Revolts and rebellions are driven purely by rage and frustration.
nodes.response: Most revolts and rebellions have a number of causes and are usually led by people with a plan and aims to achieve.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Peasants' Revolt

nodes.misconception: People at the time called the conflict the Hundred Years' War.
nodes.response: People at the time would not have known how long the wars were going to last, so this name came after the conflict had ended.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Richard II and the war in France

nodes.misconception: Historical events have one cause.
nodes.response: This will be addressed across the course of the unit, but within this lesson it is worth drawing attention to the competing causes listed in the discussion of the Peasants' Revolt.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the Black Death on England

nodes.misconception: The borders drawn during Partition were clear and accepted by all.
nodes.response: The Radcliffe Line, which demarcated the borders, was highly contentious and led to significant disputes and confusion, which resulted in violence.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Decolonisation and the partition of India

nodes.misconception: All Caribbean countries gained independence from Britain at the same time.
nodes.response: Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago were the first of Britain's Caribbean colonies to achieve independence in 1962, however, the last British colony in the Caribbean to gain independence was Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1983.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Decolonisation in the Caribbean

nodes.misconception: That Britain has no historic role in the creation of tension between Arabs and Jews over Palestine.
nodes.response: Britain's colonial role in Palestine during and after the First World War involved it making conflicting promises to both Arabs and Jews over Palestine's future.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Decolonisation in Palestine after the Second World War

nodes.misconception: Decolonisation happened in a peaceful and orderly way in all of Britain's African colonies.
nodes.response: Decolonisation in many of Britain's African colonies was mostly peaceful; however, there were exceptions. For example, in Kenya there was significant violence as the British authorities used brutal measures to suppress the Mau Mau Uprising (1952-60).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Post-war decolonisation in Africa

nodes.misconception: The British Empire was different from other European empires because Britain willingly relinquished control of its colonies and decolonisation was mostly a peaceful process.
nodes.response: While it was a peaceful process in some British colonies, decolonisation involved significant violence in other colonies. Even in colonies where decolonisation was relatively peaceful there was some violence (e.g., Accra Riots in the Gold Coast).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing decolonisation across the former British Empire

nodes.misconception: All Irish nationalists shared the same views and had the same aims.
nodes.response: Some Irish nationalists wanted Home Rule for Ireland whereas other nationalists (known as republicans) wanted complete independence from Britain. After 1921, republicans split between those who supported the Anglo-Irish Treaty and those who did not.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Decolonisation in Ireland in the 20th century

nodes.misconception: Students might believe that the king could rule without the support ot the nobility.
nodes.response: Explain that the king relied on nobles to keep law and order in society, particularly in more remote parts of the kingdom.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward IV's stable second reign

nodes.misconception: Students may believed that the Yorkists and Lancastrians were from different families.
nodes.response: The Lancastrians and Yorkists were both part of the Plantagenet family.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Henry VI and Richard of York

nodes.misconception: The belief that Margaret of Anjou was a vicious and unpleasant woman.
nodes.response: A woman who held power would have likely been criticised in the medieval period and Yorkists would also have wanted to show her in an unfavourable light.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The rule of Margaret of Anjou and the rise of Edward, Duke of York

nodes.misconception: Students may think the Wars of the Roses ended with the victory of Henry VII at Bosworth and that all historians agree with this interpretation.
nodes.response: Explain that Henry VII also faced rebellions at the start of his reign and, although the Tudors are well-known for their rule of England, few expected them to last long as a result of the rebellions and the prior decades of instability.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What the Wars of the Roses tell us about England in the fifteenth century

nodes.misconception: Students may become confused by the number of historical figures that share the same name.
nodes.response: Ensure students can differentiate between Edward IV and Prince Edward.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward V and Richard III

nodes.misconception: Students may get confused between Edward, Prince of Wales and Edward IV.
nodes.response: Explain that Edward, Prince of Wales, is the only son of Henry VI and Margaret of Anjou, and a Lancastrian.  Edward IV is the son of Richard, Duke of York, who became Edward IV, and a Yorkist.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward IV's unstable first reign

nodes.misconception: Students might not realise that women as well as men were conscripted during WW2.
nodes.response: In 1940, single women aged 20-30, and widowed women without children, were conscripted into war work.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The changing role of women in post-war Britain

nodes.misconception: Students may aassume William Beveridge was a member of the Labour Party.
nodes.response: William Beveridge was actually a member of the Liberal Party.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The aims of the post-war Labour government

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that the people had control of nationalised industries.
nodes.response: The first chairman of the National Coal Board (NCB) was the former owner of the largest coal company in Britain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Social democracy and nationalisation in post-war Britain

nodes.misconception: Students might presume that everyone the descendants of the Windrush generation had the automatic right to stay and work in Britain.
nodes.response: The children of Windrush generation did not have their own passports, and it was difficult to prove they had entered the UK legally. This led to the Windrush Scandal in 2018.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Experiences of racism in Britain

nodes.misconception: Students might believe rationing ended when the Second World War ended in 1945.
nodes.response: Rationing continued in Britain until 1954.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: British society after WWII, 1945-1970

nodes.misconception: Every element of the NHS was free for a considerable time after its creation.
nodes.response: Every element of the NHS was only free for a short time, as the overwhelming demand resulted in the need to introduce prescription fees.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The NHS and the welfare state

nodes.misconception: The Equal Pay Act (1970) led to women being paid the same as men.
nodes.response: Although the Equal Pay Act made it illegal to pay women less than men for doing the same work, many employers adjusted job descriptions for female workers to avoid paying them equally.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of women in post-war Britain, 1945-1975

nodes.misconception: Winning the right to vote in 1919 led to a radical transformation in the status and position of women in society in the 1920s and 1930s.
nodes.response: Although the Representation of the People Act of 1919 was a significant turning point, Britain in the 1920s and 1930s remained a very patriarchal society.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The right to vote and the role of women in the 1920s and 1930s

nodes.misconception: Women's suffrage led to a rapid increase in the number of female MPs in Parliament.
nodes.response: By 1931, there were only 15 female MPs in Parliament; however, women's suffrage meant that MPs were more likely to support new laws that had a positive impact on the lives of women.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The changing role of women

nodes.misconception: Medieval women completed no work other than housework and looking after children.
nodes.response: Although they were responsible for housework and childcare and did not have the same opportunities to work as men, women in the medieval period completed a range of other work; the type of work they completed was determined by where they lived.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Women and the medieval Church

nodes.misconception: The majority of women worked in factories throughout this period.
nodes.response: The work women did and whether they worked at all was largely determined by class. From the mid-19th century, legislation placed restrictions on the type and amount of work women were able to do and the number of women working in factories decreased.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Women and the Industrial Revolution

nodes.misconception: The existence of female rulers like Elizabeth I and Mary, Queen of Scots, meant that women in early modern Britain had significantly more power than in the medieval period.
nodes.response: It was extremely rare for women to wield power during this period. Early modern Britain was a patriarchal society in which society was controlled by men and the vast majority of women were excluded from all positions of power and influence.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of women in the early modern period

nodes.misconception: All French cartoons are complimentary of Napoleon and all British cartoons are critical of Napoleon.
nodes.response: Many French cartoons were critical of Napoleon and many British cartoons were critical of the British government's response to his actions.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the Napoleonic era through political cartoons

nodes.misconception: Napoleon only ever experienced success during this period, and was never defeated.
nodes.response: Napoleon faced military setbacks (particularly at sea) during this period, usually at the hands of the British.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The rise of Napoleon and his fight for the new French Republic

nodes.misconception: Revolutionary ideas failed to spread from France to other European countries.
nodes.response: Revolutionary ideas did spread to other European countries, but they did not cause any successful revolutions.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The spread of radical revolutionary ideas from France to Ireland

nodes.misconception: All contemporary British thinkers were complete supporters of the French Revolution.
nodes.response: Levels of support for the French Revolution amongst contemporary British thinkers varied.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: British responses to the French Revolution

nodes.misconception: Napoleon became Emperor of France after he seized power from the Directory in 1799.
nodes.response: Napoleon became First Consul after seizing power from the Directory, but did not crown himself Emperor of France until 1804.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The reign of Napoleon: war and legal reforms

nodes.misconception: Napoleon was only exiled once.
nodes.response: Napoleon was exiled twice. The first time to Elba after his defeat in Russia. He escaped back to France and gained support from his old troops and took power once more. He was defeated at Waterloo and exiled for the final time to St Helena.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Britain and the Napoleonic Wars

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that many of the ideas of the Renaissance were new to science, literature and art.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the Renaissance was a period during which knowledge lost in Western Europe was rediscovered, rather than created for the first time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The background to the Renaissance

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that dissection was banned by the medieval Catholic Church.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that, while dissection was not banned, there was still a taboo around handling dead bodies which limited the number of dissections that took place during the medieval period.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Italian Renaissance: science and anatomy

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that because printing presses were mechanical, they were as fast and efficient as modern machinery.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that even though printing presses were much quicker than copying by hand, it could still take a relatively long time to print books.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Italian Renaissance: humanism

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that because Renaissance architects used mathematical calculations to design their buildings, these were without subsequent problems or issues.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that these architects often made miscalculations and many subsequent improvement works were needed to ensure buildings like St Peter's did not fall down.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Italian Renaissance: art and architecture

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that some sources have a greater inherent value than others.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a source's value rests entirely upon the enquiry for which it is used and the questions asked of it. No source has inherent value unless used as part of an enquiry.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the artefacts of the Renaissance

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that we can learn little from imagery that has been produced for the purposes of propaganda.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we can learn a lot from such imagery as it is a window into the minds of those who had it produced, and helps us to understand some of their concerns and motivations.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Northern Renaissance

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that castles only had a military function.
nodes.response: Norman castles also acted as administrative centres. They had a psychological function in dominating the landscape and the people who lived there and some castles also helped trade develop.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Establishing control: motte-and-bailey castles

nodes.misconception: Paying homage, swearing allegiance, or making promises were weak obligations.
nodes.response: In fact, these promises are with the king and God. It was unlikely you would break a public and spiritual promise like this; it would not have been good for your reputation or your soul!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Norman feudal system

nodes.misconception: Lanfranc's reforms introduced new concepts like celibacy for monks, Benedictine rules for monasteries and separate courts for the Church (or even archdeacons).
nodes.response: All these were already present in Anglo-Saxon England - monasteries had been following the laws of St Benedict for centuries, for example - but Lanfranc revitalised them, ensured that they were carried out and repurposed them to boost Norman control.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Lanfranc's reforms

nodes.misconception: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were punishments for crimes.
nodes.response: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were ways of finding out who God judged as being innocent and guilty, though the ordeal was certainly punishing for both parties.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Justice and the legal system in Norman England

nodes.misconception: It took many weeks to travel from the south to the north of England in medieval times.
nodes.response: Harold and his housecarls were able to cover 185 miles in just four days in 1066: an amazing achievement.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Battle of Stamford Bridge

nodes.misconception: The Norman conquest was fully achieved by the victory at the Battle of Hastings.
nodes.response: In reality, there were many defiant Anglo-Saxons ready to carry on fighting and it took time for William to gain meaningful control over a hostile Anglo-Saxon population.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The submission of London in 1066

nodes.misconception: The Norman conquest was a brutal military occupation which resulted in wholescale change of the English Church.
nodes.response: Whilst there were significant changes, the English Church retained its basic structure and liturgy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Norman Church

nodes.misconception: In the medieval period it was expected that rulers would be ruthless in killing anyone who opposed them.
nodes.response: Rulers were expected to be just and merciful in the medieval period, and Willian faced criticism across Europe for his brutality in crushing opposition in the North of England.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Harrying of the North, 1069-70

nodes.misconception: The controversies and conflicts between the crown and the Church were specific to Norman England.
nodes.response: In fact, the controversies and conflicts between the Church and the crown happened in many kingdoms in Europe, and were more severe than in England in particular cases, especially the Holy Roman Empire.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The king and the Church in Norman England

nodes.misconception: The shield wall was not a very sophisticated or effective military tactic.
nodes.response: In fact the shield wall proved effective in holding off the Norman attacks for many hours.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Battle of Hastings

nodes.misconception: William copied the landholding system for Norman England from Normandy.
nodes.response: Landholding in Normandy was different from landholding in Norman England. William was not the owner of all the land in Normandy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Land and inheritance in Norman England

nodes.misconception: As conquerors, the Normans could make any changes they wanted to.
nodes.response: The Normans were greatly outnumbered in England and William hoped to convince most English people that his was going to rule in the same way as King Edward the Confessor.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Continuity and change in Norman government

nodes.misconception: William I introduced a whole new social system called the feudal system which was completely different from what came before.
nodes.response: In fact, many of the features of what became known as the feudal system were already in place in Anglo-Saxon England. William took the opportunity to increase his control over society to enable the extraction of wealth; his successors built on this.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Daily life in Norman England

nodes.misconception: After a monarch dies, their eldest child automatically becomes monarch after them.
nodes.response: In Anglo-Saxon England, an heir was always in a strong position, but even if there was an heir, the Witan could use their influence for someone else to be made monarch - if, for example, the heir was too young.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward the Confessor's death and the claimants to the throne

nodes.misconception: Anglo-Saxon monarchs had to be great warriors to be made king.
nodes.response: In fact some monarchs, such as Edward the Confessor, were not warriors but instead very religious men whose faith inspired others.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Anglo-Saxon kingship

nodes.misconception: The power of the Church in the medieval and modern period is equivalent.
nodes.response: The medieval Church was a very powerful institution, it was involved in governing Anglo-Saxon England (as bishops served as advisors to kings) and it was a very wealthy landholder. The modern-day Church in England has less powers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Anglo-Saxon Church

nodes.misconception: Sending the fyrd defences home in September is evidence of Harold's poor decision making.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon leaders had always struggled with the 60-day limit for the fyrd. Harold had actually kept the fyrd out for twice as long as usual: evidence of his impressive influence as a leader.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasons for William's victory in 1066

nodes.misconception: An Anglo-Saxon monarch had all the power.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon nobles could force their monarchs to do things they did not want to do. For example, King Edward was forced to allow the House of Godwin back from exile and restore them to their earldoms.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward the Confessor, the Godwins and William of Normandy

nodes.misconception: People think the survey and Domesday Book are one and the same thing.
nodes.response: In fact, the survey was ordered in 1085, and later compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Domesday Book

nodes.misconception: Towns and cities have always been where the richest people in society live.
nodes.response: For most of English history, the richest people were landowners and lived in the manor house of their manorial estate.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Life in towns in Norman England

nodes.misconception: The Normans reforms of the Church were specific to England.
nodes.response: The Church reforms were part of a much bigger European reform movement led by a succession of popes known as the Reform Papacy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Reform Papacy

nodes.misconception: After William the Conqueror was crowned King of England, he and the Normans were immediately accepted as rightful rulers and peace reigned across the kingdom.
nodes.response: In fact, William faced a hostile Anglo-Saxon population and threats of invasion from Wales and Scotland, requiring him to take measures to establish further control.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Establishing control: new earls and earldoms

nodes.misconception: Monks were all poor.
nodes.response: Although individual monks gave up all their possessions, Norman monasteries were often extremely wealthy because they held very large amount of land granted to them by the king or Norman barons and knights.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Norman reforms of English monasticism

nodes.misconception: That forest in Norman England always meant land covered by trees.
nodes.response: Forest in Norman England meant an area that was reserved for hunting and so could include open land, village land, even towns, as well as woodland.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing laws in Norman England: Forest law

nodes.misconception: William the Conqueror was hostile towards all Anglo-Saxons from the start.
nodes.response: Some Anglo-Saxons, if they had not fought against William at Hastings, were allowed to keep their land.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: William's consolidation of power

nodes.misconception: William always planned to replace Anglo-Saxons in key government positions with loyal Normans.
nodes.response: At first, William intended to boost his claim to be the legitimate heir of Edward by keeping earls Edwin, Morcar and Waltheof in place in his government of England - alongside new earls such as Earl Odo of Kent or Earl William of Hereford.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Key figures in the government of Norman England

nodes.misconception: Poor people in medieval England survived by eating potatoes.
nodes.response: Potatoes were unknown in Europe until the 16th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Work and diet in Norman England

nodes.misconception: Village life was the same all over Norman England.
nodes.response: While there were many common features, the Viking settlement of the Danelaw meant that freemen in villages in the east were much more independent of the lord of their village's manor than in other parts of the country.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Life in villages in Norman England

nodes.misconception: The Normans invented Romanesque architecture.
nodes.response: The Normans were enthusiastic adopters of Romanesque building style, but it was developed in northern Italy and France, combining Roman features with elements of Byzantine design.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The built environment of Norman England

nodes.misconception: Resistance to William’s rule of England came only from the English.
nodes.response: In 1075, two Norman earls revolted against William, and English forces helped to stop the rebellion.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Revolts against William I, 1067-1075

nodes.misconception: There were no effective responses to the Black Death.
nodes.response: No effective treatments existed in the medieval period but some preventative methods, such as quarantines, could help protect people from plague.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Black Death

nodes.misconception: The government fully implemented Edwin Chadwick's recommendations.
nodes.response: Chadwick's recommendations were included in the 1848 Public Health Act but were not compulsory, so many local authorities ignored them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvements in public health in the 19th century

nodes.misconception: The use of technology in modern medicine means doctors aren't very involved in making diagnoses.
nodes.response: Technology can help patients to monitor some health conditions themselves but many technologies that help diagnosis require a doctor to operate them or to interpret the information they provide.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern improvements in diagnosis

nodes.misconception: Florence Nightingale encouraged reforms based on her acceptance of Germ Theory.
nodes.response: A lot of Nightingale's ideas were informed by the idea of miasma and how to protect people from it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of hospital care in the 19th century

nodes.misconception: Surgery continually improved during the 19th century.
nodes.response: Improvements in anaesthetics led to more invasive surgeries which actually made infection a greater problem in the mid-19th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: A 19th century revolution in surgery

nodes.misconception: Smoking is the only cause of lung cancer.
nodes.response: Non-smokers can also develop lung cancer. Sometimes this is because of passive smoking, but other causes like air pollution can also be responsible.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The fight against lung cancer in the 21st century

nodes.misconception: London's new sewage system was built in response to John Snow's findings and recommendations.
nodes.response: Snow's work was generally overlooked by officials. Instead, London's new sewers were built in response to the Great Stink of 1858.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Fighting cholera in London in the 19th century

nodes.misconception: Alexander Fleming developed penicillin as an antibiotic.
nodes.response: Fleming did not believe penicillin would work as an antibiotic. Florey and Chain developed penicillin as an antibiotic.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The development of magic bullets and antibiotics

nodes.misconception: Development of the smallpox vaccine helped scientists to develop vaccines for other diseases.
nodes.response: It was not understood why the smallpox vaccine worked, so no new vaccines were developed until the last decades of the 19th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 19th century approaches to treatment and prevention

nodes.misconception: Germ Theory's accuracy meant that it was immediately accepted in Britain.
nodes.response: Many doctors still defended spontaneous generation and it took the additional proof provided by Robert Koch's work to convince many that microbes caused disease.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: New 19th century ideas about the causes of disease and illness

nodes.misconception: Lifestyle factors have only been considered important for a person's health in the modern period.
nodes.response: Lifestyle factors like diet have been considered important for many centuries, but before the 20th century this was often based on inaccurate ideas like the Theory of Four Humours.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern advances in understanding the causes of illness and disease

nodes.misconception: Jenner's vaccine became widespread and popular almost immediately.
nodes.response: There was considerable opposition to Jenner's smallpox vaccine which delayed widespread use of vaccination in Britain until later in the 19th century.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward Jenner and vaccination

nodes.misconception: The Great Plague was the last serious plague epidemic because a cure was found.
nodes.response: No effective cure had been developed to treat plague at the time of the Great Plague.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Great Plague of 1665

nodes.misconception: The NHS was the only feature of Britain's welfare state which supported public health.
nodes.response: The NHS was very important but slum clearance and new house building were also important features of the welfare state which benefitted public health.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The welfare state and the NHS

nodes.misconception: Vaccinations have been made compulsory to ensure uptake in modern Britain.
nodes.response: Vaccinations have been voluntary for people to receive in modern Britain but many have been provided free of charge and their benefits promoted to encourage people.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern approaches to the prevention of illness and disease

nodes.misconception: The Renaissance led to widespread acceptance of scientific ideas in medicine.
nodes.response: Opposition to change from physicians and the limits of new discoveries meant that many ideas about the causes of disease remained unchanged.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Renaissance ideas about disease and illness

nodes.misconception: Criticisms of bloodletting meant it was practiced less.
nodes.response: Bloodletting and other humoural treatments remained popular and were even used to try and treat King Charles II in 1685.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Renaissance approaches to treatment and prevention

nodes.misconception: All medieval approaches to treatment and prevention were ineffective.
nodes.response: Some effective methods, such as the use of mint in herbal remedies, existed but the scientific reason for their health benefits was not understood.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Medieval approaches to treating and preventing disease

nodes.misconception: Corrections to Galen's work were accepted virtually immediately.
nodes.response: Many medical professionals were reluctant to challenge Galen's works and so new ideas, like those of Vesalius, were not accepted immediately.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Renaissance changes in anatomy and surgery

nodes.misconception: Correcting Galen's mistakes led to immediate improvements in medical practices.
nodes.response: Despite Harvey's theory suggesting bloodletting would be dangerous, most physicians continued to recommend the procedure as a common form of treatment.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: William Harvey

nodes.misconception: There was no change in medieval surgery.
nodes.response: New developments did occur, such as the use of opium as an anaesthetic and wine to use against infection, but the impact of these was limited.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Medieval surgery

nodes.misconception: Treatments in hospitals became significantly more effective as more medical staff were employed there.
nodes.response: Treatments in most hospitals continued to be based on the incorrect Theory of the Four Humours so unhelpful practices such as bloodletting remained common.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Hospital care in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries

nodes.misconception: There was limited access to medical care in medieval Britain.
nodes.response: Although few people were able to afford physicians, most people were able to turn to other sources of care such as that offered by hospitals, wise people or members of their own family.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Medieval caregivers

nodes.misconception: Religion was the only medieval explanation for the causes of disease and illness.
nodes.response: Religion was a widespread and commonly used explanation for disease but many other theories were also used including miasma, astrology and the Theory of the Four Humours.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Medieval ideas about the causes of illness and disease

nodes.misconception: Alternative medicines were mostly abandoned during the course of the 20th century.
nodes.response: Alternative medicines, including practices like homeopathy and the use of herbal medicines, have remained popular, even in 21st century Britain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern approaches to medical treatment

nodes.misconception: That early medieval kings ruled from a royal palace.
nodes.response: In fact, early medieval kings and their courts travelled from one location to another.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The function of the White Tower

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxon Church was old-fashioned and corrupt.
nodes.response: The Normans were keen to present the Anglo-Saxon Church that way, but Edward the Confessor had kept up with reforms from the rest of Europe.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: White Tower - historical context themes

nodes.misconception: Anglo-Saxons did not have castles so therefore their settlements did not have strong fortifications.
nodes.response: Anglo-Saxon burhs were fortified settlements, surrounded by strong walls designed to deter Vikings from attacking.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: London and the events of 1066

nodes.misconception: Students commonly do not provide enough detail from their historic environment in their answers.
nodes.response: Try to back up your analysis of the question with specific facts and details from your historic environment.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The White Tower: structuring your answer to the historic environment question

nodes.misconception: William I often used the Chapel of St John for his own private worship.
nodes.response: Although this was the plan, William died before the chapel was finished.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: St John's Chapel

nodes.misconception: All Norman castles were built to the same design.
nodes.response: In fact, although we learn about the classic motte-and-bailey castle (and maybe even make models of them in school), there was a very wide variety of castle designs in England and in Normandy.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The architecture of the White Tower

nodes.misconception: The White Tower was always bustling with royal activity.
nodes.response: Royal residents were seldom present. Most of the time, the White Tower was managed by the keeper and housed a garrison of soldiers.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The residents of the White Tower

nodes.misconception: Romanesque buildings only began to be built in England after the Norman Conquest.
nodes.response: Edward the Confessor's Westminster Abbey was built in Romanesque style and completed in 1065.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: London before the Norman Conquest

nodes.misconception: There are relatively few sources for Norman England, so historians have less to say about this period than later periods of English history.
nodes.response: Historians have plenty to say about Norman England because they are able to interpret the sources available in many different ways to support many different theories.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: White Tower - sources and historical context

nodes.misconception: Students may think that the White Tower was the only castle in Norman London.
nodes.response: In fact, there were two other castles in Norman London: Baynard's Castle and Montfichet's Tower.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The site of the White Tower

nodes.misconception: Students might believe that fascism was only a factor in Nazi Germany, and be unaware of the existence of  fascist groups in Britain.
nodes.response: Fascism spread across Europe in the 1930s, including to Britain, although Britain's strong democratic tradition meant it did not take hold as it did in other countries at the time.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Racism and policing in 1950s Notting Hill

nodes.misconception: Students might fail to see the significance of the admission by the police that they acted with racist prejudice.
nodes.response: This was the first time the police had admitted to treating the black community unfairly and was a turning point in the development of civil rights.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Mangrove Nine

nodes.misconception: If a source has a limitation then it is not reliable or useful for a historical study.
nodes.response: All sources have limitations as well as strengths, which historians take account of, and does not mean that the source should not be used by a historian.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Notting Hill - sources and historical context

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that there was only rationing in Britain during WW2.
nodes.response: Rationing continued until 1954.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: National context of post-war Britain

nodes.misconception: Students can forget to use the sources provided, and instead simply rely on their own knowledge.
nodes.response: The historical environment questions are mainly source-based and therefore students should base their answers on the sources, using their knowledge to explain what is in the sources and to judge the utility of the sources.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing about Notting Hill and its sources

nodes.misconception: The discrimination and exclusion from opportunities that migrants sometimes face is just something these communities have to accept.
nodes.response: In fact, migrants set up self-help schemes and organise their own resources to ensure discrimination and lack of government help do not hold back their community and especially their children's access to opportunities.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The influence of Caribbean cultures on Notting Hill

nodes.misconception: Pupils are likely to be unaware that laws protecting UK citizens against discrimination did not start until mid-60s.
nodes.response: Prior to the Race Relations Act 1965, it was possible to discriminate against black people, for example, refuse to serve them. This was extended in 1968 to include discrimination in housing and education.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Local context of Notting Hill

nodes.misconception: Students may not make the connection between the civil rights movement in the USA and the efforts of black activists in the UK in the 1960s.
nodes.response: Explain to students that the influence of Martin Luther King Jr and Malcolm X spread outside of America.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Black activism in the Notting Hill area

nodes.misconception: Non-white soldiers and citizens of the Commonwealth played a small role during and after both World Wars.
nodes.response: Non-white soldiers and citizens of the Commonwealth played a significant role during and after both World Wars.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the World Wars on migration to and from Britain

nodes.misconception: Westward migration always refers to migration to the Americas.
nodes.response: Westward migration also includes the migration of Protestant settlers from Great Britain to Ulster.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Factors causing westward migration

nodes.misconception: Britain and competing European powers met at the Berlin Conference before the scramble for Africa had begun.
nodes.response: Britain and competing European powers had already been 'scrambling' for Africa for the majority of the 19th century. The Berlin Conference was an attempt to put an end to the fighting between European powers over Africa's land and resources.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The scramble for Africa

nodes.misconception: India was totally controlled by the East India Company at the time of the Indian Rebellion in 1857.
nodes.response: Two-thirds of India was controlled by the East India Company at the time of the Indian Rebellion in 1857.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Indian Rebellion

nodes.misconception: All migration in this period was voluntary and driven by individual choices.
nodes.response: Not all migrations were voluntary at this time. For instance, indentured labour schemes often coerced individuals into migration under harsh conditions. Additionally, Jewish migration was frequently driven by persecution.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Impact of empire on migration in and out of Britain

nodes.misconception: Migrants all experience the same hardships and migrated for similar reasons.
nodes.response: Migrants' experiences differed greatly from group to group and from person to person. Motivations amongst migrants also differed, even within particular migrant groups.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Movement within the British Empire

nodes.misconception: The Empire Windrush brought all Caribbean migrants to Britain.
nodes.response: The Empire Windrush brought the first group of Caribbean migrants to Britain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Post war migration to Britain: The Windrush generation

nodes.misconception: The British public uniformly supported imperial expansion and wars.
nodes.response: British public opinion was not monolithic; there were varied reactions to imperial policies and military actions, including support, indifference and opposition.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of imperial propaganda in the 19th century

nodes.misconception: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of South Africa.
nodes.response: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of the Cape Colony - the British colony in the region of southern Africa.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Cecil Rhodes and the Boer War

nodes.misconception: Britain was always involved in the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
nodes.response: Britain became involved in the trade in the 1500s, initially selling enslaved people onto plantations in Spanish and Portuguese colonies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Transatlantic Slave Trade

nodes.misconception: The British were the only European power trying to gain control over India.
nodes.response: The British, French and Dutch were all attempting to gain a foothold in India and expand their influence there.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The origins of British rule in India

nodes.misconception: Most of the Native Americans were killed in battle by British colonists.
nodes.response: Although many Native Americans succumbed to British violence, the overwhelming majority of Native Americans were killed by European diseases, to which they had no natural immunity.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The colonisation of North America

nodes.misconception: Decolonisation happened everywhere at once.
nodes.response: Decolonisation happened in different places at different points throughout the 20th century, for reasons specific to each area's context.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The end of the British Empire in the 20th century

nodes.misconception: All British sources on imperial expansion were positive.
nodes.response: Not all British sources on imperial expansion were positive. There was nuance due to British awareness of the realities of empire. However, British sources are more likely to be positive in outlook regarding British imperial expansion.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: What sources can tell us about the expansion of Empire

nodes.misconception: Cultural exchange between Britain and India was 'one-way'.
nodes.response: Cultural exchange between Britain and India moved in both directions, with both countries being permanently changed by the other.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of British rule in India

nodes.misconception: The European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Union (EU) have always been the same entity with identical goals and functions.
nodes.response: The evolution from the EEC to the EU over several decades, showing progressively deepening integration. This was not a seamless transition but involved significant changes in scope and objectives.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the EU on migrant experiences in Britain

nodes.misconception: Jewish persecution and antisemitism only happened in Europe during the 1930s and 1940s.
nodes.response: Jewish persecution and antisemitism had been happening for thousands of years, with Britain expelling all Jews in 1290, without letting them return for hundreds of years.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Jewish migration to Britain in the 19th and 20th centuries

nodes.misconception: The British Nationality Act of 1948 led to an immediate and easy integration of Commonwealth immigrants into British society
nodes.response: Although the British Nationality Act of 1948 allowed Commonwealth citizens to settle in the UK, many immigrants faced significant challenges upon arrival.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Experience of post-WW2 migrants in Britain

nodes.misconception: The Hundred Years' War was a war that was fought continuously for 100 years.
nodes.response: The Hundred Years' War lasted for 116 years, but there were many years during this period which saw limited or no fighting. It is better to think of this as a period of heightened animosity in which war was either present or not far off.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Hundred Years' War

nodes.misconception: England has almost never been conquered.
nodes.response: England was conquered repeatedly before and during the medieval period, and was even arguably conquered as late as 1688.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Impact of conquest and settlement on medieval Britain

nodes.misconception: The Americans won the War of Independence because they had a better army.
nodes.response: For much of the war, the American army was a poorly trained militia. Whilst they fought bravely and Washington proved to be an able general, they received significant support from France and Spain which swung the balance of the conflict.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The War of Independence

nodes.misconception: The Vikings were nothing but brutal savages.
nodes.response: Whilst the Viking aptitude for battle is well known, they were also exceptional explorers and traders. Raiding was simply another way for them to gain wealth as opposed to their only way of life.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The arrival of the Vikings

nodes.misconception: Huguenots were a separate Protestant denomination from other Protestants in Euope.
nodes.response: Huguenots were Calvinist Protestants, which was a very common form of Protestantism. The term 'Huguenot' merely means they were Protestants from France.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Huguenot migration

nodes.misconception: All those in Northern Ireland were Protestant and all those elsewhere in Ireland were Catholic.
nodes.response: Ireland was predominantly Catholic but there was a population in the north who were predominantly Protestant, who remained part of the UK as Northern Ireland after partition.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Irish migration to Britain in the 19th century

nodes.misconception: Vikings come from Norway.
nodes.response: Whilst Vikings did come from Norway, some of the most problematic Vikings from an English perspective came from Denmark. Vikings also came from Sweden.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Danish conquest

nodes.misconception: All migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent.
nodes.response: Not all migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent; however, large numbers of them were due to the discrimination they faced in newly-independent Kenya and Uganda.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Post war migration to Britain: Migration from East Africa

nodes.misconception: Plantations are large cash-crop farms found in the Americas.
nodes.response: Cash-crop plantations can be found all over the world, but the first plantations were established in Ireland. Protestants loyal to the monarch were 'planted' in Irish Catholic lands to help establish control of the area.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Ulster Plantations and Highland Clearances

nodes.misconception: The Falkland Islands have always been uncontested British territory.
nodes.response: There is a complex and prolonged sovereignty dispute with Argentina over the Falkland Islands and there were once historical claims by Spain.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Post war migration to Britain: The Falklands

nodes.misconception: Richard the Lionheart was one of the greatest English kings.
nodes.response: Although he was king of England and was born in England, Richard almost certainly did not consider himself English. He never learnt the language and only spent a maximum of 6 months in England during his 10 year reign; he didn't like the weather.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Angevin Empire

nodes.misconception: England had not been invaded before the Norman Conquest.
nodes.response: Britain had been invaded many times before the Norman Conquest: by the Romans, the tribes known as Angles and Saxons and by the Vikings.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Norman conquest (1066)

nodes.misconception: The Berlin Crisis was solely about the status of West Berlin.
nodes.response: While the status of West Berlin was a significant aspect of the Berlin Crisis, it was not the only factor. The crisis was also influenced by broader Cold War dynamics, including the arms race and competition for influence in Europe.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Berlin, 1958-61: increased tensions

nodes.misconception: Matyas Rakosi was the leader of Hungary at the start of the Hungarian Uprising.
nodes.response: Rakosi was forced to quit as leader in July 1956 when he lost the support of the USSR. Rakosi was replaced by his close friend, Erno Gero, then Khrushchev installed Imre Nagy as leader on 26th October 1956 in an attempt to end the uprising.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Hungarian Uprising (1956)

nodes.misconception: There was only significant tension between members of the Grand Alliance at the Potsdam Conference when the war had ended and Roosevelt had been replaced by Truman as US President.
nodes.response: Although tensions increased significantly by the Potsdam Conference, there was a high level of mistrust between the members of the Grand Alliance from early on. This is illustrated by Stalin's concern about the delays in opening a second front.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Causes of tension between the USA and USSR by 1945

nodes.misconception: There is agreement about why the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
nodes.response: The US decision to use atomic bombs at the end of WW2 remains deeply controversial and historians disagree about the motivation with some arguing that it was to force the Japanese to surrender while others arguing it was to intimidate the USSR.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the atomic bomb on US-Soviet relations

nodes.misconception: The German Democratic Republic (GDR) was West Germany.
nodes.response: The GDR was East Germany - the Democratic part of the name is confusing as it was not democratic in the Western sense of being able to choose freely between different political parties.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Berlin Crisis (1948)

nodes.misconception: Historians agree that the Cold War started in 1945 with the end of World War Two.
nodes.response: The breakdown of the wartime alliance and the emerging ideological rift between communism and capitalism unfolded over several years. The exact start date of the Cold War is often debated among historians.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The origins of the Cold War (1941-58)

nodes.misconception: The collapse of the Soviet Union happened suddenly.
nodes.response: The collapse of the Soviet Union was a complex process that unfolded over several years, starting with political reforms under Mikhail Gorbachev in the late 1980s and culminating in the formal dissolution in December 1991.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The collapse of the Soviet Union

nodes.misconception: NATO was established in response to Stalin setting up the Warsaw Pact.
nodes.response: The Warsaw Pact was a response to NATO's formation in April 1949 (following the Berlin Crisis and Soviet takeover of Czechoslovakia).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Cold War arms race

nodes.misconception: Détente ended suddenly following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979.
nodes.response: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan is normally considered to mark the end of Détente but US-Soviet tensions had been increasing since 1975 due to conflict over human rights issues and increased Soviet support for communist groups around the world.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Helsinki Accords and SALT II

nodes.misconception: The USA always considered it had a responsibility to protect Europe from threats.
nodes.response: Before the Second World War, the USA had a policy of isolationism which meant not getting involved in the affairs of other countries.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan

nodes.misconception: There was only one Cold War crisis involving Berlin: the USSR's blockade of Berlin in 1948 and the Berlin Airlift launched by the Western powers in response to this.
nodes.response: Berlin was a source of conflict between the USA and the USSR from the start of the Cold War. The crisis that took place between 1958 and 1963 and resulted in the construction of the Berlin Wall is sometimes referred to as the Second Berlin Crisis.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Cold War crises, 1958-70

nodes.misconception: The Soviet missile bases in Cuba were important because they provided the USSR with the ability to strike the USA with nuclear weapons.
nodes.response: The USSR had ICBMs which meant they already had the ability to attack the USA with nuclear weapons, however these were expensive and the USA had more. The USSR had more IRBMs, so placing these missiles in Cuba gave them an important advantage.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)

nodes.misconception: US-Soviet relations only began to decline when Reagan became US President in January 1981.
nodes.response: There had been a significant decline in superpower relations before Reagan became US President. For example, in 1979, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and Carter’s response led to a serious increase in tension.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The end of the Cold War, 1970-91

nodes.misconception: Gorbachev's reforms were intended to bring an end to communism and end Soviet control over Eastern Europe.
nodes.response: Gorbachev intended his reforms to strengthen communism both within the Soviet Union and its satellite states in Eastern Europe, however, once reform started in Eastern Europe, Gorbachev was unable to contain it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The fall of the Berlin Wall

nodes.misconception: The period of Détente in the 1970s did not mark the beginning of the end of the Cold War.
nodes.response: Although there was a reduction in tensions between the USA and the USSR during the early 1970s, tensions had increased again by the end of the decade.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Détente and SALT I

nodes.misconception: The Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) was fully operational when it was announced by Reagan in 1983.
nodes.response: Although they were technologically more advanced than the USSR, the USA did not have the necessary technology to launch SDI in 1983. Reagan hoped the USSR would attempt to compete and this would cause their struggling economy to collapse.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Reagan and the 'Second Cold War'

nodes.misconception: Some people underestimate the length of the Berlin Wall and believe that it only divided the city of Berlin.
nodes.response: The Berlin Wall divided the city of Berlin but it also encircled the city. The iconic stretch of wall that divided Berlin was approximately 26 miles in length. The total length of the Berlin Wall was approximately 96 miles.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Berlin, 1961-63: the Berlin Wall

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that the Iron Curtain was a real barrier (often mixing it up with the Berlin Wall).
nodes.response: The Iron Curtain was not a real barrier but metaphor for the divide imposed between East and West by the USSR, first referred to in a speech by Churchill.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Soviet influence over Eastern Europe by 1948

nodes.misconception: Alexander Dubcek was not a committed communist.
nodes.response: Dubcek was a committed communist. The purpose of the Prague Spring reforms was to preserve communist rule in Czechoslovakia and win support for communism by removing its worst features (e.g., censorship, secret police etc.)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Prague Spring (1968)

nodes.misconception: Poorer people in Afghanistan supported the communist PDPA government.
nodes.response: The PDPA's land reforms were tainted by corruption and angered many poorer Afghans because they received poor quality land. Many Afghans opposed the PDPA's attempts to create a secular society, which they saw as an attack on their faith and culture.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan

nodes.misconception: All communist countries were members of the Warsaw Pact.
nodes.response: The Warsaw Pact was primarily a European military alliance so non-European communist countries like China and Cuba were not members. Some European countries like Yugoslavia were never members while others joined and then left like Albania in 1968.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia (1968)

nodes.misconception: Castro was a communist when he overthrew Batista's government in 1959.
nodes.response: Although some people involved in the Cuban Revolution were communist, Castro was a nationalist and only declared that he was a communist at the end of 1961 after the failed Bay of Pigs Invasion led Cuba to develop a closer relationship with the USSR.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Cuban Revolution and the Bay of Pigs Invasion

nodes.misconception: Gorbachev succeeded Brezhnev as leader of the Soviet Union in March 1985.
nodes.response: Brezhnev died in November 1982. Following his death, the Soviet Union was ruled by two leaders who were in poor health and ruled only briefly: Yuri Andropov (November 1982 - February 1984) and Konstantin Chernenko (February 1984 - March 1985).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Gorbachev's 'new thinking'

nodes.misconception: According to the Bayeux Tapestry, Odo played an important role in the Norman invasion.
