nodes.response: There is reason to be sceptical about this depiction. The Bayeux Tapestry was commissioned by Odo. This perhaps explains why Odo is self-importantly shown as central to the planning and delivery of the invasion.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Bishop Odo of Bayeux

nodes.misconception: Roles were fixed in Anglo-Saxon society - a peasant would always be a peasant.
nodes.response: Anglo-Saxon society was more open to social mobility: a hard-working peasant could gain more land and become a thegn, some slaves became free and an earl could even become king!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Anglo-Saxon society

nodes.misconception: That the Normans destroyed all Anglo-Saxon government.
nodes.response: Anglo-Saxon government systems were sophisticated, perhaps more developed than Normandy’s. The Normans retained and built on the existing Anglo-Saxon governmental institutions.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Change and continuity in Norman England

nodes.misconception: People think the survey and Domesday Book are one and the same thing.
nodes.response: In fact, the survey was ordered in 1085, and later compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The significance of Domesday Book

nodes.misconception: Medieval and modern Church power is equivalent.
nodes.response: Explicitly outline the Church's organisational power: land ownership, clergy social status, and spiritual authority.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Anglo-Norman Church

nodes.misconception: Paying homage, swearing allegiance, or making promises were weak obligations.
nodes.response: In fact, these promises are with the king and God. It was unlikely you would break a public and spiritual promise like this. It would not be good for your reputation or your soul!
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The feudal system in Norman England

nodes.misconception: William always used violence to control England.
nodes.response: Although violence was a recurring tactic of William's, he also allowed some Anglo-Saxons to keep some of their land and was willing to negotiate and pay the Danes to leave England.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Northern and East Anglian rebellions

nodes.misconception: An Anglo-Saxon monarch held all the power in their kingdom.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon nobles could force their monarchs to do things they did not want to do. For example, King Edward was forced to allow the House of Godwin back from exile and restore them to their earldoms.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Edward the Confessor and the House of Godwin

nodes.misconception: William the Conqueror was hostile towards all Anglo-Saxons from the start.
nodes.response: Some Anglo-Saxons, if they had not fought against William at Hastings, were allowed to keep their land.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The legacy of Anglo-Saxon resistance

nodes.misconception: England’s monarchs always spoke English as their first language.
nodes.response: In fact, after the Norman conquest it would take over 300 years for the monarch of England to speak English as their first language.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Norman aristocracy

nodes.misconception: The Norman conquest was fully achieved by the victory at the Battle of Hastings.
nodes.response: In reality, there were many defiant Anglo-Saxons ready to carry on fighting and it took time for William to gain meaningful control over a hostile Anglo-Saxon population.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The submission of the earls in 1066

nodes.misconception: The shield wall was not a very sophisticated or effective military tactic.
nodes.response: In fact, the shield wall proved effective in holding off the Norman attacks for many hours.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Battle of Hastings

nodes.misconception: It took many weeks to travel from the south to the north of England in medieval times.
nodes.response: Harold and his housecarls were able to cover 185 miles in just four days in 1066: an amazing achievement.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The battles of Gate Fulford and Stamford Bridge

nodes.misconception: After William the Conqueror was crowned King of England, he and the Normans were immediately accepted as rightful rulers and peace reigned across the kingdom.
nodes.response: In fact, William faced a hostile Anglo-Saxon population and threats of invasion from Wales and Scotland, requiring him to take measures to establish further control.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Rewarding followers and the Marcher earldoms

nodes.misconception: The one-dimensional view of William as a violent conqueror.
nodes.response: In fact, William was very pious and he repented some of the atrocities he had committed during his reign and insisted his treasures should be used to rebuild some of the areas he had harried.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: William I and his successors

nodes.misconception: Harold Godwinson would help his brother Tostig.
nodes.response: Harold’s ambitions to be king meant he did little to help his brother Tostig. If Harold became king, he would want to avoid making enemies of Mercia and Northumbria. He wanted to show the Witan that he was loyal to England, beyond his family.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The uprising against Earl Tostig Godwinson

nodes.misconception: After a monarch dies, their eldest child automatically becomes monarch after them.
nodes.response: In Anglo-Saxon England an heir was always in a strong position, but even if there was an heir, the Witan could use their influence for someone else to be made monarch - if, for example, the heir was too young.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Claimants to the throne in 1066

nodes.misconception: Resistance to William’s rule of England, came only from the English.
nodes.response: In 1075, two Norman earls revolted against William, and English forces helped to stop the rebellion.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The revolt of the earls in 1075

nodes.misconception: In the medieval period it was expected that rulers would be ruthless in killing anyone who opposed them.
nodes.response: Rulers were expected to be just and merciful in the medieval period, and Willian faced criticism across Europe for his brutality in crushing opposition in the North of England.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Harrying of the North

nodes.misconception: Anglo-Saxon monarchs had to be great warriors to be made king.
nodes.response: In fact some monarchs, such as Edward the Confessor, were not warriors but instead very religious men whose faith inspired others.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Anglo-Saxon monarchy

nodes.misconception: England did not have any fortified settlements until the Normans built castles.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon burhs were fortified settlements, built to protect towns from Viking attacks.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Earldoms and local government in Anglo-Saxon England

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that castles only had a military function.
nodes.response: However, castles also had a psychological impact on the people of England. They served as a permanent reminder to the English of a foreign occupier in their land. They were also centres of administration.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Motte-and-bailey castles

nodes.misconception: Sending the fyrd defences home in September is evidence of Harold's poor decision making.
nodes.response: In fact, Anglo-Saxon leaders had always struggled with the 60-day limit for the fyrd. Harold had actually kept the fyrd out for twice as long as usual: evidence of his impressive influence as a leader.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasons for William’s victory at the Battle of Hastings

nodes.misconception: Church leaders had no role in how Anglo-Saxon England was governed.
nodes.response: Archbishops, bishops and other Church leaders could be part of the Witan, and that meant they were involved in advising the monarch about the government of Anglo-Saxon England.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Anglo-Saxon economy and the role of the Church

nodes.misconception: Students may think all youth blindly accepted Nazi ideas.
nodes.response: While many participated, some - like Sophie Scholl - resisted. Peer pressure, fear, and excitement all played a role.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Young people in Nazi Germany

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that most unemployed Germans turned to communism.
nodes.response: While the Communist Party gained support, many Germans, especially the middle class and business owners, feared communism and instead supported the Nazis as a defence against a potential revolution.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of unemployment and rise in support for the Communist Party

nodes.misconception: The Nazis only gained power through fear and intimidation.
nodes.response: In reality, while violence played a role, their rise was also driven by economic despair, propaganda, Hitler’s appeal, and democratic failures. Many Germans voted for them willingly, believing they offered hope and stability.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth in support for the Nazi Party

nodes.misconception: Everyone in Germany fully believed the Nazi propaganda.
nodes.response: While some people genuinely believed, many conformed due to fear, peer pressure, or habit. Propaganda created surface unity - not universal belief.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Goebbels and propaganda in Nazi Germany

nodes.misconception: All women opposed Nazi policies.
nodes.response: Women's experiences under Nazi rule varied: some embraced traditional roles and rewards, while others resisted and faced punishment, showing a complex, not uniform, response to Nazi policies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Women in Nazi Germany

nodes.misconception: The Enabling Act was passed fairly.
nodes.response: The vote was deeply manipulated: communist Reichstag members were banned, others intimidated.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Reichstag Fire and the Enabling Act

nodes.misconception: All religious leaders opposed the Nazis.
nodes.response: In reality, many remained silent or even cooperated, hoping to protect their institutions.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Nazi Party and religion

nodes.misconception: Hitler was already an all-powerful dictator by 1934.
nodes.response: While Hitler had crushed political opposition, the military remained a powerful, independent force. The SA purge was crucial to win over the army, which still had the power to challenge him.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Hitler's creation of a dictatorship

nodes.misconception: The Nazis completely solved unemployment and revived the economy.
nodes.response: While official unemployment figures dropped dramatically, some of this was due to manipulated statistics and forced labour schemes.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Employment in Nazi Germany

nodes.misconception: People “should have known” what Hitler would do once in power.
nodes.response: In reality, many elites and citizens saw the Nazis as a lesser evil amid crisis — not as future dictators. The horror of what was to come wasn’t yet clear to them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How Hitler became Chancellor of Germany

nodes.misconception: Everyone benefited from Nazi economic policies.
nodes.response: Reinforce that benefits were selective, often dependent on loyalty, and many gains were cancelled out by longer hours and lost freedoms.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Work and life in Nazi Germany

nodes.misconception: The belief that the 'stab-in-the-back' theory was based on factual evidence.
nodes.response: The theory was a narrative promoted by the military elite to distance themselves from the Armistice surrender. Germany's defeat was primarily due to military exhaustion and economic collapse, not treachery by Weimar politicians.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early unrest and the Treaty of Versailles

nodes.misconception: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 was a legally binding agreement that could prevent all future wars.
nodes.response: The pact lacked enforcement mechanisms and relied on goodwill, making it more symbolic than practical.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Stresemann's international achievements

nodes.misconception: Weimar Germany was a completely free and modernist society.
nodes.response: While it was a hub of cultural experimentation, it was also deeply divided, with strong conservative resistance and widespread political unrest. Many Germans viewed the cultural changes as dangerous and sought to restore traditional values.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Weimar culture 1924-29

nodes.misconception: Germany's recovery in the 1920s completely solved its economic problems and secured long-term stability.
nodes.response: Much of the recovery depended on American loans. What happens to Germany’s economy if those loans are withdrawn or if the US faces its own crisis? This shows how fragile the recovery really was.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Economic recovery under Stresemann

nodes.misconception: Hyperinflation affected everyone equally.
nodes.response: Some people, like businessmen who hoarded essentials to sell at inflated prices, profited during the crisis. Meanwhile, many middle-class Germans saw their savings wiped out and were forced to barter for survival.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: 1923, the Ruhr and hyperinflation

nodes.misconception: Proportional representation was purely a positive step forward because it gave a voice to smaller political parties.
nodes.response: In fact, proportional representation led to fragmentation, with many small parties gaining seats in the Reichstag. This made it difficult to pass laws because no single party had a majority.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Weimar Republic

nodes.misconception: Germany formally lost the First World War in the traditional sense, with a decisive military defeat.
nodes.response: Germany was not defeated in battle, it sought peace and agreed to an armistice. The German military leadership recognised that the war was unwinnable due to resource shortages, economic collapse, and the deteriorating morale of troops and citizens.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The First World War and the German Revolution

nodes.misconception: Germany has always existed as one country, or has existed in its current form for a long time.
nodes.response: Before 1871, 'Germany' did not exist as a single nation. It was a collection of over 30 independent, mostly German-speaking states, each with its own ruler.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Germany before the First World War

nodes.misconception: The SPD had genuine power after becoming the largest party in the Reichstag.
nodes.response: The Reichstag could debate and vote on budgets, but the Kaiser chose the chancellor, controlled the military and could close the Reichstag at will. Foreign and military policy stayed entirely in his hands, so real political power never shifted.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Industrialisation, social reform and the growth of socialism

nodes.misconception: Most Germans strongly supported the Nazis.
nodes.response: Many complied out of fear, peer pressure, or survival - not necessarily belief. Resistance was dangerous, but still present in different forms across society.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Opposition and resistance to Hitler and the Nazi Party

nodes.misconception: Nazi concentration camps and extermination camps were the same thing.
nodes.response: Concentration camps were used for imprisonment, forced labour and punishment, not initially for mass murder. Extermination camps, built later, were designed specifically for killing on an industrial scale.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Nazi racial ideology and the treatment of minorities

nodes.misconception: The Weimar Republic’s reliance on the Freikorps might suggest that the government supported right-wing ideologies.
nodes.response: The Weimar Government used the Freikorps out of desperation to suppress left-wing uprisings, but this reliance highlighted its inability to maintain order independently, rather than an alignment with right-wing ideologies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The putsches of 1919-23

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that all concentration camps in this period were death camps like Auschwitz.
nodes.response: Emphasise that early camps (1933–1939) were brutal prisons for political opponents and ‘undesirables’, but were not yet part of a systematic extermination programme. The Holocaust’s industrial death camps came later.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Nazi police state

nodes.misconception: The Kaiser could simply order naval expansion without resistance.
nodes.response: In reality, the Kaiser needed Reichstag approval for funding, so winning public support was a crucial step in pressuring parliament.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Germany’s naval ambitions before the First World War

nodes.misconception: Hitler invented antisemitism.
nodes.response: Antisemitism had deep roots across Europe and the wider world long before Hitler. The Nazis built on these longstanding prejudices, turning them into official state policy and using them to justify persecution.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The persecution of Jews

nodes.misconception: The Final Solution was decided all at once.
nodes.response: It was an evolving process. Historians have debated whether genocide was inevitable from 1933 — policies escalated over time, with many historians seeing Wannsee as marking the coordination point, not the start.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Final Solution

nodes.misconception: Students may believe Germany fully mobilised its population, including women, like the Allies did.
nodes.response: Nazi ideology restricted women's roles in industry, despite labour shortages.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Nazi economy and WW2

nodes.misconception: European countries only created colonies in Africa and the Americas.
nodes.response: European countries set up colonies all over the world, including in Asia.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: French Indochina

nodes.misconception: As a result of legal changes, there was significant progress for all black Americans by 1960.
nodes.response: Legal changes led to some change for black Americans, although a significant amount of opposition from within and outside the government led to limited change for most black Americans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The changing position of black Americans by 1960

nodes.misconception: Malcolm X's main philosophy was the use of violence in order to fight racial injustice.
nodes.response: Malcolm X supported Black Nationalism and encouraged black Americans to defend themselves by any means necessary, although this did endorse violence, Malcolm X spent much of his time with the Black Muslims supporting black Americans in poorer areas.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of Malcolm X in the civil rights movement

nodes.misconception: The work of Martin Luther King ended with the Voting Right Acts in 1965.
nodes.response: With continued violence, rioting and protests, King continued to fight for change in the North. However, he faced greater opposition than he did in the South.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: King's campaign in the North

nodes.misconception: Negotiations are quick affairs.
nodes.response: Negotiations can sometimes take place over many years before any progress is made.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The expansion of the war into Cambodia, Laos and North Vietnam, 1969-1972

nodes.misconception: Large-scale protests must mean that most people are against something.
nodes.response: A majority of people rarely, if ever, get involved in public protests, so we cannot draw absolute conclusions about what the majority thinks.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Support for the Vietnam War in the US

nodes.misconception: After Martin Luther King's famous 'I have a dream' speech, the civil rights movement continued to progress until the Civil Rights Act was passed.
nodes.response: The assassination of President Kennedy stalled the momentum the movement had gained with the events in Birmingham, he was the president that many black American had put their hope in - and many feared their hope died with him.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The peace marches (1963) and Freedom Summer (1964)

nodes.misconception: Americans were supportive of any war against a communist country.
nodes.response: Many Americans did support action against communists but an increasing number did not support the manner in which their country was fighting
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: US involvement in Vietnam

nodes.misconception: Everyone who joins the armed forces does so willingly and supports the actions of the government.
nodes.response: Conscription is common around the world, and many people are forced to join the armed forces against their will.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Opposition to the Vietnam War in the US

nodes.misconception: When the Supreme Court ordered all schools to desegregate, they were quick to follow this instruction because it came from the Supreme Court.
nodes.response: Although the Supreme Court was the highest court in the USA, many schools were slow to desegregate and some refused to desegregate until they were eventually forced.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Progress in education, 1954-60

nodes.misconception: South Vietnam needed US troops because they didn't have much of an army of their own.
nodes.response: The South Vietnamese Army was one of the largest in the world. What they lacked was modern equipment and training.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The effect of Vietnamisation on US policy in Vietnam

nodes.misconception: Jim Crow laws only impacted southern states in the US.
nodes.response: Although Jim Crow laws were implemented in every southern state, there was still some segregation in northern states.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Segregation and discrimination in the USA

nodes.misconception: The civil rights movement was always co-ordinated and led by older men and women.
nodes.response: In the 1960s, there was a shift in the civil rights movement as students began to take a leading role in the fight against racial injustice.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Greensboro and the sit-in movement

nodes.misconception: The increased success of the direct action in the 1960s was the result of minimal opposition.
nodes.response: Direct action in the 1960s was increasingly successful because of the increased opposition that was captured by national and international news reporters.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Freedom rides: protests and progress for civil rights (1961)

nodes.misconception: Martin Luther King Jr had always been part of the civil rights movement.
nodes.response: King entered the spotlight following the Montgomery Bus Boycott and became a successful, popular leader as he was not associated with any large organisations.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Martin Luther King Jr and the early civil rights movement

nodes.misconception: US presidents would only use federal intervention when pressured by the media.
nodes.response: Kennedy marked a change in the involvement of the president, as he was not pressured by the media to use federal intervention to support Meredith. Unlike in Little Rock, Kennedy's support came before the outbreak of violence from white Americans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The James Meredith case (1962)

nodes.misconception: US soldiers are highly trained, highly motivated troops.
nodes.response: Conscription generally offers a larger fighting force at the expense of a decline in quality - not everyone called to serve wants to be there.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: US weaknesses in the Vietnam War

nodes.misconception: The passing of the Civil Rights Act in 1964 marked the end of the civil rights movement.
nodes.response: While the Civil Rights Act (1964) was a landmark moment, bringing significant change, it left much to campaign for - particularly issues of voter registration amongst black Americans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965)

nodes.misconception: The Voting Rights Act (1965) marked the end of protests to fight against racial injustice.
nodes.response: Many people felt the acts were too little too late as unemployment rates remained high and daily discrimination continued - for many, in the form of poverty.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The riots of 1965-67 and the Kerner Report (1968)

nodes.misconception: The Black Power movement was entirely separate from the civil rights movement.
nodes.response: Many of the leading figures of the Black Power movement began as civil rights activists, who had grown frustrated with the lack of progress and looked to more radical methods and beliefs.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The emergence of the Black Power movement

nodes.misconception: The US lost the Vietnam War: the North had little agency or impact on events.
nodes.response: North Vietnam was a formidable fighting force who had fought several wars over many years. Their strength was a major reason why they won.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: North Vietnamese strengths in the Vietnam War

nodes.misconception: As Nixon showed little interest in the civil rights movement after his election, the movement largely regressed in the 1970s.
nodes.response: The extent of progress in the civil rights movement was largely dependent on the area of life you consider. For example, there was little change politically but there was some progress economically.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: How successful was the civil rights movement by 1975?

nodes.misconception: Foreign aid support packages, for instance Marshall Aid, are made up of just money.
nodes.response: Equipment such as heavy machinery or weapons, natural resources such as coal, as well as money, make up foreign aid support packages.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Containment and the Domino Theory

nodes.misconception: Civil rights organisations only worked in the north.
nodes.response: Civil rights organisations worked across the USA, although they would get more support from white Americans in northern states and would therefore seem more successful in the north.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Civil rights organisations in the 20th century

nodes.misconception: Opposition to the civil rights movement was limited to organisations formed by the public
nodes.response: Opposition to the civil rights movement was organised both within the public and within the US government
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early opposition to the civil rights movement

nodes.misconception: Malcolm X founded the Black Panther Party.
nodes.response: The ideas of Malcolm X in his later life would inspire the Black Power movement; this in turn inspired the Black Panther Party in the year after his death. The party was founded by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Black Panther Party

nodes.misconception: The Montgomery Bus Boycott was a successful, peaceful boycott that was carried out with minimal resistance.
nodes.response: The boycott was a peaceful means of protest, but continued despite huge resistance throughout Montgomery. Those who participated risked arrest, unemployed and sometimes their lives.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-6)

nodes.misconception: One individual, Martin Luther King, was responsible for the success of the civil rights movement from 1960 to 1965.
nodes.response: While Martin Luther King played a huge role of the success seen in these years, the success was also the result of several civil rights leaders and the work of their organisations as well an increasing support from the president.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasons why the civil rights movement was more successful from 1960 to 1965

nodes.misconception: Highly-trained members of the military and government tend not to make mistakes.
nodes.response: Everyone is capable of making errors, sometimes big and far-reaching ones, especially if they are under a great deal of stress.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Gulf of Tonkin incident

nodes.misconception: Allies are open and honest with each other, as friends should be.
nodes.response: Countries break alliances frequently and regularly act against the interests of long-time allies.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Peace negotiations to end the Vietnam War, 1968-1972

nodes.misconception: There is often confusion between guerilla and gorilla!
nodes.response: Same sound, different spelling, very different meaning!  'Guerilla' comes from the Spanish word 'guerra', meaning 'war'.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Vietcong resistance

nodes.misconception: The US has always been too large and powerful to lose a war.
nodes.response: The majority of people regard the Vietnam War as a loss for the US: they did not achieve their stated goal of containing communism.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Paris Peace agreement, 1973

nodes.misconception: A war that ended 50 years ago does not affect anybody any more.
nodes.response: Much of the Vietnamese landscape and people are still impacted or recovering from the effects of the war even today.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Impact of the Vietnam War

nodes.misconception: Wars are only won on the battlefield.
nodes.response: A variety of factors influence the outcome of a war, such as a nation's economy, geography, and popular sentiment towards the war.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Tet Offensive

nodes.misconception: Nixon was the only president who wanted to remove US troops from Vietnam.
nodes.response: Kennedy and Johnson wanted the same, but, like Nixon, found themselves getting more involved in order to prop up the South Vietnamese govt.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing US policy in Vietnam, 1969-1972

nodes.misconception: The Viet Minh gained full control over Vietnam after defeating the French.
nodes.response: Vietnam was divided in two at the 1954 Geneva Conference, leaving the Viet Minh only in control of the north.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The collapse of French Indochina

nodes.misconception: Mátyás Rákosi was the leader of Hungary at the start of the Hungarian Uprising.
nodes.response: Rákosi was forced to quit as leader in July 1956 when he lost the support of the USSR but widespread anger amongst ordinary Hungarians remained. Khrushchev installed Imre Nagy as leader on 26th October 1956 in an attempt to end protests.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Hungary and Soviet power in Eastern Europe

nodes.misconception: The CCP and KMT were under Soviet and US control.
nodes.response: Both sides in the Chinese Civil War were able to resist attempts by foreign powers to control their actions, such as the KMT in 1946 and CCP in 1949.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The growth of communism in China

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that the Iron Curtain was a real barrier (often mixing it up with the Berlin Wall).
nodes.response: The Iron Curtain was not a real barrier but metaphor for the divide imposed between East and West by the USSR, first referred to in a speech by Churchill.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Soviet influence over Eastern Europe

nodes.misconception: SALT 1 represented an end to the Cold War.
nodes.response: SALT 1 helped to moderate some elements of the Cold War such as the arms race but did not bring a complete stop to this. US and Soviet rivalry continued after 1972 and so did the Cold War.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Détente and SALT 1

nodes.misconception: The Cuban Missile Crisis made war more likely between the superpowers.
nodes.response: Both the US and USSR were shocked at how close they had come to war and were relieved to have avoided it. Further steps were agreed between both countries after the crisis had ended to make war less likely in future.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis

nodes.misconception: The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia created the risk of war between the superpowers.
nodes.response: The USA opposed the invasion but was unwilling to become involved in a military conflict involving the USSR and so limited its oppositions to criticism rather than taking steps to protect Czechoslovakia.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: International responses to the Prague Spring

nodes.misconception: The USA fought to prevent the construction of the Berlin Wall.
nodes.response: The USA believed that the construction of the wall meant they would no longer be threatened in West Berlin and used it as a valuable propaganda symbol.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Construction of the Berlin Wall

nodes.misconception: The arms race only made the superpowers more hostile towards one another.
nodes.response: The high costs and growing power of nuclear weapons developments meant both the USSR and USA were interested in finding ways to improve relations between them.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Khrushchev and peaceful coexistence

nodes.misconception: The USSR only experienced benefits from the Korean War.
nodes.response: Some new strains were created in Sino-Soviet relations due to limits on assistance from the USSR which were intended to avoid a direct conflict between the Soviets and Americans.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Consequences of the Korean War

nodes.misconception: The Bay of Pigs Invasion directly involved US combat forces.
nodes.response: JFK refused to involve US ground troops or air support in the invasion whcih relied upon a small group of Cuban exiles.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Bay of Pigs Invasion

nodes.misconception: China and the USSR fought alongside North Korea from the beginning of the Korean War.
nodes.response: China and the USSR supported the North Korean invasion but did not participate. China only joined the war at a later stage.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Outbreak of the Korean War

nodes.misconception: US assistance to South Vietnam immediately included the deployment of American ground troops.
nodes.response: The US began supporting South Vietnam in 1954 but did not deploy US ground troops there until 1965.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: US involvement in the Vietnam War

nodes.misconception: US responses to the 'loss' of China were only based on international concerns.
nodes.response: As a democracy, American policy-makers and leaders had to pay attention to domestic opinion as well as international issues. Both of these factors encouraged tough anti-communism after the 'loss' of China.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The ‘loss’ of China and the Cold War

nodes.misconception: The USSR immediately refused to cooperate with the USA after a U2 was show down in May 1960.
nodes.response: The USSR still attended the Paris Summit but walked out when the US refused to apologise for spying on it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The U2 Crisis

nodes.misconception: The USSR was in favout of the US decision to improve relations with communist China.
nodes.response: Because of the Sino-Soviet split, the Soviets worried that improved US-China relations might lead them to form an anti-Soviet alliance.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The reasons for Détente

nodes.misconception: The USA was in the lead throughout the Space Race.
nodes.response: The USSR beat the USA to launch the first satellite into orbit and to put both the first man and first woman in space.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Space Race

nodes.misconception: There was only significant tension between members of the Grand Alliance at the Potsdam Conference when the war had ended and Roosevelt had been replaced by Truman as US President.
nodes.response: Although tensions increased significantly by the Potsdam Conference, there was a high level of mistrust between the members of the Grand Alliance from early on. This is illustrated by Stalin's concern about the delays in opening a second front.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Early causes of tension between the USA and the USSR

nodes.misconception: The German Democratic Republic (GDR) was West Germany.
nodes.response: The GDR was East Germany - the Democratic part of the name is confusing as it was not democratic in the Western sense of being able to choose freely between different political parties.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Berlin Crisis, 1948-9

nodes.misconception: NATO was established in response to the USSR setting up the Warsaw Pact.
nodes.response: The Warsaw Pact was a response to NATO's formation in April 1949 (which itself followed the Berlin Crisis and Soviet takeover of Czechoslovakia).
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: NATO and the Warsaw Pact

nodes.misconception: Everybody agreed the possession of nuclear weapons made the world more dangerous.
nodes.response: Many people argued that as the US and USSR both possessed nuclear weapons this deterred them from going to war with one another - otherwise they woudl afce mutually assured destruction.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The nuclear arms race

nodes.misconception: All communist states fell under complete Soviet control because of the Brezhnev Doctrine.
nodes.response: Some states such as China, Yugoslavia, Romania and Albania became less trusting of the USSR and made increased efforts to develop their own independent relations to protect themselves against it.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Brezhnev Doctrine

nodes.misconception: Only the USSR made compromises during the crisis.
nodes.response: Both superpowers agreed to compromises in order to avoid war and resolve the crisis. Soviet missiles were withdrawn from Cuba whilst the US promised not to invade Cuba and to withdraw its own missiles from Turkey.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The 13 Days of the Cuban Missile Crisis

nodes.misconception: There is agreement about why the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
nodes.response: The US decision to use atomic bombs at the end of WW2 remains deeply controversial and historians disagree about the motivation with some arguing that it was to force the Japanese to surrender while others arguing it was to intimidate the USSR.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of the atomic bomb

nodes.misconception: The USSR did not believe that the USA would be bothered by nuclear missiles in Cuba.
nodes.response: The Soviets were aware that missile deployments to Cuba could trigger a crisis but believed they could help resolve the balance of power and deter any American attacks on Cuba.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Initial stages of the Cuban Missile Crisis

nodes.misconception: Dubček's reforms demonstrate that he was not a communist.
nodes.response: Dubček did want to liberalise politics and the economy in Czechoslovakia but he was still a communist. He considered these reforms necessary to ensure that a communist government could survive without being overthrown.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Prague Spring

nodes.misconception: Historians agree that the Cold War started in 1945 with the end of World War Two.
nodes.response: The breakdown of the wartime alliance and the emerging ideological rift between communism and capitalism unfolded over several years. The exact start date of the Cold War is often debated among historians.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The origins of the Cold War, 1941-58

nodes.misconception: The USA always considered it had a responsibility to protect Europe from threats.
nodes.response: Before the Second World War, the USA had a policy of isolationism which meant not getting involved in the affairs of other countries.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan

nodes.misconception: Castro immediately turned to the USSR for support after the Cuban Revolution.
nodes.response: Castro mainly turned to the USSR for support in 1960, after the USA had already begun restricting trade with Cuba.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: The Cuban Revolution and its consequences

nodes.misconception: From the 1950s onwards, the USSR's human rights record continually improve.
nodes.response: Under Khrushchev, more respect was shown for political and social freedoms but these restrictions were tightened again once Brezhnev took power in 1964.
nodes.subject: history
nodes.lessonTitle: Tensions between the superpowers by the late-1960s

nodes.misconception: When there's more than one subtrahend, the order cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Subtrahends can be subtracted from the minuend in any order. They can also be added together before being subtracted.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtracting to and from 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not understand that addition is commutative and are unable to 'swap' addends around.
nodes.response: Use practical equipment and small numbers to show pupils that a sum is still the same even if values are added in different orders.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add 3 numbers together using doubles and near doubles

nodes.misconception: Difference can only be found by subtracting the subtrahend from the minuend.
nodes.response: Subtract the subtrahend from the minuend when they are far apart. When close together, find the difference counting up from the subtrahend.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems involving addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be confident in representing addition problems using bar models.
nodes.response: Make connections between bar models, tens frames and 'first...then...then...now' representations. Take time to model examples.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add 3 numbers together in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils perceive the equals sign = as 'where the answer goes' and struggle with writing equations.
nodes.response: Show pupils that the equals sign represents balance and that equations are equal on both sides of the sign. Balance scales can be used.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Numbers can be added in any order

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly partition the subtrahend.
nodes.response: Partition the subtrahend to count back to ten or a tens number. Use number pairs that total ten to help subtract whatever is left.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtracting numbers that bridge through 10

nodes.misconception: Children rely on one strategy for adding to find a sum and do not consider the values.
nodes.response: Discuss when it is most efficient to use doubles, near doubles, number pairs to 10. Model efficient approaches.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add three addends efficiently using a range of strategies

nodes.misconception: Difference can only be found by counting back.
nodes.response: Difference can be calculated by subtracting the subtrahend from the minuend or by counting between the subtrahend and the minuend.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtracting small numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils partition one of the addends incorrectly to help them bridge ten.
nodes.response: Pupils use number pairs that total ten to help them partition the addend. They consider what they have to add to make ten.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Addition by bridging through 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe a pair to 10 only exists if the addends are next to one another in an equation.
nodes.response: Addition is commutative. Model the use of tens frames to show efficient addition of calculations containing number pairs to 10.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add three addends by finding pairs that total 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup ones into the tens column.
nodes.response: Model regrouping from the ones to the tens. Encourage pupils to consider the size of the numbers, thinking about an approximate sum of the two addends. Is their answer reasonable?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using column addition to add 2- and 3-digit numbers by regrouping ones

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write the minuend and subtrahend the wrong way around.
nodes.response: Model setting out column subtraction, starting with the minuend. This can be taught alongside manipulatives such as Base 10 blocks so that pupils understand that the minuend is the number that we start with.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using column subtraction to subtract without regrouping

nodes.misconception: When using adjustment (e.g. 456 − 199), pupils may forget whether they have to subtract or add 1 after they have subtracted 200
nodes.response: Ask pupils if they subtract 200 then subtract 1 more, how much have they subtracted altogether? They should see that they have subtracted 201, not 199 A number line representation will support pupil's understanding with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Decide on the most efficient subtraction strategy, including column subtraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make errors with regrouping in the ones and tens, particularly where there is regrouping in both.
nodes.response: Model examples of regrouping with the pupils, including questions where regrouping in the ones causes regrouping in the tens. If necessary, use Base 10 blocks to help with the modelling.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using column addition with regrouping in the ones and tens columns

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to use estimation to help them with checking addition equations.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to find the nearest multiple of 10 or 100 to the numbers they are adding. They will not yet be familiar with ‘rounding’. Estimated answers do not need to be really accurate, then are just an approximation and help when checking.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using known facts and strategies to accurately and efficiently use and check column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how regrouping works with column subtraction.
nodes.response: Emphasise with pupils the size of the digits, referring to the tens and the ones. Model using Base 10 blocks so that pupils understand how regrouping works with column subtraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using column subtraction with regrouping from tens to ones

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not think regrouping is needed if the tens are the same digit, but regrouping in the ones can mean regrouping in the tens.
nodes.response: Share examples where regrouping 1 ten as 10 tens means that regrouping is also needed in the tens (e.g. 345 - 148).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using column subtraction with regrouping from hundreds to tens

nodes.misconception: When finding missing numbers in column addition, pupils may find it difficult to identify whether they can add or subtract.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that addends are parts and the sum is the whole. To find a missing part, we subtract the known part from the whole. To find a missing whole, we add the known parts together. Bar models or part-part-whole models can model this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review adding 3-digit numbers using column addition without regrouping

nodes.misconception: Pupils may refer to adding numbers in the tens as 3 + 6 rather than 3 tens + 6 tens or 30 + 60
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to refer to the tens numbers as tens. In 34 + 44, we add 4 ones and 4 ones together, and then we add 3 tens and 4 tens together. This will support pupil's understanding as they progress to addition with regrouping.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review adding 2-digit numbers using column addition without regrouping

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to lay out column addition where they are adding a 3-digit number and a 2-digit number.
nodes.response: Emphasise the place value. Continually ask the pupils, 'Where is the tens column? Where is the hundreds column? How many tens does this number have? How many hundreds does this number have?' so that they begin asking these questions themselves.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use column addition to solve problems in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse column subtraction and column addition, and forget where the whole appears in both.
nodes.response: Emphasise starting with the whole. The minuend appears first in column subtraction. One part (the subtrahend) is subtracted and the difference appears beneath this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review identifying the minuend and subtrahend in column subtraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to present regrouping in column addition.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to talk about the process as they work through the problems. Model this in the lesson e.g. '5 tens add 7 tens is equal to 12 tens. 10 tens are regrouped as 1 hundred and written in the hundreds column.'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review using column addition to add 2- and 3-digit numbers by regrouping tens

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not make very accurate estimates for their calculations.
nodes.response: This lesson explores inaccurate estimations. Estimations should be quick and easy to calculate, but when adding two addends, it's sensible to make one larger and one smaller so that the estimate is as accurate as possible.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of column addition to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to make accurate use of place value, especially with numbers that have zero ones, tens or hundreds.
nodes.response: Give pupils opportunities to set out calculations such as two hundred and thirty add three hundred and four. Can they use zero correctly to represent zero ones and zero tens?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review and use knowledge of place value to correctly lay out column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misidentify the sum and addends within column addition.
nodes.response: Emphasise the use of the 'equals' symbol within the column addition. This is where the sum appears. It is important that pupils understand commutativity and that the addends can appear in any order and will still result in the same sum.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review column addition and identify the addends and sum

nodes.misconception: Pupils draw bar models with larger numbers within them, making them particularly time consuming.
nodes.response: Where larger numbers are used, encourage children to unitise numbers into units of thousands or millions. Equally, if children are secure with what each number represents, they can label each part of the bar with a label from the context itself.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use written strategies and known facts to calculate the value of a missing part

nodes.misconception: Pupils identify the correct bar model as the model with the correct numbers with equal parts.
nodes.response: Whilst this may represent the problem with regards to the numbers involved, encourage pupils to consider the size of each part in proportion to the whole as this may help when estimating answers to missing parts or wholes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of additive structure to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to draw a bar model to represent an equation without a context.
nodes.response: Refer back to the language of parts and wholes to help pupils identify which numbers in the equation represent the parts and which number represent the whole. You may like to reduce the numbers to number within 10 to emphasise the structure at first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent an equation in a part-part-whole model correctly

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to represent each problem with an accurate bar model.
nodes.response: You could continue to use number rods to represent each of the problems at first and then draw around these as a second scaffold, however, pupils do need to make the leap to representing as bar models for themselves.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a model to interpret a part-part-whole problem with three addends

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to represent the problem as a repeated subtraction equation.
nodes.response: Simplify problems by using numbers within 10 at first to reveal the structure of the problem. By doing this, you can show how both the subtraction and addition equations relate, which can help you to find the value of the missing parts or whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use mental strategies and known facts to calculate the value of a missing part

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the missing part(s) must be a different colour rod to those parts already used within the example.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with various examples, in particular examples where there are two or more of the same part, drawing on the repeated addition/multiplicative structure not just the additive structure.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify the missing part using knowledge of relationships and structures

nodes.misconception: Pupils create bar models where the parts do not equal the whole or vice versa.
nodes.response: Whilst this may be a calculation error, it is important that the context of the story is considered when looking to re-adjust the bar model. Take time to work through the context again building the bar model from the what is known.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Create stories to match structures presented in a model

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to find a way into solving the number puzzles at first.
nodes.response: It is important that pupils can identify what the whole is for each problem. Encourage pupils to draw a bar model to help link the problem to its part and wholes. This may help them identify the parts and whole and how to calculate any missing parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use part-part-whole structures to solve additive problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify appropriate sized bars that fit the problem as well as equate to the size of the whole.
nodes.response: Find parts that fit the structure of the problem first, then ask what the whole would be. Change the size of the whole and ask pupils which rod(s) would need to change. Encourage children to reason their decisions by comparing the size of the rods.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify structures within stories and use knowledge of structures to create stories

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look at each rod as representing a number rather than focusing on the colour.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the rods have no numerical value and encourage pupils discuss the rods by their colour name. They may notice proportional relationships but these should not be labelled numerically.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a combination of different parts can be equivalent to the same whole

nodes.misconception: Children may think that each group of ten is worth more than the last when we count up in tens.
nodes.response: Ensure children understand that we count all as we go along to find how many things are in a group, the last number we say tells us how many there are.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent multiples of ten in an expression or an equation

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on counting in ones rather than recognise a group of ten.
nodes.response: Encourage children to recognise groups of ten in a variety of contexts. They may need to check one e.g. a bundle of 10 straws but then should be encouraged to use comparative size to know other groups are of equal size.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that one ten is equivalent to ten ones

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on counting in tens rather than using known facts to add and subtract multiples of ten.
nodes.response: Encourage children to look for patterns as they add and subtract multiples of ten. Compare to the single-digit facts they know. Make a list of known facts to refer to.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiples of ten in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on counting in tens rather than using known facts to add and subtract multiples of ten.
nodes.response: Encourage children to look for patterns as they add and subtract multiples of ten. Compare to the single-digit facts they know. Ask 'Is there a known fact that can help you?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiples of ten

nodes.misconception: Children may get the tens and teens numbers confused and may muddle up the digits when writing the numerals.
nodes.response: Show numbers on a place value chart and talk about what each number represents. Emphasise the relative value of the digits, focusing on the groups of 10 and how this is shown. Support pupils to generalise e.g. teen numbers always have one ten.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent multiples of ten using their numerals

nodes.misconception: Children may use counting on and back strategies instead of application of known facts and therefore be inefficient when adding and subtracting multiples of 10
nodes.response: Use representations to make clear links when unitising e.g. adding 2 to 3 and then adding 2 groups of 10 to 3 groups of 10, to support children in making the link. Children should be increasingly fluent in addition and subtraction within 10
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of facts and unitising to add and subtract multiples of ten

nodes.misconception: Children may not see the link between adding or subtracting ones and adding or subtracting tens. They may not know how to use known facts to help work out equations using multiples of ten.
nodes.response: Reinforce understanding of unitising by describing groups of objects in ones or tens. Make the link between known facts and equations using multiples of ten explicit. Show it with equipment such as base ten blocks and represent on place value charts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract multiples of ten

nodes.misconception: Children may get the tens and teens numbers confused and may muddle up the digits when writing the numerals.
nodes.response: Show numbers on a place value chart and talk about what each number represents. Take time to over pronounce teen and multiples of 10 words focusing on the sound of -teen and -ty and encouraging learners to practise with silly voices.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent multiples of ten using their numerals and names

nodes.misconception: Children may not see the link between adding ones and adding tens. They may add or subtract one instead of ten or muddle addition and subtraction, so may subtract ten instead of add ten to a number.
nodes.response: Reinforce understanding of unitising by describing each group of objects in ones or tens, e.g. five cubes plus 1 cube, 5 tens plus 1 ten and talk through what is happening. Show this with equipment in tens and ones such as straws or cubes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what happens when you add and subtract ten to a multiple of ten

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to draw their own number lines accurately.
nodes.response: Encourage children to mark the midpoint and equally space the numbers by using fingers or an object to space them out.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate the position of multiples of ten on a 0 - 100 number line

nodes.misconception: May initially struggle with first and second as they do not contain the number names one and two.
nodes.response: Link these names to their shortened written forms (1st and 2nd) so children can see their relationship to one and two.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ordinal numbers

nodes.misconception: Errors in counting things that cannot be seen, touched or moved.
nodes.response: Leave only short pauses between sounds to avoid the need for children to hold numbers in their heads. Make actions clear and separate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Anything can be counted

nodes.misconception: Saying number names out of order or missing a number name in the sequence.
nodes.response: Repeat the number names in the correct order, emphasising the correction made.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting forwards and backwards within 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that a count with a missing number or number in the wrong place is incorrect.
nodes.response: Reinforce the stable order of counting to and from 10 and highlight clearly when the order is not correct or there is a number missing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding the missing numbers

nodes.misconception: May identify which number is greater than or less than another but then sequence incorrectly.
nodes.response: Encourage children to visualise each number on a number line so they can see their order. Print a number line for constant use in class.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ordering numbers to 10

nodes.misconception: Unnecessarily re-counting all objects in a group rather than counting on from an existing amount.
nodes.response: Repeat the key sentence, 'we start our count at ___, and we count ___'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting different groups

nodes.misconception: If using slides, not recognising objects have been rearranged and counting all again.
nodes.response: Gather objects to manipulate (either under a visualiser with the whole class, or in front of a small group) so that children can clearly see that none have been added or taken away.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Conservation

nodes.misconception: Mixing numerals eg. 6 and 9
nodes.response: Draw attention to each digit and explore their similarities and differences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using numerals

nodes.misconception: Reliance on counting strategies. Not recognising combinations of smaller quantities within 5
nodes.response: Play games involving dice outside of the lesson to encourage subitising of more familiar arrangements. Then, look at those unfamiliar, such as the way a group of cubes appears when dropped onto a table. 'I can see ___ and ___. I can see ___!'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subitising numbers to five

nodes.misconception: May consider the size of objects when comparing rather than the numerosity of the group.
nodes.response: Ensure any groups compared throughout the day are very obviously different before comparing more small things with fewer large things.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: More than and fewer than

nodes.misconception: Know later, when zero is added to another number, some children believe the answer is zero.
nodes.response: Secure the idea that zero shows that there is no amount in many ways. Give children zero [noun] to hold.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing zero

nodes.misconception: Missing out an object or counting one twice. Recounting without concluding how many there are.
nodes.response: Encourage using one finger to move and count each object. From the third learning cycle, repeat 'there are ___ [noun]' following a count.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting objects within ten

nodes.misconception: Inaccurate representation of the number rhymes.
nodes.response: Once again, ensure all children have access to any countable objects needed and ensure the visuals on the slides are not replied upon. Take time to revisit early counting principles, modelling how these can be used to help represent a given visual.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing counting songs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start counting on the number given and not recognise that the number before is one less.
nodes.response: Model counting back and highlight the number before alongside the manipulatives. Give opportunities for pupils to remove one from a set.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: One less with manipulatives and counting

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start counting on the number given and not recognise that the next number is one more.
nodes.response: Model the counting on and highlight the next number alongside the manipulatives. Give opportunities for pupils to add in one more to a set.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: One more with manipulatives and counting

nodes.misconception: Pupils put a digit in the ones column instead of the tenths column to represent a number of tenths.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents, linking back to the place value chart and the role of the decimal point.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe and represent tenths as a decimal number

nodes.misconception: Recording ten tenths as 0.10 rather than 1 or 1.0
nodes.response: Be sure to address this regularly with pupils whilst counting. Demonstrate the regrouping using place value counters to help.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count tenths in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that because a representation has more images/items then it is a larger number.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider the value of each image/item and say this verbally as ___ wholes and ___ tenths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order decimal numbers with tenths

nodes.misconception: Pupils write whole numbers as tenths incorrectly, for example as eight tenths not eighty tenths.
nodes.response: Reiterate that ten tenths are equal to one whole so twenty tenths are equal to two wholes. Continue this to build generalisation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe and write decimal numbers with tenths in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils think one tenth consists of one shaded part and ten un-shaded parts.
nodes.response: Encourage children to use the stem sentence to identify the whole and how many parts make it up each time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify tenths as part of a whole

nodes.misconception: Getting numbers in the wrong order when completing the stem sentences with one more and one less.
nodes.response: Use the representations to identify and support understanding of which value is one less and which is one more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding one more and one less using representations

nodes.misconception: Missing out numbers in the teens especially when counting backwards.
nodes.response: Repeat the count and stress the missing numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting to and from 20

nodes.misconception: Missing out numbers in the count or not being able to start the count if not at 1.
nodes.response: Give a three number count in to establish a pattern before asking children to join in so 7, 8, 9 given before the children say 10.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting on

nodes.misconception: Not being secure with the order of the numbers from 11 to 20 when not starting at 0 or 1.
nodes.response: Practice counting starting from different points within 11 to 20 and model the first 3 to establish a pattern.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding the missing number from 0 to 20

nodes.misconception: You can't compare and order numbers that are not next to each other in the counting sequence.
nodes.response: Start with numbers close together in the counting sequence and move on to numbers with a larger gap.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ordering numbers 11- 20 practically

nodes.misconception: Failing to match one count to one action.
nodes.response: Slow the counting and make the action and count very deliberately at the same time so pupils can imitate the modelling.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting forward to 20 and back from 20

nodes.misconception: You can compare numbers that are more than one apart and say which numbers are one more or one less.
nodes.response: Make it clear whether pupils are comparing numbers or whether they are giving the values that are one more and one less.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and ordering numbers 0-20 practically

nodes.misconception: Linking one more or one less than a number to the number after or before in the count.
nodes.response: Use objects to model one more being added or one being removed to show one less or fewer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing numbers to 20

nodes.misconception: Knowing the number before when counting backwards.
nodes.response: Giving 2 or 3 numbers to establish a pattern then reducing to 2 and then just the given number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting back from 20

nodes.misconception: Incorrect sequence of counting when recalling the next and previous numbers.
nodes.response: Start with parts of the sequence where pupils are confident to secure the concept of counting on for one more and back for one less.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding one more and one less with manipulatives and images

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency with number facts to 20 can hinder progress in applying them to multiples of ten.
nodes.response: Ensure that fluency with number facts to 20 and related subtraction facts is secure or supported so that pupils can apply them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Bridge 100 by subtracting in multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils lack fluency in pairs for 10 and so struggle to connect this to 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Promote fluency through games and chants and consider providing a scaffold of pairs for 10 which will help pupils develop automaticity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiples of 10 that total 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils not understanding what the problem is asking them to find out and identifying the operation.
nodes.response: Model the use of bar models and manipulatives to represent the problem and how to identify the operation and calculations needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using knowledge of addition and subtraction of multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency with number facts to 20 can hinder progress in applying them to multiples of ten.
nodes.response: Ensure that fluency with number facts to 20 is secure or supported so that pupils can apply them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Bridge 100 by adding in multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be less efficient if they are not fluent with bonds within 10 e.g. 3 + 6 = 9
nodes.response: Provide additional scaffolding as appropriate including examples of pairs that total 9 and 10
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to find complements to 100 efficiently

nodes.misconception: Pupils should not be encouraged to think about 'adding a zero' to the 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Make careful use of the stem sentences and representations to make sure that pupils are clear that e.g. 12 tens is equal to 120.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent 3-digit multiples of 10 in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not identify that ten tens are equal to 100 and cannot decompose 100 in this way.
nodes.response: Base ten blocks or a bead string are useful tools to allow pupils to compose and decompose 100 into equal groups of ten.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Composition of 100 in 10s and 1s

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe only multiples of 10 can compose 100 and therefore do not see four groups of 25.
nodes.response: Focus on practical representations e.g. bead strings and base 10 blocks where 100 can be composed and decomposed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Composition of 100 in 50s, 25s and 20s

nodes.misconception: Identifying the parts and wholes in a problem or given context.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentences and representations of part-part-whole and bar models to support pupils in identifying the parts and whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use place value knowledge to write addition and subtraction equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils lack fluency in pairs for 10 and so struggle to connect this to 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Promote fluency through games and chants and consider providing a scaffold of pairs for 10 for pupils to use which automaticity develops.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to find pairs of numbers that total 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils say the previous multiple of one as a whole before e.g. previous multiple of 3.4 as 2 or 2.4
nodes.response: Place the number on a number line and clarify the whole numbers it sits between.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use representations to round a decimal number with tenths to the nearest whole number

nodes.misconception: Pupils understand the equals sign as 'where the answer is' rather than equality between expressions.
nodes.response: Spend time moving addition and subtraction expressions to either side of the equals sign using numbers within 10 before moving to tenths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that decimal numbers with tenths can be composed additively

nodes.misconception: Pupils record missing part equations incorrectly.
nodes.response: Encourage children to match the equation to a representation identifying which number represents the wholes and which represent parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts and mental strategies to calculate with decimal numbers within and across a whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils write equations involving both addition and multiplication incorrectly.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to match their equation to an image provided and be clear about where the numbers in their equation come from.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that decimal numbers with tenths can be composed multiplicatively

nodes.misconception: Pupils regroup incorrectly, particularly when subtracting e.g. exchanging one ten for ten ones.
nodes.response: Build the calculation using place value counters on a grid set out like a column method. Ask pupils to represent regrouping with counters.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of column addition and subtraction to calculate with decimal numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the connection between known facts and calculating using multiples of one hundred.
nodes.response: Place value counters or Base 10 blocks may be helpful with getting children to unitise and see the connection between, for example,  14 − 7 and 1,400 − 700
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use different strategies to subtract multiples of 100

nodes.misconception: For some questions in this lesson, there is more than one possible answer, but all may not provide the solution to the problem posed. Pupils may give the first (incorrect) answer that they find.
nodes.response: For the second task, encourage pupils to distinguish between questions that only have one solution and those that have multiple solutions. Modelling your thinking throughout the second learning cycle is key to supporting pupils to access the task.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use addition and subtraction strategies to solve problems with multiples of 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not make the connection between 10 hundreds, 100 tens and 1 thousand as they may find it difficult to visualise 1,000
nodes.response: Secure understanding of 1,000 using a range of representations: counting up on number lines divided differently, showing Base 10 blocks that are equivalent to a one thousand block and even exploring within the context of money.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how many hundreds, tens and ones 1,000 is composed of

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see that larger numbers can be composed in different ways.
nodes.response: Use place value charts to show pupils how numbers can be composed in different ways (e.g. 1700 = 17 hundreds, 170 tens or 1700 ones). Make clear links to how we can read the number and how this helps us to describe what it is composed of.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use place value to compose numbers up to 2,000 using hundreds, tens and ones

nodes.misconception: Pupils may initially find it tricky to use known facts to add multiples of 100
nodes.response: When explaining that we can use 3 ones + 6 ones = 9 ones to find 3 hundreds + 6 hundreds = ___, stress that the only thing that changes here is the noun.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use different strategies to add multiples of 100

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to not immediately rush to making use of a written method such as columns addition.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to be resilient and remind them that practice makes perfect.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using redistribution with addition of decimal fractions

nodes.misconception: Lots of children will want to make use of a written method such as column addition straight away without considering the use of mental methods with jottings.
nodes.response: Encourage the children out of their comfort zone by praising efforts  and allowing them to feel motivated by any small successes in the method. Explain to them that this understanding will help them to be better mathematicians in the long run!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using redistribution with addition of integers

nodes.misconception: Often, pupils understand the equals symbol to be a big reveal or a 'ta-da!' rather than a symbol denoting equivalence. This can make the idea of a balanced equation tricky.
nodes.response: Explore pupils' understanding of the equal sign at the start of the lesson. For children who still find it a tricky concept, make use of bucket scales and plasticine to explore equivalence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a balanced equation to calculate unknown parts

nodes.misconception: Many pupils understand the equals symbol as 'makes' or a the symbol you simply place in front of the answer. This can make the idea of a balanced equation tricky, undoing concepts like adjustment.
nodes.response: Get all the pupils to write an expression (as unique as possible) that is equal to 10 and display them in the classroom. Ask the children what symbol could be placed between all of them and explore why.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how adjusting one part affects the sum
