nodes.misconception: Pupils may be very quick to try and use a written method such as columns here, particularly as the numbers get larger.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to refrain and reward them taking risks and avoiding using written methods as much as possible. Prove to them that it's quicker to do it in your head or with jottings by racing your fastest 'columns ' exponent!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve addition calculations mentally by using known facts in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: The children might be inclined not to look at previous equations to help them. They might not make use of the adjustments to the whole.
nodes.response: Practise some really simple versions. Start with 1 + 2 = 3 and then ask them to adjust 3 by a single-digit number. Write this underneath and then ask them which part has changed and by how much? How do they know?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve calculations with missing parts

nodes.misconception: The brackets are intended to make it easier for pupils to distinguish between different parts of the expression. Brackets are unfamiliar to learners so may cause errors.
nodes.response: If the brackets lead to confusion then remove them and use colour or some other signifier. Pupils needs to be able to see, understand and analyse any changes through redistribution.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using balanced equations to calculate redistribution

nodes.misconception: The idea of an extra cost being an addition and a saving being a subtraction can seem counter-intuitive to some children.
nodes.response: Talk through a more basic version using a pound for a budget and sweets at a tuck shop.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use equivalence and compensation strategies to solve addition problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils might find it hard to understand that they needn't recalculate the parts after adjustment if the question wants the new whole.
nodes.response: Show jottings and workings for two examples side-by-side. In the 1st example, calculate all the parts after adjustment as well as the new whole. In the 2nd, calculate only the new whole. Discuss with the pupils which is the most efficient and why.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use equivalence and compensation strategies to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to understand that recalculating the adjusted part is an unnecessary step.
nodes.response: Display two sets of workings side-by-side. In the 1st, show the adjusted part being recalculated. In the 2nd, show it without recalculating the part. Pupils will hopefully see that the solution emerges from both.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve addition calculations mentally by using known facts

nodes.misconception: Children may think counting stops at 100 or the regularity of the pattern does not extend past 100
nodes.response: Count beyond 100 when rote counting, trailing off after 103 or 104 and discussing what would be next to make explicit that numbers do not 'end' at 10. Show numbers past 100 on equipment used.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore the counting sequence for counting to 100 and beyond

nodes.misconception: Children may continue counting in tens when they reach the ones, e.g. count 2 tens and 3 ones completely in tens. They may think arrangement of tens and ones affects how to count them.
nodes.response: Make deliberate errors to prompt discussion and refer back to previous stem sentences, e.g. 'The objects are in ones, so I can count them in ones.' Present tens and ones in non-standard arrangements, so children practise always counting tens first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count a large group of objects by counting tens and ones

nodes.misconception: When representing two-digit numbers practically, children may start each number anew, instead of using what they know about number patterns to adapt existing representations.
nodes.response: Use the questions 'What's the same?' and 'What's different?' to draw attention to the patterns in number sequences and how these can be used. Link the abstract to the pictorial and concrete by drawing attention to what each digit represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent a number from 20 to 99

nodes.misconception: Children may only think of 'ones' in terms of the extra ones after the tens have been grouped, so may fail to see 45, for example, as 45 ones as well as 4 tens and 5 ones.
nodes.response: When objects are grouped in tens, use deliberate errors and discussion to draw attention to the total number of ones represented by the number, so children are familiar with recognising both the extra ones and the total number of ones in a number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count groups of ten and extra ones

nodes.misconception: When finding the previous multiple of ten, children may misapply what they know about counting in tens. For example, they may think 30 is before 40, so think 30 is the multiple of ten before 45
nodes.response: Make deliberate errors to discuss and encourage children to visualise, then label, their own number lines marked in tens.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a number line to position and estimate the numbers 20-99

nodes.misconception: Pupils may record two-digit hundredth values incorrectly. For example 12 hundredths as 0.012
nodes.response: Use place value counters to represent the number and demonstrate the regrouping of ten hundredths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe and represent hundredths as a decimal number

nodes.misconception: Pupils write subtraction equations incorrectly for example: 7.42 = 7 − 0.4 − 0.02
nodes.response: Create the number using place value counters and subtract parts whilst drawing a part-whole model and writing the equation alongside.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that decimal numbers with hundredths can be partitioned in different ways

nodes.misconception: When crossing the tenth boundary, pupils count ten hundredths as 'zero point zero ten'.
nodes.response: Use cardinal representations to guide the pupil's counting so ten hundredths and one tenth equivalence can be discussed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe and write decimal numbers with hundredths in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only attribute one hundredth to an area model being broken into one hundred equal parts.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils see one hundredth in both linear and cardinal examples too.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify hundredths as part of a whole

nodes.misconception: A number with more digits after the decimal point is greater than a number with fewer digits.
nodes.response: Create the numbers using place value counters or base 10 blocks and re-iterate the magnitude of each digit within the number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order decimal numbers with hundredths

nodes.misconception: Lots of children have an understanding of goal difference from experiences outside the classroom but this might be the first time some children have encountered it and it may cause confusion.
nodes.response: Consider pre-teaching if that is a possibility or introduce it in a PE context to begin with. You could even keep score of any playtime games for the days leading up to the lesson to give some real life context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use equivalence and compensation strategies to solve subtraction problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Many pupils will try to adjust the difference in the same way that the subtrahend has been adjusted without considering the use of the inverse.
nodes.response: Start simply with double-sided counters to show the concept practically.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the difference using knowledge of an adjusted subtrahend: difference structure

nodes.misconception: Known facts in this lesson include complements and two-digit subtractions which some children may find challenging to recall fluently.
nodes.response: It's a good idea, if possible, to do some pre-teaching here to develop the confidence of the children who might find the known facts aspect provides extra cognitive load. Supplying scaffolds such as key bonds to 20 and 100 may also benefit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve subtraction calculations mentally by using known facts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to understand the purpose of transforming calculations using constant difference, especially if they are less confident in calculating using mental strategies.
nodes.response: Show pupils sequences of calculations with a constant difference and get them to spot which of them is easiest to complete. Start as simply as you need to here. Constant difference is a helpful tool not a new method designed to lower confidence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how constant difference can make written calculations more efficient

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that if the subtrahend increases or decreases then so too does the difference. They might find it initially difficult to understand the idea of the inverse in the context.
nodes.response: Give lots of practical examples of this such as emptying out bottles or eating sweets demonstrating an increase in the subtrahend and its effect on the difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how adjusting the subtrahend affects the difference: reduction structure

nodes.misconception: Children might struggle to describe the changes accurately using mathematical language.
nodes.response: Make good use of your learning walls here to display the key vocabulary and stem sentences for the children to use for the description of the changes in the equations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how increasing or decreasing the minuend affects the difference

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be eager to use columnar written methods for larger integers and decimals instead of considering the values and using an efficient strategy.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of trying different mental methods so that pupils aren't reliant on written methods that prevent them from fully grasping the underlying structure of additive problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how adjusting the minuend can make mental calculation easier

nodes.misconception: Lots of pupils will want to calculate the value of the expression with the known parts in order to calculate the unknown part without considering a more efficient approach.
nodes.response: Calculating the value of one expression is efficient with simple numbers but encourage the children to try and compare the parts instead. As the numbers get harder, calculating the expression becomes much less efficient.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use constant difference to balance equations and find unknowns

nodes.misconception: The proportionality of bar models is something that children sometimes find tricky and causes them concern.
nodes.response: Remind them that accuracy is not completely necessary so long as they have roughly sized the parts (subtrahend and difference in these contexts). Alternatively, give them number rods to arrange as bar models and then draw around.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how adjusting the subtrahend affects the difference: partitioning

nodes.misconception: The concept of constant difference is difficult to understand when looking simply at abstract equations and numerals and pupils may find it challenging to 'see' the underlying structure of the maths.
nodes.response: Make good use of physical resources to reinforce the idea of constant difference. Number rods coupled with rulers or number lines can be very useful here. Take time with smaller values so pupils can generalise.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain and represent constant difference for subtraction

nodes.misconception: Children may reverse the digits in a two-digit number, not understanding the value of each digit, or partition, for example, 54 into 5 and 4
nodes.response: Return to the use of practical equipment and ask children to prove they are right using it. They could also explain their ideas to a friend to encourage them to spot their own errors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition two-digit numbers into tens and ones

nodes.misconception: Children may think that they must see both the tens and ones in a two-digit number to compare them. They may also reverse the tens and ones and compare the ones first.
nodes.response: Ensure that numbers with the ones digit hidden are given to compare so that children can appreciate the relative size of the numbers. Use practical equipment and stem sentences to consolidate understanding of the structure of two-digit numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare two-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may fail to appreciate the importance of the equals sign in an equation, e.g. making errors such as 16 = 4 + 20, or confuse the value of the digits, making errors such as 43 = 4 + 30
nodes.response: Use the language of parts and whole to activate/link to prior learning. Encourage drawing of own part-part-whole models. Encourage children to spot errors and explain why they are are incorrect and to articulate their thinking around correct answers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent addition and subtraction of tens and ones with equations

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse addition and subtraction on bar models and in problems, so may add instead of subtracting or subtract instead of adding.
nodes.response: Cuisenaire rods or strips of paper with numbers written upon them can be manipulated as bar models that represent a problem or equation. This way, the structure of the mathematics can be discussed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems by adding and subtracting tens and ones

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the importance of the order of the tens and ones digits in indicating the value of each part of a two-digit number.
nodes.response: Use place value charts, place value arrows and Gattegno charts to reinforce the value of each digit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition two-digit numbers into tens and ones using place value resources

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle crossing over the hundreds boundary (99 to 100, and back from 100 to 99).
nodes.response: It may help pupils to understand that 100 is ten lots of ten. This is the lesson focus and pupils will have lots of practise opportunities.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count across and on from 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have difficultly partitioning 10s when crossing the 100s boundary. (e.g. 125 - 40)
nodes.response: Pupils practice adding to/subtracting from multiples of 10 (e.g. 130 - 50) before exploring non-multiples of 10 (e.g. 85 + 30)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Cross the hundreds boundary when adding and subtracting any 2-digit multiple of 10

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make errors when crossing the 100s boundary, either when adding or subtracting.
nodes.response: Emphasise that ten 10s are equal to 100. When using base ten blocks, pupils should be encouraged to change ten 10s into one hundred.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find 10 more or 10 less than a given number

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not partition numbers in efficient ways to add and subtract them.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add or subtract to make 100 (e.g. when calculating 103-7, subtract 3 to equal 100, then subtract 4 to equal 96).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Bridge 100 by adding or subtracting a single-digit number

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misread numbers when using number lines (e.g. read 105 as 95).
nodes.response: Encourage children to say the 10s number before and after (e.g. the number is in between 100 and 110).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent a 3-digit number up to 199 in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may miscalculate measures questions involving unit conversions if they are not secure with the key conversions of 1 m = 1,000 mm, 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 l = 1,000 ml.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing the etymology of the words so pupils are not necessarily relying on memory and can figure out the equivalences if they cannot recall them. 'Milli' means 'thousandth' and 'kilo' means 'thousand': both relate to a thousand parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partitioning 1,000 in the context of measures

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between partitioning 100 into 2, 4, 5 and 10 equal parts and partitioning 1,000 into those equal parts.
nodes.response: You may wish to revisit partitioning 100 into equal parts, using representations familiar to pupils, to help them to understand that their knowledge of partitioning 100 can be applied to partitioning 1,000
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partitioning 1,000 and 2,000 in the context of measures

nodes.misconception: When reading bar graphs with unmarked intervals, some pupils might assume each interval equals 1. In the case of the graphs presented in this lesson, the intervals go up in 100s, 200s, 250s and 500s.
nodes.response: Encourage children to apply their knowledge of converting a unit into 1,000 (such as 1 litre being converted into 1,000 ml) and then exploring its composition in 2, 4, 5 and 10 equal parts. Check the unmarked intervals by counting in those steps.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of measure conversions to interpret graphs and tables

nodes.misconception: Pupils can be misled by the meaning of the prefix 'milli', as it sounds like one million. They therefore presume a millimetre is one millionth of a metre, or that one metre is one million millimetres.
nodes.response: The etymology of the prefixes 'milli' and 'kilo' are discussed in the lesson. You may wish to extend this by talking about other examples. Adding the words and their meanings to your Maths area will serve as a useful reminder, as will flash cards.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of 1,000 to explain common measure conversions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may need support to identify the operation(s) involved in solving a problem and when a problem is presented with mixed units and it is necessary to convert one of them.
nodes.response: Read the problems aloud. Ensure that children identify the operation(s) involved and see this as a clear step in solving the problem. Emphasise the units of measure so that attention is drawn to them and they identify whether conversion is needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use efficient strategies and common measure conversions to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Confusion between teen and decade numbers, e.g. 19 and 90, leading to errors in counting 80, 90, 20
nodes.response: Regular identification and discussion of common errors with opportunities to correct them within this lesson can be replicated beyond it.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting forwards and backwards in 10s to 100

nodes.misconception: May confuse decade number names with teen numbers e.g. thirteen, thirty.
nodes.response: Regular identification and discussion of common errors with opportunities to correct them within this lesson can be replicated beyond it.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting forwards and backwards in 10s to 50

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only consecutive numbers can be ordered.
nodes.response: Order non-consecutive numbers, then place back with other numbers on number track to consolidate understanding of their relative size.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Order and compare decade numbers on number tracks

nodes.misconception: When objects are in 10s, children may count the number of tens rather than the amount altogether.
nodes.response: Introduce errors involving confusion between the number of tens and the amount altogether for children to reason about.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count groups of 10 in decade numbers

nodes.misconception: Any group of objects can be counted in tens.
nodes.response: Identify groups that do and do not have 10 objects, drawing attention to the fact that colour, orientation and size are not relevant.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Composition of decade numbers to 100: making groups of 10

nodes.misconception: A tricky digit for many pupils to consider is 0 because the rounded number is often the same as the original number. Pupils are often tempted to round to the multiple before the one they should.
nodes.response: Spend some time establishing with pupils that occasionally when zeroes are involved, the number does not actually change when it is rounded. Number lines are a great visual support when rounding, including in this aspect.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Round a 4-digit number to the nearest hundred and ten

nodes.misconception: The tricky part when it comes to rounding is the digit 5: as the number lines in the lesson illustrate, a 4-digit number ending in 500 is equidistant to the previous and next multiples of 1,000
nodes.response: Take time to recognise the convention that when the number is equidistant to the previous and next multiple we round to the next multiple. Use examples and non-examples to show this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what rounding is and round a 4-digit number to the nearest thousand

nodes.misconception: Sometimes pupils forget to change all of the necessary digits when rounding. For example, when rounding 4,698 to the nearest hundred, they might say 4,798
nodes.response: Make sure you spend time really focusing on the parts of the slide deck that show that when rounding to the nearest thousand, the answer must be a multiple of 1,000; the same principle applies when rounding to the nearest 100 or 10
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Round a 4-digit number to the nearest thousand, hundred and ten

nodes.misconception: Zero is a tricky concept for some pupils when it comes to place value. For example, pupils might struggle to read and understand the number 2,087, or struggle to express in numbers a representation.
nodes.response: Blank place value grids are an excellent scaffold. Give pupils ample opportunities to explore using them both with concrete resources such as counters and with numerals, practising reading and writing the number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use place value and number facts to decompose 4-digit numbers in different ways

nodes.misconception: Some pupils do not realise that it is not always necessary to consider all of the digits when comparing or ordering numbers. For example, when comparing 3,974 and 7,832, the thousands are different.
nodes.response: Develop a systematic approach, such that pupils always begin by checking to see if the thousands are the same, then if necessary the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones. Counters and place value grids can really help to exemplify this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order 4-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils count the interval markers to find how many parts the whole has been divided into.
nodes.response: Identify clearly which whole you are dividing and link the bar model to the numberline to show how the intervals reveal the number of parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of decimal place value to solve problems in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when a whole is divided into x parts, they need to have x interval markers.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make connections between the bar model and the number line, drawing attention to where each whole has been divided.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that different lengths can be composed additively and multiplicatively

nodes.misconception: Where regroupings are required, pupils may not be concise in their jottings.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to articulate what each number represents in each calculation, demonstrating the calculations with place value counters.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of column addition and subtraction to calculate with decimals: tenths and hundredths

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look to adopt a formal written strategy straight away when this is not necessary.
nodes.response: Share different strategies utilised by pupils within the lesson and compare these to expand pupils' understanding of efficiency.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems with numbers with up to 3 decimal places

nodes.misconception: Pupils mistake numbers with more digits after the decimal point to be the larger number.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to build numbers with base 10 blocks, enabling them to see the magnitude of the numbers they compare.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order numbers with up to 3 decimal places

nodes.misconception: Pupils may write for example 3 cm as 0.3 m.
nodes.response: Make connections between the headings in the place value chart and images that represent metres, tenths of metres and centimetres.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of decimal place value to convert between and compare metres and centimetres

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistake the previous multiple of one for example: previous multiple of 6.38 being 5.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are given plenty of opportunities to place numbers on number lines, identifying the previous and next multiples of one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Round a decimal number with hundredths to the nearest whole number

nodes.misconception: When recording which multiple of 0.1 a number is nearest to, pupils may forget to include the ones.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils have plenty of opportunities to continue counting and rounding with multiples of 0.1 beyond one whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Round a decimal number with hundredths to the nearest tenth

nodes.misconception: Pupils use a known fact but add or subtract with different place values (e.g. 0.6 + 0.04 = 0.1).
nodes.response: Unitise through the use of language to help identify this for pupils. For example: 6 hundredths plus 4 hundredths is equal to 10 hundredths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of place value to calculate with decimal numbers up to and bridging one tenth

nodes.misconception: Pupils record numbers like 29 thousandths incorrectly as 0.0029
nodes.response: Continue to link representations of thousandths to the place value chart and use language of ten thousandths being equal to one hundredth.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read and write numbers with up to 3 decimal places

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to see that a double is two of the same thing.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring doubles that can be found in the children's immediate environment e.g. using their hands or playing a game of dominoes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recall doubles within 10

nodes.misconception: Without correct representation, children may struggle to know what to calculate.
nodes.response: If needed, provide support at this stage so that the structure of the mathematics is clear to children.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent addition and subtraction facts within 10

nodes.misconception: Children could try to apply this idea to other near-double facts that may be more easily solved using other strategies.
nodes.response: 0 + 1 and 1 + 2 are near-doubles, but these are more easily solved using the 'one more'/ 'one less' strategy. Explore this together before leading children to the most efficient strategy for calculating.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use near doubles within 10

nodes.misconception: Children may resort to counting strategies to find the difference e.g. counting back to subtract. Children may incorrectly identify the even/odd number 'before' or 'after' the one given.
nodes.response: Provide practice for children to identify numbers before/after or odd/even numbers before/after a given one. Initially, allow children to use a number line. Remove this scaffold once feeling more confident.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recall one and two more or less than numbers to ten

nodes.misconception: Children may still make errors when selecting the most appropriate strategy to aid their recall e.g. they may see 7 - 2 = and count back in ones rather than seeing that 5 is the odd number before 7
nodes.response: Always talk about the equation to solve, modelling thinking processes e.g. 'I can see... so I know.... The table in the first learning cycle, organising facts by the strategies used to recall them, can be displayed within the learning environment.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known addition and subtraction facts within 10 to solve problems

nodes.misconception: The length or height of an object is the numerical value at the end of the ruler (if not at zero).
nodes.response: If an object is not measured from zero, its length is the difference between the numerical value at the start and end of the object.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring length and height using cm and mm

nodes.misconception: E.g. 30 mm is not equivalent to 3 cm because 30 is a larger number.
nodes.response: 10 mm are equivalent to 1 cm. Millimetres are smaller than centimetres and 10 mm are needed to make an equivalent length to 1 cm.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Converting between centimetres and millimetres

nodes.misconception: Mistakes may be made on comparison problems. E.g. how much further does one child jump than another?
nodes.response: When we compare, we are finding the difference.  To find the difference, we need to subtract the smaller value from the larger value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using graphs to represent lengths and heights

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that 300 cm is bigger than 3 m because 300 is a bigger number than 3.
nodes.response: 1 m is equivalent to 100 cm. So 3 m is equivalent to 300 cm. 3 m and 300 cm are equal in length or height.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Converting between metres and centimetres

nodes.misconception: Children may mistake which unit to measure in or may struggle to estimate.
nodes.response: This is one 1 m/1 cm length.  How many of these do you think would be the same as the length/height of the object being measured?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate and measure lengths and heights and record in a table

nodes.misconception: Children may think that 10 mm are larger than 1 cm.
nodes.response: There are 10 mm in 1 cm.  1 cm is made up of 10 mm.  10 mm and 1 cm are equivalent in length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Millimetres as a unit of measure and the relationship between them and cm

nodes.misconception: 100 cm is bigger than 1 m.
nodes.response: 1 m is equal in length or height to 100 cm.  100 cm make up 1 m.  They are the same length or height.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate in metres and describe a metre in different ways

nodes.misconception: The length or height of an object is the numerical value at the end of the ruler (if not at zero).
nodes.response: If an object is not measured from zero, its length is the difference between the numerical value at the start and end of the object.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure length and height from zero using whole m or cm

nodes.misconception: Converting between units; interpreting a word problem; confusing parts and wholes.
nodes.response: When representing as a bar model, visualise the problem to help determine what the parts are and what the whole is.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving length and height

nodes.misconception: Drawing tables and graphs from scratch can be tricky for some children.
nodes.response: Provide scaffolds of tables and graphs where necessary.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving length

nodes.misconception: Confusion when counting select rows on a one hundred square, e.g. children may not use the end of the number (the ones) to help them count accurately, or may say the row ending in 40 is the 'forties'.
nodes.response: Label 'decades' throughout the lesson, and model errors in counting within these so that children get used to hearing when the count doesn't sound right.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting patterns within a decade

nodes.misconception: Difficulty finding missing numbers when more than one number missing is from a number track.
nodes.response: Encourage and model how to visualise numbers using the numbers that can be seen.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find missing numbers between 20  and 100

nodes.misconception: Confusion around the numbers which cross the tens boundary, e.g. 39, 40 may say 39, 30
nodes.response: Make errors for the children to discuss; encourage them to  explain and correct mistakes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Crossing the tens boundary counting forwards and backwards

nodes.misconception: Confusion regarding the number before the decade numbers, e.g. saying 30, 39
nodes.response: Explicitly look at the patterns in numbers that precede a decade number and discuss errors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Crossing the tens boundary counting backwards

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the number after 29, 39 etc. so saying 29,20 or twenty-none, twenty -ten.
nodes.response: Explicitly look at the numbers that follow a number ending in 9 using stem sentence to support.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Crossing the tens boundary counting forwards

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to accurately represent the story as an equation.
nodes.response: Ensure that children are able to say what each number represents in a given equation using the story as a scaffold before asking them to write their own equations to represent ‘First, then, then, now’ stories.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a 'First, then, then, now' story to add three addends

nodes.misconception: Children unable to understand that addends can be swapped but the sum will remain the same.
nodes.response: Use a number line to explore commutativity in a situation where it looks less obvious as this will show children the different structures but also different starting pints but the end pint will remain the same.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add three addends efficiently

nodes.misconception: If children record incorrectly, they could re-add an addend that has already been used to make a pair to 10
nodes.response: Carefully model how to record thinking, rewriting the new equation inclusive of 10 underneath.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add three addends efficiently by finding two addends that total 10

nodes.misconception: Using less and fewer incorrectly when describing and comparing.
nodes.response: Reinforce 'fewer' is used for things we can count (not as many) and 'less' is used for things we cannot count (not as much). Explore a range of examples of this together.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare the number of objects in two sets or difference between two measures.

nodes.misconception: Children use ten frames but use them to ‘count all’ or ‘count on’ without making 10
nodes.response: Ten frames can provide a great scaffold for all in this lesson when used to 'make 10'. Stress that we partition an addend to make 10 and that once the ten frame is full, it shows one ten so we do not need to count them all.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add two numbers that bridge through 10

nodes.misconception: Children may make mistakes when adopting more mental strategies.
nodes.response: Leave scaffolds in place until showing confidence in verbal explanation. For example, once confident visualising 'making 10' using the ten frame, remove the scaffold of the ten frame and counters.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract two numbers that bridge through 10

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand that either pair of addends can be added first and the sum will remain the same.
nodes.response: Use concrete materials to represent the addends for children to explore, discussing what is the same (the addends) and what is different (the pair being added first).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that the addends can be added in any order

nodes.misconception: Recording a subtraction to show difference incorrectly e.g. knowing that the difference between 4 and 6 is 2, but recording this as 4 - 6 = 2
nodes.response: Stress we can compare 6 to 4 or 4 to 6, but remind children that subtraction is not commutative so the whole (/ the larger number of those being compared) has to be written first in the expression. We can however change the position of the = symbol.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the difference

nodes.misconception: Children may not recognise given subtraction calculations that involve consecutive numbers and will resort to other strategies to calculate.
nodes.response: Recording equations alongside concrete or pictorial representations (such as cubes or a number line) will help children to visualise the difference and become more confident in spotting equations that contain consecutive numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what the difference is between consecutive numbers

nodes.misconception: Without correct representation, children may struggle to know what to calculate.
nodes.response: If needed, provide support at this stage so that the structure of the mathematics is clear to children.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of calculating within 20 to solve problems

nodes.misconception: When comparing the larger to the smaller number and then the smaller to the larger number, children may record this as 15 - 8 = ? and 8 - 15 = ?
nodes.response: When finding the difference, we can compare the larger to the smaller number and the smaller to the larger number. Stress that each time, we record this in the same way as subtraction isn't commutative (whole - part = part).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the difference when information is presented in a pictogram

nodes.misconception: Children may initially struggle to read and interpret the data on the bar chart / graph.
nodes.response: A ruler can be used to help children line up the top of the bar with the scale. Model this as a strategy to support accurate reading.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the difference when information is presented in a bar chart

nodes.misconception: Children think that 'counting on' is used solely as a strategy in addition.
nodes.response: Children should be made aware that the strategy for 'counting on' can be used in addition but is used as a strategy for subtraction in this lesson where we are finding the difference between two numbers close in value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the difference in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to correctly read the information presented within the pictogram/bar chart.
nodes.response: A ruler can be used to help children line up the top of the bar with the scale. Model this as a strategy to support accurate reading.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of calculating within 20 to solve problems involving statistics

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between the concrete, pictorial and abstract representations.
nodes.response: When using the part–part–whole representation, make sure you explicitly connect each number with what it represents. Ask the children to describe what they can see using the full stem sentences. 'The ___ represents the __________.'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add three addends

nodes.misconception: Trying to subtract 3 from 2 for example without regrouping and seeing the difference as 1
nodes.response: Continually acknowledge the whole and the parts in each 'column' so that children know what we have and what is being subtracted.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract 4-digit numbers using column subtraction

nodes.misconception: When using adjustment (e.g. 456 − 199), pupils may forget to subtract or add 1 to both parts.
nodes.response: The emphasis of same difference can encourage children to ensure they have subtracted or added to both parts of the calculation. Clearly display the visuals in this lesson to support with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Pupils use strategies to make solving calculations more efficient

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly aligning 3-digit and 4-digit numbers resulting in an incorrect sum.
nodes.response: Practise partitioning 3 and 4-digit numbers into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones to support when placing in columns. This will also support in understanding the relationship between the columns when regrouping.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add up to 3 four-digit numbers using column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils unable to connect scale divisions with knowledge of composition of 1,000
nodes.response: Spend time developing confidence in counting in multiples of 100 and 200 to 1,000 before making explicit links between this and scales and measures. Use 'The whole is 1,000 and we have divided it into ___ parts of ___' when doing this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how many '100s' and '200s', 1,000 is composed of

nodes.misconception: Pupils unable to connect scale divisions with knowledge of composition of 1,000
nodes.response: Spend time developing confidence in counting in multiples of 500 and 250 to 1,000 before making explicit links between this and scales and measures. Use 'The whole is 1,000 and we have divided it into ___ parts of ___' when doing this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how many '500s' and '250s', 1,000 is composed of

nodes.misconception: When objects are moved or rearranged, children may re-count them to find 'how many'.
nodes.response: Setting this lesson up practically will help reinforce that there is no need to re-count the set of objects - show they have just moved.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count a set of objects

nodes.misconception: Children may assume that taller objects have more capacity.
nodes.response: Compare real containers and demonstrate with water. Taller containers may be thinner and have less capacity.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that items can be compared using capacity

nodes.misconception: Inaccurate use of language e.g. 'Alex is longer than Sam' instead of 'Alex is taller than Sam'.
nodes.response: Encourage children to verbalise the comparisons they make eg. provide sentence scaffolds and ask them to repeat key sentences as a class.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that items can be compared using length and height

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the size of an object affects whether it is a whole or not.
nodes.response: Show whole objects in different sizes and orientations. Emphasise the language 'whole'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what a whole is

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the symbols < and >
nodes.response: Use lots of practical examples with cubes or objects inside the symbols so children can see the larger end contains the greater amount.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use equality and inequality symbols to compare the relative size of two numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may think that bigger objects, or objects that are spread out have a greater value.
nodes.response: Emphasise that we are counting the number of objects and it does not matter about the size or position.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems by comparing sets of objects

nodes.misconception: May find it hard to feel whether an object is heavier, lighter or equal to the mass of another.
nodes.response: Model using yourself as a scale in different ways - using both hands, picking one object up after another, then having one in each hand.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that items can be compared using weight and mass

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the symbols < and >
nodes.response: Use lots of practical examples with cubes or objects inside the symbols so children can see the larger end contains more objects.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use equality and inequality symbols to compare sets of objects

nodes.misconception: Children may get confused between the parts and the whole.
nodes.response: Ask the children 'What does this number represent?' and encourage them to use the stem sentences to justify their answers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using part-part-whole models with more than two parts

nodes.misconception: Children may think that smaller wholes are only a part and that parts all have to look the same.
nodes.response: Use a variety of real objects to demonstrate wholes and parts split and combined in different ways.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that a whole can be split into parts

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that a whole can be split in different ways and into more than two parts.
nodes.response: Provide lots of practical partitioning and recombining of objects and record on a part-part-whole model in different orientations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a part-part-whole model to represent partitioning into more than two parts

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to understand that a group of objects can represent a whole.
nodes.response: Use the correct language to emphasise the 'whole group of ..........' and explore what happens when a part is missing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify a part of a whole group

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that an object can represent a whole as well as a part of a whole group.
nodes.response: Explore real life examples of wholes as individual objects as well as sets of objects, e.g. sweets, eggs, chocolates, pencils in boxes etc.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that a whole can represent a group of objects

nodes.misconception: When using the part-part-whole model, children may think that the whole is also one of the parts.
nodes.response: When using the part-part-whole model, move the objects out of the whole into the parts, and replace the whole with a number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what a part-part-whole model is

nodes.misconception: When using the part-part-whole model, children may think that the whole is also one of the parts.
nodes.response: When using the part-part-whole model, move the objects out of the whole into the parts, and replace the whole with a number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a part-part-whole model to represent a whole partitioned into two parts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to cross 100s boundaries when adding 10s.
nodes.response: Base ten blocks can help with this concept. It also helps if children's attention is drawn towards the patterns in the number system.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count forwards and backwards within 3-digits

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when partitioning hundreds and tens (e.g. partitioning 340 into 220 and 120).
nodes.response: Give pupils opportunities to manipulate base ten blocks, rearranging them and partitioning both the hundreds and the tens.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition 3-digit numbers in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to connect calculating with hundreds with known facts.
nodes.response: Pupils need to be encouraged to 'unitise' hundreds to make calculation easier, seeing 500 as 5 lots of one hundred.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to add and subtract multiples of 100 within 1000

nodes.misconception: Pupils may explain the relationship with multiples of 10 as 'adding a zero' (e.g. 37 x 10 = 370).
nodes.response: Pupils should be discouraged from doing this. Instead, explore place value, reminding pupils that each 100 represents 10 lots of ten.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Write a 3-digit multiple of 10 as a multiplication equation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when adding near double multiples of ten and when crossing 100s boundaries.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use their known facts to support thinking and combine this with the use of base ten blocks, especially for crossing 100
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to solve problems involving partitioning numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find missing numbers where they are given the start and end numbers only.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the patterns in the counts (e.g. 5 and 0 of counting in 5s and 50s) so that pupils recognise multiples of numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems by counting forwards and backwards in multiples of 2, 20, 5, 50 and 25

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with positioning numbers on 0-1,000 lines.
nodes.response: Relate the positioning of numbers on 0-100 number lines with 0-1,000 number lines (e.g. 19 and 190, 37 and 370).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate the position of 3-digit numbers on unmarked number lines

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes with counting, particularly when crossing a 100s boundary.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the pattern to help them count accurately, using this to predict the next number in the count.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count forwards and backwards in multiples of 2, 20, 5, 50 and 25

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look at all the digits at once when ordering numbers and this may lead to mistakes.
nodes.response: When ordering 3-digit numbers, encourage pupils to compare the 100s digits first and then the 10s digits (and the 1s) afterwards.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ordering sets of 3-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to represent numbers where tens or ones are missing (e.g. 307 or 680).
nodes.response: Use place value grids to represent numbers, showing that there are 'no tens' or 'no ones'. Use alongside base ten block representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent a 3-digit number up to 1,000 in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make errors using the halfway steps between numbers (e.g. wrongly label 374 as 379).
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to find and label the halfway steps (e.g. the 5 or the 50s numbers).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Position 3-digit numbers on number lines

nodes.misconception: Pupils may partition numbers incorrectly when adding or subtracting across a 100s boundary.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add or subtract to first the 100s number, using number pairs that total 10 or 100.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract to and from a 3-digit number bridging 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils may need help using number pairs that total 10 to support their thinking in this lesson.
nodes.response: Make explicit connections between number pairs that total ten and the learning (e.g. 10 - 3 = 7 so 100 - 7 = 93 and 100 - 30 = 70).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to add and subtract to and from multiples of 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging when comparing numbers made from the same digits (e.g. 245 and 254).
nodes.response: Base ten blocks, place value grids and number lines can all be used so pupils can see the size of numbers and see which is larger.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and ordering numbers with 1, 2 and 3 digits

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to partition 10s numbers to help them bridge a 100s boundary.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to calculate the number of tens needed to add or subtract to the 100s number, then add or subtract the remainder.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems by adding and subtracting to or from 3-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically count back in tens to subtract a multiple of ten.
nodes.response: Discuss efficiency and compare different methods. Use practical equipment to draw attention to the relationship between adding multiples of ten in two-digit numbers and the known facts they already possess.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract multiples of ten from 2-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: When faced with problems, children may revert to using inefficient counting strategies instead of more efficient calculation strategies.
nodes.response: Record equation required to solve a problem, then explicitly discuss the most efficient strategy to solve it, drawing on prior knowledge and strategies such as use of known facts and the bridge ten strategy.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use efficient strategies to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children may focus on the ones digit rather than the tens digits. They may calculate inefficiently by counting on/back in ones rather than using the pattern in the tens digits.
nodes.response: Use Base 10 equipment alongside one hundred squares to support with understanding the structure of adding or subtracting ten and difference. Encourage children to notice what changes and what stays the same.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract 10 to and from a 2-digit number.

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically count on in tens to add a multiple of ten.
nodes.response: Discuss efficiency and compare different methods. Use practical equipment to draw attention to the relationship between adding multiples of ten in two-digit numbers and the known facts they already possess.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add multiples of 10 to 2-digit numbers.

nodes.misconception: Children may think two-digit numbers can only be partitioned into tens and ones.
nodes.response: Use practical equipment to manipulate tens and ones on part-part-whole models to help children to understand the many ways that a number can be partitioned.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition 2-digit numbers in different ways

nodes.misconception: The language of one more or one less than can confuse children, so 55 is one more than ? may be interpreted as 55 plus 1
nodes.response: Encourage children to articulate and explain in full sentences alongside number lines to support the understanding of the different ways to articulate the concept. Use stem sentences to support with this and display them around the classroom.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract one to or from a two-digit number within a decade

nodes.misconception: Children may think the multiple of ten before 43 is 30, or partition the subtrahend incorrectly when bridging, meaning they do not use the most efficient strategy.
nodes.response: Display and use the stem sentences to support articulation of how to find the previous multiple of ten. Use ten frames, number lines and one hundred squares to support with appropriate partitioning of numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract by bridging a multiple of ten

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty finding one less than a multiple of ten saying, for example, one less than 60 is 69.
nodes.response: Refer to the order of the decades counting forwards and backwards and encourage visualisation of the decades on number lines and one hundred squares to support this. Help children to generalise about the number before a decade number ending in 9
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract 1 to and from a 2-digit number crossing the tens boundary

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty knowing which operation is required to solve a problem, particularly in those involving finding the difference.
nodes.response: Encourage children to draw bar models or part-part-whole models to support their understanding of the structure of the problem and to articulate their thinking (as modelled in the lesson).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use number facts to solve addition and subtraction problems.

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty understanding the different ways in which 'difference' can be represented and the language associated with this.
nodes.response: Use a bar model to highlight the structure of the difference and create a range of problems, using different language, that could be solved using the same equation, e.g. problems which use both how many more and how many less/fewer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use number facts to solve problems in measures and data contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may partition the second addend in a way that does not allow them to make use of the multiple of ten and use their number bonds to calculate efficiently.
nodes.response: Use ten frames and number lines to support children in finding the multiple of ten and partition the addend in different ways to compare the efficiency of different ways of partitioning.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add by bridging a multiple of ten

nodes.misconception: When solving problems, particularly in new contexts, children may revert to inefficient strategies as they are focusing on the problem rather than the number involved.
nodes.response: Encourage children to record the numbers involved on bar models, number lines or in equations, then focus on what they notice about the numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use bridging to solve addition and subtraction problems

nodes.misconception: Children may default to counting in ones to find ten more or ten less.
nodes.response: Use representations that highlight the structure of the base 10 system, e.g. Base 10 blocks/one hundred squares, and also 'dual counting' to support understanding of 'unitising', i.e. that using 'ten' as a unit can help to calculate more efficiently.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find 10 more or less than a 2-digit number.

nodes.misconception: When subtracting, children may use their number bonds to ten to find the correct ones digit, but may forget to consider the previous multiple of ten, e.g. say 40-2=48
nodes.response: Encourage children to use their knowledge of decades to estimate (e.g. I know 40-2 will be in the thirties), then prove it using representations that highlight the tens structure, e.g. one hundred squares, ten frames and number lines.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use number bonds to 10 to add/subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may not recognise known facts when addends are presented in different order, e.g. they may not use 7+1 to solve 61 +7 They may also confuse tens and ones digits.
nodes.response: Focus on efficient ways of working and, when working in the abstract, partition the two-digit number into tens and ones, so the tens and ones digits can be easily identified and the commutative aspect of the ones digit can be more easily seen.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use number facts to add or subtract a one-digit number and a two-digit number.

nodes.misconception: Many polygons appear regular as all of the sides are the same length. However, it is possible (as the lesson shows) to have polygons which are the same length sides but different interior angles.
nodes.response: Pupils should have previous experience of right angles. Use a right angle 'measurer' to prove that some of the angles in a shape are greater than a right angle and some smaller; as the angles are not all equal, it is not a regular polygon.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that a regular polygon has sides that are the same length and angles that are the same size

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that, even when one of the long side and short side lengths is missing in a rectangle, they still have enough information as these are the same as the given lengths.
nodes.response: Counters are encouraged in this unit. It may be that some pupils still need the missing side lengths written on counters, but as with all scaffolding, this should only be temporary. Ask them - do you need this counter? Do you already know the number?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that the perimeter of a rectangle can be calculated by addition and multiplication

nodes.misconception: Pupils will most likely understand that different shapes can and most often do have different perimeters. They may not realise that the perimeters can potentially be the same.
nodes.response: Allowing pupils to recreate perimeters using string or number rods and rearranging themselves to make a new shape is a powerful way of showing that different shapes can have equal perimeters.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand that different shapes can have the same perimeter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overgeneralise and assume all perimeters can be calculated by multiplying one side length by the number of sides in the polygon.
nodes.response: 'Noticing' is a key mathematical skill. Encourage pupils to take their time to notice whether the shape is regular or irregular, if that information is not already explicitly given.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand that the perimeter of a regular polygon can be calculated by multiplication

nodes.misconception: Pupils often find division a trickier concept than multiplication and do not connect this to their known multiplication facts.
nodes.response: Establish the inverse relationship with multiplication and show how the division equations can be re-written as a multiplication equation with a missing factor. Support pupils in making this connection to allow them to use known facts to calculate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the side length of a regular polygon by division where the perimeter is known

nodes.misconception: When finding the perimeter of a shape, pupils may count one side twice, or not count one of the sides.
nodes.response: Examples and non-examples of perimeter are given but encourage pupils to mark a 'start point' when they find the perimeter of a shape, so that they know where to end.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that the perimeter is the distance around a 2D shape

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see a rectangle with the perimeter given and only one of the side lengths and think that there is insufficient information as there are three missing side lengths.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that because it is a rectangle, the side length opposite the given side length is in fact known. A counter can be added on and then removed again to show that they actually know two of the missing side lengths, not just one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that unknown side lengths can be calculated from the perimeter and known side lengths

nodes.misconception: Pupils may count a side twice, or miss a side, if they do not remember where their starting point was on the shape when counting the perimeter.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to mark a starting point, or use dots to mark the units they have counted.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that perimeter is measured in units of length and can be found by counting or measuring units

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that there is only one way to add the perimeter of a shape - typically clockwise, starting from the top. This is untrue and will limit the efficiency of the arithmetic.
nodes.response: The lesson presents the idea of the side lengths being given in counters. The counters can then be re-ordered, for example so that a number bond to ten can be utilised. Using counters or sticky notes or similar may support pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that perimeter can be calculated by adding together the side lengths of a 2D shape

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if they know the perimeter of a shape, and a new shape has been made from duplicates of it, they can simply multiply the perimeter by how many shapes make up the new one.
nodes.response: The lesson highlights this misconception and tackles it but it is worth being aware of it as pupils work. Point out to them that some of the sides from the original shape are now inside the new shapes so do not count as part of its perimeter.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving the perimeter and side lengths of polygons

nodes.misconception: Children may misidentify the parts or wholes in a problem.
nodes.response: Children should be encouraged to visualise the problem to help them identify the parts and whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving volume

nodes.misconception: Children further learn about the composition of 1,000 in Y4, so may make mistakes in reading scales.
nodes.response: Rehearse 1,000 is composed of two equal parts of 500 ml, four equal parts of 250 ml, five equal parts of 200 ml, 10 equal parts of 100 ml.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure volume in whole litres and millilitres

nodes.misconception: Children may estimate incorrectly or confuse where to record their measurements in the table.
nodes.response: When estimating, hold an item of known mass in one hand and the unknown in the other - compare them. Take care when reading table headings.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate then measure mass and volume and record in a table

nodes.misconception: Larger objects have a greater mass. Taller containers have a greater capacity and/or volume.
nodes.response: The size of something does not determine how much mass an object has; taller containers may be narrower and so may not hold as much liquid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and estimating mass and volume

nodes.misconception: Children may read the scale incorrectly - confusion between equal parts and marks on the scale.
nodes.response: The scale is a number line. Remember to look at the number of equal parts between the marked numbers not the marks themselves.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring the volume of liquids using millilitres.

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the terms capacity and volume.
nodes.response: Capacity is the whole amount of liquid that a container can hold. Volume is the actual amount of liquid in the container.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding capacity and volume

nodes.misconception: Children may misidentify the parts or wholes in a problem.
nodes.response: Children should be encouraged to visualise the problem (eg. act it out or draw it) to help them identify the parts and whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving mass

nodes.misconception: Composition of 1,000 is Year 4 content so children may make mistakes when giving masses in kg and g.
nodes.response: Use of stem sentences to help: 1,000 is composed of __ equal parts of __.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure mass in whole kilograms and grams

nodes.misconception: Misreading of scales by counting marks rather than equal parts in between the marked intervals.
nodes.response: Remember to look at the number of equal parts in between the marked intervals then use your knowledge of the composition of 100.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure the mass of objects using grams

nodes.misconception: When comparing masses - if the scales have different intervals or the zero is in different places.
nodes.response: Remind children that the scale is a number line and we always read number lines from zero; the further the arrow travels, the greater mass.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Become familiar with scales with different intervals when measuring in grams

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to count over the boundaries for multiples of ten thousand and one hundred thousand.
nodes.response: Ensure children focus on the number of thousands they have within the number. This should effectively be the same as counting in ones over tens and hundreds boundaries, with the exception of the unit changing from ones to thousands.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count forwards and backwards in powers of 10 to and from any multiple of 1,000

nodes.misconception: Pupils misread the values of bars on each graph.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to mark on as many gridlines that they can for themselves once they have recognised the size of the whole. This may then help pupils to estimate the value of each bar more accurately until they can do it by imagining the gridlines.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that 100,000 is composed of 50,000s, 25,000s and 20,000s

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to position five-digit multiples of 1,000 on a 0-1,000,000 number line.
nodes.response: It is important to check if pupils are secure in placing numbers on a 0-1,000 number line. This is a fundamental prerequisite to be able to achieve with this learning, so spending time securing this prior learning may be necessary.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Position 6-digit multiples of 1,000 on a marked but unlabelled number line

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify how many intervals there are on the y-axis of graphs or are less familiar with graphs and so find it more challenging.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on the gaps between each gridline as opposed to the number of gridlines there are themselves. You could generalise that there is always one fewer gridline than the number of gaps.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that 10,000 is composed of 5,000s, 2,500s and 2,000s

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to articulate larger numbers, confusing when to give the place value unit within the number.
nodes.response: Provide a sentence stem like this: _ _ _ thousand and _ _ _ , encouraging the children to notice the groupings of thousands and ones.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read and write numbers up to one million using a place value chart

nodes.misconception: Pupils attempt to learn how many tens, hundreds and thousands there are in 100,000 as a set rule rather than develop a sense for this.
nodes.response: Building and breaking 100,000 in different ways can be a really effective way to develop a sense of the number. You could use base 10 blocks to build up to 100,000 where a one cube could be redefined as 100 and then use plasticine to create 10 and 1.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how one hundred thousand can be composed

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to position five-digit multiples of 1,000 on a 0-100,000 number line.
nodes.response: It is important to check if pupils are secure in placing two-digit numbers on a 0-100 number line. This is a fundamental prerequisite to be able to achieve with this learning, so spending time securing this prior learning may be necessary.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Position five-digit multiples of 1,000 on a marked but unlabelled number line

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to create axis for their graphs that have equal intervals.
nodes.response: You could spend some time with pupils simply practising drawing each axis. Ensure pupils do not draw a line and then try to divide into equal intervals. Instead encourage marking the intervals as the line is drawn.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read the scales of graphs and measures using knowledge of the composition of 10,000 and 100,000

nodes.misconception: 10,000 of anything is the same in size.
nodes.response: Provide a range of contexts which allow pupils to see that 10,000 can be large or small, it is dependent on the context. For example, comparing 10,000 mm with 10,000 miles on a map is a good way to emphasise the difference in distances.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how ten thousand can be composed

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget the use of zero as a place holder when there are for example, 0 ten thousands in a number, e.g. 503,000
nodes.response: Encourage children to transfer the represented number into a place value chart prior to reading the number. However, it is important for pupils to be able to read numbers without a place value chart so ensure time is taken to reduce the scaffold too.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read and write numbers up to one million in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse one more and one less, particularly when finding missing numbers.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentence __ is one more / less than __ because it comes after / before it in the count.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Show one more and one less than a number using representations and describe this accurately

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse ordinal and cardinal numbers.
nodes.response: Place an emphasis on these numbers in speech throughout the day. Continue to highlight the links between them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ordinal numbers show the position of an object in relation to another

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on counting all and may not count accurately when given unfamiliar arrangements.
nodes.response: Children need to build familiarity with different arrangements of number. Comment on what you notice eg. 'I can see 3 and 1, I can see 4'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that numbers can represent how many objects there are in a set

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse one more and one less, particularly when finding missing numbers.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentence ___ is one more / one less than ___ because it comes after / before it in our count.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Show one more and one less than a number using representations

nodes.misconception: When using patterns to identify combinations, it will be easy to make errors in recording.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring the value of recording combinations within a simple table. Encourage checking, e.g. the amount of counters totals 5.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition the numbers one to five in a systematic way

nodes.misconception: As before, children may confuse the whole and the parts, or add them all up to find the total.
nodes.response: Place objects in each part of the bar model and combine them to make the whole, or starting within the whole, partition them into the parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using a bar model to represent a whole partitioned into two parts

nodes.misconception: Children may not see the bar model as proportional, so may think that the parts are equal.
nodes.response: Encourage children to see that the bars are proportional to help them get a sense of the size of the parts and whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a bar model to represent a whole partitioned into two parts

nodes.misconception: When describing the partitioning of a number, children may mix the parts and the whole.
nodes.response: Reinforce the stem sentence, ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part highlighting, the whole and each part using gestures.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition numbers one to five in different ways

nodes.misconception: Children may add the whole and one part to find the missing part.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of the stem sentence ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part, to reinforce what the numbers represent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find a missing part when one part and the whole is known

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the part and the whole, or add the whole and one part to find the missing part.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of the stem sentence ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part, to reinforce what the numbers represent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems finding a missing part when one part and the whole is known

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to recognise when an angle is greater than a right angle.
nodes.response: You can model this by trying to move the obtuse angle (though pupils don't need to know the term yet) within a right angle checker. They should be able to see that it is too large to fit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate the shapes made when rectangles are cut on the diagonal

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to look at the interior angles in the shape. They may think that an interior angle of 270° is a right angle.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we need to measure the interior angles of a shape. Show them examples of this (e.g. an arrowhead) to illustrate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that a rectangle is a four-sided polygon with four right angles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have trouble recognising right angles or lines of symmetry when shapes have been rotated.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to check every angle using a simple right-angle measurer, which can be hand made or even cut from the corner of a piece of paper. Ask them to physically manipulate the shapes so that they can identify properties more easily.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify properties of quadrilaterals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it hard to recognise right angles presented in unusual orientations.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to continue to check angles with a right angle measurer. Teach them to recognise where vertices are clearly not right angles and differentiate these from ones that could be right angles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate and draw other polygons with right angles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see other shapes and collections of lines as triangles when they are not (e.g. shapes with rounded corners, three lines that do not all meet).
nodes.response: Provide pupils with shapes, and explore shapes in the environment, classifying them as 'triangles' and 'not triangles'. Ask children, 'Does this shape have three straight sides? Does it have clearly defined, sharp vertices?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify properties of triangles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think there is only ever one right angle in an object or shape.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to explore objects and shapes that have more than one right angle and show that these are not always rectangular e.g. some trapeziums can have more than one right angle.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify and describe right angles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not correctly identify right angles within a shape to join them.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils have opportunities to identify right angles within a range of shapes prior to the lesson. If possible, encourage them to mark the right angles to help them. They should only be joining these right angles around a point.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Join four right angles at a point using different right-angled polygons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that squares are rectangles.
