nodes.response: Emphasise to pupils that all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares. Rectangles are quadrilaterals with 4 right angles, but squares have 4 sides of equal length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that a square is a rectangle in which the four sides are of equal length

nodes.misconception: Might not recognise that the arrangement is still the same when it has been rotated or flipped.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunity to explore practically and model rotating, flipping and comparing arrangements.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tetrominoes and pentominoes

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a square is not a rectangle.
nodes.response: Count the sides and vertices of rectangles (including squares) to show they all have 4 (concept is revisited throughout Year 1 and beyond).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore and recognise 2D shapes

nodes.misconception: Children may not see that a shape can have two different names e.g. a square is also a rectangle.
nodes.response: Use sorting hoops to sort rectangles and not rectangles. Then use a smaller hoop inside the 'rectangles' hoop to help identify the squares.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, discuss and identify shapes that are and are not rectangles

nodes.misconception: May think that a sphere has a circular face because when drawn, a sphere looks like a circle.
nodes.response: Physically handle and compare spheres, cylinders and cones. Explore why a sphere cannot stand but a cylinder and a cone can.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify 2D shapes within 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Children might not notice that the two small and two large triangles are the same size.
nodes.response: Lay the tangram pieces on top of each other to physically explore and compare the size of each piece.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compose tangram images

nodes.misconception: Children might mix up words that sound alike e.g. similar and cylinder.
nodes.response: Allow additional practice for children to name shapes throughout the day, particularly those that are familiar within their environment.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, recognise and compare three different 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Children may mistake some 'triangle-like' shapes as triangles.
nodes.response: Provide cut-outs of shapes to handle and explore. Make a list of properties a triangle must have and discuss them for each cut-out.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, discuss and identify shapes that are and are not triangles

nodes.misconception: Children may think that ovals are also circles.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the outside of a circle is always an equal distance from the centre by exploring and drawing around different cut-outs.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, discuss and identify shapes that are and are not circles

nodes.misconception: May not identify which pattern block will fill the shape of a space.
nodes.response: Model filling spaces using trial and error, each time describing why it does / does not fit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing pattern block images

nodes.misconception: Children might not identify the whole unit of repeat.
nodes.response: Describe the pattern aloud to hear the part that is repeated.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Copy, extend and describe repeating patterns

nodes.misconception: Children might begin to confuse 2D and 3D. For example, describe a cube as a square.
nodes.response: Use geometric construction materials to explore the 2D shapes within 3D shapes. Look for familiar 3D shapes in the environment and discuss.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognise, describe and sort 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Children may only extend in one direction, rather than in all directions beyond a central point.
nodes.response: Count the spaces to fill around the outside, and then count each pattern block as it is placed around the outside.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Radiating patterns

nodes.misconception: Might not recognise that an arrangement is still the same when it has been rotated.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities for building, rotating and comparing arrangements of cubes, and to view them from different perspectives.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Examine ways that cubes can be composed into different arrangements

nodes.misconception: Children may not recognise a 2D shape when it is presented in a different orientation.
nodes.response: Allow children to handle cut-outs of 2D shapes so they can rotate them and explore how the shapes look in different orientations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, discuss and compare 2D shapes

nodes.misconception: Children might mix up words that sound alike e.g. cube and cuboid.
nodes.response: Allow additional practice for children to name shapes throughout the day, particularly those that are familiar within their environment.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, recognise and compare three more 3D shapes

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent counting in sixes as the 6 times table

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency in 6 times tables and not understanding the divisibility rules or the problems.
nodes.response: To clearly model highlighting key words of worded problems to understand the problem and the operation required for the calculation. Continue to use language stems such as 'If I know...' 'Then I know...,' to support mathematical thinking.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiples of 6

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the key term 'adjacent,' and have difficult understanding the word problems.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between adjacent multiples of six

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the keyword adjacent and have difficult understanding the word problems.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the term to identify the known elements in worded problems. Take time to show adjacent on number lines connecting to addition and subtraction of equal groups.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between adjacent multiples of three

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent counting in threes as the 3 times table

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly write numbers by not using a placeholder zero.
nodes.response: Use place value counters or a Gattegno chart to represent the number. Are there digits for each place? If not, we need to use a placeholder zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing numbers up to 10 million

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to use unitising to make connections between the composition of 1,000 or 10,000 and one million or ten million.
nodes.response: Use the suggested stem sentences e.g. '250 is one quarter of 1,000, so one-quarter of 1,000 thousands must be 250 thousand' to support developing the unitising concept.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Composition of one million and 10 million

nodes.misconception: Children who struggle reading/writing teen numbers may struggle to read or write larger numbers. Children may group in threes from the left, rather than the right.
nodes.response: Use a place value chart to support the reading of the numbers. Remember to identify the hundreds, tens and ones first, then group in threes to the right of those.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read and write numbers up to 10 million

nodes.misconception: Children may misinterpret a word problem especially where they are insecure on the key words such as 'difference' or 'how much more'.
nodes.response: Teacher should model own thoughts when problem solving and encourage children to represent the word problems in a bar model. Construct bar models alongside a retelling of the problem so children can see where the mathematics is found.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving using knowledge of the composition of powers of 10

nodes.misconception: Children may not appreciate the size of one million or that it is composed of 1,000 thousands. Children may find grasping the concept of 'power of 10' tricky.
nodes.response: Use the place value chart and place value counters to represent the composition of one million. Use the stem sentences: 'One million is composed of 1,000 thousands' and 'Each column is ten times the value to that on its right'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Powers of 10 and their multiples

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to recognise that numbers exist to the left of zero.
nodes.response: Expose pupils to images in familiar contexts showing negative numbers. Take lots of opportunities to count bridging zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret numbers greater than and less than zero in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that subtraction is commutative and therefore equations can be written in any order.
nodes.response: Model with physical resources such as marbles in a bag that 4 - 6 results in a negative change but 6 - 4 results in a positive change.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent a change story using addition and subtraction symbols

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes answer a question like ‘What is the difference between −5℃ and 3℃?’ with ‘−8℃’.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that these differences are always positive by asking them to count forwards from the lower value to the higher value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of positive and negative numbers to calculate intervals

nodes.misconception: Fractions and decimals less than one are positioned to the left of zero or are negative in value.
nodes.response: Using a number line 0 to 1, label different fractions and decimals and show pupils that, though small in size, they are greater than zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify and place negative numbers on a number line

nodes.misconception: Pupils can come unstuck by misreading or misunderstanding the information being presented.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider what information they do know, and plot this on an empty number line, to help work out the unknown information.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving positive and negative numbers in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not write negative numbers beginning with the negative symbol e.g. writing 3- and not -3.
nodes.response: Take time to model the writing of a negative number. "I know it is negative so I begin with the negative symbol."
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read and write negative numbers

nodes.misconception: When comparing a pair of numbers such as 3 and −3, pupils may think they are of equal value.
nodes.response: Use of number lines, ideally displayed in the classroom, will help pupils to see that numbers increase in value the further right they are.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how the value of a number relates to its position from zero

nodes.misconception: Negative temperatures relate to positive e.g.  −5℃ is warmer than −3℃ because 5℃ is warmer than 3℃.
nodes.response: Emphasise directional relationship e.g. numbers decrease as they move to the right. Practical examples can help e.g. freezer temperature.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret sets of negative and positive numbers in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Inaccuracy when reading horizontally from the top of a bar to the y axis on a bar chart.
nodes.response: Model and encourage the use of rulers to follow a straight horizontal line from the top of a bar to the y axis.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of positive and negative numbers to interpret graphs

nodes.misconception: Pupils can get mixed up with which comes first, the x or y axis, when reading/plotting coordinates.
nodes.response: There are lots of aide-mémoires to remember the order. However, regular practice using a stem sentence like the one in the lesson will help.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how negative numbers are used on a coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse groups with number of items.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling of groups, demarcating groups and physically placing items into groups e.g. a bundle of straws with an elastic band.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe how objects have been grouped

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse how to find the product (total amount)
nodes.response: Model use of terminology - ask children what various parts of the multiplication equation represents. E.g. 'The 2 represents how many coins there are.' ' The 5 represents the value of each coin.' 'That is the same as 5, 2 times.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of multiplication to calcuate the product

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to comprehend groups of zero. For example children may see four empty plates as four groups of one.
nodes.response: Use a context where the number of groups is still visible when the group size is zero. Remember to make the distinction as to what is representing zero. Use the familiar stem sentences There are ___ groups of ___.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain and represent multiplication when a group contains zero or one items

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse groups with number of items in a group.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling of groups, demarcating groups and physically placing items into groups e.g. a bundle of straws with an elastic band.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that objects can be grouped in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils might confuse the number of groups with the value of the groups and therefore write incorrect expressions.
nodes.response: Once familiar with building the relevant additive expression, the multiplicative expression is introduced alongside e.g. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 is the same as 5 x 3  Take time to connect these ideas using `groups of language' and physical representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent equal groups as repeated addition

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse group size and number of groups.
nodes.response: Clearly model the number of groups by demarcating groups where possible and using familiar stem sentences such as 'There are ___ groups.' Then, move onto identifying the amount of items / objects in each group. 'There are ___ in each group.'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of multiplication to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how to represent the repeated addition expression and a multiplication expression.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to identify exactly how the equation relates to the image: with the questions ‘What does the 3 represent?’ ‘What does the 2 represent?’ ‘What does the 6 represent?’
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent equal groups as repeated addition and multiplication

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the terminology of factor and product and therefore be inaccurate when describing equations.
nodes.response: Take time to clearly model use of terminology and ask questions such as: 'What does the 3 represent?' 'What does the 5 represent?' 'What does the 15 represent?' Continue to explicitly use key terms such as factor and products within explanation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify and explain each part of a multiplication equation

nodes.misconception: Children are not able to explain the multiplication expression.
nodes.response: Children are encouraged to identify exactly how the equation relates to the image. For example 3 groups of 2 shoes: 3 x 2 - with the questions ‘What does the 3 represent?’ ‘What does the 2 represent?’ ‘What does the 6 represent?’
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent equal groups as multiplication

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify the factors in the word problems.
nodes.response: Model how to address questions. Use of familiar stem sentences to support pupils in identifying the factors: 'There are 7 bamboos. Each bamboo is a length of 5 m. 7 is factor and 5 is factor.  We can skip count in ___ to find the product.'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of multiplication to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the part and the whole, or add the whole and one part to find the missing part.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of the stem sentence ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part, to reinforce what the numbers represent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify a missing part when a whole is partitioned into two parts

nodes.misconception: Children may find it hard to draw their own number lines.
nodes.response: Place the first, last and midpoint numbers first and use fingers or cubes to space the other numbers out equally.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate where 6, 7, 8 and 9 lie on an unmarked number line

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to recognise five fingers on a hand or subitise numbers up to five in familiar arrangements such as dice patterns.
nodes.response: Play games to practise subitising and recognising five e.g. dominoes or dice games and finger games such as bunny ears. Allow regular opportunities for pupils to familiarise themselves with common patterns of numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent the numbers 6 to 10 using a five and a bit structure

nodes.misconception: Children may be so familiar with counting in ones that they might find it hard to count in twos.
nodes.response: Try saying all the numbers but whisper or clap the odd numbers to emphasise the even numbers and vice versa.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Skip count in odds and evens

nodes.misconception: Children may rely on counting from 0 rather than seeing the five and a bit structure of the numbers 6 to 10 and may therefore not partition efficiently.
nodes.response: Use fingers to expose the 5 and a bit structure. 'Grow' a number by putting up fingers one at a time while counting, 'show it' by putting up the fingers all at once, 'throw it' as you quickly throw the number of fingers forwards.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify the whole and parts of the numbers 6 to 10 using the five and a bit structure

nodes.misconception: Children may think that even numbers can only be partitioned into even parts and odd numbers into odd parts.
nodes.response: Ensure children have plenty of practical experience of partitioning representations of numbers in different ways and talk about what they notice. Using number shapes and tens frames can help to visualise the patterns.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how even and odd numbers can be partitioned

nodes.misconception: Children may see the pairs in an odd number and think it is an even number.
nodes.response: Ensure children are looking for the extra one that makes a number odd. Provide opportunities to group other odd sets e.g. pairs of socks, pairs of hands / feet and realising an odd number always has an 'odd' one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what odd and even numbers are and the difference between them

nodes.misconception: Children may see the pairs in odd numbers and think it is an even number.
nodes.response: Ensure children are looking for the extra one that makes a number odd. Provide opportunities to group other odd sets e.g. pairs of socks, pairs of hands / feet and realising an odd number always has an 'odd' one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Order and sort numbers into odd and even sets

nodes.misconception: When using patterns to identify combinations, pupils may struggle to be systematic and not identify all options systematically.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring the value of recording combinations within a simple table. Encourage checking, e.g. the amount of counters totals six. Look for patterns and support children in spotting these.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition the numbers 6 and 7 in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not connect more abstract representations of part-part-whole relationships with practical examples showing the five and a bit structure.
nodes.response: Take time to connect the representations pupils are familiar with e.g. show finger numeral representation alongside part-part-whole models and bar models to help pupils understand these all show the same relationship.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore the numbers 6 to 10 using the parts and wholes on a number line

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the inequality symbols and use them the incorrect way around.
nodes.response: Take time to practise using the symbols with hand signals or using manipulatives. Emphasise the shape of the symbols reflecting their use i.e. more cubes 'fit' into the wider end of the symbol.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare two numbers and say which is greater than or less than the other

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not understand that intervals or marks on a number line need to be equally spaced and that in these cases each mark represents one number.
nodes.response: Make connections between number tracks and number lines showing that the intervals are counted on a number line. Expose pupils to vertical and horizontal number lines showing all numbers, including beyond 10, to familiarise them with their structure.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain where 6, 7, 8 and 9 lie on a number line

nodes.misconception: Pupils are not yet fluent in number pairs and partitions of numbers 6 to 10 and so rely on counting to find missing parts.
nodes.response: Develop subitising skills so that pupils are able to recognise small partitions instantly. Encourage choral repetition of stem sentences emphasising wholes and parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition the numbers 6 to 10 in different ways

nodes.misconception: When using patterns to identify combinations, pupils may struggle to be systematic and not identify all options systematically.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring the value of recording combinations within a simple table. Encourage checking, e.g. the amount of counters totals eight. Look for patterns and support children in spotting these.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition the numbers 8 and 9 in different ways

nodes.misconception: Children may not be secure with the principles of counting.
nodes.response: Encourage any and all opportunities to count small collections of objects considering ways in which to count efficiently. Model counting using one-to-one principles and strategies such as organising collections to support counting all.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Count a set of objects and match the spoken number to the written numeral and number name

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with the language of unitising.
nodes.response: Encourage children to read aloud and spot what they notice - which known fact can they see - what is the same/different?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add multiples of powers of 10 crossing the millions boundary

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to identify or explain the pattern or to identify the number of steps from the first given number to the last instead just giving the number of missing values.
nodes.response: If children struggle to identify the pattern ask them to start by identifying the part of the number that is changing. Model the 'steps' rather than the missing parts to support children to see this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using patterns in counting sequences

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly place a number on a number line according to just counting the parts rather than working out the scale.
nodes.response: Determine the multiples that the number line is increasing in first: find the difference between the given start and end numbers and divide by the number of parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate and identify numbers on number lines

nodes.misconception: When using place value counters, children may misread a number if one of the digits is a zero and hence not represented with a counter.
nodes.response: Remember that the digits in numbers are organised into groups of three with ones, tens and hundreds in each group.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Determine the value of digits in numbers up to 10 million

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to comprehend that e.g. 1,200,000 may have a digit '2' in the one hundred thousands place but is actually composed of 12 hundred thousands.
nodes.response: Even though the digit in the 100,000s place is a 2, the number 1,200,000 is composed of 12 hundred thousands because one million is composed of 10 hundred thousands.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Composition of seven-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: A child may give the incorrect value for a digit or struggle to see how to partition larger numbers in a non-standard way.
nodes.response: Use a place value chart or counters to prove the value of the digit and use a Gattegno chart to support partitioning.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the composition of seven-digit numbers to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the greater value number is the one that starts with the greater value digit even if the number has fewer digits overall.
nodes.response: When comparing numbers, compare the value of the digits not the digits themselves. If both numbers have the same amount of digits, so we need to compare the largest place value digit that is different.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare numbers with up to eight digits

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that only one digit will change when adding two numbers where one addend has only one non-zero digit.
nodes.response: This is usually correct but what would happen if the digit changed to a value of 10 or greater? Then we would need to regroup (another lesson).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract mentally without bridging a boundary

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle with the language of unitising.
nodes.response: Encourage children to read aloud and spot what they notice - which known fact can they see - what is the same/different?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract multiples of powers of 10 crossing the millions boundary

nodes.misconception: Mis-align numbers when setting up algorithms if the numbers have different amount of digits. When finding 1 missing part out of 3 parts, children may perform two subtractions, which is inefficient.
nodes.response: When setting up the algorithm, ensure digits in the same place value place are aligned. When finding 1 missing part of 3 parts, first we add the known parts then we subtract from the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems using column addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: When using the short method, pupils may not align the digits correctly with the same place value.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents, linking back to the place value chart.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using short multiplication (no regroups)

nodes.misconception: When using the expanded method, pupils may not align the digits correctly with the same place value.
nodes.response: Use clear teacher modelling and continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents and link back to the place value chart.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using expanded multiplication (no regroups)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify the multiples of 10 a number is between when estimating.
nodes.response: Provide a number line and continue to use stem sentences to support pupils in their thinking.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate and multiply a 2-digit by a 1-digit number using expanded and short multiplication

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Ask children about the additional ten or tens as a small digit to be added in with the tens. What does this show? What is the value?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using short multiplication (regrouping 1s to 10s)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Model accurately what happens when we regroup from 10s to 100s. Why did this happen? How do we record this?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using expanded multiplication (regrouping 10s to 100s)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly if they do not understand the place value of digits in a factor.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences / array to identify when they may need to regroup.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using partitioning and representations (one regroup)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents. Demonstrate the regrouping using base ten blocks to help.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using expanded multiplication (regrouping 1s to 10s)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences / array to identify when they may need to regroup.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using partitioning and representations (two regroups)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Reiterate that if the product of the single digit and the tens number is greater than 100 then you regroup ten tens into one hundred.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using short multiplication (regrouping 10s to 100s)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not record partitioned factors as tens and ones leading to incorrect calculation.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences to support their thinking. Use the language of ___ tens to support place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using partitioning

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 10s
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: 10 frames, number lines and 100 squares and can support children to practise skip counting in groups of 10
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent counting in tens as the 10 times table

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 5s
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: 10 frame and 5 p coins can support children to practise skip counting in 5s. Then move onto counting in 5s on a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent the 5 times table in different ways

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 2 and want to count in steps of 1
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: counters can support children to practise skip counting in 2s
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent the 2 times table in different ways

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 5s
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: counters can support children to practise skip counting in 5s
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent counting in fives as the 5 times table

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the keyword adjacent and have difficulty understanding the word problems.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the term to identify the known elements in worded problems. Take time to show adjacent on number lines connecting to addition and subtraction of equal groups.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between adjacent multiples of 5

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find worded problems related to adjacent multiples challenging if they are not clear on the structure of finding previous and next multiples.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the term to identify the known elements in worded problems. Take time to show adjacent on number lines connecting to addition and subtraction of equal groups.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between adjacent multiples of 2

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse identifying the number of groups and group size.
nodes.response: Use sentence stems to support children's thinking and model writing the equation, e.g. for 2 groups of 5  we can say 2 × 5 For 5, two times we can say 5 × 2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that factor pairs can be written in any order

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly. Pupils may also not understand how to deduce the operation for the calculation.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the 2 times table to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the keyword adjacent and have difficulty understanding the word problems.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the term to identify the known elements in worded problems. Take time to show adjacent on number lines connecting to addition and subtraction of equal groups.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between adjacent multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to count in multiples of 10s and recognise this as groups of 10
nodes.response: Use of concrete resources: 10 frame and 10 p coins can support children to practise skip counting in 10s. Then move onto counting in 10s on a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent the 10 times table in different ways

nodes.misconception: Lack of understanding of key terms such as: 'digit,' 'number.'
nodes.response: Explain clearly the difference between the two key terms and encourage children to test the divisibility rule on both 3 digit and 4 digit numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the divisibility rules to find multiples of 3

nodes.misconception: Lack of understanding of key terms such as: 'digit,' 'number.' Pupils may also forget how to identify an even number.
nodes.response: Remind children that even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Explain clearly the difference between the key terms and encourage children to test the divisibility rule on both 3 digit and 4 digit numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use divisibility rules for multiples of 6

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency in the 3s and 6s times tables can lead to pupils being slower to grasp the generalisation about the relationship between the 3 and 6 times tables.
nodes.response: Use arrays and other representations to draw clear comparisons. Multiplication grids could also be provided while pupils become more fluent in recall.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between multiples of three and six

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the 3 and 6 times tables to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. This could involve drawing bar models or other representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the relationships between the 3 and 6 times tables to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children will often reverse the minuend and subtrahend because they don't always appear in the order that they would in an expression.
nodes.response: Ensure that the children spend time understanding the context, either through discussion of the problem or through visual representations such as bar models. It's also worth spending time on vocabulary by playing fun word games or charades.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Choose the most efficient strategy to subtract from a 3-digit number

nodes.misconception: On the magic squares, children will often miss the fact that it is a two step problem involving addition and subtraction. They may think you have to add the two numbers in the row/column or diagonal.
nodes.response: Start with a simpler magic square. The easier ones feature the numbers 1-9 and total 15 diagonally, vertically or horizontally. Once they understand them, introduce 2-digit and 3-digit magic squares.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use addition and subtraction to solve problems in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often know one method, such as partitioning, and stick to it without trying any others. Sometimes, some  pupils will be very reluctant to move away from written methods such as columns.
nodes.response: Reinforce the idea of bravery and courage to try new methods. Remind them that efficiency is partly about speed and they might find that other methods only become quick with practice!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Choose the most efficient strategy to add two 3-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils will sometimes remove or add ones or tens to one addend and forget to amend the other addend so that the calculation has been transformed but doesn't give the same sum as the original.
nodes.response: Encourage buddy checking of jottings as the children practise so that they can help each other to be reminded.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add 2 and 3-digit numbers by redistributing

nodes.misconception: Children will often reverse the minuend and subtrahend because they don't always appear in the order that they would in an expression.
nodes.response: Give time to ensure that the children understand the bar model representation and encourage them to discuss which number is the minuend and which is the subtrahend before engaging in a strategy for mental subtraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract 3-digit multiples of 10 by finding the difference between them

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that a tens counter has a value of ten. For example, they may think that 14 tens and 11 tens make 25 altogether, forgetting to convert 25 tens into 250.
nodes.response: Encourage counting in tens using counters to begin with. Move onto modelling questions using base ten so the children can count the tens blocks.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add two 3-digit numbers using partitioning

nodes.misconception: Children can often be overwhelmed by the amount of visual data they are presented with.
nodes.response: Expose children to graphical data as much as possible outside of maths lessons. Encourage children to make simple bar charts with cubes so they understand their formation and liken the searching for specific values to search and find books.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use addition and subtraction to solve problems involving bar charts, pictograms and tables

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often try to use a written method/algorithm which they know gives an accurate answer but don't understand why it works.
nodes.response: Encourage the pupils to be brave and remind them that this is about mental subtraction so, with practice, will be quicker than any written methods.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract 2 or 3-digit numbers using partitioning and bridging a multiple of 10

nodes.misconception: Many pupils will want to use a written method/algorithm immediately such as column method. This lesson is to support mental addition strategies.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to forget about using written procedures because they are inefficient when the addends are suited to adjustment. As class teacher, use adjustment and race the children desperate to use columns to see who is fastest!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add two 3-digit numbers using adjusting strategies

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often try to use a written method/algorithm which they know gives an accurate answer but don't understand why it works.
nodes.response: Encourage the pupils to be brave and remind them that this is about mental subtraction so, with practice, will be quicker than any written methods.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract a pair of 2-digit numbers by finding the difference

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. This could involve drawing bar models or other representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving adjacent multiples of nine

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency in 9 times tables and not understanding the problems.
nodes.response: To clearly model highlighting key words of worded problems to understand the problem and the operation required for the calculation. Continue to use language stems such as 'If I know...' 'Then I know...,' to support mathematical thinking.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts from the 10 times table to solve problems involving the 9 times table

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the keywords of this lesson and use them interchangeably or incorrectly.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the terms to identify the known elements in worded problems. Choral response can also support pupils using these words correctly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent counting in nines as the 9 times table

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. This could involve drawing bar models or other representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the 9 times table to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the keyword adjacent and have difficult understanding the word problems.
nodes.response: Model correct usage in a range of contexts including labelling abstract equations and using the term to identify the known elements in worded problems. Take time to show adjacent on number lines connecting to addition and subtraction of equal groups.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between adjacent multiples of nine

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it more challenging to use equations starting with the difference, or may make mistakes writing these.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need for balance in equations. Both sides of the equation must be equal. Equations can start with the minuend or the difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the additive relationship to rearrange subtraction equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it tricky using scales to read bar charts, especially when the scale uses multiples of five.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about where intermediate numbers are on bar charts (e.g. numbers from 10 to 15). They may count from one number to another or make marks to show approximately where numbers would be found.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using bar charts, pictograms and tables

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the parts and the whole in an equation, especially when there is a missing number.
nodes.response: Bar models are helpful for representing and understanding the parts and the whole. Ensure that pupils understand that minuend and sum both represent a whole. Allow lots of opportunities for pupils to sketch bar models.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify knowns and unknowns in addition equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle starting equations with the sum. They may think = means 'the answer is..'
nodes.response: Ensure that children understand that 'equals' means that the equation balances (i.e. both sides have the same value.) This could be achieved through using balance scales and attaching the idea of equals with balance.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the additive relationship to rearrange addition equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it more difficult to understand equations that start with the whole (e.g. 20 = 50 - 30)
nodes.response: Emphasise the need for balance in equations. To be equal, both sides must have the same value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop understanding of the relationship between addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may reorder the numbers but forget to reorder the operations too.
nodes.response: Model the problems using tens frames and number lines, ensuring that pupils understand that both the numbers and operations need to be reordered.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand why the order of addition and subtraction steps can be chosen

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to solve problems without thinking about the numbers involved.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to look at the calculations and think about the numbers involved. Pupils may not get the most efficient method first time so encourage them to think about their responses and learn from what other children have done.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve one and two-step problems in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when reordering equations where the addends and subtrahends are calculated first (e.g. 455 + 39 - 38)
nodes.response: Give pupils opportunities to explore the relationship between the addend and subtrahend. They could calculate the answers to problems where the subtrahend is one less than the addend (e.g. 45 + 10 - 9). Can they see a pattern in their answers?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve multi-step addition and subtraction problems efficiently

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rely on the same strategies to solve all problems and may find it hard to remember when to add to find the missing part and when to subtract.
nodes.response: Emphasise the use of bar models, especially for pupils who are struggling. This will help them identify whether a part is missing or if the whole is missing, and whether they should add the parts or subtract a part from the whole to get the answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify knowns and unknowns in subtraction equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the wrong operation to find missing numbers, adding when they should be subtracting or vice versa.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw bar models, focusing on the whole in the problem. They should also write problems, understanding where the missing number is and rearranging equations so that they can calculate the answers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the additive relationship to rearrange and solve equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils attempt to estimate using approximations that do not allow for quick mental calculation.
nodes.response: Spend time estimating yourself and modelling the simplicity of it. Use estimations regularly to check the magnitude of an answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use estimation to support accurate calculation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may partition numbers incorrectly and arrange grid model incorrectly.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling, ask pupils 'what does this digit represent?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 3-digit by a 1-digit number using partitioning

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly regrouping or forgetting to record a regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling. 'What does this digit represent?' 'Where do we place the regrouped amount?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 3-digit by a 1-digit number with multiple regroups

nodes.misconception: Misalignment of digits when setting out short multiplication.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling, ask pupils 'what does this digit represent?' Return to expanded layout briefly, before re-doing the problem.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 3-digit by a 1-digit number with no regroups

nodes.misconception: Children may misalign digits when arranging into the short multiplication layout.
nodes.response: Children should use unitising language to help them understand and apply this to formal written methods.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a 3-digit by a 1-digit number with one or two regroups

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty when the sum is presented on the left of the equal sign.
nodes.response: Ensure that equations are arranged with the sum both on the left and the right of equal sign. Use term 'is equal to' to stress equality.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add parts to find the value of the whole and write the equation

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that addends must be represented in a certain order.
nodes.response: Ensure parts are seen alongside objects and pictures presented in different ways so the visual always matches the given expression.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand that parts can be represented in any order

nodes.misconception: The terms minuend, subtrahend and difference may be difficult if only used occasionally.
nodes.response: Ensure the terms are used by the teacher throughout lessons and encourage children to use them when explaining their thinking.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand the relationship between addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: Children may forget to start with the whole group when writing subtraction equations.
nodes.response: Maintain a strong focus throughout on what the numbers in equations represent. Explore mistakes that are made to clarify understanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Partition a whole into two parts and write as a subtraction equation

nodes.misconception: Children may write the addends in any order when representing addition as an increase in quantity.
nodes.response: Present and discuss errors, focusing on what each number in an equation represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand addition as increasing a quantity

nodes.misconception: Children may believe the equal sign must always be placed at the end of the equation.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities to rearrange equations, initially where both addends are presented as one unit which balances the sum.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand the use of the equals sign in equations

nodes.misconception: Children may think the missing number in an equation always has to be the whole.
nodes.response: Encourage children to record their thinking, bringing attention to the missing part by underlining it.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find the missing part in an equation

nodes.misconception: Children may muddle the order of the numbers on a bar model and in a subtraction equation.
nodes.response: If children are not secure, then return to the concrete to secure understanding of this structure of subtraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using bar models to subtract

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty understanding partitioning of the whole group where one part is zero.
nodes.response: Include contexts with zero, so children can discuss and clarify their thinking.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine parts using the addition symbol

nodes.misconception: When using part-part-whole models, children may put counters in the parts and whole simultaneously.
nodes.response: Work practically, moving counters to show we can partition the whole into parts and recombine the parts to make the whole again.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding part-part-whole relationships

nodes.misconception: Children may have the misconception that multiplying always makes the number bigger and therefore 0 cannot be a product.
nodes.response: Remind children that 0 groups of something is equal to zero. You can show this practically using groups of zero. When a factor is 1 the product is the other factor.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a factor of zero or one affects the product

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. Support pupils in annotating problems and rephrasing using words such as groups to identify the factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the relationships between the 5 and 10 times tables to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that all multiples of 5 are multiples of 10
nodes.response: Show children the relationship between 5s and 10s using the multiplication chart and number line. Make clear the relationship between the multiples of 5 and 10 through using stem sentences; for every one group of ten, there are two groups of 5
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between multiples of five and ten

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the number of groups and group size.
nodes.response: Continue to use the number stems and arrays to highlight the relationship between the factors and products.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent multiplication equations in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that multiples of 5 and 10 are multiples of 10
nodes.response: Show children the relationship between 5s and 10s using the multiplication chart and number line. Make clear that even multiples of 5 are multiples of 10  Not all multiples of 10 are multiples of 5 Encourage discussions to highlight the relationship.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how groups of five and ten are related

nodes.misconception: Children may not grasp why 5 + 5 is equal to 2 × 5
nodes.response: Continue to use the stem sentences to help children understand doubling; 5 + 5 is the same as 2 groups of 5. This is the same as 2 × 5. Children can use a 2 times table chart to help them answer questions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a multiplication equation with 2 as a factor is related to doubling

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to identify the factors from the word problems.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. Pupils may benefit by highlighting which number shows the number of group size and which shows the number of groups.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what each factor represents in a multiplication story

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise that 1 can be a factor, particularly when the context includes 1 group.
nodes.response: Work with children to discuss groups and what they can see, such as 3 groups of 4   Reduce the number of groups to 2 and then 1 group and identify that 1 group can still be used. Then attach this to multiplication and expressions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what each factor represents in a multiplication story when one of the factors is one

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misunderstand the contexts or language within worded problems and therefore not understand the calculation required to solve.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the 2, 5 and 10 times tables to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misunderstand the contexts or language within worded problems and therefore not understand the calculation required to solve.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. Pupils may benefit from representing what is known and what is unknown such as by drawing a bar model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the 2, 5 and 10 times tables to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils not being able to regroup when dividing.
nodes.response: Use concrete resources to highlight regrouping of tens. Ask children 'What is the highest multiple you know?' to support with partitioning.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 2-digit by a 1-digit number using partitioning (with regrouping)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may always choose short division to solve division equations.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about other strategies that they know. Ask questions such as 'Is this the most efficient method?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use efficient division strategies to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to identify whether a question is a 1-step or 2-step problem.
nodes.response: Read and highlight key words which identify the operation. Highlight the numbers which will lead to the calculation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiplication and division in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly arrange the dividend or divisor and quotient.
nodes.response: Clear modelling. Ask children 'What does this number represent?' - 'The dividend and it is placed inside the division frame.'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 2-digit by a 1-digit number using short division (no regrouping )

nodes.misconception: Pupils not understanding and/or recording the regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Continue to use language of unitisation. For example '7 tens ÷ 3 is 2 tens remainder 1 ten.' Ask what the regrouped amount represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 2-digit by a 1-digit number using short division (with regrouping)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to arrange digits within the division frame correctly and work procedurally.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling of arrangement of digits using the division frame. Continue to use stem sentences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 3-digit by a 1-digit number using short division

nodes.misconception: Lack of understanding of place value may lead to the rise of incorrect partial quotients.
nodes.response: Encourage children to identify what each digit represents. If misconceptions persist - use place value counters to divide by skip counting.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 3-digit by a 1-digit number using partitioning and representations (no remainders)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the terminology of dividend and divisor. Pupils may regroup the incorrect amount.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils can identify the dividend and the divisor. Use language of unitisation to correct any place value misconceptions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use short division when the hundreds digit is smaller than the divisor

nodes.misconception: Working through algorithmically without having an understanding of the regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Clear modelling with PVC. Ask children 'What does this number represent?'. Continue to use sentence stems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 2-digit number using short division (with regrouping and remainders)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to record the remainder.
nodes.response: Remind children that if the ones are not divisible there will be a remainder and that this is expressed as 'r'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 2-digit by a 1-digit number using representations with exchanging and remainders

nodes.misconception: Some children may continue to share one by one when dividing.
nodes.response: Encourage children to skip count in the divisor and remind children that it is an efficient way of dividing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 2-digit by a 1-digit number using partitioning and representations (no remainders)

nodes.misconception: Pupils not understanding why they may have to regroup or what the regrouped amount represents.
nodes.response: Ask pupils 'What does this digit represent?' draw attention to place value and use continue to use language of unitisation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide using short division with regrouping and remainders

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Ask pupils what each digit represents. Continue to use skip counting when dividing each digit in the dividend.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide using partitioning and representations (multiple regroups and remainder)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be able to identify the key words leading to the operation.
nodes.response: Highlight the keyword and read back the question highlighting the context of the word problem. Words such as 'of' will need exemplifying.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiplication and division

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Encourage children to identify what each digit in the dividend represents. Ask, 'Is this digit a multiple of the divisor?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide a 3-digit number using partitioning and representations (one regroup)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with estimation, especially with thinking of numbers that are quick and easy to calculate with.
nodes.response: Pupils will probably have little or no experience of rounding but they will be able to think about the place value of numbers and give tens or hundreds numbers that are close. Number lines may be helpful for some children.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts and strategies to accurately and efficiently calculate and check column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not refer to the size of the numbers when manipulating the digit cards.
nodes.response: Encourage them to talk about the size of the numbers and whether the digit cards represent ones, tens or hundreds.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use column addition to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may regroup incorrectly, forget to write the regrouped ten or forget to add any regrouped tens when calculating the total for the tens column.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the regrouped number is a ten and that it needs to be added to the tens total. If necessary, revisit the use of base ten blocks.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use column addition to add numbers by regrouping ones

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to add the 'regrouped' hundred when calculating the total for the hundreds column.
nodes.response: Model regrouping and finding column totals clearly, reminding pupils to add together all of the numbers in the column to get the total.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use column addition to add numbers by regrouping tens

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to refer to the size of the numbers when adding and when regrouping.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to talk about the place value of the digits. Ten ones can be regrouped as a ten; ten tens can be regrouped as a hundred.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use column addition with regrouping in ones and tens

nodes.misconception: Pupils may refer to adding numbers in the tens as 3 + 6 rather than 30 + 60
nodes.response: Encourage them to refer to the tens numbers as tens, and use the language appropriately. In 34 + 44, we add 4 and 4 together and then we add 30 and 40 together. This will support their reasoning as they progress in this unit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add 2-digit numbers using column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may spend too long trying to make a very accurate estimate for their calculations.
nodes.response: Pupils need to understand that an estimation should be quick and easy to calculate. Encourage them to think about the nearest hundreds numbers so that these can be added together very quickly to give a value close enough to the answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use column addition with regrouping to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not use zero to show that there are no tens or ones number in a 3-digit number. They may also use a zero to show that there are no hundreds when adding a 2-digit to a 3-digit number.
nodes.response: Emphasise with pupils that they need to use a zero only when needed. The number 75 would not be written as 075, so should not be written like this in column addition.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add 3-digit numbers using column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find the parts and the whole in column addition.
nodes.response: Emphasise the sum as being within the 'equals' sign in column addition. Take time to write equations, bar models and column addition and make connections between these.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify the addends and the sum in column addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget to use zero to show that there are no 10s or 1s (e.g. in 60), or may use zero to show that there are no 100s when it is not needed (e.g. they may write 068).
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that zero is needed to show that there are no 10s or 1s in a 3-digit number although it isn't needed to show that there are no 100s. We don't write 68 as 068, so we do not do this with column addition either.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use place value to correctly lay out column addition

nodes.misconception: Children may inaccurately recall related doubling facts to solve halving problems.
nodes.response: Represent each problem as a bar model (as the whole and two equal parts) before solving. Encourage children to check that the two equal parts are equal to the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how doubling and halving are related

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly partitioning and halving odd multiples of 10
nodes.response: Ensure children use representations where they are able to see the partitioning of the number into an even multiple of 10 and 10 more. That way, they can clearly see they are still finding half of 30 for example.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Halve even 2-digit numbers and multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to see doubling where the numbers cannot be seen e.g. money contexts.
nodes.response: Children should be encouraged to represent the numbers using resources to support them in visualising the problem until they are confident to use mental strategies to solve.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Double 2-digit numbers and record as multiplications where one of the factors is 2

nodes.misconception: Children may be unable to see how they can use learnt strategies to solve worded problems.
nodes.response: Support children to visualise and represent each problem, first using physical resources that can be manipulated, e.g. socks to make pairs, before looking to represent the mathematics. This will help them to see what they need to calculate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify missing factors when one factor is 2

nodes.misconception: Children may revert to inefficient strategies to solve problems e.g. counting on, using fingers.
nodes.response: Within the second learning cycle, children are encouraged to evaluate strategies used by others. The most efficient strategies should be discussed together throughout the first learning cycle to support with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of doubling, halving and the 2 times table to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. This could involve drawing bar models or other representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using the relationship between 3 and 9 times table

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency in the 3s and 9s times tables can lead to pupils being slower to grasp the generalisation about the relationship between the 3 and 9 times tables.
nodes.response: Use arrays and other representations to draw clear comparisons. Multiplication grids could also be provided while pupils become more fluent in recall.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between multiples of three and multiples of nine

nodes.misconception: Lack of fluency in the 3s and 9s times tables can lead to pupils being slower to grasp the generalisation about the relationship between the 3 and 9 times tables.
nodes.response: Model using arrays and other representations. Pupils who may struggle to triple / find one third of a number may require more time to work through calculations. Multiplication grids could also be provided while pupils become more fluent in recall.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between pairs of 3 and 9 times table facts that have the same product

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Take time to act out problems particularly the game, to ensure pupils understand where the mathematics can be seen in real-world examples. Using smaller examples can help learners understand the connections.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving the 3, 6 and 9 times tables

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to solve problems or misunderstand questions.
nodes.response: Model clearly how to identify key phrases and words which will identify the operation and equation required for word problems. This could involve drawing bar models or other representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using divisibility rules for divisors of 3, 6 and 9

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the concept of 'nearest multiple of 1,000,000'
nodes.response: The nearest multiple of 1,000,000 is the multiple of 1,000,000 that a given letter or number is closest to. If a number is before than the midpoint, this will be the previous multiple and if it is after, this will be the next multiple.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding 7-digit numbers to the nearest million

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically use a formal written algorithm. Children may not see the difference between, 'How much more?' and 'How many times more?'
nodes.response: What do you notice about the numbers? Is there a more efficient way? Can you represent this in a bar model or form an equation. What do you notice about the language?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving calculations efficiently

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically use a formal written algorithm.
nodes.response: What do you notice about the numbers? What would you add/subtract to get to the nearest multiple of (a power of 10)? Can you represent this on a number line?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore mental and written strategies to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children may automatically resort to the use of the formal column algorithms. These are not always the most efficient methods.
nodes.response: What do you notice about the numbers? Is there a mental strategy that you could use?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems explaining which strategy is most efficient

nodes.misconception: Mistakes may be made when identifying the previous multiple of the power of 10 or when giving the rounded answer (missing off any digits that have a larger value).
nodes.response: Use numbers lines, the stem sentences and learning about the critical digit to support children to identify previous multiples and when giving their answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding seven-digit numbers to any power of 10

nodes.misconception: The change in amount during the 'then' part of the story may be hard to identify.
nodes.response: Draw attention to explicitly to the change, talking about it as a decrease.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret and represent subtraction stories

nodes.misconception: Some children may not relate the size of the number added/subtracted to the number at the end of the story.
nodes.response: Encourage children to predict how the number at the end of the story will change when the number added/subtracted is increased or decreased.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Create addition and subtraction stories

nodes.misconception: After exploring reduction, children may struggle to see partitioning as subtraction because a part is not taken away from the whole.
nodes.response: Make strong links between equations and different subtraction contexts by focusing on what the subtrahend represents in each case.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Furthering understanding of subtraction as decreasing an amount

nodes.misconception: Children may find the ‘then’ part of the story, where the amount changes, difficult to identify.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the change, talking about it as a decrease.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand subtraction as decreasing an amount

nodes.misconception: In the ‘then’ part of the story, the change in amount may be hard to identify.
nodes.response: Draw attention to the change, talking about it as a increase in amount.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret and represent addition stories

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand the importance of the order of the numerals in equations, so may not understand that the amount added or subtracted is of key importance when undoing a change made.
nodes.response: Present errors to discuss and correct. Encourage children to use practical equipment to demonstrate how they know they are right or to show why an error made cannot be correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that addition and subtraction are inverse operations

nodes.misconception: On recognising the subtraction symbol, children may believe that the two parts known must be subtracted from each other, regardless of which part of the equation is missing.
nodes.response: Use practical equipment on 'First, then, now' boards and on part-part-whole models to demonstrate additive relationships and encourage them to use their number sense to think about and predict plausible answers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find the missing part of a subtraction story

nodes.misconception: Children may look at the numbers but not be able to visualise the context, for example, they may try to undo 6 + 4 = 10 with 10 - 6 = 4
nodes.response: Use practical equipment to illustrate the importance of the number added and subtracted being the same. Link equations to contexts ensuring that children are secure with what each part of an equation represents when linked to a story context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: Children may not have yet formed generalisations about the increase or decrease that takes place when numbers are added or subtracted, so may predict answers that are not logical or possible.
nodes.response: Encourage children to generalise by posing errors to reason about, encouraging predictions about what will happen to the size of amounts when adding and subtracting. Encourage use of practical equipment to demonstrate their explanations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find the missing part in addition and subtraction stories

nodes.misconception: Children may add the parts instead of subtracting a part to find the missing amount.
nodes.response: Give plenty of opportunities to act out stories and solve problems with practical objects. Encourage children to think about the size of the missing part in relation to the known parts, i.e. whether it will be larger or smaller than the other parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find the missing part of an addition story

nodes.misconception: With these particular facts, children may resort to counting on in ones from five or six and you want to avoid this.
nodes.response: Begin by linking 5 + 3 in the context of 'five and a bit' to the explicit knowledge that 5 + 3 = 8  With 6 + 3, stress that this can easily be related to 6 + 4 which is a known fact. Encourage pupils to use one hand to represent 5 without counting.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems by adding 3 to 5 and 6

nodes.misconception: Children could try to apply this idea to other near-double facts that may be more easily solved using other strategies.
nodes.response: 0 + 1 and 1 + 2 are near-doubles, but these are more easily solved using the 'one more'/ 'one less' strategy. Explore this together before leading children to the most efficient strategy for calculating.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of doubles to calculate near-doubles

nodes.misconception: Children may resort to counting strategies without noticing that the relationship between the minuend and the subtrahend is that there is a difference of two.
