nodes.response: Consider pre-teaching for children who lack confidence using Gattegno chart.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the composition of 100 to multiply and divide by 100 in different ways

nodes.misconception: Many pupils believe that 'adding 2 zeros' is multiplying by 100 which can lead to difficulties later on when they are introduced to decimal numbers.
nodes.response: Don't dismiss it. It's a pattern that has been spotted and generalised. Do encourage the children to work with physical resources that don't involve the numbers themselves so they can understand that it isn't adding zero but changing place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the use of placeholders when multiplying whole numbers by 100

nodes.misconception: Many pupils believe that 'subtracting 2 zeros' is dividing by 100 which can lead to difficulties later on when they are introduced to decimal numbers.
nodes.response: Don't dismiss it. It's a pattern that has been spotted and generalised. Do encourage the children to work with physical resources that don't involve the numbers themselves so they can see that it's not subtracting 2 zeros but changing place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the removal of placeholders when dividing whole numbers by 100

nodes.misconception: Times tables recall is crucial in these lessons. It provides the platform for children to extend their understanding in combination with what they know about place value.
nodes.response: For children who struggle with times table recall, give them a times table grid to refer to. This lesson is teaching the concept of scaling, not testing their knowledge of times tables.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Scale known multiplication facts by 100

nodes.misconception: One-tenth times the size may be a confusing phrase to use because pupils are used to seeing an increase when using '___ times as many'.
nodes.response: Ensure that children understand that a one is one-tenth times the size of a ten. Base 10 is an excellent resource for this. Then gradually increase the ones and the corresponding tens.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand that dividing a number by 10 makes it one-tenth times the size

nodes.misconception: Many pupils believe that 'subtracting zero' is dividing by 10 which can lead to difficulties later on when they are introduced to decimal numbers.
nodes.response: Don't dismiss it. It's a pattern that has been spotted and generalised. Do encourage the children to work with physical resources that don't involve the numbers themselves so they can see that it's not subtracting zero but changing place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use place value to explain removing the zero in the ones from a multiple of ten when we divide by 10

nodes.misconception: Place value counters don't have proportionality in the same way that Base 10 does which can make the concepts here more abstract.
nodes.response: Smaller multiplications can be used with Base 10 to model scaling to start off with. Try 2 × 1 or 3 × 1 scaling up to become 2 × 100 or 3 × 100 with Base 10 and then put this modelling side-by-side with place value counters to make the links.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how making a factor 100 times the size affects the product

nodes.misconception: Place value counters don't have proportionality in the same way that Base 10 does which can make the concepts here more abstract.
nodes.response: Smaller multiplications can be used with Base 10 to model scaling to start off with. Try 2 × 1 or 3 × 1  scaling up to  become 2 × 10 or 3 × 10 with Base 10 and then put this modelling side-by-side with place value counters to make the links.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how making a factor 10 times the size affects the product

nodes.misconception: Place value counters don't have proportionality in the same way that Base 10 blocks do which can make the concepts here more abstract.
nodes.response: Smaller divisions can be used with Base 10 to model scaling to start off with. Try 2 ÷ 2 or 4 ÷ 2 scaling up to become 200 ÷ 2 or 400 ÷ 2 with Base 10 and then put this modelling side-by-side with place value counters to make the links.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how making the dividend 100 times the size affects the quotient

nodes.misconception: Place value counters don't have proportionality in the same way that Base 10 does which can make the concepts here more abstract.
nodes.response: Smaller divisions can be used with Base 10 to model scaling to start off with. Try 2 ÷ 2 or 4 ÷ 2 scaling up to become 20 ÷ 2 or 40 ÷ 2 with Base 10 and then put this modelling side-by-side with place value counters to make the links.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how making the dividend 10 times the size affects the quotient

nodes.misconception: Pupils may start talking of 'adding a zero' to multiply by 10
nodes.response: Don't dismiss this as it is disguising an understanding of a pattern but reassure the pupils that this will be explained later through place value discussions in the coming lessons.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between multiplying a number by 10 and multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may still not have the automaticity of times tables facts useful for this lesson.
nodes.response: Pre-teaching some tricky times tables facts by using counters for arrays will be useful. Consider allowing scaffolds within the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to calculate the area of a rectangle using multiplication

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is only one possible answer to some problems or only one way to solve a problem.
nodes.response: Discuss whether there is only one possible answer to a problem or if there are many solutions. Ensure that more than one approach to solving a problem is modelled where appropriate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of area to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: That a shape always has to be split into smaller shapes in order to calculate the area.
nodes.response: Show different ways to calculate area using the same shape. It can be split in different ways, completed and an area subtracted or a part cut and fitted into a gap.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Choose an efficient way to decompose a compound shape to calculate the area

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to split a compound shape to calculate the area.
nodes.response: Make time in the lesson to model and discuss different ways of calculating the area of compound shapes. Include strategies that move parts of the shape to simplify the shape and the calculations needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the area of shapes made from 2 or more rectangles

nodes.misconception: Calculating the length of a side when the overall dimension and part dimensions are known and understanding when a part of the overall dimension is needed to calculate part of the area.
nodes.response: Look at shapes with missing dimensions and discussing that the overall length and width of a compound rectilinear shape is the total of the shorter side lengths in a particular direction. This allows missing or overall dimensions to be calculated.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the area of compound rectilinear shapes

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not see that two rectilinear shapes can look very different but have the same area.
nodes.response: Cut out a large rectangle. Cut it into two rectangles. Ask pupils to move one of the rectangles and reposition it. Has the area changed?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the area of shapes made from 2 rectangles by decomposing the shape in different ways

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that an area of one square metre has to be in the shape of a square.
nodes.response: Take two large pieces of paper, each one square metre, and fold them in half in different ways. Bring them together to form a square metre.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure the area of flat shapes using square metres

nodes.misconception: Good multiplication skills are required for this lesson, including TO x O and HTO x O.
nodes.response: Pupils who are insecure with short multiplication will need pre-teaching. Consider giving them a scaffold such as a times tables grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the areas of rectangles using multiplication

nodes.misconception: Some pupils count fractions of a square, such as a right-angles triangle, as a whole square unit.
nodes.response: Cut out the shape to show that two ‘parts’ of a square sometimes go together to make a complete square unit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure the area of flat shapes using square centimetres

nodes.misconception: Applying known facts and strategies to solve problems involving division. Being able to break down a problem into steps when it comes to compound shapes.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities to discuss approaches and highlight the efficient strategies and approaches. Acknowledge that there is more than one way to solve a problem whilst focusing on efficient and effective strategies.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate missing dimensions in rectangles and compound rectilinear shapes

nodes.misconception: Children may start counting with the first coin they see or arranged them in a line in no particular order, leading to inefficient counting strategies instead of more efficient calculation methods.
nodes.response: Encourage children to group coins of the same value together and start with higher value coins, so they can apply the calculation strategies they already know to find the total value of a set of different coins.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate amounts up to 20 p

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully understand the concept of unitising and may confuse the number of coins with the total value. They may also count sets of coins containing 5 p coins and other coins in fives.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens with five spots alongside 5 p coins to start with to deepen the understanding of one coin representing a value of . Discuss deliberate errors, articulating thinking around why these cannot be correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the total value of the coins in a set of 5 p coins

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the number of coins with their value, so count in ones, or revert to counting in ones. They may have difficulty counting on to reach a value when some coins are already present.
nodes.response: Present situations where both 5 p and 1 p coins are used to reach the same amount to stress the difference in value. Compare sets of 1 p and 5 p coins with sets of 5 p coins drawing attention to the importance of the value of each coin.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find how many five pence coins are needed to make a given amount

nodes.misconception: Children may understand the value of each set of coins but incorrectly use a symbol ( < > = ) in comparing them.
nodes.response: Encourage reading from left to right e.g. ___ is less than / greater than ___. Ensure children have opportunities to place the coins within the symbols to understand the correct orientation of them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare sets of 2 p, 5 p, and 10 p coins

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the number of coins with their value, so count in ones, or revert to counting in ones. They may have difficulty counting on to reach a value when some coins are already present.
nodes.response: Present situations where both 10 p and 1 p coins are used to reach the same amount to stress the difference in value. Compare sets of 1 p and 10 p coins with sets of 10 p coins drawing attention to the importance of the value of each coin.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find how many ten pence coins are needed to make a given amount

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully understand the concept of unitising and may confuse the number of coins with the total value. They may also count sets of coins containing 2 p coins and other coins in twos.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens with two spots alongside 2 p coins to start with to deepen the understanding of one coin representing a value of . Discuss deliberate errors, articulating thinking around why these cannot be correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the total value of a set of 2 p coins

nodes.misconception: Children may start counting out using any coins available instead of thinking of the whole amount needed first and partitioning it into manageable parts where they can deploy known strategies.
nodes.response: Encourage children to partition teen numbers using a part-part-whole model and use what they know about making 10, and the numbers up to 10, to find combinations that use the fewest possible coins to total a given value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find and make amounts within 20 p

nodes.misconception: Children may start counting out using any coins available instead of thinking of the whole amount needed first and partitioning it into manageable parts where they can deploy known strategies.
nodes.response: Encourage children to use what they know about making 10, and the numbers up to 10, to find combinations that use the fewest possible coins to total a given value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find and make amounts within 10p

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully understand the concept of unitising and may confuse the number of coins with the total value. They may also count sets of coins containing 10 p coins and other coins in tens.
nodes.response: Use pre-money tokens with ten spots alongside 10 p coins to start with to deepen the understanding of one coin representing a value of 1. Discuss deliberate errors, articulating thinking around why these cannot be correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the total value of the coins in a set of 10p coins

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the number of coins with their value, so count in ones, or revert to counting in ones. They may have difficulty counting on to reach a value when some coins are already present.
nodes.response: Present situations where both 2 p and 1 p coins are used to reach the same amount to stress the difference in value. Compare sets of 1 p and 2 p coins with sets of 2 p coins drawing attention to the importance of the value of each coin.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find how many 2 p coins are needed to make a given value

nodes.misconception: Children may write fraction notation with the numerator and denominator the wrong way round.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentence shown in this lesson each time you write a fraction, and give children opportunities to explain what each numeral in the fraction represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read, write and understand fraction notation

nodes.misconception: Children may initially think that two quarters is larger than one-half because the numerals in the fraction are larger.
nodes.response: Try to avoid introducing the fractions in numeral form until children are familiar with recognising two-quarters in different representations such as shapes and small sets. Support understanding with stem sentences as modelled in this lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2

nodes.misconception: Children may try to make a group of 2 objects rather than share into 2 equal parts.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentence 'the whole group of _ has been divided into 2 equal parts and there are _ in each part' alongside concrete objects so that the children can experience dividing different numbers of objects into 2 equal parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find one-half of a number

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to find the whole when they are told the size of the half and may try to find half of the half.
nodes.response: Use a bar model representation to help children see the structure of double and half. Use gesture, colour and/or circling when discussing what each part of the bar model represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Relate finding half of a number to halving and doubling

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that a line drawn through the middle of something means that the whole has been divided in half.
nodes.response: Children will benefit from practical experiences where they can explore finding half of shapes and objects in different ways. Encourage them to compare the size of the parts and make sure they are equal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognise and name the fraction 'one half'

nodes.misconception: Children may think that when a shape has been split straight through the middle that the parts are equal.
nodes.response: Encourage children to compare the sizes of each part by lining them up next to each other. With paper shapes, children can cut out the parts and lay them on top of each other to see if the parts are equal or unequal in size.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Equal or unequal parts

nodes.misconception: Children may find one-quarter rather than three-quarters of an amount.
nodes.response: Use gesture, colour and/or circling to highlight three-quarters of an amount. Use the stem sentences, 'one-quarter of the whole is ___, two-quarters of the whole is ___, three quarters of the whole is ___'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find three-quarters of an object, shape, set of objects or quantity

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse finding a quarter of a number with finding 4 of the objects, or finding a third of a number with finding 3 of the objects.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentence 'the whole has been divided into ___ equal parts' and draw a bar model to represent this before children attempt to find a quarter or a third of a number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find one-third or one-quarter of a number

nodes.misconception: Children can find it difficult to see if the three parts are equal, particularly when they are presented in different orientations rather than horizontal and vertical lines.
nodes.response: Allow children to handle practical objects and cut-outs of shapes that have been divided into thirds so they can rotate them and see them in different orientations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognise and name the fraction ‘one-third’

nodes.misconception: Children can find it difficult to see if the four parts are equal, particularly when they are presented in different orientations rather than horizontal and vertical lines.
nodes.response: Allow children to handle practical objects and cut-outs of shapes that have been divided into quarters so they can rotate them and see them in different orientations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recognise and name the fraction 'one quarter'

nodes.misconception: It is not uncommon for pupils to mix up the x- and y-coordinates, meaning they end up plotting in the wrong position or giving the wrong coordinates.
nodes.response: A stem sentence has been included in the lesson which should be regularly referred to. Rhymes can also be used as an aide memoir but this should be in tandem with deep conceptual understanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw and complete simple shapes by plotting positions on the full coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to have proficiency in bridging across zero with negative numbers, in the range of −10 to 10. Grid lines that might help to support such calculations are not given in this lesson.
nodes.response: Pupils not secure will need a resource within the lesson to support their calculations, such as a number line going from −10 to 10.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving missing coordinates

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe the perpendicular height of any parallelogram to be one of its side lengths. This is only true of a rectangle.
nodes.response: Take time to exemplify perpendicular height with a focus on the right angle created. Make use of examples within the lesson and include additional unusual parallelograms to secure understanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to calculate the area of a parallelogram

nodes.misconception: When drawing triangles with a given area pupils may create a factor pair of the triangle's area when drawing the base and perpendicular height. The factor pair refers to the surrounding parallelogram.
nodes.response: For pupils who are making this mistake, encourage them to sketch the parallelogram around the triangle, reminding them to double the triangle area before finding the factor pairs.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the area of a triangle  to calculate unknown measurements

nodes.misconception: Pupils often over-generalise the word 'base' and do not recognise that the base is not always horizontal or the 'bottom' part of the shape.
nodes.response: Take time to identify that the base is related to the perpendicular height and show that one triangle can have a different base dependent on where the measurement is taken from. Pupils should consider efficiency when selecting a base.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to calculate the area of a triangle

nodes.misconception: Pupils highly familiar with finding the area of a rectangle by multiplying its side lengths might overgeneralise and multiply the base by a side length rather than by the perpendicular height.
nodes.response: Some 'red herring' examples are given in the Practice questions where the side length is given unnecessarily. You may wish to make an extra teaching point of how this is superfluous. Remind pupils of the formula, which does not include side lengths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the area of a parallelogram formula to calculate unknown measurements

nodes.misconception: One of the most common mistakes pupils make when reflecting is to flip the shape. Essentially, they translate the shape rather than reflecting it.
nodes.response: Attention is given at the start of the lesson to examples and non-examples of reflections, including the above misconception. Use real mirrors and ask pupils to reflect objects in them, noticing the direction in which the reflection is facing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflect simple shapes in the axes on a full coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils are taught to choose a vertex then count horizontally and / or vertically when translating that vertex. Pupils may forget which vertex they started with and end up translating the wrong vertex.
nodes.response: You may wish to consider asking pupils to mark the starting vertex with a small circle as a reminder of which one they started with.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw and translate simple shapes on the full coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Because area and perimeter are so often discussed alongside each other - as is the case with this lesson - pupils often get the two confused.
nodes.response: By now pupils should be very familiar with area and perimeter, so that they can apply the knowledge to problem solving. However, spend time going over the definitions at the start and ensure pupils have access to visual reminders.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving area and perimeter

nodes.misconception: Pupils may remember to scale one of the sides (or pairs of sides) of a shape but forget to scale the others.
nodes.response: Focus attention on what it means when a shape is similar, drawing on examples and non-examples to support learners to understand how scaling affects all side lengths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe the relationship between scale factors and perimeters of two shapes

nodes.misconception: Pupils might miscount the number of squares moved horizontally or vertically, resulting in an inaccurate translation.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to count the number of squares carefully from the original position, possibly using a ruler or finger to help guide their counting. Practice with simpler shapes before moving to more complex polygons.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe translations of polygons drawn on a square grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that translating a shape changes its size, shape, or orientation, rather than just its position.
nodes.response: Clarify that translation only changes the position of the shape on the grid; the shape itself remains identical in size, shape, and orientation. Use visual examples to compare the shape before and after translation to reinforce this concept.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw polygons specified by translations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up directions, for example, moving left instead of right, or up instead of down. Pupils might start their movement from an incorrect position, leading to an inaccurate final location.
nodes.response: Use clear and consistent language when teaching directions. Reinforce understanding by having students physically point or move in the indicated direction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Give directions from one position to another on a grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils might confuse the x-axis and y-axis, leading them to count along the wrong axis.
nodes.response: Reiterate that the x-axis runs horizontally (left to right) and the y-axis runs vertically (up and down). Use visual aids, like arrows or labels, to clearly mark the axes on the grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Write coordinates for already marked points in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not start counting from the origin (0,0) but from another point on the grid, leading to incorrect placement of the point.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of always starting from the origin when plotting or describing coordinates. Have students physically point to or touch the origin before plotting any point.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Mark the position of points specified by coordinates in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not correctly identify the type of polygon (e.g., rectangle, square, parallelogram), leading to errors in determining the missing coordinate.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to first identify the polygon by examining the given vertices. Review the properties of common polygons (e.g., opposite sides of a rectangle are equal and parallel). Use visual aids or models to reinforce these properties.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Complete polygons with missing coordinates

nodes.misconception: Pupils may miscount the squares when moving the shape, leading to inaccurate placement.
nodes.response: Encourage students to carefully count squares from the current position of each vertex and ensure consistency in their counting across the entire shape. Practice counting out loud as a class or in pairs. Relate it to counting on using a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Move objects including polygons on a grid according to directions and mark the new position

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistakenly plot the y-coordinate (vertical distance) first, then the x-coordinate (horizontal distance), leading to incorrect point placement.
nodes.response: Reinforce that the x-coordinate comes first by using mnemonics such as "X before Y, along the ground before you fly." Practice plotting a few points together as a class to build this habit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw polygons specified by coordinates in the first quadrant

nodes.misconception: Pupils might mistakenly alter the shape or size of the polygon during translation, thinking the process involves resizing or reshaping.
nodes.response: Emphasise that translation is a "sliding" motion that moves the shape without changing its size or orientation. Demonstrate this with cut-out shapes that can be physically moved on a grid, showing that the shape remains identical after translation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Translate polygons in the first quadrant

nodes.misconception: Pupils might write the y-coordinate (vertical distance) first instead of the x-coordinate (horizontal distance).
nodes.response: Reinforce the correct order by teaching "x comes before y" just like in the alphabet. Practice with examples and  devices like "along the x-axis, then up the y-axis" to solidify this concept.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving marking and translating points in the first quadrant on a coordinate grid

nodes.misconception: Children might want to use inequality symbols between representations showing different wholes.
nodes.response: Explain that inequalities can only be used when the whole is the same. Provide them with examples they may be familiar with such as offering half of a large and small apple and identifying that these are not the same because the wholes differ.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify when unit fractions cannot be compared

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that the greater the denominator the bigger the fraction.
nodes.response: Reinforce this using the fraction wall. Constantly refer back to it and ensure that the children become experts at using it as a tool for comparison.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare unit fractions by looking at the denominator

nodes.misconception: When looking at fraction notation, children might still be prone to considering the greater denominator to signify a greater fraction.
nodes.response: Get the whole class on board with reminding one another that the greater the denominator, the smaller the fraction. You can model this by making this mistake as you teach and the children can call you out on it - they will enjoy that!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving comparing and ordering unit fractions in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may still fall into the habit of considering the greater denominator to be a greater fraction.
nodes.response: Continue to revisit a fraction wall where possible and use real life contexts and images. Ensure that the statement, 'When the whole is equal, the greater the denominator, the smaller the fraction.' is visible and constantly refer to it.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving comparing unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Children will often fall into the trap of thinking that a greater denominator creates a bigger fraction.
nodes.response: Ensure the children have good access to fraction walls to reinforce the fact that the greater the denominator the smaller the fraction. Fraction walls that can be dismantled and arranged are very useful for this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order unit fractions by looking at the denominator

nodes.misconception: Children may misrepresent a given problem meaning they are led to calculate the solution incorrectly.
nodes.response: Children may identify the solution quickly when working with smaller numbers, but it is still important they are encouraged to visualise and represent each problem so that they know how to reveal the structure of the maths in more complex problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Addition and subtraction within 10

nodes.misconception: Children might record that numbers can only be partitioned in one way.
nodes.response: Children here have the chance to explore how numbers can be partitioned in many different ways. Narrate when exploring these different ways throughout, using  ___ is the whole, ___ is a part and ___ is a part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining and partitioning numbers within 10

nodes.misconception: Children may recall a fact incorrectly, deploying the wrong strategy to calculate.
nodes.response: Revisit strategies for calculating within 10 including using knowledge of doubling, near-doubles, odd and even numbers and one more and one less. Spend time practising recall of these facts beyond the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using known addition and subtraction facts

nodes.misconception: Mistakes when counting in ones. Children may not be able to visualise numbers to see which is more/greater than, less than or equal to.
nodes.response: Children should continue to practise counting forwards and backwards from a given number to increase confidence of counting within 100. Use number lines or one hundred squares to help children visualise numbers and support comparison.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting and comparing

nodes.misconception: Children miss out numbers when skip counting.
nodes.response: Children could have resources like number lines to refer to when counting. These can be removed once children become more confident.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Counting in multiples of two, five, ten

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between division and finding a fraction of a quantity.
nodes.response: Support children to see that the denominator of a unit fraction tells us how many equal parts the whole has been divided into and that that is the same as the divisor.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Connect division with finding a fraction of a quantity to find parts and wholes

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make connections between division and the value of a part.
nodes.response: Support children to understand and describe what they know from the information given, for example, the whole, the size of a part, or the number of parts. Also, what it is that they are trying to find. Encourage representation as a bar model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate the value of parts and wholes using understanding of division

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to construct the whole from a given part. They may misunderstand the total number of parts needed as this includes the original part.
nodes.response: Emphasise the denominator as the number of equal parts and ensure the learner sees the part they have as one of ___ equal parts. Take time to construct and deconstruct wholes from and into equal parts so learners know what to include in the count.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing a whole

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between the unit fraction and the division required.
nodes.response: The stem sentence, 'The whole is divided into ___ equal parts. Each equal part is __________ of the whole.'  supports children to grasp this. Support children to make connections between the number of equal parts and the denominator of the fraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use parts and wholes to find a unit fraction of a set of objects

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the different methods used to compare fractions of amounts and their wholes.
nodes.response: Guide through questioning. What is the same/different? Can you represent this visually? What is the size/value of the parts? What fraction of the whole is each part?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the relationship between parts and wholes to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that although parts look different, they cannot represent the same fraction of the whole.
nodes.response: Ensure multiple examples are provided where the fractional parts of the whole look different but instead are equivalent in value. You may like to create a concrete example of each shape and show how it can be manipulated so the parts are equivalent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to add related unit fractions with a representation or image

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the largest denominator of the related fraction should only be used as the common denominator.
nodes.response: Provide examples where fractions can be scaled up or scaled down to find an appropriate common denominator and encourage pupils to discuss which strategy they prefer and why.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain with and without images how to add and subtract related non-unit fractions bridging a whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils add or subtract the numerators and denominators from eachother to find the solution.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils don't move to abstract equations straight away until they are secure with how addition and subtraction of non-unit fractions can be represented pictorially. You can use unitised language: ___ fifths plus ___ fifths = ___ fifths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain with and without an image how to add and subtract related non-unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to subtract the numerators and the denominators from one another for each fraction.
nodes.response: Represent each fraction using a model that draws out the equivalence of the fractions and the need for the same counting unit (denominator). Revisit previous analogies regarding sharing a common counting unit such as animals for cats and dogs.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to subtract related unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to add both the numerators and both the denominators in order to find the sum.
nodes.response: Spend time converting related fractions so that the denominators are common. Use analogies such as adding cats and dogs and needing to rename them as animals or pets to help highlight the need for a common counting unit (or common denominator).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to add related unit fractions without a representation or image

nodes.misconception: Pupils compare expressions by only ever calculating the value of each expression before comparing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider the magnitude of the fractions they are adding or subtracting. Comparing fractions to one-half is an effective way to help identify their magnitude and whether then expression would be larger or smaller.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of adding and subtracting related unit fractions to solve problems

nodes.misconception: When adding or subtracting fractions with different denominators, you just add or subtract the denominators from each other.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to use prior generalisations such as when the numerators are the same, the fraction with the largest denominator is the smallest, to help them reason about the above misconception.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract non-related fractions with different denominators

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that any numerator and denominator can be divided by 2 even when the numerator or denominator is odd.
nodes.response: Highlight to children that although it can sometimes be helpful to think of the magnitude of a fraction when the fraction is simplified with a decimal as the numerator or denominator, fractions can only be written with whole numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of fractions in their simplest form when solving addition and subtraction problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that converting a fraction to its simplest form is the same as making the fraction smaller or making the numerator have a value of one.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils realise that the numerator and denominator are both scaled to find a different representation of the same sized fraction. Provide examples of fractions where the simplest form does not have a numerator of one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to write a fraction in its simplest form

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to make a fraction in a simpler form by finding separate factors for the numerator and denominator to simplify.
nodes.response: Share examples for why this cannot be true with images to highlight the difference in the size of the fractions. Draw attention to the fact that it is both the numerator and denominator that needs to be scaled by a common factor.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reason about how to write a fraction in its simplest form

nodes.misconception: Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase and so may not accept that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: When we multiply by a unit fraction, it is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. This results in a decrease in length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and describe lengths using knowledge of division

nodes.misconception: Children may say, 'Times longer' but this is imprecise.
nodes.response: We say 'Times the length' because this is more precise.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and describe lengths using knowledge of multiplication

nodes.misconception: Children may say 'ten times shorter' which is imprecise. Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase, and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: We say, 'ten times the original height' because this is more precise especially when the scale factor is fractional. When we multiply by a unit fraction, it is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. This results in a decrease in length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve comparison and change problems using division

nodes.misconception: Children may say 'ten times shorter' which is imprecise. Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase, and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: We say, 'ten times the original height' because this is more precise especially when the scale factor is fractional. When we multiply by a unit fraction, it is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. This results in a decrease in length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving comparison and change

nodes.misconception: Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: When we multiply an integer by a unit fraction, the effect is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. It results in a decrease.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and describe measurements involving time and money

nodes.misconception: Children may say, 'Tens times taller', which is imprecise.
nodes.response: We say, 'Ten times the original height' because this is more precise and can be used when the scale factor is fractional.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve comparison and change problems using multiplication

nodes.misconception: Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase, and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: When we multiply an integer by a unit fraction, the effect is the same as dividing the whole by the denominator. It results in a decrease.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe changes in measurement using knowledge of multiplication and division

nodes.misconception: Children may say 'ten times heavier' which is imprecise. Children are more familiar with multiplication resulting in an increase and need to appreciate that it can also result in a decrease.
nodes.response: We say, 'ten times the original mass' because this is more precise, especially when the scale factor is fractional. When we multiply by a unit fraction, it is the same as dividing the whole by the number of equal parts in it, resulting in a decrease.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and describe measurements involving mass and capacity

nodes.misconception: Manipulating equations can result in errors.
nodes.response: To find a missing factor, we can use known facts where applicable, or we can divide the product by the known factor. Always encourage children to describe each part of the equation and what it represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of multiplication and division to solve comparison and change problems

nodes.misconception: Manipulating equations can result in errors.
nodes.response: To find a missing factor, we can use known facts where applicable, or we can divide the product by the known factor. Always encourage children to describe each part of the equation and what it represents.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve comparison and change problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to understand that parts change size when the whole changes. A relative size of a part that stays the same whilst the whole changes is a tricky concept.
nodes.response: What do you notice? What is the same? What is different?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review explaining the size of the part in relation to the whole

nodes.misconception: Sometimes parts can be deceptive and look equal but are in fact unequal. For example, a rhombus that has been split into parts with lines that are equally distributed.
nodes.response: Explore this further by presenting several examples like this if needed. You could ask the children to try and think of some examples where the parts look equal but are in fact unequal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the number of equal or unequal parts in a whole

nodes.misconception: Children might think that parts are unequal just because they look different.
nodes.response: If you cut the shapes out, do they take up the same amount of space?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Secure identifying equal parts when they do not look the same

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that larger objects cannot be a part of a whole due to their size. Children may not appreciate that the same item can be a whole or a part depending on the context.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work with parts and wholes that they can handle and experience but where parts are large and have them look at example where the same object can be a whole or a part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Secure identifying a whole and the parts that make it up

nodes.misconception: Children may not include the original part when constructing a whole. E.g. if the given part is one of four equal parts of the whole, they may construct five parts together in total.
nodes.response: How many parts does your whole have?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review constructing a whole when given a part and the number of parts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to compare two time intervals when they are presented in different formats, such as five minutes to a quarter of an hour.
nodes.response: The lesson encourages converting time into minutes. Develop automaticity in recalling facts such as 15 minutes = quarter of an hour, 30 minutes = half an hour, 45 minutes = three quarters of an hour and 60 minutes = one hour.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and sequence intervals of time

nodes.misconception: The 10 on a clock is unusual as when the minute hand is pointing to 10, it is 10 minutes to the next hour. Pupils may overgeneralise, thinking, for example, when it points to 9, it is 9 minutes to.
nodes.response: As with many mathematical ideas, regular exploration and practise outside of the lesson is key to truly understanding them. Take frequent opportunities to count in five-minute intervals on a clock using minutes past and minutes to.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell and write the time to five minutes past and to on a clock face

nodes.misconception: The lesson deals with the idea of minutes past the hour to 5 minutes past. Pupils may overgeneralise and say that when sixty minutes have gone past the hour we say sixty minutes past.
nodes.response: Ensure plenty of time is spent dealing with this concept and that pupils are comfortable with the idea that when the minute hand is pointing to 12, it is an o'clock time with no minutes having gone past the hour.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell and write the time to five minutes past on a clock face

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes forget to move the hour hand when showing quarter to or quarter past, instead leaving it pointing to the o'clock time.
nodes.response: This is covered in Cycle 2 of the lesson. Continual access to a geared clock allows this idea to be revisited both in and beyond the lesson. Plan opportunities for children to see the positions of both hands at quarter past and quarter to.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell and write quarter past and quarter to on a clock face

nodes.misconception: Children may understand a day as the amount of time in which they are awake.
nodes.response: The lesson counts and names each of the 24 hours, using morning, evening and night. Take time to discuss what the children will typically be doing during these hours, including when they will usually be asleep.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know the number of minutes in an hour and hours in a day

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to compare fractions where the whole is not the same size.
nodes.response: Give an example where fractions represent different sized wholes. Discuss how fractions may not help us compare the area used/shaded if the wholes are different. Instead, highlight the show the relationship between the whole and its part(s).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to compare non-related fractions finding equivalent fractions with common denominators

nodes.misconception: Pupils automatically want to compare fractions using common denominators, following a procedure to convert fractions to an equivalent with the same denominator.
nodes.response: Spend time looking at a variety of examples that can be reasoned about without the need to convert to common denominators. It can be helpful to represent these examples using bar model help discuss the relationships between the whole and its parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to compare pairs of non-related fractions using fraction sense

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to compare fractions to a half as they mainly consider it in its simplest form.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to visualise their fractions on a number line. Also spend time thinking about the relationship between the numerator and the denominator in fractions equivalent to one-half and use this generalisation to help moving forward.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to compare pairs of non-related fractions by comparing to a half

nodes.misconception: Pupils convert to common denominators to order fractions rather then use their sense of magnitude for each fraction they are comparing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to step back at first from procedure and ask themselves what they notice about the fractions. Can they spot fractions that are equivalent to a quarter or a half?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Order sets of non-related fractions using a range of strategies

nodes.misconception: Pupils look to convert all fractions so that they have a common denominator in order to compare them.
nodes.response: The vast majority of fractions can be compared without common denominators. To support this, pupils need to have a strong sense of the magnitude of the fractions they are comparing. Do not feel you need to move away from bar models too quickly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain which strategy for comparing non-related fractions is most efficient

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse use of the Base 10 equipment. They may also confuse the equivalence between dividing by 10/100/1,000 and multiplying by 0.1/0.01/0.001.
nodes.response: The large cube now represents one whole. The smaller blocks represent decimal fraction numbers. Use stem sentences to support common mistakes: when a number is divided by ___, it is the same as multiplying by ___
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplying and dividing a number by 10, 100 and 1,000

nodes.misconception: Children may 'add' a zero when multiplying or vice versa when dividing. Children may place a zero at the end of the decimal fraction when multiplying, or vice versa when dividing.
nodes.response: When we 'add' zero, the value of the number does not change. When we multiply or divide by a power of 10, we need to move all the digits the appropriate spaces to the left/right even if this means bridging one and moving into the decimal places.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplying and dividing a number by 10, 100 and 1,000 including bridging 1

nodes.misconception: Children may 'add' a zero when multiplying or vice versa when dividing. Children may place a zero at the end of the decimal fraction when multiplying, or vice versa when dividing.
nodes.response: When we 'add' zero, the value of the number does not change. When we multiply or divide by a power of 10, we need to move all the digits the appropriate spaces to the left/right even if this means bridging one and moving into the decimal places.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1,000

nodes.misconception: The short division algorithm may not be correctly aligned.
nodes.response: Check that the decimal point aligns in the decimal fraction and the answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide decimal fractions by 1-digit numbers using written methods

nodes.misconception: Children may scale the decimal fraction inaccurately or may forget to scale the product accordingly to solve the original equation.
nodes.response: If a decimal fraction has only tenths, we multiply by 10 to form a whole number. If the decimal fraction has hundredths, we multiply by 100 to form a whole number.  Remember to adjust the product to answer the original equation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply 1-digit numbers by decimals

nodes.misconception: The short multiplication algorithm may not be correctly aligned.
nodes.response: Check that the decimal point aligns in the decimal fraction and the product. Scaffolding with place value columns may support further.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply 1-digit numbers by decimal fractions using written methods

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between multiplying by 0.01 and dividing by 100
nodes.response: When we multiply by 0.01, it is the same as multiplying by one-hundredth. When we multiply by a unit fraction, we can divide by the denominator - in this case, 100
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between multiplying by 0.01 and dividing by 100

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to make the connection between multiplying by 0.1 and dividing by ten.
nodes.response: When we multiply by 0.1, it is the same as multiplying by one-tenth. When we multiply by a unit fraction, we can divide by the denominator - in this case, 10.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between multiplying by 0.1 and dividing by 10

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly write the amount of tenths e.g. 49 tenths may be written as 0.49
nodes.response: There are ten tenths in one whole. So e.g. 49 tenths is composed of 4 ones and 9 more tenths. We write this as 4.9
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply tenths by whole numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may get confused when converting between units of measure and be unsure when they need to multiply or divide.
nodes.response: ___ are smaller than ___, so there must be more of them in the same measure so we need to multiply (and vice versa).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve measures problems using knowledge of multiplying decimal fractions

nodes.misconception: Children may scale the decimal fraction inaccurately or may forget to scale the answer accordingly to solve the original equation.
nodes.response: If a decimal fraction has only tenths, we multiply by 10 to form a whole number. If the decimal fraction has hundredths, we multiply by 100 to form a whole number. Remember to adjust the answer to solve the original equation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divide decimal fractions by 1-digit numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse when to multiply or when to divide when converting between units of measure.
nodes.response: Encourage children to think about which unit of measure is greater e.g. kg are greater than g. In a given amount, there will be fewer of the greater unit so we need to divide.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Converting units of mass and capacity

nodes.misconception: Children may think that multiplication always makes things larger. Children may scale incorrectly.
nodes.response: When a number is multiplied by a value less than 1, the product is smaller than the original number - multiplication doesn't always make things larger. Compare numbers: if one factor is made ___ times the size, the product will be ___ times the size.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Predicting the size of a product

nodes.misconception: Children may get confused with the vocabulary when we say, for example, zero point one two rather than zero point twelve. They may also confuse how we write, for example, 32 hundredths.
nodes.response: We say zero point one two to show that there is one tenth and two hundredths. 32 hundredths is composed of 30 hundredths - this is the same as 3 tenths and we have 2 more hundredths so 32 hundredths is written 0.32
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply hundredths by whole numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse when to multiply or when to divide.
nodes.response: Encourage children to think about which unit of measure is larger e.g. km are larger than m. In a given amount, there will be fewer of the larger unit so we need to divide.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Converting units of length

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse some of the terms such as 'below' and 'between'.
nodes.response: Create visuals to display which will prompt children to think about the meaning of each word. Give opportunities to explore these words in play, for example when building with blocks ask children to place the red block above the green block.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using positional and proportional language

nodes.misconception: Children may describe movements around a grid using left, right, up and down rather than using the language of turn e.g. go forward, turn left.
nodes.response: Encourage children to act out their directions practically so they can feel themselves turning and see that they are making a turn and not taking sideways steps across the path or grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Follow and give directions

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse left and right turns when someone else, whose orientation is different from their own, is making a turn.
nodes.response: Encourage children to move themselves into the same orientation as the person whose turn they are trying to describe so that they can use their own left and right to help see which directions someone else is turning.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Giving directions and describing turns

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse left and right, especially when the orientation is different from their own.
nodes.response: Encourage children to change their own orientation to match the turn they are trying to describe. Use arrows to show the direction before and after the turn and ask children to stand and make that turn. Can they feel if they're turning left or right?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding turns

nodes.misconception: Children can find it difficult to understand that another person's left is not is the same as their own - for example, when facing someone, their partner's left hand is on the opposite side to theirs.
nodes.response: Model directions from the children's own perspective - face the same way they are facing when you are describing what is on the left and right.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using directional language

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused about how to write mixed numbers. Children may say 'five and one-eight, rather than five and one-eighth.
nodes.response: As a school, establish how mixed numbers will be recorded so that you have consistency. Ensure children are accurately expressing the fraction part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a mixed number is composed

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused as to how to write mixed numbers.
nodes.response: As a school, establish how mixed numbers will be recorded so that you have consistency.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Quantities that are made up of both whole numbers and a fractional part

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused about how to write mixed numbers. Children may say 'five and one-eight, rather than five and one-eighth.
nodes.response: As a school, establish how mixed numbers will be recorded so that you have consistency. Ensure children are accurately expressing the fraction part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compose and decompose mixed numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused about how to write mixed numbers. Children may say 'five and one-eight, rather than five and one-eighth.
nodes.response: As a school, establish how mixed numbers will be recorded so that you have consistency. Ensure children are accurately expressing the fraction part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving mixed numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may write 'four-quarters' instead of 'one' or 'one and eight-eighths' instead of '2'. Children may also confuse 'part' and 'marks' when determining the unit that we are working with.
nodes.response: One is composed of four-quarters, but we write '1'. Two is composed of one and eight-eighths but we write '2'. We need to count the equal parts in between the intervals, not the marks.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Accurately label a range of number lines

nodes.misconception: Some children can struggle to identify which direction a turn is in when it does not start from a 12 o'clock position on a clock.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities to explore making clockwise and anticlockwise turns that start from many different positions and not always facing up or at the 12 o'clock position.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe turns as a quarter, half, three-quarter or full turn

nodes.misconception: Some children may mix up the direction of left and right.
nodes.response: Share different strategies for remembering left and right, such as wearing a wristband on your left, using your left hand to make an l-shape or relating left and right to which hand you write with.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review of using mathematical language to describe position

nodes.misconception: Children can find it confusing that direction is dependent on which way someone is facing, and so forwards, backwards, left or right will not always appear in the same direction.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for children to experience movement in a straight line from different starting points, e.g. chalking a grid on the floor outside for them to move around in, or describing the movement of a toy car as they drive it along a track.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use mathematical vocabulary to describe movement

nodes.misconception: Children can find it difficult to identify someone else's left and right if they are facing a different direction to them.
nodes.response: Encourage children to orient themselves so they are facing the same way as the person they are identifying the left or right side of. Experience in different ways that when someone is opposite you, their left side is the opposite side to your left.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving position, direction and rotation

nodes.misconception: Children may describe shapes as 'upside down' or 'on its side' rather than describing the rotations.
nodes.response: Display the keywords from previous lessons such as clockwise, quarter turn etc. Model describing the rotations using these keywords and provide opportunities for children to practice this when creating their own patterns.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Order and arrange objects in patterns and explain the patterns

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to compare fractions with the same numerator or denominator.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use fraction representations to help them visualise. Reference the size of the parts (same numerator, greater denominator means smaller parts) or how many there are (same denominator, greater numerator means more parts).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare non-unit fractions including those equal to 1

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to compare fractions where the wholes are not the same.
nodes.response: It's important that pupils understand that for comparison of fractions the wholes must be the same. This lesson uses one example of comparing distances in miles versus distance in kilometres as well as comparing pizzas of different shape and size.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare non-unit fractions with the same denominator

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that fractions with a higher value numerator are larger in size.
nodes.response: Show pupils images where fractions with the same numerators and denominators are equal in size (e.g. nine-ninths is equal to three-thirds).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of unit fractions to find one whole

nodes.misconception: When a number is higher, its value is greater. Pupils may struggle to understand that as the denominator gets larger / greater, the size of the parts get smaller.
nodes.response: Show pupils lots of images, comparing fractions with the same numerator (e.g. one-fifth and one-third and then two-fifths and two-thirds). Highlight that even though the number of parts we have is the same, the size of those parts is different.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare fractions with the same numerator

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see that a unit fraction with a larger denominator is smaller than a unit fraction with a smaller denominator.
nodes.response: Pupils should be supported to visualise each fraction before moving on to interpreting abstract fraction notation. Encourage them to see the connection between the number of equal parts and the relative size of the fractions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review comparing unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the concept of different shapes (and sizes, for number of objects) a little confusing.
nodes.response: Show pupils images where parts are different shapes (area fractions - parts of a whole shape) but can easily be seen to be the same size.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying equal parts in a whole in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to see the 'whole'. If several sets are presented together (e.g. different types of fruit in a bowl), is the whole the sum of all the sets or just one of them?
nodes.response: Encourage children to identify the noun they are finding a fraction of. Is it the apples or bananas, the pandas with hats on or without. From there, they can then go on to identify the part they are being asked to find e.g. the bananas in the bowl.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of non-unit fractions to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise the total number of equal parts that make up the whole and may instead just count the number they have / are shaded for example.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to count the total number of equal parts that make up the whole and then the number that are shaded. Stress that the denominator shows the number of equal parts that make up the whole and that the numerator shows the number we have.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that non-unit fractions are made of more than one unit fraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may count the number of equal parts that are shaded and write the numerator and then count the number that are not shaded and write the denominator.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils count all of the equal parts to find the denominator.  The denominator is the number of equal parts that make up whole. We encourage children to find, and then describe, the denominator before the numerator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify non-unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes when using number lines to represent fractions, especially with bar representations that do not begin at zero.
nodes.response: Link teaching to measurement. When measuring the length of a object, the measurement needs to begin at zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Place fractions between 0 and 1 on a number line

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to recall multiplication facts related to the 5 and 10 times tables.
nodes.response: Using times table charts where needed throughout this unit will support children in recalling facts and enable them to focus on seeing the relationships, e.g. between the 5 and 10 times table. These can be used until children become more fluent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify the patterns and relationships between the 5 and 10 times tables

nodes.misconception: Children assume that the answer to all questions posed is 0 because that is the focus.
nodes.response: Always encourage children to read an equation aloud and describe the role of each number within it. Relating each to a context can help children to visualise the mathematics when 0 feels abstract.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a dividend of zero affects the quotient

nodes.misconception: Children misunderstanding the difference between partitive and quotative division when discussing the problems.
nodes.response: Although they will result in the correct answers, the calculation itself will not accurately reflect the problem. Ensure children initially describe each problem and represent it visually so that they can see whether they are grouping or sharing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how times table facts can help to find the quotient (2 times table)

nodes.misconception: Children may make errors when halving 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Recap strategies for halving from previous units prior to the lesson so that the process of halving numbers does not take over the focus of this lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a division equation with 2 as a divisor is related to halving

nodes.misconception: Children may not see 2-digit numbers as divisible by 10 if they are not in their 10 times tables.
nodes.response: Encourage children to apply the knowledge that a number is divisible by 10 when it has a ones digit of 0     Examples showing this idea can be explored and displayed to reference within the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of divisibility rules when the divisor is 10 to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children misunderstanding the difference between partitive and quotative division when discussing the problems.
nodes.response: Although they will result in the correct answers, the calculation itself will not accurately reflect the problem. Ensure children initially describe each problem and represent it visually so that they can see whether they are grouping or sharing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how times table facts can help to find the quotient (10 times table)

nodes.misconception: Children may not see 2-digit numbers as divisible by 5 if they are not in their 5 times tables.
nodes.response: Encourage children to apply the knowledge that a number is divisible by 5 when it has a ones digit of 0 or 5     Examples showing this idea can be explored and displayed to reference within the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of divisibility rules when the divisor is 5 to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children misunderstanding the difference between partitive and quotative division when discussing the problems.
nodes.response: Although they will result in the correct answers, the calculation itself will not accurately reflect the problem. Ensure children initially describe each problem and represent it visually so that they can see whether they are grouping or sharing.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how times table facts can help to find the quotient (5 times table)

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly double or halve to find the missing products or factors.
nodes.response: The use of counters or visuals will help children to see the relationship between 10 and 5 in each context and support them to know when they must use doubling and when they must use halving.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain patterns and relationships between the 5 and 10 times tables

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly identify parts of the equation.
nodes.response: Multiple opportunities to label and call out the different parts of the equation will help children to become confident in using this new vocabulary.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain each part of a division equation and know how they can be interchanged

nodes.misconception: Children may revert to inefficient strategies to solve problems e.g. skip counting.
nodes.response: Within the second learning cycle, children are encouraged to evaluate strategies used by others. The most efficient strategies should be discussed together throughout the first learning cycle to support with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of division strategies to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly double or halve to find the missing products or factors.
nodes.response: The use of counters or visuals will help children to see the relationship between 10 and 5 in each context and support them to know when they must use doubling and when they must use halving.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the 5 and 10 times tables to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children are unsure as to why, when the divisor is equal to 1, the quotient is equal to the dividend.
nodes.response: Use physical resources e.g. counters or children to represent both sharing and grouping contexts to help children to visualise the idea before applying to abstract equations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a divisor of one affects the quotient

nodes.misconception: Children may not see 2-digit numbers as divisible by 2 if they are not in their 2 times tables.
nodes.response: Encourage children to apply the knowledge that a number is divisible by 2 when it is even. The distinction between even and odd numbers can be revisited prior to the lesson and displayed to reference within the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of divisibility rules when the divisor is 2 to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children are unsure as to why, when the dividend and divisor are equal, the quotient is equal to 1
nodes.response: Use physical resources  e.g. counters or children to represent both sharing and grouping contexts to help children to visualise the idea before applying to abstract equations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how the quotient is affected when the divisor is equal to the dividend

nodes.misconception: Children may compare the fractional part of the mixed number first rather than the more significant whole number part.
nodes.response: What do you notice? If the whole number is the same, we need to look at the fractional part. If the numerators are the same, we need to compare the denominators - the smaller the denominator the greater the fraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare mixed numbers when the denominators of fractional parts are different

nodes.misconception: Children may compare the fractional part of the mixed number first rather than the more significant whole number part.
nodes.response: What do you notice? If the whole number is the same, we need to look at the fractional part. If the denominators are the same, we need to compare the numerators - the smaller the numerator the smaller the fraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare mixed numbers when the numerators of fractional parts are different

nodes.misconception: Children may count the marks rather than the equal parts between integers thereby determining the unit that we are working with incorrectly.
nodes.response: Show that we need to count the equal parts in between the given integers, not the marks. You could model this with the same line with increasing parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify numbers on marked but unlabelled number lines

nodes.misconception: Children may count the marks rather than the equal parts between integers and  may compare the fractional part of the mixed number first rather than the more significant whole number part.
nodes.response: Count the equal parts in between the given integers, not the marks to determine the unit that we are working with. When comparing and ordering, consider the whole number part first - this determines which integers the mixed number sits between.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order mixed numbers using fraction sense

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to estimate the position of a mixed number on a number line if their 'fraction sense' is not secure.
nodes.response: What do you notice about the mixed number? Remember, the whole number part is the most significant part - looking at this whole number part, which integers must the mixed number sit between? What do you notice about the fractional part?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate the position of a number on a number line using fraction sense

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the product is only the fraction of the shaded part and not the fraction of the original whole.
nodes.response: Ensure precision in wording when clarifying what the question is asking of each pupil. It is important they recognise how the shaded parts relates back to the original whole each time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to divide a non-unit fraction by a whole number

nodes.misconception: Pupils automatically convert the division equation to multiply by a unit fraction regardless of the calculation.
nodes.response: Many calculations can be managed through developing a sense of fractions. Where pupils have a sense of fractional magnitude, it is often easier to solve these calculations mentally. Continue to encourage representing these equations using model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to divide a fraction by a whole number efficiently

nodes.misconception: Pupils procedurally multiply the numerators together and then multiply the denominators together to find the product.
