nodes.response: It's important pupils understand the magnitude of the fraction in relation to one another. Encourage pupils to draw images to represent each equation and notice that the magnitude of the product is decreasing in size each time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to multiply two unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils procedurally multliply the denominators and add the numerators, or vice versa. Pupils may also only mutliply the denominators and not the numerators or again vice versa.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils connect the area model to the equations and continue to visualise the magnitude of each fraction. Often mistakes are made when pupils follow a procedure with little awareness for whether their answer makes sense mathematically.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to multiply two non-unit fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils change the division symbol to a multiplication symbol and then multiply the fraction by a whole number.
nodes.response: The act of dividing the fraction part is highlighted within the representations provided. Ensure pupils are given time to explore how the area model represents the division and encourage pupils to create their own examples.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to divide a unit fraction by a whole number

nodes.misconception: Pupils find the incorrect volume of a cuboid or cube by only counting what they can see. This may be the faces or whole cubes that are forward facing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to create the cuboids or cubes for themselves as well as show pupils how the cuboids or cubes are constructed as layers of rows and columns.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to calculate the volume of a cuboid and a cube

nodes.misconception: Pupils may default to trying to use the same strategy for every shape, for example, the 'partition and add' can be applied to most shapes although it might not be the most efficient.
nodes.response: Spend time exploring each strategy with basic dimensions for compound shapes at first. Explore different strategies for the same shape and encourage children to reason which strategy might be most efficient to use.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to calculate the volume of compound shapes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the taller the object, the greater its volume.
nodes.response: Use 3D objects as much as possible to compare, so pupils can develop their appreciation for multiple dimensions that contribute to the object's volume.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what volume is in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may record different volumes for objects if they measure with inconsistent units (for example: different sized cubes).
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to compare the volume of the same object measured with two different units. Discuss what you notice and draw out the importance for a consistent unit of measure.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe the units used to measure volume

nodes.misconception: Pupils cannot visualise how to calculate the unknown dimensions on the compound shape.
nodes.response: Spend time encouraging pupils to note down 'what they know' onto each shape. Allowing pupils to manipulate the shape with concrete apparatus and to run their finger along the edges of the shape will help visualise what is known and unknown.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of calculating volume to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: There may be some confusion with pupils because Jun’s school day is likely to be sequenced differently to theirs.
nodes.response: Spend some time discussing with the class that daily timetables vary from school to school, and from person to person.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence events in the school day in chronological order

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to name which month follows December because it is the last month of the year.
nodes.response: The months of the year are presented in both linear and cyclical form. Having the latter displayed in your classroom and using it regularly to recite the months will help them to see that any of the months have a month that comes after them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use language relating to months of the year

nodes.misconception: Pupils will have lots of familiarity with linear number lines but will be less familiar with circular ones. They may not understand that in terms of time, 12 is often followed by 1
nodes.response: Take frequent opportunities outside of the lesson to practise counting around the clock so that pupils get used to the sequence ... 11, 12, 1, 2 ...
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw and label a clock face talking about the hours

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a week always starts on a Sunday, and a year always starts in January.
nodes.response: Having these displayed in your environment in a circular formation (as in the slide deck) will help to reinforce the idea that a week is any seven days in sequence and a year is any twelve months in sequence. Practise reciting using the cycles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use language relating to days, weeks, months and years

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often mix the hour hand and the minute hand, labelling each as the other.
nodes.response: The lesson presents two stem sentences which run through each cycle. The use of these stem sentences, alongside frequent opportunities to practise interpreting clocks, outside of the lesson will help pupils to secure the learning.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell the time to the hour and half hour using the hour and minute hands

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to name which day follows Saturday because it is the last day of the week.
nodes.response: In the lesson, the days of the week are presented in both linear and cyclical form. Having the latter displayed in your classroom, and using it regularly to recite the days, will help them to see that any of the days have a day that comes after them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence events across a week in chronological order

nodes.misconception: The left hand side of the clock can cause pupils problems when reading the clock to the half hour. For example, because half past nine is between nine and ten, pupils might read it as half past ten.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on the word ‘past’ - which number has it gone past?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell the time to the half hour using the hour hand

nodes.misconception: It is not a misconception to say that Monday is the first day of the week. However, generally it is accepted that the first day of the week is Sunday, which is how it will be referred to in this unit.
nodes.response: Discuss with pupils that many people regard Monday as the first day of the week because it is the first day of the working week and that while both Sunday and Monday are acceptable, Sunday is more widely accepted.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use language relating to days of the week

nodes.misconception: There may be some confusion with pupils because Jun’s day is likely to be sequenced differently to theirs.
nodes.response: Spend some time discussing with the class that people may do things in a different order to each other. For example, some people have a shower or bath in the morning and some have it in the evening.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence everyday events in chronological order

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see the minute hand as the hour hand, treating wherever the minute hand is pointing to as o'clock.
nodes.response: The lesson deliberately chooses to present clocks featuring just an hour hand to really focus in on its purpose. O'clock times with the hour hand and minute hand feature later in the unit. Explain to pupils that clocks do not only have an hour hand.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell the time to the hour using the hour hand

nodes.misconception: Children might add or subtract the denominator as well.
nodes.response: Reinforce to children that the denominator denotes the unit fraction being used in calculation so does not need changing. Count aloud with physical objects to start with before moving onto counting in unit fractions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain that addition and subtraction of fractions are inverse operations

nodes.misconception: Children often find it difficult to understand the idea that any whole can be represented by a fraction with the same numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: You might want to list down some different real life examples such as slices of pizza or pie, complete sets of sticker pages, full packs of pens/pencils. Label each example with fraction notation so the children get a firmer understanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract fractions from a whole by converting the whole to a fraction

nodes.misconception: When adding fractions with the same denominator many children may try and add both the numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: This is a misunderstanding of the unitisation. Practise counting in different set of objects such as cubes, counters, children. Move children on to counting in fractions and explain that this is simply a different unit, shown by the denominator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add on fractions with the same denominator

nodes.misconception: Children might struggle with the idea that two fractions, each with the same numerator and denominator but different numbers, can be equivalent. For example, four-fourths is equal to ten-tenths.
nodes.response: Use a fraction wall to help with this. Compare the rows and establish that the whole is the same so they are equivalent. Ask the children to list as many as they can which will help build confidence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Substitute a fraction representing a whole to solve subtraction problems

nodes.misconception: Children may develop the misconception that unit fractions must be adjacent to be part of a repeated addition.
nodes.response: When using a number line, match it with another representation where possible in which the unit fractions aren't adjacent so children see that it is about the quantity of unit fractions rather than their position.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use repeated addition of a unit fraction to form a non-unit fraction

nodes.misconception: Typically, many children add both the numerators and denominators together to get the sum.
nodes.response: Pupils need to grasp units and unitising. Get them to move around the classroom/school performing simple additions with different sets of objects. Revisit fractions explaining that they're using unit fractions and this is shown by the denominator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add fractions with the same denominator

nodes.misconception: Children will rush to subtract both the numerator and the denominator when performing a subtraction of fractions with either structure in the lesson.
nodes.response: Reinforce the concept of the unit being the fraction which is denoted by the denominator. Get children to perform subtractions using real life objects before moving them onto using fractions instead, perhaps using unit fractions to begin with.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract fractions with the same denominator

nodes.misconception: When counting, children might think that 1 comes one step after the numerator and denominator are the same. For example, "...five-sevenths, six-sevenths, seven-sevenths, 1".
nodes.response: As the teacher, count in a given unit fraction and ask the children to stand up, wave or respond in some way when you get to the unit fraction that's equivalent to 1 (when the numerator and denominator are the same).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use repeated addition of a unit fraction to form 1

nodes.misconception: Children might still try to add or subtract the denominators as well due to a misunderstanding about the denominator showing what unit-fraction is being used for calculation.
nodes.response: By this stage, buddy checking can be useful. Get the children to check each other periodically but ensure that children can also explain why this is incorrect.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: In the addition of fractions, many children will try to add together both the numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: Show the children many completed examples using representations alongside the fraction notation. Encourage them to make generalisations and spot that the denominator remains the same because it is the unit.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add fractions with the same denominator and generalise the rule

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the factor that must become the product of two factors is always the largest factor.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are provided with a range of opportunities to break down factors, identifying where it does make a calculation easier, and also where it doesn't make the calculation easier.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the reasons for changing two-factor multiplication calculations to three-factor calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils continue to work only from left to right in calculations, therefore making calculations more time-consuming.
nodes.response: Support pupils to find pairs of factors that are easy to multiply with. For example, finding factors that make a power of ten often make calculations easier as they can multiply by 10, 100 or 1000 for example at the end.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Apply commutative and associative laws to simplify multiplications

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to understand that a 3 factor calculation problem with two unknown factors can be represented as a 2 factor calculation with one unknown factor.
nodes.response: Spend time manipulating 2 factor calculations into 3 factors and vice versa. Once pupils are confident with this, apply this to a context where the numbers are kept simple to support pupils to see the structure of the problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Apply the commutative and associative laws to simplify volume calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils only ever calculate an equation from left to right.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are given time to explore where the commutative law might be best used and where the associative law might be better used. Pupils should be expected to reason why they have chosen to adopt a strategy.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the use of the commutative and associative laws when multiplying three or more numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to solve unknown factor calculations where the volume is known.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils record missing factor problems as a multiplication equation. You may choose to build up the number of missing factors from one to two. You may also choose to build up from a missing factor in a 2 factor equation to a 3 factor equation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Apply the commutative and associative laws to simplify problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that the size of the item relates to its mass and that a larger item will always be heavier than a smaller item.
nodes.response: Explore examples where the larger item is lighter and the smaller item is heavier to address this misconception. For example, compare the mass of an inflated balloon with a stone, or an empty box with a small bag full of coins.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order measurements of mass

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the same type of object, for example a pencil, can be used as a unit of measure, even when they are different lengths.
nodes.response: Read the story of Pedro's birthday quest again and discuss why the friends using their own footsteps for measuring led to them getting different results.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain why standard units of measure are needed

nodes.misconception: Children may align the end of their object with the end of the ruler, rather than zero.
nodes.response: Use a sticker or coloured pen to highlight the zero on the ruler so that children's attention is drawn to the zero when they are measuring length using a ruler.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read scales in metres and centimetres

nodes.misconception: Children may find it difficult to explain the difference between capacity and volume.
nodes.response: Look at examples of different containers containing different amounts of liquid and use these stem sentences to support their learning. 'The volume of liquid in A is _ than the volume of liquid in B.' 'The capacity of A is _ than the capacity of B.'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Volume and capacity can be measured in litres and millilitres

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a taller container always has a larger capacity.
nodes.response: Choose tall narrow containers alongside short, wide containers and compare the capacities in different ways, such as recording a measurement for each capacity as well as pouring from one container into another to see which has the greater capacity.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order measurements of volume and capacity

nodes.misconception: With larger amounts, children may miscount the number of objects.
nodes.response: Encourage children to mark where 10 objects end, and use this to count on from, rather than always re-starting at one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Length can be measured in any direction to give height, length and distance

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse the comparative language of taller, tallest, longer and longest.
nodes.response: Talk about the difference between longest and tallest. Collect examples together and label each object as tallest or longest to support children's understanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare and order lengths

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the higher the level of coloured liquid on a thermometer, the higher the temperature.
nodes.response: Explore plenty of examples of thermometers with different scales so that children can see that they need to look at the scale in order to compare two temperatures and not just the height of the coloured liquid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Temperature

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a metre and a centimetre are similar in length, due to the way they are presented in images that are not to scale.
nodes.response: Allow children to explore practically and develop a sense of the length of one centimetre and one metre. Find familiar items to reference specific lengths e.g. our classroom door is about one metre wide.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Length can be measured in metres and centimetres

nodes.misconception: Children may not read scales accurately, particularly when the type of scale changes from a horizontal line to a circular scale.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities to explore different types of scales. Find where the same mass would be on different scales and talk about what is the same and what is different about each scale.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Mass can be measured in grams and kilograms

nodes.misconception: Children may overgeneralise that parallel lines can only come in pairs or must be horizontal or vertical in orientation.
nodes.response: These misconceptions are addressed in the lesson. You may wish to use these to create additional examples and non-examples to compare and share.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying parallel lines

nodes.misconception: Pupils are not able to identify right angles and therefore struggle to identify pairs of perpendicular sides.
nodes.response: Provide children with a right angle checker. Take time to model its use, focusing on aligning one edge of the checker with a side of the angle they want to check.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate different ways of decomposing a polygon

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to identify specific quadrilaterals e.g. trapeziums when making them out of construction sticks as it can be harder to see the properties.
nodes.response: Using a ruler to draw the shape, using the inside of the construction sticks, can support pupils in seeing and identifying the key properties to help them classify a quadrilateral.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Construct quadrilaterals with and without parallel and perpendicular sides

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to recognise that the properties of composed shapes may be different from the shapes they are composed of.
nodes.response: Drawing around compound shapes can really support children thinking about this as a 'new' shape with new properties.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Make and draw shapes with and without parallel and perpendicular sides

nodes.misconception: Children overgeneralise about the appearance of polygons such as rectangles and pentagons and do not recognise them when they are less typical.
nodes.response: Ensure modelling and examples show a range of shapes. For example, show a range of rectangles and focus on the key properties of parallel and perpendicular sides to identify that they are all rectangles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw shapes with given properties

nodes.misconception: Pupils find remembering the types and properties of quadrilaterals challenging.
nodes.response: Take time to repeat and revisit the key properties within the lesson and beyond. Consider providing a scaffold for some pupils so they can create quadrilaterals without having to recall the specific properties each time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Make and draw quadrilaterals on circular geoboards

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise that the same type of shape, such as a pentagon, can have different properties such as parallel or perpendicular lines.
nodes.response: Make use of geoboards if possible to create a pentagon and physically move one vertex. Focus on the fact that the shape still has 5 vertices and discuss what is similar and different.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw shapes with given properties on a range of geometric grids

nodes.misconception: Pupils may overgeneralise about the way a triangle should look e.g. not recognising a scalene triangle as a triangle.
nodes.response: Throughout the lesson, model different triangles in different orientations. Ensure pupils see boundary examples such as scalene triangles with one very small acute angle, or long and thin isosceles triangles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Make and draw triangles on circular geoboards

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not identify when a polygon has more than one pair of parallel or perpendicular sides especially when the polygon is not a rectangle.
nodes.response: Make use of right angle checkers to identify that some shapes have more than one right angle and take time to link this to perpendicular sides.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw polygons on isometric paper

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not recognise the new shape and only identify the smaller shapes it is composed of.
nodes.response: Using plastic shapes to compose a new shape and drawing around the shape can support pupils to see the properties of the new shape. Drawing around removes the joined sides inside the new polygon.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Make shapes by joining two polygons in different ways

nodes.misconception: Children may just add the whole number part of the mixed number to the numerator or may forget to add the fractional part of the mixed number.
nodes.response: Encourage children to check their work using the stem sentence or generalisation developed in the lesson, 'first we multiply the whole number by the denominator, then we add the numerator'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Express a quantity as a mixed number and an improper fraction

nodes.misconception: Children may just add the whole number part of the mixed number to the numerator or may forget to add the fractional part of the mixed number.
nodes.response: Encourage use of stem sentences developed within the lesson. For example, there are five groups of five fifths, which is 25 fifths, and two more fifths, so that is 27 fifths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Express an amount of fifths as a mixed number and an improper fraction.

nodes.misconception: Children may subtract the incorrect parts of the mixed numbers and/or proper fractions.
nodes.response: What is the number that we are subtracting? If this number is a mixed number, partition it into its whole number part and fractional part.Use unitising to support subtraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Efficiently solve subtraction problems (within a whole)

nodes.misconception: Children may add the incorrect parts of the mixed numbers and/or proper fractions together.
nodes.response: Guide pupils through with questioning. What is the whole number part? What is the fractional part? First we add the whole number parts then we add the fractional parts using unitising.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Efficiently solve addition problems (within a whole)

nodes.misconception: Children may just add the whole number part of the mixed number to the numerator or may forget to add the fractional part of the mixed number.
nodes.response: Encourage checking of work using the stem sentence. For example, there are four groups of four quarters, which is eight quarters, and two more quarters, so that is 10 quarters. Bar models could also be used while understanding develops.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Express an amount of quarters as a mixed number and an improper fraction.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the numbers given and the percentages of them when calculating.
nodes.response: In the lesson, calculating with the numbers given (from 3 to 90) and the percentages of them (e.g. 1% to 30%) is often dealt with separately, looking at individual columns in a table. Columns can be covered when calculating to help focus attention.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of calculating any percentage of a number to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when finding 10% or 1% of numbers that include zero.
nodes.response: Draw attention to zero being a placeholder within specific numbers. Some pupils may still need to use resources such as number cards and place value charts to physically move the digits to develop their confidence in dividing by 10 and 100
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of calculating 50%, 10% and 1% of a number to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find simplifying fractions difficult and understanding that they first need to identify the highest common factor.
nodes.response: Model writing out fraction pairs and finding the highest common factor. Have worked examples displayed for pupils to reference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of fraction-decimal-percentage conversions to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not always instantly recognise that a percentage part is a factor of 100
nodes.response: Discuss factors of 100 with the pupils, for example, as factor pairs. Allow them to keep these displayed to refer to throughout the lesson if needed to help make this connection.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to solve problems where the percentage part and size is known but the whole is unknown

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find calculating 75% of a number difficult.
nodes.response: First focus on teaching one strategy for finding 75% of a number. Pupils may find it easiest to add 50% and 25% together. Show representations of this (e.g. bar models showing the proportion of the whole) alongside calculations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of calculating common percentages of a number to solve problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes when writing single-digit percentages as a decimal number (e.g. 3%).
nodes.response: Remind pupils that percentages are recorded as hundredths. Where is the hundredths column in a decimal number? Writing measurements where one unit is a hundredth of another (e.g. number of pence as a percentage of a pound) may help reinforce this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to convert percentages to decimals and fractions with a denominator of 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not convert percentages into fractions with denominators of 100 before attempting other conversions.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to always write percentages as fractions with denominators of 100 before trying to find other fraction equivalents. Show them how missing this key step can lead to errors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to convert a percentage to a fraction without a denominator of 100

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes in the second cycle, where they find the whole after a percentage change. They may think the part given (e.g. the new cost) is represented by the percentage change.
nodes.response: Use bar models to help make it clear that the price given is the part remaining after the percentage change. If pupils are struggling with this, simplify the problem by giving numbers easy to calculate with (e.g. 30% off; new price £7)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems where the known percentage part and size represents a change to the whole

nodes.misconception: When finding a price has reduced by 25%, pupils may give the answer as 25% of the number, rather than seeing it as 75% of the whole.
nodes.response: Emphasise that '25% off' means that the price has been reduced by 25%. The whole, subtract 25%, is equal to 75% of the whole. Bar models are useful for showing this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving percentages in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes when determining the percentage of different wholes that are not equal in size or value.
nodes.response: Talk about the differences between the different wholes explored. Describe percentage as a proportion of that specific whole. Compare two different wholes where the percentages of them are the same and where the percentages of them are different.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what percent means and represent a percentage in different ways

nodes.misconception: Every number has one and itself as a factor, so every number is a prime number.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils explore the different arrangements that numbers can make with tiles in arrays. Point out that the numbers which cannot be arranged in any way except for one row or column are prime numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to identify a prime number or a composite number

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to compose numbers additively using prime factors.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are confident with finding the factors of a number first before extending to finding prime factors of known factors. Give time to building numbers with prime factors in arrays to help emphasise their multiplicative composition.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to identify a prime factor of a number

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to represent numbers as an array with an unequal amount in rows and columns.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are given time to explore representing numbers as arrays and identifying where the numbers in a multiplication equation come from within their array.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain what a factor is and use arrays and multiplication and division facts to find them

nodes.misconception: Pupils record the number of factors for a square number as even as they record the same number twice when writing down the factors of the square arrangement.
nodes.response: Highlight the need to only record each number as a factor once. You may like to record this on the tail of the factor bug to help emphasise this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a complete list of factors to explain when a number is a square number

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not know when to stop looking for more factors.
nodes.response: Build up finding factors of numbers systematically by arranging into rows and columns, starting with 1 row. Encourage pupils to generalise that when the number of rows becomes larger than the number of columns, you can stop looking for factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to find all the factors of a number systematically

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully convert and may leave the fractional part of the mixed number as an improper fraction e.g. 13/5 = 1 and 8/5
nodes.response: Support via questioning: How many fifths make one whole? How many full groups of five fifths can you make?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert a number of fifths from an improper fraction to mixed number

nodes.misconception: Children may make mistakes when using the generalisation if they are unaware of the structure behind it and the reason that we multiply then add.
nodes.response: First multiply the whole number by the denominator then add the numerator. Multiplying the whole number by the denominator tells us the number of parts that can be made from the whole number part then we need to add the parts shown by the numerator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how a mixed number is converted into an improper fraction

nodes.misconception: Children may not fully convert and may leave the fractional part of the mixed number as an improper fraction e.g. 13/4 = 2 and 5/4
nodes.response: Support via questioning: How many quarters make one whole? How many full groups of four quarters can you make? Emphasise the fractional part needs to have a numerator smaller than the denominator and take time to discuss why.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert a number of quarters from an improper fraction to a mixed number

nodes.misconception: Children may make mistakes when using the generalisation if they are unaware of the structure behind it and the reason that we divide.
nodes.response: Find how many groups of the denominator can be made from the numerator by dividing. This tells us how many full groups we can make, which gives us the whole number part of the mixed number. The remainder tells us the fractional part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how an improper fraction is converted into a mixed number

nodes.misconception: Children may make mistakes when using the generalisations if they are unaware of the structure behind them.
nodes.response: Check your answers using the corresponding stem sentences or by representing the number. Ensure that, when you compare amounts that are presented as different fraction types, you convert to the same fraction type.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving converting between mixed numbers and improper fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes measuring with a protractor, reading the wrong scale to get a measurement.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to check that each answer is sensible. Is the angle greater or less than a right angle? Have they drawn an angle greater/less than a right angle? Do all the angles add up to a sum of 360°?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use understanding of angles, fractions and percentages to construct pie charts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make errors interpreting information from pie charts, especially with making links between angles, fractions, percentages and working out an answer to a question.
nodes.response: Display 'benchmarks' in the classroom, showing a pie chart with labelled sectors (e.g. showing that 10% is equal to one tenth or 36° of the chart; 25% is equal to one quarter or 90°).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret the scales used in graphs, including pie charts, to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that line graphs are only used for continuous data, where the points between those that are plotted have meaning.
nodes.response: Show children examples of graphs where there is no meaning between divisions on the x-axis (e.g. heights of children). Here, the points cannot be joined to make a line graph.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Construct line graphs representing two variables in familiar contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make mistakes converting an angle of a sector into a percentage.
nodes.response: Choose to work with angles that can easily be converted into percentages (e.g. 72° is equal to 20% of the whole chart). You could have these readily available in the classroom as part of a display to refer to throughout the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use understanding of angles, fractions and percentages to interpret pie charts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand that line graphs are only used for continuous data, where the points between those that are plotted have meaning.
nodes.response: Show children examples of graphs where there is no meaning between divisions on the x-axis (e.g. heights of children). Here, the points cannot be joined to make a line graph.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret line graphs representing two variables in familiar contexts

nodes.misconception: When showing times on clocks (for example drawing hands onto blank clock faces or manipulating mini-clocks with movable hands) pupils may not consider the position of the hour hand.
nodes.response: Frequent exposure to both examples and non-examples (such as those in the slide deck) will help pupils to see that the hour hand will not be in an 'o'clock' position if it is ___ minutes to ___.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell and write the time to the nearest minute past and to

nodes.misconception: Because the representation of numbers 1 to 3 bear a resemblance to tallies, pupils may be tempted to continue in this fashion, for example writing 4 in Roman numerals as IIII
nodes.response: Discuss with pupils the idea of Roman numerals being based around a small number of 'rules', which are never broken. One such rule is that the same letter is never used more than three times in a row. Spend time really focusing on IV and IX.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell and write the time including using Roman numerals

nodes.misconception: Pupils might instinctively believe that midnight is 12 pm. There is often confusion about the use of am and pm with midnight and midday.
nodes.response: Utilise opportunities for quickfire counting outside the Maths lesson, from different starting points. For example, 10 am, 11 am, 12 pm, 1 pm, 2pm, or 9 pm, 10 pm, 11 pm, 12 am. 1 am.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: am and pm

nodes.misconception: Pupils need to be confident with the addition and subtraction of two digit numbers to other two digit numbers to be able to work out intervals or calculate using the intervals.
nodes.response: The idea of using tracing paper to create 15 minute, 30 minute and 45 minute time intervals is suggested and modelled. This can support the arithmetic in the lesson along with counting in 5s around the clock face.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate and compare the duration of events and tasks

nodes.misconception: When first learning about seconds, pupils come to realise they are very quick. They count seconds at the same speed in which they count other numbers - usually too quickly.
nodes.response: The classic way to slow down counting speed so that it more closely matches the pace of seconds is to use 'one Mississippi, two Mississippi' etc. For most pupils that is an obscure reference point - counting elephants is suggested as an alternative.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: How many seconds in a minute

nodes.misconception: When representing the time, pupils do not always remember that both the minute and the hour hand have a role to play when showing any given time - often leaving the hour hand in the o'clock position.
nodes.response: Lots of examples and non-examples are shown in Cycle 2 of the slide deck to tackle this misconception. However, practice makes perfect. Give frequent quickfire opportunities outside of the Maths lesson for pupils to show times on mini clocks.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Tell and write the time to the nearest minute past

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget how many days are in each month. They do not particularly follow a pattern or sequence. For example, pupils might be tempted to say that August has 30 days because it follows July.
nodes.response: You could 'interrupt the forgetting' by providing frequent opportunities for pupils to recall these facts outside the Maths lesson, using flashcards for each month with the month on the front and the number of days on the back.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know the number of days in each month, year and leap year

nodes.misconception: Pupils decompose the wrong factor therefore find it difficult to find a pair of factors that are equal to 100
nodes.response: Scaffold pupil's thinking when they begin to tackle a 2 digit by 2 digit calculation. Encourage them to ask questions of the numbers, for example: 'Is one of the numbers I have to start with a factor of 100?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to use the factor pairs of 100 to solve calculations efficiently

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find factors of a number if they do not have automatic recall of their times tables.
nodes.response: Provide children with a multiplication grid to help pupils understand the process of the calculations, however ensure additional support is in place for children to build towards automatic recall of times tables.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use properties of numbers and the commutative and associative laws to simplify calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only record a prime factor once in the Venn diagram even though it might be used more than once in the composition of the number.
nodes.response: It is important the clarify that we are finding common prime factors that are used in the composition of two numbers, and this might include a prime factor being used more than once.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to identify common factors between two or more numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils who are insecure with their times tables may not be efficient at finding factors and multiples.
nodes.response: Provide children with a multiplication grid to support them in identifying factors and multiples. When finding a multiple, ask: 'Is it in the x times table?' When finding a factor, ask: 'Which times tables is this number in?'
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of properties of number to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the terminology of factors and multiples and mistake them for one another.
nodes.response: Spend time encouraging pupils to identify the factors in an array and within both multiplication and division equations. Make explicit that the product and dividend represent the multiple in each equation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to identify a common multiple of two or more numbers

nodes.misconception: Scaling values can be done using addition and subtraction.
nodes.response: The ratio relationship between the values when they are scaled must remain the same.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how and why scaling is used to make and interpret maps

nodes.misconception: Failing to spot the change in unit of measure between the scale and real life.
nodes.response: Describe the scale and identify the unit of measure used on the map or plan and the unit of measure used in real life.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of multiplication and division to solve scaling problems in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Not comparing the same or corresponding sides of related shapes.
nodes.response: Label the sides of shapes clearly and refer to them with consistent language of height and width.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify and describe the relationship between irregular polygons using scale factors

nodes.misconception: Seeing multiplication and division as inverse operations e.g. dividing by 2 and multiplying by half.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to express the relationships between values using both multiplication and division.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use multiplication and division to calculate unknown values in ratio problems

nodes.misconception: Knowing how to create a table or bar model to represent a context presented in words.
nodes.response: Discuss the context to identify the parts and the wholes in order to build an appropriate representation of the context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving ratio

nodes.misconception: Relating the elements of the multiplication and equation to the values in the bar models.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils can explain what the values in the equation represent and where they are in the bar models.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to represent ratio and to calculate unknown values

nodes.misconception: That regular polygons include all familiar shapes even if they don't meet the definition.
nodes.response: Reinforce the definition and apply to the regular shapes which appear in this lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify and describe the relationship between regular polygons using scale factors

nodes.misconception: Using addition and subtraction to connect the parts and whole in a ratio context.
nodes.response: Model all relationships at this stage using the language and notation of multiplication and division.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe the relationship between two factors in a ratio context

nodes.misconception: Using addition and subtraction rather than multiplication and division to solve problems.
nodes.response: Continue to model the use of the language and notation of multiplication to calculate missing values.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing ratio in different ways

nodes.misconception: Not identifying whether they are scaling up a part or the whole amount and how this is represented.
nodes.response: Ask if it is a part or the whole that you are being asked to work out and articulating where this is in the representation or ratio table.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving scaling and ratio

nodes.misconception: Children may not always choose an efficient strategy when adding or subtracting mixed numbers. This may result in calculation errors being made.
nodes.response: Look at the numbers in the calculation. What do you notice? Which strategy would be most efficient to use with these numbers? Check your answer using a different strategy. If you get the same answer, you are likely to be correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of mixed numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand that a one can be exchanged from a whole and the fraction rewritten. E.g. four can be rewritten as three and five-fifths to add subtraction of an amount of fifths.
nodes.response: Use of rods or drawings will support children to understand this exchange. Four is the same as three and one; one is the same as five fifths so four is the same and three and five fifths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract a proper fraction from a mixed number crossing the whole

nodes.misconception: When partitioning to subtract, children may partition correctly but then may subtract incorrectly by swapping the order of the fractional parts being subtracted.
nodes.response: Is partitioning efficient for this subtraction where the fractional part of the subtrahend is greater than that of the minuend? It may be more efficient to 'find the difference' by counting on.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Choose efficient approaches when subtracting mixed numbers

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that a smaller mixed number cannot be subtracted from a greater one if its fractional part is greater. E.g. five and three-quarters cannot be subtracted from six and one-quarter.
nodes.response: If the mixed numbers are close to each other, try to ‘find the difference’ by counting forwards on a number line from the part to the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtract a mixed number from a mixed number

nodes.misconception: Adding the fractional part of a mixed number to a proper fraction may result in an improper fraction, which may be recombined with the whole number part of the mixed number and left as improper.
nodes.response: In a mixed number, the numerator of the fractional part must always be smaller than the denominator. If it is greater, a final conversion is needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Add mixed numbers crossing the whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils are inefficient when calculating the perimeter of a rectangle or do not recognise why more efficient strategies (summing length and width and doubling) works.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to see the efficient calculation and connection with smaller integers to support the generalisation before progressing to values in the lesson. Consider adapting values for some learners where required.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to balance equations with addition or subtraction expressions

nodes.misconception: Pupils immediately calculate expressions instead of considering the relationship between expressions.
nodes.response: Take time to model interrogation of values within expressions, identifying relationships between them. Encourage this reasoning and show how it can be more efficient than calculation especially in situations with larger values.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to balance equations with addition expressions

nodes.misconception: Pupils immediately calculate expressions instead of considering the relationship between expressions.
nodes.response: Take time to model interrogation of values within expressions, identifying relationships between them. Encourage this reasoning and show how it can be more efficient than calculation especially in situations with larger values.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to balance equations with subtraction expressions

nodes.misconception: Difference can represent a rise or fall in values so the calculation can have a positive or negative answer. Difference as change is always expressed as a positive value.
nodes.response: Focus on finding equivalent changes in the data presented and ensure that pupils see that the change is a positive value that can be qualified with describing it as a rise or a fall, depending on the situation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of balancing equations to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Thinking that you can change the values of subtraction and addition expressions by making the same changes.
nodes.response: Go back and explore what happens when you change different elements of addition and subtraction equations. Use stem sentences from earlier learning to highlight what happens to the sum and difference when values are changed in equations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to balance equations with addition and subtraction expressions

nodes.misconception: Children may translate or copy a shape rather than 'flipping it' over the line of symmetry.
nodes.response: Use mirrors to support children's understanding of how a shape flips when it is reflected. Explore this idea with a wide variety of shapes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflect polygons in a line of symmetry

nodes.misconception: Children may miscount the number of squares from the mirror line when plotting each vertex to reflect the shape.
nodes.response: Encourage children to work systematically by only marking one vertex at a time to reduce the chance of errors. Also encourage use of mirrors to check.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflect polygons that are dissected by the line of symmetry

nodes.misconception: Children might find it difficult to create triangles with equal angles.
nodes.response: Allow time to play and explore constructing triangles using items such as lolly sticks and matchsticks. Develop children's understanding of angles in a triangle using angle strips to check whether the angles are equal or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore, sort and classify triangles

nodes.misconception: Children may not recognise a line of symmetry when it is neither horizontal nor vertical.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for exploring lines of symmetry practically by folding cut outs of lots of different shapes. Encourage children to view and describe these in different orientations to help them see that a line of symmetry can be in any direction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate lines of symmetry in 2D shapes by folding

nodes.misconception: Children may not identify lines of symmetry that are neither horizontal nor vertical.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for children to handle and manipulate cut outs of shapes so that they can try to find lines of symmetry in different orientations. Encourage them to describe the position of the line of symmetry to support their understanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find lines of symmetry in 2D shapes

nodes.misconception: Some children may find it harder to recognise the type of triangle when they are drawn in different positions and orientations.
nodes.response: Allow time for children to manipulate the triangles so that they can see them in different orientations and build their understanding of the properties of each type of triangle.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify different types of triangle

nodes.misconception: Children might spot the unit of repeat and draw a repeating pattern rather than a symmetrical pattern.
nodes.response: Allow children to fold and unfold painted patterns on the mirror line to see where each part of the pattern would be reflected. Printing is a great tool to create symmetrical patterns.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Complete a symmetrical pattern

nodes.misconception: Some children will think that a parallelogram is symmetrical because it can be divided in half.
nodes.response: Demonstrate with folding and by using mirrors why dividing a parallelogram in half does not result in a line of symmetry. Allow children to explore this concept with cut-outs of different parallelograms.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore symmetry by joining two identical shapes

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a rectangular flag has diagonal lines of symmetry.
nodes.response: Allow children to cut out and fold the flags to help them see that a rectangle does not have any diagonal lines of symmetry.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigate symmetry and symmetrical patterns

nodes.misconception: Children may try to reflect in a diagonal line but not at a 45 degree angle, leading to inaccuracies when marking each vertex.
nodes.response: Encourage children to work horizontally and then vertically, rather than trying to reflect in a diagonal line. Explore how this can be done in either order, orienting the paper, and notice how the same point will still be marked on the grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Diagonal lines of symmetry

nodes.misconception: Pupils consider the whole number to represent an area as well as the fraction.
nodes.response: Take time to discuss what each of the numbers in the expressions represent and link this to the context it is set in.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between repeated addition of unit fractions and multiplication of fractions

nodes.misconception: Multiplying a fraction by a larger whole number means the product will be larger.
nodes.response: In these examples, encourage children to see the whole number as a multiplier. Relate this back to representations where the fraction is shown to represent an area or a quantity. This should help to identify the fraction's magnitude when reasoning.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiplying proper fractions by whole numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupils multiply both the numerator and denominator by the whole number.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are given time to explore how equations are represented using multiple representations and avoiding 'finding the answer' initially. Encourage children to reason how each equation is linked to the representations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a proper fraction by a whole number where the product is within a whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to group items to form unitised groups.
nodes.response: Ensure time is spent labelling items in relation to the whole then move to grouping these items. Use the sentence stem: There are ___ lots of ___ _________. This is equal to ___ _________.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between repeated addition of fractions and multiplication of fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils resort to a procedure with little understanding for how we convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make connections between improper fractions and mixed numbers using both area models and number lines. Focus on reasoning by manipulating parts to complete wholes and where the wholes and parts are represented on the number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a proper fraction by a whole number where the product is greater than a whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to represent the problem as an expression or equation as they misinterpret what the whole is.
nodes.response: Draw attention to what the whole is in each example. You might like to build up each image with a whole at a time, describing the fraction of the whole that is shaded/represented.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a mixed number by a whole number not bridging a whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look to calculate each expression straight away.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are encouraged to estimate expressions, showing how this can be more efficient particularly when looking to compare expressions. The product is not always needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a mixed number by a whole number bridging a whole

nodes.misconception: Pupils may underestimate the product for example where the fractional part, when multiplied by an integer bridges over a whole.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to look at the size of the fraction each time and ask whether it will bridge a whole or not and add that onto the estimate of the whole number multiplied by the integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving multiplication of mixed numbers by a whole number

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to represent problems as a bar model.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw their own image of what the maths represents. Make connections between their own image and a bar model, linking them both to where the numbers are represented in each image.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving fractions and mixed numbers

nodes.misconception: Pupil may multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the integer therefore finding an equivalent fraction.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to represent the maths using unitised counters as this will support them to recognise the multiplicand and the multiplier.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent and multiply an improper fraction by a whole number.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will sometimes give incorrect number bond examples such as as 63 + 47 = 100
nodes.response: Model adding together the tens first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of subtraction to calculate change when paying with whole pounds or notes

nodes.misconception: Pupils use inefficient calculation strategies such as always using columnar methods.
nodes.response: Promote efficient mental strategies and model clear examples of the use of these.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of addition to add commonly used prices efficiently

nodes.misconception: Errors in column addition can occur when pupils fail to align their digits properly.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to align their decimal points before setting out the rest of the calculation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculate change when purchasing several items

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if money amount is made up of more coins it must have a higher value.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to group their coins and set them out in order. Focus on the highest value digit first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to compare amounts of money without converting

nodes.misconception: Pupils can sometimes see words like 'altogether' in a problem and assume it is an addition problem.
nodes.response: Provide lots of examples of contextualised problems and focus on mathematical language, including where it might be misleading.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve a range of problems, including finding change

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly record money, for example omitting the decimal point and using the pound notation
nodes.response: Draw attention to both correct and incorrect notation and ensure they have opportunities to see, say and record in different ways.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain and represent whole pounds and pence as a quantity of money

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly multiply and divide by 100 when converting, or multiply and divide by 10 instead.
nodes.response: Continue to emphasise the relationship between one pound and 100 pence and encourage pupils to spot patterns e.g. £2 = 200 p, £3 = 300 p
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert quantities of money between pounds and pence

nodes.misconception: When using column addition with regrouping, pupils put the regrouped digits in the wrong order.
nodes.response: Part of the first lesson cycle includes an example of a pupil getting it wrong, as well as the correct way to show the calculation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use and explain the most efficient strategies when adding quantities of money

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often default to using the column subtraction method even when it is inefficient.
nodes.response: The slide deck gives examples of when column subtraction can be replaced by quicker, more efficient methods, such as 'counting on'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use and explain the most efficient strategies when subtracting quantities of money

nodes.misconception: Pupils write 1£ because that is the order in which the expression is said.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for pupils to see and use the correct notation as well as highlighting wrong examples.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain and represent whole pounds as a quantity of money

nodes.misconception: Pupils opt to represent the problem using two separate bar models that are stacked on top of one another.
nodes.response: Whilst pupils can represent the maths how they wish, these problems tend to be more efficiently represented using a singular bar model with the whole at the top. Further iterations of these bar models can then be represented underneath.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to represent an equation with a bar model

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the removal of the multiplication symbol can result in the number becoming a two-digit number rather than two, single digits being multiplied together.
nodes.response: Using the language of 'lots of' may support pupils to see that an algebraic equation with coefficients represents multiplication. For example: 40 can be read as 'four lots of 0'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent and solve problems with two unknowns efficiently

nodes.misconception: Pupils use a trial and improvement approach to solve these problems only.
nodes.response: At first, pupils may put numbers into the equation to see what happens each time. Encourage pupils to move beyond this to notice what happens to each example. Pupils should aim to use the relationships between addends or subtrahends to help them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to balance an equation with two unknowns

nodes.misconception: Pupils cannot identify the lengths of the shapes that make up the length provided in each problem.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw a line over the sides of the shapes that represent the length within the problem. This can help pupils to see how many 'lots of' the smaller shapes length are used and how many 'lots of' the larger shapes lengths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use a bar model to represent spatial problems with two unknowns

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to understand how to represent the number rods to show the difference when trying to find the missing rod.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils spend time representing each question with an equation then match this with the number rods. This may help them to visualise the missing part as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compare the structure of problems with one or two unknowns

nodes.misconception: Pupils may draw bar models which are inaccurate and do not represent the problem effectively.
nodes.response: These types of problems lend themselves to be drawn using bar models that are lined up one on top of the other. Model creating these bar models with the pupils and explaining how you know where the numbers sit within them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain why there is sometimes only one solution to a problem

nodes.misconception: Pupils attempt to represent the problems with bar models rather than take a systematic, trial and improvement approach.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to represent each problem how they would like. Pupils should take time to notice why it is that the bar model if not appropriate to help solve these problems and identify these clues within the questions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how you know you have found all the possible solutions to a problem with two unknowns

nodes.misconception: When representing problems with more than two unknowns, pupils draw bar models all starting from the same end point and with the variables in any order.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw their bar models with the variables lined up underneath one another wherever possible. The bar model may not line up form the left, but this can help to identify the differences between each model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems with two unknowns in a range of contexts

nodes.misconception: Pupils resort to trial and improvement each time to solve every problem.
nodes.response: Pupils should look to apply what they know from previous learning and explore the structure of each problem to help them identify how best to solve it. You could come up with a checklist as a class for how best to explore a new problem each time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems with two unknowns with one, several and infinite solutions

nodes.misconception: Pupils opt for a trial and improvement approach, without working systematically either.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to identify the structure of the problem and represent the maths in a way that makes sense for them. You can then take their representations of the maths and refine them so they are more efficient.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent the structure of a problem with two unknowns in context

nodes.misconception: Pupils will need to be able to count in steps of 7 and 12 to succeed in this lesson and have a good recall of the 7 and 12 times tables. Calculation errors will occur frequently if not.
nodes.response: Consider pre-teaching pupils still insecure with this, and / or providing scaffolding such as a times tables grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert from days to weeks and months to years

nodes.misconception: It is tempting to say that we need to add 12 hours to any pm times to turn them into 24 hour times. However, it is a slight over-generalisation and does not apply to 12:00 pm up to 12:59 pm.
nodes.response: A teaching point is made of this and opportunities to apply the knowledge are given in the Practice tasks. It is worth really focusing on this as it comes up and paying attention to it while pupils are engaged with the Practice tasks.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert between times given in 12 and 24 hours

nodes.misconception: Remembering that there are 60 minutes in an hour and the values for quarter, half and three quarters of an hour. Calculations are often to and from 60 when working within an hour rather than 100
nodes.response: Make sure children have a clock face available so that they can visualise the times and see the minute hour hands. Children may find it useful to move the minute hand to count on and back in 5s to support their calculations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving writing, telling and converting the time

nodes.misconception: Part of the lesson requires pupils to decide whether times are before midday, at midday or after midday. Pupils can find categorising 12:00 and 00:00 tricky.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching points are made based around this in the slide deck. However, it is worth really focusing on these points as they come up and, when assessing the pupils during the Practice tasks, paying particular attention to those times.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Read the time on a 12 and 24 hour digital clock

nodes.misconception: Pupils will need to be able to count in steps of 6 to succeed in this lesson and have a good recall of the 6 times table. Calculation errors will occur frequently if there in insecurity in this area.
nodes.response: Consider pre-teaching pupils still insecure with this, and / or providing scaffolding such as a times tables grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert from hours to minutes and minutes to seconds

nodes.misconception: Pupils procedurally divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator without an understanding for why they do this.
nodes.response: Take time to ensure pupils link how the fraction relates to the bar model. Using the sentence stem 'The whole has been divided into ___ equal parts, and we need ___ of them,' can help to make sense of the fraction in relation to the bar model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find a non-unit fraction of a quantity using mental and written calculation strategies

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify how much the rod has been scaled by as they cannot visualise the fractional size of the new whole.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to visualise how much the whole has shrunk by. Avoid pupils using the rods to immediately  find out what size of the new whole, encourage pupils to visualise and estimate prior to checking with the rods.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiply a whole number by a proper fraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils divide by the denominator and then multiply by the numerator without any conceptual understanding for why this works.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils spend time exploring how dividing and multiplying by either the numerator or denominator works in relation to a scaling or repeated addition strategy. Encourage pupils to reason when they would use one strategy over the other.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain when a calculation represents scaling down and when it represents repeated addition

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to see the relationship between the different number rods.
nodes.response: Take time with pupils for them to explore the use of number rods if they have not done so before. You might ask pupils to find rods that are half the size of different coloured rods, so they can estimate sizes and draw attention to the relationship.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how finding a fraction of a quantity relates to multiplying by a unit fraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify how each of the expressions relate to each other.
nodes.response: Ensure connections are made between the bar models, your language and the expressions. Give particular attention to how the fraction links to how the bar model can be drawn, particularly when dividing the bar model into ___ parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how dividing by a whole number relates to multiplying by a unit fraction

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that they have to divide the shape by the denominator to create the unit fraction.
nodes.response: This is an example of where a lack of conceptual understanding can lead to procedural errors. Ensure pupils represent the maths using equal parts and label each of these parts as the fractional value they have.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find a unit fraction when the size of a non-unit fraction is known

nodes.misconception: When a unit fraction is represented as a quantity greater than one, pupils may think each part of the unit fractions quantity is itself the unit fraction of the whole.
nodes.response: Draw a circle around the quantity each time to encourage pupils to recognise that each set of objects is representative of a quantity that is one part of the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find the whole when the size of a unit fraction is known

nodes.misconception: Pupils multiply the non-unit fraction by the denominator to create the whole.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils spend time breaking down non-unit fractions back into unit fractions. Encourage pupils to recognise this as two stages. Firstly, find the unit fraction. Secondly, re-create the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find the whole when the size of a non-unit fraction is known

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the fraction part of each whole with the value of the number of items in each part.
nodes.response: Progressively build from looking at the size of each part in relation to the whole using bar models to start with. After pupils are secure with this, introduce the quantities and be clear to distinguish between the value and size of each part.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Find a unit fraction of a quantity using representations

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to unpick the maths required of them from the worded problems.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw a bar model for each problem. This will help them to identify what information is known, for example, whether the problem indicates if the whole, the value of a part, or the size of a part is known.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of multiplying a whole number by a unit fraction to solve problems

nodes.misconception: When writing the subtraction expression within the equation, children may write the parts to be divided in the order they appear in the problem, rather than putting the greatest one first.
nodes.response: Explore where the parts to be divided need to be written in a different order to how they appear in the problem. Compare this with addition and explore commutativity so that children can see how addition is commutative but subtraction is not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how the distributive law applies to division expressions with a common divisor

nodes.misconception: Children will solve an equation by working from left to right and forget that multiplication needs to be completed before addition or subtraction.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities for children to practise solving equations that cannot be solved working from left to right. You could highlight the operation symbols to draw children's attention to these before they begin to solve them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine multiplication with addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: Children may forget to use the order of operations and revert back to working from left to right.
nodes.response: Encourage them to identify all the operations in an equation before they begin to solve it so that they can apply their knowledge of the order of operations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of the order of operations to solve equations

nodes.misconception: Children may add or subtract the common factors together rather than the uncommon factors.
nodes.response: Use unitising counters or other physical resources to represent each problem and manipulate these to demonstrate the distributive law before showing children the equation that represents it.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how the distributive law applies to multiplication expressions with a common factor

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to identify the dividends and confuse these with the divisor.
nodes.response: For each problem, ask the children what each number represents and help them to describe this. For example,  'the number of sweets before they were shared and the number they are sharing between' alongside the terms dividend and divisor.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine division with addition and subtraction

nodes.misconception: You need to look carefully at a set of data to make sure that the values are reasonable and that calculation of the mean average will give a value that is useful when describing the set and comparing.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to look carefully at a set of data, identifying values that look unusual and thinking about the impact that they will have if the mean average is calculated. An outlying value in one set of data may be reasonable in another set.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain why the mean is useful and when it is not appropriate

nodes.misconception: The mean average is used to compare different sets of data. Much of the data we see in the media uses mean average values so it is important to know how these figures are calculated.
nodes.response: Discuss what the mean average of a set of data represents and perhaps look at current news stories or local papers for examples of the mean average used in the media.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to use the mean to make comparisons between two sets of data

nodes.misconception: Not realising that if you change the number of values in the set, you must divide the total by the new number of values and that this affects the value of the mean average.
