nodes.response: Use the definition of the mean average to check that the total of the set of data is correctly calculated and that the number of values in the set of data is correctly identified in all examples and contexts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how the mean changes when the total quantity or number of values changes

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that zero values do not need to be included when dividing by how many values there are in the set of data.
nodes.response: Show that even if a value is zero, it is still a value in the set of data. It doesn't affect the total of the set but does need to be included in the total number of values in the set.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how to calcluate the mean of a set of data including a value of zero

nodes.misconception: Understanding that the mean average is a way of creating one value to represent a set of data. It is calculated by sharing equally but doesn't always mean that a set is being shared.
nodes.response: Be clear about what the mean average value represents and how it might be useful in the contexts presented.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between the mean and sharing equally

nodes.misconception: When writing equations to represent part-part-whole models, children may have difficulty recording the number of groups (as this numeral is not written in the model) and revert to repeated addition.
nodes.response: Encourage children to articulate their thinking as they record, e.g. there are ___ groups of ___ and a remainder of ___
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent division by grouping with multiplication and addition equations

nodes.misconception: Rather than using the largest multiple less than or equal to the dividend, children may identify the closest multiple (one that is too high) or one that is less than the dividend but is too low.
nodes.response: Add further examples using counters to explore patterns where one more is added to draw attention to the size of the remainder compared to the divisor. Draw number lines alongside these so children begin to also visualise in a more abstract way.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain how the remainder relates to the divisor in a division equation

nodes.misconception: Children may struggle to visualise how the remainder relates to the question asked in the problem, or may solve the equation without relating back to the question asked.
nodes.response: Encourage them to write the division equation for the problem and say what each part represents, focusing particularly on the role of the remainder and how it relates to the question asked.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of division to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children may not see the link between sharing and grouping as sharing has traditionally been done by sharing out objects one by one. This becomes far less efficient when working with larger numbers.
nodes.response: To develop understanding of 'dividing between', ensure that physical objects are shared out in groups each time (forming an array beneath a bar model), rather than one by one.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Represent division by sharing with equations

nodes.misconception: Children may choose the multiple that is higher than or closest to the dividend, for example to solve 47 divided by 6, they may choose 8 x 6 = 48 instead of 7 x 6 = 42
nodes.response: Choose smaller numbers to demonstrate the concept, using practical equipment and number lines to demonstrate why the number must be equal to or less than the dividend.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use multiplication facts to answer division questions

nodes.misconception: Children may work inefficiently, e.g. they may find the digit sum of 27 to find if it is a multiple of 6, instead of first reasoning that it cannot be because it is an odd number.
nodes.response: Encourage children to consider what they know about a number first (e.g. all even numbers have even multiples) before applying other parts of rules so that they work in the most efficient way. Display models of these to enable recall of them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify when there will be a remainder

nodes.misconception: Children may have difficulty interpreting the problem and be unsure whether to ignore or include the remainder in the answer.
nodes.response: Throughout, ask and encourage children to articulate what each part of the equation represents from the problem in order to link the concrete and the abstract representation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Decide what to do with the answer to a division calculation to solve a problem

nodes.misconception: When faced with a bar model showing for example 5 parts, children often want to write a 5 in each part as they misunderstand how the grouping in fives relates to a sharing context.
nodes.response: Imagine arrays beneath the five parts of the bar model to secure understanding that the five parts represent five groups of ___ / the number of groups we are sharing between. Physically share a group of objects into these parts at any one time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve division problems involving sharing, including those with remainders

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand division as repeated subtraction because they can count forwards to find the number of equal groups in a number.
nodes.response: On a number line, show how counting forwards and backwards in multiples results in the same answer. Discuss the difficulty of using tables facts to count backwards when there is a remainder, so they understand why counting forwards is more efficient.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve division problems involving grouping, including those with remainders

nodes.misconception: Children may either choose to use a multiple higher than the dividend, e.g. 53 ÷ 9 = , or choose a multiple that is too low, e.g. 57 ÷ 8 = , which results in a remainder greater than the divisor.
nodes.response: When solving equations, refer back to the largest multiple that is less than or equal to the dividend and use number lines to allow children to visualise this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of division equations and remainders to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Thinking that the fraction and decimal use the same digits so that one fifth is 1.5 as a decimal. Some may not see that equivalent fractions and decimals represent the same value.
nodes.response: Use representations that allow pupils to see fractions as parts of 10 and 100 to secure the understanding of their equivalent decimal values. Revisit equivalent fractions to model how to convert fractions to their decimal equivalents and vice versa.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain and represent how to divide 1 into different numbers of equal parts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the connection between the common divisions of 1,000, 100, 10 and 1 and they may not see the multiplication sign representing the word of when reading the equations.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time to explore the representations of the divisions of 1,000, 100, 10 and 1 alongside each other. Encourage the equations to be read using multiplied by and also of which is more commonly used with fractions of amounts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identify and describe patterns in the number system

nodes.misconception: Knowing and understanding that one-fifth as a fraction is equivalent to 0.2 as a decimal and that counting in steps of 0.2 is the same as counting in fifths.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils have the opportunity to rehearse the fact that one-fifth is equivalent to 0.2 more frequently during the lesson and at other times when looking at fractions and decimals.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Recall common fraction-decimal equivalents

nodes.misconception: That equivalent fractions do not have the same value. Pupils can create them but do not always understand that they are equal in value.
nodes.response: Explore representations which show the same whole divided in different ways to show the same proportion of the whole. Represent equivalent fractions at the same point on a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship within families of equivalent fractions

nodes.misconception: Children do not always see the link between the numerator and the denominator in equivalent fractions. This lesson highlights that link and the fact that the proportion of the whole is the same.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentences and generalisations in the lesson to describe the fractions and to relate them to the representations used.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between numerators and denominators in equivalent fractions

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may still think that, because equivalent fractions look different, they do not have the same value.
nodes.response: Use representations such as bar models and shapes as well as number lines to ensure that this understanding is secured both in interpreting fractions as parts of a whole and as numbers with a fixed position on a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use understanding of equivalent fractions to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Children learn how to spot and create equivalent fractions without realising that they have the same value and have the same position on a number line. The understanding of equivalence is important.
nodes.response: Use the = symbol to record fractions with the same value and the language 'is equal to'. Make use of manipulatives and representations to model equivalence and highlight the equality.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the language of equivalent fractions correctly

nodes.misconception: Children may still be building understanding that the same fraction can be represented and recorded in different ways. They may still think that the larger the denominator, the larger the fraction.
nodes.response: Make use of the stem sentences to support understanding of how the recording of the fraction relates to the images and contexts used. Model the use of the keywords numerator and denominator and encourage children to use them in explanations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use representations to describe and compare fractions

nodes.misconception: The numbers in a decimal can be rewritten as a fraction so one-fifth becomes 1.5 as a decimal and that fractions and decimals do not represent equivalent values.
nodes.response: Read decimals as a number of tenths and hundredths to make the link to fractions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use knowledge of common equivalents to compare fractions and decimals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not appreciate that equivalent fractions and equivalent fractions and decimals have exactly the same value and can be substituted which may be beneficial when solving problems.
nodes.response: Model the thinking when there is a mixture of fractions and decimal representations in a problem and identify the decision as to whether to convert all to decimals or all to fractions as a step in the the problem solving process.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems using fraction-decimal equivalents

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the relationship between the numerator and denominator in a fraction as an indication of equivalence. They may only see that they can keep doubling the numerator and denominator.
nodes.response: When working with unit fractions, ensure that pupils explain that the denominator is always e.g. 3 times the value of the numerator when fractions are equivalent to e.g. one third. This will focus them on the equivalence and that key relationship.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Explain the relationship between numerators and denominators across equivalent fractions

nodes.misconception: Children need to understand that fractions can also be fractions of 1 and have an exact position on a number line. There may be confusion over labelling an exact point rather than a part of the line.
nodes.response: Use the language of labelling a point on the line and avoid talking about 'half of the line' which is the language of parts of a whole. This helps children to see that fractions are numbers in their own right with a unique position on a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use representations to describe and compare two fractions in a continuous context

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see that the fraction and its simplified version are equivalent. Pupils may not have a deep understanding of how factors relate to fractions.
nodes.response: Stress the equivalence of fractions when simplifying and make use of representations to show that fractions are equivalent using parts of a whole and position on a number line. Discuss the language of factors, common factors and prime numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the relationship between the numerator and denominator to simplify fractions

nodes.misconception: Children may think that fractions that look different cannot represent the same part of a whole. They may also still think that a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction.
nodes.response: Give plenty of opportunity to use manipulatives and representations to show sets and groups of objects divided in different ways so that they see practically that the same part of a whole can be described and represented by different fractions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use representations to describe and compare two fractions

nodes.misconception: Children need to understand that equivalent fractions must be part of the same whole and that they can be represented as parts of a whole or as a number with a unique position on the number line.
nodes.response: Use the stem sentences to draw attention to how we describe equivalence and use representations to support this. Be clear about when the representation is showing a part of a whole and when it is labelling a point on a number line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the relationship between the numerator and denominator in equivalent fractions to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not remember whether a certain larger unit is comprised of 10, 100 or 1,000 smaller units - all of these are explored at some point in this sequence of lessons.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing the etymology of the words, and have these displayed in your environment. The prefix 'kilo' means 'one thousand' while the prefix 'milli' means 'one thousandth'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert from smaller to larger units of measure

nodes.misconception: Pupils see values like 0.25 l and convert it to 25 ml.
nodes.response: The lesson presents fractions and decimals as parts of whole circles. As long as pupils know that 1 l = 1,000 ml, they should see from the representation that 0.25 l = 250 ml as 250 + 250 + 250 + 250 = 1,000
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert to and from fraction and decimal quantities of larger units

nodes.misconception: Pupils might see a number like 9.2 m and incorrectly partition it into 9 m and 2 cm.
nodes.response: It is essential that pupils are exposed to lots of examples of visual models, such as parts of circles and number lines, so that they have a secure understanding of why, in this case, the 0.2 m is equal to 20 cm.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to carry out conversions that correspond to 10 and 100 parts

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may see the prefix 'milli' and think it is related to 'million'.
nodes.response: Part of the lesson focuses on the etymology of the words and the fact that the prefix 'milli' means 'thousandth'; a millimetre is a thousandth of a litre and a millilitre is one thousandth of a litre. Consider displaying this in your environment.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert from larger to smaller units of measure

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think 8:45 + 20 mins = 8:65. As our system of time is not based around the decimal system,  this is incorrect.
nodes.response: Some pupils may still not be fully au fait with telling the time, though the lesson presumes they are. Providing them with a mini-clock with movable hands will help to reinforce the idea of bridging to and then from the o'clock time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving converting between units of time

nodes.misconception: Pupils may see, for example, 3.25 kg and convert it to 3 kg and 25 g rather than 3 kg and 250 g.
nodes.response: The lesson presents fractions and decimals as parts of whole circles. As long as pupils know that 1 kg = 1,000 g, they should see from the representation that 0.25 kg = 250 g as 250 + 250 + 250 + 250 = 1,000
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use known facts to derive common conversions over 1

nodes.misconception: Lots of practice has taken place for pupils to convert between kilometres and metres. Pupils may expect kilometres and miles to have a similar relationship and expect one mile to equal 1,000 metres.
nodes.response: Bar models and double number lines are excellent visual representations of the relationship and should help pupils to form a more concrete understanding of the equivalence between units. Displaying these will provide a prompt for pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Convert between miles and kilometres and pounds and Euro

nodes.misconception: The most common mistake pupils will make when faced with these sorts of questions is not taking into account the unit conversion that needs to take place if the units of measure are mixed.
nodes.response: You may wish to consider drawing extra attention to the fact that the units of measure are different when presenting the Practice tasks, for example highlighting them in different colours if appropriate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving converting units in different contexts

nodes.misconception: Two unrelated units of measure are called 'pounds' - the money version and the mass version. Pupils may confuse one for the other.
nodes.response: In this lesson, the word pounds (as in mass) is used with the abbreviation lb in brackets. It is recommended that you use both of these until pupils reach a point where they can automatically read lb as pounds and and record it as such.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand approximate equivalence between metric and imperial units

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may need support with the decimal representation of measures and how to convert from larger units to smaller e.g. 1.2 l into ml.
nodes.response: Allow pupils to go back to previous work completed where necessary to see the units of measure divided up into 2, 4, 5 and 10 parts and represented with decimals, to provide a scaffold for them to use whilst completing the problems in this lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solve problems involving different units of measure

nodes.misconception: Angles must always be formed with one horizontal line. Angles must also have two straight lines that are exactly the same length.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with examples where acute, obtuse and reflex angles are shown in a wide range of orientations and where the length of the lines leading into the angles differ in size to support generalising the features of each angle type.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the terms acute, obtuse and reflex when comparing angles to a right angle

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to remember the number of degrees in a triangle as they only know it as a disconnected fact.
nodes.response: Apply pupils' knowledge of angles in a quadrilateral to understanding the sum of the angles in a triangle. Spend time showing how a quadrilateral is constructed using triangles and what happens to the angles as the quadrilateral is partitioned.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Angles in triangles

nodes.misconception: Objects rotate only either less than a full turn or more than a full turn.
nodes.response: Take time to discuss the purpose of the object in question and clarify the difference between what an object should do and could do.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe rotations using the standard unit of degrees when compared to a right angle

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly place the protractor on the angle and therefore cannot measure the angle. Pupils use the incorrect scale to read the angle.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of using the middle spot on the protractor to line this up with the vertex of the angle as well as placing one of the lines on a zero line, ensuring the remaining line crosses the scale of the protractor.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure the size of angles accurately using a protractor

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have fluency in properties of 2D shapes and may therefore not notice properties of angles within quadrilaterals such as trapeziums.
nodes.response: Pre-teaching or providing a scaffold containing shape names and properties will allow pupils to see the properties and support them in making connections.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Angles in quadrilaterals

nodes.misconception: Pupils understand angles as static, created where two immovable lines meet. Pupils also believe angles are only created by two lines that are completely straight.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to use angle strips in order to create their own angles, manipulating either arm of the angle strip to create the angle. Ensure pupils are provided with examples where angles are formed by partially straight lines.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review understanding of angles as a measure of turn

nodes.misconception: Pupils significantly over or under-estimate the size of angles, particularly when the initial line of the angle is not vertical or horizontal.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to rotate the angle so that one of the lines is vertical or horizontal, or if possible, look at the angle from a different point of view which may help to view a line of the angle from a vertical or horizontal position.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimate acute and obtuse angles using the standard unit of degrees

nodes.misconception: 90 degrees is classified as an acute angle and 180 degrees is classified as an obtuse angle.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to classify angle sizes and build towards understanding that acute angles are between 0-89 degrees and obtuse angles are between 91-179 degrees. Classifying multiples of right angles as a separate group may help.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe static angles using the standard unit of degrees when compared to a right angle

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the angles on a straight line only applied to lines that are horizontal.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are exposed to straight lines in a range of orientations, encouraging them to draw on the 180 degree angle and how this can apply to both sides of the straight line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that the angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees and use this to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that composing larger polygons of smaller triangles that are not formed as a result of drawing a line from one vertex to another will help them to identify the sum of the angles.
nodes.response: Highlight how the formation of triangles within a polygon must be from vertex to vertex and demonstrate how the angles of each triangle where they meet sum to the internal angle of the polygon.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasoning about angles in polygons

nodes.misconception: The largest angle that can be created is a 360 degree angle or one full turn.
nodes.response: Explore examples in everyday life where rotations are greater than one full turn. Discuss how multiples of 180 degrees or 360 degrees are often used to describe movements in sports and other contexts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that the angles in a full turn sum to 360 degrees and use this to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the larger the size of the arc between the two lines, the larger the angle must be.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils compare the same angle where the arc has been drawn on either closer to the vertex or further away from the vertex. Generalise that the position of the arc doesn't matter, though it is convention to draw it closer to the vertex.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Use the unit of degrees as a standard unit to measure angles

nodes.misconception: Right angles are only where a horizontal and vertical line meet to create a square corner.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are shown a wide range of right angles in a variety of orientations and contexts so that pupils can better generalise the features of a right angle.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Review understanding and identification of right angles

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the whole 360 degrees must be composed of different sized angles.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are exposed to examples where two or more of the angles summing to 360 degrees are the same.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Know that the angles at a point sum to 360 degrees and use this to solve problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils draw a straight line to begin to create their angle and then place the centre of the protractor in the middle of the straight line.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to place the middle spot of the protractor on one end of the straight line as this will make it easier to mark on the second line to create the vertex once the protractor has been removed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Draw angles accurately using a protractor

nodes.misconception: Students can incorrectly insert a digit in the wrong place value column.
nodes.response: Printing or white board drawings of a place value chart will support student understanding of the different column headings and place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Place value in decimals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get mixed up between metric and imperial units.
nodes.response: You may wish to refer to Lesson 6 of this unit, which explains the metric system’s use of prefixes, and compare this with imperial measures.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Place value in imperial units

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the digit card 0 has to have significant place value.
nodes.response: If the question doesn't specify the number of digits, leading zeros can be used (and not written) to create integers with fewer digits.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of place value in integers

nodes.misconception: 40 thousands placing the 4 in the thousands column.
nodes.response: As there are 40 thousands the 4 is in the ten thousands column.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Deepening understanding of place value in integers

nodes.misconception: When making a 3-digit integer pupils use 0 as the first digit. However 057 is not a 3-digit integer.
nodes.response: Leading zeros are not written. They are not needed to preserve the place value of other digits. 057 is still a 2-digit integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of place value in integers

nodes.misconception: Kilo gram is 1000 bigger than a gram, so 40 g = 1000 x 40 kg
nodes.response: Kilo gram is 1000 bigger than a gram so 1 kg = 1000 g.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of place value in metric units

nodes.misconception: Pupils may consider non-metric units in discussion.
nodes.response: Remind them that the metric units are based around the metre, gram and litre only.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of place value in metric units

nodes.misconception: A "longer" (with more digits) number must be greater.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of ordering and comparing numbers

nodes.misconception: The number with the largest value is the greatest measurement.
nodes.response: Converting to the same unit can be helpful before comparing the place value of the digits. e.g. 0.4 m is bigger than 40 mm.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of ordering and comparing numbers

nodes.misconception: 10^3 means 10 x 3
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Exponential and fractional column headings

nodes.misconception: You have to convert to the same unit to decide if a measure is the same as another.
nodes.response: For metric units it is possible to compare the digits. Any conversion within metric has the same digits in the same order.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with place value

nodes.misconception: Not fully isolating the required variable by leaving other terms containing the variable in the expression.
nodes.response: To make a variable the subject, it must be expressed in terms of other variables only. Factorising helps isolate a variable if it is in multiple terms.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the subject where the variable appears in multiple terms

nodes.misconception: When rearranging multiplicative relationships, the values just 'swap'.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand how to manipulate multiplicative relationships properly instead of relying on a 'trick'. This will be useful in other subject areas as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of changing the subject with simple algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Thinking the multiplier for a 2% increase is either 0.02 or 1.2
nodes.response: A 2% increase is 100% + 2% of the original amount. 102% is equivalent to 1.02 as a decimal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with advanced algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Assuming that 'cross multiplying' is always the best way to solve equations with fractions on both sides.
nodes.response: Examples are included in the lesson where this results in unnecessary quadratic equations. Factorising and looking for common factors allows pupils to spot efficient methods. This also links with fraction skills of finding a common denominator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving equations with algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Trying to simplify a division calculation by identifying common factors before calculating.
nodes.response: Pupils need to understand why this works with multiplication questions to understand why this does not work with division. Encourage pupils to write their division as a multiplication of the reciprocal before identifying common factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Operations with algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the reciprocal of $$\\frac{1}{a} + \\frac{1}{b}$$ is $$a + b$$
nodes.response: $$\\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{4} = \\frac{3}{4}$$ which is not the reciprocal of 2 + 4 = 6. To find the reciprocal, it helps for the expression to be written as a single fraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the subject with multiple algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Simplifying $$\\frac{(x+4)}{(x+5)}$$ by crossing out the $$x$$ terms and getting $$\\frac{4}{5}$$
nodes.response: Refrain from crossing out factors. Instead pupils should write the numerator and denominator as products of the hightest common factor and see that HCF/HCF = 1.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simplifying algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: When solving equations with fractional coefficients, pupils may divide by the reciprocal rather than multiply. E.g. $$\\frac{1}{2}x = 8$$ pupils may just halve $$8$$
nodes.response: Start with integer coefficients, and get pupils used to the idea of multiplying by the reciprocal (not just dividing by the coefficient). This step should be written as part of the working. Answers can be checked by substitution.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of solving with simple algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: When subtracting or dividing, the largest value is found by subtracting or dividing the upper limit of a number by the upper limit of the divisor or additive inverse.
nodes.response: Drawing a number line to show  with subtraction will help students see how to achieve an upper or lower limits of an error interval calculation. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using inequality notation for errors in calculations

nodes.misconception: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
nodes.response: Within the lesson there are many examples where some zeros are significant. Relate significance back to the communication of accuracy and that some digits are significant as they preserve the place value of other digits.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding integers to one significant figure

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that repeated rounding gives the correct answer.
nodes.response: Use a number line to support pupils’ understanding. Locate the number to be rounded on the line and identify the critical values.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding to any number of decimal places

nodes.misconception: When rounding a number, pupils write the first significant digit(s). e.g 36 789 is 4.
nodes.response: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking by estimating

nodes.misconception: Incorrect use of the error interval i.e $$a ≤ x ≤ b$$ or writing the error interval as $$a ≤ x > b$$
nodes.response: As a check, encourage students to round the upper limit interval by the degree of accuracy to see if it evaluates to the rounded number.  Also,  draw a number line to show the meaning of  $$a ≤ x > b$$ and allow students to see the error.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Inequality notation to express error

nodes.misconception: Using the wrong limits when dividing or subtracting in order to find the upper limit of a calculation or lower limit of a calculation.
nodes.response: Drawing a number line to show with subtraction will help students see how to achieve an upper or lower limits of an error interval calculation. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with estimation and rounding

nodes.misconception: Division by 0.5 is the same as doubling.
nodes.response: Reiterate the division of a number is the same as the multiplication of the reciprocal e.g  The division of 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2. e.g The division of 0.1 is the same as multiplying by 10.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimating numerical calculations

nodes.misconception: When rounding a number, pupils write the first significant digit(s) only.  E.g 36 789 is 4.
nodes.response: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of rounding

nodes.misconception: Rounding prematurely during multi-step calculations.
nodes.response: Encourage to use of fractions (where possible) or the use of the ANS button.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding errors

nodes.misconception: Errors when a zero is required when rounding. E.g 5.99 rounds to 6 to 1 d.p.
nodes.response: Embedding that 6 and 6.0 may be written like that to convey the accuracy they've been rounded to. To show that 5.99 has been rounded to 1 d.p. we write it as 6.0 not 6.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding to three decimal places

nodes.misconception: When truncating, pupils are tempted to round. Also, when truncating, they cut off the number without thinking about the magnitude.
nodes.response: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value when truncating.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Truncating

nodes.misconception: The assumption that if a number ends in 2 zeros it must have been rounded to the nearest hundred.
nodes.response: Choose examples that round to the same value when rounded to the nearest ten and hundred in this case.  E.g. 398, rounds to 400 to the nearest ten and 400 to the nearest hundred.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of rounding

nodes.misconception: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
nodes.response: Designing questions that contain zero digits in a variety of positions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding integers to significant figures

nodes.misconception: When subtracting or dividing, the largest value is found by subtracting or dividing the largest rounded number by the largest rounded divisor or additive inverse.
nodes.response: Drawing a number line to show the subtraction of the smallest number will help students see how to achieve an overestimate or underestimate. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Overestimating vs underestimating

nodes.misconception: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
nodes.response: Designing questions that contain zero digits in a variety of positions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounding decimals to significant figures

nodes.misconception: Rounding prematurely during multi-step calculations.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of fractions (where possible) or the use of the 'ANS' button.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Degrees of accuracy

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that to write in completed square form they can divide through by the coefficient of x^2
nodes.response: This works for equations as equality can be maintained by dividing both sides of the equation. However if manipulating an expression, dividing through by a value changes the expression. Instead a value can be 'factored out' as necessary.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving complex quadratic equations by completing the square

nodes.misconception: That we subtract the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is positive and add the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is negative.
nodes.response: Squaring a negative value gives a positive value. Whether the constant in the bracket is positive or negative, the square of the constant must always be subtracted. This can be made clearer with algebra tiles or area models.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by completing the square

nodes.misconception: Believing the constants in the binomials must sum to the coefficient of x and multiply to the constant in the quadratic.
nodes.response: Use an area model to show what is happening when the coefficient of x^2 is not 1. Pupils should always check their answers by expanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Factorising quadratics of the form ax^2 + bx + c

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the formula for the number of days in a week is w=7d because a week has seven days.
nodes.response: Pupils should always write down exactly what the letter is representing. E.g. 'the number of days' and 'the number of weeks'. Then think about what calculation they are doing. 'To find the number of days I multiply the number of weeks by 7'. d=7w.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Further algebraic terminology

nodes.misconception: It can be hard to spot like terms where there are multiple variables with exponents. Therefore opportunities to simplify by collecting like terms can be missed.
nodes.response: When multiplying variables together, write the variables in alphabetical order. This will make it easier to identify like terms.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of simplifying

nodes.misconception: Incorrect evaluation of expressions is common when negative values are substituted. Especially where negative values are squared or pupils rely on calculators without being confident of their use.
nodes.response: When substituting, always put brackets around the value which is substituted. This helps avoid mistakes when using a calculator as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of substitution

nodes.misconception: Once shown the difference of two squares, pupils may think that squaring each term in a binomial is the correct way to expand binomials such as (x+3)^2
nodes.response: Spend time investigating where the difference of two squares occurs, use representations such as algebra tiles and area models.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Factorising using the difference of two squares

nodes.misconception: Pupils often get signs the incorrect way round in the binomials. E.g. (x+2)(x-4) instead of (x-2)(x+4)
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to always expand their binomials to check they are correct. Using representations such as an area model should reduce the likelihood of this as pupils focus on the structure and reason behind their choices.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Factorising a quadratic expression

nodes.misconception: The first two binomials have to be multiplied first.
nodes.response: Look for features of the binomials that suggest which binomials will be easiest to multiply first. Any order will give the same final product but a particular order may reduce complexity.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The product of three binomials

nodes.misconception: If a linear equation involves brackets, these always have to be expanded first.
nodes.response: Get pupils to use knowledge of factors and collecting like terms to simplify problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of solving and interpreting linear equations

nodes.misconception: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
nodes.response: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with algebraic manipulation

nodes.misconception: That the solutions are just the constants in the binomials.
nodes.response: After factorising, pupils should be writing the one step equations, equal to zero, before writing the solutions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by factorising

nodes.misconception: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
nodes.response: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with algebraic manipulation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to factorise and solve without rearranging first.
nodes.response: Being able to put the factors equal to zero only makes sense if we are using the property that if two values multiply to zero, one of them is zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by factorising where rearrangement is required

nodes.misconception: Leaving answers which are not fully factorised when they are required to.
nodes.response: There should be a focus on reading questions to decipher what they are being asked to do. When they have to fully factorise they need the highest common factor of all the terms. LC3 focuses on situations where they are not going to fully factorise.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of factorising

nodes.misconception: Missing out partial products.
nodes.response: Use an area model to demonstrate this. If pupils do not wish to draw the models they should be using the distributive law instead e.g. (x + 2)(x + 3) as x(x + 3)+2(x + 3)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of the product of two binomials

nodes.misconception: When forming expressions brackets can be missed out or incorrectly used.
nodes.response: Review priority of operations. Testing algebraic manipulations with numerical values can be useful when pupils are unsure if things are equivalent. E.g. the difference between 2(x + 4) and 2x + 4 can be shown with 2(5 + 4) and 2(5) + 4
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of forming linear equations

nodes.misconception: When rearranging multiplicative relationships, the values just 'swap'
nodes.response: Pupils should understand how to manipulate multiplicative relationships properly instead of relying on a 'trick'. This will be useful in other subject areas as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of changing the subject

nodes.misconception: Mistakes often occur when substituting into the quadratic formula with calculators, as pupils miss out brackets and change the priority of operations.
nodes.response: Values should always be put in brackets when substituted. This avoids mistakes when squaring and subtracting negative values. It also makes it easier to change the values of a , b , and c when working on a new question.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by using the formula

nodes.misconception: Pupils find simplifying expressions which are the difference of two bracketed expressions difficult.
nodes.response: There are two equivalent methods detailed in learning cycle two. Spend time on both, getting pupils to explore their equivalence. If pupils are struggling, considering subtraction as adding the negative value is the easiest to model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of expanding a single bracket

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to match up corresponding measurements on two congruent shapes when they are in different orientations.
nodes.response: Look lengths which are between any pairs of known angles or look for angles which are between pairs of adjacent  known lengths. Also, tracing paper could be used to reflect/rotate/translate one shape onto the other.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of congruence

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to spot congruent triangles if they only look for ASA.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to add any further information to diagrams, like the third angle, before starting to prove congruence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Congruent triangles (ASA and AAS)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they do not have enough information about a shape to determine whether it is congruent to another shape, when in fact they do.
nodes.response: Pupils could attempt the draw the shape based on the information that they have. They can then consider whether there are multiple way that the shape can be drawn while still satisfying all the given information.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Congruence in shapes

nodes.misconception: Pythagoras' theorem is just a relationship between the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
nodes.response: Whilst this is true, Pythagoras' theorem can more visually be represented as three squares whose sides are equal in length to the three sides of the triangle. The sum of the areas of the two smaller squares is equal to the area of the larger square.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Demonstrating Pythagoras' theorem

nodes.misconception: I need to be given a triangle in order to use Pythagoras' theorem.
nodes.response: You do not need to be given a triangle. It is an important skill to be able to sketch and label a triangle for yourself from given information, or go straight into an algebraic stage of calculation if aware that lengths given are perpendicular.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Pythagoras' theorem in context

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix up the meanings of congruence and similarity or struggle with the hierarchy of their nested sets (e.g. thinking that all similar shapes are congruent rather than the other way around).
nodes.response: Frequently refer to a Venn diagram showing the set of congruence shapes inside the set of similar shapes when examining pairs of shapes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Congruent, similar or neither

nodes.misconception: I can only use Pythagoras' theorem to find the length of a side of a right-angled triangle when the right-angle marker is labelled, so I know which side is the hypotenuse.
nodes.response: The right-angle marker doesn't need to be explicitly labelled in order to be able to identify the right-angle. You can use knowledge of "interior angles in a triangle sum to 180°" to find the right angle, given two other angles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Determining which side

nodes.misconception: When a pair of similar shapes are not in the same orientation, pupils may select an incorrect pair of lengths to calculate the scale factor.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to take a systematic approach to locating pairs of corresponding lengths by looking for the longest edge in each shape, then the second longest, third longest, etc.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of similarity

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to match up corresponding measurements on two congruent shapes when they are in different orientations.
nodes.response: Look lengths which are between any pairs of known angles or look for angles which are between pairs of adjacent  known lengths. Also, tracing paper could be used to reflect/rotate/translate one shape onto the other.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Similarity in shapes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they need to know the actual size or length to be able to prove congruence.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that if they can show that the corresponding angles or sides are the same length, then that is all that is needed. For example, if the corresponding edges are both edges of the same regular polygon, then they will be the same.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the criteria for congruence

nodes.misconception: When rotating a shape to count its order of rotational symmetry, pupils may count the starting position twice: once at the start and then again at the end of the full turn.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to be consistent with when they count the starting position, either always counting it before they begin rotating the shape or always counting it at the end of the full turn.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rotational symmetry

nodes.misconception: Pythagorean triples can be a trio of any rational numbers that, when constructed into a triangle, always produces a right-angled triangle.
nodes.response: Pythagorean triples are conventionally a trio of integer side lengths of a right-angled triangle, such as the 3, 4, 5 triangle. Other, similar triangles can be generated from Pythagorean triples, whose side lengths are rational, such as 0.3, 0.4, 0.5
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Length of the hypotenuse

nodes.misconception: The method for finding the length of a shorter side of a right-angled triangle using Pythagoras' theorem is exactly the same as when finding the hypotenuse.
nodes.response: Whilst the initial setup of "the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides equals the square of the hypotenuse" will be the same, finding the length of a shorter side will require an extra step of rearranging terms in the equation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Length of a shorter side

nodes.misconception: Every question that has a right-angled triangle must use Pythagoras' theorem to be solved.
nodes.response: It is easy to get into a habit of using Pythagoras' theorem when learning the topic, but it is likely you have seen several maths problems in the past with right-angled triangles, which ask to find areas and angles, without using Pythagoras' theorem.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with similarity and Pythagoras' theorem

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the angle doesn't need to be in between the two known sides.
nodes.response: Use the Geogebra files to demonstrate that more than one triangle can be formed at times, and therefore it does not guarantee congruence between two triangles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Congruent triangles (SAS)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that as the sides fix the angles, that this implies it is true conversely.
nodes.response: Use any regular polygon to highlight that the angles will always be the same, but the edge lengths are not always the same length. Regular polygons are always similar but not necessarily congruent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Congruent triangles (SSS)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may make assumptions about diagrams containing a right angle incorrectly.
nodes.response: Remind pupils, that they cannot assume there is a right angle, just because it may look like the two edges are perpendicular to each other.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Congruent triangles (RHS)

nodes.misconception: Pythagoras' theorem is just a relationship between the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
nodes.response: Whilst this is true, Pythagoras' theorem can more visually be represented as three squares whose sides are equal in length to the three sides of the triangle. The sum of the areas of the two smaller squares is equal to the area of the larger square.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Further demonstrating of Pythagoras' theorem

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that to write in completed square form they can divide through by the coefficient of x^2
nodes.response: This works for equations as equality can be maintained by dividing both sides of the equation. However if manipulating an expression, dividing through by a value changes the expression. Instead a value can be 'factored out' as necessary.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving complex quadratic equations by completing the square

nodes.misconception: That we subtract the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is positive and add the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is negative.
nodes.response: Squaring a negative value gives a positive value. Whether the constant in the bracket is positive or negative, the square of the constant must always be subtracted. This can be made clearer with algebra tiles or area models.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by completing the square

nodes.misconception: Believing the constants in the binomials must sum to the coefficient of x and multiply to the constant in the quadratic.
nodes.response: Use an area model to show what is happening when the coefficient of x^2 is not 1. Pupils should always check their answers by expanding.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Factorising quadratics of the form ax^2 + bx + c

nodes.misconception: Pupils can think the formula for the number of days in a week is w=7d because a week has seven days.
nodes.response: Pupils should always write down exactly what the letter is representing. E.g. 'the number of days' and 'the number of weeks'. Then think about what calculation they are doing. 'To find the number of days I multiply the number of weeks by 7'. d=7w.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Further algebraic terminology

nodes.misconception: It can be hard to spot like terms where there are multiple variables with exponents. Therefore opportunities to simplify by collecting like terms can be missed.
nodes.response: When multiplying variables together, write the variables in alphabetical order. This will make it easier to identify like terms.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of simplifying

nodes.misconception: Incorrect evaluation of expressions is common when negative values are substituted. Especially where negative values are squared or pupils rely on calculators without being confident of their use.
nodes.response: When substituting, always put brackets around the value which is substituted. This helps avoid mistakes when using a calculator as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of substitution

nodes.misconception: Once shown the difference of two squares, pupils may think that squaring each term in a binomial is the correct way to expand binomials such as (x+3)^2
nodes.response: Spend time investigating where the difference of two squares occurs, use representations such as algebra tiles and area models.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Factorising using the difference of two squares

nodes.misconception: Pupils often get signs the incorrect way round in the binomials. E.g. (x+2)(x-4) instead of (x-2)(x+4)
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to always expand their binomials to check they are correct. Using representations such as an area model should reduce the likelihood of this as pupils focus on the structure and reason behind their choices.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Factorising a quadratic expression

nodes.misconception: The first two binomials have to be multiplied first.
nodes.response: Look for features of the binomials that suggest which binomials will be easiest to multiply first. Any order will give the same final product but a particular order may reduce complexity.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The product of three binomials

nodes.misconception: If a linear equation involves brackets, these always have to be expanded first.
nodes.response: Get pupils to use knowledge of factors and collecting like terms to simplify problems.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of solving and interpreting linear equations

nodes.misconception: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
nodes.response: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with algebraic manipulation

nodes.misconception: That the solutions are just the constants in the binomials.
nodes.response: After factorising, pupils should be writing the one step equations, equal to zero, before writing the solutions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by factorising

nodes.misconception: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
nodes.response: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with algebraic manipulation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to factorise and solve without rearranging first.
nodes.response: Being able to put the factors equal to zero only makes sense if we are using the property that if two values multiply to zero, one of them is zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by factorising where rearrangement is required

nodes.misconception: Leaving answers which are not fully factorised when they are required to.
nodes.response: There should be a focus on reading questions to decipher what they are being asked to do. When they have to fully factorise they need the highest common factor of all the terms. LC3 focuses on situations where they are not going to fully factorise.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of factorising

nodes.misconception: Missing out partial products.
nodes.response: Use an area model to demonstrate this. If pupils do not wish to draw the models they should be using the distributive law instead e.g. (x + 2)(x + 3) as x(x + 3)+2(x + 3)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of the product of two binomials

nodes.misconception: When forming expressions brackets can be missed out or incorrectly used.
nodes.response: Review priority of operations. Testing algebraic manipulations with numerical values can be useful when pupils are unsure if things are equivalent. E.g. the difference between 2(x + 4) and 2x + 4 can be shown with 2(5 + 4) and 2(5) + 4
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of forming linear equations

nodes.misconception: When rearranging multiplicative relationships, the values just 'swap'
nodes.response: Pupils should understand how to manipulate multiplicative relationships properly instead of relying on a 'trick'. This will be useful in other subject areas as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of changing the subject

nodes.misconception: Mistakes often occur when substituting into the quadratic formula with calculators, as pupils miss out brackets and change the priority of operations.
nodes.response: Values should always be put in brackets when substituted. This avoids mistakes when squaring and subtracting negative values. It also makes it easier to change the values of a , b , and c when working on a new question.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic equations by using the formula

nodes.misconception: Pupils find simplifying expressions which are the difference of two bracketed expressions difficult.
nodes.response: There are two equivalent methods detailed in learning cycle two. Spend time on both, getting pupils to explore their equivalence. If pupils are struggling, considering subtraction as adding the negative value is the easiest to model.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of expanding a single bracket

nodes.misconception: Not fully isolating the required variable by leaving other terms containing the variable in the expression.
nodes.response: To make a variable the subject, it must be expressed in terms of other variables only. Factorising helps isolate a variable if it is in multiple terms.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the subject where the variable appears in multiple terms

nodes.misconception: When rearranging multiplicative relationships, the values just 'swap'.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand how to manipulate multiplicative relationships properly instead of relying on a 'trick'. This will be useful in other subject areas as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of changing the subject with simple algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Thinking the multiplier for a 2% increase is either 0.02 or 1.2
nodes.response: A 2% increase is 100% + 2% of the original amount. 102% is equivalent to 1.02 as a decimal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with advanced algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Assuming that 'cross multiplying' is always the best way to solve equations with fractions on both sides.
nodes.response: Examples are included in the lesson where this results in unnecessary quadratic equations. Factorising and looking for common factors allows pupils to spot efficient methods. This also links with fraction skills of finding a common denominator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving equations with algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Trying to simplify a division calculation by identifying common factors before calculating.
nodes.response: Pupils need to understand why this works with multiplication questions to understand why this does not work with division. Encourage pupils to write their division as a multiplication of the reciprocal before identifying common factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Operations with algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the reciprocal of $$\\frac{1}{a} + \\frac{1}{b}$$ is $$a + b$$
nodes.response: $$\\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{4} = \\frac{3}{4}$$ which is not the reciprocal of 2 + 4 = 6. To find the reciprocal, it helps for the expression to be written as a single fraction.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the subject with multiple algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: Simplifying $$\\frac{(x+4)}{(x+5)}$$ by crossing out the $$x$$ terms and getting $$\\frac{4}{5}$$
nodes.response: Refrain from crossing out factors. Instead pupils should write the numerator and denominator as products of the hightest common factor and see that HCF/HCF = 1.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simplifying algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: When solving equations with fractional coefficients, pupils may divide by the reciprocal rather than multiply. E.g. $$\\frac{1}{2}x = 8$$ pupils may just halve $$8$$
nodes.response: Start with integer coefficients, and get pupils used to the idea of multiplying by the reciprocal (not just dividing by the coefficient). This step should be written as part of the working. Answers can be checked by substitution.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of solving with simple algebraic fractions

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to tell if 174 368 is in the sequence -8,-3,2,7, ...
nodes.response: Generalising the rule for forming a given sequence can help us see if a value is in the sequence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Justifying terms of a sequence

nodes.misconception: That $$n$$ is a term in the sequence. That $$n=10$$ means 10 is in the sequence.
nodes.response: Reiterate that $$n$$ is the term number. "$$n=10$$ means the 10th term. What is the 10th term number?"
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing an arithmetic sequence

nodes.misconception: The answer to the 'handshake' problem is 15, or 15x15
nodes.response: Group pupils into 3s and ask them to record how many handshakes are made. Then group as 4s and repeat. What do they notice?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with sequences

nodes.misconception: When plotting sequences, a line must be drawn through the points.
nodes.response: Plot (1,5), (2,10), (3,15), draw a line and find other coordinates. When n = 1.5 the term value is 7.5. Is 7.5 in the sequence 5n??
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing sequences graphically

nodes.misconception: That the sequence $$3n+2$$ starts with 3 and adds 2, or starts with 2 and adds 3.
nodes.response: Calculate the first few terms. Ask, "When $$n = 1$$ what is the term value?" This is the first value for our sequence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating any term

nodes.misconception: That the sequence 6,11,16,21, ... is 5n+6 because it goes up by 5 and starts at 6.
nodes.response: Compare 6,11,16,21, ... to 5,10,15,20, ... "What is the shift? The translation? If that is 5n then this is 5n with how much more?"
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding the nth  term

nodes.misconception: Sequences such as triangular numbers which have a linear sequence in their differences are linear.
nodes.response: Terms in an arithmetic sequence have to have a common first difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Arithmetic sequences

nodes.misconception: The position-to-term rule is the initial term add the common difference.
nodes.response: Once pupils have found the additive pattern get them to write each term as a value add the difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating a sequence using a position-to-term rule

nodes.misconception: Pupils can mix up describing how patterns grow or the relationships between objects in the pattern.
nodes.response: Pupils should verbalise their description, using the keyword 'term' , making it clear which way they are describing their pattern.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Formalising a sequence

nodes.misconception: That sequences can only have constant additive or multiplicative patterns.
nodes.response: Give students two numbers and get them to carry the sequence on in different ways. Anything they come up with can be a sequence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of sequences

nodes.misconception: The difference in the given terms divided by the number of missing terms gives the common difference
nodes.response: Write the sequence out with gaps for the missing terms. Model how many additions (jumps) to get from one known term to the next.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating a sequence using a term-to-term rule

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to divide values correctly to find a multiplier, especially when fractional.
nodes.response: Pupils should write their sequence out with arrows to show which direction their multiplier is operating.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of sequences

nodes.misconception: When using a Venn diagram students often mix up HCF & LCM.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: HCF or LCM

nodes.misconception: Common factors are put into the intersection of the Venn diagram twice instead of once.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check that the product of the factors in each set is the correct integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Highest common factor

nodes.misconception: Students often use an adhoc approach to listing multiples this often leads to pairs being missed out
nodes.response: Encourage a systematic approach starting with 1 and the integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Listing factors

nodes.misconception: There is often confusion between factors and multiples.
nodes.response: Highlight that the number of dots in an array is the multiple and the number of dots in each column & row are the factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of factors, multiples, squares and cubes

nodes.misconception: All factors of all integers will appear in a 12 by 12 times table grid.
nodes.response: It is not possible to identify all factors of 24 using a 12 by 12 times table grid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of factors, multiples, squares and cubes

nodes.misconception: A common multiple of all integers is 1.
nodes.response: Get students to list multiples. This is to highlight the fact that 1 is only a multiple of 1.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Listing multiples

nodes.misconception: Students think that all numbers are square numbers as you can square any integer.
nodes.response: A square is the product of 2 repeated integers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Square and cube numbers

nodes.misconception: Identifying if integer is a multiple when its given in its prime factor form.
nodes.response: Only the bases need to be considered, not the exponents.  e.g if it is a multiple of 3 it must be a multiple of 3^2, 3^3, etc.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating integers from their prime factor expressions

nodes.misconception: 1 is a prime number
nodes.response: 1 is not a prime number as it only has one factor and a prime number has exactly two factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of prime numbers

nodes.misconception: When using a Venn diagram misplacement of factors is common.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check that the product of factors in each set is the correct integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Lowest common multiple

nodes.misconception: Use of addition instead of multiplication when the decomposing the number.
nodes.response: Reiterate that the product of prime factors is unique.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing an integer as a product of its prime factors

nodes.misconception: Students forget to scroll right to exit the exponent function.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check what they have on their screen matches the calculation exactly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Powers and roots using a calculator

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly summing the digits to identify a multiple of 3 or 9.
nodes.response: Use number bonds to sum large numbers of digits.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divisibility tests for 6 and 9

nodes.misconception: Often students only consider the last 2 digits of a number to check for divisibility for 8.
nodes.response: The last 2 digits check for divisibility for 4 not 8.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divisibility tests for 4 and 8

nodes.misconception: When different bases are used student multiply the bases.  e.g. 2 x 5^2 = 10^2
nodes.response: Calculate and compare the 2, 2 x 5^2 = 50 & 10^2 = 100
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Power notation

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly summing the digits of an integer to identify a multiple of 3.
nodes.response: Use number bonds to sum large numbers of digits.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divisibility tests for 2 and 3

nodes.misconception: Real life measurements aren't always integers. Use of integers can give more a practical application
nodes.response: e.g. find the largest with 200 blocks, the cbrt(200) is not an integer so we use 5 x 5 x 5  =125
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with factors, multiples, squares and cubes

nodes.misconception: A number is a prime if it is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 10.
nodes.response: A factor of a number can be greater than 10.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Divisibility tests for 5 and 10

nodes.misconception: The root of an integer is half of the integer.
nodes.response: The square root is the inverse of a square number. A square is the product of 2 repeated integers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Square and cube roots

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have their calculator set to radians instead of degrees.
nodes.response: The first check for understanding is designed to catch this but it is worth checking that the correct unit of measurement is being used throughout the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing the sine and cosine graphs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the incorrect trigonometric formula.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to label their triangles with the name for each side. This helps to identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of trigonometric ratios

nodes.misconception: Using any two side lengths for the sine formula.
nodes.response: It must be two side lengths and the angle between them. So any two side lengths of the triangle can be used so long as you also use the angle between them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating the area of any triangle when the height is not known

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have their calculator set to radians instead of degrees.
nodes.response: The first check for understanding is designed to catch this but it is worth checking that the correct unit of measurement is being used throughout the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Drawing the tangent graph

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain about which angle pairs with which side.
nodes.response: The angle is paired with the side length that is opposite.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The sine rule

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain over how to start a problem.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to draw a diagram if one is not provided and then to annotate the diagram with any given information as a first step. If a diagram is given then pupils should annotate that.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the sine and cosine rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the need for this rule as they have the sine rule.
nodes.response: The sine rule can be used in many cases but it is not always the most efficient. There will be problems where it will be much faster to use the cosine rule.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The cosine rule

nodes.misconception: Using any two side lengths for the sine formula.
nodes.response: It must be two side lengths and the angle between them. So any two side lengths of the triangle can be used so long as you also use the angle between them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The area of any triangle

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be hesitant to start the problems due to uncertainty.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to try an approach and then reflect on whether there has been progress towards a solution. Deducing something you didn't already know if progress even if it does not seem like it.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering the appropriate trigonometric rule

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they have to use the sine or cosine rule.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider all the trigonometric knowledge they have and choose the most appropriate piece for the problem they are dealing with.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with non right-angled trigonometry

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that the graph displayed always shows the number of solutions.
nodes.response: It is important to compare the range of values that the graph is displaying against what is being defined in the question.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting the trigonometric graphs

nodes.misconception: Pupils find the two $$x$$ values after solving the combined quadratic and declare that the solution.
nodes.response: It is important to substitute both $$x$$ values back in to one of the original equations to find the corresponding $$y$$ values. Without these, the solutions are incomplete.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a quadratic and linear pair of simultaneous equations using substitution

nodes.misconception: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
nodes.response: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: Equations always have one solution.
nodes.response: Some equations have one solution but, some have no solutions, some have two solutions, some have more than two solutions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous linear equations graphically

nodes.misconception: Pupils find the two $$x$$ values after solving the combined quadratic and declare that the solution.
nodes.response: It is important to substitute both $$x$$ values back in to one of the original equations to find the corresponding $$y$$ values. Without these, the solutions are incomplete.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a quadratic and linear pair of simultaneous equations using elimination

nodes.misconception: For a pair of simultaneous equations (one linear and one quadratic), there will always be two intersections and therefore two solutions.
