nodes.response: The linear graph might be tangent to the curve therefore only one intersection (solution). Alternatively, the straight line may never intersect the parabola and in this case, there is no solution.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a quadratic and linear pair of simultaneous equations graphically

nodes.misconception: One method is superior when solving simultaneous equations.
nodes.response: Understanding that there are often multiple ways to solve the same problem and then be able to accurately execute a variety of methods is very useful. In this topic, it can enable pupils to confirm their solutions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous equations via any method

nodes.misconception: Mistakes can be made when subtracting negative values. E.g. thinking that 5 - - 2 = 3.
nodes.response: Consider additive inverses, subtracting a negative is the same as adding the additive inverse. Pupils should be able to spot mistakes in learning cycle 1 by checking their new equation is still true.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining equations

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly expanding brackets or not using brackets when one expression is substituted into another.
nodes.response: Pupils should always use brackets when substituting. Remind them of the distributive law and that multiplying a negative value by a negative value gives a positive value. Checking final answers should catch these mistakes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous linear equations by substitution

nodes.misconception: Performing different operations on different variables. E.g. subtracting one variable to eliminate then adding the other variable and constant. Pupils incorrectly think they are adding to eliminate.
nodes.response: This is caused by negative number skills. Subtracting two identical values always gives zero even if both are negative. If a term is the same in both equations, we subtract to eliminate. Clear working is crucial here.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving algebraic simultaneous equations by elimination

nodes.misconception: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
nodes.response: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with linear and quadratic simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: Substituting with negative values.
nodes.response: Putting brackets around all substituted values is good practice.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of interpreting graphs

nodes.misconception: Subtracting the variables one way round but the constants the other way.
nodes.response: Pupils could rewrite their equations so the one they are subtracting is underneath in a column method. For this lesson, the answers are in context so pupils should spot when negative answers do not make sense.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous equations by elimination from a context

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to multiply every term in the equation when scaling or not multiplying every term by the same value.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that in order to maintain equality, the entire expression on both sides of the equals sign must be multiplied by the same value. Clear working and checking solutions can help pupils spot when they have made this mistake.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving more complex simultaneous equations by elimination

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly identifying when simultaneous equations can be formed. This can lead to pupils using the same letter in two equations to represent different things.
nodes.response: Pupils should be writing down precisely what the variable represent in context. They can then compare whether they are using the same letter to represent the same thing in two different equations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils find the two $$x$$ values after solving the combined quadratic and declare that the solution.
nodes.response: It is important to substitute both $$x$$ values back in to one of the original equations to find the corresponding $$y$$ values. Without these, the solutions are incomplete.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a quadratic and linear pair of simultaneous equations using substitution

nodes.misconception: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
nodes.response: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: Equations always have one solution.
nodes.response: Some equations have one solution but, some have no solutions, some have two solutions, some have more than two solutions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous linear equations graphically

nodes.misconception: Pupils find the two $$x$$ values after solving the combined quadratic and declare that the solution.
nodes.response: It is important to substitute both $$x$$ values back in to one of the original equations to find the corresponding $$y$$ values. Without these, the solutions are incomplete.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a quadratic and linear pair of simultaneous equations using elimination

nodes.misconception: For a pair of simultaneous equations (one linear and one quadratic), there will always be two intersections and therefore two solutions.
nodes.response: The linear graph might be tangent to the curve therefore only one intersection (solution). Alternatively, the straight line may never intersect the parabola and in this case, there is no solution.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a quadratic and linear pair of simultaneous equations graphically

nodes.misconception: One method is superior when solving simultaneous equations.
nodes.response: Understanding that there are often multiple ways to solve the same problem and then be able to accurately execute a variety of methods is very useful. In this topic, it can enable pupils to confirm their solutions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous equations via any method

nodes.misconception: Mistakes can be made when subtracting negative values. E.g. thinking that 5 - - 2 = 3.
nodes.response: Consider additive inverses, subtracting a negative is the same as adding the additive inverse. Pupils should be able to spot mistakes in learning cycle 1 by checking their new equation is still true.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining equations

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly expanding brackets or not using brackets when one expression is substituted into another.
nodes.response: Pupils should always use brackets when substituting. Remind them of the distributive law and that multiplying a negative value by a negative value gives a positive value. Checking final answers should catch these mistakes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous linear equations by substitution

nodes.misconception: Performing different operations on different variables. E.g. subtracting one variable to eliminate then adding the other variable and constant. Pupils incorrectly think they are adding to eliminate.
nodes.response: This is caused by negative number skills. Subtracting two identical values always gives zero even if both are negative. If a term is the same in both equations, we subtract to eliminate. Clear working is crucial here.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving algebraic simultaneous equations by elimination

nodes.misconception: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
nodes.response: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with linear and quadratic simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: Substituting with negative values.
nodes.response: Putting brackets around all substituted values is good practice.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of interpreting graphs

nodes.misconception: Subtracting the variables one way round but the constants the other way.
nodes.response: Pupils could rewrite their equations so the one they are subtracting is underneath in a column method. For this lesson, the answers are in context so pupils should spot when negative answers do not make sense.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simultaneous equations by elimination from a context

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to multiply every term in the equation when scaling or not multiplying every term by the same value.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that in order to maintain equality, the entire expression on both sides of the equals sign must be multiplied by the same value. Clear working and checking solutions can help pupils spot when they have made this mistake.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving more complex simultaneous equations by elimination

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly identifying when simultaneous equations can be formed. This can lead to pupils using the same letter in two equations to represent different things.
nodes.response: Pupils should be writing down precisely what the variable represent in context. They can then compare whether they are using the same letter to represent the same thing in two different equations.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: I can use outcome tables to categorise outcomes into as many events as I want.
nodes.response: Outcome tables are limited to categorising outcomes into only two events. You can use more tables to categorise outcomes into three or more events, but the number of tables you need quickly becomes massive!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing representations of outcomes for more than two events

nodes.misconception: An outcome tree doesn't have a sample space.
nodes.response: Each representation of the outcomes of a trial have a sample space as a part of it. For an outcome table, the table itself is the sample space. For an outcome tree, a sample space must always be constructed after drawing the two layers of branches.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing representations of outcomes for two events

nodes.misconception: Outcome tables and outcome trees only work for outcomes that are all equally likely.
nodes.response: Outcome tables can be separated into more rows and columns, and outcome trees split into more branches, to show outcomes that are more or less likely than other ones. This does mean these diagrams do get massive very quickly!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with possible outcomes

nodes.misconception: A small number of trials in an experiment is enough to provide conclusive findings.
nodes.response: Even in situations where we know that the different outcomes of a trial are equally likely happen, one outcome may happen more often than the others. E.g. when we flip a coin 10 times, we don't always get the exact same number of heads and tails.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Experiments to determine how likely an outcome is

nodes.misconception: The outcomes of a trial are always equally likely to occur (e.g. each of the two players in a tennis match are equally likely to win).
nodes.response: There are factors that may affect how likely one outcome is compared to another (e.g. the skill or experience of one tennis player compared to the other).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Non-equally likely outcomes

nodes.misconception: 'Equal chance' means the same as 'even chance'.
nodes.response: When a trial has more than two possible outcomes which are all equally likely to happen, each outcome has less than an even chance of happening. E.g. each number on a dice has the same likelihood of being rolled, but each is less than an even chance.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The scale of likelihoods

nodes.misconception: Every group of branches should have the same number of branches.
nodes.response: In a multi-staged trial, each stage may have a different number of outcomes. The number of branches in each group reflects the number of outcomes of a stage. This means each group of branches can be made from a different number of branches.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using an outcome tree to display outcomes for two events

nodes.misconception: Rolling a 6 on a dice is less likely to happen than rolling other numbers. Or ticket 001 is less likely to be drawn in a raffle than other tickets.
nodes.response: The random nature of picking a raffle or rolling a dice means all outcomes are equally likely as each other.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Equally likely outcomes

nodes.misconception: Pupils want to avoid writing lists of outcomes.
nodes.response: Always model and bring explicit attention to a systematic list. The benefits of working systematically is the likelihood of error is reduced.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using lists to display outcomes for more than two events

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the phrasing and language, when trying to identify the correct regions of the Venn diagram.
nodes.response: Encourage the pupils to describe each region of the Venn diagram, in context where appropriate.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using a Venn diagram to display outcomes for more than two events

nodes.misconception: An outcome tree can only have a maximum of three layers of branches.
nodes.response: An outcome tree can have as many layers of branches as needed, depending on the number of stages there are in a trial. For example, if a trial involved flipping 7 coins, then there would be 7 layers of branches! That's too probably too many to draw!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using an outcome tree to display outcomes for more than two events

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not draw the rectangle in their Venn diagrams.
nodes.response: Refer back to the rectangle hosting all possible outcomes; the sample space and therefore a vital part of a Venn diagram.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using a Venn diagram to display outcomes for two events

nodes.misconception: Pupils may worry about which event/stage of the trial should be the rows and which should be the columns in an outcome table.
nodes.response: Explain that the rows and columns can be transposed. Depending on the context AB and BA may be the same outcome, whereas in other contexts they may be two different outcomes, so a little care is needed in interpretation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using two-way tables to display outcomes for two events

nodes.misconception: Pupils want to avoid writing lists of outcomes.
nodes.response: Always model and bring explicit attention to a systematic list. The benefits of working systematically is the likelihood of error is reduced.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using lists to display outcomes for two events

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the edge length as the perpendicular height when calculating the volume.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that for any volume calculation, three perpendicular lengths are multiplied and in most pyramids the edge of a triangle is not perpendicular to the base. Also the edge of the triangles can be different in the pyramid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The volume of a pyramid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget the constant '4' when calculating the surface area.
nodes.response: Show the demonstration of the formula of the surface area using a different spherical fruit to see that it is always 4 regardless of the size of the sphere. You can also relate it to the 1/2 in the formula of the area of triangle.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The surface area of a sphere

nodes.misconception: When finding the surface area of the cone, pupils may find the curved surface area but forget to include circular base of the cone.
nodes.response: By re-reading the question, and inspecting any given diagram, pupils can check if the cone is open or closed and therefore if they need to include the circular base in their calculation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The surface area of a cone

nodes.misconception: Pupils can make errors if given the dimensions/measurements of the cylinder using different units (for example the radius is given in cm and the length in m).
nodes.response: Remind pupils to convert all measurements to the same unit (such as cm or m) before starting the calculation. Usually there is a prompt in the question to use as a guide, for example give your answer in square centimetres.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of surface area of a cylinder

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not subtract overlapping faces from their surface area calculation.
nodes.response: Ask the pupils to visualise turning around/rotating the compound solid, and consider which faces of the component solids would always be hidden.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface area of composite solids

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a cone is a pyramid.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a pyramid has a polygonal base, so a cone cannot be a pyramid as the base is a circle, which is not a polygon.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The surface area of a pyramid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if you cut the height of the cone in a half, the resulting frustrum will have half the volume of the original cone.
nodes.response: The frustrum is actually seven eighths of the volume of the original cone; the small cone that was removed to create the frustrum is one eighth the volume of the original cone if the frustrum and the small cone have the same height.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Volume of a frustum of a cone

nodes.misconception: When working out the surface area, the pupil may only find the sum of the areas of three faces of a cuboid (for example the visible sides in a 3D drawing), instead of all six faces.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch the net of the cuboid as part of their solution. This will provide a visual reminder to the pupil to find the area of all six faces, as well as making it easier to check their answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of surface area of cuboids

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the slant length (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone or frustum) with the perpendicular (or vertical) height.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to clearly label their diagrams, indicating the perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry to calculate the slant length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface area of a frustum of a cone

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the height of the cylinder may be described as the depth or length and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. Discuss which length this would be, using a diagram to support.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of volume of a cylinder

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the slant height (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone) with the perpendicular height (which is needed to find the volume of the cone).
nodes.response: Remind pupils that for any volume calculation, three perpendicular lengths are multiplied and the slant height is not perpendicular to the base in a right cone. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem to find the perpendicular height.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The volume of a cone

nodes.misconception: Pupils may multiply the radius of the sphere by the constant before cubing it.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the order of operations and the need to cube the radius before multiplying by the constants in the formula.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The volume of a sphere

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only using given measures or terms in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required to form an expression for the volume or surface area.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to clearly show how the are breaking down a compound shape, and label clearly any new or missing lengths they can determine.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming equations involving complex shape calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only using given measures in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required for substitution into a volume formula.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to show how the are breaking down a compound/composite shape. Pupils should label the diagram with any new lengths needed. They may need to use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find these new lengths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Volume of composite solids

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. They may need to evaluate a perpendicular length from other given information, using trigonometry or Pythagoras' theorem.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with further surface area and volume

nodes.misconception: Pupils can miss out some faces of the prism when calculating the surface area.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch out the net of the prism and label it clearly, to ensure that they include all faces in their calculation of the surface area. This will allow their answer to be checked more easily.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of surface area of other prisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse whether they need to calculate the volume or surface area of a 3D shape, if not told specifically to do so in a problem.
nodes.response: Use the context to decide which calculation is needed. If the question refers to packaging or painting the shape, a surface area calculation is needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with further surface area and volume

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from a product of three perpendicular lengths. The cross-sectional area uses two of the three, so identify the distance that is perpendicular to the cross-sectional face.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of volume of prisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misconfigure the net, believing that as long as the shapes of the faces are correct, the net will fold to be the desired 3D shape.
nodes.response: Have pupils mark/label/colour the edges that will join upon folding the net, this will ensure they are the correct length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of nets of solids

nodes.misconception: To draw the graph using the gradient and intercept you can just count the squares.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to look at the scales on the axes carefully when drawing a line given the gradient and y-intercept.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding the equation of the line ay + bx + c = 0

nodes.misconception: There is one answer to everything in maths.
nodes.response: We often see arithmetic and equations with one answer but, maths can be used to compare and justify multiple answers to a single problem.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with graphing linear relationships

nodes.misconception: When plotting the sequence $$3n-1$$ using technology you need to type each coordinate individually.
nodes.response: "We use technology to make things easier. There must be a quicker way!" Look for the 'table' function.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of plotting coordinates with technology

nodes.misconception: The plotted points of an arithmetic sequence form a line so we draw a line connecting them.
nodes.response: Sequences are an ordered list and do not always need to follow a rule, so we often only find and use the positive integer term numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of plotting coordinates generated from a rule

nodes.misconception: From the line $$y=x$$ to $$y=x+1$$ to $$y=x-1$$ the lines are moving left/right rather than up/down.
nodes.response: It can be shown by using a $$(x,c)$$ coordinate in desmos. That coordinate moves up and down with the change in '$$c$$'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using dynamic software to explore linear relationships

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think graphs are only linear if written in the form y=mx+c
nodes.response: Use the first learning cycle as an opportunity to show graphs in many formats. y=mx+c  makes the gradient and y intercept clear.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The equation of a straight line

nodes.misconception: Where is coordinate (−2,5)? 2 down, 5 right from the origin? 5 right, 2 down from the origin?
nodes.response: Coordinates in (x,y) form. −2 is x-instruction. From (0,0) will we travel in a positive or negative x-direction?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of plotting coordinates

nodes.misconception: The arithmetic sequence 5n+2 starts at 7 so the linear equation y=5x+2 'starts' somewhere.
nodes.response: y=5x+2 has no start and no end; it goes on infinitely. However, all linear equations have a y-intercept and this helps define them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Defining features of linear relationships

nodes.misconception: Only equations in the form $$y=mx+c$$ are linear. All equations are linear.
nodes.response: There are many forms that linear equations can take, however they always share a common feature. The variables have exponents of $$1$$.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Features of linear relationships

nodes.misconception: Writing the y intercept as a single value or getting the x and y coordinates the wrong way around.
nodes.response: Encourage writing the y intercept as a coordinate. Stating 'lines cross the y axis when x=0' can help pupils write the coordinate correctly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The intercept point

nodes.misconception: All graphs are linear and if graphs are not linear you join points with straight line segments.
nodes.response: Explore $$n+2, 2n$$ and $$x^2$$. "I see $$n$$ and 2; they must be similar" pupils think. Get them to compare numerically, then graphically.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing plotting a relationship

nodes.misconception: Writing the gradient as the constant and the y intercept as the coefficient of x.
nodes.response: Link to linear sequences where the coefficient of n is the common difference in the sequence to help pupils see why (m) is the gradient.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding the equation of the line y = mx + c

nodes.misconception: Pupils count squares to calculate gradient instead of looking at scales.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to pick points on the graph to use to find the gradient and write down the coordinates rather than count squares.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Positive rate of change from a graph

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think lines with gradients 2 and -2 are parallel.
nodes.response: Lines have to have the exact same gradient to be parallel. A line with a negative gradient will intersect a line with a positive gradient .
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Negative rate of change from a graph

nodes.misconception: When calculating gradient from coordinates, pupils get positive and negative gradients mixed up.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch the coordinates first and then always look at a positive increase in x.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rate of change from a coordinate pair

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with percentages

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease.
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating compound interest rates

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3
nodes.response: Two responses can be used to remind students that to covert a percentage into a decimal;  we divide by 100; using 3%, ask what 30% is as a decimal and 3% as a decimal. Pupils realise they cannot be the same. A place value chart also helps.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of finding a percentage

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Percentage profit and loss

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3. This error continues when increasing amounts e.g increase 40 by 3% has a multiplier of 1.3
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to covert a percentage into a decimal we divide by 100. This applies with increase too e.g 120% has a multiplier of 1.2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compound interest calculations with technology

nodes.misconception: Failing to understand the difference between simple and compound interest.  And, therefore finding the interest for one time period and multiplying it by the number of time periods.
nodes.response: Pupils can forget to transfer the year end balance as the starting balance of the next year.  Using repeated language can help.  E.g. "At the end of year 2 there was ... in the account, so, at the beginning of year 3 there was ... in the account."
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compound interest calculations

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing compound interest rates

nodes.misconception: Pupils should pay careful attention to what the question asks. Working out the overall amount after a simple or compound increase is different to working out the total interest only.
nodes.response: Pupils can underline or highlight the key instruction to the question e.g. Total amount or total interest, to remind them of the need to subtract from the original amount or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple interest calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils should pay careful attention to what the question asks. Working out the overall amount after a simple or compound increase is different to working out the total interest only.
nodes.response: Pupils can underline or highlight the key instruction to the question e.g. Total amount or total interest, to remind them of the need to subtract from the original amount or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple and compound interest

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3. This error continues when increasing amounts e.g increase 40 by 3% has a multiplier of 1.3
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to covert a percentage into a decimal we divide by 100. This applies with increase too e.g 120% has a multiplier of 1.2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of percentage increase

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of percentage decrease

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with percentages

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3, e.g. 0.54% = 0.054
nodes.response: Dividing the percentage by 100 gives the decimal equivalent i.e 0.54% = 0.0054
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple interest calculations with technology

nodes.misconception: Venn diagrams are useful when generating a complete list of outcomes and showing the probabilities of that list.
nodes.response: Venn diagrams can be very useful when categorising already known outcomes into events. The Venn diagram can then be used to calculate probabilities. However, Venn diagrams are not as useful when generating a list of outcomes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing multiple representations to calculate theoretical probabilities

nodes.misconception: Pupils may count the number of outcomes and state this as the probability.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the probability scale is between 0 and 1, so an answer of 3 is not correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from Venn diagrams (one event)

nodes.misconception: The probability of an event is the product of the probability of each outcome in the event.
nodes.response: The probability of an event is the sum of the probability of each outcome in the event seen in the sample space of a diagram. For example, in the sample space at the end of a probability tree, or by adding the outcomes in the sample space of a table.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing multiple representations to calculate theoretical probabilities for combined events

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with finding the probability of A or B, and may count the outcomes that belong to A and B twice.
nodes.response: If you use an example, such as visiting particular countries, ask the pupils how someone would respond to the question 'have you visited X or Y' if they have in fact visited both countries.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from Venn diagrams (two events)

nodes.misconception: When increasing a probability by 50%, pupils may choose to add 50% onto the existing probability rather than multiplying by 1.5.
nodes.response: Make links to any previous work pupils may have done on increasing by a percentage and emphasise that a percentage increase is being applied to the probability.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with theoretical probability

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that 'likely' from the scale of likelihoods is only equal to a specific probability (e.g. 75%).
nodes.response: All probabilities that are greater than 50% but less than 100% are equivalent to 'likely' on the scale of likelihoods.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The probability scale

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that theoretical probabilities can be also found in cases where individual outcomes are not equally likely (e.g. picking a sweet out of a box where the sweets are different shapes).
nodes.response: If the sweets in a box are different shapes then picking a sweet out of the box is not necessarily random. Someone could find their favourite flavour sweet by feeling the different shapes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from lists (one event)

nodes.misconception: A probability tree can only have two branches.
nodes.response: A probability tree can have any number of branches on a layer, but the more branches you want to include, the trickier and less practical the probability tree is to draw and use.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from probability tree diagrams (one event)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with finding the probability of A or B, and may count the outcomes that belong to A and B twice.
nodes.response: If you use an example, such as visiting particular countries, ask the pupils how someone would respond to the question 'have you visited X or Y' if they have in fact visited both countries.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from two-way tables (two events)

nodes.misconception: When finding the probability of an outcome based on a frequency table, pupils may use the number of different categories as the denominator rather than the total frequency.
nodes.response: When strawberry flavoured sweets have a frequency of 11, it means that 11 of the sweets in the box are strawberry flavoured. The box of sweets could be visually represented with each sweet being shown by the first letter of its flavour.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from a table (one event)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may list the possible outcomes in an unsystematic way, potentially causing them to miss or repeat outcomes.
nodes.response: Demonstrate how our system of counting is a systematic method for listing numbers and compare it to some of the listing strategies used in the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking listing possible outcomes

nodes.misconception: When I see a probability tree, I always multiply the probabilities.
nodes.response: If a probability tree shows a two-stage trial, then the probability of an outcome is the product of the probabilities of the outcomes at each stage. The probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of each outcome in the event.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating theoretical probabilities from probability trees (two events)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may over generalise and think that the sum of all possible events sum to 1. E.g. when rolling a standard six-sided dice, P(multiple of 6) + P(factor of 6) = 1.
nodes.response: Emphasise that probabilities sum to 1 when the events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. E.g. in the calculation P(multiple of 6) + P(factor of 6), the outcome '6' is counted twice.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Summing probabilities

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the edge length as the perpendicular height when calculating the volume.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that for any volume calculation, three perpendicular lengths are multiplied and in most pyramids the edge of a triangle is not perpendicular to the base. Also the edge of the triangles can be different in the pyramid.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The volume of a pyramid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may forget the constant '4' when calculating the surface area.
nodes.response: Show the demonstration of the formula of the surface area using a different spherical fruit to see that it is always 4 regardless of the size of the sphere. You can also relate it to the 1/2 in the formula of the area of triangle.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The surface area of a sphere

nodes.misconception: When finding the surface area of the cone, pupils may find the curved surface area but forget to include circular base of the cone.
nodes.response: By re-reading the question, and inspecting any given diagram, pupils can check if the cone is open or closed and therefore if they need to include the circular base in their calculation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The surface area of a cone

nodes.misconception: Pupils can make errors if given the dimensions/measurements of the cylinder using different units (for example the radius is given in cm and the length in m).
nodes.response: Remind pupils to convert all measurements to the same unit (such as cm or m) before starting the calculation. Usually there is a prompt in the question to use as a guide, for example give your answer in square centimetres.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of surface area of a cylinder

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not subtract overlapping faces from their surface area calculation.
nodes.response: Ask the pupils to visualise turning around/rotating the compound solid, and consider which faces of the component solids would always be hidden.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface area of composite solids

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a cone is a pyramid.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that a pyramid has a polygonal base, so a cone cannot be a pyramid as the base is a circle, which is not a polygon.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The surface area of a pyramid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if you cut the height of the cone in a half, the resulting frustrum will have half the volume of the original cone.
nodes.response: The frustrum is actually seven eighths of the volume of the original cone; the small cone that was removed to create the frustrum is one eighth the volume of the original cone if the frustrum and the small cone have the same height.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Volume of a frustum of a cone

nodes.misconception: When working out the surface area, the pupil may only find the sum of the areas of three faces of a cuboid (for example the visible sides in a 3D drawing), instead of all six faces.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch the net of the cuboid as part of their solution. This will provide a visual reminder to the pupil to find the area of all six faces, as well as making it easier to check their answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of surface area of cuboids

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the slant length (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone or frustum) with the perpendicular (or vertical) height.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to clearly label their diagrams, indicating the perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry to calculate the slant length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface area of a frustum of a cone

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the height of the cylinder may be described as the depth or length and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. Discuss which length this would be, using a diagram to support.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of volume of a cylinder

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the slant height (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone) with the perpendicular height (which is needed to find the volume of the cone).
nodes.response: Remind pupils that for any volume calculation, three perpendicular lengths are multiplied and the slant height is not perpendicular to the base in a right cone. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem to find the perpendicular height.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The volume of a cone

nodes.misconception: Pupils may multiply the radius of the sphere by the constant before cubing it.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the order of operations and the need to cube the radius before multiplying by the constants in the formula.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The volume of a sphere

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only using given measures or terms in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required to form an expression for the volume or surface area.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to clearly show how the are breaking down a compound shape, and label clearly any new or missing lengths they can determine.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming equations involving complex shape calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only using given measures in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required for substitution into a volume formula.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to show how the are breaking down a compound/composite shape. Pupils should label the diagram with any new lengths needed. They may need to use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find these new lengths.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Volume of composite solids

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. They may need to evaluate a perpendicular length from other given information, using trigonometry or Pythagoras' theorem.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with further surface area and volume

nodes.misconception: Pupils can miss out some faces of the prism when calculating the surface area.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to sketch out the net of the prism and label it clearly, to ensure that they include all faces in their calculation of the surface area. This will allow their answer to be checked more easily.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of surface area of other prisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse whether they need to calculate the volume or surface area of a 3D shape, if not told specifically to do so in a problem.
nodes.response: Use the context to decide which calculation is needed. If the question refers to packaging or painting the shape, a surface area calculation is needed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with further surface area and volume

nodes.misconception: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from a product of three perpendicular lengths. The cross-sectional area uses two of the three, so identify the distance that is perpendicular to the cross-sectional face.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of volume of prisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may misconfigure the net, believing that as long as the shapes of the faces are correct, the net will fold to be the desired 3D shape.
nodes.response: Have pupils mark/label/colour the edges that will join upon folding the net, this will ensure they are the correct length.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of nets of solids

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with percentages

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease.
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating compound interest rates

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3
nodes.response: Two responses can be used to remind students that to covert a percentage into a decimal;  we divide by 100; using 3%, ask what 30% is as a decimal and 3% as a decimal. Pupils realise they cannot be the same. A place value chart also helps.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of finding a percentage

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Percentage profit and loss

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3. This error continues when increasing amounts e.g increase 40 by 3% has a multiplier of 1.3
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to covert a percentage into a decimal we divide by 100. This applies with increase too e.g 120% has a multiplier of 1.2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compound interest calculations with technology

nodes.misconception: Failing to understand the difference between simple and compound interest.  And, therefore finding the interest for one time period and multiplying it by the number of time periods.
nodes.response: Pupils can forget to transfer the year end balance as the starting balance of the next year.  Using repeated language can help.  E.g. "At the end of year 2 there was ... in the account, so, at the beginning of year 3 there was ... in the account."
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Compound interest calculations

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing compound interest rates

nodes.misconception: Pupils should pay careful attention to what the question asks. Working out the overall amount after a simple or compound increase is different to working out the total interest only.
nodes.response: Pupils can underline or highlight the key instruction to the question e.g. Total amount or total interest, to remind them of the need to subtract from the original amount or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple interest calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils should pay careful attention to what the question asks. Working out the overall amount after a simple or compound increase is different to working out the total interest only.
nodes.response: Pupils can underline or highlight the key instruction to the question e.g. Total amount or total interest, to remind them of the need to subtract from the original amount or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple and compound interest

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3. This error continues when increasing amounts e.g increase 40 by 3% has a multiplier of 1.3
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to covert a percentage into a decimal we divide by 100. This applies with increase too e.g 120% has a multiplier of 1.2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of percentage increase

nodes.misconception: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease
nodes.response: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of percentage decrease

nodes.misconception: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens.  If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with percentages

nodes.misconception: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3, e.g. 0.54% = 0.054
nodes.response: Dividing the percentage by 100 gives the decimal equivalent i.e 0.54% = 0.0054
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple interest calculations with technology

nodes.misconception: The use of negatives are confused with subtractions.
nodes.response: Writing the negative numbers in brackets and using the additive inverse will help minimise errors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Priority of operations with positive and negative integers and decimals

nodes.misconception: Students do not see the implicit brackets. Eg. Sqrt(49 + 36) is not sqrt(49) + sqrt(36)
nodes.response: Look for extended lines or operations which indicate an implicit brackets.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Priority of operations with positive integers

nodes.misconception: When subtracting you always write the bigger number above the smaller number.
nodes.response: The context of spending money should help with this, as they will end up with a positive balance which is not possible .
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of written addition and subtraction strategies

nodes.misconception: Students often forget to scroll out of an operation or function.
nodes.response: Emphasis the cursor buttons allow users to scroll around the apps, functions and calculations on the calculator.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using your calculator efficiently

nodes.misconception: Students try to divide an integer with an integer without simplifying.
nodes.response: Student are required to convert the divisor into an integer. Simplifying the denominator into a single integer digit is preferable.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Dividing with decimals

nodes.misconception: Students often omit any place holders when subtracting decimals.
nodes.response: Encourage all place holders to be used in all written calculations so they are not omitted when they need to be there.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of arithmetic procedures with integers and decimals

nodes.misconception: Students are unsure where to start on problem solving questions.
nodes.response: Starting with one sentence at a time and isolating what the strategy is first before doing any calculation is important.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with integers and decimals

nodes.misconception: The assumption that if the calculator gives an answer then it must be correct!
nodes.response: It is really important to encourage pupils to both check calculator inputs carefully and consider the reasonableness of their answers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of arithmetic procedures with integers and decimals

nodes.misconception: Minus and a minus make a plus, 2 negatives make a positive, double negative makes a positive, etc.
nodes.response: The use of additive inverses should avoid this common misconception.  Be aware that pupils maybe already be familiar with this statement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Subtraction of positive and negative integers

nodes.misconception: 20 × 50 = 100, they partition the 2 and 5 to give 10 but count the zero as one of the 2 zeroes.
nodes.response: Make sure that partitions are written out fully.  E.g. 20 × 50 = 2 × 5 × 10 × 10 = 10 × 100 = 1000
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of multiplication and division

nodes.misconception: That addition will always make the result bigger.
nodes.response: If pupils are struggling with the concept that adding can make an integer smaller encourage them to use counters and form zero pairs.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Addition of positive and negative integers

nodes.misconception: That the difference between 3 & -9 is 6 and not 12.
nodes.response: In the early stages of the negative numbers work the use of number lines to highlight misconceptions can be very powerful.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of negative numbers in context

nodes.misconception: Using the phrase '2 negatives make a positive'.
nodes.response: Ensuring pupils understand the structure of the maths and not 'tricks' is so important. Encourage the use of correct language at all times
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplication and division where two or more values are negative

nodes.misconception: When pupils multiply decimals, they use the column method and align the decimal points.
nodes.response: If the column method is used, encourage integer multiplication and use of powers of 10 to adjust the answer to the original calculation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplying with decimals

nodes.misconception: The common multiplier is the number seen to be common eg. 1.2 x 20 + 1.2 x 30 + 1.2 x 10
nodes.response: Students can use the associative law to find more common multipliers  eg. 1.2 x 10 x 2 + 1.2 x 10 x3  + 1.2 x 10 = 12 x 2 + 12 x 3 + 12 x 1
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the associative, commutative and distributive laws together

nodes.misconception: That 0.0004 is one thousand times smaller than 4 as there are three zeros after the decimal point.
nodes.response: The use of a place value or  Gattegno chart is invaluable here to highlight this misconception .  The 4 is in the 10 thousandths column.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Simplifying multiplication and division using multiples of 10

nodes.misconception: When working with counters students may count them and not appreciate they represent negatives.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of 2 different coloured counters as there is a need to represent positive and negative integers differently.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplication and division where only one value is negative

nodes.misconception: Pupils may represent probabilities in the wrong position on the probability scale by miscounting the number of intervals required.
nodes.response: Before using any probability scale, it can be helpful to make a note of the sizes for each major and minor interval.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with conditional probability

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only one type of diagram/table can be used to solve each probability problem, or be unsure which representation to use when it is not provided to them.
nodes.response: Probability problems can often be modelled using multiple types of representation. The one you choose may depend on the information that you are trying to organise and what you then intend to do with that information.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with conditional probability

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the probability of event A given B, P(A|B), with the probability of event A and B occurring.
nodes.response: Use the context of the question to make a judgement about what probability is to be calculated. Try to avoid using, or draw attention to, potentially ambiguous language/notation. E.g. Is P(AB) referring to P(A given B) or P(B given A) or P(A and B)?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Conditional probability in a Venn diagram

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unsure whether a variable represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcome.
nodes.response: Variables can be used to represent either of these pieces of information. It can be helpful to start a problem by writing down what any variables represent (e.g. "Let x = the total number of marbles).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Probabilities involving algebra

nodes.misconception: When using the product rule, pupils may be unsure whether they should divide the product by 2.
nodes.response: Pay extra attention to the context of the problem. If the order of the two outcomes is irrelevant, then you should divide by two. If each of the two outcomes is allocated to a separate event (e.g. 1st and 2nd) then do not divide by 2.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combinations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may omit outcomes or include repetitions of the same outcomes in their lists.
nodes.response: For each problem, encourage pupils to be systematic with their ordering of outcomes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing displaying outcomes

nodes.misconception: Pupils may give the probability as a fraction with the wrong denominator.
nodes.response: Check that pupils understand the difference between the probability of event A given B, P(A|B), and the probability of event A and B occurring.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Probabilities in three event Venn diagrams

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be tempted to always use the total frequency from a tree as the denominator of any fraction.
nodes.response: The denominator of the fraction should be the total frequency of the group that is being selected from. This could be the total population or it could be a subgroup of the population.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Frequency trees

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that it possible to determine whether a coin (or other object/game) is biased by conducting an experiment with a small number of trials.
nodes.response: The greater the number of trial that an experiment contains, the closer the relative frequency of an outcome gets to its theoretical probability.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Experimental vs theoretical probability

nodes.misconception: When pupils construct probability trees for scenarios where two marbles are removed from a bag, they may mistakenly subtract 2 from the denominators of the probabilities instead of 1.
nodes.response: Even though two marbles are removed from the bag at once, you can think of it at choosing one marble and then immediately choosing a second marble. At the end of the process, two marbles have been removed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Conditional probability in a tree diagram

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any set of probabilities relating to a scenario will always sum to 1.
nodes.response: Probabilities sum to 1 when the events are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing exhaustive events

nodes.misconception: If outcome A occurs more often than outcome B, during an experiment, pupils may conclude that outcome A has a greater probability of occurring than outcome B in future trials.
nodes.response: Even when two outcomes are equally likely to happen, one may occur more often than the other due to chance. You could be more confident about your conclusion if you observe a large difference in results in an experiment with a large number of trials.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Experimental probability

nodes.misconception: Pupils may conflate the meaning of mutually exclusive with the meaning of independent.
nodes.response: Emphasise the word 'exclusive' in 'mutually exclusive' to suggest that one event excludes the other. Also, emphasise that the opposite of independent is dependent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Conditional probability in a two-way table

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only one type of diagram/table can be used to represent each probability problem and worry about choosing the correct one.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the same probability problem can often be represented using multiple diagrams or tables. In many cases, they will be able to find what they are looking for in any representation but it may be clearer to see in some more than others.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing multiple representations to calculate conditional probabilities

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused between two-way tables that show outcomes and two-way tables that show frequencies (particularly when the outcomes are numbers, such as the sum of two dice rolls).
nodes.response: Two-way tables can be either used to display the sample space of individual outcomes or the frequencies of outcomes. Therefore, when using a table, it can be helpful to note down what type of data the table shows.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing calculating probabilities from tables

nodes.misconception: When variables are used in diagrams, pupils may be unsure whether it represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcomes.
nodes.response: Variables can be used to represent either of these pieces of information. It can be helpful to start a problem by writing down what the variables represent (e.g. "Let x = the total number of marbles).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Algebra in tree and Venn diagrams

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that A ∪ B means 'to be either from A or B (but not both)'.
nodes.response: A ∪ B represents all members that satisfy at least one of the events A or B. So it could be from A, from B or from both A and B.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Set notation

nodes.misconception: There is often a lot of information to process, in order to complete a three event Venn diagram accurately. Pupils may confuse which region to complete.
nodes.response: A three event Venn diagram is easier to complete if information from intersecting events is completed first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing three event Venn diagrams

nodes.misconception: Pupils may add the probabilities along branches of a probability tree, rather than multiplying them.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that probabilities cannot be greater than 1 and demonstrate that adding across the branches sometimes results in a probability that is greater than 1. Therefore, it must be wrong.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing calculating probabilities from diagrams

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a value has to be added to each term in an expression.
nodes.response: When adding a term to an expression we can write it as a single addition and then collect like terms if necessary. Show with numbers first
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Many equations, one solution

nodes.misconception: When converting English to algebra, pupils can mix up 4x + 2 and 4(x + 2)
nodes.response: Reviewing priority of operations and expanding brackets may be helpful. The multiplier operates on all terms in the bracket.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of algebraic notation

nodes.misconception: Pupils can be unsure which values to add and which to subtract when collecting like terms.
nodes.response: Rewrite the equation with like terms grouped together before combining like terms.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing to solve two step linear equations

nodes.misconception: 10 - x = 2 means that 2 - x = 10
nodes.response: Using bar models can help pupils understand rearranging additive relationships at an early stage.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Equality in an equation

nodes.misconception: When solving equations pupils may not use the inverse operation.
nodes.response: Working out should include each step then pupils can check each step using substitution.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simple linear equations with a multiplicative step

nodes.misconception: When solving x - 5 = 10 pupils may see the -5 and calculate 10 - 5 = 5
nodes.response: Focus on understanding zero pairs and why adding the additive inverse gives the solution. Bar models are a helpful representation here.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving simple linear equations with an additive step

nodes.misconception: Trying to double an expression and only doubling one term.
nodes.response: Use the numerical examples to show why this does not work. Use of brackets in working out is also helpful.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of equality

nodes.misconception: When reading solutions from a graph pupils may read the solution as the y-coordinate.
nodes.response: The solution to the equation is the value of the variable that makes both sides balance.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solution to an equation

nodes.misconception: That we always have to use written methods to solve equations.
nodes.response: Use Desmos to show that equations like $$3x-1=17$$ and $$3x-1=x+9$$ can be solved by drawing both lines and finding the intersection.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving linear equations graphically using technology

nodes.misconception: To subtract from both the variable and numerical terms when subtracting from both sides.
nodes.response: To subtract $$2$$ from $$5x+3$$ leaves $$5x+1$$, not $$3x+1$$. Use visual representations like balance scales and bar models to show this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rearranging to solve linear equations

nodes.misconception: That "$$x$$ times five, plus three" is the same as "$$x$$ plus three, times five".
nodes.response: Use visual representations to demonstrate why and how they are different. Use algebra tiles if you have them, or get pupils to draw them.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Brackets in equations

nodes.misconception: That there is only one way to solve any given equation.
nodes.response: In maths we will often see multiple ways to solve the same one problem. To be able to use multiple methods is a demonstration of fluency.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving complex linear equations involving brackets

nodes.misconception: That algebra, in particular solving equations, is abstract and not related to the world around us.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to solve $$4(x+3)=20$$. Then show a square with length $$x+3$$, tell them the perimeter is $$20$$ and ask them to find $$x$$.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with linear equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all equations are for straight lines so can be plotted from 2 points.
nodes.response: Explore different relationships, most relationships are not linear but we focus a lot on linear relationships and their unique structure.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Different types of equations

nodes.misconception: That all brackets have to be expanded before we solve an equation with brackets it in.
nodes.response: How would you solve $$2y=50$$? You would divide both sides by $$2$$. So why not start with 'divide $$2$$' when solving $$2(y-7)=50$$?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving linear equations where brackets are used

nodes.misconception: That there is only one way to solve any given equation.
nodes.response: In maths we will often see multiple ways to solve the same one problem. To be able to use multiple methods is a demonstration of fluency.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving two step linear equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils often "multiply through by $$5$$" and turn $${{2x+1}\over5}={10}$$ into $${{10x+5}}={50}$$
nodes.response: Use equivalent fractions as opposed to multiplying through. In one simple step $${{2x+1}\over5}={10}$$ becomes $${{2x+1}\over5}={50\over5}$$
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving complex linear equations

nodes.misconception: Using the laws of indices, when dividing by a number with a negative exponent pupils can incorrectly subtract the negative exponent.
nodes.response: When the bases of all the numbers are the same, forming an equation with the exponents can reduce errors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with the laws of indices

nodes.misconception: Any number with an index of 0 equates to 0
nodes.response: Reiterate the division of any number by itself is 1. This applies with laws of indices too. E.g 8^4 / 8^4 = 8^0. Any number divided by itself gives 1, therefore 8^0 = 1. For more advanced understanding, algebraic can be used instead of numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The laws of indices - negative and zero exponents

nodes.misconception: That addition will always make the result bigger.
nodes.response: If pupils are struggling with the concept that adding can make an integer smaller encourage them to use counters and form zero pairs.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of calculations involving negative numbers

nodes.misconception: When ordering decimals, the more significant figures the greater the number.
nodes.response: When ordering decimals, having the same number of decimal places allows the pupils to see the magnitude of the number more clearly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of converting between fractions and decimals

nodes.misconception: When multiplying terms with coefficients, pupils also add the coefficients as well as the exponents.
nodes.response: Pupils should be encouraged to rewrite their expression using the associative and commutative laws, with the number parts grouped and powers grouped.  This hopefully avoids this error as they can see it is the product of the numbers.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The laws of indices - multiplication

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to raise the coefficient to the power as well as the power term.
nodes.response: Highlight that everything in the bracket is being affected by the power.  By showing examples where the bracket is written in expanded form and then the repeated multiplication helps with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The laws of indices - raising a power to a power

nodes.misconception: Any number is a square or cube number because it can be squared or cubed.
nodes.response: A square number is the result of a number being multiplied by itself. Emphasis must be on the result. A cube number is a number that has been multiplied by itself three times. Emphasis must be on the result of the repeated multiplication.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of roots and integer indices

nodes.misconception: Use of addition instead of multiplication when the decomposing the number.
nodes.response: Reiterate that the product of prime factors is unique.  This should also be helped when setting the decomposition out as products rather than just a 'tree'.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of prime factorisation

nodes.misconception: Assuming that the decimal part of the number will entirely disappear in the subtraction step.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils line up the decimal points and use squares in their books for each digit.  This should allow pupils to see the parts that cancel each other out and what is left when finding the difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Converting any recurring decimal to a fraction

nodes.misconception: When dividing terms with coefficients, pupils also subtract the coefficients as well as the exponents.
nodes.response: Pupils should be encouraged to rewrite their expression as a fraction, with the number parts grouped and powers grouped. This hopefully avoids this error as they can see the fraction line as a division.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The laws of indices - division

nodes.misconception: The incorrect input of a mixed number is common i.e some pupils press a number then the fraction button. Others inefficiently sum the integer and proper fraction.
nodes.response: Reiterating the mixed number button is located above the proper fraction button.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of calculating with fractions and decimals

nodes.misconception: When using a Venn diagram students often mix up HCF & LCM.
nodes.response: Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of LCM and HCF

nodes.misconception: Using the laws of indices, when dividing by a number with a negative exponent pupils can incorrectly subtract the negative exponent.
nodes.response: When the bases of all the numbers are the same, forming an equation with the exponents can reduce errors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with the laws of indices

nodes.misconception: Pupils multiply the base by the fractional exponent. e.g 25^(1/2) = 12.5
nodes.response: The use of a calculator allows pupils to see the index of a fraction is not to be multiplied by the base. Embedding the laws of indices where two bases are the same and each number has an index of 1/2 helps recognize the 1/2 index as a square root.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: The laws of indices - fractional exponents

nodes.misconception: Pupils may represent probabilities in the wrong position on the probability scale by miscounting the number of intervals required.
nodes.response: Before using any probability scale, it can be helpful to make a note of the sizes for each major and minor interval.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with conditional probability

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only one type of diagram/table can be used to solve each probability problem, or be unsure which representation to use when it is not provided to them.
