nodes.misconception: When plotting a sequence you should always connect the points with a line.
nodes.response: Only the (term number, term value) should be plotted. Points should not be joined as these are discrete values.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Arithmetic sequences and their graphs

nodes.misconception: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
nodes.response: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with further sequences

nodes.misconception: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
nodes.response: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying values in an arithmetic sequence

nodes.misconception: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
nodes.response: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasoning about values in an arithmetic sequence

nodes.misconception: Since there is no common difference, further terms in the sequence cannot be generated.
nodes.response: Pupils have seen sequences where the first difference is not common and seen examples of other rules. In this lesson, the concept of a second difference is introduced and this can be used to generate the next first difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing quadratic sequences

nodes.misconception: Since there is no common difference, it is impossible to find the n^th term.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle shows how we can build quadratic sequences from n^2 and a linear sequence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Quadratic sequences

nodes.misconception: Alternating sequences may cause difficulty if negative number skills are not secure.
nodes.response: A review of negative numbers would be useful. Prior lessons can be used for this review if required.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Fibonacci and alternating sequences

nodes.misconception: The common multiplier must be a positive integer for the sequence to be geometric.
nodes.response: The multiplier needs to be the same between consecutive terms but it can be any value. Examples of this can be seen in the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of geometric sequences

nodes.misconception: Arithmetic sequences only have a positive integer as the common difference.
nodes.response: Arithmetic sequences can be increasing or decreasing and can have any value for the common difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing rules for generating arithmetic sequences

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that $$u_1$$ means that $$u$$ has a value of one.
nodes.response: $$u_1$$ refers to the first term in the sequence and $$u_2$$ refers to the second term. The subscript refers to the term number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence notation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may round the wrong way when finding the term number for a particular term value.
nodes.response: By calculating the terms either side of the non-integer value of $$n$$, pupils can easily determine what the rounded value of $$n$$ should be.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Conditions in arithmetic sequences

nodes.misconception: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
nodes.response: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with further sequences

nodes.misconception: After becoming very familiar with arithmetic sequences pupils can find the difference between the first two terms and just assume the sequence is arithmetic.
nodes.response: Pupils should check the relationship between all stated consecutive terms as they now have seen a variety of sequences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of special number sequences

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with fractions and ratios

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models, ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Determining the part

nodes.misconception: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing exchange rates with ratio

nodes.misconception: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratio allow the multiplicative relationship to be seen.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing understanding of ratio as a multiplicative relationship

nodes.misconception: Only seeing multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies for ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratios allow the multiplicative relationship to be seen.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplicative relationships in context

nodes.misconception: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing more conversions with ratio

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models, ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Determining the whole

nodes.misconception: Using additive strategies instead of multiplicative.
nodes.response: Emphasise that proportional relationships maintain a constant multiplier so we are looking for a multiplicative relationship.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiplicative relationships

nodes.misconception: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratio tables can help see this more easily.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Equivalent multiplicative relationships

nodes.misconception: Pupils see the bar model and/or fraction as the whole as opposed to the proportion of the whole.
nodes.response: Emphasise equivalent fractions and equivalent bar models which show different parts to whole, but are the same proportion.  e.g 3/5 = 60/100
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing multiplicative relationships as ratios and fractions

nodes.misconception: To find one part,  some students simply divide the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio.
nodes.response: Strengthen understanding of which amount represents which part of the ratio.  Matching problems to bar models helps.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ratio language and notation

nodes.misconception: Both lines of a double number line must start at zero and these zeros must be aligned.
nodes.response: When drawing double number lines, ensure to align the zeros and the known equivalents. Showing how a graph is formed from a DNL can help.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing a multiplicative relationship

nodes.misconception: An assumption that you cannot find a fraction greater than 1 of an amount.
nodes.response: Recognising that 'of' and multiplication are equivalent should help with this , as pupils are familiar with multiplying fractions.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing finding a fraction of a given amount

nodes.misconception: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
nodes.response: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models, ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Dividing a quantity into a given ratio

nodes.misconception: Only see the amount, not proportion.  E.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
nodes.response: Referring to the whole using bar models or fractions can emphasise the amount with respect to the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Expressing one number as a fraction of another

nodes.misconception: Pupils only see the amount, not proportion. e.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
nodes.response: Referring to the whole using bar models or fractions can emphasise the amount with respect to the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of multiplicative relationships

nodes.misconception: Only seeing the amount, not proportion.  E.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
nodes.response: Referring to the whole using bar models or fractions can emphasise the amount with respect to the whole.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Deepening understanding with fractions of a given amount

nodes.misconception: When plotting a sequence you should always connect the points with a line.
nodes.response: Only the (term number, term value) should be plotted. Points should not be joined as these are discrete values.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Arithmetic sequences and their graphs

nodes.misconception: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
nodes.response: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with further sequences

nodes.misconception: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
nodes.response: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying values in an arithmetic sequence

nodes.misconception: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
nodes.response: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasoning about values in an arithmetic sequence

nodes.misconception: Since there is no common difference, further terms in the sequence cannot be generated.
nodes.response: Pupils have seen sequences where the first difference is not common and seen examples of other rules. In this lesson, the concept of a second difference is introduced and this can be used to generate the next first difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing quadratic sequences

nodes.misconception: Since there is no common difference, it is impossible to find the n^th term.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle shows how we can build quadratic sequences from n^2 and a linear sequence.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Quadratic sequences

nodes.misconception: Alternating sequences may cause difficulty if negative number skills are not secure.
nodes.response: A review of negative numbers would be useful. Prior lessons can be used for this review if required.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Fibonacci and alternating sequences

nodes.misconception: The common multiplier must be a positive integer for the sequence to be geometric.
nodes.response: The multiplier needs to be the same between consecutive terms but it can be any value. Examples of this can be seen in the lesson.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of geometric sequences

nodes.misconception: Arithmetic sequences only have a positive integer as the common difference.
nodes.response: Arithmetic sequences can be increasing or decreasing and can have any value for the common difference.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing rules for generating arithmetic sequences

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that $$u_1$$ means that $$u$$ has a value of one.
nodes.response: $$u_1$$ refers to the first term in the sequence and $$u_2$$ refers to the second term. The subscript refers to the term number.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence notation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may round the wrong way when finding the term number for a particular term value.
nodes.response: By calculating the terms either side of the non-integer value of $$n$$, pupils can easily determine what the rounded value of $$n$$ should be.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Conditions in arithmetic sequences

nodes.misconception: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
nodes.response: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with further sequences

nodes.misconception: After becoming very familiar with arithmetic sequences pupils can find the difference between the first two terms and just assume the sequence is arithmetic.
nodes.response: Pupils should check the relationship between all stated consecutive terms as they now have seen a variety of sequences.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of special number sequences

nodes.misconception: If the weather report has the rain icon, it means it will rain.
nodes.response: The rain symbol is to denote what type of rain it is likely to be should it rain. The percentage chance of rain then informs us about how likely it is to rain.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Predicting the weather

nodes.misconception: When calculating the amount of emissions per mile, pupils may forget to convert the information given from grams to kilograms.
nodes.response: Always check whether the units for any values given in the information match the units that are required for the formula.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Making a journey

nodes.misconception: When calculating the amount of electricity produced by a solar panel, pupils may forget to convert its power rating from watts to kilowatts.
nodes.response: Always check whether the units for any values given in the informatin match the units that are required for the formula.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solar power

nodes.misconception: An urban area should implement all of the strategies to make itself greener.
nodes.response: Not all strategies are viable for every urban area and some will be more effective than others depending on the location.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Making cities greener

nodes.misconception: The temperature tells us how hot it will feel.
nodes.response: The temperature given in a weather report is normally the air temperature. The 'feel like' temperature may be different depending on multiple factors.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding weather data

nodes.misconception: When performing divisions to calculate the maximum number of plants that fit into a space, pupils may round decimal answers up to the nearest integer (e.g. round 4.5 plants up to 5 plants).
nodes.response: The context would suggest that it may be more appropriate to truncate decimal answers to an integer rather than rounding them up to the nearest integer (e.g. there is not enough space available to fit the 5th plant).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing a green space

nodes.misconception: When comparing the modal class for two datasets, pupils may think that the dataset with the greatest modal class is the one which has the greatest frequency for its modal class
nodes.response: Use the frequency to identify the modal class for each dataset, but then compare the values within each class to determine which dataset has the greatest modal class.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Studying climate change

nodes.misconception: One trend line appearing higher on a graph than a different trend line means the higher line shows more change over time.
nodes.response: It is the gradient of a trend line that informs how quickly something is changing with respect to time.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Studying local climate change

nodes.misconception: Pupils may add together costs that are expressed in different units (e.g. the cost of petrol in pence and the cost of a car park in pounds) without considering the implications on place value.
nodes.response: Writing units on your answers to each stage of working can help you to double check whether numbers in subsequent calculations are expressed in the same units.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Considering a route

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using upper and lower bounds practically

nodes.misconception: Truncating the numbers rather than rounding when considering the suitable degree of accuracy.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the numbers are being rounded and therefore the digit in the next decimal place must be considered.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with rounding, estimation and bounds

nodes.misconception: When truncating, pupils are tempted to round. Also, when truncating, they cut off the number without thinking about the magnitude.
nodes.response: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value when truncating.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of rounding and truncating

nodes.misconception: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
nodes.response: Relate significance back to the communication of accuracy and that some digits are significant as they preserve the place value of other digits.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of estimating through rounding

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Upper and lower bounds

nodes.misconception: Assuming that when dividing the UB will be the result of the UB ÷ UB.
nodes.response: Get the pupils to investigate dividing numbers.  Keep the divisor the same and change the dividend.  Ask the question, "What happens as the dividend increases?".
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Upper and lower bounds in multiplicative calculations

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with rounding, estimation and bounds

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Upper and lower bounds in additive calculations

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Using upper and lower bounds practically

nodes.misconception: Truncating the numbers rather than rounding when considering the suitable degree of accuracy.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the numbers are being rounded and therefore the digit in the next decimal place must be considered.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with rounding, estimation and bounds

nodes.misconception: When truncating, pupils are tempted to round. Also, when truncating, they cut off the number without thinking about the magnitude.
nodes.response: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value when truncating.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of rounding and truncating

nodes.misconception: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
nodes.response: Relate significance back to the communication of accuracy and that some digits are significant as they preserve the place value of other digits.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of estimating through rounding

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Upper and lower bounds

nodes.misconception: Assuming that when dividing the UB will be the result of the UB ÷ UB.
nodes.response: Get the pupils to investigate dividing numbers.  Keep the divisor the same and change the dividend.  Ask the question, "What happens as the dividend increases?".
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Upper and lower bounds in multiplicative calculations

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with rounding, estimation and bounds

nodes.misconception: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
nodes.response: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Upper and lower bounds in additive calculations

nodes.misconception: An iterative formula can always be used to find the solutions to an equation.
nodes.response: This lesson addresses limitations of iteration. Some formulas will cause an error becasue we are unable to evaluate the square root of a negative or divide by 0. Other formulas may not converge. Different values of $$x_0$$ produce different results.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with iteration

nodes.misconception: Pupils are very familiar with exponents but the introduction of 'subscript' notation may confuse them. For example, they may think $$x_2$$ must be a function of $$x$$ because $$x^2$$ is.
nodes.response: Use of language helps. When talking through an iterative formula like $$x_{t+1}=8x_t +6$$ say, "The next $$x$$ value is equal to eight lots of the current $$x$$ value plus six" whilst pointing at it. Get pupils to do the same back to you.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Building on composite functions

nodes.misconception: A change in sign always indicates a solution. No change in sign means no solution.
nodes.response: A change in sign only indicates a solution if the equation is equal to zero and if the graph of the equation crosses the $$x$$ axis between those points. Where there is a repeated root or two solutions between them there may be no change in sign.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Signs of a solution

nodes.misconception: To find a solution to a given degree of accuracy an iteration can just be rounded.
nodes.response: Several successive iterations need to round to the same value to a given degree of accuracy. If in doubt efficient calculator use means many iterations can be generated easily until confident that a digit is fixed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Approximating solutions to equations

nodes.misconception: Pupils get confused between simple interest and compound interest. When presented with a compound interest problem the common error is for pupils to add the same constant amount.
nodes.response: Visual representations are helpful here. The bar models in the first part of the lesson show how compound interest grows year on year. The graphical representation also demonstrates the fundamental difference between the two forms of interest.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of compound interest calculations

nodes.misconception: Some pupils want to clear their calculator display and type every single level of iteration in each time.
nodes.response: Encourage the pupils to trust their 'Ans' button. Get them to work on an example whereby they physically type the input value in and type the whole formula again. Then get them to repeat the same question using the 'Ans' button. Time this if you can!
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating iterative formulas

nodes.misconception: Just because the sense has changed, it doesn't mean a reflection has occurred.
nodes.response: If an image has a different sense to its object, there has definitely been a reflection - the line of reflection may be at an obscure angle.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to reflections

nodes.misconception: When completing an inverse translation, students may believe they need to flip the vector.
nodes.response: Ask students to say in words how you would return to the starting point, to highlight the direction needed and then link to the vector.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with transformations

nodes.misconception: Diagonal reflections that incorrectly look like rotations or translations of the object.
nodes.response: False reflections that look like this are due to students not counting diagonals of grid squares, perpendicular to the mirror line.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflecting objects

nodes.misconception: There may be occasions when pupils cannot find the tool they are looking for.
nodes.response: Ask them to click 'more' in the toolbar, scroll down and then click 'more' again.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating transformations with GeoGebra

nodes.misconception: Pupils may want to use division instead of fractional scale factors.
nodes.response: Dividing by 2 gives the same result as multiplying by a half. However, the scale factor is defined as a multiplier, not a divisor.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing an enlargement

nodes.misconception: Enlargement only refers to an increase in size.
nodes.response: The transformation 'enlargement' refers to a change of size that can be either a stretch or a shrink.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to enlargements

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with only being able to rotate anticlockwise on Desmos.
nodes.response: Turning clockwise x degrees is equivalent to turning anticlockwise (360 - x) degrees.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating transformations with Desmos

nodes.misconception: After drawing an object on the tracing paper, you take the tracing paper off the table to rotate it.
nodes.response: This is especially dangerous if the centre of rotation wasn't drawn on the tracing paper, too. The image will lose its correct location.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Rotating objects

nodes.misconception: Line segments connecting corresponding points on an image and object can intersect each other.
nodes.response: Corresponding point line segments after a reflection never intersect. If they do, then corresponding points have not been paired correctly.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing a reflection

nodes.misconception: Students may confuse reflections and rotations depending on the object.
nodes.response: A reflection is the only transformation that changes the sense of the object, so check that first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Transformed objects

nodes.misconception: Students may translate vertically before horizontally.
nodes.response: Remind the students that the column vectors work in the same way as coordinates.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Translating objects

nodes.misconception: The centre of rotation is always in the centre of an object.
nodes.response: The centre of rotation can be anywhere. If it's outside the shape, imagine it like a pole in the ground, attached to the object by a rope.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding the centre of rotation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may initially be unsure when enlarging shapes on different background in Q2 of Task B.
nodes.response: Stress that they can use the same methods as for square or plain backgrounds (e.g. using a ruler, counting units along gridlines).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Enlarging objects

nodes.misconception: "Right means clockwise" and "left means anti-clockwise"
nodes.response: This is only true when referencing the top of the object being rotated. Rotating "left" and "right" is incorrect for all other vertices.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing a rotation's direction and size

nodes.misconception: Students may believe two shapes are congruent based purely on the shape and not the size as well.
nodes.response: Consider squares - all squares have the same angles and are visually identical but if the lengths are different they're not congruent.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking understanding of basic transformations

nodes.misconception: Students may count between the closest two vertices rather than corresponding points.
nodes.response: Remind frequently that it needs to be between corresponding vertices, labelling may help for this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing a translation

nodes.misconception: After an object has been rotated, the orientation stays the same if the image looks the same.
nodes.response: This is only true if the object is rotated through 360°. Otherwise, the orientation is different as each vertex is in a different position.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to rotations

nodes.misconception: Students may confuse the term transformation for translation.
nodes.response: Translation is one type of transformation.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to translation

nodes.misconception: I can use a protractor to measure an angle, then half that angle to bisect it.
nodes.response: Constructions, such as bisecting an angle, are methods of creating & modifying shapes & angles in ways that don't require measurement tools.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Bisecting an angle

nodes.misconception: You can't accurately draw the perpendicular to a point on a line segment close to its endpoint.
nodes.response: The perpendicular to a line segment through any point can be found; some line segments just require extending in length first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Perpendicular to a given line through a given point

nodes.misconception: When drawing circles, pupils may find that the start and end of their arcs do not join together.
nodes.response: This can be caused by the pair of compasses opening or closing mid-drawing. Hold it with one hand and rest the pencil gently on the page.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking compass skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to decide where to mark the centre point of each circle during Task A.
nodes.response: Pupils could start the task by drawing a pair of circles and labelling it with the question that presents the matching description.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Securing the skill of using a pair of compasses

nodes.misconception: You always need to draw circles that are the same size to construct any polygon.
nodes.response: Some polygons, such as kites, require you to construct two circles of different size, as long as they still intersect at two points.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with constructions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may avoid using the pair of compasses and opt for a ruler instead.
nodes.response: Emphasise the efficiency and accuracy of using compasses instead of a ruler in the construction of their triangles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing rhombi

nodes.misconception: I can use a ruler to measure the midpoint of a line segment, and a protractor to find 90°.
nodes.response: Constructions, such as perpendicular bisectors, are methods of creating & modifying shapes & angles in ways that don't require measurements.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Perpendicular bisector of a line segment

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with a diagonal of a shape being vertical or horizontal.
nodes.response: By reminding pupils of the definition, ask them to check if it fits and the shape could be rotated as well.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Diagonals of a rhombus

nodes.misconception: During tasks, pupils may use a ruler to draw or check whether points are equidistant from a centre.
nodes.response: While the tasks could be completed with a ruler, it may be quicker, easier and more accurate to use a pair of compasses.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding constructing a circle

nodes.misconception: Pupils may avoid using the pair of compasses and opt for a ruler instead.
nodes.response: Emphasise the efficiency and accuracy of using compasses instead of a ruler in the construction of their triangles.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing triangles

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with algebraic ratios

nodes.misconception: Treating the ratio as the total amount. For example sweets : chocolates in the ratio 6 : 7 and 2 chocolates are eaten, thinking the ratio must now be 6 : 5
nodes.response: Looking at how these problems are formed in learning cycle 1 will help and getting pupils to explore how the ratio changes when things are added or removed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing ratios

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of sharing in a ratio

nodes.misconception: Combining ratios without using equivalent ratios to equate the common part.
nodes.response: Pupils may need to spend extra time finding equivalent ratios and looking at when it is ok to combine ratios or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining ratios

nodes.misconception: Finding the additive relationship between two numbers instead of the multiplicative one.
nodes.response: When dealing with any proportional relationships, such as ratios, pupils should be reminded to look for the multiplicative relationship. Using 1 as a middle step can help. e.g. to connect 5 and 8, divide by 5 to make 1 and then multiply by 8.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of equivalent ratios

nodes.misconception: When $$x : y$$ are in the ratio 1 : 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
nodes.response: Show that the equation $$x = 2y$$ in a ratio table would mean the multiplier from $$y$$ to $$x$$ would be times by 2, this would mean when $$y=1 x=2$$ which is 2 : 1 not 1 : 2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Algebraic ratios

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with ratios

nodes.misconception: When $$x : y$$ are in the ratio 1 : 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
nodes.response: The bar models shown in this lesson can help to support pupils with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing equations from ratios

nodes.misconception: Not simplifying the ratio completely or over-simplifying a three part ratio when two of the parts share a further common factor
nodes.response: Link two part ratios back to simplifying fractions and remind pupils to consider if either number is a multiple of 3 as this is often missed. Remind pupils that to simplify a ratio, every part must share the common factor you are dividing by.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of simplifying and unitising ratios

nodes.misconception: Not converting the units correctly in a question or forgetting to have the same units before simplifying a ratio
nodes.response: help pupils to set out ratio tables where they include the units and work through step by step to convert correctly before simplifying. The ratio table can help organise this working.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of real world ratios

nodes.misconception: Converting a ratio e.g. 1 : 3 to 1/3 as a fraction.
nodes.response: Drawing out simple ratios using bars can help pupils to see how fractions can correctly be obtained from a given ratio.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of converting between ratios, percentages and fractions

nodes.misconception: Not referring to the context of the question when comparing the data.
nodes.response: Highlight that just saying the median or the middle 50% of data is bigger is of little use unless you know what the data was about. Check that pupils understand the context of the question.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing box plots

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with cumulative frequency and histograms

nodes.misconception: Using the highest value on the y-axis rather than the total frequency when calculating the values to read off for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that the total frequency must be used.  A graph where the y-axis goes up to 100 and the total frequency is 40 can be used to highlight this.  Then repeat with the same data, but with a graph where the y-axis goes up to 200.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting a cumulative frequency graph

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Summary statistics from histograms

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Moving between tables and histograms

nodes.misconception: Plotting the midpoint of the class against the cumulative frequency.
nodes.response: Ensure that the pupils are clear that each cumulative frequency includes all values up to the upper boundary of each group.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing a cumulative frequency graph

nodes.misconception: Not referring to the context of the question when comparing the data.
nodes.response: Highlight that just saying the median or the interquartile is bigger is of little use unless you know what the data was about.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interquartile range

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Histograms with unequal bar width

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Histograms with equal bar width

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to order the list of data before finding the 5 key pieces of information.
nodes.response: Ask some pupils to stand at the front of the classroom.  Find the person in the middle, and pose the question "is they the median sized person?" Repeat with quartiles. This should highlight the importance of putting the numbers in order first.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing box plots

nodes.misconception: When using Desmos, incorrect brackets () are used to input raw data as elements.
nodes.response: [] are used to denote a set of data elements or elements. Encourage pupils to think about set notation when using Venn diagrams. Desmos will reject the use of () as they do not denote a set of elements.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Constructing histograms and box plots using technology

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with algebraic ratios

nodes.misconception: Treating the ratio as the total amount. For example sweets : chocolates in the ratio 6 : 7 and 2 chocolates are eaten, thinking the ratio must now be 6 : 5
nodes.response: Looking at how these problems are formed in learning cycle 1 will help and getting pupils to explore how the ratio changes when things are added or removed.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing ratios

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of sharing in a ratio

nodes.misconception: Combining ratios without using equivalent ratios to equate the common part.
nodes.response: Pupils may need to spend extra time finding equivalent ratios and looking at when it is ok to combine ratios or not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining ratios

nodes.misconception: Finding the additive relationship between two numbers instead of the multiplicative one.
nodes.response: When dealing with any proportional relationships, such as ratios, pupils should be reminded to look for the multiplicative relationship. Using 1 as a middle step can help. e.g. to connect 5 and 8, divide by 5 to make 1 and then multiply by 8.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of equivalent ratios

nodes.misconception: When $$x : y$$ are in the ratio 1 : 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
nodes.response: Show that the equation $$x = 2y$$ in a ratio table would mean the multiplier from $$y$$ to $$x$$ would be times by 2, this would mean when $$y=1 x=2$$ which is 2 : 1 not 1 : 2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Algebraic ratios

nodes.misconception: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question
nodes.response: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with ratios

nodes.misconception: When $$x : y$$ are in the ratio 1 : 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
nodes.response: The bar models shown in this lesson can help to support pupils with this.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing equations from ratios

nodes.misconception: Not simplifying the ratio completely or over-simplifying a three part ratio when two of the parts share a further common factor
nodes.response: Link two part ratios back to simplifying fractions and remind pupils to consider if either number is a multiple of 3 as this is often missed. Remind pupils that to simplify a ratio, every part must share the common factor you are dividing by.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of simplifying and unitising ratios

nodes.misconception: Not converting the units correctly in a question or forgetting to have the same units before simplifying a ratio
nodes.response: help pupils to set out ratio tables where they include the units and work through step by step to convert correctly before simplifying. The ratio table can help organise this working.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of real world ratios

nodes.misconception: Converting a ratio e.g. 1 : 3 to 1/3 as a fraction.
nodes.response: Drawing out simple ratios using bars can help pupils to see how fractions can correctly be obtained from a given ratio.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of converting between ratios, percentages and fractions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may substitute incorrectly.
nodes.response: Each variable in a formula represents something. Substituting for one variable at a time may help ensure that values are in the correct places.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Construction

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unfamiliar with train timetables and how to interpret them.
nodes.response: Each column of times can be given a header of Train 1, Train 2 etc. This will make it clearer that the times in a column refer to when that train will reach a station.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Personal assistant

nodes.misconception: Pupils mix-up the sides of the right-angled triangle when using Pythagoras' theorem.
nodes.response: Pupils may benefit from labelling the right-angled triangle so that the hypotenuse is clearly identified.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Engineer

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be confused about whether to multiply or divide when dealing with reversing percentage change.
nodes.response: The first learning cycle addresses this and you may wish to display the example on a whiteboard for the entire lesson for pupils to refer to.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Running a small business

nodes.misconception: Rounding incorrectly for the stated context.
nodes.response: Pupils should consider the situation and ask - if rounding down, will there be enough? If rounding up, does this cover all cases? Thinking about the situation and trying different values to see what works can also help.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Interior designer

nodes.misconception: Substituting the wrong values into the formulas.
nodes.response: The formulas are written in words so ensure pupils check that what they are substituting is the correct value by rereading the description for each value.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Medical professional

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider the maximum of the 'bins' in learning cycle 1.
nodes.response: It can be helpful for pupils to have a running total for the values assigned to each 'bin' so that they know when it is full and no more values can be assigned there.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Operational researcher

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the mathematical conventions for rounding should apply.
nodes.response: This is rounding in a practical context and pupils should consider what the effects of rounding up and down are and how they affect the answer.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Catering

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle in the first learning cycle with where each object should be placed.
nodes.response: The closer to the observation point an object is, the larger it appears to be. So if we want an object to appear larger than something else, we need to place it closer to the camera.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Media - films and games

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be uncertain as to whether an image has rotational symmetry.
nodes.response: Tracing paper may be useful here. Pupils can trace the image and then rotate the tracing paper to determine if an image has rotational symmetry.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Graphic designer

nodes.misconception: The factors mentioned in the lesson are the only factors to consider when considering costs/profits of livestock.
nodes.response: There are many more factors to consider. Pupils could research these or brainstorm with a partner. An example could be selling the wool from any sheep owned.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Agricultural worker (animals)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that improvement comes from choosing the maximum options for training straight away.
nodes.response: In order to protect the body and give it time to adjust/grow, coaches will gradually increase the intensity of a training programme. This helps to prevent injury to the athlete.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sports coaching

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the cost per hour can be reduced if less than an hour is required (venue hire).
nodes.response: This may be possible but should not be assumed when costing for an event as otherwise this could lead to a loss rather than a profit. If unknown, assume not.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Event management

nodes.misconception: Reducing the cost to increase sales is always the best option.
nodes.response: Although this may seem a good idea, increasing the number of units sold means increasing the amount made and therefore the cost to the business. Therefore the situation needs to be carefully considered.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Sales and marketing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be convinced that a right angled triangle is formed.
nodes.response: For the model, we assume that the terrain feature is perpendicular to the surface.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Astrophysicist

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the 'and' statements in the logic part of the lesson.
nodes.response: For the statement to be true, the whole statement must be true. This refers to both clauses that are joined by the word 'and'. If even one of the clauses is not true, then the entire statement can be declared not true (even if one clause is true).
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Programmer

nodes.misconception: Pupils may substitute incorrectly.
nodes.response: Each variable in a formula represents something. Substituting for one variable at a time may help ensure that values are in the correct places.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Emergency response worker

nodes.misconception: Confusing unfamiliar units of measure.
nodes.response: Pupils may benefit from having two lists of metric and imperial measures to reference should they need to.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Agricultural worker (crops)

nodes.misconception: Direct proportion can be determined by calculating the gradient.
nodes.response: The equation of the line should be of the form y = kx and so the y-intercept should be calculated to check it is zero.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and understanding graphs showing direct proportion

nodes.misconception: Solutions for context-based problem can be listed as coordinate pairs with units e.g. 6 workers, 60 hours.
nodes.response: Solutions should always be fully interpreted in relation to the context e.g. It would take 6 workers 60 hours to paint the building.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Graphs showing inverse proportion

nodes.misconception: Perpendicular lines have to be drawn as a horizontal and vertical pair.
nodes.response: Some pupils may struggle to see that two lines are perpendicular when they are not drawn horizontally and vertically. Drawing this on paper and then rotating the paper will help them see that it is the angle between the lines that matters.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Perpendicular linear graphs

nodes.misconception: P is a point such that AP : PB is in the ratio of 1 : 3 means that point P is a third of the distance of AB from A.
nodes.response: There are 4 equal parts in total, meaning that point P is a quarter of the distance of AB from A.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced problem solving with linear graphs

nodes.misconception: Only two pairs of coordinates are needed to plot a linear graph.
nodes.response: Whilst true, this can cause issues if one pair of coordinates is calculated incorrectly. Encourage pupils to check a third point to ensure they are correct.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of drawing linear graphs

nodes.misconception: P is a point such that AP : PB is in the ratio of 1 : 3 means that point P is a third of the distance of AB from A.
nodes.response: There are 4 equal parts in total, meaning that point P is a quarter of the distance of AB from A.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Ratios in line segments on coordinate axes

nodes.misconception: The gradients of two perpendicular lines are a number and its reciprocal.
nodes.response: In order for two lines to be perpendicular, the two gradients cannot have the same sign. Therefore it is a number and its negative reciprocal.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying perpendicular linear graphs

nodes.misconception: Writing equations of the form y = mx + c and getting the gradient and y-intercept the wrong way round.
nodes.response: Graphing software can be used to show that adding a constant is a translation of the graph. Remind pupils that the y-intercept is when x is zero which is why it is the constant in the equation. They can substitute x = 0 to check.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of finding the equation of the line from the graph

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not appreciate all the steps required to prove what type of shape is shown.
nodes.response: A warm-up for the lesson could be to review properties of shapes. Consider describing a shape, one property at a time. How much information is needed before pupils can be certain they know which shape is being described?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving with linear graphs

nodes.misconception: Writing equations of the form y = mx + c and getting the gradient and y-intercept the wrong way round.
nodes.response: Graphing software can be used to show that adding a constant is a translation of the graph. Remind pupils that the y-intercept is when x is zero which is why it is the constant in the equation. They can substitute x = 0 to check.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of finding the equation of the line from coordinates

nodes.misconception: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient.
nodes.response: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient and different y-intercepts. Two lines are parallel if they are straight lines that are always the same non-zero distance apart.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Parallel linear graphs

nodes.misconception: Pupils draw x = a as a horizontal line because the x axis is horizontal. Pupils draw y = a as a vertical line because the y axis is vertical.
nodes.response: Consider the points on the line x = 5 and ask pupils to plot 2-3 points. Can they see why it must be a vertical line?
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of drawing vertical and horizontal graphs

nodes.response: Remind pupils that the x value is read from the x-axis and is read first. The y value is read from the y-axis and is read second.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Checking and securing understanding of simultaneous equations

nodes.misconception: All inequalities are graphed with solid lines.
nodes.response: When graphed, strict inequalities are indicated with a dashed line. This is important as it visually tells us that values on the line will not satisfy the inequality.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving quadratic inequalities in one variable graphically

nodes.misconception: 3 > x > 9 is a valid way to combine x < 3 and x > 9
nodes.response: Test a value to show pupils that this does not make sense. When x = 0, it is true that x < 3 but not true that x > 9 so 3 > 0 > 9 does not work.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solution set notation

nodes.misconception: We are only interested in points that are in the region satisfied by all inequalities.
nodes.response: With practical contexts, such as project management, it is useful to know when one constraint is not being met as it can suggest where additional resources (if available) should be allocated.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly interpreting the inequality diagram.
nodes.response: A filled in circle means the value is valid. An empty circle means the inequality is strict.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Inequalities on number lines

nodes.misconception: Dividing or multiplying by -1 does not change the inequality sign.
nodes.response: 2 < 3 becomes -2 > -3 when both sides are multiplied by -1.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving more complicated linear inequalities

nodes.misconception: Thinking that x = 4 is a line parallel to the x axis and that y = 4 is parallel to the y axis.
nodes.response: Consider the points along the line. Writing valid coordinate pairs lets pupils identify which coordinate stays the same and which one changes.
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving a linear inequality graphically

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly interpreting inequalities due to the phrasing in English.

nodes.misconception: Winning an election means receiving over half the vote.
