nodes.response: Music should be notated in the most effective way for it to be decoded. This is often stave notation, but can be any way of sharing the musical intention successfully, for example rhythm grids or graphic scores.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Notating a minimalist piece

nodes.misconception: Minimalism has no structure.
nodes.response: Minimalist music does have structure, but this might be on a micro level. It employs repetition of cells - a cyclical structure.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and notating a repeating minimalist cell

nodes.misconception: A musical piece or performance is unchangeable.
nodes.response: There can be many interpretations of a piece of music, even if certain directions are suggested by the composer. As the composers of your own minimalist piece, anything is changeable and each performance may also be different.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rehearsing, performing and appraising a minimalist performance

nodes.misconception: We only warm up for singing.
nodes.response: Warming up can also help us prepare for playing instruments, using our bodies and working together in an ensemble. This helps us to focus, develops our sense of pulse and improves our coordination.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rhythm grids as a form of notation

nodes.misconception: Rhythm and pulse are the same.
nodes.response: Pulse is the regular, steady heartbeat of the music as opposed to rhythm which is the pattern of sounds that we play and sing.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rhythm and beat on rhythm grids

nodes.misconception: Rhythm grid notation only shows one instruction - play and rest.
nodes.response: Rhythm grid notation can give many instructions, including which instrument to play.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Decoding more complex rhythm grids

nodes.misconception: The more complicated rhythms we use when we compose, the better our music will sound.
nodes.response: Successful music is repetitive, playable and memorable!
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing and notating on rhythm grids

nodes.misconception: Notes of short duration means the music is a really fast tempo.
nodes.response: The pulse and beat sets the tempo. It doesn't matter how many sounds fit into the beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rhythm grids and the subdivision of the beat

nodes.misconception: We always count to four in music.
nodes.response: Music can be organised into any number of beats. The first beat is always the strongest.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading stick notation on rhythm grids

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is complicated and scary!
nodes.response: Improvisation can be as simple as changing one note. Try to play what you might already be able to hear in your head. Are you planning your improvisations well?
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising longer phrases using the D minor pentatonic scale

nodes.misconception: All music is worked out beforehand and can’t be made up on the spot.
nodes.response: Improvisation is the spontaneous creation of musical melodies and rhythms during a live performance.  These musical ideas are made up on the spot and not written down so it is very hard to exactly recreate them a second time.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvisation and the minor pentatonic scale

nodes.misconception: Improvised music has no structure.
nodes.response: Jazz pieces are heavily structured around chord sequences, the head and order of improvisatons.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and performing an improvised jazz piece

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is music completely made up on the spot.
nodes.response: Improvised music is not completely made up on the spot. Preparation and the practising of musical ideas is important.  It is more a form of spontaneous reconstruction of musical ideas built upon knowledge and practice.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising a phrase using the D minor pentatonic scale

nodes.misconception: A scale uses all the notes in step with no leaps.
nodes.response: A scale is a series of notes arranged in an ascending or descending order.  Each scale has a unique pattern of intervals (the distance between notes) that defines its character and the intervals are not always the same.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing the D minor pentatonic scale

nodes.misconception: The best way to learn to play a piece is to start at the beginning.
nodes.response: We can be clever when learning pieces, looking for patterns and easy parts to fit together first whilst internalising the sounds of trickier parts.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing a minor pentatonic jazz melody

nodes.misconception: We need to sing loudly for it to be heard or for it to be 'good'.
nodes.response: Learning to sing using a range of dynamics is a key aspect of conveying the mood of a song. Pupils can explore what quality singing feels like, and the effect it can have, using a range of dynamics to suit the song.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Strong and soft singing

nodes.misconception: Singing loudly means using our shouting voice.
nodes.response: Singing loudly should be a controlled, projected sound that avoids shouting.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing stronger and feeling energised

nodes.misconception: Singing softly is easier and requires less effort.
nodes.response: Soft singing requires the same breath control as louder singing. The warm-ups and the breathing exercise help prepare for this.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: How singing softly makes me feel

nodes.misconception: We sing a song at the same dynamics all the way through.
nodes.response: We can help to convey the meaning of a song by varying the dynamics within a song. Singing with a range of dynamics also provides the listener with a broader range of sound to feel engaged with.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Controlling dynamic changes within a song

nodes.misconception: We should perform loudly and confidently so that the audience can hear us.
nodes.response: Changing dynamics can actually help an audience to feel more engaged in the singing because their ears are given more variation, and they can interpret the feeling of a song more easily.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing dynamics to perform with feeling

nodes.misconception: Conductors are for orchestras and not for singing in class.
nodes.response: Following a conductor can help us to stay together and change our dynamics together. This adds focus to our singing as well as making the song more effective for an audience.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Following a leader to change dynamics

nodes.misconception: Using just one note as a harmony would sound boring
nodes.response: Using a drone as part of a Hindustani classical performance adds an effective,  meaningful and symbolic layer to the music
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Bringing together taal, raag, and drone

nodes.misconception: Music has four beats in a bar and we always finish at the last beat in the bar.
nodes.response: Rhythm cycles in Hindustani classical music can have anything from 3 beats to 128 beats.  The rhythm is cyclical and ends on the first beat of the rhythm cycle.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing taals and speaking bols

nodes.misconception: There are only one set of names we use for notes in a scale
nodes.response: We can use pitch names of C, D, E, F, G, A, B. We can use the solfège of do, re, mi, fa, so la, ti, and in Hindustani classical we use the sargam of sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha ni. These are not fixed - meaning 'do' or 'Sa' don't have to be 'C'.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing and playing raags

nodes.misconception: The taal and raag begin and end at the same time.
nodes.response: A raag can start and end at any point in the rhythm cycle.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining taals and raags

nodes.misconception: A raag can only be played on a sitar.
nodes.response: Raags can be sung too. They can also be played on other instruments. Common instruments used in Hindustani classical music include harmonium, flute, bansuri and sarod. In the classroom, a largely accessible instrument is a glockenspiel.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing and playing a melody in a five note raag

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is complicated and hard to do.
nodes.response: Using fewer notes and focusing on creating short improvisations can be very effective and help us to introduce the idea of conveying emotion through our music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising using a five note raag

nodes.misconception: You can practise on your own and then you will play together successfully as an ensemble.
nodes.response: It is important to rehearse as an ensemble in order to perform successfully.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Ensemble performance from a graphic score

nodes.misconception: Timbre alone creates a musical story.
nodes.response: All the musical elements need to work together to create a musical story. A glockenspiel can be many things depending on how it is played - not just a polar bear.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing the timbre of instruments

nodes.misconception: Instruments can only create one sound or represent one animal.
nodes.response: There is no right or wrong when choosing instruments for their timbre.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining rhythm and timbre

nodes.misconception: Music is always notated on a score.
nodes.response: Some music is never notated, it is shared by singing and playing. Some notation uses graphic scores, or rhythm grids. Any way of sharing how the music is expected to be played is a form of notation.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Graphic score notation

nodes.misconception: Music is always notated on a score.
nodes.response: Some music is never notated, it is shared by singing and playing. Some notation uses graphic scores, or rhythm grids. Any way of sharing how the music is expected to be played is a form of notation.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading graphic scores

nodes.misconception: Timbre alone creates a musical story.
nodes.response: All the musical elements need to work together to create a musical story. A clarinet can be many things depending on how it is played - not just an orangutan.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Choosing appropriate percussive timbres to represent an animal

nodes.misconception: An ostinato is a rhythm pattern only.
nodes.response: An ostinato can be melodic as well as rhythmic. In pop music they’re often called a ‘riff’ and in electronic music, a ‘loop’. A repeated pattern can add to the texture of a piece of music and help drive it forward.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Melodic ostinato accompaniments to songs

nodes.misconception: We can play at our own tempo without listening to the other groups.
nodes.response: The songs we are layering are all played at different tempi. Feeling the steady pulse and following a conductor, as well as listening to the playing of all groups will help the class to play to the same steady pulse.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rehearsing songs with layers of instrumental accompaniments

nodes.misconception: Drones are boring because they are just a single note.
nodes.response: Drones can add depth and a focus point to a piece of music. They can sometimes even be soothing for the listener.  A piece of music can be built around a drone.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Drone accompaniments to songs

nodes.misconception: We won't be able to hear what instruments are playing when they're playing at the same time.
nodes.response: We can identify the instruments playing by their unique timbre and tune our ears to recognise each sound.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying different layers of accompaniment within a piece of music

nodes.misconception: We can only play one ostinato at a time.
nodes.response: We can have two or more groups playing two or more ostinati that can fit together when played to a steady pulse. By playing rhythms on instruments with different timbres, and adding tuned percussion, we change the sound and thickness of the texture.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Layering simple accompaniments to create a thicker texture

nodes.misconception: We play the same tune as what we're singing.
nodes.response: A melodic ostinato can add more interest to the overall sound and, with practice, we can play a different tune to the one we're singing.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing a melodic ostinato and singing simultaneously

nodes.misconception: When practising in an ensemble we need to practise at our own speed so we can play our part accurately.
nodes.response: When practising as an ensemble, we all need to play at the same tempo, we should start off slowly and speed up as we feel more confident.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising a melodic accompaniment

nodes.misconception: When we practise, we just need to repeat the music a few times.
nodes.response: Thinking about what we want to improve and choosing the best stragtegy to help us is the best way to practise.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising a rhythmic accompaniment

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing simply means playing a piece again and again.
nodes.response: To rehearse effectively, we need to work on sepcific areas for improvement to help us to play and sing together and create a balanced sound.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rehearsing as an ensemble

nodes.misconception: Once we can play the notes correctly, there's nothing we need to do to improve a performance.
nodes.response: Listening and watching the overall performance and getting feedback from others can help us to identify how to refine the performance such as adding dynamics, playing sensitively within the ensemble and playing precisely in time.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing and reflecting on the rehearsal journey

nodes.misconception: A particular piece of Folk music is always played in eactly the same way.
nodes.response: Folk music is passed down via an oral tradition and is often interpreted differently. Melodies, harmonies and instrumentation may change over time and when played in different places.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising effectively

nodes.misconception: In an ensemble performance, one part, usually the melody, is the most important part.
nodes.response: In an ensemble performance each part is crucial.  Each part adds something different to the final performance such as harmony, melody or rhythmic foundation.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing together as an ensemble

nodes.misconception: The word low is sometimes associated with quiet.
nodes.response: The word low refers to pitch.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Notating four notes on a simplified musical stave

nodes.misconception: The word low is sometimes associated with quiet.
nodes.response: The word low refers to low pitch.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Placing our new lower note on a simplified musical stave

nodes.misconception: Notes are always placed on the lines of a stave
nodes.response: Notes can be placed on, above, or below the lines on a stave
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Placing our new higher note on a simplified musical stave

nodes.misconception: The note la is placed anywhere above the high line on the stave.
nodes.response: The note la sits on top of and touches the high line of the stave.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Notating three notes on a simplified musical stave

nodes.misconception: High and low refers to volume (loud and quiet).
nodes.response: High and low refers to pitch.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: High and low notes

nodes.misconception: High and low refers to volume (loud and quiet).
nodes.response: High and low refers to pitch.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Notating high and low notes on a simplified musical stave

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the underlying feeling of uniformed beats - it is the heartbeat of the music. When organised into metres, we then feel it as beats e.g. counting 1,2,3 1,2,3. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a rhythm sequence using pictures

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Beat is the playing of the steady pulse. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing rhythm patterns to a steady pulse

nodes.misconception: We only warm up before a performance.
nodes.response: It’s really important to warm up the voice every time we are going to sing, to prevent injury and improve vocal quality.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing, moving and playing to a steady pulse

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the regular heartbeat of the music. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Echoing simple rhythm patterns

nodes.misconception: When describing an instrument’s timbre, we can say it is high or low, loud or quiet, fast or slow.
nodes.response: Timbre describes the unique sound of an instrument, not its pitch, dynamics or tempo.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying the timbre of classroom percussion

nodes.misconception: Pulse, beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the underlying feeling of uniformed beats - it is the heartbeat of the music. When organised into metres, we then feel it as beats e.g. counting 1,2,3 1,2,3. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences of differing durations.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading rhythms from pictures

nodes.misconception: Beatboxing is really difficult.
nodes.response: Beatboxing is just using your voice and sense of rhythm to mimic sounds. Humans mimic sounds all the time and this is just an extension of that.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Layering beatboxing vocal percussion sounds

nodes.misconception: Beatboxing artists use only rhythmic patterns in their music.
nodes.response: Beatboxing is not always just about drum machine mimicry. Artists like Jason Singh, combine other sounds in his recordings.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising using beatboxing techniques and vocal sounds inspired by nature

nodes.misconception: A live performance will always be exactly the same.
nodes.response: Live performances, especially of an improvisation will alter very slightly between each concert.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising a beatboxing film score

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing is just about doing something again and again.
nodes.response: In order to rehearse effectively, pupils need to discuss and question what is good or needs developing in their performance.  Repeating without analysing a performance will not improve the outcome.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating and performing a beatboxing film score

nodes.misconception: When performing in parts children often try to block out listening to the other parts and focus only on their own.
nodes.response: Children will gain in confidence when they listen to all the parts and will improve their performance.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rehearsing a texture of two or more parts

nodes.misconception: We only warm up for a performance.
nodes.response: No, it is important to warm up whenever we are making music.  Warming up will help us to focus, it will stretch and relax our vocal muscles ready for using them and will help us to listen and work as a group of musicians.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing beatboxing vocal percussion

nodes.misconception: Fusion music always requires specific, identifiable elements from each original style.
nodes.response: The fusion of styles can be so integrated that the original influences become indistinguishable.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fusing together and arranging musical ideas

nodes.misconception: Music from other parts of the world is 'traditional' and remains unchanged.
nodes.response: All music changes over time as different musicians shape it with their own creativity.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fusion and the evolution of musical styles

nodes.misconception: Fusion only refers to the blending of two contemporary styles of music.
nodes.response: Fusion is the blending of any two or more styles of music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Melody in fusion music

nodes.misconception: Once we can play the rhythms and melodies correctly, there is nothing else we need to do to prepare for a performance.
nodes.response: We can think about a range of ways to make the music more expressive, for example, adding dynamics to make our music have more impact for an audience.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing, listening and responding to each other

nodes.misconception: Musical fusion only refers to one type of blending of musical styles for example jazz and rock.
nodes.response: Fusion is a broad genre of music characterized by the creative integration of any two or more distinct styles.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fusing and layering rhythmic patterns

nodes.misconception: Fusion music is less authentic or valuable than traditional genres.
nodes.response: Fusion music is in itself innovative and musically complex and is recognised as a genre in its own right.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising repetitive cells for a fusion performance

nodes.misconception: When we compose music we always notate it using a stave.
nodes.response: Using stick notation with the notes written underneath is a quick way to notate simple melodies.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing within an ABA musical structure

nodes.misconception: Beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: The beat follows the steady pulse of a song while the rhythm follows the pattern of the words.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning a four note melody on pitched percussion

nodes.misconception: Music is always notated on a musical stave.
nodes.response: There are many different ways to notate music. Stick notation, for example, is a quick way to notate simple rhythms and melodies.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and playing using simplified notation

nodes.misconception: The longer (taller) bars on a pitched percussion instrument make a higher pitch.
nodes.response: On a pitched percussion instrument, the bars with a longer length make a lower pitch and the bars with a shorter length make a higher pitch.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing four note tonesets on pitched percussion

nodes.misconception: Improvisation is difficult and only professional musicians can do it well.
nodes.response: Improvisation is about exploring new musical ideas. Even young pupils can improvise in a fun and playful way using familiar material as a starting point.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Call and response improvisation within a four note toneset

nodes.misconception: Improvising doesn't require any thought.
nodes.response: Before we improvise, we think about what notes or rhythms we might play and how we will structure our playing, but the final product is played in the moment.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing and improvising within an ABA structure

nodes.misconception: Tempo alone can set the musical mood.
nodes.response: All the musical elements work together to help set the musical mood.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Choosing a fast or slow tempo for songs, chants and games

nodes.misconception: Beat and rhythm are interchangeable terminology.
nodes.response: The beat is the consistent audible sound of the underlying pulse. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences which can be a combination of sounds of any duration.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Keeping a steady beat as we move, sing and play

nodes.misconception: Feeling the beat doesn't need practising.
nodes.response: Singing games are really useful to help us practise the beat, especially when it is very slow or very fast. We need to practise the beat at lots of different tempi.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using tempo to tell a musical story

nodes.misconception: The tempo always stays the same throughout a piece of music.
nodes.response: Although we learn to feel the pulse and follow the steady beat, music can get gradually faster or gradually slower.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to tempo changes within a song or piece of music

nodes.misconception: Pulse and beat are the same thing.
nodes.response: Pulse is the underlying feeling of uniformed beats - it is the heartbeat of the music. When organised into metres, we then feel it as beats e.g. counting 1,2,3 1,2,3.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Feeling the pulse in music with a fast or slow tempo

nodes.misconception: Pulse and beat are the same thing.
nodes.response: Not quite! Pulse is the underlying feeling of uniformed beats - it is the heartbeat of the music. When organised into metres, we then feel it as beats e.g. counting or clapping 1,2,3 1,2,3.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Feeling the pulse in songs and chants

nodes.misconception: Improvising is music created solely on the spot.
nodes.response: Musicians might not know exactly what they are going to do, but they are building on and working from a bank of known ideas and motifs that they can draw upon, use and adapt.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising a major pentatonic melody

nodes.misconception: Warming up is fun, but we don’t need to warm up every time we practise our singing.
nodes.response: Warming-up is really important to prevent our voice from injury. It also helps to improve many of our music skills.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing major pentatonic folk songs

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing isn't important. We can just do it if we have time.
nodes.response: Rehearsing helps us to practise and prepare, so our performance can be successful.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a major pentatonic melody

nodes.misconception: Ta-di and Ta-mi are the same because they both have two notes in one beat.
nodes.response: With the Ta-di rhythm both notes divide the beat equally in half. With Ta-mi, the notes are not distributed equally - the first is longer (¾ of a beat) and the second is shorter (¼ of a beat).
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing a dotted rhythm major pentatonic melody

nodes.misconception: Ta-di and Ta-mi are the same because they both have two notes in one beat.
nodes.response: With the Ta-di rhythm both notes divide the beat equally in half. With Ta-mi, the notes are not distributed equally - the first is longer (¾ of a beat) and the second is shorter (¼ of a beat).
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Notating a dotted rhythm major pentatonic melody

nodes.misconception: The major pentatonic scale comes from a simplified version of the major (heptatonic) scale.
nodes.response: The major pentatonic scale comes from ancient civilisations and is not a simplified form of the heptatonic scale. Pentatonic music, in its various forms, is found in folk music from all around the world.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing and identifying the major pentatonic scale

nodes.misconception: Songs with a major tonality are always happy.
nodes.response: Tonality is one of the elements that gives a melody it's character. While major tonalites often feel bright, it is the combination of how all the elements of music are used that will make a song sound happy.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Major tonalities

nodes.misconception: The notes on the stave can be written like dots on the line or inbetween the lines.
nodes.response: It is important that the size of the notes matches the size of the stave. This makes the notation easier to read.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the five note major pentachord scale

nodes.misconception: A rhythmic ostinato is the same as the rhythm of the words.
nodes.response: We can make an ostinato using the rhythms of the words but often the ostinato has a different rhythm.  It can be tricky to play an ostinato and sing a different rhythm!
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and playing major melodies

nodes.misconception: When composing, to make a melody interesting, it should be complicated with lots of different notes.
nodes.response: A simple melody with lots of repetition and stepwise movement often makes a more memorable melody.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing and notating a major melody

nodes.misconception: It is common to try and play songs too quickly when learning them on an instrument.
nodes.response: It's always better to start slowly and at a steady tempo, then gradually build up speed when feeling confident.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Major melodies and the major pentachord

nodes.misconception: If we make a mistake during a performance, we should start again.
nodes.response: While sometimes we might need to re-start, practising finding our place and carrying on playing is a great skill for a performer to develop.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing major melodies

nodes.misconception: When composing, choosing a wide variety of complicated rhythms is more exciting than using simpler ones.
nodes.response: When starting composing it's often good to use mostly simpler rhythms, and to make use of repetition.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing and notating a minor melody

nodes.misconception: When writing out music notation, the exact position of the notes doesn't really matter.
nodes.response: The part that matters the most is the note head - the circle at the bottom of the stick. Where that sits (on a line or space) tells us what pitch to play, so accuracy in where it is placed is important.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading the five note minor pentachord scale

nodes.misconception: A scale always starts on the note do.
nodes.response: We are used to using the Solfège note names in the order - do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. This is only correct for major scales. A minor scale starts on the note la.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Minor melodies and the minor pentachord

nodes.misconception: If we make a mistake when performing we should always stop and start again.
nodes.response: While you might sometimes need to start again, it's good practice to try and find your place and carry on if you make a mistake when performing.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and performing minor melodies

nodes.misconception: We can play a melody quickly when we are learning it.
nodes.response: It's always better to start slow, then speed up when confidence is built.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading and playing minor melodies

nodes.misconception: Songs with a minor tonality are always sad.
nodes.response: Tonality is one of the elements that gives a melody its character. While minor tonalites often feel dark, it is the combination of how all the elements of music are used that will make a song sound sad.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying major and minor tonalities

nodes.misconception: Playing a piece of music numerous times will improve the performance.
nodes.response: Playing sections of a piece multiple times will only improve a performance if a small part is focused on and improvements are considered and rehearsed effectively.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Practising and performing composed variations on a theme

nodes.misconception: Theme and variations is the same as theme music.
nodes.response: Theme music is a musical composition which is often written specifically for video games, or films and is usually played at the beginning, end and at some point during the course of the game or film.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Theme and variation as a musical structure

nodes.misconception: Rhythms with shorter duration notes means the music is faster.
nodes.response: The speed of music is determined by the tempo.  A complicated rhythm with shorter notes can be played at a fast or slow tempo
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a rhythmic variation to a theme

nodes.misconception: Theme and variation structure only applies to orchestral music.
nodes.response: A musical structure can apply to any style of music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning a musical theme

nodes.misconception: Embellishing a theme to create a variation makes a totally new composition
nodes.response: Although each variation is different, each is based on the initial theme, and pupils will be able to recognise aspects of the original theme.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a melodic variation to a theme

nodes.misconception: Changing the tonality from major to minor will automatically make the music sound sad.
nodes.response: This is an oversimplification. All of the musical elements work together to create the character or mood of a piece of music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a further variation to a theme

nodes.misconception: Conductors are only needed to lead orchestras.
nodes.response: Conductors can direct any group of musicians - singers or instrumentalists. They can help each voice enter a round at the correct time.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Following a conductor when singing rounds

nodes.misconception: A round is where you sing a song once through but everyone starts at different times.
nodes.response: A round is a shorter song that repeats on a loop.  The start times are staggered in half, in quarters, or sometimes in thirds. Feeling the steady pulse, and counting the correct number of beats helps us know when to start singing.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounds as a singing structure

nodes.misconception: If we've rehearsed our songs, we don't need to warm up for a performance.
nodes.response: Warming up for a performance encourages everyone to feel engaged, connected and alert as well as supporting a good quality of vocal sound.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing rounds and partner songs

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing is just singing the songs through.
nodes.response: Rehearsing helps us to work out what needs further practice.  It helps us know when to start and stop singing, to feel the steady beat and is a regular reminder to follow the conductor. Feeling more confident will enable a more accurate performance.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rehearsing rounds and partner songs

nodes.misconception: Singing two songs together will clash and not sound harmonious.
nodes.response: Partner songs are made of notes that sound good together. The songs are partnered up because they fit harmoniously and can be sung following the same steady beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner songs as a singing structure

nodes.misconception: Blocking out the sound of the other song will help you concentrate on your own part better.
nodes.response: By singing more softly, we can hear the other parts and hear how partner songs fit together. This is because they share similar musical characteristics such as the key, the rhythm, the tempo and chord progression.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing partner songs

nodes.misconception: Once the performance is done, our learning is done too.
nodes.response: Watching a performance back and/or getting feedback from an audience/ director/teacher is hugely valuable in cementing our learning. We can see and hear how we used our voices and bodies to tell a story and how we applied the techniques we learnt.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflecting on a successful performance

nodes.misconception: Once on stage, it is common to focus more on the singing and drop some of the physicality.
nodes.response: We can avoid this by melding the two. How we move and how we sing can be described in similar ways. For example, legato, or smooth singing, may happen whilst we are moving in a smooth manner.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Characterful singing

nodes.misconception: If we don't read music fluently, there's no point in looking at the written music of a song. We should just use the lyrics.
nodes.response: We can build on our understanding of pitch by identifying 'melodic shapes' or 'melodic contours' in the music. We can also find clues in the music to help us know how to sing each part of the song.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Controlling our voice to convey the feeling of a song

nodes.misconception: Singing in opera is just like our everyday singing.
nodes.response: Singing in opera is all about telling a story. We can adapt the quality of our voice by using a different vocal timbre, using diction in a more percussive way or by singing with different articulation to bring our character to life.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Articulation and vocal quality when singing

nodes.misconception: Rehearsal is going over the songs until we know them.
nodes.response: Rehearsal is used to develop a character - physically, vocally, and by understanding intentions and mood. Rehearsal is also for exploring using the space to tell the story clearly as well as neatening key parts of the songs.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective rehearsal for a singing performance

nodes.misconception: When singing harmony parts, we should sing loudly to block out the other parts so that we can sing our own part correctly.
nodes.response: When singing together, it's important to listen to the other parts so that we hear how they fit together. We need to balance the sound, so that the audience can hear both parts clearly.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Balancing harmony lines in songs

nodes.misconception: Once we've performed, we don't need to keep thinking about the learning.
nodes.response: Reflecting on our performance is a valuable tool not only to feel a sense of pride in the skills we've developed, but also to see which areas of our musical learning need more focus.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Syncopation performance and reflection

nodes.misconception: When preparing for a performance, we should just focus on playing our own part accurately.
nodes.response: When playing and singing in an ensemble, the overall sound is important, we need to make the ensemble as cohesive and synchronised as possible.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and rehearsing a syncopated performance - building a tight ensemble

nodes.misconception: Syncopation means only playing on (or emphasising) the ‘weak beats’ as in emphasising the 2nd and 4th beat of a 4-beat bar, instead of the 1st and 3rd.
nodes.response: Whilst emphasising the ‘2’ and the ‘4’ is common in pop music (often called backbeat) we can also create syncopation by holding notes, missing beats, and playing what is called ‘offbeat syncopation’.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: What is syncopation?

nodes.misconception: Syncopated rhythms are really difficult.
nodes.response: Syncopated rhythms can be simple rhythms, but the emphasis on the offbeat can create an interesting, but not necessarily difficult, sound to recreate.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing and playing syncopated rhythms

nodes.misconception: Improvisation in music is only done on instruments and not the voice.
nodes.response: Scat singing, from jazz music is one type of vocal improvisation. Other types include the sargams of Hindustani and Carnatic music from India, freestyle rap, even yodelling!
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Syncopated rhythms in jazz

nodes.misconception: A commonly misused, generalised term is ‘African drumming’.
nodes.response: A popular drum from West Africa is the djembe, which is frequently referred to as ‘African drumming’. By looking specifically at Guinea, in West Africa, we can see there are many types of drum in one country within the continent of Africa.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Layering syncopated rhythms to accompany a song

nodes.misconception: All instruments can play different notes.
nodes.response: Some instruments are unpitched. This means they do not create different high and low sounds when played.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying high and low notes

nodes.misconception: Rehearsing isn't important. We can just do it if we have time.
nodes.response: Rehearsing helps us to practise and prepare, so our performance can be successful.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing a simple melody as part of a call and response song

nodes.misconception: Call and response is a singing structure.
nodes.response: The call and response structure can be found in songs, chants and instrumental music in musical styles all around the world.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Chants and songs with a call and response structure

nodes.misconception: Rhythm and beat are the same thing.
nodes.response: The beat is the playing or showing of the steady pulse, like the ticking of a clock. The rhythm is the pattern of sounds we play and sing over the steady beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a four beat rhythm

nodes.misconception: Responses are always the same in call and response songs.
nodes.response: The response can be different every time. The call can also be different. Call and response can be any kind of back and forth musical conversation.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Reading simple rhythms

nodes.misconception: Bigger or longer instruments usually create a higher pitched sound. Shorter or smaller instruments usually create a lower pitched sound.
nodes.response: Usually, the bigger the instrument, the lower the sound.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a simple high and low melody

nodes.misconception: I should sing louder so my part can be heard over the others.
nodes.response: When we all sing louder, the music becomes unbalanced. If we listen and balance each layer, our music sounds clear and beautiful.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing part singing

nodes.misconception: When we sing, we have to change pitch
nodes.response: We can sing a phrase all on one note.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a thicker texture with a sung ostinato

nodes.misconception: One instrument can only make one type of sound.
nodes.response: Our body is an instrument and we can create many different sounds, all with different timbre.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding body percussion to a song

nodes.misconception: If we know our songs well, we do not need to rehearse before a performance.
nodes.response: A rehearsal can really help to settle the nerves, helping us know what will happen and how things will feel different during the performance.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing songs with simple accompaniments

nodes.misconception: The pulse and steady beat always stays the same.
nodes.response: If the tempo changes, the pulse will change too!
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a thicker texture with a chanted ostinato

nodes.misconception: The beat is the same as the rhythm of the words.
nodes.response: The pulse is like a steady beat that stays the same, even when the rhythm of the words changes. Clap the beat whilst saying words to show how they are different.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing pulse and moving in time to the music

nodes.misconception: When singing in parts it's better to sing loudly so that you are not distracted by the other parts.
nodes.response: If everyone sings more gently, they can hear themselves, and others, properly.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Perform a melodic ostinato

nodes.misconception: When singing in harmony, we need to ignore the other parts to concentrate on our own part.
nodes.response: When singing in harmony, we need to listen carefully to the other parts to ensure our part blends with the other voices.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Harmony writing and singing in 2 or 3 parts

nodes.misconception: Pitch is the same as melodic shape.
nodes.response: Pitch refers to how high or low an individual note is. Melodic shape refers to the up and down contour pattern created by a series of pitches.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing for part work: staying in time and following melodic shape

nodes.misconception: The rhythmic ostinato matches the syllables of the song words.
nodes.response: We have composed ostinatos using the syllables of the words, but rhythmic ostinatos can be made with any rhythm pattern.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Rhythmic ostinato and practising rounds

nodes.misconception: Beat and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: The beat is the showing or playing of the steady pulse.  They rhythm is the pattern of sounds which we play in time to the beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing for part work: practising songs in rhythm names and solfège

nodes.misconception: Singing two songs together or the same song at different times will clash and not sound harmonious.
nodes.response: Partner songs and rounds have melodies that fit together harmoniously, and the parts are sung following the same steady beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner songs and rounds

nodes.misconception: Sometimes we exaggerate tempo changes, interpreting singing fast as singing 'as fast as we can'.
nodes.response: Subtle tempo changes can affect the character of the music as well as big ones.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the tempo to build excitement

nodes.misconception: Every performance of a piece is the same.
nodes.response: We can use dynamics and tempo to tell the story of the words, different conductors and performers might do this differently.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Following a conductor to create a musical mood

nodes.misconception: Everybody responds to music in the same way
nodes.response: While there are common musical features that makes a song sound happy, sad or scary, these are not always experienced in the same way. One person may find a song calm, wheras another may find it sad.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to different musical moods

nodes.misconception: Singing in a loud or cross tone involves shouting.
nodes.response: You can sing loudly and sound cross without shouting. Think of singing strongly, rather than loud to help you to do this.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing with character and feeling

nodes.misconception: If we make a mistake in a performance we should start again.
nodes.response: When performing in front of an audience it's best to carry on if we make a mistake.  Most of the time the audience won't notice.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a convincing singing performance

nodes.misconception: Everyone responds to music in the same way.
nodes.response: Loud music might be exciting, but it might also be a bit scary.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing dynamics to change the mood

nodes.misconception: C position is thumb on C in the left hand.
nodes.response: The C position is when the hand is placed in a position to play C up to G. With the right hand, this would be the thumb on C, finger 2 on D etc. With the left hand, the C position is when the little finger is on C, finger 4 is on D etc.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding bass clef

nodes.misconception: An Alberti bass is the notes of the triad played in any order.
nodes.response: An Alberti bass has a specfic, distinctive pattern which uses the lowest note, highest note, middle note, highest note of the triad in that order.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding arpeggios and Alberti bass

nodes.misconception: A ground bass pattern should finish on the tonic as it 'sounds' finished.
nodes.response: The final bar of the piece should finish on the tonic note, but until that bar, the pattern wants to repeat. Finishing on the dominant or the leading note naturally helps the music return to the first note of the pattern, which should be the tonic.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding ground bass

nodes.misconception: One iteration of the tresillo and habanera has to last for two beats.
nodes.response: The tresillo and habanera can be played in 2/4 or 4/4. The important thing is the relationship of the notes to each other. Practise clapping the rhythms twice as fast or slow to the same beat to help pupils grasp this concept.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding rhythmic variation to ground bass

nodes.misconception: An interval of a 3rd is three tones higher or lower than the first note.
nodes.response: In C major (where pupils are counting the white keys), they should count the starting note and final note, plus any in between. So an interval of a 3rd is actually two tones higher or lower than the first note. An octave would be seven notes higher.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding triadic melody to ground bass

nodes.misconception: When adding chords to a bass line, the chord has to be the same as the note in the bass.
nodes.response: In most cases the bass note should be one of the notes in the chord, but doesn't always have to be the lowest note of the chord. For a balanced chord sequence most notes in the bass lines should be the root, but not all have to be.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding triadic harmony to ground bass

nodes.misconception: You can only change the 3rd or the 6th of the scale to change the mood of the music.
nodes.response: In the lesson task any suitable chromatic movement can be used to change the feel of the motif, so pupils don't explicitly have to change the 3rd and the 6th. Play a range of motifs in the major key and change different notes so pupils can see this.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a motif

nodes.misconception: A sense of style in music refers only to the genre.
nodes.response: Style can mean genre-specific features but also can refer to compositional style and the composer using common features throughout a particular piece.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a sense of style

nodes.misconception: Any pitch and notes can work in a composition.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to think about the choice of notes in their musical ideas and listen to how it sounds.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating scary music

nodes.misconception: A soundtrack should have music all the way through.
nodes.response: Careful use of silence can heighten the tension and help to emphasise the dialogue. There is a balance and silence can be used sparingly to elevate other parts of the music and the story, particularly after a musical build up.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing music for an extended story

nodes.misconception: Using all the white notes is C major will sound cheerful
nodes.response: It's important that the home note (in this case C) is used appropriately to reinforce the notes sounding like they are in C major.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing music that doesn't sound scary

nodes.misconception: Certain timbres can only be used for certain effects.
nodes.response: Some timbres are particularly well suited to certain moods or effects but this doesn't mean that other timbres can't be used for different effects. It can also depend on the other musical features used.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The effect of timbre

nodes.misconception: The genre of the music tells us exactly what kind of film it is.
nodes.response: This is not always true. Sometimes composers deliberately use genres that go against expectations. This might be for humour, or to create a strange clash. A good example would be A Knight's Tale, which uses modern genres in a medieval film.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing mood in film music

nodes.misconception: One feature on its own will make a leitmotif have a particular mood.
nodes.response: The mood of a leitmotif comes from a combination of different musical elements, including melodic features. Changing one feature might slightly change the mood, but to create a strong mood you need to consider all different aspects of the leitmotif.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating contrasting leitmotifs

nodes.misconception: Using chords from within a minor key creates a dark mood.
nodes.response: It's more complex than that - it is important to carefully choose which chords within the key you emphasise to create a dark mood. Emphasising chord i and other minor chords helps to make it feel dark and ominous, rather than any chords from the key.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using film music to establish mood

nodes.misconception: A leimotif is just a musical theme.
nodes.response: Not quite. A leitmotif is a musical idea that must represent something else. This is usually a character, place or idea. A musical theme can exist without representing anything at all.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using leitmotif in film music

nodes.misconception: To create a contrasting version of a leitmotif, you should change lots of features of it.
nodes.response: You must be careful to not change it too much. If you do, it becomes unrecognisable and will just sound like a different leitmotif. A leitmotif represents a character, place, or idea, so we need to be able to recognise it to link it to that thing.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a leitmotif

nodes.misconception: Hooks and riffs are the same thing.
nodes.response: A riff is the more important feature in how the song fits together and tends to underpin some of the main sections in the music. It is also a more suitable musical starting point for a pop song composition.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Hooks and riffs in pop songs

nodes.misconception: Synthesiser vs synthesised sound
nodes.response: You can use a synthesiser if you have one or show a youtube clip of one in action. Use keyboard and different sounds to explain synthesised
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Instrumentation and metre in popular music

nodes.misconception: Chord sequences have to follow fixed rules exactly.
nodes.response: We use parameters as a guide to give a musical starting point for composing, but sometimes you might find other chords work. Always encourage pupils to try out a few ideas and perform their ideas so they can hear what they sound like.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a chord sequence for a pop song

nodes.misconception: The rhythm section 'plays the rhythm'. Rhythm sections are a fixed group of instruments.
nodes.response: Highlight the roles of the band and how they 'support' the singer and don't just provide rhythm for the song. There is some flexibility in the rhythm section. Not all the instruments have to be present in the music all of the time.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The rhythm section and bass lines in pop songs

nodes.misconception: For musical ideas, such as a riff or melody to contrast, they have to be totally different.
nodes.response: Songs should have to have some continuity between the different sections. Highlight ways in which two melodically different ideas might still have some similarities ie. same rhythm, same shape, same number of notes, same initial motif.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a drum beat and contrast in pop song structure

nodes.misconception: The A sections in a musical structure which has a repeated A section have to be the same.
nodes.response: Strong musical ideas usually have a balance of unity and variety, so even when a section is repeated, providing the main melodic idea is recognisable there can be some small changes which then helps to find this balance.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Extending and refining creative ideas

nodes.misconception: We can develop a composition around any element of music.
nodes.response: Using the elements of music, particularly individually, is not always helpful for pupils to make a start on a composition. Finding a musical starting point such as a set of notes or rhythm allows pupils to then explore the elements through that idea.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: How music can paint pictures

nodes.misconception: The conductor is the only person responsible for keeping the pulse and pitch is only high and low.
nodes.response: The conductor can set the tempo but all performers are responsible for keeping the pulse in a performance. Pitch as high and low is slightly limiting. Help pupils make connections to other related words that they might know.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Making and enjoying music

nodes.misconception: The description thick texture relates to the number of people performing and loud dynamics.
nodes.response: Texture is more complex than thick/thin. Use good examples early on to show that texture is related to the different layers in the music and not neccesarily the number of performers. Show how lots of performers could be performing in a thin texture.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Texture in music

nodes.misconception: A melody must feature a motif.
nodes.response: This is not necessarily true - great melodies do not have to use motifs. However, they are a useful feature to understand when learning to write melodies, because they encourage composers to balance repetition anc contrast effectively.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a melody

nodes.misconception: Using new ideas in every bar is the best way to compose a melody
nodes.response: Finding a balance of repetition and variety is usually more successful as it helps the melody become memorable.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Melodic fundamentals

nodes.misconception: A melody must be completely conjunct.
nodes.response: This is not true - great melodies often use disjunct movement. However, when learning to compose melodies, sticking to mostly conjunct movement and small intervals helps them to sound melodic.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining melody and harmony

nodes.misconception: Using chord inversions for every chord will make the chord sequence more interesting.
nodes.response: Using some inversions can make the chord sequence more interesting, but too many can sound unusual. Starting and finishing with a root position chord can help to reinforce the key.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a chord sequence

nodes.misconception: Secondary chords shouldn't be used.
nodes.response: Secondary chords are important for interesting harmony and using them is a good idea. As you become a more experienced composer, you'll learn how to effectively use them. For now, a good rule of thumb is to use them sparingly.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a chord sequence

nodes.misconception: The main thing I need to remember for long-form answers is the elements acronym (e.g. MAD T SHIRTT).
nodes.response: These acronyms do help us to remember what the elements are, but it is much more important in these longer descriptions to ensure answers are clearly structured, thorough and concise, and that correct technical vocabulary is used for each element.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing unfamiliar music

nodes.misconception: Choosing elements to discuss is just a case of thinking of the easiest ones to talk about.
nodes.response: While this might seem like the best option, it is more important that you choose elements that are relevant to the question. Remember, always link your points back to the purpose of the music, or to the style that they are part of.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Choosing elements and comparing music

nodes.misconception: A description of timbre should only describe the sound qualities heard.
nodes.response: While this should be included, it is also important to remember to describe the instruments that have been used, and if they from a particular ensemble. Remember that one instrument can also create multiple timbres.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing rhythm, tempo, timbre articulation and dynamics

nodes.misconception: Harmony and tonality are the same thing.
nodes.response: They are related, though not the same. Tonality refers to the set of notes that a piece is based on (e.g. the D minor scale) and refers to a whole piece or section of a piece. Harmony explores individual chords, chord sequences and harmonic devices.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Describing melody, harmony, tonality and texture

nodes.misconception: When describing music, just describing each element is enough.
nodes.response: For some questions, it may be appropriate just to describe each element. However, often we should give a more sophisticated response that links each element to the compositional purpose - why did the composer use that and why is it suitable?
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing musical purpose

nodes.misconception: There is a fixed and correct finger pattern for performing keyboard pieces.
nodes.response: With pieces that require a dexterous hand postition change, there are often several options. Encourage pupils to find a comfortable solution. Show examples of good keyboard technique that allows them to perform more difficult melodies with control.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: How music shapes film

nodes.misconception: A leitmotif and a film theme are the same thing.
nodes.response: Not quite. Many films have themes that represent the overall mood, and can be heard throughout the film. The difference with a leitmotif is that it explicitly represents one thing - a character, place or an idea.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing characters through music

nodes.misconception: Simply changing the instrument makes a leitmotif change mood.
nodes.response: While it does have an impact, changing other elements can make this even greater. Harmony, rhythm, dynamics, articulation and tempo are particularly useful for motivic transformation.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Motivic transformation

nodes.misconception: Music for films is always recorded and played through speakers.
nodes.response: Before technology existed to do this, film music was played live by performers in the room. It would often be a solo piano/organ player, who would improvise along with the film. Sometimes, ensembles such as orchestras would play music live instead.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Action in early movies

nodes.misconception: When a piano player plays music with a silent movie it is always completely improvised.
nodes.response: While they improvise many aspects, they often use specific musical ideas to create specific effects. This includes vamps, certain chords (e.g. diminished 7th for tension) and musical clichés like the misterioso that create certain effects.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Scoring a silent movie

nodes.misconception: A diminished seventh chord is just like any other extended chord - a triad with added notes.
nodes.response: A diminished seventh chord is quite unique as every interval is the same size (three semitones). It is different from extended chords that add notes to a triad. It has been used for centuries as a tense, dramatic chord, including in silent movies.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Tension in early movies

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the dongo and doko strikes and comfortably swapping from one to the other.
nodes.response: The dongo is a shuffle feel, whilst the doko and kara are even beats. Practise alternating from one to the other so pupils can recognise them easily and can comfortably swap from one to the other in a performance.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Taiko performance

nodes.misconception: The movements and shouts are not related to the pulse and rhythm.
nodes.response: The movements and shouts, just like the drum strikes, are rhythmically important. Reinforce the pulse when teaching the movements, shouts and strikes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The key principles of taiko

nodes.misconception: All the elements have to be achieved perfectly in order to produce a successful taiko performance.
nodes.response: There is a lot to consider when putting the performance together. Focus on playing and moving together with repeated ideas to start with. Working as a team and getting the count in and stance right is important to support the rest of the performance.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Taiko composition

nodes.misconception: Taiko is the name of the style.
nodes.response: Taiko is Japanese for 'drum' and the drums make up kumi daiko which is ensemble drumming.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Context and terminology of taiko

nodes.misconception: The solo section has to be made up in the moment.
nodes.response: The solo section can use ideas that are already planned. This is a good starting point for adding solos to build confidence and then build up to doing improvised ideas.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Kuku - structure and solo parts

nodes.misconception: Swapping comfortably and accurately from one rhythm to another with the overall structure.
nodes.response: This is quite tricky as the strucutre is complex. Break it down for pupils so they learn each section comfortably and encourage them to practise going from one rhythm to the next and think about strategies for remembering the rhythms.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Warabadon - djembe and dundun parts

nodes.misconception: You must use the given rhythms.
nodes.response: The rhythms used are variations on traditional accompaniments that are passed down orally across generations. At this stage, any rhythm can be used as a starting point for getting pupils making music but this example covers the required techniques.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Context and technique in West African drumming

nodes.misconception: The rhythm is the definitive version of the Kuku rhythm.
nodes.response: There are different versions of this piece from both Guinea and the Ivory Coast. There are also local versions within each of these. This version is a guide and can be adapted to suit your local context.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Kuku - djembe and dundun parts

nodes.misconception: Improvisation means making something up from nothing
nodes.response: You can use typical rhythms or features of the style as a basis oof any improvisation. This might mean using an establisehd idea such as a prepared triplet or syncopated rhtyhm and then extending the idea with something made up in the moment.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Warabadon - structure and solo parts

nodes.misconception: The bass line must have a different rhythm from the chords and percussion parts.
nodes.response: It can be appropriate for the bass line to use the same rhythm as another part. If it sounds effective then it is fine.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a bass line in a Brazilian song

nodes.misconception: All of the parts are necessary to make the project work.
nodes.response: Ideally pupils will record in all of the parts of the batucada, but the project will still work successfully with the core ensemble of surdo, caixa and repinique.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Polyrhythm in batucada

nodes.misconception: There is only one note that can be added to create a seventh chord, and likewise for a sixth chord.
nodes.response: There are various different types of sixth and seventh chords, which have different rules about how to form them. Here we are just learning the general principle of forming extended chords.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Extended chords in Brazilian songs

nodes.misconception: There are 'rights' or 'wrongs' in improvisation.
nodes.response: While there are rules that help us improvise effectively, a big part of learning to improvise is experimenting and seeing what works and what doesn't. Be willing to make 'mistakes' and don't fixate on doing it perfectly first time.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Improvising around a melody

nodes.misconception: The backbeat and off-beat are the same.
nodes.response: The backbeat is on beat 2 and 4 while the off-beat is on the second half of a beat (in between the beats).
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating an EDM drum beat

nodes.misconception: If a rhythm includes quavers it is syncopated.
nodes.response: This is a common misconception when first learning syncopation. Reiterate that a rhythm is only syncopated if the emphasis is in between the main beats. In practice here, that means that there will be a quaver rest at the start of a beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a syncopated EDM bass line

nodes.misconception: Adjusting EQ and/or dynamics is always musically beneficial.
nodes.response: Encourage students to use the DAW tools sparingly and reinforce the point that these tools are effective but that it is possible to overuse them. The analogy of seasoning on a meal - too much can spoil the meal - can be an effective one to use.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using DAW tools in an EDM remix

nodes.misconception: Having lots of layers of music playing simultaneously is effective use of texture.
nodes.response: It is easy to create a texture that is too thick and too busy. Encourage students to experiment with both thin and thick textures and reiterate that adding too many layers simultaneously can make music sound ineffective.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing texture and timbre in EDM

nodes.misconception: Mistaking F (or another note) for C and not understanding the impact this has on the finger prompts.
nodes.response: Reinforce 'C to the left of the two black keys', why F is a common mistake and the finger prompts only work if the C position is correct.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing a melody in the C position on the keyboard

nodes.misconception: Overdoing the emphasis on the first note of the bar and the music becoming stilted.
nodes.response: Play the pupils a non-example where the first beat is so strong it becomes unmusical and follow this with a good example.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing the melody: Ode to Joy

nodes.misconception: Pupils misinterpret the score and think the accompaniment is the second line of the melody.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to follow the score through when listening to the music and reinforce that both lines are part of the same system.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding an accompaniment to a melody

nodes.misconception: Rhythm and pulse in music are the same thing (particularly as there are a lot of crotchets used).
nodes.response: Pupils could clap/tap the beat with the audio examples to reinforce how it is different to the rhythm of the melody..
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing expressively: Ode to Joy

nodes.misconception: If the notes of a melody are changed, that just makes it a new melody.
nodes.response: Changing the notes of a melody does create a new melody, but if it is still recognisable as related to the original, we can consider it a developed version of the melody. If it is unrecognisable, then it is not a development but a totally new melody.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fundamentals of melody

nodes.misconception: If music has a key, it must be diatonic.
nodes.response: Not necessarily. A piece of music can have a key, but use notes from outside of it. This would be chromatic. It could also have a key, but use some microtones as well, meaning it is microtonal.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Tonality and intervals

nodes.misconception: Imitation and a countermelody are the same thing.
nodes.response: They are related, but not the same. Imitation has to include copying part of the melody, normally immediately. A countermelody usually tries to contrast with the main melody so that it can be heard clearly separately.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Other melodic devices

nodes.misconception: Chord IV and V sound the same, so plagal and perfect cadences sound the same.
nodes.response: They sound similar, but not identical. Picking out the bass note is the key - if you can hear that note, you can work out how it relates to the tonic, so can work out which chord (and cadence) you are listening to.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Chords and cadences

nodes.misconception: A modulation is when the chords don't use the tonic.
nodes.response: A modulation is actually when the tonic changes. Sometimes music can sound like it will modulate, but then it stays in the same key. For a true modulation, it must feel like the tonic itself has changed.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Harmonic devices

nodes.misconception: Changes between moods in a scene should always be sudden.
nodes.response: This is not always the case. Sometimes it is more appropriate to create a gradual change so that the shift isn't dramatically obvious. This might be where there is a gradual change of mood or action in a scene.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Scoring a film scene

nodes.misconception: Black notes are the same thing as chromatic notes.
nodes.response: This is not always true. Chromatic notes are any notes that are from outside of the key. If you are in C major, which only uses white notes, the black notes will be chromatic. However, in other keys the black notes might not be chromatic.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using harmonic devices in film music

nodes.misconception: All film music has to be precise to the second to fit the action perfectly.
nodes.response: Some film scenes do have to be exact where the music mirrors precisely what is happening on screen, but much film music is about creating the correct atmosphere and feel and this can be just as important when composing programmatic music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Matching music to action – using a storyboard

nodes.misconception: Chromatic and atonal are the same thing.
nodes.response: Atonal music sounds chromatic, because there is no clear tonal centre. However, chromatic music isn't necessarily atonal - a piece can be in a key, but use chromatic notes from outside of it.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Harmony and tonality in film music

nodes.misconception: Repetitive film music is not very interesting and can't build excitement.
nodes.response: Music that repeats ideas can build excitement if the composer develops aspects of it. By adding layers, changing rhythms and developing the texture, a simple repeated idea can be developed into an exciting musical soundworld.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using rhythm and texture in film music

nodes.misconception: Only advanced musicians can work out a set of notes by listening to them.
nodes.response: Anyone can work out notes by ear, if they practise the correct strategies. Identifying the melodic shape, representing it with a line, then carefully converting it into notes is an effective first step in melodic dictation.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying melodic shape

nodes.misconception: You can use the same verbalisation in compound time as simple time signatures.
nodes.response: This will create problems, because there are 3 quavers in each beat in compound time. The counting method in compound time avoids confusion by ensuring there are three quavers in each beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: More complex rhythmic dictation

nodes.misconception: Longer note values (like minims) are impossible to verbalise, because the words sound the same as a crotchet.
nodes.response: Longer note values are tricky to verbalise. A minim uses one syllable, just like a crotchet. The key is to make sure you count how many beats they last for - that will help you tell the difference between crotchets, minims and longer notes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying rhythms

nodes.misconception: Singing is only useful for singers.
nodes.response: When identifying intervals, singing is incredibly useful, even for those who aren't confident singers. Hearing the intervals back through singing or humming allows us to compare them to the reference melodies. Without this, it is much harder.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying intervals

nodes.misconception: Working out the notes of a whole melody by ear is a very difficult musical skill.
nodes.response: While it seems challenging, if you break it down into small steps - individual intervals - it is no more difficult than working out one interval. Take it one step at a time in small chunks and it is completely achievable.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing pitch dictation skills

nodes.misconception: Synthesisers are most effective for melodic lines.
nodes.response: Different types of synthesiser suit different musical roles. While synth leads are very effective for melodic lines, synth pads are well-suited to playing accompaniments, particularly sustained notes and chords.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Recreating As It Was by ear

nodes.misconception: Bass parts are normally simple and just play the lowest notes from the chords.
nodes.response: In some cases this is true, but in many cases bass lines are interesting patterns and can often be defining features of songs. This is true for both Under Pressure and Feel Good Inc.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Working out iconic bass riffs

nodes.misconception: Only highly skilled and naturally gifted musicians can work out music by ear.
nodes.response: Anyone can work out music by ear. It just takes practice and is made easier through use of effective strategies, including working out rhythm and pitch separately, and identifying individual pitches through trial and error.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Recreating Old Town Road by ear

nodes.misconception: All drum grooves have exactly the same rhythms in the kick, snare and hi-hat.
nodes.response: Many typical drum grooves do have the same features or features very close to this, however encourage pupils to identify where there are subtle differences and how the kick, snare and hi-hat patterns can be varied within these features.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Recreating Blinding Lights by ear

nodes.misconception: The C blues scale can use any of the black notes (flattened notes) on the keyboard.
nodes.response: The blues scale uses specific flattened notes - 3rd, 5th and 7th. It's important for pupils to practise finding these notes and getting used to how the scale sounds.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The blues scale

nodes.misconception: Any notes will work for improvising
