nodes.response: Find the balance between developing confidence in improvising and quality of musical ideas. Encourage pupils to think about the choice of notes, repetition, returning to a main note etc, as well as trying ideas and reflecting on what they sound like.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating an idiomatic blues performance

nodes.misconception: Playing the sequence incorrectly, particularly missing the final F in the sequence.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to learn the chord structure from memory and to think in 4-bar phrases. Highlight the last phrase specifically which has two chord changes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Blues music and the 12-bar blues

nodes.misconception: Improvisation means the notes are chosen at random.
nodes.response: Although improvising means making music up on the spot, it is based on a set of notes or scale and can use repetition. Improvisation often uses fixed stylistic characteristics such as particular rhythms, phrase structures and chord sequences.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Building an improvisation

nodes.misconception: All instruments have a fixed role and only the drums drive the music forward.
nodes.response: The guitar and piano can be melodic as well as accompanying. Different instruments can drive the music forward, and all players in the ensemble are responsible for this.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of the instruments and the bass pattern

nodes.misconception: Any note of the boogie-woogie pattern can rise and fall.
nodes.response: Whilst there are different variations of boogie-woogie, it is important that pupils keep the root the same and the 5th of the chord rises and falls.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Boogie-woogie

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to record their new ideas into one of the pitched instrument tracks.
nodes.response: Demonstrate this error before they have time to improvise new ideas.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating variation to a fundamental drum groove

nodes.misconception: Misunderstanding the meaning of acoustic because the lesson examples are played on an iPad/computer.
nodes.response: Make it clear that the iPad/computer is imitating acoustic sound.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Synthesized drum sounds

nodes.misconception: Pupils start playing on the snare because they are used to reading left to right.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the kick is the start because it is central within the drum kit.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of the kick and snare in drum grooves

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the metronome matches the rhythms they play, since they previously played crotchets.
nodes.response: Pupils should play a metronome beat while the class claps quavers to highlight the metronome shows the pulse by clicking on the beats of the bar.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of the hi-hat in a drum groove

nodes.misconception: There are no 'rules' for writing a chord sequence.
nodes.response: While to some extent this is true, in Western classical music there are very typical patterns that are used very regularly. These include the position of perfect and imperfect cadences, and what the chords do throughout the 16 bars.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a 16-bar melody

nodes.misconception: Only 3rds, 5ths and octaves work as disjunct intervals in a melody.
nodes.response: This is not true: all intervals (except sevenths) can work effectively, as long as they jump between chord tones. If intervals jump to or from non-chord tones, the melody will sound ineffective.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing effective melodies

nodes.misconception: You should use root position chords sparingly because they sound uninteresting.
nodes.response: Not necessarily. Root position chords are important because they anchor the music in the key. Most chords in a chord sequence should be root position, with some inversions used to add interst and variety.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using chord vi and using the bass harmonically

nodes.misconception: As long as the chord tones in the chord are played, it doesn't matter how these notes are split between the 2nd violin and viola.
nodes.response: This does matter. The voicing of the chord makes a big difference to how it sounds. Avoiding large intervals between those instruments, and making sure that the chords aren't very low or high pitched makes them sound effective.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Arranging for an ensemble

nodes.misconception: A countermelody is just a type of accompaniment.
nodes.response: It is actually quite different from an accompaniment, because it should be equally as prominent as the main melody, whereas an accompaniment is not. An accompaniment is usually also based on repeating patterns, whereas a melody does not have to be.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing an ensemble composition

nodes.misconception: The accompaniment part is semibreves throughout.
nodes.response: Two bars of the accompaniment is in minims. Encourage pupils to practise this bar specifically on its own when putting both hands/parts together.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing the accompaniment for Going Home

nodes.misconception: The string instruments can only be identified by pitch. The woodwind instruments are made of wood.
nodes.response: The pitch of the instruments does overlap slightly, so it's important to emphasise that the timbre of each instrument is slightly different. Most woodwind instruments were originally made of wood but the flute and the saxophone are now made of metal.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The string family and the woodwind family

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mistake another note for F when changing position.  Brass instruments can only be identified by pitch.
nodes.response: Reinforce that F is to the left of the three black keys; this has to be correct for the finger prompts to work. The ranges of the brass instruments overlap, so it's important to emphasise that the timbre of each instrument is slightly different.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The brass family and playing in the F position

nodes.misconception: Both hands change position at the same time
nodes.response: Highlight to pupils that the left hand remains in the C position even though the right hand moves to the F position and back again.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing the melody and accompaniment for Going Home

nodes.misconception: Mistaking another note for F when changing position quickly. The timpani are untuned percussion because they are drums.
nodes.response: Reinforce that F is to the left of the three black keys. Highlight that the timpani are tuned to specific pitches.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The percussion family and performing the full melody

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the number prompts but not find the correct C position on the keyboard.
nodes.response: Reinforce the position of the note C on the keyboard and ensure the pupils are sitting to play comfortably in the C position.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing an orchestral melody in the C position

nodes.misconception: A tone row is just a scale.
nodes.response: A tone row is different because it isn't just a set of notes to choose from, but a specific order. When you are composing something in C major, you can use the notes of the C major scale in any order. With a tone row, they have a specific order.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a tone row

nodes.misconception: Different voice types cannot sing any of the same notes.
nodes.response: The ranges of voices overlap, so there are some notes that can be sung by different voice types. For example, many notes that a bass can sing are also possible for tenor voices to sing.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing for voices

nodes.misconception: Retrograding breaks the rules of serialism because it changes the order of the notes.
nodes.response: Serialist composers don't consider retrograding breaking the rules. It does change the order, but the new order is still closely linked to the original tone row (by being reversed). It is therefore an acceptable and musically interesting technique.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a serialist composition

nodes.misconception: The human voice can only produce one note at a time.
nodes.response: Every sound we make has multiple different notes, its just that the main note is much louder than the others. Think about when you have a croaky voice - it almost sounds like multiple notes, because it is! Multiphonics just amplify the quieter notes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the voice creatively

nodes.misconception: Samples are always non-musical sounds.
nodes.response: This is not true - a sample is any pre-existing sound that is used in a new way. This could be traditionally non-musical sounds like machinery or speech, or it could be clips of pieces of music or individual notes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using samples

nodes.misconception: Only musical instruments (and voices) produce pitched sound.
nodes.response: Pitched sounds are everywhere. In fact, most sounds have a pitch, it is often just hard to hear it. You can probably hear a pitched sound now if you listen closely - electrical buzzing, distant speech, weather or animals all produce subtle pitches.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a sample-based composition

nodes.misconception: If the bass stays on the same note, this is a pedal.
nodes.response: This is not quite true. It is only a pedal if the bass note stays the same while the chords change above it. If the chords do not change, it cannot be a pedal.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The development of rock in the 1970s

nodes.misconception: Blues is an old style of music that isn't relevant anymore.
nodes.response: While it's true that blues first developed more than a century ago, it continued to be an important style all through the 20th century and up to the present day. It shaped many different styles (including rock) that came to be incredibly important.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The origins of rock: blues into rock ‘n’ roll

nodes.misconception: Because rock 'n' roll often uses the 12-bar blues, this means it is just a type of blues.
nodes.response: Many styles use the 12-bar blues, including pop, rock, jazz and other styles. While rock 'n' roll is closely related to blues, its defining features are quite different, and its role as a commerical pop style is far from the origins of blues.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The origins of rock: rock ‘n’ roll

nodes.misconception: Unison and homophonic textures are the same thing and unison parts have to be played in the same octave.
nodes.response: In a unison texture, both the pitch and rhythm of the part must be the same. In a homophonic texture, only the rhythm needs to be the same - the parts can play different notes or chords. Parts played in octaves are also classed as a unison texture.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fundamentals of rock

nodes.misconception: A solo should just use as many fast notes as possible.
nodes.response: To be really effective, a solo should gradually build up in intensity. If it is extremely virtuosic from the beginning, it loses its impact. Building up to a very flashy, virtuosic climax is most effective.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The guitar solo in rock music

nodes.misconception: Adjacent white notes on the keyboard are all a tone apart.
nodes.response: Most of the adjacent white notes are a tone apart but because of the pattern of the black notes on the keyboard some of the adjacent white notes are also semitones. It's important for pupils to count the notes to work out an interval.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing a melody with sharps

nodes.misconception: Sense of pulse and sense of rhythm are the same thing
nodes.response: A sense of pulse is understanding the underlying beat in the music. A sense of rhythm is understanding where the stress should be in a bar or rhythm. This is much more nuanced. At this point, encourage pupils to stress the downbeat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning the accompaniment for Fur Elise

nodes.misconception: When we refer to the A section of a piece of music (in relation to structure) they have to be exactly the same.
nodes.response: Letters are used to describe sections overall but quite often there are slight differences. Use some common examples of songs pupils will know of where sections might be labelled the same piece of music, but where there are small differences.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing hand positions in the middle of a phrase

nodes.misconception: Related keys are those with the same home (tonic) note such as C major and C minor.
nodes.response: Related keys are those with the same notes, but a different home (tonic note). Major and minor scales have different tone and semitone patterns, so they need to start three semitones apart for the notes to be the same.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fur Elise reimagined

nodes.misconception: The accompaniment patterns for section A and section B are the same and the best way to practise is to play from the start to the end of the piece repeatedly.
nodes.response: The accompaniment pattern changes slightly in section B. Highlight the difference so pupils are sure of this when practising hands together. It's more efficient to identify and practise the difficult bars in isolation first.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing fluency in changing hand positions on the keyboard

nodes.misconception: The more rubato you use the more expressive the performance
nodes.response: Rubato affects the tempo and pulse of a piece so needs to be used with subtlety. Show various examples of how Fur Elise might be played by different performers so pupils can see the variety of ways rubato can be used.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning the middle section of Fur Elise

nodes.misconception: Harmonic rhythm means the rhythm that each chord plays.
nodes.response: Harmonic rhythm means how often the chords change, not the actual rhythm that the chords play. Show examples of the same harmonic rhythm different rhythms in the chords. Changing the harmonic rhythm is a useful tool to alter the feel of music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrast in grunge

nodes.misconception: Singing a melody is only possible if you are a very strong singer.
nodes.response: Everyone can sing, but keeping to a small range of notes can help when building confidence with singing. Singing helps us to internalise the notes and really 'feel' the melody. Melodies can sound much more natural when sung.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The intro, outro and vocal melodies

nodes.misconception: Not everyone can write a good melody.
nodes.response: Writing a melody is just like writing a paragraph. Break it into small chunks (phrases). If you are finding it difficult to create a phrase, keep it simple and start by just improvising using 2 or 3 notes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Writing an instrumental melody

nodes.misconception: Power chords are any two notes of the chord triad.
nodes.response: For a chord to be a power chord it has to be the root and the fifth, not the root and the third. It also needs to be a perfect fifth. If pupils are working out their own power chords on the keyboard, some chords would use the black notes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Riffs and power chords in grunge

nodes.misconception: Rock is a specific, narrow genre in itself.
nodes.response: Rock is a very broad term for lots of different musical genres, spanning a wide range of influences and using very different musical features. There are many sub-genres of rock, including grunge, punk rock and heavy metal.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The use of the drum kit in grunge

nodes.misconception: Drum fills have to be complex and use lots of different parts of the drum kit. The tom-toms can be played in any order.
nodes.response: Drum fills can be effective using only one or two parts of the kit, such as the snare and kick. The key is that they have a distinct rhythm that separates them from the main drum groove. When using the toms, they should be played from high to low.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fills and variation in grunge drum beats

nodes.misconception: Female voices are always higher pitched than male voices.
nodes.response: While this is mostly true, alto and tenor ranges overlap. A low alto voice can be as low as a tenor. Alongside this, men can use the falsetto technique to sing much higher than their normal range, in some cases higher than female voices.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Vocal types, styles and techniques

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to memorise the timbre of all of the different instruments around the world.
nodes.response: Yes, it would be impossible. However, learning to identify some of the key instruments is valuable - these are often heard in styles across different cultures, so learning the sound of the most common is important as a well-rounded musician.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Timbre around the world

nodes.misconception: Music technology consists solely of DAWs and computer-based technology.
nodes.response: For modern musicians, computer-based tools such as DAWs are a brilliant way of using technology. However, music technology is much broader than this - synthesisers, amplification, turntables and drum machines are just a few examples.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The sounds of technology

nodes.misconception: Instrumental timbres in families can be identified with pitch.
nodes.response: This isn't always the case. Instruments such as the trombone and French horn have a similiar pitch and the oboe and cor anglais pitch ranges cross over, so it's important that pupils think about the timbres to identify instruments correctly.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding timbre: Western sounds

nodes.misconception: Homophonic and melody and accompaniment textures are the same thing.
nodes.response: Melody and accompaniment is a specific type of homophonic texture, often called melody-dominated homophony. This is different to a chordal homophonic texture. To avoid confusion, it is easiest to treat melody and accompaniment as a separate texture.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding texture

nodes.misconception: The pentatonic scale is limited to one octave on the instrument.
nodes.response: The pentatonic scale is just the names of the notes that we can use. You can use them as high-pitched notes or low-pitched notes on your instrument. Experiment with playing the scale up high and down low.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a melodic ostinato

nodes.misconception: Using the same rhythm in different ostinati creates effective contrast.
nodes.response: Using different rhythms in your ostinati is important for creating contrast. If they use the same rhythm, they will inevitably sound very similar. Try coming up with some interesting rhythm by clapping, then play them using notes on the keyboard.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating and improvising contrasting ostinati

nodes.misconception: Complicated rhythms will sound more interesting.
nodes.response: Often creating simpler rhythms is more effective. In particular, rhythms that have rests (silence) in them can create a powerful contrast between sound and silence. Try using a mix of simple and complex rhythms.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Using rhythmic ostinati in minimalism

nodes.misconception: Lots of automation changes make the dynamics effective.
nodes.response: Doing lots of dynamic changes can sound chaotic and messy. Try to limit your use of automation so that changes are gradual and slowly change the dynamics.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing your minimalist composition

nodes.misconception: It is important to constantly create variety and change in a composition.
nodes.response: We have to balance variety and repetition. Too much variety makes a piece sound messy and incoherent, too much repetition and it becomes boring. Try to find a happy medium between repeating ideas and varying things (e.g. the texture).
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Arranging reggaeton

nodes.misconception: Any melodic idea that repeats is a hook.
nodes.response: It's a bit more complex than that. In some cases, whether something is a hook or not could be a matter of opinion, not necessarily true or false. A hook must be short, memorable, and repeated.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Hooks and samples in reggaeton

nodes.misconception: An interesting, developed dembow beat should be complex.
nodes.response: Often keeping things simple is more effective than complexity. Choose one or two of the suggested ways of developing your drum beat, rather than trying to add everything in.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The global reach of reggaeton

nodes.misconception: The tresillo ('triplet' in Spanish) uses three equally spaced notes.
nodes.response: The notes in the tresillo rhythm are not equally spaced. The third note is a shorter duration. Counting the semiquavers in a 3-3-2 pattern can help us space the notes correctly (1-2-3, 1-2-3, 1-2).
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The dembow beat

nodes.misconception: Syncopation always makes music sound more energetic and driving.
nodes.response: Syncopation can make a piece feel laid back by relaxing the timing to give a 'behind the beat' effect.  Syncopated rhythms often leave gaps between sounds, which can make the groove feel more spacious and less rushed.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing an extended melody in unison

nodes.misconception: Tall vowels mean singing louder or just opening the mouth really wide.
nodes.response: Although they do help with projection, tall vowels are not about volume, they’re about the vertical space inside the mouth. If the mouth is too wide horizontally (grinning), this can tense the jaw, leading to a strained tone.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning Gumama in unison

nodes.misconception: Good balance means the parts should be the same volume all the time.
nodes.response: There is a nuance to balance and we always need to listen to other performers in the ensemble to check we can hear them and particularly hear the lead line. In Gumama all parts are of equal importance so the parts are a similar volume.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning Gumama in harmony

nodes.misconception: To add shape to a melody, the emphasis will always be on the first note of the phrase.
nodes.response: This is not always the case. Quite often, when the first note of the phrase lands on the downbeat this is naturally where the emphasis falls, however, this is more about where the main beats are rather than where the phrase starts.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing the full song

nodes.misconception: You can fit any lyrics to a melody.
nodes.response: Lyrics or melody often have to be adjusted to fit each other. This can be because there are too many or too few words to fit in a phrase, or there are too many or too few notes to fit with the words. Trial and error is the best way to address this.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing a pentatonic melody

nodes.misconception: Folk music all sounds the same.
nodes.response: Many folk traditions have shared characteristics, primarily because of the way that the music was passed between generations, but folk music is incredibly diverse, and covers lots of different types of music from different cultures and times.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Characteristics of folk songs

nodes.misconception: Sea shanties are songs for pirates.
nodes.response: Many cultures based around the sea use songs to coordinate movement on boats. Sea shanties are one example of this, and were sung by many, including sailors and fishermen. Other traditional cultures had their own songs for this purpose.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing sea shanties

nodes.misconception: Folk dances and folk songs are different names for exactly the same thing.
nodes.response: Not necessarily. Many folk songs are for storytelling or other purposes, not dancing. Some folk songs are designed for dancing, which often have different features, including an upbeat tempo, strong pulse and rhythmic drive.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing a folk melody in two parts

nodes.misconception: Hand positions should only change at the start of new phrases.
nodes.response: This depends entirely on what notes are used. Sometimes, like in Korobeiniki, it is more useful to change hand position during a phrase. When doing this, we should always practise making it seamless, so there is no obvious change in sound.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Folk dance and the minor scale

nodes.misconception: The dorian mode is the same as a minor scale.
nodes.response: There is a slight difference, with one different note. All of the modes are closely linked to major and minor scales, but have slightly different notes that help to create different moods.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Modes and sea shanties

nodes.misconception: Diction (articulation) is just about clear pronunciation.
nodes.response: Articulation is also connected to taking suitable singing breaths. If breathing is poorly controlled, consonants can sound weak or unclear, and vowels lose focus. Good breath support allows the voice to stay energised through quick or complex lyrics.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a performance

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to listen  to each other at the end of phrases and changing from one part to another.
nodes.response: Explain where pupils finish the longer notes together. They may pick a lot of this up from listening, but reinforce the importance of this in a powerful performance. Rehearse the changes from section to section to develop confidence in this.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning the full structure of the song

nodes.misconception: When pupils take a big breath, they raise their shoulders.
nodes.response: A singing breath is from the diaphragm; the upper body and shoulders should remain relaxed.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing three independent parts

nodes.misconception: The balance is the same throughout a song.
nodes.response: The balance changes depending on the parts and texture. The melody line would usually be the most prominent part. In an accompaniment texture all parts are more likely to be equal. It's important to listen and be aware of the lead line.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Singing an ostinato accompaniment

nodes.misconception: Latin dance music all sounds the same.
nodes.response: Many of the styles of music from this region include similar features, such as syncopated rhythms, Latin percussion, Spanish lyrics etc. However, they all have distinct differences that allow us to tell the different traditions apart.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Salsa and merengue

nodes.misconception: Drum beats should emphasise the start of each bar.
nodes.response: Most pop and rock drum beats do this, but many other musical styles do not emphasise beat one. The one-drop beat starts with a rest on beat one, and emphasises beat two and four.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The development of reggae

nodes.misconception: Calypso, mento and soca are different versions of the same musical style.
nodes.response: Although they have superficial similarities, these are all distinct styles with different features and histories. Soca is strongly linked to calypso and can be seen as an offshoot of that style, but mento is a completely separate tradition.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Calypso, mento and soca

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the bossa nova clave and rumba clave with each other.
nodes.response: Break the bossa nova clave into its group of 3 and group of 2. Practise the '3' on its own, identically to the son clave. Then practise the '2' with the second note delayed by a quaver. Only once the two parts are separately learnt then combine them.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Samba, bossa nova and other Latin dance music

nodes.misconception: The 2:3 clave starts on the same beat as the 3:2 clave.
nodes.response: The 2:3 clave starts with a crotchet rest. Make sure when performing or recording this that you count 'rest, 1, 2' for the '2' section of the rhythm.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Latin percussion and the clave

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of accent.
nodes.response: The regular accent is the most common, but composers often indicate more specific articulation by using other accents such as marcato and sforzando. These can be difficult to distinguish by ear, but as a performer you should be familiar with them.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding dynamics and articulation

nodes.misconception: Idiomatic rhythms are rhythms that are only used in a specific style.
nodes.response: Idiomatic rhythms are rhythms that are typically associated with that style, but can also be heard in different styles. For example, while the skank rhythm is very idiomatic in reggae, there are many other styles that also repeat off-beat quavers.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Idiomatic rhythms around the world

nodes.misconception: Compound time signatures create more complex sounding music and aren't used often.
nodes.response: This isn't strictly true. Compound time signatures are extremely common, including in popular music styles. While the theory of them is slightly more complex than simple time signatures, to compose or play using them is not particularly difficult.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding metre

nodes.misconception: Tempo markings are a precise indication of speed.
nodes.response: Most tempo markings (like allegro) are a rough indication of the speed, but not an exact measurement. Composers usually leave it up to the performers to determine the exact speed. Often in modern music they will indicate a specific speed using BPM.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Fundamentals of rhythm and tempo

nodes.misconception: Polyrhythm and cross rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: They are related, but not the same. A polyrhythm doesn't necessarily have to create different senses of pulse - it can just have different rhythms playing together. A cross rhythm has to create different senses of pulse at the same time.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Other rhythmic concepts

nodes.misconception: The orchestra has only grown through the adding of more of the same instruments.
nodes.response: The number of players has increased, but the variety of instruments has also increased. Many different instruments have been added to the orchestra since the 1600s, including brass, woodwind, percussion and keyboard instruments.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The orchestra

nodes.misconception: Harmony and tonality are the same thing.
nodes.response: Tonality is to the type of notes and chords that are used (e.g. major). Harmony is the way the notes and chords are used within that key. Think of tonality as a language (e.g. English) and harmony as the word choice and order in a sentence.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Harmony and tonality in Western classical music

nodes.misconception: Most music in the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods was written for an orchestra.
nodes.response: Although a lot of the most famous music now is orchestral, it was much more diverse than this - composers wrote for many different ensembles, large and small. These included solo compositions, duets, trios, quartets, quintets and many others.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Music for small ensembles

nodes.misconception: Oratorios and anthems are essentially the same - they are both religious, with similar musical features.
nodes.response: Anthems often are a capella, whereas oratorios always have orchestral accompaniment. Oratorios are long pieces of music, consisting of numerous songs that tell a biblical story. Anthems are shorter songs that are used as part of a Christian service.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The voice in Western classical music

nodes.misconception: Music from the Romantic period is all about love and romance.
nodes.response: The word Romantic in the musical sense has nothing to do with love or romance, this was just the name given to the period. The music was often intense, emotive and dramatic, and might sometimes link to ideas of love, but it was very varied.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: An introduction to the Western Classical tradition

nodes.misconception: Toms are only used in fills. Use of the snare/claps/clicks will automatically be a backbeat.
nodes.response: Toms can be used in the main groove just less commonly than the kick/snare. For a backbeat the snare/claps have to play on beats 2 and 4.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Timbral contrast in an R'n'B groove

nodes.misconception: Any note that precedes a strong beat is an upbeat.
nodes.response: An upbeat sounds like it musically belongs to the strong beat. Find a good non-example in a melody or drum groove to show how an upbeat both precedes the strong beat and also creates emphasis, often due to following a rest.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The feel of the kick and snare in an RnB groove

nodes.misconception: You can play an open hi-hat all the way through the bar or anywhere in the pattern.
nodes.response: The hi-hat can be played open at any point, but it shouldn't be overused, and stylistically it works well on the last quaver or off the beat.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The role of the open and closed hi-hat in an RnB drum groove

nodes.misconception: Drum fills must be more complex than the fundamental groove.
nodes.response: Show how absence of sound can be as powerful as added sound by giving an example of the groove briefly stopping.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Phrases in drum kit writing and composing a fill

nodes.misconception: Changing the voicing of a chord is the same as changing the chord inversion.
nodes.response: They are not the same thing. The inversion of the chord is determined by which note is at the bottom (the root or a different note). The voicing is how the notes are spread above this - whether they are close together or far apart.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Texture in pop ballads

nodes.misconception: To create a good countermelody, you just need two melodies playing at the same time.
nodes.response: It's a bit more complicated than that. An effective countermelody has to contrast with the main melody, so that it can be heard. This is done by choosing an appropriate timbre and octave, and using the 'space' in the main melody.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a pop ballad to a climax

nodes.misconception: Chord inversions are inserted randomly by composers.
nodes.response: Chord inversions are used to add interest by bringing subtle amounts of tension to a chord and to create smoother transitions from one chord to another. They are not chosen randomly and are used sparingly to create a particular effect.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Pop ballads from the 1970s to the 1990s

nodes.misconception: Writing a vocal melody is the same as writing an instrumental melody.
nodes.response: Many of the same principles apply, such as phrase structure and using notes from the chords and the key. However, a vocal melody has to fit the natural rhythms and mood of the words well - we don't have to consider this with instrumental melodies.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Vocals in pop ballads

nodes.misconception: The main difference between the verse and chorus is the lyrics.
nodes.response: Although that is an important difference, the verse and chorus usually have contrasting moods. This is achieved by creating contrasting chord sequences, textures, rhythms and melodies, not just using different lyrics.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Later developments in pop music

nodes.misconception: South Asian (or Indian) music is a genre itself.
nodes.response: South Asian music is as diverse as European music. There are many different styles linked to different groups of people, places and traditions. What we are looking at here are a few ways that South Asian genres have been fused with Western genres.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: South Asian and Celtic musical fusions

nodes.misconception: Afrobeat and Afrobeats are the same thing.
nodes.response: Afrobeat is a specific genre from the 1960s/1970s based on a fusion of West African music with funk and soul. Afrobeats is a broad term for many modern genres that are different fusions from across the continent, but have a few common features.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Musical fusion in the Americas and Africa

nodes.misconception: The Punjab is part of India.
nodes.response: The Punjab is an area split between modern-day India and Pakistan. It has a distinct history, culture and traditions as a region, one of which is bhangra.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The origins of bhangra

nodes.misconception: Bhangra is a style of music from South Asia.
nodes.response: Bhangra in its modern form is an example of musical fusion, between Punjabi traditional bhangra and Western popular styles of music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Bhangra as fusion

nodes.misconception: Bhangra is a traditional style of music that doesn't use music technology extensively.
nodes.response: Modern bhangra uses many of the tools that are available to musicians now, including different applications of music technology. It uses these to enhance the music, while still having its roots embedded in the traditional features of Punjabi bhangra.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing bhangra

nodes.misconception: Sudden tempo changes do not work in horizontal resequencing.
nodes.response: Sometimes tempo changes can sound jarring and unnatural, but sometimes video game composers want to create a sudden change of pace. If done carefully, tempo changes can work effectively.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Arranging and analysing video game music

nodes.misconception: In horizontal resequencing, new musical sections should completely contrast with the preceeding section.
nodes.response: There should be contrast, but there also needs to be a feeling of continuity. Using some consistent features (like tempo, key, timbre) can help to create a feeling of some continuity, while still creating a large contrast.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Horizontal resequencing

nodes.misconception: Video games composers just have to compose different music for different scenes, like a film composer.
nodes.response: To be really effective, it is more complex than this. The music they compose must be able to repeat indefinitely, while sounding musically interesting. It also has to seamlessly transition into different moods, reacting to changes in the action.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The development of video game music

nodes.misconception: Complex music sounds most exciting and energetic.
nodes.response: Not necessarily - sometimes the most energetic music is that which emphasises the pulse and uses driving rhythms. Sometimes if music is too complex, with many busy layers of sound, it can sound chaotic and messy rather than energetic.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a video game theme

nodes.misconception: Reharmonising a melody is as simple as playing it a third higher.
nodes.response: While this can be effective, for certain melodies this won't work effectively. Instead, experimenting with the harmonised melody both above and below the main melody is key, as well as experimenting with 3rds and 6ths.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Vertical layering

nodes.misconception: Teental is in 4/4.
nodes.response: Teental sounds to us like it could be in 4/4, but this is just a coincidence. North Indian classical musicians don't think of time signature in the same way that we do - the tala is what structures the time and they can be many different lengths.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Voice and rhythm in North Indian classical music

nodes.misconception: A raga is just a scale.
nodes.response: A raga is a bit more complex than being just a scale. It has specific times of day, moods and emotions associated with it, as well as rules about how it should be played.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Melody and timbre in North Indian classical music

nodes.misconception: A cross rhythm is when two players play in different time signatures.
nodes.response: A cross rhythm only sounds like there are different time signatures at the same time, but in reality they both use the same time signature (but sound otherwise).
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to West African percussive music

nodes.misconception: Dance music is usually in 4/4.
nodes.response: While the majority of modern Western dance music is in 4/4, dance music around the world (and throughout history) often uses different time signatures, including 3/.4, 6/8 and 12/8, as well as others.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Delving deeper into West African percussive music

nodes.misconception: The alap - gat - jhala structure is just about changes in tempo from slow, to medium to fast.
nodes.response: While the tempo does change, the bigger changes are around melody. The alap explores the raga freely, the gat is more structured and the jhala is heavily improvised and virtuosic.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Structure in North Indian classical music

nodes.misconception: Each period had a single defining texture (e.g. Baroque = polyphonic).
nodes.response: There were typical uses of texture for each period. For example, Baroque composers often used polyphonic textures, much more than Classical composers. However, within each period, there were examples of all textures being used and lots of variety.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Texture and harmony across the eras

nodes.misconception: Sonata form and a sonata are the same thing.
nodes.response: This is a common misconception. Sonata form is a structure in a piece that has a exposition, development and recapitulation. A sonata is a three-movement composition for solo instrument. The first movement of a sonata is normally in sonata form.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The Classical period

nodes.misconception: Non-functional harmony sounds the same as functional harmony.
nodes.response: While some of the chords might be the same, the difference is in the role. In functional harmony, chords have specific roles (e.g. V coming before I to create resolution). In non-functional harmony, any chord can be used whenever the composer wants.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Classical music in the 20th century

nodes.misconception: Romantic music is related to love and romance.
nodes.response: This is not the case - the name is not related to that. Romantic composers focused on creating expression, emotion and evocative moods in their music. Sometimes this would have links with love, but not always.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The Romantic period

nodes.misconception: All Baroque music is contrapuntal / polyphonic.
nodes.response: Textures are varied in the Baroque period, but use of contrapuntal/polyphonic textures was very common and contrasts with the later Classical period. This is a typical texture of the period, but not the only one.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The Baroque period

nodes.misconception: A piece of music has a fixed texture all the way through
nodes.response: Although we can describe some pieces of music as particular textures overall there are often sections within pieces where the texture changes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Experimenting with texture

nodes.misconception: Using disjunct intervals in a melody means the notes can be placed anywhere.
nodes.response: Disjunct intervals need a sense of order to the music and should be used in some sort of pattern in the same way that conjunct intervals should.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating a musical melody

nodes.misconception: Harmony and chords are the same thing.
nodes.response: Although the harmony is created by the different notes of the chord progression, harmony also includes all parts in the music including the melodic line.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative chord progressions

nodes.misconception: An instrument only has one timbre.
nodes.response: An instrument can have a few different timbres. Give examples of how instruments can change the sound they make.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring timbre and colour

nodes.misconception: To compose a rhythm we need to consider notation first.
nodes.response: It is important to encourage pupils not to be restricted by only rhythms they can notate and for them to experiment with rhythmic patterns that they like musically. Highlight that individual note durations such as a crotchet are not rhythms.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Composing rhythmic ideas

nodes.misconception: Piano concertos are just the same as other concertos.
nodes.response: Not quite. Because of the unique abilities of the piano - including its range and ability to play multiple lines at once - composers use it slightly differently to other instruments. This includes using it to accompany itself, or the orchestra.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The piano concerto through time

nodes.misconception: Cadenzas are always composed.
nodes.response: Many cadenzas are composed, but it is common for soloists to improvise (or slightly change) cadenzas to make them more unique and to further show off their own skill.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The concerto in the Classical period

nodes.misconception: A concerto grosso is exactly the same as a concerto, just with more than one soloist.
nodes.response: Because there is more than one soloist, composers can play around with texture and interaction more in a concerto grosso. This means that often there is more variety of interaction between parts in a concerto grosso than a solo concerto.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The concerto grosso

nodes.misconception: Melody and accompaniment is not a homophonic texture.
nodes.response: There are different kinds of homophonic texture. A chordal homophonic texture is one in which all parts play the same rhythm. Melody and accompaniment is also called melody-dominated homophony, where there is a homophonic texture with a melody above.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The baroque solo concerto

nodes.misconception: Romantic music is romantic (i.e. about love).
nodes.response: Romantic music is generally expressive and emotional, but is not necessarily linked to the emotion of love. The emotions can be anything from dramatic and terrifying to dark and mournful. The name comes from a broader artistic movement.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The romantic concerto

nodes.misconception: Broken chords have to be in the triad position where the root is the lowest note.
nodes.response: Broken chords like block chords can be played in different inversions and this can make them more interesting.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring texture and timbre

nodes.misconception: Sequence, retrograde and inversion are they only way to develop ideas and they have to be used perfectly.
nodes.response: Sequences, retrograde and inversion provide a concrete way for pupils to show development in their melodic ideas, but providing there is some similarity or recognisable quality in repeated ideas, any subtle changes within melodic ideas can work.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Making more of melodies

nodes.misconception: Contrasting sections should be totally different to other sections in a composition.
nodes.response: Contrasting sections of music can be derived from some of the same ideas but should have their own recognisable melodic and harmonic ideas.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Thinking about structure

nodes.misconception: Augmentation and diminution are not the same as augmented and diminished.
nodes.response: Augmentation and diminution are devices that affect the rhythm of music. Augmented and diminished are types of chords and refer to the harmony of music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Making more of rhythmic ideas

nodes.misconception: A pedal note is just a long, low note.
nodes.response: A pedal note is a consistent pitch usually in the bass whilst the chords change. Encourage pupils to listen to and experiment with the pitch they choose for a pedal to hear the effect it has on the harmony.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing chord progressions

nodes.misconception: The bouzouki sounds the same as a guitar.
nodes.response: The bouzouki has very specific techniques that give it its characteristic sound. These include use of tremolo, slides and thirds. Although these can be used on the guitar, they are not as common as on the bouzouki.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Melody in Greek folk music

nodes.misconception: Hand drum technique is the same across the world.
nodes.response: Techniques are very different on different hand drums around the world. Tabla, doumbek and djembe all use very different techniques, for example, the doumbek technique uses fingertips in a way that djembe does not.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: The instruments and rhythms of Palestinian folk music

nodes.misconception: There are only 12 possible notes.
nodes.response: There is an infinite possible number of notes. Imagine that an octave is a cake. We can divide it into 12 equal slices (12 Western notes) or 24 smaller slices (the Arabic system). In theory, we could divide it into any number of slices/notes.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Song, dance and maqam in Palestinian folk music

nodes.misconception: Israeli music is very similar to other Middle Eastern music because Israel is in the Middle East.
nodes.response: Israeli folk music has a very different history to other music from the region, as it was influenced by Jewish migrants from other parts of the world. Jewish folk music uses many European instruments and has similarities with European folk music.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Israeli folk music

nodes.misconception: Music for dance must have a regular pulse (in 2, 3 or 4).
nodes.response: While most Western dance music has a regular time signature, in other parts of the world it is common to dance to music with irregular time signatures, such as 5/8 and 7/8.
nodes.subject: music
nodes.lessonTitle: Understanding Greek folk music

nodes.misconception: Pupils disregard their tactics once they start playing the game, getting distracted by everything else that is going on in the game.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand their tactics and make an effort to use them during the game. Highlight and praise pupils that manage this.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Communicating to create tactics as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that leadership means being the boss and that they should be the only ones with ideas.
nodes.response: Leadership is about guiding and supporting others, not dominating. True leaders listen, include others and delegate responsibilities.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Leadership

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that teams are only successful if they score the most points or win against their opposition.
nodes.response: Scoring the most points or goals is one way you can measure success. Including all team members, playing fairly and improving are all equally important ways of being successful when competing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Collaborate effectively as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that effective communication only involves speaking clearly to someone.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that communication works two ways. Speaking clearly is important, however listening attentively is equally important to ensure the information is received.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Communication

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that all implemented tactics will always be successful.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that tactics don't always work and they may need to react quickly to adapt them.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create and use simple tactics through team challenges

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that all effective forms of communication are verbal.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that there are many different ways they can communicate through both verbal and non-verbal communication.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Communicating as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that after one attacking or defending move, their job in the team is finished and they stand still and stop following the play.
nodes.response: Often in a game, you will need to do some attacking work and some defending work.  Concentrating and reacting to the actions of others will help you to decide if you need to attack or defend.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dodging when attacking and defending

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they can only be a good team member if they score lots of points.
nodes.response: Scoring a point means everyone in the team has done their job well, not just the individual who scored.  Only some team members need to have the role of scoring points; doing your job well will help the team members whose job it is to score points.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dodging in teams

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that jumping competitions only focus on individual ability.
nodes.response: When we are competing as part of a team, our performance is a combined effort and everyone in the team can contribute in lots of different ways.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping competitions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that after agreeing a tactic, the team will be able to perform this tactic accurately every time and that when they do, it will always be successful.
nodes.response: Even when we make a great dodge into space and use a tactic, our opponents will react with a tactic of their own: this means that a tactic isn't guarenteed to be successful every time we use it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Where and why to dodge in game situation

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think they need to perform a dodge as soon as they see a defender.
nodes.response: Performing a dodge too early gives the defender time to react and move with you (shadow you).  Performing a dodge too late means you don't have space to use the best technique for your dodge.  The right timing will help you avoid the defender.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dodging in simple games

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that performing one dodge will always be successful.
nodes.response: Pupils should remember that the defender will respond to the dodge.  Pupils might need to dodge again if the defender guesses which way they will dodge and block their run into space or another defender might move into the space they are running to.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dodging

nodes.misconception: Some pupils could think that competitive games are only about scoring points and will focus on this role in a team.
nodes.response: Competitive games require attacking and defensive skills as well as team work, listening, communication, decision making, honesty, self-belief and more.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dodging in competitive games

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that their ability to jump far is fixed and cannot be changed or improved.
nodes.response: Everyone is capable of improving their performance. Practice, developing a good technique and showing self-belief can all help us to improve.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping combinations

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that jumping can only be performed in one way for one purpose.  For example, a half turn jump is used in gymnastics only.
nodes.response: There are lots of different jumping techniques which can be used in lots of different circumstances. Selecting the most appropriate jumping technique in a game can help you to be successful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Skipping and jumping in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it difficult to understand that this combination of three elements creates one jump that can be measured from the start of the hop, to the end of the jump.
nodes.response: When we combine elements into a hop, step, jump combination we can benefit from the power and momentum that builds up. By increasing the distance travelled in each element, we increase the overall distance covered in the jump combination.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping combinations: hop, step, jump

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that jumping is all about strength and do not consider the importance of coordination and technique.
nodes.response: The power needed for jumping high comes from the combined actions of a range of different body parts. The coordination of all these body parts creates a great technique for jumping high.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping higher

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think that jumping is a static action to be performed on the spot.
nodes.response: Jumping can be a dynamic movement that travels through space and can be linked in combination to gain momentum and speed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Linking jumping

nodes.misconception: Pupils move with limited or incorrect arm action such as punching their arms forwards. Pupils often run flat footed and look around at others while running instead of focusing forwards.
nodes.response: Tell pupils to run with pumping arms (pump backwards to propel forwards). Tell pupils to run with their head focused forwards and on the ball parts of the feet.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running

nodes.misconception: Pupils are confusing the techniques for hopping and skipping and sometimes run instead.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that running is a rule break. Celebrate pupils who are hopping not running and demonstrate both techniques.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hopping & skipping

nodes.misconception: Pupils run instead of hopping or skipping. Pupils get upset if points are being lost in games (beanbags are taken by the Zookeepers).
nodes.response: Remind pupils that running is a rule break and celebrate pupils who are hopping/skipping not running.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hopping & skipping in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils run instead of skipping to avoid being caught. Pupils don't follow the rules and take more than one piece of equipment at a time.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that running is a rule break and celebrate pupils who are hopping/skipping not running. Explain that this is a rule break and build in a consequence for this happening.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping in a game

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to use the correct technique for running fast. Pupils are slow to react.
nodes.response: Model the correct technique for running. Reiterate the importance of acceleration and give pupils another pupil to race against.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Accelerating when running

nodes.misconception: Pupils run out of the area to avoid being tagged.
nodes.response: Explain the consequences of running out of the area and the fact it will limit the points they score.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running in a competitive game

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus on wanting to go first in their team as opposed to their running technique. Pupils think success is all about winning.
nodes.response: Give each pupil a number and rotate who goes first to avoid the distraction. Challenge pupils to improve their own team's time instead of racing others to reinforce the point.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't land in a controlled way. Pupils don't focus forwards or use their arms when they jump.
nodes.response: Demonstrate an effective jump with a controlled landing. Explain and demonstrate jumping by swinging the arms up then down and while focusing forwards.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't land in a controlled way. Pupils do not use the correct technique for jumping. Pupils are distracted and jump looking at others.
nodes.response: Demonstrate an effective jump with a controlled landing. Demonstrate the correct technique. Reiterate the importance of jumping with heads focused forwards.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping far

nodes.misconception: Pupils will forget to use their arms and/or focus forwards when running into spaces. Pupils will run out of the area to avoid being tagged.
nodes.response: Explain and demonstrate running into space staying within the area. Explain the consequences of running off the court or pitch in a game. Model the correct technique for running and explain why it is important.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running in a game

nodes.misconception: Pupils fail to react to the commands as they aren't concentrating. Pupils run out of the space to avoid being caught by the sharks. Sharks give up when they can't catch a fish.
nodes.response: Remind pupils why it is important to focus in a game. Reiterate the consequences of running off the court or pitch in a game. Explain the importance of defenders stopping the attackers in a game and why we must speed up when we are defenders too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running at different speeds

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the techniques for leaping and jumping. Pupils focus on not being tagged and forget to jump or leap properly.
nodes.response: Demonstrate both techniques. Explain the importance of using the correct technique and demonstrate.  Bring in a rule that if pupils run instead of using their jumping skills, they have 'tagged' themselves and must stop and perform 5 star jumps.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping high

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that more space always makes an activity better or more challenging.
nodes.response: In reality, too much space can make games too easy or boring because pupils don’t have to use skills like dodging, teamwork or quick thinking to avoid others.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduce the STEP principle focusing on space

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that leadership means being the boss and that they should be the only ones with ideas.
nodes.response: Leadership is about guiding and supporting others, not dominating. True leaders listen, include others, and delegate responsibilities.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective leaders

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that the more equipment they use in an activity, the better the activity will be.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand how to use equipment to enhance the activity. Too much equipment can make it confusing and unsafe.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using equipment to adapt a task

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe talking loudly or shouting is how they should communicate as a leader.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that shouting instructions isn’t the same as giving clear, helpful directions. As well as this, good communication works both ways and leaders should allow their teammates opportunities to speak too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Communicating as a leader

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe when adapting a task that everyone needs the same level of challenge.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that everyone has different levels of skill, experience and confidence, therefore adapting a task should look to meet the needs of all the pupils engaging in it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Focusing on the task

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that adding more players and making the task bigger, makes it better and more enjoyable.
nodes.response: Too many players can mean some stand around and don’t get get chance to join in properly. Ensure the number of players, attackers and defenders is suitable for the task.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Organising people

nodes.misconception: When working in pairs, one pupil who is naturally faster moves ahead quickly from point to point, leaving their partner behind.
nodes.response: Both partners need to stay together so they can support each other with navigation and decision-making. If one person moves ahead alone, they miss the chance to communicate, plan effectively and succeed as a team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Collaborate effectively to complete a timed course

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the map the wrong way round, not matching it to their direction of travel, making it harder to locate points accurately.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils orient the map so it matches the direction they're facing. They must turn the map until the features on the map line up with what they can see around them.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Orientating a map to locate points

nodes.misconception: Pupils follow other teams assuming they’re going the correct way.
nodes.response: Highlight to pupils that orienteering is about independent navigation, and others can be wrong too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Following a set route using a map

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush off without planning a logical route, leading to wasted time or missed checkpoints.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils allow time to plan their route with their partner and that they understand the value in doing this.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Orienteering competition

nodes.misconception: When reading the face map, pupils misidentify the equipment, especially when differentiating between quoits and cones.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the key when looking at their map, rather than just looking at the objects on the face. This will help them to identify what each object represents.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduce maps working together

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that completing the course with speed is more important than completing it accurately.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of balancing speed with careful thinking and teamwork, to ensure pupils complete the course correctly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using a map to follow a route

nodes.misconception: Pupils can only stand when making letter shapes. Pupils create letter shapes back to front or they face the wrong way when they are showing others.
nodes.response: Pupils can use a range of body parts and lie, sit or stand to make letter shapes. Stress the importance of reading letters from left to right.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems by cooperating in pairs

nodes.misconception: Pupils shout at teammates when they make a mistake, causing teammates to be unmotivated and upset.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the importance of positivity and motivation, using kind and encouraging words.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems by working together to score points

nodes.misconception: Teams only take notice the ideas shared by the loudest team member.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to encourage all teammates to share ideas, so that everyone feels included, especially those who may not contribute often and remain quiet in the backgound of everything.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems with good teamwork in a challenge

nodes.misconception: Pupils shout instructions in an attempt to make themselves understood.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that using a calm voice will develop better trust and confidence in a partner.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems with communication and trust

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget the importance of clear instructions and get side tracked in just wanting to win or complete the task.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that using a calm voice and giving clear instructions will develop better trust and confidence in a partner, ultimately leading to success.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems using leadership and motivation

nodes.misconception: Pupils become too fixated on specific movements in their obstacle courses and become upset when others make adaptations.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of movement for enjoyment,and that adaptations are sometimes necessary so everyone can succeed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solving problems with a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils stand behind defenders when waiting to receive the ball. Pupils keep moving into space but don't look at the player with the ball to acknowledge they are ready to receive a pass.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to move to the side of the defender creating an angle for the pass. Support pupils to communicate (verbal and non verbal) when they are ready in a space.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine passing and receiving

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget who to mark, leaving some attackers unmarked and free to pass and move.
nodes.response: Pupils need to work as a team to agree who they are marking so they can apply pressure effectively.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending to stop an attack

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that once they have moved into a space, they can stay still and wait for the ball to come to them.
nodes.response: Pupils must be reminded to keep moving, creating angles for passes to the sides of their opposition. If they stand still, it makes it really easy for the defender to mark them.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing, receiving and creating space in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils give up if their team is not winning.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the more self-motvation, determination and  collaboration they show, the more likely they are to succeed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game application of attack and defence

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to take their time to pass and move and instead panic, rushing their passes and shooting far from the target.
nodes.response: Pupils need to have patience to support each other to pass and move towards the target, and shoot when in a suitable position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine passing, moving and shooting

nodes.misconception: Pupils recieve the ball and automatically try to shoot, regardless of their position on the pitch/court.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that their shots will not be successful if they don't give careful consideration to the position they are in before shooting.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine passing and moving to create shooting opportunities

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that balancing is only about staying completely still.
nodes.response: Activities such as riding a bike, skateboarding, surfing, throwing darts, basketball shooting, long jump etc., all need a well-balanced and controlled body position whilst the athlete is still moving.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Balance

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that coordination relates only to movement of their own body.
nodes.response: Coordination requires many different elements to work in combination. Improving balance, timing, ball tracking and the way we grip equipment can all contribute to improved coordination.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Coordination circuit

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that being able to sprint fast will always make them successful in a game or activity.
nodes.response: Being agile involves more than running quickly in one direction. Being on the balls of our feet, rotating our hips and using different footwork can help us to move quickly, react appropriately, and change direction so that we are successful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Agility

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that balance is a fixed skill that you are either good at or not.
nodes.response: There are many elements to balance: working on all of these elements contributes to overall improvement. Improving focus and concentration can help, along with developing muscular strength, proprioception and self-belief.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Balance circuit

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that working on our muscles means lifting heavy weights to make them big and bulging.
nodes.response: Healthy muscles don't need to be bulging muscles. They need to stay supple so they work well; they need rest so they don't get injured; they need to be used regularly so they don't become stiff.  This can all be achieved without lifting weights.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Agility circuit

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that being successful in sport relies on being able to run fast.
nodes.response: In many sports, having good coordination can be more valuable than speed or strength. Swimming, rowing, golf, skiing, rhythmic gymnastics, bowling and clay shooting all require coordination, but don't rely on speed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Coordination

nodes.misconception: Pupils panic when there is a defender and kick/strike/throw the ball away quickly to prevent the defender getting too close to them.
nodes.response: Explain that if we panic, we will probably lose possession in a game. Encourage pupils to take their time. Bring in walking defenders instead to slow the game down.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and receiving skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils mark the same pupil, leaving attackers open in space. Pupils swarm around and only mark the player with the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to communicate and ensure everyone is responsible for a different player. Remind pupils of the rule concerning marking. This rule is in place to enable the pupil in possession to look up and make effective passing decisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending and the concept of marking

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they are only successful if they hit a target.
nodes.response: Celebrate pupils for using the correct technique and for trying hard and provide demonstrations to support learning.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Scoring

nodes.misconception: Pupils will try and make a pass to score from too far away. Pupils run into the endzone boxes to receive a pass too early and are just standing still in the box.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to be closer to the scoring zones before trying to make a pass to score. Explain that if we just stand in the box, we aren't helping our team with a passing option.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and moving to create space

nodes.misconception: Pupils get frustrated if they aren't winning. Pupils panic and rush decisions around passing and shooting, focusing more on the competition.
nodes.response: Award points for pupils and teams that show respect and apply determination throughout. Encourage pupils to take their time and consider the options before passing or shooting so they don't lose possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking and defending in small sided games

nodes.misconception: Pupils stand still once they are in a space and just wait for the ball to come to them.
nodes.response: Explain that we must keep moving to find spaces to ensure our team always has several passing options. If we stand still, the defenders could intercept the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and creating space

nodes.misconception: Pupils turn without checking if there was actually space to turn into first. Pupils also turn when there is no need to.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to check for the space before they turn. Explain that we turn when we need to change direction to move away from a defender.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling to attack and  create space

nodes.misconception: Pupils just want to shoot and score. They forget to look up and check to see if they should pass or dribble.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that we only shoot when we are in a suitable position and should take our time to make decisions first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and passing to maintain possession and create scoring opportunities

nodes.misconception: Once in games, pupils focus too much on just wanting to shoot and to win. Pupils forget the importance of their tactics and that they need to stay focused on the task ahead.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on their tactics and to understand that it is the successful implementation of their tactics that will lead to success in the games.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attack vs defence

nodes.misconception: Pupils take strong touches of the ball and move with the ball too far away from themselves so lose control easily.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to take their time and keep the ball close to avoid losing control and possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and keeping control

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush in towards the player with the ball when defending. Often two pupils move towards the same attacker.
nodes.response: Pupils need to stay on their toes ready to react and avoid diving in. Communication will prevent players from marking the same player and risk leaving other players open.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Denying space

nodes.misconception: Pupils get frustrated when they lose possession and fail to carry out their defensive tactics.
nodes.response: Remind pupils how important it is to defend and try and stop the attack. If we give up, it's likely our opponents will score.
