nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Transition from defence to attack with a defensive focus

nodes.misconception: Pupils feel embarrassed to admit when they don't understand a tactic or don't listen when tactics are being discussed.
nodes.response: It is really important to encourage pupils to be honest if they don't understand so that their teammates can explain to them. Celebrate and praise pupils/teams who ensure everyone understands, and individuals who speak up when they need help.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking tactics in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils are deflated and lack self-motivation if their team does not have possession of the ball.
nodes.response: Get pupils to think carefully about the tactics and strategies that can be used to prevent the attack from scoring and help the defensive team regain possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defensive scenarios

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't discuss the benefits or potential problems of each tactic or power before making a selection that is right for their team at the time. One pupil takes over and rushes the decision making.
nodes.response: Explain that, for a tactic or power to have maximum impact and give their team a big advantage, they must discuss each option as a team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game application through competitions

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush when discussing their tactics as they just want to play the game. Not all pupils get to contribute to the team discussions.
nodes.response: Praise and celebrate teams who discuss their tactics thoroughly, ensuring everyone contributes and that everyone understands.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defensive tactics in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus only on winning instead of adapting their tactics to the game scenario.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils have time to plan their tactics in each scenario and highlight effective team work.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Possession scenarios

nodes.misconception: Pupils feel it isn't fair when their opponents use a tactic against them; they fail to see the importance of taking time to consider how they can use their own power to gain an advantage.
nodes.response: Celebrate teams who deploy their powers at the right time as a result of careful planning. Consider awarding bonus points for this, even if the execution isn't successful. Award points to teams who focus on their own powers and not the opposition's.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Application of 'powers' into game play to challenge tactical thinking

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise that during exercise, the depth of breathing changes as well as the speed per minute. Depth of breathing is a more abstract concept than how many breaths are taken per minute.
nodes.response: As well as taking more breaths per minute during exercise, a child will take deeper breaths each time. This is also a way for the body to get more oxygen.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Effect of exercise on our breathing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that sport and physical activity is all about competing and winning.
nodes.response: Moving and exercising is an important part of daily life, not just for organised competition. Exercising can be done for fun and is important to help our bodies and minds to stay healthy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Movement and exercise

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think exercising and physical activity are only focused on winning and being the best.
nodes.response: Exercising alone or with others can provide opportunities to have fun and try new things. Getting better at something or feeling energised can feel just as good as winning a game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Happy heart happy mind

nodes.misconception: Warming up is only needed for outdoor lessons and in the cold weather.
nodes.response: Warming up is a gentle and gradual way of getting the body and mind ready for exercise. Our bodies might not be ready for sudden, energetic movements even in warm weather or when we are indoors.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing games to make our heartbeat and breathing faster (warming up)

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that a fast heartbeat makes the body move faster rather than it being a response to exercise i.e. the heart acts like an engine and a fast heartbeat makes you run fast.
nodes.response: Your heartbeat usually changes because of an action or a feeling. When you do exercise, you need it to pump more blood to your muscles for energy so it changes its speed because of your exercising actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Effect of exercise on our heartbeat

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that success is only achieved by winning and being the best.
nodes.response: Success can be achieved in lots of different ways. You can be successful by improving your own performance (regardless of anyone else's performance), setting yourself a challenge and reaching a new target or working in cooperation with others.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing together to make our heartbeat and breathing faster

nodes.misconception: Pathways are only along the floor.
nodes.response: Pathways can be along the floor or in the air. They can also be called floor patterns and air patterns.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Space

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when performing mirroring duets they should remain on the spot.
nodes.response: Mirroring duets typically remain in situ (and may need to for safety reasons e.g. in a small space), but they should be encouraged to lean towards or away from their partner, as well as move sideways to prevent the work from becoming purely gestural.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: My moves: actions, space, dynamics and relationship

nodes.misconception: A performance needs to be on a stage, at a theatre.
nodes.response: Performing is where we show our work to another, it might be on a stage, but equally it can be a part of the lesson where we share ideas, thoughts and opinions so that we can all improve.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: My brilliant body: performing

nodes.misconception: Travelling is only a whole-body movement and involves moving around the space available.
nodes.response: Travelling can be either a whole body action or be performed by isolated body parts. As well as moving around the space it can also involve going up and down as well as turning on the spot.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions

nodes.misconception: There are only two speeds, slow and fast.
nodes.response: There are a wide range of speeds. We might think we can run fast, but a horse can run faster than us, a train can travel faster than a horse and an aeroplane can travel faster than a train.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dynamics

nodes.misconception: Mirroring and copying are the same
nodes.response: Mirroring is a type of copying, it specifically requires the movement to be translated to the opposite side of the body to produce the effect of a reflection. Copying can be a direct replication of the action.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Relationships

nodes.misconception: Pupils rely on copying others to get the steps right rather than learning the steps themselves.
nodes.response: Exaplain to pupils the importance of showing resilience and rehearsing to become more familiar with the actions, directions and patterns.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Strathspey: Scotland

nodes.misconception: Stamping is something we do when we are frustrated; it's not a dance action.
nodes.response: All actions can be used in dance. Stamping could be used to communicate frustration or could be used to add emphasis, make rhythmic sounds or show strength.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Clog dancing: England

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that pulse and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Explain that pulse is the steady, consistent beat that runs through the music and rhythm is the pattern of sounds.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Musical structure: Ireland

nodes.misconception: When you skip, you always travel forwards.
nodes.response: Skipping often involves travelling forwards, but it can also be performed on the spot or even travelling backwards.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Maypole dancing: England

nodes.misconception: When travelling around in the circle you should try to catch up with the duet ahead of you.
nodes.response: When travelling around in the circle you should aim to maintain the same distance from the duets in front and behind you.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Gay Gordons: Scotland

nodes.misconception: Emphasis in dance only means making actions bigger or more forceful.
nodes.response: Emphasis is adding stress or importance and can involve making actions bigger/more forceful or smaller/less forceful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Emphasis in dance: Ireland

nodes.misconception: You need to look at the floor to avoid the swords.
nodes.response: If working carefully, it is possible to remember where the 'sword' markings are and avoid them. This skill takes a great deal of practice.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sword dancing: Scotland

nodes.misconception: In dance, you count all music in 8's.
nodes.response: In dance, counting corresponds to the musical time signature which varies enormously. Many are 4/4 timing and can be counted in patterns of 4's or 8's, others may be in contrasting patterns such as 3/4 or 6/8, so would need to be counted accordingly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Irish Dancing: Ireland

nodes.misconception: When dancing a duet, you should always stay with the same partner.
nodes.response: Quite often, if dancing a duet, we stay with the same partner, but in some social dances we change who we dance with as part of the dance. This helps a community get to meet new people.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Barn dancing: England

nodes.misconception: Pupils often assume that using props like handkerchiefs or scarves simply means waving them in the air.
nodes.response: If using props such as handkerchiefs or ribbons in dance these can exaggerate the actions and add flow to the action. Whereas props such as sticks or swords can also add sound. Props often help to communicate the theme or origin of a dance too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using props in dance: Wales

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that all dance formations involve facing forwards, side by side.
nodes.response: In traditional dances, the performers typically look straight ahead, but the formations may involve people being side by side, one behind the other, in a circle or sometimes something different such as a star, a square or a double circle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing formations: Wales

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that contrast just means doing the opposite of someone else.
nodes.response: Contrast in dance means that you are doing something distinctly different, for example, performing different directions, levels and pathways to each other.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Contrasting dance: Wales

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can pass the ball forward. Pupils get confused with the meaning of passing the ball backwards and think that means passing over their head, rather then in relation to their attack.
nodes.response: Remind pupils of the rule that passes must go laterally or backwards, so the player receiving must not go ahead of the player in possession of the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and moving to create attacking opportunities

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget previously learnt rules and skills, leading them to chase after the ball instead of maintaining positions and structure.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that teamwork, communication, positioning and tactics can all lead to creating better chances, conceding less tries and scoring more tries.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Consolidate attacking and defending in mini games

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that when they implement a special power, they will always be successful.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of good passing and moving skills when pupils use their special power, to increase chances of success.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Application of 'powers' into game play to challenge tactical awareness

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe they can use physical contact to tackle or push their opponent.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that tag rugby is a non-contact sport and pupils can only tag their opponents or intercept a pass.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending as a team

nodes.misconception: Defenders believe they can, or they try to, take the ball when they tag an opponent.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the primary objective is to remove a tag from the ball carrier to stop their progress, rather than trying to take the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create and apply defensive tactics

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that when they use an attacking tactic it will always be successful.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that not all tactics work but they should continue to try hard and use a variety of tactics.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create, understand and apply attacking tactics in game situations

nodes.misconception: In dance we are pretending to 'be' the subject we are creating a dance about.
nodes.response: In dance we use the subject to help us think of movements that show what it is like. Pretending to be something is a drama skill that is used in some, but not all dance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather: gestures, turns, travel and jumps

nodes.misconception: Dynamics describes how fast an action is performed.
nodes.response: Dynamics involves both speed and force. Some words do mean speed, e.g. quick, whereas others only talk about force, e.g. strong. However some words might mean both, e.g. explosive would be both fast and strong.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Storms: speed and force

nodes.misconception: That dance performances do not include repetition of ideas.
nodes.response: Repeating movement material in a dance is similar to the use of a chorus in a song, it emphasises the main idea and prevents the audience from being overwhelmed. Repetitions are usually varied or developed in some way to maintain interest.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather conditions: performing as a duet/trio

nodes.misconception: A tall shape is only achieved by stretching both arms upwards.
nodes.response: Whilst stretching both arms upwards is an example of a tall shape, there are many others. These might include twists, tilts, balances etc. By encouraging the pupils beyond their initial response they will think more deeply and creatively.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sunshine and rain: size and levels

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that creating actions that communicate wind involves running fast for strong wind and walking slow for a light breeze.
nodes.response: We can create actions using changes in size, levels and direction including travelling and creating shapes to communicate wind.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Wind and clouds: travel and size

nodes.misconception: The pupils will only use their arms to communicate swirling snow.
nodes.response: Whilst arms offer a range of possible responses to suggest snow, guiding pupils to less conventional ideas such as a hip or an ear, pupils will respond with a far wider range of actions, building flexibility, control and coordination.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Snow and ice: contrast and mirroring

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can create a pathway by drawing the letter shapes in the air.
nodes.response: Drawing letter shapes in the air produces 'air pathways'. This lesson is focusing on 'floor pathways' which require the pupils to travel along the shapes of the different letters.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Curving, linear and irregular pathways: letters

nodes.misconception: Travelling sideways can only be performed by a side step.
nodes.response: There are many different ways to travel sideways, e.g. shuffling, stretching, wriggling, jumping.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Directions and levels: movement

nodes.misconception: Travelling around the room means you run in a circle. Pausing and balancing are always star shapes.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that travelling involves a wide range of actions including skipping, shuffling, marching, jumping, creeping. Also ensure pupils understand that we can balance on a range of body parts in a variety of shapes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Commas and full stops: pauses and stillness

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that a conversation only involves speaking aloud.
nodes.response: In dance, we can show a conversation by using our actions to represent the words being spoken. We can communicate the idea of dialogue without saying a word.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Question and answer: dialogue

nodes.misconception: A starting position only describes the shape you make.
nodes.response: A starting position involves both the shape you make, as well as the location. It refers to both what you do and where you do it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Location and level: paragraphs

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to make a certain shape (e.g. a wide star-shaped stretch for the letter 'X').
nodes.response: There are many possible responses - the shapes can be recreated using just part of the body or all of it. Changing between sitting, lying and standing is also an option as well as incorporating balances or jumps.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions: upper and lowercase letter shapes

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that prepositions are only used in writing.
nodes.response: Prepositions describe how things are arranged relative to other people or objects, so they can be used in all subject areas.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Formations and contrast: prepositions

nodes.misconception: Pupils create sequences and motifs that include long stops between actions as pupils fail or forget to use additional actions to aid transition.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that in order to create a sequence that flows well, we need to include addtional actions to support the transition from action to action.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A combination of actions: writing short sentences

nodes.misconception: Dynamics mean how fast or slow you perform an action.
nodes.response: Pupils think that dynamics only means how fast or slow you perform an action and forget that it is also about the force we apply.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dynamics: fronted adverbial

nodes.misconception: If working with a partner, you should always face them.
nodes.response: It can be helpful to face the people you are working with when you are deciding upon the actions you will perform. However, once you have created the action content, you can use different formations and arrangements to make the work more interesting.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dynamics: exclamation marks and fronted adverbials

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that powerful actions should be performed quickly.
nodes.response: Powerful actions can be performed at any speed. However, rushing and moving too quickly can make it difficult to control the actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Force: exclamation marks

nodes.misconception: Contrast has to be opposites.
nodes.response: Opposites are an excellent example of a contrast since they are completely different. However, there are others, e.g. to contrast 'up' you could use 'forwards' since it is a distinctly different direction.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Formations, contrast and question and answer: performing

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the curved side of their stick.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the flat side of their stick, rotating it when changing direction. Challenge pupils, but be lenient as they develop this difficult skill.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and control

nodes.misconception: Many pupils believe that the harder they hit the ball, the better their shot will be. This leads to a lack of accuracy and technique.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on using the correct technique and highlight the importance of accuracy over power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting in Hockey

nodes.misconception: Pupils hit the ball with both the flat side and the curved side of their stick.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they can only use the flat side of the stick and they lose possession if they break this rule.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Accurately passing and receiving

nodes.misconception: When defending and marking, pupils focus too much on the ball instead of watching their opponent.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to always be aware of the player they are marking by constantly checking where they are. Discourage pupils chasing after the ball when their teamate is closer to it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Denying space and defending

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can only dribble or pass and not effectively combine both, struggling to transition between the 2 actions.
nodes.response: Focus on the importance of both skills and how key decision making on when to use each action is vital.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and passing to maintain possession to create scoring opportunities

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that in a game the main role is to attack and score, forgetting about their defensive duties and stopping the opponents.
nodes.response: Highlight the value of both attacking and defending and encourage teams to work together.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attack v defence

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that learning to swim distances is more important than learning to rotate onto our backs.
nodes.response: Turning onto our back to float, and have the nose and mouth clear of the water, is an extremely important skill to learn as it means the airways are clear.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rotations whilst floating and travelling with coordination

nodes.misconception: When pupils lose their balance and fall forward into the water, they often instinctively try to place their hands onto the pool floor.
nodes.response: This significantly hinders pupils' ability to regain a standing position, often causing panic. Pupils should be taught how to regain a vertical position before, and at the start of, their first swimming lesson.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Entry and exits, travel, buoyancy and balance

nodes.misconception: Pupils keep their head away from the water.
nodes.response: Pupils should be made aware that if the face is in the water it is much easier for the legs to float.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Push and glides, streamlining

nodes.misconception: Pupils swim front paddle with their head out of the water.
nodes.response: Get pupils to lean forwards to ensure their chin or face is in the water.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Front paddle and floating

nodes.misconception: Pupils swim back paddle with a leg kick that is large, with the legs bending and the feet being low in the water.
nodes.response: The leg kick when swimming back paddle should be long and straight with small fast kicks which are near to or at the surface of the water.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Back paddle and floating

nodes.misconception: You must hold your breath and hold your nose when your face is in the water.
nodes.response: Perfrom trickle breathing; gentle continuous bubbles when the face is in the water.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Aquatic breathing, health and fitness

nodes.misconception: Pupils often swing their racket at the ball generating too much power when hitting a volley. Pupils hit the volley with their feet square to the net rather than side on.
nodes.response: The volley technique involves blocking the ball rather than swinging the racket back to hit the volley. Pupils should step into the volley so their bodies turn to the side when they hit a volley.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Volley

nodes.misconception: Pupils may switch hands if the ball is hit towards their backhand side rather than using two hands on the racket to hit the ball. Pupils may place their dominant hand at the top of the racket handle.
nodes.response: Pupils should keep their dominant hand at the bottom of the racket handle for control and place their non dominant hand at the top to play a backhand shot with both hands on the grip. Explain that the hand at the bottom provides the control.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduce backhand shots with a racket

nodes.misconception: Pupils are gaining points when they hit the ball into channels. This is only to practice creating space and pupils may think they score points in a game of tennis if they hit the ball into a channel.
nodes.response: It is important to provide pupils with the context of why they are aiming for channels to try and create space within the rally so they attempt to aim for one channel and then the other to move their opponent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop forehand (underarm shots) using rackets

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to co-ordinate, letting the ball bounce before serving underarm. Pupils struggle to aim diagonally across the court into the service box.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils are bouncing the ball in front and to the side of their body and that they are stood side on to help them make contact with the serve. Pupils need to make sure their feet are lined up correctly to help them aim diagonally.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Controlling the game from the serve

nodes.misconception: Pupils hit their shots too hard and the ball travels out of court. Pupils do not return to the ready position after every shot. Pupils struggle to rally when the ball can only bounce once.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to follow through on their swing to develop more control over the shot. Remind pupils to return to the middle and be in the ready position after every shot. Allow pupils to continue to rally even when the ball bounces twice.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Forehand (underarm shots) using rackets

nodes.misconception: When asking the pupils to hit the ball at pace, they may lose accuracy and control. You may have a wide range of abilities in your group which means that many of the games might not be competitive.
nodes.response: If pupils hit the ball too hard, remind them that accuracy and control is more important. Use the previous lessons to assess the ability of pupils so you can organise pairs who will have competitive games against one another.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game application through competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils rely heavily on using just one part of their foot, neglecting the need to use both the inside and the outside for better control.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need to alternate between both parts of the foot for greater skill and control.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop moving with the ball using our feet (dribbling)

nodes.misconception: Pupils ignore the importance of their body position when rolling the ball.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that aligning their body with the target, especially their feet and shoulders, will help increase their rolling accuracy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rolling and stopping

nodes.misconception: In this lesson, pupils may believe they can stop the ball with any part of their body.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use their hands to stop the ball rolling.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rolling and stopping in games

nodes.misconception: When dribbling with their feet in games, pupils sometimes think they can pick the ball up to protect it from defenders.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they cannot use their hands when dribbling with their feet and that they need to either use their body to protect the ball or move into open space.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling with our feet in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse dribbling with simply kicking the ball away, believing that any contact with the ball is dribbling.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of soft, controlled touches with the inside of their feet.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Moving with a ball using our feet

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw the ball focusing on throwing it hard and high, instead of passing with accuracy.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that a pass requires control and accuracy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and sending with hands

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that throwing requires a lot of strength rather than proper technique.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand that throwing too hard can lead to poor technique and less accuracy when aiming for a target.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing (underarm)

nodes.misconception: When using their fingertips to bounce the ball, pupils use the ends of their fingers.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand that using the fingertips refers to the flat part at the top of their fingers.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling with hands

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that they need to kick the ball as hard as possible to make a good pass, leading to a loss of control.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of accuracy over power and that pupils need to be able to kick the ball where they want it to go first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kicking (passing)

nodes.misconception: A fear of being hit by the ball can cause pupils to flinch, shy away or close their eyes.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that they need to keep their eyes on the ball, focusing on it until it is in their hands.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing and catching

nodes.misconception: In a game situation, pupils can panic and rush their throw without aiming or using the correct technique.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to be composed and even when under pressure to throw quickly, ensure pupils understand the importance of throwing accurately with the correct technique.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing with accuracy to win a game

nodes.misconception: In competitive situations, pupils can struggle to apply the correct technique to their actions. Pupils struggle to follow the rules of a game when trying to win.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on applying the correct technique when rolling and stopping the ball. Ensure pupils follow the rules and understand the importance of playing with honesty.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rolling (sending) and stopping skills to win a game

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that climbing out using the steps is the quickest and safest way to exit the pool in an emergency.
nodes.response: Climbing out over the side of the pool is often quicker and most appropriate when there is a whole class of students and prevents waiting or queueing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Entry and exits, regaining feet, balance and movement

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that you have to perform a font paddle arm action as quickly as you can.
nodes.response: A long and steady pull is more energy efficient and can increase propulsion.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Floating, kicking, front paddle arm action

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that you need to wear a nose clip to prevent water from going up your nose when swimming or rotating in the water.
nodes.response: Blowing out when performing rolls in the water stops water from going up your nose.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Aquatic breathing, rotations

nodes.misconception: If a pupil loses their balance, they may struggle to stand back up. Often, they instinctively put their hands on the pool floor, which can make it even harder to return to a standing position.
nodes.response: Pupils move their knees under their chest, lift their head and pull back with their hands. They can pratise adapted burpees to get used to this movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Getting ready to swim

nodes.misconception: Signalling for help in the water should be done by waving the arms about.
nodes.response: Waving the arms in an emergency could be confusing. Signal for help by raising one arm directly upwards and shouting help.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Retaining heat: heat escape lessening position and huddle position

nodes.misconception: Many pupils think that if you fall in to water you should start swimming as quickly as possible.
nodes.response: But we need to teach them that if you fall into water, you should float on your back to regain your breath and calm yourself down, before assessing the situation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Water safety code and beach flags

nodes.misconception: When dribbling in a game to score points, pupils forget to keep control and rush, causing them to kick the ball too far ahead.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of keeping the ball close and dribbling with control. Highlight how this will lead to scoring more points.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling to score a point in game activities using our feet

nodes.misconception: When in a game situation and trying to beat an opponent, pupils focus on throwing with more power and speed, rather than focusing on using the correct throwing technique.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that using the correct technique will produce better accuracy and eventually the speed and power of throws will increase.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Underarm throwing to beat an opponent

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that the throw should primarily come from the arm, rather than using their whole body.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that for greater accuracy and distance, they should also use their legs, feet, hands, hips and body.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Overarm throwing

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold onto the object too tightly and for too long, releasing it too late.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of holding the object with a relaxed grip and releasing it high for greater distance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Overarm throwing to win a game

nodes.misconception: Pupils can panic when receiving the ball in a game situation and rush to throw it away. Pupils all run towards the ball carrier rather than finding space.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of finding space and looking around to understand what to do when receiving the ball. Make sure they understand they have time to react and think before sending the ball on to their teammates.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing, receiving and dribbling to score a point using our hands

nodes.misconception: When dribbling using their hands, pupils use the tips of their fingers or their palms to push the ball towards the floor.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are using the flat part of their fingertips to push the ball towards the floor.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling to score a point using our hands

nodes.misconception: Some pupils neglect the value of, and need for teamwork, opting to try and dribble the ball each time they receive it.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make the correct decisions as when to pass and when to dribble. Also ensure to implement rules where all pupils must touch the ball before scoring.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine dribbling, passing and receiving with our hands

nodes.misconception: Pupils just stand still when receiving the ball, not understanding the importance of positioning.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to understand the importance of moving towards the ball and getting set when receiving it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and receiving using our feet

nodes.misconception: Pupils kick the ball too far ahead of them, using their toes to kick it, rather than keeping control with lighter touches.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the further the ball is away from them, the easier it is for a defender to take it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and keeping possession using our feet

nodes.misconception: Some pupils struggle with over or under throwing the ball, throwing either too hard or too soft. In game situations, pupils often all gravitate towards the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to continue to use the correct technique and focus on following through towards their target. This will eliminate the need to throw harder or softer as the technique will support accuracy. Ensure pupils are using the whole space.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and receiving using our hands

nodes.misconception: When bouncing a ball to dribble with it, pupils slap the ball down with their palms, focusing on power. Pupils dribble with their head down.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are pushing the ball down with control, using the flat part of their fingertips. Encourage pupils to keep their heads up whilst dribbling to ensure they can see space, don't bump into others and develops their peripheral view.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and keeping possession using our hands

nodes.misconception: Pupils grip the object too hard and hold onto it too long, releasing it too late.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use a relaxed grip for better control. Model to pupils the correct timing for releasing the object for greater accuracy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Application and understanding of underarm throwing

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to throw the shuttlecock over the net. Pupils often grip the racket too tightly which can reduce power and control. Pupils often stand still after throwing/hitting the shuttlecock.
nodes.response: Pupils use a beanbag instead of a shuttlecock. Lower the net/use cones. Emphasise relaxed hands for better control when gripping the racket. Returning to the ready position after every shot helps pupils develop their footwork and movement skills.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Badminton: outwitting an opponent

nodes.misconception: Pupils avoid hitting a backhand if they find it too difficult which disrupts their balance and positioning. Pupils may face the net rather than rotating their body when hitting the shuttlecock.
nodes.response: Spend time focusing on just the backhand shot to develop pupils' confidence so they will use the shot in a rally. Remind pupils to shift from the ready position, to then rotate their body to hit the shuttlecock so they can generate more power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The backhand

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to throw the shuttlecock into the correct position for their partner to hit a forehand. Pupils may struggle to hit the shuttlecock to the back of the court.
nodes.response: Pupils may need to feed the shuttlecock overarm to get enough power behind their throw to feed to their partners forehand. Place the non-racket foot forward and follow through after hitting the shuttlecock to allow for more power behind the shot.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The forehand

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to hit the shuttlecock to the back of the court due to standing square on to the net. Pupils may avoid hitting backhand shots. Pupils may hit shuttlecock into the net.
nodes.response: Pupils must work on a side on position when hitting the shuttlecock to generate more power. Pupils should work on their backhand technique to develop confidence. Remove or reduce the height of the net if pupils are struggling.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game application: consolidate outwitting an opponent

nodes.misconception: Pupils avoid hitting backhand shots. Pupils forget to return to the ready position. Pupils hit their forehands and backhands square on to the net.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time developing their backhand technique so they can use both shots in a rally. Remind pupils to return to the ready position after every shot. Pupils should have one foot slightly in front of the other so they in a side on position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying the forehand and backhand: creating space to win a point

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to make contact with the shuttlecock when serving. Pupils may struggle to serve to the back of the court. Pupils may struggle to serve diagonally across the court or over the net.
nodes.response: Pupils could revert to serving by throwing the shuttlecock. Remind pupils to be side on with a wide stance to help generate more power. Make sure pupils feet are positioned correctly to serve diagonally. You can lower the net or use cones.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Controlling the game from the serve in badminton

nodes.misconception: When pupils are batting and they run around the bases, they often run inside the bases, which is against the rules of the game.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils know the rule that they must run around the outside of the bases when running.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rounders

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that batting is more important than effective fielding, when in fact, good fielding is equally vital to success in rounders.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of good tactics in both batting and fielding. Pupils should realise that if they limit their opponents from scoring rounders, it will be easier to win the game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play with tactics

nodes.misconception: Pupils often hit the ball too hard when batting, not considering batting accuracy. Pupils hit the ball in the same space every time they bat which, if righthanded, is usually towards 2nd and 3rd base.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on accuracy and control rather than power. Encourage pupils to change the angle of their bodies, front foot and backswing to help them hit the ball in different directions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Batting tactics

nodes.misconception: When pupils are running around the bases and they have stopped on a base, they often lose concentration or do not understand when they need to run again, which can result in a run out.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that even though they have stopped, they still need to focus in order to make it round the bases without getting out. The batter can continue running again once the bowler has bowled the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play: batting and fielding

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often too slow to throw from backstop to 1st base when trying to run the batter out, resulting in the batter being able to continue running around the bases.
nodes.response: When backstop has the ball, they need to react quickly and focus on a flat, hard throw to 1st base to try and run the batter out.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game understanding focused on if the batter misses or hits the ball backwards

nodes.misconception: When pupils use the long barrier fielding technique, they do not join their heel with their knee therefore leaving a gap for the ball to roll through.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the concept of creating a barrier and that they need to ensure they leave no gaps for the ball to roll through if they miss it with their hands.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Fielding tactics

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will not want to perform to a large audience.
nodes.response: Some pupils practise performing for a small group, and if they still feel they can't perform for a larger audience, they don't have to.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Completion of pathways sequences and performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils only stand on 1 leg when asked to add a balance, or perform a straight jump off apparatus.
nodes.response: Encourage creativity by suggesting balances on different body parts or at different levels and remind them of a variety of jumps. Celebrate creativity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Zigzag pathways

nodes.misconception: The body is only balanced when it is still. Pupils find it difficult to balance still.
nodes.response: The body is always balancing whether it is still or moving (static and dynamic balances), but focusing on stillness allows pupils to show control in a static balance and feel stable. Try focusing on a fixed spot ahead of you to help keep still.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jump, roll, balance on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Pupils jump from wall bars or climbing frames.
nodes.response: Pupils should only jump from a flat surface.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Linking on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not perform quality actions because they don't point their toes. They either pull their toes towards their body, so their ankle is 90 degrees, or their foot is in a relaxed position.
nodes.response: Some pupils will need to be taught how to point their toes. Remind them to push their feet away, making their legs look longer. Practice with everyone at the beginning of the lesson.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Zigzag pathways on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't hold balances for long enough because they think they have to link straight into the next skill.
nodes.response: Holding a balance still for 4 seconds is part of the balance skill, so it should be included even when a balance is used in a linking sequence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Linking

nodes.misconception: Success means performing actions perfectly.  Pupils land a jump, and their hands touch the floor.
nodes.response: Success refers to progress relative to a starting point. Any improvements to actions should be viewed as successful. Remind pupils to land with straight backs (not rounded) to help them 'land and stand' when they land a jump.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Completion of sequences and performance

nodes.misconception: When performing sequences, some pupils perform too many actions, the sequence goes on for far too long and quality can be lost.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that sequences should have a beginning, a middle and an end so they can remember and repeat it. It is better to have a short, high quality sequence than a long, low quality one.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creation of pathway sequences

nodes.misconception: Balances are not held still for long enough.
nodes.response: Practise balancing still and remind pupils that they should be held still for about 4 seconds. Pupils can try focusing on a fixed spot to help them keep still. If they close their eyes to balance, they will wobble - try this too!
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Curved pathways on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Pupils lean backwards in a teddy bear roll, ending up on their back and getting stuck there.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of leaning to the side (left or right) on a shoulder and placing it close to their knee to start the action, then lifting the opposite leg (not both) to help you face the opposite direction.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Curved pathways

nodes.misconception: Practise makes perfect. Pupils forget the variety of shapes they can use for gymnastics skills and default to using the same basic balances and jumps in every sequence.
nodes.response: Practise might not always make a performance perfect, but it will make actions and sequences improve. Pupils can work together to help use practise time to improve. Display posters or lists of shape ideas for jumps, rolls and balances.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creation of sequences

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the top of their heads in a forward roll and forget to make their back curved. Pupils bend their backs too much when landing a jump, causing their hands to touch the floor.
nodes.response: Pupils should tuck their heads in, put their chin on their chests and use the back of their head by keeping their back rounded in a forward roll. Remind pupils to keep their backs straight so they can land upright ('land and stand').
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jump, roll, balance sequences

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mistake dribbling fast and dribbling with control, which causes them to lose control of the ball. Often pupils won't catch the ball but just move straight into a dribble.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that dribbling fast is good but dribbling with control is essential. The better control they have, the faster they will be able to dribble. Remind them that they should receive the ball and assess the best option before dribbling.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine passing and dribbling to create space

nodes.misconception: When defending in a game situation, pupils tend to follow the ball which closes up the space and leaves other players unmarked.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that they need to stay close to the player they are marking and be prepared to intercept the ball when it is passed to their opponent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending to stop the opposition's attack

nodes.misconception: Pupils often try to bounce the ball too hard, resulting in dribbling it too high. Pupils believe they can only dribble with one hand.
nodes.response: Bending your knees and dribbling lower with control will make it harder for a defender to steal the ball. You can only dribble with one hand at a time, however switching between hands is an effective way to dribble with control.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling (hand)

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that they only need to use their arms when shooting.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that shooting effectively involves the whole body, paticularly the legs that give us more power. Coordinated body movement will be more successful than just arm strength.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting and how to create shooting opportunities

nodes.misconception: Pupils often underestimate many of the learnt skills and believe that shooting from anywhere on the court is effective.
nodes.response: Remind pupils the importance of passing and dribbling into space, teamwork and positioning.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game application of attacking and defending

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that the harder they throw the ball, the better the pass will be.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of accuracy and remind the pupils that a softer, better-placed pass will be more effective and easier for teammates to receive.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing, receiving and creating space

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not move their feet when striking the ball, leading to mistimed and awkward shots.
nodes.response: Almost every shot requires some foot movement and the players stance should allow for this by being on the balls of feet and with knees slightly bent. Practising footwork using a batting tee will make applying footwork to a moving ball easier.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking the ball at different angles and speeds

nodes.misconception: When bowling, pupils focus solely on bowling powerfully and quickly every bowl, often causing them to bowl  inaccurately or without proper technique.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that the accuracy of their bowling is crucial and that varying the speed and power of the bowls can actually make it trickier for the batter to hit the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create and apply tactics, introduce umpiring and scoring

nodes.misconception: As a batting pair, pupils are often poor at communicating when to run, causing confusion and resulting in them being run out.
nodes.response: Teach pupils the importance of communication between the batters and ensure they understand the consequence of being run out.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play: game scenarios

nodes.misconception: Pupils take their eyes off of the ball when they approach it, as they look to see where they are going to throw it.
nodes.response: When pupils take their eyes off the ball, they increase the chances of misfielding it. Ensure pupils track the ball into their hands, before looking up to decide where to throw it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Stopping and returning the ball

nodes.misconception: Pupils bend their bowling arm and use an overarm throwing motion when releasing the ball, rather than using the correct cricket bowling action.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are using a straight arm and proper follow through when bowling. Pupils should focus on becoming confident with this technique before attempting to apply more speed and power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Bowling

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the bat and attempt to strike the ball using just 1 hand, like they would in similar sports, such as rounders.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that this approach can lead to a lack of control, making it difficult to play different shots. A correct 2 handed grip is essential for balance, precision and better shot execution.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The concept of cricket

nodes.misconception: Pupils jump too high and lose the quality of shapes. Pupils jump too far around in a half-turn jump and lose control of their landing. Pupils round backs on landing, causing hands to touch the floor.
nodes.response: Celebrate clear shapes over jumps that are too high. Spend time teaching what 'half-turn' means, reminding pupils to start facing one direction and end facing the opposite direction. Remind pupils to keep their backs straight so they land upright.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: High jumping

nodes.misconception: Pupils jump up with their whole body for bunny jumps. Pupils hold on to each other to support them. Pupils do not hold balances for long enough.
nodes.response: Model correct bunny jumps with hands moving first, then feet moving to hands, and repeat. Provide examples of words and advice pupils can use to support each other. Encourage pupils to hold balances for at least 3 seconds.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Low movements

nodes.misconception: Transitions mean adding a travelling option as you move from one skill to another. Gymnastics lessons always need lots of apparatus and take too long to set up.
nodes.response: Reinforce the concept of transitions as the smooth transfer of one skill moving straight into another one. Gymnastics lessons can be taught using just mats and benches, that do not take long to set up.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Transition between wide, narrow and curled movements

nodes.misconception: Pupils show balances instead of movements on the apparatus. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to be well-behaved. Pointed toes mean lifting toes towards the knees.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to travel or change their movements, not just hold still. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to show good control. Pointed toes mean pushing the toes away from the legs, making their legs look longer.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Wide movements

nodes.misconception: Peer feedback refers to liking jumps rather than the quality of skills. Pupils only practice one combination of skills. Pupils think they will be judged negatively in their performance.
nodes.response: Model good feedback, referring to the quality of skills. Encourage pupils to move around the apparatus trying a range of combinations. Encourage pupils to ensure this is a positive experience for all and that they should talk kindly to one another.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Link two movements together

nodes.misconception: Pupils queue for their favourite piece of apparatus. After a jump, pupils don't hold the landing position for long enough. Pupils jump from wall bars or climbing frames.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use all of the apparatus and find ways to enter and exit the apparatus rather than waiting in a queue. Tell pupils to 'land and stand' after a jump and hold still for 2 seconds. Tell pupils they can only jump from a flat surface.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Apparatus

nodes.misconception: In gymnastics, we only do forward and backward rolls. We bring our feet up to our bottom in a tuck jump.
nodes.response: Rolls can be sideways; as long as pupils roll silently with control, they are still successful. We bring our feet and knees up towards our chest in a tuck jump.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Curled movements

nodes.misconception: Pupils move their whole body at once in a bunny hop. Pupils point their toes the wrong way by flexing the ankle, causing the foot to point at a 90 degree angle to the leg. Pupils jump off wall bars.
nodes.response: Tell pupils to move their hands first, then their feet to their hands and repeat. Tell pupils to flex their ankles in the opposite direction and push their toes away from their leg, making the leg appear longer. Pupils only jump from flat surfaces.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: High and low on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Narrow actions are always vertical. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to be well-behaved. Pupils show empathy to others only by saying that they like their movements and balances.
nodes.response: Narrow actions can be vertical or horizontal. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to show good control. Encourage pupils to say why they liked others' gymnastics and to suggest improvements or new ideas by communicating kindly with respect.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Narrow movements

nodes.misconception: Pupils only use crawling actions to move over or under the apparatus. When reflecting on others' practice, pupils only say whether they liked or disliked their movements.
nodes.response: Give pupils other ideas to perform under apparatus, such as balance, swing, or slide, and other ideas to perform over apparatus, such as sliding or balancing on top or jumping over. Encourage pupils to be specific when reflecting on others' actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: High, low, over and under

nodes.misconception: Pupils perform gymnastics in silence to show good behaviour. Pupils don't use the floor as part of the apparatus when practicing skills.
nodes.response: Pupils perform gymnastics in silence to demonstrate good control. Pupils should use the floor and the equipment to practice and perform their skills.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The difference between wide, narrow and curled

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that moving high only means traveling on tiptoes. Pupils focus on the task rather than good movements. Pupils do not hold their balances for long enough.
nodes.response: Celebrate the different ways pupils move high. Remind pupils to move silently with control, pointing fingers and toes. Encourage pupils to hold balances for at least 3 seconds.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: High movements

nodes.misconception: Pupils panic when receiving the ball and throw it away quickly, especially if there is a defender close to them.
nodes.response: Explain that this may result in losing possession and that players have 4 seconds before they have to pass. Encourage pupils to use this time to choose the most suitable pass.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and receiving in games

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often rush their shots and look to try and score as soon as they get the ball, without considering their location in relation to the post or target.
nodes.response: Pupils must remember that they have approximately 4 seconds to prepare and then shoot. Remind pupils that using the correct shooting technique will increase their chances of success.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing, moving and scoring

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to chase after the ball and they all gravitate towards it as opposed to the player they are marking.
nodes.response: Focus on staying close to your opponent, wait for the pass to come to them and then attempt to intercept it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending and the concept of marking a player

nodes.misconception: As it is a competition, pupils tend to forget what they have learnt and rush decisions around passing and shooting. Pupils get frustrated if not winning.
nodes.response: Pupils have up to 4 seconds, so encourage them to take their time when making decisions. Award bonus points for pupils playing with integrity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking and defending in small sided netball games

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think they can freely move their pivot foot by dragging and sliding it. Pupils continue to move a few steps when holding the ball.
nodes.response: Reinforce the importance of keeping the pivot foot stationary and continue to practise the correct way to pivot. Remind pupils that stepping when holding the ball is a rule break and their team loses possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Footwork

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that by dodging they will always create space and outwit the defender. Pupils dodge to find a space then stand still waiting for a pass.
nodes.response: Pupils need to remember that the defenders role is to respond to the dodge, therefore they may need to dodge again and look for new space. Persevering with this technique will help pupils successfully outwit their opponent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and moving: creating space

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle when switching from a cooperative rally to a competitive rally. Pupils may struggle to use their backhand and rely too much on their forehand.
nodes.response: A cooperative rally involves pupils trying to help one another to play longer rallies. A competitive game involves hitting the ball into space away from their opponent. Encourage pupils to use their forehand and backhand in rallies.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The forehand and backhand

nodes.misconception: Pupils often stand with their paddle down by their side and are not in the ready position. Pupils often wait for the ball to reach them.
nodes.response: Keep repeating the ready positon throghout he lesson. Make sure pupils understand that the ball should only bounce once so they have to run to meet the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Forehand (underarm shots) using paddles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that hitting the ball into the channel is all they have to do to score a point, and they stay still after their shot.
nodes.response: Pupils aim for channels to create space to try win the overall point and hitting the channel doesn't instantly result in a point being scored. After each shot, pupils should try to return to the ready position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop forehand (underarm shots) using paddles

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often move too close to the ball and not give themselves enough room to hit the ball accurately. Pupils will often hit the ball with too much power and a lack of control.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the ball should be in front and slightly to the side of their body when they make contact with the ball. Pupils should be given time to  experiment with the amount of power needed to hit the targets, and encourage a smooth swing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating space to win a point using a paddle

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to hit the ball too hard when playing competitively. Pupils may be dishonest when scoring their own games in the competitions.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of playing accurate and controlled shots rather than focusing on hitting the ball hard. Remind pupils of the importance of respect and playing by the rules in competitive situations, and to just focus on trying their best.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The forehand and backhand in game situations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may switch hands if the ball is hit towards their backhand side rather than using two hands on the paddle to hit the ball. Pupils may place their dominant hand at the top of the paddle handle.
nodes.response: Pupils should keep their dominant hand at the bottom of the paddle handle for control and place their non dominant hand at the top to play a backhand shot with both hands on the grip. Explain that the hand at the bottom provides the control.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Backhand

nodes.misconception: When pupils perform their sequence on apparatus, they lose control, extension and flow.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils carefully consider how they can adapt their sequences to work on apparatus so they don't lose quality. Pupils can also focus on communication to help improve the quality of their sequence on apparatus.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Matching on apparatus

nodes.misconception: One pupil always leads the other. Only one pupil can perform the movement with quality.
nodes.response: Use strategies such as counting or music to help pupils move at the same time. Encourage pupils to ensure that both of them can perform the skills, and if they can't, they should work on improving or changing the movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Matching

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to distinguish between a matching and mirroring movement. Pupils struggle to execute their movements simultaneously.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work with peers to check whether a movement is matching or mirroring. Pupils should work on communication to improve their synchronisation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Matching and mirroring sequences

nodes.misconception: One pupil always leads so that their timing is out. Variations in angles of movement make the mirroring look uneven. Pupils move in the wrong direction so they are parallel instead of mirroring
nodes.response: Pupils should practise counting or using music to help them improve their timing. Pupils need to practise so they have identical body positions and use feedback to help improve this. Practise mirrored movements over and over to create muscle memory.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mirroring

nodes.misconception: There may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use when working in bigger groups. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
nodes.response: Pupils may have to delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups. Pupils may have to consider adapting their sequences when working with bigger groups.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Matching and mirroring sequences: group performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils move in the wrong direction so they are parallel instead of mirroring. When pupils perform their sequence on apparatus, they lose control, extension and flow.
nodes.response: Practise mirrored movements to create muscle memory. Pupils should adapt their sequences to work on apparatus so they don't lose quality. Pupils can also focus on communication to help improve the quality of their sequence on apparatus.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mirroring on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that teams are only successful if they score the most points or beat their opposition when they compete.
nodes.response: Competing successfully can be measured in different ways. Scoring the most points or goals is one measure. Including all team members, playing fairly or bringing positivity are all equally important ways of being successful when competing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Collaborating successfully when playing simple games

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that staying silent while someone speaks is all that is needed to show respectful listening.
nodes.response: Staying silent can be described as passive listening. Active and respectful listening uses thinking skills to understand, remember and respond to what has been said. You need to plan your next actions based on the information that has been said.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Showing respect through listening

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that trying your best means doing every role within a team.
nodes.response: Trying to do everything for a team is admirable, but one person can get tired quickly and someone else might also be more skilled at doing it. If everyone gives their best effort in their role, the combined effort can be very successful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Roles and responsibilities

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that good aim is a fixed skill that you either have or do not.
nodes.response: Accuracy and aim is closely linked to balance and technique, i.e. when a pupil can hold a steady position and perform an accurate technique, often their aim improves.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Collaborating in teams

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that when they are working in a team, everyone should stay together and do the same thing.
nodes.response: Sometimes, a good tactic to quickly complete a challenge is to split the challenge into smaller tasks and share them out amongst the team. A team can still be working towards the same goal, even if everyone is working separately on different tasks.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Cooperation and communication

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think they have to rely on others to include them and that there isn't anything they can or need to do in order to be included.
nodes.response: There are things that you can do to increase your involvement in a challenge and play a role in a team such as sharing ideas and supporting and encouraging others.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Working as a team

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that if a strategy doesn't work, they shouldn't use it again.
nodes.response: Deciding when to use a strategy is part of the challenge. A strategy that works once will not work every time or against every opponent. Having lots of strategies to try will help you find the one that works best each time.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using simple strategies

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that successful strategies need to be very complicated.
nodes.response: Simple strategies are usually most successful because everyone on the team can be clear about what they have to do and can do their part very easily and quickly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Working together and competing as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that if someone has been designated to a team, this means they have been included.
nodes.response: People can feel excluded even when they're part of a team if they are ignored or not included in the decisions being made. There are many things that you can do to help your teammates to feel included and valued in the team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Working together including everyone

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that you should only cheer and congratulate success, e.g., scoring a point or beating an opponent.
nodes.response: All players, on all teams, should be cheered and congratulated for their effort, regardless of who scores the points, who wins or which team they are playing for.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Showing respect by supporting and encouraging others

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that once a solution has been found to complete a challenge, this is the only option that should be used.
nodes.response: Many challenges and problems have various different solutions. One solution might suit the skills in your team and a different solution might suit another team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Helping my teammates

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may only think about speaking in relation to communication.
nodes.response: Information can be communicated in lots of different ways including signals, gestures, sounds, pictures and words. Receiving, interpreting and acting on the information sent is also half the process of communication.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Trust and communication

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush to complete their sequence and therefore do not perform to their potential. Pupils may give very brief, low quality feedback to their peers.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to reflect on feedback and keep striving to produce the best sequence by continually making changes to improve their performance. When pupils feedback to each other, encourage them to use key terminology and give quality feedback.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performance and giving feedback to others

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with balance due to weak core muscles. Pupils may always want to use the same apparatus in the same area.
nodes.response: Add some core strengthening exercises into the warm up and emphasise the importance of core strength in all activities. Encourage pupils to use a range of apparatus throughout the lesson to develop their confidence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Counter balance on apparatus

nodes.misconception: One partner ends up bearing more weight than the other, leading to instability. Pupils may try complex counter balances before they have mastered the foundational skills.
nodes.response: Show examples of counter balances where pupils are evenly distributing their weight. Make sure pupils can perform basic counter balances with quality before they attempt more complex balances.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequences to include counter balance on apparatus

nodes.misconception: One pupil pulls harder or doesn’t pull enough, leading to an imbalance and collapse of the position. Pupils do not have a secure grip with one another
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to communicate with their partners pulling gently at first, then increase force gradually to find the balance point. Encourage pupils to grip using wrists as an alternative to hands.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Counter tension

nodes.misconception: Now that counter tension balances and counter balances are used in the same lesson, pupils may mix them up.
nodes.response: Emphasise the difference between the two balances and that counter balances usually involve a pushing action and counter tension balances involve a pulling action.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequences to include counter balance and counter tension on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a partner balance is a counter balance.  Pupils may struggle with counter balance due to unequal weight distribution. Pupils may struggle to trust their partner.
nodes.response: Show the difference between a partner balance and a counter balance. Pupils practice positions individually and work together to adjust the balance equally. Incorporate activities that require working together and communication to build trust.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Counter balance

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush to throw the ball without checking where their opponent is positioned. Pupils may forgt to return to the ready position in the middle of the court on the baseline.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to scan the court and look for spaces away from their opponent. Remind pupils to return to the middle of the court on the baseline after every shot and adopt the ready position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: How to win a game

nodes.misconception: Pupils may change to an overarm throw when you are asking them to aim for the back of the court. Pupils may take too many risks when aiming for the perimeter and the ball goes out/hits the net a lot.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to step into their throw and follow throught towards their target to get more power behind their throw. Although we want pupils to aim away from the midle of the court, we still want them to successfully throw into the court area.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating space to win a point

nodes.misconception: When throwing underarm, pupils often struggle to release the ball so it travels forward towards the target. Pupils may forget to have their hands up ready to catch the the ball.
