nodes.response: Encourage pupils to develop a smooth arm swing when throwing towards a target and finish with a straight arm pointing in the direction of their target. Remind pupils to adopt the ready position with hands up in front of them when waiting to catch.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing with accuracy towards space

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to travel too fast without having control of the ball on the racket. Pupils may want to hit the ball over the net instead of playing 'Floor tennis'.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to move slowly to develop their hand eye coordination when using a racket before increasing their speed. Explain to pupils that floor tennis will help to develop better control when using the racket before they move on to hitting.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to Rackets

nodes.misconception: Pupils often throw the ball with too much power. Pupils step into their throw with the same foot as their throwing arm. Pupils wait for the ball to come to them instead of moving towards it.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to hold the ball loosely rather than squeezing it tightly. Remind pupils to step in with opposite foot to throwing arm. Pupils should be encouraged to move towards the ball to catch it and make sure the body is underneath the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing with accuracy

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often throw the ball from where they have caught it, and then stay in that position. Pupils throw the ball towards their opponent instead of into space.
nodes.response: Pupils should be reminded to always return to the middle of the court after throwing the ball. Pupils should always be looking to throw ito space away from their opponent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Outwitting an opponent

nodes.misconception: Pupils push or hit their partner too hard when they are the chaser. Pupils bump into each other playing tag.
nodes.response: Teach pupils how to tag and remind them to tap gently. Remind pupils to slow down or dodge to avoid collisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner activities: playing against each other

nodes.misconception: Teammates are so busy running away from taggers that they forget to look carefully and collide with others.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that to avoid collisions, they must look ahead and dodge others by changing direction and slowing down.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team activities: cooperating in a team game

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't realise it's their turn to move.
nodes.response: Players stand on a 'next player' floor marker to help them to know who's turn it is next.  Remind pupils to encourage each other with kind words when it's their turn.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team activities: decision making in a team game

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they must be standing up to create letter shapes. When creating words, pairs make their letter shapes in the wrong order, or facing the wrong way, so that the whole word is not seen.
nodes.response: Letter shapes can be formed standing or lying down. Encourage teams to imagine that they are another team looking at their word, are all letters in the correct order and facing the same direction?
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team activities: cooperating successfully

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't concentrate, so they don't realise when it is their turn. Other team members shout at them to take their turn.
nodes.response: Encourage players to pay attention to their team so they know when it's their turn. Other team members can kindly prompt them if they miss their turn.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team activities: solving problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils shout loudly thinking this will improve communication. Pupils high 5 with too much force.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of good sentences spoken at a normal talking volume. Be explicit about using gentle high 5s and ask pupils to imagine how a butterfly would high 5 their friend.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team activities: developing communication

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't perform the animal actions for a count of 6. Pupils think they have to find the cards for the animal action scavenger hunt in numerical order.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that keeping the rules demonstrates fair play and ensures everyone enjoys the game. Pupils can find and perform the animal action cards in any order.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner activities: cooperating successfully

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw equipment too high or throw overarm, and then blame their partner for being unable to catch it.
nodes.response: Encourage underarm throwing with a gentle force to help ensure all partners can catch and succeed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner activities: taking turns

nodes.misconception: Pupils shout too loudly, thinking this will improve communication. Pupils place floor markers too close together, resulting in slow movement across the river.
nodes.response: Encourage the use of good sentences spoken at a normal talking volume. Highlight pupils who place floor markers an arm's length from each other and move across the river more efficiently.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner activities: developing communication

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw the ball up too high or throw overarm and then blame their partner for being unable to catch it.
nodes.response: Encourage underarm throwing, using gentle passes so the ball makes a rainbow shape in the air. Remind pupils that teamwork requires all individuals to work together and encouraging others.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team activities: playing fairly in groups

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might dominate the partnership.
nodes.response: Cooperation and communication are key factors in any partnership: they must share roles and listen to one another's ideas.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner activities: scoring points with a partner

nodes.misconception: Pupils can only stand when making letter shapes.
nodes.response: Pupils can lie, sit, or stand to make letter shapes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Partner activities: solving problems

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't adjust their body position when preparing to stop the ball or return the hit. Instead, they stretch and try to hit the ball from an unbalanced position.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that positioning their body in line with the ball will make it easier to stop it going past them.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hitting/striking a ball with accuracy and power to beat an opponent

nodes.misconception: Some pupils forget to follow through and stop their racket immediately after hitting the ball.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that a proper follow through, towards the target, is crucial for both power and accuracy. Remind them if you see the racket stopping too early or ending up pointing to the sky or to the ground.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine hitting/striking a ball with accuracy and power

nodes.misconception: Pupils swing back and forwards quickly to hit the ball with power but take their eyes off of the ball, causing them to miss it.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of keeping eyes on the ball to ensure pupils make good contact when hitting it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking the ball into space to beat an opponent

nodes.misconception: When hitting the ball, pupils focus on power and hitting it as hard as they can, neglecting the need for technique and accuracy.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of aiming and using the correct technique for the best accuracy. It is best to master this before attempting to add more power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking the ball using a racket or bat with accuracy

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus solely on their arm movements and neglect the use of their legs and hips to create power.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand how that bending their knees and rotating their hips can create more power for bigger hits.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hitting/striking the ball with intent

nodes.misconception: Many pupils stand too close or too far away from the ball which makes it hard for them to strike the ball effectively.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to stand roughly an arm's distance away from the ball in a well-balanced stance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hitting/striking a ball into a space

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to stick with simple movements such as walking to move into balances and to link the sequence.
nodes.response: Explain that although we can walk, there are so many movement options and walking isn't the most exciting to watch. Encourage pupils to try a range of movement ideas.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence formation in pairs

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget the line of symmetry in their balances. Pupils always mirror their partner when creating symmetrical balances and always want to connect to their partner using the same body parts.
nodes.response: The content in cycle 3 will help with this but pupils will need lots of model examples to see how symmetrical balances can still be created without always mirroring their partner.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Symmetry

nodes.misconception: Pupils create 1 balance idea and think they are finished, instead of trying a range of ideas. Pupils only work on one part of the apparatus and fail to try a range of apparatus to create their ideas.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that they must try out multiple ideas and use a range of apparatus in order to be successful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Symmetrical and asymmetrical learning on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Pupils insist on including the movements and balances that they want to perform as part of the sequence, even if some members of the group cannot perform these correctly.
nodes.response: Groups need to agree on the movements and balances that they are including in the sequence and ensure everyone is able to perform them correctly and safely.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence work in groups combining concepts

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the floor to create their linking movements in unison and move around the apparatus instead of using it.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the apparatus is there to be used and that we can really enhance our creativity if we try and include a range of apparatus in our movements.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create sequences in unison on apparatus with symmetrical balances

nodes.misconception: When challenged with adding additional actions to their sequences as they finalise their work, pupils add in additional and unnecessary actions, coming away from the stipulated actions to include.
nodes.response: Explain that extra actions don't necessarily improve the sequence and will make it very difficult for someone observing to evaulate their work.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence completion and performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that moving in canon means one person moves, then there is a pause before the next person moves, so the sequence becomes disjointed.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we need to ensure that one pupil is always moving or balancing to ensure the sequence flows.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Canon in sequences

nodes.misconception: When it comes to creating a sequence, pupils include too many actions and the sequence is hard to follow as it goes on for a long time without following the rules of the structure.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of planning the sequence and use the worksheets to support with this. The sequence should only include the actions stipulated and should therefore follow a clear structure.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequences on apparatus in pairs using symmetrical and asymmetrical balances

nodes.misconception: Pupils continue to create symmetrical balances, confusing symmetry with asymmetry.
nodes.response: Provide models and continue to highlight the differenece between the two.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Asymmetry

nodes.misconception: Pupils find keeping accurate timings hard and struggle to see how to adapt the sequence to improve this and make this easier.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to slow down their movements and to include simpler movements that both pupils in the pair can perform with confidence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Unison in sequences

nodes.misconception: Pupils choose movements and balances that only one pupil can perform as they are the actions they want to perform.
nodes.response: Support pupils to understand that they need to select movements and balances that both pupils in the pair can perform.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create sequences in canon on apparatus with symmetrical balances

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the longer the sequence is, the better it must be.
nodes.response: Pupils need to understand that quality actions over quantity are essential when creating a sequence. Pupils should also be reminded to follow the sequence pattern/rules.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence completion and peer review

nodes.misconception: When you perform a canon, you have to perform the same action as each other.
nodes.response: Whilst this is often true, the actions can vary, e.g., pupils may jump apart one at a time, yet each pupil may perform a different jump, or pupils may change shape. It is the staggered timing that is the essential element.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions: the domino effect

nodes.misconception: Telling a story in dance (narrative dance) should include talking.
nodes.response: Whilst some dances include dialogue, in dance a story is usually communicated solely through actions and the performers are usually silent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Contact work: counter balances and supports

nodes.misconception: Being in a linear formation means make a line one behind the other.
nodes.response: Whilst this is an example of a linear formation, it could also involve the pupils being side by side or in a diagonal line. Linear formations can also meet or intercept to make patterns such as a 'V' or 'X' formation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Space: formations

nodes.misconception: To demonstrate changing levels, you have to stay on the spot.
nodes.response: Whilst you may wish to remain on the spot, changing levels can be incorporated into other actions such as travelling or with other spacial elements such as pathways or directions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Space: levels

nodes.misconception: Trying to move another person means you do so as forcefully as you can.
nodes.response: By starting gently, a person is able to judge the amount of effort that is likely be be required to attempt to move a solid object such as a sculpture made of stone.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dynamics: force

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when replicating Newtons Cradle, when we make contact with others, we have to bump or push them away.
nodes.response: The actions don’t have to be bumps or pushes when making contact with a partner, but instead could be any action such as a lean, a step, a jump etc.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions: Newton's Cradle

nodes.misconception: Being close together always demonstrates frienship, kindness and cooperation.
nodes.response: Being close suggests a cooperative connection between performers if the dynamic is smooth, calm and relaxed, however if the dynamic was strong, forceful and fast, the audience are likely to interpret their actions as demonstrating tension or anger.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Space: proximity

nodes.misconception: Counter balances should always involve pushing against our partner's hands.
nodes.response: We often start by connecting using our hands. Once skilled at countering our partner, we can find different points of connection or use different levels or directions to make our combined shapes more interesting and creative.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Contact work: counter balances

nodes.misconception: When being supported by someone you don't have to do anything.
nodes.response: It helps the 'supporter' if the 'supported' person is still, but they need to remain alert and actively hold their body firm, which makes it much easier for the 'supporter' to absorb their weight and return them to an upright position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Contact work: supports

nodes.misconception: There are only two speeds, fast and slow.
nodes.response: There are many speeds. Think of a race, everyone will be travelling as fast as they can but the winner will have been moving faster than the rest. Fast and slow guide us towards the rate at which we should move and may need more clarification.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dynamics: speed

nodes.misconception: When making contact you always use your hands
nodes.response: Making contact can involve different body parts, e.g. foot to foot, elbow to shoulder, back to back. Using more unusual connections can make a dance appear more interesting to the audience.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Actions: unity and cohesion

nodes.misconception: Dynamics involve either speed or force, not both.
nodes.response: Dynamics are a combination of both speed and force. We naturally use them both in every action we do, in dance we can use them to clearly communicate our dance idea, sometimes this requires greater emphasis on one or the other.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dynamics: force and speed

nodes.misconception: Representing the journey of a train or bus must include mimed actions such as pretending to turn a steering wheel.
nodes.response: Whilst pupils may wish to include such gestures, our focus is on the journey rather than the mode of transport so there is not a requirement to include the use of mime.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Travelling and stopping: journey by bus or train

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that linear pathways should follow the outline of the room.
nodes.response: Whilst there is an obvious logic to using the orientation and basic shape of the room, linear pathways can bisect the space in any way. They must simply be straight lines.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Linear/curved pathways: journey by foot

nodes.misconception: 'Briskly' means fast, so you can run.
nodes.response: 'Briskly' means quick and energetic. This does not include running.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Irregular pathways: journey by foot

nodes.misconception: To pretend to be an object such as a car, we have to use mime.
nodes.response: Miming is one way of describing an object, theme or story to an audience without using words. You will need to use your imagination to think of other ways that the audience will also understand.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Speeds: transport

nodes.misconception: Contrast is the same as opposite.
nodes.response: Opposite is an example of contrast. For example, a contrast for travelling forwards is backwards. But contrast can also mean different. For example, travelling around a bend or turning on the spot are different so would also demonstrate contrast.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Turning and directions: journey by bus or train

nodes.misconception: A performance should be to the whole class.
nodes.response: Performing can be to another person, duet or group. This can feel less daunting and is a good way to get feedback.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Journeys: performing

nodes.misconception: As pupils add more and more elements to their sequences, the quality of their performance decreases. There may be issues with group dynamics as pupils work in bigger group sizes.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of only moving on to add another element to the sequence once all members of the group are ready to move on. Pupils may have to delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Group jumping sequences; turning, canon, unison, levels and direction

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to communicate when working in bigger groups. Poor timing in unison and canon may result in a lack of flow throughout the sequence.
nodes.response: Pupils should communicate and listen to each other's ideas. Pupils should develop ways to help them improve their timing, ensuring there are no long pauses when performing in unison and canon so their sequence still flows throughout.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping on apparatus: canon and unison

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not contribute to reflections as a group as they may lack confidence to speak up in front of others. Pupils may lose flow in their sequence when they add balances.
nodes.response: Encourage every pupil to contribute in group reflection tasks and consider ways in which everyone can give feedback. Pupils should think carefully about how they will get into and out of their balances to maintain flow throughout the sequence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performance and self-reflection

nodes.misconception: Pupils may rush the jump and not be balanced before they take off from the apparatus. Pupils may misplace their feet on the apparatus. Pupils may land with stiff knees or poor body position.
nodes.response: Always check balance and engage the core before jumping. Ensure a solid stance before jumping. Pupils should bend their knees to absorb impact on landing and make sure their weight is centered over their feet.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Utilising apparatus to create moments of flight

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to bend their knees on landing. Pupils bring their head to their knees when performing a tuck jump. Pupils forget to use their arms when jumping.
nodes.response: Pupils should repeatedly practise bending knees on landing. Pupils should raise their knees towards the chest in a tuck jump. Pupils should be reminded to swing their arms to give them momentum and to use their arms in the various jumps.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Flight

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to jump high enough to turn due to a weak push off. Pupils are wobbly and unbalanced when turning. Pupils turn too much or too little.
nodes.response: Emphasise bending the knees and pushing through the balls of the feet. Pupils should practise engaging their core muscles to help them turn with control. Make sure pupils focus on rotating from the shoulders and hips not just the arms.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping and turning

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might suggest that rolling or cartwheeling is a turn to change direction.
nodes.response: Although a body rotates during a roll or cartwheel, it moves along one course, facing the same direction at the start and finish. This lesson focusses on changing the course that we are moving along which is achieved through turns and spins.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in direction

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that being a leader is the same as being 'the boss' who tells everyone what to do and has all the ideas that others must follow.
nodes.response: Being a leader can involve making suggestions and sharing ideas. They might follow your way of thinking and come up with new ideas themselves. It can also involve asking other people for their opinions and listening carefully.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence ideas

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may suggest jumping to mount and dismount apparatus as a change in level during their sequence.
nodes.response: This lesson guide focuses on a change in level in relation to the surface of the apparatus i.e closer or further away. For example, from stomach, push into a plank. Jumping off changes levels in relation to the ground which is not the intended focus.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in level on the apparatus

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not recognise the floor as a piece of apparatus.
nodes.response: The floor is a very demanding piece of apparatus because many different skills are required such as leaps, spins, splits, dance and acrobatics. In rhythmic gymnastics, additional apparatus is also used such as clubs, ribbons, hoops and balls.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in direction on apparatus

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may only consider performing their balances on top of the apparatus.
nodes.response: Apparatus can be used in variety of ways to support pupils' weight; balances can be performed on top, against or under apparatus, e.g. feet on the apparatus with hand on the floor or feet on the floor with back against the apparatus.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Application of learning onto apparatus

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that successful sequences are long and consist of lots of different movements and balances.
nodes.response: Successful sequences can be performed with control and flow. They can be short and may repeat some movements if the pupils feel this is the best decision to improve the quality of their performance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence formation combining individual and pair balances

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that a quality performance should be long and include difficult skills.
nodes.response: If a short sequence that includes easier skills is performed with accurate timings, fluidity, control and extension, this is demonstrating high quality. Evaluation should consider how something is performed as well as what is performed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence completion and peer to peer review

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that performing with flow means performing with speed.
nodes.response: Sequences need control and smoothly linked movements. This creates a steady pace that feels fluid and not rushed. Balances create stillness and are held for a least 4 seconds; flow can still be achieved even with still moments and steady movements.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in level

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that having the most skillful gymnasts in their group will make it easier to create a group sequence.
nodes.response: Creating sequences in groups needs lots of different skills which are just as important as physical skills. Groups will need to make thoughtful decisions, will need to rehearse responsibly and will need to work cooperatively.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in level and direction to create sequences in groups using apparatus

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may spend their practice time adding more actions onto the sequence instead of repeating and refining a shorter sequence.
nodes.response: Practice time can be used to repeat a skill and improve the quality of a performance, or it can be used to make changes to a sequence to improve the flow or increase the range of movements for more interest.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine balances and movements to finalise sequences in pairs

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that a performance should be perfect and if any improvements are suggested, they have failed or made a mistake.
nodes.response: Striving to be perfect is different to striving to do our best. It is good to want to perform at a high standard and it feels great when we achieve it, however, if we are seeking perfection, we might forget to celebrate everything we have achieved.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sequence completion and performance to peers

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that balancing is easy because it's just about staying still.
nodes.response: Balance requires strength and concentration to keep muscles under control in different positions. Balances should be held for at least 4 seconds and sometimes you need to make adjustments to maintain a balance. Holding a balance requires total focus.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Balances individually and in pairs

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that to communicate 'floating' they must use jumps.
nodes.response: Whilst jumping can communicate the sense of lift we associate with a balloon, the light, floating appearance comes from moving using a light, gentle dynamic which requires balance, control and coordination.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Social comment

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that to communicate an idea we have to show a picture.
nodes.response: We can communicate ideas through our dance actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Visual metaphors

nodes.misconception: When creating a motif to represent ideas from a painting, you must use the same action over and over again.
nodes.response: When creating a motif, you can demonstrate an action then repeat it by changing the size, level, direction, speed, force, using a different body part, adding an extra action, reversing the action or coordinating another action at the same time.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing motifs using question and answer

nodes.misconception: Artists just think of ideas, whatever artform they work in.
nodes.response: All artists, whether dancers, painters, actors or musicians, look to other artforms and the wider world for inspiration. Charlie Parker (musician) inspired Basquiat (painter) who later inspired Jay Z (musician).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday heroes

nodes.misconception: Pretending to be an object is drama, not dance.
nodes.response: Pretending to be an object is often categorised as 'physical theatre'. This is where dance and drama overlap and it draws upon skills from both disciplines. A similar connection is made when dancers represent characters or scenes from a story.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Multimedia

nodes.misconception: To communicate spray paint we rush around the room, making hissing noises.
nodes.response: To communicate the idea of using spray paint we need to perform smooth and flowing actions using control, balance and coordination.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Stencilling

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that in order to bring graffiti 'tags' to life through movement, you have to write in the air.
nodes.response: Creating a 'tag' using your body can involve writing in the air, but it could also include making and holding a shape, or even using the colour, style or shading as the stimulus for your actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: My tag, your tag

nodes.misconception: Posture doesn't matter in Hip hop dance.
nodes.response: Posture immediately communicates clues about a dance style, whether it is forceful and energetic like Hip Hop or light and graceful like Ballet. It enables the audience to know what to expect.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Influences: Hip Hop

nodes.misconception: A heart only symbolises love.
nodes.response: Whilst love is the most common interpretation of a heart symbol, it can also represent unity, gratitude, hope, care, comfort, friendship, romance, resisting oppression and acceptance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Refining, rehearsing and performing a dance using a combination of relationships

nodes.misconception: There can only be one correct interpretation of an action or image.
nodes.response: Interpreting meaning of a symbolic action can vary depending on your previous experience and opinions, so people may view it differently and draw various conclusions. The important thing is to be able to justify your interpretation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Breaking the code

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that interlocking requires us to connect together using our hands and arms.
nodes.response: Interlocking involves two or more things fitting together or overlapping, which could be done using a range of different body parts.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Making your mark: applying a style

nodes.misconception: A dance only has one motif.
nodes.response: Most dances will contain several motifs, these can be as short and simple as a gesture or more complex sequences. If they are performed more than once in a dance, then they are a motif.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Applying a range of motifs and structuring a dance

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that every strike requires maximum power to be good.
nodes.response: Explain that different situations need different amounts of power, such as a shorter strike. Encourage pupils to also think about technique as well as power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking a ball using a racket/bat with power

nodes.misconception: Pupils underestimate the importance of following through with their racket when pushing/ striking the ball.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that the follow through is important for accuracy and getting the right amount of power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking and pushing a ball with a racket/bat towards a target

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that hitting the ball hard is the best way to move and control it.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to keep close contol of their ball by using soft touches to keep it close.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pushing a ball with a racket/bat

nodes.misconception: When moving into space and away from defenders, pupils panic and rush which causes them to lose control of their ball.
nodes.response: Highlight the importance of always moving with control, even if it means moving a little slower at first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pushing a ball with a racket/bat into space

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to combine both power and accuracy, often focusing on just one.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that both power and accuracy are needed. Pupils should aim their hit and then think about the power when swinging through.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking a ball using a racket/bat with accuracy

nodes.misconception: When introducing defenders, pupils often neglect technique and moving with close control.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to use gentle, small touches when moving with their ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pushing a ball using a racket/bat with control

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush different relaxation techniques and actions with their bodies when performing sequences.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that mimicking different emotions requires concentration and controlled movements, which are often performed slowly in order calm our bodies.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Relaxation techniques

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to concentrate when they are freezing still or when they are deep breathing so the relaxation technique is ineffective.
nodes.response: Pupils need to be reminded that the techniques only work if they focus and are still, concentrating on their breathing / the stillness.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using relaxation techniques effectively

nodes.misconception: Once pupils start to link their mediative balances, they focus on creating a sequence of movements rather than the relaxation purposes of the process.
nodes.response: Explain that medatitive balances aren't the same as gymnastic balances and provide examples to support pupil understanding.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using props to balance in meditative balances

nodes.misconception: Pupils over complicate the balances they are holding and fail to hold them still. This also means they will not be able to focus as they try to hold the balance.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to create a stable base, enabling their body to focus throughout and successfully use the balances as a tool to relax.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing meditative balances

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to balance the imaginary stick in their pairs and create movements that wouldn't work if they were using a real stick. Pupils also lose their focus during the movements and rush them.
nodes.response: Provide lots of examples to support pupils to create movements while balancing an imaginary stick. Remind pupils of the importance of focus, control and slow deep breathing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Balancing skills in pairs using an imaginary prop

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that performing animal themed meditative balances requires acting like animals and making animal noises. This also means that pupils forget to control their breathing as they balance.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that if we make noises and actually act like animals, we are creating actions and using characterisation, not balancing to ensure calm, focus and relaxtion. We must remain silent and focus on long, slow breaths in and out.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing meditative balances in pairs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may feel uncomfortable or vulnerable when reflecting on the abstract ideas of the poem, which can make it difficult for them to focus, relax and link their work to the meaning of the poem.
nodes.response: Support pupils to open their minds to new concepts and to focus only on themself when reflecting. Explain to pupils that only by trying something with full effort and concentration can the benefits be felt.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Use mindfulness techniques to help manage emotions

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to relate to some of the negative emotions explored in the lesson and therefore don't see the benefit of practising the mime and meditative balance sequences.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it is important to practise and understand the benefits so that we are prepared for future challenges in our lives.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combine and perform mime with meditative balances

nodes.misconception: Pupils think everyone will feel the same way when they hear a piece of music and respond with the same actions and expressions.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that we might feel and respond the same way, but it is just as likely that we will feel differently as a number of factors will influence how we feel, including our mood and experiences that day.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create movement sequences to express emotions

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush their deep breathing, which reduces the impact of the technique.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it’s important not to rush deep breathing, otherwise they won’t be able to focus their minds and the technique won’t work.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing meditative balances incorporating mindfulness techniques

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that mime only refers to illustrating physical objects, e.g. a plate or a glass of water etc., and don't consider how mime can represent emotional responses too.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that mime is a powerful tool we can use to help us to understand and manage our emotions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Use mime to explore positive and negative emotions

nodes.misconception: Pupils focus on the tempo of the music, matching the beat and tempo, instead of considering the full effect of the music in creating an emotional response. (e.g., pupils run to fast music.)
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that it is important to be still and listen to the music before moving. Pupils should also be reminded to consider their facial expression, ensuing this matches their movement responses.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpret music to create expressive movement

nodes.misconception: 'The beat' and 'the rhythm' are the same thing.
nodes.response: The beat is the steady pulse of a piece of music that stays the same. Rhythm is how we mix up the beat to make patterns of sound.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: South African gumboot dance

nodes.misconception: Dance styles such as Salsa or Ballet are 'proper' dancing.
nodes.response: All dance styles were created by someone, or a group, and develop e.g. pointe work in ballet was introduced in the 1820's/1830's. New styles are still being developed. All actions can be dance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Salsa dance

nodes.misconception: Line dancing must use the feet.
nodes.response: Whilst it is typically performed with an emphasis on footwork, this can easily be adapted to use the arms or any other body part. The emphasis is on the use of a repeating pattern, with a change of direction through 90'.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: American line dancing

nodes.misconception: Moves have to be performed in a specifc order to be effective.
nodes.response: After learning a few moves, we can ask the pupils which to perform and how many. This enables them to develop their choreographic skills of selecting and sequencing actions effectively.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Traditional Greek dance

nodes.misconception: In a narrative dance you have to interpret every word into an action.
nodes.response: In a narrative dance performers aim to communicate the main parts of the story. They may add actions and join movements together to show the context and character or make it more interesting.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hula dance

nodes.misconception: Traditional dance styles are how all the people in that country dance.
nodes.response: Traditional dance styles are still danced by some people in their communities on certain occasions. They will also dance other styles too and these will change depending on whether they are in a theatre, temple or at a social event.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kathak dance

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that for an effective stretch, you should push or reach until it is painful.
nodes.response: Stretching should never be painful. You might feel tension which can be described as resistance, a pull or tightening and this indicates that the muscle should not be stretched any further. Tension might ease with some deep breathing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Improve my flexibility

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that activities for fitness are always solo tasks that don't encourage social interaction.
nodes.response: Being active with others can have lots of benefits, e.g. increased motivation, encouragement from others, and confidence. All these benefits combined, can encourage individuals to be more active, more often, resulting in increased activity levels.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Staying active, fit and healthy with others

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not recognise the heart as a muscle because we cannot consciously move it in the same way we can other muscles in the body.
nodes.response: The body has voluntary and involuntary muscles. The heart is an involuntary muscle that doesn't require conscious thought to make it contract and send blood around the body. Exercising regularly can improve the strength and endurance of our heart.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Improve my cardiovascular fitness

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that humans only need strong muscles if they want to excel in sports such as weight lifting and climbing.
nodes.response: Strong muscles are essential for humans to complete everyday tasks including breathing, blinking, sitting, lifting, chewing etc. Strong muscles also help our joints to work effectively which helps to avoid injury and pain.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Improve my strength

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that being active and fit requires gruelling, high impact activity, that maximises heart rate and leads to physical exhaustion.
nodes.response: Activities should suit the goal you are trying to achieve. High impact, exhausting activities are suited to improve cardiovascular endurance. Low impact, relaxing exercising are suited to developing other components of fitness e.g. flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Being active, fit and healthy

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think they will only be successful if they can achieve all the activities at the most challenging level.
nodes.response: Everybody is different and success is different for everyone. Anyone who tries their best and gives maximum effort should feel successful, regardless of the level of challenge they completed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Achieve a personal best

nodes.misconception: Pupils sprint and then slow up and then sprint again and slow again, especially at the start of the run.
nodes.response: Explain that having a steady rhythm may not get pupils to the front initially, but their overall time will be quicker than if they sprint and stop continuously.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to pacing

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the triple jump consists of a step, step and jump, rather than a hop, step and jump.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time to practise hopping and stepping and highlight the difference between the two. Pupils must understand that a hop requires them to land on the same foot they took off on, and a step is from one foot to the other.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping for distance: standing triple jump

nodes.misconception: Pupils transition aburptly from a lower body position leaning forwards to running upright, which causes them to slow down and lose their rhythm.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to transition smoothly as they accelerate towards top speed as doing this too quickly can cause a loss of speed. Allow opportunities for pupils to practise this and address the misconception when observed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprinting: stride pattern

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that they shouldn't start to feel fatigued if they are pacing themselves and slow down or stop if they do.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand that it is normal to feel fatigued during the run, even when they are pacing themselves, and they need to push through this using determination.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Use tactics when running for distance

nodes.misconception: Pupils grip the javelin tightly in their hand, thinking that this will help them to throw it further, however this can hinder a smooth release and lead to tension in the rest of the arm.
nodes.response: Pupils should place the javelin across their palm with their fingers wrapped around it, but not too tight. Explain to pupils that a more relaxed grip will result in a smoother release and longer throw.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing for distance: javelin

nodes.misconception: Pupils slow down before the end of the race/ sprint, preparing to stop directly at the finish line.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that they should not begin to slow down until they have crossed the finish line as it will allow other runners to catch them up and potentially overtake them.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprinting: running at speed

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that you throw the shot in the shot put event, similar to how you throw the javelin.
nodes.response: Although 'throw' is often the terminology used when competing in the shot put, pupils should push the shot which starts from under their chin. A throwing action, when using a heavier shot, would likely cause a wrist/elblow/shoulder injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that only the selected pupil performing in the event needs to focus on it.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand that the whole team has a part to play in each event. Helping with tactics, motivating and encouraging each other are ways they can all be involved.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team athletics competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that you have to be fast to be good at long distance running, overlooking the importance of endurance, breathing technique, pacing and tactics.
nodes.response: Explain that sprinting and long-distance running differ: sprinters rely on fast-twitch muscle fibres for power and speed, while long-distance runners use slow-twitch fibres for endurance and efficiency.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running for distance competition

nodes.misconception: In the triple jump, pupils collapse the middle 'step phase' rather than getting equal height and distance from every phase.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of all phases of the jump, especially the step phase and that they understand all phases of the triple jump should contribute to an equal proportion of distance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that winning is everything and become disappointed if they fail to win every race.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to focus on personal improvement, teamwork and enjoying themselves.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running for speed competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils only focus on winning and become disappointed if they don't win.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to be motivated to try and win, but to understand that performing to the best of their ability and enjoying themselves is what they need to aim for.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Individual athletics competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that tensing their body (hands, face, arms, legs), will help them generate more speed.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that this can actually slow them down, by affecting their running form and using energy inefficiently.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running for speed: sprinting

nodes.misconception: When pupils follow through on their throw, they use excessive force which causes them to lose balance, impacting the throw and often causing them to step over the throwing line.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the consequences of stepping over the throwing line - foul throw.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing: accuracy vs distance

nodes.misconception: When applying their acceleration skills to a race, pupils false start in an attempt to win.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that they need to start fast, reacting quickly to the start command, however, too many false starts can result in being disqualified.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprinting: explore acceleration

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to stand still and wait for the baton to be passed to them before they start running.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils start jogging as their teammate approaches them.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Relay

nodes.misconception: When pupils hold the relay baton, they hold it in the middle, believing that this will help them grip it best. This makes it hard for their teammate to grab the baton.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to hold the baton at the bottom when running, leaving more space for their teammate to hold when they changeover.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running for speed in a team

nodes.misconception: When building up to the jump, the pupil steps forward slightly, jumping off 1 foot.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that jumping off 1 foot or stepping forwards before jumping is a foul. They must jump and land using both feet.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping for distance: standing long jump

nodes.misconception: Moving your arms faster makes you swim faster.
nodes.response: When learning front crawl and backstroke pupils must have opportunity to catch the water and feel the water so that they are able to pull as much water as possible.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Range of skills, alternating strokes front crawl and backstroke, floating

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that swimming is the best action in an emergency situation.
nodes.response: Floating, treading water and heat retaining positions are often the best action in an emergency situation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Safe self-rescue and selecting appropriate actions during emergencies

nodes.misconception: Breaststroke is always swam with the head up.
nodes.response: Breaststroke can be swam with the head up in a survival situation or with the head submerging and lifting during each arm cycle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Range of strokes, treading water and signalling for help

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that swimming fast is most important.
nodes.response: Slow, steady and energy efficient swimming is best for longer distance swimming.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: 25m competently, confidently and proficiently, rotations, fall in entry

nodes.misconception: In emergency situations people often swim without assessing the situation first.
nodes.response: Floating for 60 seconds in a star float and then treading water to identify the most appropriate action is best for assessing a survival situation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The appropriate stroke for the intended purpose, including survival strokes

nodes.misconception: When swimming sidestroke the legs perform a breaststroke action.
nodes.response: From the starting position of one leg stacked on top of the other, the top leg moves forward and the bottom leg moves backwards, the legs then snap back together in the starting position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Safe self-rescue circuit, swimming using different survival strokes

nodes.misconception: Your fitness is fixed and cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Fitness can improve slowly and over time. Measuring our fitness only tells us what we can do on that day.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: My personal best

nodes.misconception: To become fitter you must ‘work out’.
nodes.response: Fitness can develop in many different forms. Whenever you are challenging your body physically, this will help you to become fitter.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Fitness

nodes.misconception: Some pupils might think that only oxygenated blood is transported around the body.
nodes.response: The body's cardiovascular system includes a group of organs and muscles that manage oxgenated blood and deoxygenated blood.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The cardiovascular system

nodes.misconception: Being strong is about having big muscles.
nodes.response: Being physically strong relates to how our bodies are able to overcome the forces placed upon them. Strong muscles are essential for humans to complete everyday tasks and also help our joints to work effectively which helps to avoid injury and pain.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Strength

nodes.misconception: Flexibility can only be challenged when we are holding a specific postion and staying still.
nodes.response: Flexibility of our muscles can be performed when still (static) and on the move (dynamic).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Flexibility

nodes.misconception: Rest is not good for the body as it is the opposite of being active.
nodes.response: Rest is really important to help the body recover, grow, repair and get stronger.  However too much time not moving can cause the body to reduce fitness and strength.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Cardiovascular fitness

nodes.misconception: Cold water shock only occurs in the winter.
nodes.response: Cold water shock can occur all year round in waters around the UK.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Swim safe outdoors

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that moving your arms faster makes you swim faster.
nodes.response: Catching and pulling the water slowly and effectively produces greater forward travel and increases speed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Backstroke over increasing distances and safe entry into the pool

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that they should breathe as little as often, or always breathe to the same side.
nodes.response: Breathing every 3 arms pulls maintains body position and oxygen supply to the working muscles.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Front crawl over increasing distance

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that they should kick as quickly as possible, without using a glide between each breaststroke leg kick.
nodes.response: Breaststroke is most effective when there is a short glide in the streamlined position between each leg kick.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Breaststroke, increasing distance, artistic swimming routines

nodes.misconception: Strong swimmers don't get into difficulty in the water.
nodes.response: Even strong swimmers can get into difficulty in the water if cold, tired, unwell or injured.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rookie lifeguard

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that it is okay to turn over on to your front when finishing a backstroke race.
nodes.response: When swimming backstroke you should use the flags to count your strokes so that you finish a race on your back.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Peer assessment, competitive swimming, advanced safe self-rescue circuit

nodes.misconception: When fielding, pupils retrieve the ball and run with it in order to return it to the pupil on a base.
nodes.response: Tell the pupils that when fielding, they should work together as a team. Instead of running with the ball, they should quickly pass it to another player support, who needs to be close by and supporting. This will help move the ball faster.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The concept of racing rounders

nodes.misconception: When batting, pupils focus solely on hitting the ball with power, ignoring the positioning of the fielders.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that having awareness of fielders positions willl help them to aim and strike the ball into space. A powerful strike is not as effective if it goes towards a fielder.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Batting: where and why

nodes.misconception: When fielding in games, pupils believe that retrieving the ball and running it back to the bases is the most effective and quickest way to field.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work as a team, by backing each other up and supporting each other. Ensure pupils understand that accurately throwing the ball to a teammate that is closer to the bases will be more effective and quicker than running with it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play: apply batting and fielding skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils try to generate their hitting power using just their arm, which results in them over swinging and missing the ball.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that swining smoothly and keeping their eye on the ball is important. Pupils should bend their knees slightly and use their hips to rotate and generate power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Batting: technique

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that when fielding, they only need to think about how they use their hands when attempting to catch or stop a moving ball, which can cause them to miss the ball.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand the importance of moving their feet quickly to ensure they are able to position their body behind the ball. This will increase their chances of stopping the ball from going any further.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic fielding tactics

nodes.misconception: When bowling, pupils prioritise throwing the ball with as much force as possible.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that applying force to their bowls is beneficial, but good accuracy is essential to ensure 'no balls' aren't thrown. Pupils should focus on developing excellent accuracy before attempting to apply more force.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Fielding: bowling and backstop

nodes.misconception: Pupils throw with too much force when aiming for a target.
nodes.response: Managing the right amount force of a throw requires practise and trial and error to judge how much force is needed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing underarm with accuracy

nodes.misconception: Pupils will choose to throw overarm from a distance even if this compromises accuracy.
nodes.response: Accuracy of an overarm throw takes time and practise. Pupils should try exploring both throwing techniques from different distances to judge what is their conformable throwing range.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing overarm and underarm in striking and fielding games

nodes.misconception: Pupils aim to strike the ball with a lot of power which can lead to missed timed strikes and no contact being made.
nodes.response: Power can range from the small amount of power needed to make contact, to a lot of power to make the ball travel further.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking: focus on the batter

nodes.misconception: Pupils generate a throwing action using the the arm only.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use all the body, rather than just the arm when throwing, to help generate power and balance when throwing over a greater distance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Throwing overarm

nodes.misconception: A celebration can only be shown or given when they have been successful.
nodes.response: Children may feel a lack of inclusion and encouragement if acknowledgement of their efforts are only made when they have been successful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play: apply batting and fielding skills in competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find when they move to throw/strike the ball, it goes somewhere different to where they had intended.
nodes.response: Encourage the striker/thrower to turn their body, as well as their head and shoulders towards the space they would like the ball to go.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Striking and fielding games

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes think that holding their breath or shallow breathing helps them focus or exert more power.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils stay relaxed when sprinting and understand that deep rhythmic breaths will help their muscles recieve more oxygen to generate energy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating sprinting: personal bests

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that they will set a new personal best every time they attempt to and become disappointed if they don't.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that they need to show resilience to keep trying if they don't manage to set a personal best.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating triple jump: personal bests

nodes.misconception: Pupils just use their arm strength to throw the shot, not realising the importance of using their legs to generate power.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are crouching down into their back leg and pushing off strongly to create power when releasing the shot. Remind pupils that shot put is a push, not a throw.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shot put

nodes.misconception: Pupils jump as high as possible when attempting to clear a hurdle which can slow them down and negatively effect their rhythm.
nodes.response: Pupils need to focus on their technique to help them jump the hurdles efficiently with a flat technique.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The hurdles

nodes.misconception: When pupils are receiving the baton, they turn their body to face the incoming runner to give them a better view and try to grab the baton from them.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that although this technique may seem easier, it will cause their team to lose speed. Pupils should face forwards, with their hand out behind them and communicate to ensure the exchange is successful.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Relay changeovers

nodes.misconception: Pupils dip at the wrong time, dipping too early, which has a negative impact on their running speed. Often pupils just dip their head forwards, rather than their upper body.
nodes.response: Give pupils opportunities to practise implementing the dip, aiming for around 3 steps before the finish line. Ensure pupils understand that a sprint race is measured when a runners upper body, shoulders cross the line, not their head.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Finishing a race

nodes.misconception: Pupils often place their foot too low on the wall which affects their ability absorb and redirect impact. Pupils sometimes jump straight at the wall.
nodes.response: Pupils should aim to plant their foot around knee/waist height and remind pupils to push off the wall, not into it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced movements: tic tacs and wall runs

nodes.misconception: Pupils often stop between movements resulting in poor flow and continuity. This may be due to hesitancy or lack of confidence in their technique.
nodes.response: Pupils should repeat short sequences of movements until they are performed with flow. For example, focus on linking 2-3 movements together before adding more. Focus on flow before looking at speed routes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining movement and control: putting it all together

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget to initiate the turn with their head and don't spot their landing, which leads to disorientation and a lack of control.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on looking where they want to land. You should start the spin with your eyes and your head.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing spinning movements

nodes.misconception: Pupils often look directly down at their feet which shifts their head forward and throws them off their centre of gravity. Pupils are often overly tense when balancing.
nodes.response: For safety in parkour, pupils should focus just in front/ahead of their feet. Pupils should stay relaxed especially in their arms and shoulders.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Controlling the body: balance and control

nodes.misconception: Pupils often take-off flat footed or leaning backwards and look down during their jumps.
nodes.response: Pupils should take-off from the balls of the feet with knees and hips engaged, swinging their arms for more momentum. Pupils should ensure they keep their eyes locked on the landing spot from take-off to landing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Controlling the body: jumps and landings

nodes.misconception: Incorrect hand placement when performing vaults can lead to poor balance and coordination.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils perform with the correct hand position, using one hand for the lazy vault and opposite hand to foot with the step vault. Perform the vaults slowly to build confidence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Travelling over equipment: vaulting

nodes.misconception: Little bones in the hand and foot are not considered long bones.
nodes.response: Bones are classified based on their shape, if the shaft is longer than than the width and depth of a bone it is referred to as a long bone even if it is small in size.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification of bones

nodes.misconception: A muscle will always change length when it contracts.
nodes.response: A muscle pulls on a bone to create movement. However, occasionally, if the movement is static, the muscle is still contracting and under tension but not changing length. This is known as isometric muscle contraction.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of muscle contraction (isometric, concentric and eccentric)

nodes.misconception: Little bones in the hand and foot are not considered long bones.
nodes.response: Bones are classified based on their shape, if the shaft is longer than than the width and depth of a bone, it is referred to as a long bone even if it is small in size.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification of bones applied to performance in physical activities and sports

nodes.misconception: Muscles can pull and push.
nodes.response: Muscles are only able to pull, they work in antagonistic pairs so one muscle can contract to create a movement whilst the other relaxes in opposition and then their roles are reversed to move back.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Voluntary muscles and antagonistic pairs

nodes.misconception: There can be confusion between the role of ligaments and tendons.
nodes.response: Ligaments connect bone to bone to stabilise a joint whereas tendons attach muscle to bone to enable movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Synovial joint structure and function

nodes.misconception: There can be confusion between the role of ligaments and tendons.
nodes.response: Ligaments connect bone to bone to stabilise a joint whereas tendons attach muscle to bone to enable movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Structure of a synovial joint

nodes.misconception: There can be confusion between the role of ligaments and tendons.
nodes.response: Ligaments connect bone to bone to stabilise a joint whereas tendons attach muscle to bone to enable movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification of joints

nodes.misconception: Students may mix up rotation and circumduction.
nodes.response: When you rotate the shoulder joint you draw a dot with your hand (if the elbow is fully extended) whereas circumduction draws a circle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Movements possible at different joints

nodes.misconception: Students may mix up rotation and circumduction.
nodes.response: When you rotate the shoulder joint you draw a dot with your hand (if the elbow is fully extended) whereas circumduction draws a circle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Different joints and their movements

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the different body systems and terminology used for each (for example not realising the cardio-respiratory system refers to the heart and lungs).
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that muscular means muscles, skeletal means bones, cardio means heart, vascular means blood vessels and respiratory means lungs.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Structure and function of the skeleton

nodes.misconception: Muscles can pull and push.
nodes.response: Muscles are only able to pull. They work in antagonistic pairs so one muscle can contract to create a movement whilst the other relaxes in opposition and then their roles are reversed to move back.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Muscles of the body and antagonistic pairs

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the different body systems and terminology used for each (for example, not realising the cardiorespiratory system refers to the heart and lungs).
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that muscular means muscles, skeletal means bones, cardio means heart, vascular means blood vessels and respiratory means lungs.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Bones and structure of the skeleton

nodes.misconception: Mixing up the different body systems and terminology used for each (for example, not realising the cardio-respiratory system refers to the heart and lungs).
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that muscular means muscles, skeletal means bones, cardio means heart, vascular means blood vessels and respiratory means lungs.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The functions of the skeleton

nodes.misconception: Muscles can pull and push.
nodes.response: Muscles are only able to pull, they work in antagonistic pairs so one muscle can contract to create a movement whilst the other relaxes in opposition and then their roles are reversed to move back.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Muscles and antagonistic pairs

nodes.misconception: Students may mix up rotation and circumduction.
nodes.response: When you rotate the shoulder joint, you draw a dot with your hand (if the elbow is fully extended) whereas circumduction draws a circle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Joints and their movements

nodes.misconception: Pupils may get confused with the different names of fast/ slow and type I/ type II muscle fibres.
nodes.response: The word slow has an O in it and these fibres use oxygen to contract slowly and aerobically. They are our body's first choice of muscle fibre due to fatigue resistance, hence type I.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of muscle and muscle fibre

nodes.misconception: If you can't see the outcome of your performance, you are unable to learn how to improve.
nodes.response: Receiving feedback from teammates and other pupils about your performance will enable you to learn and make progress.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Supporting others to be their best

nodes.misconception: Pupils seek the easiest opportunity to guarantee a win.
nodes.response: Winning an unfair or unbalanced race/competition is a hollow victory and greater satisfaction comes from winning a balanced contest where both individuals/teams have a good chance of winning.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Balanced competition

nodes.misconception: Winning is the only metric of success and losing is always bad.
nodes.response: You can make improvements to your own/your team's performance in many different ways, regardless of the outcome of a competition.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Redefining success

nodes.misconception: Target games must be played against people of similar ability or previous experience for it to be a fair competition.
nodes.response: Conditions can be put on specific players in target games to balance the competition, regardles of their ability or previous experience.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Create and lead a competition

nodes.misconception: All tournaments must focus solely on the outcome/winner of competition.
nodes.response: In order for all participants to feel included, tournaments can take many forms and be adapted so that everyone can enjoy an appropriate level of challenge.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tournament time

nodes.misconception: Upper body strength is the primary fitness component required for seated volleyball.
nodes.response: Core strength is fundamental to play seated volleyball effectively as it enables players to maintain their body position in the preparation and executon of skills throughout the game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: How to manage competition, in victory or defeat

nodes.misconception: Pupils think if they are struggling to achieve the guided training in the app, they have failed and have to stop.
nodes.response: The app is flexible and can be adapted to individual needs and fitness levels. Even though it is set over 9 weeks you can complete it at your own pace and revisit weeks / runs if needed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Adjusting your programme

nodes.misconception: Pupils think hitting your targets is the same as doing the maximum amount you can.
nodes.response: A target needs to be SMART. It needs to be specific to the group, one you can measure, the group agrees it and it is realistic to all the abilities and fitness levels in the group. It also needs an allocated time to achieve it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hitting your targets

nodes.misconception: Pupils think interval training is completed to increase speed and power only.
nodes.response: The rest intervals are really good to enhance stamina and cardiovascular endurance. The intense workout does develop power especially in the lower body muscles which supports injury prevention when running.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Injury prevention and the benefits of high intensity exercise

nodes.misconception: Pupils think couch to 5k is merely to start running and be able to run 5k immediately.
nodes.response: 5k is a popular distance due to the park run (a global brand). However, couch to 5k is a beginner's approach to running using a gradual training plan, over 9 weeks from walking to running.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Say goodbye to the sofa

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the race is about placing and running in the fastest time.
nodes.response: Yes placings are given, but the key focus is to complete the race in a time that you know is representative of you working to the best of your ability.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The race of your life

nodes.misconception: Pupils think squats are only limited to the gym environment.
nodes.response: A squat is a functional whole body exercise to strengthen the lower body which can completed with weights or without (just using bodyweight as resistance), and can be completed anywhere where the space if big enough.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The dangers of overtraining

nodes.misconception: fundamental movement skills (FMS) are only needed at primary school.
