nodes.response: FMS underpin good movement in any activity and in wider life, so it is essential that we continue to practise and hone these basic movements.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playground games and fundamental movement skills

nodes.misconception: A fast heart rate and feeling of nausea is dangerous and you should stop exercising.
nodes.response: This is quite normal and a sign that we are challenging our fitness. It is important to get used to the way our body feels when we start to exercise. Seek guidance if this concerns you.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Understand how your body responds to exercise

nodes.misconception: To win you must be the quickest and race to complete tasks
nodes.response: If we rush communication, we will not properly understand which will lead to mistakes. Even if we finish first, it will be irrelevant if the task is completed incorrectly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sheep pen communication challenge as a team

nodes.misconception: Rushing before figuring out a strategy and consequently making mistakes
nodes.response: Take time to plan your strategy first to avoid losing more time by being sent back to the start
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Build a successful team to cross the river

nodes.misconception: Believing that hard work involves rushing to complete the maximum number of repetitions but with poor form.
nodes.response: Doing less movements with the correct technique will have a more positive impact on fitness than blasting out lots with poor form/range of movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Fitness challenges as a team

nodes.misconception: Letting the most vocal pupils make all the decisions as they have the answers.
nodes.response: The loudest people don't always have the best ideas. If you are a dominant character it is especially important to invest time in learning how and when to be quiet, to listen or to invite others to contribute.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving challenges as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to trust others to have their back.
nodes.response: Trust is a two-way process and something that needs to be earned and then not taken advantage of.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Trust exercises

nodes.misconception: Losing track of time or becoming distracted by the freedom of navigating without the direct supervision of a teacher.
nodes.response: Focus in on school values and responsibility to retain the privilege of independence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Explore your school site

nodes.misconception: A team will still be successful as long as some of its members contribute and work hard.
nodes.response: Everyone should be given the opportunity to use their voice and have a role to ensure success. Every pupil needs to be encouraged to share their ideas and listen to others in each learning cycle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Social skill challenges

nodes.misconception: Confusion transferring the route from the map to real life.
nodes.response: By orientating the map and holding it facing the same way relative to key features/north, you can quickly navigate around and avoid confusion every time you change direction.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Orienteering

nodes.misconception: Letting the more vocal students take the lead improves team outcomes.
nodes.response: Outcomes are better if the voices of the whole group are listened to and considered.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving

nodes.misconception: Thinking the heart rate and breathing rate are zero when at rest.
nodes.response: Our body needs the energy from the oxygen we breathe in order to maintain basic living functions, hence why our heart rate is always raised above 0.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Working as a team to raise your heart rate

nodes.misconception: Feeling disappointed if some fitness test results fall below national average.
nodes.response: We all have different strengths and weaknesses and this is why we train to improve our areas of weakness.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Your current fitness and goals

nodes.misconception: Everyone needs exactly the same nutritional plan.
nodes.response: Different people have different nutritional needs, at different times in life, especially when training for different activities.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Nutritional awareness

nodes.misconception: Progress will always be made at the same rate.
nodes.response: Sometimes different factors affect level of progress (sleep, hormones, nutrition) but also training results can plateau and changes to training are needed to continue to push the body to adapt.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Future goals and healthy habits

nodes.misconception: Training a lot more will automatically improve your fitness.
nodes.response: Without adequate rest within a training programme, the individual will have a higher chance of injury, decreased performance and chronic fatigue.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sleep and recovery

nodes.misconception: Every risk can be planned for.
nodes.response: There may be some risks that cannot be planned for, so we must be able to dynamically risk assess on an ongoing basis (e.g. the piece of equipment you were planning to use breaks and becomes unfit for purpose).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Injury and injury prevention

nodes.misconception: Weight training is only for people wanting to improve muscular strength.
nodes.response: Weight training improves strength, muscular endurance, power and speed, as well as increasing bone density and joint stability while reducing the risk of injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Strength training for all

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may struggle to believe the impact your mindset can have on performance.
nodes.response: Your mindset can be the difference between giving up and persisting, through the use of mindfulness, visualisation and positive self talk anything is possible.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mental health and stress management

nodes.misconception: Expecting progress to show huge improvements.
nodes.response: different factors could affect the level of progress including frequency, effort, sleep and nutrition. Further training could show more improvement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Review your progress

nodes.misconception: Progressive overload only applies when weight training.
nodes.response: Gradually increasing frequency, intensity and time or altering the type of exercise through the manipulation of different training methods can develop all fitness components. Clear examples must be shared across activities other than weight training.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planning a training programme

nodes.misconception: Underestimating the amount of water the body needs throughout the day (not just during exercise) to maintain hydration.
nodes.response: The general recommendation is 2 litres of water per day, however when training, more should be consumed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hydration and fuelling your body for exercise

nodes.misconception: Flexibility training is only for dancers or gymnasts.
nodes.response: Flexibility training is useful for all athletes as it can improve mobility, posture and reduce muscle tension making all movements easier.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Routines for daily flexibility and mobility

nodes.misconception: Some pupils approach many fitness tasks as a race/competition and often give up as opposed to slowing down and maintaining movement until the end.
nodes.response: Reassure that a finishing position is irrelevant and instead focus on personal performance and improvement to their own fitness.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A cardiovascular base

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when you are player-to -player marking it is only about being an individual.
nodes.response: Defenders must communicate, adjust to overloads and support each other. If one defender gets beaten, others need to be ready to help. Marking your player is just one part of working together to stop the attack.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending by denying space and time

nodes.misconception: Tackling harder always makes it more effective.
nodes.response: Controlled technique, not force, makes a tackle successful and reduces the chance of injury or penalties.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Gaining confidence in contact

nodes.misconception: Pupils think if they miss a tackle, they should just give up.
nodes.response: Pupils need to show determination to chase back and continue to pressure the attack, even if they miss a tackle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Respond to challenges with persistence and focus

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that tackling a raider individually is the only option.
nodes.response: In Kabaddi, Raiders have 30 seconds to make the raid and get back across the half way line. As a result, if the defense hold up the raider until their time runs out, it is an unsuccessful raid and the raider doesn't score.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Counterattack and momentum swings

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you can constantly change directions when chasing.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that in Kho Kho, chasers cannot change direction freely. They must run around a turning pole to change direction. Turning mid-court is a foul.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Solutions to tactical challenges

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget that after making a tackle, they need to get back onside in a straight line.
nodes.response: Response: after a tackle, the whole defensive line need to be back onside 10m from the play of the ball. If you are not moving as a flat line, you leave gaps for attackers to break through.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling and getting into a defensive line

nodes.misconception: It might be believed that certain sports only require one type of practice structure.
nodes.response: Practice structures vary depending on the skills being practiced and the level of ability. Two different skills from within the same sport might benefit from different practice structures.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Massed, distributed, fixed and variable practice

nodes.misconception: Performance in sport is entirely down to physiological capabilities such as speed, strength and technique.
nodes.response: Psychological factors such as confidence, motivation and learned behaviours from similar experiences in the past have as much impact on performance sport as the level of skill players have.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Characteristics of skilful movement

nodes.misconception: A very common mistake made when classifying skills is to name a sport without the skill. For example, trying to classify 'rugby' rather than one of the many different skills within rugby.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that specific skills are required and that they can name multiple examples of skills from different sports.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification of skills on a continua

nodes.misconception: Skills must be one classification or the other, e.g. a skill is either gross or fine.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand a continua allows for skills to be classified anywhere along it, and that some skills may well fall somewhere between two different classifications.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Self-paced/externally paced and gross/fine continua

nodes.misconception: Skill and ability are interchangeable.
nodes.response: They are not interchangeable. Skill is learnt and developed through practice, while ability is a natural and inherited trait often considered innate. An ability provides an opportunity or the potential to develop a skill.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Skill and ability

nodes.misconception: A very common mistake made when classifying skills is to name a sport without the skill. For example, trying to classify 'rugby' rather than one of the many different skills within rugby.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that specific skills are required and that they can name multiple examples of skills from different sports.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The difficulty and environmental continua

nodes.misconception: A very common mistake made when classifying skills is to name a sport without the skill. For example, trying to classify 'rugby' rather than one of the many different skills within rugby.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that specific skills are required and that they can name multiple examples of skills from different sports.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification of skills continua

nodes.misconception: Pupils use both sides of the stick like they see in ice-hockey.
nodes.response: In field hockey you are only allowed to use the flat side of the stick. If the ball touches the other side or your foot it is a foul.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing smart with the ball on a stick

nodes.misconception: Pupils wait until a defender is too close before trying to make a pass and consequently lose possession often.
nodes.response: By getting control of the ball quickly, looking up to find teammates in space and passing before a defender gets too close you can keep possession better.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing smart with the ball at your feet

nodes.misconception: Pupils attack territory down the middle of the court or pitch and it becomes crowded.
nodes.response: By using accurate passing and movement of the ball out wide, you draw defenders out and create more space to invade. Similarly, by moving the ball back and then forward again, you can create more space.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing smart with the ball in your hands

nodes.misconception: Teams don't discuss tactics properly and instead focus on just wanting to play a game.
nodes.response: Forming a number of predetermined plans can be an effective way to capitalise on set play situations and being aware of which team members are the biggest threat to the opposition can leave other players more open.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Design set plays to overload the attack

nodes.misconception: Pupils are unable to adjust their team tactics based on the situation.
nodes.response: Changing the way you play as a team to include formation, tactics and roles of different players can have a huge impact on the game and a shift in momentum that disrupts your opposition.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Responding to tactical challenges in different scenarios

nodes.misconception: Some pupils commit to zone defence but others get distracted into chasing the ball, therefore moving out of position.
nodes.response: It is essential that all team members follow the same defensive strategy of player-to-player or zonal marking to avoid leaving big gaps.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Marking players, marking space and adapting on the fly

nodes.misconception: Arteries always carry oxygenated blood.
nodes.response: The pulmonary artery is the only artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood as it is pumped back to the lungs to be re-oxygenated. Consequently, the pulmonary vein is the only vein in the body that carries oxygenated blood.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Blood vessels and blood cells

nodes.misconception: Which side of the heart is the left when you look at the body and which side is oxygenated versus deoxygenated.
nodes.response: The left side of the heart is nearest your left armpit and carries oxygenated blood, the right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood (remember: LORD - left, oxygenated and right, deogygenated).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Double circulatory system and structure of the heart

nodes.misconception: Which side of the heart is the left when you look at the body and which side is oxygenated versus deoxygenated.
nodes.response: The left side of the heart is nearest your left armpit and carries oxygenated blood, the right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood (remember: LORD - left, oxygenated and right, deogygenated).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The structure of the heart

nodes.misconception: Which side of the heart is the left when you look at the body and which side is oxygenated versus deoxygenated.
nodes.response: The left side of the heart is nearest to your left armpit and carries oxygenated blood, the right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood (remember: LORD - left, oxygenated and right, deogygenated).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Structure of the cardiovascular system

nodes.misconception: Tidal volume is the amount of air breathed in and out per breath and the lungs completely empty of air when we expire.
nodes.response: Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out per breadth and it increases during exercise to enable more air and hence exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide to occur. A residual volume of air always remains in the lungs to keep them inflated.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The mechanics of breathing

nodes.misconception: Gaseous exchange only involves oxygen.
nodes.response: Gaseous exchange is when oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the lungs and the blood, and then between the blood and muscle tissues.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Air pathway from the atmosphere to alveoli and gaseous exchange

nodes.misconception: Tidal volume is the amount of air breathed in and out per breath and the lungs completely empty of air when we expire.
nodes.response: Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out per breadth and it increases during exercise to enable more air and hence exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide to occur. A residual volume of air always remains in the lungs to keep them inflated.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mechanics of breathing and interpretation of a spirometer trace

nodes.misconception: Arteries always carry oxygenated blood.
nodes.response: The pulmonary artery is the only artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood as it is pumped back to the lungs to be re-oxygenated. Consequently, the pulmonary vein is the only vein in the body that carries oxygenated blood.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Blood vessels, blood cells and the vascular shunt

nodes.misconception: The ba-dum of the heart beat represents the left then right side contracting.
nodes.response: The heart relaxes (diastole) to fill with blood then first phase of contraction squeezes blood from the top two atria down into the ventricles before the valves close off and then the second phase of contraction squeezes blood out of the ventricles.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The cardiac cycle

nodes.misconception: All of the oxygen we breathe in is used by the muscles.
nodes.response: The body only extracts a small percentage of the oxygen in each breath so it is important we keep breathing during and after exercise. You can only moves gases to an area of lower concentration so once that is equal diffusion stops.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of how the cardio-respiratory systems work together

nodes.misconception: Pupils often draw heart rate down to zero on a line graph.
nodes.response: Even at rest your heart is still beating, on average 72 beats per minute, to ensure blood is always circulating around the body to keep you alive.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output

nodes.misconception: Pupils think deoxygenated blood at the muscle tissue goes straight to the lungs rather than via the heart first (i.e. they forget they need to go through the heart twice).
nodes.response: Remind pupils the heart is a double circulatory pump consisting of a pulmonary and a systemic loop. Without this, blood pressure would be too low on return from the legs to efficiently get blood to the lungs for oxygenation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of the pathway of blood

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that only one type of guidance can be used at any time.
nodes.response: Combinations of guidance can be very effective and are common in good coaching. For example, visual demonstrations are often combined with verbal explanations.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of guidance

nodes.misconception: The input part of the model is largely based on being able to use sight to inform the brain.
nodes.response: Input is gathering data from all the senses. In sport, these can be what you see, hear, feel and touch.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic information processing

nodes.misconception: Types of feedback are often confused with types of guidance.
nodes.response: Ensure students are able to differentiate between guidance, which is infomation needed to understand how to perform a skill, and feedback which is information about how well it is being performed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of feedback

nodes.misconception: Types of feedback are often confused with types of guidance from the previous lesson.
nodes.response: Ensure students can differentiate between guidance being information needed to understand how to perform a skill, and feedback being information about how well it is being performed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of feedback to optimise performance

nodes.misconception: It is common to see variants on the SMART acronym, for example A = achievable, from other exam boards or sources. Some sources may extend the acronym to SMARTER.
nodes.response: Ensure it is understood that with the AQA exam board, SMART only ever refers to Specific, Measurable, Accepted, Realistic and Time-bound.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: SMART targets to optimise goals

nodes.misconception: It is common to see variants on the SMART acronym, for example, R = realistic, from other exam boards or sources. Some sources may extend the acronym to SMARTER.
nodes.response: Ensure it is understood that with the OCR exam board, SMART only ever refers to Specific, Measurable, Achieveable, Recorded and Timed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Goal setting and the SMART principle

nodes.misconception: It is common to see variants on the SMART acronym, for example R = recorded, from other exam boards or sources. Some sources may extend the acronym to SMARTER.
nodes.response: Ensure it is understood that with the Edexcel exam board, SMART only ever refers to Specific, Measurable, Achieveable, Realistic and Time-bound.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Goal Setting

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that just the tagger remains at the breakdown in T1 rugby.
nodes.response: After a tag/touch, 2 other defenders need to join the the tager to form a triangle at every breakdown.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming a tackle triangle and getting onside in defence

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that performance is only determined by how many tries you scored.
nodes.response: A player can have a strong impact without getting a try by helping their team keep possession, organise defence or create space for others.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: T1 rugby tournament

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when they are tagged/touched, the attacker can just give the ball (1 handed) to their teammate.
nodes.response: When tagged/touched, the attacker should present the ball with 2 hands and their teammate should rip the ball with 2 hands to keep it safe and avoid fumbles and knock ons.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ripping the ball and passing backwards

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that it is always best to pass when in a difficult situation.
nodes.response: Retaining possession through accurate kicks can at times make more yards than passing and being tagged.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kicks to restart and grubber kicks

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think it easier to hold the ball in 1 hand.
nodes.response: Holding the ball in 1 hand might feel easier at first but it reduces control, increases the risk of a knock-on and makes it harder to pass accurately in both directions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running with the ball, catching and evading in T1 rugby

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a scrum and line out in T1 rugby are contested and they push to get the ball.
nodes.response: T1 rugby is a non contact game therefore the scrum and lineouts are both uncontested. They are used to draw players into an area to create space on the pitch following a restart.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: T1 rugby restarts with lineouts and scrums

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the only way to defend is to mark 1 player on the opposite team.
nodes.response: Sometimes moving as a unit, where you shift together, can prevent any of the attackers from making a break and getting the ball up the court.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced defensive strategies and positional play

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the shooter is allowed in the D to score (like netball).
nodes.response: The only person allowed in the D is the goalkeeper, shooters have to shoot from outside the D, otherwise the goal doesn't count.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting techniques and defence

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the only movement that is important is the movement with the ball.
nodes.response: Movement off the ball is just as important, it helps create space and supports the player in possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced passing and team play

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that to take 3 steps with the ball, you have to be dribbling.
nodes.response: You only need to dribble if you want to take more than 3 steps. Once you catch the ball, you're allowed 3 steps without dribbling.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Review basic skills, rules and tactics of handball

nodes.misconception: Only the player taking the throw-off needs to be in their own half.
nodes.response: All players must be in their own half before the throw-off is taken, not just the thrower.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Full game play and strategy in action

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you should only move slowly with the ball so you don't lose posession.
nodes.response: Moving fast with the ball can create more opportunities to beat defenders, create space and keep the attacking momentum strong.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Goalkeeping and fast breaks

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a defensive player must catch the ball outright on initial contact from a shot.
nodes.response: It is sometimes more effective to bump a rebound up in the air for a teammate to catch, but it does then count as a pass. Whereas if you catch it cleanly or catch your own rebound, it doesn't use up one of your passes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defensive strategies

nodes.misconception: Pupils attack one end of the court similar to all other invasion games focused on territory and seek to tackle/intercept passes between the opposition.
nodes.response: Tchoukball is a unique game where both teams can score at both ends by throwing the ball into the rebound net and not being caught by the opposition. You are not allowed to tackle with the opposition while they are in possession of the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tchoukball and basic rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a short is associated with the height of a shot.
nodes.response: A short is when a shot misses the rebound frame completely. It results in a fault and change of possession with the defenders restarting play from behind the baseline.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils always use the same type of throw for passing and shooting (i.e. overarm with a focus on power and a direct route to the rebound frame).
nodes.response: It is easy to defend a square shot or an obvious attack angle at the rebound frame. To outwit the opposition, look to vary the type, angle and pace of shots as well as utilising fakes (e.g. a switch).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team play and game strategies

nodes.misconception: Pupils make simple ball handling mistakes due to rushing.
nodes.response: You lose possession if the ball is dropped, so whilst you need to make a pass within 3 seconds, it is essential not to make rushed decisions for passing and focus on catching the ball carefully with both hands before making your next move.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing, catching and moving with precision

nodes.misconception: Pupils always use the same type of shot.
nodes.response: Just throwing the ball harder at the rebound frame increases the risk of a fault from failing to hit the target but is also very predictable for the opposition. Therefore vary your angle, speed and deception applied when shooting.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting and then rebounding

nodes.misconception: Making loop passes are effective in attacking situations.
nodes.response: Such passes are easy to intercept as they are easy to track and often don't go very far.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Maintain possession with keep ball

nodes.misconception: Confident players shooting from out of range and failing to pass when would have been a better option.
nodes.response: Getting in a strong position with a high probability of scoring if you shoot is essential. It is important to pass to a teammate in a better position rather than shoot when out of range.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Getting into position and scoring

nodes.misconception: Route one - not utilising width or depth and just crowding the ball down the middle of the pitch/court.
nodes.response: When attacking, it is important to use the full width of the pitch/court to draw defenders out and create space for a scoring opportunity. It is also sometimes necessary to move the ball back, before moving forward again, if the space is too crowded.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking territory to score in the end zone

nodes.misconception: Crowding around the ball
nodes.response: By taking the ball out into the wide channels on a pitch/court, you draw defenders out of their area and create space elsewhere to pass to your own players and make an attack on goal.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating space

nodes.misconception: Lack of cushioning with hand or foot to keep close touch control and eyes always down to look at the ball.
nodes.response: By using kinaesthetic awareness (touch) and peripheral vision you can control the ball better with a light touch and keep your eyes up to look for space, teammates and defenders.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ball control in your hand and at your feet

nodes.misconception: Failing to remain goal side whilst keeping a view on the player and the ball.
nodes.response: Failing to remain goal side of your opposition exposes yourself to an easy scoring opportunity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defending as a unit

nodes.misconception: Pupils are unsure about situations when the body works aerobically and when it works anaerobically.
nodes.response: Aerobic exercise requires oxygen from the air we breathe to totally break down glucose to release energy for exercise. This is the most efficient mechanism but requires exercise to be at a low/ moderate intensity, whereas high intensity is anaerobic.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Aerobic and anaerobic exercise

nodes.misconception: A cool down will always prevent DOMS.
nodes.response: An active cool down supports better recovery from exercise by prolonging elevated heart and breathing rates to flush fresh oxygen through the muscles, but small micro tears in the muscles may still result in soreness 24-48 hours after exercise.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: EPOC and the recovery process

nodes.misconception: Exercise is either aerobic or anaerobic and lactic acid is bad.
nodes.response: All exercise is on a continuum from 100% aerobic (e.g. a long distance walk) to 100% anaerobic (e.g. a 1 rep max powerlifter) and the build up of lactic acid is perfectly natural and necessary to work at high intensity when insufficient O2 available.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Lactic acid and recovering from exercise

nodes.misconception: Pupils are unsure about situations when the body works aerobically and when it works anaerobically.
nodes.response: Aerobic exercise requires oxygen from the air we breathe to totally break down glucose to release energy for exercise. This is the most efficient mechanism but requires exercise to be at a low/ moderate intensity whereas high intensity is anaerobic.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Practical examples of aerobic and anaerobic exercise

nodes.misconception: Pupils may lack the confidence to officiate a game and may struggle to take control of the game. They may be biased towards certain teams depending on who they are friends with.
nodes.response: Create a safe, encouraging environment where pupils know it is acceptable to make mistakes when refereeing Reward referees when they handle challenges made towards their decision making. Ensure pupils are respecting one another's decisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating games

nodes.misconception: There is a lack of movement off the ball or teammates position themselves too close to the ball carrier therefore making it easier for the defenders to gain possession.
nodes.response: Pupils should always be moving off the ball to drag defenders out of positions. Pupils should also spread out and position themselves at different angles and distances from the ball carrier.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Positioning and creating options when attacking

nodes.misconception: Pupils may often focus on power rather than accuracy when shooting. They may also make poor decisions with regards to shooting when under pressure such as facing a goalkeeper or a defender.
nodes.response: Focus on accuracy over power, working on aiming for specific targets. Pupils should practise shooting under pressure to help them make good decisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Score and add a defender to increase complexity

nodes.misconception: There is a lack of movement off the ball or teammates position themselves too close to the ball carrier therefore making it easier for the defenders to gain possession.
nodes.response: Pupils should always be moving off the ball to drag defenders out of positions. Pupils should also spread out and position themselves at different angles and distances from the ball carrier.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a team to perform together

nodes.misconception: Pupils often dribble with their head down, focusing too much on the ball and not on teammates, spaces to move into or defenders within the space.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to develop the habit of looking up regularly to scan the area.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Movement with the ball: dribbling, receiving and turning

nodes.misconception: Pupils make a pass and stand still, waiting for the next ball. This is a common issue, especially in futsal, where quick transitions and movement are key.
nodes.response: After passing, always move to create an option. A great habit is to perform a give-and-go, where you pass the ball and immediately make a run to receive it back. This keeps the game fluid.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and movement off the ball

nodes.misconception: The more arousal you have, the better you perform.
nodes.response: The inverted-U theory recognises that after an optimal level of arousal, performance will deteriorate with any further heightening of arousal levels.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Inverted-U theory

nodes.misconception: Intrinsic motivation is always the best type of motivation.
nodes.response: Extrinsic motivation has its time and place, particularly with short term goals or with very young people. Intrinsic is much better when long term commitment and persistence is required.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Motivation: intrinsic and extrinsic

nodes.misconception: All acts of aggression involve violence and are the result of anger.
nodes.response: Some aggressive acts are controlled and are used to gain a performance advantage in sport. They are also within the rules of sports such as rugby and the combat sports.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Aggression

nodes.misconception: Mental preparation is just for elite athletes.
nodes.response: Students should understand that everyone can benefit from mental preparation techniques and that performers in many fields of work practice them. They too could benefit in their own pursuits.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Stress management techniques

nodes.misconception: This lesson gives the impression that there are only two types of people and people should be defined as one or the other personality.
nodes.response: Although the AQA specification has clear definitions of how introverts and extroverts typically behave, which will be required knowledge in the exam, students should understand that people's personality is more nuanced and goes beyond these.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Personality types

nodes.misconception: Mental preparation is just for elite athletes.
nodes.response: Students should understand that everyone can benefit from mental preparation techniques and that performers in many fields of work practice them. They too could benefit in their own pursuits.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mental preparation

nodes.misconception: Mental preparation is just for elite athletes.
nodes.response: Students should understand that everyone can benefit from mental preparation techniques and that performers in many fields of work practice them. They too could benefit in their own pursuits.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mental preparation for sports performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that a knock out tournament is always the best type of tournament to do in sport/ PE.
nodes.response: With 4 or less teams (or if you have a lot of time) a round-robin tournament is better so that all teams are able to play each other.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Organise a tournament

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that Korfball is a contact sport where you can push players.
nodes.response: Korfball allows incidental contact that is natural movement, e.g. brushing shoulders and close marking, however pushing, holding or blocking is not allowed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defensive strategies and tactics

nodes.misconception: Pupils forget that after 2 goals are scored they swap positions.
nodes.response: After 2 goals are scored in Korfball, the attackers then swap and become the defenders and the defenders swap and become attackers (on both teams).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Korfball rules and how to introduce them

nodes.misconception: Misconception: Pupils think you should always use two hands to shoot in Korfball.
nodes.response: Two-handed shots are useful, especially when you're learning, but they’re not always the best choice. In a match, you might need to shoot quickly or when a defender is close. One-handed shots can be faster and harder to block.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils think it is only defenders that screen attackers.
nodes.response: Attackers should also screen defenders to allow other attacking teammates to run into the space.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game tactics and positioning

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they only have 3 seconds to pass the ball like in netball.
nodes.response: In Korfball pupils have 4 seconds to pass the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and catching games

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think they need to take multiple touches before passing the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make quick decisions using one or two touch passes, and encourage pupils to scan before receiving the ball so they know where to pass to next.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and movement off the ball when attacking

nodes.misconception: Pupils often find passing over distance much harder and try to kick the ball too hard. Often pupils are too close together so no one is in a wide position to aim for.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to slowly increase the distance at which they pass so they maintain control and accuracy. Pupils should be encouraged to adopt wide positions when attacking, stretching defenders to create space.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Positioning and creating options in attack

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to make quick decisions and perform skills correctly when defenders are present and adding pressure.
nodes.response: Remind players to scan before receiving the ball. Use mini games or time limits in tasks so pupils are used to performing under pressure.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Score and add defenders to increase complexity

nodes.misconception: When teaching the offside rule, pupils often struggle with understanding a player is offside when the ball is passed to them not when they receive it.
nodes.response: Use cues to show the moment the ball was passed. For example, you could ask the pupils to freeze just as the ball is passed to determine whether they are offside or not.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a team to perform tactics and strategies together

nodes.misconception: Pupils make a big touch so they don't have close control of the ball. Pupils slow down after turning with the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to keep the ball close to the body so they have control at all times. Pupils should explode after the turn pushing off with their standing leg.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Movement with the ball: dribbling, receiving and turning at pace

nodes.misconception: Pupils may lack confidence when officiating and fear making incorrect decisions. They may also struggle with peer pressure and be tempted to change their decisions.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make clear, firm decisions and remind them that mistakes are part of learning. Teach referees to stand by their decisions and use short, clear explanations. Also ensure the players are respectful of those decisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating your own games

nodes.misconception: As a goalkeeper it is important to use your stick to hit away the ball.
nodes.response: It's often more effective to rely on your pads or kickers for blocking low shots and redirecting the ball to safety. The stick is mainly for high / wide shots or controlling passes, but your legs and body provide a larger surface area for most shots.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Scoring and saving a goal

nodes.misconception: When receiving the ball from the side, hitting to score is easy with the ball at the side.
nodes.response: It is easier to hit the ball with more power by controlling it and positoning it slightly to right and forward of your feet before hitting it. This allows a better angle for accuracy and power as the ball already has momentum towards the goal.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking play

nodes.misconception: It is best for lots of attackers to be near the ball so they have more chance of keeping possession.
nodes.response: Overcrowding the ball limits passing options, reduces space and makes it easier for defenders to win possession, so attackers should spread out to keep better control.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Thinking Thursdays and lessons learnt from England Hockey (game play)

nodes.misconception: When dribbling the ball eyes should always be down looking at the ball.
nodes.response: Whilst it's important to control the ball, always looking down means you can't see what's happening in the game. Keeping the head up improves decision-making, allowing players to see defenders, find passing options and spaces to dribble into.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling, passing and receiving with control

nodes.misconception: Long corners are actually taken from the corner of the pitch.
nodes.response: Long corners are taken on the 23m line, in line with where the ball went out. They used to be taken from the corners, but the rule changed in 2015.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Short and long corners

nodes.misconception: It's only the defenders that need to be good at tackling.
nodes.response: Tackling is a crucial skill for all players, not just defenders. Midfielders need to win possession and disrupt attacks, while forwards use tackling to press high up the pitch and regain the ball in attacking areas.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling and marking players

nodes.misconception: Pupils hit all shots with a similar technique and avoid high risk, powerful smashes to avoid losing points.
nodes.response: Practising smash shots is necessary in order to take your game to the next level.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Smash and defence

nodes.misconception: Pupils instinctively want to work with their best friend and/or the 'best' partner.
nodes.response: When playing matches, it's fulfilling when a competition is balanced and offers an equal chance of winning. To achieve this, pair up pupils based on current performance levels or agree a number of starting points to give to one of the people/teams.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ladder competition

nodes.misconception: Pupils swing when hitting drop shots and net shots.
nodes.response: By reducing your backswing and almost eliminating your follow through, you will be able to perform more successful drop shots and net shots that trickle just over the net and put your opponent under more pressure.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Drop shots and net play

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't adapt their court position based on where their partner is and where the shuttle has been hit.
nodes.response: Work together to cover the court. If your partner is at the front of the court then it is important to step back to cover the back of the court. However, it is typically easier to assume side-by-side positioning and cover half the court each.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Doubles strategy and communication

nodes.misconception: Pupils call their score first and get confused which side they should serve from.
nodes.response: You should always call the serving player's/team's score first. If their score is even, then they serve from the right, whereas if their score is odd, they serve from the left.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Recall of basic skills and rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils wait until their opponent hits the shuttle before starting to initiate movement to retrieve it.
nodes.response: If you wait until you know where the shuttle is going before starting to move, you will often be too late to get to it. Instead, pre-load your legs with a split step to trigger an explosive lunge to reach the shuttle faster.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced footwork and movement

nodes.misconception: Pupils fear running at speed to jump on to the springboard or are reluctant to jump on to a vault/box top. Pupils have poor technique on the springboard. Pupils fear straddling the box.
nodes.response: Build confidence by breaking the skill down. Practise without the box top or with a lower box gradually increasing height. Develop good foot positioning on the springboard before adding in the box top. Pupils could straddle on to the box first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Vaulting with control and creativity

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush their feedback and don't give detailed advice to enable pupils to make improvements. Pupils may rush to refine their routines without carefully considering how they can make improvements.
nodes.response: Provide numerous examples of high quality feedback throughout to highlight your expectations. Ensure that pupils take care over the details to improve their routine.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Reviewing, refining and improving aesthetic performance using feedback

nodes.misconception: Pupils often link pieces of apparatus together e.g. benches attached to a table which limits the use of space and options for pathways. Pupils rush to create balances that are not of high quality.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to place apparatus in spaces to allow them to explore interesting pathways and to be able to use each piece of apparatus in creative ways. Peer assessment of balances can encourage refinement and increase quality of pupils work.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Building a group routine

nodes.misconception: When working in bigger groups, there may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
nodes.response: Pupils could delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups. Pupils may have to consider adapting their  routines to help other members of their group.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing and supporting the performance of others

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to coordinate their take off on to the springboard. Pupils land on the springboard with their heels.
nodes.response: Use a short run up to develop good take off technique focusing on 1 foot to 2 feet on the springboard. Pupils should always land on the balls of their feet to get more lift from the springboard.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using apparatus to aid flight

nodes.misconception: When jumping from apparatus, pupils may rush the jump and not be balanced before they take off. Pupils may land with stiff knees or poor body position.
nodes.response: Always check balance and engage the core before jumping. Ensure a solid stance before jumping. Pupils should bend their knees to absorb impact on landing and make sure their weight is centered over their feet.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic flight using jumps and turns

nodes.misconception: Pupils always opt to perform the most simple movements. Pupils may not like performing in front of others.
nodes.response: Give pupils time to develop their movement ideas and be creative. Share creative ideas to improve the quality of movements. Encourage pupils to present in pairs to build up their confidence in performing to one another.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Different ways to move

nodes.misconception: When pupils evaluate each others performances, they overlook the important details such as performing with control, extension, flow and accurate timing.
nodes.response: Make sure pupils are using the worksheet to help them evaluate the sequences so that they focus on the fundamentals that make a sequence high quality.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating and refining sequences

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a partner balance is a counter balance. One pupil pulls harder or doesn’t pull enough, leading to a collapse of the position. Pupils do not have a secure grip with one another.
nodes.response: Show the difference between a partner balance and a counter balance. Encourage pupils to communicate with their partners pulling gently at first, then increase force gradually to find the balance point. Grip using wrists as an alternative to hands.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Point and patch balances

nodes.misconception: When pupils add more content to their sequence, they can lose flow with the sequence looking unpolished. Pupils show limited variety in their locomotive elements.
nodes.response: Practise the sequence slowly at first, focusing on smooth transitions between movements and balances. Encourage pupils to be creative and add variety to their locomotive movements throughout the sequence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating sequences with locomotion, rotation and balance

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle with spatial awareness when rotating their body. Poor posture and body alignment means pupils lose control and balance when rotating.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to practise 90 degree rotations initially and then build up to larger rotations. Encourage pupils to use visual cues so they look at a particular spot when rotating. Encourage pupils to engage their core to maintain good posture.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rotation and control

nodes.misconception: With forward rolls, pupils may not tuck their chin, leading to discomfort. They may struggle to generate enough momentum to complete the roll.
nodes.response: Emphasise tucking the chin to protect the neck and practise rocking back and forth from a crouched position to develop momentum. Break each roll down into manageable steps.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Locomotion and partner work

nodes.misconception: Anaerobic exercise is only useful for improving your ability to run fast.
nodes.response: Anaerobic training can also build muscular strength, power, endurance and improve body composition. All of these can benefit your performance in many different sports not just running.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Anaerobic exercise in action

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a circuit has to involve exercises in a circle.
nodes.response: A circuit is a series of exercises done a specific order but does not have to be set up like a circle.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Set up a basic circuit

nodes.misconception: Pupils think aerobic training is only relevant for endurance athletes like long distance runners.
nodes.response: Aerobic training is useful for any athletes that play sports that last longer than 20 minutes, e.g. rugby, netball football, hockey.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Aerobic exercise in action

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they should just include their favourite exercises in their own circuit.
nodes.response: Exercises should be selected and used to target and imporove specific areas of weakness, e.g. certain muscle groups, a components of fitness or a sport specific skill you need more practice at.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Build your own pairs circuit training programme

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that circuit training is solely to improve components of fitness but not for developing skilled sports performance.
nodes.response: While circuit training is great for improving components of fitness, it can also be designed to develop sport-specific skills. For example, in basketball, a circuit can include dribbling, shooting and passing stations, alongside fitness exercises.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sport specific circuits

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that body adaptations will occur and stay from training only once.
nodes.response: Body adaptations like stronger muscles or better endurance don’t happen after just one training session. To see improvements, you need to train regularly. If you stop training, your body can start to lose those gains – this is called reversibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Apply the basic principles of training to your circuit

nodes.misconception: Cardiorespiratory benefits only come from endurance training and muscle growth only comes from weight training.
nodes.response: Any training that regularly puts the bodily systems under more strain than they are in normal life will lead to long-term benefits to the muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory systems. However, training intensity will affect results.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Long-term effects of exercise

nodes.misconception: Cardio-respiratory benefits only come from endurance training and muscle growth only comes from weight training.
nodes.response: Any training that regularly puts the bodily systems under more strain than they are in normal life will lead to long term benefits to the muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory systems. However, training intensity will effect results.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Long term adaptations to training

nodes.misconception: A proper cool down speeds up reduction in heart rate after exercise and prevents muscle soreness.
nodes.response: An active cool down actually prolongs the elevated heart and breathing rate after exercise to help flush fresh oxygen through the muscles and improve recovery. However, DOMS may still occur due to microtears in muscles if training was intense.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of heart rate response to exercise and recovery

nodes.misconception: Cardiorespiratory benefits only come from endurance training and muscle growth only comes from weight training.
nodes.response: Any training that regularly puts the bodily systems under more strain than they are in normal life, will lead to long term benefits to the muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory systems. However, training intensity will effect results.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Long term training effects and benefits

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up what changes happen in response to exercise and what changes happen as a long term adaptation to training.
nodes.response: Short-term responses of the body are what happens as soon as we start exercising to cope with it, but if we train regularly, then the body adapts to be better able to cope with the stress of exercise and hence work more efficiently in performance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The short term responses to exercise and changes in the body

nodes.misconception: Mixing up immediate, short-term and long-term effects of exercise.
nodes.response: Immediate effects are what happens as soon as we start exercising to cope with it, whereas short-term effects are those that happen over the next 36 hours. Long-term refers to the adaptations that happen in response to training.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Immediate and short term effects of exercise on the body

nodes.misconception: Pupils often take-off with the wrong foot when performing the thief vault or they take-off too close to the obstacle.
nodes.response: Work on take-off in isolation, focusing on taking-off with the outside foot and ensuring there is enough space between them and the obstacle to ensure continued flow through the vault.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Parkour and fundamental techniques

nodes.misconception: Fear of falling or not clearing the obstacle can lead to hesitation which can then affect the flow and overall success of the vault.
nodes.response: Gradual progression and practising on lower obstacles can help build confidence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Creative movements

nodes.misconception: Poor foot placement on the wall when performing tic tacs and wall runs can result in poor technique and a weak push off. Poor control on landing is also a common issue with Tic Tacs and Wall Runs.
nodes.response: Use visual cues (e.g. chalk marks or splat spots/cones) on the wall to show the ideal contact point. Also use markers to indicate where to land and teach pupils to land quietly and stick their landing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Using walls to move

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often underestimate or overestimate the distance, leading to overshooting the jump or falling too short.
nodes.response: Emphasise that hitting the edge of the mat is crucial, therefore they should gradually increase the distance to find the correct one for them. This will also need to be adjusted when they add a run up.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Explosive movements in Parkour

nodes.misconception: Pupils may choose obstacles that don't link well and therefore don't allow for smooth transitions.
nodes.response: Provide lots of route planning support and examples/advice throughout the lesson.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Parkour: performing a route with obstacles

nodes.misconception: Pupils often look down at their feet and lack core stability when balancing, which shifts their centre of gravity so they are off balance.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on looking slightly forward on a stable point at eye level and learn how to engage their core when balancing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Balance and precision in action

nodes.misconception: Believing that only one factor can affect participation such as gender, when actally there are lots of factors that can affect participation in physical activity.
nodes.response: Some people may not face any barriers to participation, however some people may experience a number of different factors that affect whether they are able to participate in a sport or not.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The factors that affect participation

nodes.misconception: Only one value can be shown on a graph.
nodes.response: Different values can be broken down into different categories, such as the age of people and their participation in different activities, which gives a more detailed picture of participants.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Data analysis of engagement patterns

nodes.misconception: Believing that certain sports or activities are only suitable for certain types of people. For example, girls don't play rugby.
nodes.response: Some people face barriers in accessing sport or physical activity, however, these barriers should be broken down to provide opportunities for everyone to access all sport and physical activities.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Engagement patterns of different social groups

nodes.misconception: Believing that only one factor can affect participation such as gender, when actually there are lots of factors that can affect participation in physical activity.
nodes.response: Some people may not face any barriers to participation, however some people may experience a number of different factors that affect whether they participate in a sport or not.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Factors affecting participation

nodes.misconception: Provision only includes funding or money.
nodes.response: Increasing provision can also include improving facilities, time, coaching and equipment.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Strategies to improve participation

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you need to dive from a straight forward position to land in a front landing position.
nodes.response: The hips should land in the same position as the take off for the front landing. This means the hips need to lift and move backwards slightly to initiate the forward movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Front landing development

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe twisting on the vertical axis is pointless as they are keen to do tricks which are often completed around the horizontal axis.
nodes.response: Learning to twist is fundamental to overcome possible anxiety when in motion and not being able to see the cross. In addition, more challenging techniques include a twist at the start or the end, so the motor programme is required to build on this.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Trampolining safety and basic skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe that landing a somersault is achieved through speed of rotation.
nodes.response: A somersault does require some speed, but if too much power is placed on the take off, it can lead to over rotation. A somersault will appear controlled with a balanced take off and the rebound of the trampoline initiating the hips for the rotation.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Somersaults and routine development

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you need to jump backwards to land in a back landing position.
nodes.response: A back landing can feel quite scary. Jumping backwards can lead to injury and a back landing should only be attempted if your teacher has approved and is confident you will not jump backwards and will push the hips forwards when jumping upwards.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Back landing and combination

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you need to drop backwards and/or lift the legs upwards to achieve a seated position.
nodes.response: This will lead to being off balance and not allow any progressions from the seat landing. The key to the correct technique is to avoid lifting the legs and jump upwards with a hinge at the hip to then land downwards.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Seat landing and swivel hip developments

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a performance of a 10 bounce routine has to include lots of difficult skills.
nodes.response: There is judgement on difficulty through tariffs, however the performance is also linked to maintenance of height / execution with good technique. Often it is better to go simple with good execution, rather than difficult and have no control.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Routine performance and peer review

nodes.misconception: Pupils think yin yoga is boring.
nodes.response: Yin Yoga provides a chance to deeply connect with your body and mind. It can be a deeply meditative practice, allowing for self-reflection and stress relief. For many, it’s an opportunity to slow down in an otherwise fast-paced life.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Relaxation and finding inner peace

nodes.misconception: Pilates is easy and only develops flexibility.
nodes.response: Pilates builds core strength, stability and muscular endurance, and can be challenging for all types of athletes. It’s not just stretching, it’s a full-body workout that improves posture, balance and overall strength.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pilates and core strength training

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that resistance bands make exercises easier
nodes.response: Resistance bands actually add extra tension, making movements more challenging. They engage muscles throughout the entire movement, improving strength, control and stability more effectively than bodyweight exercises alone.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pilates mat work for full body strength

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that yoga is always slow and steady, and is only for relaxation.
nodes.response: Yoga can be both calming and energising, depending on the style and intention of the practice.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Vinyasa flow

nodes.misconception: Holding your breath when performing different moves or going deeper into a stretch is beneficial.
nodes.response: Holding your breath while performing movements or deepening a stretch can create tension, reduce oxygen flow and limit flexibility. Focus on steady, controlled breathing to help the body relax, move safely and maximise the benefits of each pose.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic poses and breathing techniques

nodes.misconception: I'm not flexible so I can't do yoga.
nodes.response: Flexibility develops over time with consistent practice. Yoga also improves strength, balance and mindfulness. Many poses can be modified to suit all levels, so anyone can start, no matter their current flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: 5 minutes to start your day

nodes.misconception: Believing that sponsorship only involves financial support.
nodes.response: Sponsorship can include financial support but also include equipment, clothing or facility provisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sponsorship

nodes.misconception: Believing that technology always improves performance without considering potential drawbacks.
nodes.response: Technology has both positive and negative impacts on different people in sport including performers, sponsors, spectators and officials.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Positive and negative impacts of technology on sport

nodes.misconception: Students might think that sport only benefits from media and sponsorship.
nodes.response: Media and sponsorship also benefit from the sport.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The golden triangle

nodes.misconception: NGBs only support elite sport at the top of their game.
nodes.response: NGBs provide support from grass roots level all the way up to elite level sport.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: DCMS, Sport England and NGBs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that media coverage is always beneficial for sports, without considering potential negative effects and assuming that media only affects athletes and fans.
nodes.response: Media coverage can be both positive and negative and can impact performers, sports, officials, spectators and the sport itself.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The media

nodes.misconception: The transverse plane is linked with the transverse axis.
nodes.response: They share the same name, however the transverse plane is linked with the longitudinal axis. The transverse axis is linked with the sagittal plane.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planes of movement and axes of rotation

nodes.misconception: The saggital plane is linked with the saggital axis.
nodes.response: They share the same name; however, the sagittal plane is linked with the frontal axis. The saggital axis is linked with the frontal plane.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planes and axes of movement

nodes.misconception: Any of the three planes can be paired with the three axes.
nodes.response: Planes and axes are always paired as: sagittal plane with the transverse axis, frontal plane with the frontal axis and transverse plane with the longitdinal axis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planes and axes in physical activity and sport

nodes.misconception: The transverse plane is linked with the transverse axis.
nodes.response: They share the same name, however the transverse plane is linked with the longitudinal axis. The transverse axis is linked with the sagittal plane. The frontal plane and axis however have the same name and are linked.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planes and axes

nodes.misconception: Any of the three planes can be paired with the three axes.
nodes.response: Planes and axes are always paired as: sagittal plane with the frontal axis, frontal plane with the sagittal axis and transverse plane with the vertical axis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planes and axes in sport

nodes.misconception: Any of the three planes can be paired with the three axes.
nodes.response: Planes and axes are always paired as; sagittal plane with the transverse axis, frontal plane with the sagittal axis and transverse plane with the longitudinal axis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Planes and axes in action

nodes.misconception: All joint movements require the same sort of leverage.
nodes.response: The orientation of the fulcrum (joint), the effort (muscle) and the load dictate which of the three classes of lever it is and also if there is a mechanical advantage.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Levers and mechanical advantage

nodes.misconception: The effort in a lever starts in the belly of the muscle.
nodes.response: The effort from a muscle will start from the muscle insertion. The insertion is the tendon attached to the bone which that muscle moves.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Levers in sporting actions

nodes.misconception: When drawing levers the body part needs to be included.
nodes.response: A lever will always be drawn using four shapes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Lever classification

nodes.misconception: The effort in a lever starts in the belly of the muscle.
nodes.response: The effort from a muscle will start from the muscle insertion. The insertion is the tendon attached to the bone which that muscle moves.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Levers in action

nodes.misconception: When drawing levers, the body part needs to be included.
nodes.response: A lever will always be drawn using four shapes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Levers, mechanical advantage and disadvantage

nodes.misconception: Pupils often drop their guard after blocking leaving their head and body exposed.
nodes.response: Focus on returning to the guard stance after every block and continue to prompt pupils throughout the lesson.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Blocks and defensive techniques

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that self-defence is just like fighting.
nodes.response: Self-defence focuses on escape and de-escalation. It is about avoiding harm and getting away safely.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sparring and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the pads at the wrong height or angle or keep their arms too stiff or too relaxed.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to communicate if the pads are at the wrong height or angle to give each other corrective feedback. Teach pad holders to “meet” the strike with slight forward pressure and a bend in the arms.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kicking and combinations

nodes.misconception: Pupils will often tuck their thumbs under fingers or stick them out.
nodes.response: Pupils should lock thumbs around the outside of their fist to adopt the correct guard stance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Stances and basic strikes

nodes.misconception: Pupils perform movements too fast or too slow which disrupts the flow of the kata.
nodes.response: Performing Chon-Ji at a consistent tempo and speed helps to develop cardiovascular and muscular endurance. It enhances mental focus and breath control. The different speeds simulate real combat situations which will vary in speed and acceleration.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Forms (katas) and combinations

nodes.misconception: Pupils often start exercises with too much intensity and quickly recognise that they cannot continue when performing conditioning exercises.
nodes.response: When trying to improve muscular endurance and condition, steady and continuous activity over a longer period of time gives the best results. Start at a pace that is comfortable to begin with and can be maintained as muscles start to fatigue.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kicking and footwork

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that it's ok to stop and stand mid-court.
nodes.response: It is essential to return to the middle of the court and split step as your opponent hits the ball to load elastic energy in your legs to be able to move quickly. Don't get caught standing between the baseline and non-volley line on approach to net.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A movement focus on the ready position, split step and returning to the middle

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that winning is the most important thing.
nodes.response: Learning to value a fair competition and choosing to lose in preference to cheating to win or only playing opponents you know you can beat, is a much more rewarding outlook.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing games, keeping score and competing fairly

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the best way to win is to hit ithe ball harder.
nodes.response: Sometimes just keeping the ball in and waiting for your opposition to make a mistake is the best way to win points, but it is also helpful to disrupt the rhythm by varying pace/spin, breaking the angle or using disguise to wrong foot your opposition.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Outwitting your opponents to win a point

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to swing hard at volleys.
nodes.response: When approaching the net to volley you already have momentum moving forwards into the ball which adds power so a more effective technique is to block and sometimes even cushion the pace out of the ball whilst angling it back over the net.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Forehands, backhands and volleys in action

nodes.misconception: Pupils often stand behind the ball and hit up at it rather than moving their body to get into a better position.
nodes.response: You need to move your feet quickly to get to the side of the ball to use a smooth U shaped swing on the forehand or backhand and hit through the ball towards the net.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Cooperating to build the longest rally

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need a big swing and to serve overarm.
nodes.response: When we watch pro tennis or other racket sports it looks like you need a huge swing and lots of power but when you are starting out you will get more success with a slow and controlled swing. Pickleball (like badminton) starts with an underarm serve.
nodes.subject: physical-education
