nodes.lessonTitle: Ball familiarisation and battleships serving

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may dominate the discussion with less confident pupils unwilling to take their turn at leading. Pupils might take too long explaining and not leave enough time to practise.
nodes.response: Select the numbers carefully so that pupil 1 and 2 are more confident and can model teaching first, giving less confident pupils time to get used to this process. Stress the importance of practise time and keep explanations concise.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Recap jumps and rotations

nodes.misconception: Performing group routines often means some members of the group may struggle with the choreography and therefore feel self-conscious and demotivated.
nodes.response: Stress to each group the importance of adapting choreography to suit the needs of everyone in the group. For example, some pupils could perform backward rolls whilst others perform a more basic roll. Or everyone may change the skill they perform.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Modifying and teaching routines to others

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to tuck their head when performing forward and backward rolls causing a rough landing or strain on their neck.
nodes.response: The chin should be tucked gently into the chest looking at their stomach. This will protect the neck and keep the head aligned.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Accurate replication of rolls

nodes.misconception: When pupils are teaching, they do not use the additional materials and therefore provide incorrect teaching points or unsuitable adaptations for their group.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are using the additional materials to support their understanding of each skill and make sure they know how to provide adaptations so that everyone in the group can achieve success when performing the skill.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing balances of increasing difficulty

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may struggle with the choreography, leading to frustration and disengagement.
nodes.response: Differentiate within the choreography so that pupils have choices over the skills they perform. If you would like all pupils to perform the same skill, make sure this skill is accessible for all pupils.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing a whole class choreographed routine

nodes.misconception: When performing in unison, some students may be slightly ahead or behind affecting overall synchronisation. If pupils don't move at the correct intervals in canon, the sequence looks uncoordinated.
nodes.response: Use a clear count-in or rhythm (e.g. counting beats out loud or clapping) and practise slowly before increasing speed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Small group performances in canon and unison

nodes.misconception: Pupils think conflict is negative and should always be avoided.
nodes.response: In reality, resolving conflict is an important lifeskill that can also be the catalyst for creativity and innovation. It can challenge assumptions but does need to be managed constructively.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Conflict resolution

nodes.misconception: Pupils think self-assessment is similar to being assessed in something.
nodes.response: Self-assessment is an opportunity to reflect and does not count towards any assessment. It is positive. Leaders are able to grow from self-assessments as they recognise strengths, but more importantly, identify keys areas of improvement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Summarising and reflecting on personal leadership skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils think all effective leaders are loud and shout to be heard.
nodes.response: It is common to hear a leader with a voice which is projected when communicating. However, there is so much to effective leadership beyond verbal communication, such as, active listening, knowing your team and showing empathy, to name a few.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Leadership skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils think emotional intelligence is simply about being nice or positive and is a fixed trait.
nodes.response: Emotional intelligence is recognising, expressing and managing emotions. It can be developed and improved with practice and feedback.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Emotional intelligence

nodes.misconception: Pupils think HIIT is only for experienced athletes.
nodes.response: HIIT can be modified to suit all fitness levels. It can be a valuable and quick tool to improve many components of fitness. The intervals can be shorter for beginners and the exercises less intense.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Build resilience

nodes.misconception: Pupils think to solve a problem has a just one single option.
nodes.response: Problem solving is not linear, nor is there only one universal problem solving technique. The right approach depends on the nature of the problem in a specific context.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Decision making and problem solving

nodes.misconception: Pupils think being adaptable as a leader is when there is a forced change.
nodes.response: Adaptability for an effective leader is when it is always happening and the leader is responding to how the needs of the group are being met and if the environment is working or not.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Adaptability and flexibility

nodes.misconception: Pupils think confidence is constant.
nodes.response: Fluctuations in confidence are very normal. It is not a static state and often determined by the environment your are in and any previous experience you have of that environment.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Build confidence

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a goal or a target it the end product or outcome to be achieved.
nodes.response: A goal can be based on outcome, however it can also be a goal set about the performance or process of doing something. For example, building a 3-2-1 pyramid in the quickest time compared to building the 3-2-1 pyramid without dropping any objects.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Goal setting and motivation

nodes.misconception: Pupils think leading is just about giving instructions.
nodes.response: A ledaer also requires active listening and the time and confidence to provide feedback on what has been completed well and how things can be improved.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Communication and listening skills in action

nodes.misconception: Pupils think good leaders are born like that.
nodes.response: Effective leadership is developed through experience and learning from mistakes.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Lead by example

nodes.misconception: Pupils think punctuality is merely about turning up to lessons on time.
nodes.response: Punctuality is linked to arrival time, but is also about completing tasks on time and being respectful for the time of others. This is achieved by being organised, fulfilling the task and being dependable.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Time management

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a position in volleyball is determined by their physical location on the court.
nodes.response: Rotations do occur based on court location but players are also assigned positions, with an assigned role, which they can move into directly after the serve.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team defence

nodes.misconception: The feet can not be used as a body part in volleyball.
nodes.response: Using the foot to contact the ball is legal but the foot must remain in contact with the ground. Players only tend to use this to slide the foot into the path of the ball as they simply cannot kick the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking formations and match play

nodes.misconception: Sitting volleyball is only for people with disabilities.
nodes.response: Sitting volleyball is a Paralympic sport, however it is an inclusive and adapted sport that anyone can play regardless of ability. Players have to move quickly around the court using their upper bodies frequently in a seated position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The rules and rotations of sitting volleyball

nodes.misconception: Pupils think a bump shot needs the hands to come together to make a fist.
nodes.response: The correct technique is to place the back of one hand in the palm of the other hand with the arms extended and the elbows locked creating a platform with the forearms.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Digs and sets

nodes.misconception: Pupils think serving speed is the most important factor to an effective serve.
nodes.response: The reality of a successful serve is placement and consistency.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Serving and spiking

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that a spike is performed with the hand in a fist shape.
nodes.response: A spike is performed with an open hand with the fingers together and the ball contacting the centre of the palm.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A volleyball circuit of basic skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the chest pass is only used for shorter distances.
nodes.response: The chest pass is a very versatile technique that can be used for short and longer distances. It works well as a technique to pass when aiming for the space a teammate is moving into.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Movement, space, passing and receiving

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that the opposite team to the scoring team take the following center pass.
nodes.response: The center pass is alternated throughout the game regardless of which team scores.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Transition from defence to attack

nodes.misconception: Defending in netball is mainly a role when your opponent has the ball.
nodes.response: Defending occurs in all positions and each player needs to track their opponent to try to deny them the opportunity to receive a pass.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Positional awareness to defend

nodes.misconception: An attacker should move as as soon as their teammate catches the ball.
nodes.response: A feint is an effective way to create space as we wait for the ball handler to present the ball ready to make the pass, rather than moving too early and the defender being able to catch up with you.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Outwitting opponents and ball handling under pressure

nodes.misconception: Pupils think when they go offside or do footwork they have to stand out of play as this is a penalty pass.
nodes.response: Both of these infringements do not include another player so a free pass is awarded. If a player obstructs or contacts an oppositing player a penalty pass is then awarded.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Playing and officiating your own small sided games fairly

nodes.misconception: A GS is a static position.
nodes.response: The GS can move out of the goal circle to create space for the GA to drive in and receive the ball. A shooter position requires dynamic movements such as power to jump for a rebound.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Working cooperatively to learn to shoot with precision and understanding

nodes.misconception: Fitness testing brings about improvements in components of fitness.
nodes.response: Training methods bring about improvement in fitness. Fitness testing is merely about identifying the strengths and weaknesses of a fitness component so the right training method can be allocated and used.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Reasons for and limitations of fitness testing

nodes.misconception: Starting the multi stage fitness test too quickly.
nodes.response: It can be beneficial to start the multi stage fitness test at fast walking pace to conserve energy for the faster levels.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of fitness testing - endurance

nodes.misconception: When conducting the ruler drop test, the partner or assistant will countdown so the performer knows when the ruler is going to be dropped.
nodes.response: Remind students that they need to drop the ruler randomly, rather than when the performer knows they will drop it, to really ensure validity to test reaction time.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of fitness tests: balance, coordination, agility and reaction time

nodes.misconception: Raising the knees in the sit and reach test.
nodes.response: When performing the sit and reach test, the knees should be flat along the floor to give an accurate reading of flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of speed, power, strength and flexibility fitness tests

nodes.misconception: Some students may think all athletes would require large muscle mass to be successful at sport.
nodes.response: Provide a range of examples including marathon runners, sumo wrestlers to show how diverse body compositions can be advantageous in different sports.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Body composition, balance, coordination and reaction time

nodes.misconception: Fitness testing brings about improvements in components of fitness.
nodes.response: Training methods bring about improvement in fitness. Fitness testing is merely about identifying the strengths and weaknesses of a fitness compenent so the right training method can be allocated and used.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Benefits and limitations of fitness testing

nodes.misconception: Starting the multi-stage fitness test too quickly.
nodes.response: It can be beneficial to start the multi-stage fitness test at fast walking pace to conserve energy for the faster levels.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of fitness testing and normative data for endurance

nodes.misconception: Pupils may measure their heart rate incorrectly after completing the 150 steps for the Harvard step test.
nodes.response: Before starting the Harvard step test, allow pupils an opportunity to practice finding and measuring their heart rate.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of endurance fitness testing

nodes.misconception: When conducting the ruler drop test, the partner or assistant will countdown so the performer knows when the ruler is going to be dropped.
nodes.response: Remind students that they need to drop the ruler randomly, rather than when the performer knows they will drop it, to really ensure validity to test reaction time.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of balance, co-ordination, agility and reaction time fitness tests

nodes.misconception: Pupils do not stand straight against the wall with their arm touching the wall to gain the initial mark for the vertical jump test.
nodes.response: It is important for reliable results when measuring power that the arm is against the wall and outreached as high as possible, when taking the initial measurement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of power, speed and strength fitness tests

nodes.misconception: Raising the knees in the sit and reach test.
nodes.response: When performing the sit and reach test the knees should. be flat along the floor to give an accurate reading of flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of fitness tests: speed, strength, power and flexibility

nodes.misconception: Thinking that balance is not important for games players and only useful in gymnastics.
nodes.response: Provide examples of when games players would need balance, e.g. a rugby player will need balance when kicking a conversion to provide greater accuracy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Agility, balance and co-ordination

nodes.misconception: Thinking that being physically fit means someone is automatically healthy.
nodes.response: Explain that just because someone appears physically fit, it doesn't mean they have good emotional or social health.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Health, fitness and components of fitness

nodes.misconception: Thinking that flexibility is only useful for gymnasts or dancers.
nodes.response: Discuss wider examples such as hurdlers, footballers and swimmers that will also benefit from high levels of flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Power, flexibility and reaction time

nodes.misconception: Students thinking that certain sports only need one type of component of fitness to be successful e.g. 100m sprinter just needs speed.
nodes.response: Identify all the components of fitness that are useful for each athlete, determining why they are beneficial and justifying which is most important.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of fitness components in sport

nodes.misconception: Certain sports only need one type of component of fitness to be successful, e.g. 100m sprinter just needs speed.
nodes.response: Identify all the components of fitness that are useful for each athlete, determining why they are beneficial and justifying which is most important.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Components of fitness and the relative importance to physical activity and sport

nodes.misconception: Speed is just about running fast.
nodes.response: An example of speed is moving quickly across the ground but also includes other body parts too such as the speed of arms in table tennis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, power and speed

nodes.misconception: Speed is just about running fast.
nodes.response: An example of speed is moving quickly across the ground but also includes other body parts too, such as, the speed of arms in table tennis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Cardiovascular fitness, muscular endurance, strength & speed

nodes.misconception: Thinking that being physically fit means someone is automatically healthy.
nodes.response: Explain that just because someone is appears physically fit doesn't mean they may have good emotional or social health.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between health, fitness, exercise and performance

nodes.misconception: There is only one type of strength which we usually associate with lifting heavy weights.
nodes.response: There are four types of strength: maximal, dynamic, static and explosive.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of strength

nodes.misconception: Thinking that flexibility is only useful for gymnasts or dancers.
nodes.response: Discuss wider examples such as hurdlers, footballers and swimmers that will also benefit from high levels of flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Agility, balance, co-ordination, flexibility and reaction time

nodes.misconception: Speed is just about running fast.
nodes.response: An example of speed is moving quickly across the ground but also includes other body parts too such as speed of arms in table tennis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, speed and strength

nodes.misconception: Thinking that flexibility is only useful for gymnasts or dancers.
nodes.response: Discuss wider examples such as hurdlers, footballers and swimmers that will also benefit from high levels of flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Agility, flexibility and power

nodes.misconception: Thinking that being physically fit means someone is automatically healthy.
nodes.response: Explain that just because someone appears physically fit doesn't mean they have good emotional or social health.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The relationship between health and fitness

nodes.misconception: Raising the knees in the sit and reach test.
nodes.response: When performing the sit and reach test, the knees should be flat along the floor to give an accurate reading of flexibility.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of the fitness tests that measure agility and flexibility

nodes.misconception: Certain sports only need one type of component of fitness to be successful e.g. 100m sprinter just needs speed.
nodes.response: Identify all the components of fitness that are useful for each athlete, determining why they are beneficial and justifying which is most important.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Linking sports and physical activity to different components of fitness

nodes.misconception: It is important that the pupils listen to the music before beginning to choreograph their dances.
nodes.response: Engaging pupils in the active content of the lesson is likely to improve motivation and levels of engagement. By playing the music in the background they will become familiar with it and allow it to inform the work they create.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Geology: choreography

nodes.misconception: The pupils should only use ideas introduced by the teacher.
nodes.response: Cross curricular lessons offer scope for pupils to include additional content by bringing, sharing and consolidating subject knowledge from other curriculum areas. Enabling pupils to expand the action content will increase motivation and engagement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Astronomy: performance skills

nodes.misconception: Dancers should be moving all the time.
nodes.response: Stillness is one of the five basic actions. Similar to punctuation in a sentence, it can help to bring meaning and context as well as highlight important moments. Stillness can include brief pauses as well as prolonged periods of inactivity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Geology: performance skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't like dancing.
nodes.response: Whilst no activity is attractive to everyone, most pupils enjoy dance when the tasks are open ended. This gives them the opportunity to input their own ideas and perform actions thay are comfortable with.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Astronomy: choreography

nodes.misconception: Retrograde is a term only used in dance.
nodes.response: Retrograde is a term used in many artforms, it is particularly prevalent in music and films.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Meteorology: choreography

nodes.misconception: Projection means that you have to look up.
nodes.response: Projection is effectively communicating a dance idea. This often involves looking outwards towards an audience but would not be appropriate if communicating a concept such a secrecy, nervousness or reluctance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Meteorology: performance skills

nodes.misconception: Believing that spectators always have a negative effect on performance and safety and the impact of spectators is only relevant in professional sport.
nodes.response: Spectators have positive contributions to sport like creating an atmosphere and providing home-field advantage which can not only affect professional sport, but also amateur and youth sport too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Spectator behaviour

nodes.misconception: Students may incorrectly assume that sportsmanship and gamemanship are the same thing.
nodes.response: Sportsmanship is positively conforming to the rules and etiquette of the sport, whereas gamesmanship is more negative because a performer may bend the rules to gain advantage.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sportsmanship, gamesmanship and deviance

nodes.misconception: All PEDs are automatically illegal and banned substances.
nodes.response: Not all are instantly illegal or banned. For example, some stimulants are legal such as caffeine which is used by many as a stimulant. Beta blockers are available on prescription and so have certain restrictions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Prohibited substances and methods

nodes.misconception: Students may incorrectly assume that sportsmanship and gamemanship are the same thing.
nodes.response: Sportsmanship is positively conforming to the rules and etiquette of the sport, whereas gamesmanship is more negative because a performer may bend the rules to gain advantage.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sportsmanship, gamesmanship and conduct of performers

nodes.misconception: Pupils can often confuse the x and y axis and therefore not read the correct x axis information.
nodes.response: On a bar or line graphs pupils should get into the habit of physically going along the bottom to read the information along the x axis.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpretation and analysis of data and graphs related to socio-cultural issues

nodes.misconception: Students might mistakenly believe hooliganism is limited to football.
nodes.response: Hooliganism can happen in other sports and activities but is it most widely known in football.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hooliganism

nodes.misconception: Pupils may incorrectly assume that sportsmanship and gamemanship are the same thing.
nodes.response: Sportsmanship is positively conforming to the rules and etiquette of the sport, whereas gamesmanship is more negative because a performer may bend the rules to gain advantage.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Conduct of performers

nodes.misconception: All PEDs are automatically illegal and banned substances.
nodes.response: The use of some PEDs to enhance performance is perfectly acceptable. Many sportspeople use narcotic analgesics to get through an event or drink caffeine for its stimulating effect. WADA is responsible for determining which PEDs are allowed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Drugs in sport

nodes.misconception: The fake is too subtle and not performed at a fast enough pace. Pupils make fake too early so it is easy to read.
nodes.response: Use clear and exaggerated movements when faking and shift your weight explosively. Wait until the defender is close before performing your faked movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Advanced ball handling and evasion

nodes.misconception: When soloing the ball, pupils don't flick their toe upwards causing the ball to travel in front of them. When passing, pupils throw the ball, forgetting the correct open or closed hand passing action.
nodes.response: When the foot impacts the ball, flick your toes up so the ball travels back into the hands. Pupils should spend a lot of time repeating their hand passing skills to avoid throwing the ball when under pressure.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ways to move with the ball and basic skills

nodes.misconception: Kicks may lack the necessary power or accuracy, or they might often miss their target. High catches can be intimidating and pupils may mistime their jump.
nodes.response: Focus on good technique before increasing distance or adding movements to kicks. When performing a high catch, track the ball early and use the jumping technique to meet the ball when it is at its highest point.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kicking and catching

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle to recognise the right movement to execute different strategies, which results in losing possession or missed opportunities.
nodes.response: Break down the games so you can focus on good decision making. Stop game play when a poor is decision made to ask pupils to identify and resolve the problem.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Teamwork and strategy

nodes.misconception: Pupils use the wrong hand which leads to fouls and ineffective tackles, or they dive into the tackle, allowing attackers to easily sidestep away.
nodes.response: Always use the nearest hand to flick the ball away. Stay balanced when tackling, moving your feet quickly and timing the tackle properly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling and blocking

nodes.misconception: When playing as part of a bigger team, pupils often bunch around the ball and do not hold their shape. They can also be more static off the ball thinking that teammates will be available for a pass.
nodes.response: Reduce the numbers on each team, assign clear roles or freeze the play regularly to demonstrate where players should be. Focus on movement off the ball as soon as players have passed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Full-field game and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils use short steps and run through as they hit the shuttle which leaves them out of position for the next shot.
nodes.response: Using long lunges and recovering back to the middle of the court quickly between each shot reduces the space and options available to your opposition.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective court movement and strategic thinking through throw badminton

nodes.misconception: Pupils blame each other and lose focus rather than remaining positive and regrouping.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the balanced teams mean everyone should have an equal chance of winning. Hence it is the pair who gel the best and work hard to win as many points as possible across all their matches that will win.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tournament time with performing and officiating roles in doubles pairings

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold their index finger up towards the shaft of the racket to try to get more control.
nodes.response: Letting your index finger point up the back of the grip feels like it is helping with control, but break this habit fast to prevent this technique from limiting your progress to the full range of shots that are possible with a shake hands grip.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring ways to win the point

nodes.misconception: Pupils hold the racket like a frying pan and squat lower and lower to hit overhead clears.
nodes.response: A shake hand grip and sideways stance is required to get power and accuracy into shots, but you also need to know when it is necessary to hit underarm rather than trying to hit everything above the head.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Underarm and overhead clears to maintain a rally

nodes.misconception: Pupils serve towards the middle of the court which is easy to return.
nodes.response: Aiming their serve to force a defensive shot from their opponent is a much stronger way to start the point.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Target practice serving challenges

nodes.misconception: Pupils get confused about which side to serve from and who serves next.
nodes.response: A server keeps serving after winning a point and they alternate sides each point —from the right if their score is even and left if it is odd. If the opposition wins a rally, they earn a point and the service with the other partner serving next.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Outwitting your opponents to win a point in doubles

nodes.misconception: In Salsa you have to apply tension to your whole body.
nodes.response: In Salsa it is the torso that is firmly held maintaining an upright stance, the arms are also fixed when in hold but change to some degree when moving between holds or when moving independently. The legs largely remain soft and fluid.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining and refining Salsa ideas to strive for awareness of bodily tension

nodes.misconception: Films made for entertainment are an accurate representation of a social dance style.
nodes.response: Whilst many choreographers may have researched a social dance and employed the key features, it is unlikely that it is a detailed and accurate representation, and should be considered to be 'in the style of' rather than an authentic account.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Prom night: film clips and stills as a stimulus for traditional social dances

nodes.misconception: Dance styles are set and never change.
nodes.response: Dance styles continually evolve. When studying dances from history or other places, we are able to pinpoint key attributes that were relevant at a point in time, they may remain or they may be adapted.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Prom night: the Jive

nodes.misconception: Counterbalances are always symmetrical.
nodes.response: Counterbalances can involve the same action as a partner but these can be varied by level, direction of size. Counterbalances can also use contrasting body parts to connect, e.g. the hand of one dancer pressing against the shoulder of their partner.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining and refining Jive ideas to strive for greater partner awareness

nodes.misconception: Performers have to smile all the time.
nodes.response: Performers use facial expression to communicate the mood or feelings of their character. This range can include smiling if happy, weeping if sad, a furrowed brow if worried, a cleanched jaw if angry or eye-rolling if annoyed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Combining and refining dance ideas to strive for excellence in projection

nodes.misconception: Dance actions should always be performed as big as possible so they are clear and stand out to an audience.
nodes.response: Whilst this is often the case for performance dances, social dances are often much smaller and more relaxed in their execution since they are often performed in a limited amount of space and purely for pleasure, rather than an audience.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Prom night: Salsa

nodes.misconception: Believing that a sedentary lifestyle only affects physical health through weight gain.
nodes.response: A sedentary lifestyle can have a negative impact on social and emotional health too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The consequences of a sedentary lifestyle

nodes.misconception: Personal exercise programmes are only used by people that play sport.
nodes.response: Perosnal exercise programmes can be used by everyone to increase physical activity levels.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Promotion of personal health

nodes.misconception: Believing that a sedentary lifestyle only affects physical health through weight gain.
nodes.response: A sedentary lifestyle can have a negative impact on social and emotional health too.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Consequences of a sedentary lifestyle

nodes.misconception: Students think that being physically fit means they are automatically healthy.
nodes.response: Explain the importance of social and emotional benefits too, particularly for participants such as elderly people.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical, mental and social health, fitness and wellbeing

nodes.misconception: Thinking that being physically fit means that someone is healthy.
nodes.response: It is possible to be physically fit but unhealthy. It is essential to consider social and emotional benefits/aspects of health as well as strength, cardiovascular endurance etc.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical, emotional and social aspects of health

nodes.misconception: Believing that individuals fit exclusively into one somatotype category rather than having a mix of characteristics.
nodes.response: Individuals can have a mix of characteristics from different somatotypes but can also change their somatotype depending on their lifestyle choices.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Somatotypes

nodes.misconception: Students think the only benefits to exercise are physical benefits.
nodes.response: Explain the importance of social and emotional benefits too, particularly for participants such as elderly people.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical, emotional and social health, fitness and wellbeing

nodes.misconception: Students may view lifestyle choices as something that can only be negative (e.g. fatty food, sedentary lifestyle or drugs).
nodes.response: Reframe thinking using positive examples of each factor.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Lifestyle choices and diseases

nodes.misconception: Evading space is solely about the ball carrier getting past the defender.
nodes.response: In reality, a supporting runner's positioning often determines whether an attacker breaks the gain line. A well-timed support line can draw defenders, create passing opportunities, or make a dummy pass more effective.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Evasion skills and supporting the ball carrier

nodes.misconception: Pupil think that if they go in to tackle at the legs they will get kicked in the face.
nodes.response: If you tackle low, with your head to the side and wrap their legs with your arms, they’ll go down safely and you won’t get kicked.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling and contact in rugby

nodes.misconception: I don't need to practice passing because I can already catch well and have good technique.
nodes.response: Passing isn’t just about mechanics, it’s also about teamwork. Practicing with different teammates helps improve subtle communication, like eye contact and timing, and allows you to understand how others prefer to receive the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing, receiving and breaking the gain line

nodes.misconception: It is better to move with the ball in one hand and score a try with one hand.
nodes.response: Despite it perhaps being more comfortable to have the ball in one hand (or under the arm) when running, it does not keep the ball as safe and therefore increases the risk of dropping the ball and therefore your team losing possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ball familiarisation in rugby

nodes.misconception: Play needs to be stopped by the referee at every single rule break.
nodes.response: Not every rule break means the game has to stop. The referee can play advantage, keeping the game flowing and more enjoyable. However, dangerous play, like high tackles, must be dealt with straight away to keep everyone safe.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating small-sided games

nodes.misconception: A kick is only good if it is kicked far.
nodes.response: Kicking a ball successfully involves accuracy and tactical placement to find space, kicking into touch or to allow one of your team to catch and maintain possession.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kicking, chasing and retrieving a kicked ball

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they have 6 'downs/tags' like tag rugby or rugby league.
nodes.response: In flag football, teams only have 4 downs (or attempts) to advance the ball 10 yards or score. If they don't succeed within those 4 downs, the ball is turned over to the other team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Flag football: rules and basic skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that as a defender they need to rush individually to stop the opposition.
nodes.response: Rushing alone often leaves space for the raider to escape. Defenders are more effective when they move together, stay connected and communicate to trap the raider as a team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kabaddi: tactics, strategies and game play

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they can run freely with the ball in Aussie rules.
nodes.response: In Aussie Rules, players must bounce or touch the ball to the ground every 15 metres when running with it. Running freely without doing so results in a turnover.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Australian football league: rules and basic skills

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the attacking players can block the blitzer so that the quarterback remains able to pass the ball.
nodes.response: In flag football, blocking the blitzer is not allowed. Attackers must avoid physical contact and the quarterback must rely on quick throws and good timing to avoid being tagged by the blitzer.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Flag football: tactics, strategies and game play

nodes.misconception: Pupils just stick with one payer on the opposite team and chase them.
nodes.response: The game moves too fast to just stick with 1 player, so it is better to work with teammates to create zonal defence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Australian football league: tactics, strategies and game play

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to chant "Kabaddi Kabaddi" when they are a raider.
nodes.response: Remember chanting "Kabaddi, Kabaddi" is how the raider shows they haven't taken a breath during the raid and if they forget, the raid doesn't count.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kabaddi: rules and basic skills

nodes.misconception: Dancers have to be silent when performing.
nodes.response: Whilst this is usually the case, dance often connects with other artforms and occasionally dancers may also speak, sing or make sounds through body percussion (e.g. clapping or stamping).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sound moves: space and dynamics

nodes.misconception: When performing in a group formation, this should always be in unison.
nodes.response: Unison can be highly effective in clear formations as this also communicates unity and power, but other choreographic relationships such as canon, mirroring or contact work also add interest and are visually exciting to watch.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A time and a place: formations and transitions

nodes.misconception: Performers should always look straight ahead and project to their audience.
nodes.response: In many styles, the connection to the audience is an important part of the performance. This can also be achieved by including a change of focus to communicate the performer's mood or intention, or to indicate what the audience should be looking at.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Look here: focus and emphasis

nodes.misconception: Motif variation and motif development are the same thing.
nodes.response: Variation and development are both methods of motif manipulation. However, during variation, the action content remains the same but how it is presented can be changed. Whereas, development involves significant alteration to the actions themselves.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Same, but different: relationships

nodes.misconception: The audience are always directly facing the stage/performers.
nodes.response: Whilst most theatres use an 'end on' arrangement, this isn't always the case. Fashion shows traditionally use a 'thrust' stage, lecture-demonstrations might use 'in the round' and performances such as Mummers' plays, may use 'promenade'.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Move, don’t move: relationships and stillness

nodes.misconception: It is acceptable to copy the work of others in dance.
nodes.response: Copying the work of others and passing it off as your own is known as plagiarism. However, identifying features that are common to a dance style and applying it to your choreography is different, but should remain respectful to the original source.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A certain style: style features

nodes.misconception: Training at the highest intensity is the best way to see results.
nodes.response: A balanced and accurate approach to training intensity using approximate zones is necessary to optimise fitness, recovery and avoid injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Thresholds of training

nodes.misconception: Training at the highest intensity is the best way to see results.
nodes.response: A balanced and accurate approach to training intensity using approximate zones is necessary to optimise fitness, recovery and avoid injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Thresholds of training and the Karvonen formula

nodes.misconception: Overload is negative and should not be encouraged during training.
nodes.response: Overload is encouarged as a positive aspect of traning as progression is being managed correctly to bring about adaptations to fitness. It is not to be confused with 'overtraining' which can cause injuries.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The principles of training and their application to a personal exercise programme

nodes.misconception: Overload is negative and should not be encouraged during training.
nodes.response: Overload is encouarged as a positive aspect of traning as progression is being managed correctly to bring about adaptations to fitness. It is not to be confused with 'overuse' which can cause injuries.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of training

nodes.misconception: Overload is negative and should not be encouraged during training.
nodes.response: Overload is encouraged as a positive aspect of training as progression is being managed correctly to bring about adaptations to fitness. It is not to be confused with 'overuse' which can cause injuries.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Principles of training and their application

nodes.misconception: The last two T's of the FITT acronym are interchangeable.
nodes.response: The principle is set and the first 'T' references the time used to train and the second 'T' references the specific type of training method chosen to achieve the optimal fitness gains.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The FITT principle

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they need to hit the ball hard to slice effectively.
nodes.response: Pushing and slicing require a light touch and controlled movements, not power.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pushing and slicing to keep it in play

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they should hit the ball with a flat racket face to generate topspin.
nodes.response: To create topspin, you need to angle the racket slightly downward and brush up the back of the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Topspin attack

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that deception is only about tricking your opponent with flashy shots (e.g. through the legs).
nodes.response: Effective deception is about subtle changes in timing, swing and shot placement. It doesn’t always require exaggerated fakes - small delays or slight adjustments can be just as effective in disrupting your opponent’s rhythm.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Deception

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe they can just win by hitting the ball with power.
nodes.response: Winning in table tennis isn’t just about power as control, spin, placement and consistency are just as important. A well-placed shot forces your opponent into difficult returns and increases your accuracy in rallies.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Percentage play and building a rally to create openings

nodes.misconception: In doubles, players should stand on the left and right and just hit the ball on their side (like tennis or badminton).
nodes.response: In doubles in table tennis, players have to hit alternate shots which means once you have hit the ball, you need to move out of the way so your partner can hit the next shot. Just standing on sides will make it difficult to play alternate shots.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Doubles play in table tennis

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that in a game you should always try hit the ball to the back of the table to win.
nodes.response: While hitting to the back of the table can be effective, it's not always the best strategy. Mixing up your shots, using different spins and placing the ball in various spots on the table can be more effective.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Beating your opposition in singles and doubles

nodes.misconception: Pupils are all uncomfortable with physical contact.
nodes.response: Contact must involve respect. Care should be taken to ensure any touch is appropriate. Most pupils are sensitive to this and respond appropriately. Teachers can guide this by identifying how contact should be made, e.g. touch toe to toe.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Where I’m from: my home and family

nodes.misconception: Not accepting the first action that a pupil offers is likely to put them off.
nodes.response: Challenging pupils to generate more than one response, or to find ways to refine their actions, before making their final selection, enables pupils to develop their creativity and understanding of choreographic and performance skills.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Who I like: inspirational people

nodes.misconception: Pupils are likely to focus on people who are famous.
nodes.response: It is entirely possible that pupils are naturally drawn to people who are famous, but it is still feasible to identify the qualities and behaviours that have made them successful such as hard work, determination or courage.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Who I like: my role models

nodes.misconception: When performing a 'pulling' counterbalance, pupils should hold hands.
nodes.response: There are many ways to perform 'pulling' counterbalances other than using hands, but if doing so, pupils should clasp one another's wrists to make a more secure connection.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Who I like: my friends

nodes.misconception: Pupils should 'count' the music.
nodes.response: Whilst some pupils can count music accurately, it can be an additional level of challenge for others and divert them from the task in hand. Most pupils will naturally 'feel' the music and be able to respond to the tempo and rhythm appropriately.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Who I am: my name and character

nodes.misconception: When applying dynamics, fast actions are always strong.
nodes.response: We often tend to combine fast actions with strength and slow actions with softness but this isn't always the case. Slow and strong could suggest great effort against resistence, and fast and light actions communicate fluidity and ease.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: What I like: my hobbies and interests

nodes.misconception: Throwing the baton harder increases success.
nodes.response: Kubb is a game of accuracy and control, replicating the same technique will increase accuracy and consistency with practice.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning to play Kubb

nodes.misconception: Exclusive focus on winning limits satisfaction and enjoyment.
nodes.response: Games like Kubb should be as much about the enjoyable social experience and finding ways to support each other as well as demonstrating honesty and fair play as winning the match.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Managing emotions in Kubb

nodes.misconception: To hit the ball in golf, you lift your head up to look at the target.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that in order to hit the ball successfully you need to keep your head down and focused on the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Grip, stance and swing basics

nodes.misconception: Pupils think we only get a penalty stroke if we break a rule.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that a a penalty stroke is an extra stroke added to your score as a result of breaking a rule or hitting the ball into certain areas.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play: using a variety of shots

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you can putt the ball successfully just by lining up to the ball, forgetting that the green slopes and isn't flat.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that beacuse each green is different and they aren't flat, we always have to consider where we aim and the power we apply.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Short game: putting and chipping

nodes.misconception: Golf etiquette is just about being polite.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that golf etiquette is about courtesy, consideration and respect for other players, the course and the game itself.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Design a short course

nodes.misconception: There are many misconceptions about diet, such as, the need to cut out carbohydrates or fat because they are seen as responsible for weight gain.
nodes.response: A balanced diet requires all nutrients because each has its own benefits to the body and health. Cutting any of them out completely will negatively impact overall health and performance in sport and physical activity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A balanced diet

nodes.misconception: The main consequences of dehydration are headaches and dizziness.
nodes.response: Headaches and dizziness are likely effects of dehydration, however the GCSE specification expects students to be able to understand the physiological reasons behind these such as slow blood flow, increased heart rate and body temperature.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hydration

nodes.misconception: "If I did more exercise, I'd lose weight"
nodes.response: While exercise will increase energy expenditure and could help to achieve a calorie deficit needed to lose weight, "you can't out train a bad diet." No matter how much exercise is performed, calorie intake is just as important to consider.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Energy use

nodes.misconception: There are many misconceptions about diet, such as the need to cut out carbohydrates or fat because they are seen as responsible for weight gain.
nodes.response: A balanced diet requires all nutrients because each has its own benefits to the body and health. Cutting any of them out completely will negatively impact overall health and performance in sport and physical activity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Components of a balanced diet

nodes.misconception: There are many misconceptions about diet, such as the need to cut out carbohydrates or fat because they are seen as responsible for weight gain.
nodes.response: A balanced diet requires all macronutrients because each has its own benefits to the body and health. Cutting any of them out completely will negatively impact overall health and performance in sport and phyiscal activity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A balanced diet for health and performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils often assume that a fielder needs to be stationed on each base and that it is the job of other fielders to get the ball to them while they remain with their base.
nodes.response: Use the third section of this lesson to introduce the idea that fielding positions should be fluid and that infielders, especially, should always be alert to the idea of leaving bases or covering other bases.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Fielding and throwing techniques

nodes.misconception: For many pupils, softball may be a totally new game. It's a game with a lot of different rules from the striking and fielding games they will already know such as rounders and cricket.
nodes.response: Learning the intricacies, language and rules of the game in the first lesson and playing a version which includes most of the main rules, will allow pupils to relate to, and see sense in what they learn later in the unit, to the game itself.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Softball and basic rules

nodes.misconception: Pupils who are more experienced may ignore the contribution of less able pupils, or even belittle or berate them when they don't contribute well to the team.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use their knowledge to offer feedback which can help bring about an improvement, emphasising that in team games, an individual cannot and should not perform all roles or carry the team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play and review of others' performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use a static approach to batting, perhaps using only their arms to swing the bat with.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand the whole body is involved in a good batting swing and that most of the power produced comes from the lower half of the body.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Batting techniques

nodes.misconception: Pupils often pay little attention to strategy and think only of themselves and not what the team needs. Many will only think of hitting the ball as hard and as far as they can.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider team strategy, e.g. the batting line up based on strengths of the team. Stronger hitters bring others home and in some cases, a safe hit is much more useful to a team than trying to slog and getting caught or struck out.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Base running and game strategies

nodes.misconception: Pupils may field fly balls by putting their arm up in the air then running to where they think it'll land.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to beat the ball to the landing spot by running fast - something which can't be done with one arm in the air - then position themselves to catch.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pitching and catching techniques

nodes.misconception: Hip Hop culture focuses on 'disrespecting' your opponent and mocking them.
nodes.response: As in all competitive settings, the performers are trying to succeed and employ a variety of strategies to do so, but this also includes congratulating others on their successes and supporting those who are developing their skills.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hip Hop: question and answer

nodes.misconception: Hip Hop is a dance style
nodes.response: Hip Hop is a generic term for a number of dance styles that are heavily influenced by street culture (DJing, graffiti, rapping). There are a large number of subdivisions which vary according to time and place of origin.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hip Hop: the basic movement language

nodes.misconception: In Capoeira you use pre-recorded music.
nodes.response: In Capoeira the music is played live and the tempo and style of the music dictates the style of the game that will be played.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Capoeira: improvised duets

nodes.misconception: If supporting another person you should be as far away from them as possible.
nodes.response: To support another person effectively, the performers need to be in close proximity with the 'supporter' adopting a wide base and using the large muscle groups to power the action.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Lindy Hop: contact work in duets or groups

nodes.misconception: Capoeira is based on fighting.
nodes.response: Capoeira is based on challenging your opponent, but in a game-like scenario. This is why performers are called 'players'.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Capoeira: the basic movement language

nodes.misconception: The steps learnt have to be performed in a set order.
nodes.response: In the Lindy Hop, the dancers' personal style and flair was highly prized so they would find new and inventive ways of arranging and performing the key actions seen it this style.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Lindy Hop: the basic movement language

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle with their release point when bowling underarm which results in an illegal bowling action. Pupils are too slow to throw from backstop to first base when trying to run the batter out.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on a smooth pendulum action when bowling to ensure that the ball is bowled between knee and head height and to the side of the batter. When backstop has the ball, focus on a flat, hard throw to first base to run the batter out.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: An effective bowler, backstop and first base partnership

nodes.misconception: Pupils lack the confidence to make decisions, often worrying what their peers might say if they don't agree with a decision.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with reassurance that it is acceptable to make mistakes and ensure everyone in the group is respectful of decisions made by officials.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating your own small sided rounders games

nodes.misconception: Pupils often try to hit the ball too hard or take their eyes off the ball by focusing too much on the target.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils focus on control rather than power when batting and encourage then to keep their eyes on the ball until they have hit it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Effective batting placement through Danish longball from a T

nodes.misconception: Pupils often throw with a stiff arm and do not step into their pass with the opposite foot, resulting in inaccurate and unbalanced throws.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils can throw with the correct technique from a static position before adding any movement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Catching, throwing and roller ball games

nodes.misconception: Pupils often make slow decisions when covering each other due to lack of confidence. They also panic when they are under pressure in a game situation.
nodes.response: Encourage quick and clear communication using captains and coaches to help players make good decisions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing performance and working more effectively as a team

nodes.misconception: Pupils often try to hit the ball too hard when batting. Often pupils hit the ball in the same space every time they bat which is usually around 2nd and 3rd base.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on accuracy and control rather than power. Encourage pupils to change the angle of their hips, front foot and backswing to help them hit the ball in different directions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: 3 ball rounders

nodes.misconception: Training seasons align with seasons of the year.
nodes.response: They are very different. Training seasons will align with the type of sport and their competition period. For example, the football season is currently a different time period to the netball super league and hence their seasons will be set by this.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training seasons

nodes.misconception: Each sport or activity has only one training method suited to it.
nodes.response: Perfomers in most activities can benefit from the use of multiple trianing types. For example, a marathon runner would most benefit from continuous training; however, weight training could also be used to help condition the muscles and avoid injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of training

nodes.misconception: Running is the only type of interval training.
nodes.response: Interval training can be done with any activity, as long as it involves high intensity work followed by a rest period.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of continuous, fartlek, interval training and static stretching

nodes.misconception: Running is the only type of interval training.
nodes.response: Interval training can be done with any activity as long as it involves high intesity work followed by a rest period.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of continuous, fartlek and interval training

nodes.misconception: Training at high altitude leads to permanent change in the body to support performance of an endurance athlete.
nodes.response: Adaptations to altitude are lost very quickly when returning to sea level. Therefore, an endurance athlete needs to plan carefully when to access altitude to be at optimal performance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Altitude training

nodes.misconception: That rest is not incorporated into these types of training.
nodes.response: All of these can be performed as a type of interval training and rest after each exercise / session is important to avoid the body getting injured.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of circuit, weight, plyometric and other fitness classes

nodes.misconception: Each sport or activity has only one type of training suited to it.
nodes.response: Performers in most activities can benefit from a range of training types. A marathon runner would benefit most from continuous training; however, weight training and static stretching would also help with conditioning and avoiding injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of training and how best to train

nodes.misconception: That rest is not incorporated into these types of training.
nodes.response: All of these can be performed as a type of interval training and rest is important after each exercise / session to avoid the body getting injured.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of circuits, weight and plyometric training

nodes.misconception: That rest is not incorporated into these types of training.
nodes.response: All of these can be performed as a type of interval training and rest after each exercise/session is important to avoid the body getting injured.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of circuits, weight, plyometric and HIIT

nodes.misconception: Running is the only type of interval training.
nodes.response: Interval training can be done with any activity as long as it involves high intesity work followed by a rest period.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A practical exploration of continuous, interval and fartlek training

nodes.misconception: Each sport/activity has only one specific type of training suited to it.
nodes.response: Performers in many activities can benefit from a variety of training types. For example, a marathon runner will mostly benefit from continuous training, however weight training could help to condition their muscles and avoid injury.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training methods for specific components of fitness

nodes.misconception: Pupils don't align their court positioning and often find themselves with one player forward and one back.
nodes.response: If one player is at the net and one is back on the baseline, it leaves big diagonal gaps through the court so it is essential for both be at net or both be on the baseline as much as possible.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Approach the net as a partnership

nodes.misconception: Pupils add their non dominant hand to the bottom of the grip when hitting backhands.
nodes.response: It is essential that your dominant racket hand is at the bottom of the grip and if you add your other hand for extra control or power it must go further up the racket shaft.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Bilateral movement and groundstroke consistency

nodes.misconception: Pupils rush to play full court from the baseline before they have the racket skills to direct the ball accurately and keep a rally going.
nodes.response: Tennis can be a frustrating game with a lot of fetching mis-hit balls. It is best to start slow and build your confidence with racket familiarisation and close touch control before building in more power to your shots.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Basic strokes and gameplay

nodes.misconception: Every point is equally important in tennis.
nodes.response: Break point and other points to the advantage side are far more important to avoid losing a game on your own serve or winning/losing a game respectively. In the 2019 Wimbledon final, Federer won 14 more points than Djokovic, but lost the match.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play and match practice

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they have to hit the serve as hard as possible to be effective.
nodes.response: Placement, spin and consistency are far more important when learning to serve.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Serving and returning

nodes.misconception: Pupils use a big swing for volleys and consequently regularly miss the ball or hit it out.
nodes.response: When playing close to the net, you don't need to apply much swing and instead should use the power already in the ball, combined with a step into the shot, to apply power with more of a short punching action to block the ball back.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Volleys and net play

nodes.misconception: Putting is a unique action and pupils often unwittingly revert to a throwing action which can lead to injury. Throwing is against the rules/regukations, thus it is also often illegal in competitions
nodes.response: Encourage the key technical points of holding the shot against the neck throughout the preparation and pushing the shot phases first, alsongide the key point about a straight wrist and extending elbow following behind at all times.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shot put technique

nodes.misconception: Pupils often struggle with combining the different phases of the triple jump in the correct sequence.
nodes.response: Build up to the full performance gradually, without an approach to begin with and gradually introducing one at walking pace and then jogging pace. Have a partner coach the performer to check their coordination and technique to quickly correct errors.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Supporting others to successfully triple jump

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all the power in sprinting comes from the legs and not use their arms enough when performing.
nodes.response: Power in sprinting is created by a combination of powerful legs and arms working simultaneously, hence why sprinters often have muscular arms as well as legs.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running for speed and the relationship between distance and time

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often quick to focus their feedback on something which went wrong or needs improvement, without considering the impact of identifying what is also being performed well.
nodes.response: Pupils can use methods such as the 'feedback sandwich' which encourages them to think about identifying positive aspects of performance as well as areas for improvement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Realising your potential at long jump

nodes.misconception: When perfroming the long jump, many pupils take a long step into the pit which means they land with one foot in front of the other which reduces the distance they achieve.
nodes.response: Pupils should be taught to land with feet parallel by bringing the take-off foot through and in front of them so that no distance is lost and they achieve a maximal score.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping for distance

nodes.misconception: Pupils start long distance running too fast through a mixture of excitement, copying each other and overestimating the pace they can maintain.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need to calculate and find a suitable pace and consider how sustainable a fast pace is going to be.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Running for distance and understanding pace

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be quick to get over emotional when challenged with being the official, leading to inaccurate, unfair or even biased decisions being made.
nodes.response: Pupils must learn to regulate their emotions when acting as the official to ensure competition is fair.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating your own throwing challenges

nodes.misconception: When learning the scissors technique, pupils often use an incorrect take-off foot, choosing to jump from the foot closest to the bar instead of the foot furthest away.
nodes.response: Allow pupils to practise jumping off their right foot, then their left, before performing the full action to establish which they prefer to take off with.  Be observant during full performances and be ready to suggest a pupil changes approach side.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jumping for height

nodes.misconception: There may be pupils who feel confident and enthusiastic and want to take over all officiating and not allow others to do so.
nodes.response: All pupils should take some role in officiating. Assign roles such as scorecard keeper and person in charge of reading the aims and rules at each event.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating your own jumping challenges

nodes.misconception: Pupils often perform relay changeovers with the receiver standing still until they receive the baton, then accelerating into their sprint.
nodes.response: Changeovers should be performed at high speed. The receiver begins to accelerate at just the right moment to high speed but not too far ahead of the incoming runner. This will be different for each pupil  (~3.5m is a good point to work from).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Relays

nodes.misconception: Hurdles is daunting for many pupils who may fear hitting the hurdle, falling or getting hurt, which are justifiable concerns. This causes them to do things such as stutter their approach or even stop.
nodes.response: Be careful to provide hurdles which are achievable for all abilities and gradually allow pupils to build confidence and progress to higher hurdles when ready, rather than expect them to hurdle the full height.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hurdles

nodes.misconception: A common mistake pupils make is using a 'bowling' style of throw in which the throwing arm remains straight throughout the action.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to think about pulling the javelin through, with the elbow leading first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Javelin technique

nodes.misconception: For a 9 mark answer I have to make two knowledge points, two applications and five AO3s.
nodes.response: 9 mark answers are marked holistically using a levelled response grid. Level descriptors are applied to the overall response. A quantitative approach to answering these questions can be limiting to develop the breadth of knowledge and depth of AO3.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Exam technique on the 9 mark question

nodes.misconception: For a 6 mark answer, I have to make one knowledge point, two applications and three AO3's.
nodes.response: 6 mark answers are marked holistically using a levelled response grid. Level descriptors are applied to the overall response. A quantative approach to answering these questions can be limiting to develop the breadth of knowledge and depth of AO3.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Exam technique and approaching the 6 mark extended questions

nodes.misconception: Failure to address all parts of the question.
nodes.response: The 6 mark extended answer question always requires knowledge from that exam paper (component) and the other exam paper (component) and practical application.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Exam technique and answering the extended answer questions

nodes.misconception: In long answer questions it is better to recall as much of the topic as possible.
nodes.response: It is important to recall the specific knowledge relevant to the question but then apply that knowledge and develop the knowledge based on the command word. Simply just recalling knowledge will only hit AO1 marks awarded.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Exam technique and answering extended questions

nodes.misconception: Injury prevention means injuries will not occur.
nodes.response: Nothing can guarantee that injuries will not happen, however the measures discussed in this lesson will significantly reduce the risk of injury. With the best prevention measures in place, accidents may still happen.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Injury prevention

nodes.misconception: Stretching is the first part of a warm up routine.
nodes.response: Before a muscle can be stretched it needs to have an increase in temperature and pliability. Therefore, before stretching, an individual should do a pulse raiser to increase blood flow to the muscles.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Warming up and cooling down

nodes.misconception: Injuries can be prevented in sport and physical activity.
nodes.response: We can significantly reduce the risk of injury using the measures discussed in the lesson, however nothing can guarantee an accident causing injury to a performer.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Risks and hazards

nodes.misconception: All performance enhancing drugs are illegal/banned/negative.
nodes.response: The use of some PEDs to enhance performance is perfectly acceptable. Many sportspeople use narcotic analgesics to get through an event or drink caffeine for its stimulating effect. WADA is responsible for determining which PEDs are allowed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performance enhancing drugs

nodes.misconception: Injuries can be prevented by using methods such as PAR-Q
nodes.response: Nothing can guarantee that injuries will not happen, however the measures discussed in this lesson will significantly reduce the risk of injury. Accidents will always happen.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: PAR-Qs and injury prevention

nodes.misconception: RICE is the treatment required for all injuries.
nodes.response: RICE in only suitable for soft tissue injuries such as strains and sprains. For other types of injuries , other types of medical care should be sought.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sport specific injuries and RICE treatment

nodes.misconception: Stretching is the first part of a warm up routine.
nodes.response: Before a muscle can be stretched, it needs to have an increase in temperature and pliability. Therefore, before stretching, an individual should do a pulse raiser to increase blood flow to the muscles.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Warm up and cool down

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that if they are not the fielder chasing a ball, they are not needed, even though the chasing fielder cannot throw the full distance to the wickets.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that fielders need to work together and if they think the fielder will struggle to throw the distance, they should support by positioning themselves to relay the ball.
