nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Leadership and responsibility

nodes.misconception: Some pupils don't consider the emotions of other people involved in a game which can lead to unsavoury comments after mistakes or poor play.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to consider the emotions of others and how they might be able to positively influence the emotions of others through words and actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Game play with a focus on emotional control

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not always recognise that celebrating others' achievements is an important part of their own development and contribution to the team.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils that part of the game is to show respect and to respecfully physically appreciate it when someone performs well.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Respect and sportspersonship

nodes.misconception: When wicket keeping, pupils have a tendency to stand right up to the wickets, no matter how fast the bowler is. This means they can't react quick enough to faster balls.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that they can adjust the distance between wicket keeper and stumps, depending on the speed of the bowler, so they are catching the ball around thigh height. There is no standard wicket keeper position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pressure and emotion

nodes.misconception: Pupils will swing the bat across their body like a baseball bat which increases the chance of missing the ball, edging it or getting out.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that because of the way the ball is bowled in cricket, playing with a straight bat is often the most effective way to strike and not risk your wicket.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Integrity and honesty in action

nodes.misconception: Pupils may argue about decisions, particularly close calls such as run outs. This can often lead to the decision going in the favour of the more dominant or boisterous pupils.
nodes.response: Pupils should experience the umpire role to practise making fair decisions and develop empathy, helping them understand not to challenge calls.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Teamwork and communication

nodes.misconception: Matching a similar and incorrect photo as a result of rushing.
nodes.response: During photo orienteering, it is important to take your time and look at details carefully.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Photo orienteering

nodes.misconception: Individual objects can't be used to make art.
nodes.response: If we collect a range of materials in contrasting colours and various textures, we can combine them to produce a nice composition.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: A treasure hunt

nodes.misconception: The task is impossible.
nodes.response: Each stage of the challenge is possible. A reset in order to start again may be a good strategy if you get confused.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Problem solving and team building

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that fast running throughout will be the best pace to use in trail running.
nodes.response: Using smart pacing means the pupils can use variable speeds, across different terrain, to keep safe, save engery and complete the run.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Trail running

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that walking is boring and too easy.
nodes.response: Walking can be at different speeds, does not have to be boring and is a good opportunity to be present in the moment, which enhances positive mental health.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Plan a walk in the local area

nodes.misconception: I am not a qualified first aider so I can't help someone in need.
nodes.response: Basic knowledge can allow you to help with minor injuries. Knowing what to do in certain circumstances means that you can support and hopefully make a difference for any more major situations.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Survival skills and first aid

nodes.misconception: It is too tiring to sprint the whole course.
nodes.response: Strategise and plan who will take on what role and when to spread more difficult actions/moments among the team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprint relay orienteering

nodes.misconception: Indoor caving is just about squeezing through tight spaces as quickly as possible.
nodes.response: Caving isn't just about speed. It involves planning, moving carefully, using spatial awareness and thinking ahead to create and navigate a route that is both enjoyable and challenging.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Indoor caving

nodes.misconception: You need a strong throw to be good at darts.
nodes.response: Darts is more about control and accuracy than power. A smooth, balanced stance and consistent release are more important.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Darts

nodes.misconception: It is unsafe to be blindfolded.
nodes.response: While there is an increased risk in getting injured, listening carefully to friends, trusting their guidance and being sensible will all help to reduce the risk level.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop trust within an OAA environment

nodes.misconception: Who finds it first, wins.
nodes.response: Accuracy and teamwork so we find the correct outcomes is more important than being first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Code breaking

nodes.misconception: A simple or fast resolution is not always the best resolution.
nodes.response: Sometimes deeper thinking is required to prevent further problems arising as a result of your actions.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: River crossing with a casualty

nodes.misconception: Requirement to keep checking location to ensure on track. Regular stopping and time wasting as a result of re-orientating the map.
nodes.response: Thumbing the map means tracing your route as you move along the map to represent where you are on the map at any given time.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Star orienteering

nodes.misconception: New games are often hindered by preexisting rules and scoring systems which remain the basis and stunt creativity.
nodes.response: Pupils must think outside the box and forget about pre-existing activities when creating their own games. It is important to instil the confidence to try something new even if it doesn't work.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Designing and leading your own playground games

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to align north on the compass with north on the map before navigating
nodes.response: Hold the compass next to the arrow representing magnetic north on the map and rotate your body until the arrow on the map and the arrow on the compass line up with north, then keep the map facing that way even when you change direction.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Map skills and use of a compass

nodes.misconception: Blaming others for mistakes and rushing rather than planning first and taking care over the approach.
nodes.response: Less overall time is lost if you invest in planning, negotiating and caring for each other.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Navigating the assault course as a team

nodes.misconception: All players are desperate to get the opposition's treasure so they have a high risk of getting caught and neglecting the protection of their own treasure.
nodes.response: Let pupils do it however they like first but then give time to regroup and plan a smarter team strategy.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Capture the flag

nodes.misconception: Rushing to complete the task and therforemfailing to listen to, or consider, all group members.
nodes.response: Together Everyone Achieves More, it is essential to work as a TEAM and ensure everyone is valued.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Photo finish and all aboard

nodes.misconception: Pupils in fielding positions may lose focus when they are not involved for a spell of time and then miss an opportunity to field as a result.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to communicate regularly and relay the ball back to the bowler via 1 or 2 fielders to keep everyone alert - e.g. the wicket keeper takes a catch, passes it to the slip fielder who sends it to another fielder and then to bowler.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Fielding and slip catching

nodes.misconception: Many young batters fail to move their feet when batting, instead they try to contort their bodies to deal with all sorts of line and length deliveries with little success.
nodes.response: Through practice, pupils can learn how to move their feet in response to different pitches of delivery. With short deliveries moving weight on to the back foot and changing foot position allows for pull, hook and cut shots.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Aggressive batting for maximum runs

nodes.misconception: There is certainly a misconception with many pupils that the ball should be hit out into the field whenever possible, exacerbated by the need to do this in many other striking and fielding games.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand on occasions in cricket, blocking or leaving the ball are actually preferable shots to play, rather than shots with a higher risk of getting out. It requires a different mindset to a lot of other striking and fielding games.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defensive batting

nodes.misconception: Communication after the ball is hit can be inconsistent in cricket. Having four players to coordinate means the need to communicate clearly about how many runs to make is even more important.
nodes.response: Allow pupils time to strategise about how they will communicate after the ball is hit. For example, they may nominate a captain to make all calls or decide that the batter who hit the ball makes the call.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Diamond cricket

nodes.misconception: Many pupils do not consider how adaptations and conditions can make games more enjoyable for different people, preferring to play the full version of a game even when it might be a struggle.
nodes.response: Helping pupils to be conscious of other people's motivations and understand how adaptations can make the game more accessible and enjoyable.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Teaching others to play adapted cricket games

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will think that success in bowling only comes if the ball hits the stumps.
nodes.response: In some situations, hitting the stumps is desirable, i.e., bowl a batter out / trap them lbw / win a bowl-out. However, all lengths have their uses and a good bowler can pitch the ball at a wide range of different lengths.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Games to develop spin and pace bowling

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that bowling should always be at the same length to be consistent. The phrase 'good length' might be part of the confusion.
nodes.response: Pupils should understand that as long as it is a legal ball, the length can vary. This is a good way to outwit the batter as different lengths create different challenges and keeps them guessing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Develop the overarm bowl with a run up to challenge the batting pair

nodes.misconception: Many pupils do not move their feet in response to the pitch of a ball, instead keeping their feet in the same place throughout. This leads to awkward and ineffective swings at the ball.
nodes.response: Using tees slows down the thought process so that footwork can be learned before facing a moving ball. Almost every shot requires some foot movement and the stance should allow for this by being on balls of feet and with knees slightly bent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Batting shots to outwit the fielders off a T

nodes.misconception: The most common error made when beginning to learn how to bowl in cricket is that pupils throw the ball with the elbow bending in the action which is not allowed.
nodes.response: Pupils need to understand that the action requires a straight arm and this should be emphasised throughout the lesson. It is perhaps a unique throwing action which takes time to adjust to.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Overarm bowling from a standing position

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that when they are not batting, they don't need to pay attention to what is happening on the field.
nodes.response: Being a good team member requires us to encourage our teammates and be aware of what is happening in the game, even when our turn to bat has not finished or even started yet.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Outwitting the opposition in competitive pairs games

nodes.misconception: As a batting pair, pupils are often poor at communicating when to run, sometimes even oblivious of the need to communicate at all.
nodes.response: Teach pupils a simple code that they can use and when to use it, to encourage more understanding of the need to communicate.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Batting calls and field placement

nodes.misconception: When throwing at a target, pupils will often think only of hitting the target and not the consequences of missing it - which often leads to losing more runs through overthrowing it.
nodes.response: Pupils understand the need to back up their teammate as they throw, and the need for the thrower to check that someone is backing up before throwing.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pairs throw ball fielding games

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unaware of the variety of training methods available to use for improving fitness and performance.
nodes.response: Continue to give pupils experiences which demonstrate different methods of training and ways to structure sessions, such as interval and plyometric training.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Speed

nodes.misconception: Pupils might believe that benchmarking times represent their fixed ability and that their times won’t change.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to understand that benchmarking is a snapshot in time - a starting point that effort and hard work can improve (growth mindset).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Your strengths as an athlete

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand the relationship between rest and workouts, believing that more training, equals more progress.
nodes.response: Help pupils to understand the requirement for sufficient rest and recovery time if the body is to make adaptations and improve.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training with intensity

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that improving at a physical activity requires them to perform the event in full repeatedly.
nodes.response: Help pupils to understand that training drills which overload the body are much more effective when training to achieve a goal, rather than simply repeating the full performance.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Design your programme

nodes.misconception: Pupils often struggle with setting a realistic goal for themselves, often have plans that are too ambitious for the time available or opportunity to train towards it.
nodes.response: Pupils should be aware that progress over several weeks can be marginal and that fitness gains take time and consistency. They can use the resources provided to help set realistic goals.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Setting goals for training

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe they can maintain their shorter distance pace over the longer distance, without needing to adjust.
nodes.response: Longer distances require more controlled pacing. Running a 1500m at 800m pace or a 200m at 100m pace will almost always lead to early fatigue and poor performance. Learning to distribute your effort is key to completing longer events effectively.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Adapt to different distances

nodes.misconception: PNF can sometimes be confused as a partner simply helping to deepen the stretch by pushing a bit further.
nodes.response: The method of contracting the muscle activates the nervous system which helps improve flexibility more effectively than static stretching alone.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation: flexibility

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare their progress to other pupils and feel disappointed if others have made a faster rate of progress.
nodes.response: Progress is personal and depends on many things - starting fitness, goals, technique and even how well rested you are on test day. Even small amounts of progress should be celebrated.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Measure your progress

nodes.misconception: Pupils often massively misjudge how much incremental overload can be achieved week on week.
nodes.response: Explain that small incremental increases in overload using the FITT principle will bring about results safely.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The FITT (frequency, intensity, time and type) principle

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the longer your stride, the faster you'll run.
nodes.response: Thinking about stride length and experimenting with different lengths can help pupils to understand the optimal length of stride and its relationship with cadence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Body form

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that repeating the same drills every session is the best way to improve.
nodes.response: Even performing the best drills or exercise will become boring after time. Therefore variation is required in a training programme, otherwise it will become boring and the athlete will lose interest.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Build variation into your workouts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that they need to feel hyped up or overly energised to perform well.
nodes.response: Overexcitement can lead to mistakes, such as, starting too fast or losing focus. Controlled breathing and mental rehearsal help you stay calm, focused and perform more efficiently.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Performing at your best

nodes.misconception: Graphs in exam questions will have the x and y axes labelled.
nodes.response: One of the skills assessed in GCSE PE exam questions is to label the x and y axes, as well as plot data and present as the method requested by the question.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Data collection and presentation

nodes.misconception: To analyse data you just need to explain what the data is demonstrating.
nodes.response: The analysis skill goes a little further and looks at patterns / trends / relationships in the context of data provided.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Data analysis and evaluation

nodes.misconception: Punching is an effective way of hitting the kin-ball.
nodes.response: Hitting with your hands clasped together helps to prevent injury, improve stability, ensure accuracy and enable faster, stronger hits.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking-specific skills and strategies

nodes.misconception: A team hit the kin-ball without properly nominating a team to defend.
nodes.response: Each hitting team must shout "Omnikin" followed by the colour of the bib worn by the nominated team before hitting the kin-ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Full context gameplay and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils stay upright while kneeling in the tripod position, meaning the ball is too high for hitting.
nodes.response: It is easier to hit the kin-ball when it is lower down, so be sure to bend forward in the kneeling position.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kin-ball and basic rules

nodes.misconception: Kicking the kin-ball on its side, similar to kicking a football, is considered an effective strategy.
nodes.response: It is important to kick the kin-ball on the underside of the ball to help reduce the risk of injury and maximise the chances of gaining height and therefore keeping it off the floor.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Exploring defensive strategies and kicking

nodes.misconception: The kin-ball is light as it is full of air and travels slowly so it doesn't require much strength.
nodes.response: When the kin-ball is dropping to the floor, trying to stop it with outstretched arms takes significant effort and core strength.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Building skills and confidence in kin-ball

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to get into an effective defensive position.
nodes.response: A quick transition out of a set position will reduce the chance of this occuring.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team play and advanced game strategies

nodes.misconception: Poor sporting behaviour is only related to people who spectate or support the events.
nodes.response: Everyone involved in the competition is responsible for how they behave and showing good sporting behaviour.  This includes supporters, performers and officials. Everyone's role is to ensure the event remains safe, fair and enjoyable for all.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Officiating, performing and supporting your team

nodes.misconception: Everyone's sprinting technique should look the same.
nodes.response: Everyone will have their own natural style of running. Forcing pupils to be too upright for example may be sub optimal for some. Pupils should find their natural position which may include a slight lean.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training in teams for personal bests in sprint events

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe only performers participate in competitive events.
nodes.response: Competitions depend on various roles to run safely and efficiently. Performers can only participate if officials and organisers set up the event correctly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Competing and contributing as a united team

nodes.misconception: Strength and power are more important than technique when throwing a javelin far.
nodes.response: While strength and power are both important, too much strength and not enough time focusing on technique, can impact the accuracy of the throw. A well executed throw will travel further than just force alone.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training in teams for personal bests in javelin

nodes.misconception: All throwing events have the same technique.
nodes.response: While there is a common core technique across all throwing events, each event has a unique set of technical elements that range from the grip, stance, release and recovery phases.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing performance and identifying your best events

nodes.misconception: To get faster at running middle distance you always have to train at race pace.
nodes.response: Improvements in speed and fitness for middle distance running can also come from running easy efforts. This builds aerobic fitness and gives the individual a strong base where over time the same effort will be maintained but at a faster pace.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training in teams for personal bests in middle distance events

nodes.misconception: If you get off the mat before the bar falls it will still count as a successful jump.
nodes.response: If the bar falls then the jump does not count, even if the jumper has left the mat. Every attempt should be made to clear the bar rather than rushing the landing and clearing the mat quickly.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training in teams for personal bests in high jump

nodes.misconception: Pupils wait until they have the baton before starting to run in a relay.
nodes.response: Outgoing runners need to move to the start of the exchange zone and start their run sooner to accelerate as they are handed the baton on the move. Practise the technique from stationary to running to ensure action is well rehearsed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The grand final, relays and medal tables

nodes.misconception: A belief that our identity is fixed and permanent.
nodes.response: Who we are and how that is expressed can be changed, and is likely to shift throughout our life. We can communicate who we are through our expression, how we dress, how we speak and by taking part in activities that are important to us.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mini Olympic opening ceremony

nodes.misconception: A trial is where people are judged to see who makes the cut and who doesn't.
nodes.response: A trial is an opportunity for everyone to show what they can do and also learn where they could focus on as priority areas for improvement.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Trials and team selection for a sport education season

nodes.misconception: A common mistake in the triple jump is the athlete collapses the middle 'step phase' rather than getting equal height and distance from every phase.
nodes.response: Emphasis on all phases of the jump should be practised, especially the step phase, with height and efficiency.  All phases of the triple jump should contribute to an equal proportion of distance e.g. 2m x2m x2m
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training in teams for personal bests in long jump and triple jump

nodes.misconception: You throw a shot in the shot put.
nodes.response: The shot put does not require any rotation around a joint. It is pushed from under the chin and touching the neck. A throw action will likely lead to injury due to the weight of the shot. However, "throw" is standard terminology for this event.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Training in teams for personal bests in shot put

nodes.misconception: I must include fitness test protocols and scores to show my fitness strength and weakness.
nodes.response: This is not a requirement. The analysis of the fitness components is using recent competitive performances, and justifying how it benefited or negatively affected that actual performance/s.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Non-examined assessment: preparing for analysis and evaluation

nodes.misconception: Memorising and writing the definitions from the textbook earns marks.
nodes.response: Marks are only awarded for applying your knowledge to explain the implications of fitness, skill and tactical decision making on performance. With only 14 hours to complete the coursework, it is essential to focus time on application of knowledge.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Non-examined assessment: analysing and evaluating performance

nodes.misconception: Once planned, I just need to take part in the training without writing anything down.
nodes.response: It is useful to keep up to date training logs for each session to help monitor progress (these are not included in the word count) as well as doing mid PEP fitness testing to check progress and adapt the planned training programme where needed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Non-examined assessment: writing your personal exercise programme

nodes.misconception: Pupils choose to play with one player at the net and their partner at the back of the court.
nodes.response: Splitting front and back leaves a huge gap diagonally through your court that the opposition can exploit.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Working in pairs to workout and win

nodes.misconception: Pupils think you need to be a good tennis player to participate in cardio tennis.
nodes.response: The focus is on the workout rather than the execution of shots. It is about having fun while exercising. You should prioritise keeping your heart rate elevated for the whole lesson rather than great shots or winning rallies.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Heart rate response to shuttles, shadow runs and sideline challenges

nodes.misconception: Pupils think it is not cool to sweat or that it shows they are working too hard or are unfit.
nodes.response: The sweating response is essential to homeostasis and keeping your core body temperature stable. An increased sweating response is actually an indicator of better aerobic fitness and is required when seeking a cardiovascular benefit from training.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Serves, returns, sprinting and sweating

nodes.misconception: Pupils give up when training gets tough rather than pushing themselves closer to exhaustion.
nodes.response: To get a fitness benefit, it is essential to work your body harder than it is used to and hence a little discomfort is necessary to improve. This is often referred to as no pain, no gain.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Challenging the body and brain to the max

nodes.misconception: Pupils think power comes from just the size and strength of muscles.
nodes.response: Strength is important to generate power but so are speed, timing, coordination and the combination of levers to transfer power up from the ground.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprints, smashes and side steps

nodes.misconception: Pupils think balance is only a static position, such as standing on one leg, and is only really needed in sports like gymnastics.
nodes.response: The ability to balance whilst static is essential in sport and in life, be that on one leg or two, but it is important to highlight the kinaesthetic awareness that unlocks success is also required in dynamic balances (i.e. while on the move).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Team challenges with high tempo

nodes.misconception: Pupils will tire during the latter phases of a 100m sprint race and may withdraw their effort because fatigue is setting in and they expected to perform at maximal throughout.
nodes.response: Fatigue will always feature in the final stages if the athlete is giving it their best. Recognising this by remaining determined to finish and maintaining technique will result in the best possible time.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprint performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils often throw the shot by leading with the elbow rather than push it with the elbow following behind the shot, which can sometimes lead to pain and injury, especially to the wrist.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need to push the shot by extending the arm and not trying to bring the shot behind the head to throw. Replace shot with lighter weighted balls (medicine) if necessary to avoid injury while the technique is being learned.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shot

nodes.misconception: Pupils take an approach straight towards the bar which is not conducive to performing the Fosbury flop technique and maximising height jumped.
nodes.response: Pupils should take a curved run up which is J-shaped and will allow them to perform the technique required to gain the most height in their jump. The teacher can guide them to this through the activities.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: High jump

nodes.misconception: At the beginning of a sprint performance, pupils will rise up into an upright position as soon as possible.
nodes.response: An effective drive phase of sprinting sees the body gradually rise up over the first 20m before assuming an upright position. Trying to get upright too soon after starting will hinder acceleration.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sprint training

nodes.misconception: Pupils often fail to get enough distance in the middle step phase of the triple jump and it is much shorter then the other two phases causing them to lose distance.
nodes.response: Help pupils to understand that ideally the distance covered in each phase will be similar. It might seem counterintuitive but the short step is often due to the hop stage being too long and we need to seek balance between all three stages.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Triple jump

nodes.misconception: Pupils will grip the discus by wrapping their fingers and thumb around the edges to prevent it from slipping out or dropping it.
nodes.response: The discus should sit on the palm of the hand with the edge of the discus sitting in the last joint crease of the fingers (if you turn the hand over to the top, it should fall out). The thumb should not grip the edge at all.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Discus

nodes.misconception: Pupils expend far too much energy by sprint starting instead of finding their race pace, leading them to tire in the second half of the race.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on finding their race pace, not getting over excited at the start line, beginning too fast or being influenced by others who do. Ideally, the second half of the race is completed quicker than the first (called a negative split).
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Middle distance performance

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe starting their approach from the furthest point on the runway will result in the best possible approach and jump.
nodes.response: The approach is personalised and should be measured to ensure optimal speed is reached and the take off is smooth without the need to break stride. For most, the end of the runway will not be the ideal starting point.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Long jump

nodes.misconception: Pupils may perform middle distances by jogging the majority to conserve energy and putting a sprint in at the end. This often leads to pupils wishing they had put more effort into the initial stages.
nodes.response: A well performed 800m requires a fine line between holding back some energy for the finish but also performing at around 80-90% maximum effort for around the first 600m.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Middle distance training

nodes.misconception: A common mistake pupils make is using a 'bowling' style of throw in which the throwing arm remains straight throughout the action.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to think about pulling the javelin through, with the elbow leading first.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Javelin

nodes.misconception: Position of the non striking foot changes depending on where the shot is being aimed in the goal.
nodes.response: This is a common myth, however the positioning of the non striking foot remains consistent and needs to be at the side of the ball for optimal balance and accuracy so the shot is precise and on target.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting

nodes.misconception: Ball control is mainly about dribbling.
nodes.response: Control of the ball is the fundamental skill that is the basis of other skills such as dribbling, passing or shooting. With good ball control comes an increased opportunity to maintain possession of the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ball control

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that GCSE assessment for ball control is just looking at the techniques in isolation or in a 1v1.
nodes.response: Dribbling and 1v1 needs to be seen in conditioned practices to showcase the technique when faced with the position of the defenders and decision making.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ball control on the move

nodes.misconception: In a GCSE assessment the assessor will expect to see you be on the ball as an attacker and trying to beat defenders with tricks and feints.
nodes.response: An assessor is looking for the selection of the most appropriate skill for the situation to outwit an opponent which could be a passing option or creating space. It is more about the contribution to the team performance and strategic application.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Football practical assessment

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that defending to mainly important when playing a defensive position or during set pieces.
nodes.response: Defence starts from the striker position and works all the back to the GK. Defending well as an individual leads to collective marking and reduction of attacking space and opportunities.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling and marking

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that GCSE assessment for passing is just looking at the techniques in isolation.
nodes.response: Passing needs to be seen in progressive and conditioned practices to showcase the technique when faced with opposition and decision making.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing

nodes.misconception: Pupils keep their feet planted on the ground after taking a shot.
nodes.response: Always encourage a release of a shot, moving up onto the toes, so the player is in a suitable position to move forward for a rebound.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shooting and rebounding

nodes.misconception: A player has to pivot as part of footwork to create space after landing when the ball has been caught.
nodes.response: Although a pivot may be needed to create space and is permitted, it is better to turn in the air when reveiving the ball so landing is the right position for the next pass.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Footwork and ball handling

nodes.misconception: When a penalty pass is awarded, the player infringed has to take the pass.
nodes.response: Any player can take the penalty pass if it is in a third they are permitted to go into. Players need to communicate who this player can be in order to create an attacking advantage, as the player who made the infringement has to stand out of play.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Attacking set plays

nodes.misconception: A dodge from a static position is a good place to showcase a dodge in isolation.
nodes.response: In game play, it is encouraged to be active and on the toes and thinking about a prelim movement before a change of direction or speed can be executed therefore encouraging this in early drills is advised.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dodging, passing and receiving

nodes.misconception: Once a player has released the ball, the defenders' work is done.
nodes.response: Stage 3 defending can be used to impact the next phase of play.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Defensive set plays

nodes.misconception: Each defender can only mark 1 attacker.
nodes.response: Netball positions are paired, however the competitive situation will determine if players swap, if they double mark and which stage of defence they need at that point.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Marking and defending

nodes.misconception: Spin passes are always better to use.
nodes.response: Short or soft pop passes can be more effective for quick, controlled distribution, especially in close quarters or wet conditions where accuracy and catchability matter more than speed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing and receiving

nodes.misconception: Losing a game will affect your GCSE PE moderation score.
nodes.response: For your GCSE PE moderation, you are measured against how well you can demonstrate certain skills, tactics and decision making, not the final score of your game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rugby practical assessment

nodes.misconception: Running up quickly to tackle the ball carrier is always the best thing to do.
nodes.response: Moving up quickly to tackle the ball carrier is only the right thing to do if the rest of your defensive line is with you, as you can leave gaps which makes it easy for the ball carrier to stop you and break up the pitch to score a try.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Tackling and defensive line speed

nodes.misconception: The best thing to do when a defender is about to tackle you is to (panic) pass the ball.
nodes.response: Panic passing before contact in rugby often leads to turnovers, as the pass is rushed, inaccurate, and easier for the opposition to intercept or disrupt, therefore the best decision can sometimes be to keep hold of the ball and take it into contact.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handling and carrying skills

nodes.misconception: In a rugby scrum you have to push (like in union).
nodes.response: Because the scrum half can throw the ball in at angle that is advantageous to their team, there is not much point pushing. It's better to save energy to get back to defend but if the other side are being lazy, it might be beneficial to push.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Specialist skills

nodes.misconception: Just running a hard straight line is the only way to evade defenders and break the line.
nodes.response: While running a hard straight line can be effective, varying angles like overs and unders lines, footwork, and deception through dummying, are also crucial for evading defenders and breaking the line.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Beating opponents and try scoring

nodes.misconception: Drop shots and net shots are two terms for the same thing.
nodes.response: Whilst both shots play the shuttle just over the net, a drop shot is hit from the back of the court whereas a net shot is hit from the front of the court close to the net.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Backhand shots

nodes.misconception: It is essential to attack at all times.
nodes.response: Often it can be just as effective to consistently get the shuttle back into play, keeping the shuttle in and forcing your opposition to make mistakes by varying pace and placement on the court.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shot selection

nodes.misconception: There is no advantage to delaying your shot when playing a compeititve game.
nodes.response: Delaying your shot can be effective at wrong footing your opponent.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Badminton practical assessment

nodes.misconception: Hitting it hard and fast is the highest priority.
nodes.response: It is more effective to vary the pace, angle and positioning of where you hit the shuttle to create opportunities to win the point.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Forehand shots

nodes.misconception: Getting out of position after hitting a shot.
nodes.response: Learning to lunge and recover quickly to the middle of the court requires explosive strength/power but avoids exposing space for your opposition to attack.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Footwork and court positioning

nodes.misconception: Having index finger up the back of the racket to try to control the racket in a pan handled grip.
nodes.response: Ensure all fingers are wrapped in a shake hands grip to unlock the ability to hit with more power even if it feels harder initially. Watch out for others making this mistake with their grip and correct them when you see it.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Serving long and short

nodes.misconception: If you are on the losing team, it automatically affects the score you get for your handball assessment.
nodes.response: For your GCSE PE moderation, you are measured against how well you can demonstrate certain skills, tactics and decision making, not the final score of your game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handball: full context handball game

nodes.misconception: Dribbling is always the best option to move with the ball.
nodes.response: While dribbling can be helpful to gain ground up the court, it can slow down the game, whereas passing can often be faster and more efficient at breaking through a defence.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handball: footwork and dribbling

nodes.misconception: When attacking it is always best to just dribble/ step and pass the ball straight up the court.
nodes.response: Sometimes to create more space, a flat pass across the width of the pitch or a crossover move can be used to spread, reposition or confuse defenders which can be more successful at enabling a teammate to get through the gap that is created and score.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handball: tactical play

nodes.misconception: Power is more important than accuracy.
nodes.response: Accuracy is crucial to keep the ball within possession of your team so you have more opportunities to score.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handball: passing and receiving

nodes.misconception: Screening is a defensive move only used to stop the team with the ball scoring.
nodes.response: Screening can be used by attackers to 'screen'  or block defenders to allow an attacking teammate more space to move or score.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handball: defending and marking

nodes.misconception: Players are not allowed in the D apart from the goalkeeper.
nodes.response: If you land in the goal area (the D) after taking a shot, the goal will still count as long as the ball was released before you entered the area. However, if you enter the goal area during regular play, possession is awarded to the opposing team.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Handball: attacking and shooting

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the best thing to do when a defender is about to tackle you is to (panic) pass the ball.
nodes.response: Panic passing before contact in rugby often leads to turnovers, as the pass is rushed, inaccurate, and easier for the opposition to intercept or disrupt, therefore the best decision can sometimes be to keep hold of the ball and take it into contact.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Keeping the ball safe

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they should stand next to the ball carrier when running a support line.
nodes.response: It is better to start deeper so you are able to catch the ball at full pace and have more chance of breaking the gain line
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Breaking the line

nodes.misconception: In order to get the highest marks in GCSE PE moderation I need to be very good at all the specialist skills in rugby.
nodes.response: Rugby allows for different body shapes that suit specific positions, meaning players do not need to master every specialist skill. Forwards focus on scrums, lineouts and physical contests, while backs excel in speed, passing and kicking.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Scrums, lineouts and kicking

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that spin passes are always better to use.
nodes.response: Short or soft pop passes can be more effective for quick, controlled distribution, especially in close quarters or wet conditions where accuracy and catchability matter more than speed.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Passing on the move

nodes.misconception: Pupils fail to fully commit to a tackle which allows players to break free and score.
nodes.response: Defenders must fully commit to tackle the ball carrier and keep hold until they are on the ground to avoid giving the opposition an overlap or charge through scoring opportunity.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Going into contact

nodes.misconception: Losing a game will affect your GCSE PE moderation score.
nodes.response: For your GCSE PE moderation, you are measured against how well you can demonstrate certain skills, tactics and decision making, not the final score of your game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rugby union practical assessment

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they are not permitted to jump on a free throw.
nodes.response: There is no rule stating a jump is not permitted, however the feet can not pass the free throw line so players chose to keep their feet planted on the ground.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The attacking role

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that for GCSE assessment. their defence is looked at individually.
nodes.response: In the fully competitive game, part of the assessment is showing an understanding of the different types of defence and which would is best to use depending on the situation of the game.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The defensive role

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that for GCSE assessment, passing is only required in isolation to demonstrate the correct techniques.
nodes.response: Passing needs to be seen in progressive and conditioned practices to showcase the technique when faced with opposition and decision making.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Pass and receive

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that for GCSE assessment, shooting is only required in isolation to demonstrate the correct techniques.
nodes.response: Shooting needs to be seen in progressive and conditioned practices to showcase the technique when faced with decision making. The assessment will be based on the choice of shot or drive to the basket depending on the position of the defenders.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Variety in shooting

nodes.misconception: Pupils think defence is a solo effort and only needed when marking the player with the ball.
nodes.response: Individual defensive skills are crucial, however defending as a cohesive unit leads to the attacking team being denied space and vision to move the ball.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Marking and rebounding

nodes.misconception: Pupils think they can move with the ball more than 2 steps before starting to dribble.
nodes.response: This can be seen at the elite level but will break the travelling rule.
nodes.subject: physical-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dribbling and footwork

nodes.misconception: Guru Nanak is considered a god by Sikhs.
nodes.response: Guru Nanak is not worshipped as a god but is respected as a spiritual guide and a guru.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Guru Nanak

nodes.misconception: Sikhs only do things for themselves.
nodes.response: Many Sikhs work hard to help other people and to live an honest and good life.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Guru Nanak's teachings on being honest and living a good life

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think the story is only about the physical objects (milk and flowers).
nodes.response: A clear explanation of the symbols is important, as the symbols represent the attitudes, behaviours and spiritual lessons of the story (such as purity, kindness or spiritual values).
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Guru Nanak's teachings on equality and acceptance

nodes.misconception: Guru Nanak said that money is bad and that we shouldn’t have any.
nodes.response: Guru Nanak didn’t say that money is bad. He just taught that it’s more important to help others and be kind than to focus only on money.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Guru Nanak's teachings on serving others

nodes.misconception: Sikhs believe prayer is more important than practical service.
nodes.response: Practical, selfless service (sewa) is an essential part of being a Sikh.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The legacy of Guru Nanak

nodes.misconception: Sikhs believe in more than one God.
nodes.response: Sikhs believe in only one God and they refer to God as 'Waheguru'.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sikh beliefs in God

nodes.misconception: A menorah is just a decoration for a window.
nodes.response: A menorah has a deep significance for Jews.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hanukkah and Jewish identity today

nodes.misconception: A menorah is just a decorative candle-holder.
nodes.response: A menorah has a deep significance for Jews as a symbol of G_d and the days of creation.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Hanukkah

nodes.misconception: Antisemitism is a modern experience.
nodes.response: This story shows that antisemitism goes back at least 3,000 years.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Esther and Haman

nodes.misconception: All Jews celebrate Rosh Hashanah in the same way.
nodes.response: Jews come from different backgrounds and have different cultural traditions which are marked at Rosh Hashanah.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rosh Hashanah: diverse Jewish celebrations

nodes.misconception: All festivals are solemn.
nodes.response: In this festival, Jewish children act, shout, eat and dress up.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: How Jews mark Purim today

nodes.misconception: All festivals are times of celebration and joy.
nodes.response: Yom Kippur is about reflection and penitence.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur

nodes.misconception: The story of Abraham is only relevant to Jews.
nodes.response: Christians remember this story and learn from it.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The calling of Abraham

nodes.misconception: The Bible is one book written by one person.
nodes.response: The Bible is made up from lots of books written by different authors over a long period of time.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Shared stories

nodes.misconception: The Bible says that things always go well when you believe in God.
nodes.response: Joseph, and many other Bible characters, faced great difficulties even though they had faith.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Joseph

nodes.misconception: The covenant was only made between Abraham and God.
nodes.response: The covenant was forever and continued through his descendants, including Jesus.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jesus: waiting for a promise to be fulfilled

nodes.misconception: A promise is easy to make and keep.
nodes.response: Promises are often long term and are difficult to keep.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Abraham and Sarah

nodes.misconception: Old stories have no relevance.
nodes.response: There are meanings in stories even when they are old and confusing.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Noah and the Rainbow

nodes.misconception: Friday is the only day Muslims go to Mosque.
nodes.response: Muslims pray five times a day and may do this at home or at the mosque.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mosque: finding harmony through praying together

nodes.misconception: All Muslims mark Ramadan in the same way.
nodes.response: Muslims all around the world mark Ramadan in different ways.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ramadan and harmony

nodes.misconception: The Shahadah is simply a phrase and not a belief.
nodes.response: The Shahadah is more than just words, it involves committing your life to live as a Muslim.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Shahadah: harmony through faith

nodes.misconception: Fasting during Ramadan is only about not eating food or drinking water.
nodes.response: Ramadan is about a Muslim’s whole conduct and behaviour.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sawm: finding harmony through fasting

nodes.misconception: Muslims can only pray in the mosque.
nodes.response: Muslims can pray anywhere as long as it is on clean ground, e.g., on a prayer mat.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Salat: finding harmony through daily prayer

nodes.misconception: Muslims might follow rules within Islam without a deeper understanding of God.
nodes.response: Most Muslims follow obligations or rules to bring a sense of submission and harmony with God.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Allah and harmony

nodes.misconception: Hindus only help other Hindus.
nodes.response: Hindus help all people as part of their dharma and sewa.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dharma: living the Hindu life

nodes.misconception: Hindus all have the same murti in their puja.
nodes.response: Hindus use different murti to ask for different aspects in their lives.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Puja: different Hindu expressions

nodes.misconception: Hindus worship images and murtis.
nodes.response: Hindus use murtis and images to focus their worship or to align with the energy of a murti.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Murtis and how they are used in puja

nodes.misconception: Hindus worship many gods.
nodes.response: There is one Brahman, but many Hindus believe there are many forms of Brahman. These forms are called deities. The Trimurti are the three important ways in which Hindus talk about the roles of Brahman.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Brahman: the role of deities

nodes.misconception: Hindus worship many gods.
nodes.response: Hindus worship one god in many forms.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Brahman: The story of Svetaketu

nodes.misconception: Hindus believe in heaven.
nodes.response: Hindus believe in reincarnation as part of samsara. The ultimate goal for Hindus is moksha, or being released from the cycle of samsara.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Karma, samsara and moksha

nodes.misconception: All Christians give up wealth and follow the teaching of Jesus literally.
nodes.response: Different Christians will interpret the teachings in different ways. Some may become monks or nuns and own no money. Others will campaign or support charity to follow these teachings.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting teachings on wealth today

nodes.misconception: Christians today would not challenge people in power or laws they feel are unjust.
nodes.response: Some Christians do campaign against unjust laws and have done so throughout history.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting the Good Samaritan today

nodes.misconception: Jesus was born a Christian.
nodes.response: Jesus was Jewish. He lived in a Jewish society and responded to the issues of wealth and poverty he saw around him.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jesus and generosity

nodes.misconception: All the most important people in the Jesus movement were male.
nodes.response: There are many stories in the Gospels which show that Jesus gave women power and challenged how they were treated in society.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Martha and Mary

nodes.misconception: All Christians have the same view about the role of women in the church.
nodes.response: There is diversity of opinion across different Christian denominations. Even within denominations there are different perspectives.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The challenge to power for Christians today

nodes.misconception: The Parable of the Good Samaritan is simply about kindness.
nodes.response: The Parable of the Good Samaritan answers the question, ‘who is my neighbour?’ in a radical way. Jesus has the hero of the story as someone who his audience would have considered unclean and would have been shunned by most people.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Parable of the Good Samaritan

nodes.misconception: No one celebrates Winter Solstice anymore.
nodes.response: Pagans today still celebrate Winter Solstice.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Celebrating seasons: Winter solstice

nodes.misconception: All UK Christmas traditions are linked to the nativity.
nodes.response: There are many traditions associated with Christmas that come from outside of the nativity story, for example having a Christmas tree, santa and spending family time together.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The changing nature of Christmas in the UK

nodes.misconception: Ravana is just evil and bad without any reason.
nodes.response: Ravana is not simply evil. He is a powerful king with many good qualities but is also prideful and arrogant. His flaws lead him to make poor choices, like kidnapping Sita, which makes him a complex character.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Rama and Sita

nodes.misconception: Christmas is only celebrated by Christians.
nodes.response: Data shows that Christmas is celebrated by the majority of the UK. This includes people from both religious and non-religious worldviews.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Learning from data about Christmas in the UK

nodes.misconception: Diwali is celebrated in the same way everywhere in the world.
nodes.response: Diwali is celebrated by most Hindus. However, its celebration will vary according to geographical and cultural context.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Diwali in India and the UK

nodes.misconception: The story of Rama and Sita is simply about light overcoming darkness.
nodes.response: The Ramayana has many deeper meanings. At its heart is the concept of dharma, and many Hindus look to the text and its characters as role models and for guidance in life.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Ramayana: deeper meanings

nodes.misconception: A dedication service is the same as a baptism.
nodes.response: A dedication service is different from a baptism – it involves no water.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Christians dedicate a child to God

nodes.misconception: Every Christian tradition has an infant baptism.
nodes.response: Christians have different traditions for how to welcome a new baby.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Christian baptism of a baby

nodes.misconception: Every family does everything the same way.
nodes.response: Families might welcome children in many different ways depending on their worldview
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Welcoming a new family member with or without God

nodes.misconception: Everyone has a faith ceremony.
nodes.response: Some people have a humanist naming ceremony.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Humanists celebrate new life

nodes.misconception: Every family looks the same.
nodes.response: All families look different.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Welcoming a foster child into the family

nodes.misconception: Every family welcomes new life in the same way.
nodes.response: Understand that people welcome new life in different ways.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Welcoming new life

nodes.misconception: The Khalsa was created only for warriors who fight in battles.
nodes.response: The Khalsa was created for all Sikhs who live by a set of values, such as honesty, bravery, kindness, and service to others.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of the first Khalsa

nodes.misconception: All Sikhs in the UK recently moved here.
nodes.response: There is a long historical connection between Sikhs and the UK, including their involvement in the British Empire and service in the World Wars. Many Sikh families have lived in Britain for several generations.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sikhs: the story of a British community

nodes.misconception: All Sikhs take Amrit.
nodes.response: Not all Sikhs take Amrit. Only those who choose to commit to the Khalsa, following its principles, take Amrit during a special ceremony.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Perspectives on taking Amrit

nodes.misconception: Sikhs don’t face discrimination in the UK.
nodes.response: Even though the UK supports freedom of religion, many Sikhs still face difficulties and unfair discrimination because of how they look or their religious practices.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Living as a Sikh in Britain today

nodes.misconception: Only Sikhs who have taken Amrit wear head coverings.
nodes.response: Many Sikhs, regardless of whether they have taken Amrit or not, may choose to wear a head covering like a turban or scarf to show respect for their faith and culture.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kesh, Kanga, Kachera: living as a Sikh

nodes.misconception: Only Khalsa Sikhs wear the Kara.
nodes.response: While the Kara is one of the 5 Ks worn by Khalsa Sikhs, many Sikhs wear it even if they haven’t taken Amrit, as a sign of their faith and a reminder of God.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kara: serving as a Sikh

nodes.misconception: Festivals are always serious and solemn.
nodes.response: The festival of Holi is full of fun and mischief.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The celebration of Holi

nodes.misconception: The festival of trees is only about looking after trees.
nodes.response: It is more widely concerned with caring for the world.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The festival of trees

nodes.misconception: Jewish festivals are always celebrated in the synagogue.
nodes.response: Sukkot is celebrated in the garden.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Jewish festival of Sukkot

nodes.misconception: Harvest is an English custom.
nodes.response: It is celebrated by Christians in many different countries and in many different ways.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Harvest festival around the world

nodes.misconception: Harvest is only about collecting food.
nodes.response: It is about celebrating creation, giving thanks and sharing the benefits.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Harvest festival in UK

nodes.misconception: Festivals remember happy occasions.
nodes.response: Some remember good overcoming evil.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Holi

nodes.misconception: Hindus focus on devotion to deities rather than practical action.
nodes.response: Many Hindus are deeply concerned for the planet and are taking action to make a difference.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dharma: taking action for the wellbeing of the world

nodes.misconception: Dharma is just about religious duties.
nodes.response: Dharma is about all humans do. Dharma is about making choices motivated by love and compassion.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dharma as love for all beings

nodes.misconception: Hindus have cared for the Earth only recently.
nodes.response: Ancient scriptures show that this has always been important to Hindus.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: All are one: the Earth as mother

nodes.misconception: Dharma is just about religious duties.
nodes.response: Dharma is about all human life. Dharma is about making choices motivated by love and compassion.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Krishna: reverence and gratitude for the earth

nodes.misconception: There is one Hindu creation story.
nodes.response: There are many Hindu creation stories. This is one example. The Hindu tradition is very broad and diverse.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Hindu stories of creation

nodes.misconception: Hindus think that dharma is about caring only for people.
nodes.response: Dharma is about compassion for all living things, not just people.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Dharma: Yudhishthira and the dog

nodes.misconception: Iona is only visited by pilgrims to see its historical sites.
nodes.response: People make a pilgrimage to Iona for many reasons, but many come to see the modern community that has been reestablished.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Iona: a contemporary Christian pilgrimage

nodes.misconception: Christianity spread in a similar way across Europe.
nodes.response: Celtic people developed distinctive practices and artefacts such as Celtic crosses.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Iona: a historic Christian pilgrimage

nodes.misconception: The Kumbh Mela is simply about sadhus and crowds at the Ganges.
nodes.response: The Kumbh Mela is a spiritual pilgrimage linked to the sacred rivers and sacred time. Hindus may bathe in the river, speak to and learn from the wisdom of sadhus and sadhvus. They may also offer acts of service to other pilgrims.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Kumbh Mela: a Hindu place of pilgrimage

nodes.misconception: All places of pilgrimage have remained the same.
nodes.response: Glastonbury was a famous early and medieval centre of pilgrimage in England and continues to be important today although it is different to the original centre and shrine.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Glastonbury: a historical site for Christians

nodes.misconception: Pagans and other similar spiritualities define themselves against Christianity.
nodes.response: Pagan worldviews are highly diverse. However, they share a common reverance for the earth and a tolerance towards those of other worldviews.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Glastonbury: a contemporary spiritual place

nodes.misconception: The River Ganges is sacred because the water heals people.
nodes.response: The river is sacred to most Hindus because of its earthly manifestation of the goddess Ganga.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The River Ganges: a sacred Hindu pilgrimage site

nodes.misconception: Hindu deities are often depicted in strange colours.
nodes.response: Images of Hindu deities are highly symbolic and colour often connects to deeper meanings about the deity.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of the mouth of Krishna

nodes.misconception: One of the blind men was correct and the others were wrong about the elephant.
nodes.response: All the blind men touched a different part of the elephant and so did not fully understand what an elephant was like.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of the Blind Men and the Elephant

nodes.misconception: All Hindus think this story literally happened.
nodes.response: Many Hindus will see stories such as this as helping to explain mysteries of the universe. It is not important whether the story actually happened. What is important is what the story says about humans, the universe and God.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The mouth of Krishna: deeper meanings

nodes.misconception: All Hindus see truth in the same way.
nodes.response: The Hindu worldview is pluralist, which means there are many paths to truth.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Blind Men and the Elephant: deeper meanings

nodes.misconception: All Hindu stories come from the same source.
nodes.response: There are many sources for Hindu stories. Each story helps Hindus understand more about God and the world.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of waiting for God

nodes.misconception: Namaste is simply a way of saying ‘hello’ for Hindus.
nodes.response: Namaste symbolises a deep respect and belief that all humans contain a spark of the divine.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of waiting for God: deeper meanings

nodes.misconception: Christians do not challenge society around them.
nodes.response: Christians might challenge the laws and customs of their society.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting the woman at the well

nodes.misconception: Jesus only had meaningful conversations with his disciples.
nodes.response: Jesus had a very deep conversation with the Samaritan woman.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jesus and the woman at the well

nodes.misconception: Forgiveness is easy and instant.
nodes.response: Forgiveness can be hard and complex.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting the calling of Zacchaeus today

nodes.misconception: Jesus always followed Jewish laws.
nodes.response: Jesus challenged some of the laws in Jewish society.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jesus and the lepers

nodes.misconception: The story of Zacchaeus is a parable.
nodes.response: The story of Zacchaeus is a narrative about Jesus and someone he met.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Jesus and Zacchaeus

nodes.misconception: All Christians volunteer to do the same things.
nodes.response: Christians feel called to volunteer to help in different ways.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Interpreting Jesus and the lepers today

nodes.misconception: Jesus was a special baby born as a king.
nodes.response: For many Christians, Jesus is both God and human and was born in humble circumstances.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas: deeper meanings

nodes.misconception: Christmas is only celebrated in Europe, North America and Australia.
nodes.response: Christmas is celebrated all over the world. Many Christians are found in Africa, Asia and South America. There are many different ways of celebrating Christmas depending on geographical context.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas: different ways of celebrating Christmas around the world

nodes.misconception: The Christingle is a model with sweets and fruit eaten by Christians.
nodes.response: The Christingle has different parts which help Christians remember God’s love for the world.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Christingle and its meaning

nodes.misconception: Jesus was born in a European-looking stable and it was snowing outside.
nodes.response: We do not know what Jesus or Mary looked like but he was born in the Middle East. Many artists paint this scene in line with their own culture.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Christmas: deeper meanings through art

nodes.misconception: The wise men and shepherds all visited Jesus at the same time.
nodes.response: The wise men visited at a later time after the birth of Jesus.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Christmas

nodes.misconception: All Christians celebrate Christmas in the same way.
nodes.response: Christmas is celebrated by most Christians in the UK. However, there are different traditions in different churches and groups.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Different ways of celebrating Christmas in the UK

nodes.misconception: The covenant is ancient and has no meaning for today.
nodes.response: Jews today still remember the covenant with Abraham.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Jewish people and the covenant

nodes.misconception: The Exodus story is seen as a story about distant ancestors.
nodes.response: For many modern Jews, this story continues to be meaningful to their lives and identity today.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The deeper meaning of the Exodus story

nodes.misconception: The order of the Seder doesn’t matter. You can do it any way you want.
nodes.response: The word “Seder” means “order,” and the Seder follows a special, set sequence. Each step and food is part of this order to help tell the story clearly and meaningfully.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Seder meal

nodes.misconception: This is an ancient story and has no meaning for today.
nodes.response: This story continues to be remembered and celebrated by Jews today.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Moses and the Exodus

nodes.misconception: Pesach is only for Jewish people in the past.
nodes.response: Pesach is still celebrated today by Jewish families all over the world.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Preparing for Pesach

nodes.misconception: Only men take part in the Seder and that women don’t have a role.
nodes.response: Women are an important part of the Seder. Some families even change the Seder to include stories and voices of women, so everyone feels included.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Celebrating Pesach in Britain today

nodes.misconception: The development of the Christian church is a result of the resurrection of Jesus.
nodes.response: The development of the Christian church is a result of Pentecost.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Day of Pentecost and the 'birth' of the Church

nodes.misconception: The Salvation Army is just a charity.
nodes.response: The Salvation Army is a church and a charity.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The history and work of The Salvation Army

nodes.misconception: All Christians worship in the same way.
nodes.response: There are many different Christian churches and denominations and all of these have different styles of worship.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Quakers and Pentecostals

nodes.misconception: All churches share exactly the same beliefs and history.
nodes.response: The Christian Church shares many similar beliefs but also has different beliefs and practices which have developed in different areas over time.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Christian Church in the West

nodes.misconception: All churches share exactly the same beliefs and history.
nodes.response: The Christian Church shares many similar beliefs but also has different beliefs and practices which have developed in different areas over time.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Christian Church in the East

nodes.misconception: Christianity is a western European religion and looks the same everywhere.
nodes.response: Christianity has spread to many parts of the world. In these places it has adapted alongside the culture it is in.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Christian Church in Sri Lanka

nodes.misconception: Quakers are all Christians and believe in God.
nodes.response: Quakers come from many backgrounds. Quakers speak of the light within all and that all humans are equal.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Quakers: creating a fairer and more peaceful world

nodes.misconception: Christians might be angry at the destruction of a cathedral and seek revenge.
nodes.response: The people of Coventry rebuilt their cathedral as a symbol of hope in a better world based on forgiveness and reconciliation.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The story of Coventry Cathedral

nodes.misconception: Apartheid was a system that existed in an unelected country.
nodes.response: Apartheid was the system under the South African Government.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Reconciliation: the story of South Africa

nodes.misconception: Coventry Cathedral only worked for reconciliation in Coventry after the bombing.
nodes.response: Coventry Cathedral seeks reconciliation and peace around the world.
