nodes.misconception: Renaissance and Enlightenment thinkers gave up the belief in God.
nodes.response: Renaissance and Enlightenment thinkers questioned religious authority but didn't necessarily stop believing in God, focusing instead on reason and human potential.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Renaissance and Enlightenment: religion and thought

nodes.misconception: The caste system only applied to Hindus.
nodes.response: The caste system was applied to people of different religions.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Society at the time of Guru Nanak

nodes.misconception: Sikh women are not as involved as men in religious and community life.
nodes.response: Sikh women have always played an active and important role, historically, as activists and modern day professionals.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Women in Sikhi

nodes.misconception: The Sikh diaspora are all immigrants from the Punjab region, now in India and Pakistan.
nodes.response: The Sikh diaspora includes many people from countries in East Africa e.g. Uganda.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The Sikh diaspora and identity

nodes.misconception: The kirpan is a weapon carried for violent purposes.
nodes.response: The kirpan is a ceremonial and religious article carried by initiated Khalsa Sikhs as a symbol of their duty to stand up against injustice, not to harm others. It is one of the 5 Ks that represent Sikh identity and commitment to Waheguru (God).
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of the kirpan to Sikhs

nodes.misconception: You can only have the names 'Singh' or 'Kaur' if you are a Khalsa Sikh.
nodes.response: 'Singh' and 'Kaur' have also become used as a surname.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Singh, Kaur as social levellers

nodes.misconception: Sewa in Sikhi is limited to physical labour, especially tasks like cleaning the Gurdwara, cooking in the langar (community kitchen), or serving food.
nodes.response: Sikhi emphasises that sewa can be of three types: physical service, mental or emotional service or material and financial service.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sewa: Selfless service

nodes.misconception: African women’s experiences and theology can be adequately represented by either white women or African men.
nodes.response: African women have unique experiences and should share their own stories. Others can support them, but real representation comes from their own voices, not others speaking for them.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Mercy Amba Oduyoye and African Women's theology

nodes.misconception: Christianity spread from the Middle East to Europe and that is where the most ancient forms of Christianity began.
nodes.response: The Coptic church shows that Christianity had spread to the continent of Africa many centuries before the impact of colonialism.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Coptic Christianity: Desert Fathers and Mothers

nodes.misconception: Candomblé always embraces Catholic elements.
nodes.response: Candomblé is an ancient African faith shaped by enslavement. While some include Catholic elements for tradition or protection, many focus purely on African roots. It’s a living, evolving religion adapting to each generation’s needs.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Candomblé and Brazilian spirituality

nodes.misconception: All saints canonised by the Roman Catholic Church are European.
nodes.response: Saint Rose of Lima was the first saint to be canonised from the South American continent. She was Peruvian and is seen as a patron saint of indigenous peoples.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Saint Rose of Lima

nodes.misconception: Environmental activism and protest is primarily a European concern.
nodes.response: Wangari Maathai blended her Catholic and Kikuyu beliefs to argue for environmental justice in Kenya. She framed this through a distinctively African theological lens.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement

nodes.misconception: Liberation is not always about escaping suffering.
nodes.response: Many Black women find strength in their faith and ability to survive hardship, not because God removes their suffering, but because His liberating presence sustains them.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Delores S. Williams and womanist theology

nodes.misconception: Students may think James had a clear view on the existence of God.
nodes.response: James' investigtions led him to be agnostic and open to the idea of God rather than to be a believer.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: William James and mystical experience

nodes.misconception: The God helmet experiment has been reliably replicated and proves that religious experiences are just caused by brain stimulation.
nodes.response: In reality, the experiment has not been consistently replicated, and the results have been debated.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Persinger's God helmet

nodes.misconception: Atman is just like the soul in other religions.
nodes.response: While atman is similar to the soul, in Hinduism, it's not only the individual self but also connected to the larger, ultimate reality (Brahman). So, it’s more than just an individual soul; it can be seen as part of everything.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Atman: the divine within all

nodes.misconception: Ian McCormack’s experience is unique and proves the truth of Christianity.
nodes.response: McCormack’s experience is similar to those in other religions, where people report encounters with divine beings or light, showing such experiences aren’t unique to Christianity.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Ian McCormack and near death experience

nodes.misconception: St Bernadette's visions were believed by everyone at the time.
nodes.response: Many, including her family and Church authorities, questioned her mental state, and her visions were only accepted by the Church as genuine following investigation.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: St Bernadette of Lourdes

nodes.misconception: Sufism is a branch of Islam, like Sunni and Shi'ism.
nodes.response: Sufis can be either Sunni or Shi'a, athough the majority are Sunni.
nodes.subject: religious-education
nodes.lessonTitle: Sufism and connecting with Allah

nodes.misconception: Humans are not animals. Only four legged mammals such as dogs that can be kept as pets are animals.
nodes.response: Use of humans as an example animal in this lesson. Use of a wide variety of mammals, including wild animals, as examples in this lesson.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Naming mammals

nodes.misconception: Everything that lives in water is a fish and that fish cannot breathe underwater.
nodes.response: Examples of fish and amphibians with explanation that both can live in water. Explanation that fish use gills to breathe underwater.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Naming fish and amphibians

nodes.misconception: All animals eat the same food.
nodes.response: Examples of animals that eat different types of food.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What animals eat

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all animals have the same body structure, e.g. four legs.
nodes.response: Examples of different structures, e.g. fish, birds, that clearly show that not all animals look similar or have the same body structure.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal structure

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only four-legged mammals that are pets, are animals.
nodes.response: Discuss a range of familiar animals that can be kept as pets that are not just four-legged.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Naming and grouping familiar animals

nodes.misconception: All animals have fur and four legs. Amphibians and reptiles are the same. All birds fly.
nodes.response: Range of birds and reptiles and clear explanation of what defines each type of animal.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Naming birds and reptiles

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused with the word permanent and permeable.
nodes.response: Be clear on your definition of permeable, perhaps use some actions to help them remember. Clear up at the start that although permeable sounds rather like permanent it is completely different and explain the difference using examples.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical properties of rocks: permeability

nodes.misconception: Children may use a range of observational methods to assess hardness, e.g. “heaviness” of the object, and if it breaks on impact (test for brittleness), neither of which are a test for hardness.
nodes.response: Be aware of using the correct vocabulary around testing for hardness. Explain that hardness is the ability to withstand pressure.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Mohs' scale of hardness (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: May have confusion around classification of rock – thinking rocks in the ground and materials such as concrete, tarmac and bricks are a type of rock.
nodes.response: Help children to understand the material ‘rock’ is a natural material and not an object, and that materials like brick, tarmac and concrete are human-made and therefore not the same as natural rock material.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to rocks

nodes.misconception: Geologists only look at rocks and soils collected on Earth.
nodes.response: Geologists also work with data from space.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How geologists work

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all rocks are hard. Also that if a rock is heavy it is therefore hard.
nodes.response: Share a wide range of rocks the children can handle to explore the property of hardness so they realise some rocks are much softer than others.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Physical properties of rocks: hardness

nodes.misconception: Fossils are pieces of dead animals and plants and children often think that only dinosaurs make fossils.
nodes.response: By modelling and discussing fossil formation in various ways, children will understand how fossils are formed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How fossils are formed

nodes.misconception: Children may believe all soils are the same, therefore water flows through them all at the same rate.
nodes.response: As the children carry out the practical investigation with different soil types, they will see how water flows through them at different speeds.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Soil permeability: do and review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may be confused by the difference between the words weather and climate.
nodes.response: By identifying types of weather in the early part of the lesson, you can then help pupils to understand climate by discussing how typical types of weather remain over a long period.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy soil (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: May think that rocks are all the same and can be used interchangeably for any object made from rock. Often don't know that many everyday objects are partly made from rock in its broken down form.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to research the many ways that rock is used even in objects which don't appear on first look to contain any rock material.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday uses of rocks

nodes.misconception: Children may think that soil is any dirt on the ground, or that soil was created when Earth was created. They may also think that plants make soil.
nodes.response: The activity to separate layers of soil in water allows children to make their own observations of what soil is made from.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What soils are made from

nodes.misconception: Children use the word weathering and erosion interchangeably to mean the same thing.
nodes.response: Explain the difference between these two processes, that are closely linked, through clear definitions, images and examples of where they are happening.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Weathering and erosion of rocks

nodes.misconception: Children may think that rocks are all just called 'rock' and they don't have different appearances and different names.
nodes.response: Make sure the rock samples you give them are not actual objects, e.g. an ornament, so they are not able to use usage as a way to classify. Use a wide range of rocks that are very different so the children can identify them correctly.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The appearance of rocks

nodes.misconception: All soils are the same when it comes to permeability, how wet/dry a soil is depends how much it rains.
nodes.response: By planning a practical activity, pupils will be able to measure and observe how permeable different types of soils are.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Soil permeability: plan (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: All soils are the same, they are just earth.
nodes.response: Through exploring different soil types  and their properties with the digital microscope, children will realise that soils differ depending on where and how they are formed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different types of soils (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that during the time that Mary Anning lived women did not work in science.
nodes.response: Explaining to the pupils that Mary Anning was a trail blazer and, although it was difficult for her to work in the field of science, she continued to prove new theories and develop knowledge of fossils.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Mary Anning (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that old discovered objects, like bits of pottery, coins and jewellery are fossils.  They also may believe that the fossil is always the actual plant or animal itself.
nodes.response: Being clear that only things that have been alive may become fossils, and not all living things are fossilised.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about fossil formation

nodes.misconception: Children may not make the link between types of teeth and types of food we eat.
nodes.response: Show the children, through images and practical investigation, that humans all have the same variety of teeth to eat a variety of food. It might be useful to discuss how non-meat eating humans do still have canine and incisor teeth.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different teeth for different food

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that sweet food is bad for the teeth and savoury food is good for the teeth. Also, that drinks do not contain sugar and therefore cannot be harmful to teeth.
nodes.response: As you look at the effect of different drinks on teeth, children will be able to see that it depends on the sugar content of the drink. High levels of sugar cause damage to teeth.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Looking after our teeth: plan and do  (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all teeth are the same shape and size, and that different teeth do not have different names. They often do not know that our teeth are already in our jaw when we are born.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities for children to feel and look at their own teeth for differences in shape and size.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of teeth

nodes.misconception: Some children may think that all animals' teeth are the same. They may also think that all herbivores only have molars, and all carnivores only have canines and incisors.
nodes.response: By showing images of the teeth of carnivores and herbivores, children will see how animals have different types of teeth, depending on their diet.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Carnivore, herbivore and omnivore teeth (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may believe all toothpastes are the same.
nodes.response: By investigating the effectiveness of a variety of toothpastes, children will realise there are a range of different toothpastes for different jobs.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing toothpaste (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all teeth are the same and that they perform the same job to break down food in exactly the same way.
nodes.response: Eating a few different types of food (Task A) will help children to see for themselves which teeth they are using and what they are actually doing to break down food in different ways.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The functions of teeth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all the food we eat is used by the body.
nodes.response: When pupils model the lower part of the digestive system they will see some of the food is absorbed as nutrients and other parts form waste which leaves the body.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about the journey of food

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise there are many ways to present information as well as writing.
nodes.response: By sharing many ways that information is communicated throughout the lesson, pupils will have a variety of ways that they can choose to present what they have learned about the digestive system.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting the human digestive system

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that there is a continuous system from mouth to anus that is part of a digestive system for food. Also that food goes to the tummy rather than the stomach.
nodes.response: When the pupils sketch the digestive system within the body outline, check the different parts join up to each other so food can pass all the way through. The word 'tummy' is used early on in the slide deck to highlight common misconceptions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The human digestive system

nodes.misconception: May believe diet drinks are good for teeth as they don't have sugar in them.
nodes.response: As children observe the eggshells left in different drinks, they will see that diet drinks can still cause tooth decay and discolouration.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Looking after our teeth: review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children can become confused with what some materials are called when they look at where these materials come from, e.g. paper that makes books is processed after originally coming from trees.
nodes.response: Ensure a clear distinction between the natural materials that are used to make our man-made materials, e.g. a bookshelf is made from wood and a magazine is made from paper.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Where materials come from (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all objects that can be squashed, bent, twisted or stretched may return to their previous shape (elasticity).
nodes.response: Opportunities to explore the impact of squashing, bending, twisting and stretching different materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing shape: plan and do

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all objects that can be squashed, bent, twisted or stretched will return to their previous shape.
nodes.response: Opportunities to explore the impact of squashing, bending, twisting and stretching different materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing shape: review

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials, pupils may rely purely on observation, rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities to test different materials and observe what happens.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Absorbent materials

nodes.misconception: Pupils may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Examples of different objects made from different materials to promote discussion of the properties of materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Materials and their uses

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not think that when you stretch some materials, they go back to the shape they were (and some snap).
nodes.response: Examples of different materials, some that stretch and return to their previous length, some that stretch and do not return to their previous length, and some materials that do not stretch and may snap if stretched.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Stretchy materials

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Clear explanation of how properties of materials make them suitable or unsuitable for a particular purpose.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Suitable and unsuitable materials

nodes.misconception: Saltwater is safe to drink.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain that drinking saltwater can make us ill and will explain the process of desalination.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Removing salt from seawater (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Scientific enquiry is only valid if variables can be controlled and changed.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain how some scientist cannot control variables and look for patterns in data and observations instead.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How scientists work

nodes.misconception: Changes in state and dissolving and mixing are not reversible processes.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will show which processes can be used to reverse state changes and dissolving.  This will be explored and embedded during the practice tasks.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More reversible changes

nodes.misconception: Dissolving is the same as melting.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain the difference between melting and dissolving.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Soluble and insoluble

nodes.misconception: A dissolved solid ceases to be present in the solution it forms – it turns into water. When you pass salt water through a filter paper, the salt is removed.
nodes.response: Children carry out practical activities to discover which methods can and cannot be used to recover salt from a solution.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Separating soluble solids from solutions

nodes.misconception: Bioplastics do not cause any environmental problems.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain what the limitations of current bioplastics are, and that scientists are still working on their development.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bioplastics (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that thermal insulators only keep things warm.
nodes.response: Task A specifically addresses this misconception. Children will have opportunities to investigate which cup has the best thermal insulation properties for keeping drinks cold in lesson 5 of this unit.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Thermal insulators: plan

nodes.misconception: Thermal insulators only keep warm things warm.
nodes.response: One of the learning cycles, and Practice Task B, focuses on the use of thermal insulators to keep cold things cold.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday uses of thermal insulators

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that global warming means that the weather is getting warmer everywhere.
nodes.response: Emphasise that not everywhere gets warmer all the time. Some places might experience colder weather, more storms, or other changes in climate.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Greenhouse gases (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children often think that ice, water and steam are three different substances and not water in different states, and that changes in state are not reversible processes.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will reinforce that ice (solid state), water (liquid state), and water vapour (gas state) are all water and show which processes can be used to reverse state changes.  This will be further explored and embedded during practice tasks.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reversible changes of state

nodes.misconception: Insoluble and soluble solids are separated from liquids using the same methods: dissolved solids, like salt and sugar, can be removed from solution by filtering.
nodes.response: Methods specific to the separation of insoluble solids are taught and applied in this lesson. Task A will help pupils understand that filtering does not separate dissolved solids, like salt and sugar, from a solution.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Recovering insoluble solids

nodes.misconception: All bubbles produced contain air and that it is a reversible change.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that the bubbles produced when acids react with bicarbonate of soda contain carbon dioxide and that this change is irreversible as a new material is produced.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More irreversible changes

nodes.misconception: Children may think that everyone has access to safe drinking water, and that water just 'appears' clean from a tap.
nodes.response: This lesson explains how approximately 1.6 billion people in the world today do not have access to water that is safe to drink. Also, that water is usually filtered and treated to make it safe to drink.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Providing safe drinking water (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: There is an endless supply of fossil fuels on Earth. There are no downsides to biofuels.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain that fossil fuel is a finite resource and will introduce the pros and cons of electric cars. Children will have a chance to discuss this in task B.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Burning plants as fuel (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: All materials of a given type, such as wood, metal and plastic have the same properties.
nodes.response: Children will consider examples of different objects made from different types of wood, metal and plastic to promote discussion of the properties of materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Uses of everyday materials

nodes.misconception: All materials of a given type, such as wood, metal and plastic have the same properties.
nodes.response: Children will consider examples of different objects made from different types of wood, metal and plastic to promote discussion of the properties of materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of materials

nodes.misconception: Burning, heating and melting are the same. Smoke and water vapour are the same.
nodes.response: Slides teach that heating and melting are reversible changes because the original materials can be recovered but that, with burning, the original materials cannot be recovered.  The difference between smoke and water vapour is also taught.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Burning: an irreversible change

nodes.misconception: When interpreting results, pupils may think that the greatest loss of heat has occurred in the cup which has the lowest temperature at the end.
nodes.response: Pupils will be taught they need to consider the change in temperature rather than just using the lowest end temperature to find which cup has led to the greatest heat loss.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Thermal insulators: do and review

nodes.misconception: Insulation is used only to keep houses and other buildings warm.
nodes.response: Pupils will learn that insulation is designed to slow down heat exchange between buildings and the outside, keeping buildings warm in cold seasons or climates, or cool in warm seasons or climates.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Insulating our homes and schools (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Rusting happens immediately when the correct conditions are present and it only happens in water.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that rusting is not instant and that moisture from the air provides enough water for the process to take place.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Rusting: an irreversible change

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that blood sloshes around inside the body rather than travelling through different types of blood vessels. Pupils may also think that blood can be red or blue.
nodes.response: The learning cycle focusing on representing blood vessels in the human body helps pupils to understand that blood vessels are often drawn in different colours merely to help us distinguish between them and understand their different functions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Function of blood vessels

nodes.misconception: Children may think that scientists only present information in written, formal reports.
nodes.response: This lesson encourages lots of different forms of reporting scientific information, including verbal, pictorial and written.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Circulatory system: do and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know that we need to eat food to obtain essential nutrients to keep us healthy and alive.
nodes.response: Learning about different types of nutrients found in food, such as vitamins, proteins, carbohydrates and fats will help children to remember previous learning; that we get nutrition from what we eat.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How nutrients and water are transported within humans

nodes.misconception: Children may not think it possible to replace a vital organ such as the heart with one from another person, let alone an animal bred specifically for this purpose!
nodes.response: It is important to portray a balanced argument for children to consider and debate, and for them to appreciate that no-one specifically is right or wrong.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The use of animal hearts in humans (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that blood is made in the heart and the function of blood is to clean the heart.
nodes.response: This lesson provides plenty of opportunities for pupils to learn about the different functions of blood.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Function of blood

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the lungs are part of the human circulatory system.
nodes.response: Explain how the circulatory system works to support the respiratory system by bringing blood to and from the lungs. Note: children will learn more about this in key stage 3.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The circulatory system in humans: plan

nodes.misconception: Children often think that the function of the heart is to make or clean blood. Also that the heart is 'love heart' shaped.
nodes.response: The model making in this lesson helps children to think about which objects and materials they can use to represent the heart and demonstrate how it pumps blood around the body.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Function of the heart

nodes.misconception: Children may think that bones continue to grow throughout their lives.
nodes.response: Spend time looking at the data they have collected and reinforcing the fact that our bones stop growing when we reach early adulthood.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bone length: review

nodes.misconception: Children often believe 'bendy' animals do not have a spine so classify them as invertebrates.
nodes.response: Use images of X-rays/ skeletons of snakes and eels will illustrate that they have spines and are therefore vertebrates.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal skeletons

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe if an animal has a head, extremities and an external skeleton it is a vertebrate.
nodes.response: Share images of lots of animals with exoskeletons and compare them to a knight that puts on armour to protect themselves from injury.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animals without bones

nodes.misconception: May believe that if you have small, weak muscles you can’t make them bigger and stronger.
nodes.response: Show the children that through using certain exercises most people can make their muscles stronger.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Improving muscle strength (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that bones are unbreakable.
nodes.response: Show children X-rays of broken bones and give them examples of where we wear extra protection to protect our bones.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The human skeleton: protection

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is just one huge muscle that moves the body.
nodes.response: Use diagrams that explain how muscles work in pairs and that muscles are different sizes throughout the body.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Muscles for movement

nodes.misconception: Children may think that bone is not a living thing and therefore does not grow.
nodes.response: This lesson is all about children finding out for themselves. They will find answers to the enquiry question: Do bones grow as we get older?
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bone length: plan and do

nodes.misconception: Students may think if you have big muscles you are strong, if you have small muscles you are weak.
nodes.response: Show images to illustrate a runner may be very lean and a weightlifter may have huge muscles, but both are strong, just in different ways.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Muscle strength: plan (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think their bones are not connected to each other.
nodes.response: Show the children how bones are connected to form a skeleton that supports their body.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The human skeleton: support

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the results from a few children they measured can be applied to all humans.
nodes.response: Share each group's results and see how they are different. Explain that a much larger sample may provide different results.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Muscle strength: do and review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: It always snows in winter.
nodes.response: Explanation including different kinds of weather that the pupils may experience in winter.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Signs of winter

nodes.misconception: We have the same amount of daylight in every season.
nodes.response: Explanation of how day length changes throughout the year and is shorter during winter.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Day length in winter

nodes.misconception: Pupils associate different seasons with activities rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Examples of how deciduous trees begin to change in autumn and how observational skills can help us to spot seasonal changes.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Signs of autumn

nodes.misconception: Pupils may associate sunny weather with summer and not winter.
nodes.response: Explanation that there are different types of weather in winter, but the temperature is generally cooler than during other seasons.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather in winter

nodes.misconception: Pupils associate different seasons with activities, rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Explanation of different weathers that the pupils may experience in different seasons.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather in autumn

nodes.misconception: The only problem with using fossil fuels to generate electricity is that burning them produces greenhouse gases.
nodes.response: The lesson will explore additional concerns including the finite supply of fossil fuels and the fact that burning them causes air pollution.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainable sources of electricity (non-stat Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: There is an endless supply of fossil fuels on Earth.  There are no downsides to electric cars.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain that fossil fuel is a finite resource. Children will have the chance to research the pros and cons of electric cars. Feedback slides will clarify these.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Debating the use of electric cars (non-stat Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Only scientists and electricians have careers which are associated with electricity.
nodes.response: Children will be introduced to a wide variety of careers which involve electricity and electrical technology.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical careers

nodes.misconception: All electrical appliances and circuits use the same type of switch.
nodes.response: Pupils will be introduced to a wide range of switches.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The position of switches: open and closed

nodes.misconception: Only metals are electrical conductors.  All non-metals are electrical insulators.
nodes.response: Pupils will be taught that some non-metals are poor insulators, for example, water, as it can contain dissolved minerals that act as electrical conductors.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Choosing and using conductors and insulators (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand how variables interact within a circuit and how changes in one variable can affect others.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will relate the need to control variables in a fair test to the need to do so with circuits in order to be able to relate a given variable to a measured outcome.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the volume of buzzers

nodes.misconception: The voltage of a cell is proportional to the size of the cell. Voltage is a tangible substance rather than a measure of electrical “push”.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and CfUs will clarify that voltage is a measure of the size of the push provided by a cell or other source of electricity and that cell size is not proportional to voltage.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating voltage: do and review

nodes.misconception: Electricity is stored within a cell or battery.
nodes.response: Children will model and learn that the battery provides the push to start the flow of electricity rather than being the store of it.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Components and simple circuits

nodes.misconception: Electricity was invented by humans.
nodes.response: Lesson content will teach children about early observations and explanations of natural electricity.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical discoveries and inventions (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Electrical insulators cannot conduct electricity at all.
nodes.response: Children will be taught that electrical insulators are materials that do not allow electricity to pass through them easily.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How electrical insulators keep us safe (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may not understand how variables interact within a circuit and how changes in one variable can affect others.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will relate the need to control variables in a comparative and fair test, to the need to do so with circuits in order to be able to relate a given variable to a measured outcome.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Variables in electric circuits: plan

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how variables interact within a circuit and how changes in one variable can affect others.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will explain that variables are controlled in comparative and fair tests, and that the same can be done in circuits when adjusting variables like voltage to see how they affect things like brightness of bulbs.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Variables in electric circuits: do and review

nodes.misconception: For safety reasons, electrical circuits are never used in systems or appliances which involve the use of or are used near water.
nodes.response: Slides will discuss how engineers plan for the safe use of some electrical appliances near or with water. Pupils will design their own circuit to be used near water.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical sensors: design (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: The voltage of a cell is proportional to the size of the cell. Voltage is a tangible substance rather than a measure of electrical “push”.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and CfUs will clarify that voltage is a measure of the size of the push provided by a cell or other source of electricity, and that cell size is not proportional to voltage.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Investigating voltage: plan

nodes.misconception: For safety reasons, electrical circuits are never used in systems or appliances which involve or are used near water.
nodes.response: Slides will discuss how engineers plan for the safe use of some electrical appliances near or with water. Children will design their own circuit to be used near water.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical sensors: make and review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think circuit diagrams should be drawn in 3D or that they are maps of circuits, drawn to scale with wobbly lines like roads on a map.
nodes.response: Pupils will be taught to draw and interpret circuit symbols and diagrams and will practice doing so.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Circuit symbols and diagrams

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials such as ice melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures which range from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Melting temperatures: do and review

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials such as ice melt; that materials cannot melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures which range from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Melting temperatures: research

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the water cycle only takes place when it is hot or sunny; that when water evaporates, it disappears or that precipitation only refers to rain; water in its liquid form.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain the process of the water cycle including the different forms of precipitation. The practical task addresses the misconception that the water cycle only takes place in hot or sunny weather.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaporation and condensation in the water cycle

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures, ranging from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Melting temperatures: plan

nodes.misconception: Water cannot exist in a gas form.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that water can exist as gaseous water vapour and the process of evaporation.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing state: liquid to gas

nodes.misconception: A material can only exist as a solid, liquid or gas, rather than having different forms at different temperatures.  Gases have no mass or volume.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that most materials can exist in different states and that gases have a mass and volume.  Investigations help children explore the properties of materials in different states.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of solids, liquids and gases

nodes.misconception: Children think that materials can only change from a liquid to solid state at temperatures below 0°C. They also believe that the change is irreversible.
nodes.response: Teaching slides give examples of materials which change from their liquid to solid state at temperatures higher than room temperature. Through investigation, children will observe that the change between solid state and liquid state is reversible.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing state: liquid to solid

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that water cannot exist in a gas state because they cannot see it. They may also think that evaporation only occurs at high temperatures.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain the existence of water vapour, even though it is invisible. By investigation, children observe and measure that evaporation occurs at all temperatures.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Temperature and evaporation: do and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that materials can only be heated by being placed on a warm radiator or on a stove or over a candle and don’t think of being “in the room’ as being heated.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and observations show that items which have been stored below room temperature are “being heated” when moved to room temperature. Defrosting is explained in teaching slides.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing state: solid to liquid

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that thermometers are heat sources.  They may also think that they must touch an object to measure its temperature.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain how to use a thermometer and show that you can use them to measure ambient temperature.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Thermometers and data loggers

nodes.misconception: Children may not have heard of glaciers and may think that the only year-round ice is at the poles. Melting ice caps and glaciers do not affect sea level.
nodes.response: Teaching slides introduce ice caps and glaciers and note that they are found all over the world. The effect of melting ice caps and glaciers on sea level is explained and children have a chance to model it.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Melting ice caps and glaciers (non statutory - Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that water cannot exist in a gas state because they cannot see it.  They may also think that evaporation only occurs at high temperatures.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain the existence of water vapour, even though it is invisible.  By investigation, children observe and measure that evaporation occurs at all temperatures.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Temperature and evaporation: plan

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have experience of a solid material changing to its liquid state then back to its solid state again.
nodes.response: Pupils will explore melting solid wax then watching it change back from a liquid to a solid again as it cools. The lesson provides many examples of where changing state is useful to humans in industry and every day life.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday examples of changing state: solids and liquids (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think of "condensation" as the droplets of water that form through the process of condensation, rather than the change of state from gas to liquid.
nodes.response: Teaching slides use the term "droplets of water" instead of referring to them as "condensation".
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday examples of evaporation and condensation (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Water cannot exist in a gas form. Condensation is the same as rain or only occurs during cold weather. Dew is formed by liquid escaping from plants.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that water can exist as gaseous water vapour and how condensation forms.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing state: gas to liquid

nodes.misconception: Some solids can be poured and take the shape of their containers and therefore are liquids. A material is not the same material after it has been crushed.
nodes.response: Teaching slides and investigation will help children consider the difference between one solid particle of a material and a pile of particles which behaves together like a liquid.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing and grouping solids, liquids and gases

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know how to remove only one growing condition in order to compare plants.
nodes.response: Explain that a plant without water will still require warmth and light, and discuss group A, B and C's options as a whole class.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What plants need to grow and stay healthy

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think plants appear from the ground or that big plants like trees do not grow from seeds.
nodes.response: Ensure first-hand experience of handling and planting a range of seeds, and observing them grow.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants from seeds

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a plant without light will grow less, rather than grow taller initially.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for first-hand observation of plants growing without light over an extended period of time.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants without light

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all food comes from shops. Pupils may think that all plants are edible.
nodes.response: Clear examples showing edible plants in their natural habitats. Warning that some plants can be harmful if ingested.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Grow your own food (non-statutory - Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the warmer the plant, the better it grows and the healthier it is.
nodes.response: Show that different plants need different amounts of warmth, and to expose a plant to high or low temperatures could cause it damage
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants without warmth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants grow from seeds.
nodes.response: Show everyday examples of plants that grow from bulbs, as well as plant bulbs to observe them grow.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants from bulbs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that we observe using only our eyes
nodes.response: Show how we can use other senses to observe, we might listen, smell or touch when we observe
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant health and growth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants need lots of water everyday
nodes.response: Remind pupils that different plants need different amounts of water, and a plant with too much, or not enough, water could become unhealthy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants without water

nodes.misconception: All levers work in the same way.
nodes.response: Teaching that the position of the pivot (fulcrum) and the effort compared to load can vary.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How levers can help us

nodes.misconception: All graphs can be used to present all types of data.
nodes.response: Examples given of different types of graph and sample data.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Friction: do and review

nodes.misconception: All objects experience the same amount of water resistance, regardless of their size or shape.
nodes.response: Discussion and explicit teaching. The investigation they carry out will show them that this is not true.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Water resistance: do and review

nodes.misconception: Heavy objects fall faster than light objects.
nodes.response: The activity of dropping two plastic bottles (one filled and one half-filled with water) will help children see what happens.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to gravity

nodes.misconception: All objects experience the same amount of water resistance, regardless of their size or shape.
nodes.response: Discussion and explicit teaching. The investigation they plan will, in the next lesson, show them that this is not true.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Water resistance: plan

nodes.misconception: Forces only act on moving objects.
nodes.response: Examples of forces being used to move stationary objects will be included.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Pushes and pulls

nodes.misconception: All pulleys have the wheel attached to a ceiling.
nodes.response: Examples will be given of different types of simple pulleys.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How pulleys can help us

nodes.misconception: Machines all involve engines and need a power source.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching and explanation that simple machines do not often have moving parts and do not need a power source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple machines

nodes.misconception: Air resistance does not exist or it only works vertically.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching including diagrams and examples of air resistance working in all directions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Air resistance: do and review

nodes.misconception: Gears only exist in bicycles and cars.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching of what gears are and where they are found.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How gears can help us

nodes.misconception: Friction is always unhelpful.
nodes.response: Examples given of positive uses of friction for braking and turning.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Friction: plan

nodes.misconception: All objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of their size or shape.
nodes.response: Discussion and practical exploration will address this misconception.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Air resistance: plan

nodes.misconception: Engineers only design buildings or fix things that are broken.
nodes.response: A range of examples of how and where engineers work will be given.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Design and development of machines

nodes.misconception: Engineers are only men and just like to repair or fix things.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching and discussion of the range of engineers and the different skills engineers need.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Using magnets to solve problems (non-statutory: Scientists and Engineers)

nodes.misconception: Magnetic poles may exist singly, not just in pairs.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching and examples will be used to address misconceptions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Putting magnets together: attract or repel

nodes.misconception: Kicks/throws and catches are not pushes and pulls.
nodes.response: Explicit explanation that kicks and throws are pushes, and catches are pulls; that pushes and pulls can involve short term contact.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Contact forces

nodes.misconception: Magnetic force is a contact force.
nodes.response: Through their own investigation, children will demonstrate magnetic force acting at a distance.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Magnetic force at a distance

nodes.misconception: All magnets look the same. The poles of all magnets are the ends.
nodes.response: Real examples and diagrams of different magnets and their poles will be given.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different magnets and their parts

nodes.misconception: Friction doesn’t have a direction; a force is needed to keep an object moving at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Provide examples, with images, to demonstrate the effects of friction on moving objects.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different surfaces: do and review

nodes.misconception: All metals and silver coloured objects are magnetic and are attracted to a magnet.
nodes.response: Pupils test items in classroom and explicit explanation is given that magnets attract some, but not all metals.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Magnetic force (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Friction always hinders motion therefore you always want to eliminate friction.
nodes.response: Multiple examples of positive uses of friction, including to help start motion by pushing off, are included.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different surfaces in real life (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Magnets can exert a force through paper, but not wood, a table, or other thick materials.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching and investigation will clarify that magnetic force can act through a range of materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Blocking magnetic force

nodes.misconception: Larger magnets are always stronger than smaller magnets.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching  as well as opportunities for children to explore different size magnets and their strengths.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Strongest magnet (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: All surfaces are only 2-dimensional. All surfaces are made by people (human-made).
nodes.response: Provide many examples, with images, of different types of surface including natural surfaces and 3-dimensional surfaces.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different surfaces: plan

nodes.misconception: All metals and silver coloured objects are magnetic and are attracted to a magnet.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching, including many examples, will be combined with hands-on exploration to address this misconception.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that vaping is a safe and healthy practice, or a ‘cleaner’ version of smoking.
nodes.response: Explain that, although vaping is less harmful to the body than smoking, it still has an impact on the body and, as a new practice, we are not yet fully aware of the long term effects.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of smoking

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a very narrow definition of exercise, limiting it to activities such as running or weightlifting and not including more ‘fun’ types of exercise such as dancing or trampolining.
nodes.response: Explain that any physical activity where we intentionally use a lot of effort to move our bodies is exercise, backing this up with all the examples in the slide deck.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Heart recovery time after exercise

nodes.misconception: Children may think that protein can only be provided by foods that come from animal sources.
nodes.response: Explain to children that the protein we eat can often come from both plants and animals.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy and sustainable proteins (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that being healthy can be achieved through physical fitness, not taking into account anything else.
nodes.response: Explain that a range of different factors contribute to a healthy lifestyle, including eating a balanced diet, getting a good amount of sleep and taking part in activities that help our mental well being.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Monitoring and improving lifestyle choices (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the word ‘drug’ only refers to illegal drugs due to its common usage and that taking any drug will have a negative impact on their body.
nodes.response: Using the examples in the lesson, explain that a drug is any substance which changes the way our bodies work and that they can be helpful or harmful.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Legal and illegal drugs

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that thinness automatically equates to fitness, good health and having a healthy heart.
nodes.response: Explain that having a thin body does not necessarily mean that you also have good heart health. Whatever shape your body is, it is important to exercise and keep active in order to keep your heart healthy.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy hearts

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the word ‘diet’ refers to ‘going on a diet’ and lowering calorie intake or restricting intake of fats or sugars, and in turn think that this constitutes a ‘healthy’ diet.
nodes.response: Explain that the word ‘diet’ means the things that we eat regularly, and that a balanced diet is made up of a balanced intake of different types of foods.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of a balanced diet

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that a mushroom is a plant.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that mushrooms are not plants (or animals), rather they are the fruit bodies of a group of micro-organisms called fungi (singular fungus).
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Mushrooms and mycoprotein (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think than any information written down or published online is automatically reliable and trustworthy, purely because of its appearance in the public sphere.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain how information sources, particularly those online, can vary in terms of reliability and that there are things we can do to help determine how much we can trust the information we find.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Evidence about healthy lifestyle: do and review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the heart pumps air through the body, rather than blood, as part of a pneumatic-style system that powers the muscles.
nodes.response: Explain that the heart pumps blood around the body, beating faster when we exercise because it is transporting more oxygen within blood to keep the muscles working.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Healthy heart rate

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that alcohol is safe for adults to drink because it is not illegal.
nodes.response: Explain that, although it is legal for adults to drink alcohol, it can still be harmful. This can be supported with examples of the impact alcohol has on the body (shared in the slide deck).
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of alcohol

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that scientific information communicated with the public should be presented in a complicated and ‘wordy’ way to make it more seem more intelligent or ‘official’.
nodes.response: Explain that information intended to help people make healthy lifestyle choices is best presented in a way that will allow as many people as possible to engage with it, so that they can make informed choices.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Evidence about healthy lifestyle: presentation (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that an appliance requires batteries and is not an electrical appliance as it is not 'plugged in' for use.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for children to consider a range of appliances and how they are powered by electricity to perform a function.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical appliances of the future (non-stat Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Misconceptions associated with incomplete circuits: one wire to battery; connections to the same end of the battery; wires the wrong way around; not connecting clips to metal.
nodes.response: Children will be taught about the number of wires needed and how to connect to the battery.  They will also be given the chance to explore circuit building themselves.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Building simple circuits

nodes.misconception: Jobs which use the results of science are science jobs.  Electrical engineers and electricians are both scientists because they use the results of science in their work.
nodes.response: Children will be taught the difference between doing and using science within the context of a range of jobs.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Working with electricity

nodes.misconception: Only metals are electrical conductors.  All non-metals are electrical insulators. Water is an electrical conductor.
nodes.response: Children will test materials for conductivity, but the teaching slides will note that some non-metals are electrical conductors and that it is the dissolved minerals in water that can conduct electricity, not the water itself.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical conductors and insulators

nodes.misconception: Electricity comes from the plug sockets in our homes. When electrical appliances are used, the electricity goes into them but is not part of a complete circuit.
nodes.response: Pupils will be taught where and how electricity is generated and how it is transported to our homes.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Generating and transporting electricity (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Not all metals are electrical conductors.
nodes.response: Pupils will test materials for conductivity, but teaching slides will emphasise that all metals are electrical conductors.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical conductors: testing

nodes.misconception: Misconceptions associated with incomplete circuits: one wire to battery; connections to the same end of the battery; wires the wrong way round; not connecting clips to metal.
nodes.response: Children will be taught how to troubleshoot circuits which are not working to address these misconceptions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Troubleshooting problems with circuits

nodes.misconception: All electrical appliances and circuits use the same type of switch.
nodes.response: Children will be introduced to a wide range of switches.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Switches

nodes.misconception: Some words have different meanings in day-to-day life compared to their meaning in science (cell, battery and circuit).
nodes.response: Teachings slides will discuss confusion with words circuit, cell and battery.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Components in a simple circuit

nodes.misconception: Children may think that an appliance powered by batteries is not an electrical appliance as it is not 'plugged in' for use.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for children to consider a range of appliances and how they are powered by electricity to perform a function.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electrical appliances

nodes.misconception: Different animals need different things in order to stay alive.
nodes.response: Examples of different types of animals and how they need the same things to stay alive e.g. different foods they eat.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The basic needs of animals

nodes.misconception: Children may think that there are only two stages in an animal's life; child and adult.
nodes.response: Refer to other stages in animal's lives. For example, in humans we have children, teenagers, adults and the elderly.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal life cycles

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all offspring resemble their parents.
nodes.response: Show examples of offspring that resemble their parents and of those who do not.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in animal life cycles

nodes.misconception: Children may think that an animal’s offspring is always a smaller version of the parent.
nodes.response: Include examples of animals whose offspring do not resemble them e.g. caterpillar/butterfly, swan/cygnet, tadpoles/frogs etc.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Growing up

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all offspring resemble their parents.
nodes.response: Examples of offspring that resemble their parents and of those who do not.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Young animals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that objects in space are flat, circular shapes rather than spherical
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for children to use 3D models to represent the Earth, Sun and Moon, and look at images and simulations
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The shape of Earth

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the Moon changes shape.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to observe the Moon over time, and record observations, including how it appears to change shape.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Observing the Moon

nodes.misconception: Children may believe that the Sun appears to move across the sky because the Sun moves around Earth
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for children to use models to see that it is Earth rotating that makes it look like the Sun is moving.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Why the Sun appears to move across the sky

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Sun is a planet.
nodes.response: Explain that the Sun is a star because, like other stars, it is a huge ball of glowing gas which has planets travelling around it.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about the Sun (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: The Earth, Sun and Moon are the same size, or that the Sun is much smaller than it actually is.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for children to explore diagrams and 3D models of the Earth, Sun and Moon which clearly show the differences in size.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The relative sizes of the Earth, Sun and Moon (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the Moon produces its own light, or that the Moon only comes out at night
nodes.response: Explore common reflectors of light, to enable pupils to observe how some objects, including the Moon, appear to shine as they reflect light
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How we see the Moon from Earth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a theory is just a guess or prediction that has not yet or cannot be proven.
nodes.response: Explain that theories are always based on scientific evidence and these are either strengthened or disproved as more evidence is gathered.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Scientific theories from the past (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils will think that the Moon actually does change shape, or that it becomes covered with clouds.
nodes.response: Pupils should use models to see and feel for themselves what is actually moving and how this affects the apparent shape of the Moon.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The movement of the Moon

nodes.misconception: Earth lies at the centre of our solar system, with the Sun and planets orbiting around it.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for the children to explore both diagrams and 3D models of the solar system which clearly show the Sun and planets.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The planets in our solar system (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Earth lies at the centre of the solar system, with the Sun and planets orbiting around it.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for the children to explore both diagrams and 3D models of the solar system which clearly show the Sun and planets.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The movement of the planets around the Sun

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that objects in space are flat, circular shapes rather than spherical.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for children to use 3D models to represent the Earth, Sun and Moon, and look at images and simulations.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The shape of objects in space

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that we have night when the Earth is facing the Moon or the Sun goes behind clouds.
nodes.response: Provide plenty of opportunities for pupils to use models to show the Earth rotating on its axis, next to a bright torch or lamp for the Sun.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Why we have day and night

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know how humans use different senses to stay safe.
nodes.response: Examples of different scenarios where humans use different senses to check for danger and to stay safe.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about sight, smell and sound

nodes.misconception: The human body is a single entity rather than being made of different parts that work together.
nodes.response: Examples of different parts of the body and the jobs that they do.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Body parts on the inside

nodes.misconception: A lot of people think we only touch with our hands rather than our skin. Also, that we only ever use one sense at a time.
nodes.response: Examples including touching with other parts of the body such as feet, or touching an arm against a cold metal table leg and feeling the difference in temperature.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about taste and touch

nodes.misconception: The human body is a single entity rather than being made of different parts that work together.
nodes.response: Examples of different parts of the body and the jobs that they do.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Body parts on the outside

nodes.misconception: A lot of people think we only touch with our hands rather than our skin.
nodes.response: Examples including touching with other parts of body such as feet, or touching an arm against a cold metal table leg and feeling the difference in temperature.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Body parts for our senses

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that humans are animals.
nodes.response: Clear explanation that humans are a type of animal.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Humans are animals

nodes.misconception: Plants have flowers and are grown in pots.
nodes.response: Examples of plants in different environments and different sorts of plants.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants around our school or home

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all plants have been planted by humans.
nodes.response: Clear explanation that plants can grow in the wild without need for human intervention or support.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Wildflowers

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all plants look the same/similar with the same style petals and leaves.
nodes.response: Provide examples of flowering plants with leaves and petals of different shapes, sizes and colour.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Structure of a flowering plant

nodes.misconception: Children may not realise that trees are plants.
nodes.response: Explanation that trees are a type of plant.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Structure of a tree

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all trees look the same.
nodes.response: Examples of different types of trees with differing features.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Naming trees

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants have flowers all year round and that all flowers look the same.
nodes.response: Use examples of plants at different times of the year, both with and without flowers, as well as examples of plants with flowers of various colours, shapes, and sizes.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Common flowering plants

nodes.misconception: All trees have leaves that they lose every year.
nodes.response: Show a range of examples of different types of trees including evergreen.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Deciduous and evergreen trees

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that mould is a type of plant because of its colour or the way it grows.
nodes.response: Explain that plants make their own food using photosynthesis and mould does not, so it cannot be a plant. Instead, it gets its nutrients from the organic matter that it is growing on. Also, unlike plants, mould does not need light to survive or grow.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Micro-organisms living on food: plan and do (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals are classified according to their habitat, for example aquatic animals, or by their method of movement, for example creeping animals.
nodes.response: Explain that Aristotle classified animals into water, air and land groups, but there are problems with this method, e.g. this would put birds, bees and bats in the same group. Use the examples in the lesson to make clear the correct groupings.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Carl Linnaeus and classification

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all moulds and fungi are harmful and no useful products can be extracted from them.
nodes.response: Explain that, while many moulds and fungi can be harmful to humans and other animals, many have uses in medicine such as penicillin, once they have been properly processed by scientists.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Microorganisms that help us (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that compost is just dirt or mud, or is no different from soil.
nodes.response: Explain that compost has a different composition to soil, and is full of nutrients that are beneficial to growing plants.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The 5 Rs (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think yeast is not a living thing because it doesn’t appear to have any of the characteristics of living things when we look at it dry straight from the packet.
nodes.response: Explain that yeast is a type of fungus so it is a living thing in the micro-organisms group. Throughout the lesson, reinforce the characteristics it has that makes it a living thing, such as its ability to grow and reproduce.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Growing yeast: plan (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants are green or that anything without a flower is not a plant.
nodes.response: Highlight the many examples of plants with different shapes, sizes and colours that are included in the lesson resources, reminding children that all of these are plants because they are living things that use the Sun’s light to make food.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How and why we group plants

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals with soft, flexible bodies such as snakes or fish are invertebrates, or that any animal with a hard shell is a vertebrate.
nodes.response: Explain that the external appearance of an animal does not always give us enough information to classify it as a vertebrate or an invertebrate; the presence or absence of a backbone and internal skeleton is the only characteristic that matters.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How and why we group animals

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that micro-organisms are very tiny animals or that they are not living things. Pupils may think that all micro-organisms are harmful germs.
nodes.response: Explain that micro-organisms are living things as they carry out the same processes as other living things, but they aren't animals because they have a simpler structure than animals. Explain that some helpful micro-organisms live inside our bodies.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Micro-organisms are living things
