nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider mould to be a living thing because it does not move in the ways we are familiar with animals moving.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that all living things grow, reproduce and move, and that mould can do all of these things. It is a type of fungus. Which is a living thing that is part of the micro-organisms group.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Micro-organisms living on food: review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only consider animals' characteristics to be observable if we can see them in a photo, rather than us also being able to observe their behaviour over time.
nodes.response: Explain that when scientists classify living things they make many observations of how that living thing moves, behaves and reproduces, as these are all characteristics we can observe to help us identify and classify things.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing characteristics of living things

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that organisms have, and always have had, their own names, rather than them being named by scientists and others.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain the naming process for living things used by taxonomists and other scientists.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Discovering and naming new species

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all micro-organisms are harmful and will cause us to become ill.
nodes.response: Explain that, while some micro-organisms can cause us harm, there are also many that are beneficial, such as those used in food production, water treatment or those living inside our digestive system.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Grouping micro-organisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a ‘fair test’ is one in which they all get an equal share in the roles or everyone gets to take a turn.
nodes.response: Explain that both a comparative and fair test are ones in which all variables are kept the same except for the one that is being investigated. This helps to ensure that our results show the effect of just the variable we are investigating.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Growing yeast: do and review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Food chains put living things in order of importance.
nodes.response: Explanation of interdependence of each living thing within a food chain.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Roles within food chains

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the arrows in the food chain mean "eats".
nodes.response: Explain that the arrows in a food chain mean "is food for". Provide pupils with lots of opportunities to use this language.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Introduction to food chains

nodes.misconception: A food chain shows the full detail and is a true representation of what organisms eat.
nodes.response: Include explanations that animals have a varied diet and eat many different foods. A food chain only shows one food source at a time.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing food chains

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all animals eat the same food, and also have food provided by humans.
nodes.response: Visuals to show lots of examples of different animals eating different food, and getting it in different ways.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How animals get food

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that 'ready meals' contain the same nutrients as meals we have prepared and cooked ourselves.
nodes.response: Explanation of how processed foods can contain added salt, sugar and fat.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Nutrient-rich meal: doing and reviewing (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Some food groups, e.g. fats, are 'bad' for you.
nodes.response: Explanation of how using nutritional information can help us to make informed decisions about the foods that we eat.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Nutrition from food

nodes.misconception: Foods are either 'good' or 'bad' for you.
nodes.response: Explanation of different nutrients in foods and how they can be beneficial to our health.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Types of food

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that foods containing fats are 'bad' for humans and we should not eat them.
nodes.response: Emphasise to pupils that humans need some fat as part of a balanced diet and it is a diet that is very high in fat that is not healthy for humans. The foods themselves are ok to eat as part of a balanced diet.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Fats in food: review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a ‘balanced’ diet should include equal-sized proportions of the different food groups (rather than appropriate amounts of each food group).
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need to eat different amounts of foods and that the Eatwell plate shows us the amounts of each food that we should eat.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Amounts of food

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans need to eat the same amounts of different types of food to stay healthy.
nodes.response: Emphasise that humans need to eat different amounts of different foods as part of a healthy diet.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Nutrient-rich meal: planning (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all food is produced in the same way.
nodes.response: Explanation of how foods can be produced and harvested in different ways with differing environmental impacts.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Sustainable sources of food (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unaware of the provenance of their food and the possible environmental effect of eating foods from different countries.
nodes.response: Explanation of how some foods are grown in England and how eating local, seasonal food can minimise the impact on the environment.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Food miles (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may be unaware of the provenance of their food and the possible environmental impact of eating foods from different places.
nodes.response: Explanation of how some foods are grown in the UK and how eating local, seasonal food can minimise the impact on the environment.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Local food (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: All plants and animals 'eat' food.
nodes.response: Explanation of how plants can make their own food and that animals cannot.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Making or finding food

nodes.misconception: All foods containing fats are 'bad' for us and we should not eat them.
nodes.response: Humans need some fat as part of a balanced diet but a diet that is very high in fat is not healthy for humans.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Fats in food: plan and do (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: All people eat the same foods and have the same diet.
nodes.response: Explanation that different people have different diets for a variety of different reasons, such as allergies, intolerances or their own choice.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different diets for different people

nodes.misconception: Pupils may only think that larger objects make louder sounds. They may not link the size of vibrations to the volume of sound.
nodes.response: Ensure plenty of opportunities for pupils to strike, tap, blow and shake objects to see how this affects the volume of sound produced.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Louder and quieter sounds

nodes.misconception: Children may think that sound  travels through all solid materials in the same way.
nodes.response: The investigation in this lesson allows children to find out for themselves, first-hand, that sound does not travel through all solid materials in the same way and that some materials are better sound insulators than others.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Sound insulation

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the volume of sound and the pitch of sound is the same thing, or that high sounds are loud and low sounds are quiet.
nodes.response: It is important to expose children to a wide range of high and low pitched sounds. Continue to make the distinction between volume and pitch throughout this lesson.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the pitch of sounds

nodes.misconception: Children may think that sound travels only to the person that hear it, directly from the sound source to their ear.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for children to draw diagrams of how they think sound travels, and then revisit the diagrams to make improvements or amendments with further learning.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How vibrations travel

nodes.misconception: Children may think that any sound is classified as noise, or that only very loud sounds are considered to be noise pollution.
nodes.response: Explain that unpleasant or unwanted sounds are classified as noise. Noise pollution does not have to be loud, it can be an intermittent or continuous quieter noise that becomes a problem.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Noise pollution (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that larger and longer objects vibrating produce louder sounds, without linking this to the pitch of sounds.
nodes.response: If working at school, empty the cupboard of as many musical instruments you can find to explore and demonstrate with. Encourage children who play musical instruments to share their experiences too.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Musical instruments and pitch

nodes.misconception: Children may think that the volume of sound and the pitch of sound is the same thing, or that high sounds are loud and low sounds are quiet.
nodes.response: It is important to expose children to a wide range of high and low pitched sounds. Continue to make the distinction between volume and pitch throughout the lesson.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Higher and lower sounds

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that sounds are inside the sound source waiting to come out. They may also think that the volume of sounds are the same no matter how far away from them you are.
nodes.response: Recap how sounds are made when an object vibrates. Pupils will plan an investigation to find out for themselves by measuring the volume of sounds as they move further away from the sound source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Distance from sounds: plan

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that volume of sound cannot be measured, as they may not have encountered equipment or the units of measurement for doing so.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities to measure the volume of a range of everyday sounds so that pupils become familiar with decibel levels.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring the volume of sounds

nodes.misconception: Children often think that sounds will be quieter and more muffled when travelling through a solid medium.
nodes.response: It is important for children to try string telephones out for themselves to hear how sounds can be louder and clearer travelling through a solid medium.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Vibrations and solid materials

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that sound can be produced without using any materials.
nodes.response: Ensure opportunities for children to learn about objects vibrating in order to produce sounds.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How sounds are made

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the volume of sounds are the same no matter how far away from them you are.
nodes.response: Pupils will carry out a fair test to find out for themselves how the volume of a sound decreases with distance from the sound source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Distance from sounds: do and review

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the only way for plants to reproduce is by making seeds (i.e. as a result of sexual reproduction).
nodes.response: Plants can reproduce asexually in a number of ways. Use the lesson resources to show alternative ways for plants to reproduce that don’t involve pollination, fertilisation and seed formation.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Asexual reproduction in plants

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not understand how plants of the same species can vary from one another and assume they are all the same because the differences are not obvious.
nodes.response: Explain that plants can have different characteristic within a species, such as size and shape of fruit or colour of flowers.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Selective breeding of plants (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not think that species of plants can become extinct in the same way that animals can.
nodes.response: Explain that if all of a particular species of plant, and its seeds, were destroyed then that plant would be extinct and none would ever live or reproduce again in the future.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Conservation using seed banks (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals are pollinating flowers to intentionally help them.
nodes.response: Explain that pollinators are visiting flowers to find food for themselves, rather than to help the plant; they do not pollinate flowers on purpose.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Pollinators (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that bees are the only animals that pollinate plants or that bees are the only pollinators currently in decline.
nodes.response: Explain that many types of insects, as well as some birds and mammals, can be pollinators and that many of these animal species are also in decline.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Dangers to pollinators (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that observations from enquiries should only be in written or numerical form.
nodes.response: Explain that there are many ways to represent the information we gathered during enquiries, including with diagrams, writing or even video recordings.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant reproduction from cuttings

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the only way for plants to reproduce is by creating seeds.
nodes.response: Explain that, as well as making seeds, plants can also reproduce asexually in a range of ways, including form cuttings taken from a plant by humans.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants from cuttings

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse pollination and seed dispersal, as both involve something from the flower being moved from one place to another.
nodes.response: Explain that each of these processes happen at different times and have different purposes. Pollination happens before seeds have formed and leads to fertilisation, whereas seed dispersal spreads the fully formed seeds away from the parent plant.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant life cycles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants make seeds automatically as a part of their life cycle, rather than needing pollination to take place.
nodes.response: Explain that flowers can only make seeds once pollination and fertilisation has happened.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Parts of a flowering plant and what they do

nodes.misconception: Pupils may associate different seasons with activities, rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Explanation of different weathers that pupils may experience in different seasons.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather in spring

nodes.misconception: Pupils may associate different seasons with activities rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Explanation of changes in nature that occur during spring.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Signs of spring

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that it is always sunny in summer.
nodes.response: Explanation that there are different types of weather in summer but the temperature is generally warmer than during other seasons.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Weather in summer

nodes.misconception: Pupils may associate different seasons with activities, rather than physical characteristics like the weather.
nodes.response: Explanation of changes in nature that occur during summer.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Signs of summer

nodes.misconception: We have the same amount of daylight in every season.
nodes.response: Explanation of how day length changes throughout the year and is longer during summer. You may link back to a previous lesson: Day length in winter (in the Year 1 unit: Seasonal changes: autumn and winter).
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Day length in summer

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the function of flowers is to make plants look nice or that they are there for the benefit of humans.
nodes.response: Explain that flowers are the reproductive parts of a plant that allow it to make more seeds.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The parts of a flower

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that water is taken into the plant through the leaves or flowers, due to the way water can sometimes be seen pooling there after rain.
nodes.response: Use the slide deck and lesson activities to support pupils’ understanding that water is absorbed by the roots of a plant, then transported via the stem, and that the flowers and leaves are not able to take in water.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How water is transported  in plants

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse pollination and seed dispersal, as both involve something from the flower being moved from one place to another.
nodes.response: Explain that each of these processes happen at different times and have different purposes. Pollination happens before seeds have formed and leads to fertilisation whereas seed dispersal spreads the fully formed seeds away from the parent plant.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Life cycle of a flowering plant

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that bees and other pollinators pollinate flowers to help them out, rather than it being a by-product of them getting food from the flower.
nodes.response: Explain that pollinators visit flowers to get something for themselves (nectar and/or pollen), not to intentionally pollinate flowers.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Pollination

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider plants to be living things because they do not move from place to place or have ‘babies’ in the way that many animals do.
nodes.response: Explain that plants are living things; we know this because they can move, grow and reproduce like other living things can.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What plants need: plan

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse pollen and seeds or think that pollen that is dispersed by the wind can grow into a new plant if it lands on soil.
nodes.response: Explain that pollen is different from seeds as pollen cannot grow into a new plant. It plays a part in fertilisation, which leads to seed formation, but is not a seed and cannot turn into seeds.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Seed formation and seed dispersal

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that fertiliser added to plants is their ‘food’ and so is necessary for their survival.
nodes.response: Explain that plants do not eat food in the same way that we do but they do need nutrients to survive, grow and stay healthy. They get these nutrients from soil and we can add fertiliser to soil to increase the nutrients within it.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Nutrients and fertilisers for plants (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that roots are like drinking straws that suck up water through their tips, rather than absorbing it across their whole length.
nodes.response: Share the model used in the lesson of a paper towel absorbing water to help pupils understand that water is absorbed, not sucked up, by the roots. Pupils could experience this for themselves in the classroom to help them understand and remember.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The function of roots

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants can support themselves and stay upright without roots as the stem provides support.
nodes.response: The task carried out in Learning Cycle 1 will demonstrate to pupils that plants need roots anchoring them in the soil in order to stay upright.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants without roots

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they should evaluate their investigation based on things like the neatness of their writing or how quickly they finished, rather than how they planned and carried out the enquiry.
nodes.response: Explain that scientists evaluate their investigations based on how they planned and carried them out, not on how neatly they presented their work or how quick they were to finish because this helps them to plan better investigations in the future.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What plants need: final review

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants are able to grow in any conditions and will simply adapt to their surroundings.
nodes.response: Explain that plants have certain requirements to survive and grow well, and will be unhealthy and likely die without these requirements. Results from pupils' enquiries will back this up and help them to see this first-hand.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What plants need: review

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not see the need to use a second plant in their investigation that has all of its needs met, as they will be able to observe changes in the plant from which they are removing a requirement.
nodes.response: Explain that we need an additional plant with all of its needs met so that we can make direct comparisons between this plant and the one we are depriving of something.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What plants need: do

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the purpose of flowers is to make the plant look nice or to provide food for bees, rather than them having a function for the sake of the plant.
nodes.response: Explain that the function of flowers is to allow the plant to reproduce and create more plants.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The function of flowers

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all plants need exactly the same things, in the same quantities, in order to survive and grow.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain how plant requirements differ from plant to plant.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing what plants need in different habitats

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a plant’s leaves are for the collection of water, due to their shape and the way we often appear to pour water over the leaves when we water plants.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain that the function of the leaves is to make food for the plant.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The function of leaves

nodes.misconception: Children may think that all minibeasts are insects. Children may think that all minibeasts like the same conditions (e.g. damp and dark).
nodes.response: Provide examples of different microhabitats with differing conditions, e.g. light, dark, wet etc.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting microhabitats (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: An animal’s habitat is like its ‘home’. Habitats can be divided into 'hot' and 'cold' habitats.
nodes.response: Examples and photographs showing different habitats.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal habitats

nodes.misconception: All habitats are microhabitats. All minibeasts are insects.
nodes.response: Clear explanation and definition of what a microhabitat is and how it differs from other habitats, e.g. ocean, forest, Arctic, desert etc. Examples of a variety of minibeasts including insects and non-insects.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants and animals in microhabitats

nodes.misconception: A non-living thing is something that is dead.
nodes.response: Examples demonstrating that non-living things have never been alive.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Alive, dead and never alive

nodes.misconception: Plants do not move because we cannot see them move. All things that move are alive.
nodes.response: Examples of how plants move very slowly (e.g. sunflower following sun throughout the day). Examples of things like wind-up or battery operated toys that move but are not alive.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Living things and movement

nodes.misconception: Plants are not living things because we cannot see them move.
nodes.response: Show examples of living things, including plants.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Living or non-living

nodes.misconception: Habitats can only be divided into 'hot' and 'cold' habitats. Plants are not living things.
nodes.response: Examples of different habitats where plants live and how these meet their needs, including different conditions such as underwater, desert, grasslands and savannah.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant habitats

nodes.misconception: Children sometimes don't realise plants can be in danger as well as animals.
nodes.response: Share the examples in the slide deck and give pupils time to research other plants to discover there are lots of different plants in different environments that are in danger. If time, find out if any plants in your local area are in danger.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants in danger (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that changes to the environment are negative.
nodes.response: Examples of both positive and negative changes to the environment.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Environmental changes in the news (non-stat Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children can lack awareness of the way in which living things within an environment depend upon each other. They may think that they are dependent on humans to supply them with their needs.
nodes.response: Through the lesson, children will see examples of how nature reserves and the animals and plants within it support each other.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Nature reserves (Climate change and sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may not understand the impact of an increased human population on plants and animals.
nodes.response: Discuss, using examples on the slide deck, all the repercussions of increased population. If possible, include an example relevant to their location to help them see it first hand.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Waste creation and pollution (Climate change and sustainability)

nodes.misconception: All effects of human impact on the environment are negative.
nodes.response: Examples of positive effects of human impact on the environment.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reforestation and recycling (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Humans are separate from an ecosystem and human actions cannot affect an ecosystem.
nodes.response: Using the slides and secondary sources, share with pupils the many different ways that human actions can negatively impact on animals' environments and endanger the animals that live there.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animals in danger (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the environment is just another word for nature.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to become aware of many different environments and refer to the surroundings that an animal or plant lives in.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Environments and seasonal changes (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Changes in the environment will not directly affect us.
nodes.response: Encourage the children to become aware of many different habitats and start to see how they are all interconnected and how when one thing is changed, it can impact other living things.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Land development and deforestation (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Scientists do not communicate directly with the public.
nodes.response: Explanation of the different ways in which scientists can communicate with the public.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How scientists communicate with the public (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all plants are green and have flowers.
nodes.response: Clarify with a range of examples that some plants have flowers and some don't. Discuss with the pupils if they think even flowering plants will always have a flower on them all year round.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Grouping plants

nodes.misconception: Children often believe that animals in decline are only found in faraway places like rain forests. They might not realise that the UK has its own species in decline, such as the red squirrel.
nodes.response: Through the use of the slides and doing further secondary research about their own local environment, children will become aware that there are animals in the UK that are in decline too.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting animals in decline (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that all questions need a full explanation to answer.
nodes.response: By working through the examples on the slide deck and completing the tasks, pupils will see that some questions can be answered with a simple yes or no. This is an important skill when using and creating identification keys for classification.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Identifying living things (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that it doesn't rain very much in countries with warmer climates.
nodes.response: Through the lesson, and drawing on children from other countries in your class, discuss the rainfall and weather to illustrate this is not the case. The data within the slides will help illustrate this.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Extreme weather: flooding (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that heatwaves are just a ‘hot’ day and that wildfires are always caused by humans.
nodes.response: Discuss with pupils the length and severity needed for an event to become a heatwave. Share with the pupils how the weather and conditions contribute to increased risk of wildfires occurring.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Extreme weather: heatwaves and wild fires (non-statutory CC & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle with some of the vocabulary needed for animal classification that is not used in everyday language. They may try to use an animal's habitat as an observable characteristic.
nodes.response: Model the correct classification language throughout the lesson using animals they are confident with. Although there sometimes are observable clues, you cannot be certain of an animal's habitat by looking at it out of context.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification keys to identify animals

nodes.misconception: Children may ask questions that don't have a yes or no answer.
nodes.response: Keep reminding the children that their questions need to have a yes/no answer and that this is how a classification key works to help us to group and identify unknown objects.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification keys

nodes.misconception: Pupils may try to identify plants using the habitat they are found in as opposed to their observable features.
nodes.response: Reinforce that where a plant lives is not an observable characteristic and cannot be used to identify it.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Classification keys to identify plants

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a limited view of what an animal is: mammal with fur and four legs. This can affect the way they classify animals. Also, that its habitat is an observable characteristic.
nodes.response: Use a wide range of animals including invertebrates and vertebrates, and those that live on land and in the sea, to help them look at observable characteristics when grouping.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Grouping animals

nodes.misconception: Pupils sometimes rely upon an organism’s habitat to classify it, rather than its physical features; this can lead to misunderstandings and misclassification.
nodes.response: As you model groupings, be clear to use observable features of the objects you are grouping - focus on what you can observe as a characteristic of being human.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Introducing observable characteristics

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants can decide or choose to grow in whatever way they think is best.
nodes.response: Explain that plant adaptations are inherited characteristics and the plant does not have any choice or understanding of its adaptations.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about plant adaptations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that more complicated and verbose explanations are better, regardless of target audience, as this will make them seem cleverer.
nodes.response: Explain that, when sharing information with lots of people with different levels of background knowledge, it is much better to make explanations clear and simple so it can be understood by as many people as possible.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Evolution: presentation

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a limited view of what constitutes a fossil, such as only things that resemble skeletons or ammonite shells, and not recognise things like coprolites or plant imprints as fossils too.
nodes.response: Use the range of examples used in the lesson to make it clear to pupils that there are a wide range of different types of fossil and different types of organisms that become fossils.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What fossils can tell us about the past

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that fossils can be found anywhere on Earth and in any type of rock.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain how and why fossils are mainly found in sedimentary rock and the common locations these tend to be, such as cliffs, hillsides and quarries.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Where fossils are found (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that environmental variation, such as scars, piercings or muscle size and tone, can be passed on to offspring in the same way that inherited characteristics can.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the lesson to make clear the difference between characteristics that we are born with and those that are acquired, and how only those we are born with can be passed on to offspring.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Inherited characteristics

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans as we know them have always looked the same as they do now.
nodes.response: Use the images of skulls in the slide deck to clearly show how humans’ appearance has changed over many thousands of years.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Human skulls: using evidence from the past (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the ‘fittest’, as in ‘survival of the fittest’, means the most physically fit or healthy, rather than the most suited to the environment and conditions.
nodes.response: Using the examples in the slide deck, clearly explain that when we refer to the ‘fittest’ living things surviving, we mean those that are best suited to the conditions they are living in.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The survival of the fittest

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all prehistoric living things were on Earth at the same time, rather than understanding that life on Earth changed over millions of years.
nodes.response: Use the models and information in the lesson to explain that the different layers of rock beneath our feet were formed at different times, and there are fossils of different living things buried within each.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How living things have changed over time

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals, such as finches with differently shaped beaks, have been able to change or adapt during their lifetime based on the conditions they live in.
nodes.response: Explain that adaptations take many years and generations of animals to happen and it is not possible for an animal or plant to change like this during its lifetime.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Charles Darwin and finches

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals are able to adapt during their lifetime, for example that they can change the colour of their fur to better blend in with new surroundings.
nodes.response: Explain that animals adapt slowly, over many years and generations.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal adaptations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that, while animals need to be well adapted to survive, plants do not and they simply grow where and how they can.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the slide deck to exemplify the various ways plants are adapted to survive in different environments, just like animals are.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant adaptations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think evolution is just one possible suggestion or an unproved idea about how living things change over time, due to the common use of the word ‘theory’ for an initial idea or suggestion.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the lesson to explain there is enough evidence supporting the theory of evolution for us to be certain that it is scientific fact, rather than an idea we are still unsure about.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Evolution: evidence

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that male animals get their characteristics from their father, and female animals from their mother, with no characteristics shared between offspring and parents of different sexes.
nodes.response: Use the images and examples in the lesson to make it clear that offspring share a combination of characteristics of both of their parents, regardless of sex.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Offspring: similar but not identical

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all members on a family tree are related by blood.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the slide deck to illustrate how some members of family trees are related by blood and some have joined the family through partnership.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Family trees (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all small creatures, or ‘minibeasts’, are insects.
nodes.response: Explain that an animal is only an insect if it has the characteristics of insects. Use lots of examples and non-examples to make this clear.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Insects (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that metamorphosis of an animal is the result of evolution.
nodes.response: Explain that metamorphosis is the change in form of a single animal; it’s still the same animal after metamorphosis.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the life cycles of amphibians and insects

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that animals and plants can adapt to their habitats, no matter how they change.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to make it clear that adaptations take a very long time and sometimes habitats change too fast for this to happen.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Endangered animals & life cycles (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they personally can't do anything to prevent animals becoming endangered/extinct.
nodes.response: Use the resources to explain the things pupils can do to help, and encourage them to think specifically about which are possible for them.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about endangered animals (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think the bird inside the egg is not living or that it is a small but fully formed bird.
nodes.response: Explain, using the slides, that the living bird inside the egg grows and forms until it is ready to hatch.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bird life cycles

nodes.misconception: All animal life cycles have the same stages; anything different to mammals is not an 'animal'.
nodes.response: Use the examples in the slide deck to make it clear that different types of animals have different life cycles.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing the life cycles of mammals and birds

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only birds lay eggs.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to make it clear that other animals, including amphibians, lay eggs and these can look different to bird eggs.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Amphibian life cycles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans are not animals, but something different.
nodes.response: When mammals are discussed in the lesson, remind pupils that humans are animals and mammals because of their shared characteristics.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Mammal life cycles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the insect is dead inside the pupa, or that the pupa is not a living thing.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that the insect is alive and changing inside the pupa, even if the pupa itself doesn't move.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Insect life cycles

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all sea-dwelling animals are fish or that only birds can fly.
nodes.response: Explain, with examples from the lesson, that animals are classified based on their physical features, not where they live or how they move.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal groups

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans are not animals.
nodes.response: Explain that humans are animals and are part of the mammal group. Make clear the characteristics we have that mean we fit into this group.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal gestation periods

nodes.misconception: All fat in the diet can cause ill health.
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need some fat in their diet but that they should not eat large amounts of fat regularly if they want to have a healthy diet.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Food scientists

nodes.misconception: The idea of health only relates to physical health, in particular ‘fitness’.
nodes.response: Explanation that there are different ways of staying healthy and the importance of teeth brushing.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Brushing teeth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a ‘balanced’ diet should include equal-sized proportions of the different food groups (rather than appropriate amounts of each food group).
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need to eat different amounts of foods, depending on how healthy or unhealthy they are for us. Explanation of the importance of eating different types of food.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different amounts of food

nodes.misconception: Household chores are not examples of physical activity but sports, running and climbing are. Playing, dancing and walking are not fitness activities.
nodes.response: Examples of a variety of different physical activities.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The importance of exercise

nodes.misconception: Being seen as ‘healthy’ or ‘unhealthy’ is linked to personal attributes as well as physical attributes (such as regarding an unhealthy character as lazy or untidy).
nodes.response: Reminders that there are simple measures that a human can take to help them to lead a healthy life, such as having a healthy diet, having good personal hygiene and exercising regularly.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Staying healthy

nodes.misconception: All fat in the diet can cause ill health. A ‘balanced’ diet should include equal-sized proportions of the different food groups (rather than appropriate amounts of each food group).
nodes.response: Explanation that humans need to eat small amounts of fat and sugar, but that eating too much is unhealthy. Explanation of the importance of eating different types of food. The word “balanced” is not used in this lesson.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Different types of food

nodes.misconception: Being seen as ‘healthy’ or ‘unhealthy’ is linked to personal attributes as well as physical attributes (such as regarding an unhealthy character as lazy or untidy).
nodes.response: Explanation that everyone can take steps to be healthy and that good hygiene is an important part of being healthy.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Washing hands

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know that light pollution exists nor its impact on humans and other living things.
nodes.response: An explanation of light pollution and its potential negative effects on humans and other living things.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Light pollution (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Humans can see without light.
nodes.response: Explanation of how humans can see with a little light but cannot see when no light is present.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Light and seeing

nodes.misconception: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day or when wearing sunglasses. Only lighter skin tones require protection from UV light.
nodes.response: Reminders that pupils should never look at the Sun. All skin tones require protection from UV light.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting our eyes from the Sun: do and review

nodes.misconception: All materials that let light through them are transparent.
nodes.response: Explanation of the difference between materials that are transparent and those that are translucent.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Opaque, transparent and translucent

nodes.misconception: Shadows contain details of the object, such as facial features of a human’s shadow. Also that a shadow can be a different shape to the object, and formed in between the light source and the object.
nodes.response: Explanation of how shadows are formed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Making shadows

nodes.misconception: The size of a shadow does not change.
nodes.response: Explanation of how the size of shadows change depending on the distance of the object from the light source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Shadow size: do

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all light sources are made by humans. Pupils may think that the Moon is a light source.
nodes.response: Explanation that light sources can be natural or made by humans - use examples within the lesson slides. Explanation that the Moon does not produce its own light and is not a light source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Light sources

nodes.misconception: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day or when wearing sunglasses.
nodes.response: Clear explanation that pupils should never look at the Sun, even if wearing sunglasses or if the weather is cloudy.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting our eyes from the Sun: plan

nodes.misconception: The size of a shadow does not change.
nodes.response: Explanation of how the size of shadows change depending on the distance of the object from the light source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Shadow size: review

nodes.misconception: The size of a shadow does not change.
nodes.response: Explanation of how the size of shadows can be changed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Shadow size: plan

nodes.misconception: Only mirrors and very shiny materials reflect light.
nodes.response: Explanation that lots of different materials reflect different amounts of light.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflected light: plan

nodes.misconception: All materials reflect the same amount of light.
nodes.response: Explanation that we can measure the differing amounts of light reflected by different materials.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflected light: do and review

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Reminders of the difference between the object, what it is used for, and the material it is made from. Use of real-life objects for children to explore to aid this understanding.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Materials for recycling (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Science and engineering careers are male jobs. Females cannot work in science or engineering.
nodes.response: Examples of women working in science and explanations that science jobs are for everybody.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Development of new materials (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the object with the material/s that it is made from. e.g. only fabrics are materials, building materials are materials, the word ‘rock’ describes an object rather than a material.
nodes.response: Explanation of what an object is with a definition. Opportunities to name objects. Definition of what a material is and how this is applied to objects.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Everyday objects and materials

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials children may rely purely on observation rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Ensure children have been able to test materials and generate a set of results.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Transparent and opaque materials: review

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials children may rely purely on observation rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Opportunity to use real-life results to answer questions and draw conclusions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Waterproof materials: review

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Reminders of the difference between the object, what it is used for, and the material it is made of. Use of real-life objects for children to explore to aid this understanding.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The 3 Rs (non-statutory - Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Importance of testing each material to check if we are correct and not to rely on what we think we already know. Scientists ask questions and test their ideas.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Waterproof materials: plan and do

nodes.misconception: In comparing the extent of a given property in two materials children may rely purely on observation rather than on active testing.
nodes.response: Opportunities to test each material to check if their thinking was correct.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Transparent and opaque materials: plan and do

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that soft means smooth. Younger pupils may find it hard to describe a material based only on its properties (and not its function).
nodes.response: Opportunities to rehearse expressing ideas and describing properties. Teacher to model and correct as necessary, making clear the difference between the function of an object and the properties of its material(s).
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Material properties

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans either grow at a steady rate throughout their lives or only grow on milestones such as their birthdays.
nodes.response: When pupils have completed their line graphs showing human height data, discuss the changes in height between different ages.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Representing data about human height

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that everyone goes through, or should go through puberty, at the same time.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that everybody is different and will go through puberty at different times.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes during puberty

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that height is dependent on age, so taller adults must be older than shorter ones.
nodes.response: Explain that by the time humans reach adulthood they have stopped growing. At this point, their height is not related to their age. Use examples of familiar adults such as staff members to make this clear.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in adulthood

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that population size is only affected by the number of people being born.
nodes.response: Use the lesson resources to explain that many factors have an impact on population size, with the main contributing factor currently being the increase in life expectancy.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The impact of population growth ( non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that life expectancy is a prediction for individuals or a guarantee.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that life expectancy is a measurement we can make using data that we have about human lifespans. We cannot use it to predict how long an individual or group’s life will be.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Life expectancy (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that they grow on their birthday, rather than growth being gradual and continuous.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain to children that during childhood they are slowly and continuously changing and growing.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in  childhood

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the baby grows inside its mother's stomach.
nodes.response: Using the resources, explain that babies develop in an organ called a womb.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in humans before and after birth

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans only grow on their birthdays or in short, intermittent spurts rather than growth being continuous throughout childhood and adolescence.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that growth is continuous throughout youth until adulthood.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Finding out about human height

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all elders are like their grandparents or other older people they know, whether they are fit and active or more frail and sedentary.
nodes.response: Using the resources to support, explain that all humans are different and so there'll be differences in how they age. Also make it clear that old age can span up to 40 years so there'll be differences between someone who is 65 and someone who is 95.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in old age

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not recognise the value of representing data on graphs or charts and might view it as just another task to complete.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources, clearly explain the value of presenting data in a chart or graph and how it makes information easier to understand.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing data about human height

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that human development milestones happen at the same time for everyone.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that humans are all different and so grow and develop at different rates. This is why we need surveys to find out more information, as one rule cannot be applied to all humans.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: More about human development

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the arrow in a food chain means “eats” and also that arrows should be drawn from predator to prey (rather than prey to predator).
nodes.response: This lesson reinforces the fact the the arrow in a food chain can be interpreted to mean 'is food for'.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Simple food chains

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a plant or animal can only be part of one food chain.
nodes.response: This lesson shows a number of examples of how plants and animals can be part of many different food chains. Children are encouraged to research and create different food chains for the same plant or animal.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing different food chains

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that human actions can have an impact on animals and plants but that these actions do not affect food chains.
nodes.response: Explanation of different ways in which humans can protect plants and animals in their habitats.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Protecting food chains (Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that different parts of a food chain are independent of each other and are not impacted by changes elsewhere in the food chain.
nodes.response: Clear explanation of how each part of a food chain is linked to other parts of the chain and how even small changes can have a big impact throughout a food chain.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Dangers to food chains (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the words and pictures in a food chain represent an individual plant or animal rather than populations of living things within a habitat.
nodes.response: It is made explicit within the examples in this lesson that each living thing named in a food chain represents a population of that type, or species, of plant or animal within a habitat.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes in food chains (non-statutory Climate Change & Sustainability)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a predator can always be identified by its size and ferocity in comparison to its prey.
nodes.response: This lesson gives examples of some predators that are smaller in size than their prey.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Presenting food chains

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think the arrow in a food chain means “eats” or "depends on" and also that arrows should be drawn from predator to prey (rather than prey to predator).
nodes.response: This lesson reinforces the fact the the arrow in a food chain can be interpreted to mean 'is food for'.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Creating food chains

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the consumers in a food chain are organised in order of importance.
nodes.response: This lesson focuses on food chains showing how living things depend on each other for food. Individual living things in a food chain are just as important as each other.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Consumers in a food chain

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that all animals in a food chain are predators, or that all carnivores are predators.
nodes.response: Some animals can be carnivores but not predators. These animals are scavengers because they eat meat from animals they have found or that have been killed by other animals.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Predators and prey in a food chain

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a plant is at the start of the food chain because it is the smallest organism or because it cannot eat an animal.
nodes.response: This lesson makes reference to the fact that the plant is the producer in a food chain because it makes, or produces, its own food.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Producers in a food chain

nodes.misconception: When children think of light, they do not necessarily think of it as travelling. Also that light is found only in bright areas and not in the space between.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for children to think of different ways to model and record travelling light so it is seen as a continuous straight line.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How light travels

nodes.misconception: Children may think that a shadow is cast in between the object and the light source.
nodes.response: Children need to explore shadows cast by different light sources in different positions and with different objects. They should note the position of the light source in relation to the object and the shadow each time.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The position of shadows (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Light can only reflect off shiny surface;  light does not always travel in straight lines when it bounces off a mirror.
nodes.response: Diagrams and investigations will be used to address the misconceptions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing the direction of light

nodes.misconception: Our eyes produce light, which allows us to see.
nodes.response: Pupils will be taught that we see when light enters our eyes and will model and draw this themselves.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Light enters our eyes

nodes.misconception: Light shines out of our eyes; a light ray is a long thin piece of light; light is made of light rays added together; light can only be reflected off shiny surfaces.
nodes.response: Explicit teaching about sources of light, what a light ray is; plenty of demonstrations and practice of drawing diagrams.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reflected light

nodes.misconception: To measure the angle where light hits a surface, measure in between the beam of light and the surface.
nodes.response: The lesson gives children an opportunity to explore a new concept: the normal line. They should become familiar with measuring between the beam of light and the normal line drawn at a right angle to the surface.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring reflected light: plan

nodes.misconception: Shadows only form in bright light.
nodes.response: Children will explore shadow making and images and examples will be used to show how shadows are formed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Shadow shapes investigation

nodes.misconception: One object can only cast one shadow.
nodes.response: Children will investigate how the number of light sources affects the number of shadows cast by an object.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Multiple shadows

nodes.misconception: Only shiny surfaces reflect light. Light does not always travel in straight lines when it bounces off a mirror.
nodes.response: The lesson gives the children a chance to explore reflection of light in mirrors to see for themselves that it does reflect in a straight line.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring reflected light: do and review

nodes.misconception: Children often think that light reflectors are actually light sources because they 'shine'.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for children to investigate a range of real objects for themselves. They need to know that light reflectors appear to shine because they are reflecting light from a light source.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Light sources and light reflectors (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Shadows only form in bright light; shadows and reflections are the same thing; a shadow shows the features of an object.
nodes.response: Children will explore shadow making and images/examples will be used to highlight the key features of shadows and reflections.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: How shadows form

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all types of salt cause ice to melt at the same rate.
nodes.response: Opportunity to explore different types of salt and observe firsthand the effect that each type of salt has on the ice. Pupils should use the plans they created in lesson 2 to investigate this themselves.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The effect of adding salt to ice: do and review (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is only one type of salt.
nodes.response: Explanation that rock salt is one type of salt.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The effect of adding salt to ice: plan (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is only one type of salt and that it all comes from the sea.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain how salt is produced and introduce pupils to rock salt and table salt.  Pupils make a comparison of the two.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Comparing rock salt with table salt (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Eco-anxiety can be caused by news coverage of rising greenhouse gases and global temperatures, and pupils may feel like little is being done to prevent this.
nodes.response: Use the slides to look at the many ways that scientists and engineers are working to create new technologies to capture, remove and reduce the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Carbon capture (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that carbon dioxide is inherently harmful due to the way information about climate change is often presented.
nodes.response: Explain that carbon dioxide is not necessarily harmful; it is in the air we breathe and it is vital for the survival of plants. It can, however, become problematic as levels in the atmosphere increase and cause a warming effect.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What carbon is (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that fossil fuels have been made from fossils, such as the ones they may see in the classroom or museums.
nodes.response: Explain that fossil fuels are the remains of living things that have been changed over millions of years by heat and pressure.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Fossil fuels (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that water wheels and water turbines cause water to move when they spin.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that water wheels and water turbines harness the energy of water to do work for us or to generate electricity.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Water as an energy source (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: We cannot use electricity from solar cells when it is cloudy or at night.
nodes.response: Explanation of how energy can be stored in batteries to be used when it is needed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The Sun as an energy source (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Children may think that windmills and wind turbines create wind when the sails or blades spin.
nodes.response: Teaching slide explain that windmills and wind turbines harness the energy of the wind to do work for us or to generate electricity.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The wind as an energy source (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that air pollution can be seen, and that there are no pollutants in the air if it looks ‘clean’.
nodes.response: Explain that many things that can pollute the air cannot be seen by the naked eye and air pollution can exist even when we can’t see it around us.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing air pollution (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think their carbon footprint relates only to air pollution that can be seen, such as smoke or soot.
nodes.response: Explain that greenhouse gases cannot be seen, smelled or tasted; just because we cannot see them, it doesn’t mean they are not in the air around us.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing our carbon footprint (non-statutory)

nodes.misconception: Food is absorbed without being digested; or "goodness" from food is what is absorbed.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the roles of mechanical and chemical digestion (by enzymes) of different food types into small molecules to be absorbed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Digestion and enzymes

nodes.misconception: Confusing the reagents and the substances they test for, or the results of the tests.
nodes.response: Each test is dealt with separately and the positive and negative results are discussed sequentially.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Food tests: practical

nodes.misconception: All bacteria are bad for us and make us unwell.
nodes.response: The lesson looks at how helpful bacteria in the gut help us digest our food, provide vitamins, and outcompete harmful bacteria.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bacteria in the human digestive system

nodes.misconception: That the blood and circulatory system are synonyms.
nodes.response: Blood and circulatory system are key words and introduced as specific concepts.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Absorption and transport of nutrients in humans

nodes.misconception: The role of the stomach is often misunderstood as the main or only place where digestion occurs.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the roles of the stomach and the intestines in digesting food and absorbing nutrients.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The parts of the human digestive system

nodes.misconception: An object 'has' force that provides it some kind of agency, which is independent of other objects.
nodes.response: Describe forces as interactions between two objects using the structure 'the force of object A on object B'.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The different kinds of force

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often unable to match their experience of different forces with forces in newtons.
nodes.response: Pupils are provided with opportunity to both measure and describe a range of forces.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring forces

nodes.misconception: The type of graph chosen to represent data can just be personal choice.
nodes.response: Specific kinds of graph should be chosen to represent specific kinds of data.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing friction: analysis

nodes.misconception: Friction is not a force.
nodes.response: Provide examples of friction slowing objects and preventing them from moving when they are pushed.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Friction

nodes.misconception: Energy is some sort of physical substance that objects have.
nodes.response: Energy is just a label for having certain properties. The properties are what allow objects to interact / cause change / make things happen.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Energy

nodes.misconception: A moving object has force that keeps it moving, and which runs out when it comes to rest.
nodes.response: Forces come from other objects. Forces change the motion of objects. Objects slow when forces act opposite to the direction of motion.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: What forces do

nodes.misconception: Energy can be used up.
nodes.response: Describe the mechanisms that transfer energy from one object to another, or to a system, as the energy in the original object decreases – or vice versa.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Transferring energy

nodes.misconception: The direction of the (resultant) force shows the direction of motion.
nodes.response: The direction of the resultant force shows the direction of the change (not the direction of motion). Forces make things change.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Balanced and unbalanced forces

nodes.misconception: Force arrows are often added to diagrams carelessly without regard to accurate representation.
nodes.response: Draw force arrows from the point of interaction in the correct direction with a length proportional to the size of force.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Using force arrows

nodes.misconception: Friction is only between solids that are rubbing together.
nodes.response: Highlight the different amounts of friction between the solids that are separated by different liquids.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reducing friction: practical

nodes.misconception: The MMR vaccination causes autism.
nodes.response: The study by Dr Wakefield is highly flawed, and has been discredited. Many subsequent studies have found no link between the MMR vaccination and autism. Measles is a highly infectious disease that can have devastating consequences.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating the global use of vaccination

nodes.misconception: Students often use the term "zoom in" instead of focus.
nodes.response: You must correct the term "zoom in" to focus. You are not making the image larger, you are focussing to make the image clearer.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Light microscopy: observing and identifying microorganisms

nodes.misconception: All blood cells protect us against pathogens.
nodes.response: White blood cells are part of the immune system that protects us against pathogens. Red blood cells transport oxygen to cells. Platelets are not cells, but they do help to protect against pathogens by helping to seal wounds.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Non-specific defences of the human body against pathogens

nodes.misconception: Plants have no defence against pests or pathogens.
nodes.response: Plants have physical, chemical and mechanical defences against pathogens.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant defences against disease

nodes.misconception: Plants have no defence against pests or pathogens.
nodes.response: Plants have physical, chemical and mechanical defences against pathogens.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant defences, and identifying plant diseases

nodes.misconception: Antibodies remain in the blood for years, which makes a person immune to a disease.
nodes.response: Antibodies don't stay in the body longer term, the memory cells do and they provide long lasting immunity against a pathogen.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Immunity and vaccination

nodes.misconception: Mixing up scientific terms such as antigen and antibody.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the relationship and differences between antigens, antibodies and antitoxins.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Responses of the human immune system to specific pathogens

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the atomic number and atomic mass number and get confused over which subatomic particles these represent.
nodes.response: It helps to describe the atomic number as the proton number (to help the pupils remember). Also, the provided periodic tables often have a key to help and this should be highlighted to pupils.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Using the periodic table: atomic and mass number

nodes.misconception: Pupils may use the atomic number rather than mass when calculating the relative formula mass. Also, the number of atoms can be missed for the percentage of an element in a compound.
nodes.response: Emphasise that  atomic mass is the larger number for each element on the periodic table and encourage pupils to use the key present to help them identify the mass.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Relative formula mass

nodes.misconception: Students often struggle with the idea of how small an atom actually is. In contrast, how small the nucleus is, relative to the size of the atom.
nodes.response: The use of units and numbers to show the difference in size, e.g. the atom is approximately 10, 000 times larger than the nucleus. The radius of the nucleus is 0.00001nm, compared to that of the atom which is 0.1nm.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Atomic structure (very small electron mass)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often mix up the atomic number and atomic mass number and get confused over which subatomic particles these represent.
nodes.response: It helps to describe the atomic number as the proton number to help the pupils remember. Also, the provided periodic tables often have a key to help and this should be highlight to pupils.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Atomic number and mass number

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse the subatomic particle responsible for making an atom an isotope, and how isotopes are responsible for the relative atomic masses to 1 d.p.
nodes.response: Practice determining the number of neutrons in multiple isotopes.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Isotopes

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse the subatomic particle responsible for making an atom an isotope, and how isotopes are responsible for the relative atomic masses to 1 d.p.
nodes.response: Practice determining the number of neutrons in multiple isotopes.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Isotopes and relative atomic mass

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the atomic number and mass number with regard to the number of electrons in an atom. They also can confuse the number of electrons which can be held by each shell.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the lower number (atomic number/proton number) represents the number of electrons (reference to the mass being larger can help). Practise as many electron arrangements as possible.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Modern periodic table and electron configuration

nodes.misconception: Confusion between the models and the order in which they were conceived. Also, pupils often mix up which subatomic particles are present in each model.
nodes.response: Practise is required listing the key features of each model and the subatomic particles present. A timeline with the key features present helps pupils to understand the process of discovery and how long this can take.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a model for atoms

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that the when the periodic table was devised, scientists knew about the subatomic particles.
nodes.response: Emphasise when the subatomic particles were discovered in comparison to when Mendeleev devised his periodic table.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Development of the periodic table

nodes.misconception: Students often struggle with the idea of how small an atom actually is. In contrast, how small the nucleus is, relative to the size of the atom.
nodes.response: The use of units and numbers to show the difference in size, e.g. the atom is approximately 10, 000 times larger than the nucleus. The radius of the atom is 0.1nm and the nucleus very small compared to that of the atom.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Atomic structure (negligible electron mass)

nodes.misconception: Students often think that an elemental diatomic molecule, e.g. hydrogen, is a compound because they see two atoms chemically joined together.
nodes.response: The teacher needs to emphasise the definition for compounds. Molecules are not the same as compounds, some molecules are compounds, not all.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Atoms, elements and compounds
