nodes.misconception: A palisade cell is not a specialised cell as it is used as the plant cell model. All plant cells contain chloroplasts.
nodes.response: Presentation outlines that the palisade cell is a specialised cell. Question in the check for understanding that is designed to show chloroplasts are not in root hair cells.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant cells: common structures and specialised cells

nodes.misconception: All animal cells are the same as the model animal cell. Energy is created during respiration.
nodes.response: The model animal cell simplifies the complex structure of animal cells. There are specialised animal cells that have different shapes and sub-cellular structures to help them carry out a specific function. Energy is transferred through respiration.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animal cells: common structures and specialised cells

nodes.misconception: All bacterial cells looks like the bacterial cell model.
nodes.response: Bacteria can come in different shapes and sizes, this will be outlined within the slide deck.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Common structures of prokaryotic cells

nodes.misconception: Pupils commonly convert units incorrectly, multiplying when they should divide or dividing when they should multiply.
nodes.response: It can help to relate the unit conversions in the lesson to an everyday example, e.g. pounds to pence.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The size and scale of cells: including standard form

nodes.misconception: Cells are inert 'building blocks' like bricks. Microscopes can see structures as small as molecules.
nodes.response: The lesson explores what cells are, including that they are living units, and considers what can and can't be seen using a light microscope.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Light microscopy: observing and drawing cells

nodes.misconception: Pupils commonly convert units incorrectly, multiplying when they should divide or dividing when they should multiply.
nodes.response: It can help to relate the unit conversions in the lesson to an everyday example, e.g. pounds to pence.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The size and scale of cells: the basics

nodes.misconception: All eukaryotic cells are multicellular.
nodes.response: Addressed within the slides to specifically mention that some eukaryotic organisms are unicellular.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all animals and plant are multicellular and that all unicellular organisms are bacteria.
nodes.response: Lesson explicitly addresses this misconception and the questions in Task A are designed to expose the misconception.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Cells

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to include thinking distance in the overall stopping distance, or imagine that thinking distance is too short to matter.
nodes.response: Model a situation in which a child steps out from behind a parked car 10 m in front of a driver. At 20 mph the thinking distance is about 6 m and braking distance 6 m; at 30 mph these are 9 m and 14 m.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Stopping (and estimating stopping distances)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the terms force and momentum.
nodes.response: Make explicit the understanding that forces change the motion of an object, and that the motion of an object  (that a force can change) can be described by its momentum.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Changing momentum

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that as air resistance increases, a falling object decelerates (slows down).
nodes.response: Analyse footage of a falling object played back in slow motion, or frame–by–frame, to show that the speed of a falling object increases, up to a maximum speed, and at no time does it slow down.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Terminal velocity (including graphical representation)

nodes.misconception: A common belief is that a resultant force is needed to keep an object in motion, and if no resultant force acts on an object then it must be stationary.
nodes.response: Discuss examples in which friction is very low or absent, such as a puck sliding across an ice rink or an object being dropped during a space walk and extrapolate to what would happen if friction disappeared entirely.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Resultant forces and their effects

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget to include thinking distance in the overall stopping distance, or imagine that thinking distance is too short to matter.
nodes.response: Model a situation in which a child steps out from behind a parked car 10 m in front of a driver. At 20 mph the thinking distance is about 6 m and braking distance 6 m; at 30 mph these are 9 m and 14 m.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Stopping

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that as air resistance increases, a falling object decelerates (slows down).
nodes.response: Analyse footage of a falling object played back in slow motion, or frame–by–frame, to show that the speed of a falling object increases, up to a maximum speed, and at no time does it slow down.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Terminal velocity

nodes.misconception: When applying the equation F = m × a, pupils may take F to be any one of the forces acting on the object, rather than specifically the resultant force.
nodes.response: Provide some more complex examples, in which forces act in opposite directions, so pupils are required to work out the resultant force in preparation for completing calculations.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Newton's Second Law

nodes.misconception: The distance to a pivot is always the distance along the lever, no matter which direction the force is acting in.
nodes.response: Opening a door by pushing on the handle in different directions shows it is harder to open when the shoulder of the person pushing is closer to the pivot (smaller perpendicular distance between the force and the pivot).
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Balancing

nodes.misconception: When applying the equation F = m × a, pupils may take F to be any one of the forces acting on the object, rather than specifically the resultant force.
nodes.response: Provide some more complex examples, in which forces act in opposite directions, so pupils are required to work out the resultant force in preparation for completing calculations.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Newton's Second Law (including inertia)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a lever gives you ‘something for nothing’ when used as a force multiplier.
nodes.response: Ask a pupil to lift an object by a particular height (say 10 cm) without a pivot, then with a pivot and a plank as a lever to compare the effort and distance moved in each case.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Moments, levers and gears

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that being able to complete calculations by substituting numbers into an equation is the same as fully understanding the relationship.
nodes.response: Include questions for which pupils are required to explain their understanding.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Conservation of momentum

nodes.misconception: Pupils may regard force as a property of an object, expressing ideas such as ‘the object has a force’ and ‘the object runs out of force’.
nodes.response: Describe forces as interactions between two objects, using the phrasing ‘the force of object A on object B’.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Newton's Third Law

nodes.misconception: The velocity of an object must be in the same direction as the resultant force acting on the object.
nodes.response: Invite pupils to consider situations in which the resultant force is not in the same direction as the velocity, such as an object that has been thrown upwards and is slowing down as its height increases.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Forces in two dimensions

nodes.misconception: Pupils may regard force as a property of an object, expressing ideas such as ‘the object has a force’ and ‘the object runs out of force’.
nodes.response: Describe forces as interactions between two objects, using the phrasing ‘the force of object A on object B’.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Newton’s Third Law (with free body diagrams in 2D)

nodes.misconception: The velocity of an object must be in the same direction as the resultant force acting on the object.
nodes.response: Invite pupils to consider situations in which the resultant force is not in the same direction as the velocity, such as an object that has been thrown upwards and is slowing down as its height increases.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Forces in two dimensions (including resolution of a force)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not understand clearly what is meant by stopping time and cannot explain why longer stopping times result in smaller forces.
nodes.response: Describe stopping time as the time it takes to stop ‘during which a force is acting’, and provide examples of smaller forces stopping moving objects over longer periods of time than larger forces.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Stopping safely

nodes.misconception: It is common for pupils to fail to consider the hanging mass as part of the accelerating mass.
nodes.response: Emphasise that all of the moving parts in the investigation are connected, are accelerated together, and need to be included in the measurement of the mass being accelerated.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Force, mass and acceleration  (a = Δv/t)

nodes.misconception: It is common for pupils to fail to consider the hanging mass as part of the accelerating mass.
nodes.response: Emphasise that all of the moving parts in the investigation are connected, are accelerated together, and need to be included in the measurement of the mass being accelerated.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Force, mass and acceleration (a = (v – u)/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not understand that even sub–microscopic particles have a mass and volume which affect the density of a substance.
nodes.response: Use the anomaly of ice floating on water to consolidate understanding that molecules have mass and that the spacing of water molecules can affect density.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Upthrust calculations

nodes.misconception: The pressure at a particular depth depends on the shape of the container the liquid is in.
nodes.response: Demonstrate different shaped containers with the same depth of water in each and an identical shaped hole 1 cm above the base of each. Identical sized jets of water should shoot out of each hole as the pressure at each hole is (initially) the same.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Pressure in a fluid

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the mass or weight of an object with density.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of objects of varying sizes they are going to measure the density of and, before starting to do so, ask the pupils to rank the objects in order of density with explanations. Compare results to the list after measurements.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating density and measuring volume

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not understand that even sub–microscopic particles have a mass and volume, which affect the density of a substance.
nodes.response: Use the anomaly of ice floating on water to consolidate understanding that molecules have mass and that the spacing of water molecules can affect density.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Upthrust

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have the misconception that heat is a substance that can flow.
nodes.response: Focus learning on how heating causes particles to move more quickly, and the effects that this can have on the density of a fluid.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining convection

nodes.misconception: Pressure is a weight or a force; and pressure has a preferred downwards direction in a liquid or gas.
nodes.response: Use the particle model to provide opportunities for pupils to explain the causes of pressure in a gas that is in a container, and to explain how the difference in pressure between inside and outside causes an outward force.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining changes of pressure

nodes.misconception: Pressure is a weight or a force; pressure has a preferred downwards direction in a liquid or gas.
nodes.response: Use the particle model to provide opportunities for pupils to explain the causes of pressure in a gas that is in a container, and to explain how the difference in pressure between inside and outside causes an outward force.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes of pressure

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the mass or weight of an object with density.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of objects of varying sizes that they are going to measure the density of. Before measuring density, ask the pupils to rank the objects in order of density with explanations. Compare results to the list after measurements.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring density

nodes.misconception: Pressure is a weight or a force; and pressure has a preferred downwards direction in a liquid or gas.
nodes.response: Use the particle model to provide opportunities for pupils to explain the causes of pressure in a gas that is in a container, and to explain how the difference in pressure between inside and outside causes an outward force.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining pressure changes

nodes.misconception: Thinking that the heart is part of the gas exchange system, linked to the lungs by "air tubes".
nodes.response: This lesson explores the organs that make up the gas exchange system and how air is moved into and out of the lungs,
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The human gas exchange system and breathing

nodes.misconception: Thinking that only animals respire, and that plants only photosynthesise (and do not respire).
nodes.response: This lesson uses examples of plants respiring in order to address this misconception.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Cellular respiration

nodes.misconception: Learners often assume there is only one type of cellular respiration (aerobic).
nodes.response: This lesson explores aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration in humans.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Anaerobic cellular respiration in humans

nodes.misconception: Using the term 'accurate' without understanding what it means in relation to scientific measurements. Thinking that an estimate is just a guess.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the concepts of 'accurate' and 'estimate' using simple apparatus to estimate the vital capacity of the lungs.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Estimating lung volume

nodes.misconception: Students can often confuse the word summaries for the different types of cellular respiration.
nodes.response: This lesson directly compares the different word summaries for anaerobic cellular respiration to help understand the differences between them.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Anaerobic cellular respiration and fermentation in microorganisms

nodes.misconception: Pupils often refer to the walls of the alveoli as "cell walls".
nodes.response: This lesson makes the scale of different parts of the gas exchange system clear (e.g. whether a structure is a tissue or cell).
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Adaptations of the human lungs for gas exchange

nodes.misconception: Breathing and respiration are the same thing.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the differences between breathing, respiration and gas exchange, including what they are and where they take place.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Breathing, respiration and gas exchange

nodes.misconception: Aerobic cellular respiration is a single chemical reaction.
nodes.response: This lesson uses the terms 'chemical process' and 'series of chemical reactions'.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Aerobic cellular respiration

nodes.misconception: Students struggle to distinguish between phytomining and bioleaching.
nodes.response: Reinforce that the term 'phyto' is a combining form meaning 'plant'.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Alternative methods of extracting metals: phytomining and bioleaching

nodes.misconception: LCAs only measure the carbon footprint of a product.
nodes.response: The slide deck addresses what is included in a LCA such as energy use, water use and pollutants released.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Life cycle assessments (LCAs)

nodes.misconception: Some students may think that fractional distillation produces new substances from crude oil.
nodes.response: It is important to emphasise that crude oil is a mixture, and the process of fractional distillation is to separate out the different hydrocarbons based on their boiling points.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Fractional distillation of crude oil

nodes.misconception: Thinking that oxidation and reduction are only to do with the loss and gain of oxygen.
nodes.response: Oxidation is the loss of electrons or the gain of oxygen. Reduction is the gain of electrons or loss of oxygen.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Extraction of metals by reduction

nodes.misconception: Students struggle to distinguish between phytoextraction and bioleaching.
nodes.response: Reinforce that the term 'phyto' is a combining form meaning 'plant'.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Alternative methods of extracting metals: phytoextraction and bioleaching

nodes.misconception: Not including the bonds either side of the repeating unit.
nodes.response: The slide deck states the need for open bonds to show how repeating units are bonded to each other.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Polymer structures

nodes.misconception: Cracking is the same as fractional distillation.
nodes.response: Fractional distillation separates hydrocarbons based on their boiling points. Cracking alters the molecular formula of compounds.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Cracking fractions of crude oil

nodes.misconception: Students believing that sustainability is someone else's responsibility.
nodes.response: Everyone needs to reduce, reuse and recycle to ensure sustainable development. The slide deck gives examples of products that can be recycled and the benefits of reducing, reusing and recycling.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Earth's resources and sustainable development

nodes.misconception: To show the spectator ions in an ionic equation.
nodes.response: Spectator ions are ions that remain the same throughout a reaction. They are not included in the ionic equation.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Redox reactions

nodes.misconception: Thinking that a metal and acid react together to produce salt and water.
nodes.response: Use symbol equations to show how hydrogen is produced, rather than water, due to the absence of oxygen atoms.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Developing a reactivity series for metals

nodes.misconception: That small organisms and plants don't respire (only humans and other large animals).
nodes.response: This lesson demonstrates experimentally that small organisms respire.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The effect of temperature on cellular respiration in small organisms: practical

nodes.misconception: Thinking that each enzyme can act on many different substrates.
nodes.response: This lesson reinforces understanding that each enzyme has a specific substrate, because only that substrate will fit into they enzyme's active site.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining the effect of different substrates on the rate of cellular respiration

nodes.misconception: Pupils often read the volume of gas incorrectly as they do not measure it from the bottom of the meniscus of the water in the measuring cylinder.
nodes.response: This lesson contains a detailed explanation of how to correctly measure volumes from the meniscus, and why this is important.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The effect of different substrates on cellular respiration in yeast: practical

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that plants don't respire, and that they (only) photosynthesise instead.
nodes.response: This lesson contains examples of plants respiring.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Anaerobic cellular respiration in humans and other organisms

nodes.misconception: Students sometimes think that plants don't respire, and that they (only) photosynthesise instead.
nodes.response: This lesson contains examples of plants respiring.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Anaerobic cellular respiration in humans and other organisms, including ATP

nodes.misconception: Students frequently write in exams that respiration "creates" energy.
nodes.response: This lesson contains checks and practice tasks that address this misconception.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Aerobic cellular respiration in humans and other organisms

nodes.misconception: Not appreciating that increasing temperature up to the optimum has a different effect on rate than increasing temperature above the optimum.
nodes.response: The effects on rate of increasing temperature up to and beyond the optimum are explained.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Explaining the effect of temperature on the rate of cellular respiration

nodes.misconception: Students frequently write in exams that respiration "creates" energy.
nodes.response: This lesson contains checks and practice tasks that address this misconception.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Aerobic cellular respiration in humans and other organisms, including ATP

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget that the halogens are diatomic molecules.
nodes.response: Explanation of the bonding to form molecules helps to explain why they exist as diatomic molecules.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of Group 7 (RAM 1 d.p.)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often forget that the halogens are diatomic molecules.
nodes.response: Explanation of the bonding to form molecules helps to explain why they exist as diatomic molecules.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of Group 7

nodes.misconception: Halogen solutions are coloured and sometimes it can be difficult to determine colour changes during displacement reactions.
nodes.response: Displacement of iodine gives the darkest colour change (turns brown), while bromine will provide one which is lighter (turns orange).
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Reactions of the halogens: including displacement practical

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse the trend in reactivity down the group.
nodes.response: The practical reacting the metals with water helps to memorably demonstrate the trend, however it is important to ensure that pupils can explain why this happens.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of Group 1

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse the trend in reactivity down the group.
nodes.response: The practical reacting the metals with water helps to memorably demonstrate the trend, however it is important to ensure that pupils can explain why this happens.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of Group 1 (RAM 1 d.p.)

nodes.misconception: Pupils can confuse oxidation and reduction when involving electrons. They often mistake a positive charge on an ion as meaning electrons have been added and vice versa for negative ions.
nodes.response: It is very important to teach from first principles what causes the charges and then work up to half equations where the pupils can see the electrons in the equations, finally combining these to form ionic equations.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Ionic equations: reactions of Group 1 and Group 7

nodes.misconception: Spelling of noble re- Nobel and the concept of why they were given this name, i.e. due to having a full outer shell of electrons which means they do not need to bond with other elements.
nodes.response: Explain that the name noble was due to the fact that they are so unreactive and did not need to bond with other elements due to already having a full outer shell of electrons making them so stable.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of Group 0 (RAM 1 d.p.)

nodes.misconception: Spelling of noble re- Nobel and the concept of why they were given this name, i.e. due to having a full outer shell of electrons which means they do not need to bond with other elements.
nodes.response: Explain that the name noble was due to the fact that they are so unreactive and did not need to bond with other elements due to already having a full outer shell of electrons making them so stable.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of Group 0

nodes.misconception: Many pupils are uncertain about the forces attracting or repelling particles inside an atom.
nodes.response: Extend explanations to include electrostatic forces between protons in the nucleus and introduce the strong nuclear force to explain why nuclei do not self destruct.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Unstable nuclei

nodes.misconception: A material exposed to radiation will become radioactive.
nodes.response: Take time to clearly distinguish between radioactive contamination and irradiation.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Uses of radiation

nodes.misconception: Atoms are visible under powerful optical microscopes.
nodes.response: Emphasise that atoms are far too small to see and our descriptions of atoms are models, based on evidence, that help us understand how they behave.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Evidence of atomic structure

nodes.misconception: Radioactive isotopes disappear when they decay, so that in one half-life half the mass is lost.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the mass of the nuclei at the end of a nuclear fission or fusion are almost identical to the masses of those at the start. There is a very small difference, with mass being converted to energy according to E = mc².
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Nuclear fission and fusion

nodes.misconception: Nuclear power stations continually emit radiation into the environment.
nodes.response: Clearly distinguish day–to–day processes and the lack of emissions from the generation of nuclear waste, and methods for dealing with it.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Nuclear power

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have a clear understanding of the forces acting between neutrons and protons in an atomic nucleus.
nodes.response: In simple terms, explain the reasons why some nuclei are unstable in terms of electrostatic repulsion, and include ideas about the strong nuclear force attracting protons and neutrons to each other.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Nuclear decay

nodes.misconception: Alpha and beta particles and gamma radiation are radioactive.
nodes.response: Differentiate between radioactive particles that can emit radiation and the radiation itself. Radiation consists of fast moving particles or radiation that can cause ionisation because their electric fields interact with those of outer electrons.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Ionising radiation

nodes.misconception: Nuclear power stations can explode in a similar way to nuclear bombs.
nodes.response: Explain how the fuel in power stations is not sufficiently concentrated to cause nuclear explosions, and the control rods stop them overheating which could cause a conventional explosion that releases contaminants (as happened at Chernobyl).
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Nuclear power stations

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have a clear understanding of the forces acting between neutrons and protons in an atomic nucleus.
nodes.response: In simple terms, explain the reasons why some nuclei are unstable in terms of electrostatic repulsion, and include ideas about the strong nuclear force attracting protons and neutrons to each other.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Nuclear decay (including beta–plus)

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to predict outcomes for random events such as radioactive decay.
nodes.response: Use analogies to show that random nuclear decay can lead to predictable outcomes, such as the randomness in the order popcorn kernels pop, but the predictability of how quickly all the popcorn takes to cook.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Activity and half-life calculations

nodes.misconception: It is impossible to predict outcomes for random events such as radioactive decay.
nodes.response: Use analogies to show that random nuclear decay can lead to predictable outcomes, such as the randomness in the order popcorn kernels pop, but the predictability of how quickly all the popcorn takes to cook.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Activity and half-life calculations (including complex ones)

nodes.misconception: Most pupils have difficulty in truly understanding randomness.
nodes.response: Use analogies to explain randomness.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Radioactive half-life

nodes.misconception: Atoms react because they 'want' to gain a fuller outer shell of electrons – atoms don't have feelings. Monatomic means one atom and may be confused with the term element, which means one type of atom.
nodes.response: Take care with language and avoid personifying the atoms. Make sure that definitions and terms are used correctly.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Why chemical reactions happen

nodes.misconception: Understanding that the models used to represent chemical story do not tell the complete story. Different models can be used to explain different aspects of bonding, but they all have limitations.
nodes.response: Avoid telling your class that the model is wrong; rather stress its limitations. Stress the idea that as we learn more about bonding, we will be able to use more sophisticated models to show and explain more key ideas.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Bonding models

nodes.misconception: There are several misconceptions associated with properties such as when something dissolves it disappears, electrical conductivity is a flow of electrons rather than charge.
nodes.response: When discussing electrical conductivity, emphasise the idea of electrical conductivity being a flow charge with ions behaving as charge carriers. The electron transfer that occurs during ion formation is nothing to do with conductivity.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of giant ionic structures

nodes.misconception: Ions are not formed because atoms 'want' or 'need' a full outer electron shell. Pupils often find standard notation difficult and get confused about when to use superscript and subscript.
nodes.response: It is important that pupils understand that atoms do not have 'wants' or 'needs'. Emphasise that the driving force for the formation of atoms is an increase in stability when the outer electron shell is full.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming ions for ionic bonding

nodes.misconception: Using ionic charges to determine the empirical formulae, especially with polyatomic ions. Standard notation is difficult and confusing, e.g. when to use superscripts, subscripts or brackets.
nodes.response: At this stage, pupils will need to just learn the the formulae of the polyatomic ions and accept that a full explanation will come later in their chemistry learning. Provide pupils with plenty of practice of writing and using ionic formulae.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Determining ionic formulae

nodes.misconception: Pupils often find it difficult to apply what they have learnt about alloys when asked about an unfamiliar one, or when provided with a table of data.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of different examples of alloys. Give them plenty of practice of comparing the properties of the alloy with those of the pure metal.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Alloys and their properties

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that covalent bonds are broken when any covalent structure undergoes a change of state; not just those in giant covalent structures.
nodes.response: Use physical models to show the difference between a simple covalent structure and a giant covalent structure. Explain that it is the weak intermolecular forces that are overcome when a simple covalent molecule changes state.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of covalent substances

nodes.misconception: Atoms react because they 'want' to gain a fuller outer shell of electrons – atoms don't have feelings! Monatomic means one atom and may be confused with the term element, which means one type of atom.
nodes.response: Take care with language and avoid personifying the atoms. Make sure that definitions and terms are used correctly.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Why chemical reactions occur

nodes.misconception: That the ionic bond is the transfer of electrons and not the electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions. The ball and stick model implies that there is a physical link between the ions.
nodes.response: Ensure that students have a good understanding of how ions are formed and that ionic bond forms when oppostive ions attract; before moving on to dot and cross diagrams for binary ionic substances.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Giant ionic structures

nodes.misconception: A metal is an individual atom. The property of a metal atom is the same as the bulk material. Pupils get confused between the attractive forces in the metal atoms and the metallic bond.
nodes.response: Reinforce the idea that atoms are tiny and not visible to the naked eye. The material we know as metal is many millions of atoms joined together. Revisit the structure of the atoms before introducing the idea of metallic bonding and giant structure.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Metallic structure and properties

nodes.misconception: The ionic bond is the transfer of electrons and not the electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions. Dot and cross diagrams show the empirical formula of the lattice and not an ionic molecule.
nodes.response: Ensure students have a good understanding of how ions are formed, the arrangement of ions in a giant lattice structure and empricial formula before moving on to disucss using dot and cross diagrams to model ionic bonding.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Ionic diagrams for binary ionic substances

nodes.misconception: The metallic structure model is a replication of reality. Therefore, metals contain seawater. The concept of electric current is challenging. Some may think that electrons jump from atom to atom.
nodes.response: Discuss why scientists use models with the pupils, explaining that a model is only as good as what it can explain, so it develops over time. Remind pupils how an electric circuit works before discussing why metals are good conductors.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Metal alloys

nodes.misconception: The covalent bond is the shared pair of electrons; both electrons must come from different atoms. The central atom  is responsible for the formation of covalent bonds as they want a full outer shell.
nodes.response: All chemical bonds are an electrostatic force of attraction between positive and negative charges. The sharing of electrons is the process by which covalent bonds are formed. Avoid using anthropomorphic analogies to explain how covalent bonds form.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming covalent bonds

nodes.misconception: Ions are not formed because atoms 'want' or 'need' a full outer electron shell. Pupils often find standard notation difficult and get confused about when to use superscript and subscript.
nodes.response: It is important that pupils understand that atoms do not have 'wants' or 'needs'. Emphasise that the driving force for the formation of atoms is an increase in stability when the outer electron shell is full.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Forming ions for ionic bonding (RAM 1 d.p.)

nodes.misconception: Compounds will have the same properties as the elements from which they are made.
nodes.response: Compounds usually have completely different properties from the elements from which they are made.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Compounds and their formation

nodes.misconception: Pupils often struggle with the idea of how small an atom actually is.
nodes.response: Use examples to show how many atoms make up certain things, e.g. a cell or a grain of sand.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Atoms and elements

nodes.misconception: Assuming that substances like sodium chloride (NaCl) are diatomic.
nodes.response: It is very important to emphasise that only non-metals exist as monatomic or molecules.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Molecular elements

nodes.misconception: Elements cannot have metal and non-metal properties.
nodes.response: Introduction of the metalloids and discussion of their properties.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Common elements

nodes.misconception: Students often confuse the difference between chemical and physical properties.
nodes.response: A chemical property describes how an element will react with other substances. Physical properties describes the appearance and behaviour.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Properties of elements

nodes.misconception: Students often forget to change the non-metal name to either -ide or -ate.
nodes.response: Emphasise when the non-metal reacts with a metal it changes its name to -ide. It is -ate if the non-metal is also bonded to oxygen.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Naming compounds

nodes.misconception: There are exceptions for both metals and non-metals, which have different properties.
nodes.response: Use examples such as mercury and graphite in your teaching.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Metallic elements

nodes.misconception: Writing subscript values as superscript values.
nodes.response: Subscript values show the number of the atoms, while superscript in maths is used to square a value and so does not apply to chemical formulae.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Chemical formulae

nodes.misconception: The idea that atoms can be created or destroyed when new products are formed.
nodes.response: Matter cannot be created or destroyed, only arranged differently to be formed into new products.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: A particle model of chemical reactions

nodes.misconception: It is important for the same person to take all the measurements.
nodes.response: Emphasise that if the method is a good one then everyone carrying it out carefully should get similar results that show the same pattern (the results are repeatable and reproducible).
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring instantaneous speed analysis (v=s/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring acceleration practical (v=x/t, a=(v-u)/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring acceleration practical (v=s/t, a = Δv/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring acceleration analysis (v = x ÷ t, a = (v – u) ÷ t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse displacement–time graphs with velocity–time graphs.
nodes.response: Emphasise the need for pupils to always read the axes of a graph first, before they start to think about any lines drawn on it.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating from motion graphs (a=Δv/t and v=s/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring acceleration analysis (v = s ÷ t, a = (v – u) ÷ t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often consider time in the acceleration equation to be moment in time (perhaps read from a graph) rather than a change in time.
nodes.response: Label the value of t in the acceleration as a change of time rather than just time.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Velocity-time graphs: acceleration and distance travelled (a = Δv/t)

nodes.misconception: A pair of coordinates on a s-t graph can be used to calculate the instantaneous speed or velocity at that point, but that only works for a straight line graph through the origin.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to calculate the velocity of a graph that represents a steady velocity on a line that does not go through the origin, and to check to see if dividing the values at any point on the line gives the right value for velocity.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating from displacement-time graphs: including tangents (v = s ÷ t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often consider time in the acceleration equation to be moment in time (perhaps read from a graph) rather than a change in time.
nodes.response: Label the value of t in the acceleration as a change of time rather than just time.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Calculating from velocity-time graphs (a=(v-u)/t)

nodes.misconception: Negative values on a displacement-time graph always represent motion that is backwards.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to plot a range of displacement-time graphs in real time in order for them to understand how the graph represents different motions.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Velocity on displacement-time graphs (v = s ÷ t)

nodes.misconception: When the trolley is released, it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Show a video of an accelerating trolley in slow motion identifying the distance travelled in successive equal intervals of time.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring instantaneous speed practical (v = s ÷ t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring acceleration analysis (v = s ÷ t, a = Δv ÷ t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not have an understanding of what moving at a particular speed means in the real world, and treat answers as ‘just numbers’.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of speeds through examples and questions asked (N.B. 10 m/s is approximately 20 miles per hour).

nodes.lessonTitle: Different speeds (v=s/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.
nodes.response: It is important to make sure pupils are secure in their knowledge of the vector–scalar distinction; use plenty of visual examples.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Displacement and velocity as vectors (v=s/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.

nodes.lessonTitle: Measuring acceleration practical (v=s/t, a=(v-u)/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Motion calculations: including complex ones (a=(v–u)/t, v²−u²=2as & v=s/t)

nodes.lessonTitle: Motion calculations (a=(v–u)/t, v²−u²=2ax & v=x/t)

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that if velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
nodes.response: Before teaching acceleration, consolidate an understanding of the differences between velocity and changes in velocity. Discuss how an object can be accelerating AND travelling at a constant speed (circular motion).
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Acceleration (a = Δv/t)

nodes.misconception: Travelling at exceptionally high speed through a speed camera means that it will not be able to measure your speed accurately and so it will not trigger.
nodes.response: Tell pupils that speed cameras use radio waves which travel at 300 000 000 m/s. They can accurately measure the speed of objects travelling at thousands of metres per second.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Automated measurement of speed

nodes.misconception: All DNA is genes that code for proteins; and that our characteristics are only affected by our genes
nodes.response: Most of the DNA is non-coding (non-genes), and controls when genes are expressed (i.e. when proteins are made). Changes (genetic variants) in non-coding DNA can affect characteristics (phenotype) as they control whether a gene is expressed or not.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Genetic variants in non-coding DNA can influence phenotype

nodes.misconception: Mixing up amino acids and nucleotides, also nucleotides and bases.
nodes.response: Activity checks: Nucleotides contain a base; DNA is a polymer of nucleotides that codes for the order of amino acids in a protein.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Mutations and genetic variants

nodes.misconception: DNA is the endpoint of a characteristic rather than the fact that it codes for proteins that give a protein; also that all characteristics are visible.
nodes.response: Clear examples, analogies and models to show the code in genes, leads to the order of an amino acids in a protein; examples of structural and functional proteins.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Protein synthesis

nodes.misconception: Mutations always have a negative effect on an organism.
nodes.response: Mutations can produce variation in a phenotype by producing alleles of a gene.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Genetic variants in genes can influence phenotype

nodes.misconception: Genes, DNA and chromosomes are used interchangeably rather than understanding their separate definitions; also that organisms such as animals and plants are not related.
nodes.response: Use images to show the difference between DNA, genes and chromosomes; display a phylogenetic tree so the common ancestry of all living organisms can be visualised and so the commonality of DNA between all life.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: The genetic code

nodes.misconception: That all features encoded in the genome are visible in the phenotype.
nodes.response: Give examples of structural and functional proteins that are not visible in an organism's phenotype.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The genome, the environment and phenotype

nodes.misconception: DNA is living and not necessarily a chemical.
nodes.response: Discussing that DNA is a chemical molecule and showing how it is made up of smaller chemical groups, and then modelling this chemical structure.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: The chemical structure of DNA

nodes.misconception: That all DNA codes for features rather than processes that are shared by all living organisms; also that animals are the only living organism that have DNA.
nodes.response: Make the role of DNA in features and processes explicit, using non-animal examples. Re-iterate the common processes of living organisms, and therefore why there are similarities in the genome.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The genome

nodes.misconception: DNA is living and not necessarily a chemical.
nodes.response: Discussing that DNA is a chemical molecule and showing how it is made up of smaller chemical groups, and then modelling this chemical structure.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: The structure of DNA

nodes.misconception: Pupils often do not understand what neutralisation is i.e. exactly the correct quantities of components from the acid and base combined to form water.
nodes.response: It is worth emphasising that water is formed and it is this which is neutral as it contains the hydrogen and oxygen atoms from the acid and base.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Chemical reactions: neutralisation

nodes.misconception: The difference between concentrated and dilute vs strong and weak when referring to acids and alkalis (not covered in this lesson).
nodes.response: For acids and alkalis concentration is the amount of hydrogen dissolved in a certain volume of solution. The higher the concentration, the lower the pH. Strong and weak refer to the ability of an acid to release hydrogen (not covered in lesson).
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: pH scale and universal indicator solution

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that acids ‘eat away’ materials and disappear. They observe reactions and see the loss of a reactant, but do not recognise the formation of a new soluble product.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils understand the concept of solubility and use the words soluble and dissolve when describing the production of metal salts during these reactions.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Chemical reactions: acid and metal carbonate

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to carry out a complex 3-stage practical.
nodes.response: Demonstrate the practical or do a 'follow with me' step-by-step method. If you are short on time you could just carry out the first part of the practical to produce the copper sulfate solution then stop.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Metal oxides and non-metal oxides

nodes.misconception: Pupils can expect that all reactions will be vigorous and they will see lots of bubbles being formed instantly.
nodes.response: Get pupils to leave and observe their metal + acid reactions over a period of time, e.g. 5 minutes. This will ensure that they will be able to observe bubbles forming more slowly for metals such as iron or zinc.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Chemical reactions: acid and metal

nodes.misconception: Pupils can get confused by the litmus paper test and presume that a change has to take place for it to be a positive result.
nodes.response: Use the phrases, stay red, stay blue, turn red, turn blue to help them understand that sometimes a positive test is no colour change.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Acids and bases

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the red cabbage will change to the same colours as universal indicator solution.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that there are many different indicators used to show different pH.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Practical: red cabbage indicator solution

nodes.misconception: Increasing the temperature increases the rate product is formed, and therefore think a faster reaction produces more product.
nodes.response: Increasing the temperature will make the reaction proceed faster but will not change the amount of product formed. The reactants are the limiting factor, not the temperature.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Temperature and rate: practical

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the mean rate of reaction with the instantaneous rate of reaction, thinking they are the same or not understanding the distinction between the two.
nodes.response: The tasks give pupils s the opportunity to distinguish between mean and instantaneous rate of reaction by calculating both from the same set of data.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface area and rate: analysis

nodes.misconception: Thinking that as the concentration of a solution in excess changes, so does the volume of gas produced.
nodes.response: The slide deck uses graphical data to show that the same volume of gas is produced when different concentrations are used, so long as the reacting solution is in excess.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Concentration and rate: analysis

nodes.misconception: That every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction.
nodes.response: The slide deck addresses that not every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction. The particles must collide with the activation energy in order for the collision to be successful and a new product be formed.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Collision theory

nodes.misconception: Adding a bung to the top of a conical flask does not affect volume measurements.
nodes.response: The bung can displace a small volume of gas, which can affect the accuracy of the measurements. It is essential to account for the volume displaced by the bung in calculations.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Evaluating methods for measuring the rate of reaction

nodes.misconception: That a larger surface area produces a larger volume/mass of product.
nodes.response: The experiment should help pupils realise they produce the same mass of carbon dioxide when using the same mass of calcium carbonate chips and powder.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Surface area and rate: practical

nodes.misconception: Catalysts increase the amount of product formed.
nodes.response: Catalysts do not affect the quantity of products formed. They increase the rate at which the products are formed.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Catalysts and rate

nodes.misconception: The reaction stops when the 'X' is no longer visible.
nodes.response: The disappearance of the cross only indicates that the sulfur precipitate has formed sufficiently to obscure the cross. The reaction itself continues beyond this point until all reactants are consumed.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Concentration and rate: practical using end point method

nodes.misconception: Thinking that as the concentration of a solution in excess changes, so does the volume of gas produced.
nodes.response: The slide deck uses graphical data to show that the same volume of gas is produced when different concentrations are used, so long as the reacting solution is in excess.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Concentration and rate: practical using gas collection method

nodes.misconception: To calculate the instantaneous rate of reaction by reading values from the graph at a specific time.
nodes.response: Students need to draw a tangent in order to calculate the gradient of the graph at a specific time to work out the instantaneous rate of reaction.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: The rate of a chemical reaction: including graphs

nodes.misconception: Thinking that precise and accurate are the same thing.
nodes.response: It may help to draw a bullseye target board. Precise results will all be close to each other but may not be near the bullseye. Accurate results will be near the bullseye but may be more scattered if they are not precise.
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.lessonTitle: Appropriate equipment for measuring the rate of a reaction

nodes.misconception: Particle spacing can be overemphasised at the expense of particle movement.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that although particles can move over each other, the forces of attraction mean that the particles are touching.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Melting: particle model

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to think that all gases are made of air. That gases contain no particles.
nodes.response: Ensure that pupils gain the knowledge that the particles are the substance and between the particles there is nothing.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Boiling and condensing

nodes.misconception: The idea that there is air between the particles in a gas.
nodes.response: Emphasis on explaining that air contains particles and has nothing between them.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Particle model of substances in the gas state

nodes.misconception: Some pupils can't understand that substances can change from one state to another state.
nodes.response: Ensure that the language used is solid state, liquid state and gas state, not solid, liquid and gas.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Melting: melting points and freezing points

nodes.misconception: Evaporation only occurs above the boiling point of a substance.
nodes.response: Give examples of substances other than water.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Changes of state: energy and evaporation

nodes.misconception: All the Bunsen is hot, flames are the same temperature.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to explain why they are able to turn the collar without getting burnt. Explain why it is important to select the correct flame.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bunsen burners

nodes.misconception: Students think that the particles are embedded in the substance
nodes.response: Ensure that students are reminded that all matter is made of small particles and nothing is between the particles.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Solid and liquid states

nodes.misconception: It is very common for pupils to think that uninsulated wire is needed for the coil of an electromagnet.
nodes.response: When discussing an electromagnet, always refer to the insulated wire in its core, which is necessary so the current in each turn adds to the strength of the electromagnet.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Applications of electromagnets

nodes.misconception: The magnetic field is only at the poles of a magnet.
nodes.response: Provide opportunity for pupils to plot magnetic field lines around pairs of bar magnets and to experiment with a second magnet as described in the teacher tip.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Plotting magnetic fields

nodes.misconception: Digital ammeters are always accurate to the smallest amount they display.
nodes.response: Show pupils a copy of the specifications of the ammeters they are using that show how accurate they really are.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Strength of an electromagnet

nodes.misconception: Magnets can attract or repel electric charges in a wire.
nodes.response: Explain that the correct explanation for what is happening is usually taught to pupils studying physics at university. At this point, it is sufficient to be able to describe and predict what happens when a conductor is moving in a magnetic field.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Electric generators

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it challenging to think about how current flows through the connections and around the coil in the motor.
nodes.response: Take pupils step–by–step through the building of a motor from a motor kit and provide an opportunity for pupils to build their own working motor to help them to consolidate their understanding.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: An electric motor

nodes.misconception: It is common for pupils to hold the misunderstanding that stationary magnetic fields can attract or repel electric charge or to conflate magnetic and electrostatic effects.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to explain applications of the motor effect and the generator effect in order to consolidate a scientific understanding.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Applications of motor and generator effects

nodes.misconception: It is not clear how the magnetic field around a conducting wire interacts with a uniform magnetic field.
nodes.response: Focus on observing and predicting the direction that a conducting wire is forced in by a uniform magnetic field, and openly admit that explaining this in terms of how the magnetic field interact is too challenging to include in the syllabus.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: The motor effect

nodes.misconception: Magnets can attract or repel electric charges in a wire.
nodes.response: Explain that the cause of induced current is complex and is usually taught to pupils studying physics at university. At this point it is sufficient to be able to describe and predict what happens when a conductor is moving in a magnetic field.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: The generator effect

nodes.misconception: A magnetic field is the same as the electric field around a charged object.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that an electromagnet does not attract small pieces of tissue paper, as a balloon with a static charge can do.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: An electromagnet

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not realise that the resistance of a wire varies with temperature.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are aware that the temperature of a metal wire does affect resistance and that precautions should be taken to avoid a temperature change.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Resistance of a wire at a constant temperature

nodes.misconception: To solve circuit problems you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing parallel circuits

nodes.misconception: Magnetic field effects are often mistaken for electric field effects.
nodes.response: Be explicit in teaching that electric charges and charged objects are not magnetic.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Moving electric charge

nodes.misconception: To solve circuits you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Adding components to a parallel circuit

nodes.misconception: To solve circuits, you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing series circuits

nodes.misconception: To solve circuit problems you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing parallel circuits: including complex calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that electric field lines show the movement of moving charges, rather than the force acting on them.
nodes.response: Add force arrows to electric field diagrams to show the size of the force they represent at different points.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Electric fields

nodes.misconception: To solve circuits, you need only to put numbers into equations.
nodes.response: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Analysing series circuits: including complex calculations

nodes.misconception: Pupils often use physics equations without understanding, leading to errors.
nodes.response: Develop a qualitative understanding of potential difference, current and resistance before combining them mathematically. Use the equation as a shorthand for an already understood relationship between them.
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.lessonTitle: Linking current, potential difference and resistance

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that biodiversity is the number of organisms that live in a place, rather than the number of different species that live in a place.
nodes.response: There is extensive coverage in the lesson around biodiversity being the range of species that are found in an area.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Animals are adapted for their environment

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that the biomass increases as you move to the next trophic level, presumably  because pupils incorrectly assume that biomass refers to individuals rather than populations.
nodes.response: The lesson gets pupils to estimate the biomass of populations at each trophic level to demonstrate that biomass decreases at each trophic level.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Pyramids of biomass

nodes.misconception: It is common to think that organisms, especially humans, can survive without other organisms.
nodes.response: This lesson highlights and explores the key concept that all living organisms are dependent upon other organisms for their survival.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Interdependence within ecosystems

nodes.misconception: Pupils often associate the use of quadrats to survey plants in one type of habitat. Pupils do not consider how they can be used to sample sedentary animals, e.g. barnacles or limpets on a rocky shore.
nodes.response: During the slidedeck there is reference to how quadrats can be used to sample plants and sedentary animals in different habitats.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Ecological sampling of living organisms

nodes.misconception: Biodiversity conservation can only take place in large natural habitats such as forests.
nodes.response: Biodiversity conservation can take place on a small scale, for example, by providing habitats in gardens and in urban areas. On a smaller scale still, seeds and embryos can be stored to help conserve gene pools.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Conserving biodiversity

nodes.misconception: Pupils often associate the use of quadrats to survey plants in one type of habitat. Pupils do not consider how they can be used to sample sedentary animals e.g. barnacles / limpets on a rocky shore.
nodes.response: During the slide deck there is reference to how quadrats can be used to sample plants and sedentary animals in different habitats.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Ecological sampling using a quadrat

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that the size of organisms has to increase at each trophic level within a food chain diagram.
nodes.response: The lesson addresses the misconception through exemplification. There is coverage of inverted pyramid of number to show that some producers are larger organisms that are eaten by smaller organisms.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Pyramids of number

nodes.misconception: Pupils often believe that biodiversity is the number of organisms that live in a place, rather than the number of different species that live in a place.
nodes.response: There is extensive coverage in the lesson around biodiversity being the range of species that are found in an area.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plants are adapted for their environment

nodes.misconception: Pupils often refer to the turns of a coil as the number of coils.
nodes.response: Emphasise that turns of wire can be added to a coil to make the coil longer.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Current through an electromagnet

nodes.misconception: The magnetic field is only at the poles of a magnet.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to plot magnetic field lines around a bar magnet and to experiment with a second magnet, as described in the teacher tip.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: The magnetic field of a bar magnet

nodes.misconception: A magnetic field is the same as the electric field around a charged object.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that a balloon with a static electric charge does not affect the magnet in a plotting compass.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Electromagnets

nodes.misconception: All metals are magnetic and an object with a static electric charge is magnetic.
nodes.response: Provide opportunities for pupils to test some metals that are not magnetic, and a balloon with a static electric charge with a magnet.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Magnetic poles

nodes.misconception: It is very common for pupils to think that uninsulated wire is needed for the coil of an electromagnet.
nodes.response: When discussing an electromagnet, always refer to the insulated wire in its core, which is necessary so the current in each turn adds to the strength of the electromagnet.
nodes.subject: science
nodes.lessonTitle: Using electromagets

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant diseases: Chalara ash dieback

nodes.misconception: Viruses are alive.
nodes.response: Viruses do not carry out many of the life processes required for living organisms such as respiration and reproduction.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bacterial and viral diseases in humans: Salmonella and influenza

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any health claim by a product must be true.
nodes.response: Often no scientific research has been carried out on products claiming to be healthy.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Risk factors for non-communicable diseases

nodes.misconception: The heart does not have its own blood vessels. Students often believe the heart gets oxygen and glucose from the blood circulating through it.
nodes.response: The heart has its own blood supply through the coronary arteries.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Cardiovascular disease

nodes.misconception: Malaria is caused by mosquitos.
nodes.response: Mosquitos are the vector that transfer the protist to humans.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Fungal and protist diseases in humans

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant diseases: TMV and rose black spot

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant diseases: TMV, crown gall disease and Chalara ash dieback

nodes.misconception: Only human and other animals can catch diseases. Plant diseases are not important.
nodes.response: This lesson explores examples of plant diseases, the pathogens that cause them and how they are spread, and their devastating impacts.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Plant diseases: TMV, crown gall disease and barley powdery mildew

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that viruses are alive.
nodes.response: Viruses do not carry out many of the life processes required for living organisms such as respiration and reproduction.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bacterial and viral diseases in humans: Salmonella and measles

nodes.misconception: HIV and AIDS are the same thing.
nodes.response: HIV is the virus and AIDS is a consequence of late-stage HIV infection.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Sexually transmitted infections

nodes.misconception: A person is either healthy or unhealthy.
nodes.response: Health is a range from good to ill health.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Diseases

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that people are either healthy or unhealthy.
nodes.response: Health is a range from good to ill. Fitness is one indicator of general health.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Effects of exercise on pulse rate

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that viruses are alive.
nodes.response: Viruses are not cells. They do not carry out many of the processes of living organisms such as replication and respiration.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Bacterial and viral diseases in humans: TB, cholera, Helicobacter and Ebola

nodes.misconception: Thinking that climate change affects the weather, but not human health.
nodes.response: This lesson explores direct and indirect impacts of climate change on human health.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Climate change and human health

nodes.misconception: There is nothing a person can do to decreases their risk of getting cancer.
nodes.response: Although we can't change inherited genetic risk factors for cancer, it does also have many associated lifestyle risk factors such as obesity and smoking.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Cancer

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that the excessive growth of the plants in eutrophication is the cause of a reduction in biodiversity as a result of the plants using up the oxygen in the water.
nodes.response: Steps in eutrophication are outlined. Increased minerals cause the growth of plants at the surface resulting in the death and decomposition of the plants. Decomposition results in microbes using oxygen, resulting in biodiversity loss.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Examples of human interactions with ecosystems, including use of peat

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that a small increase in greenhouse gases and a small rise in Earth's temperature will not have much impact on organisms on Earth beyond land ice melting.
nodes.response: The lesson discusses how small changes in weather patterns can have a significant impact on organisms as their habitats change and no longer provide them with food, shelter and a place to reproduce.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Climate change and biodiversity: changes in the distribution of organisms

nodes.misconception: The conservation of biodiversity can only happen on a large scale, e.g. through protecting large areas of habitat.
nodes.response: Biodiversity conservation can take place on a small scale, for example, by providing habitats in gardens and in urban areas.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Benefits and challenges of maintaining biodiversity

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have a belief that genetically engineered organisms are not safe. While there are risks with GM organisms, there are a wide range of benefits which can help humans.
nodes.response: The lesson highlights the benefits of genetically modifying crops to address food security challenges, especially in the context of a growing human population and other factors that threaten food availability.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Factors affecting human food security, and possible solutions

nodes.misconception: A misconception that is often seen is that there is a build up of biomass along a food chain.
nodes.response: The lesson outlines how biomass is actually lost between trophic levels through life processes.
nodes.subject: biology
nodes.lessonTitle: Transfers of biomass between trophic levels

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that the excessive growth of the plants in eutrophication is the cause of a reduction in biodiversity as a result of the plants using up the oxygen in the water.
nodes.response: Steps in eutrophication are outlined. Increased minerals cause the growth of plants at the surface resulting in the death and decomposition of the plants. Decomposing dead organic matter results in micro-organisms using oxygen and biodiversity loss.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Examples of human interactions with ecosystems, including fish farming

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly thinking that we can use and damage forests and oceans without negative consequences for the planet and our own survival.
nodes.response: This lesson explores the crucial role of forests and oceans as global carbon sinks that offset human carbon emissions, and the impacts of deforestation, global warming and ocean acidification.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Climate change and biodiversity: forests and oceans

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that a small increase in greenhouse gases and a small rise in Earth's temperature will not have much impact on organisms on Earth beyond polar ice melting.
nodes.response: The lesson outlines how human activities increase the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and how this links to climate change. The lesson also outlines how climate change impacts life on Earth.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: Negative human interactions with ecosystems and impacts on biodiversity

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that substances need to be at their boiling point temperature to evaporate.
nodes.response: Use plenty of real life examples of liquids evaporating in situations where pupils know that the liquid is not above its boiling point but still evaporates.
nodes.subject: combined-science
nodes.lessonTitle: State changes: evaporation and sublimation
