nodes.misconception: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando soy mayor trabajaré en un hospital'.
nodes.response: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando sea mayor trabajaré en un hospital'. After 'cuando', use the subjunctive to talk about an event that hasn't yet happened.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: De viaje: extended reading and writing (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando soy mayor trabajaré en un hospital'.
nodes.response: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando sea mayor trabajaré en un hospital'. After 'cuando', use the subjunctive to talk about an event that hasn't yet happened.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: De viaje: extended reading and writing (AQA)

nodes.misconception: To say 'my mum is a teacher', it's 'mi madre es una profesora.'
nodes.response: In Spanish, we do not need the indefinite article ('un', 'una') when referring to jobs, so we would just say 'mi madre es profesora.'
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe family members: possessive adjective 'nuestro'

nodes.misconception: To talk about completed events in the past with -ar verbs you always take off the -ar ending and add -é in the 1st person singular ('I').
nodes.response: For -ar verbs ending in -car, you remove the -car and add -qué in the 1st person singular, for example; 'sacar' - 'saqué' - 'I took out'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Describe family members: possessive adjective 'su'

nodes.misconception: To say 'better than' in Spanish I can use 'más bueno que'. To say 'worse than' I can use 'menos malo que'.
nodes.response: In English we don't say 'more good than' or 'more bad than'. We say 'better than' or 'worse than'. Spanish also has words for 'better' and worse'. To say 'better than' use 'mejor que' and to say 'worse than' use 'peor que'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Festival experiences: comparatives 'mejor que' and 'peor que'

nodes.misconception: To translate 'Where do you keep these shoes?' I need the word for 'do' in Spanish.
nodes.response: Spanish doesn't have a word for 'do' in questions. Only the main verb is used in the form that matches the subject of the question. So the translation would be '¿Dónde guardas estos zapatos?'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Shopping with friends: demonstrative adjectives 'este/a' and 'estos/as'

nodes.misconception: To compare two things in Spanish we can just change the adjective like in English, e.g. 'angry' becomes 'angrier.'
nodes.response: To compare two nouns we use a comparative structure. To express 'more ... than' we use 'más ... que' and to say 'less ... than' we use 'menos ... que'. The adjective goes in the middle and still has to agree in gender and number with the first noun.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Festival experiences: comparatives 'más que' and 'menos que'

nodes.misconception: [ge] and [gi] are a soft 'g' sound as in English. Spanish [j] is different so you can always hear the difference when you transcribe words with these sounds.
nodes.response: Spanish [ge] and [gi] sounds like Spanish [j] + e and [j] + i, so you cannot hear the difference when you transcribe. However, there is often a clue from English, e.g., 'religión' in Spanish is spelled with [gi] as in English.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Lifestyle: -er and -ir verbs 3rd person singular

nodes.misconception: Regular -er/-ir verbs in plural form always end in -en.
nodes.response: Only the 3rd person plural form ends in -en.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Online activities: -er and -ir verbs 3rd persons

nodes.misconception: Singular and plural verbs have the same endings.
nodes.response: Singular and plural verbs have different forms for first, second and third person.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Online activities: -er and -ir verbs 3rd person questions

nodes.misconception: It is easy to write Spanish from memory if I know what the words mean.
nodes.response: Knowing what words mean when you listen to or read them doesn't mean you can write them from memory.  To write from memory, you need to practise writing from memory, especially verbs, as these need to be right to communicate your message clearly.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Free time activities: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: The best way to learn vocabulary is to repeat the words and their meaning in your mind.
nodes.response: A method like look, say, cover, write, check can be more effective when learning vocabulary.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Lifestyle choices: -er and -ir verb infinitives

nodes.misconception: The verb ending -o means 'I' but only if you're a boy or man.
nodes.response: For regular verbs, the 'I' verb form always ends in 'o'. Verb endings match the person, but don't change for gender, so 'hablo' means 'I speak' for everyone.  It is adjectives that change ending -o to -a to describe a girl or woman.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Free time activities: -er and -ir verbs 1st person singular

nodes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'I will have' is 'teneré'.
nodes.response: The verb 'tener' is irregular in the inflectional future. The Spanish translation of 'I will have' is 'tendré'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: El mundo del trabajo: inflectional future - 'tendr-', 'har-', 'podr-'

nodes.misconception: Any word that ends in -é is in the preterite tense.
nodes.response: Some words that end in -é are in the inflectional future. In this case, the -é ending is added to the infinitive - 'trabajaré' (I will work) - rather than the stem, as in the preterite - 'trabajé' (I worked).
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Experiencias de trabajo: translation, extended writing

nodes.misconception: To form the inflectional future tense, take off the infinitive ending before adding -é, -ás, -á.
nodes.response: To form the inflectional future tense, add the endings -é, -ás, -á, to the infinitive.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Feria de trabajo: singular inflectional future

nodes.misconception: The plural 'you' form is the same for both -er and -ir verbs.
nodes.response: To talk to more than one person ('you all') using -er verbs in the present tense, use the ending -éis, e.g. 'comprendéis' - 'you all understand'. For -ir verbs, use the ending -ís, e.g. 'escribís' - 'you all write'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: School life: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular and plural

nodes.misconception: In Spanish the ending for 'you singular' and 'you plural' for -ar verbs is the same.
nodes.response: To refer to 'you' for one person with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -as, e.g. 'buscas'; to refer to 'you' for two or more people with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -áis, e.g. 'buscáis'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Work and jobs: 'eres' and 'sois', simple present -ar verbs

nodes.misconception: A present tense verb can be used on its own to talk about the future.
nodes.response: When using the present tense to talk about the future, it is essential to include a temporal adverb (such as 'mañana', 'la próxima semana', 'el lunes', etc.) to make the future meaning clear.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Work and jobs: 'vas' and 'vais', with simple present for future events

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, to compare things, we use 'más, menos' + adjective + 'de'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, when we're comparing two things using an adjective, we use 'más, menos' + adjective + 'que', e.g. 'más caro que', 'menos sano que'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: At a theme park: demonstrative adjectives 'ese' and 'esa'

nodes.misconception: Spanish always uses English word order when using indirect objects (subject + verb + object).
nodes.response: In Spanish, the indirect object can go before or after the verb. Both 'le doy un regalo a mi hermano' and 'a mi hermano le doy un regalo' are correct - the second just adds emphasis to who receives the gift.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Friendships: personal 'a'

nodes.misconception: It doesn’t matter whether I use 'ser' or 'estar' as they both mean 'to be,' so they’re interchangeable.
nodes.response: 'Ser' is used for permanent traits or characteristics, while 'estar' is used for temporary states, such as emotions or feelings.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: How are you feeling? 'Ser' and 'estar' 1st and 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: 'Esta' means both 'this' and 'she, he, it is'.
nodes.response: ‘Esta’ is a demonstrative adjective, it means ‘this’ and goes before a noun. ‘Está’ is a verb, means ‘she, he, it is’ and describes an state or location. As there is an accent, we must stress the last syllable.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Possessions at a crime scene: 'mío/a', 'tuyo/a' and 'suyo/a'

nodes.misconception: Spanish has only one way to say 'you are,' like English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the form of 'you are' changes depending on who you're talking to. To say ‘you are’ to one person, use ‘eres’. To say ‘you are’ to two or more people, use ‘sois’.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Where people are from: 'ser' 1st and 2nd person singular and plural

nodes.misconception: The verb ending for gustar-type verbs depends on who is affected, not on the subject.
nodes.response: The verb ending depends on the subject, i.e. what causes the feeling of liking, interest, importance or concern, etc., e.g. 'le encanta el juego' - 'the game delights him, her', 'le encantan los juegos' - 'the games delight him, her'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Friendships: gustar-type verbs

nodes.misconception: Like in English, in Spanish there is only one word for 'that' and one for 'those'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, to say ‘that’ for a singular masculine noun, use ‘ese’. To say ‘that’ for a singular feminine noun, use ‘esa’. To say ‘those’ for a plural masculine noun, use ‘esos’. To say ‘those’ for a plural feminine noun, use ‘esas’.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: At a market: demonstrative adjectives 'esos' and 'esas'

nodes.misconception: The sounds [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same in all the Spanish-speaking countries.
nodes.response: In Latin America, parts of southern Spain and the Canary Island, [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same. In the rest of Spain, [ci], [si] and [z] have different pronunciation.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: What people have: 'tener' singular and plural persons

nodes.misconception: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish and that is 'tu'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, if the possessive adjective 'your' comes before a singular or uncountable noun, we say 'tu', but if it comes before a plural noun we say 'tus'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Possessions: number agreement on 'mi' and 'tu'

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, like in English, there is only one 'the' and that is 'el'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, there are four words for 'the' - 'el' that accompanies singular and masculine nouns; 'la' for singular and feminine nouns, 'los' for plural and masculine nouns, and 'las' for plural and feminine nouns.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Spanish-speaking cities: article use and 'ser' vs 'estar'

nodes.misconception: 'Mi' and 'tu' changes according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the possessive adjectives do not change according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine. They stay the same.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Whose is it? possessive adjectives 'mi' and 'tu'

nodes.misconception: There is no difference between 'ningún' and 'ninguno'.
nodes.response: 'Ningún' and 'ninguno' look very similar but they are used differently in Spanish. 'Ninguno' is a pronoun and it replaces a masculine singular noun. 'Ningún' is an indefinite adjective and it comes before a masculine singular noun.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Madrid: indefinite pronouns 'alguno', 'ninguno'

nodes.misconception: In the inflectional future with all verbs, the endings are added to the infinitive and they are the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
nodes.response: A small number of verbs are irregular in the inflectional future and have irregular future stems.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¿Qué tipo de viaje harás? Irregular inflectional future stems 'dir-', 'saldr-'

nodes.misconception: I can translate sentences with 'desde hace' word for word.
nodes.response: In Spanish, 'desde hace' appears together with a verbs in the present tense to say how long you've been doing something. We use a different tense in English. 'Vivo aquí desde hace años' - 'I have been living here for years'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Barcelona: 'desde', 'desde hace' vs 'hace', phrases with 'llevar'

nodes.misconception: 'More than' is always translated as 'más que'.
nodes.response: 'More than' can be translated as 'más que' or 'más de'. 'Más de' is followed by numbers.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Un viaje diferente: higher numbers, plural inflectional future, irregular stems

nodes.misconception: The only factor in understanding listening tasks is vocabulary. If I know enough words, I don’t need any strategies to comprehend what I hear.
nodes.response: A strong knowledge of high frequency vocabulary is key to unlocking effective listening comprehension. However, strategies such as prediction, synonym recognition and identifying distractors can also improve listening skills.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: De compras en la ciudad: role play, develop listening

nodes.misconception: When answering questions, I can use the verb in the question to start my answer.
nodes.response: You can start your answer using the question verb but it's important to not copy the question word-for-word. If questions use 2nd person verbs, you need to change them to 1st person, changing 'you' verbs into 'I' or 'we' forms.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: De viaje en el futuro: develop understanding and answer questions

nodes.misconception: When translating from Spanish to English, I should translate each word in the order it appears in the Spanish sentence.
nodes.response: When translating from Spanish to English, make sure your translations sound natural in English. This may mean you need to change the word order from the original Spanish sentence.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Nos preparamos: reading practice (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors to do well in my listening exam.
nodes.response: Strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors are useful for listening exams, but the most important thing is to have a broad vocabulary.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Nos preparamos: listening and transcription practice (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should translate each English word individually when translating into Spanish.
nodes.response: It is important to read the whole sentence first and translate chunks of language rather than each individual word.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Nos preparamos: writing practice (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: When translating from Spanish to English, I should translate each word in the order it appears in the Spanish sentence.
nodes.response: When translating from Spanish to English, make sure your translations sound natural in English. This may mean you need to change the word order from the original Spanish sentence.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Nos preparamos: reading practice (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I should translate each English word individually when translating into Spanish.
nodes.response: It is important to read the whole sentence first and translate chunks of language rather than each individual word.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Nos preparamos: writing practice (AQA)

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors to do well in my listening exam.
nodes.response: Strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors are useful for listening exams, but the most important thing is to have a broad vocabulary.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Nos preparamos: listening and transcription practice (Edexcel)

nodes.misconception: I know 'ir' in the present tense, so it will be easy to remember it in the preterite tense.
nodes.response: 'Ir' is an irregular verb in both the present and the preterite tense. This verb is very common and therefore needs to be learnt off by heart.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Excursions and trips: 'fui', 'fuiste' and 'fue'

nodes.misconception: When 'de' appears before 'el' it becomes 'de el'.
nodes.response: When 'de' appears before a singular masculine noun with the definite article 'el' it merges with it to form 'del', e.g. 'la jugadora está fuera del estadio' - 'the player is outside the stadium'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Weekend activities: 'hice', 'hiciste', 'hizo'

nodes.misconception: To form the past participle of any verb in Spanish, remove the infinitive ending and add -ado.
nodes.response: To form the past participle of regular -ar verbs, remove the -ar and add -ado. However, to form the past participle of regular -er and -ir verbs, remove the -er/-ir and add -ido.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Hemos venido de Puerto Rico: perfect tense -er/ir regular -ido

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, 'mañana' always means 'morning'.
nodes.response: In Spanish 'mañana' has two meanings. It can mean 'morning' or 'tomorrow'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Dos idiomas, dos culturas: develop reading, practise transcription

nodes.misconception: The only way of saying 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'.
nodes.response: 'I played' could be translated as 'jugué' or 'jugaba'. The preterite verb 'jugué' implies a single, completed action in the past, whereas the imperfect verb 'jugaba' implies a habitual action in the past.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Dos idiomas, dos culturas - los Nuyoricans: imperfect for habitual actions

nodes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'it is sunny' is 'es sol'.
nodes.response: When describing weather conditions, the verb 'hace' translates as 'it is'. The Spanish translation of 'it is sunny' is 'hace sol'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Aprender un idioma: translation, extended writing

nodes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'I have' + past participle, e.g. 'I have listened', is 'tengo' + past participle, e.g. 'tengo escuchado'.
nodes.response: The Spanish translation of 'I have listened' is 'he escuchado'. In Spanish, the auxiliary verb used in the formation of the perfect tense is 'haber', not 'tener'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Ser de otro país: perfect tense -ar regular -ado, irregular past participles

nodes.misconception: To mean 'you' in an impersonal, general sense use 'tú'.
nodes.response: 'Tú' means 'you' when directed at a specific person. To mean 'you' in an impersonal, general sense use 'se' e.g. 'se puede' (you can).
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Aprender un idioma: 'hay que', 'se puede', 'se necesita', 'se debe'

nodes.misconception: The English translation of 'he visitado' is 'I visited'.
nodes.response: The perfect tense is used to express what has happened. The English translation of 'he visitado' is 'I have visited'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Ser de otro país: perfect and preterite tenses

nodes.misconception: Stem-changing verbs like 'encontrar' and 'pensar' have a stem change in all conjugations of the simple present.
nodes.response: Stem-changing verbs 'encontrar' and 'pensar' have a stem change in persons 1, 2, 3 and 6 of the simple present. The stem reverts back to the original for persons 4 and 5.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Aprender un idioma: stem-change verbs like 'encontrar', 'pensar', 'poder'

nodes.misconception: 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugé'.
nodes.response: 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'. An extra 'u' is added after the 'g' to preserve the hard [g] sound.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¿Alguna vez has ... ? Develop conversations with perfect and preterite tenses

nodes.misconception: We swap the verb and subject around to ask a closed, yes/no question as in English, e.g. 'Are we going to go on holiday?'
nodes.response: All closed questions in Spanish have the same word order as the equivalent statement, e.g.'Vamos a ir de vacaciones' ('We are going to go on holiday') → '¿Vamos a ir de vacaciones?' ('Are we going to go on holiday?').
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Summer plans: 'ir' + a + infinitive

nodes.misconception: There is no preparation needed before I read Spanish aloud.
nodes.response: Trickier sounds can trip us up when we read aloud in Spanish. Identifying any tricky sounds, then mentally rehearsing before we read aloud can help us read more accurately and fluently.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Possibilities and limits: negatives with 'pueden', 'deben' and 'quieren'

nodes.misconception: All nouns ending in 'a' are feminine.
nodes.response: There are exceptions to this, like 'problema' or 'día', that's why it is important to learn the article and the noun together.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Where people go: give statements with 'ir' in singular persons

nodes.misconception: To say where someone goes, only 'a la/al' goes before the place.
nodes.response: If the place is a city or a country, 'a' goes before the place.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: When and where people go: 'ir' 1st person plural

nodes.misconception: There are no strategies I can use to understand words in a text; I either know them or I don't.
nodes.response: I can use several strategies to help me understand a text: I can use the surrounding words that I do know, I can use my knowledge of patterns, e.g. for adjectives, and I can use cognates.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: A day on the beach: La Playa (Juan Guinea Díaz)

nodes.misconception: I need Spanish words for 'do' and 'are' to ask yes/no questions, just like in English, e.g. 'Do you go to town?', 'Are you going to the park?'.
nodes.response: Spanish yes/no questions use the same words in the same order as Spanish statements.  To make a statement into a spoken question, use raised intonation. Written questions use two question marks; the one at the start is upside down.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Where people go: ask questions with 'ir' in singular persons

nodes.misconception: I know from the sound if a Spanish word starts with 'h'.
nodes.response: The letter 'h' is a silent letter in Spanish. We need to learn the spelling of words that start with 'h' by practising vocabulary regularly.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: A day on the beach: La Playa (Juan Guinea Díaz), -ar verbs plural persons

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, we translate word-for-word from English to say 'I am going to', using 'soy' or 'estoy'.
nodes.response: Some structures do not allow for word-for-word translations between English and Spanish. To say 'I am going to' in Spanish, use the present tense of 'ir' + 'a' + 2nd infinitive verb.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Future plans: 'ir' + a + infinitive

nodes.misconception: A single 'r' is never rolled.
nodes.response: When the [r] is at the beginning of a word, we do roll it. For example, 'respeto', 'religión'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Rigoberta Menchú: -er and -ir verbs 1st and 2nd person singular (preterite)

nodes.misconception: We have to use a word like 'did' in Spanish questions.
nodes.response: In Spanish, you don't need a word like do or did to ask questions. The verb ending itself shows the tense and subject, e.g. '¿Trabajaste en el campo?' - 'Did you work in the countryside?'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Rigoberta Menchú: -ar verbs 1st and 2nd person singular (preterite)

nodes.misconception: To form the preterite tense I just take off the -er/-ir and add the correct ending (-ió - for she, he, it) to all the verbs.
nodes.response: Some verbs are irregular and don’t follow the pattern. e.g. hacer - hizo, tener - tuvo, ir - fue.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Diana Trujillo: 'fue', 'hizo' and 'tuvo'

nodes.misconception: All verbs (including -er and -ir) use -an in the present and -aron in the preterite to mean 'they'.
nodes.response: To conjugate -ar verbs for 'they', remove -ar and add -an for the present tense or -aron for the preterite tense. However, to conjugate -er/-ir verbs for 'they', remove -ar and add -en for the present tense or -ieron for the preterite tense.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Latin American women in NASA: -ar, -er, -ir verbs 3rd person plural preterite

nodes.misconception: -ar, -er, and -ir verbs all share the same endings in the present tense for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms.
nodes.response: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms, but -ar verbs have a different ending.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do at school: regular verbs 3rd person (present)

nodes.misconception: The simple present tense in Spanish is only for habitual actions, e.g. 'every week I do my homework'.
nodes.response: The simple present in Spanish is used for habitual actions and immediate plans. '¿Qué haces hoy?' means 'What are you doing today?' and 'hoy hago mis deberes' means 'today I am doing my homework'. English uses the present continuous here instead.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: What people do at school: regular 1st persons and 2nd person singular (present)

nodes.misconception: When forming a question the verb form changes in Spanish like it does in English (auxiliary 'did' + verb).
nodes.response: The verb stays the same in Spanish and only the intonation (spoken) or punctuation (written) marks the sentence as a question. There is no need to translate a form of 'do', 'did' etc.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Questions about past trips: regular preterite verbs 1st and 2nd person singular

nodes.misconception: All Spanish words with stress on the second-to-last syllable must have a written accent.
nodes.response: If a word ends in a vowel, -n, or -s, it usually has that stress naturally and doesn’t need an accent. Accents are only used when the word sounds different from the normal rule.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Famous Spanish speakers:  regular verbs 3rd person singular (preterite)

nodes.misconception: Spanish questions have the same punctuation as in English.
nodes.response: Spanish questions begin with an upside down question mark (¿).
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Estrellas y famosos: singular preterite 'dar'

nodes.misconception: 'To give' is always a natural translation of 'dar'.
nodes.response: When 'dar' appears with a noun of feeling or emotion, it is more natural to use 'to be' + adjective in English.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Estrellas y famosos: plural preterite 'dar', idiomatic uses of 'dar'

nodes.misconception: Past participles do not have gender and number marking.
nodes.response: In passive sentences with 'ser' + past participle, the past participle must agree in number with the noun it acts on.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Estrellas y famosos: 'ser' + past participle + 'por'

nodes.misconception: Just like modal verbs, 'estar' is followed by an infinitive to form the present continuous to express what is happening right now.
nodes.response: To form the present continuous, use a present tense form of 'estar' together with a present participle. To form this for -ar verbs, remove -ar from the infinitive and add -ando to the stem. For -er and -ir verbs, add -iendo to the verb stem.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Films and cinema: present continuous with -er and -ir verbs

nodes.misconception: To form the present continuous I just use 'está' + present participle.
nodes.response: To form the present continuous you first conjugate 'estar'; e.g. for 'they are' use 'están'. Then add the present participle; which is the verb stem + -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for -er/-ir verbs, e.g. 'están hablando' - 'they are talking'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Films and cinema: present continuous and modal verbs

nodes.misconception: To form the present continuous I use the present tense of 'estar' followed by an infinitive, as with other two-verb structures I know, i.e. modal verbs.
nodes.response: To form the present continuous you use the present tense of 'estar' followed by the present participle. For -ar verbs this is formed by removing the -ar ending and adding -ando, e.g. 'estoy saltando' ('I am jumping').
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Exercise and fitness: present continuous with -ar verbs

nodes.misconception: Some singular forms of 'estar' and feminine demonstrative adjectives look and sound the same.
nodes.response: The feminine demonstrative adjectives 'esta' (this) and 'estas' (these) have no accent. The 2nd and 3rd person singular forms of 'estar' have an accent on the -a: 'estás' (you are) and 'está' (she, he is). They are pronounced with stress on the -a.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Exercise and fitness: 'este' and 'esta'

nodes.misconception: 'Para' always means 'for'.
nodes.response: 'Para' often means 'for'. However, when followed by an infinitive, it means 'in order to'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Holiday plans: 'ir' + a + infinitive

nodes.misconception: -er verbs have the same ending in the 1st person plural of the present and preterite tenses.
nodes.response: Unlike -ir verbs, -er verbs do not have the same ending in these tenses. The verb ending -emos is used in the present tense and -imos is used in the preterite tense.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Holiday activities: -ar, -er, -ir verbs 1st person plural present and preterite

nodes.misconception: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by a conjugated verb.
nodes.response: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by the infinitive form of a verb.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Future trips: 'ir' + a + infinitive

nodes.misconception: The verb ending -o refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.
nodes.response: The verb ending -o refers to 'I' in the present tense. The verb ending -ó (with accent) refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Hispanic festivals: -ar verbs 3rd person preterite

nodes.misconception: 'Fue' means 'I went'.
nodes.response: 'Fui' means 'I went' and 'fue' means 'she, he, it went'. The two have similar spelling so are easily confused.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Past trips: 'hacer' and 'ir' singular persons preterite

nodes.misconception: It is important to use a range of verb tenses and complex language in role-play answers.
nodes.response: Role-play answers must consist of short words or phrases. Overcomplicating answers runs the risk of introducing ambiguity through grammatical error.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¿En qué puedo ayudarle? Formal and informal 'you' and 'your'

nodes.misconception: To tell somebody who is familiar to you to do something, use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
nodes.response: To tell somebody who is familiar to you to do something, use the affirmative imperative. For -ar verbs this ends in -a, and for -er/-ir verbs this ends in -e.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¡Cuida el planeta! Regular affirmative imperative, and 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'

nodes.misconception: The only way to mean 'you (sg)' in Spanish is 'tú'.
nodes.response: There are two ways to mean 'you (sg)' in Spanish. Use 'tú' to mean 'you' in an informal context, and 'usted' to mean 'you' in a formal context.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: De compras y en el restaurante: 'tú' and 'usted'

nodes.misconception: When performing a role-play, one-word answers are enough.
nodes.response: When preparing and performing role-plays, it is important to answer using short phrases or sentences, avoiding one-word answers.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Situaciones: role play

nodes.misconception: The only translation of 've' in Spanish is 'she, he, it sees'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the verb 've' usually means 'she, he, it sees', but it is also the affirmative imperative form of 'ir', meaning 'go'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¡Cuida el planeta! Irregular affirmative imperative 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven'

nodes.misconception: The first thing I hear correctly and understand is usually the answer to a listening comprehension question.
nodes.response: It is important to listen to the whole text before answering a listening comprehension question, as information may not be presented in an obvious order.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¡Cuida el planeta! Develop listening, practise read aloud

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, 'tú' and 'tu' mean the same thing.
nodes.response: In Spanish, 'tú' and 'tu' do not mean the same thing. 'Tú' is a subject pronoun meaning 'you' (informal), whereas 'tu' is a possessive adjective meaning 'your' (informal).
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: En el trabajo: informal and formal your - 'tu' and 'su'

nodes.misconception: When completing a photo description in Spanish, I should stick to short, simple sentences.
nodes.response: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to plan extended sentences to talk for a prolonged period of time.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Planeta tierra solo hay uno: regular and irregular imperatives

nodes.misconception: A past participle is used after 'acabar de'.
nodes.response: An infinitive is used after 'acabar de'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Las Hogueras de San Juan: acabar de + infinitive, seguir + present participle

nodes.misconception: There is always a word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish.
nodes.response: There is no word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish questions.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: La fiesta del pueblo: -er/-ir preterite 3rd person singular and plural

nodes.misconception: It is possible to describe a photo without needing to use verbs.
nodes.response: It is necessary to use full sentences to successfully describe a photo. Sentences always include a verb.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Fiestas y costumbres: photo description, read aloud

nodes.misconception: 'Estaba' only means 'I was' in the imperfect.
nodes.response: 'Estaba' means 'I was' but also 'she, he, it was' in the imperfect.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: ¿Qué estaba pasando? Imperfect continuous, preterite interruptions

nodes.misconception: Reflexive pronouns always come before the conjugated verb.
nodes.response: Reflexive pronouns can go in two plaes: before the conjugated verb or or after the infinitive, attached to it, with 2-verb modal structures.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Conflictos: imperfect 'ir', 'ver', 'ser', reflexive pronouns 'me', 'te' and 'se'

nodes.misconception: Reading and re-reading a text is always an effective way to read for understanding and get the right answers to comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Simply reading and re-reading a text isn't always the most effective way to read for understanding. Using active reading strategies such as reading the title and reading and annotating the questions can boost comprehension and accuracy in responses.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Conflictos: develop reading

nodes.misconception: The Spanish translation of 'I played football on Monday' is 'jugué al fútbol en lunes'.
nodes.response: Rather then the preposition 'en', Spanish uses the definite article before days of the week. As such, the Spanish translation of 'I played football on Monday' is 'jugué al fútbol el lunes'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Oportunidades: uses and omission of definite and indefinite articles

nodes.misconception: The inflectional future communicates what is 'going to' happen.
nodes.response: The inflectional future communicates what 'will' happen. 'Voy a + infinitive' communicates what is 'going to' happen.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Pensar en el futuro: plural inflectional future

nodes.misconception: When responding to conversation questions, it will suffice to give one-word answers.
nodes.response: Conversation answers should be consistently developed with 2-3 clauses. One-word answers are not enough.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Oportunidades: photo description and conversation practice

nodes.misconception: When conjugating verbs in Spanish, you always need to start by taking off the infinitive ending.
nodes.response: Some verb tenses, such as the inflectional future, are formed by adding the relevant ending to the infinitive. As such, the infinitive ending is not taken off.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Pensar en el futuro - entrevista a Camilo: singular inflectional future

nodes.misconception: The letter 'r' is always pronounced the same in Spanish.
nodes.response: In Spanish, 'r' is pronounced differently depending on its position within a word. 'r' in the middle or at the end of a word is pronounced as in 'pero', whereas 'r' at the beginning of a word and 'rr' are pronounced as in 'perro'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Intención o posibilidad: transcription and extended writing

nodes.misconception: When producing written work in Spanish, I should stick to short simple sentences.
nodes.response: When producing written work in Spanish, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Pensar en el futuro: extended writing

nodes.misconception: To form any verb in the conditional, add a conditional ending to the infinitive.
nodes.response: Not all verbs are regular in the conditional and some don't follow this pattern. Some verbs have irregular stems in the conditional, e.g. 'tener' ('tendr-') and 'poder' ('podr-').

nodes.lessonTitle: Yo que tú: singular and plural conditional

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, the SSC [qui] is pronounced as in 'queen'.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the SSC [qui] is pronounced as in 'equipo'.
nodes.subject: spanish
nodes.lessonTitle: Oportunidades: singular conditional, 'quisiera', 'me gustaría'

nodes.misconception: In Spanish, all adjectives must be placed after the noun.
nodes.response: The position of adjectives in Spanish can be flexible. When adjectives follow nouns, this communicates a literal, objective description. If an adjective is placed before a noun, this can communicate a figurative, subjective description.
